Processing Text: The Mg-4Sn (at.%) alloy ingot was produced by induction melting using a steel crucible under the protection of an argon atmosphere, and then cast into a steel mold. The cast alloy was homogenized at 400 °C for 6 h and cooled in the furnace. The homogenized sample was machined into cylindrical specimens with a diameter of 10 mm and a length of 14 mm for UP treatment in a modified CS-IB type hexahedral anvil apparatus. The sample was wrapped with tantalum foil and inserted in a boron nitride capsule. The hydrostatic pressure was obtained by the press along three axes. The samples were treated for 30 min at temperatures from 600 to 1100 °C under UP treatment under 4 GPa. The heating rate and time to boost pressure were 6 °C/s and 2 min, respectively. After UP treatment, the samples were cooled to room temperature by circulating water before unloading pressure. The UP-treated sample was subjected to aging heat treatment in a silicone oil bath at 200 °C, which was denoted as UPA. As a comparison, the cast alloys underwent solid solution treatment at 500 °C for 8 h, followed by aging heat treatment in a 200 °C silicone oil bath, denoted as T6. The UP-treated sample was machined into sheet specimens with the dimensions of 13 mm × 7 mm × 2 mm, and then the oxide was removed from the surface using the SiC paper. The sheet was connected to a direct current pulse power supply through Cu wires. The JT experiment was conducted at a current density of 4.5 × 10 3A/cm 2, with a voltage of 100 V, a pulse width of 80 μs and a frequency of 500 Hz. The sample was recorded by quenching every 60 s. The duty cycle is one of the main factors influencing the heat generation of the sample. Considering systematic errors, the duty cycle has been calculated to be 3-5 % in this work. Moreover, during the JT experiment, fans were utilized for supplementary air cooling, while the temperature was monitored using an infrared thermometer and maintained at about 50 °C. The JTed sample after a UPed treatment under 4 GPa at 800 °C was denoted as an ultrahigh-pressure treatment followed by Joule-heat treated (UPJTed). Processing Text: In this study, combined nanoprecipitation and gradient grain structure were introduced into a Co-Cr-Ni-based multi-principal element alloy (MPEA) using surface mechanical attrition treatment (SMAT). The alloy with low local stacking fault energy provides sufficient flow stress to reach the critical value for twinning, a phenomenon rarely observed in MPEAs with high-density L12 nanoprecipitates under quasi-static tensile conditions. The bulk ingot of CoCrNi 2(Al 0.2Nb 0.2) alloy, weighing 3 kg, was produced using electromagnetic levitation melting, as detailed in our previous work. The alloy underwent a series of treatments including homogenization, cold-rolling, recrystallization annealing, and aging to achieve the L12-strengthened structure. Subsequently, the aged CoCrNi 2(Al 0.2Nb 0.2) plate with dimensions of 55 mm × 25 mm × 1 mm was subjected to SMAT, as illustrated schematically in Fig. 1(a). During SMAT, 3 mm diameter bearing steel shots were activated at a vibrating frequency of 20 kHz, impacting each side of the alloy plate for 10 min. Samples were prepared using laser-powder bed fusion (L-PBF) from commercial gas-atomized powders of FeCoCrNi. These powders were mixed with AlSi10Mg powders for 10 h in a three-dimensional powder mixer with a mass ratio of 94:6, vacuum-dried for 4 h, and subsequently processed on a Renishaw RenAM 500E machine using a 316 L stainless steel substrate. For each layer, a scanning strategy involving 5 mm stripes was adopted, with a 67° rotation angle applied between consecutive layers. Different laser powers, ranging from 80 to 200 W, and scanning speeds, varying from 400 to 1800 mm/s, were used to prepare 32 test block samples. Based on these measurements, the processing parameters that resulted in the highest-density sample were selected: laser power was set to 200 W, scanning speed to 1400 mm/s, scanning hatch spacing to 80 µm, and thickness of each powder bed layer to 30 µm. Samples were then subjected to heat treatment at 1000 and 1200 °C for 1 and 10 h, respectively, in an argon atmosphere, followed by water quenching to investigate the thermal stability of the L-PBF (HEA) alloy. High-temperature tensile tests of the as-built alloys were conducted at 300, 600, 700, 800, 900, and 1000 °C. State: As-built

Processing Text: The spherical Ti-48Al-2Cr-2Nb (at.%) powders were produced by a plasma rotating electrode process (PREP, Sailong, China). The Ti-48Al-2Cr-2Nb alloys were produced by an EB-PBF machine (Arcam A2, GE additive, Sweden) under the high vacuum, and the dimension of the EB-PBF-built TiAl specimen was 80 mm (length) × 30 mm (width) × 30 mm (thickness). Before melting powders, the electron beam quickly scanned heating and maintaining the preheat temperature at 1000 °C. The density (ρ) of the EB-PBF-built Ti-48Al-2Cr-2Nb alloy was measured by the Archimedean drainage method (XPR226DR/AC, Mettler Toledo, Switzerland), and the densification was determined by the ratio of measured density to theoretical density (ρ0) expressed as: ρ/ρ0, where the theoretical density of the Ti-48Al-2Cr-2Nb alloy was 3.9 g cm−3. The chemical compositions of the raw powders and EB-PBF-built Ti-48Al-2Cr-2Nb alloys were analyzed by inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectroscopy (ICP-AES, iCAP 7600, Thermo Fisher Scientific, America). The microstructures and phase compositions of the EB-PBF-built Ti-48Al-2Cr-2Nb alloys were quantitatively analyzed using an optical microscope (OM, Axio Observer, Zeiss, Germany), scanning electron microscopy (SEM, SU8220, Zeiss, Germany), electron back-scattered diffraction (EBSD, Aztec X-Max80, Oxford, Britain), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM, JEM-200CX, JEOL, Japan). Specimens were mechanically polished and subsequently etched using a solution of 5 % hydrofluoric acid, 5 % nitric acid, and 90 % distilled water for OM and SEM analyses. EBSD specimens were electropolished with an electrolyte of 10 % perchloric acid, 30 % butanol, and 60 % methanol at −45 °C. Meanwhile, the EBSD test was performed at an acceleration voltage of 20 kV with a step size of 0.4 µm. TEM specimens were fabricated by twin-jet electropolishing with the same solution as that of EBSD. A tensile machine (Instron 5982, Instron Corporation, America) was used for the uniaxial tensile tests with a strain rate of 2 × 10−4 s−1. The dimension of the columnar tensile specimen was Ø5 mm × 70 mm. The loading-unloading-reloading (LUR) sheet tensile specimens were conducted at a loading and unloading strain rate of 2 × 10−4 s−1. The dimension of the LUR tensile specimens was 64 mm (length) × 9 mm (width) × 2 mm (thickness). The LUR experiment was run by the preloading program of the tensile machine. Processing Text: The Fe-Ni based alloy was prepared by vacuum induction melting with a nominal composition of 30Ni-15Cr-2.0Ti-0.3Al-1.3Mo-0.2Si-Fe bal. (wt.%). The ingot was homogenized at 1160 °C for 20 h, then forged and rolled into a bar with a diameter of 15 mm. After that, the bar was solutionized at 980 °C for 1 h followed by water cooling, to obtain a fully solid solution coarse-grain (CG) structure with an average grain size of 32 µm (referred to as SS-CG). Cylindrical SS-CG samples with an initial height of 15 mm were subjected to multiple dynamic plastic deformation (DPD) impacts at room temperature to obtain a nanograin (NG) structure (referred to as SS-NG). The final height of the sample was 3 mm after an 80% thickness reduction. To achieve their peak aging state, the SS-CG sample was aged at 740 °C for 8 h followed by water cooling (referred to as Aged-CG), while the SS-NG sample was aged at 680 °C for 30 min followed by water cooling (referred to as Aged-NG). Processing Text: For a long time, the large loss of the strength and toughness of fusion welded joints for thick near β titanium alloys has largely hindered their engineering application, which results from the few precipitations of the strengthening α phase during welding cooling. In this study, double annealing treatment was designed for electron beam welded joints of 30-mm-thick near β Ti-5Al-5Mo-5V-1Cr-1Fe alloy, with the aim of regulating the proportion of multi-level lamellar microstructures and enhancing the joint properties. Among various annealing temperatures (first annealing at 750-880 °C + second annealing at 580 °C), the 750 °C + 580 °C annealed joint exhibited simultaneously enhanced strength and toughness, with the increase in tensile strength and impact energy from 844 MPa and 8.8 J for the as-welded joint to 1129 MPa and 14.5 J for annealed joint, respectively, which were superior to those of the joints of Ti-5Al-5Mo-5V-1Cr-1Fe alloy as reported. The good coupling of α p phase and α s phase improved the precipitation strengthening and the resistance to crack propagation. The modified strengthening mechanism models were proposed by introducing the thickness and proportion parameters of the precipitated phase. This study provides a novel method via designing proper multi-level lamellar microstructures to simultaneously improve the strength and toughness of near β titanium alloy joints. Processing Text: The Mn and trace amounts of V and Nb were added to the original 300 M composition. The quenching temperature for the newly developed material was ultimately determined to be 820 °C, which is higher than the Ae 3point, ensuring the refinement of the original austenite structure. V-precipitates start form at 1048 °C and Nb-precipitates form at 1234 °C, providing precipitation and grain refinement strengthening during hot rolling and quenching processes. The material was cast into 50 kg pieces using a vacuum induction melting furnace, homogenized at 1200 °C for 6 h, and then forged into ingots measuring 80 mm × 80 mm at approximately 1050 °C. The hot rolling process involved heating the billet to 1200 °C for 2 h, hot rolling it to a thickness of 40 mm at 1100-1200 °C, further reducing it to 14 mm at 920-950 °C, and finally air cooling to room temperature. After hot rolling, the samples underwent various treatments: the hot-rolled sample was tempered at 200 °C for 1 h (denoted as sample L); the hot-rolled sample was cryogenically treated at −196 °C for 20 min and then tempered at 200 °C for 1 h (denoted as sample D-L); the hot-rolled sample was austenitized at 820 °C for 1 h and then tempered at 200 °C for 1 h (denoted as sample Q-L); the hot-rolled sample was austenitized at 820 °C for 1 h, cryogenically treated at −196 °C for 20 min, and then tempered at 200 °C for 1 h (denoted as sample Q-D-L). All cooling processes are air-cooled due to the high hardenability of the designed alloy. Processing Text: The Ti64 alloy powder with a spherical shape (between 45 and 325 µm in diameter) had an average chemical composition (wt%) of 6.15Al, 4.05 V, 0.089Fe, 0.15O, 0.01 N, 0.05C, 0.004H, and balance Ti. Laser processing parameters are as follows: laser power 7.6 kW, beam diameter 6 mm, scanning velocity 900 and 1500 mm/min, powder feed rate 500 g/h, overlap 40 %, and Z-axis increment 0.8 mm. These deposition parameters have been optimized. Solution treatment and aging (STA) was further conducted on the deposited samples at 950 °C for 2 h followed by air cooling (AC) and 550 °C for 4 h followed by AC. STA was performed in the air. After STA, the oxidative layers at the surface of the deposits were removed. The C(T) specimen in different directions from the deposited specimens after heat treatment was cut by wire electronic discharge machining. The notch direction and detailed dimensions are shown in Fig. 1(c, d). Pre-fabricated fatigue crack conditions are as follows: at the beginning, the maximum loading force is Fmax=17,000 N, and the minimum loading force is Fmin=1000 N; at the final stage, Fmax=16,000 N, Fmin=1000 N. The total number of cycles is from 18,000 to 24,000 cycles, the pre-fabricated fatigue crack length is ∼4.5 mm. Finally, fracture toughness tests were conducted in tension at a displacement speed of 1 mm/min until the C(T) specimen failed. The plane strain fracture toughness ( KIc) tests were conducted according to the Chinese standard GB/T 4161-2007, corresponding to the ASTM E399-12standard. Specimens for the electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) characterization were prepared by pre-mechanical polishing and a Leica multifunctional ion thinning instrument (Leica EM RES102) at a voltage of 6 kV for 2 h with an angle of ion beam machining of 6°. Processing Text: A 5 Kg steel ingot of composition Fe-20Mn-2Al-0.7V-0.4C (wt.%) was prepared in a vacuum levitation melting furnace under argon protection. The steel was then precision cut into 10 mm thickness rectangular plates using electrical discharge machining (EDM). The cast ingot was hot forged and annealed (see details in Fig. 1) before testing to ensure the uniform distribution of microstructure and composition. The plate with the size of Φ45 × 2.5 mm 3 was cut from the as-annealed steel and then mechanically ground up to 1000 # sandpaper, i.e., as-annealed plate. Coolant was continuously sprayed on the plate surface during USRT to avoid adiabatic warming. The spindle speed is 100 r/min, the ultrasonic frequency is 28 kHZ, the vibration amplitude is 6 μm, the static load is 400 N. Following the procedure displayed in ASTM E8 [ 32], flat tensile specimens were cut from the as-annealed plate (i.e., as-annealed specimen) and USRT plate (i.e., USRT specimen) along the forging direction (see details in Fig. 1). Tensile testing with a strain rate of 0.002 s −1 was conducted on a INSTRON 8801 machine at room temperature, the tensile strain (i.e., engineering strain) was measured by a video extensometer testing system. Processing Text: The Al-5.0Mn-1.5Mg-0.82Sc-0.76Zr (wt.%) alloy powder with a standard composition was prepared by gas atomization (Panxing New Alloy Materials Co., Ltd., China). The powder was spherical in shape, with the particles less than or equal to 22.3 µm accounting for 10% while 90% of the particles were less than or equal to 63.4 µm, as shown in Fig. 1(a, b). All the LPBF samples investigated in this work were manufactured using a BLT S210 LPBF machine equipped with a 400 W fiber laser. Constant laser power (350 W), scanning spacing (90 µm), and layer thickness (30 µm) were used with scanning velocities ranging between 450 and 1450 mm/s. Two different substrate temperatures, 25 and 200 °C, were used for each condition. The samples with the optimized process parameters had a relative density higher than 99.8 %. A bilinear scanning strategy with a scan rotation of 67° was used between the layers. The samples were printed in a high-purity argon atmosphere. Subsequently, the samples were heat-treated at 200 °C for 1 h to remove residual stresses before evaluating their microstructures and mechanical properties. The LPBF samples were prepared for microstructural characterization by mechanical grinding and polishing following a standard metallographic procedure recommended in ASTM E3-11. After polishing, the microstructural features were revealed using an etchant consisting of HNO 3(2.5 mL), HCl (1.5 mL), HF (1.0 mL), and distilled water (95 mL). The wire-cut electro-discharge machine was used to slice samples with the following dimensions: ∼5 mm long, ∼5 mm wide, and ∼1 mm thick. Prior to the EBSD characterization, the sheet samples were first mechanically polished with 400 #, 1000 #, 2000 #, and 3000 # SiC water abrasive paper, then electropolished to remove the surface deformation layer generated by mechanical grinding. Electropolishing was performed at −30 °C, with: 7 % perchloric acid, 93 % ethanol; a voltage of 25 V, and a current density of 450 mA/cm 2for about 1 min. Uniaxial tensile tests were performed using the CMT4105 universal testing machine. The gauge length and cross-sectional area of the tensile specimens were 22 mm and 1.5 mm × 4 mm. All the tensile samples were tested perpendicular to the build direction at a constant strain rate of 1 mm/min, following the standard ASTM E8. Fatigue test samples with the dimensions 60 mm × 12 mm × 1.5 mm were tested on an MTS370.02 fatigue testing machine. All samples were mechanically ground and polished prior to fatigue testing to ensure similar surface roughness. The uniaxial fatigue tests were conducted in a load control mode at a frequency of 40 Hz and stress ratio of R= 0.1, following the standard ASTM E466. The samples were tested until fracture or exhaustion till 10 7cycles. Sample: TV1; Microstructure: bimodal consisting of columnar and equiaxed grains; Scanning velocity: ~1450 mm/s; Substrate temperature: ~25 °C

Processing Text: Six ultrahigh-strength DP steels with varying microstructure but comparable tensile strength (>1400 MPa) were prepared via tailoring the heat treatment process after cold rolling. The experimental steel, with a composition of Fe-0.19C-0.26Si-3.2Mn-0.16V-0.19Mo (wt.%), underwent melting, forging, hot rolling, and cold rolling processes. The related process parameters matched those in Ref. [ 11]. The final cold-rolled sheet thickness is 1.8-1.9 mm. Then the cold-rolled sheets were heated in a tube furnace under the specified heat treatment process. Fig. 1 shows the thermomechanical processing routes. Various DP steels with different matrix phases, grain sizes, and ferrite morphologies were produced through these six routes. In this context, 'F-' and 'M-' denote ferritic matrix and martensitic matrix, respectively. 'CG' and 'FG' represent coarse-grained microstructure and fine-grained microstructure, respectively. 'P' indicates a plate-like ferrite morphology. The microstructure was examined by scanning electronic microscopy (SEM, Zeiss Sigma 300) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM, Thermo Scientific 153 FEI Talos F200X). Metallographic samples for SEM were mechanically ground and polished and then etched in a solution of 4 % (volume fraction) nitric acid. Samples for TEM were mechanically ground to a thickness of 200 µm and then electropolished in a twin-jet machine in a solution of 5 % perchloric acid in 95 % alcohol at 20 °C. Tensile tests were performed on a 100 kN Servo-Hydraulic Testing Machine equipped with an Epsilon extensometer at a strain rate of 10 -3s -1 at room temperature (20 °C). All tensile specimens are the standard subsize ones with a 25 mm gauge length and 6 mm width, machined along the rolling direction (RD) of the sheet (ASTM-E8 M). In addition, the hole expansion test was conducted on a hole expansion machine (SAS-200DT-01), with specimens being thin plates measuring 110 mm × 110 mm and featuring a central circular hole with a diameter of 10 mm (GB/T 15,825.4-1995). Compact-tension (CT) specimens were cut with a thickness (B) of 1.8 mm, and a width (W) of 18 mm. A straight-through notch was cut with a length of 8 mm, with the crack direction perpendicular to the RD. Prior to the fracture toughness measurement, fatigue pre-cracking was produced in force control with a stress ratio ( R) of 0.1, and the length of the final pre-crack was about 9 mm. Grain size: 1.06 µm (martensite); UE: 7.2%; EtF: 9.8%

Processing Text: In this work, Ti powders (∼8 μm) were used as the starting materials for preparing the composites. Fine Si powders (∼2 μm) were used to fabricate Ti 5 Si 3 reinforcements. The Ti and Si powders were first wet-mixed using acetone as the liquid medium. After mixing, the Ti/Si powder slurry was air-dried. The as-dried powders with varied Si contents were pressed and sintered in a graphite die (diameter: 12 mm) using an SPS-211Lx machine at 1050 °C with a heating rate of 100 °C/min. The sintering process included a holding time of 5 min. A consolidation pressure of 50 MPa was applied and maintained throughout the entire sintering process in a vacuum atmosphere, typically achieving a vacuum level of 10 −3 to 10 −6 Torr to prevent oxidation and contamination. The sintered compacts were then cooled to room temperature at a rate of ∼25 °C/min. For further dislodging the effect of carbon diffusion, the surface of as-sintered compacts were mechanical removed the diffusion layer. Contribution from Si solid-solution strengthening

Processing Text: Al-Mg-Mn-Sc-Zr alloy powder with high content of Sc and Zr elements was prepared by vacuum induction gas atomization. The powder granularity was 10-60 μm. The chemical composition of the Al-Mg-Mn-Sc-Zr alloy powder is shown in Table 1. The content of Sc/Zr elements is almost twice that of conventional alloys. The Mg/Mn element is also added to the alloy mainly because of its excellent solid solution strengthening. In particular, Mg element can also inhibit recrystallization to a certain extent and prevent grain growth. Processing Text: The as-received (AR) standard UNS N07718 (Alloy 718) alloy was utilized. A high-energy Nd-YAG laser (Tyrida YS120-R200A) with an 18 ns pulse width and 1064nm wavelength was employed for LSP. The 10.9 J laser pulse of 4 mm spot size produced a peak power density of 4.82 GW/cm 2. Peening was performed in a ring-wise pattern along the gauge area of the dog bone samples. Each ring consisted of 13 overlapping laser spots. Successive rings were 1.2 mm apart vertically. The calculated overlap in both the circumferential and axial directions was 70%. A thin layer of deionized water was used as the tamping medium without any ablative coating, a technique which is often referred to as LSP without coating (LSPwC) or uncoated LSP. The ex-situ hydrogen charging process was performed using a three-electrode electrochemical charging cell, incorporating a platinum foil as the counter electrode and a saturated calomel electrode (SCE) as the reference electrode, in line with ASTM G148. The electrolyte used for hydrogen charging was a 0.5M H 2SO 4solution containing 1g/L of thiourea to act as a recombination agent for enhanced hydrogen absorption. The electrochemical charging process was carried out at room temperature with a current density of 590 mA/cm 2for both 2 and 24 h, utilizing an Autolab PGSTAT302N potentiostat. Processing Text: TiZrAlMn alloy ingots were produced by melting in a vacuum non-consumable electric arc furnace. Titanium, acting as an oxygen absorber, effectively prevented oxidation. The ingots were turned and re-melted at least eight times under a pure argon atmosphere to ensure a uniform composition. Each alloy ingot, weighing approximately 65 g, displayed a coarse Widmanstätten structure composed of lamellar αphase and residual βphase. The phase transition temperatures of TiZrAlMn alloys were using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) by ASTM F2004-05 (2010) at a heating rate of 10 °C/min. The onset and end temperatures of the alloy were determined to be 785±4 °C and 869±10 °C, respectively, using the tangent method on the DSC curves. To optimize the coarse Widmanstätten structure, hot rolling was performed at different phase transition temperature regions (900 °C, 850 °C, 800 °C and 750 °C). Each TiZrAlMn alloy ingot was held in the muffle furnace for 40 min before rolling to ensure uniform heating and reaching target temperature. Button ingots, approximately 14 mm thick, were rolled to 2 mm using two-high rolls mill, achieving a total deformation of 85.7%. Between each rolling pass, the ingots were reheated in the furnace for 6 min, with a rolling reduction of 1.5 mm per pass (rolling speed: 0.5 m/s). Air cooling was used after rolling. The rolled specimens were labeled as 900-AC, 850-AC, 800-AC and 750-AC, according to their respective rolling temperatures. Specimen rolled at 900 °C; Microstructure: mixed morphology of Widmanstätten and Basket-weave structures

Processing Text: The Mg-8.5Gd-3Y-2Cu-0.5Zr (wt.%) alloy ingot, measuring 90 mm in diameter and 1200 mm in length, was successfully produced through semi-continuous casting. The ingot was subjected to a homogenization treatment at 500 °C for 12 h and then extruded at 375 °C. The extrusion process was performed at a ratio of 28:1 and a rate of 0.6 mm/s, followed immediately by air quenching to room temperature. Before undergoing multi-pass hot rolling, these plates were pre-heated to 200 °C for 30 min in a resistance furnace, with the mill rolls heated to the same temperature. The rolling involved multiple passes, reducing plate thickness by 2 %-5 % each time, accompanied by a 90° in-plane rotation after each pass, resulting in 4 mm thick sheets. After each pass, to maintain the recrystallization temperature and activate the PSN mechanism, the samples were reheated to 200 °C for 5 min and cooled in room-temperature water after rolling was completed. The 4 mm thick sheets were then subjected to a double-ageing treatment, achieving peak-aged conditions at 100 °C for 8 h and 200 °C for 36 h. Both types of Mg-RE alloys are MR + A treated. Processing Text: The IN718 components were fabricated using SLM Solutions 280HL machine, Germany. The powders were spread on the platform and melted layer by layer to generate the cylindrical specimens of dimensions 13 mm diameter and 80 mm length. An argon atmosphere was maintained in the chamber throughout the process to avoid oxidation during SLM process. A hatch style rotation of 67° was employed between the layers. The parameters utilized for SLM process like laser power of 200 W, scan speed of 1200 mm/s, hatch spacing of 90 μm and layer thickness of 30 μm. To maintain proper heat dissipation during the printing process a support structure were maintained for the samples with the same material and the supports were removed from the platform using wire cut electric discharge machine, once the printing process completed. The cylindrical specimens generated by SLM were friction welded by continuous drive KUKA friction welding (FW) machine. A facing operation was performed for the faying surfaces to remove any contaminations or oxides if present. The parameters employed for FW process such as, heating pressure of 50 bar, upset pressure of 60 bar, heating time of 6 s, upset time of 3 s and a rotary speed of 1125 rpm. An infrared thermographic (IR) camera (FLIR-make) was used to measure the temperature distribution at the interface during FW. Two cylindrical rods were considered whereas one was at stationery position and other was rotated with constant rpm during FW. The workpieces generate the frictional force in between the faying surfaces and an upset force was applied to forms the welds. The SLM samples after FW were examined for the microstructural characterization. The cross section of samples was grounded and polished with standard metallography practices to obtain scratch free surfaces. After etching with an etchant of HCl -10 ml and H 2O 2-3 ml for 10 s, the microstructures were observed under Olympus BX51 optical microscope (OM) and for higher magnification, scanning electron microscope (SEM) of Zeiss EVO MA 15 was used. The X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis was performed using Rigaku ultima IV with Cu-Kα radiation of wavelength 0.1542 nm. The step size of 0.02° was used during diffraction analysis at an angle ranging from 40° to 100°. For micro-texture analysis, a FEI TMQuanta 3D-SEM with TSL-EDX TMEBSD (electron back scatter diffraction) system was utilized. OIM Analysis TM(version 8.1) post processing software was used to analyse EBSD data. The Vickers microhardness tests were carried out with 500 g load and a dwell time of 10 s using Buehler Micromet indenter. The measurements were performed along the cross section of the specimen to cover all the zones present in the specimen. Room temperature tensile tests were conducted using Instron 8516 with a strain rate of 10 -4s -1for the as-built SLM and welded samples. The strain hardening behaviour was analysed using Kocks-Mecking plots from the tensile tests data and fracture analysis was performed on the tensile samples to evaluate the fractography features. The strength contribution from the various strengthening mechanisms were calculated for both the SLM as built and weld conditions of IN718 components. Condition: After FW (Friction Welding); Microstructure: Granular/spherical Laves phase

Processing Text: Material and methods CoCrFeNi(TiC) 0.2 HEA with a molar ratio of 1: 1: 1: 1: 0.2 was prepared in an arc melting furnace on a water-cooled hearth under a high-purity argon atmosphere. High-purity Co, Cr, Fe, Ni and TiC powders were mixed and then melted at least five times to obtain a chemically uniform ingot with dimensions of 20 mm × 20 mm × 10 mm. The as-cast ingot was cold-rolled to thin sheet, reducing the thickness by 50 %, which was then heat treated at 900 °C for 1 h and terminated by water-quenching, the formed alloy was labeled as CR-A900 hereafter. Noted that the heat treatment process was set based on previous studies [ 33–35 ], in which heat treatment at 900 °C for 1 h could obtain residual dislocations and more than half of the fine recrystallized grains. For comparison, the as-cast CoCrFeNi(TiC) 0.2 HEA was also prepared, which was labeled as as-cast. Processing Text: The Alloy 718 used in this work was a nuclear-grade material with stringent control of Co content less than 0.005 wt%. The alloy was initially produced through vacuum induction melting and cast into ingots. The ingots were soaked at 1020 °C for 1 h and subsequently hot-rolled into rods. The finish rolling temperature was 900 °C, after which the rods were water quenched. Four specific heat treatments were applied to the as-received materials to decouple the variable secondary phases. Specimen HT1 was solution annealed at 1060 °C for 1 h followed by water quench. Specimen HT2 was firstly solution annealed using the same parameters as HT1 and then a two-step aging process was applied to precipitate the γ' and γ'' phases. Specimens HT3 and HT4 were annealed at 950 °C for 1 h and 12 h, respectively, to facilitate the precipitation of micro-sized δ phases. The specimens were designed according to ASTM E8-04 and were cut using wire electrical discharge machining. To eliminate the effects of mechanical machining and ensure surface homogeneity, the gauge sections were sequentially ground with abrasive papers from 320# to 2000#, followed by polishing with diamond suspensions of 9 μm, 3 μm, 1 μm and 0.05 μm. Finally, vibratory polishing was performed to remove the surface deformation layer, ensuring no scratches or residual strain remained. Condition: Solution-annealed (HT1); Strain rate: 1E-6/s to 0.8 YS, then 4E-8/s to 2%; True strain: 2.3; Test time: 301 h

Processing Text: A master alloy with nominal composition of Ni 49Fe 20Al 17Cr 8V 6(at. %) was prepared by arc-melting Ni, Fe, Al, Cr and V elements with high purity (99.99 wt%). Each ingot was remelted at least five times to ensure chemical homogeneity. Subsequently, the molten liquid was drop-cast into a water-cooled copper mold with dimension of 70 × 10 × 10 mm. The as-cast alloys were cold-rolled with a thickness reduction of ∼90 % and then annealed at 775 °C for 2 h. Here, based on the equilibrium phase diagram of Ni 49Fe 20Al 17Cr 8V 6EHEA, we have performed a series of annealing treatment within a range temperature of 750∼900 °C for 2 h on the cold-rolled samples to achieve a superior mechanical performance. The as-cast, cold-rolled and annealed at 775 °C for 2 h were denoted as AC and CR-775 EHEAs, respectively. Processing state: as-cast; Microstructure: dual-phase lamellar structure with soft FCC/L12 and hard B2 phases

Processing Text: Initially, we prepared ten button ingots by arc-melting the different constituent elements with a purity of over 99.9 wt% under a Ti-gettered argon atmosphere. Each ingot was remelted at least four times to ensure chemical homogeneity. The next step involved remelting these ingots in a vacuum induction furnace to create a large cylindrical master alloy with dimensions of Ø29.3 mm × 55 mm (Fig. S1a). This master alloy was then vacuum-sealed in a steel sleeve under an argon atmosphere and homogenized at 1423 K for 24 h, followed by water quenching. Subsequently, the homogenized sample was preheated at 1423 K for 1 h and then hot-extruded using a four-column hydraulic press (HP32-315, Jiangsu Tiankai) at a speed of 22 ± 5 mm/s, then air-cooled. After hot extrusion, a long bar with a diameter of ∼16 mm and a length of ∼49 cm (Fig. S1b) was obtained. This uniform hot-extruded part was then cut into rectangular pieces along the extrusion direction (ED) for microstructural analysis and further cold rolling (Fig. S1c). Furthermore, a cylinder ingot of Al 0.25CoCrFeNi was obtained by pouring the liquid Al 0.25CoCrFeNi into a ceramic mold with an inner diameter of 160 mm and a height of 70 mm. The 20 plates with dimensions of 45 mm × 20 mm × 15 mm were cut from the alloy ingot by electric spark cutting followed by ∼85 % cold rolling (CR) along the longitudinal ingot direction. Then, the sheets were of a final thickness of approximately 2.25 mm. To obtain fully recrystallized equiaxial structures with three different grain sizes, the cold-rolled sheets were annealed at 1000 °C, 1100 °C, and 1200 °C for 1 h, followed by water quenching, which were denoted as CR-1000, CR-1100, and CR-1200, respectively. The crystalline structures of the as-prepared Al 0.25CoCrFeNi HEA were characterized by X-ray diffractometer (XRD, Shimadzu, MAXima XRD-7000, Japan) using Cu Kα (λ = 1.5418 Å) radiation. The voltage and current applied to the Cu target were 40 kV and 30 mA, respectively. Then the microstructure was studied on the three principal planes (perpendicular to RD (rolling direction), TD (transverse direction), and ND (normal direction) directions) of the sample by a scanning electron microscope (SEM, Helios G4 CX) equipped with energy-dispersive X-ray spectrometry (EDS, Helios G4 CX) and electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) detectors. The grain size of the alloy was measured and calculated by the EBSD statistics. The samples used for SEM and EBSD characterization were mechanically polished and then electropolished in a mixture of C 2H 5OH (90 %) and HClO 4(10 %). Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and selected area electron diffraction (SAED) were carried out on an FEI Tecnai G2 F30 microscope at a voltage of 300 kV for deformed samples. Dog-bone-shaped specimens with a gauge length of 20 mm, width of 4 mm, and thickness of 2 mm were prepared from annealed samples by electrical discharge machining. Uniaxial tensile tests were carried out with a strain rate of 10 −3s −1at 25 °C and −196 °C. The cryogenic tension tests were performed with the specimens completely immersed in liquid nitrogen. Three samples were measured for each condition. Temperature: 25 °C; Grain size: 217 μm

Processing Text: The Re 0.04Hf 0.15Ta 2.1W 0.45(TaC) 0.45 refractory medium-entropy alloy (RMEA) was successfully fabricated using mechanical ball milling and spark plasma sintering (SPS). The preparation process is shown in Fig. 1(a). First, the target composition powders were ball-milled and then loaded into a graphite mold with an inner diameter of 20 mm and an outer diameter of 30 mm. The samples were then densified using a spark plasma sintering furnace (LABOX-650F, SINTERLAND, Japan) to obtain the desired samples. The sintering temperature for the alloy was set at 1800 °C, with a holding time of 30 min. The sintering pressure was 30 MPa, and during the cooling stage, the pressure was reduced to 10 MPa. Ball milling was performed using a planetary ball mill (SQMLF-4 L, HuaWei, China) under Ar protection to minimize oxygen incorporation during the milling process. The post-milling powder handling was conducted in an argon-filled glove box. The ball milling duration was 4 h, with a rotational speed of 180 rpm and a ball-to-powder weight ratio of 8:1. To avoid the carbon contamination effect from the graphite mold during the sintering process, a 1 mm surface layer of the sintered sample was removed before conducting microstructural and mechanical property characterization. The SPS sintering curve of Re 0.04Hf 0.15Ta 2.1W 0.45(TaC) 0.45RMEA is shown in Fig. 2. The raw materials used included high-purity powders of Re, Ta, W, HfH 2, and TaC. The purity and average particle sizes of the powders were as follows: Re (99.95 wt%, 1 μm), HfH 2(99.90 wt%, 44 μm), Ta (99.95 wt%, 30 μm), W (99.95 wt%, 10 μm), and TaC (99.90 wt%, 1-3 μm). Notably, the Hf in the Re 0.04Hf 0.15Ta 2.1W 0.45(TaC) 0.45alloy originates from the HfH 2powder. Temperature: Room Temperature

Processing Text: The materials were prepared through vacuum induction melting. The C0.5 and C0 EHEAs were first subjected to solid solution heat treatment (ST) at a temperature of 1300 °C for 6h to allow complete solid solution of the alloy precipitated phases into the matrix. Subsequently, the solid solution C0.5 EHEAs were subjected to aging treatment (AT) at 500 °C, 600 °C, and 700 °C for 4 h. All the heat treatments involved in the paper were quenched in water. In order to facilitate discussion, the samples subjected to different solid solution aging temperatures are designated as (ST-C0、ST-C0.5、ST-500 °C AT-C0.5、ST-600 °C AT-C0.5、ST-700 °C AT-C0.5) EHEAs in this paper. Firstly, wire cutting was employed to prepare samples of C0 and C0.5 EHEAs in different heat treatment states. Under the conditions of 40 kV voltage and 40 mA current, phase analysis of the alloy was conducted using an X-ray diffractometer (XRD, Ultima IV, Japan) within a range of 20°-80°, at a scanning rate of 5°/min. The microstructure and elemental composition of 0.5C EHEA samples under different heat treatment conditions were characterized using a scanning electron microscope (SEM, EM30, Korea) equipped with an energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS). Before conducting SEM measurements, the samples were subjected to an etching treatment using aqua regia (HCl:HNO 3= 3:1). The electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, Oxford Symmetry S2, UK) detector (was employed to conduct a thorough microstructural characterization of the crystal orientation and phase distribution in C0.5 EHEAs after aging treatment at 600 °C. The transmission electron microscope (TEM, JEM-2100, Japan), in conjunction with High-Resolution Transmission Electron Microscopy (HRTEM), was employed to conduct a further investigation of the nanoscale precipitates at the alloy phase boundaries after aging treatment. To prevent contamination, this process was conducted in an argon-filled glove box. Subsequently, the mold was placed into a SPS system (LABOX-325R). The SPS process was conducted under the following conditions: the temperature was increased to 1050 °C at a rate of 100 °C/min, maintained for 10 min, then cooled to 300 °C at a rate of 100 °C/min, and finally cooled to room temperature within the furnace. A high vacuum of 10 −3Pa was maintained throughout the process to minimize gas contamination, and a uniaxial pressure of 50 MPa was applied. As a result, a cylindrical CoCrNi MEA block with a diameter of 20 mm and a height of 7 mm was obtained. A circular sample with a diameter of 20 mm and a thickness of 2 mm was cut from the SPSed CoCrNi using electrical discharge machining (EDM, SKD3). To induce a heterostructure, surface mechanical rolling treatment (SMRT) was applied to both surfaces of the circular sample. The SMRT parameters were as follows: a WC/Co ball penetrated the sample while sliding along its axis at a velocity of 2000 mm/min with a penetration depth of 5 μm. This procedure was repeated three times. During the SMRT process, the contact surface between the WC-Co ball and the circular sample was cooled using oil lubrication to prevent overheating. For convenience, the treated sample is referred to as MHS CoCrNi. The crystal orientation of SPSed CoCrNi was analyzed using electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, NordlysMax3) with a step size of 0.5 μm. A detailed cross-sectional analysis of MHS CoCrNi was also performed to reveal the gradient structure. Before testing, the data acquisition area of the sample needed to be treated. The test surface of each sample was first polished to remove scratches and achieve a smooth surface. Subsequently, argon ion polishing (IM4000 Ⅱ) was conducted at voltages of 5 kV, 4 kV, and 3 kV, with each stage lasting approximately 1 h. The microstructure within the grains was further investigated using transmission electron microscopy (TEM, FEI Talos F200X). Circular samples with a diameter of 10 mm and thickness of 500 μm were initially cut using EDM, followed by mechanical grinding with abrasive papers (800-2000 grade) to a thickness of 80 μm. Thin discs with a diameter of 3 mm were punched from these samples and further thinned to approximately 20 μm using a Gatan dimple grinder and ion beam thinner (Gatan Model 691). The Vickers hardness tester (Q10 A +) was used to measure the surface hardness of both SPSed and MHS CoCrNi, as well as the hardness distribution along the depth of MHS CoCrNi. The tests were conducted with a load of 50 g applied for 10 s. Dog-bone-shaped specimens with a gauge length of 5 mm and a cross-section of 2.0 × 1.5 mm 2were cut by EDM. Tensile and loading-unloading-reloading (LUR) tests were carried out on a universal testing machine (INSTRON, 68TM-50). During the LUR tensile test, specimens were initially stretched to a strain of 2 %, unloaded to 5 MPa, and then subjected to repeated cycles at designated strain levels (4 %, 6 %, 8 %, etc.). The tensile rate was 0.5 mm/min. Fracture surfaces were subsequently observed using SEM to analyze the fracture mechanism. Tensile properties; Variation: ± 80 MPa

Processing Text: Samples from the Inconel 939 powder mixture were 3D printed and casted via precision casting. The technology of precision casting into a water-based ceramic malachite shell was used to produce casting samples. AM specimens for tensile and creep tests were manufactured on the 3D printer (SLM 280 2.0, SLM Solutions Group AG) using a powder mixture in the range of 10-45 μm. The entire building cycle took place on the mentioned device with process parameters recommended by the powder supplier of the Inconel 939 material. In particular laser power was set in range 27-370 W (depends on the printing zone), scanning speed was set in range 500-7000 mm.s −1, hatching distance was determined in range 0.06-0.11 mm. The 3D printed samples exhibited a 1.2 mm allowance on their diameter. This allowance was removed by finishing operation using a cutting insert with 0.4 mm nose radius. The procedure of the heat treatment (prescribed by the powder supplier) was followed for the casted as well as for the 3D printed samples. The HIP operation was also included in the heat treatment of few samples, which combining the temperature of up to 2000 °C with a pressure of up to 2070 bar leads to the elimination of pores in the material and conversion of some undesirable structures, such as oxides, nitrides and some forms of carbides. The annealing heat treatment was performed by rapid heating (RH) to 1107 °C/2 h in a vacuum furnace followed by a slow cooling (3 °C/min) to 899 °C. After reaching a temperature of 899 °C a rapid cooling (RC) with Ar to the room temperature (RT) was carried out. Subsequent aging consisted of three steps i.e., RH to 913 °C/8 h plus RC with Ar at RT, RH to 982 °C/6 h plus RC with Ar at RT, RH to 803 °C/4 h, and quenching with Ar to RT. The HIP post-process operation was realized as a combination of the identical heat treatment with HIP at the temperature of 1200 °C/4 h and the pressure of 1000 bar. The casted samples were heat treated with homogenization annealing followed by aging. Homogenization annealing was carried out at the temperature of 1160 °C/2 h followed by cooling (30 °C) to the temperature of 700 °C followed by the air cooling to RT. The aging treatment was carried out at the temperature of 845 °C/16 h with fan cooling to RT. Few samples were subjected to the HIP process parameters at a temperature of 1200 °C/4 h and the pressure of 1035 bar in Ar atmosphere with a minimum purity of 99.995 %. The tensile tests at RT were performed using the TIRAtest 28,250 machine (TIRA GmbH). The creep resistance tests were carried out via a T-800 machine (SVUM GmbH). Condition: cast and HIP samples; Test temperature: 982 °C
Processing Word: Condition: cast and HIP samples; Test temperature: 982 °C

Processing Text: Experimental Alloy ingots of (Fe₅₀Mn₂₇Cr₁₃Ni₁₀)₁₀₀₋ₓCₓ(0, 2, 4 at.%) HEA were prepared under an argon atmosphere by arc melting in water-cooled copper crucibles. The purity of Fe, Mn, Cr, Ni, and C raw materials is higher than 99.9% (wt.%). Carbon was added as Fe₃C block to prevent being blown away. Individually, each ingot was overturned and re-melted six times to encourage compositional homogeneity. The master alloys, weighing 2 kg, were subsequently cast into a steel mold measuring 200 mm × 50 mm × 50 mm. After casting, the master alloy was sliced into rectangular samples using an electric discharge machining process. These as-cast samples were homogenized at 1200 °C for 6 h and then cold-rolled with a thickness reduction of 70%. Cold-rolled samples were sealed in a quartz tube and subjected to vacuum pumping (below 5 × 10⁻⁴ Pa) before being annealed at 800 °C for 1 h, followed by quenching in tap water. Processing Text: It was fabricated through exothermal reactions between mixed salts (high-purity reactive powders of K2TiF6 and KBF4) and molten aluminum. TiB2 particles were formed in-situ in the molten matrix. The cast ingot was homogenized at a temperature of 495 °C for 48 h. Subsequently, the hot extrusion was carried out at 450 °C with an extrusion ratio of ∼10. After extrusion, the ingot was subjected to T4 heat treatment: solution treatment conducted at 500 °C for 1 h followed by water quenching, and then kept at room temperature for over 4 days to experience potential natural aging. Dumbbell-shaped tensile specimens with a gauge length of 5 mm and a gauge section diameter of 4 mm were machined for uniaxial quasi-static and dynamic tensile tests. Cylindrical specimens with a diameter of 5 mm and a height of 4 mm were prepared by wire electrical discharge machining for uniaxial compression tests. A hat-shaped simple shear specimen with a shear zone length of 4 mm, widths of 1 mm, and thickness of 2 mm was designed and machined. All specimens were cut from the extrusion composite plate with a loading direction parallel to the extrusion direction (ED), and the surfaces of compression specimens were polished to be mirror-like using waterproof silicon carbide papers and colloidal silica polishing suspensions with different particle sizes. Both quasi-static tensile and compressive tests were performed on a DNS-100 electronic universal testing machine at a strain rate of 0.001/s. Dynamic uniaxial tensile tests were performed at strain rates from 1200/s to 4000/s using a split Hopkinson tension bar (SHTB) system and the dynamic uniaxial compression was performed using a split Hopkinson pressure bar (SHPB) system. The SHPB and SHTB systems mainly consists of three co-axial bars: the striker bar (or tube), the incident bar, and the transmission bar. For shear tests, the shear stress τ and shear strain γ can be converted to equivalent values using the relationships σeq=3τ and εeq=ln1+γ+γ2/2, respectively. The interface between loading bar ends and compression specimens were lubricated by daubing molybdenum disulfide grease. The stress, strain and strain rate of tested specimens was measured by the strain gauges on the incident and transmission bars. For the high-temperature tests, the elevated-temperature environments were obtained using an electric radiant-heating furnace. A thermocouple strapped around the specimen was used to monitor the temperature. After reaching the target value, the specimen temperature was maintained constant to within 3 K for 5 min. This process can ensure a uniform specimen temperature (both surface and internal temperature) before loading. At least three repetitive experiments in each condition were conducted to ensure repeatability of the results. Before the microstructure observation, the metallographic preparation following a three-step procedure had been conducted for the pre- and post-loading samples: grinding by using waterproof silicon carbide papers with the increasing grit size from 600 to 5000, mechanical polishing with the particulate solution on a polishing cloth, and chemical etching in a mixed solution containing 1%HF+ 1.5%HCl+ 2.5%HNO + 95 %H2O for 15 s. Flat dog-bone-shaped tensile specimens with a gage length of 6 mm, thickness of 1 mm and width of 3.5 mm were in-situ tested by a ZEISS Gemini 500 field emission SEM to characterize the microstructure evolution at specific strains under quasi-static loading and room temperature. The TEM samples were prepared by mechanically polishing to about 50 μm followed by precision ion thinning treatment. Athermal yield stress (σa) independent of temperature and strain rate

Processing Text: High-purity nickel, cobalt, and vanadium (all >99.9 % purity) were selected for the preparation of the VCoNi MPEA. The alloy was smelted using the arc-melting method under an argon atmosphere and cast into the mold of 130 mm in diameter and 150 mm in height. To ensure chemical homogeneity, the ingot was turned upside down and re-melted five times. Subsequently, the ingot was hot-forged and hot-rolled at 1423 K to form a plate with dimensions of 12 × 100 × 600 mm³. The plate underwent annealing in a vacuum at 1373 K for 2 h, followed by water quenching. Finally, cold rolling (CR) was performed with a thickness reduction of 90 % to produce sheets with a thickness of 1 mm. Heterogeneous laminated Al matrix composites reinforced by 5, 10 and 20 wt% CrCoNi medium entropy alloy lamellas were fabricated by a powder metallurgy approach with two-step ball-milling process. Spherical pure Al powders (99.9 % purity, 10 μm average particle size, Henan Yuanyang Powder Technology Co., LTD.), and spherical equiatomic CrCoNi powders (99.9 % purity, 20 μm average particle size, Beijing Yanbang New Material Technology Co., LTD.) were used as the raw materials. Firstly, the CrCoNi powders were ball milled in an attritor (Qingdao Union Process Precision Machinery Co., Ltd.) at a speed of 450 rpm in pure ethanol for 15 h, with a ball-to-powder weight ratio of 20:1. The CrCoNi slurry was then vacuum-suction filtered and vacuum dried at 333 K for 24 h to obtain CrCoNi flaky powders. Next, flaky CrCoNi powders and Al powders were mixed with 1 wt% stearic acid in a glovebox with a highly purified argon atmosphere to minimize the oxidation of Al powders. Composite powders were then ball milled in a planetary mill (QM-DY2 Nanjing NJU-instrument Co., LTD.) at 300 rpm for 8 h with the ball-to-powder weight ratio of 20:1, followed by degreasing at 673 K for 0.5 h in a muffle furnace inside the glovebox to remove the residual stearic acid. Subsequently, the composite powders were hot pressed under 900 MPa at 723 K for 0.5 h and hot extruded with the extrusion ratio of 9:1 at 573 K to obtain CrCoNi-Al composites. According to the CrCoNi content in the composite (5 wt%, 10 wt% and 20 wt%), the as-fabricated composites are designated as 5CrCoNi-Al, 10CrCoNi-Al, and 20CrCoNi-Al, respectively. Processing Text: 321 stainless steel wire with a diameter of 1.2 mm was applied as the deposition material. A 304 stainless steel plate with 150 × 300 × 6 mm 3 dimensions was used as a substrate. In the deposition process, the Fronius TPS4000 CMT welding machine was applied. Considering the deposition quality and impact requirement, a single-layer deposition with a relatively flat and smooth surface was selected to keep the process stable and ensure the impact effect. A single-point impact mode was conducted to treat the top part of the deposition after the deposition was cooled to room temperature. The process parameters were set to obtain a noticeable impact effect on the basis of ensuring the stability and sustainability of the UIT process. The impact load was applied and controlled through the KUKA robot based on the pressure sensor during this process. The UIT was applied to the single-layer deposition to better compare inter-layer thermal effects on microstructure evolution and recrystallization behavior after UIT. After obtaining 321 stainless steel bulk fabrications, samples were machined from X, Y, and Z directions to compare the impact toughness, tensile properties, and anisotropy of the fabrications with and without inter-layer UIT strengthening. Before the EBSD experiment, 10 % perchloric acid was used for electrolytic polishing of the samples. The EBSD equipment type was C-Swift manufactured by Oxford Instruments, with an accelerating voltage of 20 kV, a working distance of 15 mm, a scanning step of 1.3 μm for the macroscopic region of 0.5 × 0.5 mm 2, and 0.25 μm for the microscopic region of 0.1 × 0.1 mm 2. The macroscopic region was sampled in an area 0.5 mm away from the treated surface of the deposition to avoid the influence of interlayer remelting. The microscopic regions were located in the macroscopic region from top to bottom, with an interval of 0.1 mm. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) was performed using a FEI Scios 2 HiVac microscope. Samples were prepared using a focused ion beam (FIB) to ensure precise thinning of the regions of interest. The TEM analysis was conducted at an accelerating voltage of 200 kV, and high-resolution images were captured to examine dislocation structures and grain boundaries. The Microhardness of the bulk fabrication was tested along the Y-Z cross-section at intervals of 1 mm to analyze the microhardness distribution in different regions. The impact toughness at room temperature was conducted using the ZBC2452-C pendulum impact testing machine from MTS Industries in the USA. The AG-X plus electronic universal testing machine with a maximum load of 100 kN produced by Shimadzu Corporation from Japan was used for the tensile property testing at room temperature. Three typical temperatures (1050 °C, 1150 °C, and 1250 °C) are selected to simulate in-situ microstructure evolution influenced by UIT and inter-layer thermal effects using an ultra-high temperature laser confocal microscope. Processing Text: Multilayered Al samples were fabricated through a combined process of ARB and annealing, using 1.5-mm-thick sheets of AA3003 and AA1060 alloy as the raw materials. This thermal processing procedure consists of an initial single-pass ARB, followed by intermediate annealing, four additional ARB passes, and concluding with final annealing. For each ARB cycle, the sheets were carefully cleaned with an ethanol solution and mechanically ground by a steel brush to eliminate the greases and oxides from the surface. The sheets were then fastened with rivets and subjected to rolling at 150 °C, achieving a 50 % thickness reduction by a single pass. Since the radius of the roller, R, was ∼50 mm, and the linear velocity, V, was ∼100 mm/s, the average strain rate of rolling was around 26.6/s. After that, the bonded sheet was divided in half, preparing it for the subsequent ARB cycle. After the series of accumulative roll bonding, the final thickness of the multilayered Al sample was around 1.5 mm. Since the multilayered Al samples underwent annealing at temperatures of 600 °C and 500 °C for 1 h during the intermediate annealing, two multilayered Al samples were denoted as AA600 and AA500 samples. To better describe the microstructures evolution of AA500 and AA600 during such complex thermal processing, the intermediate-annealed, ARBed, and final-annealed AA500/AA600 samples were further designated as AA500-IA/AA600-IA, AA500-ARB/AA600-ARB, and AA500-FA/AA600-FA, respectively. The intermediate annealing was designed to prevent the plasticity instability and shear bands of harder layers caused by the accumulation of rolling strains. More importantly, different temperatures during the intermediate annealing were strategically employed to manipulate precipitation kinetics within the AA3003 alloy layers. As suggested by previous work, the nano-dispersoids start to precipitate in AA3003 layers at moderate temperatures above 300 °C, while re-dissolve at higher temperatures above 530 °C. Therefore, AA3003 layers of the AA500-IA sample should have precipitated dispersoids after the intermediate annealing, while those in the AA600-IA sample will not. This step aims to provide precursors of different heterogeneous structures in multilayered Al samples. The final annealing process was conducted at 320 °C for 1 h, which was designed mainly based on the effects of the Mn element on elevating recrystallization temperatures of Al alloys. In other words, this step mainly aimed to stimulate the full recrystallizations of AA1060 layers in multilayered Al samples. More importantly, the intermediate annealing has induced different precipitation behaviors. Given the significant effects of precipitates on recovery and recrystallization behaviors, the final annealing can lead to different recovery and recrystallization behaviors of AA3003 layers, resulting in different heterogeneous structures in AA500-FA and AA600-FA samples. Sample with dual-heterogeneous structure including bimodal grains; Uniform elongation: 15.5%; Ultimate tensile strength: 109 MPa

Processing Text: Four melts were prepared by using a medium frequency induction furnace and the chemical compositions of these prepared samples are given in Table 1. The produced stainless-steel alloys were subjected for solution treatment at 1100 °C for about 1 h, followed by water quenching. Samples were prepared through grinding and polishing sequence and etched by using 100 ml Hcl, 33 ml HNO 3, and few drops of H 2SO 4. The etched surface has been observed at high magnification using SEM in attached with EDS. Cu Kα-target diffractometer with wavelength 1.54184 A° has been used for determining the constituent phases of the observed austenitic stainless steel. Round tensile specimens are machined according to the specification of the ASTM E8 − 16b of 6 mm diameter and 32 mm gauge length. The tensile test is carried out using a 300 kN Shenzhen Wance Testing Machine at room temperature with constant crosshead velocity of 1 mm/min and strain rate 0.1 S -1. Ultimate tensile strength, 0.2 % yield strength, and elongation to fracture were estimated throughout the tensile test. Standard Charpy V-notch specimens were prepared according to the specification of ASTM A370 and tested at room temperature on PKP450 impact-testing machine to measure the energy transferred to the stainless-steel samples and the average of two tests was adopted. Specimens were corrosion tested using cyclic anodic polarization technique. The samples were prepared with mirror surface and were involved as working electrodes in 3 electrodes system, which contains saturated calomel electrode (SCE) (reference electrode) and Pt wire (counter electrode). The samples exposed area to the solution were fixed (1 cm 2) during the investigation in 3.5 % NaCl solution at the room temperature. The cyclic anodic polarization measurements were carried out starting from −0.3 V. Processing Text: High-purity Fe, Mn, Co, Cr, and C (≥99.8 wt%) were utilized as raw materials. Processing Text: The 5Ni alloy ingot was meticulously cast in an argon (Ar) atmosphere using the arc-melting technique. After casting, the ingot was homogenized at 1200 °C for 1 h in a high-temperature muffle furnace without a protective atmosphere. The homogenized ingot was then subjected to a hot and cold rolling process, reducing its thickness to approximately 1 mm. Dog-bone-shaped tensile samples, with a gauge length of 10 mm and a cross-sectional area of 3 × 1 mm 2, were fabricated using wire cutting. These samples were subsequently subjected to electric pulse treatment in air without a protective atmosphere. The oxide layer on the sample surface will be removed using sandpaper. During EPT, the sample surface temperature was continuously monitored in real time using a K-type thermocouple. An oscilloscope (Tektronix TBS1104) was used to measure various electric pulse parameters, including peak current, frequency, and pulse width. The applied pulse current exhibited a positive steep pulse spike waveform, with adjustable peak current and frequency, while the pulse width was fixed at 54 μs. S0 refers to samples after rolling without electric pulse treatment, and S1-S8 corresponds to samples treated with electric pulses. In S1-S4, the pulse peak current was the major variation, while S5-S8 had the pulse frequency adjusted. The Vickers hardness of the samples was measured using a digital microhardness tester (HXD-1000TMC/LCD). A test load of 500 mN was applied with a dwell time of 10 s. For each sample, seven hardness values were measured, with the highest and lowest values excluded. The average of the remaining five values was taken as the final hardness value. Tensile tests were performed using a microcomputer-controlled electronic universal testing machine (WANCE ETM) at a constant strain rate of 2 × 10 −3s −1. An optic extensometer (Epsilon ONE-52PT) was used to ensure accurate strain measurements. Each tensile test was repeated at least twice at the same conditions to verify the consistency and accuracy of the results. Processing Text: The QP and QP-R steels were melted in a vacuum induction melting furnace, cast into 5 kg ingots, and then the ingots were forged and cut into 20-mm-thick blocks. The blocks were homogenized at 1200 °C for 30 min and then hot-rolled in the full austenitic zone to produce a 2-mm-thick hot-rolled sheet. Subsequently, the hot-rolled sheet underwent simulated coiling at 650 °C for 30 min. The simulated coiled QP and QP-R steels underwent a standard Q&P process on the simulated continuous annealing equipment (CAS-AY Ⅱ), manufactured by Advance Riko. The heat treatment profiles for the QP and QP-R steels are shown in Fig. 1, in which the phase transformation temperature (Ae3) (806.9 °C) between austenite-ferrite and fully austenitic phase at equilibrium of the QP steel was calculated by Thermo-Calc software using TCFE 12 database. During the quenching stage, the experimentally measured Ms (the martensite start transformation temperatures) of the QP and QP-R steels are 344.6 and 340.7 °C, respectively. During the partitioning and subsequent cooling stages, no fluctuation was detected in the dilatometer curves of the QP and QP-R steels, suggesting that retained austenite was almost fully preserved after partitioning. Processing Text: The five equiatomic four-element alloys were manufactured using induction melting and yielded cylindrical ingots with a diameter of approximately 60 mm. Macroscopic observation showed the presence of dendrites in these as-cast materials. Therefore, the alloys were homogenized at 1150 ⁰C for 24 h inside stainless-steel bags to minimize oxidation and promote chemical homogenization. The cylinders were subsequently sliced into four sections longitudinally. The smaller segments were deformed to a nominal compressive strain of −0.3 in an Enerpac machine with a 100-ton capacity. The deformation could not be conducted at ambient temperature because the samples cracked; therefore, they were preheated to 400 °C. The samples were subsequently heat treated at 900 ⁰C for 1 hour in order to ensure recrystallization following deformation. These temperatures were selected due to their successful use in previous studies to ensure the homogenization of chemical elements and recrystallization. Fully recrystallized; Grain size: 70 μm

Processing Text: Hybrid manufactured components were made by depositing TC11 alloy on the rolled TC11 plates. The rolled TC11 substrate with dimensions of 225 × 40 × 100 mm3 was chosen as the substrate, and it was polished and washed with acetone and anhydrous alcohol in order to remove the oil and oxide layer. The optimized laser DED processing parameters were set as follows: the laser power of 3.5 kW, the scanning velocity of 16 mm/s, the powder feeding rate of 1000 g/h, and using the crosshatching scanning strategy along the short side. During the whole forming process, the oxygen content was always kept below 50 ppm. The TC11 titanium alloy powders with a spherical morphology for the deposition experiment were prepared by the plasma rotation electrode process method. After deposition, the hybrid manufactured TC11 sample was then immediately annealed at 530 °C for 2 h in order to eliminate residual stress and it was labeled as as-deposited sample. Three different double annealing heat treatments were conducted on the as-deposited hybrid manufactured TC11 sample. As displayed in Fig. 1d, in this study, 990 °C (below the TβSZ), 1013 °C (between the TβSZ and TβLDZ) and 1035 °C (above the TβLDZ) were chosen as the first step high annealing temperature and the second annealing temperature was all 530 °C. The soaking time for the first and second step annealing treatments were 1 h and 6 h, respectively. They both followed by air cooling to room temperature. The samples were placed directly in a furnace at the target temperature to prevent any possible changes in the microstructure during heating. These heat treatments were denoted as the 990HT, 1013HT and 1035HT in turn. The metallographic samples of the as-deposited, 990HT, 1013HT and 1035HT hybrid manufactured TC11 alloy were taken from the transverse section. These specimens were prepared using standard mechanical polishing methods and etched using Kroll's reagent (1 ml HF + 6 ml HNO3 + 43 ml H2O). After the hot rolled plate is milled to remove the surface oxide skin, it was held at 960 °C for 2 h for solution treatment, using water-cooled quenching. Processing Text: A series of CoCrFeNi(B 4C) x(x = 0, 0.01, 0.05, and 0.1) HEAs composites were fabricated via vacuum arc melting of high-purity metal elements (purity >99.95 wt%) and B 4C ceramic particles in a water-cooled copper crucible under a high-purity argon atmosphere. The samples were mechanically polished to a mirror finish, followed by vertical mechanical polishing and etching with aqua regia (HNO 3:HCl = 1:3). The samples for TEM observation were mechanically thinned to approximately 50 μm, punched into 3 mm diameter discs, and electro-polished in a solution of 10 vol% HClO4 + 90 vol% CH3OH at −20 °C, applying a voltage of 20 V. The ingots were precisely machined into cylindrical compression specimens (Φ 3 × 6 mm) using electrical discharge machining (EDM). Compressive properties were evaluated using an INSTRON-5982 universal testing machine equipped with a mechanical tensile tester, at a constant strain rate of 0.48 mm/min. Vickers hardness measurements were conducted on the samples using an FM-ARS 9000 micro-hardness tester. Nano-indentation tests were performed with a Hysitron TI-900 triboindenter integrated with an in-situ atomic force microscope (AFM). The tests were performed with the following conditions: an 8000 μN load, a loading rate of 1000 μN/s, a 2 s hold time, and an unloading rate of 4000 μN/s, using an indenter with an effective diameter of approximately 450 nm. Prior to nano-indentation, the samples were polished to eliminate surface scratches that could introduce experimental errors. Processing Text: To this end, WC nanoparticles and SiC whiskers-reinforced copper matrix composites (WC p-SiC w/Cu) were prepared by intermittent pulsed electrodeposition and spark plasma sintering. These composites are designed with a unique core-shell structure, and thereby the agglomeration of reinforcements can be effectively avoided during sintering. Subsequently, spark plasma sintering (SPS) was used to achieve CMCs with high relative density and ultra-fine grains because it has unique advantages, such as rapid heating and short holding time. The SPS was used to prepare the blocks in a graphite mold with an inner diameter of 15 mm and an applied pre-pressure of 10 MPa in a Labox-300 SPS system. During the sintering, the mold was then heated to 850 °C and lasted for 5 min while applying a pressure of 50 MPa. The sintered specimens with a thickness of 4 mm were rolled to the total accumulative reduction of 70 % at 800 °C. Compared to pure copper, yield strength is about double while maintaining high uniform elongation (15.3 %).
Processing Word: Compared to pure copper, yield strength is about double while maintaining high uniform elongation (15.3 %).

Processing Text: The original SiC powders were elongated fibers, with about a 5-8 μm length and a 0.1-1 μm diameter. To increase the nucleation sites of nanocrystalline copper by increasing the surface roughness of reinforcements, a 15-minute activation was conducted, with the pristine SiC powders pretreated in 20 % HF. The activated powders were washed in ethanol and pure water before being dried in an oven. Intermittent pulse electrodeposition was used to deposit copper on the activated powders. The activated powders (0.06 g/L for SiC powders) were placed in the electrolyte and were ultrasonically dispersed in a cell crusher for 10 min. Plating solution consisted of CuSO 4⋅5H 2O (28 g/L), (NH 4) 2SO 4(50 g/L), C 6H 8O 7(21 g/L), CuCl 2(0.04 g/L), C 7H 5O 3NS (0.05 g/L), and PEG-6000 (0.1 g/L). After dispersion, Cu 2+nucleated on the SiC powders via electrodeposition with galvanostatic conditions (8.3 × 10 2A/m 2) and a cycle of an on-time of 200 μs and an off-time of 800 μs. Subsequently, ultra-sonication was also carried out for 2 min. The above plating and sonication steps have 10 cycles, so the time of effective electrodeposition was 40 min. The electrodeposited powders were cleaned with deionized and ethanol, and then were dried at 70 °C in a vacuum drying oven for 6 ∼ 8 h. The prepared Cu@SiC were reduced in pure H 2(400 °C) for 0.5 h to remove an oxide layer in a tube furnace. YS with an uncertainty of ±2.3 MPa.
Processing Word: YS with an uncertainty of ±2.3 MPa.

Processing Text: The WNbTaVTi RHEA was successfully synthesized by spark plasma sintering (SPS) technology. The raw materials for ball milling were high-purity W, Nb, Ta, V and Ti powders. The powder was ball milled using a planetary ball mill (QM-3SP2, Nanjing Chishun Technology Co., Ltd.) with zirconia balls as the grinding media. In the process of ball milling, the ball-to-powder ratio was maintained at 5:1, and the equipment ran at a speed of 300 rpm, and alcohol was introduced as auxiliary grinding medium to promote the crushing and mixing of powders. The whole milling process was performed for 24 h with intermittent cooling to avoid excessive temperature rise. Post-milling, the powder was sieved through a 200-mesh screen to ensure a uniform particle size. The SPS process was carried out using a LABOX-350 spark plasma sintering system. The powder was loaded into a 13 mm diameter graphite die and then evacuated to a vacuum level of less than 10 Pa. A uniaxial pressure of 30 MPa was applied using a hydraulic press prior to sintering. The samples were first heated at a rate of 100 °C/min to 1200 °C and then held for 10 min to increase the solid solubility. Afterwards, the samples were heated to the target temperatures (1400, 1500, and 1600 °C) and held for 5 min. The temperature was monitored using an infrared pyrometer focused on the surface of the die. After sintering, the samples were allowed to cool naturally in the low vacuum atmosphere. Once cooled, the samples were carefully extracted and any flash or excess material was removed by gentle grinding. Sintering temperature: 1500 °C; Peak yield strength and compressive strength

Processing Text: Gas atomization, which includes free fall gas atomization (FFGA) and confined gas atomization (CGA), is a high-speed, high-pressure technique that uses gases such as helium, nitrogen, or argon to break down molten metal. In this process, inert gas is forcefully sprayed from a dedicated device or reservoir into the atomization chamber under high pressure. The forceful impact of the gas causes vigorous deformation, primary breakup, and secondary breakup of the molten metal, leading to the formation of small spherical particles. A gas atomizer system comprises essential components such as the gas storage system, metal tundish, atomizer system, spray system, and powder collection system. Research has consistently shown that gas atomization produces spherical metal powder with high production efficiency. GA offers broad applicability, excellent powder characteristics, controllable processes, and high production efficiency. The size of powders decreases with the increase of atomization pressure, gas velocity, GMR and superheat of melt. The forceful impact of the gas causes vigorous deformation, primary breakup, and secondary breakup of the molten metal, leading to the formation of small spherical particles. A gas atomizer system comprises essential components such as the gas storage system, metal tundish, atomizer system, spray system, and powder collection system. Research has consistently shown that gas atomization produces spherical metal powder with high production efficiency. GA offers broad applicability, excellent powder characteristics, controllable processes, and high production efficiency. The size of powders decreases with the increase of atomization pressure, gas velocity, GMR and superheat of melt. With the addition of copper; Alloy composition: Ti-3.5Cu

Processing Text: The material selected for the test was 45CrNiMoVA ultra-high-strength steel. The received materials were cylindrical bars with a diameter of 52 mm and a length of 200 mm. The cylindrical bars have undergone two heat treatment processes (normalizing heat treatment, quenching and tempering treatment). Slow wire cutting was used to cut a ϕ21 mm × 150 mm cylindrical sample from the cylindrical rod. After grinding the center hole, fine turning, and fine grinding, the sample is processed into a sample with a gauge length of ϕ12.5 mm × 30 mm. The cylindrical sample was electrothermally inlaid, polished, and corroded for 15 s with a 4 % nitric acid alcohol solution, and the microstructure of the cross section after roller rolling was observed on TESCAN MIRA 3 (SEM). Vickers hardness (MHVS-30AT) tester is used to hold for 15 s under 0.5 kg preload, measure the surface hardness of 10 different positions on the sample, and take the average value. In addition, a 3D laser scanning electron microscope (VK-X100, Kenyence) is used to measure the surface morphology of the sample at two ends and in the middle of the cylindrical surface. Surface morphology measurements were made using a 20× objective lens. The residual compressive stress on the specimen surface is measured by PROTO-LXRD X-ray. 1 mm aperture collimator is used. The diffraction angle is {211} Kα = 156.413°. Maximum beta is 25°. The number of beta angles is 5. Exposure time is 2 s. The surface normal residual stress was measured three times and the residual stress along the depth of the layer was measured one time. The cylindrical samples were inlaid, ground, and polished with argon ions, and the grain characteristics of the surface layers of the strengthened specimens were analyzed by using electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, JSM 7200F). The microstructure morphology of different processes was also analyzed by transmission electron microscope (TEM, FEI Talos F200X). The fracture morphology was observed using TESCAN MIRA 3 (SEM). The strengthening mechanism of the PT-DR process sequence on the surface modification of 45CrNiMoVA steel was revealed. The PT-DR process provides an effective surface strengthening method for the key structural parts with weak cold plastic deformation. The main chemical elements of the steel are shown in Table 1. The tensile yield strength of the material reaches 1639 MPa, the compression yield strength reaches 1813 MPa, and the torsional shear yield strength reaches 1249 MPa after heat treatment. The DR strengthening is carried out through the workpiece rotation speed ndrof 350 r/min, feed fof 0.028 mm/r, rolling cutter amount apof 0.8 mm, and each sample is rolled twice, as shown in Fig. 1c. A roller with arc profile is used, and the hardness of the roller is greater than that of the sample. The PT strengthening and torsional fatigue tests were conducted on the MTS 809.25 torsional fatigue testing machine, as shown in Fig. 1d. The sample was subjected to 5 repeated pre-twists with an angle of 13.7° ( θpre), a torsion loading rate of 8°/min and an unloading rate of 200 N·m/min, releasing to zero torque each time. Each group of samples was treated according to the process sequence. Under the temperature of 19 °C, three samples of each group in the final state after strengthening for the fatigue test. The maximum shear stress level τ maxis 1200 MPa with a sine waveform, the stress ratio R= 0, and the frequency is 7 Hz. The microstructure and grain characteristics of the material is characterized on the circular cross section of the sample, and the microhardness is characterized on the surface of the specimen, as shown in Fig. 1b. Condition: after heat treatment; Type: tensile yield strength

Processing Text: Cr21Ni6Mn9N (21-6-9) stainless steel has been fabricated using SLM technology. The SLM process was carried out in argon atmosphere using a 170DL printer (Avimetal AM Tech Co., Ltd.). Large bulk sample with a dimension of 73 mm × 14 mm × 8 mm was built on a 316L substrate using a laser power of 170 W, a scanning speed of 900 mm/s, a hatch distance of 80 μm and a layer thickness of 30 μm. A stripe scanning mode is adopted, with an interlayer rotation of 67°. The heat treatment experiment was carried out in a GSL-1700X-VTQ vacuum tubular furnace under a vacuum atmosphere of 5 × 10−3Pa. The SLM 21-6-9 stainless steel samples were held at 950 °C, 1050 °C, and 1150 °C, respectively, for 1 hour, and then subjected to water quenching treatment. Tensile tests were applied to the as-printed samples and the heat-treated samples using a Suns UTM5105 electronic universal tensile testing machine at a displacement rate of 0.3 mm/min. Processing state: as-printed; Context: SLM-prepared
Processing Word: Processing state: as-printed; Context: SLM-prepared

Processing Text: Using vacuum induction melting, a 50-kg ingot of steel with the composition Fe-24Mn-8Al-1C was produced. The ingot was heated to 1200 °C for two hours before being hot-forged into a slab that measured 35 mm × 100 mm in section. The slab was swan into several chunks with a length of 150 mm. The pieces were hot-rolled to 5 mm thick plates after being homogenized at 1200 °C for 2 h. Following air cooling to room temperature, the hot-rolled plates were further rolled into 1-mm-thick sheets. Some cold rolled samples were annealed at 750 °C for 5 min and then water quenched to produce heterogeneous microstructures. Besides, for comparison, other cold rolled samples were annealed between 750 and 1150 °C for 30 min respectively and subsequently water quenched in order to produce homogeneous microstructures. In order to study the effect of aging strengthening, all above annealed samples were aged at 550 °C for 30 min and then water quenched. Besides, in order to explore the potential of aging strengthening in these investigated steels, the 750-30 samples have been aged at 550 °C for 4, 6 and 8 h, respectively.
