Processing Text: Pure metals (>99.99 wt%) of Ni and Nb were used to fabricate Ni-Nb alloy targets with nominal composition Ni 60Nb 40(at.%) using a vacuum arc melting furnace and a vacuum casting machine in a high-purity Ar gas atmosphere. All ingots were remelted four times to ensure chemical homogeneity. The cast ingot was then sliced and polished into targets of ∼2 inches in diameter and ∼3 mm in thickness. The amorphous thin films were prepared on clean (100)-Si wafers in an ultrahigh vacuum direct current MS system (TA16-10D) with a base pressure of ∼2 × 10 −6Pa at different deposition power ranging from 15 W to 180 W at room temperature. The alloy target was placed directly underneath the substrate without an oblique angle, and the distance from the target to the substrate was 45 mm. During the sputtering process, the deposition pressure, substrate rotation speed, and flow rate were kept at 1.5 Pa, 3 rpm, and 40 sccm, respectively. The film thickness was controlled to be 1.0 ± 0.1 μm by changing the deposition time under various power conditions with an average deposition efficiency of ∼0.017 nm/J. The substrate temperature was measured by fixing a Ni-Cr thermocouple on the Si substrate surface (the film growth plane) to monitor the real-time temperature variation. To avoid unexpected oxidation and contamination, annealing treatments were performed in the MS chamber directly (without venting the chamber) under a base vacuum of 5 × 10 −4Pa at 613 K, 713 K, 804 K, and 843 K for 1 h. Selected Ni-Nb thin films were immersed in 0.5 M hydrochloric acid solution in water for up to 8 h. The topography of these sample surfaces was measured after different immersion durations by tapping mode AFM with stiff single crystalline Si tips (type: NCHR, manufactured by NanoSensors, Switzerland). After 8 h of immersion in an acidic solution, the chemical composition of the film surfaces was measured and compared to their composition before corrosion treatment by X-ray photoelectronic spectroscopy (XPS, K-Alpha +system, ThermoFisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). The XPS measurements were recorded with a monochromated Al Kα source (1486.6 eV, 12 kV) and a spot size of 400 μm 2in ultrahigh vacuum (UHV) conditions (base pressure below 5 × 10 −7Pa). Besides, angle-resolved XPS (ARXPS, Axis Supra +, manufactured by Shimadzu, Japan) was adopted to evaluate the thickness and structure of the oxidation layer on the film surface. The measurements were performed with Al Kα radiation. The X-ray spot had an elliptical shape with a long axis of 0.7 mm and a short axis of 0.3 mm. Estimated from micropillar compression test; Deposition power: 15 W

Processing Text: As-cast Ti45V45Cr5Al5 MPEA ingot was prepared by arc-melting the mixtures of Ti, V, Cr, and Al (purities > 99.9 wt%) under a high-purity argon atmosphere. The ingot was melted at least six times to ensure compositional homogeneity, and elliptical ingots with dimensions of 70 mm× 40 mm× 12 mm were obtained. Processing Text: This work presents the fabrication of a metastable non-equiatomic Co45Cr25(FeNi)30 MEA using PBF-LB. The alloy was printed using EOS M100 PBF-LB machine equipped with 200W Yb-fiber laser. Extensive design of experiments (DOE) was performed to optimize the printing parameters for high density. Based on the DOE results, the samples used in this study were produced with 90W of laser power, 1010 mm/s of scan speed, 0.07 mm of hatch distance, 20 μm of layer thickness, with a stripe scan strategy and a stripe width of 5 mm with 67° scan rotation between subsequent layers. The as-printed samples were metallographically prepared for microstructural characterizations by first grinding the samples using SiC emery sheets from 500 grit to 4000 grit. The ground samples were then electrochemically polished using the Struers A2 electrolyte to achieve a mirror-like finish. The preparation of TEM samples involved a two-step process. Initially, samples of approximately 1 mm thick were extracted along both vertical and horizontal cross sections from the as-printed bulk material. These extracted samples were then thinned down to a thickness of approximately 120 μm and punched into discs of 3 mm diameter. The final stage of the preparation involved twin-jet electrochemical polishing of the discs using Struers A2 electrolyte performed at −2 °C and 30 V until the hole is formed at the center of the sample. Tensile samples of 4 mm in gauge length, 1.2 mm in thickness, and 2 mm in width were extracted from the as-printed samples, using electrical discharge machining (EDM). Miniature dogbone shaped tensile samples were extracted from the as-printed samples, with a gauge length of 7 mm and thickness of 1.2 mm, using EDM. The extracted samples were then carefully mechanically ground and polished, finishing with colloidal suspension of 50 nm sized silica solution (OPS, Struers) to ensure that there was no deformed layer induced by grinding. The in-situ tensile tests were performed at a strain rate of 2.5 × 10−4s−1 to a maximum nominal strain of 40 %. Ex-situ tensile testing was performed on the Kammrath & Weiss tensile stage to obtain mechanical properties of the alloy in the as-printed state, using the displacement control mode equivalent to a strain rate of 2.5 × 10−4s−1. In-situ EBSD combined with tensile testing was performed in GEMINI 1550 SEM equipped with the velocity detector. The in-situ EBSD and tensile tests were performed using a Kammrath & Weiss tensile stage mounted inside the SEM and at a strain rate of ∼2.5 × 10−4s−1. Firstly, a carefully polished tensile sample was mounted onto the tensile stage inside the SEM and the EBSD data from the as-printed state was obtained at zero load. During the tensile testing, the loading was stopped at nominal strains of 15 %, 25 %, and 40 % to acquire EBSD data. Building direction: Horizontal; Processing state: as-printed

Processing Text: Cr, Fe, Ni and W metals with the purity of ≥99.9 wt% were used to prepare CrFeNiW0.1 MEAs. The metallic elements were melted by arc-melting technique and then solidified in a water-cooled Cu crucible under Ti-gettered high-purity argon atmosphere. The ingots were melted at least five times ensure the uniformity of the alloys, and then cast into Cu mold with the dimensions of ∼60 mm × 11 mm × 5 mm. The as-cast samples were sealed in quartz tubes and homogenized at 1200 °C for 6 h, which was subsequently by water quenching. Then, the homogenized CrFeNiW0.1 MEAs were cold rolled to a total thickness reduction of ∼78 %. The specimens cut from cold-rolled CrFeNiW0.1 MEAs were finally heat treated at 900 °C for 1 h followed by water quenching. Processing Text: The as-printed Co-free AlCrFeNi3 eutectic medium entropy alloy (EMEA) was fabricated by selective laser melting (SLM). Heat treatment as a post processing was used to improve the mechanical properties of the as-printed samples, which were subjected to solid solution treatment at 400 °C-1200 °C for 1 h in this work. No visible cracks and pores were found in the as-printed samples and the highest relative density is up to 99.57 %. The as-printed AlCrFeNi3 EMEA is consisted of FCC, B2, and intergranular BCC phases, showing a typical fish scale-like structure with ultrafine cellular and columnar substructures. The ultimate tensile strength and elongation of the as-printed alloy with relatively optimal printing parameters are 1146.9 MPa and 7.6 %, respectively. When the solid solution temperature reaches 1000 °C, the intergranular BCC phases disappeared, and the second phases are uniformly distributed in the matrix, while the ultimate tensile strength and elongation of the sample are 1335.5 MPa and 12.3 %, respectively, demonstrating an 188.6 MPa increase in strength and 4.7 % increase in ductility compared to the as-printed alloy. Pre-alloyed AlCrFeNi3 EMEA powders produced by spherical atomization of argon gas were used as the raw materials in this study. We printed multiple samples by adjusting the printing parameters, and based on the highest relative density the as-printed samples, we determined the optimized parameters as follows: laser power 185 W, scanning speed 800 mm/s, hatch spacing 100 μm, and layer thickness 30 μm. To investigate the effect of heat treatment on the microstructure and mechanical properties of the printed AlCrFeNi3 EMEA, the as-printed samples were heat treated in a muffle furnace under different conditions, including solid solution treatment at 400 °C, 600 °C, 800 °C and 1000 °C for 1 h, respectively, followed by water quenching. Processing Text: Two types of base metals (BMs) were utilized in this study: 6082-T6 aluminum alloy and WHS-T6 aluminum alloy, both provided as 2 mm thick plates. The WHS alloy represents a novel aluminum alloy, distinguished from the 6082-T6 aluminum alloy primarily by minor differences in its copper content and the composition of other alloying elements. Prior to welding, the BMs were mechanically polished to eliminate the surface oxide layer, followed by cleaning with acetone and ethanol to remove any residual contaminants. A NIR-blue hybrid laser welding system was employed to join the two BMs. This system primarily consists of a NIR laser, a blue laser, a hybrid laser head, and a dedicated welding platform. The NIR laser utilized was the Raycus RFL-C3000S, characterized by a Gaussian energy density distribution, a maximum output power of 3000 W, a fiber core diameter of 25 μm, and an emission wavelength of 1064 nm. The blue laser source was the Raycus RFL-B500D, featuring a flat-top energy density distribution, a peak power of 500 W, a fiber core diameter of 400 μm, and a wavelength of 450 nm. During welding, 99.99 % purity argon was supplied at a flow rate of 25 L/min as a shielding gas to prevent oxidation. The principal parameters used for hybrid laser welding are presented in Table 2. Welded joints were initially sectioned utilizing a wire-cut electrical discharge machine. The resulting metallographic samples underwent a systematic polishing procedure using SiC paper. Subsequently, they were refined further with diamond paste and colloidal silica solution to achieve a smooth, mirror-like surface devoid of scratches. Following these preparatory steps, the samples were subjected to chemical etching with 0.5 % HF for a duration of 25 seconds. A subset of these samples was then anodized using Barker’s reagent, a solution consisting of 7 ml of 48 % HBF 4 and 93 ml of distilled water, with the anodization current meticulously regulated between 200 and 300 mA for 30 seconds. The metallographic samples were chemically polished for 40 seconds under an electrolysis voltage of 20 V using a high-chloride ethanol solution. Processing Text: The experimental material consisted of 316L austenitic stainless steel rods with a diameter of 30 mm. The material was hot-rolled to 4 mm in thickness, followed by solution treatment at 1050 °C for 1 h. Before each rolling pass, the initial material was immersed in liquid nitrogen for 10 min. The thickness reduction per pass was kept below 5 %. Surface cracks developed when the total thickness reduction reached 70 %. Consequently, the final thickness was reduced by 70 %, resulting in a thickness of 1.2 mm for the cryo-rolled sample, which was labeled as CryoR sample. After cryo-rolling, the samples were subjected to annealing at 700 °C 20 min, 750 °C 6 min, and a sequential 700 °C 20 min + 750 °C 6 min process, followed by water quenching. These samples were labeled as 700A, 750A, and 700A-750A, respectively. All heat treatment processes were performed in a muffle furnace without a protective atmosphere. Tensile tests were conducted using a universal testing machine (5105, SSANS-CMT) at room temperature (24 °C) and liquid nitrogen temperature (−196 °C) with a strain rate of 10 −3s −1. All tensile samples were cut along the rolling direction into dog-bone shapes with a gauge length of 34 mm, width of 10 mm, and thickness of 1 mm. Each test was repeated at least three times to ensure accuracy. To evaluate inhomogeneous deformation, load-unload-reload (LUR) tests were also performed under the same conditions as the tensile tests to quantify the back stress (σ B) component. The microstructural evolution of the samples along the rolling direction (RD) was characterized. XRD analysis was conducted to examine phase transformation with a diffraction angle range of 40°-100° and a scanning speed of 2°/min, using Cu-Kα radiation at 40 kV and 150 mA. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, Oxford) was employed for quantitative analysis of the phase microstructure. After mechanical polishing, samples were electropolished using a 10 % perchloric acid solution at 20 V for 20-25 s. Processing Text: The experimental material consisted of 316L austenitic stainless steel rods with a diameter of 30 mm. The material was hot-rolled to 4 mm in thickness, followed by solution treatment at 1050 °C for 1 h. Before each rolling pass, the initial material was immersed in liquid nitrogen for 10 min. The thickness reduction per pass was kept below 5 %. Surface cracks developed when the total thickness reduction reached 70 %. Consequently, the final thickness was reduced by 70 %, resulting in a thickness of 1.2 mm for the cryo-rolled sample, which was labeled as CryoR sample. After cryo-rolling, the samples were subjected to annealing at 700 °C 20 min, 750 °C 6 min, and a sequential 700 °C 20 min + 750 °C 6 min process, followed by water quenching. These samples were labeled as 700A, 750A, and 700A-750A, respectively. All heat treatment processes were performed in a muffle furnace without a protective atmosphere. Tensile tests were conducted using a universal testing machine (5105, SSANS-CMT) at room temperature (24 °C) and liquid nitrogen temperature (−196 °C) with a strain rate of 10 −3s −1. After mechanical polishing, samples were electropolished using a 10 % perchloric acid solution at 20 V for 20-25 s. Processing Text: The GH4099 superalloy thin-walled structure was manufactured using laser-directed energy deposition (L-DED). GH4099 pre-alloyed powder with particles ranging in size from 50 to 150 μm was produced using plasma rotating electrode processing (PREP). The powders underwent a 24-h vacuum drying process at 120 °C before the L-DED process. During the L-DED, GH4099 alloy single-track walls were fabricated using a back-and-forth scanning approach. It was executed using an L-DED system equipped with a Yb fiber laser in an Ar chamber. The laser, with a beam diameter of 3 mm, operated at a power of 900 W and a scanning speed of 6 mm/s. The powder feed rate was maintained at 0.3 r/min. A protective gas (Ar) flow rate of 15 mL/min and a powder gas (Ar) flow rate of 6 mL/min were maintained consistently throughout the process to minimize the impact of impurity gases in the atmosphere. The single melt pool thickness under these parameters was 0.6 mm. The forming parameters were optimized to achieve optimal conditions and minimize the impact of forming defects on the mechanical properties of the sample. The build resulted in three cross-sectional samples perpendicular to the BD (X-Y plane) and one vertical section sample parallel to BD (Y-Z plane), dividing the entire assembly into bottom, middle, and top regions. For transmission electron microscopy (TEM) analysis, the samples were mechanically polished and then electropolished in a solution that contained 20 % sulfuric acid and 80 % methanol. This process was performed at room temperature using a voltage of 15 V. For atom probe tomography (APT), the built sample was sectioned using a focused ion beam (FIB), and needle-shaped samples were prepared along three X-Y planes at uniform heights with precise sharpness. Processing Text: Gas-atomized IN718 powder (particle size range: 15-53 μm) was used in this study. The IN718 powder was mixed with 1 wt% Ti2AlC. The mixture was mechanically stirred for 1 h to ensure uniform distribution, followed by drying at 80 °C for 2 h. The samples were fabricated using the laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) technique with optimized process parameters: 305 W laser power, 850 mm/s scanning speed, 80 μm hatching space, 40 μm layer thickness, and a 67° rotation between each printed layer, all conducted in an argon atmosphere. The specimens were initially homogenized at 1200 °C for 1 h and air-cooled to room temperature, followed by a double-step aging process: held at 720 °C for 8 h, furnace-cooled to 620 °C, and maintained at this temperature for an additional 8 h before air-cooled to room temperature. Subsequently, all samples underwent accelerated thermal exposure at 760 °C for 100, 200, 500, and 1000 h to investigate the long-term thermal stability. Processing Text: A powder metallurgy (PM) AA6061-10Cu hybrid material was fabricated by a thermomechanical consolidation technique involving hot extrusion of the compact of an AA6061 aluminum alloy and Cu powder blend. The blended powder was die-pressed uniaxially with a pressure of 750 MPa and a holding time of 5 min to produce two cylindrical powder compacts with dimensions of 52 mm in diameter and 55 mm in height. The powder compacts were induction heated to 450 °C at a heating rate for 30 °C/min, held at the temperature for 5 min, and then extruded with extrusion ratios of 9:1 and 25:1, respectively. Part of the as-extruded rod with an extrusion ratio of 9:1 was solution heated at 500 °C for a very short time of 10 min to mitigate the Kirkendall effect at the interfaces between the aluminum matrix and Cu particles, water quenched and then aged at 170 °C for 8 h to achieve a tailored-T6 heat treated state. Part of the as-extruded rod with an extrusion ratio of 25:1 was solution heated at 450 °C for 10 min to avoid excessive reactions at the interfaces between the aluminum matrix and Cu particles, water quenched and then aged at 170 °C for 8 h to also achieve a tailored-T6 heat treated state. Extrusion ratio: 9:1; As-extruded state

Processing Text: In this experiment, CuCrZr metal powder with a size of 15-53 μm was prepared by gas atomization method. The chemical composition and content of CuCrZr alloy powder are shown in Table 1. The LPBF process was used to prepare CuCrZr alloy samples, and the process parameters included a laser power (P), scanning speed (V), scanning spacing (H), and layer thickness (L). The volume energy density (Ea) was calculated using the formula: Ea = A P / (V H L). The cubes, cylinders, and tensile specimens were printed for subsequent microstructure characterization and performance testing. The samples were preheated at 150 °C before use, and the scanning strategy was a chessboard, with each layer rotated by 67°. The forming process adopted an argon atmosphere, and the oxygen content was controlled below 100 ppm. The samples were cut using an electrical discharge machining (EDM) process. The phase composition of the original powder and the sample was characterized by an X-ray diffractometer (XRD). The morphology of the original powder and the microstructure of the printed sample were studied by optical microscope (OM) and scanning electron microscope (SEM). The microstructure and phase composition of the samples were characterized by transmission electron microscopy (TEM). The density of all 10 × 10 × 10 mm³ printed samples was measured by the Archimedes method, and each sample was measured seven times. Tensile tests were carried out to study the mechanical properties of printed transverse specimens at room temperature using a universal tensile machine. The conductivity of a wafer with a diameter of 10 mm was measured using a Sigma 2008 digital eddy current metal conductivity meter. The thermal diffusivity of the sample was accurately measured by a laser thermal conductivity meter, and the specific heat capacity was detected by a specific heat capacity device. The actual density ρ of the sample was measured according to the Archimedes drainage method. Processing Text: For SPS processing, powder mixtures of nominal composition: Nb-10Hf-1Ti (wt. %), were prepared by blending the elemental powders for 24 h in a jar mill. Nb slugs were added to the powder mixture to break up agglomerates during milling. The jar milling was intended to achieve a good blending of powder particles without reducing the sizes. The blended powder was then sintered in the SPS unit (Model 10–4, Thermal Technologies, Santa Rosa, CA) using graphite dies. The sintering temperatures and times were varied to determine the optimum solid-state sintering conditions at a temperature that is significantly below the solidus line (∼2350°C). The optimum sintering temperature was determined to be 1700°C based on multiple trials in the temperature range of 1500–1800°C. At this sintering temperature, dense samples of size: 20 mm in diameter and 7.84 mm in thickness can be sintered and densified almost to full density in 2 h under a pressure of 10 MPa. The samples were heated at a rate of 50°C/min to the sintering temperature. The temperature was controlled using an optical pyrometer throughout the sintering process. The power, pressure, temperature, and ram displacement were recorded throughout the process. Nb slugs were added to the powder mixture to break up agglomerates during milling. The jar milling was intended to achieve a good blending of powder particles without reducing the sizes. The blended powder was then sintered in the SPS unit (Model 10–4, Thermal Technologies, Santa Rosa, CA) using graphite dies. The sintering temperatures and times were varied to determine the optimum solid-state sintering conditions at a temperature that is significantly below the solidus line (∼2350°C). The optimum sintering temperature was determined to be 1700°C based on multiple trials in the temperature range of 1500–1800°C. At this sintering temperature, dense samples of size: 20 mm in diameter and 7.84 mm in thickness can be sintered and densified almost to full density in 2 h under a pressure of 10 MPa. The samples were heated at a rate of 50°C/min to the sintering temperature. The temperature was controlled using an optical pyrometer throughout the sintering process. The power, pressure, temperature, and ram displacement were recorded throughout the process. Processing Text: The alloy ingots were prepared using a vacuum non-consumable arc melting furnace, with each ingot melted at least seven times to ensure composition uniformity, and the initial thickness of ingot was 14 mm. Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC, NETZSCH-STA449C) was used to measure the phase transition temperatures of T9V alloy at a heating rate of 10 °C/min. DSC revealed that the α→β transformation occurred between 679 ± 8 °C and 787 ± 6 °C. The alloy was rolled at 850 °C, 800 °C, 750 °C, and 700 °C, respectively. Before rolling, the alloy was held in a muffle furnace at the target rolling temperature for 30 min. Multi-pass rolling deformation was then performed, with the roll spacing was reduced by 2 mm per pass. After each pass, the alloy was reheated in the furnace for 3 min. Upon achieving a final deformation of 80 %, the alloy was reheated for 3 min and quenched. Based on the rolling temperature, the deformed specimens were designated as 850-HR, 800-HR, 750-HR, and 700-HR. Tensile specimens were cut from the rolled specimens along the rolling direction. The dog-bone-shaped specimens had test zone measuring 2 × 3 × 20 mm. Single-axis tensile tests were performed at a strain rate of 5 × 10 −4s −1at room temperature using an Instron 5982 universal testing machine (ASTM E8/E8M-16a). Strain measurements were obtained using the extensometer attached to the testing machine. Loading-unloading-reloading (LUR) tensile tests were carried out under the same conditions. During LUR testing, the specimens were unloaded to 20N at a rate of 200 N min −1after every 1.5 % deformation (based on extensometer), with the cycle repeated eight times. Each specimen underwent at least three tensile tests. The crystal structure and phase composition of the T9V alloy were analyzed using a D/max-2500/PC X-ray diffraction (XRD). The analysis used Cu K αradiation, step scanning with a 2 θ range of 30-80°, a residence time of 2 s and a scanning step size of 0.02°. After mechanical grinding and polishing, the specimens were etched with a solution of 2 % HF, 8 % HNO 3, and 90 % H 2O, and the microstructure was observed using a Zeiss Axiovert 200 MAT optical microscope (OM). The microstructure and fracture morphology were observed using a scanning electron microscope (SEM, Hitachi S3400). The Electron Backscattered Diffraction (EBSD) probe was also performed using this SEM. Microstructure data before and after deformation were collected by EBSD test technology with a step of 0.2 μm. Specimens for EBSD analysis were prepared via electrolytic polishing in a solution of 10 % perchloric acid and 90 % methanol at −20 °C, with an operating voltage of 20V. EBSD data were analyzed using TSL OIM 8.0 software and MATLAB scripts. Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM, Talos F200x) was used to further characterize the microstructure. Elemental analysis was conducted with energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) in this TEM. TEM was operated at an acceleration voltage of 200 kV. TEM specimens were prepared by grinding to 50 μm, punching out Φ3 mm discs, and performing twin-jet electrolytic thinning using a TenuPol-5 device. The solution and temperature were identical to those used for electrolytic polishing, with a working voltage of 15 V. Processing Text: In this work, TC4 alloy powders with a particle size ranging from 45 to 105 μm (Beijing Ruibang New Material Technology Co., Ltd.) were utilized. The DED samples exhibit a typical structure characterized by elongated, acicular phases within the β grains, which are oriented either parallel or perpendicular to one another. The primary structure of the spherical pristine powder is a densely arranged hexagonal close-packed (HCP) structure, with no evidence of a body-centered cubic (BCC) structure of the β-phase. The metallographic samples were polished and ground using #240, #400, #600, #800, #1200, #1500, #2000, and #3000 grit SiC paper, followed by polishing with a 2.5 μm diamond suspension. DED and DED-UIT samples were electrolytically polished before characterization using electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) with a Nova Nano SEM 450 (USA). Microhardness variations along the depth from the surface were measured for 10 s with a Vickers hardness tester (MMT-3 MATSUZAWA CO) under a load of 200 gf on the cross-sectional samples of the deposited layer. The tests were conducted using a computerized Instron 8801 servo-hydraulic test system (Instron, Norwood, MA, USA) at room temperature, with the strain rate set at 10−3s−1. In this work, synchronous layer-by-layer ultrasonic impact treatment (UIT) was proposed to treat laser directed energy deposited TC4 alloy, which can refine the grains and improve the mechanical properties of additive manufacturing samples in-situ. When UIT was conducted on the deposited layer synchronously, plastic deformation induced layer-by-layer. Recrystallization process occurred when subsequent laser deposition process was conducted, thus, the coarse columnar grains transformed into fine equiaxed grains. Through this synchronous layer-by-layer ultrasonic impact, recrystallization occurs layer by layer to refine the grains, the entire deposited specimen with refined microstructure is obtained and the overall mechanical properties were ultimately enhanced. The UIT system includes an ultrasonic transducer, an amplitude transformer, and an ultrasonic probe. During the LDED process, the UIT system under constant pressure (Gravity+0.2 MPa) was synchronized applied on the deposited layer, with the ultrasonic probe consistently in contact with this layer. This arrangement ensured that the deposited layer was subjected to UIT in a layer-by-layer manner. In addition, the UIT system and the LDED system were synchronized to operate with a fixed action spacing of 20 mm in this work. By controlling the loading start position of the UIT, two distinct regions can be formed on the same workpiece: the region of the DED sample subjected to UIT treatment (DED-UIT) and the region of the conventional deposited sample without ultrasonic impact treatment (DED) for comparative analysis. Processing Text: Cu/Ti composite plates with shuttle-heterostructure (SH) were prepared by accumulative roll bonding (ARB) process. Before the first ARB process, industrial pure copper and industrial pure titanium surfaces to be laminated were mechanically polished and wiped by a louver blade and industrial alcohol, respectively. Then, an 11-layer laminated billet was obtained by alternately stacking in the order of Cu/Ti. After that, the first pass of ARB at room temperature was carried out, and an intermediate billet was obtained. Subsequently, the intermediate billet was cut from the center and the surface to be laminated of intermediate billets was mechanically polished with the louver blade. After stacking, the second pass of ARB at room temperature was carried out. Repeat the above surface treatment and ARB process until 3 passes ARB at room temperature were completed, and an ARB Cu/Ti composite plate was obtained. In order to achieve interfacial microalloying of heterostructures, ARB Cu/Ti composite plates were held at 100 °C for 1 h to complete the vacuum diffusion heat treatment. Afterwards, water cooling to room temperature was carried out to obtain heat-treated Cu/Ti composite plates. Condition: After 3 passes ARB at room temperature
Processing Word: Condition: After 3 passes ARB at room temperature

Processing Text: Samples were manufactured using EOS Ti-6Al-4V grade 23 powder on an EOS M290 (EOS GmbH, Germany) LPBF machine housed at the ISO 13485 certified Centre for Rapid Prototyping and Manufacturing (CRPM) of the Central University of Technology in South Africa. Specimens were produced in three batches, and a representative portion of each batch and specimen type was selected to measure the oxygen content to ensure this was kept below 0.013 wt%. The base plate was preheated to 80 °C, and a high-speed steel blade was used as a scraper. The process parameters consisted of a 40 μm layer thickness, 280 W laser power, 1300 mm/s scan speed, 100 μm spot size and a hatch distance of 120 μm. Bidirectional scanning was used, and the scan direction was rotated by 67° between layers. This set of process parameters results in a material with less than 0.01 % porosity [ 23 ]. For tensile specimens, cylinders with a diameter of D = 10 mm and a length of L = 100 mm were produced in the vertical (Z) and horizontal (X) directions relative to the axis of the LPBF machine (and according to ASTM 59200) that is aligned with the direction in which the load is applied. For fracture toughness specimens, Compact Tension (C(T)) specimens were produced as rectangular blocks to allow for the final dimensions of a width of W = 25 mm. C(T) specimens were produced in three orientations, with the first letter indicating the direction in which the load is applied and the second letter indicating the direction in which the crack propagates, that is, ZX, XZ and XY [ 6 ], as shown in Fig. 1 . After printing, the specimens were stress-relieved (SR) at 650 °C for 3 h in a TSH 15/50/180 vacuum furnace (Elite Thermal Systems, England) and then wire-cut from the build plate. The SR treatment was chosen to allow comparison with the literature [ 15 ]. Subsequent heat treatments were conducted at the Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) in atmospheric air using a box furnace (Ultrafurn, South Africa). Therefore, at least 1 mm was removed by wire cutting or machining from all the heat-treated specimen surfaces to remove any α-case and oxide scale that may have formed. The heat treatment schedules, detailed in Table 1 , included the SR, an anneal (AN) heat treatment, chosen due to its simplicity combined with good tensile properties, and a duplex anneal (DA) heat treatment, chosen based on optimal tensile properties reported in the literature [ 6 , 25 ]. Furthermore, the heat treatments above T β (selected based on values available in the literature [ 9 , 15 ]) were combined with the stress relief (BtSR) and anneal (BtAN) heat treatments to mimic how SR or AN specimens would perform if the PBGs were equiaxed c . c It is acknowledged the above T β heat treatment is at the cost of PBG growth. Comparison to specimens with elongated PBGs is only based on orientation effects. After heat treatment, the specimens were machined and wire-cut to their final dimensions. Processing Text: The study utilized AA2195 Al-Cu-Li alloy test plates in the T8 state. The test plate was prepared through four processes: vacuum furnace smelting, semi-continuous casting, hot rolling, and heat treatment. Subsequently, wire electrical discharge machines were used to cut the material into a plate measuring 150 mm × 50 mm × 6 mm. Before welding, the oil on the surfaces of both the test plate and the welding wire was removed using acetone. The surface oxide film was then eliminated by pickling in a mixed acid solution (10 % HF, 10 % HNO 3, 20 % H 2SO 4, and 60 % H 2O) at 60 °C for 10 min. Finally, the test plate and welding wire were rinsed in flowing water and placed in a drying oven at 80 °C for 30 min. Notably, the test plate did not require the cutting of a groove. An I-shaped groove was utilized for direct butt welding. During the VPPA welding process, argon with a purity of 99.99 % was employed as both the plasma gas and the shielding gas. The ultrasonic power supply outputted a frequency of 28 kHz, with an amplitude range of 1-12 μm. A pneumatic system was used to press the ultrasonic head on the test plates with a certain pressure. Processing Text: C and N were added into the base alloy by using pure carbon and Fe 2N, and the two alloys were referred to as C-HEA and N-HEA, respectively. The two alloys were cast in a vacuum induction furnace, followed by wet chemical analysis to control the exact composition after casting. The nominal composition of the interstitial contents is 0.5 at%. However, doping N is more difficult to maintain, and the actual composition of N doping is 1 at%. The cold-rolled HEAs were notated as C-CR and N-CR for carbon-doped and nitrogen-doped HEA, respectively. To minimize significant grain growth during recrystallization and compare the effect of grain refinement and interstitial types with previous work [8,15], short-duration annealing was performed under three conditions: 800 °C for 5 minutes, 800 °C for 10 minutes, and 900 °C for 5 minutes, respectively. Henceforth, the carbon-doped TRIP alloys after annealing are designated as C800-5, C800-10, and C900-5, corresponding to the annealing conditions at 800°C for 5 minutes, 800°C for 10 minutes, and 900°C for 5 minutes, respectively. Processing Text: A series of (ZrNbTi)100-xOx (x = 0, 0.5, 1.0, and 1.5; denoted ZNTO0, ZNTO0.5, ZNTO1.0, and ZNTO1.5) MEAs were fabricated by arc melting followed by cold-rolling and annealing. O was added to the MEAs in the form of ZrO2 granules of 1 mm in diameter. The alloy ingot plates with dimensions of 8 × 2 × 70 mm3 were melted under an argon atmosphere in a water-cooled copper crucible furnace, flipped and remelted six times, and then suction cast using a water-cooled copper mold. To eliminate the micro-segregation of the AC plates and ensure a complete recrystallization of the alloy, the final plates were sealed in evacuated quartz tubes to avoid oxidation and then solid solution treated at 1000 °C for 30 min, followed by ice water quenching. Processing Text: The as-received MEA ingot with a nominal composition of (CoCrNi)94Al3Ti3 (at. %) was fabricated by arc melting in a high-purity argon atmosphere. Each element had a purity of at least 99.95%, and the ingot was remelted at least five times to ensure chemical homogeneity. The as-cast ingots were then homogenized at 1200 °C for 3 hours, followed by water quenching. Subsequently, the homogenized samples were cold-rolled to achieve a thickness reduction of approximately 70%. Then, solid solution treatment at 1100 °C for 6 minutes and water quenching was carried out to obtain completely recrystallized microstructure. Subsequently, we carried out heat treatments with different aging time at 700 °C, and finally selected the 3h aging time process with excellent hardness and cryogenic tensile properties as the research object of this work. Processing Text: The A6-B2 RHEA was prepared by vacuum arc melting high-purity (>99.9 %) elements in a water-cooled copper hearth. The alloy was produced as a ∼50 mm diameter button weighing 150 g. To remove solidification defects, the button was wrapped in a Ta foil and hot isostatically pressed (HIP'd) at 1400 °C for 4 h under a hydrostatic pressure of 207 MPa. The heating and cooling rates during the HIP process were 15 °C/min in the temperature range of 600 °C - 1400 °C. The composition of metallic elements (Al, Ti, V, Zr, Nb, Ta) was determined after HIP using electron probe micro-analysis (EPMA). Inert gas fusion was used to measure oxygen and nitrogen, while combustion infrared absorption was used to measure the carbon content, in accordance with the ASTM E1019 standard. Alloy samples were deformed by uniaxial compression to various strain levels at 25 °C, 400 °C, 600 °C and 800 °C. A constant ram speed corresponding to an initial strain rate of 10 -3s -1was used. Compression specimens had a square cross-section of 4.5 mm x 4.5 mm and a height of 7.6 mm. Room temperature tests were conducted in air, while high-temperature tests were conducted in a vacuum of 10 -5Torr or better. Temperature: 25 °C

Processing Text: A novel high strength Nb3Cr2Ti0.9W0.4Fe6 HEA was developed in this work. The spherical powders were prepared by the dual process of mechanical alloying and high temperature remelting spheroidization (DP) since such technology has combined effect of mechanical milling (plastic deformation) and temperature lifting (atomic diffusion) to achieve the composition homogenization. At the same time, the powder prepared by gas atomization (GA) method is compared, and the printed parts are compared under the same parameters of laser powder bed fusion (LPBF). The yield strength (YS), ultimate tensile strength (UTS) and average elongation (ε) of the samples measured by DP-SLM were 953 MPa, 1159 MPa and 14.8 %, respectively. The hot compression test of Nb3Cr2Ti0.9W0.4Fe6 was carried out with Gleeble-3800 thermal simulation machine. The thermal processing diagram of the alloy under different stress variables was drawn by establishing the thermal deformation constitutive equation. The DP-SLM material recovers when the deformation temperature is 1000 ℃ with deformation rate stays at 0.01 s−1. Nb3Cr2Ti0.9W0.4Fe6 alloy processed at 1050-1150°C and a strain rate of 0.005∼ 0.1 s−1 shows high power dissipation efficiency (up to 37 %) and better dynamic recrystallization structure. Nb3Cr2Ti0.9W0.4Fe6 can be considered widely used in the engine combustion chamber, guide, turbine blade and turbo disk four hot end components. The RHEA spherical powders with uniform composition were prepared by mechanical alloying (MA) and High temperature remelting spherification technology (HTRS). MA technology achieves the composition uniformity of RHEA powder through the combined action of mechanical milling (plastic deformation) and temperature raising (atomic diffusion). Nb3Cr2Ti0.9W0.4Fe6 HEA powders were prepared by mechanical alloying process. After the alloyed powder was dried sufficiently, high temperature remelting equipment was used to prepare spherical powder, provided by Shaanxi Zhiqi Kaiwu Co. The printing parameters were set: laser power reached up to 550 W with 3200 mm/s scanning speed. laser wavelength is 1.06 μm, the thickness of each layer is 0.02 mm and spot diameter is 0.1 mm. 316 steel was regarded as the basic materials (BM) and its composition is shown in Table 3. In conclusion, MA can promote the alloying of refractory elements, while HTRS could change the powder morphology (spheroidization). Processing Text: Ti-1Fe feedstocks were prepared by mechanically mixing 1 wt% of Fe powder into a gas-atomised CP-Ti powder with spheroidal morphology (TILOP-45, Osaka Titanium). Two types of Fe powders were used: a fine Fe powder of ∼5 μm (FEE16PB, Kojundo Chemical) and a coarser Fe powder of ∼25 μm (300 M, Kobe Steel, pre-sieved <45 μm mesh). Mixing was performed by rocking mill (AV-2, Asahi Rika) in 500 g batches for 1 h at a setting of 60 Hz. To promote mixing, ⌀5 mm zirconia balls were added to each mixture at a ball-to-powder weight ratio of 1:10. The prepared feedstocks were consolidated into rectangular test coupons (10 mm × 10 mm × 60 mm) using a commercial laser powder bed fusion system (TruPrint 1000, TRUMPF). Test coupons were built directly onto a pure-Ti substrate, using build parameters including laser power fixed at 160 W, layer thickness fixed at 20 μm, and varied energy densities and hatch spacings (60-S, 60-W, 120-S, 120-W, 180-S, 180-W). Tensile test specimens were extracted from the centre of each test coupon by wire electrical discharge machining with the tensile direction oriented orthogonal to the build direction and parallel to the long edge of the rectangular test coupon. The oxygen (O), nitrogen (N), and hydrogen (H) contents in the powders and built materials were evaluated by inert gas fusion analysis. The mechanical properties were evaluated by uniaxial tensile testing. Prepared from 3 to 8 μm Fe powder at higher volumetric energy densities; Satisfies ASTM requirements for PBF-LB/M Ti-6Al-4V

Processing Text: An ingot with a nominal composition of Ti-10Mo-3.5Cu (wt%) was produced through vacuum arc smelting under an argon atmosphere and was remelted three times. The composition of the prepared alloy was determined using an inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometer (ICP-OES 730). Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) coupled with Jmatpro software analysis determined the β-transus temperature (T β) of the alloy to be ∼795°C. Homogenization was carried out at 1000°C for 720 min under an argon atmosphere to ensure a uniform structure. Then, the bulk material underwent a hot rolling process at 700°C, achieving a reduction of 75 % in thickness. This was followed by solution treatment (900°C, 30 minutes, water quenched), obtaining a metastable β phase labeled as 3.5Cu-ST. Samples were then aged at different temperatures (150°C, 250°C, and 350°C) for 10 minutes and then quenched in water, represented by 3.5Cu-150A, 3.5Cu-250A, and 3.5Cu-350A, respectively. The specific aging temperatures were chosen to minimize the risk of severe ductility loss due to α phase precipitation and avoid the coarsening of ω isophases, particularly when aging above 500°C. Processing Text: Ti40Zr25Nb25Ta5Al5 (at.%) RHEA was fabricated from elemental nuggets with a minimum purity of 99.95 wt.% using an arc melting furnace (AM200, Edmund Bühler GmbH) under a Ti-getter pure Ar-atmosphere. Firstly, five alloy buttons (∼20 g) were fabricated. Each alloy button underwent six rounds of remelting to ensure chemical homogeneity, with each button flipped before each remelting cycle. Throughout each melting cycle, the alloy was kept in the liquid state for 10 min. Subsequently, all five buttons were combined and remelted together before being cast into a water-cooled Cu-mould to form a cuboidal bar with dimensions of 90 × 12 × 8 (thickness) mm3. Cross-sections of the as-cast alloy bar were ground using SiC abrasive papers and mirror-polished using 0.04 μm colloidal silica suspension (OPS) with 30 % H2O2 (10:1 by volume) for microstructural characterization. Dog-bone-shaped tensile samples with gauge dimensions of 8 mm × 2.9 mm × 1.5 mm (thickness) (Australian Standard AS 1391-2007) were prepared from as-cast bars using an electrical discharge wire-cutting machine. The entire surface of each tensile sample was ground with 600 grit SiC papers to remove the heat-affected layers from wire cutting. Tensile testing was performed on an Instron 5584 EM frame machine with a video extensometer. All tensile samples were tested at a slow strain rate of 5 × 10−5 s−1 at room temperature. The working electrodes were specimens connected with a conductive copper wire extension embedded in epoxy. A constant cross-section of 0.1 cm2 was exposed to Hank’s solution. Prior to testing, epoxy-mounted specimens were polished progressively up to 1200 grit SiC paper, degreased with acetone and ethanol, rinsed with distilled water, and dried in a compressed air stream. After 2 h immersion in Hank’s solution to attain an electrochemically quasi-stable state, potentiodynamic polarisation plots were recorded in the range −0.2 to 2.5 V in relation to open circuit potential at a scan rate of 4 mV/s. TEM samples were prepared using the standard lift-out method in a focused ion beam (FIB) system with FEI Scios DualBeam (FEI Scios DualBeam, Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA). A protective platinum (Pt) layer was deposited on sample surface prior to milling to minimize FIB-induced damage. Processing state: as-cast

Processing Text: Samples were manufactured using EOS Ti-6Al-4V grade 23 powder on an EOS M290 (EOS GmbH, Germany) LPBF machine housed at the ISO 13485 certified Centre for Rapid Prototyping and Manufacturing (CRPM) of the Central University of Technology in South Africa. Specimens were produced in three batches, and a representative portion of each batch and specimen type was selected to measure the oxygen content to ensure this was kept below 0.013 wt%. The base plate was preheated to 80 °C, and a high-speed steel blade was used as a scraper. The process parameters consisted of a 40 μm layer thickness, 280 W laser power, 1300 mm/s scan speed, 100 μm spot size and a hatch distance of 120 μm. Bidirectional scanning was used, and the scan direction was rotated by 67° between layers. This set of process parameters results in a material with less than 0.01 % porosity [ 23 ]. For tensile specimens, cylinders with a diameter of D = 10 mm and a length of L = 100 mm were produced in the vertical (Z) and horizontal (X) directions relative to the axis of the LPBF machine (and according to ASTM 59200) that is aligned with the direction in which the load is applied. For fracture toughness specimens, Compact Tension (C(T)) specimens were produced as rectangular blocks to allow for the final dimensions of a width of W = 25 mm. C(T) specimens were produced in three orientations, with the first letter indicating the direction in which the load is applied and the second letter indicating the direction in which the crack propagates, that is, ZX, XZ and XY [ 6 ], as shown in Fig. 1 . After printing, the specimens were stress-relieved (SR) at 650 °C for 3 h in a TSH 15/50/180 vacuum furnace (Elite Thermal Systems, England) and then wire-cut from the build plate. The SR treatment was chosen to allow comparison with the literature [ 15 ]. Subsequent heat treatments were conducted at the Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) in atmospheric air using a box furnace (Ultrafurn, South Africa). Therefore, at least 1 mm was removed by wire cutting or machining from all the heat-treated specimen surfaces to remove any α-case and oxide scale that may have formed. The heat treatment schedules, detailed in Table 1 , included the SR, an anneal (AN) heat treatment, chosen due to its simplicity combined with good tensile properties, and a duplex anneal (DA) heat treatment, chosen based on optimal tensile properties reported in the literature [ 6 , 25 ]. Furthermore, the heat treatments above T β (selected based on values available in the literature [ 9 , 15 ]) were combined with the stress relief (BtSR) and anneal (BtAN) heat treatments to mimic how SR or AN specimens would perform if the PBGs were equiaxed c . c It is acknowledged the above T β heat treatment is at the cost of PBG growth. Comparison to specimens with elongated PBGs is only based on orientation effects. After heat treatment, the specimens were machined and wire-cut to their final dimensions. Processing Text: The samples used for the present study were prepared by arc-melting a mixture of pure elements. The ingots were re-melted five times to ensure compositional homogeneity before being drop-cast into a copper mold. Subsequently, samples were homogenized at 1200 °C for 24 h, water-quenched, and then cold-rolled to a thickness reduction of approximately 75 %. In order to obtain samples with different grain sizes, the cold-rolled sheets were annealed at various temperatures ranging from 650 °C to 1250 °C for various time intervals. Specimens for EBSD characterization were initially mechanically ground, polished with aluminum oxide suspension, and then electrochemically polished in an electrolyte of CH 3OH:HNO 3= 4:1 at 20 V for 30 s at -40 °C. For TEM observation, specimens were firstly mechanically ground to about 30 μm, punched into 3 mm diameter disks, and finally thinned by an ion milling system (PIPS, Model 695, Gatan). Dog-bone-shaped samples with 35 mm gauge, 5 mm width, and 3 mm thickness were used for in-situ tensile loading experiments by neutron diffraction. Average grain size: ∼56.0 μm

Processing Text: The CuCrZr alloy powder used in the experiment was prepared by the plasma rotating electrode atomization process. Specimens were prepared by EB-PBF equipment (Xi'an Sailong Additive Technology Co., Ltd., China). The maximum forming size of EB-PBF equipment is 150 × 150 × 210 mm, and the maximum vacuum degree is 5 × 10 −3Pa. In order to imitate the aging heat treatment process of CuCrZr alloy in-situ to precipitate nano-precipitates, the powder bed temperatures were controlled to 300 °C, 400 °C and 500 °C during the EB-PBF process. The specific forming parameters refer to our previous research [ 14]. The powder bed temperature of the EB-PBF sample is 200 °C, the conventional sample without CPBT is labeled as EB-PBF. When printing EB-PBF samples, the powder is melted directly after the powder coating is completed. When printing CPBT samples, an electron beam is used to heat the entire powder bed after the powder spreading is completed. The thermocouple used to measure the powder bed temperature is installed under the base plate. The powder bed temperature fluctuates and cannot be controlled very accurately at present. When the powder bed temperature is too high or too low, the electron beam current will be dynamically adjusted. The samples with the CPBT at 250-350 °C are marked as 300 °C, and the samples with the CPBT at 350-450 °C and 450-550 °C are marked as 400 °C and 500 °C respectively. In this way, the sample is always maintained in the aging heat treatment temperature range during the entire printing process. This special thermal history is controlled similar to traditional aging treatment. The thermal history of different samples is shown in Fig. 1c, and the printing process parameters are shown in Table 1. The powder particle size distribution is 15-106 μm, where D50 is 43 μm and D90 is 67 μm. The elemental content of Cr and Zr in the powder was determined by inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectroscopy (ICP-AES), while the elemental content of O was determined by pulse heating inert gas fusion intrinsic absorption method. Impurities such as Fe, Si, and P were determined by ICP-AES. As-built sample with dimensions of 10 × 10 × 60 mm 3 to determine the microstructure, phase composition and mechanical properties. A Shimadzu universal testing machine AGS-X 10 KN was used to conduct uniaxial tensile experiments at a strain rate of 1 mm/min on flat dog-bone shaped samples with a gauge length of 25 × 6 × 2 mm 3 to evaluate room temperature mechanical properties. Tensile specimens were cut from the same position of the as-built specimen for comparison. All specimens were polished before tensile to ensure smooth surfaces. An eddy current metal conductivity meter (Sigma 2008B, China) was used to measure the conductivity of the specimens with a resolution of 0.01 %IACS and a measurement range of 0.8-110 %IACS. Before the conductivity was tested, the surface was polished with sandpaper to ensure that there were no large scratches. Then the surface was polished with 2.5 μm and 0.5 μm diamond spray polishing agents. Finally, the sample was cleaned and dried. Each sample was tested 3 times, and the remaining values were averaged. Optical microscopy (GX51, OM), scanning electron microscopy (Gemini SEM 300, SEM), energy dispersive spectroscopic mapping (EDS), and electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) were used to characterize the sample microstructure. Among them, the scanning step size in EBSD experiment is 1.5 μm, and the scanning area is 600∗450 μm. The mixed solution (FeCl 3/1 g, HCl/2 ml, H 2O/20 ml) was used to etch the sample surface. After etching, the samples were cleaned in C 2H 5OH and dried for observation of microstructure. The samples were prepared into thin slices with a thickness of less than 60 μm and a diameter of 3 mm, and then underwent ion beam thinning at a low temperature of 100 K. All prepared thin platinum samples were observed on a transmission scanning electron microscope (Talos F200s, TEM) operating at 200 keV. Finally, the TEM data were analyzed and processed by Digital Micrograph (DM) software. EB-PBF sample; Tensile properties tested perpendicular to the build direction

Processing Text: To ensure the uniform dispersion of SiCp in the iron powder, we dispersed SiCp and iron powder in alcohol, first using a combination of ultrasonic mixing and mechanical mixing to promote uniform dispersion. Subsequently, high-energy ball milling was conducted for 2 h with a ball-to-material ratio of 5:1. After obtaining mixed powders with different SiCp volume fractions, they were layered in a graphite mold in the order of 10 % SiCp/Fe, 3 % SiCp/Fe, pure Fe, 3 % SiCp/Fe, and 10 % SiCp/Fe. Based on the sintering parameter settings for Fe in references [ 26 , 33 ], and considering the capacity of the equipment, we chose the SPS parameters to be 900 °C, 40 MPa, and 20 min. During the sintering process, the presence of SiCp inhibited grain growth, leading to grain refinement, and the varying SiCp volume fractions across layers resulted in different grain sizes, thereby creating a gradient material with a heterogeneous structure. Processing Text: The ingot, prepared by the vacuum melt casting method, was heated to 1200 °C for 2 hours and then forged into 100 mm × 100 mm × 80 mm forgings. Once cooled to room temperature, the forgings were cut into 50 mm × 20 mm × 8 mm slabs using wire-cutting technology. Subsequently, the slab underwent homogenization at 1200 °C for 2 hours. Then, its thickness was reduced to 4 mm (50% reduction) through six hot rolling passes conducted within a temperature range of 1010 - 1150 °C, starting at 1150 °C and ending at 950 °C. After hot rolling, the sheet underwent dephosphating and was then cold rolled through ten processes, ultimately resulting in a thickness of 2.2 mm (45% reduction). Lastly, the cold-rolled sheet was annealed at approximately 1173 K for 15 mins. All heat treatments were conducted in an inert gas (argon) atmosphere to ensure material purity and prevent oxidation. A rectangular sample measuring 10 mm × 30 mm was cut from the rolled and annealed billet and then finely polished with 1500 grit silicon carbide sandpaper to achieve a uniform thickness of 2 mm. Compression testing of these thin sheet samples was conducted using the CMT5305 microcomputer-controlled universal material testing machine along the normal direction (ND), with a strain rate of 0.001 s−1. To ensure precise control of deformation, dual means of stroke and pressure control were employed in the experiments. Thickness measurements were taken at three different locations before and after the compression test, with the average values documented to reflect the initial and final thicknesses. The average thicknesses of the four samples before compression were 1.98 mm, 2.02 mm, 2.00 mm, and 2.00 mm, respectively, and they changed to 1.80 mm, 1.62 mm, 1.48 mm, and 1.34 mm after compression. Uniaxial micro-tensile tests were conducted at 298 K (room temperature) on an in-house miniature-testing machine with a load cell of 5000 N and a nominal strain rate of 0.001 s−1. The samples were cut by EDM from the pre-compressed sheet material with gauge dimensions of 5 mm × 2 mm × 1 mm. The tensile direction of the samples was strictly aligned with the rolling direction (RD). Before testing, all samples underwent mechanical grinding to ensure a smooth surface without any obvious defects. To accurately determine the tensile strain value, random speckle patterns were uniformly sprayed onto the sample surface. During the tensile process, deformation images were captured in real-time using a high-resolution camera. Subsequently, MATLAB software was utilized for image processing and analysis. Initially, the images were converted into monochrome. Then, based on the center point of the sample gauge area, a virtual extensometer was constructed from the two preset solid lines. Finally, the sample's strain was determined by calculating the displacement of pixel points between the virtual extensometers over time. In this study, two types of micro-tensile tests were conducted: in-situ tests and interrupted tests, both loaded by displacement control. The in-situ tests were designed to obtain the stress-strain curve of the sample up to fracture, and back stress was also assessed through a LUR cycle test. To ensure reproducibility, three independent tensile tests were conducted for each pre-compressed sample. During the LUR test, a strain rate of 0.001 s−1 was used for strain control during loading, while unloading was force-controlled at 25 N/s. Reloading began when the force was unloaded to 25 N. The interrupted test was designed to study the microstructure evolution, with interruptions at specific points or continuation until fracture. Additionally, to accurately characterize the microstructure evolution of the pre-compressed sample at the same position before and after tensile deformation, hardness markers were placed in the center of the target region. These markers served as reference points, facilitating accurate analysis of the microstructure evolution during subsequent EBSD characterization. Microstructure characterization was performed using EBSD on a Nova Nano SEM 230 ultra-high resolution field emission SEM. The sample preparation consisted of coarse grinding and fine grinding followed by electrolytic polishing at -20 °C using an electrolytic polishing solution of 4 vol% perchloric acid mixed with 96 vol% ethanol at a voltage of 30 V and a polishing time of 30 s. For EBSD analysis, the operating voltage was set to 20 kV, and the step size was 0.25 μm. In addition, the TEM sample was prepared from the specified sample using a focused ion beam (FIB) technique at an acceleration voltage of 30 kV. In this study, a total of two TEM observations were performed. The first observation was performed on the sample with a compressive strain of 0.4, and the second TEM test was conducted on the pre-compressed sample after stretched to 0.2. The FIB slice was taken from the central region of the sample, with the slice plane perpendicular to the RD and the slice size of 10 μm × 8 μm. The TEM sample was mechanically polished to a thickness of 30 μm, then thinned by double injection at -25 °C with an electrolyte of 10% perchloric acid and 90% alcohol at 15 V, and finally cleaned by ion grinding at 3 kV at a 2 °C angle for 10 min. Finally, the samples were observed by the TALOS F200X field emission transmission electron microscope under a 200 kV acceleration voltage. Processing Text: The steel was prepared using high-frequency vacuum induction melting and cast into ingots, which was homogenized at 1200 °C for 2h. The homogenized ingot with a thickness of 60 mm was hot rolled by seven passes to a thickness of 12 mm in the temperature range from 1050 °C to 1000 °C and cooled by water spray to RT. The hot rolled plate was further rolled with an AR mill by five passes to a thickness of 12 mm in the temperature range from 400 °C to 360 °C and cooled by water spray to RT, the stride ratio is 1:1.2. The steel plate after AR rolled was cut into four parts, which were annealing at different temperature for 10 min. The steel plate after AR rolled without annealing, and with the annealing temperature of 500 °C, 700 °C, and 900 °C are defined as AR, AR-500A, AR-700A, and AR-900A, respectively. Processing Text: 23NSS was refined using a vacuum induction heating furnace. The ingot was forged after turning. Then, after hot rolling, the forging billet was heated at 1200°C for 3 h and rolled into a 3.2-mm-thick SS plate. After the material was held at 1050°C for 20 min, the billet was water-cooled. Using an electric discharge wire cutting machine, bone-shaped tensile specimens and 10 × 10 mm tetragonal electrochemical test samples were produced along the rolling direction. The electrochemical test samples were soldered to the back of copper wire, sealed with acrylic powder, polished with 600, 800, 1000, 1200, 1500, and 2000# sandpaper, and finally cleaned with alcohol and dried. Tensile experiments were carried out on a universal test machine (SANS CMT5105) at room temperature with a crosshead speed of 3 mm/min, and the tensile strain under load was monitored by an extensometer. Bone-shaped tensile specimens were deformed in tension along the rolling direction with a marked length and parallel section width of 40 and 16 mm, respectively. In addition, 23NSS was deformed to 10, 30, and 50 % during stretching, with the stretching process stopped immediately at each stage to investigate the corrosion resistance of 23NSS under different strain states. Potentiodynamic polarization, potentiostatic polarization, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), and Mott-Schottky tests were conducted using a CS2350M dual potentiostatic instrument. All electrochemical tests were performed at 70°C in 0.0005 M H 2SO 4+ 2 ppm F −solution, which was bubbled with air to simulate the cathode environment of PEMFCs. The electrochemical tests were carried out using a three-electrode system. The counter electrode consisted of a thin platinum sheet 20 × 20 mm in size, and the working electrode had an area of 10 × 10 mm. The reference electrode consisted of a saturated mercuric sulphate electrode (MSE, 0.64 V vs. SHE, standard hydrogen electrode, all potentials relative to MSE unless otherwise stated). In addition, the reference electrode was placed in a Lagin capillary filled with saturated K 2SO 4solution, then the capillary was placed perpendicularly to the planar working electrode and counter electrode. The electrochemical tests were preceded by potentiostatic polarization of the working electrode at −1.37 V for 200 s to remove the oxides that had formed in the atmosphere. All samples were polished, cleaned, and dried prior to OCP testing. Three electrochemical test samples were used for the same treatment process, and each sample was repeated more than three times to ensure repeatability of the experiment. The potentiodynamic polarization, potentiostatic polarization, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), and Mott-Schottky tests were performed after the open circuit potential stabilized. Potentiodynamic polarization tests were initiated at a relative open-circuit potential of −0.3 V and stopped at 0.5 V relative to the reference electrode, with a scanning rate of 0.6 mV/s. Potentiostatic polarization was carried out at a potential close to the cathodic working potential of 0.23 V for 6 h. EIS tests were initiated with a 10 mV AC amplitude and frequency sweep from 10 5Hz to 10 −2Hz. Mott-Schottky tests were performed at a fixed frequency of 100 Hz with a sinusoidal excitation signal amplitude of 5 mV. The electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) samples were polished with 0.5 µm diamond abrasive and then electrolytically polished in ethanol perchloric acid solution with a volume fraction ratio of 20 % using a 20 V DC voltage for 18 s. The EBSD patterns were obtained under the following conditions: an accelerating voltage of 15 kV, sample tilt of 75°, and step size of 0.4 µm. The element distribution images were obtained by EPMA at an accelerating voltage of 20 kV with a step size of 0.4 µm. X-ray diffraction (XRD) was performed using Cu-Kα (wavelength α = 1.54 Å) radiation with a scanning range of 40-90° and scanning speed of 4°/min. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, Thermo Scientific K-Alpha) was used to determine the composition of the passive film after 120 min of open-circuit potential. Processing Text: A novel Al-9.5Ce-0.6Mg/0.7GNPs (wt. %) composite with a network co-continuous Al/(Al, Mg)11Ce3 eutectic structure was fabricated using laser powder bed fusion. The spherical Al-Ce powder with a particle size distribution of 15∼53 μm was fabricated using the gas atomization method. Commercially irregular-shaped flake-like GNPs, with a lateral size of ∼200-300 nm and a thickness of ∼5-10 nm, were used as raw materials. A low-energy ball-milling was conducted to uniformly distribute the GNPs within the Al-Ce powder while maintaining the sphericity of the Al-Ce powder particles. The ball-milling process was performed using a planetary ball milling machine (Nanjing Nanda Instrument Group Co., Ltd., China) at a rotation rate of 200 rpm for 6 h with a ball-to-powder ratio of 2:1. The as-mixed Al-Ce/0.7 wt% GNPs powder was firstly heated to 60 °C and maintained at that temperature for 6 h with a vacuum of 10−2Pa in a vacuum drying oven to evaporate residual H2O on the powder surface. A SLM 125HL machine (SLM Solutions Group AG, Germany) was used to fabricate Al-9.5Ce-0.6Mg/0.7GNPs samples with dimensions of 35 mm × 20 mm × 10 mm. The parameters used were: laser power of 330 W, laser scanning speed of 1200 mm/s, hatch spacing of 30 μm, layer thickness of 30 μm. A scanning strategy with a rotation of 67° per layer was adopted. The aluminum substrate was preheated to 200 °C before printing. Subsequently, the as-built Al-9.5Ce-0.6Mg/0.7GNPs composite was subjected to post-heat treatment. The heat treatment (HT) was operated at 400 °C for 1h followed by water quenching. Condition: room temperature; Additional properties: UTS of 452 ± 3 MPa, elongation of 5.6 ± 0.2 %

Processing Text: The Fe-Cr-Mo-Mn steel used in this study are first heated by oxidation in an electric arc furnace, then decarbonized and desulphurized, with argon stirring to achieve deoxidation and desulphurization during the refining process. Subsequently, the steel ingot was subjected to multi-pass forging on a servo-hydraulic press. The forging process was initiated at an initial temperature of 1220 °C, with the final temperature reaching 800 °C, as illustrated in Fig. 1. The H1 sample undergoes QT based on the forged state, while the Ac1 and Ac2 temperatures for Fe-Cr-Mo-Mn steel are determined to be 710 °C and 780 °C, respectively. The H2 sample is subjected to an initial high-temperature normalization at 950 °C, followed by a near-Ac3 normalization at 770 °C, before proceeding to QT. In contrast, the H3 sample receives two successive high-temperature normalizations at 950 °C prior to the QT treatment. Following a single normalization, the resulting microstructure exhibits a combination of ferrite and pearlite. However, a significant refinement in both phases occurs after double normalization, as depicted in Fig. 1. The high-temperature tempering process engenders the formation of TS, characterized by the homogeneous dispersion of carbides within a ferritic matrix. The acicular martensite formed during the quenching process undergoes decomposition into a finer TS, which is uniformly distributed within the ferrite matrix during high-temperature tempering. Moreover, the elevated tempering temperatures facilitate enhanced diffusion of carbides, promoting the coalescence and growth of precipitated carbides within the ferrite matrix into a more uniformly dispersed granular morphology. Prior to the fatigue crack propagation tests, the initial microstructures of the H1, H2, and H3 specimens of Fe-Cr-Mo-Mn steel under varying heat treatment conditions were characterized using scanning electron microscopy (SEM). Following the fatigue crack propagation tests, the three groups of samples underwent characterization using SEM and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) to provide a comprehensive analysis of the microstructure evolution. Processing Text: NiCoFeCr HEA ingots were prepared by arc-melting a mixture of pure metals (purity > 99.9 wt.%) in a high-purity argon atmosphere. After the raw materials were loaded in the arc melter, the chamber was first evacuated to ∼5 × 10−2Pa and then backfilled with pure Ar and evacuated twice to dilute the residual air inside the chamber, finally backfilled at a pressure of ∼5 × 104Pa. Before the materials were melted, a small piece of pure Ti was melted to getter any residual air that might be present in the chamber. The buttons were remelted and flipped seven times to ensure chemical homogeneity before they were suction-cast into a rectangular copper mold with the dimensions of 8 mm × 17 mm × 70 mm. After solidification, the ingots were cleaned and dried, encapsulated in evacuated quartz tubes, and homogenized for 48 h at 1250 °C to minimize any casting-related segregation and then annealed for 1 h at 800 °C in air with water quenching. The samples were cut by electric discharge machining (EDM) from the suction cast ingot and annealed sheets and then ground with SiC adhesive papers to a grit size of 7 μm and polished with diamond suspension down to 1 μm. After mechanical polishing, the microstructure and phase composition of the alloys were investigated using X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), electron-backscattered diffraction (EBSD), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) techniques. Processing Text: The gas-atomized Haynes 230 powders with the chemical composition shown in Table 1 are used as material. The LPBF manufacturing process of the Haynes 230 alloy is completed using the SLM100-N2 system equipped with a fiber laser, the maximum laser power is 450 W, the maximum forming size is 100 mm × 100 mm × 100 mm, and the double cylinders feed powders in one direction. The process parameters used are the same as in our previous study [9]. Among them, the scanning speed, laser power, thickness, and rotation angle are 2500 mm/s, 260 W, 35 µm, and 90°, respectively. Before UIT, the tensile and wear samples are grounded by a grinding machine, and the processed dimensions after the process are shown in Fig. 1(d). Then, the surface is ground step by step with SiC sandpapers until smooth, and further polished to a mirror surface. The ultrasonic impact machine (UIT-500) is used to impact treat the LPBFed Haynes 230 samples. The amplitude, out current, impact frequency, pin diameter, and overlap rate of the UIT experiment are 27 µm, 1.0 A, 20 KHz, 3.0 mm, and 50 % respectively. In this experiment, the effects of repeated impact layer times (n=1, 2, and 3) on the pore closure, microstructure, mechanical, and wear properties are emphatically analyzed. Before internal porosity and microstructure characterization, the surface is grounded step by step with SiC sandpapers (180#, 400#, 600#, 800#, 1000#, 1500#, and 2000#) until smooth and further polished to hardly any tiny scratches by nylon polishing cloth. Then, electrolytic polishing is carried out, wherein the electrolytic polishing solution is 20 mL HClO4+ 80 mL C2H5OH, the voltage of electrolytic polishing is 20 V and the polishing time is 3-5 s. In addition, electrochemical corrosion is to observe the morphology of the melt pool and sub-grain structure. The electrochemical etching solution is 15 g CuSO4+ 50 mL HCl + 3.5 mL H2SO4, the voltage is 3-5 V and the etching time is 10 s. Before tensile and wear properties tests, the top surface of all samples is slightly polished with 1500 mesh sandpaper until smooth to eliminate impact caused by rough surfaces on performance. The tensile tests are performed by employing the universal testing machine (Instron 5582, Instron Systems Corporation, America), in accordance with the GB/T 228.1-2010 standard. Three tensile samples are manufactured for each group with a strain rate of 1 mm/min, all tensile tests are conducted at room temperature and fracture morphology is observed using SEM. Furthermore, the wear tests are performed by the high-frequency reciprocating tribometer (MGW-001, Jinan Yihua Tribology Testing Technology Co., Ltd, China) at room temperature, in accordance with the ISO12156-1:1997 standard. In the wear test process, the wear ball is Si3N4 with a diameter of 5 mm, and the load force, test duration, and reciprocating distance are 20 N, 15 min, and 5 mm, respectively. The wear tests are repeated three times. Processing state: LPBF + UIT1; Uncertainty: ± 17.9 MPa

Processing Text: A Cu-Ni-Si-Ca alloy was melted using a vacuum medium-frequency induction furnace and cast in a spheroidal graphite cast iron mold, resulting in a 30 mm-thick ingot, with the chemical composition listed in Table 1 obtained by using an Inductively Coupled Plasma-Atomic Emission Spectrometer (ICP-AES). The ingot was then hot rolled at 850 °C into a plate with a thickness reduction of 90 %. The steel plate was solution-treated at 980 °C for 4 h, water quenched, and cold rolled with a 90 % thickness reduction. The plate was then cut into several 11 mm (parallel to the rolling direction) × 13 mm specimens, for the aging treatment in the temperature range from 450 °C to 550 °C for 15-1440 min. The addition of only 0.05 % Ca in this alloy is used to purify the alloy during the melting and casting process as a refinery. The DP process combined with thermomechanical treatment was exploited to expedite the precipitation kinetics, whilst the competition between DP and CP was utilized to inhibit the nucleation and growth of continuous precipitation phase (CPP). Cold deformation was conducted to further increase the nucleation rate by providing potential nucleation sites, such as dislocations and stacking faults. The growth of classic discontinuous precipitation phase (CDPP) was restricted due to the high nucleation rate of spherical discontinuous precipitation phase (SDPP) and the deformed microstructure. The aging time can be substantially shortened to introduce these metastable ordered t-Ni 3Si precipitates in the alloy. Processing Text: The LDED system (LMD300) consists of a 2 kW fiber laser with a wavelength of 1060 nm, a platform control system, and a coaxial powder feeding system. The optimized processing parameters are as follows: laser power of 1200 W, scanning speed of 7 mm/s, laser spot size of 2.5 mm, powder feeding rate of 20 g/min, overlap rate of 50% and layer thickness of ∼1 mm. The laser scanning strategy followed a zigzag path with a 90° rotation of the scanning direction between successive layers. The chamber was filled with argon gas to minimize the possibility of the melt pool oxidation during the LDED process. The deposited IN718 block in size of 75 × 25 × 15 mm 3was cut from the base metal by electrical discharge machining. Before UIT, the LDED-fabricated IN718 plate samples were prepared using wire electrical discharge machining, and the sample surfaces were ground using a grinding machine to achieve a nominal surface roughness (Sa) of 0.4 μm. The UIT setup (CO-100) is schematically illustrated in Fig. 2b. During UIT process, the impact pin (made by quenched martensitic steel) with a head diameter of 3 mm struck the horizontal surface (XY-plane) of the samples and moved along a zigzag path shown in Fig. 2c. The fixed baseline parameters for the UIT process are as follows: impact frequency of 18 kHz and travel speed of 1 mm/s. The overlap rate of 50% was chosen because an insufficient overlap rate leads to poor strengthening effects, as evidenced by the comparative results for 20% and 50% overlap rates in Fig. S3-Fig. S5in Supplementary Materials. This study mainly focuses on the influence of the key parameter—UIT output powers ( i.e., 400 W, 600 W, and 800 W)—on surface integrity, deformation microstructure, and mechanical properties. According to the proportional relationship between power and the square of amplitude, the corresponding amplitudes for each power level were ∼14 μm, ∼17 μm, and ∼20 μm, respectively. White light interferometry (UP-2000, Rtec Instruments) was employed to measure the surface topography both before and after UIT. Residual stress measurements were performed using an X-ray residual stress measurement device (LXRD-MG2000, Proto) with a Mn target and the {311} reflection. The azimuth angle of the diffraction crystal plane (ѱ) was set to 0°, 25°, 35°, and 45°, respectively. The 2θ scanning angles were defined as 150° for the initiating angle and 155° for the terminating angle, with a tube current of 25 mA, a tube voltage of 30 kV, and a spot size of 1 mm. To accurately measure residual stresses in the tensile direction (X) along the depth, surface layers were incrementally removed through electro-polishing with 10 vol% perchloric acid ethanol solution, exposing the sample surface at varying depths. Moreover, a dynamic explicit finite element model (FEM) was developed using Abaqus/Explicit software to simulate the residual stress distribution induced by ultrasonic impact treatment under single-point impact conditions. The model consists of a 5 × 5 × 2 mm 3IN718 alloy plate, meshed with 50 μm C3D8R (8-node linear hexahedral) elements, and a 3 mm diameter impact needle, meshed with 250 μm C3D10M (10-node modified quadratic tetrahedral) elements made of quenched martensitic steel. The impact needle was modeled as a rigid body due to its negligible deformation during impact. The stress field was simulated using the elastic-plastic model by using the mechanical property of IN718 alloy derived from the stress-strain curve of the as-LDEDed sample in Fig. 8c. To capture the transient dynamics of the impact process, the analysis time step was set to 0.001 s.
