Processing Text: Using powder metallurgy and hot extrusion techniques, Al5083 MMCs were then created with differing amounts of SiC/RGO. The current study used Al5083 powder for the matrix material. Initially, SiC/RGO reinforcing particles were combined with 5083 aluminum alloy powder in varying mass fractions of 0.1 %, 0.3 %, and 0.5 %. The resulting mixture was transferred to a ball milling tank, followed by the addition of 1 g of stearic acid. Afterward, the tank was flushed with argon gas, and the materials underwent milling in an ND7-1L ball mill using a ball-to-material ratio of 5:1, a rotational speed of 200 rpm, for a duration of 10 h. The 10-hour ball milling converted spherical 5083 aluminum alloy powder into flakes, enhancing sintering performance through increased surface area and mechanical interlocking. The uniformly mixed powder was subsequently transferred to a SK2-2-12TPB2 vacuum tube furnace for heating at 400 °C, the process that facilitates the removal of stearic acid from the powder. Thereafter, the SiC/RGO/Al5083 powder was placed into the cylindrical mold and use a hydraulic press to obtain the φ40 × 4 mm 3shape. Then, the mold and the cold-extruded billet were placed into the hot extrusion equipment together. Subsequent to a 30-minute hold at 500 °C, the aluminum matrix composite rods were hot-extruded according to an extrusion ratio of 1:16. Reinforcement: 0.3 wt% SiC/RGO

Processing Text: Thixomolding was conducted using a specialized thixomolding machine designed for magnesium alloys and composites. The raw material was a mixture of AZ91D magnesium chips with size of 1.2 × 1.2 × 4 mm³ and AlCoCrFeNi powder with a median particle size of 12.5 µm. Volume fraction of the reinforcements is 1.5 %. The raw materials were placed into the hopper and subjected to multi-stage heating in the barrel to achieve a semi-solid state. Seven heating stages were employed, with the barrel temperature from the feed zone to nozzle of 480, 550, 580, 615, 615, 605, and 580 °C. The screw continuously rotated at a speed of 120 rpm, shearing the semi-solid slurry, breaking up large dendrites, and making a uniform distribution of equiaxed and fine primary phases within the liquid. The semi-solid slurry exhibited thixotropic behavior, specifically shear thinning, ensuring fluidity and particle suspension. The slurry was injected into the mold at a speed of 2.8 m/s, with a cooling duration of about 5 s. The die temperature was maintained at 200 °C. Processing Text: For both CMT+P welding and OLWFW, the filler materials used were Al-Si-Cu-Mg-Zn aluminum alloy welding wires with a diameter of 1.2 mm. Table 1 shows the chemical compositions of the 6D10 aluminum alloy and the welding wire. Before welding, the top and bottom surfaces of the BM and the sides to be welded were sanded with sandpaper to remove the oxide film and cutting marks. The surfaces were then cleaned with anhydrous ethanol. During CMT+P welding, the torch introduces argon gas with a purity of 99.999 % to form a gas shield for the molten metal. The angle between the torch and base material is 58°, and the wire extension is 10 mm. The process was performed with varying synchro pulse frequencies of 2 Hz, 4 Hz, and 6 Hz to optimize porosity. In OLWFW, the welding machine is set to 'wire feeding only,' employing a forward wire feeding method with the torch at a consistent 10° angle to the vertical direction. Argon gas is used again at 20 L/min, blown diagonally downward into the molten pool. The wire extension is still 10 mm, and the laser spot center is 2.0 mm from the wire-base material contact point. The laser follows a circular oscillating path during welding, with varying amplitudes to optimize porosity. To reduce heat input in the OLWFW process, the wire is preheated with a current of 150 A. Processing Text: ER55-B2 low-alloy steel wire with a diameter of 1.2 mm was used to remanufacture a high-strength low-alloy steel 42CrMo motor shaft with a size of Φ140 × 1000 mm. The rolling temperature was maintained within the ferrite phase region. An optimal processing window was identified with a rolling temperature of 600-700 °C and 23 % rolling strain. The interlayer temperature was controlled at 180 ℃ during deposition. The deposition power source is a Lincoln direct current pulsed Tungsten Inert Gas (TIG) welding machine INVERTEC CC400-TP. Before deposition, the surface of the motor shaft was polished and cleaned with acetone. The deposition parameters are: arc current of 220 A, arc voltage of 14.3 V, wire feed rate of 175 cm/min, deposition speed of 360 mm/min, and overlap rate of 0.15. A commercial pure argon shielding gas was used with a flow rate of 15 L/min. The optimal processing window for HR-WAAM was identified by adjusting the rolling temperature (500-600 ℃ and 600-700 ℃) and rolling force (0, 20 and 25 kN). For convenience, the HR-WAAM samples subjected to rolling temperatures within the ranges of 500-600 ℃ and 600-700 ℃ were designated as RT600 and RT700, respectively. The rolling strain is determined by calculating the percentage change in layer thickness, measured before and after hot rolling. To investigate the effect of in-situ hot rolling and thermal cycling on microstructures and mechanical properties of the cladding layer, we prepared the single-layer, double-layer and multi-layer samples by HR-WAAM with a rolling force of 25 kN and rolling temperature in the range of 600-700 ℃. The width and height of the multi-layer sample are 11 mm and 12 mm, respectively. All microstructural characterization samples were sectioned along the axial direction and sequentially grounded using 240#, 400#, 800#, 1200#, and 2000# grit SiC sandpaper and polished with 1.5 µm diamond paste. The scanning electron microscopy (SEM) samples were further etched in a solution of nitric acid and ethanol with a ratio of 10:90 to reveal the microstructures. The electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) samples were subsequently vibrationally polished using 20 nm colloidal silica suspension. Microhardness tests were conducted using an INNOVATEST FALCON 500 Vickers hardness tester under 4.9 kN load with a dwell time of 10 s. 40 points were measured radially from the top of the sample across the cladding layer, the interface, and the base metal. Residual stress measurements on the specimen surface were conducted using an Xstress DR45 X-ray diffractometer, with a collimator diameter of 2 mm and an exposure time of 1 s. Measurements were conducted in both the rolling and axial directions. Prior to measurement, the specimen surface was electro-polished with a saturated NaCl solution using a VWEP-X1 electrolytic polishing machine. Stress-controlled rotating-bending fatigue tests were conducted at room temperature using a QBWP-10000 machine under various stress amplitudes. The stress ratio (R) of the tests was −1, while the waveform was sinusoidal with a nominal frequency of 100 Hz. The fatigue tests were stopped for specimens that were completely fractured (failed) or loaded for 10 7cycles (passed). For each set of process parameters, a total of 24 fatigue specimens were fabricated, with their dimensions illustrated in Fig. 2c. Among these, 15 specimens were selected to determine the fatigue limit using the staircase method. Three to five stress levels were applied, with each stress increment set at 3 %-5 % of the estimated fatigue strength, which was defined as 0.3-0.5 times the tensile strength. The remaining specimens were utilized to measure the high-stress region by the grouped-test method, with three to four elevated stress levels selected. Subsequently, the experimental data obtained from both methods were integrated to fit the fatigue curve (S-N curve). Sample condition: Unrolled

The interlayer temperature was controlled at 180 ℃ during deposition. The deposition power source is a Lincoln direct current pulsed Tungsten Inert Gas (TIG) welding machine INVERTEC CC400-TP. Before deposition, the surface of the motor shaft was polished and cleaned with acetone. The deposition parameters are: arc current of 220 A, arc voltage of 14.3 V, wire feed rate of 175 cm/min, deposition speed of 360 mm/min, and overlap rate of 0.15. A commercial pure argon shielding gas was used with a flow rate of 15 L/min. The optimal processing window for HR-WAAM was identified by adjusting the rolling temperature (500-600 ℃ and 600-700 ℃) and rolling force (0, 20 and 25 kN). For convenience, the HR-WAAM samples subjected to rolling temperatures within the ranges of 500-600 ℃ and 600-700 ℃ were designated as RT600 and RT700, respectively. The rolling strain is determined by calculating the percentage change in layer thickness, measured before and after hot rolling. To investigate the effect of in-situ hot rolling and thermal cycling on microstructures and mechanical properties of the cladding layer, we prepared the single-layer, double-layer and multi-layer samples by HR-WAAM with a rolling force of 25 kN and rolling temperature in the range of 600-700 ℃. The width and height of the multi-layer sample are 11 mm and 12 mm, respectively. All microstructural characterization samples were sectioned along the axial direction and sequentially grounded using 240#, 400#, 800#, 1200#, and 2000# grit SiC sandpaper and polished with 1.5 µm diamond paste. The scanning electron microscopy (SEM) samples were further etched in a solution of nitric acid and ethanol with a ratio of 10:90 to reveal the microstructures. The electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) samples were subsequently vibrationally polished using 20 nm colloidal silica suspension. Microhardness tests were conducted using an INNOVATEST FALCON 500 Vickers hardness tester under 4.9 kN load with a dwell time of 10 s. 40 points were measured radially from the top of the sample across the cladding layer, the interface, and the base metal. Residual stress measurements on the specimen surface were conducted using an Xstress DR45 X-ray diffractometer, with a collimator diameter of 2 mm and an exposure time of 1 s. Measurements were conducted in both the rolling and axial directions. Prior to measurement, the specimen surface was electro-polished with a saturated NaCl solution using a VWEP-X1 electrolytic polishing machine. Stress-controlled rotating-bending fatigue tests were conducted at room temperature using a QBWP-10000 machine under various stress amplitudes. The stress ratio (R) of the tests was −1, while the waveform was sinusoidal with a nominal frequency of 100 Hz. The fatigue tests were stopped for specimens that were completely fractured (failed) or loaded for 10 7cycles (passed). For each set of process parameters, a total of 24 fatigue specimens were fabricated, with their dimensions illustrated in Fig. 2c. Among these, 15 specimens were selected to determine the fatigue limit using the staircase method. Three to five stress levels were applied, with each stress increment set at 3 %-5 % of the estimated fatigue strength, which was defined as 0.3-0.5 times the tensile strength. The remaining specimens were utilized to measure the high-stress region by the grouped-test method, with three to four elevated stress levels selected. Subsequently, the experimental data obtained from both methods were integrated to fit the fatigue curve (S-N curve). Sample condition: 20 kN-RT700 (processed at 20 kN rolling force and 600-700 ºC rolling temperature)

Processing Text: The details of V powders are shown in Fig. S1(c-e) and Tables S3-S5. The melting point of V is 1890 °C. Multi-material samples were prepared using single-pass multilayers and back-and-forth scanning methods. Specifically, laser powers of 900 W were used for V. A laser spot diameter of 2.8 mm was utilized during LDED printing, with substrates composed of 316 L stainless steel. The fabrication was conducted in an enclosed molding chamber purged with argon gas (oxygen content: < 20 ppm). For LDED UHSS-Ni-Cr-V-TC4 samples, the post-heat treatment process takes into account four critical factors: temperature, duration, atmosphere, and cooling method. The optimal temperature hinges on the equilibrium phase diagrams among the representative constituents of the five materials, extrapolated from CALPHAD analyses. To prevent collapse and deformation of the samples, the holding temperature during post-heat treatment should not exceed 1347 °C. In pursuit of optimal diffusion of elements, a relatively high temperature of 1200 °C was designed. It is crucial to carefully control the holding time at this elevated temperature to avoid over-diffusion of incompatible elements. Here, a holding time of 60 min was selected. Moreover, argon was used as a protective atmosphere to avoid material oxidation. Conclusively, furnace cooling was conducted to attain a microstructure under a relatively balanced condition. Processing Text: A 2200 MPa PHS with a chemical composition (wt%) of 0.40 %C, 0.40 %Si, 1.46 %Mn, 1.99 %Cr, 0.052 %Nb and 0.17 %V was melted in a vacuum inductive furnace. Then, the molten metal was poured into square ingots for casting. The slab was annealed at 1200 °C for 1 h to homogenize the composition. Afterwards, it was hot-rolled into a plate with a thickness of 3.0 mm between 1200 °C and 870 °C. The plate was rapidly cooled from the finish rolling temperature (870 °C) to the coiling temperature (660 °C) by laminar cooling. Then, the simulated coiling process was carried out, that is, the plate was transferred to a muffle furnace, which was heated to 660 °C in advance for 1 h, and finally, furnace cooling to room temperature. After pickling, the plate was cold-rolled to a final thickness of 1.5 mm. Subsequently, the cold-rolled sheet was austenitized at 900 °C for 15 min, followed by oil quenching to room temperature. For comparison, the as-quenched specimens were subsequently tempered in a salt bath at 170 °C and 300 °C for 20 min followed by air cooling to room temperature. Specimen: OQ; Dislocation strengthening: 876 MPa; Contribution of dislocations to yield strength: 61%

Processing Text: In this work, high performance TiB2/M142 composites were prepared by powder metallurgy and hot extrusion. The results show that TiB2 particles can effectively refine the grain and the second phase, and induce more intragranular intermetallic phases. With the increase of TiB2 content, the strength increased continuously, but the ductility increased first and then decreased. The improvement of the strength of the composites are mainly attributed to thermal mismatch strengthening. The first increase in ductility is mainly due to the capture and pin of the dislocation by intragranular intermetallic phases, which makes the grains have stronger dislocation accumulation and storage capacity. The subsequent reduction in ductility is mainly attributed to the local stress concentration in the TiB2 agglomeration region, which eventually leads to the rapid failure of the composites. The starting powders used in this work were near-spherical M142 alloy powder with a size distribution of 15-53 μm (Bao-Hang New Materials Co., Ltd., Jiangxi, China) and irregular shape TiB2 powder with a diameter of about 2 μm (Macklin Bio-Chem Technology Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China). First, the weighed M142 alloy powder and the TiB2 powder (the content of TiB2 particles was 1, 3, 5 and 7 wt%, respectively) were put into a stainless steel jar filled with Ar atmosphere. The grinding medium was stainless steel ball with diameter of 10 mm, and the ball-to-material ratio was 10:1. TiB2/M142 composite powder was obtained by grinding at 200 rpm for 10 h. Secondly, the ball-milled powder was put into a Φ30 mm graphite mold and compressed at a uniaxial stress of 10 MPa through the punches. After that, the composite powder was sintered at 480 °C for 15 min by LABOX-650F spark plasma sintering (SPS) system under a vacuum pressure of less than 10 Pa. The pressure applied during sintering is 30 MPa. After cooling in the furnace, the sintered samples with a diameter of 30 mm and a thickness of 15 mm were obtained. Next, all sintered samples were hot extruded at 500 °C with an extrusion ratio of 25:1. Finally, the TiB2/M142 composite rod was subjected to T6 heat treatment (solid solution at 490 °C for 3 h, then water quenching, artificial aging at 180 °C for 6 h). The same procedure was employed to fabricate M142 alloy for comparative analysis. The effects of TiB2 particle content on the microstructure evolution and mechanical properties of the TiB2/M142 composites were investigated. Composite with 1% TiB2 addition

Processing Text: The ingots with nominal compositions of Fe-0.05C-1.6Mn-0.25Si-0.3Cr-2.5Ni-0.25Cu-0.055(Nb + Ti) (wt%) were prepared by vacuum induction melting under high-purity inert atmosphere. The as-cast ingots were forged into 170 × 85 × 120 mm (length × width × height) rectangular square billets within the temperature range of 1100-1200 °C. The forged billet was homogenized at 1200 °C for 2 h, and subsequently rough-rolled (the first stage of rolling) to 84 mm-thick plate between 1100 °C and 1030 °C. The rough-rolled plate was then air-cooled to 830 °C (plate surface) and hot-rolled (the second stage of rolling) to 50 mm in three passes at this temperature. After rolling, the steel plate was ultra-fast cooling to ∼400 °C. Subsequently, the steel plate was reheated to 830 °C and held at that temperature for 30 min to achieve thermal equilibrium between the experimental steel core specimen and the surface of the steel plate, thereby ensuring temperature uniformity throughout the experimental steel plate. Here, the reheating temperature was selected at 830 °C, exceeding the Ac3 temperature (808 °C) by 22 °C, to ensure complete austenitization of the microstructure while maintaining a moderate thermal gradient that minimizes energy consumption and prevents excessive grain growth. After that, the plate was hot-rolled (the third stage of rolling) to a thickness of 32 mm by 2 passes and subsequently laminar cooling to ∼400 °C. Finally, the rolled steel was cooled in air to room temperature, which was referred to as TPS-three-stage rolling coupling inter-pass reheating process steel. Condition: room temperature; Microstructure: ferrite-bainite mixed microstructure

Processing Text: The Al 5Ti 8(FeCoNi) 86.9B 0.1 (at.%) ingots were fabricated by melting high-purity (>99.9 wt.%) raw materials (Al, Ti, Fe, Co, Ni, and B) in a vacuum arc furnace under a protective argon atmosphere. Each ingot underwent 5 melting cycles and was then cast into a copper mold with dimensions of 50×15×10 mm 3. The samples were subsequently heated to 1200 °C and held for 2 hours to achieve homogenization. Next, they were cut using an electrical discharge machine (EDM) to dimensions of 50×15×5 mm 3 along the thickness direction. These samples then underwent multiple cold-rolling passes to achieve a 70% deformation (reducing the thickness from 5 to 1.5 mm), followed by annealing at 1050 °C for 50 s to develop a fully recrystallized microstructure, abbreviated as CRSA alloy. Finally, the samples were aged at temperatures of 765 °C and 800 °C for varying durations: 0.1, 0.3, and 4 hours for 765°C, and 4 hours for 800°C. They were labeled as 765-0.1, 765-0.3, 765-4, and 800-4 according to their aging temperature and time. After each heat treatment, the samples were rapidly cooled to room temperature by water quenching. TEM samples before deformation were first thinned to 50 μm with sandpaper, followed by punching into 3 mm discs. Deformed TEM samples were directly mounted onto a molybdenum grid after thinning to 50 μm. Finally, these TEM samples were subjected to electrochemical twin-jet thinning to obtain the desired thin areas. Dog-bone-shaped tensile specimens with a gauge length of 8 mm and a cross-sectional area of 2 × 1.5 mm 2 were obtained through EDM along the rolling direction. Tensile tests were conducted on a Zwick/Roell 5 kN tensile testing machine at a strain rate of 1 × 10 −3 s −1, with a video extensometer employed to capture the real-time deformation of the gauge section. Processing Text: MAR-M247, a nickel-based superalloy, offers excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures but suffers from poor printability due to severe cracking. This study demonstrates the successful fabrication of MAR-M247 using electron-beam powder bed fusion (EPBF) with pre-heating at 1000 °C, achieving a high relative density (>99.5 %). Pre-heating suppressed the typical solidification microstructures observed in AM-fabricated alloys and minimised residual stress, resulting in reduced cracking. The as-printed alloy exhibited superior mechanical properties, with yield strengths of 820 MPa at room temperature and 640 MPa at 871 °C, outperforming conventionally cast MAR-M247. Atom probe tomography (APT) confirmed a high volume fraction (73.1 %) of γ' precipitates, including fine secondary precipitates near grain boundaries, enhancing mechanical strength by restricting dislocation motion. However, ductility decreased at elevated temperatures due to liquation cracking along grain boundaries, driven by solute segregation (Mo, B, and Cr). Creep behaviour analysis using the Larson-Miller Parameter (LMP) indicated that the as-printed alloy exhibited a rupture life comparable to post-processed cast alloys despite the presence of liquation cracks. Primary γ' precipitates (0.2-1 μm) were the main contributors to creep resistance, while fine secondary precipitates (∼30 nm) near grain boundaries provided additional resistance. Inorganic silica coating was applied to prevent oxidation and control cooling. In order to eliminate the defects to the greatest extent and prevent the generation of cracks, the hot-rolling process was strictly selected. Specifically, the alloy ingots were held at 850 °C for 30 min in a muffle furnace, followed by multiple rolling passes with a 2 mm reduction per pass (rolling speed: 9 m/min). Processing Text: The alloy with the composition of Al-6Cu-1Ni-1Zr-1Ti(wt%) was adapted in the present work. For this purpose, the gas-atomized 2 wt% NiTi and 0.8 wt% Zr powders was added to AA2219 powder. Then, the powders were blended by mechanical mixing. To ensure homogeneity, a mixer was used to blend the powders at 100 rpm for 3 hours, changing the direction of rotation every half hour. The SLM process was conducted using an SLM 125 HL machine, which is equipped with a 400 W laser power. All SLM experiments were conducted under an argon atmosphere with the concentration of oxygen controlled below 0.1 vol%. The samples were fabricated on an Al substrate with a preheating temperature of 200 °C, using a scan strategy with a laser beam rotation of 67° between consecutive layers. The Al-Cu-Ni-Zr-Ti alloy were processed using different processing parameters, the laser power was selected within the range of 140 W to 260 W, and the scanning speed was varied between 850 ymm/s and 1750 mm/s. According to the forming quality, the optimized forming parameters were: laser power of 200 W, scanning speed of 1500 mm/s, hatch spacing of 90 μm and layer thickness of 30 mm, respectively. Cubic samples with the dimension of 10 × 10 × 10 mm 3was fabricated for the microstructure analysis, all samples for microstructural investigation were cut along the XOZ plane and mechanically ground and polished using SiC papers. The as-built samples were heat treated at 150 °C, 200 °C, 300 °C, 350 °C, 400 °C and 450 °C in the air furnace. To investigate the heat resistant of the alloy, the exposing time at 300°C and 350 °C was 200 h. Samples with the gauge dimensions of 60 mm (length) × 10 mm (width) × 1.5 mm (thickness) were machined from SLMed parts using electro-discharge machining (EDM). TEM samples cut from the SLMed Al-Cu-Ni-Zr-Ti alloy were mechanically ground and polished from ∼ 0.8 mm to 0.09 mm, followed by finally ion milling into thin foils in a Gatan Precision Ion Polishing System (PIPS). Condition: as-built

Processing Text: Ingots weighing 100 g of Al1Ti5Zr4Nb3Ta3 were fabricated in the vacuum arc-melting furnace under an argon atmosphere. Commercially pure metallic ingredients (the purity of metal elements: 99.99 wt%) were used as raw materials. Moreover, an ingot weighing 2.5 kg were melted and subsequently cast into an electrode bar with a length of 180 mm, upper inner diameter of 60 mm, and bottom inner diameter of 50 mm. Powders with different sizes in a range of 53 − 120 μm was prepared using the plasma rotating electrode process (PREP). To ensure the fluidity of powder feeding during AM process, the powders with approximately 160 mesh were selected through sieving. Pre-alloyed powders were heated up to 393 K for 2 h and cooled down to RT in a vacuum chamber to remove water vapor before use. The processing chamber was filled with high-purity argon and the oxygen content was maintained below 1000 ppm in the fabrication process, while the powder was delivered in to the laser molten on a Zr substrate through a coaxial powder delivery system. During the fabrication process, ytterbium-doped fiber laser unit with a wavelength of 1070 nm and a spot diameter of 1.8 mm was used as the power source. Before fabricating the single-wall samples, single-track experiments were carried out with a wide range of process parameters to determine the optimum process window. Optical micrographs of the transverse section of single-tracks specimens fabricated according to the Table 1 orthogonal experiment parameters are shown in Fig. 1(b). As a result, the moderate laser power P= 1400 W and laser scanning rate V= 500 mm/s are sufficient to obtain perfect molten pool morphology with the track height (Δh) of 0.36 mm and the track width (Δx) of 5 mm. The single-wall alloy with uniform distributed equiaxed grains along the deposition direction was fabricated successfully under the optimized process parameters. Then, the microstructures and mechanical properties of the LMD-fabricated alloy are characterized and tested, respectively. In comparison, a detailed analysis of the microstructures and mechanical properties of the as-cast alloy was also provided. Subsequently, the formation of microstructures mechanism and the strengthening mechanism of the LMD-fabricated alloy was discussed. Processing state: as-cast; Measured at Room Temperature (RT)
Processing Word: Processing state: as-cast; Measured at Room Temperature (RT)

Processing Text: The substrate employed in this study is a Q235 steel plate measuring 70 mm × 70 mm × 30 mm. One is spherical 316 L stainless steel powder, with a particle size ranging from 50 μm to 150 μm. The chemical composition of the 316 L stainless steel powder is provided in Table 1. The mixed powder was subsequently placed in a vacuum drying oven and preheated at 150 °C for 2 h to remove moisture and enhance flowability. The powder was then deposited as desired coating using a self-built LDED equipment equipped with a laser of 4 KW and 1060 nm wavelength (Raycus RFL-C4000). The LDED technology utilizes a coaxial powder feeding method to ensure the stability of coating properties. The optimal parameters were identified as a laser power of 1700 W, a scanning speed of 10 mm/s, a spot diameter of 4 mm, a powder feed rate of 1.2 r/min, and an overlap ratio of 50 %. With these optimized parameters, the 316 L composite coating was fabricated via multi-layer, multi-track laser processing, yielding a well-formed surface. After completing the coating process, the uneven top surface of the coating was removed using an electrical discharge wire cutting, and then cut into samples measuring 10 mm × 10 mm × 10 mm and 5 mm × 5 mm × 10 mm for subsequent tests. The metallographic samples were sequentially ground with SiC sandpaper with grades from 240# to 2000#, followed by polishing with 2.5μm diamond polishing paste. Aqua regia (HCl:HNO 3=3:1 V:V) was employed to etch the sample surface for 10-15 s, followed by ultrasonic cleaning with alcohol. The polarization test samples were mechanically polished and subsequently ultrasonically cleaned with alcohol to remove any residual polishing paste and surface impurities. Processing Text: Six alloys with varying compositions were produced by melting pure metals of aluminum, molybdenum, niobium, titanium, vanadium, and zirconium, each with a purity of no less than 99.99 %. During refining, evacuate the arc furnace chamber to a pressure below 5 × 10 −3 Pa, then fill it with high-purity argon gas to 0.02 MPa to guarantee the alloy is not oxidized during the melting process. To further reduce the oxygen concentration inside the furnace, Ti is melted once for 5 minutes to eliminate leftover oxygen in the electric arc furnace. Due to the high content of refractory elements in RHEA, increasing the current intensity and flipping times during melting is necessary. Repeated remelting ensures that any segregation or compositional inhomogeneities are minimized. The alloy ingot is melted 10 times in an electric arc furnace, each lasting 3–5 minutes, and the current is increased to 380–400 A to ensure sufficient mixing of refractory metal elements. Processing Text: These samples were built using the Laser Powder Directed Energy Deposition (LP-DED) process. The gas-atomized spherical shape powder utilized in this study demonstrated a particle size distribution ranging from 45 to 75 μm, with chemical compositions provided in Table 1. Sieve analysis, conducted in accordance with ASTM B214 on powder sampled following ASTM B215, indicated that no powder was retained on the +140 and +170 sieves, 0.2 % of the powder was retained on the +200 sieve, and 2.4 % of the powder was passed through the −325 sieve. The powder was delivered through a co-axial nozzle from an Oerlikon twin powder hopper, with argon gas serving as both the carrier and shielding gas at a flow rate of 10 L/min, and subsequently blown into the melt pool. The powder converged at a laser focal point initiating its controlled fusion and the creation of a distinct melt pool protected from atmospheric contamination by argon shielding gas. A wrought SS316 plate of dimensions 6″ length x 3″ width x 1″ thick was used as the substrate with the surface prepared by machining, followed by sandblasting. The Design of Experimentation (DOE) consisted of seven distinct configurations of DED process parameters including laser power, powder flow rate, and scan speed as shown in Table 2. Each sample, comprising six layers in height with dimensions of 2 inches in length and 1 inch in width, was fabricated in a single direction. Parameters such as layer offset (0.4 mm), hatch distance (with a step-over of 70 %), and dwell time between layers (set at 6 mins) remained constant. The implemented dwell time allowed each layer to cool adequately before the next layer was deposited, effectively minimizing the risk of overheating and reducing material variations due to uneven cooling. Additionally, to prevent any potential proximity effects, each sample was deposited with at least 1 inch of spacing between them. After AM, the entire build plate was subjected to a stress relief heat treatment at 1650 F for two hours in a vacuum furnace, a sufficient temperature to enable stress relief and the precipitation of δ phase. Each of the seven samples was then removed from the build plate using wire Electro Discharge Machining (EDM). SPT samples were extracted from each of the 7AM builds as shown in Fig. 1. After SPT samples were excised using wire EDM to an approximate thickness of 400 µm, each sample was polished on both sides with a 1200 grit polishing pad for one minute with a loading of 15 Newtons to remove the EDM recast layer. To reveal a pristine microstructure surface for Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM), each sample was progressively ground for two minutes at 150 rotations per minute and 25 Newton loading on a Struers auto-polisher with 800-, 1000-, 1200-, 2400-, and 4000 grit sandpaper. After grinding, the samples were polished for five minutes using the same auto-polisher and parameters with a 3 µm suspension followed by a 1 µm suspension. A colloidal silica polishing step followed and utilized the same parameters apart from a change to a twelve-minute duration. Finally, the samples were subjected to vibropolishing in a Buehler VibroMet Polisher using a colloidal silica/water mixture for three hours at 3 rotations per minute. Processing Text: The binary Ti-12 wt. % Mo alloy was prepared by self-consumable vacuum arc melting. The ingot was re-melted three times in order to promote chemical homogeneity. It was hot forged into square bar and then cut into several plates of 10 mm in thickness. These plates were cold rolled and followed by homogenization at 900 °C for 30 min and water quenching to obtain Ti-12Mo samples of fully β phase. These as-homogenized specimens were subsequently cold rolled at room temperature with thickness reductions of 10 %, 20 %, 40 %, respectively. The cold-rolled-40 % specimens were aged at 300 °C, 400 °C, 500 °C for 60 min, respectively, and then water quenched for modifying their microstructures via phase transformation and partial recrystallization. Processing Text: LPBF-fabricated 316L stainless steel typically exhibits a high yield strength of approximately 600 MPa due to its high dislocation density. The raw material used in this work was commercially available gas atomized 316L stainless steel powders. The average size was 42.3 μm for 316L powder. The steels were fabricated using a commercial LPBF machine, the ProX DMP 300 (3D Systems, US). Specifications of the laser are as follows: full power = 500 W, wavelength = 1.07 μm, spot size = 75 μm. Oxygen level in the printing chamber was maintained below 300 ppm using high purity Argon gas. The laser scanning direction was rotated by 90° between consecutive layers. The printing parameters are presented in Table 2. Grinding, polishing, and etching were conducted to the samples for microstructural analysis. We used gradually finer SiC sandpapers from 180 grit to 2500 grit. We used a suspension with 40 nm SiO 2particles (OPS, Struers) to polish the samples. We used a self-mixed acid solution (HF:HNO 3:H 2O = 1:4:15) to etch the samples. Various microscopes were employed to observe and study the microstructures, including a Ziess Axioskop 2 MAT optical microscope, a JEOL JSM-7600F filed-emission electron scanning microscope equipped with backscatter electron (BSE) mode. The SEM observation was conducted at the accelerating voltage of 10 kV. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, Nordlys, Oxford Instruments, Oxford) and energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS, Oxford Instruments, Oxford) were acquired using the same SEM machine at the accelerating voltage of 20 kV. A step size of 0.6 μm was used for EBSD measurements. A smaller step size of 0.2 μm was used for a higher resolution EBSD measurement. X-ray diffraction (XRD, D8 Advance, Bruker) was conducted at 40 kV and 40 mA using a 0.6° divergence slit and a step size of 0.02°. Nanoindentation tests were carried out using Nano Indenter G200 equipped with a Berkovich tip (Agilent Technologies, USA) at a strain rate of 0.05 s −1. The maximum depth of the nanoindentation was 1000 nm. A 12 by 12 array of nanoindentation with an spacing of 20 μm was performed on 316L-1TiB 2. For each LPBF-processed material, three tensile samples were tested at room temperature using an Instron 5982 universal tensile testing machine, with a constant strain rate of 10 −3s −1. Tensile strain was recorded using a non-contact Instron AVE 2 extensometer. The tensile samples, with a dog-bone shape, were machined using wire cutting. After wire cutting, careful grinding using SiC sandpapers up to 1000 grit was conducted. The gauge size was 14 × 4 × 2 mm 3, and the total length was 50 mm. Processing state: LPBF-fabricated; Microstructure: High dislocation density

Processing Text: LPBF-fabricated 316L-TiB 2composites, the core at the centre of the melt pool contains ultrafine grains and twin boundaries while the edge features columnar grains. The LPBF-processed 316L-TiB 2exhibits an excellent combination of high strength (yield strength: 858 MPa, ultimate tensile strength: 1095 MPa) and ductility (27%). Adding 1 wt% TiB 2particles significantly enhances yield strength while maintaining excellent ductility. The synergistic interaction of Ti and B elements and 316L matrix was found to drive the formation of a distinctive core-shell structure. The core is filled with fine equiaxed grains and the shell is filled with columnar grains. A detailed microstructure characterization was further carried out using SEM BSE mode before and after etching the sample. By incorporating 3 wt% TiB 2particles to 316L introduced approximately 30% ferritic phase. The X-Ray diffraction positions of TiB 2(#35-0741) are also labelled in Fig. 6. It can be concluded that no diffraction peaks belong to the TiB 2phase. By incorporating 3 wt% TiB 2, the melt pool edge became narrower. Significant grain refinement has been achieved in LPBF-fabricated 316L by doping TiB 2particles. By incorporating just 1 wt% TiB 2, the grain size was reduced to about 1 μm. The mechanism behind the enhanced efficiency of TiB 2particles in grain refinement warrants further discussion. During the LPBF process of 316L-TiB 2composites, micronsized TiB 2particles dissolve and react with the 316L matrix. The Ti released from the decomposition of TiB 2is primarily responsible for the observed grain refinement. Additionally, the B from the decomposition forms a complex network of M 2B borides (M = Fe, Cr). These borides are distributed along the grain boundaries and the cellular structure boundaries. This network of borides further enhances grain refinement through the Zener pinning effect. Adding 1 wt% TiB 2particles reduces its grain size from 25.9 μm to about 1 μm. A complex network of M 2B borides (M = Fe, Cr) forms along the grain boundaries, promoting grain refinement via the Zener pinning effect. Additionally, Ti, resulting from the decomposition of TiB 2, acts as a potent solute for further grain refinement. The addition of 1 wt% TiB 2particles significantly enhanced the yield strength of 316L to 858 MPa from 599 MPa while maintaining a high elongation of 27%. Further increases in TiB 2content improve strength but result in a reduction in elongation. Among the various particles evaluated, TiB 2demonstrated superior efficiency over other ceramic particles in grain refinement and strength enhancement for 316L. Processing Text: Alloy ingot (300 g) with a nominal composition of Ni50Co25Cr9.5Al9Ti5Ta1.5 was prepared by arc-melting a mixture of high-purity raw metals (purity > 99.99 wt.%) in a Ti-gettered argon atmosphere. The ingot was re-melted at least five times with electromagnetic stirring to ensure chemical homogeneity. The output arc current is about 600 A, and the melting duration of single cycle is about 1 min (for detailed casting process, see supplementary material). To carry out microstructure observation, the specimen was mechanically polished with SiC paper, from 60 grit to 3000 grit, to eliminate scratches. After that, the SEM sample was electrolytically polished in a mixed solution of 90 % C2H5OH + 10 % HClO4 at 30 V for 20 s and electrolytically etched using H3PO4(170 ml) + H2SO4(10 ml) + CrO3(15 g) mixed solution at 5 V for 10 s. For the EBSD sample, only electrolytic polishing was conducted to remove the surface stress layer. The preparation process of TEM sample is as follows: Firstly, the samples were mechanically ground to a thickness of 40 μm using 3000 grit SiC paper. Then, they were stamped into Φ3 mm disc, and ion-milling (Gatan 695) was carried out using a mixed solution of 90 % CH3OH + 10 % HClO4 at 15 V and 25 °C. The dog-bone-shaped tensile specimens with a gauge length of 18 mm, width of 5 mm and thickness of 1.8 mm were prepared from the ingot via wire electrical discharge machining. Quasi-static uniaxial tensile tests were performed on electronic universal tensile testing machine (Instron-5569) with a strain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1 at room temperature. The tensile samples were sequentially ground until no obvious defects could be observed. Three times tests were conducted to minimize errors, and the yield strength was determined using 0.2 % offset plastic strain method. Microstructure investigation and room-temperature tensile test with identical parameters to as-cast Ni50Co25Cr9.5Al9Ti5Ta1.5 were conducted on the annealed counterpart. Processing Text: Non-equiatomic Ti4VHf2.5Ta2.5 RHEA was fabricated by high-vacuum arc-melting using high purity raw materials (≥ 99.95 %). Before melting, high-purity Ti was first melted to absorb residual oxygen. Meanwhile, magnetic stirring was employed during the melting process to ensure uniform mixing of the liquid metal. The casted rods with a 20 mm diameter obtained by melting were directly subjected to 45 % and 90 % cold rolling individually. During cold rolling, the axis of the round rod was perpendicular to the rolling direction (RD), resulting in a final thin sheet with a thickness of 2 mm. The thin sheet obtained after 90 % cold rolling was annealed separately at 800 °C and 1000 °C for 1 h in air atmosphere. As shown in Fig. 1(a), all samples used for microstructure and mechanical properties characterization were extracted from the thin sheet using electro-discharging machine and then polished with silicon carbide paper to remove oxide layers. Condition: Annealed at 1000°C for 1 h; Loading direction: RD

Processing Text: Spherical powders with a nominal composition of Co 18Cr 15Fe 50Ni 10Mo 6.5C 0.5(at%) in a particle size range of 10-55 µm were manufactured by gas atomization (Hot gas atomization system, PSI Ltd.). A commercial LPBF machine (Mlab, Concept Laser GmbH) was utilized to build cuboidal samples from the powders in a meander scanning pattern with a 180° rotation in a layer-by-layer process. A laser power of 90 W, a hatch distance of 77 µm, a scanning speed of 500 mm/s, and a layer thickness of 25 µm were applied. The printed sample was subsequently annealed at 900 °C for 10 min, which is hereinafter denoted by A900. The temperature was determined based on our previous works on alloys with similar compositions [ 8, 10], where annealing at 900 °C promoted precipitation of carbides and μ phase. The annealing duration was limited to 10 min to avoid grain growth or excessive coarsening of precipitates. Processing state: as-built; Microstructure: cell boundaries decorated by Mo segregation

Processing Text: Under argon protection, a cast Al 0.3CoCrFeNiTi 0.3HEA with a composition purity of 99.9 % was produced using the vacuum induction levitation melting method. Cylindrical specimens with dimensions of φ4 × 6 mm were obtained using electrical discharge machining (EDM) and subjected to quasi-static compression at room temperature with a strain rate of 1 × 10 −3s −1. The samples underwent mechanical grinding and polishing, followed by electro-polishing in a solution of 10 % perchloric acid and 90 % ethanol at −25 °C, applying a current of 0.5-0.6 mA for 30 s. To facilitate microscale digital image correlation (DIC) measurements, a random speckle pattern was generated on the specimen surface by first depositing a silver film via magnetron sputtering for 60 s, then immersing the sample in a 1 % NaCl solution for 50 min to ensure uniform adhesion of nanoscale silver speckles. Subsequently, in situ DIC-assisted quasi-static compression tests were performed at room temperature at a strain rate of 1 × 10 −3s −1. The tests were interrupted at applied strains of 3 %, 6 %, and 9 % to conduct microstructural characterization via SEM. Processing Text: Ingots with a diameter of 70 mm were prepared using a vacuum induction melting furnace. A 3.5 kg ingot underwent homogenization at 1200 °C for 2 h to eliminate non-uniform microstructures formed during solidification, followed by multi-pass hot rolling with a finishing temperature of 860 °C, achieving a thickness reduction of 94.6 % (from 70 mm to 4 mm), and subsequently air-cooled to room temperature (RT). The hot-rolled steel was heated to 890 °C and held for 1 h before being furnace-cooled to 590 °C and then air-cooled. The plates were then cold-rolled in multiple passes down to 1.6 mm. Finally, the plates underwent quenching and tempering (QT) treatments. They were held at gradient temperatures (950 °C, 990 °C, 1030 °C, 1070 °C) each for 5 min and quenched in water; followed by tempering at 250 °C for 30 min and air-cooled, with the corresponding samples labeled QT950, QT990, QT1030, and QT1070, respectively. The microhardness of samples subjected to different heat treatment processes was measured using an HVS-1000 tester under a load of 0.98 N and a dwell time of 10 s. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM; ZEISS ULTRA 55) was employed to examine the microstructure, impact fracture morphology, and crack propagation path on the RD-TD plane for all samples. X-ray diffraction (XRD, Rigaku Dmax2500) experiments were performed on samples subjected to different heat treatment processes. The Cu-Kα radiation with a wavelength of 1.54056 Å was employed, with diffraction patterns recorded at a step rate of 2°/min over a 2θ range from 40° to 110°. Further characterization of the martensite microstructure was carried out using electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, ZEISS ULTRA 55). The samples were electro-polished in an ethanol solution containing 10 vol% HClO 4for 30 s, and data were collected under conditions of a step size of 0.05 μm, an acceleration voltage of 20 kV, and a tilt angle of 70°, and then processed using Channel 5 software. The phase composition and the interaction between carbides and dislocations during the impact strain process in all samples were investigated by transmission electron microscopy (TEM; JEOL-F200). TEM samples were prepared by mechanically thinning to 40 µm, and then the TEM sample with a diameter of 3 mm was twin-jetted in a 10 vol% HClO 4ethanol solution at −30 ℃. The hot-rolled steel was heated to 890 °C and held for 1 h before being furnace-cooled to 590 °C and then air-cooled. The plates were then cold-rolled in multiple passes down to 1.6 mm. Finally, the plates underwent quenching and tempering (QT) treatments. They were held at gradient temperatures (950 °C, 990 °C, 1030 °C, 1070 °C) each for 5 min and quenched in water; followed by tempering at 250 °C for 30 min and air-cooled, with the corresponding samples labeled QT950, QT990, QT1030, and QT1070, respectively. The microhardness of samples subjected to different heat treatment processes was measured using an HVS-1000 tester under a load of 0.98 N and a dwell time of 10 s. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM; ZEISS ULTRA 55) was employed to examine the microstructure, impact fracture morphology, and crack propagation path on the RD-TD plane for all samples. X-ray diffraction (XRD, Rigaku Dmax2500) experiments were performed on samples subjected to different heat treatment processes. The Cu-Kα radiation with a wavelength of 1.54056 Å was employed, with diffraction patterns recorded at a step rate of 2°/min over a 2θ range from 40° to 110°. Further characterization of the martensite microstructure was carried out using electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, ZEISS ULTRA 55). The samples were electro-polished in an ethanol solution containing 10 vol% HClO 4for 30 s, and data were collected under conditions of a step size of 0.05 μm, an acceleration voltage of 20 kV, and a tilt angle of 70°, and then processed using Channel 5 software. The phase composition and the interaction between carbides and dislocations during the impact strain process in all samples were investigated by transmission electron microscopy (TEM; JEOL-F200). TEM samples were prepared by mechanically thinning to 40 µm, and then the TEM sample with a diameter of 3 mm was twin-jetted in a 10 vol% HClO 4ethanol solution at −30 ℃. Heat treatment process: QT1070

Processing Text: A near-α Ti-6Al-2Sn-4Zr-2Mo-0.1Si-0.5Y (wt%) alloy with two distinct types of microstructures was fabricated using a powder metallurgy (PM) method involving thermomechanical consolidation (TMC) and subsequent heat treatments. The first heat treatment involved annealing at 960 ℃ for 1 h, followed by air cooling (AC), and the resulting sample was designated as 960-A. The second heat treatment consisted of annealing at 960 ℃ for 1 h, followed by water quenching (WQ), and subsequent aging at 580 ℃ for 6 h with air cooling. High temperature tensile tests at 600 °C were conducted using flat, dog-bone-shaped specimens with dimensions of 3 mm (width) × 2 mm (thickness) × 15 mm (length) at an initial strain rate of 5 × 10 −4s −1 on an AG-XPLUS 100 KN universal testing machine. The creep tests at 600 °C under applied stresses ranging from 150 to 350 MPa were performed using an ECM-100 creep testing machine. The creep specimen dimensions were 3.5 mm (width) × 2.5 mm (thickness) × 20 mm (length). Prior to loading, creep specimens were held at 600 °C for 1 h to ensure uniform temperature distribution. The temperature accuracy was maintained within ± 1 °C. Microstructure: Type 2; Condition: 600 °C; Sample designation: 960-STA

Processing Text: Alloy ingots with nominal compositions of Cu 50Ni 17.375Al 9.375Co 17Cr 3.125Ti 3.125B 0.5(at%) were fabricated by using a vacuum arc melting furnace under a high-purity argon atmosphere, and the starting materials were at least 99.9 wt%. All the ingots were repeatedly melted for 5 times to promote the chemical homogeneity, and then sucked into water-cooled copper mold with a plate shaped cavity of 80 mm × 20 mm × 7 mm. The as-cast alloys were hot-rolled with a reduction of 1.5 mm per pass at a temperature of 1000°C, resulting in alloy plates with a final thickness of 1.5 mm. To prevent oxidation of the alloy and assist in its deformation, the samples were placed in a 314 stainless steel jacket. The hot-rolled sheets were subjected to aging treatment at 900°C for 1 hour in a muffle furnace. In this work, the hot rolling process were adopted to mitigate casting defects. Dog-bone-shaped tensile specimens, with a gauge section of 26 × 5 × 1.5 mm, were cut through wire electrical discharge machining. The quasi-static tensile tests were performed on a universal testing machine (UTM5504) at room temperature, 700 °C and 800 °C using a constant strain rate of 1 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹. To ensure data reliability, three parallel tensile tests were conducted under each testing condition. The isothermal oxidation experiments were performed in a box-type resistance furnace and an electronic balance with a resolution of 0.1 mg, and the samples size were 16 × 10 × 3 mm 3. The samples were oxidized at 850 °C for 150 h under laboratory static air. Condition: room temperature; Microstructure: coherent L1₂ precipitation and grain boundary engineering

Processing Text: Specimens were cut along the diameter of the forged bar and vacuum-packaged. After solution treatment at 900°C, the specimens were cooled at a rate of 1 °C/min using temperature control equipment to temperatures between 725°C and 500°C in 25 ℃ intervals, holding at each temperature for 60 minutes, followed by water quenching to room temperature. For simplicity, these samples are referred to by their cooling temperatures (e.g., 725°C, 700°C, etc.) in the thereafter text. Dog-bone-shaped tensile specimens with a gauge length of 18 mm were used for tensile testing. The tests were conducted on a universal testing machine at a rate of 0.5 mm/min, corresponding to a theoretical tensile strain rate of 4.6 × 10−3s−1. Microstructural analysis was performed using an optical microscope (OM), scanning electron microscope (SEM), and transmission electron microscope (TEM). For electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) characterization, samples were mechanically polished and then electropolished in a mixture of 60 % methanol, 34 % n-butanol, and 6 % perchloric acid at 30 V, −30°C for ∼60 s. The metallographic structure observation was performed using a modified Kroll reagent (5 % HF + 10 % HNO₃ + 85 % H₂O) to etch the electropolished surface. Transmission specimens were wire-cut to a thickness of about 500 μm and subsequently ground with SiC abrasive paper from coarse to fine, reducing the thickness to ∼50 μm. The samples were then twin-jet electropolishing using the same electropolishing solution. Single β phase structure

Processing Text: The Al-1.5Mn alloy with a gradient microstructure was fabricated by ultrasonic shot peening (USSP). Ultrasonic shot peening (USSP) was carried out using an ultrasonic shot peening equipment (SONIC JY-P20). The ultrasonic shot peening parameters listed in Table 1 were selected for this study. Note that the parameters were selected mainly based on the mechanical responses, i.e., for peening duration 2 min the alloy manifests the best strength-plasticity synergy. The combination of 3 mm shots diameter and 15 mm peening distance can guarantee a relatively large peening intensity and in the meantime not causing surface damage such as cracks on the specimen surface. The amplitude of USSP is fixed in our device. All the surfaces of tensile specimen have been uniformly shot peened. The microstructure of Al-1.5Mn alloys with and without USSP was observed and analyzed using scanning electron microscope (SEM, Thermo Scientific Phenom XL, USA). The chemical composition of the samples was analyzed using energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) in conjunction with SEM. Phase transformations and residual stress distribution of alloys were determined by using X-ray diffraction (XRD, Bruker D-8 Focus X-ray, German). The refined microstructure of the sample was characterized by transmission electron microscopy (TEM, FEI Talos 200X, USA), electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, ThermoFisher Verios 5UC, USA) and transmission Kikuchi diffraction (TKD, ThermoFisher Verios 5UC, USA) techniques to determine the grain size and orientation changes before and after USSP. The sample was thinned using ion milling (PIPS II, USA) to prepare TEM foils. TEM-BF (bright field) imaging, selected area diffraction (SAD), STEM-BF imaging and energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) mapping were utilized. TKD test samples were prepared using the same ion-milled specimens as those used for TEM analysis. For the preparation of EBSD samples, the surface was initially ground with 600#, 1000#, and 2500# sandpapers, followed by polishing with a cloth to achieve a mirror-like finish. The samples were then subjected to vibratory polishing for 2 hours. A Vickers hardness tester (Mitutoyo HM-101, Japan) was used for hardness testing with a load of 0.1 N. At least three indentations were made at each depth position, and the standard deviation was calculated to measure the changes in the microhardness of specimens before and after shot peening. The tensile specimens, whose size is depicted in Fig. 1(c), were prepared and subjected to double-sided USSP. Uniaxial tensile tests were conducted using a universal testing machine at an initial strain rate of 10 −3s −1. The true stress-strain curves were obtained using Eqs. (1) and (2), which could provide a quantitative description of the work hardening rate. After tensile tests, fracture morphologies of Al-1.5Mn alloys were characterized by using SEM (Thermo Scientific Phenom XL, USA). In the quasi-in-situ immersion experiment, the cross-sections of Al-1.5Mn alloys with USSP treatment were ground and polished to achieve a mirror-like finish. Note that, in order to avoid the well-known interference factor of surface contamination, surface contamination layer (∼5 μm in thickness) was firstly removed by polishing before electrochemical corrosion test. This can make the to-be-studied system simpler and enable us to specifically study the influences of microstructural and residual stress changes on corrosion performance. In addition, all the specimens used for electrochemical corrosion tests had the same mirror-like finish obtained by 80 nm SiO 2 polishing. The gradient Al-1.5Mn alloy was annealed at 200 °C for 2 hours to relieve the residual stress. Condition: untreated sample
Processing Word: Condition: untreated sample

Note that the parameters were selected mainly based on the mechanical responses, i.e., for peening duration 2 min the alloy manifests the best strength-plasticity synergy. The combination of 3 mm shots diameter and 15 mm peening distance can guarantee a relatively large peening intensity and in the meantime not causing surface damage such as cracks on the specimen surface. The amplitude of USSP is fixed in our device. All the surfaces of tensile specimen have been uniformly shot peened. The microstructure of Al-1.5Mn alloys with and without USSP was observed and analyzed using scanning electron microscope (SEM, Thermo Scientific Phenom XL, USA). The chemical composition of the samples was analyzed using energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) in conjunction with SEM. Phase transformations and residual stress distribution of alloys were determined by using X-ray diffraction (XRD, Bruker D-8 Focus X-ray, German). The refined microstructure of the sample was characterized by transmission electron microscopy (TEM, FEI Talos 200X, USA), electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, ThermoFisher Verios 5UC, USA) and transmission Kikuchi diffraction (TKD, ThermoFisher Verios 5UC, USA) techniques to determine the grain size and orientation changes before and after USSP. The sample was thinned using ion milling (PIPS II, USA) to prepare TEM foils. TEM-BF (bright field) imaging, selected area diffraction (SAD), STEM-BF imaging and energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) mapping were utilized. TKD test samples were prepared using the same ion-milled specimens as those used for TEM analysis. For the preparation of EBSD samples, the surface was initially ground with 600#, 1000#, and 2500# sandpapers, followed by polishing with a cloth to achieve a mirror-like finish. The samples were then subjected to vibratory polishing for 2 hours. A Vickers hardness tester (Mitutoyo HM-101, Japan) was used for hardness testing with a load of 0.1 N. At least three indentations were made at each depth position, and the standard deviation was calculated to measure the changes in the microhardness of specimens before and after shot peening. The tensile specimens, whose size is depicted in Fig. 1(c), were prepared and subjected to double-sided USSP. Uniaxial tensile tests were conducted using a universal testing machine at an initial strain rate of 10 −3s −1. The true stress-strain curves were obtained using Eqs. (1) and (2), which could provide a quantitative description of the work hardening rate. After tensile tests, fracture morphologies of Al-1.5Mn alloys were characterized by using SEM (Thermo Scientific Phenom XL, USA). In the quasi-in-situ immersion experiment, the cross-sections of Al-1.5Mn alloys with USSP treatment were ground and polished to achieve a mirror-like finish. Note that, in order to avoid the well-known interference factor of surface contamination, surface contamination layer (∼5 μm in thickness) was firstly removed by polishing before electrochemical corrosion test. This can make the to-be-studied system simpler and enable us to specifically study the influences of microstructural and residual stress changes on corrosion performance. In addition, all the specimens used for electrochemical corrosion tests had the same mirror-like finish obtained by 80 nm SiO 2 polishing. Processing Text: The Co-Cr-Fe-Ni powders were arranged in equiatomic ratio. A 5.1 g mixture of elemental powders and 1 wt% of stearic acid as a process control agent (PCA) to prevent excessive cold welding during mechanical alloying was mixed in a hardened steel vial. The powder preparation was performed in a glove box, where oxygen and humidity levels were maintained below 0.5 ppm by continuous circulation of high-purity argon gas through a purification system. The mixture was first milled for 30 min. Next, the vials were opened inside the glove box, and 440 C stainless steel balls with a powder-to-ball radio of 1:10 were added. The vials were then sealed in the glove box, and the mechanical alloying process was carried out at room temperature for 20 h using a SPEX 8000 M/D high energy ball miller. To minimize cold welding without the need for additional PCA, the sealed vials were placed in liquid nitrogen for 5 min after every 150 min of mechanical alloying period to reduce their temperature. After mechanical alloying, the vials were placed back inside the glove box, where the as-milled HEA powders were removed and stored until sufficient milling runs were completed to generate enough powder. This was followed by annealing in an argon atmosphere at 500 °C for 1 h to remove the PCA from the as-milled HEA powders. The cold-pressed pellets were then annealed at 700 °C for 1 and 24 h, and at 900 °C for 1, 3, 6, 12, and 24 h in an argon atmosphere, followed by in-furnace cooling. The consolidated and annealed samples were ground using 800, 1200, and 2500 grits, and then polished to achieve a mirror-like surface for subsequent testing and characterization. Processing Text: In this study, (CoCrCuFe)100-xNix (x = 5, 20, 35, 50 at%) high entropy alloys (HEAs) were fabricated by vacuum arc melting technique and characterized in their as-cast condition to control microstructure and mechanical behavior via Ni alloying. The Fe, Co, Cr, Cu, and Ni elements with high purity (>99 wt%) were used as raw materials for the production of (CoCrCuFe)100-xNix (x = 5, 20, 35, 50 at%) HEAs using a vacuum arc melter with a water-cooled copper hearth. The oxidation was prevented by repeatedly evacuating and refilling the melting chamber with high-purity (>99.99 %) Ar gas. The alloys were remelted at least 5 times, and the ingots were flipped upside-down between melting runs to achieve the chemical homogeneity in the as-cast alloys. Then, the alloys were cast into the 5 mm cylindrical copper mold. Samples were ground with 600, 1200, and 2000 SiC papers and polished with 6 µm, 1 µm diamond suspension, and 50 nm colloidal silica, respectively. Freshly prepared aqua regia solution (3HCl:1HNO3) was used as an etchant for 30-50 s. Each sample was investigated before and after etching to obtain microstructural and compositional micrographs by SEM-EDS analyses. It should be noted that all the HEAs were investigated in their as-cast states. A quasi-static compression test was performed to determine the macro mechanical properties of the samples. The compression test was carried out by the Shimadzu AGS-X universal test machine under the constant strain rate (10-4s-1), which was calculated after measuring the size of each cylindrical sample under ambient temperature according to the ASTM E9-09 standard. Three samples, which have parallel surfaces with the same compositions, were tested for compression, and averaged values were used for each set of samples. Yield strength was determined by using 0.2 % offset values after the test. The Vickers microhardness test machine (Emcotest, Durascan G5) was utilized to determine the hardness values of HEAs with a load of 4.905 N (HV0.5). The average hardness values were calculated from five different points on the surface of the samples. Micromechanical properties of samples with different Ni content were determined by using iNano® system (KLA Instruments, Milpitas, CA, USA). Mechanical property mapping was obtained quickly using the NanoBlitz® 3D technique (Nanomechanics, Inc.) Firstly, the target load was determined based on a single indentation on each sample to calculate the desired indentation spacings, accounting for the overlapping of the plastically deformed zone. After the pretest, a 10 mN target load was used for 15 indentations 45 × 45 array (225 indentations) for mapping. The same regions of the indented HEAs were then investigated under SEM by backscatter electrons and EDS mapping to correlate the microstructure and indented points. Processing Text: In this paper, CoCrCu1.2FeNi high entropy alloy (HEA) was prepared by vacuum suspension melting. After 50 % cold-deformation, recrystallization annealing experiments involving the annealing temperatures of 650-950 ℃ and the annealing times of 30-120 min were carried out on the cold-deformed HEA. The recrystallization annealing process was selected as follows: annealed at 650 ℃, 750 ℃, 850 ℃ and 950 ℃ for 30 min, 60 min, 90 min and 120 min, respectively, and then cooled with the furnace. The original ingot of CoCrCu 1.2FeNi HEA was prepared by 5 five-times vacuum suspension melting. Processing Text: The alloy plate is solutionized at 743 K (470 °C) for 1 h, and quenched in water at 298 K (25 °C). The solutionized alloy is compressed to 10 % reduction in height followed by aging at 120 °C for 24 h and 160°C for 30 h. The aged plate of 200 mm in length, 50 mm in width, and 10 mm in thickness is ground and polished. The polished plate is cleaned with methanol solution and friction stir processed using an FSP machine at the jet thrust of 30 kN. The tool is made of hardened H-13 tool steel with a 20 mm shoulder diameter and traversed up to 150 mm at 1000 rpm with a rotation speed of 30 mm/minute. The pin is like a cone frustum, with a diameter of 8 mm at its wider end and a height of 6 mm. During FSP, a cylindrical tool is plunged into the workpiece and traversed along the line of interest. Specimens with a 1 cm 2cross-sectional area are taken from the top surface of the nugget zone, HAZ, and base metal of the processed plate. These samples are ground, mechanically polished, and etched with Keller's reagent (distill water: 190 ml, HNO 3: 5 ml, HCl: 3 ml, HF: 2 ml). A thin (thickness∼0.6 mm) strip is cut from the NZ perpendicular to TD and is ground to a thickness of 50 μm. A thin disk of 3 mm diameter is punched from the top, middle, and bottom of the nugget zone after FSP. Each disk is electropolished in an electrolyte solution of 20 % nitric acid and 80 % methanol at 22 V and 243 K (-30 °C) temperature using the Fischione twin-jet electropolishing of model No-110. Processing Text: This paper develops corrosion-resistant high-strength Al-Cu matrix composites (Na2MoO4@CNT/2024) by combining a new strategy of incorporating Na2MoO4 precipitant into bulk metals using the inner cavity of carbon nanotubes (CNTs) and the heat treatment. The effects of heat treatments on mechanical and corrosion properties of this novel Na2MoO4@CNT/2024 composite are comprehensively studied by microstructure characterization, tensile tests, corrosion tests and surface analysis, in comparison with its counterparts of 2024 Al alloy and CNT/2024 composite. The results show that as compared to the natural aging and peak aging treatments, the double aging (DA) and regression and re-aging treatments (RRA) can result in higher elongation (>10 %) with slightly decreased but still high strength (∼585 MPa, similar to ∼595 MPa of conventional CNT/2024 composite). This is attributed to the DA- or RRA-induced formation of precipitates and precipitation-free zone with proper sizes and distribution. Moreover, the Na2MoO4@CNT/2024 composite in any heat-treated state has excellent resistance to exfoliation corrosion (level N), intergranular corrosion (IGC depth < 8 μm) and corrosion in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution (corrosion rate < 0.02 mm/y), superior to all the other previously reported Al-Cu alloys. This results from the spontaneous release of MoO4 2- ions from the exposed CNTs promoting the formation of a protective surface film, which is independent of heat treatment. In the present work, 2024 Al alloys powders (size of ∼30 μm, purity of 99 %, Changsha TIJO Metal Materials Co., Ltd., China), industrial-grade CNTs powders (∼1000 GPa in elastic modulus and ∼100 GPa in strength, diameter of 20-30 nm, length of 20-30 μm, purity of 95 %, Nano Energy Tech Co., Ltd., China) and analytically pure Na2MoO4.2 H2O (China National Pharmaceutical Group Co., Ltd., China) were used to produce the Na2MoO4@CNT/2024 composite. Prior to preparation, the as-received CNTs were chemically purified using a mixture of concentrated sulfuric acid (18.4 mol/L) and nitric acid (8 mol/L) with a volume ratio of 3:1, to simultaneously remove the impurities and open the CNT caps for subsequent filling with the Na2MoO4 precipitants. Then, the purified CNTs and analytically pure Na2MoO4.2 H2O were added to ultrapure water with a mass ratio of 6:1 (MoO42-:CNTs), followed by heating to 35 ± 1 °C, vacuuming to fill the inner cavity of the CNTs with the Na2MoO4, filtrating, cleaning and drying in sequence, to prepare the Na2MoO4@CNT powder. More preparation details can be found in our previous work [12]. The prepared 4 wt% Na2MoO4@CNTs and as-received 2024 Al alloy powders were mixed in a mill pot and ball milled with a ball-to-material ratio of 5:1 at 200 rpm for 24 h. 4 wt% was an optimized amount for the Na2MoO4@CNTs added in the bulk 2024 Al alloy, which could improve mechanical and corrosion properties without inducing embrittlement. Then, the powder metallurgy technology and hot extrusion were used to fabricate the bulk Na2MoO4@CNT/2024 composite rod. The hot pressing of the powder metallurgy technology was operated at a temperature of 520 °C and a pressure of 10 −2Pa for 2 h and followed by hot extrusion into a rod at a temperature of 420 °C and an extrusion ratio of 17:1. Thereafter, the hot-extruded rods were heat-treated using a muffle furnace (SXL-1400C, Shanghai Jujing Precision Instrument Manufacturing Co., Ltd., China). Processing Text: The Al0.5CrNi1.5Fe2 multi-principal element alloy was designed by completely replacing Co with Fe, and partially replacing Al with Ni to avoid the formation of excessive brittle phases. The alloy was prepared using a non-consumable vacuum arc furnace. The alloying materials employed were pure metals (Al, Cr, Fe, and Ni) with a purity greater than 99.95 wt%. The alloy was remelted four times under an argon atmosphere to ensure homogeneity, with electromagnetic stirring applied to accelerate the diffusion of elements. The alloy underwent thermal mechanical treatment to induce partial recrystallization, resulting in a multi-phase, multi-scale heterogeneous microstructure. After cold rolling the Al0.5CrNi1.5Fe2 alloy to 80 % reduction and annealing at 800°C for 1 hour, a heterogeneous structure predominantly consisting of “fine-grained recrystallized regions and nano-grained un-recrystallized regions” was formed. The phase compositions of both regions included a disordered FCC matrix and dispersed ordered BCC (B2) precipitates enriched in Al and Ni, as well as disordered BCC precipitates enriched in Fe and Cr. The Al0.5CrNi1.5Fe2MPEA samples were cold-rolled at room temperature using a two-roll mill. The rolling process was carried out in multiple passes, with the rolling direction maintained constant along the length of the samples. The reduction in thickness was 80 %, and the alloy obtained after this process is referred to as CR80 in this study. To regulate the microstructure of the Al0.5CrNi1.5Fe2MPEA, the CR80 samples were annealed at 600 °C and 800 °C. The heat treatment was performed in a box-type resistance furnace under an argon protective atmosphere. During the heat treatment, the cold-rolled samples were heated along with the furnace at a rate of 20 °C/min and held at the set temperature for one hour. Processing Text: The Al-5356 alloy deposits were fabricated using the P-FSAM technique. The process optimization focuses on the ratio of actuator reciprocating frequency to tool traverse speed, ensuring adequate heat generation and particle filling for high-quality deposition. Through the implementation of an optimized stirring pin and spiral groove design, the technique facilitates Z-direction flow of thermoplastic material, resulting in enhanced interfacial bonding and material flow characteristics. During the stable deposition of single-pass multilayers of this alloy, P-FSAM requires about 1 kN thrust force, with a maximum steady-state temperature exceeding 435°C. The deposits exhibit refined grain structures due to dynamic recrystallization, nearly complete dissolution of the Al3Mg2 phase, while maintaining grain stability during thermal cycling. The deposits achieve favorable mechanical properties, with yield strength exceeding 210 MPa, ultimate tensile strength surpassing 350 MPa, and elongation over 20 % in both build and traverse directions, outperforming fusion-based additive manufacturing counterparts. The wire was first straightened and then artificially sheared to less than 1.5 mm by a high-speed rotating blade, and the shapes and statistical sizes of the particles obtained are shown in Fig. 4. Most of the particles were close to cylindrical and the statistical mean of the maximum particle size was about 1.37 mm. A commercial 6061 aluminum alloy plate was selected as the substrate to facilitate the analysis of mixing behavior between the deposited material and the substrate through post-chemical-corrosion cross-sectional observations. The substrate dimensions were 200 × 400 × 15 mm. The P-FSAM deposited components were used on a wire cutting machine to prepare samples for microstructure characterization and mechanical properties testing. The sampling area is shown in Fig. 5. The surface of the cross-sectional sample and particles was first ground and polished to a mirror finish using standard procedures, followed by etching it with weck etchant (40 %HF+45 %C3H8O+H2O). The cross-section surface was photographed on an OLYMPUS-BX53M optical microscope (OM) using a low magnification lens, and the complete cross-sectional morphology was reconstructed by synthesizing the images using Photoshop (PS) software. Microstructure samples at different heights of the component were examined in detail for grain characteristics by electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) using FEI Apreo 2 C after electrolytic polishing. The EBSD analysis was conducted with a step size of 0.2 μm. The phase composition of both the particles and the as-deposited material was identified using an X-ray diffractometer (XRD, SmartLab SE, Rigaku) with a scanning rate of 2°/min. The microstructure sample surfaces of the as-deposited materials, as well as the tensile fracture morphology, were observed using a scanning electron microscope (SEM, JSM 7200 F, JEOL). All microstructural test samples were extracted from the locations labeled ①, ②, and ③, as illustrated in Fig. 5. Nine non-standard uniaxial tensile specimens were prepared along the transverse and building directions, with their sampling locations and dimensions shown in Fig. 5. Uniaxial tensile tests were performed at room temperature on an MTS-E45 testing machine at a displacement rate of 0.5 mm/min. Vickers hardness (HXS-1000AC) was tested at a load of 100 g with a dwell time of 15 s. Processing Text: Nickel 625 solid and the first-developed TiC-containing Ni625-core wires were utilized in this study for comparative analysis. Given the differences in deposition form and current density between solid and cored wires, particularly with non-metallic ceramic particles, deposition parameters for both wires were examined separately. The optimized deposition parameters are listed in Table 3. The Q235 substrate was polished to eliminate surface impurities and oxides. The deposited components were cut to precise dimensions using a wire-cutting machine. The sample surfaces were sequentially polished using grit papers of 200#, 400#, 800#, 1200#, 1500#, 2000#, and 3000#. Further refinement was achieved using cloth polishing and a 2.5 μm diamond spray polish. A custom FeCl 3 etchant (8 g FeCl 3 + 14 ml HCl + 20 ml C 2H 5OH) was applied. The treated surfaces were analyzed using a 3D profilometry optical microscope (OLYMPUS DSX1000). High-resolution field emission scanning electron microscopy (FSEM, MAIA3 LMH) was employed to analyze particle distribution, morphology, and microstructural evolution. The porosity distribution in rectangular samples from the top of the single-wall structure was analyzed using 3D-CT. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, OXFORD C NANO+) was employed on electrolytically polished surfaces to quantify particle distribution and structural characteristics. The test was performed at 20.00 kV with a 70° sample tilt, a scanning speed of ∼198 Hz, and a 5 μm step size. A transmission electron microscope (TEM, JEM-2100F) was used for microstructural characterization. Microhardness along the deposition direction was measured using a Vickers hardness tester (HVSA-1000A). Three equidistant horizontal points at the same depth from the surface or bottom were tested, and their average was recorded. Tensile properties were measured using an electronic universal testing machine (Zwick020). A tensile speed of 0.6 mm/min was applied. Three specimens per sample, taken from the top, middle, and bottom in both horizontal and longitudinal directions, were analyzed for mechanical properties and anisotropy. Multi-layer deposition was performed under different conditions using the parameters listed in Table 3. A PC210 industrial thermal imaging camera recorded weld bead temperatures during deposition, with data analyzed using ThermoTools software. To reduce thermal accumulation, careful control of interlayer temperature is required. In this study, each layer was cooled to near-room temperature before subsequent deposition. As shown in Fig. 6f, each layer was deposited after cooling to 'room temperature - 40 °C.' Thermal imaging and temperature analysis indicate that when the interlayer is sufficiently cooled, temperature differences between arc initiation and extinction points become negligible.
