Processing Text: Thin-walled parts were produced by single-pass scanning at a speed of 0.02 m/s. The scanning path involves back-and-forth movement from left to right. After completing each layer, a 60-second interlayer waiting time is enforced. The interlayer cooling method was air-cooling to room temperature. The wire feed speed was 6.5 m/min in CMT+P mode, with a shielding gas flow rate of 15 L/min, and operating at 111 A and 18.8 V for current and voltage. The above are the process parameters for DED-Arc. The interlayer hammering was adopted after completing per layer deposition. Air hammer operated at a speed of 5500 strokes per minute, consuming 180 L/min of gas. Air hammer head moved at 0.1 m/min with a reciprocating frequency of 4 times per layer. The above surface was then cleaned with alcohol and a steel brush to prepare for the next layer deposition. When preparing the AH sample, the deposited layer cooled for 60 seconds before the hammering process. Based on the deposition and hammering process parameters, the heating platform maintained a temperature of 400℃ during the preparation of the AH+ IH sample. Both DED and hammering processes were kept at a heated state until the completion of thin-walled specimen preparation. Similar to the AH sample, a 60-second interlayer waiting time is necessary when preparing the AH+IH sample. AM, AH, and AH+ IH samples each consist of 8 layers, with average layer heights of approximately 2.15 mm, 1.63 mm, and 1.26 mm, respectively. Specimen surfaces were polished to a mirror for the following characterization. The microhardness was carried out using a microhardness tester (HXS-1000AY). Block with dimensions of 5 × 5 × 5 mm 3 was cut for CT. The phase composition was analyzed with an X-ray diffractometer (XRD, SHIMADZU XRD-6100). The diffraction angle (2θ) ranged from 20° to 90°, with a scanning step size of 0.04°. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Hitachi S-4800) was used to examine the distribution characteristics of the second phases and fracture morphology. Percentage of phases in images was calculated using Image-Pro Plus 6.0. Electrolytic polishing removed surface stress of specimens, and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, Hitachi S-4800) analyzed crystal structures further. OIM Analysis software processed initial EBSD data to relevant graphical information. Transmission electron microscope (TEM, FEI Talos F200X G2) was adopted to make the further analysis of precipitation, dislocations and substructures. Processing state: as-deposited; Microstructure: similar to DED-Arced Al-Mg-Sc alloys

Processing Text: The alloys underwent a processing sequence of casting, homogenization, hot deformation, annealing, cold deformation, solid solution treatment, followed by optional steps of cold deformation and pre-aging, and finally peak-aging. The alloys were melted under an argon atmosphere and cast into an iron mold with a size of 20 mm × 20 mm × 100 mm. The as-cast ingots were homogenized at 430 °C for 6 h and then 470 °C for 24 h, followed by hot- and cold-rolled into 2 mm thick sheets. Solid solution treatment was performed at 490 °C for 1 h, followed by water quenching to room temperature. Subsequently a two-step aging process (90 °C for 24 h followed by 140 °C to peak aging) was employed. Dog-bone-shaped specimens of the alloys in the peak-aged state were prepared with a gauge length of 9.5 mm, and tensile tests were conducted using AGS-X tensile testing machine at a tensile rate of 0.572 mm/min at room temperature, with at least three repetitions for averaging. Hardness tests were conducted to observe the aging behavior of the designed alloys, while tensile tests were performed on the alloys in their peak-aged or near-peak-aged state. Processing Text: Udimet 720Li samples were extracted from a forged disc which was solution treated and precipitation hardened (required for intended final use). Udimet 720Li samples were extracted by wire-Electro Discharge Machining (EDM) from several zones of the bulk of the forged disc, close to the inner and outer diameters, to analyse the microstructural heterogeneity. Those samples were ground, polished, and chemically etched. The cylindrical samples were extracted from multiple regions of the disc by wire-EDM, and then the top and bottom faces were ground to ensure parallelism. Uniaxial compression loading of the Udimet 720Li specimens was accomplished using a Gleeble 3500 thermomechanical testing machine (see Fig. S1) for a wide range of temperatures (20-1100 °C) and strain rates (0.01-100 s−1). Cylindrical specimens with dimensions Ø6 x 9 mm were used in the compression tests in accordance with the ASTM E9-09 and ASTM E209-00 (2010) standards. These Udimet 720Li specimens were obtained by wire-EDM from the same zones of the forged discs used for microstructural and thermophysical characterisation. Then, the flat faces of the specimens were ground to ensure parallelism and good contact with the anvils during the compression tests. Compression tests were carried out at three temperatures (20, 600, and 900 °C) and at a constant strain rate (1 s−1) for specimens extracted in each direction. More than 100 tests were carried out, varying the temperatures from 20 to 1100 °C and the strain rate from 0.01 to 100 s−1. A single temperature (20 °C) was tested for a strain rate of 0.01 s−1. For this purpose, a specimen was pre-heated to 1200 °C to completely dissolve the γ’ phase. Condition: tested at 20 °C, Strain rate: 1 s^-1

Processing Text: In this study, the low-carbon ultra-high-strength steels with precipitation-free were prepared using quenching processes, and the co-precipitation strengthening of multi-scale Cu-rich and NiAl were designed to enhance fatigue performance through quenching-tempering (QT) and quenching-partitioning-tempering (QPT) processes respectively. The designed experimental steel billet of 150 kg was melted in a vacuum furnace, and the actual chemical composition of the billet was presented in Table 1. In order to obtain sufficient multi-component Cu-rich nanoparticles during the subsequent heat-treatment process, 1.65 wt.%Cu, 5.04 wt.%Ni and 0.94 wt.%Al were added to the steel billet. The tube billet was heated to 1280 °C for 30 mins to homogenize in a rotary heating furnace, and then air-cooled to 1150 °C for rotary piercing with a reduction rate of ∼74%. Subsequently, the pierced tube billet was air-cooled to 1000 °C and continuously rolled through 5 passes to obtain a raw tube with a reduction rate of ∼46%. The rolled raw tube was reheated to 850 °C in a circulating heating furnace, and then the stretch reducing process was performed at 850 °C through 7 passes with a total reduction rate of ∼20.6%. In order to achieve a substantial improvement in fatigue strength, martensite was designed as the ideal matrix microstructure, and a two-step quenching-tempering (QT) and a multi-step QPT processes are used to precipitate multi-component nanoparticles. The one-step quenching process requires the rolled tube was heated to 900 °C for 30 min to austenitized treatment, and then water quenched to obtain sufficient martensite. Processing Text: The SS 316L powder, which was produced through gas atomization, was provided by EOS in Germany. The Hall flow rate of the powder is 12.1 s/50g, and its chemical composition is presented in Table 1. The power morphology and particle size distribution are illustrated in Fig. 1(a) and (b), respectively, showcasing a highly spherical shape (≥99 %) with a D50 size of 34.3 μm, which makes it well-suited for LPBF technology. The SS 316L was fabricated using an HBD-80 machine (Shanghai Hanbang United 3D Tech Co., Ltd., China), equipped with a YLR-500 fiber laser operating at a wavelength of 1064 nm and a beam diameter of approximately 33 μm. The schematic diagram of LPBF technology is shown in Fig. 2(a), while Fig. 2(b) depicts the laser scanning strategy. The selection of process parameters was based on Ref. [ 16], which include laser power ( P), scanning speed ( v), scanning spacing ( h), and volumetric energy density ( VED = P/hvt) [ 33], as shown in Table 2. In this work, a total of 108 tensile specimens were examined, divided into 36 groups with each group consisting of 3 replicate specimens. The 3D model, as shown in Fig. 2(c), was printed via LPBF technology. The lower section of the model was used to evaluate its relative density and microstructure. While, the upper portion of the model was divided into specimens specifically designed for conducting tensile tests and its dimensions are illustrated in Fig. 2 (e). The microstructure of the alloy parallel to the BD orientation is characterized in Fig. 2(d). The specimen density was measured using Archimedes' theory with a MAY-D80 automatic testing balance. Processing Text: The Fe 32Ni 28Cr 25Al 10Ti 5(0Nb) and Fe 31.75Ni 27.75Cr 25Al 10Ti 5Nb 0.5(0.5Nb) ingots were dripped casting by arc-melting corresponding pure metals (purity >99.9 wt%) and Al-70Nb master alloy. As-cast slats were received prime solution treatment at 1100 °C for two hours to eliminate element segregation by water quenching, and subsequently aged at ∼1000 °C for 8 h. Before trying out, the specimens were mechanically polished by Al 2O 3suspension with a volume fraction of 20 % followed by electrochemically polished (90 vol% anhydrous ethanol and 10 vol% HClO 4) with a direct voltage of 30 V. Processing Text: This study investigates the microstructure and mechanical properties of a Mg-9Gd-3Y-0.5Zr alloy fabricated by TIG-based DED-Arc with and without post-heat treatment. The results show that a tailored heat treatment (500 °C × 45 min + 225 °C × 16 h) produces a homogeneous microstructure with refined grain size and isotropic tensile properties. Solution treatment was carried out in the SO 2 atmosphere and finally water quenching. Different solution treatments (solution-treated at 500 °C for different time) and aging treatments (aging-treated at 200 °C, 225 °C, and 250 °C) were adopted. Following an optimal solution treatment for 45 min at 500 °C, aging treatment at 200 °C, 225 °C and 250 °C are adopted, respectively. 225 °C × 16h is identified as the best aging treatment for DED-Arc GW93K alloy. Processing Text: The high pure metal powder (≥99.95 wt%) of Mn, Fe, Co, and Ni with equal atomic ratio was milled for 20 h in a planetary ball mill under an argon atmosphere to produce HEA powders. To prevent severe welding of the metal powders, 1 wt% N-heptane was added to the ball mill tank. The collected HEA powders were then transferred to a vacuum hot-pressing sintering system (HPS, FUJIDEMPA HIGH-MULTI 5000). The entire sintering process was conducted under a low vacuum of 10-1 Pa and cooled with the furnace after holding at 1050 °C and 50 MPa for 1h. The sintered bulk HEAs were immersed in liquid nitrogen and cooled to its temperature before being deformed under a hydraulic press. The overall thickness was reduced by 10 %. The deformed HEA samples were then annealed at 500 °C, 600 °C, 700 °C, and 800 °C for 30 min, followed by water quenching. These samples were labeled A500, A600, A700, and A800, respectively. Before analysis, the samples were prepared through mechanical and electrolytic polishing. For transmission electron microscopy (TEM) analysis, the samples were wire-cut, mechanically polished to 50 μm, and subsequently thinned using an ion beam. Processing state: After DCD; Strength and ductility properties at Room Temperature

Processing Text: The high pure metal powder (≥99.95 wt%) of Mn, Fe, Co, and Ni with equal atomic ratio was milled for 20 h in a planetary ball mill under an argon atmosphere to produce HEA powders. To prevent severe welding of the metal powders, 1 wt% N-heptane was added to the ball mill tank. The collected HEA powders were then transferred to a vacuum hot-pressing sintering system (HPS, FUJIDEMPA HIGH-MULTI 5000). The entire sintering process was conducted under a low vacuum of 10-1 Pa and cooled with the furnace after holding at 1050 °C and 50 MPa for 1h. The sintered bulk HEAs were immersed in liquid nitrogen and cooled to its temperature before being deformed under a hydraulic press. The overall thickness was reduced by 10 %. The deformed HEA samples were then annealed at 500 °C, 600 °C, 700 °C, and 800 °C for 30 min, followed by water quenching. These samples were labeled A500, A600, A700, and A800, respectively. Before analysis, the samples were prepared through mechanical and electrolytic polishing. For transmission electron microscopy (TEM) analysis, the samples were wire-cut, mechanically polished to 50 μm, and subsequently thinned using an ion beam. Processing Text: Here, the single-phase body centered cubic (BCC) structured Ti3Zr1.5NbVAl0.25 RHEA with superior specific strength and ductility were developed by laser direct energy deposition and cold-rolling. The structures of RHEA were treated by various annealing temperatures ranging from 600 °C to 900 °C for an hour. The RHEA with a recrystallized equiaxed crystal annealed at 900 °C exhibited excellent mechanical properties such as yield strength of 976 MPa and tensile strength of 986 MPa. The elongation of 22.5 % is three times higher than original state and the specific strength of 173.1 MPa cm3·g−1 surpassed those of most RHEAs. More importantly, the enhanced yield strength can be attributed to the contributions among solution strengthening, grain boundary (GB) strengthening and dislocation strengthening. Moreover, emerging much rich dislocation microstructures make for improving strain hardening and preventing early necking for enhanced plasticity. Processing Text: The two HEAs with nominal compositions of (Cr 20Mn 24Fe 30Co 20Ni 6) 99C 1(at.%) and (Cr 20Mn 24Fe 30Co 20Ni 6) 99N 1(at.%), were cast using a vacuum induction furnace. Chromium nitride and iron-carbon were added as N and C element sources, respectively. The as-cast ingot has a cuboid shape in the dimension of 130 × 50 × 50 mm 3. Thin slices with a thickness of ∼10 mm were cut from the as-cast ingots and subsequently hot-rolled at 950 °C with a thickness reduction of 80 %. Each rolling pass reduces the thickness of 0.5-1 mm, and after every rolling pass, the sample is kept at 950 °C for 5 min. Further homogenization was conducted in an Ar atmosphere at 1200 °C for 2 h, followed by water quenching. Rectangular dog-bone-shaped tensile specimens were obtained from the as-homogenized materials using electrical discharge machining. The specimen had a total length of 130 mm and a thickness of 2 mm. The gauge area measured 50 mm in length and 10 mm in width. Tensile tests were conducted at a strain rate of 10 −3s −1using a screw-driven Zwick/Roell test rig (Z250 model) equipped with a cold chamber controlled by liquid nitrogen. The testing temperatures were set at dry ice-alcohol mixture temperature (200 K) as well as room temperature (298 K). To ensure data reproducibility, three tests were performed for each alloy state. As for the initial state, alloys were characterized using an X-ray diffractometer (XRD) machine equipped with a Cu-Kα radiation anode in order to determine the phase constitution and the lattice parameters. The samples were scanned at a 2θ angle ranging from 30° to 130°, with a scanning rate of 2°/min. To prepare specimens for electron channeling contrast (ECC) and EBSD analyses, initial grinding using silicon carbide paper was followed by polishing using a diamond suspension with a particle size of 2.5 μm. Subsequent finer polishing was carried out with oxide suspension (OPS) containing silica particles (approximately 50 nm in size). The remaining OPS particles were removed through soap polishing. Electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) analysis was conducted using a ZEISS Gemini SEM300 equipped with an electron backscatter diffractometer and an energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS), at a voltage of 20 kV, scanned with a step size of 0.15 μm and a tilt angle of 70°. For ECC characterization, a ZEISS Gemini Crossbeam 340 instrument was utilized, and optimal imaging conditions were achieved at a voltage of 30 kV and a working distance of 6.5 mm. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) was carried out for detailed characterization of the deformed microstructure using a JEOL JEM-F200 field emission high-resolution transmission electron microscope. For TEM foil preparation, the samples were polished to a thickness of approximately 80 μm using sandpaper and standard disk with a diameter of 3 mm was then punched out. Double-jet electron-polishing was employed to prepare for the TEM foils, and electron-transparent TEM foils can be obtained by utilizing 5 % perchloric acid in acetic acid at a temperature of 17 °C and a voltage of 32 V. Condition: Low Temperature (200 K); Phase: Single FCC phase

Processing Text: The experimental material consisted of 316L austenitic stainless steel rods with a diameter of 30 mm. The material was hot-rolled to 4 mm in thickness, followed by solution treatment at 1050 °C for 1 h. Before each rolling pass, the initial material was immersed in liquid nitrogen for 10 min. The thickness reduction per pass was kept below 5 %. Surface cracks developed when the total thickness reduction reached 70 %. Consequently, the final thickness was reduced by 70 %, resulting in a thickness of 1.2 mm for the cryo-rolled sample, which was labeled as CryoR sample. After cryo-rolling, the samples were subjected to annealing at 700 °C 20 min, 750 °C 6 min, and a sequential 700 °C 20 min + 750 °C 6 min process, followed by water quenching. These samples were labeled as 700A, 750A, and 700A-750A, respectively. All heat treatment processes were performed in a muffle furnace without a protective atmosphere. Tensile tests were conducted using a universal testing machine (5105, SSANS-CMT) at room temperature (24 °C) and liquid nitrogen temperature (−196 °C) with a strain rate of 10 −3s −1. All tensile samples were cut along the rolling direction into dog-bone shapes with a gauge length of 34 mm, width of 10 mm, and thickness of 1 mm. Each test was repeated at least three times to ensure accuracy. To evaluate inhomogeneous deformation, load-unload-reload (LUR) tests were also performed under the same conditions as the tensile tests to quantify the back stress (σ B) component. The microstructural evolution of the samples along the rolling direction (RD) was characterized. XRD analysis was conducted to examine phase transformation with a diffraction angle range of 40°-100° and a scanning speed of 2°/min, using Cu-Kα radiation at 40 kV and 150 mA. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, Oxford) was employed for quantitative analysis of the phase microstructure. After mechanical polishing, samples were electropolished using a 10 % perchloric acid solution at 20 V for 20-25 s. EBSD measurements were performed on a Zeiss Auriga scanning electron microscope with a step size of 100 nm at an accelerating voltage of 15 kV. Processing Text: To obtain excellent fatigue resistance and mechanical properties, a gradient-nanostructured layer was fabricated by ultrasonic surface rolling process (USRP) at the gauge section and arc transition. Severe plastic deformation (SPD) was introduced on the specimen surface by the ultrasonic vibrating motion combined with static force on the specimen applied through a rolling ball tip. The ultrasonic surface rolling processing parameters are as follows: static force 400 N, vibration amplitude 10 μm, feeding rate 500 mm/min, and repeated processing 30 times. After USRP, fatigue and tensile specimens with a thickness of 2 mm are wire-cut from the blank specimen. Microhardness distribution was measured on the cross-sections (parallel to ND) of GNS-Zr with an applied load of 200 g and a holding time of 15 s using a digital microhardness tester at room temperature. Residual compressive stress along the ND was measured using an X-ray diffractometer (XRD) with Cu-Kα radiation at the Zr {211} plane, and the diffraction angle (2θ) range was 30°-90°. Tensile tests were performed at a strain rate of 1×10−3s−1 at room temperature using a universal testing machine. The tensile properties of coarse-grained and gradient-nanostructured Zr were measured with the dimensions of 15×4×2mm3 (as shown in Fig. 1(b)). Stress-controlled fatigue tests were conducted with a frequency of 20 Hz and a stress ratio R of 0.1 using an Instron 8801 fatigue testing machine under stress control. The crack propagation rate would be calculated by the slope of two neighboring data points of the crack length versus the cycle number. The crack propagation length ∆a under different fatigue cycles was measured using a two-part silicone rubber replica method in combination with a metallographic microscope. The stress intensity factor ∆K of the single-edge notched specimens can be calculated. The test stress σmax is 270MPa, the stress ratio R is 0.1, and the frequency f is 20 Hz. Life tests were performed on notched coarse grain specimens (CG-Zr) and notched gradient nanostructured specimens (GNS-Zr). The microstructure was investigated using a Zeiss Gemini 300 field emission scanning electron microscope (SEM) fitted with an Oxford Symmetry EBSD detector, and a Talos F200X transmission electron microscope (TEM). The physical quantities of microstructure at different locations in the gradient direction were investigated by EBSD characterization. The TEM specimens were mechanically ground down to 50 μm to characterize the fine microstructure. Processing Text: A high-strength Co-free triple-phase Al10Cr12Fe35Mn23Ni20 high-entropy alloy (HEA) was successfully fabricated using Friction Surface Layer Deposition (FSLD), a bulk manufacturing method. Multiple single-layer deposits were produced by varying forging force (F) and traverse speeds (Tr) to optimize the process parameters. The optimized conditions (F = 40 kN & Tr = 200 mm/min) were then applied to manufacture a scaled-up multi-layer specimen. During FSLD, the FCC-matrix underwent continuous dynamic recrystallization due to high-temperature severe plastic deformation, forming finer equiaxed grains. Simultaneously, the BCC-dendrites fractured into smaller fragments, some of which experienced partial growth and coarsening under applied stress, resulting in an hourglass morphology. In contrast, the small B2-precipitates within the BCC-fragments dissolved during the elevated temperatures of FSLD and reprecipitated as substantially finer precipitates during continuous cooling post-FSLD. Vacuum induction melted cylindrical bars of Al10Cr12Fe35Mn23Ni20 HEA were procured from Sophisticated Alloys Inc. 25.4 mm diameter and 152.4 mm length feed rods were sectioned from the As-Received HEA bars for FSLD. A constant rotation rate of 500 rpm was used in this work to allow comparison of microstructural evolution with similar heat generation rates. The microhardness measurements were performed using a CLARK CM-802AT automatic hardness tester, and a load of 500 gf and a dwell time of 10s were used. SEM analysis has been performed on the as-received cylindrical bars of the HEA to evaluate the initial microstructure. EBSD and EDS scans were performed to identify the three different phases present in the microstructure of AR HEA. Detailed microstructural characterization has been performed on the optimized condition of the FSLD Al10Cr12Fe35Mn23Ni20 HEA to understand the microstructural evolution during processing. A multi-layer deposit of Al10Cr12Fe35Mn23Ni20 HEA comprising 7 layers was deposited consecutively layer-by-layer over the SS 304 substrate via FSLD. The optimized process parameters (condition #1: F = 40 kN and Tr = 200 mm/min) were used for this deposition. Condition: #1; Estimated from Vickers Hardness: 278 ±3.9 HV

Processing Text: High-purity (>99.9 wt%) Ni, Co, Cr, and Ti were used as raw materials to prepare alloy ingots of (Co50Cr30Ni20)95Ti5 (at.%) via arc melting under an argon protective atmosphere. To ensure a uniform chemical composition, the ingots were flipped and remelted six times, and then drop-cast into a copper mold with dimensions of 8 mm × 8 mm × 30 mm. Subsequently, the cast rods were sealed in vacuum quartz tubes and homogenized at 1473 K for 24 h to eliminate elemental segregation. The homogenized rods were then cold-rolled longitudinally at room temperature, reducing the thickness from 8 mm to 1.5 mm, corresponding to an approximate 80% thickness reduction. For the (Co50Cr30Ni20)95Ti5 samples, five different heat treatments were performed: (1) ageing at 1273 K for 1 h, followed by ageing at 1073 K for 10 h (H2); (2) recrystallization at 1423 K for 10 min (H3); (3) recrystallization at 1423 K for 10 min, followed by ageing at 1073 K for 10 h (H4); (4) recrystallization at 1423 K for 10 min, followed by ageing at 1173 K for 24 h (H5); (5) recrystallization at 1423 K for 3 min, followed by ageing at 1243 K for 72 h. All heat treatments were followed by water quenching to preserve the high-temperature microstructure. Processing Text: The Fe50.2-Mn30.0-Co5.0-Ni3.0-Cu2.0-Al9.0-C0.8 (mass%) alloy was prepared by induction melting for about 30 min in an alumina crucible under an argon atmosphere (99.9995 % purity). Later it was subsequently cast into a massive Cu mold forming an ingot of 20 × 50 × 100 mm in size. After homogenization for 4 h at 1100 °C in air and subsequent water quenching to avoid precipitation of carbides a slab of 20 × 20 mm in cross-section was subjected to hot dual axial forging (DAF) at 1050 °C in two steps. After the initial dual axial hammering out using a forging hammer the sample size was reduced to 16 × 16 mm size. Subsequent rolling using a caliber rolling mill produced the slabs of 10 × 10 mm in cross-section. Then, the sample cut in a longitudinal direction forming a 6 × 10 mm cross-section sample was subsequently cold rolled (CR) to 0.5 mm corresponding to 92 % thickness reduction (true/equivalent strain e= 2.5) in about 100 passes (∼0.1 mm size reduction per pass) at the linear passage speed of 1 cm/s. CR was performed between two stainless steel plates to protect the rolls. Then, aging temperatures of 550-600 °C, typical for Fe-Mn-Al-C alloys were applied. The samples were also aged at 200-300 °C. After homogenization, DAF and cold rolling, the chemical composition of the produced alloy was verified by the inductively coupled plasma emission spectroscopy with ARCOS FHM22 MV130 spectrometer made by SPECTRO Analytical Instruments (for metallic elements), combustion infrared absorption method with LECO CS-844 analyzer (for carbon) and helium transport melting infrared absorption method with LECO ONH836 (for oxygen). Cold-rolled sample; Tensile elongation of 4%; Annealed samples exhibited higher values.

Processing Text: The initial Al-Cu-Li alloy was first produced using spray forming and subsequently hot extruded to 30 mm thick in factory. It was then underwent cold rolling to 6 mm after annealing at 360 °C for 5 h and 420 °C for 2 h. Following this, the cold-rolled plates were subjected to various annealing treatments with different temperatures and cooling rates. A subset of cold-rolled plates was annealed at temperatures of 300 °C, 325 °C, 350 °C, 375 °C, and 400 °C for 2 h, followed by faster cooling (FC) down to 250 °C at a cooling rate of approximately 3.65 °C/min, and then air cooled to room temperature. These samples were labeled as X-FC, with “X” indicating the specific annealing temperature. Another subset of the cold-rolled plates was annealed at 400 °C for 2 h and subsequently cooled with a slower cooling rate (SC) of about 0.5 °C/min down to room temperature, which is designated as 400°C-SC. All annealed specimens were underwent a solid solution treatment (SST) at 505 °C for 60 min before being quenched in ambient water. To determine the engineering mechanical properties, the materials were ultimately aged at 152 °C for 38 h following a 5 % pre-stretch deformation. Both cold-rolled and APC specimens were annealed at 300 °C-400 °C for 30 s-3600 s. Subsequently, rapid quenching in ambient water and HV testing were performed. For the HV testing, a 500 g load was applied for 15 s with an average of 10 measurements per sample. To further explore the recrystallization kinetics of the annealed samples during SST at 505 °C, samples previously annealed at 300°C-FC, 350°C-FC, and 400°C-FC were exposed to SST at 505 °C for durations of 15 s, 30 s, 45 s, 60 s, 180 s, and 3600 s. Following the SST, immediate quenching in ambient water and HV testing were conducted. Meanwhile, APC samples also underwent annealing at 300 °C, 350 °C, and 400 °C for 2 h with a faster cooling rate. Subsequently, they were solution-treated for various durations similar to the above 300°C-FC, 350°C-FC, and 400°C-FC samples, followed by HV testing after ambient water quenching. For quasi Electron Backscatter Diffraction (EBSD) observation, the sample was marked by a hardness tester with a load of 1 Kg and a dwell time of 15 s before undergoing twin-jet electropolishing treatment. The specimens for EBSD observation were prepared through twin-jet electropolishing on MPT-1 electrolytic double sprayer. The AZtecCrystal software was employed to process the EBSD data. Processing Text: A hybrid nanostructured surface layer has been produced on interstitial-free steel by means of surface mechanical rolling treatment and subsequent chromizing treatment. As-received billets were first annealed at 850 °C for 120 min to obtain a CG structure with an average grain size of ∼200 μm, and then cut by electro-spark discharge machining to prepare cylindrical tensile specimens (for both experimental and controlled groups) with a gauge section of 4 mm in diameter and 10 mm in length. SMRT was applied to prepare a GNS surface layer on tensile specimens. After SMRT, a pure Cr layer of ∼0.30 μm in thickness was electroplated onto treated surface in an aqueous solution of 25.0 CrO 3and 0.25 H 2SO 4(in wt.%). Subsequently, Cr-coated and as-prepared (i.e. Cr-free) SMRT samples were annealed together in vacuum at 500 °C for 720 min. To preclude the possible influence on tensile properties from any residual Cr, annealed Cr-coated samples were gently polished by using an abrasive paper (5000 grit) and a surface layer of ∼0.50 μm in thickness was removed before tensile testing. Processing Text: In this study, a TiZrHf RMPEA (Ti 33.3Zr 33.3Hf 33.3, in at%) was produced using vacuum arc melting, followed by rapid solidification. Initially, high-purity Ti, Zr, and Hf metals were mechanically polished to remove surface oxides, then pre-treated by soaking in organic solvents and vacuum dried. A small quantity of high-purity Ti ingot was added to act as an oxygen-getter. The vacuum chamber was evacuated to 10 −3Pa using a mechanical and molecular pump, then filled with 0.05 MPa of high-purity argon gas for protection. During the melting process, a current of 150-350 A was applied to heat and fully melt the metals, while magnetic stirring ensured chemical homogeneity. Multiple melting cycles (5-6) were conducted to eliminate any unmelted residues. Finally, the melt was suction-cast into a copper mold (10 × 10 × 70 mm). Processing Text: Round bar tensile samples with a diameter of 6 mm and a gauge length of 30 mm were machined from a φ20 mm-rod, which was solution-heat-treated at 1080 °C for 2 min followed by water-quenching. To obtain sufficiently averaged neutron diffraction patterns across the sample's gauge part, a uniformly hydrogen-charged (H-charged) sample was prepared via thermal exposure. The sample was subjected to a hydrogen gas atmosphere at 100 MPa and 270 °C for 200 h. The hydrogen concentration (CH) was quantified using Thermal Desorption Spectroscopy (TDS) coupled with a gas chromatography having a thermal conductivity detector (JTF-20A, J-SCIENCE LAB Co., Ltd., Japan). The analysis was conducted with a time step of 5 min, spanning a temperature range from 25 °C to 800 °C. Argon gas was used as the carrier with a heating rate of 100 °C/h. In situ neutron diffraction experiments during tensile tests were conducted at the Materials and Life Science Experimental Facility (MLF) of the Japan Proton Accelerator Research Complex (J-PARC), utilizing the Engineering Materials Diffractometer, TAKUMI. During the plastic deformation, the crosshead speed was set at 0.05 mm/min, corresponding to an initial strain rate of 3×10−5 sec−1. The microstructures of the deformed samples, as well as that of the undeformed ones, were analyzed using electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) technique, equipped with a field-emission (FE-) scanning electron microscope (SEM), Sigma Zeiss, Germany. Processing Text: Austenitization was conducted by holding the annealed steel at 880 °C for 40 min. Subsequent water quenching resulted in a fully martensitic microstructure. Tempering treatments were performed by holding the as-quenched steel at subcritical temperatures of 500 °C, 550 °C, and 600 °C for durations of up to 2 h to initiate microstructural evolution followed by air cooling. The specimen preparation involved grinding with 400∼3000 grit sandpaper, followed by a 10-s electropolishing step in a solution of 10 % perchloric acid and 90 % ethanol. The specimens were extracted from 5 mm-thick heat-treated sheets utilizing a spark wire-cutting machine. Subsequently, the tensile specimens were abraded with 2000 grit emery paper and polished using 1 μm diamond paste. The specimens were then subjected to electrochemical charging to incorporate hydrogen atoms using an aqueous solution containing 0.05 mol L−1 H2SO4 and 3 g L−1 NH4SCN. A current density of 1.0 mA cm−2 was consistently maintained for 12 h at ambient temperature. To confirm that the gauge section of the specimens was exposed to hydrogen charging, the remaining components were thoroughly coated with a layer of silica gel to prevent any contact with the electrolyte solution. Immediately following the electrochemical charging, a layer of zinc was electroplated onto the surface to prevent hydrogen escape from the hydrogen-charged specimens. The protective zinc coating was applied using an aqueous solution containing ZnCl2 powder (64.3 g L−1), KCl (334.3 g L−1), H3BO4 (30.8 g L−1), and C12H25SO4Na (0.71 g L−1) at the current density of 25 mA cm−2 for 30 min. Tempering Temperature: 500 °C; Pre-charging duration: 0 h

Processing Text: The purity of Al, Co, Fe, Mn and Ni element (>99.95 wt%) were mixed, and an Al5Co21Fe21Mn17Ni36 ingot was prepared by arc melting under a high-purity argon atmosphere. To ensure the uniformity of compositions, the ingot was remelted five times. Subsequently, the ingot was solution-treated at 1150 °C for 2 h and cold-rolled to from a thickness of 8 mm-1.2 mm at RT, with a total rolling reduction ratio of 85 %. Finally, the as-rolled plates were aged at 800 °C for 1 h followed by air cooling. Samples for TEM observations were mechanically polished to a thickness of ∼40 μm and then further thinned, using a Precision ion polisher (Gatan 691). Dog-bone shaped specimens with dimensions of 15 × 5 × 1.5 mm3 were cut from the middle of the as-prepared HEA, by using an electrical discharge machine. Uniaxial tensile tests were performed on an AG-X plus pc-controlled mechanical testing system (Shimadzu Co., Ltd, Japan, with a constant strain rate of 1.0 × 10−3s−1. Three parallel samples were tested at RT and −196 °C, respectively. All tensile tests were conducted by using an extensometer to calibrate the strain. During the cryogenic tensile tests, the sample is holder located in a temperature chamber regulated by liquid nitrogen cooling at a cooling rate of 10 °C/min. Temperature: -196 °C; Phases: FCC and B2

Processing Text: The Al-1.52 Mg-1.84 Mn-0.03 Si-0.05 Fe (wt%) alloy was processed in a Nabertherm electric resistance furnace using a 99.99 %Al, 99.95 %Mg, and Al-10 %Mn master alloy and was solidified at a casting cooling rate of ∼10 K/s. A mean grain size was 170 ± 30 µm for as-cast alloy. Samples with dimensions of 9 × 9 × 18 mm and 28 × 28 × 56 mm cut from the as-cast ingot were subjected to MDF for a cumulative strain of ∑e = 14.4 (6 cycles) and strain per pass of 0.8 at temperatures of 300 and 350 °C with a strain rate of ∼10 −2 s −1. Small samples were used to analyze stress–strain behavior, bulk samples were used to study mechanical properties, the microstructure was controlled for both. The MDF process details and the stress–strain curve recalculation method are described in [18]. The room-temperature mechanical properties were determined for MDF-treated samples and MDF-treated and annealed at 300 °C samples according to ASTM E8/E8M standard using a Zwick Z250 universal testing machine with a tensile rate of 5 mm/min. Three samples with a gage size of 25 × 6 × 1 mm were tested. Processing state: MDF-treated at 300 °C; Strengthening mechanisms: I-phase precipitation strengthening and grain boundary strengthening

Processing Text: Equimolar CoCrNi MEA was prepared by arc-melting Co, Cr, and Ni mixtures with 99.99 % purity in a high-purity argon atmosphere. The ingot was remelted more than five times before the drop-cast process to ensure homogeneity. Subsequently, the as-cast CoCrNi MEA ingot was cold-forged by a 50 % reduction in thickness. Afterward, the alloy was annealed at 1173K for 1 h to reduce deformation-induced defects and promote recrystallization. Quasi-static compression tests with strain rates ranging from 1.0 × 10^−3 s^−1 to 10^−1 s^−1 were performed on CoCrNi MEA samples with a diameter of 3 mm and length of 6 mm using an Instron 5969 testing machine. Dynamic compression tests with strain rates ranging from 2.6 × 10^3 s^−1 to 6.2 × 10^3 s^−1 were carried out on CoCrNi MEA samples with a diameter of 3 mm and length of 3 mm using a SHPB system. Stop-ring technology was introduced to control the strain during the dynamic compressions. The ramp wave and shock compression experiments were conducted using the CQ-4 magnetically driven system, delivering a pulsed current with a peak value of 4 MA and a rising time of 500 ns, developed by the Institute of Fluid Physics, China Academy of Engineering Physics. Multi-level characterizations were conducted to explore the intrinsic mechanisms of CoCrNi MEA. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) was performed using a JEOL JSM-7100F field-emission scanning electron microscope (SEM). An acceleration voltage of 20 kV, a specimen tilt angle of 70°, and a working distance of 15 mm were used in the EBSD observations. A JEM-2100F transmission electron microscopy (TEM) was operated at an acceleration voltage of 200 kV to uncover microscopic deformation mechanisms. Strain rate: 10^-3 s^-1; Loading method: Quasi-static

Processing Text: Atomistic simulations of nanocrystalline HfNbTaZr RHEAs were conducted using the LAMMPS code. The interactions among Hf, Nb, Ta, and Zr atoms were modeled following the interatomic potential proposed by Maiti. A fixed timestep of 1.0 fs and periodic boundary conditions were adopted during the entire simulation. The nanocrystalline samples were constructed following the same method used by Deluigi et al., with six different average grain sizes: D=5,8,10,12,15,17nm. In short, a bcc nanocrystal with lattice parameter a0=3.63 was created with Voronoi tessellation. The nanocrystal had dimensions of 80a0×80a0×200a0, containing 272 grains for the 5 nm nanocrystal, and 23 grains for the 17 nm case. The resulting nanocrystals had ∼2.56×106 atoms. The HEA was built by randomly replacing the Hf, Nb, Ta and Zr atoms in equiatomic proportions (25 %). Processing Text: W30Cu composite materials were prepared by mechanically mixing high-purity (purity >99.9 %) W powder (average particle size 5 μm) and Cu powder (average particle size 10 μm), followed by hot pressing sintering (HPS). After mixing 70 wt% W powder and 30 wt% Cu powder, the mixture was ball-milled with a ball-to-powder ratio of 3:1. The milling was conducted at a speed of 300 rpm for 2 h, using tungsten carbide balls and a silicon nitride milling pot to ensure efficient powder milling without contamination. The milled powder mixture was then placed into a hot pressing sintering mold, which had good sealing properties, a height of 6 mm, and was made of tungsten alloy. After vacuum evacuation, HPS treatment was carried out at 1350 °C and 150 MPa for 2 h. 6 mm thick W30Cu billets were obtained by cutting after cooling with the furnace. In the first step, the W30Cu billets prepared by HPS were cut to dimensions of 30 mm × 40 mm × 6 mm and then annealed in a muffle furnace for rolling. The heating temperature was set at 500 °C with a heating time of 30 min. After annealing, the material was sent to a double-roll reversible mill for unidirectional rolling and further annealing was carried out, depending on the rolling condition of the sample, until the material thickness was reduced to 1 mm. In the second step, the 1 mm thick plates were cut to 20 mm × 40 mm × 1 mm and annealed in a muffle furnace at the same heating temperature. The heating time was extended to 45 min and the material was then sent to a four-roll reversible mill for unidirectional rolling. Annealing was performed when the sample thickness reached 0.6 mm and 0.2 mm, depending on the rolling status, and the material was rolled further until the thickness reached 0.1 mm. Samples were taken for analysis from the raw material, the 1 mm (R83%) plates after the first rolling stage and the 0.6 mm (R90%), 0.2 mm (R97%) and 0.1 mm (R98%) plates after the second rolling stage. Processing Text: The designed alloys were melted using the vacuum arc melting furnace in a high-purity argon atmosphere. The purity of raw materials was above 99.99 wt.%. After melting, the ingots were directly drop-cast into a water-cooled copper mould with the size of 10 × 10 × 55 mm 3. Processing Text: The chemical composition of A100 steel was shown in Table 1, and its heat treatment system was as follows: 885 ± 15 °C heat preservation for 60 min, quenching, oil cooling; Then, it was kept at −73 ± 8 °C for 60 min for cold treatment and reheated in air. Finally, 482 ± 3 °C insulation for 5 h tempering, air cooling. The mechanical properties of A100 ultra-high strength steels treated according to this heat treatment specification were shown in Table 2. The yield strength ( σ s), tensile strength ( σ b), elongation ( δ5) and section shrinkage (ψ) were 1920 MPa, 1998 MPa, 12.23 % and 65.82 %, respectively. In the USRP process, the static pressure and amplitude determined the intensity of ultrasonic energy, and the spindle speed and axial feed determined the coverage of processing. Parameters for the process were fine-tuned through prior orthogonal experiments and were as follows for this study: a spindle speed set at 45 r/min, an axial feed of 0.08 mm/r, static pressure fixed at 900 N, and an amplitude setting of 12 μm. Two samples were prepared for comparison—one treated with a single pass, labelled USRP-1, and the other with thirty passes, designated as USRP-30. X-ray diffraction phase analysis: The Rigaku Ultima IV X-ray diffractometer was utilized to study the specimen surface phases pre- and post-treatment, employing a Cu-Kα radiation source with a 1.5418 Å wavelength. The equipment operated at 40 kV and 35 mA, scanning at a speed of 1°/min across an angular range of 30° to 90° in 2θ. Surface topography and roughness analysis: The surface topography of USRP cylindrical specimens was observed with IFM-G4 white light surface topography instrument, and its surface roughness was measured. The average value of 3 measurements was taken as the test result of roughness. Scanning electron microscopy analysis: To scrutinize the alterations in the specimen surface microstructure pre- and post-treatment, the TESCAN LYRA3 XMU was employed, a dual-beam SEM, to capture images of the cross-sectional topography. Prior to SEM analysis, the cross-section of specimen underwent mechanical polishing utilizing a gradation of SiC sandpapers (ranging from 320 to 1200 grit), followed by a 1 μm diamond suspension. Subsequently, the sample was etched with a 4 % solution of nitric acid. Transmission electron microscope analysis: A Tecnai G2 F20 Transmission Electron Microscope (TEM) was utilized along with High-Resolution TEM to examine the surface microstructure modifications induced by USRP. Prior to TEM analysis, the specimens was meticulously prepared by grinding their surfaces to a thickness of 50 μm. Subsequently, a precision single injection thinning process on the interior perforations was employed for utilizing a solution composed of 10 % HClO 4+ 90 % CH 3OH (volume fraction). Hardness test: A Knoop HV-1000 microhardness tester was employed to gauge surface hardness pre- and post-treatment, applying a 25 g force with a 20 s dwell time. To verify the dependability of test data, five measurements for each datum was took. Residual stress test: The XL-640 system residual stress tester was utilized to evaluate surface stresses in variously processed samples. Employing Cr-Kα as the radiation source, the analyses was conducted based on the sin2ψ technique. To ascertain how residual stress altered with depth within the layers, the material was systematically stripped using an electrolytic method. This involved immersing the specimen in a concoction primarily composed of methanol (87.5 % by volume) with a sulfuric acid fraction of 12.5 %. Through this process, each layer of specimen was carefully peeled off to chart the residual stress profile depth-wise. Rotational bending fretting fatigue test method: A rotational bending fretting fatigue test was conducted using the PQ-6 tester, employing a custom fixture to facilitate the fretting fatigue load. As shown in Fig. 2, the interfacing geometry between the specimen and the bridge took the form of a curved contact, and the form of contact between the specimen and fretting pad was cylinder to camber. As the reference [20], throughout the test, the stress ring moved in unison with the specimen, and the normal forced was applied to the fretting pad by adjusting screws attached to the probing ring and was maintained at 3.6 KN using a tension sensor. The test maintained a speed of 2100 r/min, equivalent to 35 Hz, with a stress ratio set at R = -1. All testing occurred under standard room conditions, without any special atmospheric controls. The specimen size and observation method used in this paper are consistent with those in a previous paper published by us [22]. Prior to testing, all A100 steel samples were mechanically polished using a grinder to achieve the same low surface roughness. To characterize the cross-sectional surface microstructure, hardness, and residual stress distribution along the transverse direction (TD) after processing, the sample was also cut by electric discharge machining (EDM) along the TD with the Φ 6 mm × 10 mm. To study the PF and FF fracture, the samples were cut by EDM along the TD at a distance of 5 mm from the point of fracture. For the samples subjected to FF testing, the cut portion of the sample was also used to study the change in the fretting contact zone, which was located near the fretting fatigue fracture surface. In addition, to observe secondary cracks in the fretting fatigue test, the cut samples were cut in half again by EDM along the longitudinal direction (LD); these smaller sections were then mechanically polished to a mirror-like surface and etched using a 4 % Nital solution. In order to further elucidate the nano-mechanism of the martensite structure in USRP-treated A100 steel, the precipitated phase in A100 steel was characterized. In order to better confirm and characterize the morphology and type of precipitate phases, this paper focused on the analysis of the precipitate phase in the A100 steel substrate because the microstructure of the surface layer of the sample was severely refined after USRP-30 treatment, and the precipitated phase, nanocrystalline and dislocation defects were intertwined. Processing Text: Inconel 625 spherical powder from Sailong Metal Company (China) were used for the bulk HL-DED Inconel 625 and coated specimens. The powders were dried in an oven at 100 ℃ for 120 min to ensure good fluidity and to remove moisture. Bulk HL-DED Inconel 625 and coated specimens were manufactured using the ultra-high-speed laser cladding system (ZKZM-4000, ZKZM Co., China), which includes 4 kW laser, a central powder feeding system, and a computer numerical control stage. The deposition parameters were 1.8 kW laser power, 22 g/min powder feeding rate, 4 m/min laser scanning velocity, 80 % deposition tracks overlap, and 0.5 mm interlayer elevation. A single-layer Inconel 625 coating was produced moving the laser beam from left to right, while the double-layer coating was produced by laser beam passed from left to right, and then from right to left. For the double-layer coating, the endpoint of the first layer deposition served as the starting point for the second layer deposition. Based in the Inconel 625 coating defects and tensile properties discussed later, the optimal deposition parameters were 1.8 kW laser power and 4.6 Hz rotation frequency. The coating deposition rate is controlled by the rotation frequency in our experiments. The powder feeding rate was 34 g/min. The laser power was varied along with the rotation frequency. Although higher rotation speeds improve coating preparation efficiency, the maximum frequency of the computer numerical control equipment is limited to 5 Hz. Processing Text: The MEA sheets were cold-rolled to a thickness of 1.3 mm, then annealed at 1000 °C for 1 h, water-quenched, and machined down to a final thickness of 1 mm. Prior to laser welding, all material surfaces were ground with SiC papers (2400 grit) and then cleaned with ethanol under ultrasonication. The welding experiments were conducted in one pass using a continuous green laser beam with a wavelength of 532 nm and a power of 1.6 kW. Three different welding speeds of 200, 250, and 300 mm/s corresponding to heat inputs of 8, 6.5, and 5 J/mm were employed. Both PMs were mechanically fixed after being pushed together into the form of a butt joint. PWHT was then performed for 1 h at 900 °C in an electric muffle furnace, followed by rapid air cooling using a large fan at room temperature (∼25 °C). Cross-sections of the welded joints were mechanically ground with SiC paper (800-2400 grit), then polished using 3, 1, and 0.25 µm diamond suspensions, and finally polished with a 0.25 µm colloidal silica suspension. Processing Text: The test material is a 0.8 mm thick solution-treated Cu-0.98Ni-0.24 P (wt%) sheet produced by Ningbo Boway Alloy Materials Co., Ltd. The sheet was cold-rolled using a rolling mill to achieve a deformation of 75 %. After cold rolling, the sheet was subjected to aging treatments. The aging temperatures were 400 °C, 450 °C, 500 °C, and 550 °C, with holding times of 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 6, and 8 h. In the second set of experiments, the solution-treated alloy underwent a first-stage cold rolling with a deformation of 50 %, followed by aging treatments at temperatures of 400 °C, 450 °C, 500 °C, and 550 °C for holding times of 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 6, and 8 h. Following this, a second-stage cold rolling was performed with another 50 % deformation, ensuring the total deformation matched that of the R1 process. A second-stage aging treatment was then carried out at temperatures of 400 °C, 450 °C, and 500 °C for holding times of 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 6, and 8 h. Room temperature tensile tests were completed using an RDL10 electronic creep relaxation testing machine produced by Zhongji Testing Equipment Co., Ltd. All mechanical tests were conducted in accordance with the GB/T 228.1-2021 standard "Metallic Materials—Tensile Testing—Part 1: Method of Test at Room Temperature", the yield strength was determined using the 0.2% offset method. Processing Text: A series of 10 mm diameter bars were cut from the ingot using an electric discharge wire cutting machine (DK7735) as the initial sample for the whole process. A number of as-cast 7075 Al alloy bars were placed in a vacuum high temperature heating furnace (SGL-1700C). In order to reduce microstructure inhomogeneity and then improve room temperature deformability, a double-stage homogenization (DTH) 738K-24h+748K-4h was conducted on as-cast 7075 Al alloy, based on previous studies [30,41]. Subsequently, water quenching to room temperature was used and the sample transfer time was controlled within 3 s to avoid the effect of air cooling, resulting in supersaturated solid solution (SSS). Then, 7075 Al alloy was immediately placed into ECAP dies with inner angles of 120° and outer angles of 30°. At room temperature, the alloy was deformed by one ECAP pass using a four-column hydraulic press (YT-160T) at a descending rate of 3 mm/s, with each pass resulting in an effective strain of 0.622. Molybdenum disulfide (MoS 2) was used as a lubricant throughout the process to reduce the friction between the specimen and the mold. After ECAP, 7075 Al alloy was placed in CU dies and formed into fasteners, called ECAPed-CU samples. Finally, the ECAPed-CU samples of 7075 Al alloy fasteners were put into a vacuum high-temperature heating furnace (SGL-1700C) to be artificially aged (AA) at temperatures of 353 K, 383 K and 423 K at a heating rate of 283 K/min and for times of 10, 20, 60, 120 and 180 min, respectively, with specific experimental parameters and expressions shown in Table 2. The electrical discharge wire cutting machine (DK7735) was used to prepare dog-bone tensile specimens measuring 30 mm ×6 mm ×1.2 mm (with a gauge length of 10 mm) from the specimens. The specimens were ground and polished using sandpaper and polishing paste, followed by cleaning and drying using an ultrasonic cleaning machine (G-040S). The specimens were then subjected to uniaxial tensile testing at room temperature using a universal tensile testing machine (JVJ-50s) at a rate of 5 mm/min. Each specimen was tested three times to ensure the accuracy of the results. The microhardness test specimens were ground and polished to a mirror finish on a mechanical polishing machine (MP-2B). The prepared samples were subjected to microhardness testing at room temperature using a microhardness tester (MHVD-1000IS) with a load of 300gf and a holding time of 15 s. Each sample was tested 12 points independently, removing 4 points that were significantly different and taking the average of the remaining 8 points as the microhardness value to ensure the accuracy of the microhardness. DSC test samples were cut from the ECAPed-CU specimens using a wire cutter (DK7733). The samples were then machined on a mechanical grinding and polishing machine (MP-2B) to obtain a sample of approximately 3 mg. The specimens were placed in a differential scanning calorimetry (METTLER TOLEDO, DSC 3) and heated linearly in the range 303-773 K under nitrogen protection at a constant heating rate of 283 K/min to determine the order of phase precipitation during subsequent aging. X-ray diffraction (XRD, Smartlab3KW) was used to identity phases characterization and determine the dislocation density of all samples. After surface finishing, the samples were irradiated with a Cu kα (λ = 1.5418 Å) and the diffraction signals of 10-90° were collected from the samples at a scan rate of 5°/min and a step size of 0.02° at 40 KV and 30 mA. The microstructure evolution of the samples in terms of dislocations, grain boundaries and precipitation phase changes in different treatments were observed using transmission electron microscopy (TEM, JEM-F200) and high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM). Meanwhile, the samples were observed by dark field imaging using high-angle annular dark field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM). For TEM observation, the samples were first mechanically ground to 60μm, followed by further ion thinning of the samples using an ion thinning system (GATAN) in an argon ion atmosphere. Processing Text: Samples were manufactured using an MLab 200R L-PBF machine (GE Additive) equipped with a 200 W Nd:YAG fibre laser (wavelength: 1064 nm) with a 75 µm spot size. Nine parameter sets were trailed with four samples for each parameter (totalling 36 samples simultaneously fabricated). The specimens had dimensions of 10 × 10 × 25 mm 3( X-Y-Z, where Zis the build direction (BD)) and were fabricated with a support structure on top of a 316 L stainless steel build plate. An alternating 90° rotation of the laser raster direction was employed between build layers. A 25 µm layer thickness ( t) and 75 µm hatch spacing ( h) were maintained for all specimens. The following process parameters were applied: laser power ( P) between 95 and 195 W and scanning speed ( s) between 360 and 860 mm/s. A Pof 195 W and sof 860 mm/s led to the highest material density of 99.90 ± 0.07 %, as measured by using Archimedes’ principle. The middle section of the samples was sectioned using an Accutom-50 diamond saw (Struers) to prepare cross-sections in two planes: the XZplane (parallel to BD) and the XYplane (perpendicular to BD). Specimens from the XZplane were mounted in epoxy and mechanically polished to a 0.25 μm surface finish, using a combination of silicon carbide papers followed by diamond suspension polishing. Subsequently, the samples were further polished using a VibroMet 2 vibratory polisher (Buehler) with 0.04 µm colloidal silica surface finish followed by broad Ar-ion surface polishing using a PECS II system (Gatan) at 4 kV. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) was performed using a Spectra and Themis-Z (Thermo Fisher Scientific), both operated at an accelerating voltage of 300 kV, coupled with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDXS). Atom probe tomography (APT) was conducted using an INVIZO 6000 (CAMECA) equipped with a dual 257.5 nm UV laser system. Site-specific APT specimens were also lifted-out from polished EBSD specimens via standard APT lift-out techniques in the Helios G4 PFIB SEM. APT was performed at ∼50 K and ∼2.6 × 10 -11Torr. A laser power of 400 pJ and laser pulse repetition rate of 200 kHz with a detection rate of 2 % were used. Processing state: as-built; Tensile test result

Processing Text: The Ti-5411 alloy ingot was melted with high-purity sponge Ti, Zr, and Mo, Cr, V bulk raw materials by vacuum arc melting furnace. To ensure the uniformity of the composition, the ingot was turned over and melted under magnetic stirring 8 times. The β phase transformation temperature ( Tβ) of the Ti-5411 alloy was analyzed by metallographic method to be about ∼745°C. The ingot was processed in two stages, the first stage of which was multi-pass hot rolling at 800 °C to 4 mm thick plates. In the second stage, the 4 mm-thick hot-rolled sheet was kept at 800 °C for 20 min and then water-cooled, while the 0.8 mm thick sheet was obtained by multi-pass unidirectional cold rolling. The total deformation of the cold-rolled sheet was 80%. The cold-rolled sheet was held at 780 °C for 20 min and then water-quenched to obtain the microstructure of the equiaxial β-phase. The sheet was placed in a tube furnace (argon atmosphere) to prevent oxidation of Ti-5411 alloy during heat treatment. Uniaxial tensile tests were implemented on a universal testing machine (GOTECH, AI-7000-LAU10) at a tensile speed of 0.5 mm/min. In-situ tensile tests were implemented at tensile speed of 0.033 mm/min on a Gatan loading system accessory with maximum load capacity of 1800 N installed on SEM (Zeiss 300). The in-situ tensile specimens were mechanically and electrolytically polished to remove residual stresses and improve the surface quality of the tensile specimens. Electropolishing was carried out at a voltage of 40 V for 45 s in an electrolytic polishing solution at −20 °C. The electrolytic polishing solution was formulated with 5% perchloric acid, 60% methanol and 35% n-butanol (volume proportion). Metastable β titanium alloy; Water-quenched state

Processing Text: FeCoNiCr high-entropy alloys (HEAs) are often prepared by casting, resulting in a coarse-grained (CG) microstructure and low yield strength. The synthesis of FeCoNiCr HEA through mechanical alloying (MA) and spark plasma sintering (SPS) results in finer grain size, leading to high yield strength but low fracture strain. FeCoNiCr HEAs are often prepared by conventional casting, casting after purifying melts with B 2O 3, and occasionally by severe plastic deformation (SPD). Conventional casting of FeCoNiCr HEAs produces grain sizes ranging from 30 to 500 μm, yielding low strength (202 MPa) but high fracture strain (> 60 %). SPD processing of FeCoNiCr HEA can decrease the grain size to 50 μm, resulting in higher yield strength of 280 MPa and a lower fracture strain of 35 %. Casting after purifying melts with B 2O 3 causes supercooling, leading to a finer grain size of 7-20 μm, higher yield strength of 455 MPa, and a lower fracture strain of 16.8 %. FeCoNiCr HEA synthesized by MA and SPS techniques (MA-SPSed-FeCoNiCr HEA) leads to a grain size of 0.8 μm and significantly higher yield strength of 657 MPa. FeCoNiCr HEA containing 5 wt% nanoscale Y 2O 3 particles synthesized by MA and SPS techniques can even result in a grain size of 0.1 μm, leading to extremely high yield strength (1754 MPa), albeit with a low fracture-strain (5.8 %). CG FeCoNiCr (in equimolar ratio) HEAs were made via arc-melting a mixture of four elemental metal fragments. CG FeCoNiCr HEA was remelted five times to ensure uniformity and was made into an ingot weighing approx. 30 g in an electric arc furnace (Shenyang Jinyan JVAM-1B). Powders of FeCoNiCr HEA were prepared by mechanically alloying elemental Fe, Co, Ni, and Cr powders in a SPEX 8000D shaker mill for 24 h. A CS-IB cubic-anvil press was used to consolidate the as-milled powders into a bulk specimen for 30 min at 1000 °C and 4 GPa pressure. Condition: room temperature; Microstructure: coarse-grained (CG); Processing technique: arc-melting

Processing Text: The as-cast ingot with a nominal composition of Ni 61Al 17Cr 10Fe 10Mo 2(at%) was prepared by vacuum arc melting of pure metals (purity >99.95 wt%) in a titanium-containing high-purity argon atmosphere. To ensure chemical composition uniformity, each ingot was remelted at least six times before being cast into a water-cooled copper mold using a suction casting method. Initially, the cast ingots were polished to remove the surface contamination layer and then processed into rods with a diameter of 96 mm. The rods were subsequently subjected to rotational RS using a four-die swaging machine, reducing the diameter from 96 mm to 91 mm at high temperature without requiring intermediate annealing. Ultimately, the samples experienced a 10 % reduction in total cross-sectional area through the swaging process. Prior to testing, the surface of each sample underwent coarse grinding, fine grinding, and mechanical polishing until a mirror-like finish was achieved. TEM samples were prepared by wire cutting into discs with a diameter of 6 mm and a thickness of 0.5 mm, followed by grinding to 60 μm. Each sample for EBSD characterization was first mechanically polished for 4 hours, followed by further polishing with a silica suspension at room temperature. Processing Text: The alloy ingot was fabricated by arc melting and 6 times of melting were done repeatedly to guarantee compositional homogeneity. The raw materials for melting are Ti ingot (99.99 %), Nb thin plate (99.99 %), Sn shot (99.99 %) and TiO 2 powder (99.99 %). The as-produced ingot is button-like and its weight loss after melting is less than 0.1 % and can be negligible, indicating the good quality of the ingot produced. The button-like ingot was encapsulated in a quartz tube in which a vacuum atmosphere of 1.5 × 10 −5 torr was produced. Homogenization heat treatment was carried out at 1000 °C for 2 h. After homogenization heat treatment, the quartz tube was broken into ice water quickly for quenching. The homogenized ingot was processed into a sheet by cold-rolling with a reduction ratio of 98 % in thickness. The as-rolled sheets were encapsulated in a quartz tube vacuumed to 1.5 × 10 −5 torr for solution treatment (900 °C/30 min), after which ice-water quenching was accomplished by cracking the quartz tube. Condition: solution-treated (900 °C/30 min); Phase: single β phase; Microstructure: Goss texture, nanodomains in β matrix

Processing Text: Al 0.7CoCrFeNi (at%) HEA ingot was prepared by levitation melting. In this study, pure metals of Al, Co, Cr, Fe and Ni (purity ≥ 99.9 %, wt%) were used as raw materials and loaded into a vacuum levitation melting furnace. Prior to the melting, the furnace was evacuated to 1 × 10⁻³ Pa to remove gases and volatile impurities from the alloy. During the whole melting process, the melt was electromagnetically stirred to ensure a uniform distribution of heat and thus the composition. Then the melt was cast into a graphite mold with dimensions of 200 mm × 200 mm × 25 mm. The alloy was set into a resistance heating furnace (SX-G 1300 ℃) holding at 1000 °C for isothermal and at 1050 °C to 1250 °C for non-isothermal treatments, followed by water quenching. Flat dog-bone-shape specimens with a dimension of 49 mm (in length) × 9 mm (in width) × 1 mm (in thickness) were cut by wire electric discharge machining for the test of mechanical properties. The tensile tests were carried out through a universal testing machine (Shimadzu AGX-V 100 KN) at room temperature with a nominal strain rate of 1 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹. The Vickers hardness was measured using a micro-hardness tester (3S-1000QZ) with a loading force of 500 g/N for 10 s. Prior to microstructure characterizations, HEA samples were prepared by the standard metallographic method. After grinding with SiC sandpaper up to 7000 grit and polishing with diamond paste. The X-ray diffractometer (XRD, D/max-2200) and the scanning electron microscopy (SEM-5000Pro) were employed to examine the microstructure and composition. The XRD analysis was performed using Cu Kα radiation (λ = 1.5418 Å, 40 kV, 40 mA) with the range (2θ) of 20° to 100° at a scanning speed of 8°/min, and a step size of 0.026°. To observe the microstructure, samples were etched with aqua regia (HCl: HNO₃ = 3:1) and then characterized utilizing the SEM equipped with an energy-dispersive (EDS) detector, operating in the back-scatter electron (BSE) mode at a working voltage of 15 kV and a working distance of 6 mm. The phase volume fraction, average lamellar thickness, and precipitation phase size were assessed using Image-J software. The isothermal treatment at 1000 °C indicates that the prolonged holding time promotes the transformation of the BCC/B2 phases to the FCC phase. The heat-treatment duration was strictly regulated to be within 3 h. In the initial stage of exploring the combined effects of the lamellar structure and B2 precipitates, the temperature interval for non-isothermal heat treatment was precisely set at 50 °C. Subsequently, with the intention of accentuating the influence of the lamellar-strengthening effect on the mechanical properties by highlighting the variances in the morphological distribution of the lamellar phase, the temperature interval was further augmented to 100 °C. Condition: as-cast; Heat treatment: isothermal at 1000 °C (S1)
Processing Word: Condition: as-cast; Heat treatment: isothermal at 1000 °C (S1)

Processing Text: The raw materials were placed in a vacuum tungsten arc melting furnace, where Ti-24Nb-4Zr-8Sn-xN (x = 0, 0.05, 0.1 and 0.2 wt%) alloy ingots were prepared under the protection of argon. To achieve thorough and uniform mixing of the alloy components, the ingots underwent more than six repeated smelting cycles with a stirring current of 5 A. Subsequently, the alloy sample underwent cold rolling with 90 % deformation and was annealed at 900 °C for 10 min. All the samples were cut to a specified size to characterize the microstructure. The samples were ground using sandpaper ranging from 180# to 2000#, and then the surfaces of these samples were polished with an Al 2O 3 suspension. Finally, the samples were etched with a solution (5 mL of HF + 15 mL of HNO 3 + 80 mL of H 2O). The ingots were inverted and remelted five times to ensure chemical homogeneity, followed by casting into a copper mold with dimensions of 8 × 20 × 60 mm 3. The as-cast ingot was solution-treated at 1150 °C for 2 h, followed by water cooling. The homogenized ingot was cold rolled (CR) with a total thickness reduction of 86 %. Then the CR sheet was partially annealed at 700 °C for 1 h followed by air cooling. The reason for choosing the partial annealing temperature of 700 °C is shown in Supplementary Text 2. Dog-bone samples with a gage length of 15 mm, a width of 2 mm and a thickness of 1 mm were machined along the rolling direction by using a wire electrical discharge machine. Interrupted tensile tests at specific strains of 5 % and 15 % were also performed on the PR sample to evaluate microstructural evolution upon tension. TEM slices were cut from undeformed and deformed samples, mechanically grounded to ∼30μm, and then twin-jet polished in a solution of 5 vol% perchloric acid and 95 vol% ethanol at around −20 °C. The tensile samples were mechanically polished to 2000 grit size before tests to eliminate defects and impurities on the surface of the samples. Interrupted tensile tests at specific strains of 5 % and 15 % were also performed on the PR sample to evaluate microstructural evolution upon tension. TEM slices were cut from undeformed and deformed samples, mechanically grounded to ∼30μm, and then twin-jet polished in a solution of 5 vol% perchloric acid and 95 vol% ethanol at around −20 °C. Material Name: Al-3.8Ni-0.5Cr eutectic alloy with 0.15 at % Zr
Processing Text: An alloy with a nominal composition of Al-3.80Ni-0.50Cr-0.15Zr (all in atomic %) was prepared by arc melting constituent elements with 4 N purity (99.99 at %) under an argon atmosphere at a vacuum level of ∼10⁻⁵ mbar. The alloy was melted eight times, with flipping after each cycle to prevent Zr segregation. The molten button was chill cast into a split copper mold to produce a rod with a diameter of 3 mm and a length of 80 mm. After confirming the absence of solute microsegregation and verifying the bulk alloy composition using wavelength dispersive spectroscopy (WDS) in a field emission gun (FEG) electron probe microanalyzer (EPMA, JEOL JXA-8530F) operating at 30 kV, the cast alloy was sliced into small pieces and subjected to aging heat treatment at 375 °C and 400 °C for various durations, followed by water quenching. Samples for microscopic characterization and hardness measurements were prepared according to standard metallographic protocols, with initial polishing using SiC papers of varying grit sizes (1000 to 3000), followed by final polishing on a vibratory polisher (VibroMet™ 2, Buehler) using 50 nm colloidal silica. TEM samples were prepared by manually grinding 3 mm discs to a thickness of 30 µm, followed by argon ion milling using a precision ion polishing system (PIPS II, Gatan) to obtain electron-transparent regions. The preliminary aging response was confirmed by measuring the Vickers hardness (HV) using a microhardness tester (Future Tech, FM-800) at a 100 g load and a dwell time of 10 s. The yield strength of the peak-aged alloys was evaluated using a screw-driven uniaxial testing machine (Zwick/Roell) at a strain rate of 10⁻³ s⁻¹ and test temperatures of 25 °C (room temperature, RT), 200 °C, and 250 °C. The samples were preheated for 10 min to ensure thermal homogeneity in both the specimen and testing system. Compression test specimens, with dimensions of 3 mm diameter and a height of 5 to 6 mm (1.5 ≤ h⁄ d≥ 2.0), were prepared from the peak-aged rod. To investigate the deformation mechanism at RT, the sample was plastically compressed by 1.2 %. Temperature: 25 °C (room temperature, RT); Condition: peak-aged (375 °C for 20 h)
Processing Word: Temperature: 25 °C (room temperature, RT); Condition: peak-aged (375 °C for 20 h)

Processing Text: Maraging 250 steel wire was used as a feedstock material and remotely fed under the electrode to coincide with the plasma arc during printing. Before printing bulk samples, 12 single tracks were printed as a preliminary study to identify optimized printing parameters. The optimized printing parameters were set as: welding current 182 A, voltage 30 V, welding speed 5 mm/s and wire feed speed 50 mm/s. During printing, argon (99.99% purity) was applied as both shielding and welding gas. Using these parameters, thin walls of about 80 mm (length) × 20 mm (height) × 10 mm (width) with a layer thickness of 1.2 mm were printed with different interlayer dwell times of 0 min, 1 min, and 3 min to exploit the effects of thermal history on the microstructure evolution and mechanical properties of the printed maraging 250 steels. By introducing a dwell time between adjacent layers, the maraging 250 steel is cooled below the martensite start temperature, triggering thermally-driven martensitic transformation during the printing process. Thermal cycling during subsequent layer deposition results in the formation of reverted austenite which shows a refined microstructure and induces elemental segregation between martensite and reverted austenite. The reverted austenite is metastable during deformation, leading to strain-induced martensitic transformation under loading. Specifically, a 3 min interlayer dwell time produces a maraging 250 steel with approximately 8% reverted austenite, resulting in improved work hardening via martensitic transformation induced plasticity during deformation. Meanwhile, the higher cooling rate and refined prior austenite grains lead to substantially refined martensitic grains (by approximately fivefold) together with an increased dislocation density. With 3 min interlayer dwell time, the yield strength of the printed maraging 250 steel increases from 836 MPa to 990 MPa, and the uniform elongation is doubled from 3.2% to 6.5%. This intermittent deposition strategy during PAW-DED allows us to achieve an outstanding strength-ductility synergy that outperforms conventional wrought and other additively manufactured maraging steel counterparts. Processing Text: The commercially available TC4 titanium alloy bars in an annealed state with the dimensions of Ф50 mm× 200 mm were used in this experiment. The annealing process was heating at 750 ℃ for 1.5 h and then air-cooled. The rectangular billets with dimensions of 35 mm × 35 mm × 37 mm were cut from the centre of the long bar for the subsequent MDF process. The relationship between DRX behavior and strain rate was determined by hot compression experiment. The deformation temperature was selected to be 940 ℃, 880 ℃ and 820 ℃. MDF was conducted on a four-column hydraulic press. The sample was rapidly heated in the furnace to the deformation temperature and then was soaked at this temperature for 5 min. Each forging pass was involved in three steps, and the forging axis was rotated by 90° step by step (i.e. Z to X to Y to Z). The true strain for each step was 0.22, calculated from ln(h 0/h 1), where h 0and h 1were the blank height values before and after forging, respectively. Therefore, the cumulative strain per pass was approximately 0.66. The samples were re-heated in a resistance furnace to the deformation temperature after each forging pass to compensate for the temperature loss during the MDF process. The microstructures of the alloys were characterized by optical microstructure (OM, Leitz MM-6), X-ray diffraction (XRD, D/MAX2500PC), scanning electron microscope (SEM, FEI Quanta 200), electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM, Titan G2 F20). The samples for OM observation were etched in a solution of 0.5 ml hydrofluoric acid, 1 ml nitric acid and 25 ml deionised water. TEM and EBSD foils were firstly ground to 80 µm and then further prepared with a twin-jet electropolisher (a solution of 6 % perchloric acid+34 % normal butanol+60 % methyl alcohol, vol%). Mechanical properties of the alloys were characterized by tensile tests. The room temperature tensile tests were conducted on an Instron 3369 electronic universal testing machine at a constant cross-head speed of 1 mm/ min. After 2 passes of MDF at 880 °C with the strain rate of 13 s−1; Microstructure: fine uniform equiaxed α phase with a mean grain size of 3.2 μm

Processing Text: In the aviation sector, C-103 alloy and Nb521 alloy are ideal materials for manufacturing components like thrust engines and jet nozzles. A Rikagu smartlab X XRD instrument was used to collect the XRD patterns of the feedstock and as-modified powders. The wavelength of the X-ray was 0.154 nm, and the measurement angle was from 20° to 90°. A Zeiss Merlin SEM (scanning electron microscopy) was used to capture the powder morphology before and after the modification. The Imaging mode was the secondary electron mode, and the accelerating voltage was 5 kV. A Horiba EMGA-820 oxygen & nitrogen analyzer was used to measure the oxygen content of the feedstock and as-modified powders. The relative density of bulk samples fabricated by laser powder bed fusion with the as-modified powder were measured using Archimedes’s method, and their mechanical properties were obtained with a tensile test machine. Processing Text: Raw Cu, Cr, Fe, Ni, Al and Ti blocks with purity>99.8 wt % were selected to prepare the 3.5 kg CuCrFeNiTi0.8Al1.2 HEA via magnetic levitation induction melting under high purity argon atmosphere. The purity of the alloy is guaranteed by removing the oxide scale on the surface of the crude material and cleaning it in acetone by ultrasonic wave for 20 min. The melting process was repeated 4 times to achieve chemical homogeneity. In order to better study the organizational transformation behavior and solidification process during annealing, the obtained specimen was then annealed at 800 °C and 1000 °C for 24 h, followed by water quenching. Upon the introduction of annealing process, significant grain refinement was achieved. Additionally, the increase of annealing temperature led to the presence of secondary precipitated particles within the alloy. The annealed CuCrFeNiTi0.8Al1.2 HEA displays similar microstructure compared to the as-cast state. Following annealed at 800 °C, there are much more precipitates generated in the grains and several structures transformed from spherical to short-rod. Besides, note a great deal of micron-particles are precipitated from matrix. As increase the annealing temperature to 1000 °C, relatively large quantities of secondary nano-particles precipitated from α phase not just the micro-particle from DR matrix. Room temperature compressive properties and Vickers hardness of CuCrFeNiTi0.8Al1.2 HEAs were tested to study the mechanical properties. Processing state: as-cast
Processing Word: Processing state: as-cast
