Processing Text: The die casting component of the SA42 alloy was fabricated using a horizontal cold chamber die casting machine (TOYO/BD-350V5). The chemical composition range of the SA42 alloy was determined to be Mg-(4.22 ± 0.36)Sm-(2.17 ± 0.23)Al using an inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometer (ICP-OES). The processing parameters for the die casting component are detailed in Table 3. A tensile test was performed using at least three tensile bars with a gauge length of 55 mm and a diameter of 6.4 mm. The tests were conducted at room temperature with a cross-head separation rate of 1 mm/min. At least three circular disc specimens with a diameter of 5.8 mm and a thickness of 2 mm were extracted from the red rectangular box of the tensile bar, followed by carbon coating on their surface, and their thermal diffusivity was measured using the laser flash method. A densitometer was employed to determine the specimens' density utilizing Archimedes principle. A cylindrical specimen with a diameter of 6.4 mm and a thickness of 2 mm was extracted from the orange rectangular box of the tensile bar for utilization in scanning electron microscope (SEM), wavelength-dispersive spectrometer (WDS), electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), and X-ray diffractometer (XRD) analysis. SEM observations were performed at a voltage of 13 kV. WDS analyses were performed in the spot mode, under an accelerating voltage of 10 kV and a probe current of 10 nA. EBSD was also carried out on the SEM at 20 kV with a step size of 1.5 μm. In detail, the average grain size was evaluated using EBSD after the specimens were mechanically ground, polished, and etched with a special etchant for Mg alloys (29.4 g picric acid, 41 ml water, 50 ml acetic acid and 350 ml ethanol) for 5 s. The volume fraction of secondary phases was quantified using the Image-Pro Plus (IPP) software based on a minimum of three backscattered electron (BSE) images. The solute atoms present in the α-Mg matrix were analyzed using WDS. The concentration of solute atoms was derived from the mean values of ten randomly selected WDS measurements obtained from the α-Mg matrix. For phase analyses, XRD was performed. From the XRD patterns, the lattice parameters for α-Mg matrix were determined by Rietveld analysis using the MAUD program. High-quality diffraction patterns were recorded over an angular range of 10° to 90° with a step rate of 1°/min. High-pressure die casting (HPDC) Mg alloy Mg-4Sm-2Al; Exhibits improvements of 17.4% in yield strength compared to AE44

Unlike conventional rolling processes, this experiment employed a large reduction with fewer passes to achieve high strain rate deformation. The ultra-low temperature rolling process is conducted as follows: The experimental aluminum alloy sheet is immersed in liquid nitrogen for 3 min to ensure that the temperature of the aluminum sheet equilibrates with that of the liquid nitrogen. Simultaneously, liquid nitrogen is also sprayed onto the rolling mills to reduce their temperature. The aluminum sheet, now in an ultra-low temperature state, is promptly transferred into the rolling mill for rolling, with the transfer time not exceeding 0.5 s. After completing one pass of rolling, the aluminum alloy sheet is once again submerged in liquid nitrogen for cooling, and the other operational steps are consistent with those previously described. This process is repeated until the rolling experiment is completed. In this experiment, the rolling speed for ultra-low temperature rolling was set at 15 rad/s, with a roll diameter of 200 mm, resulting in a strain rate during rolling of 3.5s⁻¹. Processing Text: The material was subjected to melting in a vacuum induction furnace to yield a 50 kg ingot, followed by homogenization at 1050 °C. Subsequently, the material was forged into a 45 mm × 45 mm square bar through a process of upsetting and drawing at temperatures ranging from 1150 to 850 °C, repeated three times. Subsequent to the forging process, the material was allowed to cool in a ambient atmosphere. Cylindrical specimens (Φ3 mm × 10 mm) were extracted from the forged bar using electrical discharge machining. All the samples were austenitized at 920 °C for 2 h, and then quenched with different cooling media (water, oil, air, and furnace) to ambient temperature. Some of the water-cooling quenched specimens (Q920) were then tempered at between 560 ◦C and 700 °C. For convenience, the samples after tempering at the different temperatures of 560, 600, 640, 660, 680, and 700 °C are designated T560, T600, T640, T660, T680, and T700 respectively. After heat treatment, the specimens were processed into standard tensile samples with dimensions of Φ5 mm × 10 mm and standard Charpy V-notch impact samples with dimensions of 55 mm × 10 mm × 10 mm. They were subjected to a tensile test using a Z-150 universal testing machine and Charpy -60 °C impact test using a PIH-752H pendulum impact tester. Metallographic specimens (10 mm × 10 mm) were cut, then mechanically ground, polished, and etched with 4 % (volume fraction) nital. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) samples were prepared using a twin-jet electropolishing device. Firstly, the thickness of the thin slice specimen was reduced to less than 50 μm. Then, the specimen was punched into a 3 mm diameter disc using a punching instrument. Finally, the thin-film specimen was prepared using a twin-jet electropolishing device. The twin-jet solution contained anhydrous ethanol and 10 % (volume fraction) perchloric acid solution. Processing Text: The gas-atomized SS 310 powder supplied by Indo-MIM with the elemental composition listed in Table 1 was utilized as raw material to fabricate SLM specimens for surface quality and mechanical characterization. Before SLM fabrication, the 310 powder was kept in vacuum-drying ovens at 120°C for 2 hours to remove the volatile impurities. The test samples were built by SLM EP-M100T machine equipped with a continuous wave Ytterbium (CW Yb) fiber laser with a maximum power of 200 W, wavelength of 1.07 µm, and spot diameter of 80 µm under the shielding gas of nitrogen. The striped hatch scan pattern with a 67° rotation between each consecutive layer was chosen because it enhanced part quality. The tensile samples were prepared horizontally with respect to build direction due to their superior tensile strength. After the SLM process, the as-built samples are removed from the substrate using wire electrical discharge machining. Microstructural analysis of the SLM specimens was performed using optical microscopy (Olympus BX53M) and field emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM) (FEI Quanta 250 FEG). Elemental composition was determined using energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) in conjunction with FE-SEM. For microstructural analysis, the samples were polished using SiC grinding papers and etched by standard metallographic techniques. The SLM samples were treated with an aqua regia solution (a 1:3 mixture of nitric acid and hydrochloric acid) for 5-20 s to reveal their dendritic structure. The Vickers microhardness tester (Mitutuoyo-HB210) was used to determine the microhardness of SLM 310 specimens under 500 g load for 15 s dwell time according to ASTM E384-22. The hardness was measured on both surface PBD and surface PPBD to understand the anisotropic properties of the SLM specimen. The tensile test was performed at ambient temperature using Instron 8801 at a nominal strain rate of 10−3s−1. VED: 56 J/mm³; Laser power: 150 W; Scan speed: 750 mm/s; Fine cellular grains

Processing Text: The target nominal hypoeutectic composition of Fe–4.85Ti–0.78B (wt.%) was designed, which is equivalent to 5 vol%TiB2 (equivalent to 2.4 wt%TiB2) in an α–Fe matrix. The feedstock is a powder mixture of commercially available raw materials of gas–atomized Fe (99.99%, 15–53 μm), Ti (99.99%, 1–3 μm) and TiB2 (99.8%, 3–5 μm). Processing Text: The Zr45Ti15Nb20Ta20 RMEA fabrication process was detailed in our previous work. The as-cast samples were initially solidified at 1673 K for 2 h and subsequently aged at 773-1173 K for 6 h, 12 h, and 24 h. For ease of indicating the different heat treatments of the RMEAs, they are termed A-x-y (x = 773, 973, and 1173; y = 6, 12, and 24). The microhardness of the aged-RMEAs was measured on a Vickers hardness tester (MHVS-1000AT) with an applied load of 0.98 N and a holding time of 15 s. High-temperature uniaxial compression tests were conducted using the Gleeble 3800 thermo-simulation machine, with cylindrical specimens measuring 8 mm in diameter and 12 mm in height. Compression tests were conducted at a constant stain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1 at 1273 K, with a true stain of 0.69 (50 pct reduction in the height). The room temperature tests were performed using a universal testing machine (Instron-5582, Instron, USA) at an initial strain rate of 10−3 s−1, stopping when the cylindrical height was reduced by 50% or when the compression sample failed to fracture. The phase constituents of as-homogenized and aged RMEAs were analyzed using X-ray diffraction (XRD, Bruker d8 X-ray Diffractometer) with Cu-Kα radiation. Diffraction angles between 20° and 100° (2θ) were collected with a step size of approximately 10° per minute. The microstructure of specimens before and after compression was examined using a field emission scanning electron microscope (SEM; XL-30FEG, Holland) equipped with an electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) and energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) detector. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) (Talos F200X) was employed for additional microstructural characterization using specimens prepared by ion milling. Condition: room temperature; Processing state: aged at 773 K; Microstructure: high-density nanocubic structure formed by spinodal decomposition

Processing Text: The Iron-based MEA was fabricated using a vacuum arc melting furnace, and each raw material was sourced from pure commercial elements with a purity of at least 99.9 %. The master alloy was turned upside down five times during melting to ensure chemically homogenized alloy. During the melting process, the alloy was melted upside down five times to ensure a uniform chemical composition. The as-cast ingots were sealed in an evacuated quartz tube, homogenized at 1150 °C for 24 h, and then water quenched to room temperature. The homogenized ingots were subsequently cold-rolled to 87 % reduction in thickness using laboratory-scale rolling equipment. To obtain various grain sizes of the MEA, the tensile specimens were sealed in a quartz tube and annealed at different temperatures for various durations. The specimens were annealed at 950 °C for 100 s, 25 min, and 1 h, respectively. Additionally, in order to achieve a larger grain size within a shorter annealing time, some specimens were subjected to annealing at 1050 °C for 5 h. TEM specimens were mechanically polished using 1200-grit sandpaper to reduce the thickness to less than 100 mm and then jet-polished by an Automatic Twin-Jet Electropolisher (FISCHIONE, Model 110, applied voltage: 27 V). Tensile tests were conducted using a 100-kN-capacity universal Material Testing System (MTS, Model: 810) at room temperature (25 °C) and cryogenic temperature (−100 °C & −196 °C), with a constant strain rate of 0.001 s −1. Condition: Room Temperature; Phase: FCC; Microstructure: Dislocation + Deformation twin

Processing Text: The alloy chosen in this work was a NiCoCr-based MEA with the nominal composition Ni 51Cr 22Co 20Mo 3.5Ti 2.5Al 1(at.%). Prior to rolling, the material was solution treated at 1150 °C for 30 min followed by water quenching. Subsequently, the material was rolled to a 50% reduction in thickness to achieve the high density of nano-twins in grain interiors. The rolled sample was then annealed at 700 °C for 8, 50, 100 and 300 h, respectively. Ageing treatments resulted in the sufficient precipitation of γʹ phase, and the volume fraction of γʹ precipitate was kept at ∼14%. The γʹ-size slightly increased from 19 nm to 26 nm during the 300-h ageing. High-density nano-twins were preserved after ageing at 700 °C for up to 300 h, which demonstrated the superior thermal stability of nano-twins in the NiCoCr alloy. No recrystallized grains were observed in samples with prolonged ageing treatments up to 300 h, indicating the superior thermal stability of nano-twins and γ′ nanoprecipitates. Processing Text: The maraging steel employed in this study was Fe-18Ni-8.5Co-5Mo-0.7Ti-0.2Al (wt.%). The steel was produced using a vacuum induction melting furnace and cast into ingots with a diameter of 50 mm and a weight of 2 kg. Before melting, the furnace chamber was evacuated to 10−3Pa and filled with 0.05 MPa of high-purity argon as a shielding gas. The steel ingot was remelted five times to ensure uniform distribution of the alloying elements and subsequently homogenized at 1100 °C for 2 h to eliminate compositional segregation. Specimens for testing and observation were subjected to two different heat treatments. The first heat treatment process was solid solution treatment (SST) at 840 °C for 1 h, followed by single aging treatment (SAT) at 480 °C for 4 h. The second heat treatment process was SST at 840 °C for 1 h, followed by aging at 370 °C for 2 h (DAT-1) and at 480 °C for 4 h (DAT-2), which was denoted by duplex aging treatment (DAT). The heat treatment processes used to produce the SAT and DAT samples in this work are displayed in Fig. 1. The dog-bone shaped tensile specimens with a gauge length of 20 mm and a gauge diameter of 3 mm were machined from heat-treated samples. Room temperature tensile tests were conducted on the Instron 5969 testing machine with a laser extensometer at a strain rate of 1 × 10−3s−1. More than three independent tensile tests were performed for each sample. The fracture toughness was assessed by ASTM Standard E1820 using compact tensile C(T) specimens with a thickness of B= 4 mm and a width of W= 8 mm. All specimen surfaces were ground and polished to enable the measurement of crack length using a Leica DM4 long-distance optical microscope. Before the fracture toughness measurement, all the C(T) specimens were fatigue pre-cracked to a crack length with 0.45 W< a <0.55 Wrange using an Instron E300 electro-dynamic test instrument at a frequency of 40 Hz with a load ratio Fmin/ Fmaxof 0.1. The in-situ synchrotron experiments with a gauge size of 20 × 4 × 0.4 mm3were performed at Beamline BL22XU in Spring-8, Japan. The wavelength of the high-energy X-ray beam was 0.4131 Å. The beam size was 0.2 × 0.2 mm2. The sample-to-detector distance was 207.6 mm. A uniaxial tensile machine (Yonekura, Osaka, Japan) with a maximum loading of 2 kN was utilized for the tensile test, and the tensile strain rate was 1 × 10−3s−1. The diffraction profiles (2-D Debye rings) were recorded during the tensile deformation of the samples using a high-speed CCD camera with a dwell time for each profile of 1 s. Then, the recorded images were analyzed using Image J software. X-ray diffraction (XRD) characterization was employed on a Bruker D8 X diffractometer. Data collection was performed using Cu-Kαradiation in the 2θrange of 30-100° at a scan step interval of 0.02°. The microstructure and fracture topography were observed using the Tescan Clara S8151 scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS). Simultaneously, electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) mapping was conducted using the Tescan Clara S8151 SEM equipped with a fully automatic Oxford Instruments Aztec 2.0 EBSD system (Channel 5 software). The operating voltages of SEM and EBSD were 20 kV and 10 kV, and the scanning step size of EBSD was 0.05 μm. The EBSD sample was mechanically polished and electropolished in an electrolyte of 95 vol% glacial acetic acid and 5 vol% perchloric acid at −25 °C and 30 V. The transmission electron microscope (TEM) observations were conducted in an FEI-Tecnai G2 F20 S-TWIN microscope operating at 200 kV. The samples for TEM characterization were prepared by mechanical polishing down to a thickness of 50 μm and then punching them into discs with a diameter of 3 mm. Finally, the discs were electropolished by twin-jet electro-polishing in an electrolyte of 10 vol% perchloric acid and 90 vol% glacial acetic acid performed at −30 °C and 20 V. The Mo-enriched particles precipitated after solid solution treatment due to the low solubility and diffusion rate at low temperatures. The aging treatment conducted at 370 °C enhances the density of the Mo-enriched particles and inhibits the formation of Ni3Ti. The pre-formed precipitates act as heterogeneous nucleation sites for Ni3Ti during aging at 480 °C, increasing the nucleation rate and reducing the size. As aging continues, Mo segregates to the interface of Ni3Ti and the matrix, inhibiting the growth of Ni3Ti and forming Fe7Mo2 precipitates. Condition: Room Temperature; Microstructure: Well-regulated precipitates including Ni3Ti and Fe7Mo2; Processing state: Duplex aging treatment

Processing Text: A Cu-4Ti-0.5Cr-0.5 Mg alloy, specifically designed to achieve superior strength and conductivity, was subjected to pre-aging, cold rolling, and final aging to improve its mechanical and electrical characteristics. Cu-4Ti-0.5Cr-0.5 Mg (wt. %) ingots measuring 120 × 150 × 25 mm were produced by casting pure copper, titanium, magnesium, and chromium in an intermediate frequency furnace. After addressing surface defects, the ingot underwent hot rolling at 830 °C, reducing its thickness from 6.7 mm to 2 mm. Subsequently, the hot-rolled samples of the Cu-4Ti-0.5Cr-0.5 Mg alloy were subjected to solid-solution treatment at 900 °C for 240 min and quenched in water to obtain a supersaturated solid solution (ST). The first group was pre-aged at 450 °C for different durations (referred to as the SA group). Subsequently, the ingot was cold rolled with a total deformation of 40%. Finally, the samples were subjected to a final aging treatment at 380 °C and 450 °C for various periods (referred to as the SARA group). The second group was directly cold-rolled with a total reduction in thickness of 40% without pre-aging and ultimately aged at 400 °C and 450 °C for different times (referred to as the SRA group). Pre-aging was suggested to increase the strength and electrical conductivity of the samples prior to cold rolling. The impacts of pre-aging, cold rolling, and final aging treatment on the microstructure and mechanical performance were thoroughly examined. Through process optimization, both the strength and the electrical conductivity of the alloy were enhanced. Pre-aging, cold rolling, and final aging treatments were implemented to enhance the overall performance of the sample. Process: SARA; Temperature: 380°C; Time: 120 min
Processing Word: Process: SARA; Temperature: 380°C; Time: 120 min

Processing Text: Mg-Al-Ca alloys processed via extrusion, hot-rolling and subsequent annealing were examined, focusing on microstructures and mechanical properties. As-cast alloys were acquired by melting pure Mg and Al (purity higher than 99.9 wt%) and Mg-25%Ca master alloy at ∼700 °C in an electric resistance furnace under argon atmosphere to reduce the burn-loss rate. Stepped homogenization treatment (320 °C for 2 h, 415 °C for 3 h then 480 °C for 2 h) was conducted before extrusion. As-homogenized alloys were extruded into plates (thickness of 5 mm and width of 55 mm, the extrusion ratio is ∼20) at 400 °C under a ram speed of 0.83 m/min. Subsequently, as-extruded alloys were solutionized at 450 °C for 2 h. As-solutioned alloys were hot rolled at 300 °C to a total reduction of ∼78% (a ∼24% reduction per pass), with an inter-pass annealing at 300 °C for 10 min. At last, as-rolled alloys were annealed at 300 °C for 5 min, followed by water quenching. Processing state: annealed; Microstructure: nano-sized Al2Ca particles; Texture: weakened

Processing Text: The FeCoCrNiCu HEA ingot with an equal atomic ratio was prepared from metals with >99.9 % purity by vacuum arc smelting under argon protection. To ensure chemical homogeneity, an ingot was remelted five times and then poured into the copper mold to prepare the HEA plate. The prepared plate was further rolled at 1150 °C to reduce the thickness by 50 %, and the rolled plate was cut into a plurality of blocks with a dimension of 5 mm × 5 mm × 4 mm by the slow wire cutting. Ulteriorly, the blocks were divided into three batches for annealing at different temperatures. Specifically, the first batch of blocks was annealed at 300 °C, which was recorded as Specimen B. The second batch of blocks was annealed at 700 °C and was recorded as Specimen C. The third batch of blocks was annealed at 1100 °C and was recorded as Specimen D. All the above blocks were annealed in a vacuum tube furnace at a temperature-rise rate of 8°/min for 4 h. Meanwhile, the as-cast specimen without rolling and annealing treatments was recorded as Specimen A, as a control experimental group. Subsequently, the dynamic compression with a strain rate of 1.8 × 10 3s −1 was carried out on four types of specimens using a SHPB device. The prepared plate was further rolled at 1150 °C to reduce the thickness by 50 %, and the rolled plate was cut into a plurality of blocks with a dimension of 5 mm × 5 mm × 4 mm by the slow wire cutting. Ulteriorly, the blocks were divided into three batches for annealing at different temperatures. Specifically, the first batch of blocks was annealed at 300 °C, which was recorded as Specimen B. The second batch of blocks was annealed at 700 °C and was recorded as Specimen C. The third batch of blocks was annealed at 1100 °C and was recorded as Specimen D. All the above blocks were annealed in a vacuum tube furnace at a temperature-rise rate of 8°/min for 4 h. Meanwhile, the as-cast specimen without rolling and annealing treatments was recorded as Specimen A, as a control experimental group. Subsequently, the dynamic compression with a strain rate of 1.8 × 10 3s −1 was carried out on four types of specimens using a SHPB device. Processing Text: CBT specimens for AA6016-T4 were subjected to 2, 4, 6, 8, and 10 CBT cycles before the process was interrupted and each specimen was removed. A subsize specimen was then machined from the center of each interrupted CBT specimen and pulled in tension. The entire pre-strain process was repeated twice to produce two sets of subsize specimens which will be referred to as set 1 and set 2. CBT and ST specimens were cut from sheets of AA6016-T4 with thicknesses of 1 mm. The AA6016 alloy is heat treatable and arrived in the T4 temper state. The sheets were obtained from Commonwealth Rolled Products in 2021. The chemical compositions are shown in Table 1. The Mg and Si content in AA6016 produce Mg 2Si precipitates. The following sequence of precipitation strengthens the alloy: supersaturated solid solution → Guinier-Preston (GP) zones → needle-like β ”→ rod-like β ’+ lath-like precipitates → β + Si. These precipitates cause barriers to dislocation glide, with the β ”phases proving the most effective hardening. Optimizing parameters for AA6016-T4 was possible using one factor at a time (OFAT) testing. The maximum elongation occurs at a bend depth of 3.5 mm in RD and 4.5 mm in TD. For pull speed, the maximum elongation occurs at a value of slightly below 1.5 mm/s in RD and slightly above 1.5 mm/s in TD. To have an agreement in optimal values between the two directions the values of parameters in each direction were averaged. The result is a bend depth of 4 mm and pull speed of 1.5 mm/s as optimal parameters for AA6016-T4. The force displacement data recorded during several selected CBT tests in RD and TD compared to simple tension data is shown in Fig. 6. The optimal values of 4 mm bend depth and 1.5 mm/s pull speed are included for comparison to ST and several other CBT tests with different parameters. The CBT data shows characteristic sawtooth shapes due to the bending and unbending of the specimen as the rollers move over it. When the carriage stops to change direction after each pass there is a brief period where the specimen is not bending but is in pure tension producing the spikes seen in Fig. 6. The magnitude of bend depth and pull speed effect the tensile force required to deform the material. As bending depth increases, more plastic deformation is caused by bending rather than by tension which lowers the force output. Similarly, as pull speed decreases more deformation is caused by bending also reducing force. The forces are higher when pull speed is increased or bend depth decreased due to tension being the route of deformation. The effects of these variables allow the force on the specimen in CBT to be controlled, allowing the process to conform to any material to produce the maximum elongation. It is evident that CBT greatly increases elongation to failure of AA6016-T4. The experimental results also indicate some anisotropy between the RD and TD directions for this material. The TD direction exhibits slightly longer ETF at optimal parameters when compared to the RD direction. Fig. 10 shows the true and engineering stress strain response of the alloys obtained from specimens cut from the center of CBT specimens after CBT treatment. CBT specimens for AA6016-T4 were subjected to 2, 4, 6, 8, and 10 CBT cycles before the process was interrupted and each specimen was removed. A subsize specimen was then machined from the center of each interrupted CBT specimen and pulled in tension. The entire pre-strain process was repeated twice to produce two sets of subsize specimens which will be referred to as set 1 and set 2. The intent was to test two specimens after every pre-strain level for verification. However, the time t between testing one set of specimens to testing the other set was about three months. The specimens tested later belong to set 1, while those tested right after machining belong to set 2. The time between CBT pre-straining including machining to testing set 2 was within a month. It is known that 6xxx and 7xxx aluminum alloys are susceptible to natural aging with pre-strain influencing the aging process. The as-received specimens from 2021 did not show any natural aging effect as the natural aging processes in the alloys likely saturated. Therefore, the expectation was that the specimens will not undergo natural aging. Nevertheless, some natural aging effect on the mechanical properties is observed in the experimental results shown in Fig. 10. The observed effect shows some softening, which is the opposite of typically observed strengthening natural aging effect. Evidently the severely pre-strained structures of the alloy are unstable. The notable effect of natural aging of the pre-strained specimens in this study is seen in the decreased ultimate tensile strength (UTS) of set 1 compared to set 2. Aside from the combined pre-strain and aging effect, it is seen that the work hardening achieved via CBT results in significant increase of yield strength compared to the as-received AA6016-T4 in both RD and TD. Remarkably, yield strength exceeds 300 MPa after 10 CBT cycles, which is well above UTS. The residual ductility decreases with the increase in strength. Notably, 2 CBT cycles significantly strengthen the alloy, about 2x, but residual ductility is also appreciable, ∼10%. Fig. 12 shows the trends of plastic strain ratios r-ratios (or r-values) as a function of CBT cycles. For sheet metals the r-ratio is the resistance to thinning during plastic deformation which is important for selecting the right material for a sheet metal forming process. The r-ratio is defined as the ratio of true width strain (strain perpendicular to direction of applied load) and true thickness strain: r=εwεt. In this study DIC was used to obtain strain data in the length and width directions. Assuming volume remains constant, the equation for r ratio becomes: r=−εw(εw+εl). This equation makes it possible to calculate the r ratio without directly knowing the strain in the thickness direction. Sheet forming is impeded by pronounced anisotropic material behavior, characterized by r-ratio. It is generally understood that the anisotropy of AA sheets is mainly driven by the crystallographic texture of the sheets. However, it has been observed in 6xxx series AA that crystallographic texture by itself does not solely explain the anisotropic properties, especially for pre-strained sheets. In the present work, the r-ratio increases but then decreases with an increase in CBT cycles. The increase is likely owing to the change in texture, while the decrease could be owing to the damage accumulation. Similarly to strength, 2 CBT cycles are found to be beneficial for r-ratio. Moreover 4 CBT cycles reduce the anisotropy in r-ratio between RD and TD of AA6016-T4, which is noteworthy. After 10 CBT cycles, RD and TD

Processing Text: Fig. 11 contains the subsize ST curves recorded for AA7021-T79 which were created using the same process that was used for AA6016-T4. AA7021-T79 is much more brittle than AA6016 and was only able to be pre-strained up to 5 CBT cycles without fracture. The natural aging effect is once again observed as set 2 has higher UTS and yield strength compared to set 1. Appendix A contains numerical data for AA7021-T79. It is demonstrated that work hardening by CBT increased yield strength by over 100 MPa in both RD and TD. Evidently, the improvements are good but not as drastic as for AA6016-T4. CBT and ST specimens were cut from sheets of AA7021-T79 with thicknesses of 2.5 mm. The AA7021 alloy is heat treatable and arrived in the T79 temper state. The sheets were obtained from Commonwealth Rolled Products in 2021. The chemical compositions are shown in Table 1. Heat treatment of AA7021 (Al-Zn-Mg-Cu) results in a typical precipitation sequence as follows: supersaturated solid solution → GP zones (coherent) → η ’(metastable and semicoherent) → η (MgZn 2- incoherent resulting from over-aging). The use of AA7021 in industry is relatively small owing to its low formability at room temperature. Warm forming is a solution but increases the cost. The higher yield strength and the increased material thickness resulted in much higher forces during CBT testing. These higher bending forces resulted in the pull speed significantly changing as bend depth changed. Due to the presence of variable interactions the optimization of AA7021-T79 could not be as readily obtained using the OFAT method as it was possible for AA6016. A new method was employed that tests the effect of both variables at the same time. The Design of Experiments (DoE) method allows the experimenter to test the effect of multiple variables and their interactions on the response. The method is employed here for AA7021-T79. A 2 level, 2 variable ( 22) full factorial experiment with two center points and 1 replicate point was created using JMP statistical software for AA7021-T79 RD and TD directions. The experimental runs were set up based on two variables (bend depth and voltage) with each having two levels, a low and a high. Pull speed is not used as a variable because it is a measured response which is controlled by the voltage input to the hydraulic cylinder. Bend depth had a low of 1 mm and a high of 4 mm while voltage had a low of 1 V and a high of 9 V. The low and high levels for these variables were selected based on the machine capabilities. The purpose of low and high variable values is to be able to evaluate all possible combinations of variables in-between. For a 22 factorial experiment the area that these variable combinations form is a square with the x and y axis being the values of bend depth and voltage respectively. The area that the variable levels cover is called the experimental space. Experimental runs are carried out at combinations of low and high levels determined by the design generated in JMP. For this study the initial size of each experiment was 12 runs. After elongation data was recorded JMP can be used to analyze the results using a variety of statistical modeling techniques. A fit least squares response surface model was used to produce contour plots of the experimental space indicating regions of high elongation to failure. Additional experiments were then performed in selected regions to further close in on the optimal values of bend depth and voltage. The total number of runs to converge on optimal values for AA7021-T79 was 30 for RD and 24 for TD. The relationship between output force and the experimental variables is the same as previously explained for AA6016-T4. Evidently, the less ductile AA7021-T79 tolerated less bending and pulling speed compared to AA6016-T4. The optimal values of bend depth and pull speed were 2.5 mm and 1 mm/s for AA7021-T79. Under these conditions, the AA7021-T79 alloys elongated about 3x more compared to ST, respectively. The force displacement curves for these optimal values along with the ST test and a few other CBT tests at different combinations of bend depth and pull speed for comparisons. It is again evident that the CBT process produces much larger ETF compared to ST. It should be noted that the force displacement graphs could not be represented like those for AA6016-T4 in Fig. 6 due to the interaction between the variables. The sheet thickness and yield strength of AA7021-T79 were much higher than AA6016-T4 resulting in larger forces acting on the rollers during testing. It was discovered that these forces were large enough to slightly change the intended bend depth for a given test by moving the rollers. This created the slight variation observed between simulated and experimental results for AA7021-T79. As-received state
Processing Word: As-received state

Processing Text: Cu-0.5Cr-0.05Zr-0.15Sc alloys were prepared by vacuum melting. The hot-forged samples were cut into 5 mm thick plates and subjected to 80% reduction room-temperature rolling. Afterward, the rolled samples were vacuum aged at 350 °C-550 °C for 0-12 h. To ensure the complete dissolution of solute atoms and eliminate potential micro segregation in the as-cast structure, homogenization annealing was performed at 930 °C-990 °C (with 20 °C intervals) and at 900 °C-1050 °C (with 50 °C intervals). For the Sc-doped alloy, homogenization annealing processes of 970 °C × 2 h were applied to eliminate the micro segregation caused by Sc. Considering that some second phases precipitate after hot forging at 870 °C, both alloys were subjected to solution treatment at 1000 °C for 1 h to ensure the complete dissolution of residual second phases. For TEM sample preparation, after mechanical grinding, electro-polishing was performed at −30 °C using a solution of 70% HNO 3+ 30% CH 3OH, followed by ion milling with argon ions. EBSD samples were taken from the center of the same position on the sheet under different aging conditions, and for EBSD sample preparation, the cold-rolled samples were cut and polished on the TD plane using diamond polishing paste, followed by electro-polishing with a solution of 50% H 3PO4 acid +25% C 2H 5OH + 25% water at a current of 0.1A. Processing state: Solution treatment + 80% rolling + 450 °C × 1 h aging treatment

Processing Text: The materials were melted in a vacuum induction furnace and cast into 20 kg ingots. As shown in Fig. 1, after being subjected to homogenization at 1250 °C for 5 h, the ingots were cooled down to 1150 °C and held for 2 h prior to being forged into the Φ30 mm round bars to obtain a uniform composition and fine microstructure. The samples were held at 1000 °C for an hour to ensure complete solid solution of alloying elements, followed by water quenching to achieve a fully martensitic microstructure. Next, the samples were tempered at 600 °C for 2.5 h to facilitate the complete precipitation of MC-type nano-carbides, after which they were naturally cooled to room temperature. Thereafter, standard cylindrical tensile specimens with a threaded section diameter of 10 mm and a parallel section diameter of 5 mm were processed in the tempered samples along the forging direction. Afterwards, the 700 °C high-temperature tensile tests were performed on the MTS E45.105 tensile machine at a strain rate of 0.00007s−1/0.0014s−1 before and after yielding (GB 228.2-2015). The sample microstructures before and after high-temperature tensile tests were observed using a JSM-7000F field emission scanning electron microscopy (SEM) equipped with energy dispersive spectrum analysis (EDS) and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD). In terms of SEM observation, the samples were etched using 4% (V/V) nitric acid alcohol solution. Regarding EBSD analysis, the samples were etched using a solution which contained 10% HClO4 and 90% C2H5OH for 30 s. The EBSD measurements were performed at a step size of 150 nm. The nano- and micro-sized carbides in samples were observed by TEM (Titan ETEM, FEI) operating at 300 kV. The TEM thin foils (diameter, 3 mm) were prepared by twin-jet electropolishing with the 5% (V/V) perchloric acid alcohol solution. Processing Text: Binary Mg–5Y (wt%) alloy ingots were prepared by a multi-step process. First, high purity Mg (99.99%) and Mg–25Y (wt%) master alloys were melted within a crucible resistance furnace at ∼750 °C. This casting process was carried out under the safeguard of a protective atmosphere comprised of SF 6 and CO 2 mixed gas, with a volume ratio of 1:100. The as-cast ingots were subsequently subjected to solution treatment in a vacuum tube furnace at 530 °C for a duration of 12 h, under the protective cover of argon gas, before being cooled in ambient air. Subsequently, cylindrical billets, processing a diameter of 90 mm, were machined from the solution-treated Mg–5Y alloys by a commercial lathe. Prior to the extrusion process, these billets were preheated at 300 °C for 2 h. The extrusion procedure includes following parameters: a mold temperature was 400 °C, an extrusion temperature was 300 °C, and an extrusion ratio of 9:1. To obtain a fully dynamic recrystallized structure, the samples were air-cooled subsequent to extrusion. Ultimately, extruded Mg–5Y sheets, featuring a cross-sectional dimension of 80 × 8 mm 2 were finally fabricated. Strain rate: 800 s−1; Processing state: extruded fine-grained

Processing Text: The as-received steels were cast in vacuum furnaces and subsequently forged into billets with thicknesses ranging from 40 to 60 mm at ∼1100 °C. After homogenization at 1150 °C for two hours, the billets were hot rolled to 5 mm thickness via seven passes with the final rolling temperature over 900 °C, followed by air cooling to room temperature. Ultimately, the steels were cold rolled into 1.5 mm thick plates with a 70% reduction. The cold-rolled sheets were intercritically annealed at 680 °C for 30 min, followed by water quenching to room temperature. The temperature of 680 °C was selected to avoid cementite precipitation. Samples for synchrotron XRD and EBSD measurements were mechanically polished and then electro-polished at a voltage of 20 V for 10 s, with the electrolyte containing 10% perchloric acid and 90% ethanol. Samples for TEM characterizations were prepared using the double-jet electropolishing technique with an electrolyte containing 10% perchloric acid and 90% ethanol. The tensile samples had a gauge length of 3.4 mm, a width of 0.8 mm, and a thickness of 0.9 mm. The samples were electro-polished and then deposited using SiO 2 nanoparticles. The in situ tensile tests were performed at a strain rate of 2.75 × 10 −4 s −1 and were stopped at different global nominal strains to capture the corresponding images. Uniaxial tensile tests were carried out using an Instron 5967 machine equipped with a 30-kN load cell at room temperature with a strain rate of 1 × 10 −3 s −1. The tensile samples with the gauge length of 5 mm, thickness of 1.2 mm, and width of 2 mm were utilized. Interrupted tensile tests were also performed to investigate the deformed microstructure at different strain levels. Nanoindentation tests were performed using a Hysitron PI980 nanoindenter with a Berkovich-type tip at room temperature in a fast indentation mode. Processing state: intercritically annealed medium Mn steel; Microstructure: duplex-phase ultrafine microstructure consisting of ferrite and metastable austenite

Processing Text: In this study, we used the powder metallurgy process to prepare HSLA steel to overcome this inherent problem. The samples were composed of 4340 powder, Fe powder, FeSi6.5 powder, FeCr60 powder, FeMn80 powder, and Mo powder. The alloy powder was weighed in proportion under a high-pressure and pure argon atmosphere, and 0.6 wt% zinc stearate was added for lubrication. The powder was mixed via a planetary ball mill at a rotational speed of 300 r/min, with a material-to-ball ratio of 1:5. To avoid excessive welding resulting from the high ball milling speed, grinding was stopped for 10 min every 60 min. The samples were pressed into balls with a diameter of 60 mm at a pressure of 800 MPa. The samples were heated to the predetermined sintering temperature (1200-1350 °C) at a speed of 4 °C/min and held at this temperature for 60 min. After the insulation process was complete, the mixture was allowed to cool to room temperature in the furnace. The phases in both the powder and sintered samples were analyzed via X-ray diffraction (XRD, XPERT). Cu radiation (λ = 1.54056 Å) was used to scan in the range of 20∼90° (2θ) at a scanning speed of 3°/min. Microstructure characterization was performed via optical microscopy (OM, DSX 510), field emission scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Gemini560), electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS, data analysis software: AZtecCrystal), electron probe microanalysis (EPMA, 1720), Auger electron spectroscopy (AES, PHI-710), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM, FEI Talos F200X). When the OM samples were prepared, sandpaper was used to polish the surfaces of the samples to 3000#. After the samples were smoothed by polishing, they were corroded with a 10 vol% nitric acid alcohol solution. The EBSD samples were prepared by 15 V electrolytic polishing for 15-20 s. The sample used for TEM was ground to a thickness of 50 μm and thinned via an ion thinning instrument (GATAN695). The Archimedes method was used to measure the density of each sintered sample. The hardness of each sample was tested via the Vickers hardness test. Ten points were measured on each sample, and the mean value was obtained. A rod-shaped tensile test sample with dimensions of 12 × 4 × 1.5 mm was machined in the center of the sample. Tensile testing of the HSLA steel was performed via an electronic universal testing machine (Instron 5967) at a strain rate of 0.5 × 10 −3s −1. The samples were composed of 4340 powder, Fe powder, FeSi6.5 powder, FeCr60 powder, FeMn80 powder, and Mo powder. The alloy powder was weighed in proportion under a high-pressure and pure argon atmosphere, and 0.6 wt% zinc stearate was added for lubrication. The powder was mixed via a planetary ball mill at a rotational speed of 300 r/min, with a material-to-ball ratio of 1:5. To avoid excessive welding resulting from the high ball milling speed, grinding was stopped for 10 min every 60 min. The samples were pressed into balls with a diameter of 60 mm at a pressure of 800 MPa. The samples were heated to the predetermined sintering temperature (1200-1350 °C) at a speed of 4 °C/min and held at this temperature for 60 min. After the insulation process was complete, the mixture was allowed to cool to room temperature in the furnace. The phases in both the powder and sintered samples were analyzed via X-ray diffraction (XRD, XPERT). Cu radiation (λ = 1.54056 Å) was used to scan in the range of 20∼90° (2θ) at a scanning speed of 3°/min. A rod-shaped tensile test sample with dimensions of 12 × 4 × 1.5 mm was machined in the center of the sample. Processing Text: The samples were prepared using mechanical alloying and microwave sintering methods. Powders of Fe, Co, Ni, Cr, and Mn with a purity of 99.9 wt% were employed as raw materials, possessing an average particle size smaller than 45 μm. The FeCoNiCrMn HEAs was synthesized using an equimolar atomic ratio. Initially, steel balls with a mass ratio of 1:2:4 were utilized as the grinding medium. The ball-to-material ratio was established at 10:1, and the ball milling process was conducted for a duration of 48 h at a rotational speed of 300 revolutions per minute (r/min). Subsequently, the HEAs powder was dried in a vacuum environment at 80 °C for 48 h, after which the powder was extracted. In this procedure, 50% absolute ethanol was employed as the ball milling agent. The milling was conducted at a speed of 200 r/min for a duration of 6 h to ensure thorough mixing. Subsequently, the milled powder was dried at 80 °C. The dried Al 2O 3p/FeCoNiCrMn powder was subjected to cold isostatic pressing at 300 MPa for 2 min to create a cylindrical blank. This blank was subsequently sintered using microwave technology in a Muffle furnace. The sintering process was conducted at a temperature of 1000 °C, with a heating rate of 10 °C per minute and a holding time of 40 min. Condition: after addition of 2 wt% Al2O3

Processing Text: The CuCrZr alloy powder used in the experiment was prepared by the plasma rotating electrode atomization process. Specimens were prepared by EB-PBF equipment (Xi'an Sailong Additive Technology Co., Ltd., China). The maximum forming size of EB-PBF equipment is 150 × 150 × 210 mm, and the maximum vacuum degree is 5 × 10 −3Pa. In order to imitate the aging heat treatment process of CuCrZr alloy in-situ to precipitate nano-precipitates, the powder bed temperatures were controlled to 300 °C, 400 °C and 500 °C during the EB-PBF process. The specific forming parameters refer to our previous research [ 14]. The powder bed temperature of the EB-PBF sample is 200 °C, the conventional sample without CPBT is labeled as EB-PBF. When printing EB-PBF samples, the powder is melted directly after the powder coating is completed. When printing CPBT samples, an electron beam is used to heat the entire powder bed after the powder spreading is completed. The thermocouple used to measure the powder bed temperature is installed under the base plate. The powder bed temperature fluctuates and cannot be controlled very accurately at present. When the powder bed temperature is too high or too low, the electron beam current will be dynamically adjusted. The samples with the CPBT at 250-350 °C are marked as 300 °C, and the samples with the CPBT at 350-450 °C and 450-550 °C are marked as 400 °C and 500 °C respectively. In this way, the sample is always maintained in the aging heat treatment temperature range during the entire printing process. This special thermal history is controlled similar to traditional aging treatment. The thermal history of different samples is shown in Fig. 1c, and the printing process parameters are shown in Table 1. The powder particle size distribution is 15-106 μm, where D50 is 43 μm and D90 is 67 μm. The elemental content of Cr and Zr in the powder was determined by inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectroscopy (ICP-AES), while the elemental content of O was determined by pulse heating inert gas fusion intrinsic absorption method. Impurities such as Fe, Si, and P were determined by ICP-AES. As-built sample with dimensions of 10 × 10 × 60 mm 3 to determine the microstructure, phase composition and mechanical properties. A Shimadzu universal testing machine AGS-X 10 KN was used to conduct uniaxial tensile experiments at a strain rate of 1 mm/min on flat dog-bone shaped samples with a gauge length of 25 × 6 × 2 mm 3 to evaluate room temperature mechanical properties. Tensile specimens were cut from the same position of the as-built specimen for comparison. All specimens were polished before tensile to ensure smooth surfaces. An eddy current metal conductivity meter (Sigma 2008B, China) was used to measure the conductivity of the specimens with a resolution of 0.01 %IACS and a measurement range of 0.8-110 %IACS. Before the conductivity was tested, the surface was polished with sandpaper to ensure that there were no large scratches. Then the surface was polished with 2.5 μm and 0.5 μm diamond spray polishing agents. Finally, the sample was cleaned and dried. Each sample was tested 3 times, and the remaining values were averaged. Optical microscopy (GX51, OM), scanning electron microscopy (Gemini SEM 300, SEM), energy dispersive spectroscopic mapping (EDS), and electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) were used to characterize the sample microstructure. Among them, the scanning step size in EBSD experiment is 1.5 μm, and the scanning area is 600∗450 μm. The mixed solution (FeCl 3/1 g, HCl/2 ml, H 2O/20 ml) was used to etch the sample surface. After etching, the samples were cleaned in C 2H 5OH and dried for observation of microstructure. The samples were prepared into thin slices with a thickness of less than 60 μm and a diameter of 3 mm, and then underwent ion beam thinning at a low temperature of 100 K. All prepared thin platinum samples were observed on a transmission scanning electron microscope (Talos F200s, TEM) operating at 200 keV. Finally, the TEM data were analyzed and processed by Digital Micrograph (DM) software. Original sample; 0.2% offset yield strength

Processing Text: In this work, Hastelloy C276 alloy with exceptional strength and ultra-high elongation is fabricated using laser and arc hybrid additive manufacturing (LHAM). The specimen undergoes solution treatment at 1177 °C for 30 min, followed by water quenching. Further heat treatment (LHAM-HT) results in reduced texture strength, equiaxed grains with annealing twins and no precipitates detected. A Hastelloy C276 alloy wire (Atlantic China Welding Consumables, Inc.), 1.2 mm in diameter, was used for the deposition onto the substrate. The system comprised an IPG YLS-6000 fiber laser, a Fronius 500i welding machine, and a KUKA six-axis robot operating at 30 Hz, which were utilized for WAAM and LHAM processing of Hastelloy C276 alloy. The laser beam spot size is 0.2 mm. During the additive manufacturing process, the laser leaded, positioned at a 20° angle from the vertical to prevent reflective damage to equipment, while the CMT trailed. To manage heat accumulation, each deposited layer was cooled below 100 °C before subsequent layers are added, with the final specimens reaching a height of 40 mm. The entire process was conducted in a 99.999% pure argon atmosphere to prevent internal defects from atmospheric contamination. After deposition, the LHAM specimen underwent solution treatment, where the heating rate was set to 600 °C/h until reaching 1177 °C, followed by a 30-min hold and water quenching. For convenience, the specimens fabricated using CMT are referred to as WAAM, that fabricated by laser and arc hybrid additive manufacturing as LHAM, and the LHAM specimen after heat treatment as LHAM-HT. Processing state: after heat treatment; Microstructure: equiaxed grains with annealing twins, no precipitates

Processing Text: The intermetallic compound FeV alloy and high purity (>99.8 wt%), and Cr and W metal powders, were used to produce the as-cast (FeCr2V)1−xWxRMEAs using arc melting. First, the powders were proportioned according to the different alloy compositions and mixed evenly using physical blending. Then, the mixed metal powders were melted using arc melting technology to produce a casting ingot of approximately 30 g. The arc melting process was carried out in an atmosphere of argon to reduce the potential impact of oxidation on the sample during the process. Finally, the melting process was repeated three times to improve the uniformity of the microstructure and composition. The melted as-cast (FeCr2V)1−xWx sample was sliced into cross-sections using Electrical Discharge Machining (EDM) for observation and study of the microstructure. The standard metallographic sample preparation procedure was then followed for grinding and polishing. X-Ray Diffraction (XRD) testing was conducted on the cross-sectional sample using a CuKα radiation (λ = 1.5418 Å) with a PANalytical X’PERT PRO X-ray diffractometer to study the phase composition of the (FeCr2V)1−xWx alloy. In addition, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) equipped with an Energy Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDS) testing was conducted using a JEOL® JSM-7001F for observation of the microstructure. The JEOL® JSM-7001F and an EDS detector operated at an acceleration voltage of 15 kV were used for elemental quantification analysis. Mechanical properties of the RMEAs were evaluated through a Hysitron TI 950 Triboindenter, Struers Durascan-70 hardness tester and a Gleeble 1500 thermo-mechanical simulator. The nano-indentation tests, with an indentation load of 7 mN and a step size of 7 µm, were conducted on distinct phase areas observed in the metallographic specimens, namely the dominant phase and the minor phase regions. Vickers microhardness was measured four times for each sample using a load of 1 kg and a duration of 10 s by the Struers Durascan-70 automatic hardness tester. The compression tests were conducted on cylindrical samples (Φ6.5 mm × 8 mm), which were ground and polished according to standard metallographic sample preparation procedures using electrical discharge machining (EDM). Each alloy composition was tested under ambient conditions using a Gleeble 1500 thermo-mechanical simulator, with an engineering strain rate of 0.001 s−1. Condition: before W doping

Processing Text: The 5356 aluminum alloy samples were fabricated utilizing WAAM and U-RE-WAAM processes, respectively. Prior to additive manufacturing, the substrate surface was mechanically polished and cleaned with alcohol to remove any oxide films and oil contamination. Deposition was conducted using three distinct processes: WAAM, RE-WAAM, and U-RE-WAAM. In each process, the filler wire was melted by an electric arc under a protective atmosphere of 99.99 % argon. The torch and the molten wire moved horizontally in the Y deposition direction to form the deposited layers. By elevating the torch height in the Z building direction, subsequent layers were deposited onto the previous ones. The specific parameters for the additive manufacturing process are listed in Table 2. The parameters for the ultrasonic rotating extrusion system are specified in Table 3. In the initial layer of the additive manufacturing process, a wire feed speed of 7.5 m/min is utilized. Subsequently, the wire feed speed is decremented by 0.5 mm/min with each additional layer, down to a minimum of 5.0 mm/min. This gradual reduction in wire feed speed is necessitated by the proximity of the initial layers to the substrate, where the melting pool experiences rapid cooling and limited spread, thus requiring a higher feed rate to ensure adequate deposition width. As the number of deposited layers accumulates, the cooling rate of the melt pool decreases, necessitating a reduction in wire feed speed to 5.0 mm/min to prevent the collapse of deposited layers. The additive manufacturing process incorporates a single stack path, with interlayer temperatures strictly controlled below 50°C to maintain material integrity and process consistency. Process: WAAM

Processing Text: AlCu xCrTiV HEAs were fabricated using vacuum arc melting with pure metal particles (≥99.9 wt%). The button ingots, with a diameter of approximately 30 mm and a mass of about 40 g, were produced using a stepwise melting process. Metals with similar physical properties were melted first, followed by the sequential addition of other raw materials for remelting. To ensure homogeneity, each master alloy was remelted five times. The vacuum degree of vacuum arc melting is on the order of 10⁻³ Pa to 10⁻⁴ Pa, with a power supply of 100 kW. Samples were machined into cylindrical dimensions (Φ6 × 3 mm) and polished with 400#, 1000#, and 2000# sandpaper. After immersion in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution for 30 min to stabilize, the open circuit potential (OCP) was measured until the curve showed minimal fluctuation. Polarization curve (PPC) tests were conducted at a scanning speed of 0.005 V/s with a sensitivity of 0.01 A/V. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) tests were performed at the OCP, with a signal amplitude of 0.005 A, a rest time of 2 s, high and low frequencies of 10 5Hz and 10 −2, respectively. Both PPC and EIS tests were repeated five times, with the samples polished before each test. Processing Text: The ingot, prepared by the vacuum melt casting method, was heated to 1200 °C for 2 hours and then forged into 100 mm × 100 mm × 80 mm forgings. Once cooled to room temperature, the forgings were cut into 50 mm × 20 mm × 8 mm slabs using wire-cutting technology. Subsequently, the slab underwent homogenization at 1200 °C for 2 hours. Then, its thickness was reduced to 4 mm (50% reduction) through six hot rolling passes conducted within a temperature range of 1010 - 1150 °C, starting at 1150 °C and ending at 950 °C. After hot rolling, the sheet underwent dephosphating and was then cold rolled through ten processes, ultimately resulting in a thickness of 2.2 mm (45% reduction). Lastly, the cold-rolled sheet was annealed at approximately 1173 K for 15 mins. All heat treatments were conducted in an inert gas (argon) atmosphere to ensure material purity and prevent oxidation. A rectangular sample measuring 10 mm × 30 mm was cut from the rolled and annealed billet and then finely polished with 1500 grit silicon carbide sandpaper to achieve a uniform thickness of 2 mm. Compression testing of these thin sheet samples was conducted using the CMT5305 microcomputer-controlled universal material testing machine along the normal direction (ND), with a strain rate of 0.001 s−1. To ensure precise control of deformation, dual means of stroke and pressure control were employed in the experiments. Thickness measurements were taken at three different locations before and after the compression test, with the average values documented to reflect the initial and final thicknesses. The average thicknesses of the four samples before compression were 1.98 mm, 2.02 mm, 2.00 mm, and 2.00 mm, respectively, and they changed to 1.80 mm, 1.62 mm, 1.48 mm, and 1.34 mm after compression. Uniaxial micro-tensile tests were conducted at 298 K (room temperature) on an in-house miniature-testing machine with a load cell of 5000 N and a nominal strain rate of 0.001 s−1. The samples were cut by EDM from the pre-compressed sheet material with gauge dimensions of 5 mm × 2 mm × 1 mm. The tensile direction of the samples was strictly aligned with the rolling direction (RD). Before testing, all samples underwent mechanical grinding to ensure a smooth surface without any obvious defects. To accurately determine the tensile strain value, random speckle patterns were uniformly sprayed onto the sample surface. During the tensile process, deformation images were captured in real-time using a high-resolution camera. Subsequently, MATLAB software was utilized for image processing and analysis. Initially, the images were converted into monochrome. Then, based on the center point of the sample gauge area, a virtual extensometer was constructed from the two preset solid lines. Finally, the sample's strain was determined by calculating the displacement of pixel points between the virtual extensometers over time. In this study, two types of micro-tensile tests were conducted: in-situ tests and interrupted tests, both loaded by displacement control. The in-situ tests were designed to obtain the stress-strain curve of the sample up to fracture, and back stress was also assessed through a LUR cycle test. To ensure reproducibility, three independent tensile tests were conducted for each pre-compressed sample. During the LUR test, a strain rate of 0.001 s−1 was used for strain control during loading, while unloading was force-controlled at 25 N/s. Reloading began when the force was unloaded to 25 N. The interrupted test was designed to study the microstructure evolution, with interruptions at specific points or continuation until fracture. Additionally, to accurately characterize the microstructure evolution of the pre-compressed sample at the same position before and after tensile deformation, hardness markers were placed in the center of the target region. These markers served as reference points, facilitating accurate analysis of the microstructure evolution during subsequent EBSD characterization. Microstructure characterization was performed using EBSD on a Nova Nano SEM 230 ultra-high resolution field emission SEM. The sample preparation consisted of coarse grinding and fine grinding followed by electrolytic polishing at -20 °C using an electrolytic polishing solution of 4 vol% perchloric acid mixed with 96 vol% ethanol at a voltage of 30 V and a polishing time of 30 s. For EBSD analysis, the operating voltage was set to 20 kV, and the step size was 0.25 μm. In addition, the TEM sample was prepared from the specified sample using a focused ion beam (FIB) technique at an acceleration voltage of 30 kV. In this study, a total of two TEM observations were performed. The first observation was performed on the sample with a compressive strain of 0.4, and the second TEM test was conducted on the pre-compressed sample after stretched to 0.2. The FIB slice was taken from the central region of the sample, with the slice plane perpendicular to the RD and the slice size of 10 μm × 8 μm. The TEM sample was mechanically polished to a thickness of 30 μm, then thinned by double injection at -25 °C with an electrolyte of 10% perchloric acid and 90% alcohol at 15 V, and finally cleaned by ion grinding at 3 kV at a 2 °C angle for 10 min. Finally, the samples were observed by the TALOS F200X field emission transmission electron microscope under a 200 kV acceleration voltage. Condition: quasi-static loading; Type: tension

Processing Text: The ingot, prepared by the vacuum melt casting method, was heated to 1200 °C for 2 hours and then forged into 100 mm × 100 mm × 80 mm forgings. Once cooled to room temperature, the forgings were cut into 50 mm × 20 mm × 8 mm slabs using wire-cutting technology. Subsequently, the slab underwent homogenization at 1200 °C for 2 hours. Then, its thickness was reduced to 4 mm (50% reduction) through six hot rolling passes conducted within a temperature range of 1010 - 1150 °C, starting at 1150 °C and ending at 950 °C. After hot rolling, the sheet underwent dephosphating and was then cold rolled through ten processes, ultimately resulting in a thickness of 2.2 mm (45% reduction). Lastly, the cold-rolled sheet was annealed at approximately 1173 K for 15 mins. All heat treatments were conducted in an inert gas (argon) atmosphere to ensure material purity and prevent oxidation. A rectangular sample measuring 10 mm × 30 mm was cut from the rolled and annealed billet and then finely polished with 1500 grit silicon carbide sandpaper to achieve a uniform thickness of 2 mm. Compression testing of these thin sheet samples was conducted using the CMT5305 microcomputer-controlled universal material testing machine along the normal direction (ND), with a strain rate of 0.001 s−1. To ensure precise control of deformation, dual means of stroke and pressure control were employed in the experiments. Thickness measurements were taken at three different locations before and after the compression test, with the average values documented to reflect the initial and final thicknesses. The average thicknesses of the four samples before compression were 1.98 mm, 2.02 mm, 2.00 mm, and 2.00 mm, respectively, and they changed to 1.80 mm, 1.62 mm, 1.48 mm, and 1.34 mm after compression. Uniaxial micro-tensile tests were conducted at 298 K (room temperature) on an in-house miniature-testing machine with a load cell of 5000 N and a nominal strain rate of 0.001 s−1. The samples were cut by EDM from the pre-compressed sheet material with gauge dimensions of 5 mm × 2 mm × 1 mm. The tensile direction of the samples was strictly aligned with the rolling direction (RD). Before testing, all samples underwent mechanical grinding to ensure a smooth surface without any obvious defects. To accurately determine the tensile strain value, random speckle patterns were uniformly sprayed onto the sample surface. During the tensile process, deformation images were captured in real-time using a high-resolution camera. Subsequently, MATLAB software was utilized for image processing and analysis. Initially, the images were converted into monochrome. Then, based on the center point of the sample gauge area, a virtual extensometer was constructed from the two preset solid lines. Finally, the sample's strain was determined by calculating the displacement of pixel points between the virtual extensometers over time. In this study, two types of micro-tensile tests were conducted: in-situ tests and interrupted tests, both loaded by displacement control. The in-situ tests were designed to obtain the stress-strain curve of the sample up to fracture, and back stress was also assessed through a LUR cycle test. To ensure reproducibility, three independent tensile tests were conducted for each pre-compressed sample. During the LUR test, a strain rate of 0.001 s−1 was used for strain control during loading, while unloading was force-controlled at 25 N/s. Reloading began when the force was unloaded to 25 N. The interrupted test was designed to study the microstructure evolution, with interruptions at specific points or continuation until fracture. Additionally, to accurately characterize the microstructure evolution of the pre-compressed sample at the same position before and after tensile deformation, hardness markers were placed in the center of the target region. These markers served as reference points, facilitating accurate analysis of the microstructure evolution during subsequent EBSD characterization. Microstructure characterization was performed using EBSD on a Nova Nano SEM 230 ultra-high resolution field emission SEM. The sample preparation consisted of coarse grinding and fine grinding followed by electrolytic polishing at -20 °C using an electrolytic polishing solution of 4 vol% perchloric acid mixed with 96 vol% ethanol at a voltage of 30 V and a polishing time of 30 s. For EBSD analysis, the operating voltage was set to 20 kV, and the step size was 0.25 μm. In addition, the TEM sample was prepared from the specified sample using a focused ion beam (FIB) technique at an acceleration voltage of 30 kV. In this study, a total of two TEM observations were performed. The first observation was performed on the sample with a compressive strain of 0.4, and the second TEM test was conducted on the pre-compressed sample after stretched to 0.2. The FIB slice was taken from the central region of the sample, with the slice plane perpendicular to the RD and the slice size of 10 μm × 8 μm. The TEM sample was mechanically polished to a thickness of 30 μm, then thinned by double injection at -25 °C with an electrolyte of 10% perchloric acid and 90% alcohol at 15 V, and finally cleaned by ion grinding at 3 kV at a 2 °C angle for 10 min. Finally, the samples were observed by the TALOS F200X field emission transmission electron microscope under a 200 kV acceleration voltage. Condition: quasi-static loading; Type: compression

Processing Text: IN718 alloy produced by additive manufacturing (AM) displays significant anisotropy due to its unique microstructure. SLM-fabricated IN718 was analyzed in detail using the crystal plasticity method. Statistical analysis of SLM IN718 data identified microstructural descriptors to describe the heterogeneous microstructural characteristics adequately. A representative volume element (RVE) is constructed for CP simulations. A dislocation-based crystal plasticity constitutive model, combined with a spectral solver, is developed to elucidate the anisotropic behavior of SLM IN718 under uniaxial tension. The constructed EM-ET RVEs were subjected to uniaxial tensile deformation along the BD and TD under quasi-static loading rates ε̇=10-3s-1 and room temperature T=298 K. A 20 % strain is applied in the TD (BD). Tensile simulations were conducted on the EM-RT RVEs and RM-ET RVEs. Columnar grain morphology significantly influences the yield strength and strain-hardening behavior, especially under loading perpendicular to the BD. Loading direction: TD; Microstructure: columnar grains; Context: EM-RT RVE

Processing Text: AA7050 forgings with a longitudinal (L), long transverse (LT), and short transverse (ST) length ratios of approximately 26:4:1 were fabricated through direct-chill-casting, homogenization, multiple high-temperature (440 °C) upsetting and cogging processes. Subsequently, the forgings were solution-treated (Sol.) at 471 °C for 9 h and then water-quenched. Rectangular (15 × 15 × 5 mm 3) and dog-bone-shaped tensile samples (gauge: diameter 6 × 25 mm) were machined from the forged and solution-treated alloys. To eliminate the natural aging effect, the samples were solution-treated again in an electric furnace at 471 °C for 1 h and then water-quenched at room temperature. The solution-treated samples were first aged (FA) at 121 °C for 16 h (peak aging condition) and secondary-aged (SA) at 177 °C for different times up to 192 h, and then water-quenched. After the specimens were mechanically polished and electrically etched using a 5 % fluoroboric (HBF 4) solution with a power supply (TOYOTECH, TDP-605B) of 20 V for ∼120 s, the α-Al grain structure was observed using optical microscopy (OM; Nikon, EPIPHOT) under polarized light. Condition: Solution-treated; Direction: LT

Processing Text: The original TA4 pure Ti was cut into round bar samples measuring Φ25 mm × 150 mm, then annealed in a muffle furnace at 750 °C for 1.5 h, followed by air-cooling to room temperature. Samples underwent pretreatment, with a graphite and MoS 2 serving as lubricant. TA4 pure Ti samples with the size of Φ25 mm × 150 mm were processed using a YJ160B1 four-column hydraulic testing machine. The ECAP deformation parameters were as follows: the die channel angle was Φ = 135°, and the outer angle was ψ = 20°. Samples were pressed at a rate of 2.5 mm/s for four passes along route C. After four passes, the samples underwent CR using a Φ160 × 170 two-roll mill, with reductions set to 30 and 50 %. This process produced fine-grained TA4 pure Ti samples with dimensions of 20 mm × 20 mm × 180 mm and 12.5 mm × 12.5 mm × 250 mm. EBSD samples were prepared through an electrolytic polishing process. Thinning of samples for transmission electron microscopy (TEM) was performed using a MTP-1A double-jet electrolytic thinning instrument, with an electrolyte composed of 60 % methanol, 35 % n-butanol, and 5 % perchloric acid by volume. The voltage of thinning was 50 V and the current was 50 mA. Mechanical properties were evaluated using a WDW-300 electronic universal testing machine at a strain rate of 1 ×10 −3s −1. For microhardness testing, a 15 mm × 15 mm × 5 mm block sample was cut from the middle of each cross-section (rolling direction or RD surface) of the samples subjected to ECAP and combined ECAP-CR deformation. Testing was conducted using an HVS-10Z Vickers hardness tester with an applied load of 200gf and a holding time of 10s. Processing Text: The samples were prepared using a Renishaw AM250 printer with a molding space of 250 mm × 250 mm × 300 mm (X, Y, Z). The layer thickness was adjustable between 0.02 mm and 0.10 mm, and the laser spot diameter was 70 μm. After each layer was deposited, the grating pattern was rotated by 67° to minimize overlap between adjacent laser vectors. Samples with thicknesses of 0.5 mm, 1.0 mm, 1.5 mm, and 2.0 mm were printed perpendicular to the substrate. Adjacent samples were kept parallel, with the build plane oriented at a 45° angle to the substrate. Additionally, a block sample with a thickness of over 1 cm was printed. Pores and melt pool morphology of the treated samples were observed using optical microscopes (OM, PME3, Olympus), and dendrite structures of the samples were examined with scanning electron microscopes (SEM, LEO 1530vp and VEGA 3 LMU). A high-resolution scanning electron microscope (SEM, Mira 3, TESCAN) equipped with an electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, NordlysMax2, Oxford) probe was used to analyze grain structure, and vibratory polishing was performed to relieve surface stresses prior to characterization. Physical phase was analyzed using X-ray diffractometer (XRD, D8 DaVinci). The samples for the tensile test were prepared as flat dog-bone specimens with dimensions of 55 mm in length and 10 mm in width. Block samples were cut to a thickness of 1.2 mm. The mechanical properties of the tensile specimens were conducted using a Zwick universal mechanical testing machine with a tensile speed of 1 mm/min. Processing Text: Al-Ce alloys, known for their excellent creep resistance and thermal stability due to the Al11Ce3 phase, were optimized using CALPHAD simulations to incorporate solid solution and precipitation strengthening in addition to composite strengthening from the Al11Ce3 phase. Additive friction stir deposition (AFSD) was used to fabricate 3D builds from cast material, refining the grain size and microstructure by fragmenting Al11Ce3 lamellae into smaller, uniformly dispersed particles and inducing Al3Sc nanoprecipitates during deposition. Plates measuring 380 mm (length) × 280 mm (width) × 15 mm (thickness) were cast by pouring molten alloy at 750 °C into platens preheated to 400 °C. The cooling rate during squeeze casting was measured using fast response thermocouples placed near the center of one of the cast plates. The average cooling rate between 1025 K (the temperature where squeeze was applied) and 800 K (below the solidification temperature) was measured to be approximately 50 K/s. The squeeze cast alloys were processed by additive friction stir processing (AFSD) technique using a MELD B8 machine (MELD Manufacturing). The AFSD technique utilizes a hollow rotating tool to feed the material, which undergoes localized plastic deformation and shear deposition. The feedstock, a rod with a square cross-section of 9.5 mm × 9.5 mm × 150 mm long, was prepared by sectioning the squeeze cast plates using electrical discharge machining. Before deposition, the feedstock rods were lubricated with graphite spray to minimize friction during processing. The deposition process employed a tool made of H13 tool steel, featuring a 38.1 mm diameter shoulder with four teardrop-shaped protrusions. Two protrusions were 2 mm in height, while the other two measured 1 mm. During the plunging stage, the rotation of the tool at high speeds generated frictional heat at the tool-substrate interface, softening and plasticizing the feedstock material. Under the combined effects of frictional heat and forge load, the material was extruded beneath the tool shoulder and shear-deposited layer by layer during the tool traverse. Deposition was carried out at optimized processing parameters: a tool rotation rate of 250 rpm, a traverse speed of 7.2 mm/s, and a feed rate of 2.5 mm/s. Seven layers, each 1 mm thick, were deposited on an Al6061 substrate. Condition: Cast; Temperature: Room Temperature (RT)
Processing Word: Condition: Cast; Temperature: Room Temperature (RT)

Processing Text: The fabrication process of Cu 2- x Se bulk was prepared through solid-state sintering and hot press sintering. Cu (shot, 99.999 %) and Se (shot, 99.99 %) were weighed according to the stoichiometry of Cu 2- x Se (x = 0.07, 0.12, 0.17, 0.22, and 0.27), and subsequently loaded into a quartz ampoule containing a protective layer of pyrolytic carbon. The ampoule was then sealed under vacuum conditions. The tubes were heated to 1273 K and held for 12 h, followed by a slow cooling to room temperature. The obtained ingots were crushed into powders using an agate mortar and sieved through a 100 mesh. The raw powder was then consolidated into a high-density Cu 2- x Se bulk through hot-press sintering at 873 K under 40 MPa for 30 min. Processing Text: The vacuum induction melting inert gas atomization (VIGA) process was employed to produce the high-quality CCM alloy powders. The particle size of the obtained spherical-shaped powders was sieved into the size range of 15-53 μm. The chemical compositions of the powders were examined by inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectrometer (ICP-AES). The alloy powders were dried at 120 °C for 8 h in vacuum environment prior to LPBF fabrication. The building substrate was set at 80 °C and argon gas was filled in the building chamber to prevent oxidation. Based on our previous work, a set of optimized process parameters with the laser power of 300 W, scanning speed of 950 mm/s, hatching space of 110 μm and the layer thickness of 40 μm were chosen to ensure the sample relative density above 99.5 %. A continuous 67° rotation scanning strategy was adopted between the successive building layers. In this study, the commercial EP-M150 Plus LPBF machine equipped with a 500 W fiber laser was utilized for sample fabrication. Rectangular plate-shaped samples were fabricated with its longitude axis inclined 0°, 45°, 60°, 75° and 90° from the base substrate, which are named as V0, V45, V60, V75 and V90 samples in this context, respectively. Processing Text: A set of bulk ultrafine-grained Al alloys with nominal compositions of Al-8.5Mg-1X ( X= 0, Fe, Ti, Zr or Y) (in wt.%) were fabricated with a combined mechanical alloying and hot extrusion of powder compacts in a scalable way. Initially, powder mixtures of Al and Mg with and without the addition of Fe, Ti, Zr, or Y (purity > 99.9 %) were blended, followed by mechanical alloying under argon (Ar) atmosphere. These mechanically-alloyed powders were then compacted by a 200-tonnage hydraulic press into a cylindrical shape of 52 mm in diameter and 20 mm in height. The powder compaction was performed under a pressure of approximately 200 MPa for 5 min. Subsequently, such powder compacts were heated up to 773 K, using a conduction coil, with a heating rate of ∼30 K/min. To guarantee uniform heating, the compacts were held at 773 K for 8 min prior to extrusion. To mitigate oxidation, the compaction, heating and extrusion were all carried out in a glove box filled with Ar, maintaining an oxygen content of below 200 ppm throughout the entire operation process. An extrusion ratio of 25:1 was used to produce a rod of 11 mm in diameter. Before extrusion, the extrusion dies were preheated to 673 K to minimize the chilling of heated compacts. Tensile yield strength; Nominal composition: Al-8.5Mg

Processing Text: The steel was prepared using a vacuum induction melting furnace under an argon protective atmosphere, maintaining a vacuum level of approximately 5 MPa, and was eventually cast into a 30 kg ingot. The ingot was then held at 1140 °C for 5 h and forged into a round bar with a diameter of 60 mm. The hot rolled plate is cold-rolled with a thickness reduction of 20 %, 40 %, 60 % and 80 %, which are referred to as CR20, CR40, CR60 and CR80, respectively.
