Processing Text: Non-equiatomic CoNiMo alloys with nominal compositions of (CoNi) 88Mo 12, (CoNi) 85Mo 15, and (CoNi) 82Mo 18 (designated as M12, M15, and M18, respectively) were fabricated by vacuum induction melting (MC100V, Indutherm, Germany) using high-purity (99.95%) elements under Ar atmosphere. The ingots were homogenized at 1200 °C for 2 h under Ar atmosphere, followed by water quenching, and subsequently cold-rolled with an 80% reduction at room temperature. The HPT process was then performed on the cold-rolled sheets to significantly impose strain energy for recrystallization and the formation of a UFG structure. A total of ten turns of HPT were conducted at 1 rpm under 6 GPa on disc-shaped specimens with a diameter of 10 mm, machined from the cold-rolled sheets. To ensure sufficient ductility, the annealing temperatures predicting a high volume fraction of FCC phase were selected ( Fig. 1b-d), specifically 800 °C, 900 °C, and 975 °C for M12, M15, and M18, respectively, with a duration of 120 s. Processing Text: The samples were prepared using a Renishaw AM250 printer with a molding space of 250 mm × 250 mm × 300 mm (X, Y, Z). The layer thickness was adjustable between 0.02 mm and 0.10 mm, and the laser spot diameter was 70 μm. After each layer was deposited, the grating pattern was rotated by 67° to minimize overlap between adjacent laser vectors. Samples with thicknesses of 0.5 mm, 1.0 mm, 1.5 mm, and 2.0 mm were printed perpendicular to the substrate. Adjacent samples were kept parallel, with the build plane oriented at a 45° angle to the substrate. Additionally, a block sample with a thickness of over 1 cm was printed. Pores and melt pool morphology of the treated samples were observed using optical microscopes (OM, PME3, Olympus), and dendrite structures of the samples were examined with scanning electron microscopes (SEM, LEO 1530vp and VEGA 3 LMU). A high-resolution scanning electron microscope (SEM, Mira 3, TESCAN) equipped with an electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, NordlysMax2, Oxford) probe was used to analyze grain structure, and vibratory polishing was performed to relieve surface stresses prior to characterization. Physical phase was analyzed using X-ray diffractometer (XRD, D8 DaVinci). The samples for the tensile test were prepared as flat dog-bone specimens with dimensions of 55 mm in length and 10 mm in width. Block samples were cut to a thickness of 1.2 mm. The mechanical properties of the tensile specimens were conducted using a Zwick universal mechanical testing machine with a tensile speed of 1 mm/min. The reported mechanical property data for each thickness represent the average of three valid test results. Aged at 873 K for 4 h

Processing Text: High-purity (>99.9 %) Fe, Co, Ni, Cr, and Ti metals were arc-melted in argon atmosphere to produce ingots with the (FeCrCoNi) 95Ti 5composition. After flipping and melting five times, an ingot (diameter = 50 mm, weight = 150 g, height = 10 mm) was obtained. The ingots were hot-rolled to a thickness of 2 mm in five passes after homogenization at 1373 K for 12 h, followed by solid-solution treatment at 1373 K for 1 h and water quenching. Finally, the hot-rolled plate was aging at 873, 973, and 1073 K for 4 h, followed by water quenching. After the surface of the tensile specimen was sanded with sandpaper, its mechanical properties were tested using a universal testing machine (Zwick Z2.5 TH) at a deformation rate of 10 −3/s −1. After polishing the surface with sandpaper, the damping performance was measured using a Q800 DMA dynamic thermomechanical analyzer. Standard condition

Processing Text: The CoCrNi MPR-MEA was fabricated using laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) on mixed elemental powder blends. The powders were mixed using a planetary ball mill at 200 rpm for 7 h to ensure thorough and homogeneous blending. The Co powder had a particle size distribution ranging from 15 μm to 45 μm, with an average particle size of approximately 30 μm. The particle size distribution of the Ni powders ranged from approximately 15 μm-45 μm, with an average particle size of around 29 μm. The Cr powder exhibited a particle size distribution between 20 μm and 50 μm, with an average particle size of about 40 μm. The mixed powders were fed into an AconityMini LPBF machine. During the LPBF process, CoCrNi MPR-MEA samples were fabricated using a 316L plate as the substrate, under a high-purity argon atmosphere to prevent oxidation. The hatch spacing was fixed at 120 μm, and the layer thickness was set at 30 μm. The combinations consisted of six different laser power levels (100 W, 140 W, 180 W, 220 W, 260 W, and 300 W) and six different scanning speeds (500 mm/s, 700 mm/s, 900 mm/s, 1100 mm/s, 1300 mm/s, and 1500 mm/s), which were randomly paired for evaluation. After parameter optimization, rectangular blocks were fabricated using a laser power of 260 W and a scanning speed of 700 mm/s. The samples were prepared and cleaned using ultrasonic vibration for 5 min to remove surface contaminants. The density was measured using the Archimedes method with an AKD-310G analytical balance and distilled water as the immersion medium. Each sample was weighed in air and then in water. The measurement was repeated three times for each sample, and the average value was recorded as the final density. The relative density was calculated by dividing the measured density by the theoretical density of the reference material, CoCrNi MEA. The phase composition and crystal structure of the LPBF-fabricated CoCrNi MPR-MEA specimens were investigated using X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis. The XRD patterns were acquired using a Rigaku SmartLab diffractometer with Cu-Kα radiation operating at 40 kV and 30 mA. The diffraction patterns were collected over a 2θ range of 10-100° with a step size of 0.02° and a scanning speed of 2°/min. The morphology and elemental composition of the CoCrNi alloy powders were characterized using a HITACHI SU-1510 scanning electron microscope (SEM) equipped with an energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) detector. The SEM images were obtained at an accelerating voltage of 15 kV, and the chemical composition of the powders was determined by EDS analysis. To investigate the microstructural evolution of the LPBF-fabricated CoCrNi MPR-MEA samples, both cross-sectional and longitudinal planes were prepared following standard metallographic procedures, which included cutting, mounting, grinding, and polishing. The microstructures were examined in both as-polished and etched conditions using an Olympus GX53 optical microscope (OM) and SEM. The samples were etched using a mixture of 30 ml HCl, 10 ml HNO3, and 20 ml H2O. The fracture surfaces of the tensile tested specimens were also studied using SEM to elucidate the failure mechanisms. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) analysis was performed using a HITACHI SU-1500 SEM equipped with an EBSD detector. The EBSD data were acquired with a step size of 1.5 μm and analyzed using the TSL OIM Analysis software to determine the grain size distribution, grain boundary characteristics, and phase constitution of the LPBF-fabricated CoCrNi MPR-MEA samples. The EBSD samples were prepared by mechanical polishing, followed by electrolytic polishing in a solution containing 10 % perchloric acid and 90 % ethanol at 20 V for 30 s. The TEM analysis is conducted using a FEI Tecnai F20 transmission electron microscope, which operates at an accelerating voltage of 200 kV to obtain high-resolution images of the specimens. Prior to this characterization, the samples are carefully prepared by first mechanically polishing them to a thickness of approximately 30 μm. This is followed by an electropolishing process using a solution of 5 vol% perchloric acid and 95 vol% ethanol at −35 °C and 20 V, resulting in final specimens with a diameter of about 3 mm. The mechanical properties of the LPBF-fabricated CoCrNi MPR-MEA samples were investigated using a combination of microhardness measurements and uniaxial tensile tests. Vickers microhardness tests were performed on a fully automated Struers Duramin-40 microhardness tester with a load of 500 gf and a dwell time of 10 s. The indentations were made on both the cross-sectional and longitudinal planes of the polished samples, maintaining a minimum spacing of 5 times the indent size to minimize the influence of neighboring indentations. To ensure statistical reliability, a total of 20 indentations were made on each sample. Uniaxial tensile tests were performed at room temperature using an MTS Systems Corporation CMT-5205 microcomputer-controlled electronic universal testing machine with a maximum load capacity of 50 kN. The tensile specimens were machined from the LPBF-fabricated CoCrNi MPR-MEA samples using wire electrical discharge machining (WEDM) with a gauge length of 25 mm and a diameter of 5 mm. The tests were conducted at a constant strain rate of 1 × 10−3s−1, and the strain was measured using a clip-on extensometer with a gauge length of 10 mm. This setup allowed for accurate determination of the elastic modulus, yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation to failure. To establish the reproducibility and reliability of the results, three tensile specimens were tested for each processing condition. Processing Text: Commercial 6082 aluminum alloy rod with a diameter of 12 mm was selected for the experiment. The alloy was sectioned into a sample measuring 25 cm in length for the purpose of the UVAT experiment. In the UVAT experiment, the initial step involved establishing a connection between the aluminum rod and the ultrasonic transducer by tapping one end of the rod. However, CAT samples did not require this tapping process, and were simply cut to a fixed length in preparation for the aging process. Following the preparation, the sample underwent SS treatment at a temperature of 555 °C for 1h under Ar conditions. Subsequently, the sample was rapidly quenched to room temperature to maintain the supersaturated solid solution state. Two different aging experiments were then conducted under vacuum at a temperature of 150 °C. The first experiment involved aging CAT samples under conventional conditions, while the second experiment utilized UVAT on the samples. The ultrasonic generator operated at a vibration frequency of 20 KHz, and the power was set to 100W. Room temperature tensile tests were performed on a servohydraulic testing machine at a rate of 5 mm/min. Vickers microhardness testing was used to assess the hardness of the samples, applying a load of 0.98N for a period of 15s. The micromorphology, fracture, and elemental composition were characterized using the FEI Nova Nano SEM 450 scanning electron microscope equipped with a 15 KV energy dispersive X-ray spectrometer (EDS). X-ray diffraction phase detection was performed on the samples, involving the following parameters: V = 40 KV, A = 40 mA, 2θ = 10-90°, and a scanning speed of 5°/min. The grain structure and morphology were characterized using EBSD with a step size of μ = 0.5 μm. The samples were electrosprayed within a temperature range of −35 °C to −25 °C, followed by low-voltage ion thinning and cleaning in an angle range of ±2° to ±4° using the ion thinning instrument to prepare a thin region of an amorphous layer. Finally, transmission electron microscopy (TEM) was employed to characterize dislocations and precipitated phases of the samples. Processing Text: The as-cast ingot was first homogenized at 1373 K for 6 h, and then hot forged to a bar with section size of 45 mm × 45 mm at around 1273 K. Subsequently, the bar was further cold-rolled to sheet with thickness of 15 mm and then annealed at 1073 K for 5 min, followed by water-quenching. The statistical results of KAM values were obtained. Flat dog-bone shape specimens with gauge dimensions of 10 mm × 2.5 mm × 2 mm were cut from the sheets. Rectangular Charpy impact samples with a size of 10 mm × 10 mm × 55 mm were cut along the rolling direction. A 45° V-notch was machined in the middle of the sample with a depth of 2 mm and a radius of 0.25 mm at the root. The uniaxial tensile tests were undertaken by using a computer-controlled SUNSCMT 5105 material testing machine with a nominal strain rate of 1 × 10 −3s −1at 293 K and 77 K, respectively. The instrumented Charpy pendulum impact tests capable of recording the dynamic load-displacement curves, were performed on SANS ZBC2452-B pendulum impact testing equipment at 298 K and 77 K, according to standard GB/T 229-2020. Processing Text: Vacuum arc melting was conducted under an argon atmosphere using metal raw materials with a purity exceeding 99.9 %. The ingot was subjected to at least three flips to ensure a relatively homogeneous Fe 57.88(CrNi) 32.08Al 10.04MEA. The heat treatment process was carried out in an electric resistance furnace under an argon atmosphere, with a heating rate of 5 °C/min. The heat treatment schedules for the Fe 57.88(CrNi) 32.08Al 10.04MEA are detailed in Table 1. The selection of 1300 °C and 850 °C as the solution and aging temperatures, respectively, was based on the results of Thermo-Calc calculations. According to these calculations, the chosen solution temperature of 1300 °C exceeded the alloy's solution temperature but remained below its melting temperature. Furthermore, the aging temperature of 850 °C was primarily aimed at precipitating sufficient strengthening phase while maximizing the proportion of the alloy's soft phase (FCC phase). For simplicity, the as-cast Fe 57.88(CrNi) 32.08Al 10.04MEA was designated AC, while the heat-treated alloys were denoted 1300-HT and 850-HT, respectively. In this heat treatment process, the alloy underwent a 2-h solution treatment at 1300 °C, followed by furnace cooling. Subsequently, an aging treatment of 10 h at 850 °C, followed by water quenching, was performed. This process primarily enabled the complete precipitation of all phases within the alloy at this temperature. After annealing at 1300 °C for 1 h, followed by aging at 850 °C for 10 h, the as-cast alloy exhibited notable changes in phase composition: the FCC phase decreased from 83.66 ± 2.00 % to 78.80 ± 2.03 %, the BCC phase increased from 0.20 ± 0.05 % to 2.61 ± 0.01 %, and the B2 phase increased from 16.1 ± 0.25 % to 18.6 ± 0.01 %. Processing Text: Ti 41V 27Hf 13Nb 13Mo 6 RHEA was prepared in a water-cooled copper crucible by vacuum arc melting, and its ingot underwent remelting five times under argon atmosphere. The purity of raw materials surpasses 99.9 wt%. The as-cast samples were polished and cleaned with acetone to ensure uniform surface quality before LSR. The experiments were conducted on an LSF-Ⅲ additive manufacturing system equipped with a semiconductor laser and an inert atmosphere protection chamber (argon atmosphere with an oxygen content below 50 ppm). Processing Text: The TiZrNbHf alloy used in this experiment is melted by Ti, Zr, Nb and Hf elements with purity greater than 99.9 %. Each melting was carried out at a vacuum of 5 × 10−3Pa, followed by the introduction of high-purity argon gas to generate an arc beam. In order to ensure the uniform composition of the alloy, the ingot was turned over and remelted for 6 times. The ingot was cold rolled into sheets (80 % thickness reduction) as shown in Fig. 1. Rectangular dogbone specimens for tensile testing were then machined using an electric discharge machining (EDM) method with a mark length of 12.5 mm and a cross-sectional area of 3.2 mm × 2 mm. The specimens were annealed in vacuum quartz tubes at a vacuum of 5 × 10−3μm at a temperature of 1000 °C for 30 min. The specimens were annealed in a vacuum quartz tube at room temperature at a strain rate of 1 × 10−3s−1 strain rate on INSTRON 3382 to obtain the room temperature tensile properties of the alloy. The phase composition of the alloys was measured by XRD using Co Kα radiation at a scanning rate of 2°/minute. The microstructure of TiZrNbHf alloy was observed by SEM and TEM. The samples for EBSD characterization were prepared by electrochemical polishing in 10 % HClO4 and 90 % CH4O solution for 5 s after grinding to 3000 mesh. For the preparation of TEM samples, the samples were first mechanically polished to 50 μm and finally subjected to ion-beam thinning at low temperatures to obtain rings with a diameter of 5 μm. Subsequently, the cold-rolled sample was subjected to heat treatment at 1000 °C for 30 min to recrystallize the alloy and remove the dislocations and residual stresses generated by cold rolling. Condition: heat-treated state

Processing Text: The composition used in this study was Cu46Zr46Al8 (at.%), prepared from pure metals with a purity exceeding 99.99 %. The master alloy underwent five repeated melting cycles in a vacuum arc remelting furnace under a protective atmosphere of argon gas (purity of 99.999 %), with titanium gettering, to ensure homogeneity. BMG rods of Ø3 mm × 70 mm were produced via suction casting in a water-cooled copper mold and then cut into 1.25 mm thick disks. Samples were polished using an automatic polishing system (LMP-3S, China) to reduce disk thickness to 1.0 mm, ensuring parallelism of top and bottom surfaces. BMG rods of Ø2 mm × 70 mm were prepared and cut into cylindrical compression test samples with a length of 3 mm, ensuring parallel and orthogonal ends to minimize geometric constraints. UV treatment involved an ultrasonic vibration setup consisting of a transducer, booster, and horn connected to a control unit for parameter adjustment. During the process, the horn made contact with the sample's top surface under a preset pressure, and 20 kHz vibrations were applied. Various UV energies ranging from 50 to 400 J were employed, resulting in processing times of ∼0.6 to 1.95 s and powers of ∼83 to 205 W. The vibration amplitude and static stress were maintained at low values, specifically 40 µm for vibration amplitude and 400 kPa for static stress, to ensure the elastic nature of cyclic strains imposed by horn. The infrared imaging camera (Fotric 280d, China) with data-acquisition frequency of 30 Hz was used to capture thermal images from the BMG sample during UV treatment. AnalyzIR software analyzed temperature changes during treatment. Additionally, due to the continuous pressure applied between the horn and the sample, a K-type thermocouple with a sampling frequency of 1000 Hz was put on the struck surface to monitor temperature fluctuations throughout the process on the struck surface. Two samples were immersed in liquid nitrogen for different durations, 60 h and 10 s, respectively, followed by exposure to UV energy of 400 J. Processing state: as-cast
Processing Word: Processing state: as-cast

The powder nominal composition was Mg-4%Y-3.3%(Gd, Nd)-0.5%Zr in units of mass fraction. An HK-M300 (Huake 3D Co., Wuhan, China) commercial machine was used to fabricate samples, which equipped with an IPG 500 W fiber laser and a focused laser spot diameter of about 100 µm. In order to obtain the optimum process parameters, the LPBF printing experiments were carried out with various laser powers and scanning speeds. Based on the average particle size of the powder, the printing layer thickness was set to 30 µm to obtain a good powder spreading effect. A hatch space of 80 µm was used to minimize the Plateau-Rayleigh capillary instability and thus reduce surface roughness. A scanning strategy of 67° rotation in the scanning direction of each layer was conducted along the build direction (BD), which aimed to enhance the isotropy of the microstructure and mechanical properties. During the LPBF process, the AM50 magnesium alloy substrate was preheated to 200 °C to minimize thermal stresses caused by temperature gradients. The fabrication chamber was continuously ventilated with high-purity argon gas to reduce the risk of samples oxidation and explosion. With the process described above, the representative cubic block samples (10 × 10 × 10 mm3), dog-bone tensile samples and porous lattice structures (10 × 10 × 10 mm3) were printed. The samples were extracted from the substrate using wire electrical discharge machining (WEDM). The cubic sample densities at different process parameters were measured using the Archimedes' drainage principle. Prior to the measurements, six surfaces of the samples were mechanically ground using 400# SiC sandpaper. Pore defects were examined using an optical microscope (OM, Leica DM750M, Germany). The x-y top and y-z side surfaces were mechanically ground using 500#, 1000#, 2000#, 3000#, and 5000# SiC sandpapers in sequence, and then polished on a polyurethane pad using a diamond solution with a grit size of 50 nm to obtain a smooth surface without scratches. To facilitate the examination of the microstructure using OM and SEM, the polished surfaces were metallurgically etched with a 4% solution of nitric acid in alcohol. The crystal structure and phase composition were determined using an X-ray diffractometer (XRD-7000S, Shimadzu, Japan) with Cu-Kα radiation (λ= 1.5406 Å) operating at 40 keV and 30 mA. Morphology, distribution and size of precipitated phases were observed by backscattered electron (BSE, Quanta650 FEG, FEI, USA). The grain size, grain orientation and texture were determined via electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, GeminiSEM300, German) and the collected data were post-processed by AztecCrystal software. Prior to EBSD testing, the mechanically polished surfaces were first electrolytically polished at 30 V for 20 s, and then etched on an argon ion beam instrument (PECS II 685, USA) for 30 min to remove surface residual stresses. To elucidate the sequence of phase precipitation during the non-equilibrium solidification, thermodynamic calculations were conducted using the PanMg database within the Pandat software. Furthermore, the nano-precipitates and dislocations were identified using a field emission transmission electron microscope (FTEM, Tecnai G2 F30, Netherlands) at an accelerating voltage of 300 keV. The nano-structure were identified with the selected area electron diffusion (SAED) patterns, high-angle annular dark-field (HAADF) and energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS). The TEM thin-foil specimen was obtained by argon ion beam thinning on PECS II 695 equipment. Uniaxial quasi-static tensile tests were performed on a material mechanical properties tester (MTS-647 Hydraulic Wedge Grip, USA) at a constant strain rate of 4 × 10−4s−1 at room temperature. Elongation changes were recorded using a contact extensometer with a 20 mm scale. Tensile samples were tested at least three times to obtain the average yield strength (σy), ultimate tensile strength (σUTS) and elongation at break. The fracture morphologies were observed using SEM. Furthermore, loading-unloading-reloading (LUR) cyclic tensile tests were conducted to reveal the grain size-induced Bauschinger effect. Samples were first loaded to 1.5% strain at a strain rate of 10−3s−1, then unloaded to 20 N at an unloading rate of 100 N/min, and subsequent cycles were performed per 1% of the strain. Processing Text: The 3 wt.% SiC/ZA63 (SiC/ZA63) composites were prepared by the semi-solid stirring casting method. The Mg-6Zn-3Al alloy (wt.%, all in wt.% otherwise stated) was selected as the matrix alloy, and SiC particles (provided by Shanghai Xiangtian Nano Co, China) with the average size of 8 µm, 30 µm, and 50 µm, respectively, were selected as the reinforcement phase. Before the addition of SiC particles, the SiC particles were cleaned by 5% hydrofluoric acid solution for 24 h to remove the contaminants on the surface of particles. Firstly, the pure Mg (99.95%) was melted at 720 ℃ in a steel crucible using a resistance furnace. The Zn (99.995%) and Al (99.995%) were added into the melt when the temperature of the Mg melt reached 720 ℃, and then the melt was stirred by a graphite rod for 2 min and held for 10 min to homogenize the composition. Secondly, the melt was cooled to 600 ℃, at which the Mg-6Zn-3Al alloy was in a semi-solid condition. Subsequently, the preheated stirring paddle was inserted into the melt for stirring. After the formation of stable eddy, the SiC preheated 450 ℃ was added into the melt at a constant rate by a vibrating powder feeder. The melt was reheated to 720 ℃ after stirring and then poured into an H13 mold preheated at 500 ℃. The ingot was solidified under a pressure of 200 MPa. Afterwards, the composite ingot was homogenized at 350 ℃ for 10 h followed by quenching in water at ∼20 °C. Before extrusion, each ingot with a size of φ35 ×70 mm 3was pre-heated at 300 ℃ for 30 min, and the extrusion process was conducted at this temperature with an extrusion ratio of 12.5:1 and a ram speed of 0.1 mm/s. The diameter of extruded composite was 10 mm. Processing Text: The validity and accuracy of the model are verified using titanium alloy as a case study, followed by an analysis of the microstructure and process properties of the as-deposited. Following optimization, the average grain size in the deposited state reached 245.1 μm; the deposition efficiency increased to 22.35 mm³/s; and the energy consumption decreased to 0.41 kWh. The optimized deposited state achieved an average tensile strength of 951 MPa, an average yield strength of 869 MPa, and a microhardness of 338.3 HV1, meeting the objectives of high performance, high efficiency, and low energy consumption. Microstructure and mechanical properties remain important indicators for large-scale structural components in aerospace ( Ren et al., 2017). For the high-power/high-efficiency LDED process of titanium alloys, research hotspots mainly focus on the microstructural and properties ( Zhang et al., 2019), including the non-uniformity of microstructure, grain refinement mechanism, anisotropy of properties, and the improvement of mechanical properties ( Song et al., 2023). Through the use of the pulsed LDED process, it has become possible to produce a fully equiaxed grain structure in TC4 titanium alloy, with an average grain size of 139 μm ( Zhang et al., 2023). However, the drawback is that the tensile elongation is only 4.09%, indicating insufficient toughness ( Chen et al., 2024). Meanwhile, the introduction of external energy fields also contributes to grain refinement ( Tan et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2022, 2023). Applying high-frequency ultrasonic vibration during the deposition process can transform coarse columnar grains into fine equiaxed grains, thereby refining the grain structure and effectively enhancing tensile properties ( Todaro et al., 2020). In the LDED deposition of TC4 titanium alloy, the introduction of a transverse static magnetic field can refine the primary β grains and produce a discontinuous grain boundary α phase, thereby improving tensile ductility and reducing the anisotropy of tensile properties ( Yuan et al., 2021). Processing Text: The as-deposited state has a room temperature tensile strength as high as 1091 MPa. In this study, the base material used is TC4 titanium alloy plates with a thickness of 15 mm. Before deposition, the substrate is polished smooth with 800-mesh sandpaper to remove surface oil and oxide, and then cleaned with anhydrous ethanol. It is then placed in a vacuum drying oven and dried at 200 °C for 1 h. The deposited material is TC4 powder, with a particle size distribution ranging from 53 to 150 μm. The values of D10, D50, and D90 are 45.56 μm, 72.72 μm, and 110.31 μm, respectively. The powder has good sphericity as shown in Fig. 6. Before used for deposition, the powder is dried at 200 °Cfor 8 h. The chemical compositions of the substrate and the powder are shown in Table 2. During the experiment, the laser spot diameter on the substrate processing surface is 4 mm, with a defocus amount of 40 mm, and the powder feeder delivers 5.8 g of powder per revolution. The deposition tests are conducted using the process parameters ( P, V, F) = (3785, 24.05, 7). Microhardness measurements are conducted using the HVS-1000A Vickers microhardness tester (HV1) following the sampling method shown in Fig. 7, with samples taken from the XOY, YOZ, and XOZ planes. Fig. 23presents the Vickers hardness measurement results for the optimal process parameters ( P, V, F)=(3785, 24.05, 7) and the empirical process parameters ( P, V, F)=(3900, 25, 5). After room temperature tensile testing, the morphology of the tensile fracture surfaces is analyzed using a scanning electron microscope (SEM3100). Table 13compares the tensile properties in the horizontal direction (XOY plane) between the optimal and empirical process parameters. Compared to the empirical scheme before optimization, the optimized process parameters resulted in an average ultimate tensile strength of 950.14 MPa, an increase of 32.08 MPa. The average yield strength increased to 869.14 MPa, an increase of 26.75 MPa, while the elongation slightly decreased on average, with a reduction of 2.17%. Then, a Pareto solution set decision method based on the IWC-TOPSIS method is proposed to select the optimal solution. Compared to other schemes, the average grain size is reduced to 242.5 μm, a decrease of 20.02%. Processing Text: Here, the cost-effective Si and Cu were used to modify an Al-5.5Mg alloy for laser-powder bed fusion (L-PBF), which achieved a synergetic combination of crack-free feature and high strength. A hierarchical structure featured by the refined ɑ-Al grains, sub-micron cellular structures decorated with Mg2Si, S-Al2CuMg nanoparticles and substantial dislocation networks was responsible for the obvious strength improvement in the L-PBFed Al-5.5Mg-2Si-Cu alloy, in which the ultimate tensile strength of 560 MPa, yield strength of 453 MPa and elongation of 9.1 % have been obtained. The synergistic effects of crack elimination and precipitation strengthening induced via the incorporation of Si/Cu provide the innovative guideline to fabricate crack-free Al-Mg alloys with high strength. The pre-alloyed Al-5.5Mg-2Si-Cu powders were produced by vacuum gas atomization. The L-PBF printing was conducted using a FS271 (Farsoon, Inc, China) machine with a Gaussian beam fibre capable of 500 W output. The parameters were employed as follows: the laser power (P) ranged from 270 to 330 W while scanning speed (v) from 600 to 1200 mm/s; The parameters were maintained at a layer thickness of 30 µm, hatch spacing of 100 µm, and a focused beam diameter of 90 µm. Laser scanning strategy was defined as rotating 67° between adjacent layers. The results confirmed that the optimized processing parameters were the Pof 290 W, vof 1000 mm/s, and VED of 96.7 J/mm 3. The L-PBFed Al-5.5Mg-2Si-Cu alloy achieved a superior combination of strength and ductility, in which the UTS of 560 MPa, the yield strength of 453 MPa and the elongation of 9.1 % were obtained under as-fabricated condition. In addition to the formation of fine a-Al grains, substantial dislocation networks and supersaturated solid solution, the sub-micron Mg2Si eutectics together with inter-cellular (Mg2Si, S-Al2CuMg) nanoparticles were mainly responsible for the strength improvement. Condition: As-fabricated; Microstructure: Hierarchical structure with refined α-Al grains, sub-micron cellular structures decorated with Mg2Si, S-Al2CuMg nanoparticles, and substantial dislocation networks.

Processing Text: Haynes 230, a nickel-based superalloy with a high melting point, is prone to forming microcracks during laser powder bed fusion (LPBF). After HIP, microcracks closed with the formation of nanoprecipitates at the closure sites, accompanied by increases in both grain and nanoprecipitate sizes, which were limited by pressure. M23C6 precipitates transformed into M6C, reducing lattice mismatch. To characterize the crack inhibition process, the as-deposited samples underwent HIP treatment at pressures of 60 MPa, 130 MPa, and 180 MPa at 1210 °C for 2 h ( Fig. 1d). The nanoprecipitates grew and shifted in composition, from Cr-rich M 23C 6in the crack generation state to W- and Mo-rich M 6C after crack inhibition. Due to its high Cr (23 wt%) and W (14 wt%) content, Haynes 230 exhibits a solid-solution strengthening mechanism ( σss) [45]. In LPBF samples, the high dislocation density contributes to dislocation strengthening ( σdis). In LPBF+HIP samples, the significant coarsening of precipitates leads to precipitation strengthening ( σOro) [46]. Therefore, the strength ( σLPBF) of the as-deposited state is mainly determined by three factors: σss, σdis, and grain boundary strengthening ( σGB). After HIP treatment, the strength ( σLPBF+HIP) is primarily determined by σss, σOro, and σGB. Dislocation strengthening dominated in the as-deposited Haynes 230, with a yield strength of 517 MPa, while precipitation strengthening dominated in the HIP state, with a yield strength of 502 MPa. After hot isostatic pressing, microcracks closed, and grain and precipitate sizes increased. Higher pressure suppressed grain growth. In the crack-inhibited alloy, the secondary phase was identified as M 6C, which formed via thermodynamically driven phase transformation and exhibited various orientation relationships with the matrix. During crack inhibition, nanoprecipitates formed at junctions, bridging microcracks. The M 23C 6phase in the as-deposited state transformed into M 6C, reducing lattice mismatch, with nanotwin boundaries forming within the nanoprecipitates. Analysis of the fractured zones of crack generation and crack inhibition samples revealed changes in the deformation mechanism, transitioning from dislocation slip to the accumulation of deformation twins, nano-growth twins, and stacking faults. Synergistic enhancement in strength and ductility was observed, with strength improvement resulting from the combined effects of crack closure and nanoprecipitates hindering dislocation motion, and ductility enhancement arising from crack closure, the formation of nanotwin boundaries, and the transformation of the deformation mechanism. Processing state: as-deposited; Elongation: 5.4 ± 1.2 %; Dominant strengthening mechanism: Dislocation strengthening

Processing Text: AA7075 is widely utilized in aerospace and transportation due to its high specific strength, specific stiffness, and corrosion resistance. Hot forging is an efficient and cost-effective method for manufacturing AA7075 cylindrical rings. During hot forging, AA7075 cylindrical ring undergoes complex metal flow, resulting in anisotropy in both microstructure and mechanical properties. The present study investigated the anisotropic behaviors of microstructure and mechanical properties in AA7075 cylindrical rings along three directions: rolling direction (RD), transverse direction (TD), and normal direction (ND). The results indicated that the microstructural anisotropy contributed to anisotropy in mechanical properties both before and after hot forging. In the present study, an AA7075 extruded bar ( Table 1), measuring ø300 × 520 mm, was held at 435°C for 12 h before the initial upsetting was completed. Following the first upsetting, the material was held at 435°C for 1 h prior to the second upsetting. Following the second upsetting, the bar diameter was adjusted to ø415 mm after another hour at 435°C. Finally, the material underwent hot forging in a hot forging mold after being held at 435°C for one more hour. Fig. 1shows the hot forging die and the resulting AA7075 cylindrical ring. The tensile strength and elongation at break of AA7075 cylindrical ring were evaluated in RD, TD, and ND using uniaxial tensile testing at room temperature. Fig. 2a illustrates the relative positions of the tensile samples within the cylindrical ring, while Fig. 2b provides the detailed dimensions of these samples. Each tensile testing was performed according to the same standard procedure. Three tensile tests were conducted for each group of samples at room temperature, using a strain rate of 2 mm/min, to obtain the average values of the samples' tensile strength and elongation at break. The microstructures of three planes - RD-TD, RD-ND, and TD-ND - were examined using a scanning electron microscope (SEM) equipped with an electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) detector. Before microscopic analysis, the samples were ground and polished to achieve a suitable surface finish. This process involved three stages: grinding with sandpaper with roughness of 800, 1200, 1500, 2000, and 2500, respectively; polishing with a 1μm diamond suspension; and electrolytic polishing with electrolyte (10 % HClO 4+90 % C₂H₅OH). The SEM and EBSD test were conducted on the JSM-7800F electron microscope equipped with the EBSD detector at an accelerating voltage of 15 kV and a scanning step of 1.4 μm. Direction: RD-TD plane; Mechanism: dislocation strengthening
Processing Word: Direction: RD-TD plane; Mechanism: dislocation strengthening

Processing Text: For thin, elongated metal tapes such as 50 μm Hastelloy substrate, rolling is the most commonly employed method. However, due to the inherent hardness of alloys like Hastelloy C-276, direct rolling to a thickness as low as 50 μm is challenging and may likely require intermediate annealing. Our private communication with REBCO manufacturers revealed that they only specify the thickness and surface roughness, indicating that different Hastelloy manufacturers may provide identical 50 μm Hastelloy tapes with significantly varied grain morphologies due to distinct intermediate annealing setups during rolling. Furthermore, while nearly all REBCO tape manufacturers utilize the IBAD process, the diverse methods of superconducting layer deposition, such as PLD, MOCVD, etc., introduce varying annealing temperatures and times to the Hastelloy substrate during the layer-by-layer fabrication of the final commercial REBCO product. This effectively leads the Hastelloy tapes into different recovery stages or even initial recrystallization stages. The differing initial grain conditions of the Hastelloy, coupled with varying heat inputs during the fabrication process, can result in markedly distinct grain morphologies of Hastelloy in the final products from different manufacturers, consequently yielding different strength values. Condition: 77 K

Processing Text: An equiatomic CoCrFeNi ingot was prepared from raw materials with purities > 99.5 % in an arc melting furnace with an Ar-filled protective atmosphere, followed by solid-solution treatment at 1200 °C for 2 h. The actual composition of CoCrFeNi alloy was determined using energy dispersive spectroscopy inside the Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM), as presented in Table 1. The ingot was sectioned into two pieces and then rolled to a thickness reduction of 90 % at room and cryogenic (∼-160 ± 10 °C) temperatures, respectively, before annealing at 870 °C and 800 °C for 1 hour, respectively, followed by final quenching in water. The rolling process was carried out at cryogenic temperature to obtain a more refined grain structure as compared to room temperature due to retarded grain growth. In the following sections, the alloys rolled at the room temperature and annealed at 870 °C as well as rolled at the cryogenic temperature and annealed at 800 °C, respectively, are referred to as CG (Coarse-Grained) and FG (Fine-Grained) HEAs. The specimens for HRDIC were initially ground to #4000 grit, followed by polishing with diamond suspensions and a final chemo-mechanical polishing in a solution of 1:1.5 amorphous colloidal silica suspension to deionised water ratio to remove the surface deformation introduced during the abrasive stages of preparation. After EBSD analysis, the surface was coated with a nano-sized Au speckle pattern following the procedure developed by Gioacchino and da Fonseca [ 79]. Firstly, the specimen was coated with a ∼5 nm thin film of 99.99 % Au using an Edwards S150B sputter coater (40 mA for 315 s). Processing Text: Powder assembly and alloying process including elemental alloying and shift-speed ball milling is applied in fabrication of CNT/Al-xMg (x = 0, 2.5, 5, wt.%). Pure Al powders (mean diameter ∼30 μm), pure Mg powders (mean diameter ∼10 μm) and graphitized raw CNTs powders (30-50 nm in diameter and <10 μm in length, 1.5 wt.% added, Chengdu Organic Chemistry Co., Ltd.) are mixed together and then ball milled at 135 rpm for 10 h and 270 rpm for 2 h, respectively. The mass ratio of stainless-steel milling balls to powders is controlled to be 20:1. Low speed ball milling (LSBM) at 135 rpm flake the powders and provides sufficient surface areas for uniform dispersion of CNTs. High speed ball milling (HSBM) at 270 rpm assembles the powder flakes by cold welding. To avoid massive oxidation and cool down the planetary ball milling system, the ball milling jars are filled with Ar atmosphere and take rest for 30 min after every 2 h of working. The cold-welded particles and pure Al powders (∼10 μm in diameter) with mass ratio of 7:3 is further ball milled together at 135 rpm for another 2 h and then assembled under pressure of 70 T to form green compacts. Subsequent vacuum sintering at 813 K promotes their densification and the diffusion of Mg in Al matrix. The heating rate of the sintering furnace is 4 K/min. After cooling down at ∼0.67 K/min to room temperature, the as-sintered samples are preserved in Muffle furnace of 653K for 2h and then extruded at 653 K under pressure of 80 T. The extrusion ratio is 25:1 and the diameter of the extruded rods are ∼8 mm. After cooling down by water quenching, the extruded rods showing surface temperature of ∼300 K are preserved in freezers (∼273 K). Specimens for tensile tests, EBSD, XRD, TEM and Raman tests are cut from the extrusion rods of CNT/Al, CNT/Al-2.5 Mg and CNT/Al-5Mg. Processing Text: In the present study, a novel dual-heterogeneous structure with a bimodal grain distribution in both ferrite and austenite phases was fabricated via cold rolling and partial recrystallization annealing on solution-treated 2205 duplex stainless steel (DSS). The received hot-rolled DSS 2205 was treated with TSS treatment to obtain "TSS" samples. This process involves an initial solution treatment at 1380 °C (1653 K) for 20 min, followed by rapid water quenching, and a subsequent solution treatment at 1000 °C (1273 K) for 20 min, followed by water quenching. The comparative sample was subjected to 90 % cold rolling deformation after TSS pretreatment, and then held at 930 °C (1203 K) for 1 min, followed by quenching to room temperature, resulting in the formation of bimodal grain heterostructured 2205 DSS ((hereinafter referred to as "CRA" sample). Dog-bone-shaped tensile specimens with a gauge length of 16 mm (//RD), a width of 4 mm (TD), and a thickness of 1 mm (ND) were cut along the rolling direction (RD: rolling direction, TD: transverse direction, ND: normal direction). The sample size for tensile testing was based on a laboratory standard. Uniaxial tensile tests were conducted on a Shimadzu AG-X100KN testing machine with a strain rate of 1 × 10 −3s −1at room temperature. Additionally, cyclic loading-unloading-reloading (LUR) tests were performed on the same equipment. In the LUR tests, specimens were initially loaded to an assigned strain at a rate of 1 × 10 −3s −1, subsequently unloaded with the unloading rate of 500 N min −1to 80 N, and then reloaded to the specified strain at the same rate of 1 × 10 −3s −1. To ensure the reliability of the results, three parallel tensile tests were repeated for each sample at the same strain rate. Electron backscattering diffraction (EBSD) mapping of undeformed samples was conducted on an Apreo field emission scanning electron microscope (SEM) equipped with a NordlysMax2 EBSD detector from Oxford instrument. The accelerating voltage was set at 15 kV, and the scanning step size was 0.2 µm. The detailed microstructures of the CRA sample before and after stretching were characterized by JEOL-2001F transmission electron microscopy (TEM). The sample was initially mechanically polished to achieve a thickness in the range of 50-60 µm. Further thinning was conducted using the TenuPol-5 automatic twin-jet electrolytic polishing equipment operating at 28 V and −20 °C. The electrolyte consisted of 10 vol.% perchloric acid and 90 vol.% ethanol. In situEBSD and SEM characterization techniques were used to observe the microstructural evolution of the experimental steel during deformation. The in-situtensile specimen was cut into a dog-bone shape with dimensions of 2 mm (//RD) × 1.8 mm (//TD) × 1.2 mm (//ND). EBSD characterization was performed using a Gemini 300 Zeiss SEM equipped with an Oxford Symmetry Series detector and an MTEST 2000 Gatan in situtensile stage. The parameters included a 20 kV accelerating voltage, 0.1 µm scanning step, and a 0.05 mm/min tensile loading rate. Both undeformed and in-situtensile samples were electropolished at 30 V for 25 s using a reagent consisting of 90 vol.% ethanol and 10 vol.% perchloric acid. Processing state: Solution-treated (TSS sample)

Processing Text: Microlattices are 3D-extruded with inks containing a blend of precursor Ti + Nb + TiAl3 powders, and their struts are then densified through a series of heat treatments to eliminate organic binder, sinter porosity, and achieve compositional Ti2AlNb homogeneity. The phase evolution of an as-printed filament (representative of a microlattice strut) is examined using in-situ X-ray diffraction, revealing a series of steps: (i) TiAl3 decomposition, starting at 710 °C and ending at 780 °C, to form TiAl; (ii) Nb and Al interdiffusion, initiating at 820 °C, accompanied by the formation of Nb2Al and Nb3Al phases; (iii) the α→β Ti phase transformation and (iv) Ti3Al formation, starting at 870 °C. Fully-homogenized Ti2AlNb microstructures with low residual porosity, comprising a B2 matrix and two types of α2 and O (orthorhombic) secondary phases, are achieved after sintering at 1300 °C for 5 h. The as-printed microlattices and heat exchanger were subjected to a three-step heat-treatment: (i) debinding at 450 °C for 30 min to decompose PS and remove residual DCM; (ii) pre-sintering at 750 °C for 2 h to remove any remaining organic materials; and (iii) sintering at 1300 °C for 5 h, followed by furnace cooling at a rate of 10 °C/min. Both the debinding and pre-sintering steps were carried out in an MTI GSL-1500 tube furnace with Ar (99.999 % pure) flowing at a rate of 500 sccm, with a Ti foil as an oxygen getter. For the sintering step, the pre-sintered microlattice was wrapped with Mo foil and vacuum-encapsulated in a quartz tube (OD: 19 mm, ID: 15 mm, residual Ar pressure: 190 mbar). Test temperature: 1000 °C; Compressive measurement; Ductility: 48%

Processing Text: The Al x(CoFeNi 1.5) 100-xHEA in atomic fraction was designed and a button ingot of 100 g was fabricated using an arc melting furnace in a Ti-gettered argon atmosphere. The ingot was flipped, melted and electromagnetically stirred for six times, in order to ensure chemical homogeneity. Samples were cut from the as-cast button (designated as AC) and cold rolled down to 80 % reduction (designated as CR). The CR samples were recrystallized in a muffle furnace at 1010 °C for 15 minutes followed by water quenching (which is denoted here as CRR) to achieve the full FCC microstructure. Subsequently, these samples were annealed at 500, 550, 575 and 600°C for 36, 54, and 72 hours, respectively, to achieve nano-lamellar structure. The schematic diagram of heat treatment with sample dimensions are shown in Fig. 1(a-b). The samples are denoted as, for example, CRR500-36 and CRR550-72, in which the first number from the left indicates the aging temperature and the second number indicates the aging time. The microstructures of these samples were examined via scanning electron microscope (SEM; ZEISS, SUPRA 55) and transmission electron microscope (TEM: FEI Talos F200X). The samples for SEM were prepared by grinding with SiC papers (grit sizes: 240-2500), polishing with 0.01μm colloidal silica solution, and finally etching in a 300 mL solution containing 25 % HNO 3, 25 % HF, and 50 % H 2O. The chemical composition was measured using energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) coupled with SEM. The samples for TEM imaging were prepared by using the Gatan ion thinner method and TEM investigation was performed at a voltage of 250 kV. Flat dog-bone tensile specimens were machined on a wire-cut electric discharge machine, with dimensions of 6 mm × 2 mm × 1 mm (length × width × thickness). All tensile specimens were ground to 1200 grit emery paper and then cleaned with acetone to remove surface defects. Tensile tests were performed using a universal double-column testing machine (Instron 45582 100KN) at room temperature with an initial strain rate of 1 × 10 −3s −1. Two specimens were tested for each aging condition. The fracture surfaces after tensile testing were examined by SEM. Sample ID: CRR500-72; Aging at 500°C for 72 hours

Processing Text: The reinforcement, a high-entropy ODS-(CoCrFeNiMn)100-x Al x (where x = 0, 5, 10, 20 at%) powder, was incorporated into the BCC-structured ODS-FeCrAl alloy by powder metallurgy processing. First, high-energy MA of elemental powders was conducted using a planetary mill (Fritsch P5) to separately produce the matrix and four types of reinforcement alloy powders. The MA process was carried out in an argon atmosphere at a rotational speed of 250 rpm for 50 h. Subsequently, each of the four MAed reinforcement powders was individually mixed with the MAed matrix powder using a powder mixer (GM55-4) at a speed of 100 rpm for 2 h, with the reinforcement powder content set at 15 wt%. Finally, the mixed alloy powders were sintered at 1100 °C for 5 min using a SPS device (LABOX-210). Compressive yield strength (σ sc)

Processing Text: The FeMnCrTi 0.1alloy was prepared using arc melting, with high-purity metal powders (purity >99.5 %) sourced from Beijing Xingrongyuan New Materials Co., Ltd. Prior to melting, the chamber was repeatedly purged with high-purity argon gas, and a molten titanium ingot was employed to further adsorb oxygen. Each alloy ingot underwent five cycles of remelting, during which electromagnetic stirring was applied to enhance compositional homogeneity. The details of contents of the FeMnCrTi 0.1alloy was shown in Table 1. Samples were irradiated with hydrogen ions up to 100 dpa. Hardness test results for the FeMnCrTi 0.1alloys after hydrogen ion irradiation were obtained, including hardness-depth curves and average hardness values. The alloy exhibits a yield strength of over 1000 MPa and a fracture strain exceeding 25 % at 650 °C. After irradiation with hydrogen ions up to 100 dpa, the material shows no significant segregation or dislocation loops. The average bubble size is less than 2 nm, and the bubble density and swelling rate is lower than that of CLAM (China Low Activation Martensitic) steel under similar irradiation conditions. Additionally, the irradiation hardening rate of this alloy is lower compared to common HEAs. Condition: at 650 °C

Processing Text: The medium Mn steel used in this study was initially a hot-forged plate with a thickness of 35 mm. Before the cyclic treatment, the hot-forged plate was heated to 1200°C and held for 2 h before being hot rolled. The final rolling temperature exceeded 850°C, with a total of 7 passes. The final rolled thickness was 5 mm, corresponding to a reduction of 85.7 %. After hot rolling, the medium Mn steel was water-cooled to room temperature. For ease of reference, the hot-rolled medium Mn steel is referred to as HR in this study. The sequence includes the first intercritical annealing (denoted as I1), followed by the first cold rolling (C1), progressing to subsequent cycles of annealing and rolling—specifically, the second (I2, C2), third (I3, C3) as well as fourth (I4, C4) intercritical annealings and cold rollings. According to simulations using Jmatpro 7, the A1 and A3 temperatures for medium Mn steel were 500°C and 750°C, respectively. In this study, 700°C was selected as the intercritical annealing temperature. The entire process and the corresponding detailed parameters are presented in Table 2 and Fig. 1. As previously mentioned, medium Mn steel is prone to cracking during cold rolling. When the reduction exceeds 25 %, surface cracks develop, preventing further processing. Therefore, the cold rolling reduction was limited to 25 %. The microstructures of medium Mn steel in various states were characterized using scanning electron microscopy (SEM, JSM-7100F), electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, JSM-7100F, OIM), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM, FEI Tecnai F30). For SEM, samples were ground with sandpaper, mechanically polished, and electrolytically etched in a 10 % perchloric acid alcohol solution at 15 V for 25-30 s. SEM examination was performed at 15 kV. For EBSD, samples underwent mechanical polishing followed by electrolytic polishing using the same 10 % perchloric acid alcohol solution at 20 V for 15-25 s. EBSD was conducted at 20 kV. The scan parameters were as follows: 80 μm × 80 μm with a step size of 0.5 μm for HR; 8 μm × 8 μm with a step size of 0.1 μm for I2 and I3; and 40 μm × 40 μm with a step size of 0.2 μm for I4. For TEM, samples were thinned to below 50 μm, cut into 3 mm discs, and further thinned using an MTP-1A twin-jet electrolytic polisher in 4 % perchloric acid alcohol at −40°C with 75-100 V. TEM was conducted at 200 kV. Element distribution in the C3 sample after tensile testing was analyzed using electron probe microanalysis (EPMA, JXA-8530F). Samples were ground and polished. EPMA was conducted at 15 kV, with scan parameters as follows: 100 μm × 50 μm, step size 0.2 μm for HR and C1; 10 μm × 5 μm, step size 0.1 μm for I2; and 20 μm × 10 μm, step size 0.1 μm for I3 and C3. Phase content was analyzed using X-ray diffraction (XRD, Rigaku) with Cu Kα radiation. Samples were electrolytically polished to reduce residual stress using the same parameters as EBSD preparation. The scanning range was 40°-100° at 3°/min. The austenite volume fraction ( fγ) was calculated using Eq. (1)[32]. (1)fγ=1.4Iγ1.4Iγ+Iαwhere Iγis the integrated intensity of austenite and Iαis the integrated intensity of α or α’-phase, which were calculated based on the integrated intensities of (200)α, (211)α, (200)γ, (220)γ, and (311)γ diffraction peaks. Hardness measurements for each layer were conducted using a Vickers microhardness tester (TMVS-1). A load of 10 g and a dwell time of 10 s were applied, with at least five points tested per layer, and 5 layers per each type of multilayer structure. Tensile testing (UTM5105X) was performed on dog bone-shaped specimens, with an initial tensile speed of 1 mm/min. The longitudinal direction of the tensile test specimen was consistent with the rolling direction. The gauge length of the specimen was 10 mm, and the width was 2.4 mm. If the plate thickness exceeded 2 mm, the specimen thickness was 2 mm; otherwise, the specimen thickness matched the plate thickness. Three specimens of each parameter were tested in tensile test. The deformation behavior of the tensile specimens in various states was assessed using DIC. Images during the tensile loading process were captured using an Elphel NC353L camera, which provided high-resolution images of 1224 × 614 pixels, with a physical resolution of 0.021 × 0.021 mm/pixel. The camera's sampling frequency was set to 5 frames per second. Before conducting the tensile tests, the facet of DIC specimens was uniformly sprayed with black paint, followed by the application of white paint using a spray gun for contrast enhancement. Processing Text: Elemental powders of tungsten (W), niobium (Nb), tantalum (Ta), and vanadium (V) with purities exceeding 99.5 % were employed to fabricate the equal-atomic ratio WNbTaV RHEA samples. Processing Text: A356 matrix composites with dual-structured reinforcements (monolithic τ2-phase particles and core (Ti)-shell (τ2) structured particles) and matrix (Si-rich regions and Si-lean regions) were fabricated via solid-state sintering and subsequent die forging. The achieved green billets were subsequently sintered under vacuum at 555 °C for 3 h, 4 h, 5 h, and 6 h, respectively. Once the sintering was completed, the billets were swiftly moved to a preheated steel mold cavity (300 °C) positioned on a hydraulic machine, and forged at 190 MPa for 20 s to densify the microstructures, and finally formed cakes with dimensions of Ø50 mm × ∼10 mm. Processing Text: The starting materials for this study were a Ni single crystal of 99.999 % purity. The cylindrical Ni single crystal rod had 70 mm length and 15 mm diameter. The Ni single crystal was prepared using the standard Czochralski method. Cylindrical specimens were cut using an electrical discharge machine (EDM) in three different crystallographic orientations, namely [100], [110], and [111], from the Ni single crystal rod and annealed at 500 °C for 1 h. The specimens were prepared using standard metallographic procedures followed by polishing with colloidal silica and finally electropolishing (Struers LectroPol 5) using A2 solution (90 ml distilled water, 730 ml ethanol, 100 ml butoxyethanol, 78 ml perchloric acid) at 20 V for 15 s at ambient temperature. Compression samples were extracted from nickel single crystals such that the [111], [110], and [100] direction was parallel to the compression axis. All the samples were tested in a Dartec servo-hydraulic universal testing machine with an initial strain rate of 10−3s−1 at ambient temperature up to 10 % true strain. Processing Text: Traditional commercial hot-rolled AZ31 sheets were obtained from commercial suppliers, with thicknesses in the normal direction (ND) of 0.5 mm. They were cut into rectangular sheets measuring 22 mm ×60 mm along the transverse direction (TD) and rolling direction (RD). All sheets underwent grinding and polishing to achieve a mirror finish, followed by ultrasonic cleaning. To prevent bonding between the punch and the samples, the upper and lower punch surfaces were coated with graphite paper. During DB, a WE43 sheet was sandwiched between two AZ31 sheets to form an “AZ31/WE43/AZ31” heterostructured sample. High-purity argon was used as a protective gas to protect surfaces from oxidation. The DB experiment was performed according to specified process parameters, including bonding temperature, holding time, and bonding pressure. The heating rate was set to ensure simultaneous attainment of the specified bonding temperature and pressure. Following DB process, the sample was air-cooled. SEM and EBSD samples were taken from the RD to ND slice for both the DBed and initial materials. Tensile testing samples, shaped like a dog’s bone, with 45 mm length and 11 mm width, were extracted from the specimens using an electric spark cutting machine. Processing Text: A 50 kg ingot was cast in a vacuum induction furnace, reheated to 1200 °C for homogenisation annealing, and forged into billets with a cross-sectional area of 1500 mm × 20 mm at 950-1200 °C. The forged plates were hot-rolled (HR) at 1050 °C to a thickness of 5.5 mm and air-cooled to room temperature. The HR plates were further subjected to WR at 650 °C to a thickness of 1.6 mm. During WR, the HR plates were first heated to the target temperature, maintained for 15 min, and rolled five times, which decreased the total thickness by approximately 71 %. The WR plates were intercritically annealed (IA) at 620 °C for 5 h to soften the steel, and then cold-rolled (CR) to reduce the thickness by 15 % to 1.36 mm. Finally, the ART samples were annealed at 600-750 °C for 5 min and then air-cooled to enhance their ductility; the final samples were named WCR600, WCR675, and WCR750. Processing Text: Argon gas atomised Al-Ni-Sc-Zr powder was used for LPBF fabrication. The chemical composition of the powder determined by Inductively Coupled Plasma Atomic Emission spectroscopy (ICP-AES) was Al-5.61Ni-0.63Sc-0.09Zr (wt.%). After optimising the laser parameters, the components were built using a laser power of 285 W, scanning speed of 1500 mm/s, hatch space of 90 μm, layer thickness of 30 μm, and island scanning strategy with a 90° rotation between layers. The fabrication process was carried out in a high-purity argon atmosphere with an oxygen content of <200 ppm. After the LPBF process, the as-built alloys were separated from the base plate using electrical discharge machining. Subsequently, the as-built alloys were then subjected to direct ageing at temperatures ranging from 200 to 375 °C, with ageing times ranging from 1 min to 70 h. Processing Text: The experimental steel was prepared by smelting in a high-frequency vacuum furnace using high-purity raw materials. The cast ingot was hot forged into a plate of 30 mm thickness and then homogenized at 1100 °C for 2h. The Ac 3and Ms temperatures of the as-obtained steel were 818 °C and 170 °C, respectively, as determined by a DIL-805A quenching thermal dilatometer. The austenitization temperature and the first-stage austempering temperature were determined to be 910 °C and 240 °C, respectively. Thermal simulation experiments were conducted using cylindrical samples ( φ6 mm × 70 mm) on a Gleeble-3500 simulator. All samples were austenitized at 910 °C for 30 min. For the TA-4.5 treatment, samples were quenched to 240 °C immediately after austenitizing and held for 4.5h. When the bainite transformation had progressed to 30 %, the samples were rapidly cooled to 180 °C to continue the second austempering stage until the bainite transformation was complete (approximately 16h). For the TA-8.5 treatment, after 8.5h of the first austempering stage at 240 °C (when 70 % of the bainite transformation had occurred), the samples were immediately cooled to 150 °C and held for 3h. This holding time slightly exceeded the incubation period of bainite transformation, enabling the refinement of BRA through localized BF formation in carbon-depleted regions. According to the calculations from JMatPro software, the samples were held at 240 °C for 8.5h and 20h before being brought down to ambient temperature, designated as SA-8.5 and SA-20, respectively. Processing Text: An Al-1%Si alloy was prepared using high-purity aluminum (99.99 %) and an Al-20%Si alloy by melting in a clay graphite crucible at 730 °C in an electric furnace. The melt was stirred with a graphite rod, degassed using hexachloroethane, and then cast into a graphite mold preheated to 200 °C. The ingot was sectioned into plates for solution treatment and subsequent rolling deformation. The as-cast (AC) samples underwent solution treatment at 570 °C for 10 h, followed by water quenching. The solution-treated samples are called AS for short. Processing Text: A commercially pure Ti (Grade 2) featuring a composition of Ti-0.03 % N-0.08 % C-0.015 % H-0.3 % Fe-0.25%O ((weight percent) was prepared in the present study. The initial bulk underwent vacuum annealing at 800 °C for 2 h to achieve a homogeneous CG structure. The primary bar, measuring Ø160 mm × 300 mm, was subjected to multiple unidirectional extrusion at 500 °C. At the beginning of extrusion, a diameter reduction of 5–8 mm per pass was applied with no any rotation. When the rod diameter is decreased to 50 mm, the diameter reduction per pass was changed to 2–4 mm. A final bar with a diameter of Ø24 mm was obtained. Plates with a thickness of 10 mm were cut and subsequently rolled in multiple passes to a final thickness of 1 mm, i.e., 90 % thickness reduction under liquid nitrogen temperature. Five sets of rolled samples were subsequently annealed at 450 °C for 1 h, 500 °C for 1 h, 600 °C for 1 h, 700 °C for 1 h, and 800 °C for 2 h to achieve varying sizes of recrystallized grains. Processing Text: Ingots with the nominal composition of Ni 41.8Co 19Cr 10Fe 10Al 15Ti 2Mo 2Hf 0.1B 0.1were prepared by arc melting in a Ti-gettered high-purity argon atmosphere. Each ingot was re-melted at least four times for chemical homogeneity and then drop-casted into a water-cooled copper mold with a dimension of 100 × 12 × 5 mm 3. Processing Text: In this study, hierarchical heterostructures were introduced into CoCrFeMnNi HEA via an in-situ rolling (ISR) assisted laser cladding (LC) process. The coating was fabricated by overlapping individual tracks with a 30 % overlapping ratio. Following the preliminary testing, the distance D between the laser head and the roller was set to 13 mm. In this work, static pressures of 0 N, 1000 N, 2000 N, 3000 N, and 4000 N were applied, and the corresponding coatings were referred as un-ISR, ISR1, ISR2, ISR3 and ISR4, respectively. Annealed 45 steel with dimensions of 100 mm × 100 mm × 10 mm was chosen as the substrate. To minimize the interference of oxides and other impurities, an angle grinder was used to remove the oxide layer from the substrate surface, followed by cleaning with anhydrous ethanol. The powder used in this study was CoCrFeMnNi HEA powder with a particle size range of 45-105 μm, produced by high-temperature gas atomization. Before the experiment, place the powder in a vacuum drying oven (Shanghai Jiecheng Experimental Instrument Co., Ltd., DZF-6050) and dry it at 100 °C for 2 h to ensure its uniformity and fluidity. The coating was prepared by using a semiconductor laser (HWL-1500) with a wavelength range of 910-1050 nm and a DPSF scraper powder feeder to transport CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy powder coaxially. Laser spot diameter 2 mm, laser power 1500 W, scanning rate 3 mm/s, powder feed 7 g/min, overlapping ratio 30 %. High purity argon is used as melt pool shielding gas with a flow rate of 3 L / min. The prepared coating was cut into cuboid specimens with dimensions of 15 × 15 × 10 mm 3using a high-speed wire electrical discharge machining machine tool (Fangzheng CNC Machine Tool Co., Ltd., DK7720). The specimens were then hot - mounted using a metallographic specimen mounting machine (Laizhou Hengyi Test Instrument Co., Ltd., XQ-2B). Subsequently, the cross - section of the specimen was ground using SiC sandpapers of grit sizes 60 mesh, 400 mesh, 800 mesh, 1500 mesh, and 2000 mesh in a wet - grinding manner on a metallographic specimen grinding and polishing machine (Laizhou Hengyi Test Instrument Co., Ltd., MP-2B). After grinding, the specimens were polished with diamond polishing paste until no obvious scratches were visible under an optical microscope. The specimens were placed in anhydrous ethanol and cleaned in an ultrasonic cleaner for 5 min. To prepare the surfaces for electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) analysis, the specimen was pre-ground and polished using the metallographic pre-grinding machine (Hua Xing Test Instrument Co., Ltd.). The surface was then ion-polished with a precision ion thinning instrument (GATAN PIPS II 695) to remove the damage layer caused by mechanical polishing. The microhardness was measured using a Vickers hardness tester (Laizhou Hengyi Test Instrument Co., Ltd., NVM-1000 A). The load was set at 0.3 kg, and the dwell time was 15 s. Each value was measured three times to ensure accuracy. The tribological properties of the coatings at room temperature (25 °C) were evaluated by a ball-on-disk wear tester (Lanzhou Zhongke Kaihua Science and Technology Development Co., Ltd., HT-1000) with a Si 3N 4ball as the counterpart. The tests, performed under dry sliding conditions in accordance with the ASTM G99-17 standard, were repeated three times. The test parameters included a loading force of 10 N, a friction radius of 3 mm, a rotation speed of 600 r/min, and a wear time of 30 min. Condition: Untreated; Measurement: Room Temperature
Processing Word: Condition: Untreated; Measurement: Room Temperature

Processing Text: Forged H13 steel, supplied in a spheroidized annealed state with dimensions of 100 × 100 × 50 mm 3, was used as the substrate for metal deposition in the WA-DED process. H13 wire with a diameter of 1.6 mm was used as the deposition material. Two different process routes were designed to fabricate the hybrid samples, as shown in Fig. 1. (i) WA-DED was performed directly on the forged H13 substrate which is in the annealed state, and then the hybrid components fabricated by forging/WA-DED were austenitized at a temperature of 1030 °C for 2 h, and quenched in oil, and then double-tempered at 580 °C for 2 h, referred to as WQT ( Fig. 1(a)); (ii) the forged H13 substrate was first austenitized at 1030 °C for 2 h, and quenched in oil, and then WA-DED on the quenched H13 substrate, followed by double tempering at 580 °C for 2 h, referred to as QWT ( Fig. 1(b)). The WA-DED process was accomplished by a GMAW-based WA-DED system consisting of a YASKAWA AR1440 robot and a YASKAWA MOTOWELD-RD500 welding power source. H13 blocks with dimensions of approximately 80 × 80 × 60 mm 3were deposited on the forged substrate using the composite path of Contour + Zigzag. Adjacent layers use cross-over deposition paths (see Fig. 1). The detailed process parameters of the WA-DED process are shown in Table 2. Processing Text: The AFMAR alloys were prealloyed and gas atomized by CEIT (Spain). The powders were then sintered through Spark Plasma Sintering (HPD-25 equipment, FCT System GmbH, Germany) in a graphite die 20 mm in diameter. A tungsten foil of 25-50 µm was placed between the inner walls of the die and the powder, isolating the alloy from the graphite and preventing carbon contamination. A heating rate of 400 °C/min was used to reach a sintering temperature of 1100 °C and held for 5 min while applying a 50 MPa uniaxial pressure under a 10 -2mbar low vacuum. This sintering cycle was chosen because it had been previously optimized with the same die geometry for a similar alloy. AFMAR samples were cut into semi-circles of 20 mm in diameter and approximately 2 mm in thickness. All samples were grounded to a 1200-grit surface finish and cleaned with ethanol prior to the corrosion tests. The samples were placed in rectangular alumina crucibles with molten lead. Samples of commercial alloys 316 L and T91 were placed in a separate crucible from the AFMAR alloys and were used as reference. The lead exposure tests were conducted in a COSTA (COrrosion test STand for liquid metal Alloys) facility located at KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm, developed by the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT). The alumina crucibles containing the samples, and the lead were positioned inside a sealed quartz glass tube. To control the oxygen concentration in the atmosphere inside the tube, one extreme had inlet and outlet gas tubes. Since the oxygen partial pressures needed for the test are much lower than what can be provided in commercial bottles (≅ 10 -18bar), a flowing gas mixture of Ar, H 2and H 2O is used. An Ar gas flow is bubbled through water, carrying water vapor as it moves. Then, the humidified-Ar flow is mixed with an Ar-5 %H 2gas flow at the inlet of the gas tube. By controlling the flow rate of both gases, it is possible to adjust the H 2/H 2O ratio and achieve the desired oxygen partial pressure of the gas phase inside the glass tube (p O2). A Zirox SGM5 oxygen analyzer placed at the gas outlet was used to monitor the p O2. Corrosion tests at 550 °C and 650 °C were performed, lasting up to 1000 h each. Condition: after 500 h in molten lead at 550 °C

Processing Text: The alloy components were weighed according to the designed composition and thoroughly melted in a ZG-25-A vacuum induction furnace at a temperature of approximately 1450 °C. The molten alloy was then poured into a sand mold to form 12 kg Al0.3CoCrFeNiTi0.15 ingots. A portion of the original ingot was subjected to further melting process to improve material homogeneity, remove impurities, and obtain the cast sample (noted as C-1 sample). For the LPBF process, the remaining primitive initial ingots were processed into 32 mm bars. The pre-alloyed Al0.3CoCrFeNiTi0.15 powders were generated by the plasma rotating electrode process (PREP) (the schematic view is shown in Fig. 1(a)) from the prepared bars. The particle size ranges from 10 to 53 μm. The 3 × 3 × 3 mm3 cuboid samples (noted as 0A ∼ 9J) were built on a commercial machine (TruPrint 1000) with a build chamber of Φ100 mm*80 mm (Figs. 2(a ∼ b)). Employing a laser power (P) of 175 W, and a layer thickness (h) of 30 μm, the laser was rotated at a 67° angle (α) for each scanning layer (Fig. 2(d)) for homogenous microstructure. The argon atmosphere was maintained during the deposition with an oxygen environment below 100 ppm to prevent oxidation. Meanwhile, the hatching space (d) ranged from 30 to 70 μm and the scanning speed (v) varied from 500 to 2400 mm/s, corresponding to changes in laser volumetric energy density (E=Pvhd) from 33.7 to 388.9 J·mm−3 (Table S1). These parameters were meticulously selected to build Al0.3CoCrFeNiTi0.15 specimens. In addition, to reduce the effect of pore characteristics (including shape, size, location and number) on stress concentrations (Fig. S1), the remelting technology was undertaken to further enhance the performance, as depicted in Fig. 2(c) (noted as R-2). Finally, 33 × 17 × 7 mm3 samples were deposited under the same optimized laser conditions to analyze their mechanical properties (Fig. 2(d)). The tensile test specimens perpendicular to the building direction, with a gauge length of 12.5 mm, a width of 4.0 mm, and a thickness of 1.5 mm (Fig. 2(d)), were cut out by a wire-cut electrical discharge machine. Then the tensile tests at 20 °C and 700 °C were conducted on the INSTRON 5982 and ZWICK universal testing machine (Z250SH) with a tensile rate of 5 × 10−3 s−1. A digital image correlation sensor was used to measure the strain at RT, the displacement at 700 °C tensile testing was measured by a ceramic contact extensometer. The microhardness was conducted by an XHVT-10Z Vickers hardness tester with a load of 1 kg for a dwell time of 20 s. Each reported hardness value is the average value of five measurements. The metallographic specimen was cut in the middle zone of cuboid samples, as depicted in Fig. 2(d), which were first ground with SiC papers up to 5000 grit and then polished. Defects and morphology (aqua regia etching: 15 mL HCl + 5 mL HNO3) were observed by optical microscope (OM) (SOPTOP RX50M). The microstructures and grain orientation were achieved using a TESCAN MIRA3 scanning electron microscope (SEM) equipped with an electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) detector and energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS). The grain size, texture, misorientation between grains, and Kernel average misorientation (KAM) map were investigated using EBSD analysis (MTEX). The microstructures and precipitations were also characterized by the FEI TALOS F200X transmission electron microscope (TEM). The 3 mm foils (thickness less than 50 μm) were polished to electron transparency by a twin-jet electro-polisher (5 % perchloric acid +95 % ethanol) at −15 °C and 30 V. Processing state: LPBF (R-2 sample); Condition: Room Temperature

The molten alloy was then poured into a sand mold to form 12 kg Al0.3CoCrFeNiTi0.15 ingots. A portion of the original ingot was subjected to further melting process to improve material homogeneity, remove impurities, and obtain the cast sample (noted as C-1 sample). For the LPBF process, the remaining primitive initial ingots were processed into 32 mm bars. The pre-alloyed Al0.3CoCrFeNiTi0.15 powders were generated by the plasma rotating electrode process (PREP) (the schematic view is shown in Fig. 1(a)) from the prepared bars. The particle size ranges from 10 to 53 μm. The 3 × 3 × 3 mm3 cuboid samples (noted as 0A ∼ 9J) were built on a commercial machine (TruPrint 1000) with a build chamber of Φ100 mm*80 mm (Figs. 2(a ∼ b)). Employing a laser power (P) of 175 W, and a layer thickness (h) of 30 μm, the laser was rotated at a 67° angle (α) for each scanning layer (Fig. 2(d)) for homogenous microstructure. The argon atmosphere was maintained during the deposition with an oxygen environment below 100 ppm to prevent oxidation. Meanwhile, the hatching space (d) ranged from 30 to 70 μm and the scanning speed (v) varied from 500 to 2400 mm/s, corresponding to changes in laser volumetric energy density (E=Pvhd) from 33.7 to 388.9 J·mm−3 (Table S1). These parameters were meticulously selected to build Al0.3CoCrFeNiTi0.15 specimens. In addition, to reduce the effect of pore characteristics (including shape, size, location and number) on stress concentrations (Fig. S1), the remelting technology was undertaken to further enhance the performance, as depicted in Fig. 2(c) (noted as R-2). Finally, 33 × 17 × 7 mm3 samples were deposited under the same optimized laser conditions to analyze their mechanical properties (Fig. 2(d)). The tensile test specimens perpendicular to the building direction, with a gauge length of 12.5 mm, a width of 4.0 mm, and a thickness of 1.5 mm (Fig. 2(d)), were cut out by a wire-cut electrical discharge machine. Then the tensile tests at 20 °C and 700 °C were conducted on the INSTRON 5982 and ZWICK universal testing machine (Z250SH) with a tensile rate of 5 × 10−3 s−1. A digital image correlation sensor was used to measure the strain at RT, the displacement at 700 °C tensile testing was measured by a ceramic contact extensometer. The microhardness was conducted by an XHVT-10Z Vickers hardness tester with a load of 1 kg for a dwell time of 20 s. Each reported hardness value is the average value of five measurements. The metallographic specimen was cut in the middle zone of cuboid samples, as depicted in Fig. 2(d), which were first ground with SiC papers up to 5000 grit and then polished. Defects and morphology (aqua regia etching: 15 mL HCl + 5 mL HNO3) were observed by optical microscope (OM) (SOPTOP RX50M). The microstructures and grain orientation were achieved using a TESCAN MIRA3 scanning electron microscope (SEM) equipped with an electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) detector and energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS). The grain size, texture, misorientation between grains, and Kernel average misorientation (KAM) map were investigated using EBSD analysis (MTEX). The microstructures and precipitations were also characterized by the FEI TALOS F200X transmission electron microscope (TEM). The 3 mm foils (thickness less than 50 μm) were polished to electron transparency by a twin-jet electro-polisher (5 % perchloric acid +95 % ethanol) at −15 °C and 30 V. Processing Text: The material used is annealed low-carbon steel (LCS) sheets with a thickness of 2 mm and a nominal composition (wt.%) of 0.2C-0.5Mn-1.0Si. In order to introduce a gradient distribution of interstitial atoms, a diffusion bonding treatment was used. The detailed process is given as follows: 0.1 mm graphite was stacked between two steel sheets to form a sandwich plate; then, the stacked sandwich was diffusion bonded under a pressure of 5 kPa and under the protection of argon gas. The target bonding temperatures of 1200 °C and 1220 °C were used, respectively, with a holding time of 30 min. Subsequently, the bonded plates were hot rolled at 1000 °C with a thickness reduction of 50 % to tailor the grain morphologies. Hereafter, the hot-rolled specimens via diffusion bonding at 1200 °C and 1220 °C are referred to as CGS1200 and CGS1220, respectively. Multi-gradient microstructure with variations in grain size, volume fraction, and lamellar spacing of pearlite; gradient distribution of interstitial C-atoms; strength-toughness combination is excellent; compared to high-performance steels
