Processing Text: The material is entirely melted in an electric furnace at roughly 720 °C, with a combination of protective gases (SF 6: CO 2= 1: 99) to avoid oxidation, then it is transferred into a hot steel mold and allowed to air-cool, producing cylindrical ingots 90 mm in diameter. Afterward, the ingot is heated to 500 °C for 24 h and then allowed to cool in the air to achieve homogenization. The alloy was extruded at 400 °C, maintaining a speed of 2 mm/s with extrusion gradient: T1. The temperature as a single variable adds 300 °C, 350 °C, and 450 °C, while other parameters remain unchanged according to the T400S2T1. Similarly, speed as a single variable additionally adds 1 mm/s and 4 mm/s, and gradient as a single variable additionally adds T0 and T2 (angle α is 0 and 2 respectively, as shown in Fig. 1). Different mixed grain structures can be achieved in this work by adjusting extrusion parameters like speed, gradient, and temperature. By altering extrusion parameters to influence the DRXed process, different proportions, distributions, and types of coarse grains in Mg-5Y-1Sn alloy were obtained. The extrusion gradient refers to the number of modulus angles α in the forming strip. Extrusion conditions: T300S2T1

Processing Text: The Mn0.3CoCrFeNi was prepared via vacuum-induction melting using elements that are over 99.9 % in purity. The Co, Cr, Fe, and Ni in equimolar ratio were first added to an alumina crucible in a muffle furnace and melted. Afterward, Mn was added in an upper funnel in its respective molar ratio; this was done to achieve the best possible uniform alloy composition since Mn has a smaller molar ratio compared to CoCrFeNi, and to avoid possible oxidation/evaporation of Mn since it has a lower melting point compared to CoCrFeNi or its constituent elements. The furnace was vacuumed to a pressure of 0.1 Pa, filled with argon up to 100000 Pa, and then the furnace was turned on to melt all elements at 1600 °C for 75 min and continuously stirred for uniform mixing. An additional 2 min was spent for refining (removing impurities and fully fusing), and then the mixture was cast into ingots of 300 × 200 × 20 mm plate for each alloy. Alloys were then air-cooled. For each of the alloys, the as-cast samples (hereafter called AC) were split into 200 × 24 × 12 mm coupons; one of them was homogenized and cold-rolled (hereafter called CR). The homogenization was conducted at 1250 °C for 4 h using a high-temperature Carbolite furnace followed by water quenching to ensure chemical homogeneity. The cold rolling was conducted using a 2HI Lab Rolling Mill (IRM MODEL #3350) to achieve ⁓30 % thickness reduction at a final dimension of ⁓270 × 25 × 8 mm. A portion of the CR plates for both HEAs were further split, and half was annealed at 1250 °C for 1 h, followed by water quenching to ensure chemical homogeneity, recovery, and recrystallization (hereafter called CRA). Processing conditions: AC-Mn; Quasi-static compression

Processing Text: The TA15 alloy was fabricated using laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) technology. After annealing, L-PBF TA15 samples exhibit excellent mechanical properties at medium to high temperatures. Heat treatment was conducted in a resistance furnace, with the samples coated with a ceramic protective layer to prevent oxidation. The heating rate was set at 10 °C/min, followed by a 2-h dwell at a temperature of 850 °C, and then cooled by air. The fine needle-like αʹ martensite transitioned into lamellar α + β phases after annealing treatment. Samples were tensile tested in the range of 500-750 °C. The as-built TA15 alloy consists of αʹ phase, which can be decomposed into α + β after annealing treatment. The TA15 alloy processed by L-PBF demonstrates exceptional high-temperature tensile properties, with a tensile strength of 686 ± 12 MPa and an elongation of 18.5 ± 2.1 % at 500 °C. Processing Text: Invar 36 alloy samples were fabricated using the in-situ rolling-assisted laser directed energy deposition (LDED) process, and the effect of in-situ rolling on the microstructure, mechanical properties and coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE) was investigated. The plastic deformation introduced by in-situ rolling facilitated the recovery and recrystallization of the pre-solidified layers. The yield strength was significantly enhanced due to grain refinement strengthening and work hardening. The refinement of grains and the increase in residual stress induced by in-situ rolling enabled these samples to maintain an ultra-low CTE. Gas atomized Invar 36 alloy powders were utilized as raw material, and the HAM experiments were performed on an IR-LDED system. The deformation of the deposited material was achieved by adding a rolling unit next to the deposition head and ensuring the synergistic movement of the two, and the distance between the rolling unit and deposition head was 35 mm. The rolling load was obtained in real-time through a sensor, and can be adjusted by controlling the lifting amount of the rolling unit in each layer. The dimension of the rolling head was ϕ50 mm × 20 mm, and a detailed description of the IR-LDED procedure can be found in our previous publication [ 16]. The scanning speed of rolling unit and deposition head was 8 mm/s, and the laser power and overlap rate were 1300 W and 40 %, respectively. Samples with dimensions of 70 mm × 5 mm × 50 mm were fabricated by the IR-LDED process under loads of 0 kN, 5 kN and 10 kN, and the corresponding lifting amount of the rolling unit in each layer were 0.55 mm, 0.38 mm and 0.28 mm, respectively. Processing Text: The (CoCrFeNi)84(AlTi)16 M/HEA system was fabricated using MA + SPS. The high purity (≥99.7 wt %) elemental powders of Co, Cr, Fe, Ni, Al and Ti (particles size ≤10 μm) were used as raw materials in specific atomic ratios. The compositions (via at. %) were synthesized in the current work as shown in Fig. 1. To attain M/HEAs with a nanocrystalline structure, the elemental powders were mechanically alloyed by planetary ball mill machine using stainless bowl and balls. The ball milling was conducted at a rotation speed of 300 rpm under Ar atmosphere for 70 h after mixing of 0.3 wt% stearic acid as a process control agent to improve milling efficiency. The milled M/HEA powders were consolidated (Ø25 mm × 10 mm) in the graphite mold under pressure of 40 MPa at temperature of 1000 °C using SPS for 8 min in a vacuum. The morphologies and microstructures followed by chemical composition/elemental maps (micro sized areas) of the MA and SPS processed (CoCrFeNi)84(AlTi)16 M/HEAs were characterized via the field emission scanning electron microscope (FESEM, Mira3 TESCAN) equipped with energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX). Also, the morphologies of the fracture/worn surfaces and corresponding chemical compositions were determined using FESEM/EDX analyses. Topographies of the worn surfaces and the roughness of the M/HEAs were determined by atomic force microscopy (AFM, multiple mode RAR). The phase identification of the MA processed M/HEA powders and SPS processed M/HEA specimens was examined using X-ray diffraction (X-ray diffractometer (XRD), λ = 1.54056 Å, D8 ADVANCE, BRUKER) in a 2θ scanning range of 20-80°. The diffraction spectra were investigated using Xpert software to consider full width half maximum of the FCC/BCC Bragg peaks to estimate the crystallite size (C.S), lattice parameter (L.P), lattice strain (L.S) followed by dislocation density (D.D). The C.S and L.S values estimated from Eq. (1) were used to calculate D.D by following relationship [ 77]: (2)D.D = 2√3 (L S/(b × C.S)) where b is Burger's vector. The room temperature mechanical properties of the SPS processed (CoCrFeNi)84(AlTi)16 M/HEAs were considered by the Vickers micro hardness tester (Qv-1000DM) and a universal testing machine (Zwick 250/Roell). The Vickers micro hardness test was done on the polished surfaces with 200 g applied load for 10 s. Uniaxial compressive tests were done on the cylindrical specimens (Ø 3 mm × 6 mm) at an initial strain rate of the 10−3s 1 and the stress-strain curves and the strain hardening rate (SHR) versus true strain were also plotted. The wear tests were carried out in the wear testing machine (AMI, via rotating abrasive plate (Ø 70 mm with a Rockwell hardness of ∼ 60 Ra)). The tested M/HEA specimens (Ø 5 mm × 10 mm) were sliding under contact conditions with a normal load of 50 N for 1500 s and sliding velocity of 450 rpm without lubricant. Friction force was automatically recorded during the wear test. The friction coefficient was estimated via normal load and friction force, where the wear rate of the tested M/HEA specimens was determined using the volume loss method. Condition: compressive yield strength (CYS); System: 3 M/HEA system

To ensure homogeneity, each ingot was remelted at least ten times. The phase stability of TiZrV 0.5Nb 0.3Al 0.2alloy was simulated using CALPHAD methodology, ensuring the formation of a single BCC phase while preventing the formation of brittle phases. Processing Text: Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) with varying laser scan speed under constant power was utilized to manufacture specimens of 316L stainless steel containing keyhole (KH) and lack of fusion (LoF) flaws. Optimal fully dense (FD) specimens were also manufactured. Rods of 15 mm in diameter and 100 mm in length were built horizontally (Y) and vertically (Z) for making FD specimens and vertically (Z) for making KH and LoF specimens. To ensure consistent particle size distribution, the powders underwent a sieving process using a 75 μm mesh screen for 15 min, following the guidelines specified in ASTM B214 for sieving metallic powders. For the laser powder bed fusion process, an SLM 125HL system (SLM Solutions Group AG, Lübeck, Germany) equipped with continuous laser beam was employed. The system utilized a single 1070 nm wavelength fiber laser with a maximum power of 400 W and a beam diameter of approximately 70 μm (IPG Photonics, Oxford, MA, USA). A preheated 316 L SS build-plate at 100 °C was used to minimize potential thermal mismatch issues. Argon was chosen as the protective atmosphere to maintain an O2 content below 0.1 % during the laser powder bed fusion process. The study maintained consistent parameters throughout, including a laser power of 200 W, a hatch distance of 0.12 mm, a layer thickness of 0.03 mm, a stripe width of 10 mm, a stripe overlap of 0.08 mm, a scanning rotation of 67° between subsequent layers, and a stripe scanning strategy. Contouring, up-skin, and down-skin parameters were deactivated. Based on previous research findings, the laser scanning speed (mm/s) was adjusted to achieve different density levels. This adjustment allowed to produce specimens with keyhole (KH) flaws (speed of 400 mm/s) and lack-of-fusion (LoF) flaws (1500 mm/s). Additionally, near fully dense (FD) specimens (99.9 %) were produced using a scanning speed of 800 mm/s. Prior to grain and texture characterization, the samples underwent a series of preparation steps. These steps involved sectioning, mounting, grinding, and polishing. To begin, the samples were carefully sectioned and then mounted using a graphite-based conductive mounting powder. Next, a sequence of abrasives with varying grit sizes (320, 600, 800, and 1200), all based on Silicon-Carbide, was employed for grinding the samples. Subsequently, the samples underwent a polishing stage using glycol-based polycrystalline diamond suspensions from Allied High Tech, specifically with particle sizes of 3 μm and 1 μm. The polishing process was carried out on Buehler TexMet C polishing cloth. For the final polishing step, Allied High Tech products were utilized, including a 0.05 μm colloidal silica suspension and Chem-Pol polishing cloth. To perform the grinding and polishing procedures, an automated Buehler AutoMet 250 Pro Polisher Grinder was employed. Processing Text: Alloy ingots with nominal compositions of NbTa xTiV ( x= 0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5 in relative molar ratio) were fabricated using pure Ti, V, Nb, and Ta metals (purity ∼99.95 wt%) in a non-consumable vacuum arc melting furnace (HVAM-B, China) under a high-purity argon atmosphere. All ingots were subjected to a minimum of six flips and remeltings to guarantee chemical homogeneity. The dimensions of the as-cast ingots were approximately 25 mm in diameter and 7 mm in thickness. The as-cast ingots were rolled into 1 mm-thick sheets using a double-high rolling mill with a rolling speed of 150 mm s −1(JH-RZH-110, China) at room temperature. Subsequent cold rolling was performed in a multi-pass rolling process with consistent directionality and a per-pass deformation of 0.01 mm, culminating in plates approximately 1 mm in thickness. Multiple dog-bone-shaped samples were extracted from the cold-rolled sheets along the rolling direction using an electrical discharge machine (DK77, China) for subsequent tensile tests. The tensile samples had dimensions of approximately 16 mm in gauge length, 4 mm in gauge width, and 1 mm in thickness. The tensile samples were encapsulated within a quartz tube under a vacuum pressure of 0.005 Pa, followed by annealing at 1200 °C for 45 min to recrystallization and relieving residual stress. After annealing, the samples were quenched in water to preserve the solid solution phase. Subsequently, the annealed samples were polished prior to tensile testing. Tensile tests were conducted at a strain rate of 1 × 10 −3s −1at room temperature. Each alloy underwent at least three repeated tensile tests for consistency and reliability. The microhardness of the alloys was assessed using a Vickers hardness tester (MHV-1000, China) with a 0.3 kgf load applied for 15 s. Each sample underwent more than ten hardness tests to ensure statistical reliability. The dynamic elastic modulus and Poisson's ratio of the alloys were determined using an ultrasonic pulse-echo measurement system (Teclab UMS-100 system, France). The mass density of the alloys was measured utilizing the Archimedes drainage method (JHY-300W, China) in accordance with the international standard ASTM B962-17. The phase structure of the as-cast alloys was detected using an X-ray diffractometer (XRD) (Rigaku Smartlab SE, Japan) operating within a diffraction angle (2 θ) range of 20°-90° with Cu-Kα radiation ( λ= 0.15406 nm). Microstructural characterization was performed using a field emission scanning electron microscopy (SEM) (Tescan Amber, Czech) operating at 20 KV voltage and 10 nA current. The chemical compositions of the as-cast alloys were examined using an energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS) (Oxford Ultim Max 40, UK). The samples used for XRD and SEM testing were prepared using a mechanical lapping method. The samples were grinded successively with abrasive papers ranging from 300-grit to 3000-grit abrasive papers, followed by final polishing using polishing pastes. Grain orientation and misorientation were analyzed using an electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) camera (Oxford Symmetry, UK) with a scanning step of 1.5 μm. The EBSD samples were polished using a broad argon ion beam system (Gatan 685 PECS II, USA) for approximately 2 h at 7 kV voltage prior to analysis. Ta content: Ta 0.0; Measurement: Yield stress

Processing Text: The Al-5.0Mn-1.5Mg-0.82Sc-0.76Zr (wt.%) alloy powder with a standard composition was prepared by gas atomization (Panxing New Alloy Materials Co., Ltd., China). The powder was spherical in shape, with the particles less than or equal to 22.3 µm accounting for 10% while 90% of the particles were less than or equal to 63.4 µm, as shown in Fig. 1(a, b). All the LPBF samples investigated in this work were manufactured using a BLT S210 LPBF machine equipped with a 400 W fiber laser. Constant laser power (350 W), scanning spacing (90 µm), and layer thickness (30 µm) were used with scanning velocities ranging between 450 and 1450 mm/s. Two different substrate temperatures, 25 and 200 °C, were used for each condition. The samples with the optimized process parameters had a relative density higher than 99.8 %. A bilinear scanning strategy with a scan rotation of 67° was used between the layers. The samples were printed in a high-purity argon atmosphere. Subsequently, the samples were heat-treated at 200 °C for 1 h to remove residual stresses before evaluating their microstructures and mechanical properties. The LPBF samples were prepared for microstructural characterization by mechanical grinding and polishing following a standard metallographic procedure recommended in ASTM E3-11. After polishing, the microstructural features were revealed using an etchant consisting of HNO 3(2.5 mL), HCl (1.5 mL), HF (1.0 mL), and distilled water (95 mL). The wire-cut electro-discharge machine was used to slice samples with the following dimensions: ∼5 mm long, ∼5 mm wide, and ∼1 mm thick. Prior to the EBSD characterization, the sheet samples were first mechanically polished with 400 #, 1000 #, 2000 #, and 3000 # SiC water abrasive paper, then electropolished to remove the surface deformation layer generated by mechanical grinding. Electropolishing was performed at −30 °C, with: 7 % perchloric acid, 93 % ethanol; a voltage of 25 V, and a current density of 450 mA/cm 2for about 1 min. Uniaxial tensile tests were performed using the CMT4105 universal testing machine. The gauge length and cross-sectional area of the tensile specimens were 22 mm and 1.5 mm × 4 mm. All the tensile samples were tested perpendicular to the build direction at a constant strain rate of 1 mm/min, following the standard ASTM E8. Fatigue test samples with the dimensions 60 mm × 12 mm × 1.5 mm were tested on an MTS370.02 fatigue testing machine. All samples were mechanically ground and polished prior to fatigue testing to ensure similar surface roughness. The uniaxial fatigue tests were conducted in a load control mode at a frequency of 40 Hz and stress ratio of R= 0.1, following the standard ASTM E466. The samples were tested until fracture or exhaustion till 10 7cycles. Testing temperature: Room Temperature; Heat-treated at 300 °C for 6h

Processing Text: A 50 kg ingot of the investigated steel was prepared by vacuum induction melting. The ingot was soaked at 1200 °C for 3 h and then hot-forged into a slab with a sectional dimension of 35 mm ×100 mm. Once the chunks were reheated to a temperature of 1200 °C for a duration of 3 h, they were then subjected to hot-rolling in order to form plates with a thickness of 5 mm. After the hot-rolled plates were air cooled to room temperature, they were directly rolled into 1 mm thick strips. It can be summarized as the following two steps: (1) First stage annealing: the cold-rolled samples were annealed at 700 °C for 45 min in order to obtain a micrometer-scaled granular ferrite/austenite and partially recovered austenite microstructure and subsequently water quenched. The first heat-treated samples with a partially recrystallized microstructure are referred to as “PRX”; (2) Second stage annealing: the PRX samples were annealed at 800 °C for 30min and subsequently water quenched to form heterogeneous microstructure. To elucidate the impact of heterogeneous microstructures on mechanical properties, some cold-rolled samples were annealed at 800 °C for 30 min to obtain homogeneous microstructures. When the cold-rolled samples were annealed at 700 °C (first stage annealing), the κ carbides, ferrite and austenite grains nucleated at the primitive grain boundaries. The microstructures consisted of the mixture of recrystallized and non-recrystallized matrix. After that, the PRX samples were annealed at 800 °C (the second stage annealing). Due to the pinning effect of the κ carbides, ferrites and the high stored dislocation energy, the heterogeneous microstructure possessed fine ferrite, fine austenite, and coarse austenite. Through cold rolling and subsequent annealing, Fe-24Mn-10Al-1C lightweight steel with a heterogeneous structure was produced. Processing Text: The Mo-11%Hf alloy (also called Mo-11Hf) was produced in the form of ∼250 g button by mixing and arc melting high purity (>99.9 %) elements. The arc melter operated at ∼20 V and 600 A. To obtain homogeneous distribution of the alloying elements in the liquid state, the button was flipped over and re-melted 6 times, being in the molten state for ∼1-2 min between each melting stage. To heal casting defects and homogenize the cast microstructure, the alloy button was wrapped in Ta foil to minimize possible interstitial elements pickup during processing and hot isostatically pressed (HIP’d) at 1400 °C for 5 h under a hydrostatic pressure of high-purity argon of 207 MPa. The heating and cooling rates were controlled to 15 °C/min at temperatures above 600 °C during the HIP process. Several SC alloy samples were wrapped in a Ta foil, placed in two quartz tubes, which were pulled under vacuum and purged with high-purity argon several times, and sealed under the argon pressure of 0.179 Torr. The samples in one quartz tube were additionally annealed at 1400 °C for 1 h and water quenched and in the other quartz tube annealed at 1400 °C for 50 h and water quenched. The average alloy composition was measured after HIP processing using direct current plasma emission spectroscopy (ASTM E 1097-12) for metals, inert gas fusion (ASTM E 1019-18) for oxygen and nitrogen and combustion infrared detection (ASTM E 1019-18) for carbon, and the results are given in Table 1. Compositions of the alloys in WQ1 and WQ2 conditions were measured using SEM/EDS. X-ray diffraction (XRD) was conducted from polished surfaces of alloy samples using a Bruker D2 Phaser diffractometer operating with Cu-K α1radiation in the 2θ range of 20°-100°. Microstructure, phases and local chemical compositions were studied using a TFS Apreo C field emission scanning electron microscope (FEG-SEM) equipped with a backscatter electron (BSE) detector, forward scattered electron (FSE) detector, calibrated Oxford X-Max energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) detector and Oxford Symmetry electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) detector. The average concentrations of the alloy samples in WQ conditions were determined by SEM/EDS from 10 randomly selected regions, with the total surface area of ∼10 mm 2per each condition. Local chemistries were determined using a point analysis at the dwell time of 60 s per point, electron probe current of 0.8 nA and accelerating voltage of 20 kV. The reported concentrations of the Mo-rich matrix and Hf-rich regions and particles were probed and averaged from 40 to 60 points per alloy condition/constituent. Grain size distributions and average equivalent circular grain diameter (ECD) in the alloy after different heat treatment conditions were determined using EBSD analysis and AztecCrystal software by Oxford Instruments. Compression samples with dimensions 4.5 mm × 4.5 mm x 7.5 mm were extracted from the middle section of the alloy button by wire electrical discharge machining (EDM). Mechanical tests were conducted by compression at 25 °C-1400 °C at a constant ram speed of 0.0075 mm/s that corresponded to an initial strain rate of 0.001 s −1. Room temperature tests were conducted in air and high-temperature tests were conducted in vacuum of ∼10 −5Torr or better. Condition: SC; Temperature: 600 °C

Processing Text: The Al 0.8Nb 0.5Ti 2V 2Zr 0.5LRHEA pre-alloyed powder was prepared by Induction Levitation Melting (ILM) and Plasma Rotating Electrode Atomization (PREP) process with the high sphericity. The particle size ranged from 53 to 114 μm with an average size of 75 μm measured by the laser particle analyzer (Mastersizer 2000). The elemental compositions were quantitatively measured by the inductive coupled plasma atomic emission spectrometer method (ICP, Agilent 725). The LRHEA products were prepared by a LDED device equipped with a YAG fiber laser (wavelength 1064 nm, maximum power 6000 W) under an argon atmosphere with oxygen content below 100 ppm. The process parameters employed were a laser power of 1200 W, a layer thickness of 600 μm, a scanning speed of 10 mm/s and a scanning spacing of 1500 μm. The SEM in the backscattered electron (BSE) mode was employed to investigate the elemental distribution of LRHEA sample, and the EPMA was used to further explore the element segregation between the dendrite and inter-dendrite region. Processing Text: In the work, cold rolling and annealing were applied to powder plasma arc additively manufactured (CoCrNi)94Al3Ti3 medium-entropy alloy (MEA) to efficiently attain different types of lattice defects and heterogeneous structures, thereby enhancing the strength of the alloy. The microstructure and mechanical properties of cold rolled samples (50 % thickness reduction) annealed at 1073-1273 K for 1 h are compared. It has been shown that the MEAs prepared by additive manufacturing accumulate a large amount of deformation energy within the grains during the cold rolling process. At annealing temperatures ≤1173 K, the recrystallized grain size has not been coarsened, the coarse and fine grains formed a heterogeneous grain structure, leading to significant back stress strengthening. The specimens were cold rolled (CR) at 50 % in the direction shown in Fig. 1(b) at room temperature with an electro-hydraulic universal testing machine. Subsequently, the cold rolled specimens were annealed (RA) at 1073, 1173 or 1273 K for 1 h, followed rapid by water quenching. The PPA-AM with subsequent a single-step cold rolling (CR) and annealing (RA) is used to produce different types of lattice defects, heterogeneous structures, and fine-grained structures in the (CoCrNi)94Al3Ti3 MEA. For the cold-rolled samples, short-time annealing treatment was carried out, and the evolution of the alloy's microstructure and mechanical properties was studied in detail. The (CoCrNi)94Al3Ti3 MEAs powders used in this study were composed of Co, Cr, Ni, Al, and Ti mono metal powders (the particle size of the mono metal powders is 150-250 mesh and the purity was over 99.5 %). The monolithic metal powders were configured according to the proportions and then processed for homogeneous mixing with a high-energy ball mill (YXQM-12L, MITR Ltd, Hunan, China) for 6 h. The (CoCrNi)94Al3Ti3 MEAs were prepared with PPA-AM equipment (PPA-AM, DML-VO3AD, Duomu Company, Shanghai, China). Processing Text: An ingot of Co 17.5Cr 12.5Fe 55Ni 10Mo 5 (atomic percent, at%) MEA was fabricated using a vacuum induction melting equipment (MC100V, Indutherm, Germany) under a high-purity argon atmosphere. The raw materials, with a purity exceeding 99.9 %, were used for casting. A rectangular ingot with dimensions of 100 x 35 × 8 mm 3 was homogenized at 1250 °C for 6 h in an argon atmosphere. The homogenized ingot was then milled precisely to a thickness of 7 mm to remove surface oxides and roughness. Afterwards, cold rolling was carried out, reducing the thickness from 7 mm to 1.5 mm. The laser surface treatment was performed on the cold-rolled plate using three distinct scanning patterns: single scan that covers the surface once, a single scan at low speed for long-term exposure of the laser heat source to the material's surface, and a triple scan that repeats the laser scanning three times over the same track. Laser scanning was performed with a laser power of 250 W and a beam diameter of 400 μm under argon atmosphere, using a laser module (YLR-300-MM-AC, IPG photonics, USA). The hatch space during laser scanning was 2 mm, with a scan speed of 10 mm/s for SS and TS and 5 mm/s for SSLS. Both surfaces of the plate underwent laser scanning under the same conditions. For comparison, a typical annealing treatment was carried out on the cold-rolled plate. The cold-rolled plate was annealed in a furnace at 900 °C for 1 h under an argon atmosphere and then quenched in water. Condition: Annealed

Processing Text: HEA ingots with a nominal composition of Al 0.5 Cr 0.9 FeNi 2.5 V 0.2 were melted in a vacuum electromagnetic induction furnace, and the ingots were remelted at least eight times to ensure compositional homogeneity. To reduce micro-segregation during the casting process, the samples were heated slowly to 1150 °C, held at this temperature for 24 h, and then water-quenched to room temperature. The samples were finally aged at 700 °C for 1 h, followed by furnace cooling. Plates with dimensions of 100 (length) × 20 (width) × 1 (thickness) mm³ were cut from the samples for remelting experiment. A fibre laser (FF-M180 machine, Fastfotm) was used to fulfill the remelting experiment. The spot size, laser power, and scanning speed of the fibre laser were 125 µm, 400 W, and 75 mm/s, respectively. The direct spacing of each remelted track in the lamellar-structured samples was 750 µm. Processing Text: The experiments were conducted using SS316L as both the powder bed material and the substrate material. The powder particles had a size distribution of 15-53 µm. In the first stage, nine cubic samples with dimensions of 10 mm x 6 mm x 5 mm were fabricated using the L-PBF process with processing conditions specified in Table 2. In the second stage, half of the top surface of each sample was polished using the LR parameters specified in Table 3. The L-PBF and LR experiments were performed using a Tong-Tai AM-160 machine, which is equipped with Ytterbium Fiber Laser YLR-1070 (wavelength 1070 nm) in a chamber filled with nitrogen and an oxygen concentration lower than 2000 ppm. For each as-built samples shown in Fig. 8, the top surface topology was measured using a confocal laser-scanning microscope (as shown in Fig. 13). and the corresponding values of Sa was determined as shown in Fig. 14. The feasibility of the proposed L-PBF+LR method is experimentally demonstrated using SS316L powder as the feedstock material. Tensile test specimens fabricated using the optimal processing conditions show an overall tensile strength of 550 ±7.8 MPa and an overall yield strength of 420 ±5.9 MPa. Compared to a conventional L-PBF process performed with a layer thickness of 30 µm, the mechanical properties of the optimal printed specimens are improved by 96 %, while the fabrication time is reduced by approximately 48 %. Tensile test specimens with the configuration and dimensions shown in Fig. 10 were fabricated using the L-PBF and in-situ LR process to investigate the effect of the re-melting process on improving the mechanical properties of the built parts. Tensile testing was performed at room temperature on an HT-2420 system at a displacement speed of 1 mm/min. In this study, the main purpose of density measurement is to observe the relationship between the SR and density of the L-PBF processed part. Thus, for each cubic samples, the average SR of each sample was measured, and the samples were then cut into two separate specimens to determine the density. In accordance with the procedure described in [55], polished cross-sectional images with different SR values were acquired using an optical microscope. The topology of the top surface of each specimen was measured after both the L-PBF construction process and the LR operation using a confocal laser-scanning microscope (KEYENCE VK-200) at 10-x magnification. The values of Sa and Sq, i.e., the arithmetical mean height and root mean square height, respectively, were computed from the measured surface profiles using MATLAB software. The autocorrelation function showing the spectral relationship between the surface height and the separation distance between surface points was also extracted from the SR profile. The correlation length, Cl, was determined as the point at which the autocorrelation function declined to 1/e [41]. The accuracy of the CFD model was verified by comparing the simulated depth of the melt pool ( Fig. 11) for three combinations of the L-PBF parameters with the results reported in [56]. The corresponding results are presented in Table 4 and Fig. 12. The reliability of the trained ANN model was evaluated by conducting a regression analysis of the ANN predictions for the melt pool depth and the SR results obtained by the CFD model. Note that the initial surface roughness was assumed to be 12 μm in both cases. The melt pool depth results presented in Fig. 19 indicate that the RSME has a value of 0.695. In order to examine the relationship between the SR and density of the built parts, a series of L-PBF experiments were conducted using different printing parameters to fabricate cubic parts with a size of 10 mm x 10 mm x T x No, as indicated in Table 5. After completing the printing process, the SR of each part was observed and the density value was calculated. In the present study, the mechanical properties and manufacturing efficiency were evaluated for three different printing strategies: LPBF30 (powder layer thickness of 30 µm); LPBF60 (powder layer thickness of 60 µm), and LPBF+LR60 (powder layer thickness of 60 µm and LR processing). Fig. 32 shows the arrangement of the different samples on the build table. Table 6 lists the L-PBF and LR parameters used for the different sample types. Finally, when the L-PBF and in-situ LR experiment finished, the tensile parts were conducted mechanical tests. Tensile strength was examined and compared between parts produced through L-PBF and in-situ LR and conventional L-PBF process. The mechanical properties of the samples fabricated using the different L-PBF and LR methods were evaluated through tensile testing. The results obtained for the yield strength, ultimate tensile strength (UTS), and elongation of the various samples are shown in Fig. 33. Fig. 34 shows the stress-strain curves for different methods namely LPBF60, LPBF30, LPBF+LR60 and EOS60. Note that the results for an EOS60 (powder layer thickness of 60 µm) standard components given in literature [62] are also shown for comparison purposes. The results have shown that the specimens fabricated using the LR method have an overall tensile strength of 550 MPa and an overall yield strength of 420 MPa. The corresponding standard deviation values are less than 7.8 and 5.9 MPa, respectively. These values are close to those of the optimal LPBF30 sample with no LR, that is, 564 ± 3.5 MPa and 425 ± 18.5 MPa, respectively. The elongation value of the LPBF+LR60 sample is greater (27 %) than that of the L-PBF60 and EOS60 samples. Processing Text: The raw materials used in this study include Al, Cr, Fe, Ni with a purity of 99.95 % and sizes from 45 μm to 105 μm. The Fe, Cr, Ni powders are nearly spherical with good flowability, the Al powder is irregular. The powders are blended by three-dimensional powder mixer with 150 revolutions per minute (rpm) for 12 h. The designed molar ratio of the HEA powder is 0.8(Al): 1(Cr): 2(Fe): 2(Ni), and the chemical composition are listed in Table 1. Fig. 1(b) displays a schematic of the blended powders and LMD process. The laser deposited system equips with a 2000 W continuous wave fiber laser, a powder feeder with argon as the powder carrier gas, a KUKA six-axis robot and a cladding head. Meanwhile, the whole process is carried out under argon protection. The main process parameters include laser power (P), laser scanning speed (V), and powder feeding rate (F) that have a significant influence on the geometrical accuracy and quality. Table 2 lists the ranges of the process parameters. The corresponding parameter combinations are P=1000 W, V=10 mm/s, and F=12 g/min. A suitable combination of parameters is selected from the process window to accomplish the deposition of multilayer thin-walled parts. Subsequently, the microstructure and mechanical anisotropy of the thin-walled parts of Al 0.8CrFe 2Ni 2HEA are investigated, the abrasion resistance is evaluated at 25 ℃ and 400 ℃. Processing Text: The Mg-5Bi-3Al alloy was prepared by using pure Mg (99.95, all in wt.% otherwise stated), pure Bi (99.99 wt.%), and pure Al (99.995 wt.%). The preparation process was as follows: the pure Mg was melted in the steel crucible with a resistance furnace at 700 °C, and then the melt was subjected to a 20 min holding period after the addition of pure Al and Bi. The whole process was operated within a protective atmosphere of CO 2and SF 6mixed gas. After that the melt was poured into a steel mould preheated at 250 °C. The actual composition of the alloy was determined using inductively coupled plasma-atomic emission spectroscopy (ICP-AES), and the result is 5.12 wt.% Bi, 3.15 wt.% Al and Mg in balance. The solid solution treatment process of Mg-5Bi-3Al ingot with a size of φ35 × 70 mm at 420 °C for 4 h and then 505 °C for 20 h. Subsequently, the ingots were extruded at 240 °C and 300 °C, respectively, after preheating at the corresponding extrusion temperature for 30 min. The extrusion ratio and extrusion rate were 25:1 and 0.1 mm/s, respectively. The alloys extruded with different temperatures were denoted as E240 and E300, respectively. The extrusion direction-transverse direction (ED-TD) plane of each sample for microstructure observation was ground and polished by the traditional metallographic sample preparation method and then etched with 4% nitric acid alcohol for as-cast samples, and picric acid etchant (2 g picric acid, 10 mL water, 5 mL acetic acid, and 35 mL ethanol) for extruded samples. Processing Text: The raw material used in this study is Ti-11 wt.% V (hereinafter referred to as Ti-11V) binary titanium alloy block, which was supplied by the Northwest Institute for Nonferrous Metal Research, China. The actual chemical composition of the block is titanium with 10.6 wt.% V whilst the β-transus temperature ( Tβ) is ∼730 °C. The solution treatment (ST) was performed at 950 °C for 2 h and water quenched to ambient temperature. In order to activate deformation kinking in microstructure, cold forging was carried out on the ST block with a thickness reduction of 10 % at ambient temperature. The as-forged sheet was subsequently cold-rolled to a total rolling reduction of 70 % at ambient temperature, followed by the aging at 620 °C for 2 h. As a contrast, the other group of Ti-11V block was treated at the same process route except the absence of cold forging. The rolled sheet remain the same total thickness reduction of 70 % as before. After cold rolling, the sheets were aged at 620 °C and 660 °C for 2 h, respectively. For the sake of brevity, the three types of process routes will be respectively referred to as ‘F + R-620 °C’, ‘R-620 °C’ and ‘R-660 °C’ in the sections below. Sample: R-620 °C; Condition: aged at 620 °C

Processing Text: The MEA ingot with a nominal composition of Ni 46Co 23Cr 23Al 2Ti 2Nb 4(at.%) was fabricated by arc melting in a high-purity argon atmosphere. Processing Text: The experiments utilized 2195 Al-Li alloy (Al-3.75Cu-1.07Li-0.52Mg-0.39Ag-0.12Zr), provided by the China Space Technology Research Institute. The sheets underwent solid-solution at 510°C for 30 min, followed by natural aging (NA) for at least three days to reach a steady state. After natural aging, the sheets were pre-rolled under either room temperature or cryogenic conditions, with reduction ratios of 3∼15 %. The rolling process was carried out with 80 mm diameter working rolls at a speed of 1 m/min. In regard to CPR, the sheets were immersed in liquid nitrogen for 30 min prior to rolling, with a transfer time of less than 5 s. After pre-rolling, artificial aging was performed at 160°C for 0.5 h ∼ 60 h. Samples that underwent RPR with rolling reduction ratios 0 %, 3 %, 6 %, 10 %, and 15 % were labeled as RPR0, RPR3, RPR6, RPR10, and RPR15 respectively. The CPR samples, with rolling reduction ratios of 3 %, 6 %, 10 %, and 15 % were labeled as CPR3, CPR6, CPR10, and CPR15. The microstructural examination and grain size analysis of the pre-rolled samples were conducted using optical microscopy (OM, Mshort MJ42). The RD-ND plane was mechanically polished and anodized in a fluoroboric acid solution (5 ml HBF 4, 100 ml H 2O). The aged samples’ microstructure was characterized using transmission electron microscopy (TEM, FEI TECNAI G2 T20, 200 kV). High-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) and high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) were used to observe precipitates. The samples were mechanically thinned less than 0.1 mm, and 3 mm diameter discs were wafered using a perforator. The wafers were then thinned using a twin-jet machine with a mixed solution (CH 4O: HNO 3= 7:3). The thinning process was conducted at −25℃, with a voltage of 25 V and a current voltage of 80 mA. X-ray Diffraction (XRD) tests were performed to determine the pre-rolled samples’ dislocation density using instrumentation (D8 ADVANCE Davinci). The scanning speed was 1°/min, with a scanning step of 0.02°, and an angular range of 30° ∼ 90°. The {111}, {200}, {220}, and {311} diffraction peaks were fitted using the Voigt method to calculate full width at half maxima (FWHM). The modified Williamson-Hall formula [24,25], was utilized for determining the dislocation density. Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) analysis was performed using a differential scanning calorimeter (Netzsch DSC 200 F3). The experiments were conducted in a high-purity nitrogen atmosphere, with the samples placed in a pure aluminum crucible. The heating rate was 10 °C/min, and the temperature range spanned from 50°C to 500°C. The sample weight was measured to be about 10 mg. A Vicker's hardness tester (HXD-2000TMC/LCD 181101X) was used to measure the hardness, applying a 300 gf load for a 15-s dwell time. Samples for tensile testing were prepared along the rolling direction and tested at 1 mm/min using a Shimadzu AGS-X 10 kN tensile machine. Each condition was tested three times, with strain monitored by a video extensometer (TRViewX). Scanning electron microscopy (SEM, TESCAN MIRA3 LMU) was employed to examine the fracture surfaces. Intergranular corrosion (IGC) test was performed in accordance with the ISO 8407 standard. Before the corrosion tests, samples were pretreated by immersion in a 10 wt% sodium hydroxide (NaOH) solution at 50°C for 2 min, followed by a brief immersion in concentrated nitric acid (HNO3, 1.4 g/ml) solution for another 2 min and thorough rinsing. Subsequently, the samples were immersed in a corrosive solution containing sodium chloride (NaCl, 30 g/L) and concentrated hydrochloric acid (HCl, 14 g/L) at ambient temperature for 24 h. Electrochemical characterization was performed utilizing a standard three-electrode setup within an electrochemical workstation. Polarization tests were conducted at a scan rate of 2 mV/s with an exposed electrode area of 1 cm². For the electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) measurements, the polished samples were briefly immersed in a sodium chloride solution (NaCl, 3.5 wt%) for 10 min to attain a stable open circuit potential. The EIS tests were performed with a sinusoidal perturbation amplitude of 5 mV, spanning a frequency range from 10 −2to 10 5Hz. All electrochemical tests were conducted three times to ensure reliability of the results. Peak-aged state, room-temperature pre-rolled (RPR) samples

Processing Text: The multi-level heterostructured Cu-Ni-Al-Sn-Si (Co-free alloy) and Cu-Ni-Al-Sn-Si-Co alloys (Co-containing alloy) are successfully fabricated and systematically investigated. The alloy compositions involved in this study are shown in Table 1, and all the as-cast alloys used were fabricated through a vacuum arc furnace with a high purity argon atmosphere. To chemically homogenize and reduce elemental segregation of the as-cast alloy, the ingots were solution-annealed for 4 h at 1000 °C followed by quenching in water. Processing Text: In-situ titanium boride (TiB) reinforced titanium matrix composites (TMCs) were fabricated via selective laser melting (SLM) technique. The Ti6Al4V alloy powders were mechanically mixed with 0.5 wt% and 1 wt% TiB 2nanoparticles, respectively, using a three-dimensional mixer (JXHY-2L). The mixing process included a speed of 80 rpm/min and a duration of 4 h. To avoid the adverse effect of energy on the properties of the alloy powders during the mechanical mixing process, the machine was paused for cooling at room temperature for 10 min after every 20 min of mixing, ensuring mixed uniformly. The process parameters for fabricating samples with Ti6Al4V powders and 0.5 wt% TiB 2/Ti6Al4V powders, respectively, were as follows: a laser power of 180 W, a scanning speed of 1000 mm/s, a hatching spacing of 120 μm, and a layer thickness of 30 μm; additionally, a short linear scanning strategy was implemented with an interlayer rotation angle of 67°. To alleviate residual stress accumulation during processing, the substrate was preheated to 180 °C. In comparison to Ti6Al4V, TiB 2exhibits a higher melting point and enhanced laser absorption characteristics, necessitating increased laser energy densities when fabricating samples with elevated TiB 2content. Consequently, when the TiB 2addition reached 1 wt%, adjustments to the process parameters were made: specifically, increasing the laser power to 200 W while reducing the scanning speed to 800 mm/s and modifying the hatching spacing to 100 μm. Prior to processing, the powders underwent drying in a vacuum oven at 80 °C for 8 h; high-purity argon gas was introduced to maintain oxygen levels below 100 ppm to prevent oxidation within the melt pool. Processing Text: The substrate employed in this study is a Q235 steel plate measuring 70 mm × 70 mm × 30 mm. One is spherical 316 L stainless steel powder, with a particle size ranging from 50 μm to 150 μm. The chemical composition of the 316 L stainless steel powder is provided in Table 1. The mixed powder was subsequently placed in a vacuum drying oven and preheated at 150 °C for 2 h to remove moisture and enhance flowability. The powder was then deposited as desired coating using a self-built LDED equipment equipped with a laser of 4 KW and 1060 nm wavelength (Raycus RFL-C4000). The LDED technology utilizes a coaxial powder feeding method to ensure the stability of coating properties. The optimal parameters were identified as a laser power of 1700 W, a scanning speed of 10 mm/s, a spot diameter of 4 mm, a powder feed rate of 1.2 r/min, and an overlap ratio of 50 %. With these optimized parameters, the 316 L composite coating was fabricated via multi-layer, multi-track laser processing, yielding a well-formed surface. After completing the coating process, the uneven top surface of the coating was removed using an electrical discharge wire cutting, and then cut into samples measuring 10 mm × 10 mm × 10 mm and 5 mm × 5 mm × 10 mm for subsequent tests. Aqua regia (HCl:HNO 3=3:1 V:V) was employed to etch the sample surface for 10-15 s, followed by ultrasonic cleaning with alcohol. Processing Text: Spherical pre-alloyed FCC-type CoCrNi powders, with a particle size range of 15-45 µm, were utilized to prepare CoCrNi(Al0.6TiFe)x (x = 0, 0.13, 0.20, 0.28) alloys on 304 stainless steel substrate using an LDED system. The powders were fed with a double-hopper powder feeding system and mixed in a blender before feeding through the nozzle. All the bulk samples (50 ×20 ×6 mm 3) were fabricated with optimized process parameters where the laser power, scanning velocity, powder feed rate, and laser beam diameter were optimized and set at 570 W, 1200 mm min −1, 5.4 g min −1, and 1.3 mm, respectively. Deposit layer thickness was around 0.5 mm. A rotation of 90° was conducted between the adjacent layers. The overlapping rate was set at 50 %. Tensile coupons with a gauge dimension of 25 × 6 × 4 mm 3 were extracted from the bulk samples by wire cut electrical discharge machining. Uniaxial tensile testing was carried out on the MTS E45 universal test machine. The nominal engineering strain rate was set to be 0.6 mm min −1. A non-contact and digital image correlation (DIC) technique (Correlated Solution, Inc.) with one 12MP (3000 × 4000 pixels) camera was used to monitor the displacement and strain fields during tensile tests. The DIC system was synchronized with tensile test machine, and the frame capture speed was set to 2 Hz during loading. The microstructure observation was performed in the cross-section parallel to the build direction. The samples were ground with fine SiC papers and then polished with diamond polishing paste, finally etched with an etchant (5 g CuCl 2 in 100 ml HCl and 100 ml of ethanol) for 2 minutes. The phase identification was conducted by X-ray diffraction (XRD, PANalytical Empyrean) with Cu Kα radiation source at 30 kV and 30 mA with a step size of 0.01° and scanning speed of 0.6 °/min. The microstructures were observed using optical microscope (OM), scanning electron microscope (SEM, FEI Apreo2S Lovac), energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) and electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD). The accelerate voltage values were 10 kV and 20 kV for SEM and EBSD observation, respectively. The transmission electron microscope (TEM) foils were prepared by a twin-jet electro-polishing with a mixture of 5 vol% perchloric acid and 95 vol% ethanol. TEM, high-resolution TEM (HRTEM) and selected area electron diffraction (SAED) were performed by using a FEI Talos F200X G2 device at an acceleration voltage of 200 kV. High angle annular dark field (HAADF)-scanning TEM (STEM), annular dark field (ADF)-STEM, annular bright field (ABF)-STEM and EDS analyses were carried out by the same TEM instrument. Processing method: LDED; Condition: base alloy without additional elements

Processing Text: A room-temperature strength-ductility matching Ti2AlNb intermetallic was successfully prepared with hot-pressing sintering and following by a single-step solution heat-treatment in O + B2 dual-phase region. As-sintered Ti2AlNb intermetallic mainly contained the O phase and a little of B2 and α2 phases, showing brittle characteristics. A solution treatment at 950℃ for 2 h and then water quenching was conducted. The brittle α2 at the grain boundaries transformed into O phase and the O phase dissolved into the soft B2 phase partially, resulting in a much higher increase in elongation with 10.4 % and its yield strength still remained at 867.3 MPa compared with the sintered ones. Along with the EBSD analysis, this strength-ductility matching mechanism was mainly attributed to the decrease of the brittle hexagonal α2 and orthorhombic O phase, and the increase of the soft cubic B2 phase. The spherical Ti2AlNb pre-alloyed powder (Particle size: 75-125 μm) with a nominal composition of Ti-22Al-25Nb (at%) fabricated by plasma rotating electrode process, and purchased form Xi'an Sailong Additive Technology Co., Ltd. The pre-alloyed powder was filled into high-strength graphite molds and then uniaxially hot pressed for 2 h at 1300℃ and 35 MPa under vacuum condition of 10 -2Pa, followed by furnace cooling to fabricate Ti2AlNb alloy billet. The HT samples were obtained by solution treatment at 950℃ for 2 h followed by water quenching. The phase constitution in the pre-alloyed powder and sintered alloy were analyzed using the X-ray diffraction (XRD, X’PERT) with a Cu-Kα radiation. The room-temperature tensile properties were tested on an electro-mechanical universal testing machines (AGXplus) with a speed of 0.5 mm/min and an electronic extensometer was used to measure the strain. Processing Text: Specimens with cylindrical shapes measuring 40 mm in diameter and 60 mm in height underwent carburization in an Aichelin carburizing furnace. The bottom face of the cylindrical specimens was carburized. In contrast, the other surfaces were treated to prevent carburization. A droplet carburizing atmosphere activated by methanol and isopropyl alcohol was used, and methanol and isopropyl alcohol were added successively during the carburizing heating process. The specimens were subjected to intensive carburizing treatment at 900 °C. Subsequently, diffusion carburization at 900 °C for 2 h was performed, followed by austenitization at 830 °C, quenching in oil, and tempering at 180 °C for 15 h. Then the carburized specimen was strengthened by USRP. USRP tests were carried out on carburized specimens under different static pressures (200, 300, and 400 N). The ultrasonic rolling ball was a silicon nitride (Si3N4) ceramic ball with a diameter of 8 mm and a hardness of 1500 HV. The rolling surface with static pressure of 500 N presented quality defects, poor surface morphology, and uneven surface processing. Because of the rolled-surface quality problem, the surface did not meet the expected smoothness and consistency standards. On the basis of these parameters, the effects of 200, 300, and 400 N static pressures on surface integrity and corrosion resistance were the primary focus of this study. Initially, the specimens were ground, polished, and chemically etched with a 4 % nitrate alcohol solution, then observation of the microstructure was conducted using optical microscopy (VHX-2000E, Keyence) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM; ZEISS Auriga). In addition, for a deeper examination of the specimens' microstructure, the specimens were observed by electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD; Thermo Scientific/Helios G4 CX). The EBSD analysis was conducted at a voltage of 20 kV. Before the EDS experiment, the specimen was soaked in alcohol and placed in ultrasonic cleaning equipment for cleaning. Specimen: Combined-200 N

Processing Text: The study is carried out on a cold-rolled 304 stainless steel sheet. For the bulging simulations and experiments, a 304 stainless steel cold-rolled sheet with a nominal thickness of 0.80 mm and an out diameter of 200 mm is used. The uniaxial tension specimens are designed and processed in accordance with the GB/T 228.1-2021 standard. Mechanical properties are tested at angles of 0 °, 45 °, and 90 ° with respect to RD. In uniaxial tension tests, the strain is measured synchronously by GOM-ARAMIS at a strain rate of 0.01 /s. Using the plastic strain data from these uniaxial tension tests, the Lankford coefficient and the degree of in-plane anisotropy are calculated based on the GB/T 5027-2016 standard. In this model: the sheet metal is configured as a deformable shell, discretized into four-node curved shell elements (S4R) with dimensions of 1 mm × 1 mm, and the Hill48 yield criterion is employed to define the anisotropy of the sheet metal. The dies used in the experiment are identical to those in the simulation, with all dies having a radius fillet of 5 mm at the cavity entrance. The radius value is set according to ISO 16,808-2022. Consistent with the uniaxial tension test, the strain rate of the feature points in the bulging area is designed to be around 0.01/s in the bulging test. The pressure loading curve is pre-set to the hydraulic station with a linear increase of 0.5 MPa/s, and then gradually reduces in slope until it reaches the burst pressure. Angle: 0°

Processing Text: The austenitic steel in this study has a composition of 16 %Ni-8 %Mn-4 %Al-1 %C-Fe (in wt. %). The casted steel is hot-rolled above 1000 °C to produce strips with a thickness of 5 mm. Afterward, the hot-rolled strip is cold-rolled (CR) at room temperature down to 1.5 mm thick, labeled as CR steels. The first strip is annealed at 650 °C for 60 mins, referred to as the An sample. The second strip is put into an 850 °C furnace for 3 mins for partial recrystallization, referred to as the PRex sample. Some 650 °C-annealed samples are further heated at the 850 °C furnace for 3 mins, labeled as the An-PRex sample. For the tensile tests, dog-bone samples with a gauge dimension of 12 mm×4 mm×1.5 mm are cut from the heat-treated plates along the rolling direction. The quasi-static tensile tests are performed using an MTS810 machine at a quasi-static strain rate of 0.001/s under ambient temperature, with the strain measured by a 10 mm extensometer. For microstructure characterization, samples are ground with sandpapers to achieve mirror-like conditions and then electropolished using a mixture containing 10 % perchloric acid and 90 % glacial acetic acid. The polished samples are examined using a Zeiss Sigma 300 scanning electron microscopy (SEM) equipped with an Oxford electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) detector. Microscale digital image correlation (μ-DIC) characterization during tensile tests is performed on a Kammrath & Weiss in-situ tensile stage. Nanoindentation tests are performed within the SEM facility using a Hysitron PI-88 PicoIndenter under displacement-control mode, with a maximum force of 2 mN. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) samples are prepared by site-specific lift-out method with Thermo Scientific Helios 5 CX dual-beam focus ion beam (FIB). The TEM and electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS) characterization are performed using a Thermo Fisher scientific Talos F200X STEM at 200 kV and an aberration-corrected Themis ETEM at 300 kV. The prepared TEM samples are also used for transmission-EBSD (T-EBSD) characterization with a voltage of 30 kV and a step size of 10 nm, using the same SEM and EBSD facilities. For atom probe tomography (APT), needled-shaped samples are prepared by FIB, and the measurements are performed using a local electrode atom probe (Cameca LEAP 6000XR) at 50 K in laser mode with 25 pJ pulse energy and 200 kHz pulse rate. Synchrotron-based X-ray diffraction (Sync-XRD) measurements with an energy of 22.7 keV are performed at the BL02U2 surface diffraction beamline of the Shanghai synchrotron radiation facility (SSRF). Processing Text: With its inherent lightweight characteristics, magnesium (Mg) alloy has become a key material in industries such as aerospace and rail transportation. To broaden its application scenarios, adding various alloying elements has become a common method for customizing its performance characteristics [1-3]. Among them, the addition of heavy rare earth (RE) elements such as Gadolinium (Gd) and Yttrium (Y) has been proven to be extremely effective in improving the YS of Mg alloys. For example, Wang et al. [4]reported that by adding more than 12 wt% of rare earth elements and combining with the extrusion process, a YS as high as 385 MPa could be obtained. In addition, various elements such as Manganese (Mn), Tin (Sn), and Zinc (Zn) are also used to improve the performance of Mg alloys. Mn could effectively improve the corrosion resistance of the alloy. At the same time, it could act as a heterogeneous nucleation point in the alloy during solidification, and then refine the grains [5]. The Sn element could also form a new MgSnRE phase with RE elements, which could form fine grains and tiny precipitates within grains and boundaries, hinder dislocation slip, and improve the comprehensive performance [6]. The solubility of Zn element in Mg is very high, which has a good solid solution strengthening effect and helps to improve the tensile properties [7]. Five solute elements, including Sn, Zn, Ca, Mn, and Al, were adopted by our team in the early stage, to design an alloy with the proportions of these solute elements being nearly equimolar. Its specific chemical composition is Mg-0.29Sn-0.35Zn-0.52Ca-0.30Mn-0.36Al (at%). After extrusion, this alloy showed excellent mechanical properties, with a YS of 280 MPa, a UTS of 310 MPa, and an EL of 20.3 % [8,9]. The significant improvement in mechanical properties is mainly attributed to the synergistic effects of fine grain strengthening, dislocation strengthening, and the uniform and dispersed distribution of nanoscale granular phases in the alloy matrix. The strengthening and toughening effects of adding Gd, Y, Zn, Mn, and Sn to Mg alloys are fully documented and widely recognized in the literature [10-16]. However, there are relatively few studies on their addition to the Mg matrix in nearly equimolar ratio. In addition, at present, there are not many studies on the microstructure evolution, mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance of Mg alloys prepared by the above method. It is necessary to conduct in-depth research on these systems to broaden the application range of Mg alloys. The purpose of this study is to study the microstructure evolution of the Mg-Gd-Sn-Y-Zn-Mn alloy system synthesized in nearly equimolar ratio and evaluate its mechanical properties and corrosion resistance in the extruded state. Optical microscopy (OM), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), electron backscattering diffraction (EBSD), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) are used to clarify the comprehensive influence of these multi-element additions on the alloy microstructure and final properties. Processing Text: W/AlSi10Mg composite powders were prepared using a solvent-assisted dispersion method, followed by low-energy ball milling and drying processes. The procedure entailed dispersing W nanoparticles (average size ∼500 nm, 272 g, 6.4 wt%) onto the surface of spherical AlSi10Mg powders (average size ∼32 μm, 4 kg, 93.6 wt%) in an ethanol medium. Following this, low-energy ball milling was performed for 4 hours at 150 rpm, with a ball-to-powder ratio of 1:1. The composite powders were dried at 80°C and then sieved through a 200-mesh screen. W/AlSi10Mg composite samples were fabricated using an SLM 280 HL machine (SLM Solutions GmbH, Germany). This equipment, equipped with dual fiber lasers with a maximum power of 400 W and a spot diameter of 80 μm, enables high-precision and high-performance metal 3D printing. The forming chamber was evacuated and filled with high-purity argon, maintaining the oxygen content below 100 ppm to prevent material oxidation during fabrication. The substrate was preheated to 150°C to mitigate residual stress and deformation caused by rapid heating-cooling cycles. Considering surface quality, densification, and production efficiency, the following process parameters were determined: powder layer thickness (t) of 30 μm, hatch spacing (h) of 80 μm, and laser power (P) of 300 W. To investigate the influence of laser scanning speed on the microstructure and properties of the composites, three representative scanning speeds (v) were selected: 1800 mm/s, 2200 mm/s, and 2600 mm/s. A stripe scanning strategy was employed, with adjacent layers rotated 67° to improve the anisotropy of the fabricated parts. Based on these parameters, the volumetric energy density (Ev) was calculated using the equation Ev = P/(v·h·t). The calculated Ev values were 69.4 J/mm³, 56.8 J/mm³, and 48.0 J/mm³ for the three scanning speeds of 1800 mm/s, 2200 mm/s, and 2600 mm/s, respectively. Samples included standard tensile specimens for mechanical testing and 8 × 8 × 8 mm³ cubes for microstructural analysis. Processing Text: Additive friction stir deposition (AFSD) provides an innovative solution for the additive manufacturing of Al-Zn-Mg-Cu alloys and composites with poor printability due to their high hot crack sensitivity. The fine grains exhibit excellent stability during heat treatment due to the pinning effect of dispersed TiB2 particles. After heat treatment, these non-uniform features can be eliminated, and the η-Mg(Zn,Cu,Al)2 precipitates dissolve into matrix. Numerous homogenous nano-sized precipitates (∼4.8 nm, GPII zone and η’ phase) form at grain interior, and the interface precipitates (η-Mg(Zn1.5Cu0.5)) form at the interface between TiB2 particle and Al matrix. In addition, the heat-treated composite achieves uniform mechanical properties across different height positions, with a hardness of 219 HV, tensile strength of 644-650 MPa, and ductility of 13-14.6 %. During AFSD, the material is deposited layer by layer at high temperature and high strain rate through severe plastic deformation. Unlike fusion-based AM, no solidification-related defects are generated because feedstock is performed in the solid state without re-melt process. Based on this thermomechanical processing nature, the alloys fabricated by AFSD show fine, equiaxed microstructure due to dynamic recrystallization, thereby behaving the enhanced mechanical properties. The feedstocks (3.5 wt% TiB₂/7055 composite) were fabricated by two steps, including the preparation of the as-cast composite by the in-situ mixed salt method and hot extrusion. Step 1: the pre-weighted mixture salts of KBF4 and K2TiF6 were added into Al melt to fabricate in-situ TiB2 reinforced Al composite ingot (master composite). Subsequently, pure Zn, pure Mg, and Al-50Cu master alloy were added into the re-melted master composite to fabricate as-cast composites. Step 2: the as-cast composites were homogenized at 470 °C for 24 h, followed by air cooling to room temperature. The as-homogenized specimens were extruded at 420 ℃ to rods (diameter: 20 mm) with an extrusion ratio of 30:1 and extrusion speed of 0.5 mm/s. The actual composition of the feedstock rods was measured by inductively coupled plasma atomic emission analysis as 8.23 wt% Zn, 2.10 wt% Mg, 2.33 wt% Cu, 3.60 wt% TiB2 (∼2 vol%) with balanced Al. The AFSD process was carried out by the solid-state friction-based deposition equipment which was developed by Tianjin University. The feedstock was softened by the friction heat generated between the feedstock and the surface of the substrate, and then deposited onto the substrate by moving the shoulder. Here, a multilayer deposit (25 layers) was prepared under the suitable parameters of stirring head, i.e. the rotation speed of 300 r/min and traverse speed of 100 mm/min. The preset layer thickness and deposition length were 2 mm and 250 mm, respectively. Additionally, the rods were added individually when preparing the final 25-layers deposit. The as-deposited composite (named as AD composite) was subjected to solution treatment at 477 ℃ for 1 h, followed by water quenching, and then aged at 120 ℃ for 24 h to achieve T6 heat treatment state (named as HT composite). Unlike fusion-based AM, no solidification-related defects are generated because feedstock is performed in the solid state without re-melt process. The as-homogenized specimens were extruded at 420 ℃ to rods (diameter: 20 mm) with an extrusion ratio of 30:1 and extrusion speed of 0.5 mm/s. The feedstock was softened by the friction heat generated between the feedstock and the surface of the substrate, and then deposited onto the substrate by moving the shoulder. The preset layer thickness and deposition length were 2 mm and 250 mm, respectively. Additionally, the rods were added individually when preparing the final 25-layers deposit. Processing Text: The Ti54Nb14Zr15Mo17 alloys were prepared by arc-melting. The Ti54Nb14Zr15Mo17 alloys, with high Mo Eq, Bo, and Md values, fall within the range of β-titanium alloys. Prior to the tests, graphite plates coated with tantalum sheet lubricant were placed between the specimens and the dies to reduce friction. Four different testing temperatures (950 ℃, 1000 ℃, 1050 ℃, and 1100 ℃) and four different strain rates (0.001 s⁻¹, 0.01 s⁻¹, 0.1 s⁻¹, and 1 s⁻¹) were utilized. After the hot compression tests, the deformed alloys were water-quenched immediately to maintain the deformation microstructure. True stress-strain curves were obtained through hot compression tests, and a constitutive equation was derived to relate flow stress to hot deformation parameters. A hot processing map was constructed based on the dynamic material model and verified by deformation microstructure. The mechanical properties of the alloys were tested by selecting the optimal hot processing parameters from the map, and the orientation distribution function (ODF) method was employed to quantitatively investigate the texture evolution under different deformation conditions. Processing Text: The raw alloy ingots of Al 0.3CoCrFeNi (atomic percent, at%) with dimensions of 275 × 96 × 38 mm 3 were produced via arc-melting high-purity metals (purity > 99 % wt%) in an argon atmosphere. To ensure chemical homogeneity, the ingots underwent at least two re-melting cycles. To minimize casting defects, the ingots were held in a furnace a 1250 ℃ for 1 h and then underwent multi-pass hot rolling, reducing the thickness by 80-85 %. Subsequently, they were heat-treated at 1250 ℃ for 24 h to refine their microstructure. Following homogenization, the samples underwent severe cold rolling, reducing the thickness by 85-90 %. The samples were annealed at 700, 750, 800, and 850 °C for 1 h, followed by water quenching. Specifically, cold-rolled specimens were subjected to recrystallization annealing at 1150 °C, followed by 50 h of annealing at 600°C for the FCC+L12 microstructure; direct 50 h annealing at 600 °C after cold rolling for the FCC+B2 + σ microstructure; and direct 1 h annealing at 800 °C after cold rolling for the FCC+B2 microstructure. Processing Text: Samples were cut into cylindrical shapes with dimensions of (Φ) 5 mm × 6.8 mm from cast ingot solidified under normal pressure. Subsequently, the samples were wrapped in an insulating layer and a graphite tube. The pressure device of the LPR1000 2-6-8 multi-stage high-pressure apparatus consists of an axially cylindrical pressure chamber, resembling to a piston-cylinder system. Pressure is applied to the octahedral talc sample assembly through primary and secondary pressure transmission modules, driven by the press. Graphite is used as the heating element, and the heating temperature is controlled by adjusting the heating power. The sample was heated to 1550 °C under an external pressure of 6 GPa for 60 minutes, after which the heating device was turned off and the pressure was released to atmospheric levels. The SSS and HPS alloys were subsequently aged at 400°C, 450°C, and 500°C in an argon atmosphere for varying durations up to 10 hours. The samples were ground using SiC paper and polished with diamond suspension. A solution with the composition of FeCl 3(2 g), HCl (3 ml), and C 2H 5OH (100 ml) was used as the etchant. The microstructure was observed using a HITACHI SU50000 field emission scanning electron microscope (SEM) and an FEI Talos F200X transmission electron microscope (TEM). Image Pro Plus 6.0 software was used to measure the area fraction and size of various precipitates based on TEM images. The foil thickness in the beam direction was determined by measuring the spacing of Kossel-Mollenstedt fringes in a {111} αreflection in a < 011 > αtwo-beam convergent beam electron diffraction (CBED) pattern. X-ray diffraction (XRD, X’PERT X-ray, Holland) with diffraction angle (2θ) ranging from 30° to 100° and a scanning speed of approximately 1°/min was utilized to determine the crystal structure of the alloys. The DC conductivity measurement at room temperature (300 K) was conducted using the traditional four-probe technique. The samples measured are approximately 3 mm in length, 1 mm in width, and 0.3 mm in thickness. Four platinum wires were affixed to the samples using conductive silver paste. The DC resistance of the samples was initially measured using a physical property measuring system (PPMS, Dynacool-14T, USA) and subsequently converted to DC conductivity. Vickers hardness testing of the specimens was performed using a Huayin HV-1000A microhardness tester with a load of 200 g and an indentation time of 15 seconds. The reported hardness values represent the average of eight separate measurements. The compression test was conducted using a SANS CMT6000 universal testing machine with a compression speed of 0.5 mm/min. The compression specimen measured are 2 mm in diameter and 3 mm in length. At least three measurements were taken for each sample to minimize experimental errors. Peak aging state; Aged at 450 °C

Processing Text: A 50 kg ingot of lightweight steel with a composition of Fe-18Mn-8Al-1C-5Ni (wt%) was prepared in a vacuum induction melting furnace (chemical composition analyzed by spark optical emission spectroscopy: Fe-18.20Mn-7.98Al-1.03C-5.02Ni wt%). The as-forged steel was hot rolled to 5 mm at 1200°C with a total reduction of 93 %, followed by water quenching (referred to as "WQ"). The hot-rolled steels were homogenized at 1200°C for 1 hour and then cold-rolled to a final thickness of 1 mm with a total reduction of 80 %. Three types of heat treatment schedules were applied to the cold rolled specimens in the present study, as illustrated in the Fig. 1. The cold-rolled strips were at 1000°C for 50 minutes to obtain full recrystallization (referred to as "AN50"), and annealed at 850 °C for 5 minutes to induce partial recrystallization (referred to as "AN5"), followed by WQ. Pre-straining was conducted in the AN5 specimen with several tensile strains of 0 %, 5 %, and 15 %. Subsequently, these AN5 specimens with different pre-strains were annealed at 850°C for 7 minutes with WQ. These pre-strained and sequent annealed specimens were denoted as "0 %-AN7", "5 %-AN7", and "15 %-AN7," respectively. Processing Text: Ni 0.35Al 0.3(CoFe) 0.2Cr 0.15-xMo x(x=0,0.05) HEA ingots were prepared by using Al, Co, Cr, Fe, Ni, and Mo metal particles (purity >99.9 %) as raw materials in a high-purity argon atmosphere through a DHL-500 II nonconsumptive vacuum arc melting furnace. Cylindrical Φ4 mm×6 mm samples were obtained from the ingots via EDM, and the samples were polished with 180--2000 mesh SiC sandpaper to remove oxides on the surface of the samples, polished with diamond polishing paste to remove scratches on the surface of the samples, and finally cleaned with an ultrasonic cleaning machine. Finally, the treated samples were made so that no obvious scratches could be seen under the optical microscope. The experimental transmission samples were cut into Φ4 mm × 0.5 mm circular slices via wire cutting, and the samples were ground with sandpaper to a thickness of less than 50 μm. Processing Text: Ingots were meticulously crafted with a precise nominal composition of (FeCoNi)86-Al7Ti7 through the process of arc melting. This involved blending constituent elements of exceptional purity exceeding 99.9 % mass, within a meticulously controlled Ti-gettered high-purity argon atmosphere. Each ingot underwent no less than five times of melting to guarantee the utmost chemical homogeneity. Subsequently, the molten alloy ingot was cast into a copper mold, precisely crafted to dimensions of 60 mm × 15 mm × 3 mm. To ensure the accuracy of collected data, grinding and polishing, approximately 2 mm in depth, were carried out on the surrounding area of the characterization sample. The resulting as-cast sheet then underwent a homogenization process at 1150 °C for approximately 2 h, followed by a water quenching process. This was followed by cold rolling, reducing the thickness by approximately 65 %. The cold-rolled thin sheet was then subjected to a recrystallization process, achieved by heating at 1150 °C for approximately 1.5 min. Subsequent to this recrystallization, the samples were meticulously subjected to a 4-hour aging treatment, also followed by a water-quenched process, at a series of temperatures of 580 °C, 650 °C, 690 °C, 720 °C, 780 °C, and 820 °C. Processing Text: Samples of the (CoNiV) 97Al 3MEA were prepared with high-purity (> 99.99 at%) Co, Ni, V, and Al in a vacuum smelting furnace (argon enclosure). To obtain a homogeneous alloy, the ingot needed to be turned over and remelted four times, and then a strip alloy ingot with dimensions of 70 mm × 30 mm × 10 mm was prepared by casting and molding. The melted alloy ingot was encapsulated in a quartz tube protected by argon gas and homogenized at 1200°C for 24 h. Then, the as-cast alloy ingot was polished with sandpaper to remove the surface oxidized skin and a small amount of impurities. The grain size and phase composition of the alloys were optimized by combining the large deformation cold-rolling and high temperature annealing treatment, and the toughening mechanism of the alloys was evolved. To refine the grains within the alloy, a cold rolling process was required to reduce the total thickness of the alloy plate by 85 % to 1.50 mm. The ultrasonically cleaned samples were annealed at 900°C, 950°C, and 1000°C for 60 min, and then they were removed from the furnace after cooling. They were then cleaned with alcohol and deionized water and dried to facilitate subsequent mechanical property testing and characterization. Each thinned alloy was machined into a tensile specimen in the shape of a flat dog-bone (size 34 mm × 8 mm × 1.5 mm) by electrical discharge machining wire cutting. The sample was sanded with #240 to #3000 SiC sandpaper to obtain a smooth, metallic luster. Quasi-static uniaxial stretching (at 25°C) was carried out at a fixed strain rate of 1 × 10 −3s −1, which was accompanied by a scalar 10 mm extensometer. A sample with dimensions of 10 mm × 10 mm × 1.5 mm was cut by wire-cutting, and the hardness was measured by an HXD-1000 Vickers Hardness Tester with 500 g loading for 10 s. Each specimen was tested at 10 points in different areas, the maximum and minimum values were removed, and the average of the remaining eight points was taken as its hardness value. To observe the microstructural morphologies of the alloys, all samples were polished on the surface using #400 to #7000 silicon carbide sandpaper and ground with 0.5 μm diamond polishing paste to a mirror-like luster. The physical phase identification of the (CoNiV) 97Al 3alloys was performed by X-ray diffraction (XRD). The detailed parameters for XRD characterization were as follows: Cu-Kα rays (λ = 1.5406 Å), scanning angle of 20°-90°, voltage of 30 kV, current of 30 mA, and scanning rate of 5°/min. An EDS-equipped scanning electron microscopy (SEM) system and a laser scanning confocal microscope were selected for characterizing the microstructures, grain sizes, and elemental distributions of the samples. Crystallographic information was collected and analyzed via electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) test and the TSL OIM analysis software. The samples were thinned to a thickness of 50 nm using an ion beam at 100 K. Corresponding selected area electron diffraction (SAED) and high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) results were obtained from a field-emission transmission electron microscope (Tecnai F30) operated at an accelerating voltage of 300 kV. Processing Text: In this study, two novel Co-free medium entropy alloys (MEAs) with compositions of Cu20Cr10Fe35Ni35 (Cu20) and Cu10Cr20Fe35Ni35 (Cu10) were successfully prepared by a combination of mechanical alloying (MA) and spark plasma sintering (SPS). High-purity (>99 %) Cu, Cr, Fe, and Ni powders (purchased from Kojundo Chemical Lab. Co., Ltd., Saitama, Japan) were used as the starting materials, and their average particle sizes were 75 μm, 63 μm, 4 μm, and 3 μm, respectively. The alloy powders with nominal atomic ratios of Cu20Cr10Fe35Ni35 and Cu10Cr20Fe35Ni35 (hereinafter denoted as Cu20 and Cu10, respectively) were synthesized by MA under an argon atmosphere using a high-energy ball milling device (Zoz Simoloyer CMJ-02SS) equipped with a water-cooling system. Cr-steel balls with chemical compositions of 0.95-1.1 wt% C, 1.3-1.6 wt% Cr, 0.15-0.35 wt% Si, <0.5 wt% Mn, <0.025 wt% P, and <0.025 wt% S (JIS SUJ-2) were used as the milling media, and the ball to powder weight ratio was 15:1. The milling operations were carried out at optimized cycles of 1200 rpm and 700 rpm for 6 h with time intervals of 45 s and 15 s, respectively. The progress of milling was monitored by taking out a small amount of powder every 1 h and examining it using XRD analysis. The 6 h-MAed powder was consolidated by SPS in a graphite die at 1000 °C for 10 min under uniaxial pressure of 30 MPa in vacuum.
