Processing Text: Bulk samples of HEA matrix-MXene composites were prepared by spark plasma sintering (SPS) using a mixture of CrMnFeCoNi HEA powder that contained 2 wt%, 4 wt%, 6 wt%, 10 wt% of MXene phase. The microstructure evolution, phase structure, and compressive mechanical properties of the samples were investigated at room temperature. The fractions of the MXene phase played important roles in the nanostructural evolution and grain refinement of the HEA-MXene composites. The densities of SPS-processed (SPS-ed) CoCrFeMnNi-MXene composites were measured using the Archimedes method. The X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis was used to characterize the phase and crystal structure of both the powder and bulked HEAs-MXene composites. The microstructure of the CoCrFeMnNi-MXene composites was characterized using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) with energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS), backscattered diffraction (EBSD) system attached to the field emission scanning electron microscope (FE-SEM), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM). The mechanical properties of the HEAs were evaluated using compression tests at an initial strain rate of 10−3, and the hardness of the gas-atomized and bulk samples was measured using a Vickers micro-hardness test with a load of 1000 g and a holding time of 10 seconds. The tribological characteristics of the SPS-ed CoCrFeMnNi-MXene composites were conducted at ambient conditions on a ball-on-disc tribometer. MXene content: 10 wt%; Condition: room temperature; Microstructure: FCC and HCP phases

Processing Text: In this study, hierarchical heterostructures were introduced into CoCrFeMnNi HEA via an in-situ rolling (ISR) assisted laser cladding (LC) process. The coating was fabricated by overlapping individual tracks with a 30 % overlapping ratio. Following the preliminary testing, the distance D between the laser head and the roller was set to 13 mm. In this work, static pressures of 0 N, 1000 N, 2000 N, 3000 N, and 4000 N were applied, and the corresponding coatings were referred as un-ISR, ISR1, ISR2, ISR3 and ISR4, respectively. Annealed 45 steel with dimensions of 100 mm × 100 mm × 10 mm was chosen as the substrate. To minimize the interference of oxides and other impurities, an angle grinder was used to remove the oxide layer from the substrate surface, followed by cleaning with anhydrous ethanol. The powder used in this study was CoCrFeMnNi HEA powder with a particle size range of 45-105 μm, produced by high-temperature gas atomization. Before the experiment, place the powder in a vacuum drying oven (Shanghai Jiecheng Experimental Instrument Co., Ltd., DZF-6050) and dry it at 100 °C for 2 h to ensure its uniformity and fluidity. The coating was prepared by using a semiconductor laser (HWL-1500) with a wavelength range of 910-1050 nm and a DPSF scraper powder feeder to transport CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy powder coaxially. Laser spot diameter 2 mm, laser power 1500 W, scanning rate 3 mm/s, powder feed 7 g/min, overlapping ratio 30 %. High purity argon is used as melt pool shielding gas with a flow rate of 3 L / min. The prepared coating was cut into cuboid specimens with dimensions of 15 × 15 × 10 mm 3using a high-speed wire electrical discharge machining machine tool (Fangzheng CNC Machine Tool Co., Ltd., DK7720). The specimens were then hot - mounted using a metallographic specimen mounting machine (Laizhou Hengyi Test Instrument Co., Ltd., XQ-2B). Subsequently, the cross - section of the specimen was ground using SiC sandpapers of grit sizes 60 mesh, 400 mesh, 800 mesh, 1500 mesh, and 2000 mesh in a wet - grinding manner on a metallographic specimen grinding and polishing machine (Laizhou Hengyi Test Instrument Co., Ltd., MP-2B). After grinding, the specimens were polished with diamond polishing paste until no obvious scratches were visible under an optical microscope. The specimens were placed in anhydrous ethanol and cleaned in an ultrasonic cleaner for 5 min. To prepare the surfaces for electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) analysis, the specimen was pre-ground and polished using the metallographic pre-grinding machine (Hua Xing Test Instrument Co., Ltd.). The surface was then ion-polished with a precision ion thinning instrument (GATAN PIPS II 695) to remove the damage layer caused by mechanical polishing. The microhardness was measured using a Vickers hardness tester (Laizhou Hengyi Test Instrument Co., Ltd., NVM-1000 A). The load was set at 0.3 kg, and the dwell time was 15 s. Each value was measured three times to ensure accuracy. The tribological properties of the coatings at room temperature (25 °C) were evaluated by a ball-on-disk wear tester (Lanzhou Zhongke Kaihua Science and Technology Development Co., Ltd., HT-1000) with a Si 3N 4ball as the counterpart. The tests, performed under dry sliding conditions in accordance with the ASTM G99-17 standard, were repeated three times. The test parameters included a loading force of 10 N, a friction radius of 3 mm, a rotation speed of 600 r/min, and a wear time of 30 min. Condition: room temperature (RT)

Processing Text: The ingots with nominal compositions of Al x(MoV) 100-x(x = 0, 15, 33, and 50 at%, henceforth denoted as Al0, Al15, Al33, and Al50, respectively) were fabricated using vacuum arc melting (VAR). The VAR process was conducted under a Ti-gettered Ar atmosphere, followed by rapid quenching in a water-cooled copper mold. To enhance chemical homogeneity, each ingot underwent a series of flipping and remelting at least 5 times. Thermodynamic calculations for the present alloy were conducted using Thermo-Calc software (version 2023b, Thermo-Calc Software, Sweden). Crystallographic analysis was performed using X-ray diffraction (XRD: D8-Advance, Bruker, Germany) with Cu Kα radiation scanning from 20° to 100° with a step size of 2°/min. To investigate the chemical composition and phase distribution, a field-emission scanning electron microscope (FE-SEM: JSM-7100F, JEOL Ltd., Japan) equipped with backscattered electron (BSE), electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), and energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) detectors were utilized. The samples for EBSD were mechanically ground using 1200-grit abrasive paper, followed by polishing with a 1 μm diamond suspension and a 40 nm colloidal silica solution. To characterize the nanoscale microstructure, a field-emission transmission electron microscope (FE-TEM: JEM-2100F, JEOL Ltd., Japan) equipped with an EDS detector, was operated at 200 kV. The samples for TEM were prepared using a focused ion beam instrument (FEI: Helios Nanolab G3 CX, FEI company, USA) operated at 5 kV and a 3° incidence angle of the Ga +ion beam. Compression and hardness tests were conducted to evaluate the mechanical properties of these alloys. Vickers hardness was measured using a microhardness tester (FM-700, Future-Tech Corp., Japan) with an indentation load of 500 gf and a dwell time of 10 s. To ensure reliability, the indentation process was repeated more than 10 times. For compression tests, cylindrical samples with a diameter of 4 mm and a height of 6 mm were prepared using an electric discharge machine (EDM). Compression tests were carried out at a quasi-static strain rate of 10 −3s −1using a universal testing machine (UTM: Instron 5582, Instron Corp., USA). The digital image correlation method (ARAMIS 12 M, GOM Co., Germany) was employed to accurately measure strain during compression tests. To ensure data reproducibility, the compression test was repeated more than 3 times. Processing state: as-cast; Microstructure: single-phase BCC structure

Processing Text: Alloys were prepared through cold crucible induction melting using high-purity elements. Ingots with masses between 300 and 2500 g have been first cast. Subsequently, a portion of each ingot was remelted under a nitriding atmosphere with controlled pressure and time to promote nitrogen absorption in the liquid alloy. In the case of the Y3 matrix, various nitrogen contents were introduced (ranging from 0.1 to 0.3 wt% N) by adjusting the time under the nitriding atmosphere. After casting, the ingots were homogenized at 1200 ∘C during 2 h and then hot forged at approximately 1000 ∘C to produce 14 mm diameter bars. Forged bars were annealed at 1100 ∘C during 90 min followed by air cooling to produce the reference state of the materials. For Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM) observations and Energy-Dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) analyses, all the samples were ground with SiC papers down to 1200 grade. Final preparation was made by electropolishing (6 % HCl in ethanol, at 10-12 ∘C, at 25 V during 30 s). Processing Text: Hastelloy X was additively manufactured using the LPBF technique, forming a vertical rod measuring 120 mm in length and 22 mm in diameter. The as-built material was stress-relieved at 1050°C for 1 h. Subsequent to stress relief, the material was subjected to heat treatment at two distinct temperatures isothermally, i.e., 800 °C and 950 °C, for the duration of 500 h. The specimen subjected to 800 °C for 500 h will be referred to as S1, while the specimen subjected to 950 °C for the same duration will be referred to as S2 hereafter. Micro tensile specimens, with gauge dimensions measuring 6 mm x 2 mm x 1 mm, were precision machined from the additive manufacturing (AM) rod along the build direction (BD) using electrical discharge machining (EDM). Tensile tests were carried out utilizing a universal testing machine (Zwick/Roell Z100) at a strain rate of 10−3s−1 under both ambient temperature (25 °C) and 800 °C conditions. Before each tensile test, the specimen underwent a heating process with a rate of 10 °C/min and was held at 800 °C temperature for 30 min to ensure specimen homogenization using a three-zone furnace. Condition: room temperature; Processing state: isothermally aged at 800 °C; Microstructure: uniform distribution of μ phase

The extrusion process was conducted at a ram speed of 1 m/min and an extrusion ratio of 25:1. Following this, the extruded bars underwent electrical discharge wire-cutting to fabricate tensile samples (diameter: 5 mm, length: 25 mm) and compressive samples (diameter: 6 mm, length: 10 mm). Tensile and compressive tests were conducted using a CMT5105 material testing machine, maintaining a consistent strain rate of 10−3s−1 at room temperature. Processing state: as-extruded

Processing Text: The base alloy (90W-7Ni-3Fe) and the alloy compositions with Mo and Nb addition of (1.25, 2.5, & 3.75 wt%) independently were sintered in a reducing atmosphere at 1500 °C for 60 min. Alloys of different compositions with Mo and Nb addition were prepared using elemental powders. The base composition was modified by adding elements Mo and Nb independently in the steps of 1.25 wt%. For all the compositions, a constant Ni to Fe ratio of 7:3 was maintained. The required quantity of powder for each alloy was measured carefully and hand-mixed in a mortar and pestle for 20 minutes. The hand-mixed powder was further mixed rigorously in a turbo mixer at 80 rpm for 60 minutes without any medium. The mixed powder was compacted using a uniaxial press at 350 MPa pressure to obtain cylindrical samples of a diameter of 6 mm and height of 3 mm and cylindrical samples for compression testing of 6 mm diameter and 8 mm height. Further, these compacts were sintered in a tubular horizontal furnace (Tehreek, India) at a sintering temperature of 1500 °C for 60 min under a flowing hydrogen atmosphere (0.1 lpm). Samples were heated at a heating rate of 5 °C/min from room temperature to 1000 °C and dwelled for 40 min. Further temperature increments were done as 4 °C/min till 1200 °C and 3 °C/min till 1500 °C. Finally, samples were furnace cooled at 5 °C/min. The samples were sectioned along a plane parallel to the vertical axis of the sintered sample for microstructure and phase analysis and hardness measurements. The sintered samples were ground using emery paper till 3000 grit size, followed by cloth polishing using alumina and colloidal silica. Derived from combined hardness (H=3450 MPa) via the relation H = 3σ_y; Strengthening mechanisms include tungsten grain boundary strengthening, matrix solid solution strengthening, and matrix grain boundary strengthening

Processing Text: Spherical TC17 powder was prepared using the vacuum plasma rotating electrode atomization method, with a particle size ranging from 45 to 106 μm and a flowability of 19.7 s/50 g. To remove moisture from the powder, it was treated in an electric thermostatic drying oven at 110 °C for 1.5 h. TC17 specimens with dimensions of 60 mm × 50 mm × 12 mm were prepared on a TC4 substrate using an n-shape scanning strategy. The specimens were subjected to vacuum heat treatment in a TL1400 tube furnace. The heat treatment process referenced the heat treatment standard for titanium and titanium alloy parts (GB/T 37584-2019). Due to the limited effect of annealing and solution treatment on the strength-ductility balance, three aging treatments at varying temperatures were conducted after these treatments. The specific heat treatment procedures are shown in Table 3, with all cooling methods being furnace cooling. Samples with dimensions of 15 mm × 15 mm × 8 mm were cut from the specimens for wear testing, while the dimensions for other tests were 6 mm × 6 mm × 8 mm. The phase analysis was conducted using an X-ray diffractometer (D/MAX-2500, Cu target), with the experimental parameters set as follows: 2θ = 10-90°, a step size of 0.02°, and a scanning speed of 1°/min. The polished TC17 samples were chemically etched for 10 s using a mixed solution with a volume ratio of HF, HNO 3, and H 2O of 2:3:40. Measurements were taken every 100 μm under a load of 200 g and a dwell time of 10 s, with 30 points measured for each sample. Dry sliding wear tests were carried out using an MPX-3G pin-disc wear tester, with a 6 mm diameter GGr15 steel ball as the counterface. A normal load of 20 N was applied, the rotational speed was set to 300 r/min, the friction radius was 1.5 mm, and the wear time was 45 min. Annealing at 840 °C and solution treatment at 800 °C promoted the precipitation and growth of lath and plate-like primary α phase (α P), as well as continuous and discontinuous grain boundary α phase (α GB). Aging induced the preferential precipitation of secondary α phase (α S) around the grain boundaries, but it did not fully occupy the PFZ region. As the aging temperature increased, both the α P and α S underwent coarsening. Sample: Deposition

Processing Text: The eutectic Fe-B alloy with compositions of Fe-3.8B (wt%) was fabricated in a 10 kg-capacity vacuum induction furnace with the charge materials of pure iron, ferroboron (Fe-18.8 wt% B) and cast as ingots with the dimension of 200 × 150× 40 mm. Substrates of 150 × 100 × 10 mm in size were cut from the ingots via wire-electrode cutting for LR treatment, followed by surface grinding using a grinding machine, cleaned with acetone and dried. A Trumpf TruLaser Cell 7020 (TRUMPF SE + Co. KG, Germany) equipped with a TruDisk 3001 solid state laser was carried out for LR treatment. The specific laser process parameters are listed in Table 1. The interval spacing between the two scans was 1.5 mm, and Argon shielding gas (flow rate of 20 SCFH) was used during the LR process to prevent oxidation. To characterize the architectured nano-lamellar structure, TEM samples were prepared using a focused ion beam (FIB) from specimen A3. STEM samples were lifted out using a ultra-high-resolution FIB/SEM system (GAIA3, TESCAN, Czech). The foils were thinned with a 30 kV Ga beam to about 250 nm and then polished at progressively lower voltages to gradually reduce the sample thickness to around 50 nm. Processing Text: The AA 2024 alloy was melted using susceptor-assisted microwave heating, and the molten alloy was then directionally solidified in-situ at five solidification rates (50, 100, 150, 200, and 250 μm/s) under microwave irradiation. Processing Text: A Fe35.4Ni24Cr21Co9Mo2Cu1.6Al3Ti4 multi-principal element alloy (MPEA) reinforced by L12 nanoprecipitates was fabricated with four different grain sizes (∼19, ∼50, ∼127 and ∼361 μm) to optimize mechanical and corrosion properties. In a high purity argon protective atmosphere, the Fe 35.4Ni 24Cr 21Co 9Mo 2Cu 1.6Al 3Ti 4(at%) MPEA ingots were prepared by vacuum induction arc furnace. The purity of each element was ≥ 99.9 wt%, and the ingots were remelted at least 6 times in a water-cooled copper cavity to ensure the uniformity of the chemical composition. Then, the ingots were homogenized at 1180 °C for 8 h in muffle furnace with high purity argon atmosphere. Subsequently, the ingots underwent multiple cold rolling, with a cold rolling reduction of ∼82 % (from a thickness of ∼8.3 mm to ∼1.5 mm). As shown in Fig. S1, the annealed temperature was initially determined based on the phase diagram, followed by preliminary experiments to identify the specific temperature and duration required to achieve the desired grain size. Thus, cold-rolled plates underwent recrystallization annealing at 1180 °C for durations of 60 s, 300 s, and 900 s, respectively, to obtain the MPEA with different grain sizes, and followed by aging at 700 °C for 2 h. Note that following aging, the samples were quenched into water. The resulting three samples were denoted as An60s-Ag2h, An300s-Ag2h, An900s-Ag2h, respectively. Meanwhile, an ingot without cold rolling underwent the identical homogenization and aging treatment, and this sample was named as Ag2h. Grain size: ∼50 μm; Microstructure: L12 nanoprecipitates embedded in the FCC matrix

Processing Text: A dual-phase (DP) Co-free HEA was manufactured by SLM and annealed at 900 °C in this work. Cube samples with a dimension of 10 × 10 × 10 mm, and dog-bone shape samples with a gauge length of 25 mm, width of 5 mm, and thickness of 2 mm, were fabricated under an argon atmosphere using a HANS-M-100 SLM machine (HAN’s Laser, Shenzhen, China). A 500 W fiber laser with a focused beam diameter of 50 μm and a wavelength of 1070 nm was equipped into the SLM machine. The following SLM parameters were used during the SLM process: laser power of 160 W, scanning velocity of 1000 mm/s, interlayer scanning angle of 67°, hatch spacing of 60 μm, and layer thickness of 30 μm, which resulted in the final specimens having a relative density higher than 99 %. Annealing samples were achieved in a SX2-5-12 furnace (LICHEN, Shanghai, China) after heat treatment at 900 °C for 1 h, then cooled in air. Previous research by our team has indicated that the as-printed dual-phase (DP) Co-free HEA Fe32Cr33Ni29Al3Ti3 demonstrates high yield strength but low elongation [13]. So this work tries to increase the ductility of the SLM-processed dual-phase (DP) Co-free HEA Fe32Cr33Ni29Al3Ti3 and heat treatment at 900 °C for 1 h was chosen. Thus, annealing at 900 °C for 1 h and then cooling in air was tried in this work. Gas atomization produced pre-alloyed Fe32Cr33Ni29Al3Ti3 (at%) powder from vacuum induction melted ingots for SLM. The particle size has a characteristic of D50 = 32.7 μm, as shown in Fig. 1(b). In this study, the as-printed dual-phase Fe32Cr33Ni29Al3Ti3 HEA was annealed at 900 °C for 1 h. During annealing, spinodal decomposition occurred with element redistribution. Processing Text: The Al-4Ni-0.4V-0.2Zr-0.2Ti (ANV-ZT) alloy was prepared from a commercial-purity Al ingot, an Al-10Ni master alloy, an Al-5V master alloy, and Al-5Zr and Al-5Ti master alloys. The alloy was melted in a ZnO-coated clay-graphite crucible in a resistance furnace at a temperature of 800 °C. Argon was used for degassing, and the alloy was allowed to settle for 10 min. The melted alloy was then poured into a permanent mold (cooling rate 7 °C/s) at 750 °C. The permanent mold was preheated to 220 ± 5 °C before the alloy was poured into it. Isochronous and isothermal annealing experiments were conducted on the ANV-ZT alloys. For isochronous annealing, the duration was 8 h, with temperature ranging from 200 to 500 °C, in 50 °C increments. After determining the optimum annealing temperature, isothermal annealing kinetics experiments were performed, varying the holding time from 2 to 120 h. The samples were positioned similarly to those used for microstructure observations. Sample dimensions were 8 × 8 × 8 mm. All annealing was carried out in air, and the samples were cooled in water at 60 °C after annealing. The sampling locations are shown in Fig. 1(a). After casting and annealing, the samples were ground, polished, etched with a 0.5 % HF aqueous solution. Their microstructures were observed using an optical microscope (DMM-580C, Caikon, China). The average grain size of the primary α-Al (as cast) was measured using a lineal intercept image analysis method (ImageJ), with the average calculated from ten visual fields for each sample. The eutectic Al 3Ni phases were observed using scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Nova Nano SEM 450, FEI, Netherlands), and the intermetallic compounds were analyzed using energy dispersive spectroscopy spectrometer (EDS). The samples were further etched with a 10 % HCl aqueous solution and the three-dimensional morphology of the eutectic Al 3Ni phase was observed using SEM. Multiple fields of view were selected for each sample, and at least 300 rod-like eutectic Al 3Ni phases from different eutectic colonies were measured using ImageJ software to determine the average diameter and spacing of the Al 3Ni phases. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM, Tecnai G2 F30, FEI, Netherlands) was used to observe the morphology and distribution of the precipitated phases. TEM samples were prepared from the ANV-ZT (isothermal peak annealing) alloy. The sample was initially to 50 μm and then thinned using a double-spray method (TenuPol, Struers, Denmark). The double-spray electrolyte was a nitrate methanol solution, with a voltage of 18-20 V, and a temperature of −25 °C. The microhardness of the alloys was measured under a load of 4.9035 N for 30 s using a Vickers hardness tester (430 SVD; Wilson, USA). Each sample had 10 measurement points selected randomly, and the average hardness value was calculated. Tensile tests were conducted using a universal testing machine (AG-IC/100kN, Shimadzu, Japan) at a loading speed of 1.0 mm/min, with a strain rate of 1.4×10 −6s −1. The positions and sizes of the tensile samples are shown in Fig. 1(b). The elevated-temperature tensile test tests were performed at 350 °C. The samples maintained at this temperature for 10 min before stretching, and the tensile strength and elongation were determined from the average of at least three samples. Condition: annealed at 350 °C for 8 h; Temperature: room temperature

Processing Text: The alloy was developed through in-situ alloying with Al, Si, Ti, Mo and V elemental powders to fabricate quintenary alloy of Ti-Al-Si-Mo-V. The samples were deposited onto the metal plate substrates of Ti6Al4V alloy through in-situ laser alloy deposition of powders. The LENS machine deposition head has a four-way feeding nozzles made of copper which deposits powders co-axially on the base plate while a beam of laser instantaneously dissolves the powder materials. Using three externally attached powder feeders (GTV Verschleiss-Schutz Gmbh, Luckenbach, Germany), to supply the Si, V, and Mo powders while the Ti and Al powders were deposited by powder feeders of the LENS machine. This resulted in a five-way powder feeding system, as opposed to two that the manufacturer had originally installed. A heating platform was introduced to control and/or reduce thermal gradient during sample fabrication based on our observation from the simulation results. The ceramic heating platform had a heating element and thermostat controller attached to it; this was used to continuously keep the temperature of the base plate constant to prevent cracking. The samples were built based on the pre-programmed CAD file using a cross-hatch pattern of deposition strategy along axes of x and y. The alloys were generated at a laser power of 450 W, 10.58 mm/s scan speed, and 25 l/min center purge gas rate. With the intention of varying the composition of alloy samples deposited, each elemental powder flow rates were approximated following calibration of the powder flow rate in rpm (revolution per minute) and converted to mass flow rate in g/min. The samples were heat-treated for 60 minutes at temperatures of 1200 °C and 1400 °C, with subsequent furnace cooling (FC). The heat treatment furnace (Kejia Furnace, China) was applied for the post-processing in an inert atmosphere having an inlet for the continuous supply of Ar (99.99 % purity) to prevent contaminations and oxidation during HT. After ramping the temperature from RT to the desired temperature at 20 °C per minute, FC was done after holding for 60 minutes at the set temperatures. Processing Text: A series of Hf xNbTaTiV ( x= 0.00, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00 in molar ratio) alloy ingots with different Hf content were synthesized from high purity (>99.95%) metals by vacuum arc melting within a Ti-gettered ultra-high purity Ar (>99.99%) atmosphere. The as-cast ingots were flipped and remelted at least six cycles to ensure chemical homogeneity. The button-shaped ingots were rolled into thin sheets approximately 1 mm in thick at room temperature using a precision rolling mill (JH-RZH-110, China). More than three dog-bone-shaped samples were sliced from the rolled sheets for each alloy component along the rolling direction using an electrical spark erosion wire cutting machine (DK77, China). The size of the dog-bone samples was about 16 mm in length, 12 mm in width, and 1 mm in thickness. The dog-bone samples were sealed in an evacuated quartz tube maintained about 0.67 Pa vacuum and annealed at 1200 °C for 45 min and quenched in water to achieve recrystallized microstructures. The tensile tests of the annealed samples were performed at a strain rate of 0.001 s −1by an electronic universal testing machine (ETM205D, China). The microhardness (HV) of the as-cast alloys was tested using a Vicky MHV-1000 hardness tester. The phase composition of the alloys were determined by X-Ray diffraction with Cu-Kα radiation ( λ= 0.15406 nm) and a 2 θangle range of 20°-90° using an X-ray diffractometer (Rigaku Smartlab SE, Japan). A recrystallization anneal at 1200 °C for 45 min was applied to cold-rolled Hf xNbTaTiV sheets to eliminate deformation textures and defects. Condition: Annealed samples; Fracture strain ratio: 26.9%

Processing Text: In this study, the ingots with a nominal composition of a chemically complex alloy consisting of Ni 45 Co 21 Fe 15 Cr 10 Al 4·5 Ti 4.5 (at. %) were arc-melted under a high-purity argon atmosphere with the elements Co, Cr, Ni, Al and Ti (>99.99% pure). The ingots were re-melted a minimum of five times. All button ingots were finally cast into a copper mold with a dimension of 10 × 10 × 100 mm³. After homogenizing at 1323 K for 2 h and subsequent water quenching, the resultant ingots were cold-rolled in steps at 293 K along the longitudinal direction to a total thickness reduction of ∼85%. No intermediate annealing process was implemented during the cold-rolling process. Ultimately, the as-rolled sheets were subjected to water quenching after being aged at 850 °C for 1 h and 550 °C for 36 h. Processing Text: Heterogeneous lamella structures in m- & n-SiCp/2024Al composites were architected by assembling building blocks with different microstructures via planetary ball milling, mechanically mixing, hot pressing and extrusion, as schematically shown in Fig. 1. 57 wt% 2024Al powders and 3 wt% n-SiCps were first planetary ball milled at a rotational speed of 250 rpm for 6 h to uniformly disperse n-SiCps and refine substructures, by which brittle n-SiCp/2024Al UFG building blocks were obtained. Ball milling was conducted in stainless steel jars filled with Ar at 1 atm atmosphere and Φ6 mm steel balls at a ball to powder ratio of 20:1. 1 wt% stearic acid was also added as process control agent. Then, another 28 wt% raw coarse-grained 2024Al powders as ductile FG building blocks and 12 wt% m-SiCps were mechanically mixed with cold-welded n-SiCp/2024Al powders using nylon jars at a rotational rate of 120 rpm for 8 h. Φ6 mm ZrO 2balls following a ball to powder ratio of 5:1 were added. The above powder mixtures were hot pressed into billets at 853 K for 2 h using a uniaxial pressure of 300 MPa and a vacuum pressure of 10 −3Pa. To tailor differentiated heterogeneous lamella structures and study microstructure related strengthening and toughening behaviors, the sintered billets were hot extruded into rods at 673 K with extrusion ratio of 9:1, 16:1 and 25:1. Corresponding samples were abbreviated as E9, E16 and E25, respectively. Subsequently, the extruded rods were solid solution treated at 768 K for 2 h and quenched in water, followed by artificial aging treatment at 443 K for 4 h (T6 state). Finally, three heterogeneous lamella m- & n-SiCp/2024Al composites were fabricated. Sample: E16; Exhibits simultaneously improved tensile properties
Processing Word: Sample: E16; Exhibits simultaneously improved tensile properties

Processing Text: The gas-atomized (FeCoNi) 86 Al 7 Ti 7 HEA powders (provided by Zhongyuan New Material Technology Co., Ltd., Ningbo, China.) were used as feed-stock powders in the present study. The sizes of the particles D 10 , D 50 , and D 90 are calculated to be ∼20.17, ∼34.73, and ∼57.53 μm, respectively. A selective laser melting HBD-100 printer (Hanbang United 3D Tech Co. Ltd., Shanghai, China) equipped with a fiber laser (wavelength of 1064 nm) was used to prepare the HEA samples. The laser offers an output power of 200 W, and a spot diameter of 60 μm. To avoid oxidation, the PBF process was conducted under an argon atmosphere with an oxygen content <100 ppm. The optimized processing parameters were set as follows: layer thickness ( t ) - 30 μm, hatch spacing ( h ) - 50 μm, laser power ( P ) - 160 W, scanning speed ( v ) - 1200 mm/s, and 304 stainless steel was used as the substrate. A 67° scan rotation between the successive layers was employed to minimize the thermal residual stresses generated during the PBF process. Condition: tested at 77 K (cryogenic temperature)

Processing Text: The filler wires used in the welding process were ER4047 and ER5183, representing silicon-rich and magnesium-rich compositions, respectively. The CMT-laser oscillation hybrid welding was conducted using a Fronius CMT TPS 500i arc welding machine and a CWX-3000 fiber laser. A beam scanning frequency of 100 Hz was selected to achieve stable and uniform energy distribution, preventing both local underreaction and overreaction. The beam incident angle was configured at 10° to mitigate porosity by stabilizing the keyhole. The angle between the specimen and the CMT welding gun was approximately 60°. Argon was selected as the shielding gas, with a flow rate of 25 L/min. The circular oscillation parameter mode was calibrated based on earlier studies that demonstrated its efficacy in reducing porosity. The specific process parameters implemented in this investigation are detailed in Table 2. For sample preparation, the welded joints were sectioned using a wire cutting electrical discharge machine to facilitate subsequent microstructural observation and mechanical testing. Processing Text: The representative Ni-22Al-7Ti eutectic alloy with a dual-phase lamellar microstructure possesses an ultra-high fracture strength of 3500 MPa and an admirable fracture strain of 30 % under compression at room-temperature. The representative Ni-22Al-7Ti eutectic alloy with a dual-phase lamellar microstructure possesses an ultra-high fracture strength of 3500 MPa and an admirable fracture strain of 30 % under compression at room-temperature. It also possesses a super-high strength of 1180 MPa at 700 °C, overperforming their single-phase counterparts. The superior mechanical property can be attributed to the synergetic deformation of the eutectic structure, R characterization (abnormal yield effect) and the Ti alloying enhanced phase stability at elevated temperatures. The non-equilibrium solidification induced super-saturation also results in the super-high strength at room-to-medium temperature and a unique softening mechanism via the formation of the two-fold composite structure. Alloy ingots with nominal compositions (at. %) of Ni-25Al-7Ti, Ni-22Al-8Ti, Ni-22Al-7Ti, Ni-22Al-6Ti, Ni-Al and Ni-25Al were prepared by using the arc melting technique under Ar-atmosphere. All samples were melted five times to ensure composition homogeneity. The four-section (diameter: 3-2.5-2-1.5mm) Ni-22Al-7Ti alloy rods were prepared under the same experimental conditions, for subsequent mechanical tests and microstructure characterizations. The samples were annealed at 800 °C and 1000 °C for 100h followed by air cooling to RT for stability evaluation. The thermal behavior of the as-cast alloy was analyzed by a HT differential scanning calorimeter (DSC, Mettler TGA/DSC3+) under an Ar-atmosphere at heating and cooling rates of 40 K/min and 10 K/min. The density of the alloy was measured by the Archimedean method, and the precision of balance was 0.1 mg. Phases of alloys were identified by utilizing an X-ray diffractometer (XRD, Bruker D8) with a Cu-Kα radiation. The microstructure was analyzed by using the optical microscopy (OM, DMi8) and scanning electron microscope (SEM, JEOL JSM-IT800). Before observation, samples were mechanically polished, and then chemically etched for 10 s with a mixed solution of 20% HF + 10% HNO 3+ 70% H 2O (volume fraction). The crystalline structures of different phases and dislocation distribution were further identified by the transmission electron microscope (TEM, TALOS F200S) coupled with the selected area electron diffraction (SAED) equipment. The phase chemical composition was analyzed by using the energy-dispersive spectrometer (EDS) in SEM and TEM. The Vickers hardness was measured by a hardness tester (Leica Duramin 40 Micro-Hardness), with a load of 500 gf for 15 s. Compression tests were carried out on the universal mechanical testing machine at RT-1000 °C with commonly used rates of 10 -4s −1and 10 -3s −1. For the sample soften at HT, the high strain rate is used to shorten the testing time to evading the aging effect. The cylindrical samples with 3 mm in diameter and 6 mm in length, cut from the as-cast ingots for compression show small anisotropy. The strain-stress curves were corrected according to the modulus. Processing Text: The experimental material consisted of 316L austenitic stainless steel rods with a diameter of 30 mm. The material was hot-rolled to 4 mm in thickness, followed by solution treatment at 1050 °C for 1 h. Before each rolling pass, the initial material was immersed in liquid nitrogen for 10 min. The thickness reduction per pass was kept below 5 %. Surface cracks developed when the total thickness reduction reached 70 %. Consequently, the final thickness was reduced by 70 %, resulting in a thickness of 1.2 mm for the cryo-rolled sample, which was labeled as CryoR sample. After cryo-rolling, the samples were subjected to annealing at 700 °C 20 min, 750 °C 6 min, and a sequential 700 °C 20 min + 750 °C 6 min process, followed by water quenching. These samples were labeled as 700A, 750A, and 700A-750A, respectively. All heat treatment processes were performed in a muffle furnace without a protective atmosphere. Tensile tests were conducted using a universal testing machine (5105, SSANS-CMT) at room temperature (24 °C) and liquid nitrogen temperature (−196 °C) with a strain rate of 10 −3s −1. All tensile samples were cut along the rolling direction into dog-bone shapes with a gauge length of 34 mm, width of 10 mm, and thickness of 1 mm. Each test was repeated at least three times to ensure accuracy. To evaluate inhomogeneous deformation, load-unload-reload (LUR) tests were also performed under the same conditions as the tensile tests to quantify the back stress (σ B) component. The microstructural evolution of the samples along the rolling direction (RD) was characterized. XRD analysis was conducted to examine phase transformation with a diffraction angle range of 40°-100° and a scanning speed of 2°/min, using Cu-Kα radiation at 40 kV and 150 mA. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, Oxford) was employed for quantitative analysis of the phase microstructure. After mechanical polishing, samples were electropolished using a 10 % perchloric acid solution at 20 V for 20-25 s. EBSD measurements were performed on a Zeiss Auriga scanning electron microscope with a step size of 100 nm at an accelerating voltage of 15 kV. Processing Text: To investigate the impact of new phase addition of Invar 36, B4C particles, known for their high melting point, were used as reinforcement phases to fabricate B4C/Invar 36 composites through laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) technology, which offers high design flexibility. The Invar 36 powder (15-55 μm) and the B4C particles examined in this study were supplied by Shandong Lianhong New Material Technology Co., Ltd., China. As illustrated in Fig. 1(a), the gas-atomized spherical Invar 36 powder is uniformly distributed, with a mean particle size of 26.24 μm, making it well-suited for the LPBF powder laying process. Fig. 1(b) presents the 99.9 % purity irregularly shaped B4C powders. The chemical composition (in wt.%) of the precursor powders is detailed in Table 1 and 2. To achieve a homogeneously mixed feedstock composite powder containing 2 wt% B4C, a ball-milling process was conducted using a QM-3SP4-1 planetary ball mill at a rotation speed of 150 rpm for 2 h. Following this optimized ball-milling duration, the B4C particles were nearly all firmly embedded within the relatively soft surface of the larger Invar 36 powders, without any significant alteration to the original spherical particle shape or size distribution (Fig. 1(c)). It is noteworthy that the composite powder was dried at 80 °C for 120 min prior to the experiment. The LPBF apparatus utilized was the Hans-M100, which was equipped with a YLR-200/500 YAG fiber laser, featuring a wavelength of 1060 nm, a laser spot size of 70 μm, and a maximum power output of 500 W. The layer thickness, stripe width, and stripe overlap were consistently maintained at 0.03 mm, 10 mm, and 0.08 mm, respectively. Additionally, after the construction of each layer, the scanning direction was rotated by 67°. The influence of laser scanning speed on the relative density, microstructural evolution, and mechanical properties of the B4C/Invar 36 composites was systematically examined. The results indicate that B4C/Invar 36 composites with nearly full density (99.32 %) were successfully produced at a laser power of 150 W and a laser scanning speed of 700 mm/s. B4C particles exhibited a strong heterogeneous nucleation effect on Invar 36 grains; the increase in nucleation sites contributed to grain refinement, ultimately enhancing the mechanical properties of the samples. The yield strength of the samples reached 410.17 MPa, while the ultimate tensile strength reached 729.27 MPa. Calculations reveal that grain refinement strengthening is the primary mechanism by which B4C enhances the Invar 36 matrix, with other strengthening mechanisms serving as auxiliary contributors to achieve synergistic strengthening. Processing Text: The ingots of TiZrHfNbx HEAs were produced by vacuum arc melting (Edmund Buhler AM/0.2) mixtures of high purity raw elements (purity >99.95 % wt) in Ti-gettered argon atmosphere. The ingots were turned and remelted at least six times to achieve chemical homogeneity. The as-cast ingots were polished in parallel to 10 mm and cold rolled to 2 mm with thickness reduction about 80 %. The rolled plates were cut into small pieces and encapsulated into vacuum quartz tubes, followed by thermal annealing at 850 °C for 30 mins with water quenching. The dog-bone shaped tensile samples with gauge length of 4 mm and cross-section area of 1 × 2 mm 2 were cut from the recrystallized HEA plates by wire cutting machine. All the specimens were ground using SiC sandpapers with grind size from 180 to at least 1200 grit in order to remove potential oxidations and sampling defects. The TEM sheet samples were firstly mechanically grinded to a thickness about 40 μm, then punched into discs with diameter of 3mm. The sheet discs samples were further thinned using ion-beam milling to a thickness of electron transparency in a Precision Ion-beam Polish System (PIPS, PIPS II 695, Gatan). Processing Text: In the present work, a single-pass multi-layer wall structure of Monel 400 alloy was deposited using the CMT-WAAM technique. The microstructure was analysed in the building direction, where finer equiaxed dendrites were observed in the bottom region, gradually transforming into coarse elongated dendrites in the top region of the deposited structure. Along with the change in microstructure, a variation in average microhardness was observed in the building direction, decreasing from 286 HV0.1 in the bottom region to 249 HV0.1 in the top region. The tensile specimens tested along the building direction fractured in the gauge length towards the top region of the wall, with an average yield strength of 353 MPa, ultimate tensile strength of 718 MPa, and percent elongation of 39 %. The electrochemical corrosion test in a 3.5 wt% NaCl solution was performed at the central region of the deposited structure. The CMT-WAAM deposited Monel 400 showed an exceptionally low corrosion rate of 0.03 mm/year. The experimental results confirmed that CMT-WAAM deposited Monel 400 exhibits mechanical and corrosion properties similar to or superior to conventional Monel 400, establishing the credential of the process for marine applications. In current study, a single-pass multi-layer wall structure of Monel 400 alloy was deposited using the CMT-WAAM technique. Systematic experimental work was conducted to examine the microstructural features and mechanical properties of the deposited structure at different locations within the build. In addition, the corrosion performance of the deposited Monel 400 alloy in a 3.5 wt% NaCl solution was evaluated. In the present work, Monel 400 has been deposited using CMT equipped Fronius TPS 400i metal inert gas welding machine integrated with an ABB IRB 1500 six-axis robotic arm also known as CMT-WAAM. This approach offers welding without spatter with minimal heat input, and rapid deposition rate. The wire feed rate was calibrated in accordance with the welding voltage and current, enabling the thorough fusion of the furnished wires. The deposition process was carried out in an argon shielding atmosphere by keeping the torch perpendicular to the substrate and moving it horizontally. Layer-wise deposition was carried out on the horizontal plane by moving the torch along the Z-axis. In order to prevent the build-up flaws caused by the intermittent start-stop of deposition process at the extremities, the deposition direction was altered for each layer. The microstructure development may be controlled by the initial circumstances present before the deposition of each layer. Therefore, in order to reduce its impact, deposited material was cooled to nearly 93°C before the next pass. Additionally, this method has the benefits of maintaining a consistent thickness of the weld bead with reducing overflow. Processing Text: 316L ASS powders and Ti nanoparticles were employed as deposition materials. The powder morphology and composition of 316L ASS were investigated with a ZEISS Merlin SEM, as illustrated in Fig. 1, with a size distribution between 15 and 53 μm. Ti nanoparticles were incorporated into the base powders at varying concentrations: 0.0 wt%, 0.5 wt%, and 1.0 wt%. To ensure the formation of a homogeneous mixture, 316L ASS powders and Ti particles were mechanically blended via ball milling for 3 h under an inert argon (Ar) atmosphere. The ball milling procedure was conducted with a ball-to-powder weight ratio of 5:1 and a rotational speed of 125 rpm. All the laser processing parameters involved were optimized as follows: the laser power is 600 W, the scanning speed is 4 mm/s, the lifting increment is 0.5 mm, the overlapping rate of 50 % between each track, and the laser beam diameter of 0.5 mm. During the LMD-processed, high purity argon gas was utilized as a protective gas to minimize oxidation as it carried the powders. For microstructural analysis, the specimens were etched with aqua regia, a mix of HCI and HNO 3 in a ratio of 3:1 by volume, for 30 s. They were then examined with an optical microscope (OM). Phase analysis was conducted using a Bruker D8 ADVANCE XRD instrument. The diffraction experiments were carried out in a continuous mode, spanning a 2θ range from 5° to 90° with a scanning speed of 3°/min. Following this, the grain boundary and the phase distribution of the samples were examined using EBSD at an accelerated potential of 15 kV. The sample preparation process involved an electro-polishing procedure in a 9:1 vol ratio mixture of perchloric acid and ethanol at a DC current of 25 V for 50 s, in which the process temperature was maintained at −30 °C. To obtain a more detailed view of the microstructure, thin foils for TEM were obtained using a Struers TenuPol-5 twin-jet electrolytic thinning system. Subsequently, the test was examined using a JEOL JEM-F200 TEM. Deformation temperature: 77 K

Processing Text: The substrate material utilized was 38CrMoAl steel, measuring (100 × 100 × 10) mm3, and its elemental composition (wt%) is outlined in Table 1. The 38CrMoAl steel was manufactured by China Northeast Special Steel Group Co., Ltd. Fe50Mn30Co10Cr10 HEA powder was manufactured by Shandong Jirek Metal Materials Co., Ltd., China. Its chemical composition (a.t. %) is detailed in Table 2. Fig. 1 depicted the particle size distribution and morphology of Fe50Mn30Co10Cr10 HEA powder. The powder morphology was a spherical powder with some satellite particles. The particle size distribution of the Fe50Mn30Co10Cr10 HEA powder was measured utilizing a laser particle size tester, revealing a particle size range of 30-140 μm. Prior to the laser cladding experiment, the 38CrMoAl steel was cleaned with industrial alcohol to remove contaminants, and then allowed to dry for 4 min. The laser cladding equipment is a German TruDisk 6006 machine equipped, which utilizes a 6000 W disc laser and is equipped with a KUKA robotic arm. A schematic diagram of the laser cladding process was manifested in Fig. 2(b). The Fe50Mn30Co10Cr10 specimen were tested by wire cutting into (10 × 10 × 10) mm3 cubes. The specimens were sequentially ground with SiC sandpaper (320#, 800#, 1200#, 2000# and 3000#), followed by polishing with diamond suspension. After polishing, the samples were etched utilizing aqua regia for 10 s. Under the optimal laser processing parameters, 20 × 20 × 5 mm3 cubes were prepared by laser cladding to prepare compressed specimens, as depicted in Fig. 2(c). As manifested in Fig. 3(a), the geometry of the coating (height, width, and depth) was characterized using a metallurgical microscope. The porosity of the coating was calculated by ImageJ software. The phase composition was analyzed using Philips Xpert-Pro-type X-ray diffraction equipment with Cu Kα radiation. The test parameters are: scanning rate 8°/min, angle range 20°−100°. The microstructures were analyzed using a Hitachi-SU5000 scanning electron microscope and an electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) detector. As depicted in Fig. 3(b), the depth profile of the microhardness from the Fe50Mn30Co10Cr10 coating to the substrate was measured using a Dura scan-70G5 Vickers microhardness tester. The test conditions were a load time of 15 s and a load capacity of 2 N. To guarantee data precision, three points were measured at the same depth within the coating to assess the microhardness values. The compression properties of Fe50Mn30Co10Cr10 coatings were tested using the E44 304 universal testing machine at 5 %, 6 % and 7 % compression speeds. Prior to constructing the parameter optimization model, preliminary experiments were conducted by manipulating individual variables including laser power (Pp), scanning speed (V), and powder feeding speed. The details of the processing parameters used in the pre-experiments were shown in Table 3. The optimal processing parameters were identified as follows: laser power at 1750 W, scanning speed at 8.0 mm/s, and powder feed rate at 11.5 g/min. Compression rate: 5%

The metallographic samples were electrochemically polished in a mixture of 90 % ethanol and 10 % perchloric acid before examining the microstructure with an optical microscope (OM). The samples intended for backscattered electron (BSE) characterization, energy dispersive spectrometry (EDS) mapping analyses, and electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) were characterized by TESCAN MIRA-Ⅲ equipped with an EBSD detector. EBSD data were acquired with a step size of 0.6 μm for a large region and 0.04 μm for an individual grain and processed with Aztec-HKL software. A representative bulk sample with 10 mm × 10 mm × 10 mm was extracted from the deposited alloy via wire electrical discharge machining. Texture characterization was conducted on a neutron texture diffractometer at the China Advanced Research Reactor (CARR), the China Institute of Atomic Energy (CIAE). Using the Euler cradle, the pole density Pℎ kl( α, β) for a specified plane (hkl) can be obtained by rotating the sample through the χ(0°-90°) and φ(0°-360°) axis with a certain angle interval, which aligns the various sample orientations along the (hkl) scattering vector while recording the diffracted neutron intensities at each step using a detector set at the 2θposition of the (hkl) reflection. The step of the Euler cradle was set as 5°. The horizontal direction (X) of the chosen sample was φ=0°, and the deposition direction (Z) was parallel to the φ=90°. The pole figures and orientation distribution function (ODF) can be calculated from the diffracted neutron intensities and polar coordinates using LaboTex software. Ambient-temperature and elevated-temperature uniaxial tensile testing was conducted on a TSMT mechanical testing platform at a strain rate of 1 × 10−3s−1in air. The rectangular dog-bone-shaped tensile specimens with a gauge geometry of 12.5 mm × 3.0 mm × 2.0 mm were sectioned in the middle of the deposited sample along the Z direction and examined, and each sample was repeated at least twice to verify the reproducibility. An extensometer was employed to directly monitor the strains for ambient-temperature tensile tests, while for the testing at 600-800 °C, strains were determined indirectly from the load displacement. A thermocouple was used to measure the temperature of the upper, middle, and lower ends of the tensile sample to ensure an even distribution of circumambient temperature. To eliminate the effect of temperature fluctuation at the high-temperature tensile test, the samples were heated to the preset temperature at a heating rate of 10 °C/min and kept for 5 min before testing. Processing Text: The ingots of Fe x(CoCrNi) 100-x (x = 25, 40, 50, 62, 64, 66, and 71, at.%) MEAs were produced using an arc-melting technique in a water-cooled copper mold under high-purity argon. The as-cast materials, with a thickness of approximately 7 mm through hot rolling at 1000 °C, were homogenized at 1200 °C for 24h under argon gas, followed by furnace cooling. Processing Text: The Ni 50Cr 20Co 15Al 10V 5(at. %) HEAs in this work were synthesized using an arc-melting furnace in a Ti-getter, high-purity Ar atmosphere. High-purity Ni, Cr, Co, Al, and V metals (>99.9 wt %) were melted to cast the alloys. To ensure compositional uniformity, the alloys underwent more than seven repeated melting cycles under electromagnetic stirring. The alloys were then cast into a water-cooled copper mold, producing ingots measuring 10 mm × 10 mm × 80 mm. Subsequently, homogenization treatment was carried out at 1200 °C for 24 h in an Ar atmosphere, followed by water quenching. The homogenized ingots underwent cold rolling, resulting in an 80 % reduction in thickness. Following cold rolling, the alloys were recrystallized at 1100 °C for 10 min and then water-quenched to room temperature. After that, the recrystallized samples were subjected to aging treatments at 700 °C for 1 h and 12 h, respectively. These alloys for the study were named as aged-1h, aged-12 h, and recrystallized samples, respectively. The samples for examination underwent initial sanding with SiC sandpapers ranging from 400# to 2000#, followed by polishing with a 50 nm oxide polishing suspension (OPS) solution to remove surface stress. Samples for TEM analysis were first ground with SiC sandpapers to a thickness of less than 100 μm. Following this, the samples were further thinned using a precision Ar ion-beam milling system (Gatan 691) to achieve electron transparency. Samples for tensile tests were obtained with a gauge length of 10 mm and width of 2 mm using electric spark cutting. Before testing, the surface of all samples was sanded with SiC sandpapers ranging from 400# to 2000#. For analyzing the deformed microstructure, samples were additionally polished with OPS solution for EBSD and ECCI measurements. Processing state: Recrystallized
Processing Word: Processing state: Recrystallized

Processing Text: FeCoCrNiMnP xHEAs were cast by arc melting in a high-purity argon atmosphere. The Fe, Co, Cr, Ni, and Mn particles were obtained in Kairui New Materials (Beijing) Technology Co., Ltd. P was added in the form of FeP (the P content is 22 wt%). The all particles were ultrasonically cleaned in alcohol and weighed according to their design ratios. The particles are then placed in a copper mold crucible in order of their melting point from lowest to highest. Before melting the alloys, the pure metal Ti is melted first in order to remove residual oxygen from the furnace chamber. To ensure uniform composition, the alloys were repeatedly melted five times in an argon atmosphere and subsequently cooled with the furnace. The ingot is homogenized at 1100 °C for 6 h respectively. The two alloys were denoted as P0-CG and P2-CG HEAs (CG: coarse grains). Processing Text: The alloy ingots of these four compositions were prepared using vacuum arc melting in a water-cooled copper hearth under an argon atmosphere. Prior to melting, the raw materials (Mo, Nb, Ta, V, and Al) with a purity of 99.99 % were mechanically ground to remove the surface oxidation and then ultrasonically cleaned in ethanol for 3 min. High-purity Ti was employed as a degassing substance to remove residual oxygen in the vacuum chamber. In order to ensure chemical homogeneity, the button ingots were remelted for six times. Rectangular specimens with dimensions of 5 × 5 × 10 mm were machined from the button ingots. All surfaces were mechanically polished to a mirror-like finish. The microstructure were characterized using an X-ray diffractometer (XRD-6000, Shimadzu) with Cu-Kα radiation and a scanning electron microscope (SEM, Nova NanoSEM 450) equipped with an energy-dispersive spectrometer (EDS) and a backscatter electron (BSE) detector. Elemental micro-segregation was characterized by electron probe micro-analysis using an EPMA-8050G operating at an accelerating voltage of 15 keV. Vickers microhardness was examined by a 430SVD Micro-hardness test system on polished surfaces using a 136° Vickers diamond pyramid under 3000 g load applied for 15 s. 10 random indentations were inducted to get the average hardness. The ambient temperature compression properties were tested on a mechanical testing machine (AG-IC 100 kN) using the rectangular specimens with a strain rate of 10 −3s −1. Besides, the uniaxial compression tests at 600 °C, 800 °C, 1000 °C and 1200 °C were conducted on a Gleeble 3500-GTC system. During the tests, specimens were heated to the target temperature at a rate of 5 °C/s and held for 30 s, then uniaxially compressed with a strain rate of 10 −3s −1. The density measurements were performed on a JD200-3 electronic balance with a sensitivity of 0.1 mg, based on Archimedes' Law. Condition: before Al doping

Processing Text: In this research, focusing on low-carbon steel, a martensite-ferrite heterogeneous structure dual-phase (MFDP) steel with a network morphology where ferrite is surrounded by martensite was obtained via cyclic annealing and subcritical quenching heat treatment processes. With the initial microstructure of ferrite and lamellar pearlite, a spherical pearlite and martensitic structure surrounding the ferrite was first obtained by applying the cyclic annealing process near the Ac1 temperature. Subsequently, the annealed structure was subjected to subcritical quenching heat treatment, thereby establishing a network-like martensite-ferrite dual-phase heterogeneous structure and named N-760 °C and N-780 °C. The heat treatment experiment was carried out in a box-type resistance furnace, and the model was YFX16/120-GC. Through the previous heat treatment attempt, the microstructure obtained by different cycle time and cycle times was observed. Finally, it was concluded that the martensite can effectively wrap the ferrite structure after seven cycles of 690 °C holding for 2min and 700 °C holding for 8min. The specific process is as follows. (i)The sample is subjected to a heat treatment process in a resistance furnace at a temperature of 700 °C for 2 min, followed by cooling the furnace to 690 °C and maintaining it for 8 min. The temperature transition from 700 °C to 690 °C occurs over 7 min. Subsequently, the furnace is reheated to 700 °C and held for 2 min, during which the temperature rises from 690 °C to 700 °C over 12 min. This cycle is repeated 7 times to achieve a uniform ferrite-pearlite structure. After the cyclic annealing, the sample is air-cooled for 30 min.(ii)The sample was kept at the temperature of the two-phase region for 60 min, and finally water quenching was carried out to obtain the network martensite-ferrite dual-phase (MFDP) steel. The sample is subjected to a heat treatment process in a resistance furnace at a temperature of 700 °C for 2 min, followed by cooling the furnace to 690 °C and maintaining it for 8 min. The temperature transition from 700 °C to 690 °C occurs over 7 min. Subsequently, the furnace is reheated to 700 °C and held for 2 min, during which the temperature rises from 690 °C to 700 °C over 12 min. This cycle is repeated 7 times to achieve a uniform ferrite-pearlite structure. After the cyclic annealing, the sample is air-cooled for 30 min. The sample was kept at the temperature of the two-phase region for 60 min, and finally water quenching was carried out to obtain the network martensite-ferrite dual-phase (MFDP) steel. In Fig. 1 (b), the sample was placed in a heat treatment resistance furnace with a temperature of 950 °C for 30 min for homogenization heat treatment to eliminate internal defects in the structure and obtain a more uniform structure. Processing Text: The alloy was identified as a promising single-phase FCC candidate through systematic thermodynamic calculations using the Calculation of Phase Diagrams (CALPHAD) method and Thermo-Calc software, with validation from X-ray diffraction analysis of the as-cast alloy. The strengthening effects of carbon are attributed to solid solution strengthening and mechanisms such as twinning. The alloy was identified as a promising single-phase FCC candidate through systematic thermodynamic calculations using the Calculation of Phase Diagrams (CALPHAD) method and Thermo-Calc software, with validation from X-ray diffraction analysis of the as-cast alloy. Microstructural characterization using X-ray diffraction, scanning electron microscopy, and electron backscatter diffraction revealed no alteration in the FCC structure, but a refinement of grain size from 10 μm to 5 μm and a more random crystallographic texture. Additionally, transmission electron microscopy (TEM) analysis demonstrated dense, parallel deformation twins in the alloy with 1 atomic percent of carbon, confirming that twinning significantly contributes to improved ductility and strain hardening. The strengthening effects of carbon are attributed to solid solution strengthening and mechanisms such as twinning. These non-equiatomic HEAs were fabricated via arc melting, using 99.9 % pure elements. The melting process was conducted within an inert Ar gas environment in the crucible. To guarantee optimal chemical uniformity, the ingots were subjected to at least five additional remelting cycles. The as-cast samples were homogenized in the atmosphere of argon at 1373 K for 4 h to ensure complete diffusion of alloying elements and minimize phase segregation. Following homogenization, the samples were cold-rolled, reducing their thickness by 65 % to refine the microstructure further and enhance mechanical properties. After cold rolling, all samples were annealed for 1 h at 1173 K to relieve internal stresses and stabilize the microstructure, followed by air cooling. Condition: as-cast; Carbon concentration: 0 at.%; Microstructure: single-phase FCC

Processing Text: An 30 g ingot with a nominal composition of (CrHfMoNbTaTiVZr) 84Si 16was produced by vacuum arc melting of pure (> 99.95 wt%) metals. Rectangular samples measured 6 × 4 × 4 mm 3were cut from the as-cast ingot. Samples for XRD and SEM analysis were prepared by careful mechanical polishing to mirror surfaces using Buehler MasterMet 2 Suspension. For TEM examinations, thin foils were prepared using a Tenupol-5 twin-jet electro-polisher with an electrolyte containing a mixture of 600 ml of methanol, 360 ml of butanol, and 60 ml of perchloric acid at − 35 °C and 29.5 V; more details can be found elsewhere [ 17]. The surfaces of the samples for the hardness measurements were prepared by careful mechanical polishing to mirror surfaces using Buehler MasterMet 2 Suspension. Microstructural investigations were performed using X-ray diffraction (XRD, Rigaku Ultima IV; Cu Kα radiation having the wavelength of 1.5406 Å and a scanning rate of 3°/min from 20° to 80° (Fig. S1)), scanning electron microscopy (SEM; FEI Quanta 600 FEG and Nova NanoSEM 450), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM; JEM JEOL-2100 and Thermo Fisher Scientific™ Talos™ F200X G2) together with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS). The hardness measurements of constitutive phases were performed using a Shimadzu DUH-211S Dynamic Ultra Micro Hardness Tester fitted with a Berkovich tip. The measurements were conducted using a 10 × 10 grit with a distance of ∼50 μm between the indents. The maximum load of 50 mN was applied for 5 s; a loading speed was 6.6620 mN/s. The hardness and elastic moduli were obtained by using the Oliver and Pharr method [ 18]. After the measurements have been completed, the area was analysed by SEM (in a back scattered electron (BSE) regime) and EDS mapping to correlate the indents and phases (Fig. S2). The indentation fracture toughness, K C, also known as indentation fracture resistance, was evaluated at room temperature using by Digital Vickers Hardness Tester under a load of 98 N, following the formula [ 19]: (1)Kc=0.009EH0.4Phl0.5where E is the elastic modulus, which was equal to 120.1 GPa and derived from the indentation tests (using DUH-211S Dynamic Ultra Micro Hardness Tester under a load of 1961 mN and Oliver and Pharr method [ 18]); H is the measured microhardness; P is the indentation load; h is the length between the center and the corner of a remnant imprint; l is the length between the corner of the indent and the tip of the crack. For calculations, all the indents (10 independent measurements) that showed at least one crack were considered, according to [ 19]. Isothermal compression of the specimens measured 6 × 4 × 4 mm 3was carried out at 22, 800, 1000, 1200, and 1400 °C. Room-temperature compression tests were performed in the air using an Instron 5882 test machine. High-temperature compression test were conducted in vacuum (10 −4Torr or better) using a REM-600 A test machine. The specimens tested at 800, 1000, 1200, and 1400 °C were placed in the furnace, evacuated, heated (20 °C/min) to a target temperature, and held for ≈ 10 min to equilibrate the temperature before testing. The temperature of the specimen was controlled by a thermocouple attached to its side surface. No forced cooling was applied after the termination of the test. The initial strain rate was 10 −4s −1both for room- and high-temperature tests. Testing was carried out to the fracture of the specimens or to 50 % of strain. At least two samples at each temperature were tested. Oxidation tests were carried out using a Nabertherm furnace under the static laboratory air at 1200 °C. Priorto the tests, surfaces of the samples were mechanically gritted, polished, and ultrasonically cleaned in isopropanol. During the testing process, samples were placed in alumina boats, put into the preheated furnace, and removed after 0.5, 1, and 6 h of the oxidation test and cooled in the laboratory air for mass measurements. The mass of the specimens before and after oxidation was measured using an HR-200 analytical balance with an accuracy of 0.1 mg. Cross-sectional morphologies of the oxidised specimens were examined by SEM and EDS (Fig. S3). Compression test at 1000 °C

Processing Text: Commercial Zircaloy-4 tubes with a diameter of 9.5 mm and wall thickness of 0.57 mm were procured with a nominal composition in Table 1. The 2 µm and 7 µm geometries were prepared in the axial direction using a gallium ion FIB and plasma xenon FIB with two varying tensile geometries shown in Fig. 1. In addition to this, four 2 µm and seven 7 µm of the tensile bars were made from an irradiated tube of Zircaloy-4. This irradiated tube with an ID of “R-05″ was part of the Accident Tolerant Fuels 2 (ATF-2) experiment and was irradiated at the Advanced Test Reactor (ATR) Loop 2A at Idaho National Laboratory (INL). This rod was able to achieve a burnup of 9.27 GWd/tHM at temperatures ranging from 250 °C to 280 °C. Kamerman et al. calculates this rod's fast fluence as 1.98 х 10 25n/m 2using a coupled Monte Carlo N-Particle (MCNP) and ORIGEN methodology. Rough milling of the SSMT tensile samples was conducted at 30 kV and 60-2000nA while final cleaning used 30 kV and 0.5-10nA. The meso‑scale 80 µm tensile specimens were prepared from a 100 μm thick foil sample of Zircaloy-4 tubing which was sectioned using a high-speed diamond saw. The sample surface on both sides was polished from 600 grit sandpaper to a final solution of 1 μm diamond suspension. The foil was machined using an 8 W Spirit One fs-laser combined with a Newport microfabrication workstation to control movement. The laser system was run at a power of 3 W, a laser wavelength of 1040 nm, a pulse duration of 332fs, and a repetition rate of 50 kHz using a Mitutoyo NIR 10x objective lens which has a focused spot size of ∼10 μm. A compressed air gas flow was used to assist in removing ablation particles during cutting. Following laser machining, the tensile bars were quickly immersed in a bath of ethanol in an ultrasonic cleaner to remove excess ablation particles on the surface. Microstructural examination was performed using a Thermo Fisher Scios 2 DualBeam SEM equipped with an Oxford Symmetry S3 electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) detector. Prior to examination the surface was mechanically polished from 600 grit sandpaper to a 0.02 μm colloidal silica solution and then cryo-electro polished at 0 °C for one minute. Processing Text: The raw material was prepared by suspension melting of elemental ingredients (purity >99.9 wt. %) in high-purity argon atmosphere. To ensure uniformity, the ingot was re-melted at least five times. Then, the as-cast ingot was homogenized at 1200 °C for 24 h followed by air cooling. Finally, a measured composition of 2.11Al-25.59Co-23.63Cr-25.43Fe-23.24Ni (at. %) was determined by energy disperse spectroscopy. The heterostructure was produced by cold rolling and partial recrystallization. The as-homogenized material was rolled to 0.5 mm thick after 20 rolling passes with a thickness reduction of 90 %, using a customized machine with rolls fully immersed in liquid nitrogen, to obtain severely refined nanostructure with as high as possible stored energy. By trial and error, the annealing parameters for expected heterostructure, 550 °C for 1 hour followed by air cooling, were identified, by which the resulting microstructure of constituent zones conforms to the key design principles of strong-yet-tough material. To ensure uniformity, the ingot was re-melted at least five times. Then, the as-cast ingot was homogenized at 1200 °C for 24 h followed by air cooling. Processing Text: B4C particles (B4Cp) reinforced highly alloyed Al-Zn-Mg-Cu-Zr matrix composite was successfully fabricated through ball-milling, cold isostatic pressing, vacuum degassing, hot isostatic pressing (HIP), homogenization, hot extrusion, solution treatment, and aging treatment. The pressure of cold isostatic press was 200 MPa, and the vacuum degassing was implemented with the pressure of 140 MPa at 525 °C for 48 h. The vacuum degree in the vacuum degassing process was set as the maximum of 2 × 10−3Pa. The sintering duration, temperature and pressure of HIP were 4 h, 525 °C and 140 MPa, respectively. After removing the can, the sintered ingots were annealed in a resistance furnace (RX-30-13) with the system of 250 °C × 6 h + 350 °C × 6 h + 450 °C × 12 h, followed by furnace cooling. They were primary extruded using an extruding machine (1450 US ton, YUEN-SUN Machinery Co., Ltd) with the extrusion temperature and ratio of 480 °C and 10:1, respectively. The secondary extrusion with the ratio of 10:1 was conducted on a hydraulic press (YQ32-100), in which the extrusion temperature was 440 °C. The resistance furnace (RX-30-13) was adopted again for solid solution treatment with the system of 490 °C × 2 h + 510 °C × 2 h + 525 °C × 2 h, accompanied with water quenching. The T6 aging treatment (110 °C × 14 h) were carried out in a blast oven (DHG-9030), and the T4 aging treatment (natural aging at ∼ 25 °C for 360 h) was implemented in the air. Processing Text: A solution-treated Cu-0.5Cr-0.05Zr-0.05Ti (wt.%) alloy was drawn into a large-depth cup implementing a two-stage deformation process in the present study, firstly using a ∅ 50 mm cylindrical punch and subsequently redrawn by a ∅ 34 mm punch. The redrawn cup wall was subjected to aging heat treatment up to 400 °C, 500 °C, and 600 °C for 2 h followed by water quenching to understand the microstructural evolution and its correlation with mechanical properties. The as-received sheets were solutionized at 950 °C for 30 min, followed by water quenching to enhance the deep drawability. These solution-treated sheets were considered for the two-stage deep drawing experiment as illustrated in Fig. 1(a). The first stage involved the deep drawing of a circular blank into a cylindrical cup, followed by the second stage, which involved redrawing the fabricated cup to increase the cup height. The deep drawing experiment was performed using a deep drawing die setup comprised of a cylindrical punch of 50 mm diameter and a die of 55 mm diameter. Similarly, the redrawing test was carried out using a 34 mm diameter punch and a redrawing die. A maximum cup depth of 38.5 mm and 58.5 mm was achieved in the deep-drawn and redrawn cups, respectively, from an initial blank of 100 mm diameter. Before the experiment, 2.5 mm circular grid patterns were marked over the blank surface to determine the post-deformation strains. The major and minor strain distributions of the drawn-cups were evaluated by mapping the deformed circular grid dimensions using the circular grid analysis technique [ 25]. Therefore, the redrawn cups were subjected to aging treatment at different temperatures, as illustrated in Fig. 1(b), to analyze the microstructural and mechanical property variation in the deformed components under thermal exposure prior to the actual use in the space application. Microstructural characterizations of the redrawn cup wall and aged specimens (referred to as aged-redrawn cup, henceforth) were performed using SEM (ZEISS Merlin) equipped with EBSD and energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) facilities. The specimens for microstructural examination were extracted from the redrawn cup wall as depicted in Fig. 1(b). The specimen surfaces were prepared using a standard metallographic procedure and then etched with an etchant containing 2 gm K 2Cr 2O 7, 8 ml H 2SO 4,and 100 ml distilled water. For the EBSD analysis, the surfaces were further electropolished at −5 °C using a solution of 25 ml HPO 3, 25 ml C 2H 5OH, and 50 ml deionized water at 6 V for 20 s. The EBSD scans were performed with a step size of 0.25 μm, and the data were processed in a commercially available TSL-OIM software to evaluate grain size, grain boundary characteristics viz., high-angle grain boundaries (HAGBs with misorientation angle 15°-65°) and low-angle grain boundaries (LAGBs with misorientation angle 2°-15°), grain orientation spread (GOS), and Kernel average misorientation (KAM). Further, a detailed investigation of precipitate characteristics was done using high-resolution TEM (HRTEM, JEOL3000) technique. The TEM specimens were prepared using mechanical thinning followed by focused ion milling for final thinning and dimpling. Further, X-ray diffraction (XRD) method was utilized to determine phase composition, micro-strain, and crystallite size in all the specimens using a diffractometer (Bruker D8, Germany) equipped with a Cu target. The mechanical properties of the redrawn and aged-redrawn cup specimens were evaluated to comprehend the effect of aging temperature. Hence, miniature tensile specimens were cut from the redrawn cup wall region using a wire electro-discharge machine, as per the dimension given in Fig. 1(b) [ 26]. These specimens were then subjected to aging, and uniaxial tensile tests were performed in a 50 kN universal testing machine at 2 mm/min. The tests were repeated on three specimens in each condition. Moreover, hardness variation in the cup was estimated along a curvilinear distance from the cup bottom center to the cup top edge, and compared with aged-redrawn cup specimens. A Vickers hardness tester was used to apply an indentation load of 100 gf. Condition: Solution-treated
Processing Word: Condition: Solution-treated

Processing Text: WAAM is based on the development of traditional arc fusion welding. During WAAM process, wire melted and then deposited layer by layer to form the parts. Heat accumulation is prone to occur during deposition in layers, which would result in some defects (such as pores, cracks, residual stress and distortion). One kind of the main metallurgical defects of Al-Zn-Mg-Cu alloys manufactured by WAAM is pore. The presence of pores significantly reduces the mechanical properties of the materials. Strategies for reducing pore defects include vibrating the workpiece, using Cold Metal Transfer (CMT) technology, and applying thermal deformation. Solidification cracks and liquefaction cracks are also common defects. Strategies for reducing crack defects include optimizing alloy composition, adding grain nucleating agents, and using CMT technology. Direction: Horizontal; Condition: As-deposited + PHT process

Processing Text: The 2 wt.% Ti particle reinforced Mg-6 Zn alloy composites with different contents (0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2 wt.%) of Mn were prepared using semi-solid stirring assisted ultrasonic treatment followed by hot extrusion. Approximately 1 kg matrix alloy was melted in an electronic resistance furnace at 720 °C under the protective atmosphere of 99 vol. % CO 2 and 1 vol. % SF 6. Once the alloy was fully melted for 2 h, the floating slag was removed, and the temperature was lowered to 650 °C to achieve a semi-solid state. The pre-heated 2 wt.% Ti particles (200 °C for 2 h) were quickly added into the molten melt for 6-min mechanical stirring. After stirring, the mixed melt was reheated to 680 °C to reach a liquid state and subjected to ultrasonic treatment for 5 min. The ultrasonic power was 1.5 kW and the frequency was 20.1 kHz. Before water quenching, an additional 30 s of mechanical stirring was applied following the ultrasonic treatment. At last, the as-cast Ti particle reinforced Mg-6Zn- xMn composites were obtained. In order to eliminate the segregation of second phases, the ingot with a diameter of 80 mm was homogenized at 420 °C for 4 h. The composite ingots were extruded at 360 °C with an extrusion ratio of 25:1 with a speed of 0.5 m/min. Room temperature; Microstructure: fine/coarse bimodal structure; Interfacial bonding: tightly Ti/Mn2Ti bonding and Mn2Ti/Mg coherent orientation relationship
Processing Word: Room temperature; Microstructure: fine/coarse bimodal structure; Interfacial bonding: tightly Ti/Mn2Ti bonding and Mn2Ti/Mg coherent orientation relationship

Processing Text: In the PBF [ 39 ], the material is deposited by melting a powder bed in a layer-by-layer pattern using a heat source ( Fig. 4 (a)). The main difference between the two main categories of PBF, SLM and EBM, is the heat source used to melt powder: the former uses a laser, and the latter uses an electron beam. Various scanning strategies and process parameters used in PBF are shown in Fig. 4 (b). The most popular scanning strategies include unidirectional, bidirectional, spiral, zigzag, and crosswise; in each instance, neighboring tracks are overwritten with a hatch spacing lower than the track width to ensure complete melting. The directional hatch policy is usually rotated in the subsequent layers by a 67 o rotation. Rotating scanning helps to break down the epitaxy of columnar growth [ 40 ]. One of the most critical aspects of AM is the identification of the process parameters that affect the final product microstructure and quality. These include the scan speed, power source density, scanning strategy and spacing, and layer thickness [ 41 ], which affect the microstructural phases formed inside material, layer patterns and orientations, type of defects, and residual stresses. Strain rate: 10⁻³ s⁻¹, relative density: ∼0.25-0.34

Processing Text: This experiment utilized commercially available hot-rolled and annealed AZ31B magnesium alloy sheets. Strips with a thickness of 4 mm, a length of 130 mm, and a width of 100 mm were cut from the sheets for rolling. During the rolling process, the rolling speed for both passes was set at 50 mm·s−1, with a reduction rate of 25 % per pass. Prior to rolling, the sheets were heated to 350 °C and held at this temperature for 30 min before the first pass. After the first pass, the sheets were reheated to 350 °C and held for 15 min before the second pass. SR was performed using a two-roll synchronous rolling mill with a working roll diameter of 320 mm. ASR and AAR were conducted using a two-roll asymmetrical rolling mill with working roll diameters of 320 mm and 280 mm, respectively. The heated magnesium alloy sheet is placed on a conveyor roller table, and then the angle between the rolling centerline and the length direction of the plate is controlled by adjusting the pushing mechanism located on both sides of the sheet. Based on previous research on sheet shape, this study selected a rolling angle of 40° for the first pass and 80° for the second pass in the AAR process. Process: SR; Tension direction: 45°
