Processing Text: To address this issue, bimodal-structured AZ80 Mg alloys with varying heterogeneity levels were fabricated via low-temperature extrusion in this work. Commercial Mg-8.46Al-0.66Zn-0.23Mn (AZ80, wt.%) was employed in this study. To minimize oxidation, an as-cast billet was prepared by melting an AZ80 ingot in an electric resistance furnace at 720 °C under a CO 2+SF 6(99:1) protective atmosphere. The molten metal was held at 740-750 °C for 30 min and then was poured into a steel mold (Ø 60 mm×200 mm) preheated to 210 °C. Before extrusion, as-cast billets and extrusion mold were preheated to 230 °C, 250 °C, and 270 °C for 40 min, respectively. Direct extrusion was conducted at 230 °C, 250 °C, and 270 °C (denoted hereafter as EX230, EX250 and EX270 alloys, respectively) with a ram speed of 1 mm/s and an extrusion ratio of 11.1. After extrusion, the samples were immediately quenched in water, and extruded rods with a diameter of 12 mm were obtained. Processing Text: The steel was melted in a vacuum induction furnace into an ingot of 25 kg, followed by hot-forging and hot-rolling (HR) into 12 mm thick plate. The hot-rolled plate was firstly machined into a dilatometric sample with a diameter of 3 mm and a length of 10 mm. The dilatometric sample was then heated to 1100 ℃ at a rate of 10 ℃/min. For quenching and tempering (QT) treatment ( Fig. 1c), the sample was austenitized at 900 ℃ for 30 min followed by water-quenching, and then tempered at 650 ℃ for 30 min. For step quenching and tempering (SQT) treatment ( Fig. 1c), the specimen was initially austenitized at 900 ℃ for 30 min, followed by slow cooling (∼10 ℃/min) to the intercritical temperature (780 ℃) for 20 min, and then water-quenching to room temperature. Such quenching treatment is referred to as step quenching. Finally, the specimen was tempered at 650 ℃ for 30 min. Standard cylindrical tensile specimens with a gauge length of 44 mm and diameter of 7 mm were prepared from the QT and SQT plates. Uniaxial tensile testing (MTS machine) was carried out at ambient temperature using an initial strain rate of 10 −3s −1. To quantify the evolution of HDI stress, a load-unload-reload (LUR) process was conducted under tensile tests using the MTS machine at a strain rate of 10 −3s −1. Tensile strain was measured using an extensometer. Processing Text: The Al-Mg alloy plates used for the study were prepared by depositing AA5087 wire (1.2 mm in diameter) onto AA5A06 plates via the WADED system. The WADED system mainly includes an ABB six-axis robot and a Fronius CMT Advanced 4000R welding system. During the WADED process, the filler wire was melted by the arc in a protective atmosphere (99.99 % Ar), and the CMT torch moved horizontally (Y-depositing direction) with the molten wire to form a deposited layer. Deposition of the next layer was performed on the previous layer by raising the torch height (Z-building direction). The WADED Al components were finally removed from the substrate using electrical discharge machining (EDM) and double-side milling to 6 mm thickness. The LSP experiment was carried out in a self-built LSP system, which mainly included a Nd: YAG pulsed laser (with a wavelength of 1064 nm and a pulse duration of 15 ns) and a six-axis robot. WADED Al plate was ground and polished before LSP, and then fixed on six-axis robot to adjust position. The Al foil with a thickness of 100 µm and the flowing water layer were covered on the surface of WADED Al plate as absorbing layer and constraining layer, respectively. The front and back sides of the WADED Al plate were strengthened in turn. The pulsed laser with energy of 5 J was focused by a convex lens into a circular spot with a diameter of 2 mm. Both sides of sampling region were treated twice by LSP at a 50 % overlapping rate to prevent the distortion and obtain the unform residual stress distribution. The as-deposited samples after LSP treatment were further annealed at 200 °C for 1 h to study the effect of the LSP + annealing process on the WADED Al alloy. Processing state: as-deposited

Processing Text: The master FeCoCrNiCuAl0.4 alloys with a mass of 170 g were prepared by high-frequency induction melting using high purity of 99.99 wt% Fe, 99.99 wt% Co, 99.99 wt% Cr, 99.99 wt% Ni, 99.99 wt% Cu, and 99.99 wt% Al elements. The experiments were performed by a self-designed 3D ultrasonic solidification apparatus for metallic alloys. Three ultrasonic transducers with an operating frequency of 20 kHz were set up vertically by locating TC4 ultrasonic rods with 5 mm diameter end faces at the center point of the outer walls of the mold through X, Y and Z directions with elastic contact. There were two 1045 steel rods with fixed bases coaxially arranged on the opposite sides of the ultrasonic horns along X and Y directions, and a fixed cover plate using the same steel material with a central window to stabilize along Z direction. The mold was optimized to ensure the ultrasonic solidification system was in resonance, which internal and external sizes were 30×30×55 mm and 20×20×50 mm, respectively. During the experiments, the master alloys were melted and heated to 1873 K using high-frequency induction melting and subsequently poured into a cubic graphite casting mold, which was preheated to 1273 K and has a protective coating. The ultrasonic transducers were turned on, and one-dimensional Z, two-dimensional Y and Z, and three-dimensional X, Y, and Z ultrasonic waves, all with an amplitude of 18 μm, were selected to be applied to the melt through the casting mold. Meanwhile, a self-designed high-temperature sound field detecting system and K-type NiCr-NiSi thermocouple were used to monitored the acoustic field and temperature synchronously by immersing them at a distance of 30 mm below the highest alloy melt liquid level and 5 mm from the side wall. When the liquid alloys completely solidified and the temperature reached to 1273 K, the ultrasonic powers supply were turned off, and the solidified samples of FeCoCrNiCuAl0.4 alloy were finally obtained. After experiment, the alloy samples were cut longitudinally and polished. A Netzch 404 C Differential Scanning Calorimeter (DSC) was used for thermal analysis of static specimen at a scan rate of 10 K/min. The phase constitution was analyzed by a D8 discover A25 X-ray diffractometer (XRD) with a wavelength of 0.179021 nm. The solidification microstructures and crystallographic information were characterized by a Zeiss Gemini 500 scanning electron microscope (SEM). The electron backscatter diffraction images (EBSD) and energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS) results were taken by Oxford Instruments Nordlys detectors. The EBSD samples were electropolished with a mixed solution of HClO4: C2H7O2: CH4O=1: 2: 7 and the electric voltage of 18 V at 293 K for 15 s. A FEI Talos F200X transmission electron microscope (TEM) was used to characterize the crystal structure. Mechanical tensile tests were performed at the loading rate of 1×10−3s−1 by an Instron 3382 universal testing machine equipped with a Lve-Pro video extensometer. The gauge section of the dog bone-shaped sample was 10×3×1.2 mm. Electrochemical corrosion studies were performed in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution via a CHI660E electrochemical workstation. After the open circuit potential (OCP) was stabilized, the potential dynamic polarization curve was recorded at a potential scanning rate of 10 mV/s, and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was performed in the frequency range of 10−2∼105Hz, with a sinusoidal perturbation of amplitude 5.0 mV around the obtained OCP values for each sample. Processing state: statically solidified

Processing Text: The materials used in this study were commercial CuCrZr alloys (grade C18150). The commercial copper alloys had undergone cold deformation and annealing treatment, resulting in mostly deformed grains and a large number of precipitates. To improve the uniformity of the microstructure and composition of the copper alloys and minimize the dissolution of precipitates back into the matrix, the alloys were initially subjected to a solid solution treatment at 950 ℃ for 2 hours before cryogenic treatment. Subsequently, they were rapidly cooled using water as the medium to achieve a solid solution state. Cryogenic treatment was conducted using the SLX-30B cryogenic treatment box, developed by the Institute of Physics and Chemistry, Chinese Academy of Sciences, with nitrogen supplied from a pressure tank. It should be noted that the cryogenic box controlled the temperature and cooling rate by adjusting the flow rate of liquid nitrogen. In this study, the latent heat of vaporization of liquid nitrogen was used to cool the sample, and the cooling rate was set at 3 ℃/min. Cryogenic treatment duration: less than 8 hours; Tensile strength around 245 MPa

Processing Text: Disk-shaped ingots of the Co 40(CrFeNi) 60alloy with a thickness of 10 mm and a diameter of ∼ 40 mm were produced in a vacuum arc melter. Each ingot was flipped and re-melted five times to improve the chemical homogeneity. The as-cast ingots were trimmed to obtain samples with parallel sides along an intended rolling direction (RD), after which the samples were cold-rolled 80 %. Dog-bone-shaped specimens with a gauge size of 6 × 3 × 1 mm 3and the tensile axis along the RD were machined from the rolled samples. Several tensile specimens and specimens for microstructural examinations were annealed at 600 °C for 15 min, 1 h and 10 h to produce material at different stages of recrystallization. This plane was electrochemically polished and then examined using electron channeling contrast (ECC) imaging and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD). EBSD step sizes were 40 nm for the as-rolled material and 80 nm for the annealed samples. Processing state: as-rolled; Microstructure: heterogeneous containing deformation twins, low misorientation bands, and shear bands

Processing Text: Gas-atomized AISI 4140 powder was used as the additive material. The powder is spherical in shape, with an average particle size of approximately 40 μm. 95 % of the particles have diameters ranging from 25 to 53 μm. The experimental setup for conducting the LMD and EHLA processes is depicted in Fig. 2. The machine employed in this study consisted of a focusing optic PHFQ-H1-C, a coaxial powder nozzle, and a spindle. A diode laser with a maximum power of 4000 W was used as the beam source. Powder feed was accomplished through the coaxial powder delivery system of the laser head using a pneumatic twin powder feeder. Argon gas was used for powder delivery and specimen shielding to prevent oxidation, and the purity of argon gas is 99.99 %. A water-cooling system was implemented to cool the laser system and laser head. In the LMD process, the interaction time between the laser beam and the powder particles is short, resulting in a high ratio of laser energy being absorbed by the substrate. The powder particles melt in the melting pool, leading to a relatively large heat-affected zone. Conversely, in the EHLA process, the laser-powder reaction occurs along the powder delivery path. Consequently, most of the powder particles melt above the surface and enter the melting pool as liquid drops. The EHLA process employs higher laser power to ensure a pore-free, less-cracked, and metallurgical-bonded layer. We studied divergent parameter combinations for a single layer and investigated the microstructure (pores, cracks, bonding quality, thickness, etc.) of the cross-section of the deposition accordingly, and those results feeded back to the process parameters. Through trial and error, the process parameters for a single layer with low porosity, metallurgic bonding between the substrate and the layer, and without any cracks were finally selected. The parameters used for LMD and EHLA are presented in Table 2. In the process strategy, the workpiece rotates using a fixed lathe chuck while the powder nozzle moves horizontally above the substrate. The overlap ratio between two tracks in the same layer is approximately 70 %. All experiments were conducted using a meandering scan path. Case 1: a single layer with multiple tracks using LMD, following the process parameters outlined in Table 2(LMD process parameters). Case 2: a single layer with multiple tracks using EHLA, following the process parameters described in Table 2(EHLA process parameters). Case 3: a 3D structure using LMD on a cylindrical base material. The dimensions of the deposition were 10 mm in the thickness direction (BD, R) and 100 mm in the length direction (SD, Z). In order to mitigate potential hot cracking caused by high temperatures during continuous deposition and to conduct comparative IHT experiments, we fabricated a total of 22 layers (10 mm) and allowed a dwell time of 15 min for cooling the deposition to 60 °C. Case 4: a 3D structure using EHLA on a cylindrical base material. The dimensions of the EHLA deposition were identical to those of the LMD deposition. However, since the thickness of an EHLA layer is approximately one-fourth to one-fifth of an LMD layer, we deposited a total of 95 layers to achieve a structure with a 10-mm thickness. To study the IHT effect and compare the resulting microstructure with LMD, we implemented a cooling time of 15 min after each set of five continuous deposited layers in order to facilitate cooling to 60 °C. Due to the high-power input and limited time available for heat transfer, the EHLA deposited structure exhibited some burnt edges, with a zig-zag burnt position of 5 mm at a 45-degree angle to the horizontal direction at each edge. This phenomenon is primarily attributed to the zigzag scanning strategy, as it results in a brief period of secondary heating at both ends and insufficient time for heat dissipation. The as-built deposition was sectioned along the cross-sectional (R-Z) direction for microstructural characterization. The samples were carefully examined under a microscope (Axio Imager Objective A-Plan 50×) to ensure minimal pores, crack-free deposition, and a sound metallurgical interface. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM, ZEISS Sigma 300) was used to analyze the microstructural composition after etching with a 2 % Nital etchant (97 % ethanol and 3 % nitric acid) for 10 s. Electron dispersive spectroscopy (EDS, ZEISS) analysis was conducted to determine the element distribution in selected regions. Prior to texture analysis, vibration polishing with Al2O3 powders was performed. Texture analysis was carried out using an electron backscattered diffraction detector (EBSD, Oxford C-Nano) for both single-layer and multi-layer samples. Nanoindentation tests (FISCHERSCOPE HM2000, Germany) were used to measure the nanohardness of single layers, while the hardness of multi-layer samples was determined using a Vickers hardness tester as per DIN EN ISO 6507-1. To mirror the measurement errors, the hardness test was performed on three 3 positions from the edge to the middle (along Z direction) of the cross section, and three lines was defined for each position. The mean value of each point at three lines was used for the final results. The Vickers test was performed with a force of 0.98 N and a dwell time of 10 s. The distance between the clad edge ZB and testing position Z1 was approx. 2 mm. The horizontal distance between two testing lines Z1 and Z2 was 50 μm, and the vertical distance between two testing points R1 and R2 was 25 μm. A total length of approx. 3.5 mm consisting of deposition, heat affected zone (HAZ) and part of the substrate were tested. Similarly, three replicates were performed, and the mean value was used for the nanoindentation test, and a force of 300 mN was applied with a dwell time of 25 s according to standard ISO 14577-1 Metallic materials — Instrumented indentation test for hardness and materials parameters. A volume with thickness of 10 mm and length of 100 mm for the manufacturing of tensile test samples was produced for both LMD and EHLA process. Tensile tests were performed according to the DIN EN ISO 6892 standard, and the round tensile samples adhered to the dimensions specified in DIN 50125. Processing Text: AlSi10Mg was typically employed as a primary material for components utilized in SLM manufacturing due to its favorable mechanical properties, heat resistance, corrosion resistance, and lightweight characteristics [7-10]. In order to further enhance the mechanical properties of AlSi10Mg and meet specific requirements, heat treatment can be used to modify its atomic structure and nature [11-16]. The heat treatment process was Solution Heat Treatment (SHT, 525 °C), and the heat treatment time includes 1 h, 2 h, and 3 h. Cooling methods consist of Refrigerant Cooling (RC), Water Cooling (WC), Air Cooling (AC), Oil Cooling (OC), and Furnace Cooling (FC). As the cooling rate decreases and the heat treatment time increases, the size of the formed Si phase particles varies from small to large, and the distribution deviates from inhomogeneous to homogeneous. In addition, the number of precipitated particles increases and then decreases. To investigate the impact of cooling rates and heat treatment time on the mechanical properties of AlSi10Mg alloys, quasi-static tensile and compression tests were performed. On the other hand, the tensile strength of the heat-treatment samples decreases while the ductility increases, and the Vickers hardness of the samples also decreases with decreasing cooling rate and increasing heat treatment time. The samples treated at 525 °C - 2 h - AC exhibited the highest tensile and compressive properties. Selective laser melting (SLM) was a form of additive manufacturing (AM) that employs metal powders to fabricate components. The experimental samples were fabricated using AlSi10Mg powder aerosol obtained from Beijing Research State Technology Company. SLM uses an EOS 280 3D printer (400 W, 100 μm) with a Yb fiber laser. To mitigate the risk of embrittlement caused by the reaction between oxygen and Al or magnesium during the manufacturing process, the sample specimens were produced in an air-free environment. Argon gas was employed to maintain the oxygen concentration below 0.6 %. The printer uses a laser power of 300 W, a scanning rate of 1000 mm/s per second, a layer thickness of 30 μm, and a hatch spacing of 120 μm. The AlSi10Mg specimens produced through SLM were subjected to various heat treatments, as outlined in Table 2. The primary heat treatment was Solution Heat Treatment (SHT), with a temperature of 525 °C [33-35]. One noteworthy method was RC, which employs a refrigerant spray to lower the temperature of the sample to ambient temperature. In the process of OC, the quenching oil was heated to 60 °C. Subsequently, the sample was submerged in the heated oil and allowed to cool to the ambient temperature. The cooling rates associated with the various cooling methods were ranked in descending order as follows: V (RC)> V (WC)> V (AC)> V (OC)> V (FC). Additionally, argon gas was employed to safeguard the samples against oxidation during the heat treatment. The solid block samples were subjected to heat treatment before polishing. After polishing, the samples were subjected to corrosion for 20 s using Keller's reagent (2.5 ml HNO 3, 1.5 ml HCL, 1.0 ml HF, and 95 ml H 2O). Condition: Fastest cooling rate after SHT (525 °C - 2 h)

Processing Text: The experimental material was a cylindrical ingot of Mg-12.8Gd-3.8Y-1.9Zn-0.5Zr (wt%) alloy, which was produced by semi-continuous casting process. The alloy ingot was homogenized at 520 °C for 16 hours and cooled at RT. Before the experiment beginning the homogenized alloy ingot underwent a series of pretreatment steps. Firstly, the alloy ingot underwent one pass of upsetting-extruding experiment. Subsequently, one pass of backward-extruding experiment was performed. Finally, the backward-extruded sample ring was cut into rectangular initial alloys of 70 mm × 56 mm × 120 mm. The deformation temperature for both the upsetting-extruding and backward-extruding experiments were 450 °C, and the dies were preheated at 450 °C × 8 h before the experiments. The size of the alloy after upsetting experiment was Φ465 mm, and the extrusion ratio was 1.9:1. Two passes of forging experiments were conducted on the initial alloy, with each forging direction perpendicular to the axial direction of the backward-extrusion experiment. The detailed experimental steps are as follows: Firstly, the initial alloy was pre-aged at 200 °C. Based on previous research, it was found that the sample was in peak aging state at 120 h. The first pass of forging was performed on the pre-aged samples. The die and initial alloy were preheated at 460 °C and 450 °C, respectively, and held for 30 minutes before the experiments, and cooled at RT after forging. The sample after the first pass of forging was defined as PF sample. The PF sample was treated with low-temperature solid solution at 460 °C for 8 hours. After the treatment, it was put back into the die for the second pass of forging. Prior to the experiment, both the die and sample were preheated and held at the same temperature and holding time as the first pass. The sample after the second pass of forging was defined as PFSF sample. The second pass of forging was performed directly on the PF sample, as well as the die and sample were also preheated and held at the same temperature and holding time before the experiment. The sample after the second pass of forging was defined as PFF sample. Initial state

Processing Text: In this study, low-density (< 6 g/cm3) AlCrFeTiX (x = Co, Ni, Cu) high-entropy alloys were produced by mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering (SPS), and their structures and mechanical properties after SPS and annealing at 1000 °C for 24 h were reported. The commercial powders of Al (99.7 wt%, particle size < 30 μm), Cr (99.7 wt%, particle size in the range 10-30 μm), Fe (99.9 wt%, particle size < 75 μm), Ti (99.5 wt%, particle size < 45 μm), Co (99.8 wt%, particle size < 70 μm), Cu (99.97 wt%, particle size < 60 μm), Ni (99.9 wt%, particle size < 30 μm) were used as the precursors. 18 g batches of an stoichiometric Al:Cr:Fe:Ti:Co (1:1:1:1:1:1 mol), Al:Cr:Fe:Ti:Cu (1:1:1:1:1:1 mol), and Al:Cr:Fe:Ti:Ni (1:1:1:1:1:1 mol) mixtures were used for mechanical alloying at 694 rpm (jar rotated at 1388 rpm) for 60 min in a water-cooling double-station planetary ball mill (Activator 2S, Activator, Russia), which is high energy planetary ball mill and allows reaching centrifugal acceleration more than 90 g. Before the milling, a stainless steel jar of 250 ml capacity was vacuumed, filled with the 99.98 %-purity argon having a pressure of 4 atm and then sealed. The powders were unloaded from jars and loaded to graphite die for SPS in a glove box in an argon atmosphere. Cylindrical graphite die (the inner diameter of 30 mm) was filled with a desired amount of the mixed powders. Then, the powders were consolidated using a SPS apparatus (Labox 650, Sinter Land, Japan) using the following parameters: heated in vacuum (15-20 Pa) at the rate of 100 °C/min, the temperature of 900°C, under uniaxial loading of 50 MPa, and dwell time of 10 min. After sintering, the specimens were free cooled in vacuum; cooling time to room temperature was ∼15 min. Disc-shaped samples of 30 mm in diameter and 7 mm thick were obtained. The specimens measured 3 × 3 × 5 mm 3 were cut from the disc-shaped samples after SPS using electrical discharge machining. A part of the specimens were annealed at 1000 °C for 24 h with further air cooling. Prior to annealing, the specimens were sealed in a vacuumed (10 −2 torr) quartz tube filled with titanium chips to prevent oxidation. Temperature: 600 °C; State: after SPS
Processing Word: Temperature: 600 °C; State: after SPS

Processing Text: Buttons of CrFeNi are firstly prepared using vacuum arc melting in the water-cooled copper hearth utilising 99.9 % pure Fe, Cr, and Ni elements. The buttons were remelted 5 times at argon atmosphere for homogeneity. The casted buttons were cleaned and polished removing the oxide layer from the button surface. Further buttons of 48 gms for CrFeNi were cast into a rod of 10 ×10 x 50 mm 3 using suction casting. The suction casting was carried out at 10-7 mbar pressure. The rods were homogenised at 1100˚ C for 24 hours in an argon atmosphere followed by water quenching to attain a single-phase FCC structure. Consequently, the homogenised rods were cold rolled up to 50 % thickness reduction to minimise the casting defects. The rods were then further subjected to annealing at 1373 K for 2 hours to remove all the residual stress and attain a fully recrystallised microstructure in the rods before further processing. The rods were then rolled at room temperature (300 K) up to 90 % rolling reduction with a 5 % reduction in each pass. The samples at different rolling reductions of 20 %, 40 %, 60 % and 90 % were cut and kept for further characterisation. The rolled samples were prepared by polishing on SiC paper up to 2500 grade followed by alumina cloth polishing and vibromet polishing with colloidal silica. Condition: Annealed
Processing Word: Condition: Annealed

Processing Text: Master alloys with nominal composition of Co 68Al xFe 24.7-xV 4.8Cr 2.5(x = 16.5, 17 and 18 at.%) were prepared by arc-melting high-purity (99.95 wt%) Co, Cr, Fe, V and Al, which was denoted as Al-16.5, Al-17 and Al-18 samples, respectively. Each master alloy was remelted five times to ensure chemical homogeneity, and the molten liquid was subsequently drop-cast into a water-cooled copper mold of 70 × 10 × 10 mm 3. The crystal structure was analyzed by X-ray diffraction (XRD, Bruker AXS D8 Advance) with Cu Kα radiation with a scanning range of 20° ∼ 100°. The microstructure of the samples was characterized by field emission scanning electron microscopy (SEM, FEI Quanta 250F). The samples were ground with 400-2000# SiC sandpapers until the surface was smooth, and finally polished with 0.25 μm diamond suspension. Then, the polished samples were electrochemically etched, and the corrosive solution was a diluted aqua regia solution of HNO 3: HCl:C 2H 5OH = 1:3:8 vol%. The phase structure and chemical composition were characterized by FEI Talos F200X transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS). For the TEM sample preparation method, the sample was first punched to circle sheets with radius of Ф3 mm and then ground to about 50 μm. Twin-jet electropolishing was performed at a temperature of about 233 K using a mixed solution of HNO 3:CH 4O = 1:4. An Oxford symmetry S2 detector was installed on the JEOL-JSM-IT800 instrument and electron back-scatter diffraction (EBSD) measurements were performed. Vickers hardness measurements were performed using a hardness tester (HVS-1000) at a load of 500 gf and a load time of 10 s. Average hardness was obtained after at least 5 measurements of each sample. A rectangular specimen with 2 × 2 × 4 mm 3was cut from the ingot with an electric discharge machine, and a room temperature compression test was performed at a strain rate of 2 × 10 −4s −1. Compression tests were performed on three samples of each material to confirm repeatability. Nanoindentation test (KLA-Nano Indenter G200) was measured at least four times to ensure data reliability. Microstructure: eutectic structure; Processing state: as-cast

Processing Text: Master ingots of present HEA with a nominal composition of Al 0.3CoCrFeNi were fabricated by vacuum-levitation melting method. All elements (Al, Co, Cr, Fe, and Ni) used as raw materials have the purity higher than 99.9 wt%. The ingots were remelted four times to ensure chemical homogeneity. Original HEA plates with dimensions of 150 mm (length) × 60 mm (width) × 20 mm (thickness) were obtained by drop casting method using a steel mold. Then, the plates were annealed at 1150 °C for 24 h for homogenization and water-quenched. The homogenized plates were cold-rolled to sheets with a thickness of ∼2 mm (90 % reduction) and then cut into specimens with dimensions of 5 mm (length) × 5 (width) × 3 mm (thickness) for recrystallization annealing. These small specimens were annealed at 750 °C, 850 °C and 950 °C in an electric box furnace (SX-1600 °C) for various durations and water quenched. To investigate microstructures at higher temperatures, additional specimens were annealed at 1000 °C, 1100 °C and 1200 °C for 1 h, and water quenched. The microstructural evolution of Al0.3CoCrFeNi high entropy alloy after cold rolling and annealing treatment (at 750 °C, 850 °C and 950 °C) was investigated by scanning electron microscopy and electron backscatter diffraction. Processing Text: A novel Ti35Zr35Nb15Mo5Fe5Cr5 complex concentrated alloy (CCA) with potential for biomedical application was developed by vacuum arc melting. Metal pieces of Ti, Zr, Nb, Mo, Fe, and Cr with high purity (greater than 99.95 %) were used to produce Ti 35Zr 35Nb 15Mo 5Fe 5Cr 5CCA in a vacuum arc melting furnace. The sample was melted in a high vacuum melting chamber (vacuum pressure ∼ 10 −6mbar) under a high-purity argon atmosphere using a Ti getter. It was then solidified on a water-cooled copper hearth. For chemical homogeneity, the sample was remelted five times, and each time, the sample was flipped before melting. In accordance with ISO 2738, the density of the as-cast CCA sample was determined by applying Archimedes' principle. For annealing treatment, the as-cast specimens were vacuum-sealed in a quartz tube and annealed at temperatures of 700˚C, 900˚C, and 1100˚C for a duration of 20 h using a muffle furnace. All the as-cast and annealed specimens were metallographically prepared for microscopy using emery papers for polishing and Kroll's reagent (6 ml HNO 3, 2 ml HF, and 92 ml H 2O) for etching. Processing Text: The CLAM steel, with a chemical composition (in wt.%) of Fe - 8.91% Cr - 1.4% W - 0.54 % Mn - 0.15% Ta - 0.15% V- 0.09% C - 0.06% Si, was melted in a vacuum induction furnace prior to casting an ingot with dimensions of 100 mm × 100 mm × 120 mm. The ingot was solution treated in an air furnace at 1200 °C for 2 h to homogenize the microstructure and completely dissolve primary carbides, prior to hot and then warm rolling to extensively elongate the prior-austenite grains along the rolling direction. To prepare the lamellar grain structure in the CLAM steel, the steel was directly tempered at 700 °C for 15 min to transform the martensite into ferrite but to prevent the ferrite grains undergoing complete recrystallization. Evolutions of the mechanical properties for the top (a) and bottom (b) AlSi7Mg samples in relation to the direct-aged conditions (Table 2). The starting points at 0.1 and 70 h represent the as-built conditions for both the top (a) and bottom (b) samples. They indicate the different exposure times at the build platform temperature (150 °C). Variations of both the Vickers microhardness values and size of Si-eutectic particles in relation to the direct aging temperatures of top (dotted lines) and bottom (continuous lines) samples. Evolutions of the mechanical properties of the artificially aged AlSi7Mg (a) and AlSi10Mg (b) samples. When the as-built AlSi7Mg samples underwent a solution heat-treated for 4 h (Fig. 7a), the yield and ultimate tensile strengths reached (125±10) MPa and (285±12) MPa, respectively, due to the microstructural changes affecting of Si-eutectic and grain sizes (see Fig. 3 and Fig. 4). Following a similar heat treatment, Bosio et al. [46] demonstrated that the significant strengthening contributions related to the α-Al cell size decreased the strength by approximately 82 %. They further showed that the α-Al cells confer 52 MPa compared to only 11 MPa conferred by the grain boundaries, as describe the following Hall-Petch equation: (8)σHP=k(1dcell+1dgrain) where σHP is the strength ruled by the Hall-Petch law, k is a material constant (40MPam1/2), dcell and dgrains([μm]) are the average cell (Fig. 3c,d) and grain sizes. As also reported by [11, 47], softening effects were also caused by a reduction in the percentage of alloying elements within the crystal lattice, as discussed in the Introduction section. True elongations increased from 0.135 to 0.180. Both the artificial aging treatments at 150 and 175 °C restored the mechanical performance of each solution heat-treated sample, bringing them to the peak-aged conditions (see yellow rectangle in Fig. 7). Other intermediate conditions, including peak-aging at 200 °C (see Table 2), fell between the maximum (peak-aging) and minimum value (175 °C × 512 h). Processing Text: The Zn-xCu (x= 0, 2, 4 and 8 wt%) alloys ingots were purchased from Beijing Zhongnuo New Material Technology Co., Ltd. The actual chemical compositions of the as-cast Zn-xCu alloys were measured by ICP-OES, as listed in Table 1. The plates with a size of 100 mm × 60 mm × 20 mm were prepared from the as-cast Zn-xCu (x= 0, 2, 4 and 8 wt%) alloys, and then were homogenized at 350 °C for 9 h. In order to crush coarse cast microstructure and obtain fine equiaxed grains, the as-cast Zn-xCu (x= 0, 2, 4 and 8 wt%) alloys plates were rolled down to 8 mm by 15 % reduction in thickness per pass after preheating at 200 °C for 5 min. Subsequently, the rolled samples were annealed at 300 °C for 1 h. The annealed Zn-xCu (x= 0, 2, 4 and 8 wt%) alloys plates were sequentially further rolled to 65 % rolling reduction in thickness by multi-pass after preheating at 250 °C for 10 min. The tensile specimens of the Zn-xCu (x= 0, 2, 4 and 8 wt%) alloys with a gauge length of 20 mm and a width of 3 mm were prepared from the rolled samples. The tensile specimens were cut along the rolling direction. The thickness of tensile specimens was equal to that of the rolled sheets. Specimens for microstructure characterization were ground, polished and etched with an acid solution (20 g CrO3, 1.5 g Na2SO4 and 100 mL distilled water), then were characterized by the optical microscope. The microstructure at high magnification and the chemical compositions of phase were analyzed by scanning electron microscopy with energy dispersive spectrometry (EDS). The phase compositions of the Zn-xCu (x= 0, 2, 4 and 8 wt%) alloys were identified using an X-ray diffractometer analysis (XRD) with a Cu-Kα irradiation and the XRD patterns were collected over the 2θ range of 30-80° at a scan rate of 2° per min. Moreover, microstructure and texture evolution of the Zn-xCu (x= 0, 2, 4 and 8 wt%) alloys during hot-rolling were characterized by the electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) analysis. To further characterize the microstructures of Zn-xCu alloys after hot-rolling, TEM observations were carried out by a Tecnai G2 transmission electron microscope. The TEM samples were prepared by mechanical grinding to below 50 μm, and then ion thinning in a 4 wt% perchloric acid alcohol solution. Processing Text: Pure W, W-0.8wt % (HfNbMoZrTi)B2 and W-1.0wt % (HfNbMoZrTi)B2 materials were fabricated using mechanical ball milling and spark plasma sintering. The W materials blocks were fabricated through a sequence of mechanical ball milling, high-temperature sintering, and subsequent annealing. The powders were ball milled in a planetary mill under a pure argon atmosphere to minimize oxidation and enhance sintering activity. The milling process was conducted at a rotational speed of 300 rpm for 6 hours, using tungsten carbide balls as the milling medium with a ball-to-powder weight ratio of 10:1 to minimize impurity introduction and maximize milling efficiency. Subsequently, the milled powder was loaded into a graphite mold with a diameter of 30 mm, pre-compacted at room temperature, and then heated to 1600 °C under a pressure of 64 MPa for consolidation. The sintered W blocks were then annealed at six different temperatures: 1000 °C, 1100 °C, 1200 °C, 1300 °C, 1400 °C, 1500 °C, 1600 °C, 1700 °C, 1800 °C, 1900 °C, and 2000 °C for 1 h, each for 1 h under argon protection. Processing Text: A commercial pure Mg cast ingot with a diameter of 80 mm was utilized in this work. The initial processing step involved extruding the an as-cast Mg ingot at 523 K with a high extrusion ratio of approximately 17:1 and the extrusion speed is 5∼6 mm / s. Processing Text: A 2 kg ingot (20 × 40 × 300 mm) of the Cr40Co40Ni20 (at.%) alloy was produced with commercially pure elements (>99.7 %) by vacuum induction melting with non-forced cooling using an alumina crucible. The ingot was homogenized at 1100 °C for 2 h, and the thickness was gradually reduced by several hot rolling steps to a final thickness of ∼1.7 mm at around 1100 °C. The plate was cold rolled up to a final thickness of ∼1.0 mm (final cold rolling thickness reduction of ∼40 %). Tensile test specimens were obtained by electrical discharge machining and a schematic of the sample geometry is provided in the supplementary material (Section S1). Samples were recrystallized under four different conditions (1: 800 °C/20 min; 2: 900 °C/30 min; 3: 1000 °C/2 h; 4: 1100 °C/2 h) to obtain four different grain/crystallite sizes, followed by water quenching. The heat treatment conditions were chosen based on the grain growth kinetics of the Cr40Co40Ni20 alloy, studied by Bertoli et al. (2021). Samples with different grain/crystallite sizes were analyzed by in-situ SXRD during tensile testing. SEM-EBSD analysis were performed on the recrystallized and deformed samples, in the grip section and in the gauge length, respectively, after the tensile tests. Samples were carefully prepared according to standard metallographic preparation, up to a final stage of at least 15 h in a vibratory polisher with a 0.04 μm colloidal silica suspension. In-situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction (SXRD) was performed during uniaxial tensile testing at Sector 1-ID at the Advanced Photon Source (APS), Argonne National Laboratory, IL, USA, at room temperature with a constant strain rate of 2 × 10-4 s-1. A monochromated 71.6 KeV high-energy beam was used, with a corresponding wavelength of 0.1731 Å. CeO2 powder was used as a standard for the calibration of the instrument parameters and to determine the sample-to-detector distance, which was calculated to be 2129 mm. Four GE-41RT area detectors were used to capture the 2D raw Debbye-Scherrer rings at different stress/strain levels. Each diffraction pattern was obtained through the summation of 10 individual images with an exposure time of 0.3 s. A dark image was recorded before each test for background subtraction. The 2D Debye-Scherrer rings were converted into conventional 1D intensity vs 2θ diffraction patterns by integrating along the full azimuthal angle (φ range from 0 to 360°) and the 10° transverse direction (TD) (φ range from −5 to 5°) using the General Structure Analysis System (GSASII) software. The HCP phase fraction was quantified by two methods: via EBSD and via SXRD. SEM-EBSD analysis were performed on the recrystallized samples to assess their microstructure, phases and average grain/crystallite size. Processing Text: The single-phase β coarse-grained (CG) specimens of metastable Ti25Nb (at.%) alloy were subjected to solution treatment in the β phase region, followed by aging at 300 °C for 60 min to obtain CG60. The resulting CG specimens were then subjected to low-temperature aging at 300 °C for 60 min, 660 min, and 1440 min, followed by water quenching to obtain CG60, CG660, and CG1440, respectively. The Ti 25Nb (atomic percent, at.%) ingot (length × width × thickness: 200 mm × 55 mm × 6.5 mm) was produced by arc melting pure titanium and niobium metals in an argon atmosphere, with at least three remelting cycles to ensure uniform distribution of elements. The ingot was then cold-rolled at room temperature to produce sheets with a thickness of 0.65 mm, resulting in a 90 % reduction from the original 6.5 mm thickness. The sheets were then cut into dog bone-shaped tensile specimens with dimensions of 10 mm in total length and 3 × 1 × 0.45 mm 3 (the gauge dimensions: length × width × thickness) using an electrical discharge wire cutting machine. To obtain specimens with coarse grains (hereafter referred to as CG), the dog bone-shaped specimens were first placed in a quartz tube furnace and annealed at 825 °C for 30 min, followed by water quenching. Processing Text: A heterogeneous lamella structure was produced in a single-phase Fe55Mn20Cr15Ni10 MEA via two-step rolling and annealing. The received Fe55Mn20Cr15Ni10 MEA was melted at least four times from the starting elements with a purity exceeding 99.9% in a magnetic levitation melting furnace. The ingots underwent homogenization at 1373 K for four hours under vacuum, followed by water quenching. Subsequently, a two-step rolling and heat treatment process was conducted. Initial room-temperature rolling (50% reduction) and annealing at 973 K for 10 min, followed by quenching, were carried out to obtain a refined grain structure. Subsequently, cryorolling was conducted with a reduction of 67%, followed by annealing at 923 K for 10 min and quenching. The samples thus obtained are denoted as T0. The samples annealed at 1023 K for 10 min after cryorolling were also prepared to achieve a coarse-grained (CG) structure for comparison. For cryorolling, the sheets were immersed in liquid nitrogen for 10 min before each pass and rolled immediately to minimize the increase in deformation temperature. The per-pass reduction was maintained below 0.1 mm, and final sheets with a thickness of 0.5 mm were obtained. Following the final annealing, dog-bone-shaped tensile specimens with gauge dimensions of 3 × 22 mm were sliced along the rolling direction and ground with SiC papers up to 2000 grit. Cryo-pre-straining at varying degrees (6, 12, 21, and 36%) introduced hexagonal close-packed (HCP) phase, high-density dislocations, twins, and stacking faults, leveraging the reduced stacking fault energy at cryogenic temperatures. The Shimadzu AGS-X 10 kN universal testing machine was employed for cryo-pre-straining at 77 K and subsequent tensile tests at 293 K. For the T0 samples, tensile experiments at 77 K with a crosshead movement speed of 0.75 mm/min were interrupted at plastic strains of 6, 12, 21, and 36% to obtain the cryo-pre-strained samples with different deformation amounts (denoted as T1, T2, T3, and T4, respectively). During cryo-pre-straining, the samples were fully immersed in liquid nitrogen, and the strains were determined by measuring the changes in the displacement of the Vickers microindents (300 gf) before and after loading. The annealed sample and cryo-pre-strained samples were further subjected to tensile testing at 293 K with a constant strain rate of 1 ×10−3s−1 until fracture, and the strains were measured using a digital video extensometer. Condition: uniform coarse-grained structure

The received Fe55Mn20Cr15Ni10 MEA was melted at least four times from the starting elements with a purity exceeding 99.9% in a magnetic levitation melting furnace. The ingots underwent homogenization at 1373 K for four hours under vacuum, followed by water quenching. Subsequently, a two-step rolling and heat treatment process was conducted. Initial room-temperature rolling (50% reduction) and annealing at 973 K for 10 min, followed by quenching, were carried out to obtain a refined grain structure. Subsequently, cryorolling was conducted with a reduction of 67%, followed by annealing at 923 K for 10 min and quenching. The samples thus obtained are denoted as T0. The samples annealed at 1023 K for 10 min after cryorolling were also prepared to achieve a coarse-grained (CG) structure for comparison. For cryorolling, the sheets were immersed in liquid nitrogen for 10 min before each pass and rolled immediately to minimize the increase in deformation temperature. The per-pass reduction was maintained below 0.1 mm, and final sheets with a thickness of 0.5 mm were obtained. Following the final annealing, dog-bone-shaped tensile specimens with gauge dimensions of 3 × 22 mm were sliced along the rolling direction and ground with SiC papers up to 2000 grit. Cryo-pre-straining at varying degrees (6, 12, 21, and 36%) introduced hexagonal close-packed (HCP) phase, high-density dislocations, twins, and stacking faults, leveraging the reduced stacking fault energy at cryogenic temperatures. The Shimadzu AGS-X 10 kN universal testing machine was employed for cryo-pre-straining at 77 K and subsequent tensile tests at 293 K. For the T0 samples, tensile experiments at 77 K with a crosshead movement speed of 0.75 mm/min were interrupted at plastic strains of 6, 12, 21, and 36% to obtain the cryo-pre-strained samples with different deformation amounts (denoted as T1, T2, T3, and T4, respectively). During cryo-pre-straining, the samples were fully immersed in liquid nitrogen, and the strains were determined by measuring the changes in the displacement of the Vickers microindents (300 gf) before and after loading. The annealed sample and cryo-pre-strained samples were further subjected to tensile testing at 293 K with a constant strain rate of 1 ×10−3s−1 until fracture, and the strains were measured using a digital video extensometer. Processing Text: The equiatomic CoCrFeNi alloy was produced by melting high-purity metal billets in a vacuum induction furnace and by repeated melting of the obtained ingot in a vacuum arc melter, as described in the previous publication [ 9]. The alloy was cold rolled by multiple passes to achieve a total thickness reduction of 80 %, which was slightly less than that achieved in the previous work. Several samples of the as-rolled plate were annealed at 600 °C for 8 min, 15 min, 30 min and 3 h, followed by microstructural investigations and mechanical tests. One additional sample was annealed at 600 °C for 6 h, and its microstructure was examined to analyze the effect of the extended heat treatment on the recrystallization kinetics. For microstructural investigations, the plane containing the rolling direction (RD) and the normal direction (ND) of the samples was polished mechanically and then electrochemically. The HEA samples' microstructure with different deposition strategies were explored by optical and scanning electron microscopy, as well as the electron backscatter diffraction method. Microhardness and tensile tests were used to evaluate the mechanical properties of different samples. CoCrFeNiMo0.2 HEA wire was used for CMT-WAAM. Three deposition strategies (single-pass (SP), oscillation (OS), and multi-parallel pass (MPP)) were adopted to prepare metal walls of different thicknesses. The hardness of the alloy was measured along the building direction (BD) using a Vickers hardness tester (Shimadzu HMV-2T) with a load of 1 kg and a dwell time of 10 s. Processing Text: The metals of Ti, V, Nb, Mo and Cr with purities higher than 99.9 % were used for alloying. The alloys were prepared by arc-melting through more than 6 times under an argon atmosphere. All the alloy ingots (100g in weight) were subsequently homogenized in vacuum at 1200 °C for 24 h, followed by water quenching (WQ). The plate samples were cold-rolled at room temperature with a thickness reduction of 75 % (from 6.0 mm to 1.5 mm). Subsequently, all the rolled plates were heat treated at 900 °C/60min for recrystallization, as well as for solutionizing in case of possible precipitates in the alloys, followed by WQ. After then, the plates were aged, respectively, at 600 °C/8 h, 500 °C/24 h and 400 °C/60 h. Aged at 400 °C for 60 h, the alloys with VEC of 4.30 and 4.35 contained large volume fraction of the large-sized α phase, playing a great role in strengthening. Processing Text: Ni30Co30Cr10Fe10Al18W2 EHEA was additively manufactured using the laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) technique. The pre-alloyed powder of Ni30Co30Cr10Fe10Al18W2EHEA was prepared through vacuum induction gas atomization. The Ni30Co30Cr10Fe10Al18W2EHEA samples were fabricated using a TruPrint 1000 3D printer (TRUMPF, Germany). The printer is equipped with a Nd:YAG fiber laser, which can generate a maximum laser power of 200 W with a spot diameter of 80 μm. High purity argon gas was used as the protective atmosphere during fabrication to maintain minimum oxygen content (below 200 ppm) inside the printing chamber. A 5 × 5 mm2 checkerboard scanning strategy was employed to suppress cracking and reduce stress. An angle of 67° between successive layers was used to control the anisotropy. A polished 316 stainless steel with a diameter of 98 mm was used as the substrate. The volumetric energy density (VED) has been used as a direct parameter to describe the incident laser energy, which can be calculated as E=P/(νsht) where P is the laser power, νs is the scanning speed, h represents the hatch spacing, and t is the layer thickness. By conducting the parameters optimization process, the optimal combination (laser power: 120 W, scanning speed: 1100 mm/s, hatch spacing: 0.07 mm, layer thickness: 0.02 mm, VED: 77.92 J/mm3) was then decided based on the sample having the highest density of 99.73 %. These parameters were then used to build samples with dimensions of 30 × 14 × 5 mm3 for subsequent microstructural characterizations and mechanical tests. After printing, the samples were annealed at temperatures of 750, 800, 900, and 1000 °C for 1 h with a heating rate of 20 °C/min, followed by water quenching. For SEM, specimens were all vibratory-polished to obtain mirror finish of surface and eliminate residual stress from mechanical polishing. For transmission electron microscope (TEM) sample preparation, selected specimens were mechanically polished to a thickness of less than 60 μm and then punched into 3 mm circular discs. The samples were further thinned to approximately 40 nm using ion milling. Tensile tests were performed using a servo-hydraulic 810 MTS testing machine (MTS Corp., USA). The tensile strain was measured using an ARAMIS v6.1 digital image correlation (DIC, GOM Optical Tech., Germany). Uniaxial testing was conducted at a strain rate of 10−3 s−1 at room temperature, with three repeated tests for each condition. Processing state: Heat-treated; Temperature: 750°C for 1 h

Processing Text: The raw materials are sponge titanium, vanadium blocks, molybdenum sheets, chromium particles, sponge zirconium and aluminum particles which the purity are exceeding 99.9 %. 300g ingots were melted in a vacuum non consumable electric arc furnace. In order to ensure uniform composition, the ingots were repeatedly melted three times. After sealing the melted alloy ingot with argon gas and annealing at 1000 °C/6h and water cooling for homogenization treatment, cut it into rectangular original specimens using a wire cutting machine. The sample was subjected to multiple passes of cold rolling (with a reduction rate of less than 10 % per pass), and the thickness reduction of the sample after cold rolling was 20 %, 60 % and 85 %, respectively. The alloy with a 60 % reduction is annealed at 800 °C for 30 min, while the alloy with an 85 % reduction is annealed at 800 °C for 20 min. This is because the time to complete recrystallization decreases with increasing deformation. After testing its organization as recrystallized equiaxed β grains, it was subjected to aging treatment at 550 °C for 5–10 h. After annealing and recrystallization

Processing Text: The designed alloys were prepared using constituent elements of 4 N (99.99 at %) purity. A 100 g batch of each alloy was produced using a laboratory-scale vacuum arc melting unit filled with argon and equipped with a water cooled copper hearth and a non-consumable tungsten electrode. The alloy was melted 6 to 8 times with flipping after each cycle to avoid macro-segregation of elements. The melted samples were subsequently cast into rods (ϕ × l- 3 mm × 80 mm) and slabs ( l× w× t- 80 mm × 10 mm × 6 mm) using a vacuum suction casting unit attached with a water-cooled split copper mould. The cast rods were solutionized at 1175 °C for 20 h and aged at 900 °C for 20 h followed by water quenching. Bulk composition determination and elemental mapping of the cast and solutionized alloys were performed in an electron probe micro analyzer (EMPA, JEOL, JXA-8530F) with both energy and wavelength dispersive detectors (EDS and WDS). The chemical in-homogeneity/segregation of the cast microstructure is removed by solutionizing heat treatment above the solvus temperature. The sub-solvus temperature was determined by thermodynamic calculations using Thermo-Calc. Backscattered SEM micrographs of the peak aged 5Fe alloy (aged at 900 °C for 20 h) show cuboidal shape precipitates distributed uniformly within the matrix. The Fe addition results in the slight change of average γʹ precipitate size (< r> ± σ) of 71 ± 1.1 nm. The Fe addition does not significantly affect the γʹ volume fraction (57 ± 3 (%) for the 5Fe alloy). The lattice misfit across the γ/γʹ interface is measured by performing synchrotron X-ray diffraction analyses on the 5Fe alloy aged at 900 °C for 20 h. The lattice parameter value of γʹ precipitates is measured to be 3.6052 Å for the 5Fe alloy. The lattice misfit values for the 5Fe alloy are measured to be +0.56. Atomic-scale compositional measurements were performed using atom probe tomography (APT, LEAP™ 5000XS, Cameca Instruments), operating in a laser pulsing mode. The laser pulse repetition rate of 250 kHz, a pulse energy of 40 PJ with base temperature of 30 K and 0.5 % detection rate were used for the measurements. The Ga ion milling was performed at 30 kV, with final cleaning at 2 kV and 8 pA current to remove the severely damaged regions. γʹ dissolution temperature of peak aged alloys was determined by heating 50 mg weighted samples in a differential scanning calorimetry (DSC, STA449F3 NETSCH). The sample was heated under an inert argon atmosphere at 10 °C/min till 1250 °C, followed by cooling to 50 °C at a cooling rate of 10 °C/min. Room temperature density measurement was performed using Archimedes principles, as described in ASTM 311-17. Room temperature mechanical property was evaluated by performing a uniaxial tensile test on the flat dog bone-shaped specimen with a gauge dimension of 10 × 1.2 × 1 mm 3in a Gatan micromechanical testing platform at a constant strain rate of 6.7 × 10 -4s -1. For high-temperature mechanical properties, uniaxial compression tests were carried out in a servo-hydraulic driven universal testing system (UTS, DARTEC) at a constant strain rate of 10 -3s -1. Cylindrical samples with dimensions of 3.1 mm in diameter (ϕ) and 5.5 mm in length (L), maintaining an L/ϕ ratio of 1.5-2.0, were used for the compression tests. The samples were heated at a rate of 100 °C/min in a split tube furnace, followed by an isothermal hold at the testing temperature for 10 min to ensure uniform temperature distribution. Processing Text: The Co-Cr-Fe-Ni powders were arranged in equiatomic ratio. A 5.1 g mixture of elemental powders and 1 wt% of stearic acid as a process control agent (PCA) to prevent excessive cold welding during mechanical alloying was mixed in a hardened steel vial. The powder preparation was performed in a glove box, where oxygen and humidity levels were maintained below 0.5 ppm by continuous circulation of high-purity argon gas through a purification system. The mixture was first milled for 30 min. Next, the vials were opened inside the glove box, and 440 C stainless steel balls with a powder-to-ball radio of 1:10 were added. The vials were then sealed in the glove box, and the mechanical alloying process was carried out at room temperature for 20 h using a SPEX 8000 M/D high energy ball miller. To minimize cold welding without the need for additional PCA, the sealed vials were placed in liquid nitrogen for 5 min after every 150 min of mechanical alloying period to reduce their temperature. After mechanical alloying, the vials were placed back inside the glove box, where the as-milled HEA powders were removed and stored until sufficient milling runs were completed to generate enough powder. This was followed by annealing in an argon atmosphere at 500 °C for 1 h to remove the PCA from the as-milled HEA powders. The cold-pressed pellets were then annealed at 700 °C for 1 and 24 h, and at 900 °C for 1, 3, 6, 12, and 24 h in an argon atmosphere, followed by in-furnace cooling. The consolidated and annealed samples were ground using 800, 1200, and 2500 grits, and then polished to achieve a mirror-like surface for subsequent testing and characterization. 3D-printed; No AlTi addition

Processing Text: The CoCrFeNi powder (Yijing New Material Technology Co., Ltd, China) with purity of 99.85 wt% and the AlTi powder (Zhongkeyannuo New Materials Technology Co., Ltd, China) were prepared by gas atomization. The size range of both powders is 13-53 μm. AlTi powders were added into CoCrFeNi powders in a ratio of 2.5, 5 and 7.5 wt% using a custom-made tumbling powder mixer. Each proportion was blended for 8 h to ensure uniform mixing. All powders were stored in the glove box to maintain purity. Before each printing, powders were heated to 80 °C for 2 h, which is aimed to reduce the moisture of the powders. A 50 × 50 mm 2 size 316L stainless steel substrate was used, and all the samples were fabricated in an argon protection atmosphere with a purity level of 99.98 %. The CoCrFeNi(AlTi) xwt%(x = 0, 2.5, 5 and 7.5) HEAs samples were produced using a 3D printer (SLM 125, SLM solution, Germany). The total printing process was divided into two stages. In the first stage, we printed the CoCrFeNi specimens for parameter optimization. Table 2 summarizes six groups of parameters for optimization printing. Each group was designed according to a different VED, which can be calculated by the following equation [ 26]: VED=pv.h.tWhere p, v, hand tare laser power (W), scan velocity (mm/s), hatch spacing (mm), and layer thickness (mm), respectively. Fig. 1(a) shows the 3D printed density blocks, which were tested the density by using Archimedes method [ 27]. Three density blocks were tested for each group to minimize the error of the measured density. For the second part, we used the parameters of group 2 to produce CoCrFeNi(AlTi) xwt%(x = 0, 2.5, 5 and 7.5) HEAs samples, because samples from group 2 showed the highest relative density of 98.3 %, which is shown in Fig. 1(b). Density blocks with a dimension of 5 × 5 × 6 mm 3 and dog-bone-shaped specimens with a dimension of 45 × 10 × 1 mm 3 were cut from the 316L substrate with wire-electrode cutting. All structural and phase characterization samples were sanded with 1500 grits and polished with diamond and magnesium oxide powders. The samples for scanning electron microscope (SEM) were etched for 10 s in aqua regia consisting of hydrochloric acid (75 vol%) and nitric acid (25 vol%). A model microhardness tester (HV-1000, Yanrunguangji Technology Co., Ltd, China) was used to measure the Vickers hardness with a testing load of 200 gf and loading for 10 s. Each sample was tested for three points to obtain the average microhardness values on the surface. A universal tensile tester (UTM5105, Keshen Electron Co., Ltd, China) was used to perform tensile tests at room temperature. The tensile rate is 10 −3s −1, the width of the specimen is 2 mm, the thickness is 1 mm, and the extensometer with a 10 mm gauge is used. 3D-printed; AlTi addition (x = 7.5)

Processing Text: Samples, with a thickness of 10 mm, were obtained by cutting from the ingots along the rolling direction (RD). These samples were solution-treated at 1050 °C for 1 h followed by water quenching. Subsequently, cold rolling was performed on a laboratory rolling mill to achieve a total thickness reduction of 90 % ± 0.5 %. Next, the cold-rolled samples were annealed at temperatures ranging from 850 °C to 1000 °C (in 50 °C intervals) for 2 min followed by water quenching to obtain samples with non-uniform multi-scale grain structure, hereafter referred to as short-term annealed (SA-temperature) samples. For comparison, the cold-rolled samples were annealed at 1000 °C for 30 min to prepare samples with uniformly sized grains, hereafter referred to as long-term annealed (LA-1000 °C) sample. Electron Backscatter Diffraction (EBSD) samples were prepared by mechanical grinding, polishing, and subsequent electrochemical polishing. The samples intended for EBSD analysis were electro-polished for 40 s in a solution consisting of 10 % perchloric acid and 90 % ethanol at a current of 1 A. Samples of 1 × 1 cm were obtained using an electrical discharge machining (EDM) apparatus, with the back of each sample welded with a lead wire and embedded properly. Processing Text: The steel was heat treated and isothermally held at 300 °C for 2 h above Ms temperature to obtain bainitic microstructure. The heat-treated steel was subsequently subjected to cold-rolling and cryo-rolling (10 % reduction in thickness). The steel used in the present study was melted and cast as a block of size 5 × 7 × 4.5 cm 3. The as-cast material underwent a 60 % rolling reduction through hot rolling and was then homogenized at 1100 °C for 2 h. Following homogenization, the steel was furnace-cooled to room temperature to eliminate segregation of alloying elements and achieve a uniform microstructure. Plates of 1.8 mm thickness were used for heat treatment and further cold-rolled and cryo-rolled by dipping in liquid nitrogen for 5 min after each pass in a two-high laboratory rolling mill. A 10 % reduction was carried out in multiple passes. The condition for treatment 1 corresponded to heating the steel to an austenization temperature of 1000 °C, holding it there for 5 min, quenching and isothermally holding at 300 °C for 2 h, and air cooling it to room temperature. Treatment 2 corresponds to room temperature cold rolling after treatment 1 while treatment 3 corresponded to cryo-rolling following treatment 1. Processing Text: The present study utilized gas atomized pre-alloyed HX powder as the feedstock for the LPBF process. A BLT-S320 LPBF system (Xi'an Bright Laser Technologies Co., Ltd., Xian, China) was employed, with optimized process parameters to produce nearly fully dense samples: laser power of 300 W, scanning speed of 1000 mm/s, hatch distance of 0.09 mm, and layer thickness of 0.06 mm. A strip scanning strategy with a rotation angle of 67° was employed to perform sequential layer-by-layer fabrication, as illustrated in Fig. 1a. Tensile cylindrical bars with dimensions of Φ14 × 80 mm were built in both horizontal and vertical orientations. Following the LPBF procedure, the tensile sample bars underwent full heat treatments, consisting of HIP followed by ST. The HIP was conducted at 1180 °C and 150 MPa for 3 h with furnace cooling. Then, the ST was conducted at 1180 °C for 1 h with argon quenching. Both HIP and ST were performed under a vacuum of less than 1 × 10 −2Pa. To investigate the effect of temperature on deformation behavior, a series of tensile tests were performed on dog-bone shaped specimens ( Fig. 1c) machined from fully heat-treated (HIP + ST) tensile bars. These tests were performed at temperatures ranging from −50 °C to elevated temperatures. The tensile tests were conducted at a rate of 0.5 mm/min to ascertain the yield strength and 2.5 mm/min to fracture, using a universal testing machine. Specimens were cooled or heated to the test temperature and soaked for 15 min prior to the application of tension. The initial stage of tensile tests (first 0.2 % strain) was measured using an extensometer to ensure precise yield strength (YS) calculations. The tensile tests were repeated three times to quantify the standard error for each type of samples. The specimen used to examine the initial microstructure was obtained from the extremity portion of the tensile bar before testing. The specimen for deformation microstructure analysis was extracted from the gauge section of the tensile specimen, specifically near the fracture region. Temperature: -50 °C; Condition: fully heat-treated (initial hot isostatic pressing followed by solution treatment)
Processing Word: Temperature: -50 °C; Condition: fully heat-treated (initial hot isostatic pressing followed by solution treatment)

Processing Text: MD simulations were performed by Large-scale Atomic/Molecular Massively Parallel Simulator (LAMMPS) software package [32]. In order to study the influence of grain orientation on the plastic deformation behavior of W under Berkovich tip, simulation boxes with 〈001〉, 〈011〉, and 〈111〉 crystal orientations along z→direction (or indented direction) were created. For each simulation box, the lowest bottom layer with a thickness of 1 nm was fixed to stabilize the box, a thermostatic layer with thickness of 2 nm above the fixed layer was set to keep a constant temperature during simulation, and the rest region above thermostatic layer was a Newton layer, as shown in Fig. 1(a). The interactions between W-W atoms were described with the embedded atom method (EAM) potential formulated by Zhou et al. [33]. Before indentation simulation, periodic boundary conditions were set in x→, y→, and z→directions, and the W substrate was relaxed for 50 ps under the NPT ensemble to reach a thermodynamically stable state at 300 K. The thermostatic layer and Newton layer were controlled by a velocity-scaling thermostat and the microcanonical ensemble (NVE), respectively. The simulation temperature and time step were set to 300 K and 1 fs, respectively. The indenter moved along - z→direction with a speed of 20 m/s until the indentation depth reached 2.5 nm. Then, the indenter was held at 2.5 nm for 20 ps and unloaded to 0 nm. Crystal direction: within 10 degrees of 〈100〉 pole

Processing Text: Samples were subjected to a two-step partitioning heat treatment, comprising intercritical annealing (IA) followed by low-temperature partitioning (LTP). Pre-quenched samples were heated to 745 °C or 765 °C for an IA holding time of 40 min and then oil quenched, named as IA 745 or IA 765, respectively. IA 745 or IA 765 samples were reheated to 380 °C, held at this temperature for 30 min for LTP and then oil quenched. Thus, the samples subjected to 745 °C or 765 °C IA process followed by 380 °C LTP treatment are named as IA 745+LTP or IA 765+LTP. Choosing 745 °C and 765 °C as the IA temperature is based on the thermodynamic calculations in Fig. S1(c), which indicates that a sufficient amount of RA can be obtained at room temperature. The temperature for LTP, 380 °C, was selected to sufficiently partition C atoms while avoiding the precipitation of cementite (Fig. S1a). Before conducting the two-step partitioning heat treatment, all specimens were subjected to a pre-quenching treatment, i.e. austenitizing at 950 °C for 20 min and then oil quenched, to obtain a structure of full martensite. The steel was melt using a 25 kg vacuum induction furnace. After casting, the ingot was homogenized at 1200 °C for 12 h and hot-forged to square bars with a cross-sectional size of 40 mm × 40 mm. Sample: IA 745; Processing: Intercritical annealing (IA)

Finally, all steels were solution treated at 1323 K for 1 h, followed by water quenching. For convenience, X2Mn30, X1MnN30-0.3 and X2MnN30-0.6 steels in the solution treated state were defined as 0 N, 0.3 N and 0.6 N, respectively. Plate-type tensile specimens were cut from bars with the central axis parallel to the rolling direction (RD), and the gauge dimension was 15 × 3 × 3 mm3 according to the standard GBT 228.1-2010. Deformed 0.3 N and 0.6 N steels with the true strains of 0.25, 0.40 and 0.55 were obtained by interrupting the stretching at a strain rate of 10-3s-1. The sample surfaces were mechanically polished and then electrochemically polished in an electrolyte of 10 % perchloric acid and 90 % alcohol at 253 K and 39 V. Processing Text: In this study, hierarchical heterostructures were introduced into CoCrFeMnNi HEA via an in-situ rolling (ISR) assisted laser cladding (LC) process. The coating was fabricated by overlapping individual tracks with a 30 % overlapping ratio. Following the preliminary testing, the distance D between the laser head and the roller was set to 13 mm. In this work, static pressures of 0 N, 1000 N, 2000 N, 3000 N, and 4000 N were applied, and the corresponding coatings were referred as un-ISR, ISR1, ISR2, ISR3 and ISR4, respectively. Annealed 45 steel with dimensions of 100 mm × 100 mm × 10 mm was chosen as the substrate. To minimize the interference of oxides and other impurities, an angle grinder was used to remove the oxide layer from the substrate surface, followed by cleaning with anhydrous ethanol. The powder used in this study was CoCrFeMnNi HEA powder with a particle size range of 45-105 μm, produced by high-temperature gas atomization. Before the experiment, place the powder in a vacuum drying oven (Shanghai Jiecheng Experimental Instrument Co., Ltd., DZF-6050) and dry it at 100 °C for 2 h to ensure its uniformity and fluidity. The coating was prepared by using a semiconductor laser (HWL-1500) with a wavelength range of 910-1050 nm and a DPSF scraper powder feeder to transport CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy powder coaxially. Laser spot diameter 2 mm, laser power 1500 W, scanning rate 3 mm/s, powder feed 7 g/min, overlapping ratio 30 %. High purity argon is used as melt pool shielding gas with a flow rate of 3 L / min. The prepared coating was cut into cuboid specimens with dimensions of 15 × 15 × 10 mm 3using a high-speed wire electrical discharge machining machine tool (Fangzheng CNC Machine Tool Co., Ltd., DK7720). The specimens were then hot - mounted using a metallographic specimen mounting machine (Laizhou Hengyi Test Instrument Co., Ltd., XQ-2B). Subsequently, the cross - section of the specimen was ground using SiC sandpapers of grit sizes 60 mesh, 400 mesh, 800 mesh, 1500 mesh, and 2000 mesh in a wet - grinding manner on a metallographic specimen grinding and polishing machine (Laizhou Hengyi Test Instrument Co., Ltd., MP-2B). After grinding, the specimens were polished with diamond polishing paste until no obvious scratches were visible under an optical microscope. The specimens were placed in anhydrous ethanol and cleaned in an ultrasonic cleaner for 5 min. To prepare the surfaces for electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) analysis, the specimen was pre-ground and polished using the metallographic pre-grinding machine (Hua Xing Test Instrument Co., Ltd.). The surface was then ion-polished with a precision ion thinning instrument (GATAN PIPS II 695) to remove the damage layer caused by mechanical polishing. The microhardness was measured using a Vickers hardness tester (Laizhou Hengyi Test Instrument Co., Ltd., NVM-1000 A). The load was set at 0.3 kg, and the dwell time was 15 s. Each value was measured three times to ensure accuracy. The tribological properties of the coatings at room temperature (25 °C) were evaluated by a ball-on-disk wear tester (Lanzhou Zhongke Kaihua Science and Technology Development Co., Ltd., HT-1000) with a Si 3N 4ball as the counterpart. The tests, performed under dry sliding conditions in accordance with the ASTM G99-17 standard, were repeated three times. The test parameters included a loading force of 10 N, a friction radius of 3 mm, a rotation speed of 600 r/min, and a wear time of 30 min. Processing Text: The Al0.2CrNbTiV high-entropy alloy was prepared by vacuum arc melting. The raw materials of Al, Cr, Nb, Ti and V elemental metal blocks with a purity in excess of 99.9 wt% was placed in a water-cooled copper crucible, evacuate to a vacuum degree of less than 2 × 10−3Pa, then melt in a high-purity argon atmosphere to avoid oxidation. The ingots were repeatedly melted and turned over at least 5 times to eliminate segregation and ensure the uniform distribution of different elements. The alloy ingot size obtained is about 56 mm in diameter and 20 mm in height. The annealing temperature was determined based on the thermal analysis results. During the annealing experiments, the Al0.2 alloy specimens were placed in a crucible and sealed in a vacuum quartz tube, heated to the corresponding annealing temperature at a heating rate of 5 °C/min, held for 12 h then cooled slowly with the furnace. The annealing temperatures of 650 °C, 850 °C and 1050 °C were determined in this paper to further analyze the changes in the structure and properties of Al0.2 alloy after annealing at different temperatures. Room temperature (25 °C) compression experiments were carried out using an MTS EM-type material testing machine with 6 × 4 × 4 mm3 rectangular specimens of the alloy, with an initial strain rate of 10−3s−1, and loaded to a strain of 50 %. The annealed specimens were ground and polished to a mirror surface using the mechanical polishing method, ultrasonically cleaned in ethanol for 30 min and dried. The hardness of the annealed alloy was measured using a micro-Vickers hardness tester with an experimental load of 200 g and a loading time of 15 s, each specimen was measured at least eight times to take the average value. The annealed alloy was subjected to reciprocal dry friction test at room temperature (25 °C) using UMT-TRIBOLAB multifunctional material surface mechanical property tester to analyze the friction and wear properties of the annealed alloy. Experimental normal load of 10 N, stroke of 5 mm, frequency of 2 Hz, time of 20 min, for Si3N4 ceramic balls of φ6 mm, each sample was repeated 3 times to calculate the average friction coefficient; meanwhile, the profile shape and volume loss of the worn samples were scanned using a matching 3D profiler. Processing Text: The RHEAs for experimental verification were fabricated using the vacuum arc melting from pure elements (purity greater than 99.98 wt%). To prevent oxidation of the ingot, the furnace chamber underwent 5 cycles of evacuation and backfilling with high purity Argon prior to melting. In addition, a Ti-getter was used to remove any remaining oxygen before remelting the ingots. To ensure homogeneity, the ingots were flipped and remelted for 6 times on the water-cooled copper hearth. The ingots were kept in liquid state for 2 min at the last melting round. After solidification and cool-down, cylindrical samples with a diameter of 3 mm and a length of 6 mm for compression test were obtained from the ingots using wire electrical discharge machining (EDM) as compression test samples. Samples were compressed at a deformation rate of 0.001 mm/s until either the maximum displacement of 3 mm was reached or the sample fractured. The end surfaces of compression testing samples were ground carefully with sandpaper up to a grit size of 2000 to minimize the friction between the punch and the samples. Processing Text: Ingots of the nominal composition Fe3.75Cr1.25NiAl0.6-xTix (x = 0, 0.15, 0.30 and 0.40, molar ratio) with a weight of 100 g were prepared by arc-melting raw elemental metals (with purities ≥99.9 wt %) under Ti-gettered argon atmosphere. Each alloy was melted four times to ensure chemical homogeneity in an arc melter (Hotstar). The as-cast alloy plates with dimensions of 10 mm × 5 mm × 80 mm were prepared by copper mold pour casting (Edmund Bühler). The samples cut from the as-cast alloy plates were characterized by means of X-ray diffraction (XRD, Philips PW 1050, Cu-Kα) at a scanning speed of 10°/min, scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Zeiss Supra 55), transmission electron microscopy (TEM, Talos F200) attached with energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS). The etching solution used for sample preparation for SEM observations contains 6 % HClO4+ 35 % CH3(CH2)3OH + 59 % CH3OH (volume fraction). TEM samples with a diameter of 3 mm were mechanically ground to a thickness of about 50 μm, thinned by twin-jet electro-polishing in a solution of 10 % HClO4+ 90 % C2H5OH (volume fraction) at a cryogenic temperature of 243 K, and then further ion-milled in a Gatan 691 device. Statistical analysis on the volume fraction of each phase and particle size of precipitates were performed with at least 3 SEM micrographs, using the Image J 1.52V software. Tensile tests were conducted on a universal testing machine (Instron 5582) at a nominal strain rate of 2 × 10−4s−1 at room temperature. The tensile samples were in dog-bone plate shape with a gauge dimension of 14 mm × 2 mm × 0.8 mm. An extensometer was used to measure directly the tensile strain, and at least three specimens of each alloy were tested. Processing Text: A novel NiAlCrFeMo high entropy superalloy was prepared using the vacuum arc melting method, followed by annealing at 800 °C, 1000 °C, and 1200 °C for 10 h. The NiAlCrFeMo high-entropy alloy ingot was prepared by melting bulk Ni, Al, Cr, Fe, and Mo metals of no less than 99.9 % purity using a non-consumable vacuum arc furnace. To ensure the homogeneity of the chemical composition, the alloy ingot was remelted at least four times on both sides before being suction-cast into a water-cooled copper mold. Prior to annealing heat treatment, the cast ingot was sectioned into cylindrical rods with a diameter of 10 mm and a length of 110 mm, as well as other cylindrical and thin sheet specimens, using a DK7735 electrical discharge wire cutting machine. The former was used for high-temperature tensile testing, while the latter were prepared for electron microscopy and XRD analysis. Various samples were first subjected to heat treatment at different temperatures. The annealing temperatures were set at 800 °C, 1000 °C, and 1200 °C, using an SGL-1700C heat treatment furnace, with a heating rate of 10 °C/min. Upon reaching the target temperature, the samples were held for 10 h, followed by water quenching to preserve the high-temperature microstructure. High-temperature tensile tests were conducted on the tensile specimens using a Gleeble-3800 thermal simulation machine, with a strain rate of 0.001 s⁻ 1 and a deformation temperature of 1000 °C. The heating rate was set at 10 K/s, and the specimens were held at the target deformation temperature for 4 min to ensure uniform heating before water quenching to maintain the high-temperature microstructure. During the tensile tests, the stress-strain curves were corrected for adiabatic heating effects to eliminate thermal influences on the results. A NiCr-NiSi thermocouple was welded to the center of each specimen using a spot welder to monitor the temperature in real-time during deformation. The true strain values were calculated based on the specimen's geometry and temperature variations. SEM samples were embedded in phenolic resin, polished to 2.5 μm by PRESI automatic polishing machine, etched in 30 ml HCL +30 ml HNO 3+ 1g CuSO4·5H 2O solution, and placed under Zeiss Sigma 500 SEM equipped with EDS for microstructure and chemical composition observation. The polished surface was subjected to microhardness testing for 15s under a load of 500g using an MHVD−1000IS Vickers microhardness tester. At least 50 measurements were taken for each sample to obtain an average value. The microstructure was further characterized using a JEM-F200 Japanese JEOL field emission transmission electron microscope (TEM). TEM samples were mainly mechanically polished to 30 μm and then ion thinned using a precision ion thinning instrument (Gatan 691).
