Some of them were mixed in an agate jar by the ball milling machine (PM4L, DROIDE, Shanghai, China) at a speed of 150 rpm for 30 min. Specimens measuring 10×10×10 mm 3 were produced (detailed manufacturing information is in supplementary materials Fig. S1 and Table S3). The relative density (RD) of samples with good formability was measured using the Archimedes method using a density meter (ZMD-2, FANGRUI, Shanghai, China). Samples with the highest density among these samples manufactured by different parameters were selected to do the X-ray diffraction (XRD) analyses. XRD analyses were determined on the X-Y plane using an X-ray diffractometer (D8 Advance, Bruker, Karlsruhe, Germany) with Cu Kα radiation at a scanning rate of 10° min −1, and a 2θ angle ranging from 20° to 120°. Processing Text: The (Ni2CrCo)94Nb3V3 high-entropy alloy variable-width thin-walled structures were fabricated by directed energy deposition. The raw materials used in the work are CrCoNi, Ni, Nb, V powders, and their sizes range between 45-105 μm. The mixed powder was obtained by ball milling for 30 min at speed 200 rpm, and the ball to powders ratio is 2:1. The manufacturing process of the variable-width thin-walled structure sample was carried out on a five-axis additive and subtractive hybrid CNC machine tool (SVW80C-3D), and the process parameters are as follows: laser power 900 W, scanning speed 7.0 mm/s, Z-axis lift 0.35 mm, laser spot diameter 3 mm. Printed samples were annealed at 1403 K for 1 h and directly aged at 923 K for 110 h, and then water quenched to room temperature. Printed, annealed, and directly aged samples are named DED, AN, and DA, respectively. Sample: DED(Narrow); State: Printed

Processing Text: Mo compacts with different microstructures were prepared via SPS of the prepared Mo composite powders. In detail, 45 g of the prepared powders were sealed into the graphite mold with an inner diameter of 30 mm. The powder was then heated to 1100 and 1200 °C with a heating rate of 100 °C min-1, and held for 10 min at a pressure of 40 MPa. Then, bulk samples with a diameter of 30 mm and a height of approximately 6 mm were obtained. The phase compositions of prepared Mo nanocomposite powders were measured by an X-ray diffraction system (XRD, Rigaku D/max-2500). The oxygen contents of powders and sintered bulks were measured by an oxygen and nitrogen analyzer. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM, JEOL JSM-7500F) and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, Oxford Nordlys Max 3) were employed to characterize the microstructure of powders and sintered Mo composites, and the intragranular/intergranular Al2O3 nanoparticles were characterized by transmission electron microscope (TEM, FEI Tecnai G2 F20). The apparent density of samples was calculated by the Archimedes method. Quasi-static compressive tests were conducted by an electronic universal testing machine (UTM5105X) at room temperature with a constant loading rate of 0.1 mm min-1, using cylindrical specimens with a diameter of 4 mm and a length of 6 mm. Three-point bending strength was tested with a span length of 15 mm on 1.5 mm × 2 mm × 25 mm specimens. Vickers hardness test was performed on a polished surface, and holding pressure for 20 s under a load of 1 kg. The wear resistance was evaluated by the dry sliding wear tribometer using a rotation speed of 200 mm min-1 for 30 min, with a friction stroke length of 5 mm and a load of 10 N. Condition: Room Temperature; Sintering temperature: 1100°C; Strain to fracture: 6.3%
Processing Word: Condition: Room Temperature; Sintering temperature: 1100°C; Strain to fracture: 6.3%

Processing Text: Mg-1Zn-0.2Ca-1.0MgO (wt.%) was prepared by pure Mg (99.99 wt.%), pure Zn (99.99 wt.%), Mg-25Ca (wt.%) master alloy and MgO NPs (mean particle size ∼50 nm). Raw materials were added into a box-type furnace with a mixed N2 and SF6 protection atmosphere. The pre-heated MgO NPs were then added when the melt temperature reached 780°C. A shear stirring equipment and an ultrasonic device were then used to disperse MgO NPs for 15 min. Finally, the melt was poured into a steel mold at 720°C. The ingot was firstly solution-treated at 420°C for 16 h and then was extruded using an extrusion ration of 56 and a ram speed of 0.2 mm/s at 270°C. Heat treatment was applied to the extruded samples at 200°C, 275°C, 350°C for 30 min. An ultra-fine grained (UFG) Mg-1Zn-0.2Ca-1.0MgO composite with an average grain size of 0.49 µm as well as an excellent combination of yield strength (379 MPa) and ductility (10.1%) was produced by one-step extrusion. Subsequent heat treatment at 200 ℃ for 30 min further improved its yield strength to 420 MPa and elongation to 12.1% with a slight grain growth to 0.76 µm. Processing state: one-step extrusion; Microstructure: ultra-fine grained (UFG) with an average grain size of 0.49 µm
Processing Word: Processing state: one-step extrusion; Microstructure: ultra-fine grained (UFG) with an average grain size of 0.49 µm

Processing Text: Steels 'NM79′ and 'NM610′ were labeled to indicate the Mn content of 9 and 10 wt% while keeping (Ni + Mn) fixed at 16 wt%. The steel ingots were homogenized at 1250 °C for 2 h and subsequently rolled into plates with a thickness of 14 mm at 1100 to 900 °C. The hot-rolled plates were annealed at 1150 °C for 30 min, and water-quenched. The steel specimens were electro-polished in a solution of (90% CH 3COOH + 10% HClO 4) or mechanically-polished using 1 μm diamond suspension combined with colloidal silica. Tensile tests were performed on plate-type-bar specimens (gage length: 25 mm, width: 6 mm, thickness: 1 mm, longitudinal orientation) of H-uncharged steels at room temperature with a cross-head speed of 10 mm min −1 (strain rate: 6.67 × 10 −3s −1) using a universal testing machine (5982, Instron, USA) with a capacity of 100 kN. Optical extensometer (One-78pt-200, Epsilon, USA) was used to measure the tensile strain during the test. A long-term high-pressure H-charging method was implemented on Charpy specimens at 10 MPa and 300 °C for 33 days, ensuring uniform equilibrium H concentration throughout the entire specimen. Immediately after H-charging, Charpy impact tests were carried out on the Charpy specimens in the temperature range of 25 to −196 °C using a pendulum impact tester (PSW750, Zwick Roell, Germany). Thermal desorption analysis (TDA) was performed on four steels using thermal desorption mass spectra (Bruker, G4 Phoenix, Germany). Processing state: as-annealed
Processing Word: Processing state: as-annealed

Processing Text: A near-dense LPBF CoCrFeNi HEA was manufactured by fine-tuning the parameters. The LPBF was conducted via the HY-M300 LPBF system (Huayang New Material Technology Co., Ltd.). The LPBF machine is mainly composed of a Yb-fiber laser (wavelength 1060-1100 nm; maximum output power 500 W; spot diameter 80 μm), a laser galvanometric scanning system with an available maximum scanning velocity of 7000 mm/s, an automatic powder delivery system, a building platform with an effective forming space of 300 × 300 × 450 mm 3. The 304 stainless steel plate was chosen as the building substrate upon LPBF with a preheating temperature of 373 K. To avoid excessive oxidation, the LPBF experiment was performed in a protective atmosphere (Ar) with an oxygen concentration below 100 ppm. Various printing parameters were investigated in the LPBF experiment. In this experiment, the samples were fabricated with varied laser power ( P: 220-420 W) and scanning speed ( v: 450-1350 mm/s) at a constant hatch spacing ( h: 90 μm) and layer thickness ( t: 50 μm) to investigate the effect of processing parameters on the microstructure and mechanical properties of the as-printed HEA specimens. The scanning strategy was chosen as the strip scanning strategy, keeping the interlayer rotation angle of 67°. The samples with two geometries were prepared by LPBF: cuboid samples with a dimension of 9 × 9 × 5.5 mm 3for microstructural analysis and cuboid samples with a dimension of 50 × 15 × 2.5 mm 3for mechanical test. Dog-bone-shaped tensile specimens with a gauge length of 12 mm were prepared via electro-discharge machining. For microstructural observation, the samples were first mechanically grounded by SiC sandpapers from 400 grit to 2000 grit, followed by electropolishing using 20 % nitric acid and 80 % ethanol at 20 V. The tensile test was performed on the HUALONG 50KN universal testing machine at a strain rate of 0.001 s −1at room temperature. The surface of the tensile specimens was grounded by 2500 grit SiC sandpapers before the tensile test. Condition: as-printed; Processing method: LPBF; Associated with superior mechanical properties including over 50% ductility
Processing Word: Condition: as-printed; Processing method: LPBF; Associated with superior mechanical properties including over 50% ductility

Processing Text: Molybdenum-rhenium alloys has a low recrystallization temperature and insufficient high temperature strength, making it unable to serve as structural parts for a long time in high temperature environments above 1300 ℃ for a long time. The Mo-5 wt% Re and Mo-5 wt% Re-1 wt% ZrO 2alloys were prepared by liquid-liquid doping method (Abbreviations are Mo-Re and Mo-Re-ZrO 2). (NH 4) 2Mo 4O 13(99.99 % purity, CMOC Group Limited), Zr(NO 3) 4·5 H 2O (99.99 % purity, MACKLIN), CO(NH 2) 2(99.99 % purity, MACKLIN), and Re powder (99.99 % purity, MACKLIN) as raw materials, the precursor powder of ZrO 2was prepared by hydrothermal method at 180 ℃ for 16 h. (NH 4) 2Mo 4O 13was then dissolved in distilled water. The Re powder was dispersed by a cell crusher for 30 min, and the obtained suspension was mixed and stirred with (NH 4) 2Mo 4O 13. The hydrothermal preparation of ZrO 2precursor powder mixing with the above solution, after ultrasonic oscillation and mechanical mixing, drying in vacuum drying furnace. After drying at 100 ℃ × 48 h, the mixed precursor powder was obtained, calcined at low temperature, and reduced at high temperature with two stages of hydrogen. Then, the composite powder was sieved and put into a rubber leather sleeve with an inner diameter of 30 mm, and compressed at a pressure of 200 MPa through a cold isostatic press for 20 min. The pressed blank was kept warm for 72 h in a medium frequency sintering furnace at 1900 ℃. The Mo-Re alloy rods obtained by sintering was cut into cylindrical compression samples of 6 × 9 mm along the direction parallel to the axial direction, and the samples were subsequently polished. The room temperature compression experiment used a SHI MADZU AG-I250 kN precision universal testing machine with a diameter of 6 mm and a length of 9 mm, and a strain rate of 1 s −1. The high temperature compression tests were carried out on a Gleeble 1500D thermal simulation tester. The specimens were subjected to heating to the deformation temperature and then tested at a heating rate of 20 ℃/s and a holding time of 5 min. The hot compression test temperatures were 1100 ℃, 1200 ℃, 1300 ℃, and 1400 ℃, with a strain rate of 1 s −1. Condition: room temperature compressive yield strength

The process parameters used for the deposition are - laser power: 800 W, scan speed: 0.3 m/min, spot overlap: 50 % and laser beam diameter: 2 mm. The 67⁰ interlayer scan rotations are deployed for the bulk deposition. The sample sectioning for metallographic characterization and mechanical testing is done using a wire cut - EDM (make & model: Concord, DK-7732). Microhardness testing is performed at a load of 200 g and a dwell time of 10 s using the Economet VH-1MDX Vickers hardness tester. The Shimadzu AGX-V universal testing machine is deployed to evaluate the tensile properties. Processing state: LDED-built Co40 alloy; Context: Higher yield strength compared to equiatomic Co33 alloy without much compromising its ductility

Processing Text: The powder feedstock for L-PBF was supplied by the Volgograd-Russia Aluminum Plant (UC RUSAL) with the following particle size distribution: d 10= 17.3 μm, d 50= 26.7 μm, and d 90= 40.75 μm using the molten metal spraying method. Cylindrical bars having a diameter of 20 mm and a length of 100 mm were manufactured with the building direction (BD) parallel to the bar's length under a controlled Ar atmosphere. A commercial SLM280HL printer (Selective Laser Melting Solutions Group AG, Lübeck, Germany), was used to make samples, operating with the following parameters: a scan speed of 1650 mm/s, a power of 370 W, a hatch spacing of 130 µm, layer thickness of 50 µm and a scanning rotation of 67° between consecutive layers. These parameters yielded a laser energy density of 1.72 J/mm 2, leading to a porosity fraction lower than 0.18 %. Annealing in the temperature range of 20 °C to 500 °C for one hour led to evolutions in the as-built L-PBF cellular structure, including partial fragmentation of the cell boundaries between 20 °C and 300 °C; the breakdown and transformation into ultrafine Si-enriched particles in the range of 300 °C to 400 °C; and subsequently coarsening at temperatures exceeding 400 °C. Uniaxial tensile tests were conducted at room temperature at an initial strain rate of 1 × 10 −3s −1using miniature bone-shaped samples (4 mm in length, 1.3 mm in width, 2 mm in thickness and 1 mm radius (R)) oriented parallel to the BD. The samples for the mechanical testing were fabricated from the as-built bars using electrode discharge machining, which resulted in uniformly smooth surfaces. Vickers microhardness using a square-based pyramidal diamond indenter were carried out for the as-built and annealed samples. A constant load of 1.8 N and a dwell time of 15 s were used. In situ high-energy synchrotron X-ray diffraction (HEXRD) analysis was carried out during isothermal annealing heat treatments at 400 °C and 500 °C with a holding time of one hour each using cylindrical samples of 5 mm diameter and 8 mm length. To mitigate the impact of sample size on strain calculation, the so-called digital image correlation (DIC) method was used. The DIC system was implemented on a universal tensile machine employing a 12-megapixel digital camera operating at 32 frames per second with an acquisition time of 2 s and a pixel size of 0.04 mm. The acquired data was subsequently processed in Matlab, utilizing the open source software Ncorr. To ensure more reliable results, all tensile samples were tested in the weakest direction, i.e., the tensile loading direction parallel to the BD. In order to establish a correlation between synchrotron measurements and the microstructure and mechanical properties at various temperatures, a series of samples from the as-built material were subjected to annealing treatments with a holding time of one hour at temperatures of 200 °C, 300 °C, 400 °C, and 500 °C. Subsequently, these samples were evaluated using EBSD, hardness, and tensile testing. Condition: after annealing at 400 °C

Processing Text: The 35Co-34Ni-24Cr-7Mo alloy, with the chemical composition presented in Table 1, was prepared as described previously [45]. The solution-treated plate was cold rolled to the thickness of 1.5 mm (88 % reduction in thickness) and annealed at 950 °C for 750 s in an electrical furnace with an ambient atmosphere. Based on the ASTM E8M standard, sub-size dimensions (gage length: 25 mm, width: 6 mm, thickness: 1.5 mm), were used for the tensile test samples, which were prepared along the rolling direction by a wire-cutting process followed by polishing to achieve a smooth surface. The tensile tests were performed with a computer-controlled GOTECH AI 7000-10 tones tensile tester machine at a constant speed of 3 mm/min. To provide different deformation temperatures, samples were pre-cooled for 5 min in liquid nitrogen (∼ 77 K), dry ice + ethanol (∼ 195 K), and an ambient (∼ 295 K) environment, and then tensile tests were performed in a chamber with the mentioned environments to keep the temperature stable during deformation. To observe the microstructure before and after deformation, the center of the gage in the tensile test sample (RD-ND plane) was electro-polished and, consequently, electro-etched by the electrolyte of 35 vol% H 2SO 4in methanol with the voltage of 6 V. The samples were mechanically polished up to 1200 grit SiC papers and subsequently electropolished with a 92 % HCl + 8 % CH 3COOH solution. For this purpose, samples with a diameter of 3 mm and a thickness of 60 μm were prepared using a jet polish technique with HNO 3acid. Condition: Room Temperature (295 K)

Processing Text: A Ti-4Al-6V-5Mo-3Cr-1Zr (wt%) cylindrical rod with a diameter of ∼150 mm was used in this work. The as-received alloy has a bi-modal microstructure and its β-transus temperature was determined to be 830 ± 5 °C through metallographic examination. A sub-transus solution treatment was performed at 820 °C for 30 min and the sample in this condition will be referred to as “ST820”. Afterwards, ST820 was subjected to a dual-step aging treatment where the first-step aging was conducted at 300 °C for 5 h, 10 h or 100 h, and the second-step aging at 520 °C or 600 °C for 2 h. Hereafter, the Ti-46531 alloy in these dual-aged conditions will be referred to as “300°C/Xh+520°C” or “300°C/Xh+600°C” (X = 5, 10, 100). In addition, single-step aging was also conducted at 300 °C for 5 h, 10 h or 100 h, respectively. These specimens will be denoted as “300°C/ Xh ( X= 5, 10, 100)”. To clarify the nucleation mechanism of the α-phase, further short-term aging experiments were performed or 5 min at 520 °C or 600 °C on the 300°C/100 h sample, and these two specimens will be accordingly referred to as “300°C/100h+520°C/5min” and “300°C/100h+600°C/5min”. Each sample was wrapped in pure titanium foil and encapsulated in an evacuated quartz tube (vacuum level ∼ 5 × 10 −3Pa) to minimize the oxidation during the heat treatment. All samples were water quenched by breaking the quartz tubes immediately after the heat treatment. Aged at 600 °C; Dual-aged sample
Processing Word: Aged at 600 °C; Dual-aged sample

Processing Text: The RHEAs with nominal composition Ti50Nb(20-x)V20Al10Six (x=0, 0.5, 1, 1.5 at%) were fabricated by vacuum melting furnace using 99.95 % (wt%) purity raw materials under a Ti-gettered argon atmosphere. The Nb-V (melting current ∼500 A, melting time ∼90 s) and Ti-Al-Si (melting current ∼300 A, melting time ∼90 s) intermediate alloys were prepared separately to prevent the volatilization of Al and Si. Processing Text: Cu 45Mn 8Ni 40Sn 7medium entropy bronze alloy was fabricated using copper, manganese, nickel, and tin powders as raw materials in a vacuum induction furnace (VIF-1, TianJin Muffle Technology Co.). The multi-stage heat treatment of the alloy is performed using a high-temperature box-type resistance furnace in air atmosphere. The appropriate temperature for each step in the heat treatment process was primarily determined based on differential scanning calorimetry (DSC, DMA242E, NETZSCH) analysis of the alloy and previous studies of Cu-Ni-Sn alloys [28,29]. To reduce compositional segregation, the ingots with dimensions of Φ25 × 20 mm were homogenized at 820 ℃ for 4 h, followed by furnace cooling. The solution treatment temperature was selected at 900 ℃, and water quenching was performed after holding for 1 h. Aging treatment was conducted at 450 ℃ for 5 h to ensure sufficient formation of the precipitated phase. The alloy, treated by homogenization (820 ℃/4 h)-solution (900 ℃/1 h)-aging (450 ℃/5 h), exhibits a hardness of 362 HV, yield strength of 626 MPa, ultimate strength of 1229 MPa, compressive strain of 47.2 %, fracture toughness of 20.7 MPa·m1/2, and maintains a low wear rate of 1.72×10−5 mm3·N−1·m−1. The processes of homogenization and solution treatment reduce dendrite segregation of elements and eliminate the detrimental lamellar structure at the grain boundaries. During the aging treatment of the alloy, sub-micron scale needle-like precipitates are formed, which play a significant role in enhancing its mechanical properties. Processing Text: Non-equiatomic ratio (TiZrNb-based) 100-xOx (x= 0, 2 at%) RHEAs were prepared by vacuum induction melting in argon atmosphere in a water-cooled copper crucible. According to the concentration of oxygen added in the RHEAs, the following are named O0 and O2 RHEAs, respectively. The purity of each element (Ti, Zr, Nb, etc.) is above 99.95 %, and oxygen is added in the form of TiO2 (purity > 99 wt%). The ingot is remelted at least three times to guarantee its chemical homogeneity. Finally, the ingot with a diameter of ∼90 mm and a height of ∼100 mm was obtained. Then, the as-cast alloys were homogenized at 1100 ℃ for 2 h and forged on a hot press with a deformation of 50 %. The strain rate is about 5 s−1. Then, repeat the heat treatment and forging process. The forged sample was recrystallized and annealed at 800℃ for 2 h, and then the O0 and O2 RHEAs were water-quench (named O0-WQ and O2-WQ, respectively). In addition, after recrystallization and water-quench treatment, the RHEAs were isothermally annealed at the temperature ranging from 500℃ to 700℃ for 1 h, 2 h, 4 h, 10 h and 24 h. All heat treatments were carried out in Ar-filled quartz tubes to avoid oxidation and environmental effects on the material. Condition: after water quenching

Processing Text: The EHESs ingots with nominal compositions of Ni70-xCo10Cr20Alx (x= 17, 18, 19 at%, denoted by Al17, Al18, and Al19, respectively) were prepared by vacuum arc-melting a mixture of pure metals (purity > 99.9 wt%) in Ti-gettered high-purity argon atmosphere. The ingots were flipped and smelted at least five times to ensure chemical homogeneity and then were drop-cast into water-cooled copper molds with dimensions of 10 ×10 ×65 mm3 and 13 ×13 ×50 mm3. Part of the cast bars were annealed at 750 ℃ for 7 d. The density of the EHESs is measured by the Archimedes drainage method. Phase identification was investigated by X-ray diffraction (XRD) with Cu Kα radiation (Rigaku Kmax 2500 V). The microstructure and chemical composition were characterized by using a ZEISS SUPRA 55 scanning electron microscope (SEM) in secondary electron (SE2) and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) modes as well as an F20 transmission electron microscope (TEM). The SEM and EBSD samples were prepared by electrolytic polishing in the solution with 90 % ethanol and 10 % perchloric acid at 30 V. The TEM samples were thinned by ion-milling. Tensile tests at ambient temperature and 750 ℃ in air were carried out at a strain rate of 10−3s−1. The dog-bone-shaped specimens with gauge geometry of 15 ×3 ×2 mm3 were used in the test. An extensometer to directly monitor strain was employed in the ambient-temperature tensile test. For the 750 ℃ tensile test, strains were determined indirectly from the load displacement and were further confirmed by measuring changes in sample gauge length before and after testing. As for the tensile load-unload-reload tests, the unloading-reloading process began at an engineering strain of 1 % and then was unloaded in a load-control mode to 40 N at an unloading rate of 10−3s−1, followed by reloading whenever the engineering strain increases 1 % until the fracture. Condition: ambient temperature; Microstructure: lamellar FCC(L12) and B2(BCC) phases with nano-precipitates

Processing Text: The (TiZr)65-x-yNb15Mo20SixAly (x=5,10,15,20,y=0; x=9.5,19,y=5) ingots were prepared by melting a mixture of pure elements of Ti, Zr, Nb, Mo, Si and Al (with purity above 99.9 wt%) in a consumable electrode vacuum arc furnace with the protection of an Ar atmosphere. Given the high melting point of Nb and Mo, the Nb and Mo alloys were melted initially, followed by adding other pure metal elements. To guarantee the homogeneity of the composition, each ingot was repeatedly melted at least six times. The compressive tests were conducted at room and high temperature (800℃) with a strain rate of 10−3 on an AGXplus (JPN) machine. The compressed specimen is a cylinder of Ф4 mm×6 mm. The equipment is first heated to 800°C at a rate of 10°C per minute. Once the temperature stabilizes, the specimen is maintained at 800°C for ten minutes before testing. All samples for mechanical properties should be ground and polished to ensure that the upper and lower surfaces are parallel. Three samples were tested in each component to ensure the accuracy of the experimental results. Specimens for high-temperature oxidation tests with nominal dimensions of 6 × 4 × 4 mm3 were obtained from the as-cast ingots using an electric discharge machine. The surfaces of specimens were mechanically gritted, polished, and ultrasonically cleaned in an alcoholic solution. To eliminate the influence of impurities in the crucible on the experiment, the crucibles were calcined at 1000°C for 6 h prior to the oxidation test. Each treated specimen was placed in a crucible for weight measurement, and the initial weight was recorded as M0. The oxidation tests were performed using an open-tube muffle furnace. The specimens were heated at a rate of 10°C/min until reaching 1000°C and held at that temperature for 6 h. Afterward, the specimen is removed and air-cooled. Once it is completely cooled, it is weighed. Our oxidation experiments were conducted in a cyclic oxidation mode, with multiple cycles following the procedure described above. We used an electronic balance with a precision of 0.1 mg to measure the weight of each oxidized specimen. To minimize errors, we selected three specimens from each oxidation test group and calculated the average weight gain. Processing Text: To prepare the Ti/W composites, industrial pure titanium (D 50 = 10 μm) and tungsten (D 50 = 2 μm) powders are mixed using a planetary ball mill. The tungsten content is varied at mass fractions of 10 %, 15 %, 20 %, and 25 %. The ball milling process involves a rotational speed of 200 rpm, a ball-powder weight ratio of 10:1, and a total milling time of 10 hours. In order to minimize the temperature rise during the milling process, a single ball grinding time is 30 minutes, with an interval of 10 minutes between each milling session. Anhydrous ethanol is used as a process control agent. After milling, the powder and anhydrous ethanol mixture is vacuum dried at 60°C for 24 hours to obtain the composite powder. Next, the Ti/W composite powder is introduced into a graphite mold with a 20 mm inner diameter, and graphite foil is added to facilitate lubrication and facilitate sample removal after sintering. The composite powders are pre-compacted at 10 MPa uniaxial pressure for 10 minutes and then subjected to vacuum sintering using the sparking plasma sintering system (SPS-3 T-3-MN, Chen Hua, China). The sintering process involves a temperature of 1400°C, a heating rate of 100 °C/min, an applied pressure of 40 MPa, and a sintering time of 10 minutes. Subsequently, the samples are cooled to room temperature in the furnace. Processing Text: The experiment utilized vacuum-atomized 15-5PH stainless steel powder produced by Oerlikon Metco, Switzerland. The powder exhibited good sphericity, with a smooth surface and uniform morphology. The particle sizes for D10, D50, and D90 were 19.4 μm, 33.2 μm, and 50.9 μm, respectively. The primary chemical composition of the powder (wt. %) was Fe-12.48Cr-3.55Ni-3.04Cu-0.18Nb-0.48Mn-0.46Si-0.0509C. Subsequently, the 15-5PH samples required for this experiment were fabricated using the HBD 280 metal LPBF system from Guangdong HanBang Laser Technology Co., Ltd. Each layer was printed with a 67° rotation relative to the previous one. Based on previous studies, the optimal process parameters were: laser power ( P) of 260 W, hatch space ( H) of 0.06 mm, scanning speed ( V) of 1200 mm/s, and layer thickness ( T) of 0.04 mm. The two heat treatment processes adopted afterwards were ST-AT (solid solution at 1040 °C for 40 min, water cooling, aging at 482 °C for 1 h, then air cooling) and AT (aging at 482 °C for 1 h, then air cooling), respectively. The chemical composition of the powder was analyzed using inductively coupled plasma emission spectroscopy, while the particle size distribution was measured with a Bettersize 2600 laser particle size analyzer. After the sample (10 × 10 × 10 mm 3) was polished and ground, it was corroded for 15 s at 25 V in a 15% HF (vol. %) aqueous solution. Utilizing a mixed solution of 5% HClO 4+95% CH 3COOH (vol%), the electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) sample was corroded for 30 s at a voltage of 25 V. The microstructure was then examined using a Leica DMI3000 M-type metallographic microscope (OM) and the crystal structure, texture analysis and dislocation characteristics were examined Gemini SEM 300 type scanning electron microscope (SEM). Tiny cylinders, 3 mm in diameter and less than 0.5 mm thick, were cut from a substrate via wire cutting, then manually ground to 60 μm. Finally, transmission electron microscope (TEM) samples were further thinned using the ion thinning method and examined using a JEOL JEM-2100F SEM. Phase analysis was performed with a SmartLab X-ray diffraction (XRD) system carrying Cu Kα. The V-notch impact test specimen (55 × 10 × 10 mm³, notch depth 2 mm, root radius 0.25 mm) underwent Charpy impact testing using a JBN500 metal pendulum impact tester. Rod-shaped tensile specimens with a gauge diameter of ϕ5 mm and the gauge length of 25 mm were subjected to room temperature tensile performance tests on a DN200 universal tensile testing machine at a strain rate of 1.3 × 10 −3s −1. The hardness was measured using an HRS-150 Rockwell hardness tester with a load of 1470 N and 10 s dwell time. The morphologies of the tensile and impact fractures were examined using SEM (Gemini SEM 300). Processing state: AT (heat-treated); Microstructure: dual-phase α-martensite and γ-austenite
Processing Word: Processing state: AT (heat-treated); Microstructure: dual-phase α-martensite and γ-austenite

Processing Text: CoCrFeNiMo 0.35(at.%) HEA ingot was prepared by vacuum induction melting of pure metals Co, Cr, Ni, Fe and Mo (purity >99.9 at.%) under argon atmosphere. In order to achieve good homogeneity of the alloy, the melting is repeated at least five times, and the ingot size is φ 100 × 150 mm. Then, several cuboidal specimens of 60 mm × 30 mm × 15 mm were cut out of the ingot by means of wire cutting. Before rolling, the specimens were put into a heat treatment furnace and heated to 900 °C for 30 min. Then the multi-pass rolling method was used to roll along the length direction. The rolling reduction of per pass was 5%, and the rolling speed was 0.1 m/s. The rolled plate was placed back into the heat treatment furnace for 10 min following each pass of rolling, and then the next pass was rolled. Water quenching immediately after rolling. Before the formal experiment, the pretreatment experiment was carried out to determine the processing parameters of hot rolling. The edge cracking occurred when the alloy was rolled with 60% reduction, so the maximum reduction was determined to be 50%. The reduction rate of rolling is 10%, 20%, 30%, 40% and 50%. X-ray diffraction (XRD, Rigaku D/MAX-2400) was used to determine the crystal structure of the five groups of specimens after hot rolling. The acceleration voltage used in the test is 40 kV, the target is Cu target Kα radiation, and the scanning range is 20°-80° at 4°/min. Energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) coupled with scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Apreo-S) was used to analyse specimen microstructure and phase distribution. In addition, the grain orientation, phase content and grain size distribution were studied by electron backscattering diffraction (EBSD, Zeiss Gemini300). The EBSD samples were electropolished for 10 s at room temperature with the electrolyte HClO 4: C 2H 5OH = 1: 9, and the test voltage was 20 kV. The nano-indentation test at room temperature was carried out with the nano-indentation instrument (Anton Paar Step 500), the peak load was 40 mN, the load holding time was 10 s, and each characteristic phase was tested six times. Tensile tests were performed at room temperature using an Instron 5569 universal tensile tester with a tensile load of 100 kN and a strain rate of 0.5 mm/min. Processing state: after hot rolling; Reduction: 50%

Processing Text: Solid cylindrical samples of AM 316H SS were fabricated using a Concept Laser Mlab 100R powder bed fusion system (GE Additive, Boston, MA, USA). The process employed a laser power of 90 W, a scan speed of 1275 mm/s, a layer thickness of 25 μm, and a laser focus diameter of 50 μm. Printing occurred in an argon gas environment, with all specimens printed vertically. For the AM SS specimens, we first 3D printed cylindrical samples measuring 3 cm in height and 1 cm in diameter. Subsequently, these samples underwent precision machining via electrical discharge machining (EDM) to attain final specimens with a diameter of 10 mm and a thickness of 2 mm. Tensile specimens were 3D printed in a vertical orientation with a nominal gage length section of 5 x 2.5 × 1 mm 3, employing printing conditions similar to those for the cylindrical specimens. The AM 316H SS and conventional SS specimens were mechanically ground and polished using a Struers Tegramin-25 automatic polisher. Grinding was done on an MD-Piano 220 grinding surface, while polishing was carried out using an MD-Plan cloth with 9 μm diamond suspension. Final polishing utilized an MD-Chem cloth with 0.25 μm fumed silica. The as-built polished AM SS and the conventional SS samples were irradiated using a 3SDH Pelletron accelerator (National Electrostatics Corporation, Middleton, WI, USA) at ambient temperature. Irradiation was performed with an H +ion beam, with fluences of 1.49577x1016and 1.49577x1017ion/cm 2corresponding to damage of 0.6 and 6 displacements per atom (dpa), respectively. During irradiation, the incident ions exhibited an average energy of 0.5 MeV with an average beam current of 300 nA. Hardness testing was conducted on AM and conventional SS specimens to assess the radiation damage and hardness changes before and following irradiation, using a Shimadzu HMV-M3 Vickers hardness tester (Shimadzu Scientific Instruments, Kyoto, Japan). Each measurement involved applying a 50 g indenter load with a dwell time of 15 s. The selection of the specific weight for the study was deliberate, ensuring that the penetration depth remained within the affected irradiated volume. For each irradiation level studied, at least five hardness measurements were conducted on two samples, ensuring a representative dataset for subsequent analysis. Uniaxial tensile testing was conducted using an INSTRON®servo-hydraulic (Instron Company, Norwood, MA, USA) load frame with a 100 kN load cell. All tension tests were performed under displacement control (0.1 mm/s). The strain was measured using digital image correlation (DIC), and the engineering strain was extracted using the digital extensometer method. The Young's modulus, yield strength (YS), total elongation (TE), and ultimate strength (UTS) were calculated from the resulting stress-strain curves. We employed an environmental scanning electron microscope (SEM), specifically the FEI Quanta™ FEG 450 ESEM(FEI Company, Hillsboro, OR, USA), to examine the cracked surfaces resulting from the uniaxial testing. Processing Text: Al-Mg-Sc-Zr alloys with flat surface, low porosity and excellent mechanical properties were prepared by Laser Metal Deposition (LMD) and annealed (A) using secondary recycled Al-Mg-Sc-Zr powders in an open environment. The optimal LMD parameters are laser power 1800 W, scanning speed 5 mm/s and scanning spacing 3 mm The Al-Mg-Sc-Zr alloy deposited by multi-layer multi-track under optimal parameters and subsequent annealing treatment displays a flat surface, porosity of 2.08%, hardness of 134 HV, ultimate tensile strengthen (UTS) of 348 MPa, yield strength (YS) of 235 MPa and uniform elongation (εu) of 16.71%. The in-situ heat treatment induced by the subsequent multi-layer multi-track deposition transformed the alternately distributed coarse and fine equiaxed grain structure into a homogeneous grain structure. The Al-Mg-Sc-Zr alloy, developed by adding Sc and Zr elements to the traditional Al-Mg alloy, has attracted much attention due to its high specific strength, corrosion resistance, and weldability. In order to eliminate the internal stresses generated during the manufacturing process, the LMD-prepared Al-Mg-Sc-Zr alloy was annealed (A) at 300 °Cfor 2 h. The initial powder is argon atomized HS5501 powder produced by Jiangxi Baohang New Materials Co., Ltd. This study is collected all unmelted the argon atomized HS5501 powder after LMD under a closed argon protective atmosphere. Then, this recycled powder was filtered through a 150 μm sieve to ensure the removal of spatter and powder agglomerates. Then put secondary recycled Al-Mg-Sc-Zr powders into a vacuum drying oven at 120 °C to be dried for 2 h. The LMD experiments were carried out in an open environment using a LMD facility equipped with a 2000 W semiconductor fiber laser with an argon protected airflow at the nozzle. The processing parameters are as follows: laser power (P) was 1200-1800 W, the scanning speed (v) was 3-5 mm/s, the scanning space (l) was 2-3 mm, the spot of the laser was 3 mm, the flow rate of the protective gas was 10 L/min, the flow rate of the powder feed gas was 15 L/min, and the scanning strategy was unidirectional reciprocating scanning. Since aluminum alloy has high reflectivity, in order to prevent the reflected laser from damaging the cladding head, the LMD process makes the laser beam at an angle of 80° to the substrate. Processing Text: The binary Ti-12 wt. % Mo alloy was prepared by self-consumable vacuum arc melting. The ingot was re-melted three times in order to promote chemical homogeneity. It was hot forged into square bar and then cut into several plates of 10 mm in thickness. These plates were cold rolled and followed by homogenization at 900 °C for 30 min and water quenching to obtain Ti-12Mo samples of fully β phase. These as-homogenized specimens were subsequently cold rolled at room temperature with thickness reductions of 10 %, 20 %, 40 %, respectively. The cold-rolled-40 % specimens were aged at 300 °C, 400 °C, 500 °C for 60 min, respectively, and then water quenched for modifying their microstructures via phase transformation and partial recrystallization. Processing Text: A CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy (MEA) with gradient hetero-structure (GHS) composing of gradient nanostructured surface layer and hetero-structured matrix was prepared via a two-step process: pre-cold rolling (CR) deformation and subsequent annealing followed by surface mechanical grinding treatment (SMGT) and secondary annealing. The equiatomic CrCoNi MEA was electromagnetic levitation melted under a high-purity argon atmosphere and cast into ingot with dimensions of 10 × 70 × 800 mm 3. The chemical composition of the trial alloy is 32.05Cr-35.85Co-32.1Ni, in at.%. The 5 kg ingot was homogenized in an argon atmosphere at 1150 °C for 2h, followed by water cooling. The homogenized ingot was then cold rolled (CR) for multiple passes into sheets of 1.5 mm thickness with a total reduction of about 82%. The CRed sheets were then annealed at 650°C-800 °C to obtain HS samples, which were designated as HS650, HS700 and HS800 samples, respectively. The HS700 sample was selected for SMGT processing. A polished WC/Co ceramic ball with a diameter of 8.0 mm was pressed into the surface of the HS700 plate sample to obtain a gradient structured SL. The room-temperature SMGT processing was conducted under lubricating oil, with a pressing amount of 25 μm per pass and a total processing number of 15 passes. Both the surfaces of the plate sample were processed by SMGT, with the plates itself undergoing a synchronous alternation of positions in both the up-and-down and forward-and-backward directions at each processing interval. The sample obtained from the SMGT processing of the HS700 sample is designated as the GHS sample. In order to optimize the surface grain size gradient structure to maintain high strength and further restore intragranular dislocation plasticity in SL, the GHS sample was subjected to an additional annealing treatment at 625 °C for 1h, resulting in an optimized GHS sample, which is designated as the GHS625 sample. Processing Text: In this study, hierarchical heterostructures were introduced into CoCrFeMnNi HEA via an in-situ rolling (ISR) assisted laser cladding (LC) process. The coating was fabricated by overlapping individual tracks with a 30 % overlapping ratio. Following the preliminary testing, the distance D between the laser head and the roller was set to 13 mm. In this work, static pressures of 0 N, 1000 N, 2000 N, 3000 N, and 4000 N were applied, and the corresponding coatings were referred as un-ISR, ISR1, ISR2, ISR3 and ISR4, respectively. Annealed 45 steel with dimensions of 100 mm × 100 mm × 10 mm was chosen as the substrate. To minimize the interference of oxides and other impurities, an angle grinder was used to remove the oxide layer from the substrate surface, followed by cleaning with anhydrous ethanol. The powder used in this study was CoCrFeMnNi HEA powder with a particle size range of 45-105 μm, produced by high-temperature gas atomization. Before the experiment, place the powder in a vacuum drying oven (Shanghai Jiecheng Experimental Instrument Co., Ltd., DZF-6050) and dry it at 100 °C for 2 h to ensure its uniformity and fluidity. The coating was prepared by using a semiconductor laser (HWL-1500) with a wavelength range of 910-1050 nm and a DPSF scraper powder feeder to transport CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy powder coaxially. Laser spot diameter 2 mm, laser power 1500 W, scanning rate 3 mm/s, powder feed 7 g/min, overlapping ratio 30 %. High purity argon is used as melt pool shielding gas with a flow rate of 3 L / min. The prepared coating was cut into cuboid specimens with dimensions of 15 × 15 × 10 mm 3using a high-speed wire electrical discharge machining machine tool (Fangzheng CNC Machine Tool Co., Ltd., DK7720). The specimens were then hot - mounted using a metallographic specimen mounting machine (Laizhou Hengyi Test Instrument Co., Ltd., XQ-2B). Subsequently, the cross - section of the specimen was ground using SiC sandpapers of grit sizes 60 mesh, 400 mesh, 800 mesh, 1500 mesh, and 2000 mesh in a wet - grinding manner on a metallographic specimen grinding and polishing machine (Laizhou Hengyi Test Instrument Co., Ltd., MP-2B). After grinding, the specimens were polished with diamond polishing paste until no obvious scratches were visible under an optical microscope. The specimens were placed in anhydrous ethanol and cleaned in an ultrasonic cleaner for 5 min. To prepare the surfaces for electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) analysis, the specimen was pre-ground and polished using the metallographic pre-grinding machine (Hua Xing Test Instrument Co., Ltd.). The surface was then ion-polished with a precision ion thinning instrument (GATAN PIPS II 695) to remove the damage layer caused by mechanical polishing. The microhardness was measured using a Vickers hardness tester (Laizhou Hengyi Test Instrument Co., Ltd., NVM-1000 A). The load was set at 0.3 kg, and the dwell time was 15 s. Each value was measured three times to ensure accuracy. The tribological properties of the coatings at room temperature (25 °C) were evaluated by a ball-on-disk wear tester (Lanzhou Zhongke Kaihua Science and Technology Development Co., Ltd., HT-1000) with a Si 3N 4ball as the counterpart. The tests, performed under dry sliding conditions in accordance with the ASTM G99-17 standard, were repeated three times. The test parameters included a loading force of 10 N, a friction radius of 3 mm, a rotation speed of 600 r/min, and a wear time of 30 min. Sample: annealed at ~1023 K; Temperature: ~77 K

Processing Text: An irregular shape of pure Cr powder (>99% purity, JFE Material, Japan) was supplied as a starting material. The average particle size was measured using a Mastersizer 3000E particle size analyzer (Malvern Panalytical, UK), and the laser absorption of powder was determined using an ultraviolet-visible near-infrared spectrophotometer (V-770, Jasco, Japan). In addition, a rotary-drum-type powder flowability measuring device (Revolution Powder Analyzer, Mercury Scientific, US) was used to measure the rest fractal, avalanche angle. As described in Fig. 1(b), an L-PBF machine (EOS M290, EOS, Germany) equipped with a 400 W Yb-fiber laser as the primary heat source was used to fabricate the samples with dimensions of 10 mm × 10 mm × 5 mm along the x-, y-, and z-axes, respectively. Preheat temperatures of 80 °C and 200 °C were applied. The 80 °C preheat temperature was used to avoid unexpected temperature fluctuations caused by laser energy input during the manufacturing process and to maintain a constant fabrication condition. For the 200 °C preheat temperature, the maximum preheat temperature setting of the equipment used. Furthermore, shorter scan length samples were fabricated in size of 5 mm × 5 mm × 5 mm at a preheat temperature of 200 °C to maximize the heat accumulation effect. A bi-directional scanning with 90° rotation between layers was used to minimize the residual stress, and various input energy density (ED) conditions were attempted to optimize the process parameters. The densification of the as-built Cr samples was measured by the Archimedes principle using ethanol at room temperature. The theoretical density of 7.19 g/cm3 for pure Cr was used to determine the relative density. The specimens were then sectioned on the yz-plane representing the x-scan direction by wire electrical discharge machine, and prepared as mirror polish surface quality. The relative densities of specimens were additionally evaluated for representative samples using an optical microscope (OM; Eclipse LV-150, Nikon, Japan) and ImageJ software. The phase analysis of the as-built Cr specimens was carried out by X-ray diffraction (XRD, RINT-2500V, Rigaku, Japan) using Cu Kα radiation with a wavelength of 0.154 nm. The XRD data were obtained through point scanning in the 2θ angular range from 30° to 90° with a step size of 0.02° and a scan time of 2 s per step at room temperature. Microstructural characteristics were analyzed using FE-SEM equipped with electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD; NordlysMax 3, Oxford Instruments, UK), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM; JEM-ARM200F, JEOL, Japan). In terms of the mechanical properties evaluation, hardness was assessed using Vickers (HMV-G, Shimadzu, Japan) and nanoindentation (ENT-1100a, ELONIX, Japan) tests. The former test was performed with a test force of 0.2 kgf, while the latter test was carried out using a Berkovich tip at a force of 10 mN. Furthermore, compression tests (AG-X, Shimadzu, Japan) at room temperature were conducted at a nominal strain rate of 1.7 × 10−4s−1 condition employing the rectangular shape of the test samples with dimensions of 2 × 2 × 5 mm. The laser heat source behavior of multi-scan tracks was estimated by using a finite element thermal model simulation (COMSOL Multiphysics 6.1, COMSOL Inc., Sweden). Processing Text: The deformation production of the ferrite in the wire is simply dislocation, which subsequently transforms to subgrain boundary and high angle grains boundary. The microstructural evolution of ferrite is simpler. The dominant deformation mode in ferrite is dislocation. Thus, the deformation structure at small strain is mainly manifested as the dislocation cells with LAGB. However, due to the higher drawing strain in this study, these subgrains with LAGB evolved into HAGB via continuous rotation, thus refining the ferrite grains. Therefore, when the drawing strain reaches ε= 6.65, the boundary spacing in the ferrite phase decreases to 56 nm in average. The contribution of yield strength is the sum of dislocation strengthening and grain boundary strengthening. Contribution to yield stress based on boundary strengthening, solid solution hardening, and lattice friction

Processing Text: The deformation product of stainless steel with different Md30 versus deformation true strain. The boundary spacing in ferrite and austenite versus the drawing strain. The deformation mechanism of austenite phase in single phase austenite stainless steel or duplex stainless steel has previously been well summarized to follow the steps: dislocation gilding, formation of stacking fault, formation of twinning or ε-martensite and finally formation of α′-martensite from ε-martensite or twinning. The microstructure characterization confirms that twinning plays the key role in the deformation mechanism of the austenite during the drawing process, while α- or ε-martensite phase is formed after cold drawing even at the drawing stain ε= 6.65. The formation of ε-martensite or deformation twinning depends on the stacking fault energy (SFE) of the austenite phase. For measuring the SFE of the austenite during drawing deformation, 2507 DSS rod was tensile strained to 2% strain at ambient temperature. A TEM experiment was employed to measure the SFE of the austenite at room temperature. The yield strength of the austenite phase in 2507 DSS can be calculated according to the Hall-Petch equation. Processing Text: The pre-alloyed Ti-45Nb powder used in this study was provided by Ningxia Orient Ta Ind Co. With a powder particle size of 15-53 μm, and the powder was vacuum-dried before use. A process parameter with a laser power of 380 W, a scanning speed of 550 mm/s, a layer thickness of 0.03 mm, and a hatch distance of 0.08 mm was selected for producing LPBFed Ti-45Nb specimens using a DiMetal-100 device under a protective argon (99.99%) atmosphere. Based on the phase diagram of the Ti-Nb alloy, five types of heat treatments (at temperatures of 250 °C, 500 °C, 750 °C, 1000 °C, and 1250 °C, respectively) were used to investigate the phase transition. The as-built specimens and heat-treated specimens were named RT, HT250, HT500, HT750, HT1000, and HT1250, respectively, and are listed in Table 1. The heating rate for all heat treatment processes was 2 °C/min. All LPBFed specimens were heated to the preset temperature, held at that temperature for 24 h, and then cooled to 25 °C in the furnace. Heat treatment was carried out in a vacuum tube furnace (KSL-1500X-S). The phase formation and microstructural features were characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD, Rigaku MiniFlex 600, Cu Kα). Microstructure characterization was performed by scanning electron microscope (SEM, Phenom pro). Furthermore, grain orientation was characterized by using FE-SEM with an electron backscatter diffraction device (EBSD, EDAX-TSL system). Room temperature compression tests were carried out using a universal testing machine (E44.304, MTS Co., China) at a speed of 0.001 mm/s. To ensure the repeatability of the results, at least 5 specimens were measured for each condition, and an extensometer was also used to ensure the accuracy of the strain measurements. The slope of the linear portion of the stress-strain curve was used to determine the Young's modulus for each specimen, and the Young's moduli of all specimens was calculated 8 times to minimize errors. Microhardness testing was performed on different types of specimens using an indenter (FM-110, Future-Tech) with a maximum load of 100 gf and a 10 s dwell time; the distance between individual indents was 80 μm. Each specimen was tested for 36 indentations to ensure the accuracy of the data. Sliding wear tests were carried out by a pin-disc wear instrument (Rtec, MFT-5000, USA) at room temperature under dry conditions with loads of 20 N and 40 N, a test-disc speed of 400 rpm, a wear radius of 20 mm, and a wear time of 60 min. The annealed GCr15 plate, with a hardness of 58-62 HRC, was used for the grinding disk, while the tested specimens served as pins during the wear test, and its working principle is shown in Fig. 1. The coefficients of friction (COFs) were automatically recorded as a function of the time of the cycle. In addition, the average COF was measured using a separate load system in contact with the continuous lever arm and recorded using a Nanovea Tribometer system. All of the data (specific wear rate and average COF) were measured at least three times to ensure the accuracy of the results. Condition: RT (Room Temperature); Microstructure: mainly β-TiNb phase

Based on the phase diagram of the Ti-Nb alloy, five types of heat treatments (at temperatures of 250 °C, 500 °C, 750 °C, 1000 °C, and 1250 °C, respectively) were used to investigate the phase transition. The as-built specimens and heat-treated specimens were named RT, HT250, HT500, HT750, HT1000, and HT1250, respectively, and are listed in Table 1. The heating rate for all heat treatment processes was 2 °C/min. All LPBFed specimens were heated to the preset temperature, held at that temperature for 24 h, and then cooled to 25 °C in the furnace. Heat treatment was carried out in a vacuum tube furnace (KSL-1500X-S). The phase formation and microstructural features were characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD, Rigaku MiniFlex 600, Cu Kα). Microstructure characterization was performed by scanning electron microscope (SEM, Phenom pro). Furthermore, grain orientation was characterized by using FE-SEM with an electron backscatter diffraction device (EBSD, EDAX-TSL system). Room temperature compression tests were carried out using a universal testing machine (E44.304, MTS Co., China) at a speed of 0.001 mm/s. To ensure the repeatability of the results, at least 5 specimens were measured for each condition, and an extensometer was also used to ensure the accuracy of the strain measurements. The slope of the linear portion of the stress-strain curve was used to determine the Young's modulus for each specimen, and the Young's moduli of all specimens was calculated 8 times to minimize errors. Microhardness testing was performed on different types of specimens using an indenter (FM-110, Future-Tech) with a maximum load of 100 gf and a 10 s dwell time; the distance between individual indents was 80 μm. Each specimen was tested for 36 indentations to ensure the accuracy of the data. Sliding wear tests were carried out by a pin-disc wear instrument (Rtec, MFT-5000, USA) at room temperature under dry conditions with loads of 20 N and 40 N, a test-disc speed of 400 rpm, a wear radius of 20 mm, and a wear time of 60 min. The annealed GCr15 plate, with a hardness of 58-62 HRC, was used for the grinding disk, while the tested specimens served as pins during the wear test, and its working principle is shown in Fig. 1. The coefficients of friction (COFs) were automatically recorded as a function of the time of the cycle. In addition, the average COF was measured using a separate load system in contact with the continuous lever arm and recorded using a Nanovea Tribometer system. All of the data (specific wear rate and average COF) were measured at least three times to ensure the accuracy of the results. Processing Text: This study aimed to explore the impact of in-situ formed nitride and oxide precipitates on the properties of Fe12Cr6Al alloy by using a nitrogen-rich atmosphere and incorporating nano-sized Y2O3 (0.45 wt %) during laser powder bed fusion (LPBF). As a result of adding Y2O3 nanoparticles to the Fe12Cr6Al alloy, the grain size decreased from 70 μm to 40 μm, and the Al-O, Al-N, and Al-N-O precipitates were replaced by Y-O, Y-Al-O, and Y-N precipitates. Additionally, the nitrogen contents increased from 220 ppm to 470 ppm. The sample with Y2O3 exhibited higher mechanical properties, with yield strength, tensile strength, and hardness (HV) increasing by 80 MPa, 112 MPa, and 23 HV, respectively. This study deviates from previous research on Y2O3-containing FeCrAl alloys by investigating the impact of in-situ synthesized Y-N nitrides on Fe12Cr6Al. The objective is to elucidate the combined effects of these precipitates on the properties of Fe12Cr6Al alloy in comparison to literature-reported oxide dispersion-strengthened (ODS) FeCrAl alloys, which were fabricated in an argon (Ar) atmosphere. Fe12Cr6Al powders were sourced from MK Co. in South Korea and fabricated using gas atomization, along with Y2O3 powders also sourced from MK Co. The Fe12Cr6Al powder ranged from 15 to 45 μm, while the Y2O3 powder had particle sizes from 50 to 100 nm. The test powder was prepared by blending Fe12Cr6Al powder with 0.45 wt % Y2O3 powder. The Fe12Cr6Al and Y2O3 powders were mixed at 6000 RPM for 6 min to ensure a uniform distribution. Two samples were fabricated using the LPBF machine (Metalsys-250, WINFORSYS): one without Y2O3 and one with Y2O3 in the Fe12Cr6Al alloy. The chamber was continuously supplied with N2 gas during the fabrication, maintaining the O2 content below 100 ppm. All samples were fabricated using the laser processing parameters (laser power: 200 W, scanning speed: 400 mm/s, layer thickness: 30 μm, scanning distance: 100 μm, spot size: 100 μm) identified as optimal for achieving superior properties. The alloys were printed in a striped pattern, with each layer's scan direction rotated by 90°, and were fabricated with dimensions of 30 × 10 × 10 mm³ for property examination. The elemental compositions of the powders and the as-built samples were determined using inductively coupled plasma-optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES, QSG-750, OBLF). The oxygen and nitrogen content in the as-built samples, particularly, was measured using a nitrogen/oxygen analyzer (LECO, ON-836, Japan). For tensile testing (three tests for each sample), the as-built dog bone specimens were precision-cut from the 316 L substrate parallel to the building direction, with a gauge length of 6.4 mm and a gauge width of 2.5 mm. Their tensile properties were evaluated at room temperature using a Universal Testing Machine (Instron-582, INSTRON) with a strain rate of 10⁻³ s⁻¹. Vickers hardness measurements were also conducted on cross-sections of the specimens using a Mitutoyo/HM-220B microhardness tester. Hardness values were determined by averaging the results of ten indentations made on each specimen under a load of HV 0.5 for a dwell time of 10 s. During the LPBF process, Fe12Cr6Al melts within a nitrogen atmosphere, promoting nitrogen absorption. This environment facilitates the dissociation of nitrogen gas molecules, leading to the formation of reactive nitrogen species that can subsequently interact with the molten metal and contribute to the formation of Al-N and Y-N precipitates. Processing Text: Equimolar CoCrNi MEA was prepared by arc-melting Co, Cr, and Ni mixtures with 99.99 % purity in a high-purity argon atmosphere. The ingot was remelted more than five times before the drop-cast process to ensure homogeneity. Subsequently, the as-cast CoCrNi MEA ingot was cold-forged by a 50 % reduction in thickness. Afterward, the alloy was annealed at 1173K for 1 h to reduce deformation-induced defects and promote recrystallization. Quasi-static compression tests with strain rates ranging from 1.0 × 10^−3 s^−1 to 10^−1 s^−1 were performed on CoCrNi MEA samples with a diameter of 3 mm and length of 6 mm using an Instron 5969 testing machine. Dynamic compression tests with strain rates ranging from 2.6 × 10^3 s^−1 to 6.2 × 10^3 s^−1 were carried out on CoCrNi MEA samples with a diameter of 3 mm and length of 3 mm using a SHPB system. Stop-ring technology was introduced to control the strain during the dynamic compressions. The ramp wave and shock compression experiments were conducted using the CQ-4 magnetically driven system, delivering a pulsed current with a peak value of 4 MA and a rising time of 500 ns, developed by the Institute of Fluid Physics, China Academy of Engineering Physics. Multi-level characterizations were conducted to explore the intrinsic mechanisms of CoCrNi MEA. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) was performed using a JEOL JSM-7100F field-emission scanning electron microscope (SEM). An acceleration voltage of 20 kV, a specimen tilt angle of 70°, and a working distance of 15 mm were used in the EBSD observations. A JEM-2100F transmission electron microscopy (TEM) was operated at an acceleration voltage of 200 kV to uncover microscopic deformation mechanisms. Condition: Base material; Processing state: as-cast

Processing Text: The high-Mn steel plates were produced using a blast furnace. The cast ingot underwent solution treatment, followed by hot rolling to a thickness of 20 mm and controlled cooling. A single-mode 20 kW fiber laser (IPG, YLS-20,000-S2T) was used for welding. The bead-on-plate process was applied to specifically focus on manganese vaporization behavior, using Ar shielding gas (20 l/min), a welding velocity of 8.3 mm/s, and laser power of 3 kW. The focusing lens had a focal length of 300 mm. The laser beam had a diameter of 200 μm, a wavelength of 1080 nm, and a beam parameter product of 8 mm mrad. The laser defocusing (LD) was set to 0, +10, and +20 mm above the surface; for convenience, these three conditions are referred to as ‘LD0’, ‘LD10’, and ‘LD20’ in the study. The heat input was 361 J/mm, and the energy density ranged from 188 to 2302 J/mm² with respect to the various LDs. The tensile specimens (Shimadzu, AG-X Plus 300 kN) with a 5 mm gauge length and 1.5 mm thickness were prepared in the transverse direction from the top surface of the laser-welded specimens. Processing Text: Alloy ingot with nominal compositions of AlCrFeNiTi 0.2 were prepared by non-consumable electrode arc-melting in a Ti-gettered, high-purity argon atmosphere on a water-cooled copper hearth. The ingot was flipped and remelted at least seven times to ensure compositional homogeneity. For microstructural analysis, specimens were cut from the as-cast AlCrFeNiTi0.2 ingot by electrical discharge machining (EDM). The metallographic specimens were abraded on SiC papers to 2000 grit, and then final polished on a Buehler Vibromet using 0.05 μm colloidal silica for 30 min. The slight alkalinity of the colloidal silica could potentially produce an etched surface; therefore, no additional etchant was applied prior to microscopic observation. In order to observe the dendritic microstructure more clearly, aqua regia etching was used to distinguish the two main phases (A2 and B2/L2 1) of the as-cast AlCrFeNiTi 0.2 HEA. A series of small cylinders with a diameter of Φ2.5 mm and a length of 5 mm were cut and polished from the as-cast AlCrFeNiTi 0.2 ingot for the purpose of conducting compression tests. Compression tests were conducted at a compressing speed of 0.5 mm/min on a SASTest CMT4305 universal testing machine. The microhardness of the as-cast AlCrFeNiTi 0.2 HEA was measured using a QATM Qness 60 A + EVO microhardness tester according to ASTM E384. The tester has an accuracy range of ±2% to ±5%. The applied load is 200 g and the holding pressure time is 15 s. Furthermore, an Agilent G200 nanoindentation tester was employed to assess the hardness of distinct regions. The maximum indentation depth was 1000 nm using the indentation depth control mode. Processing Text: This research aimed to enhance the strength and ductility of spray formed (SFed) 7050 aluminum (Al) alloy through hot extrusion and subsequent heat treatment. The as-deposited samples were heated at (300°C@24h + 470°C@24h) and cooled in air (pre-treated state). Afterwards, the billets were axially extruded into rods at 420 °C using different ERs (5, 9, 16, 25) with an extrusion speed of 0.8 mm/s. Processing Text: The powders used in this investigation were a Mar-M247 superalloy with size distributions ranging from 15 to 53 μm. The chemical composition of the Mar-M247 powders was analyzed as Ni-8.7Cr-10.12Co-10.3W-5.6Al-1.3Hf-3.1Ta-1.1Ti-0.74Mo-0.14C (in wt.%). SLM-100 system (Shandong Charmray Laser Technology Co., Ltd) was used to prepare specimens with the following parameters: laser power 140-240 W, scanning speed 800-1200 mm/s, interlayer rotation angle 67°, reciprocating scanning strategy, layer thickness 30 μm, and hatch spacing 80 μm. Progressive remelting has been proposed to slowly raise the temperature field and reduce the peak stress by multiple cycling at low laser power. The identical parameters of progressive remelting: laser power 60-90 W, scanning speed 600-800 mm/s, interlayer rotation angle 60°-90°, layer thickness 30 μm, hatch spacing 60-70 μm and building parameters: laser power 120-150 W, scanning speed 700-800 mm/s, interlayer rotation angle 60°-90°, layer thickness 30 μm, hatch distance 70-80 μm. Cuboidal specimens 5 mm × 5 mm × 5 mm for microstructure characterization, tensile samples 8 mm × 2 mm × 55 mm along the building direction for room temperature, and tensile samples 15 mm × 1.8 mm × 48 mm along the building direction for 900 °C were fabricated on 316L stainless steel build-plates. In order to promote the nucleation and growth of γ′ phase and improve the mechanical properties at elevated temperature, a standard heat treatment used for investment casting is conducted in a KSL-1200X furnace with solution treatment at 1185 °C (below γ′ phases solvus and in order to ensure the complete dissolution of γ′ phase) for 2 h with air-cooling and followed by a double-aging treatment at 1100 °C for 4 h, and 871 °C for 20 h cooled in the air (to make the alloy close to the equilibrium state) as well. Optical microscopy (OM) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) were used to observe the microstructures of the samples and the square samples were cut along the building direction, after which the cut sample was ground and polished. In order to obtain the microstructure, the samples were etched with a solution of 5 g CuSO4 + 20 ml HCl +20 ml H2O. SEM images and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) data were obtained by a JEF 7800 field emission scanning electron microscope. TEM observation was performed using FEI Talos F200X to investigate the microstructures of Mar-M247. Tensile tests at room temperature were performed along the building direction using an Instron 5584 machine at a constant crosshead velocity of 0.02/s. Tensile tests at 900 °C were performed along the building direction using an AG-X Plus Series Dual Column Electromechanical Test Frame at a strain rate of 0.0008/s in accordance with ISO 6892-2:2011. The identical parameters of progressive remelting: laser power 60-90 W, scanning speed 600-800 mm/s, interlayer rotation angle 60°-90°, layer thickness 30 μm, hatch spacing 60-70 μm and building parameters: laser power 120-150 W, scanning speed 700-800 mm/s, interlayer rotation angle 60°-90°, layer thickness 30 μm, hatch distance 70-80 μm. Cuboidal specimens 5 mm × 5 mm × 5 mm for microstructure characterization, tensile samples 8 mm × 2 mm × 55 mm along the building direction for room temperature, and tensile samples 15 mm × 1.8 mm × 48 mm along the building direction for 900 °C were fabricated on 316L stainless steel build-plates. In order to promote the nucleation and growth of γ′ phase and improve the mechanical properties at elevated temperature, a standard heat treatment used for investment casting is conducted in a KSL-1200X furnace with solution treatment at 1185 °C (below γ′ phases solvus and in order to ensure the complete dissolution of γ′ phase) for 2 h with air-cooling and followed by a double-aging treatment at 1100 °C for 4 h, and 871 °C for 20 h cooled in the air (to make the alloy close to the equilibrium state) as well. The tensile sample is shown as a dog bone in Fig. 3, and the size of the transmission test sample is 10 * 10 * 0.5 mm. The as-cast samples were ground, polished and electrolytically corroded. The transparent thin foil for transmission electron microscope (TEM) observation was prepared by mechanical grinding, polishing and double jet electrolytic polishing technology, after the sheet with a thickness of 500 μm was cutting from the alloy. The tensile samples like dog bone with a gauge length of 7 mm, a width of 4 mm, and a thickness of 2 mm were subjected to tensile tests at room temperature on a universal electronic testing machine (MTS-E45) with a strain rate of 10 −3mm·s −1. Processing Text: The (FeCoNi)90Al10 MEA was produced in a 2-kg vacuum induction furnace using high-purity raw material of Fe (99.91 wt %), Co (99.98 wt %), Ni (99.98 wt %), and Al (99.7 wt %). The alloy ingots were kept at 1100 °C for 1 h, and then forged into 40 × 26 × 13 mm3 plates within the temperature range of 1000-1100 °C. The plates were solution treated at 1200 °C for 1 h, followed by water quenching, then cold rolled to 1.4 mm thickness (reduction rate 78 %). The cold rolled sheets were solution treated at 1210 °C for 3 min, followed by water cooling. Finally, the sheets were aged at 620 °C for 30, 45, 60, and 120 min, respectively, followed by water cooling. The heat treatment process was determined using the TCHEA4 database of Thermo-Calc software. The solution treatment at 1210 °C could ensure both 0C and 0.2C alloys exhibited a single FCC structure, and ageing treatment at 620 °C ensured a sufficient L12 phase and a few B2 phases. Processing Text: Samples were cut into cylindrical shapes with dimensions of (Φ) 5 mm × 6.8 mm from cast ingot solidified under normal pressure. Subsequently, the samples were wrapped in an insulating layer and a graphite tube. The pressure device of the LPR1000 2-6-8 multi-stage high-pressure apparatus consists of an axially cylindrical pressure chamber, resembling to a piston-cylinder system. Pressure is applied to the octahedral talc sample assembly through primary and secondary pressure transmission modules, driven by the press. Graphite is used as the heating element, and the heating temperature is controlled by adjusting the heating power. The sample was heated to 1550 °C under an external pressure of 6 GPa for 60 minutes, after which the heating device was turned off and the pressure was released to atmospheric levels. The SSS and HPS alloys were subsequently aged at 400°C, 450°C, and 500°C in an argon atmosphere for varying durations up to 10 hours. The samples were ground using SiC paper and polished with diamond suspension. A solution with the composition of FeCl 3(2 g), HCl (3 ml), and C 2H 5OH (100 ml) was used as the etchant. The microstructure was observed using a HITACHI SU50000 field emission scanning electron microscope (SEM) and an FEI Talos F200X transmission electron microscope (TEM). Image Pro Plus 6.0 software was used to measure the area fraction and size of various precipitates based on TEM images. The foil thickness in the beam direction was determined by measuring the spacing of Kossel-Mollenstedt fringes in a {111} αreflection in a < 011 > αtwo-beam convergent beam electron diffraction (CBED) pattern. X-ray diffraction (XRD, X’PERT X-ray, Holland) with diffraction angle (2θ) ranging from 30° to 100° and a scanning speed of approximately 1°/min was utilized to determine the crystal structure of the alloys. The DC conductivity measurement at room temperature (300 K) was conducted using the traditional four-probe technique. The samples measured are approximately 3 mm in length, 1 mm in width, and 0.3 mm in thickness. Four platinum wires were affixed to the samples using conductive silver paste. The DC resistance of the samples was initially measured using a physical property measuring system (PPMS, Dynacool-14T, USA) and subsequently converted to DC conductivity. Vickers hardness testing of the specimens was performed using a Huayin HV-1000A microhardness tester with a load of 200 g and an indentation time of 15 seconds. The reported hardness values represent the average of eight separate measurements. The compression test was conducted using a SANS CMT6000 universal testing machine with a compression speed of 0.5 mm/min. The compression specimen measured are 2 mm in diameter and 3 mm in length. At least three measurements were taken for each sample to minimize experimental errors. Process: P1; Final peak-aged state

Processing Text: Bulk specimens were produced by BLT-S310 Selective Laser Melting machine from gas-atomized powder with compositions of Al-4Cu-2Mg-0.3Sc-0.7Zr (wt.%). The powder was dried in a vacuum drying oven at 120 °C for 15 h before SLM processing. Based on a series of process parameter optimizations, the parameters of preparing the bulk specimens (70 × 70 × 15 mm 3) were: a laser power of 200 W, laser scanning speed of 540 mm/s, layer thickness of 0.03 mm, hatch spacing and laser spot of 0.1 mm, and a scan direction rotation of 67°. The as-fabricated and aging treatment samples were cut, ground and polished for microstructure analysis and microhardness analyses. The microstructures of the samples were characterized by scanning electron microscopy (SEM, SIGMA 500 of Ziess Company) equipped with an energy dispersive x-ray spectrometer (EDS) and an electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD). The microstructure was further characterized using an Thermo Fisher Talos F200S G2 transmission electron microscopy (TEM) operating and high angle annular dark field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) with EDS. The tensile samples with a gauge length of 25 mm were tested on an Instron 3382 machine with a constant cross head moving speed of 1 mm/min. Strain was measured with a 12.5 mm gauge length extensometer. Samples were aligned perpendicular to the build direction as shown in Fig. 2. The phase transformation point was measured by differential scanning calorimetry (DSC). Differential scanning calorimetry was performed using a NETZSCH STA 449C Simultaneous Thermal Analyzer by heating rates of 4 °C/min in nitrogen inert atmosphere. The DSC sample weight is between 5 and 10 mg, was cut from the as-fabricated samples to fit into the alumina crucibles (Ф5 × 4 mm 3) for the analysis. Based on the DSC peaks observed, the temperatures for direct heat treatments were chosen in such a way that the peak temperature of each possible phase transition (local minimum points) and the possible phase transition termination temperature. The sample underwent a significant melting reaction after 520 °C, therefore, heat treatment at temperatures of 520 °C was performed. From all the above considerations, the aging treatment used were 203 °C, 225 °C, 282 °C, 320 °C, 440 °C, 465 °C, 496 °C and 520 °C for 2.5 h followed by water cooling. Aged at 440 °C for 2.5 h; Fine secondary Al3(Sc, Zr) precipitates contributed to strengthening

Processing Text: Alloys with a nominal composition of Co 37Cr 14Ni 37Al 6Ti 6(at. %), hereinafter referred to as Al 6Ti 6, were prepared in a vacuum furnace by arc-melting a mixture of the constituent elements with a high-purity (>99.9% pure) supplied by Beijing Ryubon New Material Technology, LTD. All ingots were melted at least four times with magnetic stirring, then suctioned into a copper mold (10× 100 × 2 mm 3). The as-cast ingots were homogenized at 1200 °C for 2 h to eliminate elemental segregation during solidification, followed by oil quenching. The samples were cold rolled along the longitudinal direction with ∼65 % reduction in thickness, followed by a recrystallization annealing (RA) at 1050 °C for 2 min, and oil quenching, hereinafter referred to as Al 6Ti 6-RA. Part of the RA sheets was subjected to aging (RAA) at 700 °C for 4 h, followed by water quenching, hereinafter referred to as Al 6Ti 6-RAA. The aging temperature of 700 °C was chosen because it facilitates the formation of a hierarchical precipitation microstructure. All the heat treatments were conducted under an argon atmosphere in a high-temperature vacuum Muffle furnace. Notably, the heat treatment conditions of Al 6Ti 6alloy include solution treatment, cold rolling, RA, and aging, which were widely used for L1 2phase alloys in the previous reports [ 8-10, 14]. In addition, it is noted that the concentration of Cr element in the Al 6Ti 6alloy is lower than that of Co and Ni since an excessive concentration of Cr can result in the precipitation of a brittle phase. Condition: deformed at cryogenic temperature (77 K); Microstructure: hierarchical L1 2 precipitates

Prior to ECAP deformation, the solid solution alloys were treated at 950 °C for 1 h before quenching in water. ECAP samples with the dimensions of 80 × 10 × 10 mm 3 were cut from solid solution alloys along the hot rolling direction. Subsequently, the aged samples were directly cold-deformation (CD) by rolling with an 80 % reduction, then aging at 400 °C, 450 °C, and 500 °C for different durations. Processing Text: The IN738LC powder was produced using the gas atomization method in an argon atmosphere. The IN738LC alloy was fabricated using an EOS M290 LPBF system. Argon gas was employed as an inert atmosphere to prevent oxidation during the printing process. The laser beam scanning was bidirectional, with a 67° rotation between successive layers. The scanning strategy, layer thickness (τ= 40 μm), hatch spacing (h= 90 μm), and laser power (P= 270 W) were kept constant for all samples. The scanning speed (V) was varied from 600 to 1400 mm/s to adjust the VED within a defect-free processing range. Three typical laser scanning speeds―600 mm/s, 1000 mm/s, and 1400 mm/s―were employed to investigate the effect of LPBF heat input on recrystallization behavior. According to VED= P/(V·τ·h), the VED values for the three scanning speeds are 125 J/mm3 (VED-125), 75 J/mm3 (VED-75), and 53 J/mm3 (VED-53), respectively. HIP treatment was conducted at a supersolvus temperature of 1210 °C, with a pressure of 180 MPa and a holding time of 3 h, to investigate recrystallization behavior. Subsequently, the HIP-treated samples underwent a SHT consisting of two stages: holding at 1120 °C for 2 h, followed by 850 °C for 24 h. The AB samples were electrolytically etched using a solution containing 12 ml H3PO4, 40 ml HNO3 and 48 ml H2SO4 at a voltage of 6 V for 5-10 s to observe the cellular structure and MC-type carbides. The heat-treated samples were etched using the Kalling's reagent No.2 (5g CuCl2 in 100 ml hydrochloric acid and 100 ml ethanol) to reveal the grain boundaries, carbides and γ′ phases. Samples for examination by TEM were prepared as 5 mm diameter discs with a thickness of 50 μm and milled using an ion beam with a Gatan 695 ion mill. All tensile samples were treated by HIP and subsequent SHT (i.e., HIP + SHT). Temperature: 23 °C; Recrystallization fraction: lowest
