Processing Text: In this work, a high-strength-ductility Ti2AlNb alloy is fabricated by hot rolling the compact prepared by spark plasma sintering. The microstructure and tensile properties of the rolled sheets were controlled by changing the thickness reduction and rolling pass. The starting material was pre-alloyed Ti2AlNb powders, which were fabricated by gas atomization. The powders had a composition of 20.3 % Al, 24.7 % Nb and 55.0 % Ti. The powders were sintered in a ZLY-60 sintering furnace. High-strength graphite was used as the sintering die. A glass tube, with the main function of preventing the current from flowing through the sintering die, was assembled between the die and the powders. The graphite paper and TC4 slice were placed between the graphite electrode and the powders to prevent the diffuse of C element. The vacuum degree during sintering was below 10−3Pa. The sintering temperature, pressure and time were 1060 °C, 50 MPa and 10 min respectively. The sintered compact had a diameter of 40 mm and a height of 15 mm. After sintering, the compact was cut into square blocks with dimensions of 28 mm × 28 mm × 3 mm. Then, these blocks were coated with parting agent (ZrO2) before assembled in the packs. The packs were made of 304 stainless steel. It has two main functions. The first is protecting the block from oxidation. The second is providing a compressive stress, avoiding the edge cracking of the sheet. The rolling machine was 400 two-roll asynchronous hot rolling machine. Before rolling, the sealed pack was heated to 1030 °C in a high temperature furnace and kept for 15 min. A box-type high temperature furnace named MXX1400-40 was used during preheating and reheating. The rolling temperature was 1030 °C. The sealed pack was held at 1030 °C for 15 min before the first rolling and then reheated for 5 min between each rolling pass. The sheets were water cooled after each rolling pass, and their microstructures and properties were tested. The microstructure and tensile properties of the rolled sheets were controlled by changing the thickness reduction and rolling pass. The multiple rolling process causes the increase in ultimate tensile strength (UTS) and yield strength but decrease in elongation (EL). Reported in the work of Niu et al.
Processing Word: Reported in the work of Niu et al.

Processing Text: IN738LC superalloy samples were fabricated using a Bright Laser BLT-S210 system equipped with a 500W IPG-YLR laser with a Gaussian spot size of 80 μm. The rectangular samples (20 mm × 20 mm × 40 mm) were fabricated under an argon atmosphere with oxygen content lower than 100 ppm using optimized processing parameters with a laser power of 280 W, a scanning speed of 1200 mm/s, a hatch distance of 80 μm, and a layer thickness of 40 μm. Two scanning strategies namely 67° rotation and chessboard 67° rotation between the adjacent layers were selected for producing the specimens. To investigate the effect of preheating platform temperature on microstructure evolution and mechanical properties, one batch of specimens was printed at a preheating temperature of 25 °C and 350 °C, respectively. The printed rectangular samples were cut from the substrate by electrical discharge machining (EDM). The use of a chessboard scanning strategy and substrate preheating was found to be beneficial for achieving a larger melting pool size, coarser dendrite/cellular arm spacing, and a larger volume of carbide precipitates due to enhanced heat accumulation during the LPBF process, which was verified by finite element analysis. Processing Text: Alloy ingots with a nominal composition of Cr 29.41Fe 29.41Ni 29.41Al 8.24Si 2.65Ti 0.59Cu 0.29(in at.%) were synthesized by melting the mixture of pure Cr, Fe, Ni, Al, Si, Ti, and Cu (with purities above 99.9 wt%) under a high-purity argon atmosphere. Processing Text: Commercial pure Ni powders (>99.9 %, Shanghai Pantian Powder Materials Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China) with a particle size of ∼500 nm and macroporous Ni foams with a pore count of 130 per inch and a thickness of 2 mm (Yiyang Foammetal New Material Co., Ltd., Yiyang, China) were used as raw materials. The Ni foams were first ultrasonically cleaned with acetone and deionized water for 30 min each, followed by annealing at 1000 °C for 20 min in a horizontal tube furnace using a mixture of Ar/H 2gas to remove surface oxides and contaminants. The 3DGN were grown on the Ni foams skeletons through CVD method using a mixed gas of Ar, H 2, and CH 4(1000, 300, and 5 standard cubic centimeter per minute, respectively) at a temperature of 1000 °C for 10 min. Subsequently, the Ni powders were ultrasonically dispersed and evenly filled into the pores of the Ni foam/3DGN, maintaining a precise mass ratio of 4:6. The stacked Ni/3DGN foams were then consolidated for 5 min using spark plasma sintering (SPS) under a pressure of 50 MPa at 1100 °C. Finally, the sintered composite coins, with a diameter of 30 mm and a thickness of 5 mm, were cold-rolled to a thickness of 1 mm and then vacuum-annealed at 400 °C for 1 h. Processing Text: The samples used for the present study were prepared by arc-melting a mixture of pure elements. The ingots were re-melted five times to ensure compositional homogeneity before being drop-cast into a copper mold. Subsequently, samples were homogenized at 1200 °C for 24 h, water-quenched, and then cold-rolled to a thickness reduction of approximately 75 %. In order to obtain samples with different grain sizes, the cold-rolled sheets were annealed at various temperatures ranging from 650 °C to 1250 °C for various time intervals. Specimens for EBSD characterization were initially mechanically ground, polished with aluminum oxide suspension, and then electrochemically polished in an electrolyte of CH 3OH:HNO 3= 4:1 at 20 V for 30 s at -40 °C. For TEM observation, specimens were firstly mechanically ground to about 30 μm, punched into 3 mm diameter disks, and finally thinned by an ion milling system (PIPS, Model 695, Gatan). Dog-bone-shaped samples with 35 mm gauge, 5 mm width, and 3 mm thickness were used for in-situ tensile loading experiments by neutron diffraction. Processing Text: The pipes possess an outer diameter and wall thickness of 6 mm, while the plates are sized at 100 x 100 × 6 mm. Nine unique experiments were planned using the Taguchi orthogonal array method, with the welding tool remaining constant. Three independent variables (travel speed, rotation speed, and shoulder diameter) were altered at three different levels for each variable. The joint's surface flange was FSW-welded. The plates were subjected to FSW on the face side, resulting in a weld depth of 5 mm. AA 6061 pipes with an outer diameter of 50 mm and a wall thickness of 6 mm are considered for the friction stir welding process. Pipe AA 6061 has been subjected to friction stir welding. The dimension of the plate is 100 × 100 × 6 mm. The rotational speed was set to 1800 rpm after several trial and error experiments, and the traverse speed was 5 mm/min. The weld quality has been assessed through visual inspection. Tensile and load bending tests have been done to determine the weld's mechanical properties. The pipes are bent after being broken in half to flatten them. Tensile testing specimens have been produced following ASTM-E standards. The mechanical characteristics of an Al 6061 weld under ASTM- E8 (or AWS) conditions must be specified. The welded sample was cut into the required size for the tests. Tensile testing was also used to evaluate the joint's strength. The operating limitations for each of the FSW parameters, such as travel speed, tool rotational speed, and shoulder diameter, were defined to decrease flaws and improve the tensile strength in the FSW joint. The pipes to the plate are first clamped in a specially made spindle-mounted apparatus for FSW that may rotate at various speeds. Welding is done with EG-85- FSW equipment. The foundational parts of the FSW equipment are depicted in Fig. 2, which also contains the base, motor, pulley, chuck for holding shafts, shaft with removable bolts, and tail. Fig. 2 depicts a fixture that comprises a shaft and bolts and displays the fixture's geometrical dimensions. The welding setup for friction stir welding (FSW) is depicted in Fig. 3. Processing Text: In this work, we developed a Ti20W alloy using powder metallurgy and hot extrusion, which combined remarkable mechanical properties and good corrosion resistance. High-purity powders of Ti (<45 μm), and W (<10 μm) were mixed for 6 h under an argon atmosphere to obtain the Ti20W (weight fraction, wt.%) powder mixture. Subsequently, the Ti20W powder mixture was compacted through cold isostatic pressing (CIP). The parameters for CIP included the pressure of 180 MPa, the holding time of 1 min, and the temperature of 298 K. Then, the compact Ti20W samples were set in a vacuum furnace for sintering. The details for the sintering process involved the heating rate of 10 °C/s, the sintering temperature of 1350 °C, the holding time of 4 h, and furnace cooling to the room temperature. The as-sintered billets were further machined into cylindrical samples with a diameter of 120 mm in preparation for extrusion. Before extrusion, the cylindrical samples were set into a die at 950 °C for 2 h. The subsequent hot extrusion process was conducted at 950 °C with an extrusion ratio of 4, followed by air cooling to the room temperature. Cylindrical samples with a diameter of 60 mm were obtained and labeled as Ti20W-60. Then, the Ti20W-60 samples were extruded at 950 °C to get the cylindrical rods with a diameter of 30 mm, labeled as Ti20W-30. Processing Text: High-purity metals (>99.95 wt%) of Ti, Zr, Nb, Ta, Al were used to prepare Ti 40Zr 40-xNb 10Ta 10Al x(x = 0, 5, 8, 10 at%) RHEAs. Processing Text: High-purity elements (Co, Cu, Fe, Ni ≥ 99.99 wt%, and Ta ≥99.95 wt%) were used for casting. To ensure uniform dispersion of elements, the ingots were flipped over and remelted at least five times. The thoroughly homogenized ingots called the As-casted (Ac-) samples, were subsequently cast into copper molds to achieve the final dimensions of 4 cm × 4 cm × 9 cm. The Ac- samples were then annealed at 1100 °C for 2 h to optimize their microstructure and they were named Heat-treated (Ht-) samples. Compression tests were conducted on both Ac- and Ht-samples to evaluate the mechanical properties using a UTM4000 electronic universal testing machine from the Three-Sides All-Round Company. The tests were performed at a strain rate of 1 × 10 −3mm/s on cylindrical samples with a dimension of Ф6 × 9 mm. The Vickers hardness test used a TH-300 hardness tester with a 49.03 N (HV5) load. The final hardness value was determined by averaging five individual measurements. During heat treatment, Cu outwards diffused from γ′(Cu-rich) into γ matrix, γ′(Ta-rich) phase and δ phase. The accumulation of Cu and Ta into the δ phase strongly promoted its growth. After heat treatment, the γ′ phase became much less and was accumulated along the δ phase. Cu outwards diffused from the γ′(Cu-rich) phase into the γ matrix, γ′(Ta-rich) phases, and δ phases. Finally, γ′(Cu-rich) phases transformed into γ matrix. At the same time, the accumulation of Cu and Ta into δ phases significantly promoted its growth, which resulted in the increase of δ phase volume fraction from 3% to 6%. Processing Text: ER 2319 aluminum welding wire with a diameter of 1.2 mm was chosen as the fill wire, and a 2A12 plate with a thickness of 12 mm was used as the substrate. Before the WAAM process, the surface oxide layer and contaminants of the substrate should be removed by a weak alkaline solution and a special polishing wheel. Then, the treated substrate surface needed to be cleaned with alcohol and acetone and then dried for use. The WAAM system comprised a cold metal transfer heating source (TPS 400i, Fronius, Austria), a robot (ABB robot), a the wire feeding mechanism, and a control system. The welding wire was melted by the heat of the arc to form the molten pool, which solidified to build a deposition layer. Then, after forming a deposition layer, raising the torch, repeating the manufacturing process of the previous deposition layer to form the next deposition layer, and cycling the deposition layer by layer to fabricate the as-deposited wall of 150 mm × 220 mm in size. Finally, the as-deposited wall was milled on both sides into a thin plate with a thickness of 5 mm. The WAAM 2319 aluminum alloy underwent a T4 heat treatment process within the KSL-1200× muffle furnace prior to LSP, involving a solution treatment followed by natural aging. The sample was introduced into the muffle furnace at an initial temperature of 25 °C and then gradually heated to the solid solution temperature of 535 °C at a rate of 200 °C/h. Following a 60-min dwell time, the sample was extracted from the furnace and promptly immersed in a cooling medium for quenching, which consisted of water at a temperature of 20 °C. Subsequently, the sample was placed in a room temperature environment for a minimum of 48 h. LSP experiments were carried out by an SGR-Extra-15 Nd: YAG high power pulse laser (Beamtech, Beijing china) with a wavelength of 1064 nm, a pulse width of 10 ns, a frequency of 5 Hz, and a spot diameter of 3 mm. During the LSP experiment, a 100 um thick 3 M special aluminum foil needed to be pasted on the surface of the specimen as an absorptive layer. To raise the peak pressure of the laser shock wave, a confining layer of running water with a thickness of roughly 1-2 mm was applied to cover the peening area. Both sides of the thin plate should be subjected to LSP treatment. The other main experiment parameters used were: the number of impacts was 2 times, the laser energy was 5 J and 10 J, and the spot overlap rate of the longitudinal and transverse direction was 50 %. The tensile investigations of specimens before and after LSP with different energies were performed at room temperature with a constant strain rate of 10 −3s −1 and a tensile rate of 1.5 mm/min using the 8801 servo-hydraulic testing equipment (Instron, USA). The hole fatigue specimens were examined on a high-frequency fatigue machine (QBG-100, Qianbang, china) with a stress level of 130 MPa, a frequency of about 96 Hz, and a stress ratio of 0.1. Processing Text: The T42 RHEA sample was additively manufactured using a mixture of pure Ti, Hf, Nb, and V powders (all with purities exceeding 99.95 %). The particle size of the powder mixture was determined via a particle analyzer (Malvern Mastersizer 3000), giving an average particle size of ∼81 μm. X-ray diffraction (XRD, λ = 1.54 Å for Cu Kα) testing was applied, showing the phase structure of well-mixed elemental powders. During the LENS process, a remelting procedure involving ultra-high energy input was performed to maintain a uniform elemental distribution and prevent the presence of un-melted elemental powder. Argon was introduced into the LENS machine's (Optomec LENS MR-7) working chamber to maintain a low oxygen content (below 200 ppm). The fabrication process involved a scanning speed of 5 mm/s, hatching space of 381 μm, working laser power of 550 W, remelting power of 800 W, and a layer thickness of 200 μm. After the LENS procedure, a bulk RHEA sample measuring 70 × 12 × 5 mm was obtained for further testing. The tensile tests were conducted on the as-deposited samples at various temperatures, including RT, 673 K, 773 K, 873 K, and 1073 K, at a strain rate of 1 × 10 −3s −1. The tests were carried out using a ZwickRoell Proline universal testing machine equipped with a heating chamber, and strain evaluation was performed using digital image correlation (DIC). The tensile bar used in the experiments had a gauge length of 6 mm and a thickness of 1 mm. Prior to the hot tensile experiment, the tensile bar was preloaded at 30 N to compensate for thermal expansion during the heating process. A heating speed of 10 K/s was employed to reach the target temperature, and the hot tensile test commenced after a 10-min thermal insulation period at the target temperatures in the heating chamber. SEM specimens, including the deformed samples, were ground with 2000-grit SiC paper, polished with 1 μm micro-sized polycrystalline diamond solutions (Struers), and then finished with a finer polishing using a 50 nm sized SiO 2particle solution (OPS, Struers). Subsequently, the samples underwent ion polishing by an Ion Beam Etching machine (EM TIC 3X, Leica) at 5 kV for 1 h. Processing Text: An ingot of equiatomic CoNiV (at. %) multicomponent alloy was produced using a conventional laser powder bed fusion (LPBF)-printing method. Argon-atomized CoNiV pre-alloyed powders were used in the current study. A commercial 45# steel plate was used for the building substrate during the LPBF process. The substrate was sandblasted and then thoroughly cleaned using acetone before the printing, and then preheated to a temperature of 100 °C. A piece of alloy bulk with a dimension of around 90 mm × 40 mm × 15 mm was produced using an FS271 laser melting facility equipped with a 5000-W Gaussian beam fiber laser protected by an inert high-purity Argon atmosphere, and the oxygen level was kept below ∼0.04 % during the LPBF process. The laser spot size was ∼100 μm in diameter, and the laser melting was conducted at 160 W and 800 mm/s scanning speed. The powder layer thickness was controlled at ∼20 μm during printing, and the hatch spacing was set as ∼0.1 mm. The laser scanning direction was anticlockwise rotated by ∼67° between each adjacent printing layer to lower the internal stresses. The printed specimen was naturally cooled to room temperature inside the chamber with the Argon atmosphere. Subsequently, a piece of alloy specimen was cut from the as-printed MCA bulk and then sealed into a quartz tube with a vacuum state. After that, the sealed alloy plate in the quartz tube was then heated to 500 °C in an oven and aged for 24 h, followed by water quenching. Condition: as-printed; Temperature: ~298 K

Processing Text: Alloy rods, weighing approximately 500 g, were fabricated from constituent elements (>99.95 at.% purity) by arc melting in an argon atmosphere on a water-cooled copper vessel. Prior to alloy melting, the furnace chamber was evacuated, flushed and backfilled with high purity argon. The alloy rods were remelted at least five times to ensure the homogeneity and dropped into a copper mold with dimensions of Φ 20 mm × 200 mm. The as-cast ingots were hot-rolled at 1200 °C from 20 to 2 mm in thickness, followed by water quenching. The specimens were solid solution treated at 1050 °C for 1 h and quenched in ice-water mixture, followed by cryogenic treatment in liquid nitrogen for 8 h in order to obtain single-phase martensite (labeled as ST). The sheets were then aged at 480 °C for 15, 30 (labeled as SA30), 120, 300 (labeled as SA300), 3,000, 12,000 and 30,000 min (labeled as SA30000), respectively. Condition: after aging treatment; Associated with tensile strength of ∼1910 MPa and total elongation of ∼10.5%

Processing Text: A series of TiZrHfNbSi x(x = 0, 0.05, 0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00, molar ratios) HEAs, named Si0, Si0.05, Si0.10, Si0.25, Si0.50, Si0.75, and Si1.00, were produced using a vacuum arc melting system (NMS-DRⅢ, Chengdu Zhongke New Materials Technology Engineering Co., Ltd, China). High-purity raw materials with purities exceeding 99.95 % were employed, including Ti, Zr, Hf, Nb, and Si. To prevent oxidation of the specimens during melting, the furnace chamber was maintained at a vacuum level of 3 × 10 −3Pa. Subsequently, the melting furnace was filled with argon protective gas, and pure Ti ingots were melted for a minimum of 5 min to eliminate residual oxygen from the furnace chamber. The samples, approximately 20 g, were melted in a water-cooled copper mold. To enhance the chemical homogeneity of the alloys, five melting cycles were performed under electromagnetic stirring, each lasting over 4 min per smelting cycle. The samples were flipped between cycles to ensure uniformity. The density of the alloys was measured using the Archimedes method. The phase components of the samples were analyzed using an X-ray diffractometer (XRD, D8 Advance, Bruker, Germany) with Cu-Kα radiation. Scanning was performed at a rate of 5°/min within the range of 20°-80°. The microscopic morphology of the sample was observed using a scanning electron microscope (SEM, Crossbeam 350, Zeiss, Germany), and the cross-sectional analysis of chemical composition and element distribution was conducted using energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) at an acceleration voltage of 15 kV. An SEM (Merlin, Zeiss, Germany) equipped with Oxford Symmetry software was employed to determine the grain size, grain orientation, and phase distribution of the sample through electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, C-nano, Oxford, UK). The surfaces of the samples for SEM and EBSD, dimensions of 10 mm × 10 mm × 2 mm, were mechanically polished after sequential sanding with 400-5000 grit sandpaper, followed by final argon ion polishing. The Vickers hardness of the samples was measured using a Vickers hardness tester (MHVS-1000AT, Shanghai Aolong Xingdi Testing Instrument Co., Ltd, China) with a 98 N load applied for 10 s. The Young's modulus was determined by measuring the sound velocity with a sample size of 10 mm × 10 mm × 2 mm. Room temperature mechanical properties of the surface-polished samples were evaluated under uniaxial compression conditions using an electronic universal mechanical testing machine (AGX-VD, Shimadzu, Japan) with a strain rate of 5 × 10 −4s −1. The compressed samples, wire-cut using electrical discharge machining (WEDA), had dimensions of 2 mm × 2 mm × 4 mm. To analyze crack propagation and fracture morphology during the compression process, SEM analysis was employed. Corrosion resistance evaluations of TiZrHfNbSi xHEAs in Hank's balanced salt solution at 310 K were conducted using an electrochemical workstation (Ivium-n-Stat, Ivium Technologies, Netherlands) with three-electrode electrolytic cell. Samples for electrochemical testing were cut and encapsulated with epoxy resin after connecting the wires with conductive adhesive to avoid crevice corrosion. The electrodes have a working area of 5 mm × 5 mm and grounded with 400-2000 grit sandpaper. The dynamic potential scan ranges from −0.5 V to +1.5 V relative to the open circuit potential. Processing Text: An 80 kg steel ingot was smelted using a high-frequency vacuum induction furnace, which was then forged into billets with the dimension of approximately 60 mm × 60 mm. The billets were heated to 1250 °C for 1.5 h and then hot rolled to 3 mm by 8 passes. The finished rolling temperature was approximately 900 °C. After undergoing laminar cooling, the hot-rolled plates were transported to an insulation furnace, which was pre-set and maintained at 660 °C. The power of the insulation furnace was turned off after that the plates had been insulated in the furnace for 1 h. The plates were, thereafter, slowly cooled to room temperature within the furnace. The plates were, thereafter, cold-rolled to a thickness of 1.5 mm. The critical temperatures of the cold-rolled sheets, A c1and A c3, were determined as 709 °C and 908 °C, respectively, using a thermal dilatometer. As the next step, the cold-rolled samples were subject to an austenite-reverted-transformation (ART) annealing process. The annealing process was performed in one step at the temperatures of 715 °C, 735 °C, and 755 °C for 0.5 h. The corresponding samples were labelled as ART715, ART735, and ART755, respectively. In addition, a two-step annealed sample was completely austenitized at 920 °C for 0.1 h, then quenched to room temperature, and finally reheated to 735 °C and kept isothermal for 0.5 h. This sample was labelled Q-ART735. Furthermore, tensile samples with a gauge length of 50 mm have been prepared along the rolling direction. Tensile tests were, thereafter, performed by using a CMT5105-SANS electronic universal testing machine at RT. Also, microhardness measurements were performed by using an FM-700 Vickers hardness tester with a load of 200 g and a holding time of 15 s. The reported hardness value for each annealing process was an average of ten measurements and the standard deviation was also presented. Furthermore, the TI 950 TriboIndenter, with a constant load of 2 mN, was used in a nanoindentation study. Also, the HER was measured using a ZWICK BUP1000 forming testing machine. Hole expansion samples, with a dimension of 100 mm × 100 mm and a 10 mm diameter hole in the center, were used for these tests. These holes were formed by punching or wire-electrode cutting, with a punching clearance of 5 %. All samples with punched holes have been tested in the burr-up position at a speed of 0.3 mm/s. After a through-thickness crack had been detected, the HER was calculated using a crack propagation monitoring system. The following equation was used for these calculations: (1)HER(%)=Dh−D0D0×100where D0and Dhare the hole diameters before and after the test, respectively. For each annealing process, the reported HER value was an average of the HER values for three samples. Furthermore, microstructure characterizations were performed by using field-emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM) and electron backscattering diffractometry (EBSD). A microscope (Zeiss Ultra-55) equipped with an electron backscattering diffractometer was used for the EBSD analyses. Also, the micromorphology of the retained austenite was analyzed by transmission electron microscopy (TEM; Tecnai G 2F20), and the Mn content in the retained austenite was examined by energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) during TEM analysis. Moreover, X-ray diffraction (XRD; D/max2400) was used to measure the volume fraction of the retained austenite, before and after tensile deformation. The samples used for SEM analysis were polished and etched with a 4 vol% nital solution. Also, the samples used for EBSD and XRD analyses were electropolished with a perchloric acid alcohol solution, which had the following composition: alcohol: perchloric acid: distilled water = 14:1:1. The TEM samples, with a diameter of 3 mm and a thickness of 50 μm, were electropolished using a twin-jet machine. The electrolyte that was used in the experiments was an 8 vol% solution of perchloric acid in alcohol. In addition, the experiments were conducted at a working voltage of 30 V and a temperature of −10 °C. Discontinuous yield behavior; Annealing temperature not explicitly mentioned

Processing Text: The AlCrCuFeNi high entropy alloy (HEA) with two FCC and BCC crystalline phases was successfully synthesized through 60 h of mechanical alloying (MA) followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS). The AlCrCuFeNi HEA was synthesized using elemental powders of Al, Cr, Cu, Fe, and Ni, each with a purity exceeding 99 % (Merck Co., Germany) and particle sizes below 45 μm. These powders were blended in equal atomic proportions (20 %) and subjected to MA using a planetary ball mill (QM-3SP4, Nanda Co., Ltd) within a steel vial containing hardened chromium steel balls, with a ball-to-powder weight ratio of 10:1. The powders underwent milling at a speed of 350 rpm for a duration of 60 h, all under a protective argon gas atmosphere to prevent oxidation. To prevent powder agglomeration, approximately 2 wt% of stearic acid was introduced to the powders as a process control agent (PCA). Following MA, the AlCrCuFeNi milled powders were compacted using spark plasma sintering (SPS) (KPFVT Company, Iran). The powders were pressed into a graphite die with a diameter of 40 mm under a pressure of 45 MPa for 6 min within a vacuum environment. This technique employs direct current (DC), low pulse voltage current, and uniaxial force in a low-pressure environment to achieve rapid powder sintering. The sintered samples were processed at three distinct temperatures of 850 °C, 900 °C, and 950 °C. The sample sintered at 900 °C, exhibiting a relative density of 94 %, was identified as the optimal sintered sample. This sintered AlCrCuFeNi alloy was determined to comprise two solid solution phases (BCC and FCC) alongside an intermetallic compound known as σ. Estimated using shear punch testing; Room temperature

Processing Text: In this investigation, graphene nanoplatelets reinforced pure titanium matrix (GNPs/TA1) composites were synthesized via short-term ball milling followed by spark plasma sintering. Spherical TA1 powder (with a diameter of 45-105 μm) was provided by Beijing Gongcheng New Material Technology Co., Ltd. Multilayer graphene nanoplatelets (GNPs) with a purity of 99.9 % and a lateral diameter of 5-15 μm was obtained from Shanghai Yaotian New Material Technology Co., Ltd. The fabrication of graphene-reinforced pure titanium matrix composites is detailed in Fig. 1and comprises two primary stages: (1) Preparation of the mixed powder: Initially, 0.03g of aggregated graphene nanoplatelets is dispersed ultrasonically in 500 mL of anhydrous ethanol. After being uniformly dispersed for 1 h, the graphene solution is combined with 14.97g of spherical TA1 powder and introduced into a 500 mL tungsten carbide ball mill jar. The mixture was ball-milled at a ball-to-powder ratio of 1:10 and a rotation speed of 300 rpm for 2.5 h. The slurry was then transferred to a vacuum rotary evaporator and processed for 1 h to remove a small amount of anhydrous ethanol. Finally, the slurry was placed in a vacuum drying oven at 85 °C for 10 h to obtain the mixed drying powder. (2) Preparation of GNPs/TA1 composites via SPS technology: The mixed powder was placed into a steel mold and subjected to a pressure of 30 MPa. The temperature was increased at a rate of 100 °C/min up to 730 °C. The material is maintained under vacuum at this temperature and pressure for 10 min, followed by natural cooling to yield a cylindrical billet. Cylindrical specimens with a diameter of 5 mm and a height of 6 mm were fabricated from billets using an electric discharge wire cutting machine. These specimens were employed for both quasi-static and dynamic compression testing, as depicted in Fig. 2. Quasi-static compression tests were executed on a SUNS universal testing machine (maximum load capacity of 100 kN) at strain rates of 10 −3s −1, 10 −2s −1and 10 −1s −1. Dynamic compression tests were carried out at strain rates of 1730 s −1, 2480 s −1and 3000 s −1utilizing a standard split Hopkinson pressure bar (SHPB) system. Processing Text: The smelting of high-Mn damping steel was carried out using a 50 kg-capacity vacuum induction furnace. After casting, the riser was cut off, and then forged at 900 °C-1050 °C to produce steel slabs with a cross-sectional size of 80 mm × 50 mm. The chemical composition of the high-Mn damping steel was Fe-0.05C-17.2Mn-0.45Si-0.36Cr-0.05V (in wt pct). After heating the forged slab to 1200 °C and holding for 2 h, the slab was rolled into a 2.5 mm thick plate using a two-roll hot rolling mill (ϕ450 mm). The starting rolling temperature was 1000 °C and the final rolling temperature was 820 °C. After rolling, it was air-cooled to room temperature. Three steel plates with a length of 100 mm were cut from the hot rolled sheet and then subjected to solution treatment at 1100 °C for 1 h and subsequent water quenching to room temperature. After that, three steel plates were pickled and cold rolled with reduction ratios of 10 %, 40 % and 50 %, respectively. The cold rolled sheets with reduction ratios of 10 %, 40 % and 50 % were annealed at 700 °C for 30 min and water cooled to room temperature, and the corresponding samples were denoted as CR10, CR40 and CR50, respectively. The specimens for tensile test were taken from the annealed sheets along the rolling direction and the gauge size was 25 mm × 6 mm. The tensile test was conducted on the AI-7000-LAU10 tensile testing machine at a tensile speed of 3 mm/min, and the deformation area was fully monitored using a laser extensometer. Room temperature damping test was carried out using Dynamic Mechanical Analyzer (DMA Q800, TA Instruments, USA) in single cantilever beam mode and the sample size was 35 mm × 5 mm × 1 mm. The in situ tensile specimen was mechanically grinded to 0.5 mm thick and then electrolytically polished at 25 V for 25 s in the mixture of 10 vol% perchloric acid and 90 vol% alcohol solution. In situ EBSD test was conducted on Zeiss Gemini SEM 300 equipped with GATAN tensile testing machine. Microstructure characterization was characterized by scanning electron microscope (SEM, Zeiss Gemini 300, Germany) equipped with electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, Oxford Instruments Symmetry, United Kingdom), transmission electron microscope (TEM, FEI Tecnai G 2F30, USA) and X-ray diffractometer (XRD, Smart Lab diffractometer, Rigaku, Japan). The ϕ3 mm thin foil for TEM observation was mechanically grinded to 40 μm and electrolytically double-jet polished in the mixture of 10 vol% perchloric acid and 90 vol% alcohol solution at −25 °C and 25 V. EBSD and XRD samples were subjected to electrolytic polishing after mechanical grinding. Average AGS: about 4.0 μm; Synergetic effects of grain refinement strengthening and multiple martensitic transformations

Processing Text: The Cu-10Al-5Fe-5Ni-xMn alloys (x = 0, 1.5, 4.5, 7 wt%) were prepared by a medium-frequency induction furnace. Ingredients of pure Cu, Al, Fe, Ni, and Mn elements with a purity of at least 99.9 wt% were used as raw materials. The surface of the molten alloy was covered with cryolite powder to prevent oxidizing. Each sample was cut off from the middle of the ingot to get consistency. The whole casting process is shown in Fig. 1. The samples with different Mn content were denoted as S1, S2, S3 and S4, respectively, as shown in Table 1. The chemical composition of the NAB-xMn (x = 0, 1.5, 4.5, 7 wt%) ingots were detected by X-ray Fluorescence (XRF, Shimadzu XRF-1800). X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis was performed by a Bruker D8 Focus diffractometer equipped with a Cu radiation target to identify the crystalline phase. To further analyze the microstructure evolution of NAB alloys, the samples were polished and then etched in a solution containing 95 ml C 2H 5OH + 2 ml HCl +3 g FeCl 3for microstructural observation and composition analysis. Microstructural observation was carried out on a scanning electron microscope (SEM, IT 800 HSL) equipped with an energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS), and a transmission electron microscopy (TEM, JEM-2100F). The TEM samples were prepared by twin-jet electro-polishing in a solution containing 30 % HNO 3and 70 % CH 3OH at −30 °C. Tensile tests were carried out using a universal tensile machine (Instron 5569, Instron Corp., America) at room temperature. The Digital Image Correlation (DIC) system (NCM-2D) was used to accurately measure the strain of samples. Fig. 1shows the size of tensile samples, the gauge was 15 mm in length and the tensile rate was 5 × 10 −4s −1. To ensure the accuracy of the data, at least three tensile samples were tested for each condition. The hardness test was measured by using a Vickers hardness tester under a constant load of 500 g for 15 s. Each sample was tested 6 times and took the average value to decrease the error. Processing Text: Invar 36 alloy samples were fabricated using the in-situ rolling-assisted laser directed energy deposition (LDED) process, and the effect of in-situ rolling on the microstructure, mechanical properties and coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE) was investigated. The plastic deformation introduced by in-situ rolling facilitated the recovery and recrystallization of the pre-solidified layers. The yield strength was significantly enhanced due to grain refinement strengthening and work hardening. The refinement of grains and the increase in residual stress induced by in-situ rolling enabled these samples to maintain an ultra-low CTE. Gas atomized Invar 36 alloy powders were utilized as raw material, and the HAM experiments were performed on an IR-LDED system. The deformation of the deposited material was achieved by adding a rolling unit next to the deposition head and ensuring the synergistic movement of the two, and the distance between the rolling unit and deposition head was 35 mm. The rolling load was obtained in real-time through a sensor, and can be adjusted by controlling the lifting amount of the rolling unit in each layer. The dimension of the rolling head was ϕ50 mm × 20 mm, and a detailed description of the IR-LDED procedure can be found in our previous publication [ 16]. The scanning speed of rolling unit and deposition head was 8 mm/s, and the laser power and overlap rate were 1300 W and 40 %, respectively. Samples with dimensions of 70 mm × 5 mm × 50 mm were fabricated by the IR-LDED process under loads of 0 kN, 5 kN and 10 kN, and the corresponding lifting amount of the rolling unit in each layer were 0.55 mm, 0.38 mm and 0.28 mm, respectively. Processing Text: Two types of steel (Fe-0.3 %C and Fe-0.7 %C wt.) used in the tensile armor of flexible ducts, differing in chemical compositions and thermomechanical treatments, were analyzed, both exhibiting HE in a hydrogen-rich environment. Sample A showed a decrease in yield strength from 810 MPa in air to 687 MPa after hydrogen charging, with total elongation reduced from 11.15 % to 7.38 %. For Sample A, the average YS was recorded at 810 ± 15 MPa, while Sample B showed a higher YS of 1216 ± 6 MPa, indicating a significant increase of approximately 50 % attributable to the higher carbon content. Similarly, the UTS for Sample A was measured at 876 ± 64 MPa, compared to 1311 ± 51 MPa for Sample B, revealing an enhancement of nearly 50 % as well. The elongation percentage, a measure of ductility, was inversely affected; it decreased from 11.15 ± 0.7 % in Sample A to 8.52 ± 1.7 % in Sample B, reflecting a reduction in ductility by approximately 24 % due to the increased carbon content. YS of sample A decreases under both hydrogen exposure conditions, highlighting its vulnerability to HE. These morphologies demonstrate distinct mechanical behaviors, where spheroidized cementite provided embrittlement, while lamellae provided resistance to HIC. Sample A has lower carbon content, presented 34 % of elongation reduction. Condition: Air
Processing Word: Condition: Air

Processing Text: In this contribution, we utilized the laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) technique to produce a high-Mo maraging steel with a nominal chemical composition of Fe-13Ni-12Co-10Mo-1W-1Ti (wt.%). Notably, the ultrafast cooling rate inherent to L-PBF successfully suppresses the formation of coarse Mo-enriched precipitates. The co-precipitation of high-density Ni3Ti and Mo-enriched nanoprecipitates within the direct-aged martensitic matrix was observed. As a result, despite containing ∼16% soft reverted austenite, the direct-aged samples exhibit an ultrahigh yield strength (YS) of ∼ 2.34 GPa and an ultrahigh ultimate tensile strength (UTS) of ∼2.57 GPa, with an acceptable uniform elongation (UE) of around 2.7%. Gas-atomized powders with particle sizes ranging from 15 to 53 μm were utilized to make bulk samples. The chemical composition of the pre-alloyed powder is detailed in the Table 1. Sample blocks with dimensions of 70 (x) × 22 (y) × 14 (z, building direction (BD)) mm 3( Supplementary Fig. S2) were fabricated in an L-PBF machine BLT-S210 (BLT, Inc, Xi'an, China). The printing was conducted with optimized parameters of a laser power of 170 W, a hatch spacing of 80 μm, a scan speed of 1000 mm/s, a layer thickness of 20 μm, and a scan strategy with 67° rotation between layers. Post-printing heat treatments were conducted using a DIL-805 A/D type dilatometer with both the heating and cooling rates set at 10 °C/s. In reference to aging parameter used by Kwon et al. [ 25] for an ultrahigh UTS of 2.4 GPa in a high-Mo maraging medium-entropy alloy (56.89 Fe-25.01 Co-9.96 Ni-8.14 Mo in wt.%), the as-built samples of this study were performed an aging treatment at 550 °C for 10 min, followed by cooling to ambient temperature (denoted as direct-aged samples). In addition, to replicate conventional heat treatment process, the as-built samples underwent annealing at 1000 °C for 1 h, followed by cooling to ambient temperature (denoted as annealed samples). This annealing temperature is higher than the standard 820 °C typically used for 18 Ni maraging steels, aiming to suppress the formation of Mo-enriched precipitates during the annealing. These annealed samples were then subjected to the same aging treatment at 550 °C for 10 min, facilitating comparative analyses between different fabrication techniques. Vickers hardness tests were performed under an applied load of 9.8 N and a dwell time of 10 s, and at least ten indentations were conducted per sample. Uniaxial tensile tests were conducted at a strain rate of 10 -4s -1at ambient temperature. Dog-bone-shape tensile specimens with the gauge dimensions of 8 × 2 × 1 mm 3were prepared along the x-axis direction using electrical-discharge machining, and then polished to 5000-grid SiC paper. Processing state: direct-aged; Contains ~16% soft reverted austenite; Strengthened by high-density Ni3Ti and Mo-enriched nanoprecipitates

Processing Text: The high power laser cladding (HPLC) process with laser power of 15 kW was used for the first time to fabricate 17-4PH alloy coatings. The experiment utilized 17-4PH powder smelted through vacuum gas atomization technology as the laser cladding material. The powder particles' morphology are near-spherical and the size ranges from 40 μm to 220 μm. The powder was dried for 2 h in a vacuum oven at 100 °C before the experiment. The HPLC system and details of the coating preparation: the HPLC system, the laser spot size (20 mm × 2 mm), the top view morphology, transverse morphology, and transverse dimensions of a single-track coating, respectively, the preparation process and final morphology of multi-track and multi-layer coating, respectively. Under a cladding speed (VC) of 10 mm/s, the build rate (η) was calculated to be about 272 mm3/s via the formula. Based on the preparation process and the process parameters, a multi-track and multi-layer coating with dimension of 170 mm × 190 mm × 7.2 mm (length × width × thickness) were prepared on the 0Cr13Ni5Mo substrate. In order to facilitate the heat treatment, the coating was divided into five groups (A-E) along the overlapping direction (X+). The group A did not undergo heat treatment, while groups B to E were first uniformly solution-treated at 1040 °C for 1 h, followed by natural cooling in the air. Subsequently, they were subjected to aging treatment at corresponding temperatures of 300 °C, 400 °C, 480 °C, and 550 °C for 4 h each, followed by natural cooling in the air. The metallographic specimens were obtained from each coatings (A-E) using a wire cutting machine. After grinding and polishing the XOZ plane, the specimens were corroded for 5 s in a corrosive agent, and then the microstructures were observed via a scanning electron microscope (SEM). The ground and polished specimens (XOZ plane) were submerged in perchloric acid solutions with a volume fraction of 8 %, subjected to electrochemical polishing at 20 V for 40 s, and then etched for 30 min at 4 kV and 3° in a precision etching coating system. Crystallographic data of the coatings were analyzed by an electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) probe. In addition, the phases were analyzed via X-ray diffractometry (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM). The micro hardness was tested along the direction of Z- with a spacing of 0.5 mm, a load of 0.5 kg, and pressure retention of 20 s. The tensile specimens (three specimens per group) were taken from the coatings (A-E) and the forged substrate (F) respectively. All tensile specimens were tested at a strain rate of 1.4 × 10−3s−1. The CE test specimens (three specimens per material) were taken from the coating and substrate material respectively. The heat treatment process of the coating CE specimens were consistent with the heat treatment process parameters of the tensile test specimen with the best plasticity. Subsequently, the tested surfaces were polished. The CE test was performed according to ASTM G32-16. Before testing, the specimens were cleaned, dried, and weighed. Subsequently, each specimen underwent a 4-hour CE test in deionized water with temperature of 25 ± 2 °C using a magnetostrictive induced cavitation facility resonating at 20 kHz with an amplitude of 60 μm. After the CE test, all specimens were cleaned, dried, and weighed again to calculate the mass loss. Finally, the surface and transverse morphologies of the CE specimens were observed by SEM. The elastoplasticity of the 17-4PH coating specimens for CE test was probed through an instrumented nanoindentation method using a Berkovich-type indenter. Processing Text: WCAWs were prepared by liquid phase sintering (LPS) and laser ultrashort-time liquid phase sintering (LULPS) respectively. The 93 wt% W-CoAlW cuboid samples prepared by laser ultrashort-time liquid phase sintering were denoted as LULPS WCAWs. The oxygen content was kept below 50 ppm through a continuous flow of argon in the process chamber. The laser power, scan speed, and feed rate are 1400 W, 15 mm/s, and 20 g/min, respectively. Processing Text: Equimolar CoCrNi MEA was prepared by arc-melting Co, Cr, and Ni mixtures with 99.99 % purity in a high-purity argon atmosphere. The ingot was remelted more than five times before the drop-cast process to ensure homogeneity. Subsequently, the as-cast CoCrNi MEA ingot was cold-forged by a 50 % reduction in thickness. Afterward, the alloy was annealed at 1173K for 1 h to reduce deformation-induced defects and promote recrystallization. Quasi-static compression tests with strain rates ranging from 1.0 × 10^−3 s^−1 to 10^−1 s^−1 were performed on CoCrNi MEA samples with a diameter of 3 mm and length of 6 mm using an Instron 5969 testing machine. Dynamic compression tests with strain rates ranging from 2.6 × 10^3 s^−1 to 6.2 × 10^3 s^−1 were carried out on CoCrNi MEA samples with a diameter of 3 mm and length of 3 mm using a SHPB system. Stop-ring technology was introduced to control the strain during the dynamic compressions. The ramp wave and shock compression experiments were conducted using the CQ-4 magnetically driven system, delivering a pulsed current with a peak value of 4 MA and a rising time of 500 ns, developed by the Institute of Fluid Physics, China Academy of Engineering Physics. Multi-level characterizations were conducted to explore the intrinsic mechanisms of CoCrNi MEA. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) was performed using a JEOL JSM-7100F field-emission scanning electron microscope (SEM). An acceleration voltage of 20 kV, a specimen tilt angle of 70°, and a working distance of 15 mm were used in the EBSD observations. A JEM-2100F transmission electron microscopy (TEM) was operated at an acceleration voltage of 200 kV to uncover microscopic deformation mechanisms. Processing Text: A novel Co-free Al0.7CrFeMnNi1.3 high-entropy alloy (HEA) was prepared and followed by annealing treatment at 400-1000℃ for 2 h to investigate the effect of microstructure evolution on compression and tribological properties. The as-cast alloy ingots of Al 0.7CrFeMnNi 1.3were prepared using the vacuum arc melting under high purity Ar atmosphere, remelted at least 5 times to reduce element segregation, and then water-cooled directly in the copper crucible. The as-cast alloy ingots were then placed in the muffle furnace for annealing treatment followed air cooling, and the annealing temperature is set to 400, 600, 700, 800, 900 and 1000℃for 2 h, which were marked the as-annealed alloy. Annealing treatment results in the reversible transformation of matrix phase, and the phase transformation mechanism is discussed based on experimental and thermodynamic calculation. Processing Text: The composition of high-Mn austenitic steel was carefully designed to make the twinning behavior sensitive to changes in strain. The high-Mn steel is chosen here for the easy-controlled SFE and twinning behavior. The SFE of high-Mn steel is adjusted to close to 20 mJ/m2 by designing the Mn and C content. According to the Olson-Cohen thermodynamic model, a steel composition of Fe-20Mn-0.9C-5Mo (all in wt%) was designed, with a calculated SFE of 24.7 mJ/m2. The steel was prepared via vacuum induction melting. The as-cast ingots underwent homogenization at 1473 K for 2 h and hot forged at 1300 K to produce a round bar with a diameter of 80 mm. The forged bar is finally processed into a hollow tube with an inner diameter of 56 mm and a wall thickness of 10 mm. Then, the tube billets were forward power spinning at room temperature using a spinning machine with two symmetrically distributed rollers. Artificial spray emulsion was used to fully cool the contact part between the spinning wheel and the workpiece. After three spinning passes, the wall thickness is reduced from 10 mm to 8.5 mm, and the total wall thickness reduction is 15 %. The rollers are R type, with a diameter of 446 mm and a tip radius of 12.5 mm. The mandrel was rotated at a speed of 55 rpm, and the feed rate of the rollers was 0.5 mm/r. Additionally, a plate with a thickness of 4 mm was cut from the forged bar and underwent cold rolling for comparison. Initial state; Single-phase austenite

Processing Text: We fabricated a non-equiatomic Ni35Co27.5Cr27.5Al5Ti5 HEA consisting of spherical L12 nanoprecipitates and FCC matrix using casting, homogenization and aging. Notably, both the homogenized and aged Ni35Co27.5Cr27.5Al5Ti5 HEA samples exhibit equiaxed grains, with the latter showcasing uniformly distributed spherical L12 nanoprecipitates in the FCC matrix. The average size and volume fraction of these nanoprecipitates in the aged HEA are ∼10.9 nm and ∼41.9 vol%, respectively. Processing Text: Equimolar CoCrNi MEA was prepared by arc-melting Co, Cr, and Ni mixtures with 99.99 % purity in a high-purity argon atmosphere. The ingot was remelted more than five times before the drop-cast process to ensure homogeneity. Subsequently, the as-cast CoCrNi MEA ingot was cold-forged by a 50 % reduction in thickness. Afterward, the alloy was annealed at 1173K for 1 h to reduce deformation-induced defects and promote recrystallization. Quasi-static compression tests with strain rates ranging from 1.0 × 10^−3 s^−1 to 10^−1 s^−1 were performed on CoCrNi MEA samples with a diameter of 3 mm and length of 6 mm using an Instron 5969 testing machine. Dynamic compression tests with strain rates ranging from 2.6 × 10^3 s^−1 to 6.2 × 10^3 s^−1 were carried out on CoCrNi MEA samples with a diameter of 3 mm and length of 3 mm using a SHPB system. Stop-ring technology was introduced to control the strain during the dynamic compressions. The ramp wave and shock compression experiments were conducted using the CQ-4 magnetically driven system, delivering a pulsed current with a peak value of 4 MA and a rising time of 500 ns, developed by the Institute of Fluid Physics, China Academy of Engineering Physics. Multi-level characterizations were conducted to explore the intrinsic mechanisms of CoCrNi MEA. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) was performed using a JEOL JSM-7100F field-emission scanning electron microscope (SEM). An acceleration voltage of 20 kV, a specimen tilt angle of 70°, and a working distance of 15 mm were used in the EBSD observations. A JEM-2100F transmission electron microscopy (TEM) was operated at an acceleration voltage of 200 kV to uncover microscopic deformation mechanisms. Before gradient nanotwinning refinement

Processing Text: Bulk CoCrFeNiCu-based high entropy alloy was fabricated using a combination of short-term high energy ball milling and rapid spark plasma sintering. Commercial powders of Co (99.7 % pure, mean particle size 3 µm), Cr (99.35 %, >71 µm), Fe (99.96 %, 10-20 µm), Ni (99.5 %, 45-60 µm), and Cu (99.5 %, 45-60 µm) were used as starting materials. The powders were mixed in equiatomic proportion Co+Cr+Fe+Ni+Cu, then 20 g of the mixture were placed in steel jar of the planetary ball mill Activator-2S («Chemical Engineering Plant» Ltd, Russia) together with 400 g of steel milling balls (each ball was 6 mm in diameter, mass of one ball was about 0.86 g). High energy ball milling (HEBM) was carried out in Ar atmosphere (4 bar), without any liquid agent addition. After 120 min of HEBM at rotating speed 694 rpm for Sun disk and 1388 rpm for the jar (in laboratory coordinate system), mechanically alloyed powder CoCrFeNiCu was obtained. The extremely high rotating speed in combination with permanent water cooling of the jars available in the Activator-2S mill, allowed relatively fast mechanical synthesis of the alloy: less than 2 h instead of 5 - 65 h required in the air-cooling mills with rotating speed 200-350 rpm. As-prepared alloy powders were SPS-consolidated in vacuum using a Labox 650 apparatus (Sinter Land, Japan). The powder mixture was placed into а cylindrical graphite die (inner diameter 30 mm) and uniaxially compressed at 50 MPa. The sample was heated at а rate of 100°С/min up to the preset sintering temperature ∼ 1073 K by passing rectangular pulses of electric current through the sintering media. The dwell time at sintering temperature was 10 min. SPS-produced disks were 5 mm thick and 30 mm in diameter. Processing Text: Alloy ingots with nominal composition of the Al x CrFe 2 Ni (x = 0.3, 0.4, 0.5 and 0.7 in mole ratios), denoted as Al x, or Al 0.3, Al 0.4, Al 0.5, and Al 0.7, respectively, were manufactured by arc melting in a high purity argon atmosphere with high purity (> 99.8 wt%) Al, Cr, Fe, and Ni raw materials. To ensure a homogeneous composition the ingots were repeatedly melted five times. Rectangular plates of 70 mm × 14 mm × 2 mm for the four MEAs were prepared by the copper mold injection casting. The crystal structure of the as-cast Al x CrFe 2 Ni MEAs was identified by X-ray diffraction (XRD, Shimadzu 7000) at a speed of 4 ◦/min with Cu K α radiation. The scanning electron microscopy (SEM) equipped with energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) was used to observe the microstructure and detect the elemental distributions of the alloys. The volume fraction and distribution of the different phases in the alloys were observed by electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD). Besides, the structure of each phase of the as-cast alloys was also characterized by the transmission electron microscope (TEM, JEM-2100). Hysteresis lines of different samples were measured using an integrated physical property measurement system (VSM, Micro Sense EZ9). The strain gauge type BX120-5AA (5×3) was used to measure the magnetostriction coefficient of the alloys with a resistance value of 120 Ω and a strain measurement range of 1-19999 ppm. The magnetic domains of alloys were tested using the magnetic force microscope (MFM) module of the atomic force microscope. The damping capacity of the as-cast alloys were characterized by the dynamic mechanical analyzer (DMA, Q800, single cantilever mode), and the damping capacity was estimated using the internal friction Q−1 (Q−1 = tan δ, where δ is the phase lagged between the applied cyclic stress and the resulting strain). A universal mechanical testing machine (MTS-E45) was used to test the tensile sample at tensile rate of 1 × 10 −3 s −1. Processing Text: The series were made from ternary master alloys of CuPdPt and AuCuPd to ensure their constant ratio. The two additional elements were further added to pieces of the master alloy in different concentrations. All masses were weighed according to the stoichiometric composition of the desired alloy and melted under Ar atmosphere on a water-cooled Cu plate in an arc furnace (Arc Melter AM 200 Edmund Buehler GmbH). To enhance the homogeneity of the samples, they were flipped over and melted again four times. Finally, the samples were cast into a graphite mould (4 mm in diameter and 75 mm in length). The samples were homogenized at a homologous temperature of approx. 0.9 in sealed quartz ampules under Ar atmosphere and quenched in ice water. Afterwards, the samples were deformed by rotary swaging (UR2–4, Heinrich Müller Maschinenfabrik, Pforzheim) up to a true strain of ε = 0.71 (ε = ln A i / A f, where A i and A f are the initial and final cross-section area, respectively), while the degree of deformation per step was ε ≈ 0.24. Recrystallization heat treatment was done for one hour at the same temperature as the homogenization treatment with subsequent quenching in ice water to maintain the single-phase microstructure [18]. Processing Text: The SPD processes can be classified as bulk-SPD, surface-SPD and powder-SPD methods. In bulk-SPD, the goal is to modify the bulk microstructure of a material with reasonably large sizes. In surface-SPD, only surface and sub-surface layers are modified. In powder-SPD, the material is in the form of powder, and strain is introduced on the surface layer and core of the powder particles usually by ball milling methods. Different methods based on rolling, torsion, forging and extrusion can satisfy the required conditions for SPD processing of bulk material. The most known method for inducing SPD in powders is high-energy ball milling. Recent trends in SPD methods include hydrostatic pressure methods, upscaling disc samples to rods using HPTE, pipe sample processing using t-HPS, sheet processing using IF-HPS, cryogenic-SPD, and ultra-SPD. Processing Text: Cu47.5Zr45.1Al7.4 and Zr41.2Ti13.8Cu12.5Ni10Be22.5 BMGs prepared by vacuum arc melting and vacuum die casting processes were purchased from Peshing New Metal Co., Ltd. The size of BMG samples was 20 mm × 20 mm × 2 mm. Before CE experiments, the samples were polished with water sandpaper and diamond paste to mirror the surface and then were ultrasonically cleaned in ethanol solution for 10 min. The CE test of two types of samples was carried out in deionized water by an ultrasonic vibration apparatus that conforms to ASTM G32-16 standard. The BMG samples were held stationary below the amplitude transformer with a diameter of 15.9 mm at a distance of 0.5 ± 0.01 mm and immersed in water at a depth of 12 ± 4 mm. CE tests were operated at a frequency of 20 kHz, an amplitude of 50 μm (peak-to-peak), a duration of 12 h and a water temperature of 25 ± 2 °C controlled by a circulatory system. After every interval of 1 h, the mass loss of the samples before and after CE was measured by an electronic analytical balance with an accuracy of 0.1 mg, and then converted to volume loss according to their densities. The amorphous structure of Cu47.5Zr45.1Al7.4 and Zr41.2Ti13.8Cu12.5Ni10Be22.5 BMGs was verified by X-ray diffractometer (XRD, D/Max-2400, Philips, Netherlands) with a Cu-Kα radiation (40 kV, 40 mA) over a 2θ range of 20°-90°. The thermal stability of the two types of samples was evaluated by differential scanning calorimeter (DSC, Netzsch STA 449 F5, Germany) from 298 to 1073 K at a heating rate of 20 K min-1 in high-purity nitrogen. Their morphologies and elements distribution of polished surfaces were measured by the JSM-5600LV scanning electron microscope (SEM, JEOL, Japan) coupled with an energy-dispersive spectrometer (EDS). A FIB-SEM system (Helios G4 PFIB, FEI, Netherlands) was used to prepare TEM samples of the CE zone of BMGs and a transmission electron microscopy (TEM, JEM-F200, JEOL, Japan) was employed to investigate the microstructure of BMGs and to study whether nanocrystalline precipitates were formed after CE. In addition, positron annihilation lifetime spectroscopy (PALS, Ortec, United States) measurements were performed using a fast-fast coincident method and a 12.5 μCi 22Na position source sandwiched between two pieces of the same specimen. The density values of the two types of samples were obtained by calculation, which can be expressed as the following formula: ρ=mV where m is the mass of the sample, accurately measured by an electronic analytical balance with an accuracy of 0.1 mg, and V represents the actual volume of the sample, measured with an AccuPyc 1330 Rycnometer-type densimeter (Micromeritics, USA) in high purity helium. The microhardness of polished surfaces of BMGs was measured by a microhardness tester (MH-5-VM) at a load of 300 g and a dwelling time of 10 s, and the average value of 10 points was taken. Their nanoindentation tests before and after CE were carried out by an NHT02 nanoindentation instrument with a triangular pyramid indenter at a maximum load of 30 mN, a loading/unloading rate of 60 mN min-1, a dwelling time of 10 s, and a collection frequency of 10 Hz, and each test was repeated five times at least. In addition, under the sinus mode of the NHT02 nanoindentation instrument, the true stress-strain curves of the two BMGs were tested to obtain yield strength using a spherical indenter with a radius of 10 μm at a maximum load of 50 mN, a sinus frequency of 10 Hz, an amplitude of 5 μm, a holding time of 10 s and a loading-unloading rate of 100 mN min-1, and each test was repeated five times at least. Processing Text: In this work, in-situ alloyed NbMoTaWTix (x=0, 0.125, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75) RHEAs were additively manufactured using the laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) process. For the LPBF process, a HBD 100 metal printer equipped with a 200 W fiber laser, and elemental powders of Nb, Mo, Ta, W and Ti with the particle sizes in the range of 15-53 μm and ∼99.9 % purity were used. The powders were mixed by using a mechanical planetary ball mill for 12 h under an argon atmosphere. The content of O, N and H elements in the powder was measured using a high-power electrode combustion device (LECO-ONH 836). The powder was dried in the oven at 120 ℃ for 4 h under vacuum before their use. All the samples were prepared in a high purity argon environment (O < 300 ppm), and the processing parameters for LPBF process are: laser power ∼200 W, scanning speed ∼400 mm/s, layer thickness ∼30 μm, hatch spacing ∼0.10 mm, and the laser focus diameter ∼60 μm. A linear scanning strategy was used during the process, and the scan rotation of ~67° between successive layers was employed. Condition: compressive yield strength at 1600 °C

Processing Text: TiVNbTa RHEA was prepared from high purity (99.95 wt%) Ti, V, Nb, Ta by vacuum levitation melting (VLM), with ingot size of Φ50∗60 mm. Electromagnetic stirring in the VLM process allows the molten liquid alloy to be fully mixed, with a uniform and accurate composition. In addition, during the melting process, the alloy is suspended in the crucible, so that pure alloy can be prepared without pollution. RT tension and compression was tested using an Instron 5967 machine at a strain rate of 5 × 10 −4s −1on plate specimens with a gauge dimension of 3 × 1.9 × 1 mm and rectangular specimen with a size of 2 × 2 × 4 mm, respectively. In order to obtain the high-temperature (HT) mechanical properties of the VLM TiVNbTa alloy, a Gleeble 3500 testing machine was used for compression test at HT. The test temperature was 1273 K and the sample size was 10 mm diameter by 15 mm high. The preparation process for HT samples was similar to those for tension and compression at RT. For comparison with related studies, the strain rate was set to be 10 −3s −1. Condition: as-cast; Context: accompanying with a high yield strength

Processing Text: Materials and methods Argon atomized pre-alloyed (CoCrNi) 94 (TiAl) 6 powder with a particle size range of 15–53 μm was used in this study. The powder particles were processed under a modulated pulsed laser mode using a Renishaw AM 400 system. Samples of 60 × 10 × 12 mm 3 were fabricated in argon for microstructural characterization and tensile test. A mender scanning strategy was used for hatch scanning on each layer and the scanning direction was rotated by 67° for each layer [ 44 ]. To tailor microstructure to achieve the optimum combination of mechanical properties, samples were subjected to ageing treatment at different temperatures including 600 °C, 650 °C, 700 °C, 800 °C and 900 °C for 2 h, respectively. Some samples were aged at a specific temperature (e.g., 700 °C) for different durations such as 10 min, 30 min and 2 h to investigate the influence of ageing duration on microstructure and mechanical properties. Processing Text: Alloys with a nominal composition of Al 0.2Cr 0.9FeNi 2.2Ti 0.2were fabricated by arc melting high-purity raw materials (Al, Cr, Fe, Ni, and Ti with purity higher than 99.9 %) in a Ti-gettered argon atmosphere. To ensure compositional homogeneity, the ingots were inverted and remelted seven times with electromagnetic stirring before drop-casting into a 6 × 25×45 mm copper mold. The as-cast ingots were first solid solution treated at 1150 ℃ for 4 h and then water quenched to room temperature. The solid solution treated ingots were then multipass cold-rolled along a lengthwise direction, with a total reduction of 80 %. Subsequently, the as-rolled ingots were annealed at 1050 ℃ for 10 min followed by air cooling. Finally, the as-annealed ingots were isothermally aged at 600 ℃, 700 ℃, and 800 ℃ for 8 h, respectively. The aged samples are hereinafter denoted as 600A, 700A, and 800A based on their corresponding aging temperatures. To prevent the harmful effects of oxidation during the extended heat-treatment process, the ingots were enclosed in quartz tubes and filled with high-quality argon gas prior to the heat treatment. Processing Text: A straightforward processing route, involving hot rolling followed by annealing, was utilized to produce single-phase FCC HEAs. The (Co 3Cr 1.6FeNi) 100-xCu xHEAs with a nominal composition was fabricated through vacuum melting using a mixture of constituent metal elements (purity >99.95 wt%), under an argon atmosphere containing Zr-gettered material. The melting process was repeated 6 times to ensure the uniformity of the chemical composition. Subsequently, electric discharge machining (EDM) was utilized to machine the button ingot to an 8 mm thickness, then homogenized at 1200 °C for 2 h and subsequent air cooling. Following hot rolling, the samples were heat treated at 700 °C for 1 h and subsequently quenched in water, labeled as Cux (x = 0,2). Processing Text: Ti 1.5Ta 0.5NbZrMo 0.5RHEA was prepared by LPBF. Specifically, this study focuses on how the structure of the precipitates and dislocation tangles affects the high-temperature creep resistance and microstructural evolution. The pure metal powder being used are Ti (20∼74 μm, purity: 99.9 %), Nb (20∼74 μm, purity: 99.9 %), Ta (20∼74 μm, purity: 99.9 %), Zr (53∼105 μm, purity: 99.7 %) and Mo (20∼74 μm, purity: 99.9 %), as shown in Fig. 1a. The powders were mixed according to the nominal composition of RHEA and stirred with a planetary ball mill (Pulverisette-4) for 40 h to achieve the purpose of mechanical alloying, as shown in Fig. 1b. Fig. 1c shows the powder morphology obtained after ball milling and it can be found that a large amount of crushed powder has adhered to the intact spherical powder particles. To check the mixing effect, EDS with a working voltage of 20 kV characterized the mixed powder and the results showed that the Ti 1.5Ta 0.5NbZr 0.5Mo RHEA powder had completed the preliminary mechanical alloying, which ensured the compositional homogeneity of the billet samples prepared by the subsequent rapid prototyping ( Fig. 1d). Cylindrical samples (diameter: 5 mm, height: 7.5 mm) were prepared using commercial LPBF equipment (M2 multi-laser) under an Ar atmosphere. The laser power, scanning speed and layer thickness were 240 W, 1700 mm/s and 0.05 mm, respectively. The Ti 1.5Ta 0.5NbZr 0.5Mo RHEA cylinders were prepared using the LPBF technique and the laser scanning strategy is shown in Fig. 1f. The Archimedes density (ρ A) of the as-built sample was measured by an analytical balance with pure ethanol, according to ASTM B962-08standard. The samples for microstructural characterization are mechanically polished using SiC papers up to 2000 grits and then are precision polished with Cr 2O 3. The microstructures were observed using scanning electron microscopy (SEM, TESCAN VEGA 3), energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), with a working voltage of 20 kV. The grain size distribution is investigated via electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) (MIRA 3, TESCAN, Czech Republic). The step sizes of the EBSD maps were 0.25 μm. The obtained EBSD data was analyzed using the channel 5 software. The nanoscale microstructures were characterized by Transmission electron microscope (TEM). The TEM samples were processed by EDM wire cutting, then ground to 50 μm thickness with abrasive paper, thinned to perforation with argon ions and observed by JEM 2100F. High-angle annular dark-field scanning TEM (HAADF-STEM) images were observed using a Talos F200X G2 with an operating voltage of 200 kV and the GATAN Digital Micrograph software was used to measure the crystal plane spacing and to calibrate selected area electron diffraction (SAED) patterns. Tensile Creep tests were carried out according to ASTM E139 and dimensions of the creep specimen are shown in the Fig. S1. The length direction of the creep samples is perpendicular to the building direction. The tensile creep tests were conducted at 923 K, 973 K, and 1023 K in vacuum of 1 × 10 -4Pa controlled by an oil diffusion pump. The tensile creep tests were conducted under stresses of 30, 60, 90, 120 and 150 Mpa, as shown in Table 1. The strain of the material during creep is measured by a resistance-strain high-temperature extensometer (2632 series, Instron). Experimental value; Prepared using LPBF; Error margin ± 14.7 MPa

Processing Text: Experimental The powder for PBF-LB was obtained by atomization of the vacuum induction melted Fe 65 Co 12.5 Ni 12.5 Cr 9.5 C 0.5 alloy using a US35 atomizer from ATO LAB. PBF-LB of the alloy was carried out in an argon atmosphere using a 3D printer DMP Flex 200 (3D Systems Inc., Rock Hill, SC, USA); the laser power (P) was 200 W, the scanning speed (V) was 1600 mm/s; a 316L steel plate was used as the substrate. The flow rate of the shielding gas (argon) was 5 L per minute. To improve the quality of the workpieces, the direction of laser movement was changed by 67° during fusion of each subsequent layer [ 67 ]. The distance between tracks and the beam diameter were 50 μm and 70 μm, respectively. All the parameters of PBF-LB were selected based on our earlier trials [ 43 ]. Samples for heat treatment, microstructure analysis, and mechanical testing were cut out of the as-produced alloy using an electric discharge machine. The samples were annealed for 60 min in a muffle furnace in air in a temperature range 800–1100 °C; then the specimens were cooled in air. For the sake of convenience, the Fe 65 Co 12.5 Ni 12.5 Cr 9.5 C 0.5 alloy samples produced using PBF-LB were denoted hereafter as PBF-LB (as-sintered), PBF-LB - 800, PBF-LB - 900, PBF-LB - 1000, and PBF-LB - 1100 (annealed at 800, 900, 1000 or 1100 °C, respectively). Samples measured 20 × 10 × 11 mm 3 were cut out using the electric discharge machine and then cold rolled at room temperature. Unidirectional multi-pass rolling of the samples was carried out to a total thickness reduction of 80 % (from 11 to 2.2 mm) with a reduction of 3–5% per pass without intermediate annealing. After cold rolling, the specimens were cut from the sheets and annealed in the muffle furnace at 800 °C for 60 min followed by air cooling. The cold-rolled and annealed conditions were marked hereafter as PBF-LB - CR and PBF-LB - CR-800, respectively. Condition: Cryogenic Temperature (77 K); Processing state: Cold-rolled

Processing Text: The substrate employed in this study is a Q235 steel plate measuring 70 mm × 70 mm × 30 mm. One is spherical 316 L stainless steel powder, with a particle size ranging from 50 μm to 150 μm. The chemical composition of the 316 L stainless steel powder is provided in Table 1. The mixed powder was subsequently placed in a vacuum drying oven and preheated at 150 °C for 2 h to remove moisture and enhance flowability. The powder was then deposited as desired coating using a self-built LDED equipment equipped with a laser of 4 KW and 1060 nm wavelength (Raycus RFL-C4000). The LDED technology utilizes a coaxial powder feeding method to ensure the stability of coating properties. The optimal parameters were identified as a laser power of 1700 W, a scanning speed of 10 mm/s, a spot diameter of 4 mm, a powder feed rate of 1.2 r/min, and an overlap ratio of 50 %. With these optimized parameters, the 316 L composite coating was fabricated via multi-layer, multi-track laser processing, yielding a well-formed surface. After completing the coating process, the uneven top surface of the coating was removed using an electrical discharge wire cutting, and then cut into samples measuring 10 mm × 10 mm × 10 mm and 5 mm × 5 mm × 10 mm for subsequent tests. The metallographic samples were sequentially ground with SiC sandpaper with grades from 240# to 2000#, followed by polishing with 2.5μm diamond polishing paste. Aqua regia (HCl:HNO 3=3:1 V:V) was employed to etch the sample surface for 10-15 s, followed by ultrasonic cleaning with alcohol. The polarization test samples were mechanically polished and subsequently ultrasonically cleaned with alcohol to remove any residual polishing paste and surface impurities. Processing Text: This study employed LPBF to fabricate TiN/GH5188 Co-based superalloy composites with alternative TiN nanoparticle contents (0, 0.5, 1, and 1.5 wt%). A series of TiN/GH5188 composites were synthesized by incorporating nano-TiN particles (obtained from Guangdong Yinna Technology Co., Ltd., China, with an average particle size of ∼100 nm) into gas-atomized GH5188 powder from AVIC Metal Powder Metallurgy Technology Co., Ltd., China. The preparation process, depicted in Fig. 1a, involved premixing the powders, followed by high-energy ball milling using a planetary mill (Retsch, Haan, Germany) at a speed of 280 rpm for 8 h. Silicon dioxide (SiO 2) served as the milling media, with a powder-to-ceramic ball mass ratio of 1:4. Mixed powders were dried in an oven at 100 °C for 20 min to remove moisture before being ready for printing. An LPBF machine (DiMetal-100, Guangzhou Laseradd Additive Technology Co., Ltd., China) was used for sample fabrication, equipped with an IPG fiber laser (maximum output power of 200 W) and a galvanometer (Hurryscan20-1080 nm-XY2, SCANLAB GmbH, Puheim, Germany). GH5188 and TiN/GH5188 composite samples were fabricated on a #45 steel substrate using optimized process parameters. Apply a laser power and scanning speed of 180 W and 900 mm/s, respectively. The layer thickness is 0.03 mm, and the hatching space is fixed at 0.07 mm. Block-shaped samples and tensile specimens were created using an orthogonal scanning strategy with a 45° angle to the airflow and a 90° rotation between layers. The dimensions of the block-shaped samples are 8 × 8 × 8 mm³, while the shape and dimensions of the tensile specimens are shown in Fig. 2c. The block-shaped samples were polished according to standard metallographic procedures, etched by a mixed solution of concentrated HCl and 3.3 wt% H 2O 2in a volume ratio of 4:1 for 60 s to prepare metallographic samples. The surfaces paralleled to the building direction were subjected to argon ion polishing using an ion grinding instrument (IM4000plus, HITACHI, Japan) at a voltage of 4 kV, an angle of 3°, and a duration of 2 h. Processing Text: The Ni 1.5FeCrCu 0.5HEA was fabricated using the vacuum induction melting (VIM) technology, employing high-purity Fe, Ni, Cr, and Cu metals at 99.5 %. The as-cast HEA ingot underwent machining to remove surface layers and was cut using a wire-cut machine into samples with dimensions of 80 × 30 × 50 mm³. Subsequently, the specimens underwent a process of cold rolling to achieve different thickness reductions of 24, 45, 65, and 85 %. A rolling machine, with a load of 20 tons and a roll diameter of 140 mm, was utilized for this process. Following each reduction, samples were strategically cut along the ND-RD cross-section to explore and analyze the intricate microstructure. To investigate the microstructure through the electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) technique, the specimens were polished with 6-, 3-, and 1-μm polishing pads for 3 min after sanding. Following this, the samples were placed on a vibratory machine with oxide polishing suspensions (OPS) for 16 h. Additionally, the central layer of the RD-TD section was mechanically polished to examine the bulk texture. Eventually, specimens for tensile testing were created, having a gauge length of 6.4 mm and a width of 2.5 mm. Deformed samples' phase and texture evolution were comprehensively analyzed with a Philips-XPERT X-ray Diffractometer (XRD) equipped with Cu-Kα radiation (λ = 0.15406 nm). The microstructure of the deformed alloys underwent study using a scanning electron microscopy (SEM) equipped with a high resolution (1244 × 1024 pixels) Oxford electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) Symmetry® S3 detector (CMOS sensor technology) integrated with the AZtecHKL software. Observation of the microstructure of deformed materials at 200 keV was undertaken using a transmission electron microscope (TEM) (JEM-2100F, JEOL, Japan). Using the same electrolyte as for EBSD samples, the TEM samples (about 100 mm thick) were created in a twin jet Tenupol-5 electrolytic polisher at 10 °C with a flow rate of 10, and voltage of 24 V. Micro-hardness tests were carried out under a force of 10 kg for 30 s to determine Vickers hardness. Tensile tests, conducted at room temperature according to ASTM E8Mstandard, utilized a universal uniaxial testing machine (Hounsfield H25KS). Subsequently, SEM was employed to assess the fracture surfaces after tensile tests. Processing state: 85 % cold rolled

Processing Text: The experimental material used in this study was Hastelloy C276 wire with a diameter of 6 mm produced by Nanye Metal products Technology Co., Ltd. (Jiangsu, China). A four-roll mill with a diameter of 70 mm was employed to carry out the cold rolling pre-experiments of three different series of deformations. The samples using 10% single-pass deformation have been conducted 20 passes in total and the final total deformation is 87.8%. The samples using 20% single-pass deformation have been conducted 10 passes in total and the final total deformation is 89.3%. The samples using 40% single-pass deformation have been conducted 4 passes in total and the final total deformation is 87.0%. In the subsequent heat treatment experiments, samples with a total deformation of 49.7%, 71.3%, and 79.9% were selected for strip samples A, B, and C. To ensure that surface cracks do not occur, all three types of samples were rolled with a 10% single-pass deformation. Sample A requires 5 passes, B requires 9 passes, and C requires 13 passes, respectively. Then A、B、C were conducted by heat treatment. The heat treatment temperature was chosen from 1070 to 1190 °C and conducted an experiment every 30 °C, while the soaking time was selected at 5, 10, 20, and 40 min, followed by water cooling. Hence, twenty sets of heat treatment experiments were performed. The final substrate is prepared by alternating heat treatment and rolling, and the surface of the substrate is mechanically polished using 0.5CR alumina solution and argon ion polished under 3-5 keV for 60 min by IM4000II to obtain the final nanoscale roughness.
