Processing Text: A lightweight steel having a chemical composition, in wt. %, of Fe-26Mn-8Al-3Mo-1.2C-0.02Nb (wt.%), was cast in an induction furnace under Ar atmosphere and then hot rolled into plates. Subsequently, after the plates were solution treated at 1050 °C for 1 h followed by water quenching, they were cold rolled to obtain a reduction in thickness of 55 %. Finally, the samples cut from the plates were annealed at various temperatures (750, 800, 825, 850, and 900 °C) for 1 h, and then cooled in water. The microstructure after annealing consists of heterogeneous recrystallized, unrecrystallized grains containing nanoscale Mo 2C precipitates, and intergranular Mo-enriched carbides. As the annealing temperature increases, the fraction of recrystallization grains, and average Schmid factor increase, while the average grain sizes and the volume fraction of Mo 2C decrease. Annealing at 825 °C results in a desirable heterogeneous structure with normal bimodal grain distribution and uniform dispersion of nanoscale Mo 2C particles. Annealed at 800°C

Processing Text: The ingot with nominal composition Fe40Ni30Cr20Al5Ti5 (at.%) HEA was fabricated by vacuum arc-melting technology under an argon atmosphere. All alloy ingots with a mass of about 120 g were then drop-cast into a copper mold to form plates with dimensions of 6 × 12 × 60 mm3, subsequently homogenized at 1200 °C for 2 h, followed by water-cooled. And then cold rolled to ∼1.2 mm with a thickness reduction of ∼80 %. A two-step heat treatment scheme was applied on the cold-rolled sheets: annealing for 3 min at 1150 °C followed by water cooling (referred to as A0) to achieve fully recrystallized microstructure, the final aging treatment was carried out for 4 h at different temperatures (700 °C, 800 °C, 900 °C, referred to as A700, A800, A900), also followed by water quenching. The EBSD and SEM specimens were polished with 3000-grit SiC papers and followed by twin-jet electropolishing in a solution of 90 % ethanol and 10 % perchloric acid at −25 °C under a direct voltage of 20V. TEM samples with a diameter of 3 mm were first mechanically ground to a thickness of 50 μm, then twin-jet polished in a solution of 90 % ethanol and 10 % perchloric acid at around −25 °C under a direct voltage of 25V. For the tensile tests, the specimens were cut into dog-bone shapes with gage dimensions of 1 × 2 × 15 mm3 and were machined and polished. Room temperature tensile tests were performed on the Instron 5582 testing machine at a strain rate of 1 × 10−3s−1. Aging treatment: 800 °C for 4h; Phases: sigma and L21 co-precipitated in FCC matrix

Processing Text: A Ti-23Nb at.% alloy was prepared by cold crucible levitation melting using 99.99% pure Ti and 99.9% pure Nb. Ingots were homogenized at 1273 K for 120 min followed by water quenching, and hot rolling at approximately 1173 K. The resulting ingot was cut into chips that were cold-rolled to a 60% thickness reduction, achieving a final thickness of approximately 2 mm at room temperature. These sheets were then fully recrystallized at 1123 K for 15 min in a pure Ar atmosphere, followed by water quenching to attain the solution-treated (ST) alloy. Some ST samples were cut into cuboids with cross-sectional dimensions of 10.5 × 2 mm, which were annealed at 573 K for 10 min and then cooled in air and furnace to produce the air-cooled (AC) and furnace-cooled (FC) samples, respectively. The samples with gage dimensions of 3 × 15 × 2 mm 3 for the tensile tests were cut by an electric discharge machine along the rolling direction (RD). Full α″-type ST samples of a Ti-23Nb alloy were annealed at 573 K to induce the α″ → β reverse martensitic transformation and ω precipitation. Thereafter, ω-strengthened β-type Ti-23Nb samples were acquired by slowly cooling the annealed samples via either air cooling (AC samples) or furnace cooling (FC samples). Sample type: ST (solution-treated); Microstructure: full α″ martensites

Processing Text: The bulk MoNbTaW RHEA was fabricated by laser energy deposition on the TC4 substrate. Prior to the process, the substrate was washed using alcohol and then dried in a drying furnace at 200 °C for 2 h. The raw powders were blended using a ball mill for 12 h to obtain the mixed powder, which was dried in a furnace at 120 °C for 3 h. The pre-experiments were conducted in order to obtain samples without any macroscopic cracks and holes on the surface. The deposition path has been designed to ensure the flatness of the sample surface and reduce the formation of cracks and holes. The optimized process parameters are as follows: a powder feed rate of 0.2 r min−1, a protecting argon gas flow of 15 L min−1, a laser power of 1200 W, and a scanning speed of 10 mm s−1. The wire-cutting method was utilized to prepare the cuboid samples measuring 12*12*5 mm3 for composition analysis and wear testing and 5*5*2 mm3 for oxidation tests. In addition, cylinder samples with a diameter of 3.6 mm and a height of 5.4 mm were prepared for the compression tests. The oxidation tests were performed with a heat-treatment furnace (KSL-1200×-M) in an air environment. The cuboid samples were ground with sandpaper to remove the oxide layer from their surfaces. Afterward, the processed samples were cleaned with alcohol to eliminate any impurities. To investigate the impact of temperature on oxide behavior, the oxidation tests were conducted using temperature gradients of 500, 650 and 800 °C. Additionally, the weight of the samples was recorded before and after the oxidation test to draw oxidation kinetics curves. The oxide scales collected from the surface on oxidation samples were ground using a circular glass container to obtain a mixed powder of oxidation products. This mixed powder was subsequently sieved to meet the XRD observation requirements. To improve the repeatability of experiments, each experiment was repeated three times to calculate the average value of mass gain. The wear behavior of the MoNbTaW RHEA was investigated through the reciprocating sliding wear tests at 500 and 600 °C. Under specific conditions, the wear tests are conducted using the multifunctional wear tester (UMT-TriboLab). The applied normal load is 4 N, with a wear time of 20 min, a wear frequency of 2 Hz, and a stroke length of 10 mm. The Si3N4 balls with a diameter of 6 mm have been chosen as frictional pairs. The 3D white light profiling system (Bruker Contour GT-K) is utilized to obtain the wear volume and wear coefficient. Additionally, the microstructure and composition of the wear surface are analyzed by SEM. Condition: at 1400 °C; Reported by Senkov et al.
Processing Word: Condition: at 1400 °C; Reported by Senkov et al.

The process parameters adopted for DED were laser power of 400-650 W, laser scanning speed of 4 mm/s, layer thickness of 76 μm and a hatching distance of 305 μm. Processing Text: Four types of ingots, namely Cu-3Ni-1Ti, Cu-3Ni-1Ti-0.1Zr, Cu-3Ni-1Ti-0.3Zr, and Cu-3Ni-1Ti-0.5Zr, were fabricated utilizing copper rods (with a purity of 99.95 wt%), nickel particles (with a purity of 99.95 wt%), titanium particles (with a purity of 99.95 wt%), and a Cu40Zr intermediate alloy (containing 40 % Zr) as raw materials. The fabrication process was conducted in a vacuum induction melting furnace operating under an argon atmosphere. These ingots were subsequently subjected to homogenization treatment at 850 °C for 12 h in a resistance furnace, followed by hot-rolling to reduce their thickness by 50 %. Afterward, a solid solution treatment was carried out at 950 °C for 1 h, followed by rapid water cooling. Subsequently, the ingots were subjected to multiple cold-rolling passes to achieve 90 % cold deformation. Finally, aging treatment was performed at temperatures ranging from 450 °C to 550 °C for durations varying from 0 to 15 h. To comprehensively analyze the microstructure of the samples, a variety of advanced techniques were employed. Initially, a scanning electron microscope (SEM, TESCAN MIRA3 LMH) equipped with an energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS) was used to examine the microstructural features of samples in different states: as-cast, solid solution, and cold-rolled conditions. Following the SEM analysis, a scanning electron microscope with electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) capability (∑IGMA, Carl Zeiss) was employed to further elucidate the crystallographic structure and grain boundary characteristics of the aged samples. Sample preparation for SEM and EBSD involved meticulous polishing using different grades of SiC sandpaper, followed by electrolytic polishing using a solution comprising 30 % HNO 3and 70 % alcohol. To investigate the distribution, structure, and composition of precipitated phases within the samples, a transmission electron microscope (TEM, Tecnai G2 20) was utilized for detailed examination and analysis. The preparation procedure for TEM samples included slicing into thin sections using a wire electric discharge machine to achieve approximately 800 μm, followed by mechanical grinding down to around 60 μm. Subsequently, a dual-jet electrolytic polishing method was employed, utilizing a methanol solution containing 35 % nitric acid at a temperature range of −30 ± 5 °C. Furthermore, we also conducted hardness, ultimate tensile strength, and conductivity tests. The hardness test was performed using a micro Vickers hardness tester (Huayin 200HVS-5) with an experimental load of 0.5 Kg and a holding time of 15 s. At least five measurements were recorded for each sample, and the average of these measurements was used as the final result. The ultimate tensile strength test was carried out using a universal electronic testing machine (UTM 4204) at a testing rate of 0.1 mm/s. Additionally, the conductivity test was conducted using an eddy current conductivity tester (Sigmascope SMP350, SIGMASCOPE), and the final conductivity value was determined as the average of five data points. Processing Text: Argon atomized equiatomic AlCoCrFeNi HEA powder and high purity Ni powder (>99.9 wt%) both with a particle size range of 15-53 μm were blended for 6 h at a rotation speed of 28 rpm in an argon atmosphere using a three-dimensional (3D) swing powder mixer to prepare AlCoCrFeNi2.1 HEA powder. The mixed powder was then processed by L-PBF under a modulated pulsed laser mode using a Renishaw AM 400 system equipped with a ytterbium fiber laser. The oxygen level in the building chamber was reduced to below 50 ppm prior to sample fabrication. A laser power of 325 W, a point exposure duration of 60 μs, a powder layer thickness of 50 μm, a point distance of 60 μm and a hatch distance of 90 μm were used for the sample building. A Meander scanning strategy was used for hatch scanning on each layer and the scanning direction was rotated by 67° after each layer. Some of the as-printed samples were subsequently subjected to an aging treatment at 500 °C, 600 °C, 700 °C and 800 °C for 5 h in vacuum (∼10−6Pa), respectively, followed by air cooling. The as-built samples and the L-PBF-processed plus aged samples were sectioned along the build height direction by electrical discharge machining (EDM) and ground using SiC papers from 320 grit up to 2400 grit before being polished using 3 μm diamond suspension and colloidal silica suspension (or OPS solution). The samples were then electrolytically etched in a solution containing 10 g Oxalic acid and 100 mL water for microstructural characterization by optical microscopy (OM) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) via a SUPRA55 electron microscope. Prior to the TEM study, disc specimens of 3 mm in diameter were machined out of the materials, ground to a thickness of 40-50 μm and then electropolished in a solution made from 5 vol% perchloric acid and 95 vol% alcohol using a twin-jet electro-polishing system. Tensile specimens with a gauge length of 23 mm and a reduced section diameter of 4 mm were machined out of the horizontally built samples. Uniaxial tensile tests were conducted at a nominal strain rate of 5 × 10−4/s. Condition: directly cast; Microstructure: lamellar duplex-phase with L12 ordered FCC and B2 phases

Processing Text: A commercial 304 ASS with a chemical composition of Fe-18.16Cr-8.06Ni-0.85Mn-0.41Si-0.06C (mass%) was used in this study. To fabricate an ultrafine-grained microstructure, a two-step cold rolling and annealing process was employed. The as-received plate (25 mm thick) first underwent multi-pass cold rolling to achieve a thickness of 4 mm, followed by annealing at 750 ℃ for 10 min and subsequently quenching in water. Subsequently, the plate was further cold rolled to 1.2 mm and annealed at 700 ℃ for 10 min, followed by water quenching. The UFG 304 ASS, fabricated by simple cold rolling and annealing, consisted of quasi-full austenite with a mean grain size of 0.35 μm and 7 % retained martensite. Processing Text: A 3 Kg CoCrFeNiAl 0.5Ti 0.1HEA ingot, with elemental purity exceeding 99.9 %, was fabricated using the vacuum arc melting method four times. The alloy ingot was annealed at 1100 °C for 4 h. Subsequently, it was forged into a rod with a diameter of 21 mm using a 400 kg forging machine. The initial billet temperature was approximately 1050 °C, decreasing to about 900 °C by the end of forging. TEM samples were first mechanically ground to a thickness of 30 μm, then twin-jet electro-polished using a solution of HNO 3:CH 4O = 1:4. Cylindrical tensile specimens, 15 mm in gage length and 3 mm in diameter, were machined from forged rods. These specimens were then polished using SiC paper up to 2000 grit. The samples were initially sanded with SiC paper up to 2000 grit to ensure a smooth surface. Then samples were polished with a polishing machine using a sequence of decreasing abrasive sizes until the surface was scratch-free. The polished samples were cleaned with ethanol and dried to remove any debris or contaminants. For high-temperature tests at 873 K, 1073 K, and 1273 K, the samples were heated by convective heat transfer from an induction-heated stainless steel susceptor at a rate of 1 K/s. Once the desired temperature was achieved, it was maintained for 15 min to allow the material to equilibrate. Temperature: 77 K

Processing Text: Ti2NbVAl0.3Zrx (x = 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1) LRHEAs were prepared by the vacuum arc melting furnace under the protection of high-purity argon gas. Metal particles with purity >99.95 % were used as raw materials. In order to avoid melting losses and melting segregation, Ti-Al and Zr-V-Nb intermediate alloys were prepared. Finally, the intermediate alloys were combined and melted six times repeatedly. Before melting, the air pressure in the chamber was reduced to 3*10−3Pa and the chamber underwent five purging cycles with high-purity argon gas. This was followed by melting Ti ingots to remove residual oxygen in the chamber and prevent sample contamination. SEM samples were polished using a 0.3 μm alumina suspension, followed by metallographic etching using a solution of HCL, HNO3, and HF in a ratio of 10:3:1. TEM samples were mechanically ground to 50 μm and subsequently thinned using an ionic thinning machine (Gatan 695). Tensile tests were conducted on the specimens using an electronic universal testing machine (Instron 68 MT-55) at a quasi-static strain rate of 1*10−3S−1. The tensile samples were identified with a section size of 5mm × 2mm × 1.5 mm and were mechanically ground to 2000 mesh prior to the commencement of the experiment. Vickers hardness of the samples was measured using TMHV-1000Z with a load of 200g and a force holding time of 15s. The corrosion behavior of the current alloy system was tested using an electrochemical workstation (VersaSTAT 3F) in a 3.5 wt% NaCl solution. The sample size was 10mm × 10mm × 4 mm, with a test area 1 cm2, and was mechanically ground to 2000 mesh prior to testing. Electrochemical tests were conducted in a three-electrode electrolytic cell setup, with the sample serving as the working electrode, the saturated calomel electrode (SCE) as the reference electrode, and the platinum electrode as the auxiliary electrode. The open circuit potential was initially stabilized for 1800s, followed by potentiodynamic polarization (PDP) and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) tests. The PDP test was conducted at a scan rate of 0.333 mV/s, starting from an initial potential of −0.3V SCE(vs. OCP) and ending at 2V SCE(vs. OCP). EIS measurements were carried out with an amplitude of 5 mV/s and a frequency range from 105Hz to 10−2Hz. Each sample underwent three tests under identical conditions to ensure result accuracy. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS; Thermo Scientific K-Alpha) analyzed the oxide film formed on the sample surface. Fracture elongation: ∼9.4 %
Processing Word: Fracture elongation: ∼9.4 %

Processing Text: Spherical and non-porous powders were prepared using the plasma rotating electrode method. The particle sizes ranged from 45 μm to 220 μm. To improve the powder's fluidity during the deposition process, the powder was dried in a vacuum environment at 100 ± 10 °C for 4 h. A TC4 sheet measuring 150 mm × 150 mm × 30 mm was selected as the substrate. Before testing, the upper surface was polished with a grinding wheel and cleaned with ethanol and acetone to improve the laser absorptivity. The LDED equipment consists of a laser system, a powder delivery system, a CNC motion system, and an argon gas protection chamber. The laser beam created a molten pool on the substrate's upper surface during deposition. Three coaxial nozzles powered by argon gas inject and melt the titanium alloy powder into the molten pool. The robot drove the movement of the laser head assembly to form a layer-by-layer molten metal track on the surface of the substrate. The serpentine reciprocating scanning strategy was adopted. Throughout the entire procedure, the sample was kept in a clean argon environment (O₂ < 0.02 %, H₂O < 0.05 %) to avoid oxidation. The near-α titanium alloy was annealed by standard heat treatment. Temperatures ranging from 650 to 850 °C were selected for stress relief annealing temperature. 950 °C was chosen for recrystallization annealing. The super-transformation treatment temperature exceeded the β-transformation temperature (1030 ± 5 °C). Consequently, the super-transformation annealing temperature was 1050 °C. The specimens were air-cooled after being annealed for 4 h in an SA2-9-12 TP air resistance furnace. Condition: As-deposited; Direction: H
Processing Word: Condition: As-deposited; Direction: H

Processing Text: The multi-component ingots, with a nominal composition of Fe2Ni2CrAlx (x =0.9, 1.1, 1.2, 1.3), was prepared through the vacuum arc melting technique. The elemental metals, with boasted a purity exceeding 99.9%, were melted within a water-cooled copper mold. Arc melting were conducted under an atmosphere of ultrahigh-purity argon (Ar). The ingots experienced at least 5 re-melting cycles. The microstructures of the alloys were analyzed using electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) measurements, which were carried out using a SEM equipped with a EDAX detector and TSL OIM data collection software. Density of the Fe2Ni2CrAlx MPEAs were measured by using the Archimedes method. Each sample underwent five measurements to obtain averaged values. The solidus and liquidus temperatures were determined using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC). The DSC scans encompassed a temperature range from 25 °C to 1500 °C, at a rate of 10 °C/min during the heating cycles. It maintains a continuous flow of argon (Ar) during the process. The mechanical properties of the samples were evaluated using compressive tests at elevated temperatures. The compression tests of Φ4mm×6mm cylindrical samples were performed on the AG-X Plus 250 kN/50 kN Electronic Universal Testing Machine. The initial strain rate was 2 mm/min and the temperature was 200 °C, 400 °C, 600 °C and 800 °C. The testing was performed until the fracture of the samples or reaching a reduction of 70%, whichever was earlier. Three compression tests were conducted to derive the average value. Temperature: 200 °C
Processing Word: Temperature: 200 °C

Processing Text: The specimens were produced from a plate of S690QL steel with 20 mm of thickness. The S690QL steel is a high-strength structural steel compliant with the British Standard BS EN 10025-6: 2004+A1: 2009. The sample was grounded using silicon carbide papers #80, #180, #220, #400, #600, #800, #1200 and #2500 in succession and in this order, polished and then etched with Nital (2% nitric acid). The specimens were prepared by grinding them successively with silicon carbide papers #400, #800, #1000, and #2000, followed by cleaning in an ultrasonic bath with ethanol. This process served two crucial purposes: removing naturally formed oxides and degreasing, thus achieving uniformity across all specimens. The grips were safeguarded from corrosion by applying a coating of spray paint on both sides, a layer of black electrical tape followed by a coating of silicone on the side that would be immersed in the solution. The specimens were stored in a desiccator until testing to prevent premature corrosion. To induce pre-corrosion, the specimens were placed in a three-electrode cell setup consisting of: the working electrode, which is a specimen of the S690 QL steel; the platinum wire counter electrode; the silver chloride electrode (Ag/AgCl electrode) reference electrode; and a water-based solution of 3.5% sodium chloride (3.5%NaCl) as the electrolyte. The specimens were left for 30 min in open circuit to reach a more stable surface state. At the end of that period, a current of 0.25 A was applied to the system for 8745 s (≈2 h 26 min) using the potentiostat’s Galvanostatic Scan function. All tests were conducted at room temperature. After corrosion, the specimens were cleaned under running water and brushed with a light plastic bristle brush, followed by an ultrasonic bath in ethanol. Quasi-static tensile tests were performed on four round-type specimens complying with the standard ASTM-E8/E8M-22. An extensometer with a 50 mm gauge length was employed to measure strain, and the tests were performed under displacement control at a velocity of 1 mm/min. Processing Text: The wire-cut specimens were extracted from 10H2M steel pipe sections of 1 m long delivered in both, the as-received state and after extensive exploitation for 280,000 h at high temperature equal to 540 °C under the internal pressure of 2.9 MPa, as specified by the power plant maintenance service. The hourglass specimens used for either standard tensile or fatigue tests were wire-cut and machined from the as-received and exploited pipelines made of 10H2M steel. Uniaxial tensile tests were executed to determine material characteristics and typical strength parameters like the yield strength for example under strain rate equal to 2 × 10 −4s −1. Fatigue tests identified another important effect, namely, due to exploitation a significant decrease of the fatigue lifetime was observed for the entire range of stress amplitudes considered. Two sets of selected specimens (as-received and exploited) after fatigue tests at four stress amplitudes (±320 MPa, ±350 MPa, ±370 MPa and ± 400 MPa) were analysed. SEM analysis confirmed, that the long-term exploitation of the 10H2M steel in the power plant working conditions strongly effects its fracture mechanisms, and a consequence, its ability to further safe work. Processing Text: The EHEA with a nominal composition of Al 21Co 19.5Fe 9.5Ni 50 was prepared by arc-melting a mixture of constituent elements with a purity higher than 99.99 wt.% in a high-purity argon atmosphere. Before the melting process, the surfaces of each metal block were mechanically cleaned to remove surface oxides. Each alloy sample was melted five times for one minute and flipped over each melting to ensure complete mixing and chemical homogeneity. Solution treatment at 900 and 1100 °C followed by furnace cooling to room temperature leads to a significant precipitation of L1 2 phases within the FCC phases. Furthermore, solution treatment at the same temperature, followed by rapid water quenching, results in the appearance of numerous L1 0 phases within the B2 phases. After solid-solution treatments at 900 °C for 1 h, the samples were cooled to room temperature using three different cooling methods: furnace cooling (at a rate of 5 °C min -1), air cooling, and water quenching. These samples were named as 900F, 900A, and 900W, respectively. Subsequently, following a 1-h solid-solution treatment at 1100 °C, the specimens were cooled to room temperature using the same cooling methods, resulting in samples named 1100F, 1100A, and 1100W, respectively. Solution treatment: 900 °C/1 h/Furnace cooling (900F)

Processing Text: The equimolar CoCrFeNi HEA ingot used in this work was prepared by vacuum induction levitation melting from pure Co, Cr, Fe, and Ni metals with 99.9 wt.% purity constituent elements. The ingot was remelted four times to promote chemical homogeneity and then dropped into a rectangular cross-section copper mold with a length of 300 mm and an inner diameter of 25 mm. The ingot was cut to a rod of diameter 20 mm and length 200 mm, which was then homogenized at 1473 K for 24 h. The rod was first hot-rotary swaged to 8 mm in diameter along the longitudinal direction after preheating at 1173 K for 1 h, and then hot-drawn to 1 mm in steps at 1023 K. Subsequently, the HEA wires of diameter 1 mm was subjected to multi-pass cold-drawing at ambient temperature with an areal reduction of ∼10% followed by annealing at 1173 K for 1 h in each step, resulting in a final diameter of ∼70 μm with a length of more than 300 m. The CoCrFeNi microfibers were further treated by ECT. The electric current was applied parallel to the length direction of the treated microfiber using a precision direct current (DC) power supply for 480 s with various current densities of j= 100, 120, 140, 160, 180, 200 A/mm 2, and the corresponding specimens are labeled as ECT100, ECT120, ECT140, ECT160, ECT180 and ECT200, which reach a stable temperature of 623 K, 747 K, 850 K, 943 K, 1013 K, and 1075 K during the ECT, respectively, as measured by an FLIR A325sc infrared camera. For comparison, CHT was also performed on another batch of CoCrFeNi microfibers at 623 K, 747 K, 850 K, 943 K, 1013 K, and 1075 K for 480 s, with the samples labeled as CHT623, CHT747, CHT850, CHT943, CHT1013 and CHT1075, respectively. Processed with electric current treatment (ECT) at a current density of 140 A/mm²; Microstructure: homogeneous ultrafine grains, low dislocation density, and dense 9R phase
Processing Word: Processed with electric current treatment (ECT) at a current density of 140 A/mm²; Microstructure: homogeneous ultrafine grains, low dislocation density, and dense 9R phase

Processing Text: The AlNbTiVZr RHEA powder was prepared by plasma rotating electrode process (PREP), and the atomic percentages of each element are shown in Table 1. The morphology of the alloy powder is shown in Fig. 1(a). The XRD pattern shown in Fig. 1(b) reveals that the alloy powder is composed of the body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solution phase. The process was conducted in a laser direct energy deposition system, as shown in Fig. 1(c). The deposition process was carried out on a TA15 substrate with the X scanning direction. A zigzag scanning strategy in XOY plane was adopted to deposit each layer. The zigzag scanning strategy was adopted and the reasons were as below: firstly, this path ensured that the laser beam evenly deposits energy on the surface, thus achieving uniform heating and alloying of the workpiece surface; secondly, the Z-shaped path could effectively reduce the residual stress and deformation of the material, thereby improving processing quality and accuracy [22,23]. The process parameters were as below: the diameter of the laser beam was 3 mm; the laser power was 1600 W; the powder feeding rate was 7 g/min; and the scanning speed was 10 mm/s. The entire preparation process was carried out in an argon-protected atmosphere with an oxygen content below 100 ppm. Cylindrical specimens with a diameter of 4 mm and a height of 6 mm were prepared by cutting the deposited block using the wire electrical discharge machining (WEDM) technique. The surface of the compression samples were cleaned with sandpaper before conducting the hot compression tests at room temperature, 600 ℃, 700 ℃, and 800 ℃ using a DSI-Gleeble 3500 equipment. The samples were heated from room temperature to preseted temperature using a heating device with a ramp rate of 10 ℃/s and held for 300 seconds after reaching the preseted temperature. The compression tests were performed at a strain rate of 0.001 s -1 with a strain of 50%. Condition: Room Temperature; Processing state: synthesized by levitation melting

Processing Text: Metallic-glass-crystal composites of Cu47.5Zr47.5Al5 are obtained by flash-annealing of metallic-glass ribbons. Metallic glasses are typically prepared by rapid cooling from the liquid state. Master alloys with the nominal compositions of Cu47.5Zr47.5Al5 were prepared from high-purity elements (> 99.98%) by arc melting under Ar atmosphere (5 N). Glassy ribbons (1.2−1.4 mm wide, 30−35 μm thick) were obtained from the master ingots by using the melt-spinning technique. From these ribbons, ∼5.4 cm long pieces were cut for resistive annealing (an actively heated length was 3 cm) in a device custom-built at IFW Dresden. Cu47.5Zr47.5Al5 MGCCs with the predominant B2 CuZr phase were obtained via single-step annealing at Φ ≈ 1200 ± 100 K s−1. The power was shut immediately when Tx was reached, detected by a resistance drop. About 3 cm long samples were cut out from as-spun MG ribbons for the tensile tests. In situ high-energy XRD measurements during mechanical testing were carried out at the P21.1 beamline, PETRA III synchrotron radiation source at the Deutsches Elektronen-Synchrotron DESY Hamburg. In order to increase the strength of fully-crystalline Cu46.5Zr48Al4Nb1.5 samples while maintaining their ductility, more attention was subsequently paid to the role of the Cu10Zr7 phase. To eliminate the effect of the remaining glassy phase on mechanical properties and to further understand the role of the crystalline phases in the deformation mechanism, two-step annealing in vacuum was carried out with Cu47.5Zr47.5Al5 MG ribbons. The grain size and volume fraction of the Cu10Zr7 phase were controlled by adjusting the annealing time of the second step in which the phase transformation PT1 (Cu10Zr7 → B2 CuZr) and even PT2 (Cu10Zr7 → τ4) occurred. Cu47.5Zr47.5Al5 MG has a wide Φ-processing window for the formation of MG-B2 composites with a minimum Φ of ∼500 K s−1. To fabricate MGCCs containing predominantly the B2 CuZr phase, an optimum Φ of ∼1200 K s−1 was chosen in the present work. The volume fraction of crystalline phases identified by Rietveld-refinement of XRD data is given in Table 2. The measured stress-strain curves (σ-ε) are plotted in Fig. 2(a). The corresponding microstructures of fractured samples of a fully-crystalline sample (Al5C) and two composites (Al5GC#1 and Al5GC#2) are shown in Fig. 2(b-d). The measured mechanical properties are listed in Table 2. The introduction of B2 crystals into the glassy matrix decreased the yield stress σy but improved the ductility conforming to the study of flash-annealed MGCCs of Cu47.5Zr47.5Al5 MG ribbons. The higher strength of the MGCC in the present study can be explained by the significantly smaller diameter of B2 CuZr crystals, i.e., ∼10 µm on average. In situ XRD measurements of Cu47.5Zr47.5Al5 MGCC (sample Al5GC#1) carried out in the present study showed that tensile deformation was accompanied by a remarkable martensitic transformation (MT, B2 CuZr ↔ B19′/B33 CuZr) initiated upon yielding. Fig. 4 shows cycled tensile loading/unloading experiments of Cu47.5Zr47.5Al5 MGCC (sample Al5GC#2). The stress required for the MT onset showed an apparent decrease from 969 ± 20 to 514 ± 20 MPa between the 1st and 4th cycles. The volume fraction of the remained B19′/B33 martensite increased from ∼0% in the 1st cycle to ∼14% in the 4th cycle (∼41% remaining) after unloading. Processing Text: Al-6.54Mg-0.36Sc-0.11Zr (wt%) components were successfully manufactured by WAAM with an interlayer temperature at 100 °C (named IW) and continuous printing (named CP). The WAAM system mainly consists of a Fronius welding system, an ABB six-axis robot system, and a computer system. The Fronius welding system includes a cold metal transfer (CMT) welding power supply, a wire feeder, a cooling water tank, and a gas feeding system. The first layer adopted CMT + P mode with a current of 177 A. CMT + Adv mode was selected for the second and subsequent deposition layers. The current and scanning speed were 100 A and 6 mm/s respectively. Before WAAM, the preheating temperature of the substrate was 150 °C. The oxide film on the surface of the 5A06 substrate was removed by a wire brush and the surface was cleaned by acetone. The WAAM conditions included controlling the interlayer temperature at 100 °C and continuously printing. After printing, the components were subjected to aging heat treatment at a temperature of 325 °C, a heating rate of 10 °C/min, and an aging time of 6 h. The as-deposited component was named AD and the heat-treated component was named HT. Condition: as-deposited (AD)

Processing Text: The principal consumable materials were synthesized in powdered form utilizing commercially available Fe-based flux-cored wire, denominated as G6. The investigated feedstock powder exhibited a nearly spherical morphology and was atomized using nitrogen gas atomization. The average particle diameter of the feedstock powder was determined to be 94.7 μm, with particle sizes ranging from 58.2 μm (D 10) to 139 μm (D 90), as shown in Fig. 1. The chemical composition of the G6 powder was analyzed using inductively coupled plasma-optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES), which revealed a nominal composition of Fe-9.3Cr-2.3Si-0.4 C-0.38Mn in weight percent (wt.%). Five distinct laser power settings were selected based on their substantial influence on the energy density across various parameter sets, thereby affecting the average grain size in the central region of the deposit. Each deposited block consisted of 10 layers, with the deposition area maintained constant throughout all the deposition processes. The laser power was determined through a preliminary series of experiments conducted prior to this study, which yielded stable tracks with uniform geometry (see Fig. 2 (b)). The design of experiments for single parts included various laser powers ranging from 300 W to 900 W, with intervals of 150 W. The powder deposition rate, scanning velocity, and coaxial gas flow were consistently maintained at 5 g/min, 850 mm/min, and 8 L/min, respectively. A beam diameter of 1 mm and a layer thickness of 250 μm were consistently applied for the deposition of each layer across all specimens of the Fe-Cr-Si based hardfacing alloy. It was observed that surface quality at power settings of 750 W and 900 W was significantly inferior, whereas the surface quality and geometric accuracy improved markedly at the setting of 450 W. The highest hardness observed in an additively manufactured part was at 600 W, achieving an average hardness of 554 HV. It is evident that a laser power of 450 W facilitates a notably enhanced surface morphology, and thus, was selected as the optimized laser power condition for processing parameters during repair operations. For microstructural characterization, the laser repaired G6 were sectioned along the middle of the edge in the XZ plane. To minimize the influence of temperature, unintended phase formation, strain, and residual stress on the microstructures, the specimens were machined using wire electrical discharge machining (wire-EDM). Subsequently, metallographic specimens were subjected to a series of grinding steps utilizing SiC grinding papers up to a grit size of 4000. The specimens were then polished using colloidal silica with a particle size of 0.04 μm and rinsed with ethanol to remove any residual silica from the surface. To reveal the boundaries of the melt pools (MPBs) and examine the microstructure, Beraha's reagent was used to etch the deposits [ 51]. Microstructural imaging was conducted using a Zeiss A1 optical microscope (OM) and a JEOL 7800F field emission scanning electron microscope (FE-SEM) equipped with Aztec Energy Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDS). The specimens were analyzed using a Rigaku SmartLab X-ray diffraction (XRD) instrument equipped with a Cu Kα anticathode (λ = 1.5412 Å). XRD was operated at 45 kV and 200 mA in a theta-2theta scan mode to identify the phases present. The diffraction angle ranged from 30° to 100°, with a scan rate of 2°/min. Processing Text: To reduce the initial sheet thickness for both alloys to 3 mm, cold-rolling and solution treatment at a temperature of 1100 °C was performed, followed by water quenching. FSW was conducted on a research-type FSW apparatus. The rotational speed, travel speed, and tile angle of the stir tool were 500 rpm, 40 mm/min, and 2.5°, respectively. In addition, the plunge depth of the shoulder was set to be 0.25 mm. The N-HEA and N-steel sheets were positioned on the advanced side (AS) and retreated side (RS), respectively. The samples for metallography were cut perpendicular to the welding direction. First, the sample was etched using 6 ml of hydrochloric acid, 6 ml of hydrogen peroxide, 6 g of copper sulfate, and 12 ml of water. Subsequently, the sample was gently polished with a polishing machine to remove the corrosion products from the N-steel side. Finally, the sample was etched with a solution of 10 g of picric acid, 5 ml of hydrochloric acid, and 100 ml of ethanol. Using electrical discharge machining, flat dog-bone-shaped specimens with standard dimensions of 22 mm in length, 4 mm in width, and 3 mm in thickness were cut. Condition: 77 K

Processing Text: CoCrFeNi(SiC)x (x = 0, 0.1, 0.2, and 0.3) HEAs were prepared through laser metal deposition. Highly pure powders (purity >99.5 %, particle size >100 μm) of Co, Cr, Fe, Ni in equal atomic ratios of 100, 90, 80, and 70 at.% were weighed on a JS20-01 electronic precision balance (accuracy ±0.1 g). Before the start of alloying, 0, 10, 20, and 30 at.% SiC particles (purity >99.9 %, particle size <30 μm) were added, and the resulting specimens were labeled as 0-SiC, 10-SiC, 20-SiC, and 30-SiC, respectively. The formulated powders were mixed in a high-energy ball mill (YXQM-12L, MITR Co. Ltd., Hunan, China) at 100 r/min for 300 min. During the grinding process, the mill is stopped sequentially for 5 min at 15-min intervals to minimize the occurrence of cold-welding. A stainless steel bottle and Al2O3 balls with a diameter of 3-5 mm were used as the grinding medium under argon atmosphere protection. The weight ratio of balls to powder was 2:1. The substrate material was 304 stainless steel with dimensions of 180 mm × 100 mm × 10 mm. AM was performed by using an LMD machine (RFL-A3000D, Wuhan Lijiang Laser Technology). The laser power was 1500 W, scanning speed was 4 mm/s, spot size was 2.7 mm, and overlap rate was 50%. Pure argon was used as the powder feeding and protection gas. The specimen deposition height was approximately 10 mm. Specimens were cut into 10 mm × 10 mm × 2 mm blocks by using an electric spark wire cutter. The sample blocks were gradually sanded with sandpaper. The prepared samples were corroded with copper chloride solution (CuCl2:HCl:C2H5OH = 1:1:1). Specimen: 10 at.% SiC; Ultimate tensile strength: 799.67 MPa; Elongation: 8.17%
Processing Word: Specimen: 10 at.% SiC; Ultimate tensile strength: 799.67 MPa; Elongation: 8.17%

Processing Text: Rods of polycrystalline Ni with a diameter of 10 mm were selected as raw material and the energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS) analysis was carried out to measure the chemical composition of pure nickel (listed in Table 1). Processing Text: The SAF2507 duplex stainless steel with the heterogeneous structure is produced through cold rolling (ε = 90%) and subsequent 1-min normalizing at 1273 K. The original material with a thickness of 11 mm was normalized at 1523 K for 2 h to obtain the homogeneous coarse grains (CG) structure, refer as the CG sample. Then, the normalized steel plate was cold rolled (CR) with a thickness reduction of 90%, refer as the CR90% sample. The cold rolled plate was cut into the dimensions of 150 mm × 10 mm × 1.1 mm (length × width × height) using the wire-electrode cutting, and the small plates were sealed using a vacuum sealing machine (MRVS-3002, Partulab, Wuhan, China). Subsequently, in order to ensure that only partial recrystallization of the grains of the samples occurred, vacuum-sealed samples were placed as soon as the furnace temperature reached 1273 K and held for 1 min When the time was up, the samples were quickly removed and air cooled, refer as 90%-1273 sample. Dog-bone-shaped tensile samples with a gauge length of 49 mm, width of 9 mm, and thickness of 1.1 mm were cut from the steel plates with the longitudinal axes parallel to the rolling direction. Uniaxial tensile test and loading-unloading-reloading (LUR) experiment were performed at room temperature using a SHIMADZU-100kN Universal Tester (Shimadzu Corporation, Tokyo, Japan) with a quasi-static strain rate of 6.6 × 10 −4s −1, and used a dual camera non-contact extensometer as a strain gauge for mechanical property testing. The X-ray diffraction (XRD, Empyrean, Malvern Panalytical, Holland) with Cu Kα radiation, scan rate: 1°/min, step size: 0.02°, and 2θ angle ranging from 40° to 100° was carried out to confirm the fraction of constituent phases and determine the dislocation densities of the specimens. The microstructures in the RD-TD plane were observed using a field emission scanning electron microscope (FE-SEM, NOVA Nano SEM 450, FEI company, Hillsboro, OR, America) equipped with the electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, NordlysMax2 detector, Oxford Instrument, Abingdon, UK) and the X-ray energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS, X-MaxN50 electrically cooled, Oxford Instrument, Abingdon, UK) plugin. The EBSD tests selected step sizes of 2 μm, 0.2 μm, and 0.1 μm corresponding to CG, CR90%, and 90-1237K samples, respectively. The substructures of the steel samples were analyzed using a transmission electron microscope (TEM, FEI-Tecnai-F30, FEI company, Hillsboro, OR, USA) operated at 300 kV with selected area electron diffraction (SAED) and the EDS plugin. Processing Text: The experimental material is 3.6 % copper-containing austenitic antibacterial stainless steel. After hot rolling-cold rolling-antibacterial heat treatment, the antibacterial heat treatment temperature is 800 °C, and the aging time is more than 6h. The copper-containing antibacterial stainless steel specimens were prepared using wire-cutting method and the wire-cutting marks around the specimens were removed using sandpaper. Tensile tests were conducted on the samples at room temperature (25 °C) and low temperatures using the Shimadzu AGS-100KN universal testing machine. The low temperature tensile test was carried out on a tensile testing machine equipped with a temperature control experimental chamber. Liquid nitrogen was introduced into the low temperature experimental chamber, and the temperature in the box was set to −20 °C, −60 °C, −100 °C, and −140 °C, respectively. Prior to the low-temperature tensile test, the sample was required to acclimatize in the low-temperature chamber for 5 min. The tensile speed during the test was set at 1 mm/min. The wire cutting method was employed to cut out the observation samples near the fracture tip of the tensile samples at different temperatures. In order to prevent the oxidation of the sample after cutting the sample, the fracture morphology was observed under the scanning electron microscope as soon as possible to clarify the fracture mode and morphology of the sample during tensile testing at different temperatures. The samples were cold inlaid and polished with 600#, 1000#, 1500#, 2000# sandpaper in turn, followed by electrolytic polished. The electrolyte was 10 ml 70% perchloric acid and 90 ml anhydrous ethanol. In order to eliminate the residual stress on the surface of the sample and obtain high-precision calibration. The sample was cut into a thickness of 0.3 mm by wire cutting, and then ground to a thin sheet with a thickness of 30-50 μm by 2000# sandpaper. The thin sheet sample was punched into a circle of Ф3 mm, and the RL-2 electrolytic double spray thinning instrument was used for thinning. The solution was 50 ml 70% perchloric acid and 450 ml anhydrous ethanol. The voltage was set to 25V and the polishing temperature was −25 °C. Condition: tested at room temperature (25 °C)

Processing Text: Three alloys were selected for experimental validation, including one non-equimolar counterparts with higher yield strengths (V32 alloy). The three HEAs were prepared by vacuum arc melting using raw materials of purity greater than 99.9 % for pure Nb, Ti, V, and Zr metals in an argon gas atmosphere. These ingots of 60 g were remelted at least six times to ensure chemical homogeneity. The samples were electrodischarged machined cut into Φ 4 mm × 6 mm for subsequent compression tests, and then mechanically polished to remove machining marks. Compression tests were conducted at room temperature using an INSTRON 3382 testing machine, with a compression rate of 1 × 10-3 s−1. Phase identifications were conducted by X-ray diffraction (XRD, D8 DISCOVER A25) with Co Kα radiation. The microstructures of alloys were determined by a ZEISS Sigma 300 scanning electron microscope (SEM) with energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) detector. The EBSD sample was prepared by first mechanically polishing, then vibratory polishing. Condition: Room Temperature; Processing state: as-cast; Microstructure: Not explicitly mentioned, but contains Laves phase

Processing Text: The 24CrNiMoY alloy steel powder was prepared by vacuum induction melting gas atomization (VIGA), and the fine powder with a particle size of 15-53 μm was obtained by vibration sieving. The powder particle size distribution was measured by LA-920 laser particle sizer, and the powder morphology and particle size distribution are shown in Fig. 1. It can be seen that the powder particle size distribution ranges from 5 to 80μ m, and the average powder particle size is 34.3 μm, and the alloy steel powders are well sphericalized, which is suitable for the SLM printing block. The SLM 24CrNiMoY alloy steel samples with good surface formation and high tensile strength along with high elongation were printed by varying the laser power, i.e., energy density, using a 1000 W fiber laser SLM 3D printer with no change in other parameters. The SLM device used an AFS-M260 model equipped with a 1000 W fiber laser manufactured by Beijing Long yuan Company for sample preparation, and the standard x/y grating alternate scanning mode was used. In order to minimize porosity and further melt the upper layers of unfused powder and pore defects, a cross-scanning strategy was used, where the laser scanning direction was periodically rotated by 67° between adjacent layers. Q235 steel was selected as the substrate, which was preheated to 80 °C to reduce the temperature gradient. During the forming process, argon was continuously injected into the cavity as a protective gas to ensure that the oxygen content was less than200 ppm. Two kinds of samples were prepared, one of which was 10mm × 10mm × 10 mm for microstructure analysis and hardness testing, and the other was a tensile specimen of 30mm × 7mm × 1 mm for testing the mechanical properties. The wire-cut samples were ultrasonically cleaned with acetone solution, then sequentially sanded and polished, and then corroded using a solution of HNO3 (2 ml) and C2H5OH (48 ml) in conjunction for 3-5s. The cubic specimen blocks were ground and polished to reduce their surface roughness, and the microhardness of the samples was tested with a Qness Q10A + type microhardness tester under a load of 4.9 N and a holding time of 15S. The tensile specimens were designed according to the ISO 6892-1 standard, and the tensile tests were carried out at room temperature using an AG-X plus 100 kN electronic universal testing machine at a tensile speed of 0.5 mm/min, and the fracture morphology was observed using SEM equipment. The results show that with the optimized laser power over 400 W, the powder layer thickness can be increased to 60 μm, and the theoretical productivity reaches 7.2 mm3/s, which is more than two times of the normal SLM technology. As the laser energy density increases, the structure of melt pool changes from a thermal conduction mode to a keyhole mode, and the microstructure mainly consists of martensite, bainite and pre-eutectic ferrite, and the phase composition of the specimen is α-Fe phase and a small amount of Fe3C,with fine grain size and irregular orientation. When the laser energy density is 68 J/mm3, the microhardness of the specimen is 410HV0.2, the tensile strength reaches 1121 MPa and the percentage elongation after fracture is 11.5%, which realizes a good match between strength and ductility. The fine tempered martensite and lower bainite in the microstructure is the key to excellent strength and ductility. In order to avoid the keyhole mode of the molten pool, it is necessary to reduce the laser power or increase the powder thickness. The pristine powder was prepared by vacuum induction melting gas atomization (VIGA) technique and the powder quality was good. The relative density of 24CrNiMoY specimens shows a trend of increasing and then decreasing with the increase of EVD, and when the laser energy density is 68 J/mm 3, the density of the specimen is the highest, which reaches 98.42%, with the best surface molding quality and fewer internal defects. When the laser energy density reaches 72 J/mm 3, due to the high laser energy density, the "keyhole effect" appears at the bottom of the molten pool, which reduces the molding quality of the specimen. The microstructure of 24CrNiMoY specimen is mainly dominated by martensite, lower bainite and granular bainite, and with the increase of EVD, the HAZ area increases, and the proportion of bainite organization increases, which reaches the optimum when the laser energy density is 68 J/mm 3. At this time, the grain size is fine, the weaving strength is the weakest, and the orientation is irregular, thus obtaining a uniform specimen organization, which is conducive to improving the strength of alloy steel. Under the optimized scanning strategy, the best microhardness of 410 HV, tensile strength of 1121 MPa, yield strength of 1080 MPa, elongation after break of 11.5% were obtained for 24CrNiMoY specimens when the laser energy density was 68 J/mm 3. By increasing the layer thickness to 60 μm, not only can we obtain SLM specimens with good molding performance, but the molding rate also reaches 7.2 mm 3/s, which is 2 times higher than that of the low-layer-thickness molding. A CrCoNi 5Cu 1.5alloy ingot (100 × 35 × 8 mm 3) was fabricated by vacuum induction (MC100V, Indutherm, Walzbachtal-Wössingen, Germany) melting using high-purity (99.9%) Cr, Co, Ni, and Cu elements. The ingot was subjected to a solution treatment at 950 °C for 6 h to obtain a uniform elemental distribution. The homogenized ingot was cold-rolled along the longitudinal direction with a thickness reduction of 80%. Thin films were fabricated for 400 min with a thickness of 20.5 μm, referred to as F specimen. The recrystallized target (R) and sputtered film (F) were subsequently aged at 300 °C and 200 °C, respectively, for 24 h in the Ar atmosphere, followed by water quenching. Processing Text: A CoFeNi-based HEA with a hierarchical structure with heterogeneous microstructure, consisting of body-centered cubic (BCC) bands, ultra-fine grained dual-phase and non-recrystallized lamellae (NRL) zones containing a high-density of nanoprecipitates, was fabricated and finely tuned by cold rolling (CR) and annealing. Processing Text: The Mg-8Li dual phase alloy was deformed by multi-directional compression with different passes. Multi-directional compression was carried in Zwick ZH250SH at room temperature. Mg-8Li (wt.%) ingots were used, which actual chemical composition is 7.97(wt.%) of Li. Processing Text: The microstructure and its relationship with the mechanical properties of an Inconel 718 superalloy fabricated by selective laser melting (SLM) technology were investigated under different post processes, including HT1, HT2, HT2+HIP and as-built conditions. Specifically, HT1 involved solution treatment at 960 °C for 1 h followed by air cooling (AC) and aging treatment at 720 °C for 8 h with furnace cooling (FC) to 620 °C for 8 h. HT2 involved solution treatment at 980 °C for 1 h followed by AC and aging treatment at 760 °C for 1 h with FC to 650 °C for 1 h. HT2+HIP included the same solution and aging treatments as HT2, with an additional Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP) at 1170 °C for 4 h at 100 MPa. The AM IN718 superalloy was fabricated by selective laser melting (SLM) of gas-atomized IN 718 superalloy powders produced by Höganäs Corporation. The SLM parameters were as follows: laser power of 300 W, scanning speed of 1150 mm/s, hatch spacing of 110 μm and layer thickness of 30 μm. Following HT2+HIP treatment, the rod-like γ″precipitates appears comparatively shorter and thicker in comparison to the HT1 condition, albeit with a slight decrease in dimensions as shown in the blue window in Fig. 5. During HIP treatment, the Laves phase located between dendrites dissolves into the matrix at elevated temperatures, liberating a substantial quantity of Nb element. Consequently, this process yields a notable augmentation in the γ″precipitates generated through the aging treatment as shown in Fig. 5 (b). Condition: as-built; Temperature: room temperature
Processing Word: Condition: as-built; Temperature: room temperature

Processing Text: The Al2O3P/CoCrFeMnNi composites were fabricated by mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering (SPS). The base matrix is prepared using Co, Cr, Fe, Mn, Ni pure metal powder with a purity higher than 99.5 wt% and the particle size less than 48 μm. The Al2O3 powder of different sizes was used as the reinforcement, which contains nano and micro Al2O3. The size of nano-Al2O3 is 20-30 nm with purity of 99.8% and the values of micron-Al2O3 powder are 20-30 nm and 99.9%, respectively. In the process of SPS, infrared thermometer was used to determine the sintering temperature of the material by adding holes to the graphite mold. Processing Text: The Cu-20 wt% Fe alloy was produced in a conventional VIM (Vacuum Induction Melting) furnace. For that, commercially pure Fe (99.97 wt%) and Cu (99.92 wt%) elements were poured into a graphite crucible, followed 10 min of metallurgical homogenization of the molten bath before solidification. The Cu-Fe alloy was solidified in a stepped Cu mold using centrifugal casting so that rapidly solidified samples could be generated. Rods having 7, 9 and 11 mm were produced in duplicate so that more samples for microstructural and mechanical properties analyses could be examined. The alloy was melted in situ since the heating system was able to control it. After attaining the desired temperature of the melt, the heating system was turned off and the mold rotated. As such, the molten alloy filled the stepped cylindrical internal cavity of the Cu mold, before solidification naturally started. For metallographic examination of the different sectors along the rods, the samples were polished and etched with a solution (5 g of FeCl 3+ 50 ml of HCl + 100 ml of H 2O) for 10 s, and then examined using an optical microscope. Hardness tests were performed on the transversal sections of the different rod sectors using a test load of 200 gf and a count time of 15 s. Great attention has been paid to the hardness tests to ensure that the indentation size was sufficiently large to encompass all microconstituents, thereby enabling a comprehensive response from the entire microstructure. The average of at least 20 measurements was used to determine the representative hardness value for each sample. Uniaxial engineering compressive tests on the cylindrical rods were performed by using a universal testing machine (Instron model 5500R) at a strain rate of 5 × 10 −4s −1(with constant crosshead speed). The tested specimens’ geometry was 5 mm in diameter and 7.5 mm in length. XRD analysis was carried out to identify the formed phases, using a Bruker D8 Advance ECO, within an angular range varying from 5° to 90° (2θ) with a step size of 0.02° and a count time of 0.25 s per step. Processing Text: The tensile specimens were cut by electrical discharge machining (EDM) along the rolling direction (RD) of the steel plate with a gauge length of 25 mm, a thickness of 3 mm and a width of 7 mm. Tensile tests were performed at a crosshead speed of 3 mm/min in a Gotech electronic universal testing machine, where a laser extensometer was used to monitor the tensile strain. At least three tensile specimens of each steel were deformed to fracture to ensure reproducibility. To reveal the microstructural evolution during straining, interrupted tensile tests to engineering strains of 3% (or 5%) and 10% were performed. The microstructure was analyzed by scanning electron microscopy (SEM), electron back-scatter diffraction (EBSD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM). EBSD was performed in a Zeiss Ultra55 scanning electron microscope, and specimens were prepared by vibration polishing with 50 nm colloidal silica for 2.5-24 h in a Buehler-VibroMet 2. TEM was performed on a FEI Tecnai G2 F20 instrument operating at 200 kV. The TEM specimens were cut by EDM with a thickness of 1 mm and then first ground into foils with a thickness of <80 μm. Subsequently, the foils were further thinned using Struers TenuPol-3 electrochemical double-jet equipment, which was formed into an electrolyte of 10 vol% perchloric acid and 90 vol% ethanol at a voltage of 20 V and a temperature of −30 °C. Processing Text: In the present work, the AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 EHEA was hot rolled in multiple passes at different temperatures and reductions. The hot rolling process of as-cast AlCoCrFeNi 2.1EHEA is shown in Fig. 1(b) , involving four rolling temperatures (800 °C, 900 °C, 1000 °C and 1200 °C). Among them, the condition of 1200 °C and 60% reduction was tested as a control group to further explore the improvement of the mechanical properties. Taking the deformation of hot rolling at 1000 °C as an example, the sheet is heat-treated by annealing for 10 mins at 1000 °C, and then hot rolling operated at ∼10% reduction. Upon successful completion of the rolling process (i.e., absence of sheet edge cracking and uniform sheet thickness), the 10% reduction sample is reintroduced into the furnace and annealing for 10 mins again. Subsequently, the ∼20% reduction rolling stage is initiated, and the process is repeated. The deformation achieved during the final successful rolling represents the hot rolling reduction at this temperature. After completing all the hot rolling tests, sheets with 10% reduction at 800 °C, 40% reduction at 900 °C, 60% reduction at 1000 °C and 60% reduction at 1200 °C are obtained (denoted as H81, H94, H106 and H126, respectively). The specific samples of SEM were first polished to 3000-grit SiC abrasive paper, and then electrolytically polished for 50 s in a reagent mixture (electrolyte is a mixed solution of 10% perchloric acid, 30% n-butanol and 60% methanol). After polishing, the samples were etched in a solution (etching solution is a mixed solution of 3% hydrofluoric acid, 7% nitric acid and 90% deionized water) for 3 s to complete the SEM sample preparation. The TEM specimens were prepared by means of ion milling on a GATAN 691. High purity elements (Al, Co, Cr, Fe, Ni with purity above 99.9%) were used to prepare AlCoCrFeNi 2.1EHEA ingots in a vacuum induction magnetic levitation melting furnace under high purity argon atmosphere. To ensure the chemical homogeneity of the ingots, the melting process was repeated for more than five times. The melt was cast into the water-cooled copper mold, and finally AlCoCrFeNi 2.1EHEA ingots were obtained. The material with Φ74 × 100 mm was cut from the center of the ingot as the raw material used in the experiment. Subsequently, a circular sheet with a diameter of 74 mm and a thickness of 4 mm was fabricated as a hot-rolled specimen. Condition: H106; Processing state: Hot-rolled

Processing Text: In the present work, the AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 EHEA was hot rolled in multiple passes at different temperatures and reductions. The hot rolling process of as-cast AlCoCrFeNi 2.1EHEA is shown in Fig. 1(b) , involving four rolling temperatures (800 °C, 900 °C, 1000 °C and 1200 °C). Among them, the condition of 1200 °C and 60% reduction was tested as a control group to further explore the improvement of the mechanical properties. Taking the deformation of hot rolling at 1000 °C as an example, the sheet is heat-treated by annealing for 10 mins at 1000 °C, and then hot rolling operated at ∼10% reduction. Upon successful completion of the rolling process (i.e., absence of sheet edge cracking and uniform sheet thickness), the 10% reduction sample is reintroduced into the furnace and annealing for 10 mins again. Subsequently, the ∼20% reduction rolling stage is initiated, and the process is repeated. The deformation achieved during the final successful rolling represents the hot rolling reduction at this temperature. Processing Text: A series of (FeCoCrNi) 100-XTi X(X = 0, 1, 3, 7, and 9 at. %) HEAs were synthesized via arc-melting followed by thermo-mechanical treatment. These samples were derived from high-purity element powders of Fe, Co, Cr, Ni, and Ti (> 99.95 wt. %). The raw powders were blended in stoichiometric proportions and ball-milled for 4 h. To mitigate splashing during the melting process, the mixed powders were compacted into cylinders (φ10mm × 12 mm) under 15 MPa pressure. Each ingot underwent four remelting cycles to ensure uniform mixing, resulting in button-like as-cast samples. The as-cast samples were heat-treated at 1000 °C for 2 h, followed by hot compression deformation and annealing treatments (1000 °C for 2 h), and quenched in water to achieve homogenization. The as-homogenized samples were subsequently cold-rolled to achieve approximately 70% thickness reduction, then annealed (1000 °C for 5 min) before being quenched in water, resulting in as-recrystallized samples for further analysis. Processing Text: We used vacuum arc melting method to fabricate a single-phase FCC Fe 41Ni 20Co 20Cr 10Al 5V 4HEA, followed by rolling and annealing at different temperatures. As-cast HEA Fe 41Ni 20Co 20Cr 10Al 5V 4(at. %) was produced by arc-melting a mixture of high-purity raw elements (> 99.99 wt%) in an argon atmosphere. The ingot was remelted at least six times to ensure chemical homogeneity. The chemical composition of the as-cast HEA was measured by inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS). The resulting ingot was first homogenized at 1100 °C for 10 h and then hot-rolled at 1200 °C with a total thickness reduction of approximately 73%, followed by water-quenching. Hot-rolled HEAs were solution treated at 1100 °C for 30 min and then cold-rolled along the longitudinal direction with a 70% reduction in thickness. The rolled HEAs were cut by electro-discharge machining (EDM) to obtain sheets measuring 62 × 16 × 2.8 mm. These sheets were then annealed at 700 °C, 800 °C, and 900 °C for 1 h. All the heat treatment was conducted in a vacuum tube furnace and quenched in water. The dog-bone-shaped tensile specimens with dimensions of 16 mm (length) × 4 mm (width) × 1 mm (thickness) were cut from the bulk samples along the rolling direction using EDM. Tensile tests were performed on an Instron 3369 mechanical testing machine using a 10 mm extensometer at room temperature (25 °C), with a strain rate of 1.0 × 10 −3s −1. Furthermore, the microhardness of the specimens was assessed using Vickers indentation tests performed on the polished surfaces, applying a load of 1 kg and a dwell time of 15 s. The experimental results are the average of five measurements taken at several locations for each sample. Grain Size: ~2.79 ± 0.28 μm; Annealed state

Processing Text: Ti-6Al-4 V alloy and its composites were prepared using ball milling, SPS and hot rolling with multi-pass. The fabrication steps are as follows: (1)The 90 g HDH-Ti, 10 g Al V and 0.15 g rGO powders were mixed using planetary ball milling (QM-3SP2, China) under 300 r/min in a ball mill tank filled with an Ar atmosphere to prepare rGO/Ti-6Al-4 V mixtures. Similarly, 10 g Al V powder was mixed with 90 g HDH-Ti powder in the same way to obtain Ti-6Al-4 V mixed powder for control experiments. The ratio of stainless steel balls to powder in the mixing process is 3:1. After that, two types of mixed powders of Ti-6Al-4 V and 0.15 wt% rGO/Ti-6Al-4 V were obtained, i.e., the rGO content was 0 wt% and 0.15 wt%, respectively.(2)The two types of mixed powder obtained in step (1) were densified for 5 min at 1050 °C under vacuum conditions and 45 MPa pressure using spark plasma sintering (SPS). For simplicity, the as-rolled Ti-6Al-4 V and 0.15 wt% rGO/Ti-6Al-4 V composites were labeled as TMC0 and TMC1, respectively. Processing Text: The width of the fusion region in bimetallic SS/IN parts joined using LPBF was reported to be 100-200 μm. Both additively manufactured SS and Inconel formed columnar grains in the z-direction because of the thermal gradient induced by the building process. However, stainless steel formed wider and more equiaxed grains compared to the finer Inconel grains due to the difference in thermal expansion between the two alloys. One of the first studies on dissimilar joining of SS/IN via LPBF was presented by Mei et al., in 2019, where the authors printed a 316SS/IN718/316SS sandwich structure and reported the presence of microcracks on both interfaces, specifically on the stainless-steel segment of each interface. This crack formation is likely caused by the residual thermal stresses at the interfaces. Notably, microcracks were more dominant at the IN718/316SS interface, while lack-of-fusion pores were more dominant at the 316SS/IN718 interface. A similar observation was made by Wits et al. in graded IN718/316L builds, where cracking occurred in the Fe-rich regions. Axial force applied parallel to interfaces

Processing Text: The IN718 components were fabricated using SLM Solutions 280HL machine, Germany. The powders were spread on the platform and melted layer by layer to generate the cylindrical specimens of dimensions 13 mm diameter and 80 mm length. An argon atmosphere was maintained in the chamber throughout the process to avoid oxidation during SLM process. A hatch style rotation of 67° was employed between the layers. The parameters utilized for SLM process like laser power of 200 W, scan speed of 1200 mm/s, hatch spacing of 90 μm and layer thickness of 30 μm. To maintain proper heat dissipation during the printing process a support structure were maintained for the samples with the same material and the supports were removed from the platform using wire cut electric discharge machine, once the printing process completed. The cylindrical specimens generated by SLM were friction welded by continuous drive KUKA friction welding (FW) machine. A facing operation was performed for the faying surfaces to remove any contaminations or oxides if present. The parameters employed for FW process such as, heating pressure of 50 bar, upset pressure of 60 bar, heating time of 6 s, upset time of 3 s and a rotary speed of 1125 rpm. An infrared thermographic (IR) camera (FLIR-make) was used to measure the temperature distribution at the interface during FW. Two cylindrical rods were considered whereas one was at stationery position and other was rotated with constant rpm during FW. The workpieces generate the frictional force in between the faying surfaces and an upset force was applied to forms the welds. The SLM samples after FW were examined for the microstructural characterization. The cross section of samples was grounded and polished with standard metallography practices to obtain scratch free surfaces. After etching with an etchant of HCl -10 ml and H 2O 2-3 ml for 10 s, the microstructures were observed under Olympus BX51 optical microscope (OM) and for higher magnification, scanning electron microscope (SEM) of Zeiss EVO MA 15 was used. The X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis was performed using Rigaku ultima IV with Cu-Kα radiation of wavelength 0.1542 nm. The step size of 0.02° was used during diffraction analysis at an angle ranging from 40° to 100°. For micro-texture analysis, a FEI TMQuanta 3D-SEM with TSL-EDX TMEBSD (electron back scatter diffraction) system was utilized. OIM Analysis TM(version 8.1) post processing software was used to analyse EBSD data. The Vickers microhardness tests were carried out with 500 g load and a dwell time of 10 s using Buehler Micromet indenter. The measurements were performed along the cross section of the specimen to cover all the zones present in the specimen. Room temperature tensile tests were conducted using Instron 8516 with a strain rate of 10 -4s -1for the as-built SLM and welded samples. The strain hardening behaviour was analysed using Kocks-Mecking plots from the tensile tests data and fracture analysis was performed on the tensile samples to evaluate the fractography features. The strength contribution from the various strengthening mechanisms were calculated for both the SLM as built and weld conditions of IN718 components. Reference baseline

Processing Text: ODS-NbTaTiV RHEAs were prepared utilizing powder metallurgy (P/M) method with high-purity elemental powder (Nb, Ta, Ti, V, >99.5%, <45 μm, equiatomic) and Y 2O 3powder (30-50 nm, 0.35 wt%). The powders were ground in a planetary ball mill (MITR-YXQM-4 L) at 250 rpm for 20 h. Tungsten carbide vials and balls were used as milling media with the ball-to-powder mass ratio of 10:1. The miller was interrupted and reversed every 5 min, and then stopped for another 5 min to avoid overheating. Then, the milled powders were consolidated via spark plasma sintering (SPS, LABOX-325R) at 1300 °C, 1400 °C, and 1500 °C to produce the cylindrical bulks (Φ 20 × 10 mm) with a heating rate of 100 °C/min and a pressure of 40 MPa for 10 min. Cylindrical specimens (Φ 6 × 9 mm) for ambient/elevated temperature compression tests were machined using an electric discharge machine. The surface of the specimens was mechanically polished to remove the defects and lubricated with graphite to reduce the friction coefficient between the specimens and the indenter. Compression tests at ambient temperature were employed using a hydraulic testing machine (Instron 8802). Compression tests at elevated temperatures were employed using a dynamic thermal simulator (Gleeble-3180) in a vacuum environment (4 × 10 −3Pa). The specimens were heated to a set tested temperature (700 °C, 800 °C, 900 °C, and 1000 °C, respectively) with a heating rate of 5 °C/s and soaked for 3 min. Afterward, the specimens were compressed to 35% engineering strain with a strain rate of 0.001 s −1. Processing Text: In this study, a Ti3Zr1.5NbVAl0.25 HEA was produced by DED. The experimental Ti 3Zr 1.5NbVAl 0.25HEA powder was prepared using the plasma rotating electrode process, with specific parameters such as an alloy rod rotation speed of 21,000 r/min, a plasma arc current of 1500 A, and an electrode movement speed of 1.4 mm/s ( Fig. 1(a) ). The effects of process parameters on single track cladding layer (STCL) were studied by response surface methodology (RSM), and the parameters were optimized accordingly. The ranges for P, v, and fare 1200-1800 W, 8-11 mm/s, and 0.7-1 r/min, respectively. The DED equipment comprises an ytterbium fiber laser system (YLS-4000-U-K, Germany), a multi-axis linkage robot arm (KUKA, Germany), a coaxial powder feeder, circulating water cooling equipment, etc. ( Fig. 2(a) ). The molten pool forming process is shown in Fig. 2(b), where the high energy laser melts and deposits the powder onto the substrate. During the printing process, the shielding gas flow is maintained at 15 L/min, and the laser spot diameter is 3.85 mm. The process is conducted under high-purity argon, with an oxygen concentration below 50 ppm throughout. A total of 20 groups of experiments were designed, each requiring the printing of a 30 mm STCL. Microhardness testing was performed using a Vickers hardness tester (Innovatest Falcon 500) with a load of 200 g and a dwell time of 13 s, measuring at intervals of 0.5 mm between adjacent points. Nanoindentation experiments of the molten pool and HAZ were carried out using an Agilent G200 instrument, with 10 measurement points in each region and a spacing of 30 μm between adjacent points. For microstructure and elemental distribution analysis, a field emission SEM (Tescan MIRA3-LMH) was utilized. Additionally, the crystal orientation of grains in the molten pool was determined using electron backscattering diffraction (EBSD). The EBSD sample was prepared through electrolytic polishing in an electrolyte solution (10 vol% HClO 4+ 90 vol% CH 3OH), using a voltage of 25 V and a temperature of −30 °C for 30 s. Resulting in optimal values of P= 1615.51 W, v= 8 mm/s, and f= 1 r/min. Considering the precision of the laser equipments, a laser power of 1600 W was selected for the next experiments. Processing Text: The mixture of element powders of Co, Cr, Ni and nano-TiC powders was used to alloy the CoCrNi-TiC composite in-situ by LPBF. To begin with, the mixed powders were tumble blended for 4h, and ball milled for 4h at a powder ratio of 4:1 at 300 rpm. Then, the obtained powders were alloyed in-situ by LPBF on the BLT s200 laser printing machine with a laser wavelength of 1070 nm and a laser spot diameter of 80 μm. The hatch space was set to 80 μm, and the scan direction rotated 67° between each building layer. The strip scanning strategy with a strip width of 10 mm was adopted to minimize the thermal stress within the sample during preparation. According to the nominal composition of CoCrNi-4wt%TiC, the nano-TiC particles with an average diameter of 40 nm and spherical elemental powders of Co, Cr, Ni with an average diameter of around 40 μm were mixed. The laser scanning strategy that combines high scanning speed and high laser power can effectively disperse the agglomeration of the nano-TiC particles. Also, the high times taken by remelting in each building layers facilitates the in-situ alloying of the blended elemental powders containing high melting point Cr powders. This high depression force applied during the keyhole mode melting leads to the heterogeneous distribution of nano-carbides with a higher number density and a smaller particle size at the bottom of the melting pool. The addition of high fraction nano-TiC particles significantly improves the strength of the composite to 1886 MPa at 77K, 1456 MPa at 298K, 528 MPa at 1073K, 300 MPa at 1173K, respectively. Meanwhile, plasticity is maintained at a reasonable level. Test temperature: 77 K; Strengthening mechanisms include lattice friction, second-phase, grain-boundary, and dislocation strengthening

Processing Text: Nano-lamellar structured Cu-0.1 at.% Zr alloys are prepared by the combination of equal channel angular pressing and subsequent cryogenic rolling. A vacuum induction furnace was used to produce a 5 kg ingot (> 240 mm length × 50 mm height × 50 mm width) of the Cu-0.1 at.% Zr material starting from the pure constituent elements (purity ≥ 99.9 wt.%). After homogenizing the cast samples at 1200 K for 6 h and removing the oxidation layer, equal channel angular pressing (ECAP) processing via route B C was applied at room temperature for 12 passes using a die with a channel angle of 90°. This processing treatment introduced an equivalent Von-Mises strain during each ECAP pass of about 1, which was expected to significantly refine the as-cast coarse grained microstructure after the total strain increased up to about 12 to an approximately saturated ultra-fine-grained microstructure. Rolling billets (60 mm length × 50 mm height × 25 mm width) were cut from the center of the ECAP-processed samples along the extrusion direction. The details and underlying principles of ECAP processing and subsequent rolling at cryogenic temperatures, namely cryogenic rolling (CYR), can be found in our previous work [ 21]. After multiple repeated cryogenic cooling and CYR processes, the rolling billet thickness was finally reduced to 5 mm. The total thickness reduction and equivalent Von-Mises strain were about 90 % and 2.3, respectively. Post-deformation annealing treatments were conducted at temperatures between 523 K and 823 K for various durations to obtain different LB spacings. Processing Text: The Ti4Al3 MEA was fabricated in an arc-melting furnace (Shenyang Jinyan New Material Preparation Technology Co., Ltd). The starting elemental materials, at least 99.95 weight percent (wt. %) pure, were supplied by ZhongNuo Advanced Material (Beijing) Technology Co., Ltd. Before the arc melting, the furnace chamber was purified by melting high purity Ti. The melting of MEA ingots was repeated for five times to ensure the homogeneity of alloying elements. After the melting, the melt alloy was cast into a copper mold (50 mm × 20 mm × 5 mm in dimension). The alloy ingots were first homogenized at 1150 °C for 3 h in vacuum (less than 0.005 MPa), then water-quenched to room temperature, and finally cold rolled. The cold rolling was performed with the reduction in thickness per pass below 0.2 mm and a total reduction in thickness of 70 %. The HP heat-treatment was carried out in a CS-IB type cubic-anvil apparatus (Guilin Guiye Machinery Co., Ltd.). A specimen (20 mm in diameter and 1.5 mm in thickness) was compressed to a HP of 4 GPa by six orthogonal pistons. Under a HP of 4 GPa, the specimen was first heated to 1150 °C, held for 10 min for recrystallization, then cooled to 600 °C and remained at 600 °C for 60 min for aging, and finally water-cooled to room temperature to achieve the HP-treated specimen (named HP MEA). For comparison, the specimens were also synthesized using the above recrystallization-ageing treatments at atmospheric pressure (named AP MEA). As-processed (AP) condition
