Processing Text: These alloys were prepared from commercial pure Al, battery-grade pure Li, pure Mg, Al-Cu and Al-Zr master alloys under the protection of high-purity Ar. The melt temperature was 710 °C before being transferred into the steel molds, which had been preheated to 250 °C. The molds include a T-shaped mold for evaluating HTS, a spiral mold for measuring fluidity, and a regular bottom-injection permanent mold for subsequent mechanical performance optimization. Some of the alloy ingots (Alloys 1-4) were subjected to a well-designed double-stage solid solution treatment under the protection of Ar. Then, they were quenched in water and aged at 175 °C. According to our previous studies [ 1, 38], the first-stage treatment parameters should be set as 480 °C/32 h. The second-stage treatment parameters are closely related to the melting point of (Cu, Mg)-rich secondary phases at the grain boundaries, which was measured to possess a lower limit of ∼535 °C derived from the DSC curve. Hence, the temperature was set to 530 °C (∼5 °C lower than the melting points) and the time was set to 24 h based on our work on diffusion kinetics. Consequently, the solid solution treatment scheme was determined as 480 °C/32 h + 530 °C/24 h. The aging treatment scheme was determined to be 175 °C/64 h. Processing Text: LPBF builds of pure Nb, with a relative density of 98 %, exhibited an YS of 490 MPa, UTS of 609 MPa, and ductility of 9 % with appreciable strain hardenability. Spherical Nb powders were acquired from Atlantic Equipment Engineers (AEE), and powder size distribution (PSD) analysis was performed using the Microtrac S3500 laser diffraction analyzer. The D 90 upon doing the PSD analysis was found to be 48 μm. The Nb powder was also tested for O contamination using the LECO ON736 infra-red analyzer. Based on the LECO elemental analyzer data, the O and N concentrations in the starting powders were found to be 316 ±11 ppm and 190 ±10 ppm respectively. Nb samples of dimensions 15 mm × 15 mm x 10 mm were printed on the Trumpf TruPrint 1000 equipped with a 55 μm laser beam diameter using the following parameters - laser power of 180 W and 200 W; laser scanning speeds of 200, 400, and 600 mm/s; hatch spacing of 60 μm; layer thickness of 50 μm. The depositions were carried out in an inert Ar atmosphere, and the oxygen in the chamber was maintained below 100 ppm during the process. The sub-sized tensile specimens with a gauge length of 5 mm, and thickness of 1 mm, were machined from 180 to 600 condition using a KENT USA (WSI-200) electron discharge machine. The bulk specimens were uniaxially tensile tested at room temperature at a strain rate of 10 −3s −1. Compression tests were performed using the MTS 322 load frame (MTS Systems Corp., Eden Prairie MN) equipped with a 500 kN load cell. Cylinders of diameter 8 mm and height of 10 mm were compression tested at a strain rate of 10 −3s −1 at room temperature. The tests were conducted up to deformation with ∼80 % height reduction. Three tests each for both tension and compression modes were performed on the build with the optimized parameter. Imaging and Electron Back-Scattered Diffraction (EBSD) was performed using the FEI Nova NanoSEM 230, and Apreo SEM using a step size of 0.25 μm. The EDAX-OIM Analysis™ software was employed to analyze the EBSD scans. Rigaku Ultima III XRD with a Cu Kα target was used for the measurements with a step size of 0.025°. A dual-beam focused ion beam milling system (FEI Nova 200 Nanolab FIB/SEM) was utilized for the preparation of atom probe tomography (APT) tips and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) foil. The foils prepared for TEM were analyzed using the FEI Tecnai G2 F20 ST TEM operating at 200 kV with scanning and transmission modes capability. The APT was operated in laser mode using the CAMECA LEAP 5000XS with the specimen's base temperature at 50 K, pulse rate of 200 kHz, pulse energy of 50 pJ, and a target detection rate of 5-10 ions detected every 1000 pulses. Data analysis was performed using the software package AP Suite 6.1. Processing Text: The two studied steels, Fe18Mn0.6C (medium carbon) and Fe18Mn1.0C (high carbon), were fabricated in a vacuum induction furnace. To ensure compositional homogeneity, the ingots underwent annealing at 1150 °C for 4 h under an inert argon atmosphere, then hot-forged into billets with cross-sectional dimensions of approximately 35 mm × 45 mm, and subsequently air-cooled to room temperature. To achieve comparable grain sizes, Fe-18Mn-0.6C and Fe-18Mn-1.0C steels were solution treated at 900 °C for 25 min and 15 min, respectively, and then followed by quenching in water. The initial microstructure of both steels exhibited a fully austenitic structure, with an average grain size of approximately 45 μm (excluding annealing twin boundaries), as illustrated in Fig. 1. Tensile tests were conducted at 298 K and 223 K using an MTS tensile machine at a strain rate of 2 × 10 −3s −1. To investigate the evolution of microstructures, the tensile tests were interrupted at engineering strains of 10 % and 30 % (corresponding to true strains of 9.5 % and 26.2 %, respectively) or continued until fracture. Dog-bone shaped tensile specimens were obtained from heat-treated plates via electrical discharge machining. The specimens had a total length of 65 mm, a gauge length of 15 mm, a width of 4 mm, and a thickness of 2 mm. The strain for all specimens was measured using a standard contact extensometer with a gauge length of 10 mm during the tensile tests. For the tensile tests conducted at 223 K, a low-temperature chamber was attached to the testing machine. This chamber was connected to a liquid nitrogen tank, and the temperature of the tensile test was regulated by the evaporative cooling process of the liquid nitrogen. Following the tensile tests were completed, microscopic observations were performed on the deformed specimens, to investigate their deformation behavior. X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns were inspected on Rigaku D/max-2500/PC (Cu radiation). To ensure sufficient diffraction intensity, a slow scan rate of 1° min −1and a range of 40-100° were employed for detection. Prior to XRD analysis, specimens were mechanically grinding with SiC paper and polished with 3 μm and 1 μm diamond paste. The specimens for electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) observation were selected from the deformed tensile specimens. Then, these specimens subjected to a series of mechanical grinding and polishing procedures, followed by ion milling to eliminate any damaged surfaces. The ion milling was performed using the Hitachi IM 4000, which was operated under the conditions of 75° for 15 min. Subsequently, EBSD maps were gathered using AZtec software in a Hitachi SU 5000 scanning electron microscope (SEM) with an operating voltage of 30 kV and a step size of 200 nm. For the microstructural examination of fractured specimens, a FEI Talos F200X transmission electron microscope (TEM) operated at 200 kV acceleration voltage was applied. TEM specimens with a diameter of 3 mm were cut from the near tensile fractures and then ground to a thickness of approximately 30 μm by SiC paper, followed by thinning to perforation via ion polishing in a Gatan 694 ion polishing system. Processing Text: Alloy ingots were fabricated by arc-melting in a water-cooled copper cavity under a Ti-gettered ultra-high purity argon atmosphere, using a mixture of Ti, Nb, Cr, and V pure metals (purity higher than 99.95 wt.%). A plate with dimensions of 40 × 20 × 6 mm3 was cut from the as-cast ingot, followed by homogenizing at 1300 °C for 4 h in a high-purity argon atmosphere. The cold-rolled plate was subsequently annealed at 1100 °C for 3 min followed by water quenching to produce a fully recrystallized microstructure (named as CRRA sample). Processing Text: A simple two-step process including the ultrasonic dispersion of ceramic particles and the volatilization of liquid medium by stirring was employed to synthesize Y2O3 nanoparticle modified CoCrNi matrix (Y2O3/CoCrNi) composite powders, which were subsequently processed for L-PBF to make samples. Y2O3 particles were dissolved firstly into alcohol with a powder-to-alcohol weight ratio of 1:200, and then dispersed under ultrasound condition to eliminate the inherent agglomeration. The ultrasonic process was last for 20 min at an input power of 270 W. Afterwards, the CoCrNi powders were poured into the solution, and the mixture was continuously stirred at a constant temperature of 120 °C until the liquid phase medium was completely evaporated. Finally, Y2O3/CoCrNi composite powders were dried in a vacuum furnace at 80 °C for 10 h to remove the moisture. The samples (10 mm × 10 mm × 5 mm and 30 mm × 10 mm × 5 mm) were produced using an EP-M150 facility equipped with a fibre laser at a maximum power of 500 W and a spot size of 70 μm. The substrate was preheated to 70 °C prior to printing and the oxygen content in the building chamber was strictly maintained below 100 ppm with the protection of argon atmosphere. A short linear scanning strategy with 67° rotation between adjacent layers was applied. To determine the optimal parameters, the h was kept constantly (60, 90 and 120 μm) with varying P from 150 to 350 W. The layer thickness (t) was kept at 40 μm. The scanning speed (v) was optimized in advance and the constant value of 800 mm/s was applied. The volumetric energy densities Ev=P/vht were calculated to explore the effects of processing parameters on the printing quality and microstructural evolution. The surface defects and microstructural characteristics of the specimens were detected by optical microscope (OM) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Tescan Mira3) equipped with energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS). Before observation, the samples were polished using 1-3 μm diamond and 40 nm colloidal silica suspensions, and followed by etched in a solution of 5 g CuCl2+10 ml ethanal +10 ml HCl for 60 s. Thin foil samples were prepared for TEM by the precision ion polishing system (PIPS) at a voltage of 5 kV/2 kV and an incident angle of 3-7°. The room-temperature tensile test using a universal tensile machine (MTS Alliance RT30) was performed on dog-bone-shaped samples with a gauge dimension of 25 mm × 7.5 mm × 1.5 mm, which were sliced by electro-discharge technique machining (EDM). The tensile direction was perpendicular to the building direction and the strain rate was set at 1 × 10−3s−1. Processing Text: The HfMoNbTaTi alloys were prepared by mechanical alloying (MA) and subsequent spark plasma sintering (SPS). Hf, Mo, Nb, Ta, and Ti pure elemental powders (＞99.5 %) with 325 mesh particle size (＜45 μm) were selected as raw materials. The raw material powders were weighed by equal atomic ratio in a vacuum glove box filled with high-purity argon. The total mass of powders in each jar was 50 g. The stainless steel balls with diameters of 5 mm, 8 mm, and 10 mm (1:1:1 mass ratio) were selected as the milling medium. The powders and milling balls were filled into stainless steel jars according to the 10:1 ball-to-powder weight ratio and sealed. QM-3SP4 (Nanjing Nanda Instrument Plant) planetary ball mill was employed for high-energy ball milling to achieve alloying between different elements. The parameters of MA process were as follows: rotational speed: 265 rpm, autorotation speed: 400 rpm, and milling duration: 50 h. To reduce the introduction of impurity elements, no process control agent (PCA) was employed during the MA process. The pre-alloyed powders were taken out in a vacuum glove box and sealed for storage. The pre-alloyed powders were loaded into graphite molds with a diameter of 20 mm in the air. To facilitate demolding, graphite papers (thickness: 0.15 mm) were used to separate the powder from the mold. Subsequently, the combination of powder and mold was placed into a spark plasma sintering furnace (SPS-20T-10, Shanghai Chenhua Technology Co., Ltd.) and preloaded with an axial pressure of 10 MPa. Once the vacuum level reached 7.5 × 10−3Pa, the sintering procedure was started. The sintering procedure comprised the following steps: (1) Heating-up stage: The combination body was heated up to the target sintering temperature at a heating rate of 50 °C/min. The sintering temperature was set to 1400°C-1700 °C at 50 °C intervals. Simultaneously, the sintering pressure was uniformly increased to 50 MPa. (2) Holding stage: The combination body was maintained at the sintering temperature and pressure for 15 min. (3) Furnace cooling stage: At the conclusion of the holding stage, the sintering pressure was rapidly decreased. The combination body was cooled to room temperature within the furnace. The sintering temperature was detected by an infrared pyrometer. The as-sintered alloys were ground using a standard metallographic procedure to 2000# of SiC papers and mechanically polished with a diamond suspension. Cylindrical specimens of dimensions φ4 × 6 mm were randomly obtained from the as-sintered alloys using the electric spark cutting. The specimens’ axes were aligned parallel to the axis of the sintered block’s axis. The specimen’s surfaces were ground by 1500# SiC paper. Instron 5569 electronic universal testing machine was used to conduct the room temperature compression experiments at a strain rate of 10−3s−1. Processing Text: The Inconel 718 powders used in LDED. (a) Typical SEM micrograph, (b) particle size distribution. The Inconel 718 powders utilized in this investigation were fabricated using the plasma rotating electrode process (PREP). Table 1 shows the chemical composition (wt.%) distribution of these powders. The microscopic morphology and particle size distribution of the raw Inconel 718 powders were illustrated in Fig. 1(a) and (b). The average dimension of these powders was 82.637 μm, with Dv(10) = 52.994 μm, Dv(50) = 90.261 μm, and Dv(90) = 146.319 μm. Before LDED, the powders were desiccated in a vacuum drying oven at a preset temperature of 120 °C for 4 h and then cooled to room temperature in a vacuum. LDED processing was performed on a laser deposition system developed by Nanjing-Rui Optoelectronics Technology Co., Ltd. The system mainly combines a fiber laser (DF6000-60), a 6-axis robot (STAUBLI RX160), a laser water cooler (MCWL-200DTR), a powder feeder (HR-spfh-dt1h06), and a vacuum environment bin. The Ar gas of 99.99 % purity was used as a protective and powder feed gas during LDED. Meanwhile, the entire LDED process was conducted within an Ar-filled environmental chamber with a water and oxygen level under 50 ppm to eliminate oxidation. The TSH facility is a far-infrared graphite microcrystalline heating platform mainly composed of graphite microcrystalline panels and an induction heating coil. It can realize excellent heat transfer with the substrate and display the temperature of the substrate in real time on the LCD screen. Before LDED processing, the substrate was first placed on the heating platform, then heated to the preset temperature, and finally, LDED was performed. For accuracy, the temperature of the heating substrate was additionally assessed by an infrared temperature measurement instrument to verify that the predetermined temperature was achieved. Notably, the heating platform was continuously operated during LDED and kept the preset temperature constant. The optimized parameters used in LDED processing are illustrated in Table 2. Fig. 2(a) presents the schematic diagram of the TSH coupled with LDED, where the laser scanning paths of two neighboring deposited layers were perpendicular to each other for releasing RS. The LDEDed Inconel 718 alloy with the substrate at room temperature (RT), heating 100 °C, heating 200 °C, and heating 300 °C were named T RT specimens, T 100 specimens, T 200 specimens, and T 300 specimens, respectively. Meanwhile, to investigate the effects on the microstructures and mechanical properties of LDEDed Inconel 718 alloy in different building directions, the specimens perpendicular to the building direction and parallel to the building direction were named the 0° specimen and the 90° specimen, respectively. Firstly, original block specimens with a size of 35 mm × 35 mm × 30 mm (height) were fabricated by LDED at different TSH temperatures. Then, these original specimens were cut to avoid the influence of possible metallurgical defects (porosity, inclusions, etc.) in the peripheral regions, and only the centermost portion of 30 mm × 30 mm × 25 mm (height) was retained. The sampling positions of the block specimens for microstructure observations, microhardness tests, and residual stress tests are illustrated in Fig. 2(b). All test surfaces (10 mm × 10 mm red-marked surfaces in Fig. 2(b)) were abraded with 180 # - 3000 # SiC sandpapers and polished with diamond spray polish (1.5 μm). Subsequently, these polished surfaces were etched with aqua regia (HCl: HNO 3= 3:1, vol) for 15-20 s, immediately rinsing with anhydrous ethanol and air-dried in moving air. Microstructure observation was first performed using an OLYMPUS-GX71 optical microscope (OM) and a JSM-7800F scanning electron microscope (SEM). Then, the grain size, orientation, and boundary distribution were analyzed using a ZEISS-G300 type electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD). Eventually, a focused ion beam (FIB) prepared FIB flakes for further microstructure observation at the nanoscale in a JEOL 2100 PLUS type transmission electron microscope (TEM). Moreover, the primary dendrite arm spacing (PDAS) values of the typical OM images in the specimens were quantitatively analyzed using Image-J software. All the tested surfaces in the specimens were polished and sanded identically before the microhardness test. The microhardness was performed using an FM-ARS900 Vickers hardness tester with a spacing of 0.5 mm and a load of 100 gf for 15 s. The average of 10 measurements was taken as the definitive microhardness figure to ensure accuracy and rationality. Before the RS test, all the test surfaces were polished using a Leica EM RES102 argon ion polisher to avoid the introduction of excessive mechanical stress. The RS tests were performed on an X-350A X-ray residual stress tester. The fixed ψ method with angles of 0°, 25°, 35°, and 45° was used for residual stress measurements. The cross-correlation method determined the peaks, and the 2θ angle scanning step was set to 0.10° and the counting time to 0.50 s. The high voltage of the X-ray tube was 22.0 kV, the current was 6.0 mA, the collimator diameter was 2 mm, and the stress constant was constant at −601 MPa/°. The measurements were taken at 50 μm intervals on the surface of the specimen, and a total of four points were taken to obtain the residual stresses on the surface of the specimen. The three-dimensional dimensions of the tensile specimen are shown in Fig. 1(c). The tensile tests were performed on a Germany-DOLI-DDL200 tensile testing machine with a 0.5 mm/min tensile loading rate at room temperature. After the tensile experiments, the failed specimens were immediately examined with an SEM to get the fracture morphology without pollution. Specimen orientation: 90°; Condition: T RT (Room Temperature)

Processing Text: The directed energy deposition (DED) technique was used to deposit a CoCrNiWC medium entropy alloy (MEA) through a robotic-assisted laser additive manufacturing (LAM) machine. The microstructural features, including solidification grains, structural defects, and phase transformations, along with uniaxial tensile behavior in different orientations, were comprehensively studied. A quantitative assessment was carried out to evaluate the contribution of strengthening mechanisms through apprising stacking fault constant of 11362 MPa nm for the developed MEA, enrolling the impact of FCC to HCP crystal structure transition for the cobalt matrix after rapid cooling LAM solidification in the solid-state board. The presence of numerous ordinary screw dislocations interacting with each other, stacking faults (SFs), nanotwins, and refined grains led to their hindering as the critical factor for strengthening. The SF intersections resulted in the formation of effective Lomer-Cottrell (LC) locks and nanotwins, which were barriers to slip and attributed to dislocation interactions. The rapid cooling solidification of the LAM process contributed to impressive mechanical properties of deposited CoCr-based MEA with remarkable yield and tensile strengths of ∼895 and 1410 MPa, confirming the direct contributions of statistically stored dislocations upon impact SF and nanotwining strengthening. Processing Text: An ingot with the nominal composition of (CoCrFeMnNi) 98 · 4 B 0 · 8 N 0.8 alloy (in at%, hereinafter denoted by BN-HEA) was fabricated via vacuum induction melting using elemental pellets with purities higher than 99.95 %. Interstitial atoms of B and N were added by the high-purity FeB and MnN compounds. The ingot was homogenized at 1100 °C for 6 h under an Ar atmosphere, followed by water quenching. Cold-rolling was applied to the BN-HEA ingot with a thickness reduction ratio of ∼79 %. Disks with a diameter of 10 mm and a thickness of 1.5 mm were obtained from the rolled BN-HEA for the HPT process. Before the HPT process, the samples were annealed at 800 °C for 1 h and mechanically polished with SiC papers up to 1200 grits. The recrystallized disks were subjected to the HPT process under a pressure of 6 GPa and a revolution of 5 turns at 1 rpm. The HPT-processed disks were annealed at temperatures of 700 and 800 °C for 15 min in an Ar atmosphere, followed by water quenching. Processing state: annealed sample A700

Processing Text: Three AlxHfTaTi alloy button ingots (x = 0, 0.3, 0.5 at.%, hereafter referred to as A0, A3, A5 alloy) with each weight of about 50 g were cast in a vacuum induction furnace using pure metals (99.9 wt.% purity) in an argon atmosphere. Using a heated asynchronous rolling mill (ZKWS8A-3), the ingots were cold-rolled into sheets with the thickness of about 1 mm (reduction ratio of about 87 %) at room temperature. Processing Text: The precipitation behavior, mechanical properties, and strengthening mechanisms of FeCrNi-based medium entropy alloys fabricated by laser powder bed fusion and followed by aging treatment were investigated. Subsequently, precipitates were introduced into these LPBF-fabricated FeCrNi and (FeCrNi) 94Ti 3Al 3MEAs through post-heat treatment. The as-built samples were subsequently aged at temperatures of 800 °C for 2 h followed by water quenching. For the (FeCrNi) 94Ti 3Al 3alloy aged at 800 °C for 2 h, the discrete needle-shaped precipitates are observed in the FCC matrix. Processing Text: The steel bars were austenitized at about 900 °C for 1 h, quenched in water, and tempered between 650 °C and 700 °C to the desired strength for 2 h. Two kinds of specimens were produced utilizing different heat treatment routes. The first type of specimens was subjected to the conventional quenching and tempering procedure, described above, and these samples are denoted as SQT (single quenched and tempered). SQT samples were further exposed to a replicated tempering step, similar to the first one. In this way, a second type of specimens designated as DQT (double quenched and tempered) was obtained. After heat treatment, decarburized layers were removed in order to machine the specimens for hydrogen-related experiments. The surface of all specimens was mechanically ground with 600 grit carbide silicon abrasive paper, rinsed with deionised water, and degreased in ethanol. Tensile specimens with a gauge diameter of 25 mm were machined from original steel bars and fixed into the electrochemical cell with surrounding Pt-mesh. Hydrogen uptake was initiated prior to in-situ testing by electrochemical pre-charging using 3.5 % NaCl solution with 1 g/L of CH 4N 2S as recombination poison, at an applied current of 1 mA/cm 2for 24 h, to maintain equilibrium and constant hydrogen content. Subsequently, the electrochemical cell was mounted on a uniaxial tensile test machine (BETA 501, ZwickRoell, Germany) and in-situ charging was continued while performing a tensile test at a strain rate of 1.0 × 10 -6s −1. Specimens for TDS analysis were manufactured as thin plates with geometry 30 × 6 × 1 mm and served as cathode during electrochemical charging. Charging of specimens was conducted in a similar solution from , at 25 °C with a current density of 1 mA/cm 2. After charging, specimens were rinsed with acetone and immediately placed into liquid nitrogen to prevent the escape of hydrogen. Measuring system was calibrated with a gas mixture consisting of N 2and 5 % H 2,and the carrier gas for the measurements was a high-purity N 2.TDS spectra were recorded in the heating range from 30 °C to 950 °C, at four different heating rates (200, 400, 800 and 1200 K/h). Electrochemical permeation experiments were conducted on specimens with rectangular geometry (40 × 40 × 1.2 mm). Grinding step, up to 1000-grit SiC paper, was implemented to reduce the thickness of the specimens to 1 ± 0.005 mm prior to the application of the palladium layer on the oxidation side. The method utilized to adhere Pd- coating on specimens was physical vapor deposition. The entry side was galvanostatically charged at constant current density (1 mA/cm 2) in a solution of 3.5 % NaCl with 1 g/L CH 4N 2S, at 25 °C. Test environment: Air

Processing Text: The Cu-18Ni-17Zn alloy ingot, with a thickness of 20 mm and a width of 300 mm, has been manufactured by horizontal continuous casting. The as-cast billet was cold rolled into a plate with a 50 % reduction. The rolled plate was then heat treated at 800 °C for 2 h and water quenched at room temperature. This step was followed by cold-rolling to a thickness of 2 mm. Finally, the cold-rolled samples were found to have a rolling strain (η) of 0.8. The formula for the rolling strain is presented in eq. (1): (1)η= (h0-h)/h0 where h represents the uniform thickness of the plate cross-section after rolling, and h0 is the initial uniform thickness of the plate cross-section. The cold-rolled samples were subjected to annealing treatments at temperatures ranging from 350 °C to 900 °C for various durations. Furthermore, Vickers hardness measurements were performed with a 200HVS-5 hardness tester, with an applied load of 1 kg for 15 s. The tensile tests were conducted at a strain rate of 10−3s−1 using a universal tensile testing machine at room temperature. In the EBSD analyses, the specimens were firstly ground with waterproof emery papers up to a grit of #5000. They were then ion milled using an ion mill at an accelerating voltage of 3 kV and a gun angle of 7°. The EBSD measurements were performed by scanning electron microscopy (SEM; Zeiss ΣIGMA); the microscope was equipped with an EBSD system. The applied voltage was fixed at 20 kV, and a nominal beam current value of 6.4 nA was used. The working distance, tilt angle, binning level, and step size were 15 mm, 70°, 4 × 4, and 0.5 μm, respectively. Furthermore, the samples were characterized by XRD with an X'pert X-ray diffractometer and Cu-Kα radiation. The scanning range and step size were 35°-100° and 0.02°, respectively. Processing Text: Alloy ingots with the nominal composition of Ni66-xFe28AlxV6 (x = 16, 17, 18 at%), were prepared by vacuum arc-melting the mixtures of high-purity elements (Ni, Fe, Al and V; 99.99 wt%) in an argon-filled atmosphere. Each ingot was remelted as least five times to guarantee chemical homogeneity. Subsequently, the molten liquid was drop-cast in a water-cooled copper mold with dimensions of 70 × 10 × 10 mm3. The as-cast Ni66-xFe28AlxV6 (x = 16, 17, 18) alloys were denoted as Al-16, Al-17 and Al-18 alloys, respectively. TEM samples were first mechanically ground to 45 μm in thickness and then punched to Ф3 mm circle sheets, followed by a twin-jet electro-polishing with the voltage of 28 V and current of 60 mA. The mixed solution is HNO3:CH4O = 1:4. Microhardness of these as-cast alloys was determined by the nanoindentation tests (KLA-Nano indenter G200) with the maximum load of 500 mN. Uniaxial tensile tests were performed at a strain rate of 2 × 10−4 s−1. The shape and dimension of tensile sample possess the gauge length of ∼6.5 mm, width of ∼2 mm and thickness of ∼1.2 mm, respectively. In order to guarantee the experimental repeatability, each alloy (Al-16, Al-17 and Al-18) needs to be tested at least three times. Processing Text: Spherical 316L stainless steel (STS) powders for LPBF, with an average particle size of ∼30.7 μm, were prepared using gas atomization. Processing Text: Firstly, the sample design and sample processing of the failure die with different depths and directions were carried out. The material composition, hardness and metallographic structure of the samples were analyzed, and the tensile and impact properties were tested by direct-reading spectrometer, Rockwell hardness tester, optical microscope, scanning electron microscope, MTS testing machine and impact testing machine, etc. Meanwhile, with the help of Deform-HT software and JMatPro software, the coupling simulation of hardness, temperature and structure of the heat treatment of NOS525 steel was realized, and the hardness change of the material after heat treatment was predicted and verified by heat treatment test. Direct reading spectrometer was used to analyze the chemical composition of the samples. The literature shows that the heat treatment quenching process of NOS525 material was 650℃ (1 h) + 850℃ (2 h) + 950℃ (2 h) + 1030℃ (3 h). The cooling method was oil cooling for 8 min and then air cooling for 5 min. The temperature of the die after quenching was about 120℃, and the die was tempered three times in succession. The tempering process temperature was 560℃ (6 h) + 600℃ (6 h) + 600℃ (6 h), and the three times of tempering were all air-cooled cooling, and the die temperature was reduced to below 50℃. By combining Deform-HT software and JMatPro software, the coupling simulation of hardness, temperature and structure of NOS525 steel heat treatment process was carried out, and then the mechanical properties were evaluated according to the results of hardness simulation, and finally the optimization of heat treatment process was guided. The quenching simulation temperature was set to 1000℃, 1030℃, 1060℃, and 1090℃, and other heat treatment parameters were maintained unchanged from the existing heat treatment scheme. According to the sample size, the heat treatment holding time was determined, the quenching holding time is 12 min, and the tempering holding time is 22 min. The heat treatment tests were carried out at different quenching temperatures, the quenching temperatures were 1000℃, 1030℃, 1060℃ and 1090℃ respectively, and the other parameters were consistent with the existing process. A heat treatment model is established to optimize the quenching temperature. Through the coupling simulation of hardness, microstructure and temperature of the die material, combined with the heat treatment test, the heat treatment process temperature of the die material was optimized, that is, the quenching temperature is 1090℃, the first tempering temperature is 560℃, the second tempering temperature is 600℃, and the third tempering temperature is 600℃. Processing Text: The spherical pre-alloyed powders were prepared using Ar gas atomization. The mean particle sizes of D10, D50, and D90 are 8.4, 28.4, and 64.8 µm, respectively. The chemical composition of pre-alloyed powder, measured by inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectrometry, is Al-5.14Mg-2.15Si-3.05Zn-0.62Mn-0.24Fe (in wt.%). Prior to the LPBF process, pre-alloyed powders were dried at 100 °C for 10 h under a vacuum condition. The samples were fabricated using by EP-M150 laser powder bed fusion system equipped with a 500 W ytterbium fibre laser under the Ar atmosphere. The optimized processing parameters are shown in Fig. 1(c). The substrate was preheated at 60 °C before the LPBF process, and a rotation of 67° was conducted between adjacent layers to alleviate residual stress during the LPBF process. Considering the superior combination of strength and ductility in the horizontal tensile samples, the as-LPBFed samples for tensile testing were processed perpendicular to the building direction. Several samples with the size of 60 mm × 10 mm × 10 mm were made for testing and analysis. Precipitation analysis was carried out using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) under argon atmosphere from 20 to 500 °C, with a heating rate of 10 °C/min. As-LPBFed samples were directly aged at 120, 150, and 180 °C in a muffle furnace, followed by air cooling. The selected ageing temperatures were also confirmed to effectively facilitate the precipitation of prospective β- and η-type phases. The relative density of as-LPBFed samples was measured using the Archimedes method, and the density of 99.7 % was obtained via optimized process parameters. Phase identification of as-LPBFed and as-aged samples was carried out by X-ray diffraction (XRD) with the Cu Kα radiation source (wavelength = 0.15406 nm). Before microstructural characterization, both the as-LPBFed and as-aged samples were ground with SiC grinding paper up to the 3000 grit size and then polished using 0.3 µm SiO 2suspension. Microstructural characteristics were first detected by an optical microscope (OM) and then further characterized by a FEI Nova Nano230 scanning electron microscope (SEM) equipped with an electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) detector. The polished samples for SEM observation were etched using Keller's reagent. Grain morphology was investigated by EBSD with a step size of 1.0 µm. The grain size distribution was calculated based on the statistics from TSL OIM software. The samples for EBSD analysis were prepared by electropolishing (immersed in the methanol-nitric acid solution for 10 s at 15 V). To further characterize the microstructures in detail, the Talos F200X transmission electron microscope (TEM) equipped with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) was used. Both selected area electron diffraction (SAED) and high-resolution TEM (HRTEM) were applied to determine the orientation relationship of precipitation phases. TEM samples were polished using the Gatan 691 ion polishing system. To estimate the average size of the precipitates in the aged samples, Image-Pro-Plus software was used for the statistical analysis of a series of TEM images. The tensile samples with a gauge size of 15 mm × 4 mm × 2 mm were cut perpendicular to the building direction. The samples were ground using SiC papers to remove surface oxide layers before tensile testing. The tensile properties were conducted on the Alliance RT/30 system with a strain rate of 1 × 10 −3s −1. The loading direction of the tensile tests was perpendicular to the building direction, the tensile tests were repeated three times for each condition of samples. To accurately reflect the hardness values of samples, the micro-hardness across the molten pool boundary (MPB) area from one molten pool (MP) to another MP was measured using the Buehler-5104 microhardness tester under a load of 200 g and 15 s dwell time. The average micro-hardness values were obtained from ten different areas on the same surface. Processing state: as-built; Microstructure: nanosized eutectic Mg2Si cells

Processing Text: In this study, we fabricate near-fully dense and crack-free AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 EHEA samples with an alternating nano-scale eutectic lamellar structure composed of disordered face-centered cubic (FCC) and ordered B2 phases using the laser directed energy deposition (LDED) method. By using a novel and simple interlayer pause strategy, we have found that the eutectic lamellar structure can be significantly refined, achieving approximately 40% greater refinement compared to the case without interlayer pause. The optimized EHEA exhibits an exceptionally high strength of 1214 MPa and a sufficient uniform elongation of 16.3%, outperforming the non-interlayer-pause counterpart by 14% in strength and 47% in uniform elongation. Pre-alloyed AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 EHEA powders. The LDED processes were performed on a metal LDED AM machine (BLT-C400B) equipped with a laser system with a maximum output power of 1000 W and a focused laser spot diameter of 1 mm. Before printing, the raw atomized powder was dried in a furnace with a vacuum atmosphere at 80 ℃ for 4 hours to ensure excellent powder flowability during the LDED process. Meanwhile, to reduce the potential for oxidation, high purity argon gas was introduced during printing to ensure that the oxygen content in the chamber being less than 100 ppm. The schematics of the scanning strategy and the dimension of the tensile specimen are shown in Fig. 2(b) and (c), respectively. The optimum printing window was acquired through orthogonal experiments, and the specific parameters involved in the orthogonal experiments include laser power (750 W to 950 W) and scanning speed (400 mm/min to 600 mm/min). The optical images representing the average porosity rate of the samples along DD-TD direction are shown in Fig. 3, where the lowest porosity of 0.12 % was obtained with a power of 900 W and scanning speed at 600 mm/min. In line with previous studies, we generally selected a scan spacing equivalent to 40∼50 % of the melting pool width to ensure an ideal overlap. The interlayer rotation angle was carefully chosen according to previous investigations. Based on the powder feed rate contingent upon the motor speed of the powder reservoir, we quantitatively assessed the feed rate by conducting three separate measurements of powder output quality per minute. The argon gas flow rate was set in accordance with the recommendations provided by the equipment engineer. Accordingly, the final optimal process parameters are established: the laser power of 900 W, scanning speed at 600 mm/min, scanning spacing of 1 mm, powder feed rate of 4-6 g/min, interlayer rotation angle of 67° and lens-protecting argon gas flow rate of 8-12 L/min. The pause time between interlayers was changed to 0, 15, 30, 60, and 120 seconds to print EHEA blocks with dimensions of 50×20×5 mm 3 for tensile specimens. Sample without interlayer pause; tensile strength: 1070 ± 12 MPa; uniform elongation: 11.1 ± 0.6%; processing state: LDED (Laser Directed Energy Deposition).

Processing Text: The designed Ti-4.5Al-4.5Mo-7V-1.5Cr-1.5Zr alloy was fabricated by a vacuum arc melting furnace. After casting, the ingot was subjected to two different forging processes. The first one takes place in the β-phase region, followed by water quenching (WQ). By contrast, the second one was performed with a starting temperature slightly above Tβ and a finishing temperature below it (β trans forging), followed by air cooling (AC). The single reduction for both processes was set to be ∼40 %. After the forging process, the alloy underwent an aging treatment at 480 °C for 6 h, followed by AC. The whole thermomechanical process is shown schematically in Fig. 2. The present forged and aged Ti alloys were subjected to various microstructure characterization facilities, including scanning electron microscope (SEM, Hitachi-SU6600), electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, Oxford instrument), transmission electron microscope (TEM, JEM-F200), and scanning transmission electron microscope (STEM, Hitachi-HF5000). The specimens for SEM and EBSD were prepared following standard metallographic procedures. For TEM analysis, the samples were ground to a foil with a thickness of ∼50 μm and punched into 3 mm discs. To produce electron-transparent regions in these punched disks, twin-jet polishing was conducted at -30 °C and 50 V in a solution of 65 % methanol, 30 % butyl alcohol, and 5 % perchloric acid. The X-ray diffraction (XRD, PANalytical X'Pert-PRO diffractometer) pattern was obtained using a Cu anode at 45 kV, the diffraction angular is in a range from 30° to 90°. The flat dog-bone tensile specimens with a gauge length of ∼12 mm and gauge width of ∼5 mm were cut using an electrical discharge machine (EDM). Quasi-static uniaxial tensile tests were performed on an INSTRON 1195 testing machine with a crosshead speed of 1 mm/min (corresponding to an initial strain rate of 1.4 × 10 -3) at room temperature. Tensile properties such as yield strength ( σ0.2), ultimate tensile strength ( σUTS), and total elongation at fracture ( ɛf) were measured using standard operation. Loading-unloading-reloading (LUR) cycles were conducted to measure the back stress evolution. In each cycle, the specimen was first stretched with a crosshead speed of 1 mm/min to a designated strain ε, and then it was unloaded using the load-control mode to 20 N at a rate of 200 N/min, followed by reloading at a rate of 1 mm/min again to the next designated strain. At least three samples were performed to ensure the repeatability of the testing. Processing state: aged; Microstructure: multi-architectured α precipitates in β-domains

The homogenized ingot was rolled at room temperature from 7 to 1.3 mm thickness (a reduction ratio of 81.4%). Three different groups of samples were investigated: as-rolled, as-annealed, and laser-treated samples. The as-annealed samples were obtained through recrystallization annealing the as-rolled plate at 1073 K for 10 min, followed by water quenching. To develop a dual-gradient structure, the as-rolled sheet was laser-treated on both surfaces along a rolling direction. Laser treatment was conducted under an argon atmosphere using a laser module (YLR-300-MM-AC, IPG photonics, USA) with a wavelength of 1.07 μm and a beam diameter of 400 μm. The processing parameters for the laser treatment are listed in Table 1. To establish the distribution of mechanical heterogeneity on the present samples, Vickers microhardness tests were performed with microindent equipment (FM-700, Future-tech) with 100 gf and a dwell time of 10 s on the cross-section. Processing Text: Samples were manufactured using EOS Ti-6Al-4V grade 23 powder on an EOS M290 (EOS GmbH, Germany) LPBF machine housed at the ISO 13485 certified Centre for Rapid Prototyping and Manufacturing (CRPM) of the Central University of Technology in South Africa. Specimens were produced in three batches, and a representative portion of each batch and specimen type was selected to measure the oxygen content to ensure this was kept below 0.013 wt%. The base plate was preheated to 80 °C, and a high-speed steel blade was used as a scraper. The process parameters consisted of a 40 μm layer thickness, 280 W laser power, 1300 mm/s scan speed, 100 μm spot size and a hatch distance of 120 μm. Bidirectional scanning was used, and the scan direction was rotated by 67° between layers. This set of process parameters results in a material with less than 0.01 % porosity [ 23 ]. For tensile specimens, cylinders with a diameter of D = 10 mm and a length of L = 100 mm were produced in the vertical (Z) and horizontal (X) directions relative to the axis of the LPBF machine (and according to ASTM 59200) that is aligned with the direction in which the load is applied. For fracture toughness specimens, Compact Tension (C(T)) specimens were produced as rectangular blocks to allow for the final dimensions of a width of W = 25 mm. C(T) specimens were produced in three orientations, with the first letter indicating the direction in which the load is applied and the second letter indicating the direction in which the crack propagates, that is, ZX, XZ and XY [ 6 ], as shown in Fig. 1 . After printing, the specimens were stress-relieved (SR) at 650 °C for 3 h in a TSH 15/50/180 vacuum furnace (Elite Thermal Systems, England) and then wire-cut from the build plate. The SR treatment was chosen to allow comparison with the literature [ 15 ]. Subsequent heat treatments were conducted at the Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) in atmospheric air using a box furnace (Ultrafurn, South Africa). Therefore, at least 1 mm was removed by wire cutting or machining from all the heat-treated specimen surfaces to remove any α-case and oxide scale that may have formed. The heat treatment schedules, detailed in Table 1 , included the SR, an anneal (AN) heat treatment, chosen due to its simplicity combined with good tensile properties, and a duplex anneal (DA) heat treatment, chosen based on optimal tensile properties reported in the literature [ 6 , 25 ]. Furthermore, the heat treatments above T β (selected based on values available in the literature [ 9 , 15 ]) were combined with the stress relief (BtSR) and anneal (BtAN) heat treatments to mimic how SR or AN specimens would perform if the PBGs were equiaxed c . c It is acknowledged the above T β heat treatment is at the cost of PBG growth. Comparison to specimens with elongated PBGs is only based on orientation effects. After heat treatment, the specimens were machined and wire-cut to their final dimensions. Processing Text: Fe60Ni25Cr15, Fe60Ni30Cr10, and Fe64Ni15Co8Mn8Cu5 alloys were fabricated using a vacuum induction melting (MC100V, Indutherm) with pure metal (> 99.99 wt%). The 150 g ingots, measuring 50 mm in length, 35 mm in width, and 7 mm in thickness, were subjected to homogenization treatment at 1100 °C for 6 h under an Ar atmosphere. These ingots were then cold-rolled to a final thickness of 1.5 mm, corresponding to a total thickness reduction of 78.5%. To obtain a single face-centered cubic (FCC) phase, the cold-rolled specimens were annealed at 800 °C for 10 and 30 min, and at 900 °C for 30 min, respectively. Calculated value for σ0*; ΔE = 100.33 kJ⋅mol−1

Processing Text: A series of y (TiC)-Fe 1.4Co 0.8Ni 0.8Cr (y = 0, 2.5, 5.0, 7.5 and 10.0 % in volume fraction, respectively.) composites were prepared by mechanical milling in combination with the vacuum induction melting. Firstly, commercial high purity Fe, Ti and C (size from 0 to 50 μm) powders were weighted and followed mechanically mixed using a planetary ball milling machine. For mechanical alloying, the rotational speed was maintained at 250 r/min, the ball-to-materials ratio was closed to 10:1 and the milling time was set to 8 h. The homogeneous mixed powders were dried in a vacuum drying oven at 110 °C for 90 min, and subsequently shaped into a thin block using a hydraulic press at 15 MPa. The thin block was mixed with Ni, Co and Cr metal particles in a ceramic crucible and then put them into the smelting furnace. As the mixture become melted solution, poured it into a water-cooled copper crucible and cooled in the furnace. The addition of Ti and C element cause lattice distortion of the fcc structure, which in turn boosts the solid solution strengthening in L7.5 composite. Room temperature; Microstructure: fcc phase with submicron/micron TiC; Strengthening mechanisms: grain refinement, dislocation strengthening, precipitation strengthening
Processing Word: Room temperature; Microstructure: fcc phase with submicron/micron TiC; Strengthening mechanisms: grain refinement, dislocation strengthening, precipitation strengthening

Processing Text: Tensile tests were performed at RT using a smooth round bar, the SP test, and fracture toughness tests using single-edge notched tension (SEN(T)) and compact tension (C(T)) specimens. Two tensile tests using the smooth round bar specimen extracted from the longitudinal direction of the pipe were performed at a strain rate of 1 × 10−4/s. For the fracture toughness test, an SENT test using the specimen shown in Fig. 7(a) was conducted according to BS8571. In addition, a C(T) test using the 0.5T specimen was performed according to ASTM E1820 at RT under monotonic loading with a constant velocity of 1 × 10−4 mm/s. SP tests were conducted in air and hydrogen at various hydrogen partial pressures. The maximum load in the SP tests decreased with increasing hydrogen partial pressure and increased with decreasing temperature. Both the C(T) and SEN(T) tests were performed in air, and the C(T) test was performed in hydrogen (under two different hydrogen partial pressures). Specimen: #1; Test condition: Room Temperature

Processing Text: Nominal TiZr-based (MoTiZr, NbTiZr, MoTiVZr, NbTiVZr, and NbMoTiZr) alloys were prepared by arc melting under an argon atmosphere. Each ingot (∼60 g) was fabricated from pure elemental metal of over 99.9% purity and remelted six times to achieve a uniform distribution of the alloying elements. The specimens for cell cultivation were prepared by cutting into Φ14 mm × 1 mm pieces using electrical discharge machining. The surfaces of these samples were mechanically polished using SiC sandpapers with a maximum grit size of #5000. Prior to the cell cultivation experiments, the samples were washed with acetone and ethanol in ultrasonication, heated at 180°C for three hours, and then exposed to ultraviolet light for 24 hours to ensure their cleanness and sterility. Processing Text: The Ti6Al4V scaffold was fabricated using laser-based powder bed fusion (PBF-LB), then immersed in molten Zn while utilizing an oxide film to prevent merging of the two materials. The pre-alloyed Ti6Al4V powder particles utilized in creating the Ti6Al4V scaffold were spherical powders produced through the gas atomizing method (D10=23.0μm, D50=36.2μm, D90=55.0μm, Avimetal Powder Metallurgy Technology Co., Ltd, China). Argon gas was employed to maintain an inert protective atmosphere during the PBF-LB manufacturing process ( Fig. 1a). A PBF-LB additive manufacturing machine was used to manufacture the specimens (S210, Xi’an Bright Laser Technologies Co., Ltd.). The parameters for laser power, scanning spacing, scanning speed, and layer thickness were set to 180 W, 60 μm, 800 mm/s, and 20 μm, respectively. This set of parameters is selected to achieve optimal density and mechanical properties. The open-cell rhombic dodecahedron structure was selected for processing, with a design porosity of 80 %. The PBF-LB-processed Ti6Al4V scaffold was immersed in a chemical solution with a fixed ratio ( Fig. 1b), containing nitric acid (HNO 3), hydrofluoric acid (HF), and deionized water in a volume ratio of 40:10:50. The initial concentrations were 4 mol/L for HNO 3and 22.5 mol/L for HF (Yantai Shuangshuang Chemical Co., Ltd., China). The chemical polishing solution was placed in a water bath and kept at 20°C with a magnetic rotor at 150 r/min. The chemical polishing process lasted 2 minutes. Subsequently, the polished Ti6Al4V scaffold underwent ultrasonication in ethanol for 15 minutes, followed by drying and weighing [66]. A Zn block was heated to 700°C in a graphite crucible, while a Ti6Al4V scaffold was preheated in a 700°C air environment for 30 minutes. 0.1 g of NH 4Cl is applied to the surface of molten Zn, followed by placing the Ti6Al4V scaffold and adding heavy objects on top to prevent floating ( Fig. 1c). The depth of molten Zn exceeds the height of the Ti6Al4V scaffold to ensure complete filling of Zn. Subsequently, the crucible was cooled in the air, and once the Zn solidified, the heavy object was removed. Water cooling aided in removing the IPCs from the crucible without miscible of Zn and Ti6Al4V. Sandpapers were used to smooth the surface, remove excess Zn on the surface, and expose the Ti6Al4V scaffold. Samples were encapsulated in epoxy resin, leaving only 1 cm 2of area exposed to the SBF solution [68]. Compression test
Processing Word: Compression test

Processing Text: Nano-sized graphene incorporated Al-5.5 wt% Cu alloy matrix composites were produced via powder metallurgy. Nano-sized graphene powders obtained via the arc-discharge method were incorporated into Al and Cu powders in varying amounts (0-5 wt%) by applying a high-energy ball milling (HEBM) process for different durations. The consolidated composites were prepared by the succeeding uni-axial pre-compaction and pressureless sintering stages. The raw powders were mixed in a powder shaker for 2 hours to obtain more homogenous starting mixtures for the milling process, and they were named as as-blended or non-MAed powders. Stearic acid (C 18H 36O 2, ZAG, 99.5 % pure) was added to the powder blends as the process control agent (PCA). The milling vials were loaded with as-blended powders with a ball-to-powder weight ratio (BPR) of 8:1 under an Argon atmosphere in a glove box to avoid oxidation during the milling process. The hardened steel milling vial with a 55 ml capacity and balls with a 1 mm diameter were used to process 8 g powder for each batch. The high-energy mechanical milling at 1200 rpm with different durations (2, 4, and 8 hours) was applied to determine the optimum processing time. The as-blended and mechanically alloyed (MAed) powders were compacted under 650 MPa uniaxial pressure as cylindrical samples with a diameter of 12 mm. The removal of PCA before the sintering step was applied in an MSE tube furnace at 420 °C for 2 hours under an Argon atmosphere. Following the de-binding step, the pressureless sintering process was carried out in a Protherm PZF12/105/900 tube furnace under a flow of Argon gas with a 5 °C/min rate of heating and cooling at 600 °C for 2 h. All three alloy variants were manufactured using an EOS M290 machine with a 100 µm spot size and 370 W nominal power Yb-fibre laser. Samples were processed in an inert argon atmosphere with a standard oxygen level set and controlled at a maximum of 0.1 %. The samples were printed at 370 W power, 1300 mm/s laser scanning speed, 0.13 mm hatch distance and 0.03 mm layer thickness to produce fully dense samples (>99.8 % relative bulk density). These parameters were selected based on previous work where process optimisation was done utilising a design of experiments approach [32]. Scan rotation of 67° between each layer of material deposition was applied. The heat treatments for all the samples were conducted in a radiation-controlled furnace with a temperature control of ± 2 K. The samples were heated to optimum heat treatment temperature (623/ 648 K) at 10 K/min. The optimum heat treatments are based on previous work [32]. After heat treatment, the samples were air-cooled. The samples for room temperature (RT) tensile testing were heat treated as per specifications summarised in Table 2and then machined to the final shape (see Fig. 1) from the original cylindrical shape. The samples for high-temperature tensile testing were heat treated as summarised in Table 2and then machined to the final shape (see Fig. 1). Processing Text: The GH4099 powder prepared by vacuum induction-melting inert gas atomization (VIGA) method was used as the experimental material, with powder particle sizes distributed in the range of 15-53 μm. Before the experiment, the powder was dried in a vacuum drying oven at 80 °C for 8 hours to remove moisture. The GH4099 samples were fabricated using commercial L-PBF equipment (3D Systems ProX-200) for microstructure observations and mechanical performance testing. The fiber laser has a maximum power of 300 W, a wavelength of 1070 nm, and a spot diameter of 75 μm. During the L-PBF experiment, a protective argon gas atmosphere (purity of 99.9 %) was introduced to reduce the oxygen content to below 500 ppm. The laser scanning vector between layers rotates by 90 degrees. Based on optimization based on densification, the processing parameters for the L-PBF of GH4099 blocks include the laser power of 290 W, scanning spacing of 50 μm, layer thickness of 30 μm, and various scanning speeds of 1100 mm/s, 1300 mm/s, 1500 mm/s, and 1700 mm/s. After the L-PBF process, the samples are directly removed from the building platform using wire EDM (electrical discharge machining), without additional stress-relieving heat treatment. For convenience, the L-PBF GH4099 samples fabricated at different scanning speeds of 1100 mm/s, 1300 mm/s, 1500 mm/s, and 1700 mm/s are designated as V1, V2, V3, and V4, respectively. Processing Text: This study describes a new nonequiatomic proportional cast Co40Cr20Ni30Al4.5Ti5Mo0.5 high-entropy alloy prepared by a vacuum induction melting technique. The samples were then cut into 10 mm × 10 mm × 4 mm blocks and annealed in a KSL1400 high-temperature chamber furnace at 700 °C, 800 °C, 900 °C, or 1000 °C for 2 hours. After annealing at 800 °C, the alloy demonstrates excellent corrosion resistance, characterized by a low passivation current density, a large passivation range, and a high corrosion potential. The microstructure of the alloy was examined using optical microscopy (OM), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS), and X-ray diffraction (XRD). Furthermore, various corrosion evaluation methods, such as total immersion experiments, potentiodynamic polarization experiments, and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, were employed to assess the corrosion performance of the HEA in a 3.5 % NaCl solution. The alloy composition and heat treatment process were carefully designed. According to this strategy, the selected alloy composition is Co40Cr20Ni30Al4.5Ti5Mo0.5. In this study, a Co40Cr20Ni30Al4.5Ti5Mo0.5 HEA was prepared by arc melting the raw materials under a vacuum argon atmosphere. Co, Cr, Ni, Al, Ti, and Mo metal particles with a purity of 99.99 wt% were used as the raw materials. To ensure the chemical homogeneity of the alloy, the button-shaped ingot was remelted six times before being cast into a mould. Subsequently, homogenization was conducted at 1200 °C for 2 hours to obtain rectangular bars measuring 10 mm × 10 mm × 100 mm. Afterwards, the specimens were sanded and polished using SiC metallographic sandpaper and a polishing machine. Uniaxial tensile tests were conducted on these specimens using an Instron 5569 universal testing machine equipped with an optical extensometer. The loading speed was set at 0.5 mm/min. Additionally, hardness measurements were performed using an HXD-1000TMC/LCD microhardness tester. Electrochemical testing was conducted using a PARSTRT 4000 A workstation. Prior to testing, wires were spot welded to the specimens using a HIMAX TW50 stacker welder. The samples were then sealed with resin, leaving a 10 mm × 10 mm working area. Subsequently, the samples were polished using 180-2000 mesh sandpaper and W2.5 diamond polishing paste until the surface was free of scratches and exhibited a mirror effect, signifying completion of the polishing process. Finally, the samples were rinsed with water and anhydrous ethanol and dried. For the electrochemical tests, a standard three-electrode system was employed. The SCE reference electrode was chosen, with a platinum sheet serving as the auxiliary electrode. A 3.5 % NaCl solution was utilized in the experiment, which was conducted at room temperature (25 °C). Initially, an open-circuit potential (OCP) test was performed for 1800 s. Subsequently, an electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) test was conducted under OCP conditions. The frequency range was set from 100 kHz to 10 mHz with an amplitude of 10 mV. Equivalent circuit diagrams were plotted and fitted using ZView software to obtain the fitted EIS data. Adopting the measurement rate of 0.5 mV/s, potentiodynamic polarization experiments were then carried out, starting from a potential of −1 V (vs. Ref) and ending at 1 V (vs. Ref). The corrosion potential (Ecorr), corrosion current density (icorr), and other relevant data were obtained by fitting the curve using Tafel analysis. Annealing temperature: 700 °C; Processing state: annealed

Processing Text: The CrCoNiSi 0.3 MEA was prepared by arc-melting the mixtures of high-purity metals (purity > 99.9 wt%) in a high-purity argon atmosphere. The ingots were melted eight times to ensure chemical homogeneity, followed by drop-casting in water-cooled copper mold with dimension of 2 × 10 × 100 mm 3. The as-caste plates were homogenized at 1100 °C for 5 h. Subsequently, the homogenized plates were rolled to a reduction ratio of 70 %, followed by annealing at 900 °C for 1 h, as same as the previous study [26] for comparison. Dog-bone-shaped tensile specimens with gage geometry of 10.0 × 4.0 × 0.6 mm 3 (length, width, and thickness) were cut from the plates for quasi-static and dynamic tension samples. The quasi-static tensile tests were conducted with a Instron 5969 testing machine under a strain rate of 0.001 s −1. Dynamic tension tests were performed using a split Hopkinson tensile bar (SHTB) under a strain rate of 2100 s −1. Especially, the specimens were immersed in liquid nitrogen for 30 min to completely reach the temperature of 77 K before testing. At least three samples were conducted to ensure the experimental reliability in both quasi-static and dynamic tensile tests. In quasi-static tensile tests, the deformation strain was calibrated through extensometer. The fracture strain under dynamic tension was determined by the post-mortem measurements of the specimens because of the large fracture strain and incomplete records [25]. The samples were cut from the uniform deformation section after tensile deformation for microstructure characterization. Condition: Cryogenic temperature; Quasi-static tension

Processing Text: The material used in this study was commercial AISI 304 stainless steel. 304 stainless steel bars were solution heat-treated at 1100 °C for 60 min and subsequently quenched in water to obtain a coarse-grained (CG) full austenitic microstructure. The USRP process mentioned in previous work [27-29] was employed on CG rod samples to prepare surface gradient nanostructures. Based on the exploration of a large number of USRP parameters and orthogonal experimental results, the USRP parameters in this study were customized under the premise of avoiding surface spalling: the surface static pressure was 0.4 MPa, the rotational speed of the main shaft was 300 rev/min and the axial feeding velocity of the WC/Co impact ball was 36 mm/min. The samples were processed 10 passes to obtain a thick deformation layer, which was referred to as the USRP sample. Then, a set of USRP samples was welded to a thermocouple and placed in an induction coil, and heated to 700 °C, followed by air-cooling to obtain annealed USRP samples, and the corresponding samples were labeled USRP-700. To reveal the influence of USRP and annealing on the mechanical properties of the material, the Vickers microhardness (HV) test was carried out on the cross-section of all the samples by the HVS-1000 automatic microhardness tester with a load of 25 g and a holding time of 10 s. Uniaxial tensile tests of USRP, USRP-700 and solution-treated (SS) coarse-grained samples (diameter of 5 mm and gauge length of 25 mm) were carried out on a servohydraulic testing machine (MTS810) at a constant cross-head speed of 1 mm/min, and the high-resolution extensometer was used to accurately measure the elongation of the sample to calculate the yield strength of material during the tensile process. To obtain the back stress, loading-unloading-reloading (LUR) tensile tests were performed at a strain rate of 1 × 10−4s−1 at room temperature, and the back stress was analyzed using Yang’s method [30]. Tensile fracture morphology and cross-sectional microstructures were characterized using a ZEISS SUPRA55 field emission SEM with electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) and cross-sectional backscattered electron (BSE) detectors, the step size of EBSD is 50 nm. The TEM specimens were sliced by electrical discharge machining, mechanically ground to a thickness of ∼ 50 µm, and then twin-jet thinned using a solution of 10 vol% perchloric acid and alcohol. Processing Text: Samples were built using a SLM280HL (SLM Solutions, Germany) machine equipped with a maximum power of 400 W fiber laser and a laser spot size of 80 µm. To minimize the thermal residual stress, the 316 L stainless steel substrate plate was pre-heated to 200 °C. The following parameters were applied: laser power of 320 W, layer thickness of 30 μm, hatch distance of 70 μm, and scanning speed of 1000 mm/s. A 67° rotation between layers was applied. The as-built samples were annealed for the duration of 12 h at 500 °C - 1000 °C, followed by water quenching. The nomenclature used for the heat-treated condition was AM-HT. Alloy with a nominal chemical composition of Ni 35Co 35Cr 25Ti 3Al 2 was also prepared in conventional vacuum arc melter under argon atmosphere. Repeated melting was carried out at least five times to ensure chemical homogeneity and then dropped into water-cooled copper molds with the dimensions of 50 × 10 × 5 mm 3. The cast ingot was cold rolled to ∼12 % total thickness reduction and thereafter isothermally annealed at 700 °C. The condition was called CR-12 %-HT. All samples for EBSD and electron channeling contrast imaging (ECCI) were prepared by standard metallography plus electropolishing. The final electrochemically polishing was carried out using a 10 % perchloric acid and 90 % ethanol electrolyte solution with a voltage of 30 V for 30 s at ambient temperature. Samples for SEM studies were then electro-chemical etched in 10 % phosphoric acid water solution at a voltage of 2 V for 5 s. EBSD was employed to evaluate the recrystallized volume fraction and GB statistics with step sizes of 1 μm (scan area of 500 × 500 μm 2) and 150 nm (scan area of 100 × 100 μm 2), respectively. The smaller scanning step size was utilized for the accurate determination of TB content. TEM foils were first mechanically ground to ⁓50 µm in thickness and then punched into 3 mm diameter disks. Disks were electro-polished using 10 % perchloric acid in ethanol with a twin-jet polisher. The dislocation density analysis of the samples was carried out using X-ray diffraction (XRD; D8 Discover A25, Bruker, Co K α) based on the convolutional multiple whole profile fitting (CMWP) procedure. Hardness tests were carried out using a Vickers hardness tester with a load of 1 kg and a duration of 15 s. For tensile testing, a universal testing machine TSMT EM6.504 equipped with an extensometer was used. Tests were performed at room temperature under quasi-static conditions at a strain rate of 10 −3s−1 on dog-bone-shaped samples with the gauge dimensions of 12.5 × 3.2 × 2 mm 3. A mechanical extensometer was used to monitor the tensile strain. To investigate the microstructural evolution during deformation, interrupted in-situ tensile experiments were conducted using a Kammrath & Weiss tensile stage with an initial strain rate of 10 −3s−1. The in-situ tensile specimens with a gauge dimension of 8 × 2 × 1 mm 3 were fabricated by electrical discharge machining (EDM). For LPBF Ni 35Co 35Cr 25Ti 3Al 2 alloy, all tensile tests were conducted with the loading direction oriented perpendicular to the build direction. Processing state: as-built

Processing Text: The Co 34.46Cr 32.12Ni 27.42Al 3Ti 3 MEA were repeatedly melted under protection of argon atmosphere in an induction melting furnace to reach chemical homogeneity. The as-received ingots were homogenized under a very high temperature of 1423 K to achieve composition homogeneity, and then hot-forged into plates with thickness of 18 mm. The plates were homogenized again under 1423 K, followed by water quenching. These 18 mm thick homogenized plates were then cold-rolled (CR) by multi-passes (0.1 mm thickness reduction per pass) into plates with thickness of about 1.5 mm. The CR plates were annealed at a selected temperature of 1273 K for 1 h followed by water quenching, to obtain a coarse-grained (CG) structure with single FCC phase. Single-graded structure was obtained by SMGT processing on the CG plates. During SMGT, both sides of the CG plates were processed for 15 min by high-strength steel balls with a diameter of 4 mm and an average impact speed of about 20 m/s. The single-grade structure was aged at 973 K for varying times (10, 30, 120, 240 min) to obtain different dual-graded structures (hereafter referred as DG_10, DG_30, DG_120 and DG_240). Processing Text: ARB process combined with subsequent low-temperature annealing was utilized to produce the HM/NLS in pure Cu. Firstly, fully annealed (annealing at 450 °C for 2 h) and 98% cold-rolled pure copper sheets with different initial thicknesses were used as the original materials for this work. To obtain CRed-Cu/FAed-Cu laminated composites with different layer thickness ratios, we fixed the initial FAed-Cu sheet thickness and changed the CRed-Cu sheet thickness. To promote bonding, both of the CRed-Cu and FAed-Cu sheets were ultrasonically cleaned in acetone bath. Then the CRed-Cu and FAed-Cu sheets were stacked in a sandwich-like structure with an order of FAed-Cu/CRed-Cu/FAed-Cu and roll-bonded at room temperature using 2-high rolling mill (Φ 200 × 300 mm) with a nominal thickness reduction of 50%. Subsequently, the roll-bonded tri-layer structural FAed-Cu/CRed-Cu/FAed-Cu sheet was cut in half along the rolling direction (RD). Thereafter, a repeating sequence of cleaning, stacking, roll bonding and halving was performed. Through repeating the above process to 6 cycles, FAed-Cu/CRed-Cu laminated composite sheets with average layer thickness h = 20 μm can be fabricated. The ARB processed FAed-Cu/CRed-Cu laminated composites were annealed at 200 °C for 30 min under vacuum protection and water quenched to finally obtain the HM/NLS. Through using aforementioned fabricate process, a series of HM/NLSed Cu samples with different layer thickness ratios (corresponding to different volume fraction of coarse/fine grains) can be obtained by changing the initial thicknesses ratio of the CRed-Cu sheet to the FAed-Cu sheet. Thickness ratio (R_CGed/NSed) = 2:3; Achieves high strength-ductility synergy

Processing Text: The alloy Nb80Mo10Zr10Cr10Al5B0.1, denoted by NbMoZrCrAlB, was prepared by vacuum arc melting. The raw materials purity is larger than 99.9%, and the element B was added as AlB3. To insure the purity and homogeneity, the ingot was melted in a high-purity argon atmosphere and re-melted by at least 5 times. The microstructure of the unirradiated sample was observed using scanning electron microscopy (SEM, JSM-7001F) equipped with energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) detector. The mechanical property was measured by universal testing machine (AG-X Plus 100 kN), using Φ4 × 6 mm cylinder specimen at an initial strain rate of 1 × 10−3s−1. The samples were irradiated with 5 MeV Xe+ ions to a fluence of 2.1 × 1015 ions/cm2 at 350 °C and 750 °C, respectively. Transmission Electron Microscope (TEM, JEM-2100F) was used to characterize the microstructure of the irradiated samples. The cross-section TEM samples were prepared using focused ion beam (FIB, Helios CX5) with lift-out technique. Then, Ga ion beam was used to reduce the thickness to about 50 nm for all the samples, and the number densities statistics of Xe bubbles and dislocation loops were estimated according to the thickness value. Processing Text: The challenges in Wire Arc Directed Energy Deposition (Wire-DED) of super duplex stainless steels (SDSS) are the growth of large columnar grains and undesirably high austenite content. Here we report the additively manufactured SDSS with the addition of TiN inoculant via Wire-DED. Commercial ER2594 SDSS wire (Cr 24.851 wt%; Ni 9.651 wt%; Mo 3.778 wt%; Mn 0.465 wt%; Si 0.471 wt%; Al 0.022 wt%; Ti 0.008 wt%; N 0.264 wt%; C 0.010 wt%; Nb 0.018 wt%; Fe 60.297 wt%.) with a diameter of 1.2 mm was used for fabricating the SDSS thin-wall slabs, and the fabrication of the SDSS component was carried out using WAAM in conjunction with cold metal transfer (CMT) technology. Furthermore, a shielding gas consisting of 98% argon (Ar) and 2% carbon dioxide (CO 2) with a flow rate of 20 L/min was selected. The specific processing parameters were provided in Table 1. Processing Text: The 304L γ-austenitic stainless steel with FCC structure was processed by the L-PBF technique. The L-PBF equipment was a BHGD-LM150 laser melting 3D printer equipped with a 200 W IPG fiber laser generator. The whole L-PBF process was performed in a pure argon (99.9%) atmosphere. The gas-atomized powders with nominal sizes ranging from 15 to 53 μm were used for the L-PBF process. The following L-PBF processing conditions were adopted: laser power of 140 W, scanning speed of 900 mm/s, hatch spacing of 50 μm, and layer thickness of 30 μm. Prior to the L-PBF process, the substrate was preheated to 100 °C. The chessboard scanning strategy with a size of 4 × 4 mm 2 was used, and the adjacent blocks were rotated by 90°. After scanning each layer, the scanning direction of the subsequent layer was rotated by 67°. Ten rectangular blocks with a geometric dimension of 140 mm (length) × 32 mm (width) × 3.5 mm (thickness) were prepared with the L-PBF process. Five rectangular blocks were heated isostatically pressed at 1365 °C and 130 MPa for 3 h. These HIP parameters were selected based on our previous results, which could achieve an isotropic microstructure similar to that of traditionally manufactured materials. The samples under two conditions were hereinafter referred to as “as-received” and “HIPed” samples, respectively. The crossbeam 550 focuses ion beam field emission scanning electron microscopy (FIB-FESEM) equipped with a symmetry electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) detector was used to investigate the grain characteristics, including grain shape, grain size, grain boundaries (GB), and crystallographic orientations. The voltage for gathering energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) mappings was 15 kV. Before EBSD observation, the printed bulks were firstly prepared with the metallographic polishing process (400, 800, 1000, 1500, and 2000-grit sandpapers, as well as 2.5 and 1.5-μm diamond polishing pastes). The metallographically polished bulk samples were electroetched in a 10% oxalic acid solution using the following parameters: 15 V DC voltage, 15 s duration, room temperature, with a galvanized iron sheet as the cathode material. The step size for EBSD observation was 0.55 μm. The acquired EBSD data was processed and analyzed by Aztecrystal software. The grain interfaces with the misorientations of 2-15° and > 15° were classified as low-angle grain boundaries (LAGBs) and high-angle grain boundaries (HAGBs), respectively. Based on Brandon's criterion, twin boundaries were defined as Σ3 coincidence site lattice (CSL) 60° rotations with a tolerance angle of 8.66° around the <111> crystallographic direction. The Σ3 CSL boundaries with <111> 60° ± 8.66° misorientation were defined as twin boundaries (TBs). An FEI Talos F200X transmission emission microscopy (TEM) equipped with a high-angle annular dark field (HADDF) detector and an X-ray EDS system was used to analyze the dislocation distribution and atomic structures. The TEM foils were prepared with the mechanical polishing process (2000-grit sandpaper), electrochemical polishing process (10% perchloric aid solution), and ion thinning process (Gatan 691 thinning equipment). The rectangular blocks were processed into dog-bone-shaped tensile samples by electro-discharge machining (EDM) and surface polishing. The geometric dimension of the dog-bone-shaped samples conforms to the ASTM E8 standard. The length direction, width direction (building direction), and thickness direction of the printed rectangular blocks were hereafter referred to as LD, WD (BD), and TD directions, respectively. The surface roughness of the dog-bone-shaped samples was <0.4 μm after surface polishing using up to 2000 grit sandpaper. Tensile tests were performed using a Shimadzu 200 kN fatigue testing machine with a strain rate of about 1.1 × 10 −3s −1. To eliminate the adverse effect of subsurface defects on the mechanical testing and fulfill the ASTM E8 standard requirement, an additional surface grinding process with a removal depth of 250 μm was undertaken. Processing Text: Gas-atomized CM247LC powder (LPW Technology Ltd., Britain) was used for the LPBF process. An LPBF machine with an IPG-YLR-500 fiber laser and a Gaussian spot size of approximately 80 μm (DiMetal-100H, South China University of Technology, China) was used to manufacture CM247LC samples. The laser linear energy density El and volumetric energy density Ev was determined by: (1)El=Pv(2)Ev=Pvht where P is the laser power (W), v is the scan speed (mm/s), h is the hatch spacing (mm), and t is the layer thickness (mm). Different linear energy density values of remelting Er (i.e., 0.1 J/mm, 0.2 J/mm, 0.3 J/mm) and remelting scan strategies (i.e., parallel remelting PR, and orthogonal remelting OR) were used in the LPBF process. In the PR scan strategy, the rotation of 0° was applied between the prior melting and remelting, while the rotation of 90° was applied in OR. To remelt the layer sufficiently and eliminate lack-of-fusion pores, the hatch spacing of remelting (40 μm) was half of the prior melting (80 μm). A scan strategy with 90° rotation between layers was adopted in the prior melting. The laser remelting strategy was employed to each printed layer for manufacturing the CM247LC alloy via LPBF. The effects of laser remelting parameters on the microstructure, cracking behavior and mechanical properties of the LPBF-processed CM247LC alloy were systematically investigated. The impact of the energy density and scan strategies of remelting on the crack behavior and the underlying crack inhibition mechanisms of laser remelting were discussed. Based on the effects of laser remelting on the cracking behavior of LPBF-processed CM247LC samples, optimized-remelting parameters (P= 100 W, v= 1000 mm/s, h= 40 μm, remelting scan strategy = OR) were obtained. The LPBF-processed CM247LC samples with enhanced strength-ductility (ultimate tensile strength of 1280 MPa, yield strength of 885 MPa and elongation of 11.9%) were obtained by optimized-remelting parameters. Processing Text: A fine-grained duplex steel with a composition of Fe-5Mn-2Al-0.6C (wt.%) was fabricated using a powder metallurgy (PM) technology of thermomechanical consolidation by hot extrusion of powder compact. The Fe, Mn, Al, and C powders used had average particle sizes of 35, 8, 14, and 4 μm, respectively, with purities of 99.5 %, 99.9 %, 99.9 %, and 97.0 %. They were proportionally placed in four containers to achieve a nominal composition of Fe-5Mn-2Al-0.6C. and then the powder blend was subjected to planetary ball milling with stainless steel balls in an argon atmosphere at 400 rpm for 48 h with a ball-to-powder weight ratio of 5:1. 1 wt% of stearic acid was added as a process control agent, which also introduced additional C and O to the powder. The milled powder was die-pressed into a cylindrical compact with a pressure of 940 MPa at 400 °C in an argon atmosphere. The powder compact was induction heated to 1200 °C at a rate of 50 °C/min, held the temperature for 5 min, and then extruded into a rod. The extrusion ratio was set at 16:1. Subsequent heat treatment was performed to adjust the microstructure and mechanical properties. A portion of the as-extruded rod was subjected to heat treatment in order to change its microstructure. The austenitization temperature of the material, with a nominal composition of Fe-5Mn-2Al-0.6C, was determined to be 858.7 °C using J-MatPro software. To ensure complete austenitization of the material's microstructure, it was homogenized at 1000 °C for 30 min, followed by quenching in water and tempering at 200 °C for 2 h. The short low-temperature tempering period is intended to prevent grain growth and martensite decomposition into bainite or pearlite, while relieving internal stresses within the material.
