Processing Text: Subsequent heat treatment was performed to adjust the microstructure and mechanical properties. The results show that the heat treatment caused the precipitation of nanoscale carbide within the martensite, which significantly increased the yield strength from 792 MPa to 1078 MPa. The Fe-5Mn HT sample exhibits equiaxed martensite grains with a similar average grain size of about 1.6 μm. The Fe-5Mn HT sample exhibits the presence of nanoparticles within the α′-martensite grains, as confirmed by the selected area electron diffraction (SAED) plot, indicating their precipitation from within the α′-martensite. The orientation relationship between these nanoparticles and the matrix is consistent with ε-carbides commonly found in α′-martensite, following a Jack orientation expressed as α′[011]//ε-carbide [1100]. Heat treatment induces the precipitation of ε-carbide particles within α′-martensite. This is attributed to the uniform distribution of C atoms within the grains at elevated temperatures. The rapid transformation of austenite to martensite during water quenching prevents C atoms from diffusing back to austenite, causing them to be trapped within the martensite structure. During tempering, C atoms precipitate out of the martensitic lattice as carbides, which reduces the distortion level of the martensitic lattice and enhances its stability. As a result, the Fe-5Mn HT sample exhibits the presence of nano-sized carbide particles within the martensite structure. Processing Text: The as-received material was AISI 316 L stainless steel sheet (0.01C-17.3Cr-10.1Ni-1.0Mn-2.0Mo, wt%) with austenitic structure and an average grain size of 25 μm. Room-temperature multi-pass cold rolling with thickness reductions (r) in the range of 12.5 to 75% based on both UR and CR routes were used during rolling, where during the CR route the rolling direction was altered by 90° around the normal direction after each pass. In each pass, the reduction in thickness was ∼3% for each step in both UR and CR routes. Afterwards, annealing at 825 °C for different holding durations up to 135 min was applied for the purpose of reversion and recrystallization. The choice of this temperature was based on the results of Sohrabi et al. [27] for the successful reversion and recrystallization of AISI 316 L stainless steel. Metallographic sample preparation included grinding, mechanical polishing, electro-polishing (40 V, 50%H3PO4-50%H2SO4 solution), and electroetching (2 V, 60% HNO3 solution) to reveal the microstructures using an OLYMPUS VANOX optical microscope and a Zeiss Sigma field-emission scanning electron microscope. Using an MTS universal testing machine, tensile tests at room temperature with constant cross-head speed of 0.3 mm/min (initial strain rate of 6 × 10−4s−1) were applied to the subsize JIS Z 2201 specimens (rectangular specimens with a gauge length of 8 mm and gauge width of 3 mm), for which the repetition of tests was considered to ensure the reproducibility of results. Processing Text: CoFeNiCr xcomplex concentrated alloys (x = 0 - 25 at%) were fabricated using L-DED technique by systematically varying the Cr concentration. The AM deposits were fabricated using pre-alloyed equiatomic CoFeNi and CoFeNiCr powders as precursor materials. The depositions were made in a Optomec LENS-750 L-DED unit with 300 W laser power, 12.7 mm/s laser traverse speed, 0.5 mm beam size, and 0.25 mm beam track overlap (hatch distance). A multi-track, multi-layer scanning strategy was used to achieve a final deposit dimension of 5 mm × 5 mm x 5 mm on a 316 L stainless steel substrate. A bidirectional scanning strategy was employed within each layer and the laser head was rotated 90⁰ after each layer, i.e., 90⁰ rotation of scanning plane, for optimum thermal management during deposition. The Cr concentration of the AM deposits was monitored by adjusting the feed rate of the pre-alloyed powders from the hoppers. The AM printed deposits possessed relative densities between 98 % and 99.5 % and contained the mean Cr xcomposition of x = 6, 12, 18, and 24 at% respectively. Further detailed descriptions on the processing conditions and parameters are provided in Ref. [25]. To experimentally determine the lattice parameters of CoFeNiCr xalloys, X-ray diffraction on the L-DED printed samples was performed in a Rigaku Ultima III high resolution diffractometer operated at 40 kV/44 mA with Cu K αradiation. The diffraction patterns were obtained for 2θ angles between 40⁰ and 100⁰ with a step size of 0.2⁰ and scanning speed of 0.2⁰/min. Precise lattice parameters of L-DED printed CoFeNiCr xalloy samples were estimated from X-ray diffraction patterns using Nelson-Riley [26]method. The evolution of microstructures and phases in AM printed alloys were characterized using electron back scattered diffraction (EBSD) technique in a Thermo Fisher Apreo 2 C scanning electron microscope (SEM) attached with an EBSD detector. The orientation image (OIM) micrographs obtained from EBSD were analyzed using TSL-OIM 8 analysis software to estimate the dislocation density and grain size. Nanoindentation experiments were carried out to estimate the elastic modulus values of L-DED printed CoFeNiCr xalloy samples using a KLA iMicro nanoindenter in continuous stiffness measurement (CSM) mode with a maximum load of 50 mN and a diamond Berkovich indenter. The elastic modulus values were determined from the initial slope of the unloading segment of the load-displacement curve using Oliver-Pharr method [27]. For better statistics and consistency in determination of elastic modulus values, 20 indents were carried out on each alloy composition. The profilometry-based spherical indentation plastometry (PSIP) technique was employed to determine the nominal stress-strain behavior and yielding characteristics of the L-DED printed CoFeNiCr xalloys. The technique involved indenting the surface with a hard spherical ball indenter (indenter radius of 1 mm), measuring the profile of the indent with a contact-type profilometer and iterative finite element modelling (FEM) to fit the profile of the residual indent using Voce hardening equation ( Eq. 1) [28]. Processing Text: The AISI D2 tool steel powder feedstock was fabricated by Eloi Materials Lab (Korea) through gas atomization in the N 2 gas atmosphere. Four rectangular blocks with dimensions of 12 × 12 × 6 mm 3 were fabricated by an L-DED system 3D printer equipped with a ytterbium fiber laser (YMD-250, EML CO., Ltd, Korea), with a scan rotation of 90° at each layer. The detailed processing parameters are provided in Table 1. Two samples of D2 tool steel fabricated via L-DED were initially preserved in their as-built condition, with one undergoing no further treatment (labeled as B) and the other subjected to DCT. The DCT involved immersion in a liquid nitrogen chamber for 1 h, and this sample is referred to as B-D. Additionally, another set of two B samples was processed using a modified version of the ASTM standard heat treatment, which included pre-heating at 850 °C for 20 min, followed by homogenization at 1200 °C for 20 min, and then water quenched. One sample from this heat treated pair was further treated using the same DCT process as the B-D sample, resulting in the labels BH (for the solely homogenized sample) and BH-D (for the homogenized and DCTed sample), respectively. Samples for microstructural characterization were mechanically ground to 1200 grit SiC paper and then polished using a diamond suspension of 3 and 1 μm. The samples were finally polished using colloidal silica of 0.25 μm for 1 h. The polished samples were chemically etched using 10 % Nital solution for 1 min before observation through SEM (Quanta FEG250, FEI, United States). Processing Text: Commercial 316 L stainless-steel powder (0.01 wt% C, 17.24 wt% Cr, 10.65 wt% Ni, 2.0 wt% Mo, 1.7 wt% Mn, 1.8 wt% Si, 0.02 wt% O, and balanced Fe) with a diameter of 25-53 μm was used. The EHLDED and EHLR specimens were processed into cubic size of 10 × 10 × 6 mm by wire cutting, and subsequently were ground, polished, and etched in an aqua regia corrosive agent (containing 25 vol% HNO 3and 75 vol% HCl) for 60 s to produce a clear contrast among the different crystal structures. A cubic specimen with dimensions of 3 × 3 × 1 mm was cut from the center for porosity detection. Multilayer coatings with 16 layers have been prepared, as shown in Fig. 2e, and specimens for the tensile test were prepared with dimension of 20 × 6 × 1 mm (length × width × thickness) from the center of the multilayer coatings, as shown in Fig. 2f. Tensile tests were conducted at room temperature at a crosshead speed of 0.6 mm/min using a Zwick Z2.5 TH tensile testing machine equipped with a high-precision LaserXtens Compact laser extensometer. The tensile properties were measured from three repeated tests to ensure the precision of the data; the average results and standard deviations were plotted. Processing Text: Sponge Ti (≥99.9 wt %), sponge Zr (≥99.7 wt %), industrially pure Al (99.9 wt %), and granule Mn (≥99.7 wt %) were used as raw materials to prepare Ti-25Zr-4Al-1.5Mn (wt. %) ingots. To prevent oxidation during the smelting process, the alloys were melted under an argon atmosphere using Zr as an oxygen absorber in a vacuum non-consumable electric arc furnace. The rolling temperature was raised to 750 °C, 800 °C, 850 °C, 900 °C separately. Each TZAM sample was then heated in the furnace at the corresponding temperature for 30 min before undergoing multi-pass rolling using a two-high mill. During rolling, the samples were re-heated at the corresponding temperatures for 4 min before the next pass of rolling. The pressure applied during each pass was approximately 1.2 mm, with the total deformation reaching 88.5 % of the original ingot thickness. Once the desired thickness was achieved, the ingot was placed in the furnace for 4 min and then rapidly quenched. An inorganic silica coating was used to protect the specimens from oxidizing and cooling. According to the different hot rolling temperatures, the prepared samples were defined as 750-WQ, 800-WQ, 850-WQ, 900-WQ. The prepared samples were cut into thin flake tensile specimens of bone rods, with an effective area of 2 × 3 mm in the middle and an effective length of 20 mm. Single-axis tensile tests were conducted at room temperature until failure using an Instron 5982 testing machine, and the strain was measured with an extensometer at an initial strain rate of 5 × 10 −4s −1. Tension was applied parallel to the rolling direction. To ensure accuracy, each set of tensile specimens was tested at least three times. The microstructure of hot-rolled TZAM alloy was observed by optical microscope (OM, Ax 200 MAT), electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD, equipped in Hitachi S3400 SEM), and transmission electron microscope (TEM, Talos F200x). For OM observation, samples were abraded with sandpaper until fine scratches appeared on the surface in a uniform direction, mechanically polished with 0.02 μm silica suspension and chemically etched by using a solution of 10 % hydrofluoric acid (HF), 20 % nitric acid (HNO 3) and 70 % distilled water. For EBSD observations, samples were sandpapered until no rough scratches remained, followed by electrolytic polishing at 19 V and −23 °C using a solution containing 10 % perchloric acid and 90 % methanol until the surface was smooth. The EBSD scanning utilized a step size of 0.2 μm, and three regions were sampled per specimen to ensure data fidelity. An X-ray diffractometer (XRD, D/max-2500/PC) equipped with Cu Kα emitters was used to analyze the phase composition and crystal structure of hot-rolled TZAM samples. XRD was performed in step scan mode with a 2θ range of 30-80° and a scan rate of 2° per minute. For TEM sample preparation, the thin slice was ground to 30 μm by twin-jet electrochemical polishing and thinned with a solution containing 10 % perchloric acid and 90 % methanol at 13.5 V and −23 °C. The thinning time was determined according to the hole transmittance value. Under vacuum conditions, the acceleration voltage is selected to be 200 KV. Three blocks with different strains in each single compression pass, i.e., 5 %, 7.5 %, and 10 %, were fabricated via the TCC processing for 5 cycles, respectively. Each cycle includes three compressions at different orthogonal directions. The first compression was conducted parallel to the ED along the a-axis. In other words, compression was initially applied to the A plane, followed by subsequent compressions on the B and C planes, respectively. Taking the material compressed with 5 cycles under 5 % strain in each pass as an example, we name it the “5 %-5 cycles” material. The accumulative equivalent true strains of 5 %−5 cycles, 7.5 %−5 cycles, and 10 %−5 cycles materials are 0.37, 0.72, and 1.01, respectively. The samples were first loaded to one specified strain at a strain rate of 10−3s−1, and then unloaded to 60 N at an unloading rate of 200 N min−1 with the stress control mode, followed by reloading at the same strain rate of 10−3s−1 to the specified strain. The alloy was cut into rectangle blocks with a dimension of 14 mm × 14 mm × 15 mm with a long axis parallel to the extrusion direction (ED). Then the TCC processing was performed on the blocks. The compression was conducted at a strain rate of 10−3s−1 on the Shimadzu AG-Xplus 100 KN equipment and the processing route is schematically shown in Fig. 1(c). Three blocks with different strains in each single compression pass, i.e., 5 %, 7.5 %, and 10 %, were fabricated via the TCC processing for 5 cycles, respectively. Each cycle includes three compressions at different orthogonal directions. The first compression was conducted parallel to the ED along the a-axis. In other words, compression was initially applied to the A plane, followed by subsequent compressions on the B and C planes, respectively. Taking the material compressed with 5 cycles under 5 % strain in each pass as an example, we name it the “5 %-5 cycles” material. The accumulative equivalent true strains of 5 %−5 cycles, 7.5 %−5 cycles, and 10 %−5 cycles materials are 0.37, 0.72, and 1.01, respectively. Dog bone-shaped tensile specimens with a gauge length of 3 mm (// a-axis), a width of 2 mm (// c-axis), and a thickness of 1.2 mm (// b-axis) were prepared, with the coordinate system referred to Fig. 1(c). The room-temperature uniaxial tensile tests were conducted on the Shimadzu AG-Xplus 100 KN equipment equipped with a digital image correlation (DIC) equipment with a tensile rate of 10−3s−1. To ensure the repeatability of uniaxial tensile tests, more than 8 samples taken from a region above 3 mm away from the surfaces of the TCC processed blocks were tested, and these samples showed similar mechanical properties. The loading-unloading-reloading (LUR) testing was also conducted on this device. The samples were first loaded to one specified strain at a strain rate of 10−3s−1, and then unloaded to 60 N at an unloading rate of 200 N min−1 with the stress control mode, followed by reloading at the same strain rate of 10−3s−1 to the specified strain. Nanoindentation tests were conducted on the triboincenter equipment produced by Hysitron Company. Apply a maximum load of 1500 μN to the surface of the sample using a diamond indenter. The nano-indentation tests were performed in a 4 × 6 matrix with a spacing of 15 μm for the 10 %-5 cycles material. The samples for electron back-scattered diffraction (EBSD) mapping were also taken from the area at least 3 mm away from the block surfaces, with a sample size of 4 mm (// a-axis) × 3 mm (// c-axis) × 1.2 mm (// b-axis). Using 2000#, 3000#, and 5000# sandpaper, the oxide layer of the samples was removed. Subsequently, electrolytic polishing was performed in a solution with perchloric acid (5 vol.%) and ethanol (95 vol.%) to release residual stress on the sample surfaces and also to achieve a mirror-like effect. The polishing process was carried out on the LectroPol-5 equipment produced by Struers company. The polishing voltage and polishing time were set to 25 V and 25 s, respectively, and the temperature of the electrolytic polishing solution was maintained at 0 °C. EBSD tests were performed on Thermo Scientific Apreo scanning electron microscope (SEM) with an accelerating voltage of 15 kV and a scanning step size of 0.8 μm. Detailed microstructures of the materials are further characterized by the JEOL-2001F transmission electron microscopy (TEM). The samples were first mechanically polished to a thickness of 50-60 μm, followed by thinning using the TenuPol-5 automatic twin-jet electrolytic polishing equipment. The electrolyte was a solution of perchloric acid (3 vol.%) and ethanol solution (97 vol.%). Processing Text: Oxygen-rich 47Zr alloy reinforced by spherulite ZrO phase was prepared by in-situ semi-solid processing. The material used for the experiments was an as-forged oxygen-rich 47Zr-45Ti-5Al-3 V (47Zr-O, wt%) alloy with an oxygen atom content of 2280 wt. ppm. The XRD pattern and TEM images show that the as-forged alloy is composed of acicular α and β phases, which is a typical widmanstatten microstructure, and the average width of the acicular α phase is 53 nm. According to the calibration results of PDF cards (JCPDS cards 44-1294, 65-7479, 44-1288, and 20-0684), α'' and ZrO phase is generated in the alloy after SSP as well as the normal α and β phases. The phase fractions were quantitatively determined using software Jade 6.5 and the reference intensity ratio (RIR) method. The as-forged alloy contains 63 wt% and 37 wt% β and α phases, respectively. Subsequently, α'', β, and ZrO phase content first increases and then decreases with increasing semi-solid temperature, achieving maximum α'', β, and ZrO phase content at 1500°C. The tensile tests were performed at 500°C using an Inspekt Table-100KN universal testing machine at a set strain rate of 0.6 mm/min. Condition: As-forged; High temperature (500°C) mechanical properties

Processing Text: CNT/2024Al matrix composites were prepared by powder metallurgy and hot extrusion, followed by T6 aging treatment. 2024Al powders (Al-4 wt.%Cu-1 wt.%Mg-0.5 wt%Si) and multi-walled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs) were used as raw materials. 2024Al powders, 1.5 wt% CNT, and stearic acid (used as processing control agent) were added to the jar, and the ball-to-powder weight ratio was 20:1. Processing Text: MPCM ceramic is synthesized with MgO, TiO2, Cr2O3, ZrCl2O·8H2O and Al2O3, SiO2 via solid state reaction at 1600 °C. MPCM ceramics were prepared by solid phase sintering method. With MgO (AR, Tianjin Tianli Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd, China), TiO2(99 %, Shanghai Macklin Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd, China), Cr2O3(99.95 %, Shanghai Macklin Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd, China), ZrCl2O·8H2O (AR, Sinopharm Group Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd, China), Al2O3(99.99 %,Shanghai Macklin Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd, China), SiO2(AR, Tianjin Kio Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd, China) as raw materials, the mass ratio of each oxide was designed as 0.07:0.14:0.26:0.53:1.3:0.5. The first four oxides had a total mass of 1 g and approximate equal molar ratios, and the molar ratio of Al2O3 and SiO2 was determined to be 3:2 according to the molar ratio. The raw material and absolute ethanol were mixed by ball-milling (XQM-20, Changsha Tencan Powder Technology Co., Ltd, China), the ball-milling time was 9 h at 300 r/min, and the slurry was dried in a drying tank (101-2ABE, Shanghai Kuntian Experimental Instrument Co., Ltd, China) and passed through a 200 mesh screen. Processing Text: The preparation involved arc-melting high-purity raw materials, including Ti, Al, Cr, and Nb ingots, and irregular-shaped ZrO2 powders under an Ar atmosphere in a water-cooled copper crucible. Before drop-casting into a water-cooled copper mold with a dimension of 5×12×100mm3, all ingots underwent six cycles of flipping and repeated melting. Subsequently, the as-cast specimens were cold-rolled with a thickness reduction of ∼80% along the long axis. Processing Text: A high-strength crack-free TiN/Al-Mn-Mg-Sc-Zr composite was fabricated by laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF). The L-PBF process involved the partial melting and decomposition of TiN nanoparticles under high temperature, leading to the formation of L12-Al3(Ti, Sc, Zr) nanoparticles. Before and during the L-PBF processing, the chamber was filled with high-purity argon to maintain a low level of O2 (lower than 0.1 vol.%) and the substrate plate was preheated to 200 °C. A 67° rotation scanning strategy was employed. Optimized L-PBF parameters used to produce dense alloy and composite samples are as follows: laser power P= 300 W and scanning speed v= 800 mm/s for specimen S 0; P= 200 W and v= 1200 mm/s for specimen S 1.5, S 3.0, and S 4.5. Other parameters are hatch spacing h= 100 μm and layer thickness t= 30 μm. Cubic specimens with a size of 10 mm × 10 mm × 10 mm were prepared for microstructure characterization. Processing Text: To investigate the effect of Nb addition on the microstructure and mechanical properties of the current iHEA, 0.5 wt.% Nb powder (99.95 % purity) was mixed with 99.5 wt.% iHEA powder. The particle morphology of elemental Nb powder is shown in Fig. S1(b). These two powders were mixed in the mixer of the powder feeder for 24 h. The LMD process was carried out using a 3 kW IPF Photonics fiber laser with a wavelength of 1.07 μm. The following optimized printing parameters were used for the fabrication of the iHEA-Nb bulk sample: laser power of 1500 W, scanning speed of 350 mm s-1, and overlap ratio of 50 %. A scanning pattern with 180° angle rotation between two consecutive deposition layers was applied, and ST37 carbon steel plates were used as the substrates. For both iHEA-Nb and iHEA reference samples, tensile specimens with gauge dimensions of 11.5 mm × 3.5 mm × 1 mm were obtained with the long axes parallel to the laser scanning direction using electrical discharge machining. Prior to the tensile tests, the specimens were sequentially ground using SiC sandpaper from 320 to 2000 grit. Uniaxial tensile tests were conducted using a Kammrath-Weiss tensile module in displacement-controlled mode at the strain rate of 10-4 s-1, and the machine displacement was used to measure tensile strain. Tensile tests were repeated at least 3 times for each condition to ensure the reliability and repeatability of the results. In situ micropillar compression tests were performed on differently oriented grains ([001] and [111], respectively) to study the micromechanical properties of the as-built iHEA-Nb sample. The micropillars were prepared using a focused ion beam (FIB) and the detailed preparation parameters can be found in our previous work [27]. Processing Text: Inconel 718 pre-alloyed powder with a spherical morphology was produced via argon gas atomization. The D10, D50, and D90 values were equal to 23.1, 31.3, and 42.6 μm, respectively. The chemical composition (wt.%) of Inconel 718 powder was determined via inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectrometry. A 316 L stainless steel plate with dimensions of 250 mm × 250 mm × 10 mm was used as the building substrate that was preheated to 100 °C before LPBF processing. All LPBF specimens (16 mm × 16 mm × 100 mm) were manufactured using an EOSINT M280 LPBF printing system (EOS, Germany) equipped with a Gaussian beam fiber laser source with a maximum power of 400 W under an argon atmosphere. A 67° rotation angle between the successive layers was adopted during LPBF processing. A schematic of the LPBF process and its main parameters are shown in Fig. 1(c). They include a layer thickness of 40 μm, hatch spacing of 110 μm, scanning speed of 960 mm/s, and laser power of 258 W. After LPBF processing, some specimens were subjected to annealing at 1200 °C for 10, 30, and 60 min followed by water cooling. To enhance the alloy properties for engineering applications, a double-aging treatment involving heating to 720 °C, 8 h/furnace cooling at 55 °C/h to 620 °C, and 8 h/air cooling were performed to precipitate the γ'' and γ' phases. The double-aging treatment did not influence the fraction of twins or alloy morphology because of its high-temperature stability. Thus, the directly heat-treated specimens were denoted as LPBF-HT-10, LPBF-HT-30, and LPBF-HT-60. Other LPBF-fabricated specimens were soaked in liquid nitrogen for 7 d (168 h), recovered at ambient temperature, and held for 1 h (“DCT specimens”), which ensures that more homogeneous stress can be effectively introduced into the matrix. Subsequently, the DCT specimens were subjected to the same annealing and aging treatments described above and denoted as DCT-HT-10, DCT-HT-30, and DCT-HT-60. A schematic of the heat treatment and DCT processes is shown in Fig. 1(d). Condition: tensile loading; Microstructure: finer grains + high-density twins + precipitates; Properties: high strength and excellent plasticity

Processing Text: Three ingots weighed 500 g of non-equiatomic TiZrHfNb x (x = 0.5, 0.55, 0.6) alloys were prepared by levitation melting in a cold crucible under argon atmosphere. The purity of the raw materials of Ti, Zr, Hf, and Nb blocks was above 99.9 wt. %. The ingots were melted at least four times to achieve a homogeneous distribution of alloy elements. After the last melting process, the alloy melts were finally dropped to the bottom of the crucible and solidified into ingots. The ingots were annealed at 1300 °C for 10 h in a circulating argon atmosphere to homogenize the microsegregation, followed by water quenching. The cold rolling with a total thickness reduction of about 80 % (from 10 to 2 mm) combined with recrystallization treatments at 1000 °C for 30 min was used to acquire microstructures with equiaxed grains. Processing Text: IN738LC is now widely used in gas turbine and aero-engine turbine components due to its excellent high-temperature strength, creep resistance, and corrosion resistance. IN738LC has been widely used in hot-end components owing to its excellent high-temperature performance, while it has still suffered from metallurgical defects during laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) due to its high crack sensitivity. This study investigated forming behavior, microstructure evolution and mechanical property of LPBF-processed IN738LC samples at different parameters (laser power of 150-300 W, scanning speed of 500-1500 mm/s). The IN738LC alloy powder used in this study was manufactured by aerosolization method. The particle size statistics of the powders are shown in Fig. 1(a), with the powder range from 13 μm to 60 μm. The D 10, D 50and D 90are 23.7 μm, 36.9 μm and 57.1 μm respectively. SEM images of the powders are shown in Fig. 1(b), where some of the powders were observed to have satellites. The flowability of the powder determined by the Hall method was about 15.4 s., proving the good roundness and flowability of the powder. The composition of the element of IN738LC powder is shown in Table 1. The LPBF forming experiments were performed with a system equipped with a 500 W continuous fiber laser. Five different laser powers and scanning speeds were selected for the 5*5 forming experiment. Substrates with different parameters were first fabricated to take over the fabrication of single tracks. Material Name: CoCrNi-based MEA containing 5% Al and 5% Ti
Processing Text: The MEA specimens were printed using a PPA-AM equipment (DML-VO3AD, Duomu Company, Shanghai, China). The following processing parameters were used: deposition current 110 A, scanning speed 25 mm/min, interlayer waiting time 4 min, torch to sample distance 10-12 mm, powder feeding gas (high purity Ar) flow 2.5 L/min and powder feeding rotor speed 20 r/min. The first group of experimental samples were untreated after AM deposition (As-built), the second group of samples were first heat-treated at 1200 °C for 10 h and quenched in water, then aging-treated at 700 °C for 1.5 h and quenched in water (HT-AT). The other two groups of samples were heat treated at 1200 °C for 10 h (HT-1200) and aging treated at 700 °C for 1.5 h (AT-700) and then quenched in water. The samples were ground using 320-2000# SiC sandpaper in sequence, polished using 0.25 μm diamond spray. The EBSD samples were electropolished in a solution of 20% perchloric acid and 80% alcohol for 60-80 s at a temperature of −30 °C and voltage and electric current were set at 30 V and 0.2-0.5 A, respectively. The Vickers hardness of different MEA samples was measured by a digital microhardness tester (HVS-1000 A) under 9.8 N applied load and 15 s loading time. Hardness tests were performed at 1 mm intervals along the build direction. The tensile properties of the dog-bone shaped tensile specimens were carried out by displacement rate of 0.6 mm/min in a universal testing machine (Instron 5900) at room temperature (RT), and each group of samples was repeated at least three times to ensure the accuracy. Processing Text: In this study, vanadium microalloying was employed to prepare high-nitrogen austenitic stainless steel with excellent comprehensive mechanical performance. The high nitrogen stainless steel was prepared by high-purity iron, chromium, electrolytic manganese, molybdenum, vanadium, and chromium-nitrides within a vacuum induction furnace. The steel was synthesized at 1550 °C with a nitrogen pressure of 0.1 MPa. Then, the induction melting synthesized steel was subjected to a high-temperature austenization process at 1150 °C for 1 h. Then, the steel was hot-rolled 5 times within the temperature range between 1150 °C and 950 °C until the thickness of the steel was reduced to 2 mm, followed by water quenching down to room temperature immediately. Subsequently, the hot-rolled steel plates were subjected to solid solution treatment at high temperatures of 900 °C, 1000 °C, 1100 °C, and 1200 °C for 1 h, followed by a water quenching process, respectively. Processing Text: Multistage thermomechanical treatment experiments were conducted on Cu-Ni-Co-Si-Mg alloy strip prepared by the Heating Cooling Combined Mold (HCCM) horizontal continuous casting-cold rolling process. The tensile strength, yield strength, and electrical conductivity of Cu-Ni-Co-Si-Mg alloy can reach 894 MPa, 855 MPa, and 47.1 %IACS after a third-stage of thermomechanical treatment (TTMT). The cold rolling in first-stage of thermomechanical treatment (FTMT) not only caused work hardening of the alloy but also promoted the precipitation of solute atoms and the growth of second phase particles, limiting the increase in strength. Second-stage of thermomechanical treatment (STMT) effectively hindered the excessive growth of second phase particles in FTMT but shortened recrystallization process. The superior performance of Cu-Ni-Co-Si-Mg alloy after TTMT was attributed to dispersive precipitation of Ni, Co, and Si elements as (Ni, Co) 2Si phases in the copper matrix, strengthening the interaction between the precipitates and dislocations. A short process of HCCM horizontal continuous casting-cold rolling-thermomechanical treatment was developed to produce a high strength and highly electrically conductive Cu-Ni-Co-Si alloy strip used in lead frames. Cu-Ni-Si alloy is a typical aging-strengthening alloy, and its excellent performance is mainly attributed to the precipitation of small and dispersed Ni 2Si phases from the matrix during subsequent heat treatment. This article utilized HCCM horizontal continuous casting technology to produce Cu-Ni-Si alloy slabs. The Cu-1.3Ni-1.0Co-0.9Si-0.1 Mg alloy strip underwent a second-stage of thermomechanical treatment (STMT) process: (940 °C/1.5 h solid solution treatment→ 60% cold rolling → 450 °C/1 h aging → 70% cold rolling → aging). Processing Text: The commercial IN738LC alloy powder with the composition shown in Table 1 was prepared using the argon atomization method. The powder was approximately spherical with a few satellite spheres on the surface with D50 about 30.97 μm (Fig. 1(a and b)), meeting the basic requirements for the printing process. An EOSINT M290 machine equipped with a YLR-400GIA fiber laser was used for printing, and the printing process was executed under argon protection with an oxygen concentration of less than 0.1%. The substrate was preheated to 100 °C before printing, and the specific printing parameters were: laser power of 270 W, the spot diameter of 80 μm, scanning speed of 1437 mm/s, layer thickness of 40 μm, scanning spacing of 72 μm, and rotational scanning strategy of 67° within the layer (Fig. 1(c)). Sample blocks measuring 10 mm × 10 mm × 3 mm were cut using EDM wire-cutting equipment for subsequent experimental studies of heat treatment and hot corrosion. Table 2 shows the heat treatment regime for the samples, which consists of super solution treatment and standard solution heat treatment followed by aging. To prevent oxidation, the heat-treated samples were enclosed in an argon-filled ampule and placed in an SK-G08163-2-600 tube furnace (Tianjin Zhonghuan Electric Furnace). The furnace was heated to the target temperature at a ramp rate of 5 °C/min and kept for a specified time, then air-cooled (Fig. 1(d)). Three sets of samples were cut into 10 mm × 10 mm × 3 mm specimens, polished to 2000 mesh, and then measured for surface dimensions using vernier calipers. The mass of each sample was obtained using an analytical balance (Lichen FA1004). The samples were then ultrasonically cleaned in alcohol for 5 min, degreased in acetone, and dried for later use. The spare samples were immersed in a sealed alumina crucible containing a corrosive medium of 25% NaCl+75% Na2SO4. Hot corrosion tests were conducted in a box furnace at a target temperature of 900 °C. Samples were removed at 10 h intervals and washed with boiling deionized water to eliminate surface molten salts. To prevent damage from washing to the oxide layer, the samples were wrapped in filter paper during the cleaning process. After cleaning, the samples were dried in a vacuum oven at 100 °C and weighed to record the final mass change. The samples underwent three rounds of testing and the results were averaged. According to the literature, salt-coating method experiments were also conducted for comparison, and the detailed description is as follows: three sample groups using the same measurements were heated at 250 °C in a box furnace. A saturated 25%NaCl+75%Na2SO4 aqueous solution until a uniform salt mixture of 1 ± 0.1 mg/cm2 was sprayed onto the surface of the samples for the hot corrosion experiments at 900 °C (The corrosion kinetics curves are shown in Fig. S1). The samples were removed and weighed at regular intervals, which resulted in a significant degree of oxide layer shedding, and this directly affected subsequent observation as well as characterization analysis. Thus, the same crucible full-impregnation method as described in the literature was employed for this experimental (see Refs. [38, 41, 42]). Processing Text: The antibacterial Ti-xCu alloys (x = 3, 5, and 7 wt%) were fabricated by powder metallurgy (PM) technique using spark plasma sintering (SPS) route. The gas-atomized CP-Ti powder with a mean particle size of 113 μm (98% purity) and Cu powder with mean particle size of 51 μm (99% purity) were filled in the ball milling tanks in a glove box with argon gas. The mixed powders (Ti-3Cu, Ti-5Cu, and Ti-7Cu, wt.%) were milled for 6 h with a speed of 200 r/min and a ball-to-material ratio of 5:1, and the anhydrous ethanol was added as the process control agent. Processing Text: Ingots of the (TiNbZr)89(AlTa)11 (at. %) RHEA were produced using a vacuum-melting furnace. The constituent metals, sourced commercially, had a purity level exceeding 99.9 %. During arc melting, a mixture of these constituent elements was melted in an atmosphere consisting of argon gas. The specific operational procedure for melting involves the amalgamation of the alloy’s source components within the crucible. The technique utilizes an arc current ranging from 60 to 70 A. When the arc is initiated, it is initially melted on a crucible holding pure Ti for a duration of 1-2 min. This step serves to eliminate the oxygen present in the furnace, hence preventing oxidation of the HEA during the melting process. Afterwards, the alloy is melted using a smelting current ranging from 200 to 300 A. The alloy samples underwent multiple cycles of melting, with a minimum of 10 repetitions, in order to achieve consistent melting and enhance their chemical uniformity. Following casting, a homogenization treatment was performed at 750 °C for 3 h and then at 1,050 °C for 4 h to achieve a consistent microstructure. Cylindrical specimens, measuring 4 mm in diameter and 4 mm in length, were prepared for dynamic and quasi-static-compression tests. The quasi-static-compression tests were conducted at room temperature. Dynamic-compression tests with strain rates ranging from 1.0 × 103 to 3.5 × 103 s−1 were carried out using a split Hopkinson pressure bar (SHPB). Following this step, a solution treatment was applied to the samples at 1,000 °C for 30 min, succeeded by water quenching. Subsequently, the alloy underwent ageing at 600 °C for varying durations: 0 h, 2 h, 4 h, 8 h, 12 h, 16 h, 24 h, 48 h, and 72 h. This heat treatment aimed to determine the maximum hardness for microstructure analysis utilizing an ISO 6507-standard HV-1000Z micro-Vickers hardness tester at 10 kg-force loads for 15 s. The hardness of the alloy was measured to assess the effect of the heat treatment. Strain rate: 1.0 × 10^3 s^-1

Processing Text: The experimental material consisted of 316L austenitic stainless steel rods with a diameter of 30 mm. The material was hot-rolled to 4 mm in thickness, followed by solution treatment at 1050 °C for 1 h. Before each rolling pass, the initial material was immersed in liquid nitrogen for 10 min. The thickness reduction per pass was kept below 5 %. Surface cracks developed when the total thickness reduction reached 70 %. Consequently, the final thickness was reduced by 70 %, resulting in a thickness of 1.2 mm for the cryo-rolled sample, which was labeled as CryoR sample. After cryo-rolling, the samples were subjected to annealing at 700 °C 20 min, 750 °C 6 min, and a sequential 700 °C 20 min + 750 °C 6 min process, followed by water quenching. These samples were labeled as 700A, 750A, and 700A-750A, respectively. All heat treatment processes were performed in a muffle furnace without a protective atmosphere. Tensile tests were conducted using a universal testing machine (5105, SSANS-CMT) at room temperature (24 °C) and liquid nitrogen temperature (−196 °C) with a strain rate of 10 −3s −1. All tensile samples were cut along the rolling direction into dog-bone shapes with a gauge length of 34 mm, width of 10 mm, and thickness of 1 mm. Each test was repeated at least three times to ensure accuracy. To evaluate inhomogeneous deformation, load-unload-reload (LUR) tests were also performed under the same conditions as the tensile tests to quantify the back stress (σ B) component. The microstructural evolution of the samples along the rolling direction (RD) was characterized. XRD analysis was conducted to examine phase transformation with a diffraction angle range of 40°-100° and a scanning speed of 2°/min, using Cu-Kα radiation at 40 kV and 150 mA. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, Oxford) was employed for quantitative analysis of the phase microstructure. After mechanical polishing, samples were electropolished using a 10 % perchloric acid solution at 20 V for 20-25 s. EBSD measurements were performed on a Zeiss Auriga scanning electron microscope with a step size of 100 nm at an accelerating voltage of 15 kV. Processing Text: The heavy warm rolling promoted the transformation of metastable austenite (∼12.2 vol%) into hard domain α’ martensite. After 600 °C re-annealing, the hard domain α’ re-reversed to α + γ. The austenite content of WRA (71.9 %) significantly increased compared to WR. It was deduced that the hard domain α’ martensite was re-reversed into α + γ, and the heterogeneous microstructure disappeared during re-annealing. It was found that the austenite content (48.0 %) in WRT decreased slightly compared to WR, which was attributed to the decomposition of a small amount of metastable austenite into cementite and ferrite during tempering. In addition, the low temperature tempering further promoted C enrichment of soft domain γ without the re-reversion of α’ martensite (400 °C below Ae1 temperature point), thus further improving the thermal stability of soft domain γ while maintaining the heterogeneous microstructure. The microstructures of WR, WRA and WRT were characterized by the EBSD band slope (BS) images superposed by the inverse polar figure (IPF) maps of austenite. Austenite was represented by the color region. For WRA, the durable high-temperature re-annealing promoted the re-reversion of the hard domain α’ martensite into newly nucleated γ L, while the pre-existing γ Lin WR recrystallized and grew into globular grains (γ G) with random crystallographic orientations, the austenite size was also coarsened (0.45 → 0.57 μm). In addition, the internal stress was released after a durable re-annealing. Homogeneous microstructure; Heat treatment: high temperature annealing

Processing Text: The initial material was melted and cast, and then held at 1200 °C for 60 min, and then water cooled. The as-cast plates were subjected to cold rolling with a total reduction of ∼80 % to 5 mm by multiple passes. EBSD samples underwent mechanically polishing followed by a 20-second electrolytically polish at 25 V in a 7 % perchloric acid solution, using HKL Channel 5 software for analysis. TEM specimens were prepared by a twin-jet electrochemical polisher (25 V in a 7 vol% HClO 4acetic acid electrolyte), and examined in a scanning transmission electron microscope (JEOL JEM 2100F field emission, STEM) operated at 200 kV. 3D atom probe tomography (APT) using a local electrode atom probe (LEAP 3000 HR) was employed to study the microstructure of nanoprecipitates, conducted at 50 K under ultra-high vacuum (4.5 × 10 −11Torr) with a pulse fraction of 0.2 and a pulse repetition rate of 200 kHz. Processing Text: Commercial 316L stainless steel with a chemical composition of Fe-16.4Cr-10.6Ni-2.3Mo-0.8Mn-0.5Si (wt.%), measured using X-ray fluorescence (XRF; ZSX Primus II), was annealed at 1000 °C for 5 h and water quenched. The specimen was pre-cooled in the chamber using liquid nitrogen for 2 h and then the chamber was filled with liquid helium to attain a temperature of 4.2 K. Dog-bone shaped tensile specimens with a gauge length of 25 mm, width of 6 mm, and thickness of 1.2 mm were used, then the specimen was pre-strained up to a strain of 3.5 % at 4.2 K. The surface of the specimens was mechanically polished with silicon carbide papers (#400-#2000) and 1 µm diamond suspension. To effectively remove the microstrain by mechanical polishing, the specimens were mirror-polished with colloidal silica with a particle size of 50 nm for 5 h. Finally, the specimens were cleaned using ethanol to remove silica particles. Condition: as-annealed; Temperature: room temperature

Processing Text: All samples were fabricated by the SLM technique using a commercial EOS M290 machine and a Yb:YAG fiber laser in an Argon atmosphere. The precursor material was gas atomized AISI 316 L SS powder with spherical morphology and an average particle size of 15–55 µm. Samples with 50 × 50 × 50 mm³ dimensions were printed on a 10 mm thick AISI 316 L SS substrate. Fig. 1 (a–b) display the fabrication of specimens via SLM, with parameters detailed as: laser power (280 W), scanning speed (960 mm/s), layer thickness (40 µm), hatch spacing (110 µm), and scan angle (67° between layers). To study annealing–induced hardening, they were annealed at six temperatures from 400 °C to 900 °C, with a step size of 100 °C, and the step size of annealing time is carried out in a proportional sequence of 2 h. Then, these samples were quenched in water, obtaining samples with 24 kinds of heat–treated conditions. Before microstructural analysis, the samples were mechanically ground with SiC papers from 800 to 3000 grit, and then polished with water–based diamond suspensions from 9 µm to 1 µm, and finally vibratory polished using a 0.05 µm OP–S colloidal silica suspension for 5 h. Phase composition and microstructures were analyzed using X–ray diffraction (XRD) with a Rigaku Smart–lab diffractometer, employing Cu Kα radiation at 40 kV and 40 mA. Dog bone tensile sample (Fig. 2 (b)), annealed at 500 °C for 8 h, was polished before quasi–in situ EBSD analysis. Annealed at 500 °C; High-density tangled dislocations, cellular/wall dislocation structure, nano-particles (O, Cr, Mo, and Si), high proportion of LAGBs
Processing Word: Annealed at 500 °C; High-density tangled dislocations, cellular/wall dislocation structure, nano-particles (O, Cr, Mo, and Si), high proportion of LAGBs

Processing Text: The prototypical material used in this study is a binary metastable β-Ti alloy Ti-11V (wt.%), which was supplied as hot-rolled block by the Northwest Institute for Nonferrous Metal Research, China. The actual chemical composition of the block consists of 10.6 wt.% V and Ti in balance, while the β-transus temperature (T β) is ∼730 °C. The block was cut into sheets for heat treatment and subsequent cold working. The solution treatment (ST) was performed at 950 °C for 2 h following water quenched (WQ) to room temperature. After heat treatment, the ST sheets are divided into two groups for cold working. In the first group, a combination of cold forging (CF) and cold rolling (CR) was applied. The CF was first performed on the ST sheets at room temperature with a thickness decrease of 10 % to induce deformation kinking in microstructure. Subsequently, these CF sheets underwent cold rolling at room temperature with a thickness decrease of 30 %. For convenience, these cold-worked sheets will hereafter be referred to as the F+ R-40 % ones. To investigate the effects of larger thickness reduction during cold rolling on mechanical properties, several CF sheets were subjected to a thickness reduction of 60 %, henceforth referred to as the F+ R-70 % ones. In the second group, individual CF or CR was applied separately. Some ST sheets underwent cold forging with a thickness decrease of 10 % (referred to as the F-10 % sheets), while others were directly subjected to cold rolling with a thickness decrease of 40 % (referred to as the R-40 % sheets). Processing state: R-40 % (cold rolling with 40% thickness reduction)

Processing Text: The Co-Cr-Fe-Ni powders were arranged in equiatomic ratio. A 5.1 g mixture of elemental powders and 1 wt% of stearic acid as a process control agent (PCA) to prevent excessive cold welding during mechanical alloying was mixed in a hardened steel vial. The powder preparation was performed in a glove box, where oxygen and humidity levels were maintained below 0.5 ppm by continuous circulation of high-purity argon gas through a purification system. The mixture was first milled for 30 min. Next, the vials were opened inside the glove box, and 440 C stainless steel balls with a powder-to-ball radio of 1:10 were added. The vials were then sealed in the glove box, and the mechanical alloying process was carried out at room temperature for 20 h using a SPEX 8000 M/D high energy ball miller. To minimize cold welding without the need for additional PCA, the sealed vials were placed in liquid nitrogen for 5 min after every 150 min of mechanical alloying period to reduce their temperature. After mechanical alloying, the vials were placed back inside the glove box, where the as-milled HEA powders were removed and stored until sufficient milling runs were completed to generate enough powder. This was followed by annealing in an argon atmosphere at 500 °C for 1 h to remove the PCA from the as-milled HEA powders. The cold-pressed pellets were then annealed at 700 °C for 1 and 24 h, and at 900 °C for 1, 3, 6, 12, and 24 h in an argon atmosphere, followed by in-furnace cooling. The consolidated and annealed samples were ground using 800, 1200, and 2500 grits, and then polished to achieve a mirror-like surface for subsequent testing and characterization. Processing state: As-rolled

Processing Text: The as-received MP159 alloy in a cast-and-wrought state is prepared by Central Iron and Steel Research Institute. And the original ingot of MP159 alloy was prepared by vacuum induction melting. Solution treatment at 1000 °C for 1h is then conducted, followed by water quenching. We hereafter denote the solution treated MP159 sample without annealing as WA-MP159. All the heat treatments were carried out in the air condition. Tensile tests on cylindrical specimens with a diameter of 5 mm and a gage length of 30 mm were conducted on an Instron 3369 universal testing machine at RT, 400 °C, 500 °C, 600 °C, 650 °C and 700 °C, respectively. The tensile strain rate is set to be 1.5 × 10 −4s −1. TEM samples were prepared by dual jet polishing at Specimens for using an electrolyte of perchloric acid (10 %) and ethanol (90 %). Processing Text: Equimolar CoCrNi MEA was prepared by arc-melting Co, Cr, and Ni mixtures with 99.99 % purity in a high-purity argon atmosphere. The ingot was remelted more than five times before the drop-cast process to ensure homogeneity. Subsequently, the as-cast CoCrNi MEA ingot was cold-forged by a 50 % reduction in thickness. Afterward, the alloy was annealed at 1173K for 1 h to reduce deformation-induced defects and promote recrystallization. Quasi-static compression tests with strain rates ranging from 1.0 × 10^−3 s^−1 to 10^−1 s^−1 were performed on CoCrNi MEA samples with a diameter of 3 mm and length of 6 mm using an Instron 5969 testing machine. Dynamic compression tests with strain rates ranging from 2.6 × 10^3 s^−1 to 6.2 × 10^3 s^−1 were carried out on CoCrNi MEA samples with a diameter of 3 mm and length of 3 mm using a SHPB system. Stop-ring technology was introduced to control the strain during the dynamic compressions. The ramp wave and shock compression experiments were conducted using the CQ-4 magnetically driven system, delivering a pulsed current with a peak value of 4 MA and a rising time of 500 ns, developed by the Institute of Fluid Physics, China Academy of Engineering Physics. Multi-level characterizations were conducted to explore the intrinsic mechanisms of CoCrNi MEA. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) was performed using a JEOL JSM-7100F field-emission scanning electron microscope (SEM). An acceleration voltage of 20 kV, a specimen tilt angle of 70°, and a working distance of 15 mm were used in the EBSD observations. A JEM-2100F transmission electron microscopy (TEM) was operated at an acceleration voltage of 200 kV to uncover microscopic deformation mechanisms. Condition: As-built; Measurement context: UTS of 656.6 MPa, elongation to failure of 32.6%
Processing Word: Condition: As-built; Measurement context: UTS of 656.6 MPa, elongation to failure of 32.6%

Processing Text: A layer-wise heterostructured MEA (denoted as HS MEA) sample was fabricated by alternate deposition of pre-alloyed CoCrNi MEA and blended Al7Ti7 MEA powders from two hoppers. The laser processing parameters were optimized as follows: focused laser diameter of 4 mm, laser power of 1600 W, laser scanning rate of 600 mm/min, powder feeding rate of 13 g/min, overlapping rate of 40 % and deposition head lift height about 1 mm. The specimens were first solution-treated at 1150 °C for 2 h and then water quenched, followed by aging at 800 °C for 2 h and then air-cooling to room temperature. Condition: As-built; Measurement context: UTS of 799.1 MPa, elongation to failure of 24.5%

Processing Text: Green pellets with a diameter of 10 mm were produced using a 25-ton manual press (Kimaya Engineers, India) at a pressure of 520 MPa. The compacts were sintered in a tube furnace (Swam Equip, India) under a continuous flow of 99.99 % pure argon gas. The green samples were subjected to a sintering temperature range of 560-650 °C, with a 30 °C interval, at a heating rate of 5 °C/min. The duration of sintering was 90 min, followed by controlled cooling within the furnace. Bulk density measurements were performed using the Archimedes principle with a Sartorius Secura YDK03 instrument. Phase analysis was conducted using a Panalytical X-pert powder X-ray diffractometer (Make: Panalytical, Model: X-pert powder). The instrument was equipped with Cu-Kα radiation (λ = 0.15406 nm) for data profile acquisition. The process involved a voltage of 45 kV and a current of 30 mA, with a step size of 0.02 and a duration of 25s/step. Optical microscopy (Quasmo ISI Microscope) and scanning electron microscopy (VEGA 3 LMU TESCAN) were employed to characterize the microstructure. Quantification and mapping of elements were performed using a Field Emission Gun Scanning Electron Microscope (FEGSEM) (JEOL, model: JSM 7800F) equipped with an Energy Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDS) detector. For TEM analysis, specimens were obtained by cutting 300-micron-thick discs from the sintered samples, followed by metallographic polishing to a thickness of less than 100 μm. Subsequently, ion beam milling was applied to the specimens. The crystal structure and lattice imperfections, such as stacking faults, dislocations, and precipitation and their boundaries at the atomic scale, were investigated using a High Resolution- Transmission Electron Microscope (HR-TEM) (Model: JEOL JEM 2100, at an operating voltage of 200 kV). Nanoindentation measurements were performed using a Berkovich diamond indenter with a radius of 150 nm, featuring an included angle of 142.30° and a half angle of 65.27°, within a NANOINDENTER device (BRUKER'S HYSITRON TI PREMIER). A 2 mN load was used for the nanoindentation study and the distance between the two consecutive indentations was 3 μm to evaluate the hardness and modulus. The load-displacement curves were used to generate hardness and elastic modulus profiles across the matrix, intermetallic, and particle interfaces. The room temperature and isothermal compressive strength (at 200 °C, 250 °C, and 300 °C) of the composite were assessed using cylindrical samples (φ10mm x l = 15 mm) with an aspect ratio (l/d) of 1.5. The test was performed using a Universal Testing Machine (Jinan, WDW-100S) following the ASTM E−09standard. For the isothermal compression test, a furnace setup was employed. All samples were sintered at 620 °C due to its verified superior density in line with our previous findings. All samples were subjected to a strain of 0.5 and then water-quenched to facilitate microstructural observation. The strain rate for both room temperature and isothermal tests was set at 10 −4S −1. Room temperature; Pressureless sintering without heat treatment

The sample using reciprocating scanning strategy is labelled as thin-wall 1, and the sample using alternate scanning strategy is labelled as thin-wall 2. The schematic of a single-track sample is shown in Fig. 1(c3). After LDED, The XY-section and XZ-section samples were sequentially ground, polished and electro-etched using concentrated sulfuric acid and methanol electrolytic solution (15 V, 10 s). Flat dog bone specimens (at least three of each) were cut along the scanning direction (SD) and building direction (BD) with the dimensions shown in Fig. 1(d) to test the tensile properties of the LDED samples at room temperature. All tensile tests were measured using an Instron 68MT-50 testing machine with a speed of 0.6 mm/min. The microhardness test was performed along the deposition height of the sample using a micro-Vickers hardness tester with a load of 500 g and a holding time of 10 s. Processing Text: The Co 44Ni 44Mo 9W 3alloy was synthesized by vacuum arc melting using high-purity metals (>99.9 %). The melt was drop-cast into a rectangular water-cooled mold with sizes of 60 mm × 30 mm × 10 mm. The as-cast ingot was homogenized at 1250 °C for 12 h followed by water-quenching, and then cold-rolling (CR, with a reduction of 75 % in thickness) at RT. In order to obtain fully-recrystallized FCC microstructure with various average grain sizes, the cold-rolled alloy was annealed at different temperatures (i.e., 900 °C, 1100 °C, and 1200 °C, respectively) for 70 s and then water-quenched. These temperatures were chosen to ensure a single-phase structure based on thermodynamic calculation results using Thermo-Calc software (with a TCNI9 database). Dog-bone shaped tensile specimens (with gage length, width and thickness of 8 mm, 2 mm, and 1 mm respectively) were machined by an electro discharge machine with the loading axis parallel to the rolling direction. Tensile tests were performed using an Shimadzu AGS-X universal testing machine equipped with a RVX-112 video extensometer. The tests were conducted in air at RT under a nominal strain rate of 1.0 × 10 −3s−1. To understand deformation mechanisms, the microstructural evolution was characterized by a Zeiss Sigma 300 scanning electron microscope (SEM, equipped with electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) and energy dispersive X-ray (EDX) detectors) and an FEI Talos F200X transmission electron microscope (TEM). Samples for SEM and EBSD investigations were prepared by conventional mechanical grinding and electro-polishing. EBSD imaging was performed with a step size of 0.12 μm, and the data were analyzed using AZtecCrystal software. TEM samples were further prepared using a Twin-Jet electro-polisher with electrolyte of 95 % methanol and 5 % perchloric acid solution. Conventional bright-field (BF) and dark-field (DF) TEM imaging was conducted at 200 kV. Condition: Ambient temperature; Microstructure: FCC single-phase
Processing Word: Condition: Ambient temperature; Microstructure: FCC single-phase

Processing Text: Ni20Cr3Al and nano Ti powders were mechanically milled in an atmosphere of Ar+20%Air. Ti powder was partly oxidized to be TiO2 during the milling and spark plasma sintering. The others are dissolved into the nickel-based alloy and form coherent intermetallic phase of Ni3Ti. Owing to the higher affinity of Al than Ti to O, most TiO2 particles were transformed to be in-situ nano Al2O3 dispersoids with good coherency to the alloy matrix as well. Grain refinement and precipitates strengthening contribute largely to the greatly improvement of mechanical strength of the NiCrAl-2Ti alloy, of which the yield strength reaches 884 MPa and ductility is 10.72%. Besides, the refined grains promote the selective oxidation of Al, ensuring an extremely high oxidation resistance. Its oxidation rate constant (kp) is as low as 9.7 × 10−8 mg2 cm−4 s−1 at 900 °C. Commercially available powders of Ni20Cr3Al (28-50 μm, Institute of Metal Research, Chinese Academy of Sciences), Ti (≤60 nm, Tijo Co., Ltd, China), and TiO2(≤25 nm, Shanghai Aladdin Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd, China) were used as the original materials. Ensuring the same mass fraction of Ti elements in alloys (2 wt%), nano TiO2 and Ti powers were added to the Ni20Cr3Al alloy powder to get NiCrAl-3TiO2 and NiCrAl-2Ti, respectively. Then the mixed powders were placed in a vacuum glove box filled with Ar. The NiCrAl-TiO2 and NiCrAl-2Ti powders were pumped to −0.1 MPa and 0.02 MPa (i.e. 0.2 atm) by the air pump, respectively, then filled with Ar. Subsequently, powders were milled by a high-energy ball-milling (HBM) machine (XQM-4 L, Changsha Tencan Powder, China) with a ball-to-powder weight ratio of 10:1 at 300 rpm for 4 h. Thereafter, the mixtures were sintered by a spark plasma sintering technique (HPD 250, FCT Group, Germany) at 1150 °C under a pressure of 40 MPa for 20 min in Ar atmosphere. The others are dissolved into the nickel-based alloy and form coherent intermetallic phase of Ni3Ti. Owing to the higher affinity of Al than Ti to O, most TiO2 particles were transformed to be in-situ nano Al2O3 dispersoids with good coherency to the alloy matrix as well. Grain refinement and precipitates strengthening contribute largely to the greatly improvement of mechanical strength of the NiCrAl-2Ti alloy, of which the yield strength reaches 884 MPa and ductility is 10.72%. Besides, the refined grains promote the selective oxidation of Al, ensuring an extremely high oxidation resistance. Its oxidation rate constant (kp) is as low as 9.7 × 10−8 mg2 cm−4 s−1 at 900 °C. Commercially available powders of Ni20Cr3Al (28-50 μm, Institute of Metal Research, Chinese Academy of Sciences), Ti (≤60 nm, Tijo Co., Ltd, China), and TiO2(≤25 nm, Shanghai Aladdin Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd, China) were used as the original materials. Ensuring the same mass fraction of Ti elements in alloys (2 wt%), nano TiO2 and Ti powers were added to the Ni20Cr3Al alloy powder to get NiCrAl-3TiO2 and NiCrAl-2Ti, respectively. Then the mixed powders were placed in a vacuum glove box filled with Ar. The NiCrAl-TiO2 and NiCrAl-2Ti powders were pumped to −0.1 MPa and 0.02 MPa (i.e. 0.2 atm) by the air pump, respectively, then filled with Ar. Subsequently, powders were milled by a high-energy ball-milling (HBM) machine (XQM-4 L, Changsha Tencan Powder, China) with a ball-to-powder weight ratio of 10:1 at 300 rpm for 4 h. Thereafter, the mixtures were sintered by a spark plasma sintering technique (HPD 250, FCT Group, Germany) at 1150 °C under a pressure of 40 MPa for 20 min in Ar atmosphere. Balanced mechanical properties with high yield strength and moderate ductility (10.72%); Grain refining and precipitation strengthening contribute largely to improvement of mechanical strength

Processing Text: Spherical 1060 pure aluminum (Al) powders (purity＞99.6 %) and CuO powders (purity＞99.9 %) were used as raw powders, whose average diameters were 5 μm and 1 μm, respectively. The milling time and ball-to-powder ratio were 10 h and 10:1, respectively. The milled powders were pre-compacted at 200 MPa for 60 s by a cold tubular mold. Then, the round preform was placed in the Al mold and was sheared and stirred by a processing tool. The rotational velocity of the tool was varied during the preparation process to introduce more substructure in materials. The rotational velocity was initially set at 500 rpm and changed to 100 rpm when the sample was only 1.5 mm (h 1in Fig. 1) in thickness. Then, keep it until 1 mm (h 2in the Fig. 1) and hold for 10 s. The detailed schematic of the whole preparation process is given in Fig. 1. Al-5wt.%CuO prepared with a constant rotational velocity of 500 rpm was used as the control group. Processing Text: The IN718 components were fabricated using SLM Solutions 280HL machine, Germany. The powders were spread on the platform and melted layer by layer to generate the cylindrical specimens of dimensions 13 mm diameter and 80 mm length. An argon atmosphere was maintained in the chamber throughout the process to avoid oxidation during SLM process. A hatch style rotation of 67° was employed between the layers. The parameters utilized for SLM process like laser power of 200 W, scan speed of 1200 mm/s, hatch spacing of 90 μm and layer thickness of 30 μm. To maintain proper heat dissipation during the printing process a support structure were maintained for the samples with the same material and the supports were removed from the platform using wire cut electric discharge machine, once the printing process completed. The cylindrical specimens generated by SLM were friction welded by continuous drive KUKA friction welding (FW) machine. A facing operation was performed for the faying surfaces to remove any contaminations or oxides if present. The parameters employed for FW process such as, heating pressure of 50 bar, upset pressure of 60 bar, heating time of 6 s, upset time of 3 s and a rotary speed of 1125 rpm. An infrared thermographic (IR) camera (FLIR-make) was used to measure the temperature distribution at the interface during FW. Two cylindrical rods were considered whereas one was at stationery position and other was rotated with constant rpm during FW. The workpieces generate the frictional force in between the faying surfaces and an upset force was applied to forms the welds. The SLM samples after FW were examined for the microstructural characterization. The cross section of samples was grounded and polished with standard metallography practices to obtain scratch free surfaces. After etching with an etchant of HCl -10 ml and H 2O 2-3 ml for 10 s, the microstructures were observed under Olympus BX51 optical microscope (OM) and for higher magnification, scanning electron microscope (SEM) of Zeiss EVO MA 15 was used. The X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis was performed using Rigaku ultima IV with Cu-Kα radiation of wavelength 0.1542 nm. The step size of 0.02° was used during diffraction analysis at an angle ranging from 40° to 100°. For micro-texture analysis, a FEI TMQuanta 3D-SEM with TSL-EDX TMEBSD (electron back scatter diffraction) system was utilized. OIM Analysis TM(version 8.1) post processing software was used to analyse EBSD data. The Vickers microhardness tests were carried out with 500 g load and a dwell time of 10 s using Buehler Micromet indenter. The measurements were performed along the cross section of the specimen to cover all the zones present in the specimen. Room temperature tensile tests were conducted using Instron 8516 with a strain rate of 10 -4s -1for the as-built SLM and welded samples. The strain hardening behaviour was analysed using Kocks-Mecking plots from the tensile tests data and fracture analysis was performed on the tensile samples to evaluate the fractography features. The strength contribution from the various strengthening mechanisms were calculated for both the SLM as built and weld conditions of IN718 components. Processing Text: Fe-Cr-Al alloys, owing to their absence of allotropic transformation, require multiple cycles of rolling and recrystallization annealing processes to achieve substantial grain refinement, ultimately leading to the attainment of outstanding mechanical properties. Simply using warm rolling for an ultra-coarse-grained Fe-Cr-Al alloy to introduce lamellar kink bands (KBs) into the matrix, the mechanical properties can be significantly improved. To improve their mechanical properties, the alloys would experience multiple plastic deformation and heat treatments to regulate their textures, substructures, second phase, grain size, and other microstructural characteristics [3-10]. This was followed by a simple warm rolling process to introduce KBs into the matrix, obtaining a new microstructure composed of original ultra-coarse grains and their internal KBs. Table 1 shows the nominal composition of hot-rolled Fe-Cr-Al slabs with a thickness of 6 mm. A solution treatment at 1150 °C for 6 h was performed to dissolve the Laves phase and also coarsen the grains. The as-soluted plates were then warm rolled to a thickness of 2 mm (with 66 % thickness reduction) at 400 °C by four rolling passes. Finally, the plates were annealed at various temperatures (700, 750, 800, and 850 °C) for 0.5 h to investigate the effect of temperature on hetero-deformation induced (HDI) strengthening effect of KBs. The warm-rolled samples are annealed at different temperatures (700, 750, 800, and 850 °C) for 0.5 h to eliminate residual stress (named KBs-700 °C/0.5 h, KBs-750 °C/0.5 h, KBs-800 °C/0.5 h, and KBs-850 °C/0.5 h). In this work, substantial KBs were introduced into an ultra-coarse-grained Fe-Cr-Al alloy by warm rolling. Processing Text: The as-cast GZ151K alloy ingots were solution treated (T4) at 520 °C for 12 h, quenched into water at 90 °C, and then cut into 110 mm diameter, 2 mm thick semicircular pieces with a wire cutting machine. All GZ151K alloy sheets were accurately ground to get the same degree of roughness before USRP with air pressure and the amount of rolling set at 0.3 MPa and 0.2 mm, respectively. The rolled alloy sheets were then held in a high-temperature resistance furnace at 450 °C with different annealing time (5 min, 15 min, 30 min, 60 min) and then cool in water to room temperature, named RUed 450-5 min, RUed 450-15 min, RUed 450-30 min and RUed 450-60 min, respectively. For OM and SEM, the samples were first cut by a wire machine, and the ND-RD plane (ND: normal direction, RD: rolled direction) of the samples was selected as the surface to make mosaic samples. After that, all the samples were ground and polished carefully, then etched using an etchant for 4∼6 s containing 4.2 g C 6H 3N 3O 7, 10 mL CH 3COOH, 80 mL C 2H 6O, and 10 mL H 2O at room temperature. X-ray diffraction analysis (XRD) was used to investigate the phases of GZ151K after annealing treatment. A transmission electron microscope (TEM, JEM-F200) with an operating voltage of 200 kV, was used to analyze the structure, size, and morphology of the nano phases in RUed GZ151K alloy. The foil samples for TEM observation were prepared by twin-jet polishing under a voltage of 30 V with 2% HClO 4alcohol solution. A SEM equipped with a field emission gun (EBSD, Sigma 500) was used for the qualitative analysis of the twinning type of USRPed samples. Microhardness was measured on the cross-sections (parallel to ND) of the samples by using a nanoindentation tester (Fischer, HM2000) and a digital microhardness tester (HXS-1000A) were conducted to characterize the distribution of microhardness along thickness at cross-section (parallel to ND) after annealing treatment. The load of the nanoindentation and digital microhardness testers were 300 mN and 200 g and the holding time was 10 and 20 s, respectively. At each depth, the average and deviation of the microhardness values were calculated using ten measurements. The tensile tests were measured on the SHIMADZU Universal Tester (HMV-2T) with the strain rate of 1 × 10 −3s −1, and three samples with the dimensions of 30 × 6 × 2 mm 3were tested to repeat the experiment in each state at room temperature. Processing Text: In this paper, three distinct types of heterostructures were constructed in Mg-2.77Y (wt.%) alloy by applying simple thermomechanical processing. The initial material was then cut into a dimension of 60 mm (ED) × 14 mm × 2.5 mm for cold-rolling (CR) and the total thickness reduction was 42% (the single-pass reduction did not exceed 2%). The cold-rolled sheets were annealed (“A”) at 325 °C, 350 °C, 362 °C, 375 °C and 400 °C for 180 s, respectively, followed by water quenching. During the whole annealing process, the temperature fluctuation did not exceed ± 5 °C. Taking the sample annealed at 375 °C as an example, it is denoted as the “CRA-375 °C” material. Room-temperature uniaxial tensile tests were carried out on Shimadzu AG-Xplus 100 KN equipment at a strain rate of 10 -3s -1. The samples were loaded to one specified strain (e.g., 1%) at a strain rate of 10 -3s -1, and then unloaded to 80 N at an unloading rate of 250 N∙min -1 with the stress control mode, followed by reloading at the same strain rate to the specified strain (e.g., 2%). The samples for electron back-scattered diffraction (EBSD) mapping were cut from the annealed materials and polished with sandpaper. The RD-ND surface of each sample was electrochemically polished with a time less than 30 s to remove the strained layer. The electrolyte consists of perchloric acid (5 vol.%) and ethanol solution (95 vol.%). EBSD tests were carried out on the Thermo Scientific Apreo scanning electron microscope (SEM) equipped with the nordlysmax2 EBSD detector of the Oxford instrument. The accelerating voltage was 15 kV and the scanning step size was 0.15∼0.35 µm. The RD-TD surfaces of CRA-362 °C and CRA-375 °C materials were electropolished. Then, EBSD characterizations during uniaxial tensile deformation were carried out on the Gemini300 Zeiss scanning electron microscope equipped with symmetry series EBSD detector and MTEST series in-situ tensile stage. The acceleration voltage was 20 kV and the scanning step size was 0.1∼0.2 µm. The loading rate was 0.033 mm/min. Processing state: cold-rolled and annealed at 325 °C

Processing Text: Plastic deformation at room temperature followed by post-annealing is one of the best methods to achieve fine-grained metals and alloys. In this research, the high-temperature annealing behavior of cold-rolled electrolytic tough-pitch (ETP) copper sheets was studied. 90 % asymmetric cold rolling followed by high-temperature post-annealing at 673 K for 1, 2, 5, 10, 30, 60, and 120 min were applied on the copper. The microstructure was significantly changed with increasing annealing time from 1 to 2 min owing to full recrystallization. With increasing the annealing duration, the grain size is increased. The formation of equiaxed grains with a smaller size (∼9 μm) compared to the full-annealed (initial) sample (∼68 μm) is observed after the longest time of post-annealing (120 min) due to the pinning effect of Cu2O particles. The post-annealed copper sheets processed by asymmetric rolling (in this work) exhibited a more homogeneous microstructure through the thickness compared to the symmetric rolling due to more uniform stored strain energy. The results showed that the first deformed grains that undergo recrystallization during post-annealing are Goss-oriented grains. With an increase in the post-annealing time, the S and Copper components were eliminated and a strong Cube and P texture orientations were formed. Interestingly, after 1 min of post-annealing, the yield and tensile strength enhanced to 410.2 MPa and 418.6 MPa owing to the annealing hardening phenomenon. The hardness and strength reached a constant value after the post-annealing for 10 min and above. With the increase of post-annealing time from 1 min to 120 min, the electrical conductivity was increased from 77.6 to 97.5 %IACS. From the obtained results, it can be concluded that the asymmetric cold rolling followed by high-temperature post-annealing is capable of strength improvement and maintaining electrical conductivity in copper. Post-annealing at 673 K for 2 min

Processing Text: Zr48Cu47.5Al4Co0.5 amorphous powder with better forming ability was utilized as raw material and printed by selective laser melting (SLM) technique with high cooling rate. Through parameter adjustments and proactive design of amorphous fractions, gradient metallic glasses (GMGs) based on Zr has been successfully prepared. The scanning distance was 100 μm for parameters 1-4 and 80 μm for parameter 5, and the printed samples had a layer thickness of 25 μm, a spot size of 50 μm, a joint thickness of 0.02 mm, and a layer thickness of 5 μm at the joints. The cylinders were prepared with a diameter of 7 mm, height of 8.06 mm. Before applying SLM technology, the surface of the titanium substrate needs to be sandblasted to enhance the adhesion of the parts. High purity argon gas is used to purify the room and reduce the oxygen content. When the oxygen level drops to 0.2 %, the substrate is preheated to 130 °C. In order to prepare the gradient structure, the parameters in the homogeneous structure were screened according to their correspondence with the amorphous fraction, and four parameters were finally identified. The specimens were corroded using a mixed solution of HF and H2O (in the ratio of 1 ml of HF and 100 ml of H2O). During corrosion, the sample was immersed in the corrosion solution. After 10s, the sample was taken out and washed under clear water, then washed with anhydrous ethanol, and finally dried for use. Processing Text: Samples were cut into cylindrical shapes with dimensions of (Φ) 5 mm × 6.8 mm from cast ingot solidified under normal pressure. Subsequently, the samples were wrapped in an insulating layer and a graphite tube. The pressure device of the LPR1000 2-6-8 multi-stage high-pressure apparatus consists of an axially cylindrical pressure chamber, resembling to a piston-cylinder system. Pressure is applied to the octahedral talc sample assembly through primary and secondary pressure transmission modules, driven by the press. Graphite is used as the heating element, and the heating temperature is controlled by adjusting the heating power. The sample was heated to 1550 °C under an external pressure of 6 GPa for 60 minutes, after which the heating device was turned off and the pressure was released to atmospheric levels. The SSS and HPS alloys were subsequently aged at 400°C, 450°C, and 500°C in an argon atmosphere for varying durations up to 10 hours. The samples were ground using SiC paper and polished with diamond suspension. A solution with the composition of FeCl 3(2 g), HCl (3 ml), and C 2H 5OH (100 ml) was used as the etchant. The microstructure was observed using a HITACHI SU50000 field emission scanning electron microscope (SEM) and an FEI Talos F200X transmission electron microscope (TEM). Image Pro Plus 6.0 software was used to measure the area fraction and size of various precipitates based on TEM images. The foil thickness in the beam direction was determined by measuring the spacing of Kossel-Mollenstedt fringes in a {111} αreflection in a < 011 > αtwo-beam convergent beam electron diffraction (CBED) pattern. X-ray diffraction (XRD, X’PERT X-ray, Holland) with diffraction angle (2θ) ranging from 30° to 100° and a scanning speed of approximately 1°/min was utilized to determine the crystal structure of the alloys. The DC conductivity measurement at room temperature (300 K) was conducted using the traditional four-probe technique. The samples measured are approximately 3 mm in length, 1 mm in width, and 0.3 mm in thickness. Four platinum wires were affixed to the samples using conductive silver paste. The DC resistance of the samples was initially measured using a physical property measuring system (PPMS, Dynacool-14T, USA) and subsequently converted to DC conductivity. Vickers hardness testing of the specimens was performed using a Huayin HV-1000A microhardness tester with a load of 200 g and an indentation time of 15 seconds. The reported hardness values represent the average of eight separate measurements. The compression test was conducted using a SANS CMT6000 universal testing machine with a compression speed of 0.5 mm/min. The compression specimen measured are 2 mm in diameter and 3 mm in length. At least three measurements were taken for each sample to minimize experimental errors. Predicted using a Gated Recurrent Unit deep learning model based on experimental data
