Processing Text: Argon gas atomized powder with diameters ranging from 15 to 53 μm was subjected to LPBF fabrication. The LPBF experiments were conducted using a commercial ProX DMP 200 machine (3D Systems, USA) equipped with a 300 W fibre laser. The laser spot size is 75 μm and the wavelength is 1070 nm. The optimal processing parameters were identified, which can be used to achieve the highest relative density. After the optimisation of process parameters, both cubic-shaped and dog bone-shaped samples were built with a laser power of 285 W, scan speed of 1500 mm/s, hatch space of 90 μm, and layer thickness of 30 μm. A separate-area scanning strategy was adopted with a 90° rotation between layers. The angle between the scanning direction and the X-axis is 45° for every layer. The fabrication process was performed in a high-purity argon atmosphere with an oxygen content below 200 ppm. The alloy was exposed at 250℃ for 100 h and shows no apparent decrease despite increasing the exposure time to 500 h. The tests were carried out on a material testing machine (Zwick Roell, Germany) at ambient temperature and an elevated temperature range of 200-300℃, with a strain rate of 10−3s−1. A 10 min hold before tensile testing was applied to the samples for uniform temperature. Vickers hardness tests were performed using a 10 kg load with a dwell time of 15 s. Condition: Room Temperature (25℃); Processing state: as-built

Processing Text: In this work, through the combination of austenite reversion treatment (ART) and subsequent flash austenitizing (FA), nanoscale chemical heterogeneity was successfully introduced into a low-cost UHSS prior to the aging process. The steel with a nominal chemical composition of 0.25 C-5 Ni-5 Mn-5 Co-1 Cr-2 Mo-1 Al (wt.%) was prepared through levitation melting and cast into an ingot of ∼ 5 kg. The as-cast ingot was homogenized at 1150 °C for 10 h and subsequently hot-forged into a square bar with a cross section of 20 mm × 20 mm, followed by air-cooling. The as-forged bars were hot-rolled at 1000 °C with a reduction of thickness from 20 to 5 mm. Then the hot-rolled plates were solution-treated at 900 °C for 1 h and then oil-quenched to ambient temperature, immediately subjected to cryogenic treatment (CT) at −196 °C for 2 h (denoted as CT sample). Subsequently, the CT samples were held at 580 °C for 5 h (denoted as ART sample). After ART, the ART samples were further FA at 830 °C with a heating rate of 30 °C/s and a cooling rate of 60 °C/s (denoted as FA sample). Then the FA samples were isothermally aged at 550 °C for 2 h (denoted as AG sample). During subsequent aging, a high number density of fine Ni(Al,Mn) and (Mo,Cr) 2C nanoprecipitates were concurrently introduced and the presetting austenite further grew with the consumption of substitutional Mn and Ni from the martensitic matrix. Processing Text: Ingots with the nominal compositions of Al 5 Cr 20 Fe 35 Co 35 Ni 5 were fabricated by induction melting under vacuum and subjected to homogenization treatment at 1373 K for 6 h. Plates with a thickness of 4 mm were cut from the ingots and rolled at room temperature to a thickness of 0.75 mm, corresponding to the final thickness reduction of 81.3 %. High-ratio differential speed rolling (HRDSR) with a rolling-speed ratio of 2 was applied (by setting the upper and lower roll speeds to 6 rpm/min and 12 rpm/min, respectively) to impose severe plastic deformation (SPD) on the materials during the rolling process. The rolled materials were annealed in an argon atmosphere at various temperatures ranging from 923 K to 1373 K, along with different annealing duration times ranging from 10 min to 72 h. After each annealing treatment, the samples were subjected to rapid cooling by immersing them in water. Processed by High-ratio differential speed rolling (HRDSR); Limited ductility of 2.2 ± 0.6%

Processing Text: Samples used for subsequent experiments were obtained by directly cutting heat-treated wires using electrical discharge machining (EDM). The three types of aged wires, namely Ti6554, Ti6554-0.05B and Ti6554-0.1B ones, were machined into dumbbell-shaped tensile samples with a gauge portion of 3 mm in diameter and 15 mm in length along the rolling direction (RD). Uniaxial tensile tests were conducted on an INSTRON 1195 testing machine at a strain rate of 5 × 10−4s−1at ambient temperature. To ensure experimental repeatability, at least three samples for each alloy were measured. Tensile properties such as yield strength (σy), ultimate tensile strength (σb) and total elongation at fracture (εf) were recorded after testing. The samples for microstructural characterization were mechanically ground using a series of SiC abrasive papers and subsequently electropolished in a solution of 10 % HClO4and 90 % CH3COOH (vol%). Then, the metallographic samples were etched in a Kroll's reagent of 2 vol% HF, 8 vol% HNO3, and 90 vol% H2O. Phase constitution analysis of the aged samples was examined utilizing a Rigaku D/MAX-RB X-ray diffractometer (XRD) with Cu-Kαradiation source at an acceleration voltage of 40 kV and a current of 100 mA. Metallographic analysis was performed on Nikon MA200 optical microscope (OM) and Hitachi SU6600 scanning electron microscopy (SEM). Crystallographic information in both initial and deformed samples were captured by employing Oxford electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) detector mounted on Zeiss GEMINI 500 field-emission scanning electron microscope (SEM). Transmission electron microscope (TEM) foils were thinned to approximately 50 μm through mechanical grinding. Electron transparency was achieved by twin-jet electropolishing at 10 V in a solution of 65 % (volume) methanol, 30 % ethylene glycol, and 5 % perchloric acid at 243 K. The TEM foils were examined in a field-emission transmission electron microscope (JEOL JEM-F200 TEM) operating at an accelerating voltage of 200 kV. Aged for 1h

To study the static mechanical behaviors of the steel considering heat treatment conditions, quasi-static tensile experiments are taken in this paper. The experiments are taken on a WDW-300-1 microcomputer-controlled electronic universal testing machine of Bairoe Company at a lower tensile rate (1 mm/min). Three quasi-static tensile experiments were performed with each heat treatment condition to ensure good consistency of experimental results. To study the evolution mechanism of grains, SHPB experiments are applied for the dynamic mechanical behaviors of 18CrNiMo7-6 steel at high temperature and high strain rates. The strain rates are 3000 s −1, 5000 s −1, 8000 s −1and 10,000 s −1. At the same time, the equipment also has a high-temperature heating system, which can realize the rapid rise of the experimental temperature (up to 800 °C) and maintain a constant temperature. Subsequently, the sample is heated to the picked temperature, and bullet fired bar are fired to shock-compress the workpiece. This study proposes that dynamic mechanical behavior curves of 18CrNiMo7-6 steel during normalizing heat treatment (NHT), quenching heat treatment (QHT), and carburizing and quenching heat treatment (CQHT) are obtained by carrying out impact mechanical experiments under different strain rates and different temperatures based on Split Hopkinson pressure bar (SHPB) experiments. The microstructure of 18CrNiMo7-6 steel is investigated with three common heat treatment conditions. Then, with taking Split Hopkinson pressure bar (SHPB) experiments, this paper studies the microstructure, grain boundary, Schmid factor, local misorientation and recrystallized fraction of 18CrNiMo7-6 steel with three heat treatment conditions at high temperature, stain and strain rate. Processing Text: The NiCoCr multi principal element alloy (MPEA) was prepared by thermal-mechanical processing. NiCoCr ingots were prepared by arc-melting a mixture of pure metals (purity > 99.9 wt%) in a high-purity argon atmosphere. The buttons were remelted and flipped five times to ensure chemical homogeneity before they were dropped cast into a cylindrical copper mold (Ф20 mm × 50 mm). Five alloy samples were cast under different vibration parameters and corresponding named Ax-y, where x represents the vibration frequency (x = 30, 50; the dimension of quantity is Hz), y represents the amplitude (y = 1, 2; the dimension of quantity is mm), and sample A0 means no vibration. After mechanical polishing, microstructure and phase composition of the alloys were investigated using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM). The distribution of elements was analyzed using energy-dispersive X-ray spectrometry (EDS) equipped on SEM device. The samples were cut by electric discharge machining from the lower parts of the ingots and room-temperature tensile properties were measured using a Shimadzu AG-100 kN testing machine at strain rate of 10 −3s −1. The densities of alloy specimens were tested by the Archimedes principle. Processing Text: The as-cast Mg-9 wt.% Li-5 wt.% Al-4 wt.% Zn alloy (LAZ954) plate was prepared using pure Mg (99.9 wt.%), Al (99.9 wt.%), Zn (99.9 wt.%), and Li (99 wt.%). Processing Text: Gas-atomized IN718 powder, supplied by Renishaw plc (Staffordshire, United Kingdom), was utilized for the LPBF production with a particle size range between 15 and 35 μm. LPBF was performed using a Renishaw AM250 SLM system (Staffordshire, United Kingdom) with a Ytterbium fiber laser. Two bulk IN718 samples with dimensions of 60×60×40 mm 3were LPBF-ed. A single laser beam was utilized in continuous mode with a wavelength of 1070 nm, a spot size of 100 µm, a power of 300 W, a scanning speed of 1050 mm/s, a hatching distance of 90 µm, and a layer thickness of 0.04 mm, which led to the energy density of 71.4 J/mm 3. The substrate temperature was set at 80 ˚C. A striped scanning strategy using a hatch angle of 67° was chosen to minimize the microstructure anisotropy in perpendicular transverse directions. A bi-directional scanning method was implemented to ensure efficient melt-pool fusion and minimize residual stresses. Subsequently, vertical sheets with dimensions of 60×60 mm were wire-cut with a thickness of 3 mm to cut the tensile and fatigue specimens. Each sheet yielded either six tensile or three fatigue samples. For sample preparation, specimens were ground using a 2000# SiC sandpaper, then polished and vibration polished with a 0.03 µm alumina suspension. The TD-BD cross-section was chosen for the EBSD mapping to show the anisotropic microstructure along these two directions. EBSD maps were collected using the NOVA NanoSEM 230 scanning electron microscope (SEM) device with the Oxford Instruments® AZtec™ system at a voltage of 20 keV, a tilt angle of 70˚, a working distance of 13 mm, and a step size of 1 µm. The surface was polished similarly to the EBSD sample preparation before the XRD tests. Tensile tests were conducted according to the ASTM E8/E8M standard using the engineering strain rate of 0.001 s −1. Moreover, stress-controlled fatigue tests were carried out based on the ASTM E466/E466M with maximum stress values ranging from 550 MPa to 750 MPa, a stress ratio of 0.1, and a frequency of 15 cycles per second. Direction: Transverse (TD); Experimental result
Processing Word: Direction: Transverse (TD); Experimental result

Processing Text: The powder feedstock for L-PBF was supplied by the Volgograd-Russia Aluminum Plant (UC RUSAL) with the following particle size distribution: d 10= 17.3 μm, d 50= 26.7 μm, and d 90= 40.75 μm using the molten metal spraying method. Cylindrical bars having a diameter of 20 mm and a length of 100 mm were manufactured with the building direction (BD) parallel to the bar's length under a controlled Ar atmosphere. A commercial SLM280HL printer (Selective Laser Melting Solutions Group AG, Lübeck, Germany), was used to make samples, operating with the following parameters: a scan speed of 1650 mm/s, a power of 370 W, a hatch spacing of 130 µm, layer thickness of 50 µm and a scanning rotation of 67° between consecutive layers. These parameters yielded a laser energy density of 1.72 J/mm 2, leading to a porosity fraction lower than 0.18 %. Annealing in the temperature range of 20 °C to 500 °C for one hour led to evolutions in the as-built L-PBF cellular structure, including partial fragmentation of the cell boundaries between 20 °C and 300 °C; the breakdown and transformation into ultrafine Si-enriched particles in the range of 300 °C to 400 °C; and subsequently coarsening at temperatures exceeding 400 °C. Uniaxial tensile tests were conducted at room temperature at an initial strain rate of 1 × 10 −3s −1using miniature bone-shaped samples (4 mm in length, 1.3 mm in width, 2 mm in thickness and 1 mm radius (R)) oriented parallel to the BD. The samples for the mechanical testing were fabricated from the as-built bars using electrode discharge machining, which resulted in uniformly smooth surfaces. Vickers microhardness using a square-based pyramidal diamond indenter were carried out for the as-built and annealed samples. A constant load of 1.8 N and a dwell time of 15 s were used. In situ high-energy synchrotron X-ray diffraction (HEXRD) analysis was carried out during isothermal annealing heat treatments at 400 °C and 500 °C with a holding time of one hour each using cylindrical samples of 5 mm diameter and 8 mm length. To mitigate the impact of sample size on strain calculation, the so-called digital image correlation (DIC) method was used. The DIC system was implemented on a universal tensile machine employing a 12-megapixel digital camera operating at 32 frames per second with an acquisition time of 2 s and a pixel size of 0.04 mm. The acquired data was subsequently processed in Matlab, utilizing the open source software Ncorr. To ensure more reliable results, all tensile samples were tested in the weakest direction, i.e., the tensile loading direction parallel to the BD. In order to establish a correlation between synchrotron measurements and the microstructure and mechanical properties at various temperatures, a series of samples from the as-built material were subjected to annealing treatments with a holding time of one hour at temperatures of 200 °C, 300 °C, 400 °C, and 500 °C. Subsequently, these samples were evaluated using EBSD, hardness, and tensile testing. Processing Text: The GH4099 superalloy was fabricated using the laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) technique. An optimal parameter combination was established using the response surface method (RSM) design and the variance method, resulting in the optimal parameter combination of PLP= 317 W, vSS= 900 mm/s, and HS =0.08 mm. The as-deposited GH4099 alloy is primarily composed of columnar crystals grown epitaxially and M23C6 carbides without the generation of the γ′-phase. After solution treatment, recrystallization and grain growth occurred, with the alloy remaining as large, irregularly shaped polygonal columnar crystals. The aging process precipitated substantial γ′-phase, which internally existed as a mixture of equiaxed and columnar crystals. Subsequently, the partial samples were subjected to solution and aging treatments. Specifically, solid solution S1130 (1130 ℃ × 2 h and then water-cooling) and solid solution-aging treatment SA800 (1130 ℃ × 2 h and then water-cooling + 800 ℃ × 9 h and then air-cooling) were carried out for part of deposited samples. The samples were separated from the matrix using a wire-cutting method. An ultrasonic cleaning device JP-010 was used to clean the as-deposited samples to remove adherent powder and impurities. The polished samples were etched using Kalling's No.2 reagent (5 g CuCl 2, 100 mL HCl and 100 mL ethanol). Electrolytic polishing was performed at 12 V in a 10% perchloric acid solution for 30 s. Room temperature and high-temperature (800 ℃ and 900 ℃) mechanical tests were conducted using a CMT5105 electronic universal testing machine at a strain rate of 1 mm/min, with three repeated tests for each sample under different conditions. Processing Text: The specimens are cylindrical with a diameter of 8 mm and a length of 12 mm. The specimens were heated to 1073 K at 10 K/s and compressed by 50% after being held at this temperature for 120 s for soaking. Dynamic compression tests with cylindrical specimens of 4 mm diameter and 4 mm length were carried out at mean strain rates of 2500-5500 s−1 using the SHPB system as shown in Fig. 1. Elevated temperatures were obtained with a radiant-heating furnace and the thermocouple arrangement was used to ensure the testing temperature. The specimens were heated to 1073 K and held for 2 min to ensure temperature uniformity before the dynamic tests. The temperature was maintained constant during the test with a fluctuation of ±3 K. Within 1 to 2 s after compression, the specimens were immediately quenched to room temperature using water to freeze the high temperature deformed microstructure. For the dynamic compression experiments, the diameter and length of the impacting rod were 19 mm and 200 mm, respectively. The length of both the incident and transmitted rods was 1200 mm. By adjusting the output gas pressure push the impactor bar, impinging the incident bar velocity can be controlled to obtain different strain rates (2500 s−1-5500 s−1). For SHPB tests at elevated temperatures, it is necessary to heat the specimen to the required uniform temperature while the incident and transmitted bars are in suitable low temperatures. To ensure conditions appropriate for uniaxial deformation and to minimize the friction effect, a vaseline lubricant was used between the sample surface and the indenter before compression. All the tests were repeated at least three times at each strain rate to the accuracy and reproductivity of the experimental data. After deformation, the specimens were cut by electrical discharge machining along the compression axis from the center. The specimens were ground using waterproof silicon carbide paper, mechanically polished, and then etched with 1 ml HF, 1.5 ml HCl, 2.5 ml HNO3, and 95 ml H2O at room temperature for metallographic observation. The specimens for EBSD were electrolytically polished using a mixture of 10vol pct perchloric acid and 90vol pct ethyl alcohol solution at room temperature. Processing Text: Laser directed energy deposition (LDED) has attracted as a progressive additive manufacturing technique in fabricating the stainless steel components. The rapid melting and solidification velocity under LDED process induces the appearance of pores and the columnar dendritic, which degrades the strength of alloys. Here, a self-developed LDED-UR (ultrasonic rolling) synchronous manufacturing equipment is developed to fabricate the 316L stainless steel, and the characterization of microstructure and mechanical properties are studied. Results show that the size and fraction of pores are significantly reduced by LDED-UR processing, and fine equiaxed grains are obtained under the combined effects of ultrasonic vibration and roller pressure. With the severe plastic deformation, the average grain size of LDED-UR sample is decreased from 76.10 μm to 26.23 μm (LDED sample), and high angle grain boundaries transforms to low angle grain boundaries. Meanwhile, the dislocation density in LDED-UR sample is increased compared to the LDED sample. Owing to the grain refinement and dislocation strengthening, the average microhardness, yield strength, ultimate tensile strength and elongation of the LDED-UR sample reach 268.18 ± 13.90 HV0.2, 442 MPa, 771.2 MPa, and 49.8 %, respectively, which are larger than those of LDED sample (214.13 ± 13.76 HV0.2, 396 MPa, 682 MPa, and 45.5 %). 316L stainless steel, as a structural metallic material, has been extensively utilized in various industrial sectors for its superior mechanical properties, including aerospace and marine facilities. 316L stainless steel plate with dimensions of 100 mm × 100 mm × 16 mm is fabricated as the substrate. The 99.99 % Ar gas is employed as the shielding gas to prevent oxidation of deposition layers. 316L stainless steel powders (Avimetal Powder Metallurgy Technology Co., Ltd, China) is employed in this study, and it is manufactured by gas atomization method. Processing state: LDED-UR; Microstructure: grain refinement and dislocation strengthening

Processing Text: The steel was melted in a high-frequency vacuum induction melting furnace with a capacity of 50 kg and casted into a mold with a diameter of 110 mm. Thereafter, the casting ingot was homogenized at 1200 °C for a duration of 3 h. Then the ingot was cooled down to 1100 °C and directly radial forged into bars in a diameter of 16 mm with downward pressure of about 20 % per forging stroke. The starting and final forging temperatures were 1100 °C and 950 °C, respectively, and the forging temperature range was in the dual phase region. This was followed by cooling down to room temperature (RT) in air circumstance. Quasi-static uniaxial tensile were carried out using the specimens cut from the forged bars by electrical discharge machining (EDM). The uniaxial tensile tests were performed on a universal material testing equipment (Shimadzu AG-100 KN) at a strain rate of 5×10−4s −1and at RT. Standard miniaturized compact tension (CT) specimens for the fracture toughness tests were cut from the forged bars by EDM. A miniature CT specimen with a width W of ∼12.0 mm and a thickness B of ∼3.0 mm was used. In order to obtain a sharp initial crack front, the CT specimens were first notched to a depth of ∼4.0 mm by electrical discharge machining, and then fatigue pre-cracked in a tension-tension mode at a frequency of 2 Hz until an initial total crack length a0of ∼6.0 mm was reached. In order to improve the surface stress constraint and make the crack extend straightly, side grooves with a total depth of 0.2B were additionally machined on both surfaces of the fatigue pre-cracked CT specimens. The fracture tests were carried out on an Instron 5982 testing machine with a load capacity of 5 kN under displacement control at a speed of about 0.1 mm/min to stimulate crack extension. The hardness of the specimens was measured by a Shimadzu HMV-G 31DT Vickers hardness testing machine and both the loads applied to ferrite and martensite were 98.07 mN with a 15 s dwell time. All surfaces of the samples for tests and characterizations were mechanically ground by SiO 2papers and electrically polished in a solution of 20 % perchloric acid and 80 % ethanol (vol%) performed at −25 °C with a potential of 30 V and corroded in a solution of 5 % nitric acid and 95 % ethanol (vol%). Condition: RD samples; Offset: 0.2%; Associated with high strength and ductility

Annealed 45 steel with dimensions of 100 mm × 100 mm × 10 mm was chosen as the substrate. To minimize the interference of oxides and other impurities, an angle grinder was used to remove the oxide layer from the substrate surface, followed by cleaning with anhydrous ethanol. Before the experiment, place the powder in a vacuum drying oven (Shanghai Jiecheng Experimental Instrument Co., Ltd., DZF-6050) and dry it at 100 °C for 2 h to ensure its uniformity and fluidity. The coating was prepared by using a semiconductor laser (HWL-1500) with a wavelength range of 910-1050 nm and a DPSF scraper powder feeder to transport CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy powder coaxially. The specific chemical composition (wt.%) of the LPBF Ti6Al4V alloy powder is listed in Table 1. The following processing parameters were used for printing: the scanning speed of v= 2000 mm/s, the laser power of P= 330 W, the hatch spacing of h= 0.09 mm and the layer thickness of t= 0.03 mm. The printing process was carried out in a 99.99 % inert argon atmosphere and the corresponding laser energy input density E= P⁄ ( v∙ h∙ t) was 61.11 J/mm 3. The continuous interlayer rotation scanning strategy “cross-hatching” in Fig. 3(a) was adopted to improve anisotropy and reduce defects [47,48]. The round rods (with a diameter of 12 mm and a length of 68 mm) and blocks ( 72×32×33mm3) were manufactured with the same process parameters along the Z direction (build direction, BD), as shown in Fig. 3(b). The substrate was preheated to 35 ℃ to prevent powder spatter and to reduce the effect of the heat-affected zones on the microstructure. To relieve the residual stress produced in the LPBF process, the printed rods and blocks were first heated to 800 ℃ for 4 h, and then cooled to room temperature in an argon atmosphere. After heat treatment, the tensile and fracture specimens were prepared by cutting the original round rods and blocks, respectively. The LPBF round bars were machined to standard dog bone specimens with a gauge length of 27 mm and a diameter of 5 mm to obtain the tensile properties in accordance with the GB/T 228-2010, as shown in Fig. 5(a). According to ASTM E399-20 [49], 1/2 compact tensile (CT) specimens (1/2 T) with different thickness ( B) and crack length ratio ( a/W, a− crack length, W− specimen width) were fabricated to determine KIC. The melting and casting processes were protected by an argon atmosphere throughout, and the chemical homogeneity of the material was ensured by five repeated melting cycles. Subsequently, the flake specimens were treated under argon protection at 1373 K for 10 h to obtain homogenized specimens. Then, using a multi-roll mill at room temperature, the homogenized specimens were cold rolled to different degrees of 30 %, 50 %, 70 %, and 90 %, and represented by CR-30 %, CR-50 %, CR-70 %, and CR-90 %, respectively. Subsequently, the cold-rolled sheets were annealed under vacuum conditions with a holding time of 1.5 h at 1223 K, followed quickly by water quenching to obtain annealed state specimens with different cold rolling ratios (represented by CR30%-A, CR50%-A, CR70%-A, and CR90%-A, respectively). Finally, the thin plates subjected to different treatments were cut into dog-bone-shaped tensile specimens using electric discharge machining. Processing Text: The alloys were cast using arc melting under the protection of Ar atmosphere. The raw materials used were pure metals (purity>99.9 wt%). The dimensions of the ingots were 60 × 12 × 8 (length × width × thickness) mm³. Each ingot was kept at 1200 °C for 4 h followed by water quenching. After that, a multi-pass hot rolling process was conducted at 1100 °C with a total reduction in thickness of 50 %. Then the hot-rolled plates were homogenized at 1200 °C for 4 h, followed by water quenching. The obtained alloys were denoted as the homogenized (HOMO) materials. To achieve the refined microstructure, the HOMO materials then underwent multi-pass cold rolling with a total thickness reduction of 60 %, and the cold-rolled (CR) materials were obtained. The materials in the CR state were then annealed for 3 min in a salt bath furnace and water-quenched. The materials annealed at 750 °C and 900 °C were denoted as the partially recrystallized (PRX) and the fully recrystallized (FRX) materials, respectively. Processing Text: Ti 50 Zr 16 V 16 Nb 10 Al 5 Mo 3 (henceforth designated as Ti-CCA) is produced from high-purity metals (>99.9 %), with each alloying element sectioned into smaller pieces beforehand, and the weight was confirmed to have an accuracy of 0.005 g. Processing Text: The Al-5.0Mn-1.5Mg-0.82Sc-0.76Zr (wt.%) alloy powder with a standard composition was prepared by gas atomization (Panxing New Alloy Materials Co., Ltd., China). The powder was spherical in shape, with the particles less than or equal to 22.3 µm accounting for 10% while 90% of the particles were less than or equal to 63.4 µm, as shown in Fig. 1(a, b). All the LPBF samples investigated in this work were manufactured using a BLT S210 LPBF machine equipped with a 400 W fiber laser. Constant laser power (350 W), scanning spacing (90 µm), and layer thickness (30 µm) were used with scanning velocities ranging between 450 and 1450 mm/s. Two different substrate temperatures, 25 and 200 °C, were used for each condition. The samples with the optimized process parameters had a relative density higher than 99.8 %. A bilinear scanning strategy with a scan rotation of 67° was used between the layers. The samples were printed in a high-purity argon atmosphere. Subsequently, the samples were heat-treated at 200 °C for 1 h to remove residual stresses before evaluating their microstructures and mechanical properties. The LPBF samples were prepared for microstructural characterization by mechanical grinding and polishing following a standard metallographic procedure recommended in ASTM E3-11. After polishing, the microstructural features were revealed using an etchant consisting of HNO 3(2.5 mL), HCl (1.5 mL), HF (1.0 mL), and distilled water (95 mL). The wire-cut electro-discharge machine was used to slice samples with the following dimensions: ∼5 mm long, ∼5 mm wide, and ∼1 mm thick. Prior to the EBSD characterization, the sheet samples were first mechanically polished with 400 #, 1000 #, 2000 #, and 3000 # SiC water abrasive paper, then electropolished to remove the surface deformation layer generated by mechanical grinding. Electropolishing was performed at −30 °C, with: 7 % perchloric acid, 93 % ethanol; a voltage of 25 V, and a current density of 450 mA/cm 2for about 1 min. Uniaxial tensile tests were performed using the CMT4105 universal testing machine. The gauge length and cross-sectional area of the tensile specimens were 22 mm and 1.5 mm × 4 mm. All the tensile samples were tested perpendicular to the build direction at a constant strain rate of 1 mm/min, following the standard ASTM E8. Fatigue test samples with the dimensions 60 mm × 12 mm × 1.5 mm were tested on an MTS370.02 fatigue testing machine. All samples were mechanically ground and polished prior to fatigue testing to ensure similar surface roughness. The uniaxial fatigue tests were conducted in a load control mode at a frequency of 40 Hz and stress ratio of R= 0.1, following the standard ASTM E466. The samples were tested until fracture or exhaustion till 10 7cycles. Laser power: 300 W; Scanning speed: 1600 mm/s
Processing Word: Laser power: 300 W; Scanning speed: 1600 mm/s

Processing Text: Tensile specimens were cut from the side wall using wire-electrode cutting. Tensile specimens were solution treated at 470 °C for 43 min, water quenched, and pre-aged at 92 °C for 16 h (termed “PA” sample). Warm tensile tests were performed at 185-215 °C with strain rates ranging 0.001-0.01 s−1. Processing Text: The LPBF samples were prepared using a self-developed HP-LPBF300 system which possesses a continuous wave IPG YLR-2000 single-mode fiber laser (near-Gaussian mode laser beam; 2000 W maximum output power; 1070 nm wavelength). Spherical 300M steel powders with a particle size ranging from 15 μm to 56 μm, which were produced by gas atomization, were used as the feedstock for sample building. A series of cuboid samples and tensile test samples designed according to ISO 6892-1-2009 standard were deposited using the process parameters listed in Table 2. The as-built sample reveals a microstructure composed of tempered martensite and a minor amount of residual austenite. Before heat treatment, the phase transition temperatures of the LPBF-fabricated 300M samples were verified by using a NETZSCH DIL402C thermal dilatometry (TD) instrument with a heating rate of 10 k/min from room temperature to 1400 °C. The obtained thermal expansion curve displayed in Fig. 1 shows the start temperature of austenitization (A s) for the as-built sample was approximately 708 °C, while the finish temperature of austenitization (A f) is around 856 °C. Accordingly, the quenching temperature in this study was chosen as 870-1100 °C. The holding time (1 h) and the cooling method (oil quenching) were selected in accordance with the conventional quenching process applied to 300M forged components. In terms of selecting the tempering temperature, considering that tempering treatment for 300M forgings is commonly carried out at approximately 300 °C, the chosen tempering temperature range for this study spans from 200 °C to 400 °C. Furthermore, because two times of tempering treatment leads to more thorough release of residual stresses in the microstructure and thus more improved toughness and more enhanced stability of the workpiece compared to a single tempering treatment, the tempering treatment was conducted twice for every tempered sample in this study. The LPBF-fabricated samples were heat treated in a KSL-1400×-A2 muffle furnace with a heating rate of 10 K/min. The details of the different heat treatment conditions are summarized in Table 3. To investigate the evolution of microstructural morphological and crystallographic textures of the LPBF-fabricated samples with the heat treatment conditions, the bulk specimens were first ground and polished according to the standard metallographic preparation procedure and then etched by using an etchant of 4% nital solution before being observed with a Nikon Epiphot-300 optical microscope (OM) and a GeminiSEM-300 scanning electron microscopy (SEM) equipped with an electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) detector. In addition to mechanical polishing, the samples used for EBSD analysis were further electrolytic-polished in a mixture of 6 mL perchloric acid and 94 mL ethanol at 18 V for 2 min. Phase identification was conducted employing a PANalytical X'Pert PRO X-ray diffraction (XRD) using Cu Kα radiation with a scan step size of 0.02°. Moreover, a Tecnai G2 F30 transmission electron microscope (TEM) was used to characterize the dislocations, deformation twins, stacking fault and other substructures like carbide precipitation. TEM samples with a diameter of 3 mm were ground using 2000-grit SiC abrasive paper until the thickness reaches approximately 50 μm, and then electropolished in a 10/90% perchloric acid/ethanol solution at −20 °C using an automatic twin-jet electropolisher. Room temperature microhardness and tensile properties were characterized to assess the mechanical performance of LPBF-fabricated 300M steel before and after different heat treatments. Microhardness measurements of the samples were carried out via an HVS-1000 tester using a 4.9 N load and a 20 s dwell time. Tensile properties tests were conducted using a Shimadzu AG-100 kN tester with a strain rate of 10 −3/s, and the tensile load was perpendicular to the build direction of LPBF-fabricated samples. Processing Text: The ingot of the Co 68Al 18.2Fe 6.5V 4.75Cr 2.55alloys were fabricated by arc-melting the mixtures of high-purity constituent elements in a Ti-gettered argon atmosphere and the ingot was remelted at least five times to ensure chemical homogeneity. Following the last re-melting step, the melt was drop-cast in a rectangular copper mold of dimensions: 60 mm × 10 mm × 5 mm (height × length × width). The as-cast MEA was characterized by Bruker D8 X-ray diffractometry (XRD) with Cu Kα radiation and the scanning range of 2θ is 20°-100°. The samples were ground with SiC abrasive papers with grits of 400, 800, and 1,200, and finally polished with 0.25-μm-diamond suspension. The microstructure and fracture morphology of the as-cast MEA were observed by FEI Quanta 250F scanning electron microscope (SEM) with SE detector. The phase structure and chemical composition of the as-cast MEA were characterized by a FEI Talos F200X transmission electron microscope (TEM) at a voltage of 200 kV with an energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS). Electron back-scattered diffraction (EBSD) measurement was conducted on JEOL-JSM-IT800 instruments equipped with an Oxford Symmetry S2 detector. The scanning step size and the scanning area are 0.16 μm and 60 × 60 μm 2, respectively. The nanoindentation tests with the maximum load of 30 mN was conducted on KLA-Nano indenter G200 machine. Rectangular specimens with dimensions of 2 × 2 × 4 mm 3were cut from the as-cast ingot by electric discharge machine and tested for room-temperature compression and high-temperature compression tests. Room-temperature compression tests were conducted on an Instron 5969 universal testing machine at a strain rate of 2 × 10 −4s −1. High-temperature compression tests of 600 °C and 800 °C were performed on a SUNS-UTM5305H machine equipped with a radial heating furnace at a strain rate of 2 × 10 −4s −1. Condition: room temperature; Processing state: as-cast; Microstructure: dual-phase FCC + B2

The HEA powders and Si powders were then weighed according to a molar ratio of 90:10 to obtain the designed composition (Fe 50Mn 30Co 10Cr 10) 90Si 10(at%) and mechanically mixed using a three-dimensional shaker mixer (Turbula) for 10 hours at a spindle speed of 30 r/min to ensure a uniform powder mixture. After three remelting passes, with sufficient diffusion time to promote the blending of the mixed pure Si in the Fe 50Mn 30Co 20Cr 20HEA matrix, the printed HESMA exhibits an outstanding recoverable strain of 5.2 % combined with a high yield stress of 500 MPa. Processing Text: The lattice constants of a= b= 2.932 Å and c= 4.684 Å are employed to construct the unit cell of Ti-7Al. Afterward, ∼12 % Al atoms are randomly located on the crystal to ensure a perfectly substitutional alloy. The consequent alloy structure takes the form of a cuboid, as depicted in Fig. 1, with final dimensions of 80.63 Å× 85.49 Å× 81.97 Å. Utilizing a consistent approach, 160 different samples are prepared for MD studies by keeping the indistinguishable dimension while introducing random variations in the positions of Al atoms on the α-structure. The force field of the atoms of the single-crystal structure has been defined by 2NN MEAM potential parameters. In each computation, the periodic boundary conditions are applied to all three directions of the samples, effectively diminishing the influence of the boundary/edge effect on the structure. Before subjecting the structures to a constant strain rate, a comprehensive energy minimization process is undertaken to achieve equilibrium among all atoms. The minimization involves a two-stage combined optimization method. First and foremost, the NVT (stands for the number of atoms, volume, and temperature of the structure) canonical ensemble is conducted for a total time of 5 picoseconds. This is aimed at the determination of the positions and velocities of each atom using non-Hamiltonian equations in the Nose-Hoover method at every time step. Following this, the simulation is extended for an additional 50 picoseconds, utilizing the NPT (stands for the number of atoms, pressure, and temperature of the structure) isothermal-isobaric ensemble where the objective of this phase is to resolve the kinematics parameters, such as linear/angular positions, orientations, and velocities of all atoms at every time step. The NPT ensemble is employed to keep constant temperature and pressure in conjunction with the imposition of uniaxial deformation along the [ 10 0] direction, featuring a specified strain rate of 10 10s −1at a temperature of 300 K. Prior to going through the NPT tension process, the samples are completely stable in terms of temperature and pressure; 5 ps of NVT ensemble has been employed to settle down the temperature at 300 K and successively 50 ps of NPT ensemble relaxed the samples to keep the zero pressure. At a constant strain rate of 10 10s −1(= ε˙11=dε11/dt), the main stress-strain simulation is conducted in [1 0 0] direction ( ε¨11= 0, ε22≠ 0, ε33≠ 0) at previously achieved constant pressure and temperature through next 30 ps. Processing Text: This letter successfully used double-wire arc additive manufacturing technology to prepare a new type of Al20.33Co21.60Fe30.45Ni27.62 EHEA. In particular, the double-wire feeding system uses combined cable wire (CCW) as the main welding wire and locates the eutectic point by adjusting the bypass Al wire feeding speed, which greatly improves the flexibility of alloy design. For the first time, this paper adopts D-WAAM technology, using self-designed CCW as the main welding wire and Al wire as the side axis feeding wire to locate the eutectic point and prepare an Al20.33Co21.60Fe30.45Ni27.62 eutectic high entropy alloy with a strength plasticity balance. In this paper, cold metal transfer smart arc additive manufacturing equipment was used to prepare EHEAs. As the main welding wire, CCW is transported vertically by CCW equipment, and the Al welding wire is transported by a side-axis wire feeder. It consists of two Fe wires, two Co wires and three Ni wires. The wire diameters are all 0.6 mm. The wire feeding speed is 7 m/min. The Al wire is a pure Al wire with a diameter of 0.8 mm, and the wire feeding speed is 3.4 m/min. The phase structure of the deposited samples was analyzed using an X-ray diffractometer (XRD). The XRD test voltage was 40 kV, the current was 150 mA, the scanning angle range was 20°-100°, and the scanning speed was 6°/min. A universal testing machine was used to conduct tensile experiments with a tensile rate of 0.6 mm/min. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) were used to observe the microstructure and tensile fracture morphology. Processing Text: An alloy with a nominal composition of Ni 40 Co 30 Cr 20 Al 5 Ti 5 was produced by arc-melting a mixture of various high-purity metal elements (purity >99.95 wt%). Processing Text: Commercially sourced gas-atomized CoCrNi pre-alloy powders were utilized, characterized by spherical geometry. The powders demonstrated a Hall flow rate of 18.8 s/50 g, a loose powder density of 4.31 g/cm³, and a tapped density of 4.80 g/cm³. Particle size analysis revealed a median particle diameter (D₅₀) of 43.4 μm, with a size distribution spanning from D₁₀ = 27.4 μm to D₉₀ = 65.5 μm, and an average particle size of 45.7 μm. Elemental distribution within the CoCrNi pre-alloy powders was found to be uniform. The SLM apparatus was equipped with a three-cylinder forming system and an IPG YLR-AC 1000 W laser, with a laser spot diameter ranging from 90 to 110 μm. A specific scanning strategy was employed, incorporating a 67° rotation angle between successive layers with a thickness of 40 μm to reduce anisotropy. An orthogonal experimental design was applied to systematically adjust the process parameters, namely laser power (p), scanning speed (v), and hatching space (d), set within the ranges of 80–140 W, 300–450 mm/s, and 80–110 μm, respectively. The parameter samples were fabricated with dimensions of 10 × 10 × 4 mm³ (length × width × thickness). The density of these samples was measured using the Archimedes drainage method, with at least three repetitions, and compared to the density of cast counterparts (8.2687 g/cm³). The optimal processing parameters were identified as p = 120 W, v = 350 mm/s, and d = 110 μm, achieving a density of 8.2191 g/cm³ and a relative density of 99.4%. Minimal microporosities were detected through electronic computed tomography (CT) imaging, indicating excellent forming quality. Condition: room temperature; Processing state: as-printed; Associated tensile strength: 892.78 MPa; Elongation: 33.28%

Processing Text: Fe-Si alloys with a nominal Si content of 5%, 10% and 20% were fabricated. Gas atomized Fe (purity 99%) and Si (purity 99.95%) powders, with a particle size ranging from 63 to 150 µm, obtained from American Elements (United States) and Tosoh SMD Inc (United States), were used in an Optomec Laser Engineered Net Shaping (LENS 150) equipment. The Fe-Si samples were printed by a LENS 150 equipment equipped with an IPG YLR-400 laser with a maximum laser power of 400 W and a laser beam diameter of 0.4 mm. This system was equipped with multiple powder feeders (PF), of which 2 feeders were used. Argon (Ar) was used as the inert carrying gas to transport powder from the powder feeder through the pipeline system to the powder delivery nozzle. Ar was also used as a shielding gas to control the environment during deposition. Three batches of samples were printed vertically along the z-axis. The first batch consisted of samples of Fe-5Si, Fe-10Si and Fe-20Si, each with dimensions of 5 mm ×5 mm ×6 mm, for density, hardness, and magnetic property measurements. The second batch included samples of Fe-3.5Si, Fe-5Si, Fe-10Si and Fe-20Si, each with dimensions of 5 mm ×5 mm ×25 mm, printed for tensile test measurements. The third batch comprised of samples of Fe-10Si and Fe-20Si, both with dimensions of 5 mm ×5 mm ×15 mm, printed for the compression tests. All samples were printed using optimized parameters from our previous work, i.e., laser power of 350 W, layer thickness of 0.20 mm, hatch spacing of 0.20 mm, stage speed of 8.4 mm/s, a protective gas centre purge of 20 litre per minute (lpm) and a powder supply gas flow of 4 lpm. The powder flow rates used on each powder feeder (PF1: Fe powder only, PF2: Fe+20% Si) were as follows: PF1: 3.75 rpm, PF2: 1.25 rpm for Fe-5Si. The printed samples were separated from the substrate using an electric discharge wire-cut equipment. Subsequently, the columnar sample was sectioned parallel to the build axis into two halves. Cross-sectioned surfaces were mechanically polished progressively, from Grit500, Grit2000, Grit4000 to a 0.03 µm polishing suspension, for characterization and property measurements. Processing Text: The Al-5.0Mn-1.5Mg-0.82Sc-0.76Zr (wt.%) alloy powder with a standard composition was prepared by gas atomization (Panxing New Alloy Materials Co., Ltd., China). The powder was spherical in shape, with the particles less than or equal to 22.3 µm accounting for 10% while 90% of the particles were less than or equal to 63.4 µm, as shown in Fig. 1(a, b). All the LPBF samples investigated in this work were manufactured using a BLT S210 LPBF machine equipped with a 400 W fiber laser. Constant laser power (350 W), scanning spacing (90 µm), and layer thickness (30 µm) were used with scanning velocities ranging between 450 and 1450 mm/s. Two different substrate temperatures, 25 and 200 °C, were used for each condition. The samples with the optimized process parameters had a relative density higher than 99.8 %. A bilinear scanning strategy with a scan rotation of 67° was used between the layers. The samples were printed in a high-purity argon atmosphere. Subsequently, the samples were heat-treated at 200 °C for 1 h to remove residual stresses before evaluating their microstructures and mechanical properties. The LPBF samples were prepared for microstructural characterization by mechanical grinding and polishing following a standard metallographic procedure recommended in ASTM E3-11. After polishing, the microstructural features were revealed using an etchant consisting of HNO 3(2.5 mL), HCl (1.5 mL), HF (1.0 mL), and distilled water (95 mL). The wire-cut electro-discharge machine was used to slice samples with the following dimensions: ∼5 mm long, ∼5 mm wide, and ∼1 mm thick. Prior to the EBSD characterization, the sheet samples were first mechanically polished with 400 #, 1000 #, 2000 #, and 3000 # SiC water abrasive paper, then electropolished to remove the surface deformation layer generated by mechanical grinding. Electropolishing was performed at −30 °C, with: 7 % perchloric acid, 93 % ethanol; a voltage of 25 V, and a current density of 450 mA/cm 2for about 1 min. Uniaxial tensile tests were performed using the CMT4105 universal testing machine. The gauge length and cross-sectional area of the tensile specimens were 22 mm and 1.5 mm × 4 mm. All the tensile samples were tested perpendicular to the build direction at a constant strain rate of 1 mm/min, following the standard ASTM E8. Fatigue test samples with the dimensions 60 mm × 12 mm × 1.5 mm were tested on an MTS370.02 fatigue testing machine. All samples were mechanically ground and polished prior to fatigue testing to ensure similar surface roughness. The uniaxial fatigue tests were conducted in a load control mode at a frequency of 40 Hz and stress ratio of R= 0.1, following the standard ASTM E466. The samples were tested until fracture or exhaustion till 10 7cycles. Condition: as-fabricated; Microstructure: dense and crack-free with fine grain size of 3.51 μm

Processing Text: To produce the Al-20%Mg2Si composite, an ingot of A413 aluminum alloy was melted in a graphite crucible located in an electrical resistance furnace, and pure magnesium (99.9%) was immersed by a graphite-coated steel plunger at 750 ± 5 °C. The melt was protected from oxidation and gas absorption by using coverall flux. The melt was held for 10 min at 750 ± 5 °C for homogenization, then poured into a graphite-coated and preheated Y-block steel mold. In another set of experiments, the optimal amount of the Cu-8%P master alloy was added into the melt to investigate the effect of the modification. The specimens were annealed at 490 °C ± 2 for 8 h to eliminate any internal and residual stresses. The specimens were hot rolled at 400 °C for 10%. Deformed specimens were heated to the semi-solid temperature of 570 °C. The specimens were held at the semi-solid temperature for 25, 35, and 45 min, then they were quenched into the water. They were heated to the selected semi-solid temperature for the appropriate time in an electrical resistance furnace and placed in a 500 °C preheated H13 tool steel mold. Subsequently, they were hot pressed into 27% reduction by using a hydraulic press at the conditions of a cross-head speed of 20 cm/s, pressure of 40 tons, and specimens with the dimensions of 3 × 25 × 85 mm 3 were produced. The solutionizing treatment was carried out at 490 °C ± 2 for 4 h in an inert gas atmosphere then, the specimens were quenched into the water, and finally, they were age-hardened at 170 °C ± 1 for 2 h. Processing Text: NbTaTiZrX RHEAs with BCC structure constructed by SQS method. The relationship between the elastic constant, elastic modulus, hardness, strength, and plasticity of NbTaTiZrX RHEAs with elements is systematically analyzed both by SQS and VCA methods. The calculated results show that alloying of Mo, W and Re with high elastic modulus can enhance the strength and the hardness of RHEAs. For alloying of V and Hf, the ductility of RHEAs is improved. The reduction of pseudo energy gaps and the formation of Hf-Hf strong metallic bonds further confirm its metallic ductility from the electronic density of states and charge density. The lattice constants (Å) of NbTaTiZrX RHEAs are calculated. Elastic constants (GPa) of NbTaTiZrX RHEAs are calculated by SQS method. Yield strength (GPa) of NbTaTiZrX RHEAs is calculated. Energy factors of NbTaTiZrX RHEAs are calculated by SQS method including screw dislocation (Ks) and edge dislocation (Ke); mixed dislocation (Km). Total density of states for NbTaTiZrX RHEAs is calculated by SQS method. Charge density contour of NbTaTiZrX RHEAs along the crystal plane (1 1 0) is analyzed. Common parameters of NbTaTiZrX RHEAs are calculated. Calculated using SQS method; Notably higher than other considered high-entropy alloys

Square specimens of 32.8 mm (length) × 10 mm (width) × 2 mm (height) and 5 mm × 5 mm x 5 mm were cut from the ingot using wire cutting. Room temperature quasi-static compression test was conducted using a universal testing machine (CMT 5205, US) at a strain rate of 0.1 s −1. According to the ASTM E209-18standard [ 30], a dynamic thermal simulator (Gleeble-3500, US) was used to test in an argon environment with a temperature range of 800-1200 °C (in increments of 100 °C). The strain rate was 0.1 s −1and the strain was 50%. Homogenized for 15 min before deformation to eliminate the thermal gradient of specimens. After cutting along the mid-plane parallel to the compression axis, the internal organization of the section was observed using SEM with equipped electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, Oxford Symmetry, US) to further investigate the microstructural evolution. Processing Text: The Ti-4V-2Mo-2Fe alloy (referred to as TVMF hereafter) was prepared in a vacuum suspension melting furnace utilizing high-purity Ti, V, Mo, and Fe particles as raw materials. Throughout the smelting process, argon gas serves as the protective atmosphere. The ingot undergoes six times of melting to ensure uniform chemical composition. The β phase transition temperature of the TVMF alloy was determined to be approximately 753 ± 3 °C via a differential scanning calorimeter (DSC). Subsequently, the alloy ingot undergoes three forging stages using a four-column hydraulic press, with temperatures maintained at 1000 °C, 950 °C, and 900 °C for 30 min before each forging cycle. Each forging pass induces approximately 40% deformation, and the alloy was air-cooled after the final forging. Next, the alloy was subjected to deformation using a two-high mill at temperatures of 700 °C, 750 °C, 800 °C, 850 °C, and 900 °C, denoted as 700HR, 750HR, 800HR, 850HR, and 900HR for ease of identification. Prior to rolling, the alloys were preheated in a muffle furnace for 30 min. The initial thickness of the alloy was 20 mm, with a pressure of 1 mm applied per pass and a total deformation of approximately 90% after a 3 min hold following each pass. Following the final rolling, the alloy was subjected to a 3 min keep warm and subsequently quenched in water. Processing Text: In the present work, cold rolling and subsequent high-temperature annealing processes were employed to the Cu1.2NiMnFe0.5Cr0.5Al0.2 high-entropy alloy. After subsequent aging treatment at 400 °C, spinodal decomposition occurred within the matrix, leading to enhanced strength. High-entropy alloy ingots of Cu 1.2NiMnFe 0.5Cr 0.5Al 0.2(at.%) were prepared by induction melting of commercial purity metals (>99%) and casting into a cylindrical steel mold (Φ35 × 275 mm). To minimize elemental loss, the furnace chamber was evacuated and filled with argon gas. The as-cast ingots were heat-treated at 950 °C for 24 h to enhance chemical homogeneity. Subsequently, samples measuring 100 × 10 × 5 mm 3were cut from the ingots and cold-rolled with a 60% rolling reduction ratio, reducing their thickness from 5 to 2 mm. The cold-rolled plates were annealed at 950 °C for 2 h (depicted as the AN sample) and then water-cooled to obtain fully recrystallized microstructure, and sequential aging at 400 °C for xh (x = 2,4,6,8,10) and then air-cooled (designated as the 2H, 4H, 6H, 8H, and 10H samples, respectively), were conducted to acquire spinodal-decomposed microstructure. The samples for TEM were grounded to a thickness of 50 μm and then ion-milled. And the samples for electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) analysis underwent electropolishing in a solution containing perchloric acid and ethanol with a volume ratio of 9:1, the polishing process was conducted at 26.5 V for a duration of 5 s. Sharp tip specimens for atom probe tomography (APT) were made by a two-step electrochemical polishing. The 0.3 mm × 0.3 mm blanks were cut by low-speed diamond saw, followed by electrochemical polishing using 10% perchloric acid at a direct voltage of 15 V, the tips were then polished by using weaker electrolyte (2%) of perchloric acid at a direct voltage of 8 V. Processing Text: Ti40Zr25Nb25Ta5Mo5 (at.%) HEA was fabricated from commercially pure (purity ≥99.95 wt.%) nuggets of each element using an arc melting furnace (AM200, Edmund Bühler GmbH, using a Vario hybrid 400-DC-HF generator). The furnace was engineered to incorporate a water-cooled copper crucible equipped with multi-purpose mould cavities. Each ingot was prepared in a batch of 20 g and loaded in a water-cooled copper mould cavity in the order of high melting point metals stacking on top of lower melting point metals to minimize evaporation. After that, the chamber was closed, evacuated to about 5 Pa by a rotary pump, and then flushed with a flow of high-purity argon for 15 min. This process was repeated twice. Then, the chamber was further evacuated to a high vacuum condition (∼10 −4Pa) by a diffusion pump. Finally, the chamber was refilled with high-purity argon for the arc-melting process. CP-Ti nuggets were used as an oxygen getter. The materials were then melted by the arc which was controlled by the generator and an arc-driving arm. Each ingot (20 g) was melted six times and flipped after each melting. During each cycle of melting, the molten alloy was held in the liquid state for 10 min for chemical homogeneity (inverted each time before remelting). Five ingots were then melted together and cast into a water-cooled copper mould to form a cuboidal bar with dimensions of 90 × 12 × 8 mm 3. Finally, specimens were cut from the as-cast alloy bar, ground with SiC abrasive papers and mirror-polished with 0.04 μm colloidal silica suspension (OPS) with 30% H 2O 2(10:1 by volume) for characterisation. Processing state: as-cast; Microstructure: nearly equiaxed grain structure with dendritic structures enriched in Ta, Nb, and Mo

Processing Text: A commercially extruded Mg-Y-Nd-Gd-Zr alloy (∅15 × 100 mm) was utilized as the experimental specimen. The alloy underwent an initial partial solution treatment (450 °C, 2 h) in a resistance furnace (SX-G04133), followed by cooling in hot water at 80 °C (ST). The samples treated with a solid solution after the 1st, 4th, 8th, and 9th rolls are denoted as ST+1P, ST+4P, ST+8P, and ST+9P, respectively. The microstructures of the samples were examined by optical microscopy (OM, Olympus GX51) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Gemini300, Zeiss). The cross-sectional surface of the Mg alloy bar was observed. The microstructural evolution of the samples was analyzed by X-ray diffraction (XRD, D8 Advance), electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, C-nano, Oxford), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM, FEI Talos F200X, 200 kV). The XRD measurement utilized a Cu target as the radiation source, with an incident wavelength of 1.5406 A. The test voltage was set to 40 kV (in increments of 1 kV per step) and the tube current was maintained at 30 mA. The angle range (2θ) for scanning was specified as 20-80°, and the scanning rate was set to 2°/min. For EBSD sample preparation, argon ion polishing was performed on the OM samples at 5, 4, and 3 kV for 45 min with an inclination angle of approximately 4.5°. EBSD observations were conducted using an Oxford C-nano EBSD system (Zeiss) in conjunction with a Gemini300 scanning electron microscope operating at a test voltage of 25 kV. The image resolution was set to 311 × 256 pixels, and the scanning step size was 0.5 mm. The tensile properties and hardness of the samples were evaluated using an MTS Landmark material-testing system (MTS810, 250 KN) and an HVS-1000 digital Vickers microhardness tester. The surface of the ST sample, without undergoing the USRP treatment, has a rough texture with an arithmetic mean deviation (Ra) of 0.65 μm and a micro-roughness 10-point height (Rz) of 6.92 μm. Following the USRP treatment, the surface roughness of the ST+1P sample significantly decreases, with Ra and Rz values measuring 0.17 and 1.44 μm, respectively. The surface smoothness of the ST+4P sample improves as all burrs disappear, resulting in Ra and Rz values of 0.06 and 0.55 μm, respectively. With a further increase in the USRP-induced deformation, surface burrs reappear on the ST+8P sample, exhibiting a rougher texture than that of the ST+4P sample; correspondingly, Ra and Rz increase to 0.24 and 1.87 μm, respectively. However, spalling occurs on the surface of the ST+9P sample, leading to morphological damage; at this stage, the Ra and Rz values of the Mg alloy are approximately 3.29 and 20.59 μm, respectively. The optimal surface roughness of the Mg-Y-Nd-Gd-Zr alloy is achieved after four passes. The depth of the gradient layer increased with each additional USRP pass, ranging from 650 μm (1 pass) to 910 μm (8 passes). The USRP induced the largest plastic deformation at the top surface of the sample, leading to the continuous proliferation of high-density dislocations and stratification, which in turn triggered DRX and ultimately resulted in numerous dislocation-rich and stratified nanocrystals with HAGBs on the top surface. The plastic deformation in the subsurface layer was slightly lower than that in the surface layer, which still consisted of HAGBs nanocrystals wrapped in dislocations; however, their sizes were slightly smaller than those on the surface layer. Owing to the low fault energy of Mg alloys, abundant DTs were observed. As the depth increased, the number of DTs decreased while transitioning into tension twins with a relatively low CRSS. Eventually, a composite gradient structure, characterized by an increasing grain size, decreasing dislocation density, decreasing layer fault density, and decreasing twin density, was formed. The microhardness of the Mg alloy decreased exponentially with increasing depth from the surface treated using the USRP under the same number of rolling passes. Simultaneously, with an increase in the number of passes, a continuous enhancement in the microhardness of the topmost layer was observed, ranging from 106.3 Hv at one pass to 115 Hv at four passes and reaching up to 119.7 Hv at eight passes. After one USRP treatment, the YS of the Mg alloy increased by approximately 34.2%. As the number of USRP treatments increased, a continuous increase in the depth of the gradient layer and gradual consumption of the twin crystals was observed, resulting in an elevated work-hardening rate for the Mg alloy. Simultaneous transitioning from a brittle fracture mechanism to a ductile fracture mechanism resulted in ongoing improvements in the UTS and EL. Untreated ST sample
Processing Word: Untreated ST sample

Processing Text: The concentrations of Al and Ti are systemically adjusted for the propose to obtain high volume fraction of γ′ precipitates, good alumina-forming ability, and in the meantime minimizing the formation of harmful phases. Alloy ingots of 200 g were prepared from the constituent elements (Fe, Ni, Cr, Al, Ti, and so on, purity >99.9 wt%) by arc melting in an Ar atmosphere. The alloy buttons were flipped and remelted more than five times to ensure thoroughly mixing of all elements and then drop cast into a water chilled Cu mold (12.5 × 12.5 × 120 mm 3). The drop cast ingots were homogenized at 1225 °C for 8 h, then quenched in water. The homogenized ingots were cold rolled along the longitudinal direction to a thickness reduction of ∼70%. The cold rolled plates were recrystallized at 1000 °C for 1 h and then aged at 700 °C for 24 h. All the heat treatments were carried out in an argon-protected tube furnace. Dog bone shaped specimens with gauge sections about 3.2 × 2.0 × 12.7 mm 3 were cut from the aged plates by electro-discharge machining (EDM). The surface of the gauge section was mechanically ground by 1200 grits SiC paper to eliminate defects on the surface of the tensile specimen. Tensile tests were conducted in the laboratory atmosphere on a screw-driven mechanical testing machine equipped with an induction heater. Before load applying, the specimens were held at the testing temperature for 15 min to ensure the temperature being stable. All specimens were tested at a strain rate of 10 −3s −1, which corresponds to a displacement rate of 0.75 mm/min. For each alloy at each temperature, at least three specimens were tested to ensure data reproducible. The elongation to fracture (EF) was calculated by measuring the length of the specimen before and after fracture. The yield strength (YS) was obtained by using the 0.2% offset method. Specimens with a dimension of 10.0 × 10.0 × 2.0 mm 3 were cut by EDM and ground to 2000 grit SiC paper before test. Oxidation tests were conducted at 750 °C for 480 h in air. Before and after oxidation, weights of specimens were weighed by using an electronic scale with the accuracy of 10 −4g. The scanning electron microscopy (SEM) samples were ground with 1200 grit SiC paper and then mechanical polished or electropolished. TEM images and selected area electron diffraction (SAED) were captured with a spherical aberration corrected FEI Titan G 2scanning TEM and a FEI Tecnai G 2F20 TEM, both of which were operated at 200 kV and equipped with an annular dark field (ADF) detector and a high angle annular dark field (HAADF) detector. Temperature: 25°C to 650°C

Processing Text: The samples were cut along the rolling direction (RD) and transverse direction (TD) and then subjected to a sequential annealing process in an air-circulating furnace, involving a temperature increase to 350 °C at 10 °C/min followed by a 50-min hold at this temperature, followed by rapid quenching in water. Surface finishing was achieved through sequential grinding with sandpapers of increasing fineness (800#, 1000#, 1500#, and 2000#), polishing with a 3 μm diamond suspension, and electropolishing at −20 °C in a solution of 10 % perchloric acid and 90 % anhydrous ethanol. Tensile specimens, designed in a flat dog-bone shape, were extracted from the plate centers in RD and TD orientations. These specimens were prepared with dimensions of 20 mm in gauge length, 2 mm in thickness, and 6 mm in width, consistent with quasi in-situ tensile testing specifications. The tensile behavior was assessed at room temperature (298K) and low temperature (77K) using an MTS C43.105 full-temperature field tensile testing machine equipped with extensometer at a strain rate of 1.2 × 10−3s−1. To achieve and maintain the desired low-temperature environment, the chamber was filled with liquid nitrogen, ensuring that the sample was completely submerged and constantly exposed to liquid nitrogen throughout the test. Prior to initiating the tensile test, the setup was equilibrated for approximately 25 min. Quasi in-situ EBSD testing was conducted to monitor the evolution of grain orientation at strain levels of 0 %, 5 %, 10 %, 15 %, and 20 %. Grain boundaries and dislocation configurations were analyzed using a FEI TECNAI F30 transmission electron microscope (TEM), with sample preparation via twin-jet electropolishing in a 30 % nitric acid and 70 % absolute alcohol solution at −20 °C. The ingots were melted by a vacuum arc melting furnace under the protection of argon gas, and followed by being cast into a graphite mould. The as-cast ingots were chemically analyzed by X-Ray Fluorescence (XRF, ZSX Primus IV). Subsequently, the ingots were homogenized at 900 °C for 1 h and quenched in water. The as-homogenized ingots were then cold rolled and cold drawn to wires with the diameter of Φ 0.5 mm. During the process of cold deformation, the intermediate annealing at 900 °C for 1 h was performed. The deformation of each pass was controlled at 15%, and the deformation accumulation of 90% was gained. The isochronous aging treatment was performed at the temperature range of 200°C-600 °C for 1 h, and the isothermal aging treatment was carried out at 300 °C and 400 °C for various durations from 1 h to 5 h. To avoid the oxidation during aging, vacuum tube furnaces were used for protection. Condition: cold-deformed

Processing Text: Pre-alloyed Al0.5CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) powders were prepared via gas atomization and followed by hot-pressing sintering (HPS) at 1200 °C for 1 h to fabricate bulk materials. The gas-atomized HEA powders were held in a 12.5 mm-diameter graphite die and subsequently hot-pressing sintered (HPSed) at 1200 °C for 1 h under a pressure of 60 MPa in the ZT-25-20YVHP equipment. Moreover, the annealing experiments were conducted at 200, 400, 500, 600, 800, 900, 1000, and 1200 °C for 10 min, and the alloys were cooled down naturally in the air to investigate the thermal stability and phase evolution of the as-atomized powders. Processing Text: The experiment utilized 15-5 PH stainless steel powder produced by using vacuum atomization method (Oerlikon Metco., Switzerland). The powder exhibited excellent sphericity, presenting a smooth and fully formed structure ( Fig. 1(a)). The particle size distribution was mostly within 15∼53 μm, with D10, D50, and D90 being 19.4 μm, 33.2 μm, and 50.9 μm, respectively ( Fig. 1(b)). The primary chemical composition of the powder was Fe-12.48Cr-3.55Ni-3.04Cu-0.18Nb-0.48Mn-0.46Si-0.0509C (wt. %). Subsequently, the 64 sets of small square samples (10 × 10 × 10 mm 3) with different process parameters were fabricated using the L-PBF equipment (HBD 280 Metal 3D Printer). The chosen process parameters included a range of Pat 200 W, 260 W, 320 W, and 380 W, Vat 800 mm/s, 1200 mm/s, 1600 mm/s, and 2000 mm/s, Hat 0.06 mm, 0.09 mm, 0.12 mm, and 0.15 mm, respectively, and a fixed scanning layer thickness ( T) of 0.04 mm. The printing strategy involved rotating the current printing layer by 67° compared to the previous layer. Subsequently, well-formed (no visible defect) process parameters were selected for the fabrication of tensile and impact samples. The particle size of the powder was determined using a laser particle size analyzer (Better Size 2600), while the chemical composition was analyzed through inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectroscopy. Subsequently, the ground and polished samples underwent corrosion in a 15 % HF aqueous solution at a voltage of 25 V for 15 s. Microstructural observations were conducted using optical microscope (OM, Leica DMI3000 M) and scanning electron microscope (SEM, Gemini SEM300). The electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) samples were prepared using a mixed solution of 5 % HClO 4+95 % CH 3COOH (vol%) at a voltage of 25 V for 30 s. The crystal structure and texture of the samples were examined and the EBSD data were further analyzed using the software of OIM. The phase structure was analyzed by X-ray diffractometer (Smart Lab) carrying Cu Kα. Utilized the Archimedes drainage method for precise determination of the density of the formed samples. The bar shaped tensile test sample (gauge length specification: φ5 mm × 25 mm) was subjected to room temperature tensile performance testing on a universal tensile testing machine (DN200), with a strain rate of 1.3 × 10 −3s −1. The samples were subjected to HRC testing using the hardness tester (HRS-150), applying a loading force of 1470 N for a duration of 10 s. Additionally, the V-notch impact samples (size 55 × 10 × 10 mm 3) were subjected to Charpy impact testing on the metal pendulum impact testing machine (JBN500), featuring a notch depth of 2 mm and a root radius of 0.25 mm. The morphology of both tensile and impact fractures was observed under the SEM. Sample 21#, processed via L-PBF with P = 260 W, H = 0.06 mm, V = 1200 mm/s; Exhibits a heterogeneous layered structure of FCC + BCC dual-phase, fine-grain and coarse-grain layers.
Processing Word: Sample 21#, processed via L-PBF with P = 260 W, H = 0.06 mm, V = 1200 mm/s; Exhibits a heterogeneous layered structure of FCC + BCC dual-phase, fine-grain and coarse-grain layers.

Processing Text: Gas-atomized FeCoCrNiMo 0.2HEA powders were adopted as the raw materials for SLM, with an average particle size of ∼67.1 μm. SLMed samples were fabricated using an FS273 M machine (Farsoon, China) equipped with a YAG fiber laser, which has a maximum output power of 500 W and a laser beam diameter of 90 μm. Before initiating the selective laser melting (SLM) process, the chamber of the SLM machine underwent vacuuming and subsequent filling with high-purity argon gas, ensuring a low oxygen content of less than 100 ppm. Cube-shaped samples (10 mm × 10 mm × 8 mm) and sheet-shaped samples (70 mm × 12 mm × 8 mm) were built for microstructural observation and mechanical test, respectively. All the SLM samples were annealed at 400 °C in a vacuum furnace for 3 h with a subsequent furnace cool to mitigate residual internal stress. Sample density was measured according to the Archimedes method. For microstructural examination, samples underwent electro-polishing in a solution composed of 60 % methanol, 34 % n-butyl alcohol, and 6 % perchloric acid at an applied DC voltage of 20 V. Tensile tests were performed on an Instron 3369 machine at room temperature, maintaining a constant strain rate of 1 × 10 −3s −1, with the tensile direction oriented perpendicular to the building direction. The microstructure of the fractured samples at the energy density of 47 J/mm 3 was analyzed using EBSD and TEM. Processing Text: The production process of the bar involved several steps, as illustrated in Fig. 1. Initially, a casting ingot with dimensions of 530 mm in width and 410 mm in thickness was heated at a temperature of 1210 °C ± 30 °C for a duration of 11 h. Subsequently, the ingot was rolled into a square middle billet measuring 240 mm × 240 mm. The middle billet was further hot-rolled into a cylindrical bar with a diameter of 130 mm, within a temperature range of 900 °C-950 °C. Before the isothermal heat treatment, the bainitic transition temperature of sample steels were obtained by the thermal expansion experiment. The thermal expansion experiment was carried out on the thermal simulation testing machine Gleeble-3500, the experiment process and the sample size are shown in Fig. 2(a). The thermal expansion curves obtained from the thermal expansion experiment are shown in Fig. 2(b). The bainite transformation temperatures range of 0Nb-steel and 0.015Nb-steel measured by the tangent method were 400∼521 °C and 381∼505 °C, respectively. For the isothermal quenching experiment, several cylinder rods with a diameter of 15 mm and a length of 70 mm were extracted from the low carbon bainitic microalloying steel rods. The isothermal process parameters and route are depicted in Fig. 3 and presented in Table 1. In the first step, the samples were austenitized in a KSL-1400X box-type high-temperature furnace. The austenite temperature (AT) was set at 950 °C, and the soaking time was 60 min. Subsequently, the samples were removed from the high-temperature furnace and directly placed into a salt bath furnace for isothermal treatment, where the salt used was nitrate salt. The temperature range of bainitic transformation, calculated by JMatPro, was determined to be 370∼550 °C. Consequently, the IT were set at 400 °C, 450 °C, and 500 °C, respectively, with each isothermal time set at 10 min. Finally, the samples were removed from the furnace and air-cooled to room temperature. Furthermore, two additional experiments were conducted with different austenitizing temperatures. The samples were austenitized at 900 °C and 1000 °C, respectively. Following the austenitization process, the samples were transferred from the high-temperature furnace to the salt bath furnace for isothermal treatment at 450 °C for 10 min. The ASTM grain size grades after austenitizing at 900 °C, 950 °C, and 1000 °C were determined to be 6, 7.5, and 8, respectively. Thermal expansion experiments were performed using the DIL 805A dilatometer, with specimen dimensions of φ4 × 10 mm. The heat treatment process involved an austenitizing temperature of 900 °C for 30 min followed by a 10-min soaking at 450 °C, as depicted in Fig. 3. The optimal isothermal quenching process for achieving a balance between strength and toughness is as follows: the steels were austenitized at 900 °C for 30 min and then subjected to an isothermal treatment at 450 °C for 10 min. Processing Text: Nearly equiatomic AlCoCrFeNi alloy samples were prepared by induction melting and mechanical alloying (MA) combined with spark plasma sintering (SPS). Pure powders of each element (Co 99.8%, Cr 99%, Fe 99.9%, Ni 99.5%, Al 99.7%) were used in appropriate amounts to prepare the equiatomic alloy. A total amount of 20 g of the powder mixture was put in the jar along with milling balls, both made from AISI 420 stainless steel. The balls-to-powder weight ratio was 1:15. To decrease the undesired cold welding, 4 wt% of n-heptane was used as the process control agent (PCA). The sealed vessel was then flushed with argon of 99.996 purity (2 l min−1 for 2 min) to prevent any oxidation during the alloying process. The MA was carried out in 30 min intervals followed by 10 min breaks between them until the straight time of the MA reached 8 h. The rotation speed was 400 rpm. The prepared powder alloy was sintered in SPS device FCT Systeme HP D 10. An amount of 10 g of the powder was put in a graphite mould with a diameter of 20 mm and sealed with graphite paper. The sintering temperature was set to 1000 °C with a heating speed of 200 °C min−1 and a pressure of 48 MPa being applied after reaching the sintering temperature. The sample was held under these conditions for 10 min, which prevents excessive coarsening of the microstructure. Eventually, the sample was cooled down to laboratory temperature with the maxima cooling speed of the machine, which is determined by the temperature gradient between the mould and both the water-cooled pistons of the SPS machine. The other AlCoCrFeNi specimen was prepared by induction melting. Small chunks of the individual base metals in precise weight ratios were melted in an Al2O3 crucible at 1800 °C under an argon atmosphere. The melted alloy was homogenized by eddy currents for several minutes before casting. Afterwards, the alloy was cast in a steel mould 14 mm in diameter. Thin foils from the cast material were electropolished (T = −30 °C, U = 15 V) in a TENUPOL 5 (Struers) unit filled with a solution of 20% HNO3 in methanol, a lamella from the sintered alloy was prepared by a Ga+ focused ion beam (FIB, FEI Quanta DualBeam). The mechanical properties were examined by Vickers hardness and compressive stress-strain tests. The hardness was measured with a load of 30 kg and a load time of 10 s. The average value was calculated after measuring 10 indents. The compressive tests were performed on the LabTest 5.250SP1-VM machine using block-shaped specimens with a height corresponding to 1.5 times the side of the base. The deformation speed was set to 10−3 s−1, and each alloy was tested using at least three samples to provide sufficient statistical reliability. The compressive tests were performed at room temperature, at 800 °C, and at room temperature after being annealed at 800 °C for 100h.
