Processing Text: The steel was designed to have a low stacking-fault energy (SFE, 17.8 mJ/m²) to introduce high density of nanotwins through pre-deformation. The steel was prepared by arc-melting high-purity metals in argon. The ingots were homogenized at 1200 °C for 1 h, then hot-rolled to 4 mm in thickness and water quenched (labeled as HR). The HR samples were then cold-rolled 40% at room temperature to 2.4 mm in thickness (labeled CR40). Finally, the CR40 samples were annealed at 100-600 °C for 10 min, followed by water quenching. The samples annealed at 300 °C and 400 °C are respectively denoted as ANN300 and ANN400. A subsequent intermediate annealing was applied to control the reverse phase transformation from ε-martensite to austenite to enhance the deformation ability of the nanotwinned steel (rising tensile elongation from 5 to 16%). The microstructures of samples CR40, ANN300, and ANN400 were characterized in the plane containing rolling direction (RD) and normal direction (ND) of the sheets by transmission electron microscopy (TEM), electron backscattering diffraction (EBSD), and X-ray diffraction (XRD). Thin foils for TEM examinations were prepared by mechanical polishing down to 100 μm in thickness, followed by ion thinning using a Gatan 695 instrument, and observed using a 200 kV TEM (FEI Talos F200X). The samples for EBSD and X-ray diffraction were electropolished in a solution of 10% perchloric acid and 90% acetic acid at room temperature. X-ray diffraction (XRD) with Cu-Kα radiation (Bruker D8 Advance) was used to determine the phase composition. The scanning range was 35-95°, with a scan rate of 1°/min. The volume fractions of austenite ( Vγ) and ε-martensite ( Vε) were measured by a direct-comparison method. The microhardness of the samples was measured using an HVS-1000Z micro-Vickers hardness tester, with a loading force of 9.80 N and a loading time of 15 s. Tensile testing was performed at a strain rate of 10−3s−1 using a SUNS testing machine with a contact extensometer. Condition: CR40 (Cold-Rolled); Microstructure: Nanotwins and ε-martensite
Processing Word: Condition: CR40 (Cold-Rolled); Microstructure: Nanotwins and ε-martensite

Processing Text: Ti-30Zr-5Mo alloy was triply melted by consumable vacuum arc-melting sponge Ti, sponge Zr, and Ti-32Mo master alloy. The ingot was homogenized at 1100 °C for 6 h in vacuum and then forged at 1100 °C and air cooled to room temperature. Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC, Netzsch STA449F3) measurements were carried out at 20 °C/min. According to the DSC results, the α to β phase transformation temperature of Ti-30Zr-5Mo alloy was determined to be approximately 700 °C. To obtain body-centered-cubic Ti-30Zr-5Mo materials with different β grain sizes, different heat treatment processes were conducted. The samples were solution treated at varied temperatures (700-950 °C) in β phase region with different annealing times (30-60 min) in vacumm and followed by water quenching. SIMRT was used to obtain finer grain sizes. The ingots were cold rolled with a reduction ratio of 30%, and then solution treated at 700 °C for 2 min. The above process is one loop, and all the processes are shown in Fig. 2b. Tensile specimens with a total length of 40 mm, gauge a length of 13 mm, a width of 3 mm, and a thickness of 1.5 mm were prepared by electrical discharge wire cutting. The SHIMADZU AG-XPLUS 100 KN tensile testing machine was used for tensile tests at room temperature with a strain rate of 3 × 10 -4s -1. Three samples of each grain size were prepared to minimize errors. Before optical microscopy observation using an optical microscope (OM, ZESS AXIO), the materials were mechanically polished and then chemically etched using a solution of 3.5 pct hydrofluoric acid (HF), 10 pct nitric acid (HNO3) and 86.5 pct distilled water (H2O). The phase constitutions of the tensile materials before and after deformation were determined by X-ray diffractometer (XRD, Smart Lab). The samples after deformation for XRD acquisition are taken near the fracture of the tensile specimens after fracture. In-situ tensile tests in scanning electron microscopy (SEM, JEOL JSM-7001F) and electron back-scattered diffraction (EBSD, Oxford instrument Symmetry) systems were used to analyze the microstructural evolution of materials during tensile deformation. Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC, Netzsch STA449F3) measurements were carried out at 20 °C/min. According to the DSC results, the α to β phase transformation temperature of Ti-30Zr-5Mo alloy was determined to be approximately 700 °C. To obtain body-centered-cubic Ti-30Zr-5Mo materials with different β grain sizes, different heat treatment processes were conducted. The samples were solution treated at varied temperatures (700-950 °C) in β phase region with different annealing times (30-60 min) in vacumm and followed by water quenching. SIMRT was used to obtain finer grain sizes. The ingots were cold rolled with a reduction ratio of 30%, and then solution treated at 700 °C for 2 min. The above process is one loop, and all the processes are shown in Fig. 2b. Tensile specimens with a total length of 40 mm, gauge a length of 13 mm, a width of 3 mm, and a thickness of 1.5 mm were prepared by electrical discharge wire cutting. The SHIMADZU AG-XPLUS 100 KN tensile testing machine was used for tensile tests at room temperature with a strain rate of 3 × 10 -4s -1. Three samples of each grain size were prepared to minimize errors. Before optical microscopy observation using an optical microscope (OM, ZESS AXIO), the materials were mechanically polished and then chemically etched using a solution of 3.5 pct hydrofluoric acid (HF), 10 pct nitric acid (HNO3) and 86.5 pct distilled water (H2O). The phase constitutions of the tensile materials before and after deformation were determined by X-ray diffractometer (XRD, Smart Lab). The samples after deformation for XRD acquisition are taken near the fracture of the tensile specimens after fracture. In-situ tensile tests in scanning electron microscopy (SEM, JEOL JSM-7001F) and electron back-scattered diffraction (EBSD, Oxford instrument Symmetry) systems were used to analyze the microstructural evolution of materials during tensile deformation. Processing Text: High-purity Ti, Zr, Mo, and Hf (wt % >99.99) metal were melted through arc melting in high purity argon atmosphere. The ingots were then re-melted by turned over six times to ensure their chemical homogeneity. The molten alloy buttons were poured into a copper mold to obtain a long rod-shaped MPEAs sample. For the preparation of the SEM specimens, mechanical polishing and electrolytically polishing with HClO4, CH3(CH2)3OH and CH3OH solutions at −25 °C for 90 s were conducted. The samples were first cut into thin slices with a thickness of 0.3 mm using wire cutting, then polished with 2000-grit sandpaper to a thickness of approximately 0.05 mm, and finally subjected to ion thinning for final thinning. Condition: As-cast; Microstructure: Single BCC phase

Processing Text: The Fe30Mn10Co10Cr2.5V1.5C MPEA was produced by ingot casting followed by solution annealing under an argon atmosphere for 5 h at 1150 °C. Subsequently, hot-rolling was applied at 1150 °C to reduce the material thickness to 4 mm. After air cooling, the material was cold-rolled to a thickness of 2 mm (50 % cold-rolling degree). Two different annealing strategies were performed: (a) recrystallization and aging route (RX+A), (b) aging treatment after cold-rolling (CR+A). The first annealing strategy (RX+A) comprised a recrystallization treatment at 1150 °C for 10 min followed by aging with varying temperature (600 - 900 °C) and time (0.5 - 24 h). In the second annealing strategy (CR+A), the aging treatments were performed after cold-rolling without recrystallization for 15 min to 16 h at temperatures in the range between 500 and 1000 °C. Processing Text: A hot-draw stick of commercial Inconel 718 alloy with a diameter of ∼40 mm was utilized. The friction welding experiments were carried out using an HWI-IFW-130 friction welding machine developed by Harbin Welding Institute. One IN718 stick was fixed at the center of the flywheel in the welding machine and then rotated by a constant speed of 2500 r/min during the later friction welding process. Another IN718 stick was applied to tightly contact with the MCA intermedium along the axial direction of the fixed stick. The forge pressure was controlled at 400 MPa, as well as the first friction pressure at 300 MPa. The moment of inertia was kept to be constant at 1.18 kg m 2. For comparison, another friction weld joint was directly produced on two directly contacted IN718 sticks without the in-between MCA intermedium layer under identical welding conditions. The contact surfaces of the used IN718 stick were initially ground by sandpapers and polished using diamond paste, to remove any possible contaminants or oxides for better contact of the following welding. A two-step ageing treatment was performed, namely heated to 720 °C and hold for 8 h, then slowly cooled to 620 °C inside the furnace by 50 °C/h and held for another 8 h, followed by air cooling to room temperature. Flat dog-bone-shaped tensile specimens with a thickness of 1.5 mm were machined from the center part of the weld joints by using electrical discharge machining (EDM). Uniaxial tensile tests were then carried out at room temperature of ∼20 °C using an MTS landmark testing system at a constant strain rate of 1 × 10 −3s −1. The surfaces of the specimens before and after the tensile experiments were mechanically ground with silicon carbide abrasive paper (from P180 to P5000), and then fine polished using 3 μm diamond suspensions. Last polishing with ∼100 nm SiO2 suspension was carried out to remove the strained layer induced by prior mechanical grinding for a better resolution of electron microscopic characterization. The microstructural examination was conducted on a TESCAN CLARA scanning electron microscope (SEM) equipped with an electron back-scattered diffraction (EBSD) detector microscope at different regions of the attained specimens. Transmission electron microscopic (TEM) investigations including high-resolution atomic imaging and the selected area electron diffraction (SAED) analysis were conducted by using a FEI Talos F200X microscope operated at 200 kV. The elemental distribution of the weld joint was also investigated using energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) instrumented in the Talos TEM device. Thin foils for the above TEM study were prepared from the zone near the interface boundary between the IN718 and IN178 or MCA intermedium, and they are produced using the Helios 600i Focus ion beam (FIB)-SEM system. The transverse distribution of nano-hardness values in the weld zone was also measured on the polished specimens using a KLA G200X nano-indenter. The indentation tests were performed under a load-control mode with a maximum force of 4 mN with a loading rate of 0.04 mN/s (i.e., a nominal strain rate of 0.01/s) at room temperature. For higher reliability, three indents were repeated at each location under identical conditions. Condition: as-weld; Compared with counterpart without MCA intermedium layer (~530 MPa)

Processing Text: The heterostructured Al-Mg-Si-Cu alloy profile modified by TiB2-TiC particles was prepared by conventional extrusion and solution treatment. The solution treatment was performed at 560 °C for 3 h, followed by rapid quenching to room temperature in cold water, and then the sample was artificially aged (AA) at 175 °C for different times to explore the age hardening response. The gauge section of the tensile specimens were controlled to be 15 mm (width) × 6 mm (thickness), and the gauge length was determined by 5.65 S0 (Where S0 represents the cross-sectional area of the gauge section). The tensile tests were performed on the CMT5105 tensile test machine at room temperature. The tensile speed was controlled to be 1 mm/min first and then 10 mm/min after yield. Three parallel tensile specimens for each sample were tested to obtain reproducible tensile properties. In addition, the loading-unloading-reloading (LUR) tensile test at room temperature was carried out on instrument LD26.105 electronic universal test machine. The gauge dimension of the LUR specimens is 10 mm (length) × 3 mm (width) × 3 mm (thickness). Five loading-unloading loops were performed in the LUR test. The strain rate is controlled to be 5 × 10−4 s−1 to the specified strain (such as 1%). Next, it is unloaded to 50 N in a stress-controlled mode with an unloading rate of 400 N min−1. Repeat the above operation for the next cyclic tensile tests. The standard grinding and polishing processes were employed to prepare the samples for optical microstructure, which was analyzed with a ZEISS Axioskop. The microstructure of the alloy profile was also analyzed by Zeiss ∑IGMA field emission scanning electron microscope (SEM) equipped with energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS) and electron backscattering diffractometer (EBSD). After grinding with fine emery paper and polishing with diamond powder, the EBSD samples were electrolytically polished for 10 s at 21 V using a solution of 10 vol% perchloric acid and 90 vol% ethanol. The HKL Channel 5 software was used to analyze EBSD results. The transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) observations were performed by an FEI Tecnai G2 F20 transmission electron microscopy operating at 200 kV. The TEM samples were prepared by standard mechanical grinding process to a thickness of around 80 μm and then punched into disks with a diameter of 3 mm. The twin-jet electro-polishing was employed to prepare the TEM samples using a solution of 30 vol% nitric acid and 70 vol% methanol at the temperature range of −25 to −40 °C. Condition: Peak-aged (AT-6); Tensile strength: 385 MPa; Elongation: 4.8%

Processing Text: High-entropy alloy ingot was prepared by vacuum arc-melting in an argon atmosphere with a nominal composition, Ni 2CoCrFeTi 0.24Al 0.2. The composition elements were supplied by Zhong Nuo Advanced Material (Beijing) Technology Co., Ltd with 99.95 wt.% purity. We remelted the ingot at least four times to promote the chemical homogeneity and dropped it into a water-cooled copper mold with a dimension of 50 × 10 × 5 mm 3. Alloys were next homogenized at 1200 °C for 2 h followed by cold rolling with a total thickness reduction of ∼70 %. According to our previous works, we selected 800 °C as the annealing temperature to obtain the concurrent recrystallization and precipitation microstructures. Meanwhile, 75 min, 90 min and 105 min were further chosen as the annealing time to obtain different recrystallization fractions. All annealing treatments were conducted in air followed by water quenching. Detailed thermal-mechanical processing routes are shown in Fig. S1. The dog-bone-shaped tensile samples were cut from the annealed sheet by electron discharge machine (EDM) with a gauge length of 12.5 mm and width of 3 mm. We ground the surface by 240#, 800#, 1500#, 2500# SiC papers and carried out the quasi-static tensile tests on the TSMT universal tensile machine (TSMT EM6. 504) with a strain rate of 10 −3s −1. Processing Text: The 316LSS samples were produced via SLM (DiMetal-100H) using gas-atomized powders with the powder size distribution of 15-53 μm. Tensile and cubic samples of 316LSS were printed two times under various laser powers (70 W, 140 W, 210 W, and 280 W) at fixed scanning speed (200 mm/s), layer thickness (0.03 mm) and hatch spacing (0.1 mm). A combined stripe and meander pattern within each layer, along with a 67° scan angle between adjacent layers, was employed to minimize the impact of printing strategies on anisotropy. The laser energy density E was determined as follows: E = P / (v * h * t) where P refers to the laser power, v is the scanning speed, and h and t are the hatch spacing and layer thickness, respectively. The laser energy density in this work fell in the range from 116.7 to 466.7 J/mm³. Once the laser power increased from 70 to 280 W, the relative density of SLM316LSS parts initially increased and then subsequently decreased. The peak value of relative density (nearly 99.0%) was attained at a laser power of 140 W. The porosity of the SLM316LSS parts gradually disappeared as the laser power increased, which was due to the powder fusion. However, once the laser power increased to 210 W, gas pores and crack defects began to form. Processing Text: Accordingly, we designed and prepared Mg-0.5Al-0.4Mn-0.2Ce and Mg-0.5Al-0.4Mn-0.2Ce-0.4Zn alloys by melting pure Mg (99.90 wt.%), pure Al (99.90 wt.%), pure Zn (99.90 wt.%), Mg-3.35Mn wt.%, and Mg-25Ce wt.% master alloys in a resistance furnace under the mixed protective atmosphere of CO 2and SF 6(the volume ratio of CO 2and SF 6was 99:1). After heating and melting at 993 K and holding for 20 min, the melts were poured into a mold preheated at 523 K to obtain the alloy ingots of 90 mm × 160 mm in diameter and height. The ingots were homogenized at 623 K/2 h + 693 K/10 h, followed by water cooling at room temperature. The homogenized ingots and the extrusion die were kept at 673 K for 30 min. Subsequently, hot extrusion was carried out to obtain sheets with a cross-sectional area of 40 mm × 5 mm via an extruding machine (630 tons) equipped with an extrusion cylinder of 95 mm in diameter. The extrusion ratio and extrusion temperature were ∼ 35:1 and 673 K respectively, and the extrusion die-exit speed reached ∼7.5 m/min. As-extruded sheets were then air-cooled to room temperature. Afterward, the extruded sheets were hot rolled from 5 mm to 1 mm in 4 passes with a reduction of roughly 20 %, 25 %, 33.3 %, and 50 %, respectively. The roll temperature was kept at 373 K. The inter-pass annealing was conducted at 573 K for 10 min during the whole rolling process. Finally, all rolled sheets were annealed at 623 K for 5 min. Condition: Annealed; Tensile direction: RD (Rolling Direction); Trace Zn addition enhancing GB cohesion

Processing Text: FeCoNiCrMnTix (x = 0, 2, 4, 6 wt%) HEAs were prepared using vacuum arc melting. The FeCoNiCrMnTix HEAs were melted using a ZHF30-3 vacuum arc furnace under high-purity argon protection and conditions with a vacuum degree of 3 × 10-3 Pa. The process was repeated three times to avoid the presence of any other impurity gases in the cavity. The initial arc current is restricted to a maximum of 500 A, and the arc is initiated within approximately 10 min. The alloy particles are melted into a liquid state within water-cooled copper molds before being cast into ingots with a button-like shape. Strictly following the operational procedures, the alloy ingot melts back five times, with every subsequent melting requiring the ingot to be turned over. This process ensures the alloy composition remains uniform, thus preventing the segregation phenomenon. Since the mass loss of the alloy ingot during melting is less than 0.5%, the alloy composition is assumed to be the nominal composition, and the size of the ingot is approximately 30 mm × 30 mm × 15 mm. Cubic specimens measuring 8 mm × 8 mm × 6 mm (OM/SEM/HV test), 6 mm × 6 mm × 1 mm (XRD), 10 mm × 5 mm × 1.5 mm (Tensile test), and 6 mm × 8 mm × 3 mm (Wear test) were sequentially cut using the DK7720 EDM CNC wire cutting machine and grinded using metallographic sandpaper ranging from 400 to 2000 grit. After polishing treatment with diamond abrasive paste on a polishing machine and cleaning with isopropyl alcohol, the specimens for OM/SEM/HV test were electrolytically corroded in a 10% oxalic acid solution. All observations and tests were conducted on the upper surface of the cut material. Alloy A1, single FCC phase
Processing Word: Alloy A1, single FCC phase

Processing Text: Commercial pure Al sheet AA1060 with a thickness of 15 mm was selected as the original material for this study. A CG Al sheet with completely recrystallized structure was obtained by homogenization at 773 K for 3 h, whose average grain size is 45 μm. Then the CG Al sheet was deformed to high strain of 2.7 by cold rolling (CR) with a 10% reduction per pass, and the final thickness after deformation is 1 mm. The severely rolled microstructure with a grain size of 0.8 μm and high dislocation density is shown in Fig. 1. Then the CR samples were annealed at different temperatures for 1 h to obtain samples with different grain sizes. The CR samples were annealed at different temperatures of 373 K, 473 K, 523 K, 573 K, 623 K and 673 K for 1 h to obtain samples with different grain sizes, as presented in Fig. 3. The average equivalent grain size of the annealed samples measured by electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) is 0.8 μm, 0.9 μm, 1.7 μm, 2.1 μm, 16.8 μm, and 22.4 μm, respectively. Based on the difference in grain size, these samples can be divided into three categories: UFG, fine grain (FG) and CG. Therefore, the annealed samples are defined as UFG-0.8, UFG-0.9, FG-1.7, FG-2.1, CG-16.8, and CG-22.4 samples, respectively. Grain size: UFG-0.9; Temperature decrease from 298 K to 77 K

Processing Text: The multidirectional forging (MDF) experiments of Mg-Gd-Y-Zn-Zr alloy were performed. The MDF process step is shown in Fig. 1. Surface A of sample was first forged and then turned over 90° to forge the surface B of sample. Finally, the surface was again turned over 90° to forge surface C. Each press underwent one pass at initial forging temperatures of 400 °C, 450 °C, and 500 °C, respectively. In addition, a no-load pressing rate of 10 mm/s was set, such that the temperature of the sample gradually reduced from contact with air during forging. The heating temperature of the upper and lower chopping boards was measured to be 450 °C. The chopping boards were continuously heated during deformation, and the sample was air-cooled after deformation. The effects of temperature and cumulative strain on microstructure and mechanical properties of multi-directional forged Mg-Gd-Y-Zn-Zr alloy were studied. The results showed that the recrystallization ratio of the alloy gradually increased with the initial forging temperature after 3 passes of MDF. Under the condition of the initial forging temperature of 500 °C, the grain size was gradually refined with increasing MDF passes, and the average grain size was refined to 1.49 μm after 12 MDF passes. With the increase in MDF passes, the maximum texture density of the alloy gradually decreased. The mechanical properties gradually increased with the MDF passes. In the first 6 MDF passes, the mechanical properties greatly increased, but after that, the increase gradually slowed down with additional MDF passes. The optimal mechanical properties were obtained after 12 MDF passes, and the tensile strength, yield strength, and elongation after fracture were 362 MPa, 294 MPa, and 14.5%, respectively. Optimal mechanical properties after 12 MDF passes; Tensile strength: 362 MPa; Elongation after fracture: 14.5%

The Zn-Cu-Ti alloy rod was first cut lengthwise to expose its internal structure for analysis. The test surfaces of these sections were then prepared through a two-step process: grinding and polishing. The grinding was performed sequentially starting with a coarser 240# sandpaper and progressing to a much finer 3000# sandpaper. Following the grinding, the test surfaces were polished using diamond sprays, first with a 3 μm spray and then with a finer 0.5 μm spray. Hot-rolled samples were sourced from six regions of the Zn-Cu-Ti alloy rod and then homogenized at 370 °C for 2 h. The EBSD samples were similarly prepared but underwent ion polishing. Processing state: as-cast

Processing Text: Powder bed fusion (PBF), along with subsequent heat treatment, plays a crucial role in enhancing the impact toughness of FeCoNiCrMo0.2 high-entropy alloys (HEAs). In this study, the dynamic-mechanical properties and microstructure of the as-built PBF-FeCoNiCrMo0.2 HEAs and quenched PBF-FeCoNiCrMo0.2 HEAs heated at 600-750 °C for 8 h were investigated. As the heating temperature increases, the columnar grains and cellular structures undergo coarsening and the dislocation density gradually decreases. Moreover, higher heating temperatures facilitate the precipitation of Mo-rich second phases. The μ phases are predominantly distributed along the boundaries of the cellular structures. In the quenched Q700 specimen (heated at 700 °C for 8h), the size and volume fraction of the μ phases are measured to be 63.4 nm and 3.59%, respectively. Additionally, under the same condition, the Q700 specimens also exhibited a relatively slight increase in the size of the cellular structures. The preparation method for the pre-alloyed powder involved initially melting pure metal powders in a vacuum induction furnace to form pre-alloyed ingots. Subsequently, the pre-alloyed ingots were subjected to high-speed airstream in an atomization chamber, resulting in their fragmentation into small droplets that solidified to form fine powder. The cylindrical specimens were placed inside a vacuum glass tube. Then, the vacuum tube was purged with argon gas for a minimum of three cycles to remove any residual air inside the glass tube. Later, the glass tubes containing the specimens underwent a high-temperature sintering process for 10 min to ensure an airtight seal, thus providing an inert gas protective environment during the heating process. The treatment was carried out at temperatures of 600, 650, 700, and 750 °C with specimens labeled as Q600, Q650, Q700, and Q750, respectively, using the DZSX2-10-12NP (Yun Yue, P.). These specimens were heated for 8 h, then quenched with industrial oil to prevent the growth of grains and second phases. Processing Text: Hot-rolled STSs 308 L plates with thicknesses of 20 mm were used. A V-shaped groove was cut from the base metal along a 45° diagonal with a root gap of 10 mm. The all-weld metals were prepared using 12 flux-cored arc weld passes. The welding process involved a welding current of 240 A and arc voltage of 32 V. The specimens for the FE-SEM and EBSD observations were prepared through mechanical polishing using colloidal silica. The polished specimens were etched using a solution with 40 ml of HCl, 50 ml of nitric acid, and 100 ml of ethyl alcohol. All specimens were mechanically ground using #2000 grit SiC sandpaper, followed by electropolishing in an etchant solution (10% HCLO 4+ 90% CH 3OH) at 9 V for 100 s at −30 °C. Hydrogen was electrolytically charged for 48 h in a 3% NaCl + 0.3% NH 4SCN solution. A direct-current power supply was connected to the specimen as the cathode, and a Pt sheet was used as the anode. For the H-charging process, the current density and temperature were 100 A/m 2and 90 °C, respectively, to promote hydrogen diffusion into the specimen. After H-charging, the specimens were promptly immersed in liquid nitrogen to ensure hydrogen retention prior to subsequent analysis. Condition: Air; Temperature: 25 °C
Processing Word: Condition: Air; Temperature: 25 °C

Processing Text: The materials used in this study were from the same batch, and their chemical composition is provided in Table 1. The materials were prepared in a vacuum induction melting furnace, and heat isostatic pressing (HIP) was employed during the preparation process to reduce casting porosity that may affect tensile properties. Subsequently, a two-stage heat treatment, including solution treatment and aging treatment (1185 °C/2h/argon cooling and 871 °C/20 h/air cooling), was conducted to refine the γ-γ' eutectic structure at grain boundaries and increase the proportion of γ' for further enhancing the material strength. To accurately investigate the effect of SP on the microstructural evolution of the blade surface layer and the tensile fatigue properties, samples were taken from the BM along the blade direction in this study. In this study, the SP treatment was performed using S230 cast steel shots with a diameter of approximately 0.58 mm. The air pressure employed during the treatment was approximately 0.35 MPa, and the mass flow rate of the shot was around 12 kg/min. The coverage rate achieved was 150 %. Type A Almen specimens were used to assess the strength, and the average value of the three arc heights tested was found to be 0.32. SP was independently conducted on the sample plate, the high cycle fatigue specimen, and the tensile specimen. The specific areas subjected to SP treatment on different specimens are depicted in Fig. 1(c). The cutting method used in this study was Electrical Discharge Machining (EDM) wire cutting. For obtaining the micromorphology of the surface layer, the square specimens shown in Fig. 1(c) were mechanically polished using silicon carbide sandpapers with different grit sizes, namely 400 mesh, 1000 mesh, 2000 mesh, and 3000 mesh. After polishing, the specimens were corroded with a mixture of 10 ml HCl,10 ml HNO 3, 0.3 g H2MoO 4, and 15 ml H 2O. Finally, the micro-morphology of the surface deformation layer was observed by SEM (JEOL JSM-6510LV, Japan). For the EBSD analysis, the sample underwent the same milling process as described above. Electrolytic polishing was then performed to remove the residual stress layer generated during the grinding process. The polishing solution comprised 7 % perchloric acid and 93 % ethanol, and the current density was set at 450 mA/cm2 for approximately 1 min. To measure the microhardness on the surface layer of both the BM and the SP, a Vickers microhardness tester (SHIMADZU HMV-G31DT, Japan) was utilized. Prior to testing, the cutting surfaces were ground and polished to eliminate the effects of cutting on hardness measurements. A test load of 0.98 N, a dwell time of 15 s, and a test depth gradient of 50 μm were used. To ensure the accuracy of the test results, each depth was tested three times, and the average value was taken. In order to measure the residual stress after SP treatment, the Hole-drilling method was used, and the measurement standard was ASTM-E837-13A [38]. The SINT MTS3000 Hole-drilling strain gauge was employed to measure the shot peened samples. The distance between each test point was approximately 10 mm to avoid mutual influence between the test points. The BM and SP specimens were subjected to uniaxial tensile tests using a universal testing machine (AG-100KNXPSTDW/0, Japan) at RT besed on the standard of ASTM E8M [39], and the strain rate of both specimens was 2.5 × 10 −4s −1. In addition, high cycle fatigue tests were also carried out using a high-frequency fatigue testing machine (QBG-100, China) for BM and SP at RT (R = −1). SP was independently conducted on the sample plate, the high cycle fatigue specimen, and the tensile specimen. The SINT MTS3000 Hole-drilling strain gauge was employed to measure the shot peened samples. The distance between each test point was approximately 10 mm to avoid mutual influence between the test points. The BM and SP specimens were subjected to uniaxial tensile tests using a universal testing machine (AG-100KNXPSTDW/0, Japan) at RT besed on the standard of ASTM E8M [39], and the strain rate of both specimens was 2.5 × 10 −4s −1. In addition, high cycle fatigue tests were also carried out using a high-frequency fatigue testing machine (QBG-100, China) for BM and SP at RT (R = −1). Processing Text: Samples were manufactured using EOS Ti-6Al-4V grade 23 powder on an EOS M290 (EOS GmbH, Germany) LPBF machine housed at the ISO 13485 certified Centre for Rapid Prototyping and Manufacturing (CRPM) of the Central University of Technology in South Africa. Specimens were produced in three batches, and a representative portion of each batch and specimen type was selected to measure the oxygen content to ensure this was kept below 0.013 wt%. The base plate was preheated to 80 °C, and a high-speed steel blade was used as a scraper. The process parameters consisted of a 40 μm layer thickness, 280 W laser power, 1300 mm/s scan speed, 100 μm spot size and a hatch distance of 120 μm. Bidirectional scanning was used, and the scan direction was rotated by 67° between layers. This set of process parameters results in a material with less than 0.01 % porosity [ 23 ]. For tensile specimens, cylinders with a diameter of D = 10 mm and a length of L = 100 mm were produced in the vertical (Z) and horizontal (X) directions relative to the axis of the LPBF machine (and according to ASTM 59200) that is aligned with the direction in which the load is applied. For fracture toughness specimens, Compact Tension (C(T)) specimens were produced as rectangular blocks to allow for the final dimensions of a width of W = 25 mm. C(T) specimens were produced in three orientations, with the first letter indicating the direction in which the load is applied and the second letter indicating the direction in which the crack propagates, that is, ZX, XZ and XY [ 6 ], as shown in Fig. 1 . After printing, the specimens were stress-relieved (SR) at 650 °C for 3 h in a TSH 15/50/180 vacuum furnace (Elite Thermal Systems, England) and then wire-cut from the build plate. The SR treatment was chosen to allow comparison with the literature [ 15 ]. Subsequent heat treatments were conducted at the Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) in atmospheric air using a box furnace (Ultrafurn, South Africa). Therefore, at least 1 mm was removed by wire cutting or machining from all the heat-treated specimen surfaces to remove any α-case and oxide scale that may have formed. The heat treatment schedules, detailed in Table 1 , included the SR, an anneal (AN) heat treatment, chosen due to its simplicity combined with good tensile properties, and a duplex anneal (DA) heat treatment, chosen based on optimal tensile properties reported in the literature [ 6 , 25 ]. Furthermore, the heat treatments above T β (selected based on values available in the literature [ 9 , 15 ]) were combined with the stress relief (BtSR) and anneal (BtAN) heat treatments to mimic how SR or AN specimens would perform if the PBGs were equiaxed c . c It is acknowledged the above T β heat treatment is at the cost of PBG growth. Comparison to specimens with elongated PBGs is only based on orientation effects. After heat treatment, the specimens were machined and wire-cut to their final dimensions. Condition: as-received

Processing Text: The material used in this work is cold-rolled 316L austenitic SS seamless tubes with an outside diameter of 12 mm and a thickness of 2 mm. The 316L SS tubes were bright annealed at 1080 °C followed by rapid water quench and subsequently machined into specimens. The surface of the specimens was mechanically ground and polished to obtain a smooth surface by uniformly distributing the machining marks in the longitudinal direction, thus reducing the effect of surface quality. Multiaxial non-proportional cyclic pre-hardening (CPH) treatment was performed in a circular path, with a 90° phase shift between the axial and torsion loads, over 10 cycles at the strain amplitude of 0.4 %. At the end of the CPH process, the axial strain is at its peak value (0.4 %) and the equivalent shear strain is controlled to 0. Subsequently, the axial strain reaches the minimum value of the corresponding uniaxial fatigue tests to start the uniaxial stage while the equivalent shear strain is controlled at 0 throughout the whole uniaxial stage. Monotonic tensile tests were carried out under displacement control mode at a displacement rate of 0.06 mm/s. Strain-controlled uniaxial fatigue tests at the strain amplitudes of 0.2 % and 0.4 % were performed on AR and CPH materials in a fully-reversed triangular waveform (R = -1) with a fixed strain rate of 5 × 10 -3s −1. Microstructure observations were made using electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, Edax) equipped on a scanning electron microscope (SEM, Apreo S LoVac). The samples for EBSD observations were obtained along the axial direction of the specimen and at a distance of 5 mm away from the fracture surface. Mechanical ground and polished processes were carried out using 180, 400, 1000 and 2000 grit SiC sandpapers, followed by electrochemical polishing using a 10 % perchloric acid ethanol solution at a voltage of 20 V and a current of 5 A. The EBSD characterization were performed at a voltage of 20 kV, a working distance of 17.4 mm and a scan area of 400 μm × 300 μm with a step size of 0.8 μm. Due to the small scan area, two to four areas were scanned for each condition of the sample. The thin slices for TEM observation were also taken along the specimen axial direction at a distance of 5 mm away from the fracture surface. The sample preparation process consisted of mechanical grinding on both sides with SiC sandpaper grits of 400, 800, 1000, and 2000 under maintained horizontal conditions. Samples were thinned to ∼ 60 μm with 2000 grit, followed by twin-jet electro-polishing with a 10 % perchloric acid ethanol solution. Condition: As-received (AR)
Processing Word: Condition: As-received (AR)

Processing Text: Herein, we designed and fabricated a multiphase Ti-Mo-Ag composite (TMA) with heterogeneous triple-phase precipitation (TPP) structure by spark plasma sintering. The mixed powders were ball milled at 300 r/min for 12 h, which were then sintered by a spark plasma sintering furnace (HPD 250, FCT Group, Germany) following parameters of vacuum 0.1 Pa, pressure 40 MPa, heating rate 50 °C/min, final sintering temperature 1000 °C and a holding time 15 min. After sintering, a ‘triple-phase precipitation (TPP)’ structure was built up without any complicated heat treatment, and mechanical strength was notably enhanced. Processing Text: During the powders mixing process, FeCoCrNiMn powder was blended with 2.5 wt%, 5 wt%, and 7.5 wt% of TiC particles in a planetary ball mill. The milling operation was conducted at a speed of 400 rpm for 4 h, with a ball-to-powder weight ratio of 1:1. To avoid container overheating, the ball mill operation was paused for 10 min after every 20 min milling, and the rotation direction was then altered. For the 3D printing process, 25 cubic samples with dimensions of 5 mm × 5 mm × 5 mm were printed using an SLM machine (FORWEDO LM-120, Forwedo). The SLM machine was equipped with a fiber laser device, featuring a maximum output power of 500 W, a wavelength of 1.06 µm, and a spot diameter of 80 µm. The laser power (P) ranged from 240–320 W, while the scanning speed (v) varied from 200–1000 mm/s. The layer thickness (t) was fixed at 50 µm, the laser beam diameter was 80 µm, and the hatching space (h) was 100 µm. To minimize the thermal stress of the printed sample on the building plane (X and Y directions), we employed a scanning strategy where the laser scanning was rotated 90° between adjacent layers. Condition: after addition of TiC; Effect: slight decrease in plasticity

Processing Text: A polycrystalline ingot of MnCu2Al was prepared using a combination of arc melting and furnace annealing according to previous investigations. Elemental Mn (Sigma Aldrich, chips, 99%) was cleaned of its native oxides by annealing in an evacuated silica ampule for 8 h at 1000 °C. Starting materials of cleaned Mn, Cu (Alfa Aesar, wire, 99.99%), and Al (Alfa Aesar, wire, 99.9995%) were weighed with a 1:2:1 stoichiometry, totaling a mass of 3.0 g. An additional excess of Mn (10 mg) was added to compensate for volatilization during melting. The materials were arc melted four times in an Ar atmosphere, flipping the ingot between melts for homogeneity, with a total mass loss of 1.3%. The resulting ingot was wrapped in Ta foil, sealed in an evacuated silica ampule, and homogenized at 850 °C for 7 days to create a large-grained microstructure, then quenched into water. To ensure structural homogeneity, the ingot was divided and pieces were sampled from opposing faces of the ingot, ground into a fine powder, and sieved through a 140 mesh (106 μm particle size) for a synchrotron powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) sample. The powder sample was again sealed within an evacuated fused silica ampule and tempered at 320 °C for 1 h to resolve any pre-existing crystallographic defects. Microscopy and mechanical testing were performed on pieces of the ingot that were tempered under the same conditions. Specifically, the nanoindentation test specimen was created from a tempered piece of the arc melted ingot that was mounted to an aluminum puck using crystal bond, ground using SiC paper, polished using diamond suspensions down to 1 μm, and vibratory polished using colloidal silica to a mirror finish. While mounted to the aluminum puck, the polished surface was imaged using SEM and mapped using EBSD, to characterize the crystallographic orientation of visible grains. Nanoindentation experiments were performed to test the mechanical properties of each grain orientation using a Nanomechanics iMicro Nanoindenter equipped with a 1000 mN load cell and Berkovich tip diamond indenter. All nanoindentation data were collected using a continuous stiffness method operating at a frequency of 100 Hz, to a total depth of 1000 nm, and each data point reported in this investigation is representative of at least 10-20 indents per crystallographic orientation, collected between depths of 400 nm-1000 nm. Data recorded during the initial 400 nm of each indentation were excluded to account for surface roughness and possible surface artifacts introduced by polishing. To create an accessible base for micro-pillar experiments, the polished specimen was remounted to an angled polishing puck and polished into a wedge-shaped geometry. Using EBSD mapping near the edge of the wedge-shaped specimen, several grains of interest were identified, and were femtosecond laser machined in situ into single-crystalline pedestals using the TriBeam microscope, a laser-equipped TFS Versa 3D FIB-SEM. Micro-compression pillars were produced directly from the single-crystalline pedestals using the FIB to mill the pillar tops and sides perpendicular to the wedge surface with a slight taper, before removing all material from the faces to create pillars with a 1:1:2 aspect ratio to mitigate the potential impact of buckling. A square pillar cross-section was employed to aid in the identification of active slip systems. Micro-compression experiments were performed in situ in an TFS Apreo S SEM equipped with a Femto-tools FT-NMT04 Nanomechanical Testing System designed to optimize alignment during small-scale mechanical testing. Each pillar was loaded in a series of load vs. displacement tests until the point of yield using a displacement-controlled method. Following SEM imaging, a detailed microstructural investigation was performed on an electron-transparent lamella micro-machined from the [11 8 2]-oriented pillar, using STEM imaging and a g⋅b analysis in the TEM. As the deformed material had high internal strains, the foil was prepared with three electron-transparent windows, framed by thicker regions for stabilization. Processing Text: The ingots were prepared via vacuum induction melting furnace under 10 −3Pa. The purity of the raw materials is 99.9%. The quality of the ingot obtained by smelting is between 20 and 25 kg. After annealing at 1473 K for 1 h, the ingots were forged into a 6 mm thick plate at 1373 K, and then hot rolled to plates with a thickness of 3 mm at 1373 K, and quenched in an ice brine solution. The plates were then cold-rolled to 0.35 mm thick strip with a reduction of 90%. The samples were electric-discharge machined from the rolled strip. Following this, the cold-rolled samples were annealed in a dry 5% hydrogen/95% argon mixed atmosphere at 1123 K for different durations ranging from 0.5 h to 3 h. After annealing, specimens were water quenched. Tensile tests were conducted at a speed of 0.0017/s on the AG-X plus instrument. The axial directions of all the tensile specimens are perpendicular to the rolling direction (RD) of the cold-rolled strip. Soft magnetic properties for the as-rolled and annealed samples were measured using MATS-2010SD loop tracer. Microstructure characterization was performed by Zeiss SUPRA55 scanning electron microscope (SEM) and FEI Tecnai G 2F30 transmission electron microscope (TEM) equipped with energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS). SEM specimen was etched by a mixture solution of 4 vol.% nitric acid and 96 vol.% alcohol. TEM samples were thinned by twin-jet electropolishing using an electrolyte of 10 vol.% perchloric acid and 90 vol.% alcohol around −20 °C. Electrolytic extraction technique was employed to dissolve the matrix, 50% nitric acid solution was used for the electrolyte and after vacuum filtration the content of element remaining in the matrix was tested using ICP-AES. XRD fine-scan measurements were carried out on the finely polished samples to measure the dislocation density using a Cu-Kα radiation source. Processing Text: The non-equiatomic Ni46.3Fe21Cr18.5Al10V4.2 (at%) [referred to here as: (NiFeCrAlV)] CCA ingot was prepared through arc melting under an argon atmosphere with 99.9% purity constituent elements. The as-cast ingot was homogenized at 1200 ℃ for 8 h with water-cooling (WC). Subsequently, it was subjected to severe plastic deformation through cold rolling (CR), reducing its thickness from 10 mm to 1 mm. The CR specimens were annealed at 700 ℃, 800 ℃, 900 ℃, and 1000 ℃ for 1 h with a WC, which were marked as CR700, CR800, CR900, and CR1000, respectively. Processing Text: In this work, selective laser melting (SLM) process is used to prepare the AlNi6TiZr alloy. By analyzing the printing quality and mechanical properties of the printed specimens with different process parameters, the SLM forming window of AlNi6TiZr is obtained. The relative density of the sample printed with 270 W-1100 mm/s (laser energy density: 82 J/mm3) reaches 99.7%, exhibiting excellent mechanical properties (yield strength (YS): 421.7 MPa; ultimate tensile strength (UTS): 480.4 MPa). After an aging treatment of 325 °C-12 h, the YS and UTS of the sample increased to 494 MPa and 550.7 MPa, respectively. The hard-shell structure (HSS) formed by the Al3Ni phase at the grain boundary significantly strengthened the grain boundary strength. The precipitated Al3(Ti, Zr) phases at the grain boundaries prevent grain growth and dislocation movement. The Al3Ni and Al3(Ti, Zr) phases have good thermal stability that can still maintain excellent enhancement effects at high temperature. The raw material was a gas-atomized 6060 aluminum alloy powder (2.5-50 μm) produced by Jiangxi Baohang Advanced Materials Co., Ltd. Some microalloying powders including Ni powder (0.5-2 μm), Ti powder (70-90 nm), and high-purity Zr powder (3-7 μm) were mixed with the raw material by ball milling method, and the optimized parameters (ball powder ratio (wt%): 5:1, milling speed: 280 rpm, milling time: 10 h, protection gas: argon (> 99.99%)) of powder mixing process was according to Refs. [ 32, 44]. The mixed alloy powder was dried at 10 Pa and 120 °C for 8 h in a DZ-201 vacuum drying oven (Changsha Mitr Instrument Equipment Co., Ltd., China), and then cooled in the equipment to room temperature. The bulk and tensile specimens were printed using a LiM-X150A SLM device (Tianjin LiM Laser Technology Co., Ltd., China), which is equipped with an IPG 500 W fiber laser (wavelength: 1064 nm, spot diameter: 40-60 μm). First, the substrate ( Table 2) was fixed on the printing platform and preheated to 35 °C. Then, the printing process started under argon protection, in which the oxygen content was below 100 ppm. To optimize the printing parameters of AlNi6TiZr alloy, several sets of laser power and scanning speed were selected. The aging treatment (AT) process was conducted in an SX-B07123 electric box furnace (Tianjin Zhonghuan Electric Furnace Co., LTD, China), and the AT parameters were 325 °C for 6, 12, and 24 h, respectively. After aging treatment, the AT-ed specimens were air-cooled. The bulk specimens with a size of 10 mm × 10 mm × 10 mm were mechanically polished using a 2.5 μm diamond grinding paste on a polishing machine to obtain a mirror surface. Then, it was chemically etched with the Kellar reagent (HF:HCl:HNO 3:H 2O = 2:3:5:195) for 20 s. Condition: as-printed (AB); Relative density: 99.7%; Laser energy density: 82 J/mm³
Processing Word: Condition: as-printed (AB); Relative density: 99.7%; Laser energy density: 82 J/mm³

Processing Text: In this work, a full composition with different mixing proportions (100 % Cu to 100 % Ni) was fabricated in a single printing process through in-situ alloying based on our process of micro laser powder bed fusion. The powder feeding system was designed to facilitate the smooth transfer of powder materials from 100 % Cu to 100 % Ni. In our system, we place a flat partition along the longer diagonal of the powder hopper, creating separate spaces for filling powders, Cu and Ni, according to their respective allocation areas. Below this hopper is a cylindrical powder mixer, with the axis of the cylinder aligned in the X direction. The mixer mixes the powders along the width of the hopper (Y direction) and maintains the desired gradient of the composition along the X direction. The gradient powders then fall into the powder recoater and are spread onto the substrate. This method enabled the fabrication of functionally gradient materials comprising Cu-Ni alloy with continuous composition variation in the X direction perpendicular to the spreading direction. Dog-bone-shaped samples with gauge dimensions of 15 mm ( L) × 4 mm ( W) × 1.5 mm ( H) were used for tensile tests. Rectangular bars measuring 30 mm ( L) × 2 mm ( W) × 2 mm ( H) were used for electrical conductivity testing. Cubes with a side length of 5 mm were prepared for microstructure inspection. For metallographic observations, 10 equally spaced specimens were cut from the fabricated Cu-Ni alloy parts along the direction of the composition gradient variation and prepared in accordance with ASTM E3-11 standards. The morphology and compositions of the received powders and chemical compositions of the as-printed samples were measured and analysed via scanning electron microscopy (JCM-6000PLUS) using energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) and X-ray fluorescence spectrometry (XRF, Bruker M4 Tornado). The particle size distributions of the as-received powders were measured using a laser particle size analyser (Bettersize3000). The apparent densities of the powders were measured by a loose densitometer (HR-S3 Scott volumeter). The powders of Cu and Ni had similar material densities, while the mixed powders had an acceptable apparent density that was not notably affected by the similar particle size distributions of pure Cu and Ni powders. The compositions of GA were characterised via EDS. Measurements were made at positions with element ratios (Cu/Ni) designed at 0 %, 5 %, 15 %, 25 %, …, and 100 % to validate the accuracy of gradient element distribution along the GD. An X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis of components was conducted using a high-resolution Rigaku SmartLab X-ray diffractometer. The 2θ scan angle ranged from 20° to 90° and the scanning speed was 5°/min. The microstructure and grain texture studies were conducted using an electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) system (EDAX Velocity Plus) with a step size of 0.5 μm and a scan area of 200 μm × 200 μm. The EBSD data were analysed using an open-source Matlab toolbox (MTEX 5.7.0). The corresponding misorientation angles were measured to calculate the grain boundaries (GBs). Misorientation angles in the range of 2°-15° were defined as low-angle GBs (LAGBs) whereas misorientation angles exceeding 15° were defined as high-angle GBs (HAGBs). The grain size was calculated according to the HAGBs, and the Williamson-Hall method was adopted to determine the dislocation density. The electrical resistance ( ρ) was evaluated using a micro-ohmmeter (YP2511) and calculated according to the equation ρ= RA/ L, where R is the measurement made by the micro-ohmmeter, A is the cross-sectional area of the bar, and L is the measurement length. Before the cross-sectional area was measured, the bars were polished with SiC sandpaper (1200 and 2500 grit) to ensure measurement accuracy. Five lengths (15, 18, 21, 24, and 27 mm) were measured to calculate the final mean values. The coefficient of linear thermal expansion (CTE) was measured using a thermal mechanical analyser (TMA 7, Perkin Elmer) following ASTM E831-19. Microhardness was measured with a hardness tester (Decca HV-1000) adopting a load force of 200 g and a hold time of 10 s. Measurements were made at 10 points, and the average values were recorded as the final microhardness. Tensile properties were evaluated by conducting uniaxial tensile tests at a constant speed of 0.96 mm/min on a tensile machine (Tinius Olsen H5KS). Three tensile bars were tested for each sample to minimise measurement errors. Cu content: 100 % (Cu 1Ni 0)

In our system, we place a flat partition along the longer diagonal of the powder hopper, creating separate spaces for filling powders, Cu and Ni, according to their respective allocation areas. Below this hopper is a cylindrical powder mixer, with the axis of the cylinder aligned in the X direction. The mixer mixes the powders along the width of the hopper (Y direction) and maintains the desired gradient of the composition along the X direction. The gradient powders then fall into the powder recoater and are spread onto the substrate. This method enabled the fabrication of functionally gradient materials comprising Cu-Ni alloy with continuous composition variation in the X direction perpendicular to the spreading direction. Dog-bone-shaped samples with gauge dimensions of 15 mm ( L) × 4 mm ( W) × 1.5 mm ( H) were used for tensile tests. Rectangular bars measuring 30 mm ( L) × 2 mm ( W) × 2 mm ( H) were used for electrical conductivity testing. Cubes with a side length of 5 mm were prepared for microstructure inspection. For metallographic observations, 10 equally spaced specimens were cut from the fabricated Cu-Ni alloy parts along the direction of the composition gradient variation and prepared in accordance with ASTM E3-11 standards. The morphology and compositions of the received powders and chemical compositions of the as-printed samples were measured and analysed via scanning electron microscopy (JCM-6000PLUS) using energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) and X-ray fluorescence spectrometry (XRF, Bruker M4 Tornado). The particle size distributions of the as-received powders were measured using a laser particle size analyser (Bettersize3000). The apparent densities of the powders were measured by a loose densitometer (HR-S3 Scott volumeter). The powders of Cu and Ni had similar material densities, while the mixed powders had an acceptable apparent density that was not notably affected by the similar particle size distributions of pure Cu and Ni powders. The compositions of GA were characterised via EDS. Measurements were made at positions with element ratios (Cu/Ni) designed at 0 %, 5 %, 15 %, 25 %, …, and 100 % to validate the accuracy of gradient element distribution along the GD. An X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis of components was conducted using a high-resolution Rigaku SmartLab X-ray diffractometer. The 2θ scan angle ranged from 20° to 90° and the scanning speed was 5°/min. The microstructure and grain texture studies were conducted using an electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) system (EDAX Velocity Plus) with a step size of 0.5 μm and a scan area of 200 μm × 200 μm. The EBSD data were analysed using an open-source Matlab toolbox (MTEX 5.7.0). The corresponding misorientation angles were measured to calculate the grain boundaries (GBs). Misorientation angles in the range of 2°-15° were defined as low-angle GBs (LAGBs) whereas misorientation angles exceeding 15° were defined as high-angle GBs (HAGBs). The grain size was calculated according to the HAGBs, and the Williamson-Hall method was adopted to determine the dislocation density. The electrical resistance ( ρ) was evaluated using a micro-ohmmeter (YP2511) and calculated according to the equation ρ= RA/ L, where R is the measurement made by the micro-ohmmeter, A is the cross-sectional area of the bar, and L is the measurement length. Before the cross-sectional area was measured, the bars were polished with SiC sandpaper (1200 and 2500 grit) to ensure measurement accuracy. Five lengths (15, 18, 21, 24, and 27 mm) were measured to calculate the final mean values. The coefficient of linear thermal expansion (CTE) was measured using a thermal mechanical analyser (TMA 7, Perkin Elmer) following ASTM E831-19. Microhardness was measured with a hardness tester (Decca HV-1000) adopting a load force of 200 g and a hold time of 10 s. Measurements were made at 10 points, and the average values were recorded as the final microhardness. Tensile properties were evaluated by conducting uniaxial tensile tests at a constant speed of 0.96 mm/min on a tensile machine (Tinius Olsen H5KS). Three tensile bars were tested for each sample to minimise measurement errors. Cu content: 0 % (Cu 0Ni 1)

Processing Text: Pre-alloyed AlCo0.4CrFeNi2.7 (atomic percent %) hypoeutectic HEA powders produced via argon-gas atomization were used as raw materials for the L-PBF processes. The particle sizes were measured using a laser particle-size analyzer distributed in the range of 15-53 μm. The BLT-A300 apparatus (Xian, China) equipped with a maximum 500 W fiber laser operating in a continuous wave mode was employed for the L-PBF processes. A Gaussian energy intensity distribution and a focus beam-spot size of 76 μm were used during L-PBF. To reduce thermal stress, the substrate material of 304 stainless steel was preheated to 200 °C before printing. In addition, a 67° interlayer rotational angle was adopted during L-PBF. Based on our previous work [4], the following optimal scanning parameters were used during the L-PBF processes: laser power of 250 W, scanning speed of 800 mm/s, hatch spacing of 80 µm, and layer thickness of 40 µm. A block sample with the dimensions of 60 mm × 50 mm × 5 mm (length × width × height) was fabricated. Subsequently, to further improve the mechanical properties of the alloy, the as-printed sample was annealed at different temperatures (600 ℃, 700 ℃, 750 ℃, 800 ℃, and 1000 ℃) for 1 h in a tube furnace at a heating rate of 10 °C min−1 under an argon protective atmosphere, followed by water quenching. These samples were marked as HT600, HT700, HT750, HT800, and HT1000, respectively. The phase constitutions of the alloy were characterized using X-ray diffraction (XRD, BRUKERD8 Discover) with a Cu Kα radiation. The 2θ scanning was analyzed in the range of 20-100° with a scanning speed of 4°/min. The morphologies and phase constitutions of the alloy were investigated through a Zeiss Supra55 field emission scanning electron microscopy (SEM) equipped with an electron back-scattering diffraction (EBSD) spectrometer. The samples for SEM characterization were prepared using mechanically polished with oxide polishing suspension. The EBSD specimens were prepared by mechanically grinding them using 5000-grit SiC papers and then electrochemically polishing them in a mixture of 90 vol% (volume percent) ethanol and 10 vol% perchloric acid. A direct voltage of 22 V and a current of 1.5 A were used during the electrochemical polishing at room temperature. The scanning step of EBSD was 0.15 μm. The more detailed microstructures were characterized utilizing a transmission electron microscope (TEM, Tecnai F30). Disc-shaped TEM samples with a diameter of 3 mm were mechanically ground to a thickness of 40 μm and then thinned to be electron-transparent using double-jet electron polishing in a solution of 90 vol% ethanol and 10 vol% perchloric acid at a temperature of −25 ℃. The volume fraction and size of precipitates were measured from STEM images using Image J software. The tensile tests were carried out using a CMT4105 universal electronic tensile testing machine with an initial strain rate of 1.0 × 10−3 s−1 at room temperature. Dog-bone-shaped tensile samples were cut by electrical discharge machining and then were mechanically ground to 2000 grit size with lengths of 50 mm and cross sections of 5 mm × 1.5 mm. For each state of the alloy, at least three samples were tested. Before testing, the samples were fixed on a jig, and the strains were examined using an extensometer during tensile tests, with a gauge length of 15 mm. Processing state: as-printed; Microstructure: dual-phase nanolamellae (FCC + BCC)

Processing Text: To obtain a high-entropy alloy characterized by high strength and plasticity, (NiCoV)100-xGax (x = 0, 5, 7) was successfully prepared, cold-rolled, and heat-treated. The (NiCoV) 100-XGa x(x = 0, 5, 7) series alloys (purity >99.9 %) were prepared by arc melting furnace. Each sample was melted four times and turned over before the next melting process to ensure chemical homogeneity. The resulting samples were cold rolled to approximately 20 % of the original size and then cut with a wire cutter to obtain flat dog bone-style samples (length: 35 mm; width: 3 mm). Small squares of dimensions 10 mm × 10 mm were formed. The resulting drawn samples and squares were annealed at 900 °C, 950 °C, and 1000 °C for 1 h. The surface of the small square was polished with sandpaper from low to high grinding to 2500 grain. The surface was etched with aqua regia solution, the surface was rinsed with water immediately after etching for 10 s, and then the surface was cleaned with alcohol. Finally, the sample microstructure was observed with XP-550 polarizing microscope made by MikeVision. Annealing temperature: 900 °C

Processing Text: The alloy ingots with nominal compositions of Ni30Co30Cr20Fe20-xRex (x=0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 9 at.%, denoted as Rex), and Ni30Co30Cr20Fe20-yMoy (y=2, 4, 6, 8, 10 at.%, denoted as Moy) were prepared by arc-melting method in Ti-gettered high-purity argon atmosphere. The purity of each metal is at least 99%. Co-Re and Mo-Fe intermediate alloys were first re-melted four times, then flipped and smelted at least five times with other raw materials to ensure compositional homogeneity. These ingots were drop-cast into a water-cooled copper mold with dimensions of 8 mm × 8 mm × 40 mm. The as-cast bars were homogenized at 1473 K for 12 h. To ensure a single-phase FCC structure, the homogenization temperature of Mo8 and Mo10 HEAs are selected as 1573 K for 12 h. Then all the bars were cold-rolled to a reduction 60% in thickness and annealed at 1473 K for 1 h. All the thermo-mechanical procedures were performed in vacuum and finally quenched with water. Phases identification and lattice parameters for these HEAs were conducted by X-ray diffraction (XRD) with Cu Kα radiation (Smart Lab 9 kV). The shear modulus and Poisson's ratio of the alloy were measured by UMS-100 ultrasonic echo analysis technique. The microstructures of the HEAs were characterized by ZEISS SUPRA 55 scanning electron microscope (SEM) equipped with an electron backscatter diffraction detector (EBSD). Processing Text: A series of HfNbTaTiV x alloys with various V contents (x= 0.00, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75 and 1.00 in molar ratio) were fabricated from high purity (>99.95 %) metals by using vacuum arc melting in a water-cooled copper crucible under argon atmosphere. The cast ingots were flipped and remelted at least six cycles to achieve chemical homogeneity. Ultimately, several button-shaped ingots were prepared with about 7 mm in thickness and 30 mm in diameter. The cast ingots were subjected to a series of cold rolling using a precision rolling mill (JH-RZH-110, China) to forming sheets about 1 mm in thickness (thickness reduction >85 %). Multiple dog-bone-shaped specimens were extracted from the rolled sheets utilizing an electrical spark erosion wire cutting machine (DK77, China). The dimension of the dog-bone-shaped specimens was 16 mm in length, 12 mm in width, and 1 mm in thickness, respectively. The obtained specimens were annealed at 1200 °C for 45 min inside an evacuated quartz tube maintained about 0.67 Pa vacuum. Subsequently, the specimens were promptly quenched in water. Afterward, tension tests were conducted on the dog-bone specimens at a strain rate of 0.001 s −1, using a universal testing machine (ETM205D, China). The tensile axis was aligned parallel to the rolling direction. The hardness of the alloys was evaluated using a Vicky MHV-1000 tester under 0.3 kgf load with duration of 15 s. Processing Text: TaMoNbCrTix (x = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1) RHEAs were fabricated through mechanical alloying (MA) and spark plasma sintering (SPS). The mechanical alloying process was performed using a planetary ball mill (QM-3SP4, Nanjing Nanda Instrument Co., Ltd., China) under an argon atmosphere. The milling duration was set to 50 h, while the milling speed was maintained at 350 rpm. The powders were sintered under vacuum conditions using spark plasma sintering equipment (SPS-825, Sumitomo Coal Mining Co., Ltd., Japan) with a sintering temperature of 1200 °C, a sintering pressure of 40 MPa and a holding time of 10 min. By employing severe deformation of the ball-milled powder, short sintering time, and the inhibition of precipitated phases on grain growth, the resulting RHEAs exhibited ultrafine grains measuring less than 1 μm. Processing Text: A novel type of Ni-based alloy containing the gadolinium neutron absorption unit and the tungsten gamma ray shielding unit were successfully fabricated. The designed and fabricated Ni-based alloys had excellent hot workability between 1100 °C and 1200 °C. A series of Ni-based alloys with different Gd and W contents were designed and melted in a vacuum induction melting furnace and cast in a copper mould with water cooling. The raw materials for smelting were prepared using high-purity materials, namely pure chromium (99.9 wt%), pure gadolinium (99.9 wt%), pure nickel (99.9 wt%), and NiW (W content = 60 ± 0.1 wt%) alloy. The casting ingots weighing about 1 kg possessed a dimensions of 60 mm × 15 mm × L mm (L: length). The ingots were hot-rolled into thin plates with a thickness of 3 to 4 mm at 1100 to 1200 °C and then annealed at 1150 °C. After that, the partial annealed plates were cold-rolled into sheets with a thickness of about 1.5 mm and then solution treatment was carried out at 1150 °C. The density of all the prepared specimens was determined though the Standard Archimedes method. Tensile tests at room temperature were performed on an MTS-CMT 5205 testing machine with a tensile rate of 0.9 mm/min. High temperature tensile tests were carried out on a Gleeble 3500 testing machine with a strain rate of 0.001 s −1. The phase of the alloys was determined by D/max2200 X-ray diffractometer (XRD) analysis with Cu K αradiation. The microstructures were observed and analysed by Keyence VHX-100 optical microscopy (OM), Phenom XL scanning electron microscope (SEM), and JSM-2010F transmission electron microscope (TEM). Energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) was used to analyse the chemical compositions of the alloys. The phase diagrams of the alloys were calculated by Thermo-Calc thermodynamic simulation software. The ion-beam thinning method was used to prepare the TEM foils, including cutting thin slices from the specimens, mechanically grinding them, and finally thinning the samples with an argon ion beam under different angles. Condition: room temperature

Processing Text: MEA ingots with a nominal composition of Co33.33Ni33.33V33.34(at.%) were produced by the vacuum arc melting technique in a high-purity argon atmosphere, in which a mixture of pure metals (purity over 99.9 %) was used. The samples were first remelted a minimum of four times to ensure chemical homogeneity. Following the hot rolling deformation at 1000 °C (0.5 h of treatment at this temperature before rolling resulted in a 40 % decrease in rolling volume), the ingots were annealed at 1000 °C for 2 h before being quenched in water. After reducing the samples from 10 mm to 2 mm via cold rolling, they were annealed at 1000 °C for 10 min followed by water quenching. The electrical discharge machining method was employed to obtain samples measuring 1 × 1 × 200 mm, which were then subjected to subsequent cold-drawing processes. CoNiV fibers, with a diameter of 300 μm, were produced through multipass cold-drawing at room temperature, with approximately a 10 μm reduction in diameter in each drawing step. To precisely control the content of precipitated phases, the CoNiV fibers underwent further annealing at temperatures of 1000, 900, 880, 865, and 850 °C for 10 min each. Subsequently, water quenching was performed after all the aforementioned drawing steps. The aforementioned samples were designated as 1000-10, 900-10, 880-10, 865-10, and 850-10 for convenience. Processing Text: Commercial Ni, Al, and Cr powder were used as raw materials. The particle size of Ni powder and Al powder is 10 μm and the purity is 99.85%. The particle size of Cr powder is 45 μm and the purity is 99.5%. Weigh NiAl-30Cr according to the ratio of Ni: Al: Cr of 35 at.%: 35 at.%: 30 at.%, and mix them uniformly in a ball mill. The ball mill was set to run at 40 rpm for 8 h. Then, the uniformly mixed powder was pressed into a cylindrical prefabricated blocks at a pressure of 60 MPa. The prefabricated blocks were placed in a thermal explosion furnace for combustion synthesis and hot pressing. The furnace was programmed with a heating rate of 30 °C/min. As the temperature of prefabricated block increased rapidly, a pressure of approximately 40 MPa was promptly applied. Microhardness measurements were performed on a hardness testing system (HTS, 1600-5122VD Micromet 5104, USA) under a load of 50 g and holding time of 10 s. Processing Text: Mg-9.5Gd-4Y-2Zn-0.3Zr alloy wires with a diameter of 1.2 mm were fabricated by a multistage drawing process with a cumulative area reduction (CAR) of 96% at 500 °C using as-extruded rods with a diameter of 6 mm as the raw material. The extrusion was carried out at 500 °C, with an extrusion ratio of 23:1, using cylindrical billets with a diameter of 70 mm and length of 400 mm. Then, cylindrical rods with a diameter of 6 mm were obtained. Mg-9.5Gd-4Y-2Zn-0.5Zr alloy wires were fabricated using a multi-pass drawing process at 500 °C. The drawing speed was between 20 mm/s and 35 mm/s. The strain of the drawing process was calculated by area reduction using Eq. (1): (1)AR=A0−AfA0where A 0and A fdenote the initial and final cross-sectional areas of the wires, respectively. The strain was between 10% and 12% per pass. Finally, the Mg-9.5Gd-4Y-2Zn-0.3Zr alloy wires with a diameter of 1.2 mm were obtained with a CAR of 96%. Samples for transmission electron microscopy (TEM, Thermofisher Talos F200X at 200 kV) were mechanically thinned to a 50-60 μm thickness, followed by electrolytic polishing in a 5% HClO 4and 95% C 2H 5OH solution at −30 °C and 30 V, then ion milling (Gatan 695) at 3°-6° incidence angle and 3-4 kV voltage. Samples for TEM were prepared using a focused ion beam (FIB, Thermo Scientific Scios 2 SEM) and an Omniprobe manipulator. The mechanical properties were evaluated through Vickers hardness (HVS-1000Z) and tensile testing (Instron 5582). The Vickers hardness tests were conducted with an applied force of 2 N for a duration of 10 s, in accordance with the ISO 6507-1 standard. Processing Text: The starting material used in this work was a commercial AISI 316L stainless steel rod with a chemical composition of Fe-0.065C-2Mn-16.1Cr-10.02Ni-2.02Mo-Si-0.045P (wt.%). The rod with a diameter of 5.5 mm was drawn to 0.98 mm through 18 passes drawing with an average area reduction of 17% every pass. The drawing speed was set to be 0.1-0.2 m s−1, which is equal to a strain rate at a magnitude of 10−1s−1. The total drawing strain εis 3.44 (ε= 2ln (d0/ dw), where d0is the diameter of the rod, and dwis the diameter of the drawn wire). The 316L samples for X-ray diffraction analysis and electron microscopy investigation were sectioned along the longitudinal direction of the original rod and drawn wires. The samples were ground and polished. The samples were etched by Na2SO3: HCl: H2O solution before microstructural examination under scanning electron microscopy (SEM) using a second electron detector. For the transmission kikuchi diffraction (TKD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) experiments, the thin foil samples from the longitudinal section of the rod and wires were ground to a thickness of 50 μm and then prepared by double-jet electrolytic polishing or ion milling with a GATAN Model PIPS system. The tensile test of 316L samples were carried out using a CMT5105 universal material testing machine at room temperature (∼25 °C) and 120 °C (simulating the temperature during drawing). The total length and the gauge length of the tensile specimens are 15 mm and 5 mm, respectively. The strain rate of the tensile test was set to be 6.0 × 10−3s−1. Three samples for each strain were measured to ensure the accuracy and reliability of the mechanical testing results. X-ray diffraction (XRD) experiments were performed on a Rigaku D-max2100 diffractometer operating with Cu radiation, and the scanning speed was 5°/min. The SEM experiments were carried out in a FEI Siron-200 SEM. The electron back scattered diffraction (EBSD) and TKD were carried out in a ZEISS Crossbeam 550 SEM equipped with a Symmetry S2 detector. The scanning steps are at the range of 6-100 nm based on the boundary spacing of the microstructure in the samples. Acceleration voltages for EBSD and TKD were set to be 20 kV and 30 kV, respectively. The detailed microstructure and atomic resolution observation of the samples were examined using either an FEI-Tecnai G2 or Talos F200X high-resolution (HR) TEM, both operated at 200 kV. Processing Text: MEAs of nominal compositions FeCr2V and FeCr2VWx (x = 0.1, 0.3, 0.5) were fabricated by arc melting using raw powders that are readily available in the market, including FeV alloy powder and commercially pure (>99 wt%) Cr, W elemental powders (all sourced from Beijing Ranbond Technology Co., China). The raw powders were mixed according to the designed nominal compositions and then placed into a water-cooled copper mold for arc melting with a vacuum arc furnace under an argon atmosphere. The ingots were flipped over and remelted three times to enhance the homogeneities of the final microstructure and chemical distribution of the obtained materials. A button-shaped ingot with the weight of approximately 30 g and dimensions of about Φ20 mm x 12 mm was obtained for each composition (referred to as W0, W0.1, W0.3, W0.5 hereinafter, based on their W composition). Vickers microhardness was measured four times for each sample of as-cast alloys under a load of 1 kg and a duration of 10 s using a Struers Durascan-70 automatic hardness tester. Processing Text: The equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi HEA materials with different carbon contents are provided by Beijing Yanbang New Materials Co. After homogenization at 1200 °C for 3 h, the samples are cold rolled at room temperature, and the final thickness is reduced from 2.5 mm to 1.0 mm (reduced by 60%). To achieve similar grain sizes (∼50 μm), the C0.5 or C1.0 samples are annealed at 1200 °C for 1 h or 1.5 h, respectively. Dog-bone-shaped specimens are harvested from the annealed sheet, and have a gauge length of 4 mm, a width of 4 mm and a thickness of 1 mm for both quasi-static and dynamic tensile experiments. Quasi-static uniaxial tensile tests are conducted with a mechanical universal testing machine (SUNS, model number UTM6000) at the strain rate of 0.001 s−1. Dynamical tests are carried out at the strain rate of 5200 s−1 using a standard split Hopkinson tension bar (SHTB) apparatus. Prior to the EBSD and TEM characterizations, all the specimens are grounded and mechanical polished, and then electro-polished. Test: C0.5-S; Strain rate: 0.001 s^-1; Quasi-static loading

Processing Text: The alloys employed in the current study were prepared by vacuum arc melting using powder with purity above 99.95 wt%. Finally, NiFe 20 was obtained. The sandpaper and SiO 2polishing solution were used to polish the experimental samples to a mirror-like surface. To eliminate processing defects and maintain the "mirror" state, NiFe 20 was annealed at 800 °C for 1 h. Electrochemical charging with 0.1 mol/L NaOH and 0.5 g/L CH 4N 2S heavy water solutions under identical experimental conditions were conducted. All samples were charged at a constant current of 50 mA/cm 2for 24 h at room temperature in a heavy aqueous solution containing 0.1 mol/L NaOH and 0.5 g/L CH 4N 2S. The deuterium charged samples were put into TDS within 24 h for deuterium concentration measurement. The TDS measurements were heated from room temperature to 800 °C under high vacuum (10 −5Pa) at a constant heating rate of 1 °C/s. Slow strain tensile tests were performed for pristine and the deuterium-charged samples using an Instron 5565 tensile testing machine equipped with a video extensometer, with a strain rate of 4 × 10 −4/s and a loading rate of 0.12 mm / min at room temperature. All samples were analyzed using EBSD along the normal direction (ND), with a scanning step size of about 0.25 µm. The TEM thin sample were prepared using standard electropolishing techniques. Firstly, a disk with a diameter of 3 mm was cut near the fracture surface using electrical discharge machining (EDM). The 3 mm disk was thinned to a thickness of about 80 µm using mechanical polishing. Finally, the sample thickness was further reduced to electron transparency using a 5% perchloric acid and 95% ethanol solution on a TJ100-SE twin-jet polisher with an instrument voltage of 20 V and a temperature of − 20 ± 4 °C. Deuterium charged conditions: 24 h

Processing Text: WNbMoTaZr RHEA ingots (46 ± 0.5 g) were prepared by the vacuum arc melting method, using raw elements with purities higher than 99.9 wt%. Twelve times of re-melting in a water-cooled cropper crucible, under an argon atmosphere, were employed to ensure the homogeneity. The ingots were sliced into three layers, as shown in Fig. 1c (top, middle, and bottom). Nine samples with dimension of 4 mm × 4 mm × 2 mm at each layer, as shown in Fig. 1d, were cut using wire electronic discharge machine (WEDM). The polished upper surface of each layer was utilized for microstructure inspection. The Vickers hardness of each specimen was tested at the top surface by a micro-hardness tester. Compression tests were conducted on a universal Materials Testing System (MTS). The specimens were cut from the region close to the middle of the ingots, as shown in Fig. 1c.
