Processing Text: Pre-alloyed powders (Ti 41V 27Hf 13Nb 13Mo 6in at%) were fabricated by the plasma rotating electrode-comminuting process (PREP) in Sailong Metal Materials Co., Ltd. The process was conducted in a Ytterbium Laser System (YLS-10000) with a 10 KW laser, a coaxial powder feeding device, and a real-time monitoring camera. The laser scanning direction was set as X with a rotation angle of 90° between adjacent layers, and the deposition direction was Z. The process parameters were set as follows: laser power of 1800-2000 W, scanning speed of 6-8 mm/s, powder delivery rate of 11 g/min, layer thickness of 0.5 mm, and laser beam diameter of 5 mm. Low line energy density (η) under 2000 W-8 mm/s (η= 250 J/mm) and high line energy density (η= 300 J/mm) under 1800 W-6 mm/s were adopted ultimately. The processing chamber was filled with argon and purged at a constant flow rate of 4 liters per minute to avoid oxidation, forming bulk specimens (12 mm × 12 mm × 35 mm). The RHEAs with grain-size graded microstructure were successfully created using the optimized processing conditions (laser power: 1800 W, scanning speed: 6 mm/s). The ambient-temperature tensile specimens with a gauge geometry of 4.0 mm × 1.5 mm × 1.0 mm were sectioned using electrical discharging. All specimens were mechanically polished to ensure surface regularity and tested along the Z direction. The uniaxial tensile testing was conducted on a Kammrath & Weiss mechanical testing platform at a strain rate of 1 × 10−3s−1. Before being tested for digital image correlation (DIC) analyses, the speckle patterns were coated on the surface of tensile specimens, and the resulting deformed characteristics were captured by a high-speed camera (frame rate, 1 Hz). In-situ tensile tests were conducted under EBSD. The tensile rate was 3 μm/s, and the gauge dimensions of the in-situ tensile samples were 3.0 mm × 1.2 mm × 0.8 mm. The samples for transmission electron microscope (TEM) observation were mechanically ground to ∼40 μm thickness, followed by ion milled, and finally identified by a double Cs corrector TEM (Themis Z). The laser scanning direction was set as X with a rotation angle of 90° between adjacent layers, and the deposition direction was Z. The process parameters were set as follows: laser power of 1800-2000 W, scanning speed of 6-8 mm/s, powder delivery rate of 11 g/min, layer thickness of 0.5 mm, and laser beam diameter of 5 mm. Low line energy density (η) under 2000 W-8 mm/s (η= 250 J/mm) and high line energy density (η= 300 J/mm) under 1800 W-6 mm/s were adopted ultimately. The processing chamber was filled with argon and purged at a constant flow rate of 4 liters per minute to avoid oxidation, forming bulk specimens (12 mm × 12 mm × 35 mm). The RHEAs with grain-size graded microstructure were successfully created using the optimized processing conditions (laser power: 1800 W, scanning speed: 6 mm/s). The ambient-temperature tensile specimens with a gauge geometry of 4.0 mm × 1.5 mm × 1.0 mm were sectioned using electrical discharging. All specimens were mechanically polished to ensure surface regularity and tested along the Z direction. The uniaxial tensile testing was conducted on a Kammrath & Weiss mechanical testing platform at a strain rate of 1 × 10−3s−1. Before being tested for digital image correlation (DIC) analyses, the speckle patterns were coated on the surface of tensile specimens, and the resulting deformed characteristics were captured by a high-speed camera (frame rate, 1 Hz). In-situ tensile tests were conducted under EBSD. The tensile rate was 3 μm/s, and the gauge dimensions of the in-situ tensile samples were 3.0 mm × 1.2 mm × 0.8 mm. The samples for transmission electron microscope (TEM) observation were mechanically ground to ∼40 μm thickness, followed by ion milled, and finally identified by a double Cs corrector TEM (Themis Z). Processing Text: The PBF-LB process was implemented using an SLM Solutions 125HL machine with a 400 W continuous 1060 nm wavelength (CW) fiber laser. The manufacturing process was conducted in a high Ar-content atmosphere with less than 0.1% oxygen to protect the samples from oxidation. Build plate preheating at 200 ℃ was used to reduce thermal stresses. A bidirectional scanning strategy was used in this work with a 45° angle between scanning direction and the normal direction (ND, X axis) on the first layer and a 90° rotation for each subsequent layer. Laser power and scanning speed were considered as processing variables while hatch spacing and layer thickness were held constant. Volume energy density (VED) of each process parameter set was calculated according to: (1)VED=Pv⋅h⋅twhere P, v, hand trepresent the laser power, laser scanning speed, hatch distance, and layer thickness, respectively. CoCrNi cubes with dimension of 5 × 5 × 5 mm 3and 2 mm support structure were printed with the range of processing parameters. Vickers microhardness testing was conducted on both the XY and XZ planes for 5 indents using a Struers Duramin-40 automated hardness tester with a 10 kg indent force, 10 seconds dwell time and 1 mm spacing. Tensile samples with a cross-section of 1.5 mm × 1.5 mm and a gauge length of 4 mm were cut from each PBF-LB/CoCrNi cube (15 mm × 15 mm × 15 mm) using electrical discharge machining (EDM) in both the vertical orientation (long axis parallel to the build direction) and horizontal orientation (long axis perpendicular to the build direction). The example graph of a tensile sample after EDM cutting is shown in Fig. S1eto reveal the surface quality. Two samples per orientation were characterized for six sets of PBF-LB processing parameters. Tensile tests were carried out using a Deben micro-tester equipped with a 2 kN load cell with a 0.4 mm/min displacement rate. A black and white color speckle pattern was spray painted on the surface of each sample before testing to measure the strain using digital image correlation (DIC). A video of the speckle painted sample surface was taken to record the tensile deformation for each sample. Strain data was obtained by analyzing the videos using the GOM correlation software package (Zeiss). In-situ tensile tests were conducted under an optical microscope (OM) for samples in both orientations for the E106 processing parameters. This testing method allowed a correlation between the deformation mechanisms and microstructural features. For in-situ testing, the surface of each tensile specimen was mirror polished and etched to reveal the microstructural features (melt pool and grain boundaries) under the optical microscope. The samples were step-loaded to failure with 0.6 mm displacement-controlled intervals at a displacement rate of 0.4 mm/min. After each interval step, testing was paused and OM images of the entire gauge section were taken to evaluate the deformation characteristics and microstructure evolution. The gauge area was marked by indents to perform EBSD analysis of the same location before and after deformation to reveal the texture and deformation relationship. Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations were conducted to analyze the melt pool shapes, temperature distributions, and cooling rates (T′) for the various PBF-LB processing parameters. Single track PBF-LB simulations were carried out using the commercial CFD solver Flow-3D which simulates both the powder bed and the laser printing process. Thus, powder particle motion and the recoating process were considered in the powder bed model establishment. Additionally, mass, momentum, and energy conservation were maintained during each simulation. Sample: E144; Orientation: Horizontal; Energy Density: Highest; Texture: <111>//LD

Processing Text: Although equiatomic CoCrFeNi medium-entropy alloys (MEAs) show excellent ductility, their strength is not high enough for the use in various engineering applications. Interestingly, the LPBF-fabricated CoCrFeNi MEAs have been found to exhibit both poor ultimate tensile strength (UTS) (∼582 MPa) and uniform elongation (δu) (∼11.7 %), attributed to the formation of hot cracks. In order to investigate the effect of TiC particles on the microstructure and mechanical properties of CoCrFeNi MEAs, pure CoCrFeNi MEAs (named as as-built MEAs) are fabricated by using the parameter iv. The relative density of as-built MEAs is measured as 99.4 %, and the microstructure of as-built MEAs is examined. Their metallographic microstructure is shown in Fig. 3(a), which presents the MPs with a typical “fish scale” shape, and the boundaries of semi-elliptical MPs can be clearly found. Fig. 3(b) displays that the cellular, cellular/columnar dendritic and elongated cellular sub-grains are formed in MPs. As-built MEAs are composed of some columnar grains which grow along the building direction (BD). Furthermore, some hot cracks occur and propagate along the boundaries of columnar grains in as-built MEAs. To explore the distribution of elements around hot cracks, the EDS characterization is carried out. The results can indicate that Co, Cr, Fe and Ni elements are evenly distributed in the columnar grains, and no obvious element segregation is found. For as-built MEAs, based on the IPFs of FCC phase and the orientation map of the IPFs of FCC phase in BD, they show an apparent preferred orientation (<110>) which is parallel to BD. As shown in Fig. 3(h), the fractions of low angle grain boundaries (LAGBs) and high angle grain boundaries (HAGBs) in as-built MEAs are 75.7 % and 24.3 %, respectively. The formation of LAGBs is mainly caused by the rearrangement of dislocations. Additionally, the grain size of FCC phase is confirmed as 169.8 ± 37.8 μm. For the alloys fabricated by LPBF technique, it was proved that the thermal residual stress and high dislocation density could be produced to promote the formation of solidification sub-structure. According to the KAM map, some relatively high KAM values are found within coarse grains, indicating that many dislocations are generated within these grains, which is attributed to the formation of many sub-grains surrounded by substantial dislocation networks and some LAGBs. Processing Text: Quaternary RMPEAs of Cr7Mo18Nb35V40 were prepared from pure elements of Cr, Mo, Nb, V, with 99.9% purity feedstock (American Elements, Los Angeles, USA). Using an Arcast 200 (Arcast, Maine, USA) arc melter, 10 mL buttons were melted on an actively cooled Cu hearth in an ultra-high purity (UHP) Ar environment. The melt chamber was evacuated to a vacuum level of 10 mTorr and purged three times with UHP Ar before every melt. Electromagnetic stirring enhanced mixing of the melt, and the buttons were flipped and remelted 5 times to avoid dead zones and improve mixing to achieve an overall homogenous melt. The buttons were then remelted on a vacuum arc suction cast mold into multiple cylindrical rods of 70 mm length and 8 mm diameter to achieve a more homogenous solidification. Temperature: 1250 °C; Processing state: as-cast

Processing Text: To overcome this limitation, we have successfully designed a strong and stiff magnesium-lithium alloy (LAZWMGT) by using Sn and RE (Gd, Y) nuclei to refine HCP α-Mg grains and forming secondary Mg2Sn inside primary Mg grains. All raw materials were melted in a fully automatic vacuum melting furnace under an argon protective atmosphere and kept at 730 °C for 10 min before pouring the melt into a copper mold to obtain cast ingots whose diameter was 150 mm, and the height was 30 mm, as shown schematically in Fig. 1. To obtain higher strength and Young′s modulus, the cast ingots were subjected to a heat treatment (solid solution (T4): 350 °C-4 h+ 400 °C-1 h, aging (T6): 85 °C-3 h). The microstructure, morphology, and elemental compositions and their distributions of the specimens were characterized by using a scanning electron microscope (SEM, S4800, Japan) equipped with an energy-dispersive X-ray spectrometer (EDS, QUANTAX) and optical microscope (OM, ZEISS). The phase analysis was carried out using an X-ray diffractometer (XRD, RigakuD/max-2500) with a copper foil target and a scanning speed of 4°/min. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, ESCALAB 250Xi, Thermo Scientific, USA) with an Al K α source was used to determine the surface chemical composition of the Mg-Li alloy, and the C (1 s) line of the amorphous carbon with a binding energy of 284.8 eV was used to standardize the absolute binding energy. According to the Williamson-Hall method, the grain size and microstrain were also quantified for LAZWMG and LAZWMGT specimens [17]. The full width at half-maximum of the peak was obtained as a measurement of peak broadening by fitting the peaks to the XRD using the Pearson-VII software. To evaluate the strength of the specimens under different heat treatments, the samples in cast and heat treatment states of 48 mm in length and 10 mm in width, and 1.5 mm in thickness were stretched at an initial strain of 1 × 10 -3S -1using an electronic universal tensile tester (CMT5205, MTS Systems Corporation, USA) according to ASTM E8/E8M-2011. Under each condition, four specimens were tested to ensure the accuracy of the experimental data. The samples (size: 60 mm × 10 mm ×2 mm) were evaluated on an IET-01 non-destructive test instrument for the dynamic elastic modulus of solid materials using the pulse excitation method following ASTM E 1876-2009. Processing Text: Experimental procedure Commercial Ti6Al4V powder with the size range of 45∼ 120 µm and pure Ta powder with the size range of 15–50 µm were used in this study. Ti6Al4V and Ta powders were mixed by the ball milling process with rotational speed of 150 r/min for 3 h, then dried in a vacuum furnace at 120 ℃ for 2 h to remove residual moisture. The Ti6Al4V-xTa alloys were prepared using a laser cladding system, including a 6 kW ﬁber laser cladding head equipped with the coaxial powder feeding. The substrates plates were made of forged Ti6Al4V alloy with the geometric size of 100 × 100 × 20 mm. The surface of the substrates was ground using 800 grit SiC papers then cleaned with alcohol before cladding. The laser power, scan speed and powder feed rate were chosen as 2000–2200 W, 480 mm/min and ∼5.4 g/min, respectively. The diameter of laser beam was estimated to be around 3 mm. The working chamber was ﬁlled with argon gas and the oxygen level was kept less than 20 ppm to prevent oxidation of alloy during LAM process, and argon could also provide shielding to prevent contamination of the laser lens. During the multi-layer deposition process, the layer thickness was set as 0.6 mm in the depositing direction. The overlapping fraction between the two parallel tracks was set as 30 % to achieve a continuous building. Condition: room temperature; Processing state: LAMed; Microstructure: finest uniform basketweave microstructure, weakened α-variants selection

Processing Text: A new Co-rich Co50Cr20Ni20Fe5Mn5 HEA was synthesized by vacuum arc remelting and processed through homogenization, cold rolling, and recrystallization. The Co 50Cr 20Ni 20Fe 5Mn 5and Co 20Cr 20Ni 20Fe 20Mn 20high entropy alloys were prepared using vacuum arc remelting (VAR) in a water-cooled copper crucible using the commercially pure metals of Co, Cr, Fe, Ni, and Mn with a purity greater than 99.9%. In addition, pure Ti was melted and utilized as an oxygen-getter within the VAR chamber. The arc was formed in a high-purity Ar atmosphere (99.999%) using a non-consumable tungsten electrode. Each ingot was sliced into 5-6 pieces and the pieces were flipped over and underwent six remelting cycles to promote thorough mixing. To ensure reasonable homogenization, the as-cast ingots were hot-forged to a 54% height reduction across their width and subsequently homogenized at 1100 °C for 24 h in a vacuum, followed by water-quenching. The homogenized alloys were analyzed for their chemical composition using inductively coupled plasma-optical emission spectrometry (ICP -OES). Following the homogenization treatment, the alloys were hot rolled at 1000 °C with a 68% thickness reduction. To ensure nearly isothermal hot deformation, the specimens were heated at 1000 °C for 15 min before the first and for 5 min before each subsequent rolling pass. After hot rolling, the samples were annealed at 1000 °C for 5 min, followed by water quenching. Further grain refinement of the alloys was achieved through cold-rolling at room temperature with a thickness reduction of 68%, followed by recrystallization annealing at 900 °C in a vacuum for 7 min, followed by water quenching. Condition: Room Temperature; Phase: FCC + 6%HCP; Grain Size: 7.1 µm; Microstructure Characteristics: TWIP-TRIP effect

In addition, pure Ti was melted and utilized as an oxygen-getter within the VAR chamber. The arc was formed in a high-purity Ar atmosphere (99.999%) using a non-consumable tungsten electrode. Each ingot was sliced into 5-6 pieces and the pieces were flipped over and underwent six remelting cycles to promote thorough mixing. To ensure reasonable homogenization, the as-cast ingots were hot-forged to a 54% height reduction across their width and subsequently homogenized at 1100 °C for 24 h in a vacuum, followed by water-quenching. The homogenized alloys were analyzed for their chemical composition using inductively coupled plasma-optical emission spectrometry (ICP -OES). Following the homogenization treatment, the alloys were hot rolled at 1000 °C with a 68% thickness reduction. To ensure nearly isothermal hot deformation, the specimens were heated at 1000 °C for 15 min before the first and for 5 min before each subsequent rolling pass. After hot rolling, the samples were annealed at 1000 °C for 5 min, followed by water quenching. Further grain refinement of the alloys was achieved through cold-rolling at room temperature with a thickness reduction of 68%, followed by recrystallization annealing at 900 °C in a vacuum for 7 min, followed by water quenching. Processing Text: The ingots of (Ti-V-Al) 100-xN xshape memory alloys with different N additions (x = 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, at.%) were prepared by using a non-consumable arc-melting furnace under Ar atmosphere. High pure titanium (99.9%), vanadium (99.9%), aluminum (99.99%), and TiN particle powder were selected to be the raw materials. To ensure homogenization of the alloy composition, the ingots were melted and flipped six times. After melting, the (Ti-V-Al) 100-xN xsamples were sealed in quartz tubes under high vacuum. Then samples were solution treated at 1000 °C for 3 h, followed by water-quenching. Subsequently, the (Ti-V-Al) 100-xN xingots were hot-rolled to obtain thin plates measuring 4 mm in thickness. These plates were further cold-rolled to achieve a final thickness of 1 mm. Finally, the (Ti-V-Al) 100-xN xspecimens were cut into materials of different sizes (20 mm × 10 mm × 2 mm, 40 mm × 2 mm × 2 mm) using wire cutting to meet the requirements of various analytical experiments. After this, all samples were subjected to solution treatment at 900 °C for 3h under higher vacuum conditions, followed by water-quenching. The phase composition and structural information of the (Ti-V-Al) 100-xN xshape memory alloy were determined through X-ray diffraction (XRD) using the CuKα radiation source at room temperature. Optical microscopy (OM) was used to observe the microstructural evolution of the Ti-V-Al shape memory alloy with varying Nitrogen (N) content. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) combined with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) was utilized to examine the surface morphology, analyze the elemental composition of the second phase, and investigate the fracture surfaces. The specimens for SEM observation underwent polishing using SiC sandpaper with grit sizes ranging from #240 to #2000, followed by cloth polishing using a SiO 2solution with a particle size of 50 nm. To prepare the specimens for OM experiments, they were etched using a solution consisting of HF:HNO3:H2O in a ratio of 1:5:10. Bright-field transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images and corresponding selected area electron diffraction (SAED) patterns were used to study the martensitic variants and morphology of the second phase in the (Ti-V-Al) 100-xN xshape memory alloy. The twin jet-polishing was employed to prepare the specimens for transmission electron microscope (TEM) observations. The specimens were immersed in a solution containing 6% perchloric acid, 60% methyl alcohol, and 34% n-butyl alcohol, at approximately −20 °C. Furthermore, the martensitic transformation behavior of the (Ti-V-Al) 100-xN xshape memory alloys was investigated by conducting differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) analysis over a temperature range of −50 to 400 °C, with a heating/cooling rate of 20 °C/s. The mechanical properties of the (Ti-V-Al) 100-xN xshape memory alloy at room temperature, including tensile strength, were assessed using a tensile testing machine at a rate of 0.2 mm/min. The Vickers hardness of (Ti-V-Al) 100-xN xshape memory alloys was measured at room temperature using the nanoindentation technique with a 50g load applied for 10s. To ensure accuracy, measurements were taken at five different points on the same sample. To evaluate the friction and wear properties of the (Ti-V-Al) 100-xN xshape memory alloy under dry conditions at room temperature, a ball-on-disk tribometer (HSR-2M, Zhongke Kaihua) was used with a load of 10 N. Maximum yield strength observed; N content adjusted; Alloy features solid solution strengthening, grain refinement, and precipitation strengthening.

Processing Text: The 4032 aluminum alloy (12.74 wt% Si, 0.33 wt% Fe, 1.29 wt% Cu, 1.00 wt% Mg, 1.15 wt% Ni, 0.059 wt% Ti, residual Al) was melted in a 60 kg capacity crucible using a resistance furnace. During the melting process, the temperature of the resistance furnace was controlled at 720 °C. A total of 30 kg of the alloy melt was prepared, and this melt was homogenized for 1 h. Subsequently, the Al-10Sr intermediate alloy was added, and the alloy melt was subjected to outgassing and smelting for 15 min. After resting for 15 min, the desired alloy melt was obtained. The casting process was carried out using an injection speed of 0.1 m/s, a squeeze pressure of 150 MPa, a pouring temperature of 710 °C, and a mold temperature of 220 °C. Subsequently, standard sample blocks were cut from the test bar for T6 heat treatment according to the following procedure: heating of the solid-solution at 525 °C for 2.5 h, water quenching to room temperature, aging at 175 °C for 10 h, and air cooling to room temperature. The yield strength of the refiner-free 4032 aluminum alloy (hereinafter referred to as alloy CS1) in the as-cast state was determined to be 169 MPa, the tensile strength was 249 MPa, and the elongation was 1.55 %. Subsequently, alloy CS1 was subjected to T6 heat treatment, according to the following parameters: solid-solution temperature of 525 °C, solid-solution heating insulation time of 2.5 h, aging temperature of 175 °C, aging insulation time of 10 h. After the T6 heat treatment (hereinafter referred to as alloy AS1), the tensile strength of the alloy increased to 364 MPa, the yield strength increased to 334 MPa, and the elongation remained relatively constant at 1.56 %. Processing Text: a developed multi-step hot deformation process was employed to regulate the grain boundaries (GBs), hetero-phase boundaries (PBs) and dislocation structure for dual-phase titanium alloy. The effects of accumulative thermal deformation ratios from 33% to 75% (2-8 cycles) on the microstructure and mechanical properties have been investigated. The sintered sample shows a typical Widmanstätten structure without obvious pores and micro-cracks. However, with the increase of the deformation ratio, for the hexagonal close packed (HCP) Ti, the crystal orientations of { 01 1 ‾ 0 } and { 1 ‾ 2 1 ‾ 0 } were gradually transformed into {0001}, with the change of high-angle grain boundaries (HAGBs) to low-angle grain boundaries (LAGBs). The density of stored geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs) density raised dramatically from 1.95 × 1014 m−2 to 6.5 × 1014 m−2, and various types of dislocations have been characterized. For the β phase, in the thermal deformation process, high density α-precipitates with an average thickness below 20 nm had formed with Burgers relationship of {110}BCC//{0001}HCP and < 1 ‾ 11 > BCC//< 2 1 ‾ 1 ‾ 0 > HCP. Finally, the yield strength of the dual-phase titanium alloy increased dramatically from 881 MPa to 1178 MPa, and the ductility can still maintain at above 8.5%. The enhanced strength was mainly contributed by the increase of geometrically necessary boundaries (GNBs) and nano-lamellae boundaries (NLBs). Processing Text: The aluminum alloy sheet was divided into four small sheets which had been annealed at 460℃ for 0, 30, 60 and 120 min separately and all were followed by water quenching. The four sheets were named AN0, AN30, AN60 and AN120, corresponding to 0, 30, 60 and 120 min of annealing time respectively. The texture components (Brass, Copper, S, Cube and Goss) were characterized by electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD), which was performed on a MIRA4 LMH field emission scanning electron microscope equipped with a NordlysMax2 EBSD detector. The accelerating voltage was 20 kV, and the working distance was about 15 mm at a magnification of 200× with a specimen tilt of 70°. The EBSD specimens were prepared with the assistance of standard metallograph technology. Finally, electropolishing was carried out with electrolyte at 20 V for 20 s. Uniaxial tensile tests were carried out using an Instron 3369 universal testing machine at a tensile rate of 2 mm/min. The tensile mechanical performance test specimens were taken from the rolled annealed AN0 and AN60 sheets, and the tensile specimens were cut along three directions 0°, 45° and 90° to the RD on the rolling surface. In order to ensure the reliability of results, the tensile testing of each data point was repeated three times. The in-plane anisotropy was measured by the plastic strain ratio r-values ( r=εwidth/εthickness) along the three directions. In order to measure the r-value under quasi-static conditions, we used a vernier caliper to measure the transverse and thickness strain of the tensile sample, and took the average value of three samples. The crystal plasticity simulations in this work were performed through the open-source software DAMASK which enables us to conduct the crystal plasticity simulations together with a spectral solver. The material orientations obtained from EBSD were employed as input data for the CPFFT simulations, and material properties were assigned to the grains in the RVE model using a material configuration file. Assuming that the elastic behavior of the material conforms to Hooke’s law, the cubic crystal elastic constants C11=107.3GPa, C12=60.9GPa and C44=28.3GPa, which are typical values for face-centered crystal (FCC) aluminum alloy. The phenomenological constitutive law was used to describe the plastic deformation behavior of materials, and the material parameters were determined by fitting the stress-strain curve through the trial-and-error method. The loading condition was set in the simulation with uniaxial stretching along the x-direction, and the iso-static strain rate was 1×10 −3s −1. The periodic boundary condition was applied as, (11)Ḟ=[1000*000*]×10-3s-1&P=[****0***0]Pa. In order to determine the in-plane anisotropy and calculate the r-value more conveniently, an equivalent method was used for the uniaxial tensile testing, and the rotation of the loading direction was realized by rotating the Euler angles of grains. The RVEs of AN0 and AN60 samples were generated using DREAM.3D software. The generated RVEs shown in Fig. 4(a-b) has 500 grains at a grid resolution of 80×80×80, and assigned the grain orientations of AN0 and AN60, with different colors representing different grain orientations. Processing Text: In this study, 316 L stainless steel specimens with 0 and 2 wt% Nb were fabricated using direct energy deposition, and heat treatment was performed at various temperatures. All the specimens were additively manufactured in a cubic shape (30 mm × 30 mm × 30 mm) using a DED machine (MX-3, Instek). The process parameters were as follows: a laser power of 400 W, scan speed of 0.85 m/min, overlap of 0.5 mm, powder feed rate of 3 g/min, hatching distance of 0.5 mm, and layer thickness of 0.25 mm. The scan strategy involved the use of a cross-snake-hatching method in which each layer was rotated by 90°. The additively manufactured 316 L stainless steel specimens were maintained at 800 °C and 900 °C, respectively, for 1 h for heat treatment, and then water quenched. The specimens that were not heat treated were denoted by “As,” and those treated at the lower and higher temperatures were denoted by “LHT” and “HHT,” respectively. Processing Text: Laser aided additive manufacturing (LAAM) of stainless steel 316L (SS 316L) in a controlled argon environment was investigated. The controlled argon environment can significantly reduce the oxidation and fundamentally change the process conditions. It was found that after inhibiting oxidation, the surface of the deposited SS 316L showed remarkably high reflectance (71%) to laser radiation, which minimised heat accumulation. Subsequently, stable melt pool temperature and high cooling rate (4.1 × 10^4 K/s) were also observed. Furthermore, nano-sized oxides were found to be nucleated owing to excessively low internal oxygen content (220 ppm). The unique process condition resulted in enhanced strengthening effect due to cellular structure refinement and dispersed nano-sized oxides. Gas-atomised SS 316L powders were employed as the feedstock material. The SEM photo in Fig. 1(a) depicts a near-spherical morphology of the SS 316L powders, with observable satellite attachments on the surfaces. Some irregularly shaped powders can also be observed. A median particle size of 69.4 μm was characterized using laser scattering particle size analyzer. The oxygen content of the deposited SS 316L was measured through inert gas combustion method with an oxygen/Nitrogen/Hydrogen elemental analyzer (LECO ONH836). Quasi-static tensile test at the strain rate of 10^-3 s^-1 was conducted on Instron 5982 universal tensile test machine at room temperature. Dynamic tensile tests with an average strain rate of 3150 s^-1 were conducted using a Spilt Hopkinson Tensile Bar (SHTB) apparatus. The microhardness of the deposited SS 316L was measured using a HVS1000 microhardness tester, with the load set as 500 g and the dwell time 15 s. The specially designed Ar chamber in this paper successfully minimizes the oxidation level to achieve a very low oxygen content of 220 ppm. The oxide particles obtained are fine, with an average size of 131.4 ± 68.5 nm. Reduction of oxidation not only influences the surface condition of the deposited material, but also leads to high reflectance of laser energy. The resulting shiny and smooth surface exhibits a reflectance of 71%. This, combined with controlled Ar environment, resulted in significantly reduced thermal accumulation, stable melt pool temperature, and high cooling rate during the LAAM process. Consequently, refined grains (24.8 μm) and cellular structures (2.4 μm) can be achieved. Quasi-static tension at strain rate of 10^-3 s^-1; As-deposited material

Processing Text: The Ti-5.7Al-3.2Sn-5.4Zr-0.5Mo-1.0Nb-0.4Si-0.2Er (all in wt%) alloy (IMI834) was procured from Yunnan Titanium Industry Co., Ltd (CHN), which ingot with a diameter of 200 mm and length of 400 mm was produced by vacuum arc remelting (VAR) technology triple times. The β/(α + β) transus-temperature of the Ti alloy was measured as 1005 °C by differential scanning calorimetry. The ingot is first forged at 1150 °C to obtain a cubic billet with a cross section of 50 mm. Then, forged at 980 °C to obtain a rectangular billet with a lengthwise cross-sectional side length of 40 mm. The forged bar was solution treated at 990 °C for 1 h to obtain a bimodal structure with equiaxed primary α phase. The second step is to obtain the LPS-HS by hot rolling in the α+β phase region (920,960 and 990 °C) this Ti alloy after solution treated. The sheets with a BM are annealed at a specified temperature for 15 min. During the rolling process, the reduction was 15% per pass, with annealing 5 min after per pass. This rolling process is repeated for 8 passes, and a total rolling reduction of 81%. Subsequently, the aging treatment was carried out at 700 °C for 5 h. The cooling method is air cooling(AC). We conducted a 990 °C/1h/AC heat treatment on the alloy after forging. To ensure experimental consistency, the deformation amount during rolling was kept the same, with rolling performed at temperatures of 920, 960 and 990 °C in the (α+β) phase region. The alloy after rolling is subjected to a 5 h aging treatment at 700 °C. Room Temperature tensile properties

Processing Text: Copper matrix composites reinforced by copper-coated graphite and Ti3AlC2 were fabricated using the hot-pressing sintering. The preparation of copper matrix composites mainly includes three stages. Firstly, a ball milling process was used to mix raw materials. The powder mixture of Ti3AlC2, electrolytic copper, and copper-coated graphite powders was put into 304 stainless steel jars and mixed using a planetary ball mill at 180 rpm for 8 h with weight ratio of ball to powder of 5:1. Secondly, the powders mixture was poured into a Cr12MoV die of Φ 30 mm and was cold pressed into a green compact at a pressure of 300 MPa for 5 min. Thirdly, the green compact was sintered at 1223 K below 1× 10−2 Pa by a vacuum hot-pressing under the pressure of 25 MPa followed by furnace cooling. Processing Text: In the present work, a Ni3(Al, Ti)-type multicomponent alloy of Ni43.9Co22.4Fe8.8Al10.7Ti11.7B2.5 was successfully fabricated using laser metal deposition (LMD) technique. Mixed powders of Ni, Co, Fe, Al, Ti and B with purity ≥99.99% were used as raw materials. The mixed powders were mechanically mixed for 3 h and dried at 393 K for 3 h. An in-house developed LMD printing system was employed, and the powder was fed into the laser melt pool on the GH4169 high-temperature alloy substrate using a coaxial nozzle under a high-purity argon gas atmosphere (≥99.99%). The variables that followed were the applied optimal process parameters: laser power of 1400 W, laser scanning speed of 400 mm/min, gas flow rate of 3 L/min and powder feed rate of 1.4 rad/min. The Ni43.9Co22.4Fe8.8Al10.7Ti11.7B2.5 alloy prepared by LMD consists of dendrite γ + γ′ phases, γ′ envelopes and interdendritic γ + γ′ phases, with discontinuous acicular TiB2 precipitates in the interdendritic γ + γ′ region. During the solidification process, TiB2 and γ dendrites preferentially precipitate, and the residual liquid phase reacts with γ dendrites to form γ′ envelope layer. Subsequently, γ and γ′ phases are co-precipitated from the residual interdendrite liquid phase. During the deposition process, the interdendrite γ′ phase coarsened and merged, and the cubic γ′ phase precipitated inside the γ dendrite. Condition: maximum value at 973 K

Processing Text: Be/Al composites containing varying volume fractions of beryllium were fabricated via the pressure infiltration method. Under pressure infiltration conditions, the molten aluminum successfully repaired the defects in the beryllium swarf. Be/Al composites with volume fractions of 30%-60% were prepared using the pressure infiltration method, and the process flow diagram is shown in Fig. 1. The treated beryllium swarf was compressed to a predetermined volume content in a steel mold with a diameter of 52 mm to obtain a preform. Subsequently, the steel mold containing the Be preform was kept at 600 °C for about 3 h. At the same time, Al was heated to above 800° and kept warm, and molten Al liquid was obtained under argon (Ar) protection. Subsequently, the prepared preform and mold were placed on the press table, and the molten Al liquid was poured into the mold cavity for mechanical pressing. According to the preparation of Be/Al composites with different body parts, the pressure range is between 50 and 100 MPa, the infiltration speed is 1-50 mm/s, and the holding time is 5min. With the full immersion of molten Al liquid into the cracks of the beryllium swarf and the gaps between the swarf, residual gas in the pores is simultaneously discharged, greatly improving the density of composite materials, and finally preparing Be/Al composites with beryllium volume fractions of 30%, 40%, 50%, and 60% respectively. Processing Text: The bulb flat steel with a yield strength of 1292 MPa, elongation of 18.5 % and an impact energy of 53 J at − 196 °C is obtained by quenching and tempering process. In order to reveal the tempering response and strengthening mechanism during the quenching and tempering process of bulb flat steel, multi-scale characterization is carried out to explore the microstructural evolution and nano-precipitation behavior of the ultralow temperature bulb flat steel under different tempering processes. After holding the cast ingot at 1200 °C for 3 h, it is forged into a rectangular billet of 150 mm * 150 mm * 2000 mm. The billet is heated and held in a three-stage heating furnace (600 °C in the preheating section, 1130 °C in the heating section and 1250 °C in the soaking section) and hot rolled after descaling. The opening rolling temperature is 1150 °C and the final rolling temperature is 920 °C. The bulb flat steel of HP140*11 specification is prepared by 12 passes of groove rolling and air cooled to room temperature. The temperature parameters of QT process are selected based on the results of phase transformation temperature determination. In this study, the quenching temperature was taken as 830 °C, and the holding time was 30 min to make the specimens fully austenitized, and then water quenched to room temperature. Subsequently, the specimens were tempered at 450 °C, 500 °C, and 550 °C for 5 h respectively. Finally, the specimens were removed and air cooled to room temperature. The QT process route is shown in Fig. 2(b). The mechanical properties of the bulb flat steel were tested by tensile and impact tests, respectively. The tensile tests at room temperature were performed on an electronic tensile testing machine with an extensometer at a strain rate of 10 -3s −1. The low temperature impact tests were performed on a TB50 impact testing machine using liquid nitrogen as the cooling medium. The sampling positions and dimensional diagram are shown in Fig. 3. The microstructures of the ultralow temperature resistant bulb flat steel after heat treatment were characterized using a SUPRA55 SEM. The samples are cut from the sampling position in Fig. 3, and the longitudinal section of the sample is polished and etched (HNO 3: alcohol = 1 ml: 10 ml). The diffraction peak profile of the specimen was measured by a German Bruker D8 ADVANCE XRD. The measurement range is 20°-140°, the measurement step is 0.02°, and the test speed is 2°/min. The crystal structure of the blub flat steel was characterized by EBSD. The specimen was ground with abrasive paper, followed by electropolishing with 5 % perchloric acid alcohol solution. The parameters of electropolishing were: voltage = 30 V, polishing time = 40 s. The microstructure of the bulb flat steel was characterized using an FEI Titan themis G2 60-300 TEM. For TEM observation, the thin foils were prepared by twin-jet electropolishing. Needle samples for APT analysis were prepared by two-step electropolishing method. The data were collected by the atom probe under vacuum of < 10-8 Pa in the analysis chamber, the sample was cooled to 50 K, the pulse voltage frequency was 200 kHz, and the pulse fraction was 20 %. Processing Text: The Ni 40Co 18Cr 18Fe 14Al 5Ti 5HEA was fabricated using an FS273M SLM machine (Hunan Farsoon High-Technology Co., Ltd, China). The fiber laser of this SLM instrument has a spot diameter of 55 μm and a maximum output power of 500 W. Before printing, the chamber of the SLM device was vacuumed and then filled with high-purity argon gas to ensure the oxygen content remained below 1000 ppm. The build substrate was preheated to 100 °C to reduce thermal stress. A wide range of printing parameters including adjustments in laser power ( P), scanning speed ( V), and scanning pitch ( h), were explored. Specifically, Pranged from 260 to 300 W, Vranged from 800 to 1200 mm·s −1, and hranged from 60 to 140 μm, all while maintaining a consistent layer thickness ( t) of 40 μm. The laser beam scanned each layer in a unidirectional manner, with the scanning direction altered by 67° for each subsequent layer (as shown in Fig. 1b), aiming to minimize defects and residual stress [26]. The densities of the SLM-produced samples were determined using Archimedes' drainage method. Phase analysis of the powders and as-printed samples was conducted using a Cu Kα radiation X-ray diffractometer (XRD, 7000SX, Shimadzu). The microstructure was characterized using optical microscopy (OM), scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Nova Nano SEM 450), electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM, FEI Tecnai G20, 300 kV). For the TEM analysis, the samples were initially mechanically polished to a thickness of approximately 30 μm and then further thinned using an ion polishing system (Gatan PIPS II 695). Tensile testing was conducted on seven representative SLM-produced HEA samples, each prepared with varying printing parameters (denoted as P1, P2, …, P7) encompassing a wide range of laser power, scanning speed, and scanning pitch. Processing Text: The Fe-28Mn-10Al-1.2C-xMo (wt.%, x = 0, 3, 5) low-density steels in this work were prepared under near-rapid solidification. First, the alloy ingot was prepared from high purity Fe (99.99 %), Mn (99.9 %), Al (99.9 %), C (99.8 %), and Fe-Mo intermediate alloy (55.1 wt% Mo) in a cold-crucible suspension induction melting equipment. Then, the alloy ingot was re-melted by induction heating in Ar atmosphere, and poured into a copper mold at a rotating speed of 660 r/min, thereby obtaining a steel strip with a size of (60-80) mm × 60 mm × 2.5 mm. To promote the precipitation of nano-particles, some of the steel strips were aged at 450 °C for 9 h under a high vacuum of 5 × 10 −3Pa and then cooled in furnace. The actual compositions of steel strips were detected by an Inductively Coupled Plasma Mass Spectrometry (ICP) and a CS2800 carbon-sulfur analyzer. Processing state: as-cast

Processing Text: CrMnFeCoNi HEA with 5 at.% SiC nanoparticles addition was fabricated by LMD. The size of the pre-alloyed spherical equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi powder and SiC powder that were analyzed using laser particle size analyzer (Microtrac s3500) are approximately 120 μm and 40 nm, respectively. Two powders were fully mixed and dried in a vacuum environment at 120 °C for 2.5 h prior to additive manufacturing. Under the protection of argon gas, the mixed powders were delivered into the chamber through a coaxial nozzle at an argon gas flow 15 L/min and a feeding rate of 7-9 g/min. Successive layers were deposited on a 316L steel substrate, ultimately forming walled-samples. The heat treatment processes of the samples were carried out in a vertical vacuum tube quenching furnace, which quenched immediately after 2-h heat treatment at different temperatures (700/900/1100 °C). The tensile tests of the samples were performed at an engineering strain rate of 10 −3s −1 in an Instron 5982 static testing machine. Each group of samples was retested three times to obtain their average value. The tensile samples with a gauge length of 10.0 mm, gauge width of 2.0 mm, and thickness of 1.6 mm were cut from to the center of LMD-fabricated wall, and the tensile direction was parallel to deposition direction (DD). The samples under different heat treatment temperature were subjected to corrosion treatment in equal proportion of FeCl 3-HCl-H 2O solution for 30 s before SEM observation. Condition: Room Temperature (25°C)

Processing Text: Heterostructured (HS) 2024Al alloys with various heterogeneity levels, consisting of soft domains (CGs) and hard domains (FGs, Al3Tip, and eutectic compounds), were fabricated via adjusting the mold temperature of powder thixoforming. A powder mixture was produced by combining 3.5 wt% Ti p and 96.5 wt% 2024Al p in a planetary ball-milling machine (ND7-21). The ball-milling process was carried out for 8 h at a speed of 135 rpm/min with a ball-to-powder ratio of 5:1. To prevent overheating, the ball milling was stopped for 10 min after running for 10 min. Following ball milling, the resulting powder mixture was subjected to hot-pressing in a steel mold using a vacuum hot-pressing furnace (GWL-VSF-1200RY) to form Φ 45 mm × ∼16 mm green compacts. Processing Text: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA powder (Beijing Yanbang New Material Technology Co., Ltd., China) was purchased and used as a feedstock for cold spray deposition. The powder size distribution was 15-53 μm (a d50 value of 29.351 μm). Al 6061 alloy substrate (5 mm thickness) was used for CS deposition. Prior to deposition, the substrate was grit-blasted using an alumina grit blasting pressure of 3 bar. The CrCoFeMnNi HEA powder was cold sprayed on Al6061 substrate using the cold spraying facility of Impact Innovations (GmbH, Germany) using nitrogen as processing gas. The gas temperature and pressure were set at 600 °C and 4.2 MPa, respectively; the gas flow, the scan velocity, and the standoff distance from the nozzle exit to the substrate surface were set at 100 m3/h, 30 mm/s, and 25 mm, respectively. About 70 mm × 70 mm × 8 mm freestanding CrMnFeCoNi HEA plate was successfully printed. The as-spared samples were heat treated at temperatures of 600 °C, 900 °C, 1100 °C, 1200 °C, and 1250 °C in a muffle furnace for 1 h with a heating rate of 10 °C/min, followed by furnace cooling. Before microstructural characterization, the as-sprayed CrMnFeCoNi HEA deposit was carefully sectioned from the substrate via a Wire Electrical Discharging Machine (EDM). Then, the piece of samples was cut using EDM (5 mm × 5 mm × 2 mm) from the as-sprayed deposit for microstructural characterization. Both the as-sprayed and sintered samples followed the standard sample preparation process. Hence, the CrCoFeMnNi HEA deposit is unsuitable for chemical etchants, so we used the standard sample preparation procedure of ion polishing methods. The prepared samples have been ground mechanically using 400#, 1000#, 2000#, and 5000# water sanding papers to obtain a smooth and delicate surface, and then polished by Leica EMRES102 argon ion polishing instrument, with an applied voltage of 5 KeV, 4 KeV, and 3 KeV for 1 h for each polishing process. The cylindrical samples with 6 mm × Ø4 mm for quasi-static and 4 mm × Ø4 mm for dynamic compression test were prepared via wire cutting machine (EDM) from the as-sprayed deposit. Room temperature quasi-static compression behavior was tested by using a standard GB/T7314-2017 metallic materials testing system with a strain rate of 1 × 10−3s−1. An electronic universal material testing machine, (INSTRON5985, US) was used for this quasi-static test. The dynamic behavior of the as-sprayed and sintered samples was carried out by the split Hopkinson pressure bar (SHPB) facility at room temperature. Processing Text: Pre-alloyed Ti–20Zr–23Nb (TZN) powder, obtained from Guangzhou Sailong Additive Manufacturing Co., China, with an average particle size of 50 μm, was utilized in this research work. Pristine TZN powder was milled at 100, 150, 200, and 300 rpm for 3 h using a planetary ball mill (Pulverisette 5, Fritsch). WC balls and vials were used with a 10:1 ball-to-powder ratio, while keeping the argon atmosphere inside the vials tightly closed to prevent air from entering. Subsequently, the milled TZN powders were blended with pristine powder in equal-weight proportions (1:1) through a 3-h milling session at 125 rpm using a low-energy horizontal ball mill. This secondary milling operation, performed in an air atmosphere with plastic bottles and WC balls at a 5:1 ball-to-powder ratio, was specifically employed for the purpose of uniform powder mixing. The pristine and milled-mixed (1:1 mixing of as-received and milled powders) TZN powders were sintered using spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1200 °C for 10 min with a heating rate of 100 °C/min, using a 13 mm graphite die for SPS. Processing Text: The W-W interatomic interactions were described using the embedded atom method (EAM) interatomic potential developed by Marinica et al., 2013. This potential was specifically designed for studying the irradiation effects and dislocations in tungsten and has undergone extensive validation through ab initio and experimental values. The simulation box with dimensions of 40.0 nm × 22.3 nm × 23.1 nm, containing approximately 1.4 million atoms, was used. The x-, y-, and z-axes of the simulation box were oriented as [111], [-110], and [-1-12], respectively. To create the edge dislocation along the z-axis whose normal direction of the slip plane is along the x-axis, the ATOMSK software package was employed. This edge dislocation, characterized by the x slip direction and a Burgers vector of a/2<111>, was introduced, where a represents the lattice constant, measuring 3.14 Ȧ. The construction of the dislocation model referred to the method developed by Osetsky and Bacon (2003). Two types of dislocation loops with Burgers vectors of a<100> and a/2<111> were introduced at the center of the simulation box, referred to as ‘perfect loop’, to account for all possible dislocation loop scenarios. The construction process involved the insertion of the dislocation, and then the energy minimization. Subsequently, the dislocation loop was inserted, and another energy minimization step was launched to obtain the initial static equilibrium configuration. Subsequent to these steps, dynamic relaxation was carried out. Initially, all atoms were assigned random velocities to produce the desired initial temperature, T. With two vacuum regions at the edge of simulation box along the y-direction, an isobaric-isothermal (NPT) ensemble was employed to obtain thermal equilibration configuration. The time step employed for dynamic relaxation was set at 1.0 fs. In this simulation, the velocity-load mode for shear strain was applied, with a corresponding strain rate of 1 × 10^7 s−1. The timestep for the dynamic shearing process remained consistent at 1.0 fs. The major simulations were conducted at a temperature of 318 K. Additionally, temperatures range is from 100 K to 900 K with the aim of improving the applicability of the study. The study focuses on dislocation loop sizes ranging from 1.0 to 10.0 nm. Additionally, the Burgers vectors of the dislocation loops, including 1/2<111> and <100>, were also taken into consideration to explore their effect on the interactions in this study. The sample was firstly annealed at 1273 K for one hour to remove the damage associated with the electric discharge machine cutting and to recrystallize the grains. An EBSD scan is performed over an area of 800 μm × 600 μm where the mean size of grain is 37.5 μm. Condition: unirradiated; Temperature: 300 K

Processing Text: The LDX 2101 material was prepared in an electric arc furnace, with an argon oxygen decarburizer, ladle refining furnace and continuous casting process. After casting, the LDX 2101 material was homogenized by heat treatment at 1250 °C for 1 h. After heat treatment, three samples were cut (10 mm thick) from LDX 2101 material for hot rolling at 1250 °C. In order to study the influence of different distributions of hot rolling reduction on the microstructure and mechanical properties, a reduction of 50 % is distributed in the first pass, and the thickness decreases to 10 mm→5 mm→4 mm→3 mm. In addition, a reduction of 50 % was distributed in the middle pass, and the thickness decreased to 10 mm→8 mm→4 mm→3 mm. Finally, the 50 % reduction is distributed in the last pass, and the thickness decreases to 10 mm→8 mm→6 mm→3 mm. After the rolling experiment, each sample was quenched in water to retain the deformed structure. After rolling, samples were prepared along the rolling direction (RD) for microscopy and mechanical testing. The microstructure of the specimens was analyzed by DM2500 optical microscope (Quanta FEG 450), and the specimens were etched in 10 % oxalic acid solution for 25 s. The dog bone-shaped tensile specimens with length of 15 mm, width of 5 mm and thickness of 3 mm were machined (by electric discharge machining) from the rolled plate along the RD. The tensile test at room temperature at a displacement rate of 1 mm/min was carried out on mTS810 tensile machine. The phase structure after deformation was determined by XRD. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) was used to analyze the grain, stress-strain distribution and deformation mechanism of the phases. In order to remove the surface stress, electrolytic polishing was performed in 10 % perchlorate ethanol at 30 V for 20 s. Lastly, transmission electron microscopy (TEM, 200 kV JEM-2200FS field emission electron microscope) was performed to investigate the microstructure of LDX 2101 material after different rolling distribution. Sample: B50; Rolling reduction distribution: large deformation applied at the end

Processing Text: Raw powders with a purity of 99.99 wt% for titanium (Ti) and 99.9 wt% for molybdenum (Mo) were purchased from a reputable commercial supplier. Ti and Mo powders were mixed in a high-energy ball milling machine at a weight ratio of 90 to 10 using stainless steel balls with a diameter of 9 mm. The ball-to-powder ratio is 10:1, rotating at a speed of 1725 rpm for a duration of 10 min. Mixed powders were then subjected to loading at a pressure of 400 MPa for 5 min to prepare preform blanks. Some preform blanks were subsequently transferred into a hot-pressing furnace where they underwent a sintering process. Those preform blanks were heated to 850 °C and simultaneously pressurized to 65 MPa within 10 min followed by holding for 3 min. Finally, the sintered specimen was cooled down to 300 °C inside the furnace before being air-cooled to room temperature. After hot-pressing sintering, specimens underwent sequential diffusion and annealing heat treatments to adjust their microstructure. A diffusion temperature of 900 °C was selected. Additionally, taking into account the highest temperature of BCC phase separation (802 °C) and the eutectoid temperature (673 °C), specimens were annealed respectively at 650, 750, and 850 °C for 2 h. The subsequent VED values range between 30 and 127 J/mm3, with the benchmark combination found in batches with 1700 mm/s and 350 W, yielding a VED above 100 J/mm3. Processing Text: The elemental powders used in this investigation -Titanium (Ti), Aluminum (Al), and Vanadium (V)-were purchased from Alfa Aesar, USA, with an average size of 45 µm and a purity of more than 99%. The elemental powder was weighed using a digital weighing balance in the weight percentages of Ti (89 wt%), Al (6 wt%), and V (5 wt%). Milling was performed at different durations to drastically modify the internal structure (achieve more grain refinement) and investigate the influence of particle size on microstructure and mechanical performance. A powder sample of 5 g was taken from the vial at intervals of 20 h for characterization during the synthesis of Ti-6Al-5 V alloy powders. XRD analysis was performed using a Philips PANalytical instrument with a CuKα radiation source (λ = 0.1541 nm). The mean crystal size and strain were determined by X-ray peak profile analysis, taking into account the major reflection peaks in the 2θ range of 30° to 90°. HR-SEM (FEI Quanta FEG 200 microscope) and HR-TEM (JEOL Japan, JEM-2100 Plus microscope) were used for microstructural observations of the milled powder samples. SPS was used to make bulk samples using the M/s FCT Systeme GmbH machine at 1050 °C with 50 MPa pressure. A heating rate of 100 °C/min was used, and the SPS was performed under a vacuum atmosphere. Each sample was taken around 6 min during SPS, and the samples were consolidated inside a graphite die-set, producing φ 15 mm and 10 mm (height). Quanta FEG 650 FE-SEM attached with an EBSD detector was used for detailed microstructural analyses. HR-TEM was also carried out on the spark plasma-sintered sample after making the sample a thin foil with a size of around 120 nm. Vickers micro-hardness tests were conducted on sintered specimens. A 50gf load was applied with a dwell duration of 5 s. Testing was performed at 10 different locations, and the average result was used for interpretation. Cylindrical samples with dimensions of ϕ 8 mm and 10 mm (height) were fabricated from the spark plasma-sintered sample, following the ASTM E9 standard. Ti-6Al-5 V-0 h and Ti-6Al-5 V-120 h samples were subjected to compression tests. Three trials were conducted for each alloy in the compression test, and the average result was used for investigation. Processing route: MA+SPS; Mechanical Testing: Compression; Ref: [19]

Ti and Zr powder were manufactured by gas atomization, Nb and Ta powder were manufactured by plasma rotation electrode process (PREP). The powder granules are spherical. High purity Ar was used as a protective atmosphere, oxygen content <100 ppm, build platform using pure titanium substrate, which was preheated to 200 °C. Processing Text: The feedstock powder utilized in this work were commercially available MoO2 and Mo powders (average particle size <300 nm and <200 nm, purity >99.9 %) supplied by Xi'an Rare Metal Materials Research Institute Co., LTD. The Mo composites were fabricated successively via low-energy ball-milling, hydrogen reduction and spark plasma sintering (SPS). Initially, the mixed MoO2 and TiC powders in a weight ratio of 99/1 were uniformly blended in a planetary mill for 4 h using ZrO2 ceramic jar and ball, where anhydrous ethanol was served as the grinding medium. The rotating speed is 350 rpm and the ball-to-powder mass ratio is 8:1. Subsequently, the ball-milled mixture was subjected to reduction process in a flowing dry hydrogen (≥99.999 %, 1 L/min) at 850 °C for 2 h and 900 °C for 1 h. Then the as-reduced composite powders were consolidated by SPS technique at 1100 °C, 1200 °C, and 1300 °C for 10 min with a heating rate of 50 °C/min and a pressure of 40 MPa. For comparison, a sample designated as pure molybdenum prepared through the same procedures was created as a control group, where the sintering circumstances identical to those of MT2, including 4 h ball-milling of Mo powder, then sintered the powder at 1200 °C. Processing Text: Electron beam freeform fabrication (EBF3) additive manufacturing technique has been successfully employed to print the non-weldable Al-5Cu thin-walled parts through an optimized set of process parameters. The process parameters were optimized, and the grain evolution mechanism with inherited characteristics is disclosed by both experimental and simulation methods. The composition of Cu: 4.90, Mn: 0.29, Ti: 0.14, V: 0.09, Cd: 0.29, Zr: 0.09, Fe: 0.08, Si: 0.03, Al: balance, wt% was determined by using the inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) method. The multiple sets of process parameters with various traveling speeds and feeding speeds were designed to build the single-track walls (height: 60 mm and length: 80 mm). Prior to the EBF3 printing, the wire material and the ground substrates were dried in an oven at 80 °C for 4 h. In order to obtain the temperature field of single-track walls, especially within melt pools, a numerical model was built using the ANSYS software. The “element birth and death” technique was applied to model the layer-by-layer deposition process. The numerical model was validated by the experimental results of melt pool morphology and in-situmonitored thermal cycle curves of substrate. The as-built sample with the optimum set of process parameters was subjected to solid solution treatment at 530 °C for 2 h and then water quenching at room temperature, followed by artificial aging treatment at 170 °C for 8 h. Post-heat treatment is conducted to engineer the desirable microstructure containing multiple nanostructures, i.e., the nanoscale θ"" and θ' precipitates, stacking faulted zones and Al-Cu-Cd clusters, leading to a high-strength Al-5Cu alloy with good ductility. After solution and aging heat treatment, Al-Cu-Cd nanoclusters (∼ 2 nm in Dia.) are generated, which facilitates the formation of nanoscale stacking faulted zones (∼11 nm). Meanwhile, as heterogeneous nucleation sites, Al-Cu-Cd nanoclusters effectively promote θ'-Al2Cu phase (∼ 19 - 114 nm) precipitation to enable the coexistence with fine θ""-Al3Cu precipitates (∼ 7 - 37 nm). Condition: As-built
Processing Word: Condition: As-built

Processing Text: Ingots of Ni34Co28Cr28Al10 MPEA were fabricated by vacuum arc melting (VAM) in Ar protecting atmosphere. High-purity elemental metal powders of Ni, Co, Cr and Al, > 99.99% purity for each, were mixed to achieve the targeted composition. The mixtures were melted and then solidified in a button-shaped water-cooled copper mold to obtain bulk ingots. To ensure uniform distribution of each element, all ingots were flipped and remelted at least five times. Additionally, electromagnetic stirrer was used during the last two remelting to further enhance elements homogeneous distribution of elements. Finally, these ingots were obtained by molding in copper mold with baguette shape, each measuring approximately 60 × 25 × 10 mm3. To eliminate the possible segregation of elements, as-cast samples were homogenized at 1200 ℃ for 4 h followed by water-quenching, and these samples were named HT. Subsequently, selected HT samples were aged at 700 ℃ for 2 h respectively and then quenched in water, and the corresponding samples were termed as Aged700. In the end, three types of samples were obtained: AC (as-cast), HT, Aged700. All the heat treatment was carried out under argon gas protection to prevent excessive oxidation of the samples. Sample: AC; Microstructure: FCC phase with L1 2 precipitates and B2 phase with BCC precipitates

Material Name: Mg alloy and Al composite (ARB processed)
Processing Text: Before roll bonding, each sheet was brushed and degreased. The surface-treated layers were stacked as a sequence of Al/Mg/Al and were tightly fastened by steel wire. The first process, conventional accumulative roll bonding (ARB), was carried out with seven passes. In the first pass, a 78% reduction in thickness was applied to achieve strong adherence between layers. In the next six passes, a 50% thickness reduction was applied. Between passes, the rolled composites were cut in length to achieve equal portions. They were then surface-treated and stacked together. The second process, cross-accumulative roll bonding (CARB), was completely similar to the previous procedure with only one difference. The rolling direction (RD) was changed 90° with respect to the normal direction (ND). In the third procedure, before employing the CARB method, the Al and Mg AZ31 sheets were kept in a furnace at 400 °C for 120 min, to remove imperfections and improve deformability. In all three procedures, room-temperature roll bonding was employed. Initial pass, before changing the strain path and pre-annealing treatment

Processing Text: Cylindrical ingots (110 mm diameter; 90 mm high) of the vanadium-free MEA Ni43.4Co25.3Cr25.3Al3Ti3 (at.%) were cast by a magnetic suspension melting technique, using the same melting parameters. A 10 mm thick piece of each MEA was cut off via electrical discharge machining and homogenized at 1150 °C for 4 h. Subsequently, the pieces were cold rolled to a total thickness reduction of 80 % with a 5 % reduction in thickness for each pass. The vanadium-free MEA was aged at either 700 °C for 24 h or 900 °C for 24 h, which are referred to as V07 and V09, respectively. In addition, both the cold-rolled vanadium-free MEA were annealed at 1100 °C for 24 h to compare the microstructure with the aged MEA. All the heat treatments (i.e. homogenization, annealing, and aging) are conducted in an argon atmosphere, all of which are followed by water quenching. Temperature: 77 K

Processing Text: Ti 1.5 NbVAl x (0.25, 0.5, 0.75 and 1) RMEAs were prepared by vacuum arc melting in a water-cooled copper crucible under argon atmosphere, referred to as Al0.25, Al0.5, Al0.75 and Al1, respectively. After placing the raw material in the crucible, the chamber was evacuated to 3*10 −3 Pa. Subsequently, high purity argon gas (99.999 %) was repeatedly used to purge the air for five times. The argon gas is pressurized to 0.05Mpa before the melting alloy. During melting, the Ti ingot is first melted to absorb any residual oxygen and other impurities in the furnace chamber. To prevent the volatilization of the Al element and the segregation of the Nb element, a two-step approach was adopted. First, Ti–Al and Nb–V intermediate alloys were prepared(low-melting-point metal materials were placed at the bottom of the crucible). Each intermediate alloy ingot was remelted by inversion three times. Subsequently, the intermediate alloys were combined, flipped and remelted for five times. Each melting time lasted for 2 min to ensure a more homogeneous composition of the alloys, and then cast into a 150 mm × 15 mm × 15 mm cuboid using copper mold flip casting technology. Test: Tensile; Condition: Room Temperature; Processing state: as-cast
Processing Word: Test: Tensile; Condition: Room Temperature; Processing state: as-cast

Processing Text: The required plate thicknesses, impact velocities, volumetric velocities of sound, and free surface velocity histories are taken from the experimental papers for copper [90]. Processing Text: In order to develop high-strength Al-Cu-Mg-Ag alloys used in the aerospace, this paper studied the mechanical properties and microstructure of Al-Cu-Mg-Ag alloys with T6I4 secondary aging and T6I4 secondary aging combined with deep cryogenic treatment. The alloy used in the experiment was quenched in water immediately after solution treatment at 515 °C for 1.5 h. The combination of DCT and secondary aging is divided into three parts: pre-aging process, aging the alloy at 185 °C for 2 h; DCT process, the same batch of samples were put into the liquid nitrogen tank, and using liquid nitrogen to cryogenically cool the alloy sample at − 196 °C for 0.5 h, 1 h, 2 h, and 4 h, respectively. The samples after cryogenic cooling were air warmed for 1 h and conducted aging.; Re-aging process, the DCT alloys are aged at 120 °C for 9 h. In this experiment, 99.99% industrial pure Al, pure Ag, pure Mg and master alloys of Al-Cu, Al-Zr and Al-Ti were used for smelting. Heat the alloy to 750 °C and keep it warm for a period of time. After the metal is completely melted, add C 2Cl 6and wait for 10 min for degassing and slag removal, and use a metal mold for casting. The size of the ingot is 70 mm × 50 mm× 150 mm. The sample was mechanically punched to a final thickness of 50 µm, and the samples for TEM observation were prepared by the standard twin jet electropolishing method using 70% methanol and 30% nitric acid solution at − 30 °C. Processing Text: High-purity Ti, Zr, V, and Ta (purities are all higher than 99.95 wt.%) were used as raw materials, and Ti 1.5ZrV 0.5Ta 0.5 alloy was fabricated by arc melting which was repeated at least 5 times in a water-cooled copper crucible to improve the chemical homogeneity. The as-cast samples were homogenized at 1200 °C for 6 h and then quenched in water. The homogenized samples were subsequently aged at 400 and 600 °C for 6 h, respectively, and the corresponding samples are named T400 and T600. Tensile tests were performed on a Zwick Z2.5 TH testing machine at room temperature with a strain rate of 5 × 10 -4s -1, using rectangular dog-bone-shaped tensile plate specimens with a gage dimension of 5 mm × 2 mm × 1 mm. The compression tests at room temperature were performed using WDW-200D universal testing machine at a strain rate of 1 × 10 -3s -1. The high-temperature mechanical properties of the alloy were tested by the Gleeble-3500 simulation machine with a strain rate of 1 × 10 -3s -1. The heating rate of the test temperature was 10 °C s -1 and held for 5 min. The compression tests, including room temperature and high temperature, were performed on cylindrical specimens with dimensions of φ6 mm × 9 mm. Condition: Room Temperature; Microstructure: Single-phase solid solution bcc1 phase

Processing Text: In this study, we fabricated a ductile Ti42Hf21Nb21V16 RHEA for additive manufacturing using a directed energy deposition (DED) technique, with a focused laser serving as the energy source. The feedstock powders used for RHEA fabrication include plasma rotation electrode atomized spherical titanium (Ti, purity> 99.95%), niobium (Ti, purity> 99.95%), hafnium (Hf, purity> 99.95%) and vanadium (V, purity> 99.95%) powders， ranging in size from 50 µm to 100 µm (D 50=75 µm). The powders exhibit a perfect spherical shape, indicating good flowability. Initially, the powders were blended in a powder mixer (Turbula, T2F) at room temperature for 2 h, with a revolving speed of 200r/min, within a sealed container. The bulk RHEA sample of size 12 × 70 × 4 mm was fabricated on a pure Ti substrate by additive manufacturing in the form of LENS (Optomec LENS MR-7). The LENS MR-7 is a coaxial powder feeding 3D printer that utilizes a high-powered laser system within a closed chamber filled with argon. The laser, with a spot size of ∼ 600 µm, was used to form the melt pool and remelt the previous path. To ensure a uniform elemental distribution, a remelting procedure was employed in our study. The scanning strategy for the fabrication process is as follows, 1)Layer building: The first layer was scanned in a zigzag strategy, with a powder feed rate of 4 g/min and a laser power of 550 W;2)Remelting procedure: After the first laser stopped, the powder delivery nozzle moved upward by 200 µm (offset value) and the remelting process began. The procedure involved a 45°rotation compared to the previous layer. No powder was delivered to the molten pool during this step and the laser power was increased to 800 W;3)Layer building: Once the remelting process was completed, the powder delivery nozzle was immediately raised by 200 µm, and the powder feed rate was initiated. The working laser power was set to 550 W, and a 45°rotation was applied for layer building;4)Remelting procedure: A scan rotation of 45°, compared to the previous layer, was applied, and a similar remelting procedure (2) was applied to remelt the previously built layer. Layer building: The first layer was scanned in a zigzag strategy, with a powder feed rate of 4 g/min and a laser power of 550 W; Remelting procedure: After the first laser stopped, the powder delivery nozzle moved upward by 200 µm (offset value) and the remelting process began. The procedure involved a 45°rotation compared to the previous layer. No powder was delivered to the molten pool during this step and the laser power was increased to 800 W; Layer building: Once the remelting process was completed, the powder delivery nozzle was immediately raised by 200 µm, and the powder feed rate was initiated. The working laser power was set to 550 W, and a 45°rotation was applied for layer building; Remelting procedure: A scan rotation of 45°, compared to the previous layer, was applied, and a similar remelting procedure (2) was applied to remelt the previously built layer. The four steps were repeated periodically until a bulk specimen with a thickness of ∼ 4 mm was built. The other parameters used in this study remained constant, including a working distance of 10 mm, a scanning speed of 5 mm/s, and a hatching space of 381 µm. Before the experiment, flowing argon was used to reduce the oxygen level to ∼ 200 ppm in the atmospheric chamber which was maintained throughout the entire printing process. After a whole procedure, the actual composition of LENS-fabricated RHEA was determined by energy disperse spectroscopy (EDS). Due to the application of high remelting laser power during the fabrication of the LENS-fabricated sample, severe residual stress was produced. To mitigate this stress and enhance the mechanical performance of the LENS-fabricated sample, a vacuum annealing approach was employed, referred to as-HT state. The annealing process involved heating the samples to 1273 K for 4 h, with a heating rate of 10 K/min and subsequent furnace cooling. The LENS process involves high cooling rates (∼10 3- 10 4K/s), which deviates the microstructure from the equilibrium calculations. Processing state: as-LENS; Fracture strain: 22.5%

Processing Text: Pure Fe, Cr, and Ni powders were used as raw materials. A high-throughput in-situ alloying technique based on Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) was employed to synthesize 80 Fe-Cr-Ni alloys. In-situ alloyed Fe-Cr-Ni samples were fabricated using a self-developed High-Throughput Additive Manufacturing System (HTAMS) developed by the CISRI Group. HTAMS is a modified LPBF machine equipped with automated powder mixing and spreading capabilities. It uniformly deposits powders of varying compositions in a pre-defined ratio on a build platform with four composition-variable zones. The build process was conducted in a high-purity Ar 2 atmosphere, with an oxygen level maintained below 100 PPM. Each sample measured 12 × 10 × 2 mm (XYZ) and featured bevels at the border for facilitating identification of the interface between samples. Samples were divided into two parts using distinct process parameters. For the top and bottom parts of the sample, low power and speed were used to sinter the powders, aiding in distinguishing sample boundaries during subsequent tests, such as microhardness. For the middle part of the sample, sintering + triple remelting strategy was used to promote element diffusion. The laser scan strategy was 'No pattern, zig-zag'. High laser energy (240 W) and a small spot diameter (60 µm) were employed to increase the melt pool temperature; slow laser scanning speed (700 mm/s) was utilized to extend the melting time of the melt pool; multiple remelting strategies were employed to subject individual positions of the sample to repeated melting and solidification cycles. All samples were cut along the YZ plane and then mounted in epoxy resin for subsequent characterization. The sample matrix was ground with 180# to 1500# sandpaper and subsequently polished with 5 µm and 0.5 µm diamond polishes. Four compositions of 2Cr, 12Cr, 12Cr6Ni, and 20Cr7Ni were selected for tensile property testing and top melt pool morphology analysis. Three rectangular specimens, measuring 7 × 40 × 7 mm (XYZ), were fabricated utilizing the sintering + triple remelting processing parameters listed in Table 3. These specimens were subsequently machined according to the dimensions depicted in Fig. 3 prior to undergoing tensile property testing. Additionally, a rectangular specimen with dimensions of 7 × 10 × 7 mm (XYZ) was fabricated and cut along the YZ plane to facilitate analysis of the top melt pool morphology. The tensile tests for the 2Cr, 12Cr, 12Cr6Ni, and 20Cr7Ni were carried out at room temperature with an elongation rate of 0.05 mm/s. Processing Text: The samples were prepared using Co, Ni, Al, Ta, and Cr of high purity (99.9 wt%). The raw materials underwent ultrasonic cleaning with anhydrous ethanol. To achieve a homogeneous composition, the metal material was melted at least 8 times in an arc-melting furnace. For heat treatment, the samples were encapsulated in a quartz tube under vacuum conditions and filled with a small amount of argon gas as a protective atmosphere. They were then quenched in cold water to obtain the desired microstructure at the target temperature. All alloy samples underwent solid solution treatment at 1250 °C for 12 h, and then were aged at 800 °C for 24 h ∼ 200 h to obtain fine γ/γ′ microstructure. To determine the oxidation rate of the sample, the bulk samples were cut into small regular geometries and then placed in a tube furnace at the appropriate temperature under an air atmosphere. During the oxidation tests, the specimens were placed in alumina crucibles, allowing for the measurement of the total weight gain, including any oxide products that may have spalled off. Various specimens were subjected to oxidation for 50 h, 100 h, 200 h, 300 h. The weight gain of each specimen was determined with a high level of accuracy, up to 10−4g. Subsequently, each specimen, along with its respective crucible, was removed from the furnace and weighed together to obtain the mass change by subtracting the initial weight of crucibles. Condition: room temperature

Processing Text: The material used in this work was an as-cast non-equiatomic metastable Fe42Mn28Co10Cr15Si5 (at. %) HEA, obtained by vacuum induced melting under an argon atmosphere. Standard metallography was used to prepare the samples, which were etched with Kalling's-2 reagent (5 g CuCl2, 100 ml HCl and 100 ml C2H5OH) at room temperature for 40 s. Dog-bone shaped specimens for tensile testing with a cross section of 1.5 x 2 mm2 and gauge length of 16 mm were used. Tensile testing was performed at room temperature with a 1x10-3s−1 strain rate. High energy synchrotron X-ray diffraction was used to investigate the deformation behavior of the metastable Fe42Mn28Co10Cr15Si5 HEA during the loading process. Experiments were performed at the P07/High Energy Materials Science beamline of Petra III at the DESY synchrotron, Germany. A monochromatic X-ray beam with a fixed energy of 87 keV was used. A Perkin Elmer 2D detector with a pixel size of 200 x 200 μm2 collected the scattered intensity in the form of Debye-Scherrer rings at 12 different loading stresses. The beam size was set to 700 x 700 μm2. The sample-to-detector distance was of 1.226 m, which was determined by calibration with LaB6 powder. To complement and gain a deeper insight into the evolution of microstructural changes induced during tensile testing to failure of the present metastable HEA, an in-situ Electron Backscatter Diffraction (EBSD) analysis was also performed. The in-situ tensile testing was performed using a Kammrath & Weiss tensile module at room temperature with a strain rate of 3 × 10-4s.
