Processing Text: In this paper, we present a straightforward method for fabricating graphene/Cu composites with an oriented bimodal structure through an in-situ synthesis process combined with hot rolling. Dendritic copper powder, mechanical exfoliation graphene and polyacrylonitrile were used as the raw materials. The graphene/Cu composite with oriented bimodal grains achieves a good balance between strength, ductility and electrical conductivity. Both the fine grains arising from the raised fine particles of dendritic copper powder and the graphene coated on the surface of fine grains facilitate the load transfer, resulting in improved strength of the composites. Furthermore, the formation of coarse grains during sintering and hot rolling deformation contributes to enhanced ductility. Simultaneously, the oriented structure of these coarse grains and graphene sheets establishes an efficient charge transport pathway, ensuring high electrical conductivity. The tensile yield strength of the oriented bimodal composite measures 315 MPa with 0.073 wt% carbon content, while its fracture elongation is 12.4%, and the electrical conductivity remains at 95.7% IACS. This study not only sheds light on the synergistic effects between graphene and copper in a bimodal composite system but also introduces a methodology for tailoring the microstructure to achieve a desired balance between mechanical strength, ductility, and electrical conductivity. Dendritic copper powder, mechanical exfoliation graphene and polyacrylonitrile (PAN) were used as the raw materials. PAN is a common raw material for the preparation of carbon fiber, which is easy to obtain and can be uniformly coated with copper powder and has a significant tendency to graphitization. We obtain bimodal structure by preserving the small raised fine copper particles by transforming PAN to graphene on the surface of dendritic copper powder during heat treatment and sintering process, and then obtain oriented structure by hot rolling. Copper powder (200 mesh electrolytic copper powder), Polyacrylonitrile (PAN) and N, N-dimethylformamide (DMF) were purchased from Aladdin Company. The mechanical exfoliation graphene (G M) was purchased from Xiamen Kaina Graphene Technology Co., Ltd. The amounts of raw materials used for each sample is shown in Table 1. G Mand the PAN were added to DMF for magnetic stirring for 12 h, and then 33 g of copper powder was added to continue stirring for 1 h. The obtained slurry was filtered and put into a copper boat for heat treatment. Heat treatment was performed at 250 °C for 2 h and at 800 °C for 5 min at a heating rate of 10 °C/min under H 2/Ar atmosphere (with a H 2volume fraction of 17%) for all samples. Processing Text: The (CoNiV) 95 Al 3 Ti 2 (at.%) MEA was first melted by electromagnetic levitation under the protection of an argon atmosphere. The melting process was repeated five times to ensure chemical homogeneity, and subsequently, the material was cast into ingots. Following the casting, the ingots were solution-treated at 1373 K for 8 h in a vacuum environment, followed by water quenching. Afterwards, they were cold rolled to achieve a 90 % reduction in total thickness through multiple cycles, with each rolling cycle reducing the thickness by 0.1 mm. Finally, the cold-rolled plates were annealed under vacuum conditions at varying temperatures: 1373 K for 8 h, 1273 K for 3 min, and 1273 K for 1 min. Processing Text: The as-received 321ss rods were machined into a dog-shaped torsion specimens with a gauge dimensions of ∼60 mm in length and ∼5 mm in radius (R). The 321ss torsion specimens were austenitized at 1100 °C for 2 h to eliminate the effect of previous processing and obtain a single-phase γaustenitic coarse-grained (CG) microstructure. Then, the CG 321ss were subjected to small angle cyclic torsion (CT) processing with torsion angle of 5∼30°, torsion rate of 60°/min and cycle number of 200. The CT-treated samples were defined as CT-5, CT-10, CT-20, CT-30 (the numbers stand for CT torsion angle). The phase compositions and volume fractions of the strain-induced martensites at different radii in the radial direction of the CT-20 and CG 321ss before and after tensile deformation were measured by both micro-XRD (Bruker DB discover) with a diffraction beam of 1 mm and EBSD characterizations (JSM-7200F) with a step size of 0.3 μm and scanning region of 900 × 900 μm 2. The micro-XRD were taken at the cross-section of sample and the positions were shown in Fig. 1. To fix the position where micro-XRD is taken, the target positions are determined through an optical microscope, as a result, the fixed point measurement can be carried out. The volume fraction of α′martensite was estimated from the peak intensities Ihkl, and calculated using the formula, Vα′= Ibcc(110)/( Ibcc(110)+ Ifcc(111)) [ 25]. The EBSD raw data were further analyzed by OIM Analysis to acquire the average γgrain size, misorientation angle, grain boundary and GNDs density distributions. The microstructures at the surface of the CT-20 sample before and after tensile deformation with various strains were deeply characterized by TEM and SAED investigations (FEI Talos F200X). Interrupted tensile tests were carried out at various engineering strains to investigate the evolution of microstructures by TEM during tensile deformation. The samples for EBSD and TEM investigations were mechanically polished followed by ion thinning. The Vickers microhardness (HV) at different locations in the radial direction from the surface to the center of the CG and CT-treated specimens before and after tensile deformation were conducted with a load of 9.8 N and a duration of 10 s. Each HV average was obtained from four repeated measurements at the identical radius. The tensile tests of the CG and CT-treated samples were performed at a nominal strain rate of 5 × 10 −4s −1, and the tensile strain was measured by a contact-type extensometer with a gauge length of 25 mm. The loading-unloading-reloading (LUR) tests were conducted at a loading speed of 1.2 mm/min and an unloading speed of 2000 N/min. Condition: CT treatment of 5°
Processing Word: Condition: CT treatment of 5°

Processing Text: FeCrNi MEA was successfully fabricated using laser powder bed fusion. The pre-alloyed powders of FeCrNi consisted of Fe (32.97%), Cr (35.46%), and Ni (31.57%) in atomic percent. The powders were prepared by gas atomization. All samples were fabricated by the LPBF method. For the LPBF process, the as-building samples were fabricated by HBD − 150 (Shanghai Hanbang United 3D Tech Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China). The spot size of laser is 50 μm. LPBF samples were prepared on a building substrate pre-heated to 100 °C under protected Ar atmospheres. The FeCrNi MEA was manufactured using the same parameters as FeCrNi-TA MEA, which included a scanning speed of 800 mm/s, a layer thickness of 30 μm, and the scanning direction rotated 67° between each layer. X-ray diffraction (XRD, Bruker D8 ADVANCE) measurements were operated at 40 kV and 40 mA between 30° and 110° (2θ) with a step size of 3°/min. Specimens were mechanically ground and polished, and then electrically polished with a solution of 10% HClO4 and 90% C2H5OH at 25 V for 30 s at room temperature. The TEM samples were ground to a thickness of 30 μm, made to circle sheets (Ф3 mm), and finally thinned by a standard double jet polishing with an electrolyte solution of 90% ethanol and 10% perchloric acid. Room temperature uniaxial tensile tests (INSTRON 5982 tension machine) were conducted at an engineering strain rate of 1 × 10−3s−1. Three tensile tests were performed for each alloy. The as-built FeCrNi sample demonstrates a notably high relative density, reaching a maximum value of 99.976% (VED = 95.83 J/mm3). Processing state: as-built; Microstructure: single FCC structure

Processing Text: χZr-Ti-5Al-2.5Sn (χ = 0, 10, 20, 30 and 35, wt%, χZTAS) ingots used in this study were prepared by utilizing raw materials of sponge Ti (99.9 wt%), sponge Zr (Zr + Hf ≥ 99.5 wt%), industrially pure Al (99.9 wt%) and Sn (99.9 wt%). The as-cast ingots were prepared by a vacuum non-consumable electro-arc furnace with a Ti-gettered high-purity argon atmosphere. To ensure the chemical homogeneity, the ingots were flipped and remelted at least six times. Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC, NETZSCH-STA449C) was carried out at a heating rate of 10 °C/min by following ASTM: F2004-05(2010) standard to confirm the temperature range of α + β phase region of TiZrAlSn alloys ( Fig. 1a ). According to the DSC curves of as-cast TiZrAlSn alloys, a medium hot-rolling temperature of 920 °C was selected. The TiZrAlSn ingots were put in a vacuum furnace with an argon atmosphere for 30 min at 920 °C before rolling. The 15 mm button-ingots were rolled five passes by using two-high mill rolls to obtain final 5 mm thin plates, and the plates were placed in the furnace for 1 min to keep the sample temperature at 920 °C and water quenched. A holding time of 5 min was also carried out between every two rolling passes. The rolling reduction was ∼2 mm per pass (rolling velocity: 0.4 m/s) and the total deformation was ∼65%. Processing Text: Elements of equal mass and purity of 99.97 % Pt, 99.99 % Au, 99.99 % Cu and 99.99 % Ni were selected and loaded into a cylindrical alumina crucible of Φ 16 mm after ultrasonic cleaning, and then the alumina crucible was placed in a cylindrical graphite crucible of Φ 18 mm. Then the DHL-400 high vacuum arc melting furnace produced by Shenyang Scientific Instrument Research Center of Chinese Academy of Sciences is used to cast Φ 16 mm × 50 mm Pt-25Au-25Cu-25Ni (wt. %) alloy ingots, in which the vacuum in the furnace is 3 × 10 −3Pa, the melting time is 60 s and the melting temperature is 1800 °C. The ingot of length 50 mm is cut off 5 mm by DK7735 EDM, and then cold rolled into thin sheets with thickness of 0.5 mm. Twenty 5 × 5 mm sheets were cut from the middle of the cold rolled sheet alloy as annealed samples, which were used to observe the microstructure and XRD analysis of the alloy after annealing at different temperatures. The remaining alloy ingots are drawn into Φ0.6 mm alloy wire for tensile tests. The total deformation is 90 %, less than 5 % each time for the rolling and drawing process. In order to prevent the alloy wire from slipping in the tensile test, copper sheets should be clamped and fixed at both ends of the chuck. In the experiment, the alloy samples were annealed in an SK-G08123K vacuum tube annealing furnace. The annealing temperature range is 250-950 °C, and the holding time is 1 h. Condition: Post-aging at 350°C for 1 hour

Processing Text: Herein, we report a LPBFed multiphase Fe-18Mn alloy (γ-austenite, ε-martensite, and α-ferrite) fabricated from pre-alloyed powders. After annealing at 650 °C, the alloy with a uniform microstructure displays a high 1 GPa tensile strength, a good fracture elongation of 16 %, and an extremely high work-hardening rate of 8500 MPa. The grain size of a few hundred nanometers provided the excess Gibbs free energy, resulting in an increase in the stacking fault energy (SFE) to 23.9 mJ/m2. Gas atomized pre-alloyed Fe-18Mn (nominal, wt%) powders with a size range from 15 to 53 μm were used for the LPBF processing. The powder's morphology is shown Fig. 1a. Prior to LPBF experiments, the powders were dried at 80 °C for 4 h. The chemical compositions of the powder and processed part are shown in Table 1. The Fe and Mn contents were measured using inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES, Agilent 720, USA), while the O was measured using an oxygen-nitrogen analyzer (ON-3000, NCS, China). The LPBF processing was carried out using a FS271 M LPBF system (Farsoon, Inc., China) under a protective Ar atmosphere, in which the O content was kept below 0.2 vol.%. The laser parameters were a hatch spacing of 80 μm, and a layer thickness of 30 μm, a laser power of 210 W and a scanning speed of 700 mm/s. Inter-layer rotation between scans of 67° was employed to prevent excessive heat accumulation, as shown in Fig. 1c. The heat-treatments were carried out in a SX2-12TS high-temperature vacuum atmosphere furnace, with a heating rate of ∼10 °C/min. To investigate the effects of a simple stress-relieving anneal, samples were annealed at 450 °C, 550 °C, or 650 °C. To investigate the effects of solution annealing, samples were annealed at 750 °C, 850 °C or 1050 °C. All samples were annealed for 2 h, followed by furnace-cooling to room temperature. Processing state: as-built
Processing Word: Processing state: as-built

Processing Text: 316L ASS powders and Ti nanoparticles were employed as deposition materials. The powder morphology and composition of 316L ASS were investigated with a ZEISS Merlin SEM, as illustrated in Fig. 1, with a size distribution between 15 and 53 μm. Ti nanoparticles were incorporated into the base powders at varying concentrations: 0.0 wt%, 0.5 wt%, and 1.0 wt%. To ensure the formation of a homogeneous mixture, 316L ASS powders and Ti particles were mechanically blended via ball milling for 3 h under an inert argon (Ar) atmosphere. The ball milling procedure was conducted with a ball-to-powder weight ratio of 5:1 and a rotational speed of 125 rpm. All the laser processing parameters involved were optimized as follows: the laser power is 600 W, the scanning speed is 4 mm/s, the lifting increment is 0.5 mm, the overlapping rate of 50 % between each track, and the laser beam diameter of 0.5 mm. During the LMD-processed, high purity argon gas was utilized as a protective gas to minimize oxidation as it carried the powders. For microstructural analysis, the specimens were etched with aqua regia, a mix of HCI and HNO 3 in a ratio of 3:1 by volume, for 30 s. They were then examined with an optical microscope (OM). Phase analysis was conducted using a Bruker D8 ADVANCE XRD instrument. The diffraction experiments were carried out in a continuous mode, spanning a 2θ range from 5° to 90° with a scanning speed of 3°/min. Following this, the grain boundary and the phase distribution of the samples were examined using EBSD at an accelerated potential of 15 kV. The sample preparation process involved an electro-polishing procedure in a 9:1 vol ratio mixture of perchloric acid and ethanol at a DC current of 25 V for 50 s, in which the process temperature was maintained at −30 °C. To obtain a more detailed view of the microstructure, thin foils for TEM were obtained using a Struers TenuPol-5 twin-jet electrolytic thinning system. Subsequently, the test was examined using a JEOL JEM-F200 TEM. Processing state: A700-60 sample; Microstructure: nano-scale sigma precipitates, nano/ultrafine-grained microstructure
Processing Word: Processing state: A700-60 sample; Microstructure: nano-scale sigma precipitates, nano/ultrafine-grained microstructure

Processing Text: The Cast_33 superalloy was produced by arc melting under an Ar atmosphere. Then, the Cast_33 sample was homogenized at 1250°C for 24 h and subsequently aged at 900°C for 24 h (same heat treatments as for AM_33), to obtain a γ/γ' microstructure. The γ' microstructural stability of the Cast_33 superalloy at high temperatures was analyzed after long-term aging heat treatments at 800°C, 900°C, and 1000°C for 24 h, 100 h, 200 h, and 500 h. The homogenized samples were sealed in quartz glass capsules filled with Ar; subsequently, aging heat treatment was performed under the abovementioned conditions. The Cast_33 superalloy retained cuboidal γ' precipitates up to 1000°C for 500 h. Moreover, the γ' coarsening was confirmed to follow the LSW model at 800°C and the TIDC model at 900°C and 1000°C in terms of both the size and number density of γ' precipitates. By APT analyses, the sluggish interface diffusion of Co and corresponding interfacial energy reduction induced transition of γ'-coarsening mechanism from LSW to TIDC. Condition: room temperature; Compared to reference superalloys

Processing Text: Both sides of the welded plate were machined into an X-groove, and anchor welds were deposited. The area in the middle of the welded plate for prefabricating cracks was machined into a Y-groove, with a root gap of 2 ± 0.2 mm. Anchor welds were welded before the area for pre-cracking. According to the GB50661-2011 standard [ 26], carbon dioxide arc welding with an electrode YCJ501-1 whose nominal radius equals to 1.2 mm can be used for the anchor weld. Carbon dioxide arc welding with the same electrode YCJ501-1 as the anchor weld was also used for the pre-cracking area, but the welding conditions and interval time were different. The welding process was divided into two steps: first, only the priming weld was deposited for pre-cracking. And then 10 days later, the remaining weld was continuously filled by multi-layer and multi-pass welding. The priming weld was deposited without preheating or drying of the electrode to increase the amount of diffusible hydrogen in the weld. And the priming weld was located at the position of the change in the cross section dimensions where the stress concentration was prominent. Cracked Area Ratio: 16.77%; Fractured at Weld Metal

Processing Text: Samples were fabricated on an SLM125HL machine with powders provided by Höganäs. Cylinders with a height of 96 mm and a diameter of 13 mm were manufactured under argon flux, with a pre-heating of the baseplate to 100 ∘C, and the LPBF parameters recommended by SLM for 316 L stainless steel. The baseplate used in this study was full of vertical samples (45 samples, dimension of baseplate: 125 mm × 125 mm) and so, the building time was approximately 48 h. The chessboard laser scan strategy with islands containing 20 scan vectors (2.4 mm × 2.4 mm) was used. A 67 ∘rotation of the pattern was applied between the layers. PMHT were conducted under secondary vacuum on AB samples. The furnace used is a secondary vacuum furnace which allows to realize heat treatments in a controlled atmosphere. It is equipped with a cold shelter and a sliding carriage facilitating the insertion of samples into the high-temperature zone once the desired temperature is attained, all while maintaining the furnace's vacuum integrity without necessitating its opening. The PMHT was conducted for a duration of 2 h at the prescribed temperature, after which the furnace was gradually cooled under vacuum conditions until the ambient temperature in the high-temperature region was reached. Specifically, in this investigation, samples are introduced into the preheated region of the furnace once it has reached the prescribed temperature, and subsequently held for a duration of two hours. Tensile specimens are machined from the cylinders built with the LPBF process (diameter = 13 mm, height = 96 mm). Heat treatments are realized after the machining in order to relief probable residual stresses induced by machining. Dislocation structures were studied by bright-field TEM for samples in the AB state, and after PMHT at 500, 650, 900 and 1200 °C. TEM analysis were carried out on thin foils extracted from samples in the AB state and heat treated at 500, 650, 900 and 1200 ∘C. Processing state: PMHT at 1200 °C; Contribution source: dislocations
Processing Word: Processing state: PMHT at 1200 °C; Contribution source: dislocations

Processing Text: The cast ingot with an actual composition of Mg-10.15Gd-2.88Dy-2.15Sm-1.51Ag-0.24Zr (wt.%) was prepared from highly pure Mg (99.99 wt%), Ag (99.9 wt%), Mg-22Gd (wt.%), Mg-21Dy (wt.%), Mg-25Sm (wt.%), and Mg-30Zr (wt.%) master alloys in an electric resistant furnace under the atmosphere of pure argon by the water-cooled permanent mold casting method. After standing at ∼750 °C for 20 min and reducing the temperature to 730 °C, the alloy melt was poured into the mold with diameter of ∼90 mm to obtain the as-cast ingot. The ingot was solid solution-treated at 510 °C for 7.5 h, cooled in air for 2 min and then quenched into warm water of ∼80 °C to avoid the generation and propagation of cracks caused by stress during direct quenching in cold water. The solution-treated ingot was machined into the cylindrical-shaped billets with diameter of 80 mm, and then extruded into bars at 350 °C with an extrusion ratio of 28 under an extrusion ram speed of 0.3 mm s−1. The as-extruded sample was named as E. One part of the specimens was heat treated at 480 °C for 2 min (i.e. ESHT) and the other for 20 min; they were both subsequently quickly quenched into warm water of ∼80 °C, which were named as ES2 and ES20, respectively. The aging treatment of the extruded and heat treated samples were aged at 190 °C, and the age-hardening curves were obtained. The samples in peak-aged condition of ES2 and ES20 were named as ES2A and ES20A, respectively. Sample: E; Processing state: as-extruded
Processing Word: Sample: E; Processing state: as-extruded

Processing Text: The Iron-based MEA was fabricated using a vacuum arc melting furnace, and each raw material was sourced from pure commercial elements with a purity of at least 99.9 %. The master alloy was turned upside down five times during melting to ensure chemically homogenized alloy. During the melting process, the alloy was melted upside down five times to ensure a uniform chemical composition. The as-cast ingots were sealed in an evacuated quartz tube, homogenized at 1150 °C for 24 h, and then water quenched to room temperature. The homogenized ingots were subsequently cold-rolled to 87 % reduction in thickness using laboratory-scale rolling equipment. To obtain various grain sizes of the MEA, the tensile specimens were sealed in a quartz tube and annealed at different temperatures for various durations. The specimens were annealed at 950 °C for 100 s, 25 min, and 1 h, respectively. Additionally, in order to achieve a larger grain size within a shorter annealing time, some specimens were subjected to annealing at 1050 °C for 5 h. TEM specimens were mechanically polished using 1200-grit sandpaper to reduce the thickness to less than 100 mm and then jet-polished by an Automatic Twin-Jet Electropolisher (FISCHIONE, Model 110, applied voltage: 27 V). Tensile tests were conducted using a 100-kN-capacity universal Material Testing System (MTS, Model: 810) at room temperature (25 °C) and cryogenic temperature (−100 °C & −196 °C), with a constant strain rate of 0.001 s −1. Grain size: 6.7 μm; Deformed at room temperature

Processing Text: PM-HIPed GH3535 specimens were prepared via a typical PM-HIP process. Argon atomized powder with chemistry listed in Table 1 was used, and the HIPing scheme used was 1175 °C/150 MPa/4 h, and the samples extracted from the PM-HIPed block was not subjected to any further heat treatments. Forged GH3535 specimens were extracted from a forged bar with diameter of 50 mm, and this bar was annealed at 1180 °C after the forging process. Samples with dimensions of 10 × 10 × 1 mm were cut from the forged/PM-HIPed material blocks using a wire-cutting machine. One side of each specimen was polished to mirror finish using SiC paper from 600 grit to 1600 grit and 50 nm Al2O3 powder. Finally, specimens were electropolished at 36 V for 10 s using an electrolyte (50 % H2SO4, 40 % glycerol, and 10 % deionized water) at 0 °C. The polished specimens were irradiated by 1 MeV He+ ions with a dose of 3 × 1016 ions/cm2 at both room temperature and 650 °C. The damage profile was predicted using Stopping Range of Ions in Matter (SRIM) 2013 software in the 'Quick Calculation' Kinchin-Pease mode with displacement energies of 40 eV for Ni, Cr and Fe elements, and 60 eV for Mo element. The specimens for microstructure characterization were prepared using the same methods the samples for irradiation. The general microstructure of the materials was examined using an optical microscope (OM) and a Zeiss Merlin Compact SEM equipped with an electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) detector. The samples for OM observation were etched with a solution consisted of 3 g CuSO4, 10 ml H2SO4, 40 ml HCl and 50 ml H2O. Electron back-scattered diffraction (EBSD) was performed on the electro-polished specimens to analyze the orientations distribution and grain boundary characteristics. The He bubbles and dislocation loops in the irradiated samples were observed using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) (Tecnai G2 F20) with a maximum accelerating voltage of 200 kV. Focus ion beam (FIB) was employed to prepare the cross-sectional TEM samples, thickness of the samples was measured using convergent beam electron diffraction (CEBD). Size and distribution of the helium bubbles in the irradiated samples were characterized using the through focus technique. The dislocation loops were characterized under bright field (BF) mode and dark field (DF) mode. Both the as-received and irradiation specimens were subjected to uniaxial tensile experiments, which were conducted at a constant strain rate of 8.3 × 10−4 s−1 in a uniaxial tensile testing machine (Zwick/Roell Z100) at room temperature. The yield strength of specimens was defined as the stress of 0.2 % strain, and the ultimate tensile strength was derived from the maximum stress. An MTS G200 nano-indentation device with a Berkovich indenter was used to measure the hardness of the samples before and after irradiation both at room temperature. The indent penetration depth was set at 2000 nm and no less than 10 indentation tests were performed on each sample to confirm the statistical significance and the correctness of the test results. Irradiation Temperature: RT; Calculated based on He bubbles and dislocation loops

Processing Text: An ingot of the Fe 50Ni 25Cr 15Al 10 HEAs was produced using an arc-melting furnace. The purity of the raw materials for each element was above 99.95 wt %, and the metal mixture was loaded into a Cu crucible cooled with water. To ensure chemical homogeneity, the HEA ingot was remelted six times. Subsequently, the HEA was drop-casted onto a sheet with dimensions of 25 mm × 4 mm × 80 mm. The sheet was subjected to homogenisation treatment at 1100 °C for 2 h, followed by CR until the thickness was reduced by 60%. The deformed sheet was annealed at 1000 °C for 1 h, after which aging treatment was performed for 10 h at different temperatures (550, 600, 700, and 800 °C); this process was termed as cold rolling and aging (CRA). Before SEM and EBSD, the samples were polished to a mirror surface and then electropolished in a solution of 10 vol% HClO 4 and 90 vol% C 2H 5OH (volume fraction) at a cryogenic temperature of −25 °C. The TEM samples were mechanically ground to a thickness of approximately 40-50 μm and then twin-jet electropolished. Processing state: after 600°C CRA
Processing Word: Processing state: after 600°C CRA

Processing Text: Laser shock peening (LSP) was implemented to treat aircraft landing gear 50CrVA alloy to improve mechanical properties. The LSP treatment was carried out on the LSP experimental equipment with a wavelength of 1064 nm, a pulse width of 20 ns, and a repeat rate of 10 Hz. In the present work, the laser energy was 7.3 J, the spot diameter was 3 mm, an S-shaped loading path was selected, and the overlap was 50 %. The LSP treatment was carried out on an area of 72 mm × 45 mm in the center of the sample, and the pulse laser beam was always perpendicular to the surface of the sample. The absorbing layer applied was a 0.1 mm thick black tape and the confining layer was a transparent running water layer approximately 1-2 mm thick. Material Name: CoCrFeNiMn HEA with the addition of Y2O3
Processing Text: The bulk CoCrFeNiMn high entropy alloy with the addition of Y2O3 is fabricated by directed energy deposition, and its microstructures and mechanical properties were investigated in relation to laser power. The substrate is Q235 steel (Mn < 1.4 %, Si < 0.35 %, S < 0.05 %, P < 0.045 %, C < 0.22 %) with dimensions of 12 cm × 15 cm × 10 cm. It was polished using sandpaper, and afterwards, was washed employing alcohol prior to the laser process. Based on the pre-experiments, it has been observed that the deposited layer showed excellent quality when using a powder feeding speed of 0.2 r/min and a spot diameter of 2 mm. During the laser printing process, high-purity argon gas with a flow rate of 15 L/min was used as a shielding gas to prevent oxidation in the melting pool. The deposition strategy was designed to minimize cracks caused by the disparity in thermal expansion coefficients between the substrate and CoCrFeNiMn HEA. The bottom layer, serving as a transition area, was prepared using a laser power of 300 W. This was followed by deposition at gradually increasing laser power. The vertical axis was adorned with an alternating 90-degree crosshatch pattern. The process parameters are as follows: laser power of 700 W, 800 W and 1000 W, scanning speed of 10 mm/s, and an overlapping rate of 50 %. The bulk samples with dimensions of 38 mm × 10 mm × 12 mm were prepared to utilize the same processing parameters and deposition strategy for material characterization and mechanical tests. The samples for material characterization and mechanical test were removed from the Q235 substrate by employing wire electrical discharge machining (EDM). Then, the samples were polished and washed prior to the test. The sample was ground using SiC sandpaper (400#, 800#, 1200#), and then further ground with 2000# sandpaper in water. Then, the samples were electro-polished in a mixed solution prepared with 45 mL absolute alcohol and 5 mL perchloric acid. During the process, the process parameters were set as follows: a voltage of 30 V, a temperature of -30℃, and an etching time of 30 s. The raw materials for CoCrFeNiMn HEA consist of five powders with non-spherical shapes. The Y2O3 powder with a size of about 50-150 um is employed to enhance the strength of HEA. The powders were blended with a ball crusher for 12 h and then dried at a temperature of 120 °C for a minimum of 2 h. Sample: AM-700; Laser Power: 700 W
Processing Word: Sample: AM-700; Laser Power: 700 W

Processing Text: Four alloys with a nominal composition of Fe-13Cr-4.5Al-1Nb-2Mo- xSi ( x= 0, 0.5, 1, and 2 wt.%) were prepared by arc-melting and cast in the copper moulds with a size of about 55 mm × 22 mm × 15 mm. All cast ingots were first homogenized at 1300 °C for 1 h, followed by air cooling (AC) to room temperature. For the conventional processing route, the alloy ingots were heated to 1300 °C at a heating rate of ∼30 °C/s and rolled at this high temperature to avoid the formation of coarse Laves precipitates. Then, the plates after hot rolling (HR) were further subjected to 300 °C warm rolling (WR) and recrystallization annealing (RX). To introduce the nanoprecipitates into the alloy matrix, a novel processing route was designed. The 15-mm thick alloy plates were first heated to 1100 °C at a heating rate of ∼30 °C/s and hot rolled to 10 mm, and then thinned to 5 mm at 800 °C to refine the coarse grain of the homogenized alloys and produce Laves submicron precipitates, followed by AC to room temperature (RT). The 5 mm-thick alloy plates underwent 300 °C WR with 70% thickness reduction to further refine the layered grain obtained by HR but also introduce more substructures such as dislocation cells. The WR samples experienced fast annealing (FA) to 1150 °C at the heating rate ∼100 °C/s for ∼3 s to promote RX and regression of Laves precipitates obtained in the HR process, followed by water quenching (WQ) to RT. To enhance the density of nucleation sites of Laves nanoprecipitates and promote their uniform distribution in grain interiors during aging, 15% pre-rolling at RT was applied to the alloys to introduce more nucleation sites (e.g. dislocations) before aging with the thickness reduction to ∼1.25 mm. The aging treatment at 600 °C for 1 h was finally performed, followed by AC to RT, rendering a high density of Laves nanoprecipitates prepared uniformly in grain interiors. Processing Text: HEAs are generally categorized into two elements, as depicted in Fig. 6. Recently, HEAs have more potential in many industries than typical alloys. High entropy alloys (HEAs) are hard, strong, and have many properties, including thermostability and corrosion resistance. HEAs also had exceptional chemical and mechanical characteristics. As a result, these alloys offer enormous development potential [ 34]. Till Jan. 2022, more than 300 high entropy alloys have been processed along with more than 35 principal elements. The concept of HEAs is different from traditional alloys because HEAs are not made up of just one or two components. HEAs have been defined in two ways by researchers: the first is based on composition, while the second is based on entropy [ 35]. So, based on composition, high entropy alloys contain a minimum of 5 main elements in the equimolar or near equimolar ratios, as depicted in Fig. 7. The atomic % of each element for these alloys lies between 5 % to 35 %. Although several additional elements were included in the high entropy alloys, the overall percentage of these elements are <5 % [ 36]. However, based on entropy, the HEAs are defined as the random blending of distinct features that yields configurational entropy (ΔSconf.). Further, these alloys are categorized into three types of alloys, as shown in Fig. 8. These materials are termed as high entropy alloys owing to the fact that their random solid & liquid state has basically higher entropies as compared to those in conventional alloys. The evolution of HEAs from conventional alloys is shown in Fig. 9. The main properties of HEAs are as given below: a) High hardness and strength. In the case of HEAs, the uneven atomic radius of distinct elements causes an intensive lattice distortion effect. These types of effects obstruct the dislocation movement, leading to very high hardness and strength [ 34]. The lattice distortion of HEA containing chromium is shown in Fig. 10. Li et al. [ 35] also reported that severe lattice distortion could occur in the high entropy alloy, and each element has its unique and specific atomic size. The Fe51 CCA ingot (2 kg) with a nominal composition of Fe-35.5Ni-4Cr-6.3Al-3.2Ti (at.%) was vacuum induction cast using pure elemental metallic ingots (99.9 wt% purity) and a high-purity argon atmosphere. The cast ingot was homogenised at 1100 °C for 4 h in a muffle furnace purged with argon. The plates with a dimension of 40 mm × 60 mm × 25 mm were cold rolled (CR) to an engineering thickness reduction of 60%. Cold rolling comprised several passes with 5% true strain at each pass to achieve the required reduction in thickness. The recrystallisation temperatures of 900, 950, and 1000 °C were selected from the γ-only phase field (relatively low temperature with single-phase FCC structure to minimise grain growth and to achieve recrystallisation). The cold rolled ingot was subjected to recrystallisation annealing at three different temperatures (900, 950 and 1000 °C) for various durations (5-200 min) followed by water quenching to analyse the kinetics of recrystallisation and grain growth. They were then aged at 630 °C for 16 h to form a γ+γ′-only phase structure with the precipitation of a significant volume fraction of γ′ phase (24%; Fig. 1). The chemical composition of the Fe51 CCA was measured using SEM-EDS and the actual composition was found to be Fe-35.6Ni-4.3Cr-6.1Al-3.5Ti (at.%). d^-0.5 (µm^-0.5) is 0.0280269058295964

Processing Text: WNbMoTaZr RHEA ingots (46 ± 0.5 g) were prepared by the vacuum arc melting method, using raw elements with purities higher than 99.9 wt%. Nine samples with dimension of 4 mm × 4 mm × 2 mm at each layer, as shown in Fig. 1d, were cut using wire electronic discharge machine (WEDM). The effect of sample aspect ratio (1.5, 2, and 2.5, with cross-sections of 3 mm × 3 mm) on the uniformity of the mechanical properties was also examined. Group is 2.968586387434556

In this work, a eutectic high-entropy alloy, CoCrFeNi(TiNb)0.325, was successfully prepared via vacuum arc melting. The CoCrFeNi(TiNb)0.325EHEA master ingot was prepared by vacuum arc melting with a cold copper crucible. After three cycles of argon gas purging, melting and cooling were conducted under vacuum conditions at 0.01 atm. The alloy was remelted a minimum of five times to ensure chemical homogeneity. Subsequently, the thermal behavior was analyzed using high-temperature differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) under a flowing argon atmosphere with a heating rate of 10 K/min. Based on the DSC curve, a heat treatment process was formulated. The sample was annealed in an air environment at 850 ℃ and 1160 ℃ for 12 h, respectively, followed by furnace cooling to room temperature. Samples is 850

The nature of the chemical bonding was analyzed by the LOBSTER package. Then equilibrium phase fraction plots were extracted by CALPHAD with Thermo-calc software. Further, to validate computational results RHEAs were prepared by TIG arc melting and microstructural and phase analysis was done by SEM and XRD. The elastic and mechanical properties were measured by Vickers hardness tester and ultrasound phase spectroscopy. Arc-melted ingots were fabricated under a Ti-gettered high-purity argon atmosphere in a water-cooled copper hearth. The melted ingots were subjected to several runs of remelting and flipping to ensure chemical homogeneity. The as-received MP159 alloy in a cast-and-wrought state is prepared by Central Iron and Steel Research Institute. And the original ingot of MP159 alloy was prepared by vacuum induction melting. Solution treatment at 1000 °C for 1h is then conducted, followed by water quenching. We hereafter denote the solution treated MP159 sample without annealing as WA-MP159. All the heat treatments were carried out in the air condition. Tensile tests on cylindrical specimens with a diameter of 5 mm and a gage length of 30 mm were conducted on an Instron 3369 universal testing machine at RT, 400 °C, 500 °C, 600 °C, 650 °C and 700 °C, respectively. The tensile strain rate is set to be 1.5 × 10 −4s −1. TEM samples were prepared by dual jet polishing at Specimens for using an electrolyte of perchloric acid (10 %) and ethanol (90 %). And the preparation temperature of TEM samples was −30 °C. APT needle samples were milled and prepared using FEI Helios NanoLab G3 UC dual-beam scanning electron microscopy. Temperature is R.T.

Processing Text: Green pellets with a diameter of 10 mm were produced using a 25-ton manual press (Kimaya Engineers, India) at a pressure of 520 MPa. The compacts were sintered in a tube furnace (Swam Equip, India) under a continuous flow of 99.99 % pure argon gas. The green samples were subjected to a sintering temperature range of 560-650 °C, with a 30 °C interval, at a heating rate of 5 °C/min. The duration of sintering was 90 min, followed by controlled cooling within the furnace. Bulk density measurements were performed using the Archimedes principle with a Sartorius Secura YDK03 instrument. Phase analysis was conducted using a Panalytical X-pert powder X-ray diffractometer (Make: Panalytical, Model: X-pert powder). The instrument was equipped with Cu-Kα radiation (λ = 0.15406 nm) for data profile acquisition. The process involved a voltage of 45 kV and a current of 30 mA, with a step size of 0.02 and a duration of 25s/step. Optical microscopy (Quasmo ISI Microscope) and scanning electron microscopy (VEGA 3 LMU TESCAN) were employed to characterize the microstructure. Quantification and mapping of elements were performed using a Field Emission Gun Scanning Electron Microscope (FEGSEM) (JEOL, model: JSM 7800F) equipped with an Energy Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDS) detector. For TEM analysis, specimens were obtained by cutting 300-micron-thick discs from the sintered samples, followed by metallographic polishing to a thickness of less than 100 μm. Subsequently, ion beam milling was applied to the specimens. The crystal structure and lattice imperfections, such as stacking faults, dislocations, and precipitation and their boundaries at the atomic scale, were investigated using a High Resolution- Transmission Electron Microscope (HR-TEM) (Model: JEOL JEM 2100, at an operating voltage of 200 kV). Nanoindentation measurements were performed using a Berkovich diamond indenter with a radius of 150 nm, featuring an included angle of 142.30° and a half angle of 65.27°, within a NANOINDENTER device (BRUKER'S HYSITRON TI PREMIER). A 2 mN load was used for the nanoindentation study and the distance between the two consecutive indentations was 3 μm to evaluate the hardness and modulus. The load-displacement curves were used to generate hardness and elastic modulus profiles across the matrix, intermetallic, and particle interfaces. The room temperature and isothermal compressive strength (at 200 °C, 250 °C, and 300 °C) of the composite were assessed using cylindrical samples (φ10mm x l = 15 mm) with an aspect ratio (l/d) of 1.5. The test was performed using a Universal Testing Machine (Jinan, WDW-100S) following the ASTM E−09standard. For the isothermal compression test, a furnace setup was employed. All samples were sintered at 620 °C due to its verified superior density in line with our previous findings. All samples were subjected to a strain of 0.5 and then water-quenched to facilitate microstructural observation. The strain rate for both room temperature and isothermal tests was set at 10 −4S −1. The compacts were sintered in a tube furnace (Swam Equip, India) under a continuous flow of 99.99 % pure argon gas. The green samples were subjected to a sintering temperature range of 560-650 °C, with a 30 °C interval, at a heating rate of 5 °C/min. The duration of sintering was 90 min, followed by controlled cooling within the furnace. Bulk density measurements were performed using the Archimedes principle with a Sartorius Secura YDK03 instrument. Phase analysis was conducted using a Panalytical X-pert powder X-ray diffractometer (Make: Panalytical, Model: X-pert powder). The instrument was equipped with Cu-Kα radiation (λ = 0.15406 nm) for data profile acquisition. The process involved a voltage of 45 kV and a current of 30 mA, with a step size of 0.02 and a duration of 25s/step. Optical microscopy (Quasmo ISI Microscope) and scanning electron microscopy (VEGA 3 LMU TESCAN) were employed to characterize the microstructure. Quantification and mapping of elements were performed using a Field Emission Gun Scanning Electron Microscope (FEGSEM) (JEOL, model: JSM 7800F) equipped with an Energy Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDS) detector. For TEM analysis, specimens were obtained by cutting 300-micron-thick discs from the sintered samples, followed by metallographic polishing to a thickness of less than 100 μm. Subsequently, ion beam milling was applied to the specimens. The crystal structure and lattice imperfections, such as stacking faults, dislocations, and precipitation and their boundaries at the atomic scale, were investigated using a High Resolution- Transmission Electron Microscope (HR-TEM) (Model: JEOL JEM 2100, at an operating voltage of 200 kV). Nanoindentation measurements were performed using a Berkovich diamond indenter with a radius of 150 nm, featuring an included angle of 142.30° and a half angle of 65.27°, within a NANOINDENTER device (BRUKER'S HYSITRON TI PREMIER). A 2 mN load was used for the nanoindentation study and the distance between the two consecutive indentations was 3 μm to evaluate the hardness and modulus. The load-displacement curves were used to generate hardness and elastic modulus profiles across the matrix, intermetallic, and particle interfaces. The room temperature and isothermal compressive strength (at 200 °C, 250 °C, and 300 °C) of the composite were assessed using cylindrical samples (φ10mm x l = 15 mm) with an aspect ratio (l/d) of 1.5. The test was performed using a Universal Testing Machine (Jinan, WDW-100S) following the ASTM E−09standard. For the isothermal compression test, a furnace setup was employed. All samples were sintered at 620 °C due to its verified superior density in line with our previous findings. All samples were subjected to a strain of 0.5 and then water-quenched to facilitate microstructural observation. The strain rate for both room temperature and isothermal tests was set at 10 −4S −1. Processing Text: Pure metals Al, Co, Cr, Fe and Ni with a purity of 99.5% were weighed according to the nominal composition, and the pre-alloyed ingots were melted by non-consumable vacuum arc furnace. Each pre-alloyed ingot was melted 5 times, and the ingot was turned over before each re-melting to ensure homogeneous composition. Metal rods with a diameter of 7 mm were cut from the pre-alloyed ingot by spark machining, and the surface was polished and cleaned to serve as a material for directional solidification. The metal rods with a total length of about 10 cm were placed in the ceramic tubes and then placed in the Bridgeman directional solidification furnace, where the rods were melted by radiative heat transfer through graphite and held for 50 min to ensure complete melting and uniform temperature distribution. The alloy melt was withdrawn into the Ga In liquid using a pulling system with withdrawal speeds of 5 μm/s, 50 μm/s, 100 μm/s, 150 μm/s and 200 μm/s, respectively. When the withdrawal distance reached 4 cm, the alloy melt was rapidly pulled into the Ga In liquid and quenched to retain the solid-liquid (S-L) interface morphology. Finally, a directional solidification rod with a length of about 10 cm was obtained, including non-directional solidification zone, directional solidification zone and quenching zone. Directional solidification rods were cut along the direction parallel to the heat flow to prepare specimens for microstructure observation and mechanical property testing. The phase composition was analyzed by X-ray diffraction (XRD, MXP21V AHF) using Cu Ka radiation in the range of 20°-100° at a rate of 8°/min. The microstructure and element distribution were analyzed by scanning electron microscope (SEM, TM4000) and transmission electron microscope (TEM FEI Talos F200). Electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD, Zeiss Super55) was used to determine the phase structure and strain distribution. The EBSD samples were electro-polished in a mixture of 90% alcohol and 10% perchloric acid with an applied voltage of 15 V for 10-12 s at room temperature. The mechanical properties were tested using an Instron 5569 universal tensile testing machine at a tensile speed of 1 mm/min. The tensile specimen is dog-bone shaped, with a gauge length of 16 mm, a thickness of 1.8 mm, and a width of 2 mm. The specimens under each directional solidification condition were tested three times to ensure the accuracy of the data. The nano-hardness of different phases was tested by G200 nanoindentation, and the maximum depth was set to 300 nm. Solidification rate(µm/s) is 4.838709677419345

Processing Text: All specimens were manufactured by an EOS M290 L-PBF machine, equipped with a 400 W Yb-fiber laser with a laser spot size of 80μm in diameter. The printing laser power was 210 W and the laser moved in a stripe printing pattern with a 50μm hatch distance. The printing head scanning speed was 1750 mm/s and the powder layer thickness was 20μm. After each layer was printed, the subsequent layer was rotated by 67 ∘ as indicated in Fig. 1a for the coherence of microstructure through whole specimens. After the printing process, several heat treatments were implemented on all specimens. The first step was hot isostatic pressing (HIP) at 1200 °C for 4 h under 200 MPa. The following step was standard solution heat treatment at 1120 °C for 2 h. The final step was aging at 850 °C for 24 h. After heat treatments, all specimens were machined in dog-bone shaped tensile bars as shown in Fig. 1c. The gauge length was 24.5 mm and the gauge diameter varied from 3 mm to 5 mm in Fig. 1d. Uniaxial tensile tests were carried out on an Instron 5982 universal testing system with a 100 kN loading capacity and crosshead movement speed ranging from 0.0001 to 1016 mm per minute. The temperature was measured by three temperature sensors at three zones of the furnace. An extra sensor was attached to the middle of specimens for accurate measurement of temperatures at the surface. The testing temperature ranged from 650 °C to 950 °C for different specimens. A dwell time of 2 h after reaching the target temperature was used before the start of tests to achieve a homogeneous thermal distribution as well as for stabilizing the thermal expansion of the specimens. The strain rate was 10 −3, that is, a displacement rate of 1.47 mm/min. The strain was measured by means of a 7361C extensometer attached to the middle of the specimens. Once the strain measured by the extensometer reached 2%, the strain data was read from the crosshead displacement. Pristine specimen’s surfaces and cross sections from the near fracture surface were mechanical polished. For the phase identification, the surfaces were etched in a 10% phosphoric acid solution. A field emission scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Hitachi SU70) with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) and Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) was occupied for morphology observation at an acceleration voltage of 20 kV. The corresponding chemical composition was determined by EDS and analyzed in the Oxford Instruments’ INCA software. EBSD was measured via an Oxford NORDLYS EBSD detector and acquired by Flamenco software. nan is 650.8403361344538

The equimolar CoCrFeNi HEA ingot used in this work was prepared by vacuum induction levitation melting from pure Co, Cr, Fe, and Ni metals with 99.9 wt.% purity constituent elements. The ingot was remelted four times to promote chemical homogeneity and then dropped into a rectangular cross-section copper mold with a length of 300 mm and an inner diameter of 25 mm. The ingot was cut to a rod of diameter 20 mm and length 200 mm, which was then homogenized at 1473 K for 24 h. The rod was first hot-rotary swaged to 8 mm in diameter along the longitudinal direction after preheating at 1173 K for 1 h, and then hot-drawn to 1 mm in steps at 1023 K. Subsequently, the HEA wires of diameter 1 mm was subjected to multi-pass cold-drawing at ambient temperature with an areal reduction of ∼10% followed by annealing at 1173 K for 1 h in each step, resulting in a final diameter of ∼70 µm with a length of more than 300 m. The CoCrFeNi microfibers were further treated by ECT. The electric current was applied parallel to the length direction of the treated microfiber using a precision direct current (DC) power supply for 480 s with various current densities of j= 100, 120, 140, 160, 180, 200 A/mm², and the corresponding specimens are labeled as ECT100, ECT120, ECT140, ECT160, ECT180 and ECT200, which reach a stable temperature of 623 K, 747 K, 850 K, 943 K, 1013 K, and 1075 K during the ECT, respectively, as measured by an FLIR A325sc infrared camera. Processing Text: The Inconel 718 superalloy was fabricated using spark plasma sintering (SPS) technology with varying sintering temperatures and heating rates. The raw Inconel 718 superalloy powders were sourced from Jiangsu Vilory Advanced Materials Technology Co., Ltd., China. The powders primarily consist of Ni (51.5 %), Cr (22.48 %), Fe (19.67 %), Nb (3.78 %), Al (1.31 %), Ti (1.25 %), etc. The powders were provided in sizes ranging from 30 to 70 µm. In order to decrease particle size, increase contact area, and enhance interparticle integration during the sintering process, ball milling was employed. The parameters used for ball milling can be found in Table 1. Cylindrical sintered specimens were then prepared using a spark plasma sintering system (SPS-mini, Shanghai Chenhua Science and Technology Co., Ltd., China). The sintering system had a maximum current of 3000 A, a maximum voltage of 30 kV, a maximum heating rate of 300 °C/min, and a minimum vacuum of 10 −4Pa. Sintering tests were carried out using various temperatures and heating rates under a sintering pressure of 50 MPa and a holding time of 5 min, as indicated in Table 2. The resulting 5 sets of sintered specimens were named S-1 to S-5, respectively. To investigate the effect of pulse current on the sintering neck formation process in the heating stage, 4 specimens were sintered with a heating rate of 100 °C/min, and the sintering time is listed in Table 3. When the target sintering time was reached, the sintering process was immediately halted, obtaining a sintering specimen with the characters of that time. The Inconel 718 superalloy powders after ball-milling were weighed using a balance, and loaded into graphite molds. Before filling the powders into the mold, the graphite spray was evenly sprayed on the inner wall of the mold cavity and the surface of the punches, to prevent the powder from sticking to the mold cavity and the punches when sintering, improving the dimensional accuracy of the sintered specimens. The experimental molds and punches are composed of hot-pressed graphite material (type GTTKG347) with a compressive strength of 100 MPa, supplied by Shanghai Chenda Company, China. A miniature temperature-measuring hole is located at the center of the outer surface of the mold, which is aligned with the temperature-measuring device during installation to facilitate real-time measurement of the sintering temperature. nan is S-1

The fabrication process was conducted in a vacuum induction melting furnace operating under an argon atmosphere. Processing Text: Ti2NbVAl0.3Zrx (x = 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1) LRHEAs were prepared by the vacuum arc melting furnace under the protection of high-purity argon gas. Metal particles with purity >99.95 % were used as raw materials. In order to avoid melting losses and melting segregation, Ti-Al and Zr-V-Nb intermediate alloys were prepared. Finally, the intermediate alloys were combined and melted six times repeatedly. Before melting, the air pressure in the chamber was reduced to 3*10−3Pa and the chamber underwent five purging cycles with high-purity argon gas. This was followed by melting Ti ingots to remove residual oxygen in the chamber and prevent sample contamination. SEM samples were polished using a 0.3 μm alumina suspension, followed by metallographic etching using a solution of HCL, HNO3, and HF in a ratio of 10:3:1. TEM samples were mechanically ground to 50 μm and subsequently thinned using an ionic thinning machine (Gatan 695). Tensile tests were conducted on the specimens using an electronic universal testing machine (Instron 68 MT-55) at a quasi-static strain rate of 1*10−3S−1. The tensile samples were identified with a section size of 5mm × 2mm × 1.5 mm and were mechanically ground to 2000 mesh prior to the commencement of the experiment. Vickers hardness of the samples was measured using TMHV-1000Z with a load of 200g and a force holding time of 15s. The corrosion behavior of the current alloy system was tested using an electrochemical workstation (VersaSTAT 3F) in a 3.5 wt% NaCl solution. The sample size was 10mm × 10mm × 4 mm, with a test area 1 cm2, and was mechanically ground to 2000 mesh prior to testing. Electrochemical tests were conducted in a three-electrode electrolytic cell setup, with the sample serving as the working electrode, the saturated calomel electrode (SCE) as the reference electrode, and the platinum electrode as the auxiliary electrode. The open circuit potential was initially stabilized for 1800s, followed by potentiodynamic polarization (PDP) and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) tests. The PDP test was conducted at a scan rate of 0.333 mV/s, starting from an initial potential of −0.3V SCE(vs. OCP) and ending at 2V SCE(vs. OCP). EIS measurements were carried out with an amplitude of 5 mV/s and a frequency range from 105Hz to 10−2Hz. Each sample underwent three tests under identical conditions to ensure result accuracy. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS; Thermo Scientific K-Alpha) analyzed the oxide film formed on the sample surface. Engineering Strain (%) is 5.998217468805704

Processing Text: Fabrication of CrCoNi alloy by pulsed-wave laser powder bed fusion (LPBF). (a)A schematic of pulsed-LPBF of pre-alloyed CrCoNi powder with an inserted crystalline lattice structure of the MEA. (b)A schematic showing the comparison of emission mode between pulsed-wave and continuous-wave lasers. (c)As-built microstructural features of the pulsed-LPBF CrCoNi alloy at various length scales from the cross-section view. The pulsed-wave laser induces extra thermal cycles, generating additional pre-existing dislocations that are uniformly distributed within the interiors of solidification cells, a phenomenon distinct from conventional AM. The first batch of CrCoNi alloy samples was printed by a customized LPBF machine equipped with a 200 W SPI fiber laser source, as schematically shown in Fig. 1a. In contrast with the continuous-wave lasers used in typical LPBF processes, the laser in this work was emitted in repeated pulses at a frequency of 1000 kHz ( Fig. 1b). The working duration of each pulse was ∼250 ns. The wavelength and the spot size of the laser were 1060 nm and 100 µm respectively. The prints employed gas-atomized CrCoNi powder with a nominal composition shown in Table S1. The particle size of the spherical powder ranged from 20 to 53 µm. The pulsed-LPBF prints were conducted in a nitrogen atmosphere and maintained at a constant parameter set including a laser power of 200 W, a powder layer thickness of 40 µm, and a scan rotation of 90° between layers. Initial optimization of process parameters was conducted with cubic CrCoNi samples (6 mm × 6 mm × 6 mm) using scanning speeds of 400-1000 mm/s and hatch spacings of 40-100 µm. After observations of polished cross-section surfaces by optical microscopy, the optimized pulsed-LPBF process window was refined to scanning speeds of 500-800 mm/s and hatch spacings of 60-100 µm, ensuring the relative density of the printed MEA is higher than 99.8% ( Fig. S1a). The surface roughness generated within this refined process window is in a range of 10-20 µm ( Fig. S1b). These cubic samples were printed starting with a 0° laser scan followed by a 90° rotation. The samples (30 mm length × 10 mm width × 6 mm height) for mechanical tests were printed starting with a 45° laser scan followed by a 90° rotation. To compare the effect of continuous-wave and pulsed-wave lasers on microstructure and mechanical properties, a second batch of CrCoNi samples was printed with the same geometric size using a commercial LPBF machine (EOS M290). The continuous-wave laser used in this batch had the same wavelength (1060 nm) and spot size (100 µm) as the pulsed-wave laser used in the first batch. To decouple the influence of other factors, the print parameters were selected from the process window optimized in the first batch print: a laser power of 200 W, a scanning speed of 500 mm/s, a hatch spacing of 80 µm, a layer thickness of 40 µm, and a scan rotation of 90°. The relative density of the fabricated sample was also higher than 99.8% ( Fig. S1c). Uniform elongation (%) is 1.6252390057361374

Processing Text: A Ti6242 bar was employed in the as hot-rolled condition with a chemical composition of Ti-6.31Al-1.95Sn-4.12Zr-1.91Mo-0.1Si (wt.%), and its β transition temperature ( Tβ) was measured to be approximately 1006 °C by a DIL805A/D type dilatometer. The samples were subjected to three-step heat treatment to obtain heterogeneous structure. Firstly, the samples were solution treated at 950 °C for 1 h, and then quenched in the water (WQ), designated as Step 1. Secondly, the samples were rapidly up-quenched to the single β phase region for 12 s by high-frequency induction heating to transform the equiaxed α pphase to β phase, but maintained the solute partition in the two phases as the limited solution time was not enough for the homogenization of alloying elements (Step 2). Finally, the samples were aged at 590 and 620 °C for 8 h, respectively, and then cooled in air (AC) to precipitate heterostructure with different thicknesses of α lamella (Step 3). The two samples after three-step heat treatment were called HS-590 and HS-620. For comparison, the EM samples with homogeneous microstructure were prepared using the same treatments in steps 1 and 3, and designated as EM-590 and EM-620. Elongation (%) is 2.2935916542473898

Processing Text: Tungsten heavy alloys (WHAs) prepared using laser additive manufacturing (AM) exhibit intricate geometries, albeit with limited mechanical properties. Here we designed a high-strength WHA featuring a FeCrCoNi high entropy alloy (HEA) binder via the laser metal deposition (LMD) technique. Due to the distinctive thermal cycle and rapid cooling rate, the as-deposited alloys exhibit microstructures with hypoeutectic, eutectic-like, and spot-like characteristics. The μ phase precipitated out from the supersaturated solid solution, thereby nucleating massive dislocations on the FeCrCoNi matrix to increase the work hardening rate. Furthermore, the μ phase formed an ultrafine intermetallic compound (IMC) layer around the W grain, reducing the hole or crack between the W grain and FeCrCoNi matrix. Processing Text: In-situ titanium boride (TiB) reinforced titanium matrix composites (TMCs) were fabricated via selective laser melting (SLM) technique. The Ti6Al4V alloy powders were mechanically mixed with 0.5 wt% and 1 wt% TiB 2nanoparticles, respectively, using a three-dimensional mixer (JXHY-2L). The mixing process included a speed of 80 rpm/min and a duration of 4 h. To avoid the adverse effect of energy on the properties of the alloy powders during the mechanical mixing process, the machine was paused for cooling at room temperature for 10 min after every 20 min of mixing, ensuring mixed uniformly. The process parameters for fabricating samples with Ti6Al4V powders and 0.5 wt% TiB 2/Ti6Al4V powders, respectively, were as follows: a laser power of 180 W, a scanning speed of 1000 mm/s, a hatching spacing of 120 µm, and a layer thickness of 30 µm; additionally, a short linear scanning strategy was implemented with an interlayer rotation angle of 67°. To alleviate residual stress accumulation during processing, the substrate was preheated to 180 °C. Prior to processing, the powders underwent drying in a vacuum oven at 80 °C for 8 h; high-purity argon gas was introduced to maintain oxygen levels below 100 ppm to prevent oxidation within the melt pool. Processing Text: The ingots of Al 5Ti 8(FeCoNi) 86.9B 0.1(at. %) HEA were fabricated from metals with purity exceeding 99.9 wt.% in a vacuum arc melting furnace. Each ingot underwent five remelting cycles to ensure chemical homogeneity before being cast into a water-cooled copper mould measuring 50 × 15 × 10 mm 3. Subsequently, the cast ingots were homogenized at 1200 °C for two hours and then subjected to multi-pass rolling at room temperature to achieve a 50 % reduction in thickness (from 10 mm to 5 mm). Following rolling, the samples were heat-treated at 1165 °C for 10 min to achieve a recrystallized FCC-type grain microstructure (abbreviated as HT alloy). Afterwards, the samples underwent further multi-pass rolling to achieve an 80 % reduction in thickness (from 5 mm to 1 mm), abbreviated as the CR alloy. The cold-rolled samples were then annealed in the FCC+L1 2two-phase region ( Fig. 1) at 760 and 800 °C for two hours and were designated as CR760 and CR800 alloys, respectively. Processing Text: The spherical pre-alloy powders of the CoCrNi HEA and Fe 50Mn 30Co 10Cr 10HEA were prepared by vacuum induction melting gas atomization. The laminated HEAs were printed by a direct energy deposition method. During printing, the CoCrNi HEA and the Fe 50Mn 30Co 10Cr 10HEA were alternately deposited up to a desired height. The scanning path follows a zigzag pattern, where the scanning direction is rotated by 90° between each adjacent layer to minimize residual stress. Here, the laminated HEAs were successfully fabricated with three different layer spacings of 0.1 mm, 0.3 mm, and 0.5 mm, denoted as LH0.1, LH0.3 and LH0.5, respectively. The laser diameter is 1 mm, and the powder feeding airflow and protective airflow are fixed at 5 and 10 L/min, respectively. Sample is LH0.1

Processing Text: Elemental powders of tungsten (W), niobium (Nb), tantalum (Ta), and vanadium (V) with purities exceeding 99.5 % were employed to fabricate the equal-atomic ratio WNbTaV RHEA samples. A planetary ball-mill (QM-3SP2, Nanjing Chishun Technology Co., Ltd.) was utilized to mix raw powders for 24 h at 300 rpm with tetrafluoroethylene tank, ZrO 2balls and ball-to-powder ratio of 5:1. Following ball milling, the powders were consolidated using SPS (LABOX-350, Sinterland, Japan) apparatus. As observed, the prepared powders were loaded into a graphite mold, and sequentially heated to target temperatures (1300, 1400, 1500, and 1600 ℃) at a rate of 100 ℃/min. Each temperature was sustained for 5 min under a uniaxial pressure of 30 MPa, followed by cooling to room temperature in the furnace. Specifically, the powder body was held at 1200 ℃ for 10 min during heating to facilitate the solid solution formation among the powders. After the SPS process, the samples underwent grinding and polishing for subsequent observation and experiments. Sintering temperature (°C) is 1300

Processing Text: Raw Cu, Cr, Fe, Ni, Al and Ti blocks with purity>99.8 wt % were selected to prepare the 3.5 kg CuCrFeNiTi0.8Al1.2 HEA via magnetic levitation induction melting under high purity argon atmosphere. The purity of the alloy is guaranteed by removing the oxide scale on the surface of the crude material and cleaning it in acetone by ultrasonic wave for 20 min. The melting process was repeated 4 times to achieve chemical homogeneity. In order to better study the organizational transformation behavior and solidification process during annealing, the obtained specimen was then annealed at 800 °C and 1000 °C for 24 h, followed by water quenching. Upon the introduction of annealing process, significant grain refinement was achieved. Additionally, the increase of annealing temperature led to the presence of secondary precipitated particles within the alloy. The annealed CuCrFeNiTi0.8Al1.2 HEA displays similar microstructure compared to the as-cast state. Following annealed at 800 °C, there are much more precipitates generated in the grains and several structures transformed from spherical to short-rod. Besides, note a great deal of micron-particles are precipitated from matrix. As increase the annealing temperature to 1000 °C, relatively large quantities of secondary nano-particles precipitated from α phase not just the micro-particle from DR matrix. Room temperature compressive properties and Vickers hardness of CuCrFeNiTi0.8Al1.2 HEAs were tested to study the mechanical properties. Temperature(°C) is 800

Processing Text: This work utilizes a consolidation technique that uses high-pressure & high-temperature (HPHT) to produce an ultrafine-grained (UFG) FeCrCoNi HEA. The high consolidation pressure has two effects: 1) reducing interparticle distances due to the enforced plastic deformation of individual granules, making for high bulk density, and 2) reducing the diffusivity, thereby reducing the growth speed of grains. The high strain is primarily the result of a reduction in the diameter and content of Cr-Mn-O-rich oxides - which reduce the interface area between the soft matrix and hard oxides, thereby suppressing the sources of crack generation - due to the utilization of high pressure. UFG FeCoNiCr HEA was prepared by MA and HPHT techniques. Applying a substantial consolidation pressure (4 GPa) leads to the UFG FeCoNiCr HEA achieving a relative density near 99 %. The consolidated UFG FeCoNiCr HEA exhibits an average grain diameter of approx. 181 nm and displays exceptionally high yield strength of approx. 1526 MPa - significantly higher than the yield strength (162 MPa) of CG FeCoNiCr HEA - and a high fracture of 35 %. The high yield strength is predominantly brought about by the UFG matrix. The achievement of the UFG matrix can be attributed primarily to the application of a high consolidation pressure, which has two effects: 1) reduces interparticle distances because of the enforced plastic deformation of the individual powder particles and 2) reducing the diffusivity, thereby reducing the rate of grain growth. The high strain is predominately induced by fine diameter and low content of coarse Cr-Mn-O-rich oxide. High sintering pressure suppresses the oxides to grow, reducing the interface area between soft matrix phases and hard oxides, and thus decreasing the sources of crack generation. Strain (%) is 4.959349593495936

Material Name: RHEAs containing both W and C
Processing Text: Raw materials with purities higher than 99.95 wt.% were used to prepare the W-Ta-Ti-V-C RHEAs by vacuum arc melting under a Ti-gettered, high-purity argon atmosphere. Here, the C element was introduced by adding WC particles. To ensure the homogeneity of RHEAs, W-Ta and Ti-V-WC middle-alloys were firstly prepared by 4 melting times respectively. The middle-alloys were then merged to fabricate ingot, which was flipped and remelted 12 times, and maintained a liquid state for about 5 min in each melting. The compressive samples with dimensions of 3 mm × 3 mm × 6 mm were cut from the prepared ingots by wire electrical discharge machining (WEDM) and the mirror-like surfaces were achieved by mechanical polishing for the following microstructural observation. The phase structure of prepared RHEAs was inspected by performing standard X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) observation on an X-ray diffractometer (PANalytical X-Pert PRO MPD, Netherlands) and high-resolution transmission electron microscope (Talos F200X G2, China), respectively. The TEM foils were prepared by ion milling (Gatan 695, USA) and focused ion beam (FIB, Crossbeam 350, Germany) lift-out technology. The phase stability of the RHEAs was inspected by differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) using a simultaneous thermal analyzer (Netzsch STA449F3, Germany) under an argon atmosphere with a heating rate of 10 °C/min from 25 °C to 1400 °C. Annealing treatment was also performed to examine the phase stability of the RHEAs in a muffle furnace (KSL-1100X, HF-Kejing, China) under an argon atmosphere with a heating rate of 10 °C/min from 25 °C to 1000 °C and a soaking time of 24 h. The microstructure of RHEAs was observed on the field-emission scanning electron microscopes (SEM, Hitachi SU8020, Japan and Gemini 500, Germany), and the element distribution was detected using the equipped energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS). Material Name: RHEAs containing both W and C
Processing Text: Raw materials with purities higher than 99.95 wt.% were used to prepare the W-Ta-Ti-V-C RHEAs by vacuum arc melting under a Ti-gettered, high-purity argon atmosphere. Here, the C element was introduced by adding WC particles. To ensure the homogeneity of RHEAs, W-Ta and Ti-V-WC middle-alloys were firstly prepared by 4 melting times respectively. The middle-alloys were then merged to fabricate ingot, which was flipped and remelted 12 times, and maintained a liquid state for about 5 min in each melting. The compressive samples with dimensions of 3 mm × 3 mm × 6 mm were cut from the prepared ingots by wire electrical discharge machining (WEDM) and the mirror-like surfaces were achieved by mechanical polishing for the following microstructural observation. The phase structure of prepared RHEAs was inspected by performing standard X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) observation on an X-ray diffractometer (PANalytical X-Pert PRO MPD, Netherlands) and high-resolution transmission electron microscope (Talos F200X G2, China), respectively. The TEM foils were prepared by ion milling (Gatan 695, USA) and focused ion beam (FIB, Crossbeam 350, Germany) lift-out technology. The phase stability of the RHEAs was inspected by differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) using a simultaneous thermal analyzer (Netzsch STA449F3, Germany) under an argon atmosphere with a heating rate of 10 °C/min from 25 °C to 1400 °C. Annealing treatment was also performed to examine the phase stability of the RHEAs in a muffle furnace (KSL-1100X, HF-Kejing, China) under an argon atmosphere with a heating rate of 10 °C/min from 25 °C to 1000 °C and a soaking time of 24 h. The microstructure of RHEAs was observed on the field-emission scanning electron microscopes (SEM, Hitachi SU8020, Japan and Gemini 500, Germany), and the element distribution was detected using the equipped energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS). Deformed TEM samples were directly mounted onto a molybdenum grid after thinning to 50 μm. Finally, these TEM samples were subjected to electrochemical twin-jet thinning to obtain the desired thin areas. Dog-bone-shaped tensile specimens with a gauge length of 8 mm and a cross-sectional area of 2 × 1.5 mm 2 were obtained through EDM along the rolling direction. Using powder metallurgy and hot extrusion techniques, Al5083 MMCs were then created with differing amounts of SiC/RGO. The current study used Al5083 powder for the matrix material. Initially, SiC/RGO reinforcing particles were combined with 5083 aluminum alloy powder in varying mass fractions of 0.1 %, 0.3 %, and 0.5 %. The resulting mixture was transferred to a ball milling tank, followed by the addition of 1 g of stearic acid. Afterward, the tank was flushed with argon gas, and the materials underwent milling in an ND7-1L ball mill using a ball-to-material ratio of 5:1, a rotational speed of 200 rpm, for a duration of 10 h. The 10-hour ball milling converted spherical 5083 aluminum alloy powder into flakes, enhancing sintering performance through increased surface area and mechanical interlocking. The uniformly mixed powder was subsequently transferred to a SK2-2-12TPB2 vacuum tube furnace for heating at 400 °C, the process that facilitates the removal of stearic acid from the powder. Thereafter, the SiC/RGO/Al5083 powder was placed into the cylindrical mold and use a hydraulic press to obtain the φ40 × 4 mm 3shape. Then, the mold and the cold-extruded billet were placed into the hot extrusion equipment together. Finally, as shown in Fig. 1(d), graphite dies with a diameter of 24 mm filled with the ground powders was placed in the SPS chamber between two graphite electrodes and the powders were sintered. Mechanical alloying of powders was achieved by vertical planetary grinding (LC-PBM-6L, Shanghai Lichen Instrument Technology Co., LTD). The parameters of ball milling were formulated as follows: The ZrO 2vials and balls were utilized as the milling media with balls to powders mass ratio of 10:1. The powders were milled in planetary ball millers for 30, 40 and 50 h at 300 rpm in a vacuum atmosphere, and some anhydrous ethanol (30 ml) was added in the vials. To prevent the grain growth of NbTaTiV RHEAs, the samples (with the cylindrical shape of Φ 24 ×7 mm) of NbTaTiV alloys were fabricated by spark plasma sintering technique (SPS, SPS-PM-20/60, Shanghai Jinghua Technology Co., LTD, China). The composite powders were sintered under a pressure of 50 MPa at a sintering temperature of 1200 °C, 1300 ℃ and 1400 ℃ with a heating rate of 100 °C/min, and the gradient heating method was used to prevent temperature overshoot ( Fig. 2a). The pressure was held all time in the hole process, and the vacuum degree was 0.2 × 10 −5Pa. Then, the samples were cooled to room temperature in the furnace. Rectangular 12 mm × 12 mm × 12 mm samples comprising the processed MMC powder feedstocks were fabricated using the LPDED process ( Fig. 1(b)). An LPDED system (InssTek MX-4) with a 1 kW Yb fiber laser (IPG Photonics, wavelength 1070 nm), a ring-type powder feeding system, and a 0.8 mm laser beam spot diameter were employed. The samples were produced using constant process parameters: a laser power of 420 W; deposition speed of 15 mm/s; powder feeding rate of 2.8 g/min; 90° rotational zigzag scanning strategy; and a hatch distance of 0.47 mm between the tracks. After forming each layer, the laser nozzle head was moved upward by 0.38 mm. The samples were fabricated by repeating the layer formation on a stainless-steel 316 plate with dimensions of 120 mm × 120 mm × 12 mm. A specific heat treatment cycle was employed to optimize the mechanical properties of Inconel 718, particularly to promote the precipitation of the γ 'and γ ''phases, which are crucial for high-temperature performance. The samples were subjected to a standard double-aging heat treatment process: Solution Treatment: The samples were first held at 1100 °C for 1 h and then rapidly cooled by water quenching. This step is designed to dissolve the existing phases and create a supersaturated solid solution. Aging Step 1: The samples were then aged at 720 °C for 8 h, followed by controlled furnace cooling at a rate of 100 °C/h. During this aging step, the primary γ 'precipitates form, which significantly contributes to the material's strength. Aging Step 2: Finally, the samples underwent a second aging process at 620 °C for 10 h before being air-cooled. This step facilitates the further precipitation of γ '', enhancing the alloy's mechanical properties, particularly its creep resistance and stability at elevated temperatures. Samples machined along the build direction using EDM were polished according to standard metallographic procedures, including ion milling (IM4000 PLUS CTC, Hitachi). Tensile tests were conducted using dog-bone specimens with a 3.5 mm gauge length at room temperature, employing a strain rate of 10 −3/s under a digital image correlation system. Each sample category was subjected to five replicates to validate the results ( Fig. 1(c)). For compression tests, cylindrical specimens measuring 3 mm in diameter and 5 mm in height were heated at a rate of 10 °C/min in a heating chamber and tested 30 min after reaching the target temperatures (650-1000 °C) at a compression rate of 10 −3/s.
