Processing Text: Ingots with the nominal compositions of CoCrFeNi and Al 0.3CoCrFeNi HEAs were fabricated from Al, Co, Cr, Fe, and Ni pure elements (purity >99.9 wt %), using the vacuum-arc-melting facility. The melting chamber was initially evacuated to a pressure of 10 -5torr. Then, the mixed elements were melted, remelted, superheated, and poured into a high-purity graphite crucible with an inner length of 200 mm, upper inner diameter of 65 mm, and bottom inner diameter of 50 mm. After casting, the resultant CoCrFeNi and Al 0.3CoCrFeNi HEAs were cut into several disks with identical dimensions (diameter of 30 mm and thickness of 1.0 mm). To obtain a uniform surface roughness and a strong interfacial bonding, both surfaces of the CoCrFeNi and Al 0.3CoCrFeNi sheets were brushed with steel wool pads to remove surface oxides and contaminants, and they were then cleaned in an ultrasonic acetone bath for 5 min. After the surface cleaning treatment, ten Al 0.3CoCrFeNi sheets and nine CoCrFeNi sheets were stacked alternatively to form a stacked laminate (with the outermost layers being Al 0.3CoCrFeNi). The stacked laminates were placed in a graphite die for confinement and pressed under a pressure of 40 MPa at 1100 °C for 2 h in a vacuum hot-pressing furnace to obtain hot-pressed Al 0.3CoCrFeNi/CoCrFeNi laminated composites. Subsequently, the laminated composites were cold rolled to achieve a total thickness reduction of 90 % after multiple passes. To determine the best annealing temperature for optimizing the properties of the multilevel HLSed HEAs, the rolled Al 0.3CoCrFeNi/CoCrFeNi laminated composites were annealed in Ar atmosphere at a series of temperatures in the range between 500 °C and 700 °C for 24 h, and they were subsequently water-quenched. The thermo-mechanical processing triggers Al element diffusion from the Al 0.3CoCrFeNi layer into the adjacent CoCrFeNi layers, resulting in the formation of numerous fine-scale B2 and σ precipitates adjacent to the layer interfaces in both the CoCrFeNi and Al 0.3CoCrFeNi constituent layers and thus enhancing the interface bonding. Processing Text: The Mg-8.5Gd-3Y-2Cu-0.5Zr (wt.%) alloy ingot, measuring 90 mm in diameter and 1200 mm in length, was successfully produced through semi-continuous casting. The ingot was subjected to a homogenization treatment at 500 °C for 12 h and then extruded at 375 °C. The extrusion process was performed at a ratio of 28:1 and a rate of 0.6 mm/s, followed immediately by air quenching to room temperature. Before undergoing multi-pass hot rolling, these plates were pre-heated to 200 °C for 30 min in a resistance furnace, with the mill rolls heated to the same temperature. The rolling involved multiple passes, reducing plate thickness by 2 %-5 % each time, accompanied by a 90° in-plane rotation after each pass, resulting in 4 mm thick sheets. After each pass, to maintain the recrystallization temperature and activate the PSN mechanism, the samples were reheated to 200 °C for 5 min and cooled in room-temperature water after rolling was completed. The 4 mm thick sheets were then subjected to a double-ageing treatment, achieving peak-aged conditions at 100 °C for 8 h and 200 °C for 36 h. Both types of Mg-RE alloys are MR + A treated. Processing Text: CoCrNi MEA powders (0-25 μm, Chengdu Kotilon alloy., Ltd.)) with high purity (99.99 %) were used as raw materials in this study. The morphology of the powders was characterized using scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Nova Nano SEM450). The powders were then loaded into a 20 mm diameter mold. To prevent contamination, this process was conducted in an argon-filled glove box. Subsequently, the mold was placed into a SPS system (LABOX-325R). The SPS process was conducted under the following conditions: the temperature was increased to 1050 °C at a rate of 100 °C/min, maintained for 10 min, then cooled to 300 °C at a rate of 100 °C/min, and finally cooled to room temperature within the furnace. A high vacuum of 10 −3Pa was maintained throughout the process to minimize gas contamination, and a uniaxial pressure of 50 MPa was applied. As a result, a cylindrical CoCrNi MEA block with a diameter of 20 mm and a height of 7 mm was obtained. A circular sample with a diameter of 20 mm and a thickness of 2 mm was cut from the SPSed CoCrNi using electrical discharge machining (EDM, SKD3). To induce a heterostructure, surface mechanical rolling treatment (SMRT) was applied to both surfaces of the circular sample. The SMRT parameters were as follows: a WC/Co ball penetrated the sample while sliding along its axis at a velocity of 2000 mm/min with a penetration depth of 5 μm. This procedure was repeated three times. During the SMRT process, the contact surface between the WC-Co ball and the circular sample was cooled using oil lubrication to prevent overheating. For convenience, the treated sample is referred to as MHS CoCrNi. The crystal orientation of SPSed CoCrNi was analyzed using electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, NordlysMax3) with a step size of 0.5 μm. A detailed cross-sectional analysis of MHS CoCrNi was also performed to reveal the gradient structure. Before testing, the data acquisition area of the sample needed to be treated. The test surface of each sample was first polished to remove scratches and achieve a smooth surface. Subsequently, argon ion polishing (IM4000 Ⅱ) was conducted at voltages of 5 kV, 4 kV, and 3 kV, with each stage lasting approximately 1 h. The microstructure within the grains was further investigated using transmission electron microscopy (TEM, FEI Talos F200X). Circular samples with a diameter of 10 mm and thickness of 500 μm were initially cut using EDM, followed by mechanical grinding with abrasive papers (800-2000 grade) to a thickness of 80 μm. Thin discs with a diameter of 3 mm were punched from these samples and further thinned to approximately 20 μm using a Gatan dimple grinder and ion beam thinner (Gatan Model 691). The Vickers hardness tester (Q10 A +) was used to measure the surface hardness of both SPSed and MHS CoCrNi, as well as the hardness distribution along the depth of MHS CoCrNi. The tests were conducted with a load of 50 g applied for 10 s. Dog-bone-shaped specimens with a gauge length of 5 mm and a cross-section of 2.0 × 1.5 mm 2were cut by EDM. Tensile and loading-unloading-reloading (LUR) tests were carried out on a universal testing machine (INSTRON, 68TM-50). During the LUR tensile test, specimens were initially stretched to a strain of 2 %, unloaded to 5 MPa, and then subjected to repeated cycles at designated strain levels (4 %, 6 %, 8 %, etc.). The tensile rate was 0.5 mm/min. Fracture surfaces were subsequently observed using SEM to analyze the fracture mechanism. Tensile properties; Variation: ± 80 MPa

Processing Text: It was fabricated through exothermal reactions between mixed salts (high-purity reactive powders of K2TiF6 and KBF4) and molten aluminum. TiB2 particles were formed in-situ in the molten matrix. The cast ingot was homogenized at a temperature of 495 °C for 48 h. Subsequently, the hot extrusion was carried out at 450 °C with an extrusion ratio of ∼10. After extrusion, the ingot was subjected to T4 heat treatment: solution treatment conducted at 500 °C for 1 h followed by water quenching, and then kept at room temperature for over 4 days to experience potential natural aging. Dumbbell-shaped tensile specimens with a gauge length of 5 mm and a gauge section diameter of 4 mm were machined for uniaxial quasi-static and dynamic tensile tests. Cylindrical specimens with a diameter of 5 mm and a height of 4 mm were prepared by wire electrical discharge machining for uniaxial compression tests. A hat-shaped simple shear specimen with a shear zone length of 4 mm, widths of 1 mm, and thickness of 2 mm was designed and machined. All specimens were cut from the extrusion composite plate with a loading direction parallel to the extrusion direction (ED), and the surfaces of compression specimens were polished to be mirror-like using waterproof silicon carbide papers and colloidal silica polishing suspensions with different particle sizes. Both quasi-static tensile and compressive tests were performed on a DNS-100 electronic universal testing machine at a strain rate of 0.001/s. Dynamic uniaxial tensile tests were performed at strain rates from 1200/s to 4000/s using a split Hopkinson tension bar (SHTB) system and the dynamic uniaxial compression was performed using a split Hopkinson pressure bar (SHPB) system. The SHPB and SHTB systems mainly consists of three co-axial bars: the striker bar (or tube), the incident bar, and the transmission bar. For shear tests, the shear stress τ and shear strain γ can be converted to equivalent values using the relationships σeq=3τ and εeq=ln1+γ+γ2/2, respectively. The interface between loading bar ends and compression specimens were lubricated by daubing molybdenum disulfide grease. The stress, strain and strain rate of tested specimens was measured by the strain gauges on the incident and transmission bars. For the high-temperature tests, the elevated-temperature environments were obtained using an electric radiant-heating furnace. A thermocouple strapped around the specimen was used to monitor the temperature. After reaching the target value, the specimen temperature was maintained constant to within 3 K for 5 min. This process can ensure a uniform specimen temperature (both surface and internal temperature) before loading. At least three repetitive experiments in each condition were conducted to ensure repeatability of the results. Before the microstructure observation, the metallographic preparation following a three-step procedure had been conducted for the pre- and post-loading samples: grinding by using waterproof silicon carbide papers with the increasing grit size from 600 to 5000, mechanical polishing with the particulate solution on a polishing cloth, and chemical etching in a mixed solution containing 1%HF+ 1.5%HCl+ 2.5%HNO + 95 %H2O for 15 s. Flat dog-bone-shaped tensile specimens with a gage length of 6 mm, thickness of 1 mm and width of 3.5 mm were in-situ tested by a ZEISS Gemini 500 field emission SEM to characterize the microstructure evolution at specific strains under quasi-static loading and room temperature. The TEM samples were prepared by mechanically polishing to about 50 μm followed by precision ion thinning treatment. Athermal yield stress (σa) independent of temperature and strain rate

Processing Text: Multilayered Al samples were fabricated through a combined process of ARB and annealing, using 1.5-mm-thick sheets of AA3003 and AA1060 alloy as the raw materials. This thermal processing procedure consists of an initial single-pass ARB, followed by intermediate annealing, four additional ARB passes, and concluding with final annealing. For each ARB cycle, the sheets were carefully cleaned with an ethanol solution and mechanically ground by a steel brush to eliminate the greases and oxides from the surface. The sheets were then fastened with rivets and subjected to rolling at 150 °C, achieving a 50 % thickness reduction by a single pass. Since the radius of the roller, R, was ∼50 mm, and the linear velocity, V, was ∼100 mm/s, the average strain rate of rolling was around 26.6/s. After that, the bonded sheet was divided in half, preparing it for the subsequent ARB cycle. After the series of accumulative roll bonding, the final thickness of the multilayered Al sample was around 1.5 mm. Since the multilayered Al samples underwent annealing at temperatures of 600 °C and 500 °C for 1 h during the intermediate annealing, two multilayered Al samples were denoted as AA600 and AA500 samples. To better describe the microstructures evolution of AA500 and AA600 during such complex thermal processing, the intermediate-annealed, ARBed, and final-annealed AA500/AA600 samples were further designated as AA500-IA/AA600-IA, AA500-ARB/AA600-ARB, and AA500-FA/AA600-FA, respectively. The intermediate annealing was designed to prevent the plasticity instability and shear bands of harder layers caused by the accumulation of rolling strains. More importantly, different temperatures during the intermediate annealing were strategically employed to manipulate precipitation kinetics within the AA3003 alloy layers. As suggested by previous work, the nano-dispersoids start to precipitate in AA3003 layers at moderate temperatures above 300 °C, while re-dissolve at higher temperatures above 530 °C. Therefore, AA3003 layers of the AA500-IA sample should have precipitated dispersoids after the intermediate annealing, while those in the AA600-IA sample will not. This step aims to provide precursors of different heterogeneous structures in multilayered Al samples. The final annealing process was conducted at 320 °C for 1 h, which was designed mainly based on the effects of the Mn element on elevating recrystallization temperatures of Al alloys. In other words, this step mainly aimed to stimulate the full recrystallizations of AA1060 layers in multilayered Al samples. More importantly, the intermediate annealing has induced different precipitation behaviors. Given the significant effects of precipitates on recovery and recrystallization behaviors, the final annealing can lead to different recovery and recrystallization behaviors of AA3003 layers, resulting in different heterogeneous structures in AA500-FA and AA600-FA samples. Processing Text: The QP and QP-R steels were melted in a vacuum induction melting furnace, cast into 5 kg ingots, and then the ingots were forged and cut into 20-mm-thick blocks. The blocks were homogenized at 1200 °C for 30 min and then hot-rolled in the full austenitic zone to produce a 2-mm-thick hot-rolled sheet. Subsequently, the hot-rolled sheet underwent simulated coiling at 650 °C for 30 min. The simulated coiled QP and QP-R steels underwent a standard Q&P process on the simulated continuous annealing equipment (CAS-AY Ⅱ), manufactured by Advance Riko. The heat treatment profiles for the QP and QP-R steels are shown in Fig. 1, in which the phase transformation temperature (Ae3) (806.9 °C) between austenite-ferrite and fully austenitic phase at equilibrium of the QP steel was calculated by Thermo-Calc software using TCFE 12 database. During the quenching stage, the experimentally measured Ms (the martensite start transformation temperatures) of the QP and QP-R steels are 344.6 and 340.7 °C, respectively. During the partitioning and subsequent cooling stages, no fluctuation was detected in the dilatometer curves of the QP and QP-R steels, suggesting that retained austenite was almost fully preserved after partitioning. Processing Text: Cr, Fe, Ni and W metals with the purity of ≥99.9 wt% were used to prepare CrFeNiW0.1 MEAs. The metallic elements were melted by arc-melting technique and then solidified in a water-cooled Cu crucible under Ti-gettered high-purity argon atmosphere. The ingots were melted at least five times ensure the uniformity of the alloys, and then cast into Cu mold with the dimensions of ∼60 mm × 11 mm × 5 mm. The as-cast samples were sealed in quartz tubes and homogenized at 1200 °C for 6 h, which was subsequently by water quenching. Then, the homogenized CrFeNiW0.1 MEAs were cold rolled to a total thickness reduction of ∼78 %. The specimens cut from cold-rolled CrFeNiW0.1 MEAs were finally heat treated at 900 °C for 1 h followed by water quenching. Processing Text: The as-printed Co-free AlCrFeNi3 eutectic medium entropy alloy (EMEA) was fabricated by selective laser melting (SLM). Heat treatment as a post processing was used to improve the mechanical properties of the as-printed samples, which were subjected to solid solution treatment at 400 °C-1200 °C for 1 h in this work. No visible cracks and pores were found in the as-printed samples and the highest relative density is up to 99.57 %. The as-printed AlCrFeNi3 EMEA is consisted of FCC, B2, and intergranular BCC phases, showing a typical fish scale-like structure with ultrafine cellular and columnar substructures. The ultimate tensile strength and elongation of the as-printed alloy with relatively optimal printing parameters are 1146.9 MPa and 7.6 %, respectively. When the solid solution temperature reaches 1000 °C, the intergranular BCC phases disappeared, and the second phases are uniformly distributed in the matrix, while the ultimate tensile strength and elongation of the sample are 1335.5 MPa and 12.3 %, respectively, demonstrating an 188.6 MPa increase in strength and 4.7 % increase in ductility compared to the as-printed alloy. Pre-alloyed AlCrFeNi3 EMEA powders produced by spherical atomization of argon gas were used as the raw materials in this study. We printed multiple samples by adjusting the printing parameters, and based on the highest relative density the as-printed samples, we determined the optimized parameters as follows: laser power 185 W, scanning speed 800 mm/s, hatch spacing 100 μm, and layer thickness 30 μm. To investigate the effect of heat treatment on the microstructure and mechanical properties of the printed AlCrFeNi3 EMEA, the as-printed samples were heat treated in a muffle furnace under different conditions, including solid solution treatment at 400 °C, 600 °C, 800 °C and 1000 °C for 1 h, respectively, followed by water quenching. Condition: As printed

Processing Text: The GH4099 superalloy thin-walled structure was manufactured using laser-directed energy deposition (L-DED). GH4099 pre-alloyed powder with particles ranging in size from 50 to 150 μm was produced using plasma rotating electrode processing (PREP). The powders underwent a 24-h vacuum drying process at 120 °C before the L-DED process. During the L-DED, GH4099 alloy single-track walls were fabricated using a back-and-forth scanning approach. It was executed using an L-DED system equipped with a Yb fiber laser in an Ar chamber. The laser, with a beam diameter of 3 mm, operated at a power of 900 W and a scanning speed of 6 mm/s. The powder feed rate was maintained at 0.3 r/min. A protective gas (Ar) flow rate of 15 mL/min and a powder gas (Ar) flow rate of 6 mL/min were maintained consistently throughout the process to minimize the impact of impurity gases in the atmosphere. The single melt pool thickness under these parameters was 0.6 mm. The forming parameters were optimized to achieve optimal conditions and minimize the impact of forming defects on the mechanical properties of the sample. The build resulted in three cross-sectional samples perpendicular to the BD (X-Y plane) and one vertical section sample parallel to BD (Y-Z plane), dividing the entire assembly into bottom, middle, and top regions. For transmission electron microscopy (TEM) analysis, the samples were mechanically polished and then electropolished in a solution that contained 20 % sulfuric acid and 80 % methanol. This process was performed at room temperature using a voltage of 15 V. For atom probe tomography (APT), the built sample was sectioned using a focused ion beam (FIB), and needle-shaped samples were prepared along three X-Y planes at uniform heights with precise sharpness. Region: middle; Represents decrease in yield strength relative to the bottom region

Processing Text: For SPS processing, powder mixtures of nominal composition: Nb-10Hf-1Ti (wt. %), were prepared by blending the elemental powders for 24 h in a jar mill. Nb slugs were added to the powder mixture to break up agglomerates during milling. The jar milling was intended to achieve a good blending of powder particles without reducing the sizes. The blended powder was then sintered in the SPS unit (Model 10–4, Thermal Technologies, Santa Rosa, CA) using graphite dies. The sintering temperatures and times were varied to determine the optimum solid-state sintering conditions at a temperature that is significantly below the solidus line (∼2350°C). The optimum sintering temperature was determined to be 1700°C based on multiple trials in the temperature range of 1500–1800°C. At this sintering temperature, dense samples of size: 20 mm in diameter and 7.84 mm in thickness can be sintered and densified almost to full density in 2 h under a pressure of 10 MPa. The samples were heated at a rate of 50°C/min to the sintering temperature. The temperature was controlled using an optical pyrometer throughout the sintering process. The power, pressure, temperature, and ram displacement were recorded throughout the process. Processing state: SPS-processed; Microstructure: nearly fully dense with very little residual porosity (∼1.3 vol. %); Compared to wrought, EB-PBF, and LB-PBF processed versions.

Processing Text: The alloy ingots were prepared using a vacuum non-consumable arc melting furnace, with each ingot melted at least seven times to ensure composition uniformity, and the initial thickness of ingot was 14 mm. Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC, NETZSCH-STA449C) was used to measure the phase transition temperatures of T9V alloy at a heating rate of 10 °C/min. DSC revealed that the α→β transformation occurred between 679 ± 8 °C and 787 ± 6 °C. The alloy was rolled at 850 °C, 800 °C, 750 °C, and 700 °C, respectively. Before rolling, the alloy was held in a muffle furnace at the target rolling temperature for 30 min. Multi-pass rolling deformation was then performed, with the roll spacing was reduced by 2 mm per pass. After each pass, the alloy was reheated in the furnace for 3 min. Upon achieving a final deformation of 80 %, the alloy was reheated for 3 min and quenched. Based on the rolling temperature, the deformed specimens were designated as 850-HR, 800-HR, 750-HR, and 700-HR. Tensile specimens were cut from the rolled specimens along the rolling direction. The dog-bone-shaped specimens had test zone measuring 2 × 3 × 20 mm. Single-axis tensile tests were performed at a strain rate of 5 × 10 −4s −1at room temperature using an Instron 5982 universal testing machine (ASTM E8/E8M-16a). Strain measurements were obtained using the extensometer attached to the testing machine. Loading-unloading-reloading (LUR) tensile tests were carried out under the same conditions. During LUR testing, the specimens were unloaded to 20N at a rate of 200 N min −1after every 1.5 % deformation (based on extensometer), with the cycle repeated eight times. Each specimen underwent at least three tensile tests. The crystal structure and phase composition of the T9V alloy were analyzed using a D/max-2500/PC X-ray diffraction (XRD). The analysis used Cu K αradiation, step scanning with a 2 θ range of 30-80°, a residence time of 2 s and a scanning step size of 0.02°. After mechanical grinding and polishing, the specimens were etched with a solution of 2 % HF, 8 % HNO 3, and 90 % H 2O, and the microstructure was observed using a Zeiss Axiovert 200 MAT optical microscope (OM). The microstructure and fracture morphology were observed using a scanning electron microscope (SEM, Hitachi S3400). The Electron Backscattered Diffraction (EBSD) probe was also performed using this SEM. Microstructure data before and after deformation were collected by EBSD test technology with a step of 0.2 μm. Specimens for EBSD analysis were prepared via electrolytic polishing in a solution of 10 % perchloric acid and 90 % methanol at −20 °C, with an operating voltage of 20V. EBSD data were analyzed using TSL OIM 8.0 software and MATLAB scripts. Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM, Talos F200x) was used to further characterize the microstructure. Elemental analysis was conducted with energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) in this TEM. TEM was operated at an acceleration voltage of 200 kV. TEM specimens were prepared by grinding to 50 μm, punching out Φ3 mm discs, and performing twin-jet electrolytic thinning using a TenuPol-5 device. The solution and temperature were identical to those used for electrolytic polishing, with a working voltage of 15 V. Specimen: 800-HR; Context: reloading yield strength (σr) from the first hysteresis loop

Processing Text: In this work, TC4 alloy powders with a particle size ranging from 45 to 105 μm (Beijing Ruibang New Material Technology Co., Ltd.) were utilized. The DED samples exhibit a typical structure characterized by elongated, acicular phases within the β grains, which are oriented either parallel or perpendicular to one another. The primary structure of the spherical pristine powder is a densely arranged hexagonal close-packed (HCP) structure, with no evidence of a body-centered cubic (BCC) structure of the β-phase. The metallographic samples were polished and ground using #240, #400, #600, #800, #1200, #1500, #2000, and #3000 grit SiC paper, followed by polishing with a 2.5 μm diamond suspension. DED and DED-UIT samples were electrolytically polished before characterization using electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) with a Nova Nano SEM 450 (USA). Microhardness variations along the depth from the surface were measured for 10 s with a Vickers hardness tester (MMT-3 MATSUZAWA CO) under a load of 200 gf on the cross-sectional samples of the deposited layer. The tests were conducted using a computerized Instron 8801 servo-hydraulic test system (Instron, Norwood, MA, USA) at room temperature, with the strain rate set at 10−3s−1. In this work, synchronous layer-by-layer ultrasonic impact treatment (UIT) was proposed to treat laser directed energy deposited TC4 alloy, which can refine the grains and improve the mechanical properties of additive manufacturing samples in-situ. When UIT was conducted on the deposited layer synchronously, plastic deformation induced layer-by-layer. Recrystallization process occurred when subsequent laser deposition process was conducted, thus, the coarse columnar grains transformed into fine equiaxed grains. Through this synchronous layer-by-layer ultrasonic impact, recrystallization occurs layer by layer to refine the grains, the entire deposited specimen with refined microstructure is obtained and the overall mechanical properties were ultimately enhanced. The UIT system includes an ultrasonic transducer, an amplitude transformer, and an ultrasonic probe. During the LDED process, the UIT system under constant pressure (Gravity+0.2 MPa) was synchronized applied on the deposited layer, with the ultrasonic probe consistently in contact with this layer. This arrangement ensured that the deposited layer was subjected to UIT in a layer-by-layer manner. In addition, the UIT system and the LDED system were synchronized to operate with a fixed action spacing of 20 mm in this work. By controlling the loading start position of the UIT, two distinct regions can be formed on the same workpiece: the region of the DED sample subjected to UIT treatment (DED-UIT) and the region of the conventional deposited sample without ultrasonic impact treatment (DED) for comparative analysis. Processing Text: Samples were manufactured using EOS Ti-6Al-4V grade 23 powder on an EOS M290 (EOS GmbH, Germany) LPBF machine housed at the ISO 13485 certified Centre for Rapid Prototyping and Manufacturing (CRPM) of the Central University of Technology in South Africa. Specimens were produced in three batches, and a representative portion of each batch and specimen type was selected to measure the oxygen content to ensure this was kept below 0.013 wt%. The base plate was preheated to 80 °C, and a high-speed steel blade was used as a scraper. The process parameters consisted of a 40 μm layer thickness, 280 W laser power, 1300 mm/s scan speed, 100 μm spot size and a hatch distance of 120 μm. Bidirectional scanning was used, and the scan direction was rotated by 67° between layers. This set of process parameters results in a material with less than 0.01 % porosity [ 23 ]. For tensile specimens, cylinders with a diameter of D = 10 mm and a length of L = 100 mm were produced in the vertical (Z) and horizontal (X) directions relative to the axis of the LPBF machine (and according to ASTM 59200) that is aligned with the direction in which the load is applied. For fracture toughness specimens, Compact Tension (C(T)) specimens were produced as rectangular blocks to allow for the final dimensions of a width of W = 25 mm. C(T) specimens were produced in three orientations, with the first letter indicating the direction in which the load is applied and the second letter indicating the direction in which the crack propagates, that is, ZX, XZ and XY [ 6 ], as shown in Fig. 1 . After printing, the specimens were stress-relieved (SR) at 650 °C for 3 h in a TSH 15/50/180 vacuum furnace (Elite Thermal Systems, England) and then wire-cut from the build plate. The SR treatment was chosen to allow comparison with the literature [ 15 ]. Subsequent heat treatments were conducted at the Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) in atmospheric air using a box furnace (Ultrafurn, South Africa). Therefore, at least 1 mm was removed by wire cutting or machining from all the heat-treated specimen surfaces to remove any α-case and oxide scale that may have formed. The heat treatment schedules, detailed in Table 1 , included the SR, an anneal (AN) heat treatment, chosen due to its simplicity combined with good tensile properties, and a duplex anneal (DA) heat treatment, chosen based on optimal tensile properties reported in the literature [ 6 , 25 ]. Furthermore, the heat treatments above T β (selected based on values available in the literature [ 9 , 15 ]) were combined with the stress relief (BtSR) and anneal (BtAN) heat treatments to mimic how SR or AN specimens would perform if the PBGs were equiaxed c . c It is acknowledged the above T β heat treatment is at the cost of PBG growth. Comparison to specimens with elongated PBGs is only based on orientation effects. After heat treatment, the specimens were machined and wire-cut to their final dimensions. Processing Text: The A6-B2 RHEA was prepared by vacuum arc melting high-purity (>99.9 %) elements in a water-cooled copper hearth. The alloy was produced as a ∼50 mm diameter button weighing 150 g. Compression specimens had a square cross-section of 4.5 mm x 4.5 mm and a height of 7.6 mm. Processing Text: An ingot with a nominal composition of Ti-10Mo-3.5Cu (wt%) was produced through vacuum arc smelting under an argon atmosphere and was remelted three times. The composition of the prepared alloy was determined using an inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometer (ICP-OES 730). Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) coupled with Jmatpro software analysis determined the β-transus temperature (T β) of the alloy to be ∼795°C. Homogenization was carried out at 1000°C for 720 min under an argon atmosphere to ensure a uniform structure. Then, the bulk material underwent a hot rolling process at 700°C, achieving a reduction of 75 % in thickness. This was followed by solution treatment (900°C, 30 minutes, water quenched), obtaining a metastable β phase labeled as 3.5Cu-ST. Samples were then aged at different temperatures (150°C, 250°C, and 350°C) for 10 minutes and then quenched in water, represented by 3.5Cu-150A, 3.5Cu-250A, and 3.5Cu-350A, respectively. The specific aging temperatures were chosen to minimize the risk of severe ductility loss due to α phase precipitation and avoid the coarsening of ω isophases, particularly when aging above 500°C. Processing Text: Ti40Zr25Nb25Ta5Al5 (at.%) RHEA was fabricated from elemental nuggets with a minimum purity of 99.95 wt.% using an arc melting furnace (AM200, Edmund Bühler GmbH) under a Ti-getter pure Ar-atmosphere. Firstly, five alloy buttons (∼20 g) were fabricated. Each alloy button underwent six rounds of remelting to ensure chemical homogeneity, with each button flipped before each remelting cycle. Throughout each melting cycle, the alloy was kept in the liquid state for 10 min. Subsequently, all five buttons were combined and remelted together before being cast into a water-cooled Cu-mould to form a cuboidal bar with dimensions of 90 × 12 × 8 (thickness) mm3. Cross-sections of the as-cast alloy bar were ground using SiC abrasive papers and mirror-polished using 0.04 μm colloidal silica suspension (OPS) with 30 % H2O2 (10:1 by volume) for microstructural characterization. Dog-bone-shaped tensile samples with gauge dimensions of 8 mm × 2.9 mm × 1.5 mm (thickness) (Australian Standard AS 1391-2007) were prepared from as-cast bars using an electrical discharge wire-cutting machine. The entire surface of each tensile sample was ground with 600 grit SiC papers to remove the heat-affected layers from wire cutting. Tensile testing was performed on an Instron 5584 EM frame machine with a video extensometer. All tensile samples were tested at a slow strain rate of 5 × 10−5 s−1 at room temperature. The working electrodes were specimens connected with a conductive copper wire extension embedded in epoxy. A constant cross-section of 0.1 cm2 was exposed to Hank’s solution. Prior to testing, epoxy-mounted specimens were polished progressively up to 1200 grit SiC paper, degreased with acetone and ethanol, rinsed with distilled water, and dried in a compressed air stream. After 2 h immersion in Hank’s solution to attain an electrochemically quasi-stable state, potentiodynamic polarisation plots were recorded in the range −0.2 to 2.5 V in relation to open circuit potential at a scan rate of 4 mV/s. TEM samples were prepared using the standard lift-out method in a focused ion beam (FIB) system with FEI Scios DualBeam (FEI Scios DualBeam, Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA). A protective platinum (Pt) layer was deposited on sample surface prior to milling to minimize FIB-induced damage. Processing state: as-cast

Processing Text: The ingot, prepared by the vacuum melt casting method, was heated to 1200 °C for 2 hours and then forged into 100 mm × 100 mm × 80 mm forgings. Once cooled to room temperature, the forgings were cut into 50 mm × 20 mm × 8 mm slabs using wire-cutting technology. Subsequently, the slab underwent homogenization at 1200 °C for 2 hours. Then, its thickness was reduced to 4 mm (50% reduction) through six hot rolling passes conducted within a temperature range of 1010 - 1150 °C, starting at 1150 °C and ending at 950 °C. After hot rolling, the sheet underwent dephosphating and was then cold rolled through ten processes, ultimately resulting in a thickness of 2.2 mm (45% reduction). Lastly, the cold-rolled sheet was annealed at approximately 1173 K for 15 mins. All heat treatments were conducted in an inert gas (argon) atmosphere to ensure material purity and prevent oxidation. A rectangular sample measuring 10 mm × 30 mm was cut from the rolled and annealed billet and then finely polished with 1500 grit silicon carbide sandpaper to achieve a uniform thickness of 2 mm. Compression testing of these thin sheet samples was conducted using the CMT5305 microcomputer-controlled universal material testing machine along the normal direction (ND), with a strain rate of 0.001 s−1. To ensure precise control of deformation, dual means of stroke and pressure control were employed in the experiments. Thickness measurements were taken at three different locations before and after the compression test, with the average values documented to reflect the initial and final thicknesses. The average thicknesses of the four samples before compression were 1.98 mm, 2.02 mm, 2.00 mm, and 2.00 mm, respectively, and they changed to 1.80 mm, 1.62 mm, 1.48 mm, and 1.34 mm after compression. Uniaxial micro-tensile tests were conducted at 298 K (room temperature) on an in-house miniature-testing machine with a load cell of 5000 N and a nominal strain rate of 0.001 s−1. The samples were cut by EDM from the pre-compressed sheet material with gauge dimensions of 5 mm × 2 mm × 1 mm. The tensile direction of the samples was strictly aligned with the rolling direction (RD). Before testing, all samples underwent mechanical grinding to ensure a smooth surface without any obvious defects. To accurately determine the tensile strain value, random speckle patterns were uniformly sprayed onto the sample surface. During the tensile process, deformation images were captured in real-time using a high-resolution camera. Subsequently, MATLAB software was utilized for image processing and analysis. Initially, the images were converted into monochrome. Then, based on the center point of the sample gauge area, a virtual extensometer was constructed from the two preset solid lines. Finally, the sample's strain was determined by calculating the displacement of pixel points between the virtual extensometers over time. In this study, two types of micro-tensile tests were conducted: in-situ tests and interrupted tests, both loaded by displacement control. The in-situ tests were designed to obtain the stress-strain curve of the sample up to fracture, and back stress was also assessed through a LUR cycle test. To ensure reproducibility, three independent tensile tests were conducted for each pre-compressed sample. During the LUR test, a strain rate of 0.001 s−1 was used for strain control during loading, while unloading was force-controlled at 25 N/s. Reloading began when the force was unloaded to 25 N. The interrupted test was designed to study the microstructure evolution, with interruptions at specific points or continuation until fracture. Additionally, to accurately characterize the microstructure evolution of the pre-compressed sample at the same position before and after tensile deformation, hardness markers were placed in the center of the target region. Processing Text: 23NSS was refined using a vacuum induction heating furnace. The ingot was forged after turning. Then, after hot rolling, the forging billet was heated at 1200°C for 3 h and rolled into a 3.2-mm-thick SS plate. After the material was held at 1050°C for 20 min, the billet was water-cooled. Using an electric discharge wire cutting machine, bone-shaped tensile specimens and 10 × 10 mm tetragonal electrochemical test samples were produced along the rolling direction. The electrochemical test samples were soldered to the back of copper wire, sealed with acrylic powder, polished with 600, 800, 1000, 1200, 1500, and 2000# sandpaper, and finally cleaned with alcohol and dried. Tensile experiments were carried out on a universal test machine (SANS CMT5105) at room temperature with a crosshead speed of 3 mm/min, and the tensile strain under load was monitored by an extensometer. Bone-shaped tensile specimens were deformed in tension along the rolling direction with a marked length and parallel section width of 40 and 16 mm, respectively. In addition, 23NSS was deformed to 10, 30, and 50 % during stretching, with the stretching process stopped immediately at each stage to investigate the corrosion resistance of 23NSS under different strain states. Potentiodynamic polarization, potentiostatic polarization, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), and Mott-Schottky tests were conducted using a CS2350M dual potentiostatic instrument. All electrochemical tests were performed at 70°C in 0.0005 M H 2SO 4+ 2 ppm F −solution, which was bubbled with air to simulate the cathode environment of PEMFCs. The electrochemical tests were carried out using a three-electrode system. The counter electrode consisted of a thin platinum sheet 20 × 20 mm in size, and the working electrode had an area of 10 × 10 mm. The reference electrode consisted of a saturated mercuric sulphate electrode (MSE, 0.64 V vs. SHE, standard hydrogen electrode, all potentials relative to MSE unless otherwise stated). In addition, the reference electrode was placed in a Lagin capillary filled with saturated K 2SO 4solution, then the capillary was placed perpendicularly to the planar working electrode and counter electrode. The electrochemical tests were preceded by potentiostatic polarization of the working electrode at −1.37 V for 200 s to remove the oxides that had formed in the atmosphere. All samples were polished, cleaned, and dried prior to OCP testing. Three electrochemical test samples were used for the same treatment process, and each sample was repeated more than three times to ensure repeatability of the experiment. The potentiodynamic polarization, potentiostatic polarization, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), and Mott-Schottky tests were performed after the open circuit potential stabilized. Potentiodynamic polarization tests were initiated at a relative open-circuit potential of −0.3 V and stopped at 0.5 V relative to the reference electrode, with a scanning rate of 0.6 mV/s. Potentiostatic polarization was carried out at a potential close to the cathodic working potential of 0.23 V for 6 h. EIS tests were initiated with a 10 mV AC amplitude and frequency sweep from 10 5Hz to 10 −2Hz. Mott-Schottky tests were performed at a fixed frequency of 100 Hz with a sinusoidal excitation signal amplitude of 5 mV. The electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) samples were polished with 0.5 µm diamond abrasive and then electrolytically polished in ethanol perchloric acid solution with a volume fraction ratio of 20 % using a 20 V DC voltage for 18 s. The EBSD patterns were obtained under the following conditions: an accelerating voltage of 15 kV, sample tilt of 75°, and step size of 0.4 µm. The element distribution images were obtained by EPMA at an accelerating voltage of 20 kV with a step size of 0.4 µm. X-ray diffraction (XRD) was performed using Cu-Kα (wavelength α = 1.54 Å) radiation with a scanning range of 40-90° and scanning speed of 4°/min. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, Thermo Scientific K-Alpha) was used to determine the composition of the passive film after 120 min of open-circuit potential. Processing Text: The LDED system (LMD300) consists of a 2 kW fiber laser with a wavelength of 1060 nm, a platform control system, and a coaxial powder feeding system. The optimized processing parameters are as follows: laser power of 1200 W, scanning speed of 7 mm/s, laser spot size of 2.5 mm, powder feeding rate of 20 g/min, overlap rate of 50% and layer thickness of ∼1 mm. The laser scanning strategy followed a zigzag path with a 90° rotation of the scanning direction between successive layers. The chamber was filled with argon gas to minimize the possibility of the melt pool oxidation during the LDED process. The deposited IN718 block in size of 75 × 25 × 15 mm 3was cut from the base metal by electrical discharge machining. Before UIT, the LDED-fabricated IN718 plate samples were prepared using wire electrical discharge machining, and the sample surfaces were ground using a grinding machine to achieve a nominal surface roughness (Sa) of 0.4 μm. The UIT setup (CO-100) is schematically illustrated in Fig. 2b. During UIT process, the impact pin (made by quenched martensitic steel) with a head diameter of 3 mm struck the horizontal surface (XY-plane) of the samples and moved along a zigzag path shown in Fig. 2c. The fixed baseline parameters for the UIT process are as follows: impact frequency of 18 kHz and travel speed of 1 mm/s. The overlap rate of 50% was chosen because an insufficient overlap rate leads to poor strengthening effects, as evidenced by the comparative results for 20% and 50% overlap rates in Fig. S3-Fig. S5in Supplementary Materials. This study mainly focuses on the influence of the key parameter—UIT output powers ( i.e., 400 W, 600 W, and 800 W)—on surface integrity, deformation microstructure, and mechanical properties. According to the proportional relationship between power and the square of amplitude, the corresponding amplitudes for each power level were ∼14 μm, ∼17 μm, and ∼20 μm, respectively. White light interferometry (UP-2000, Rtec Instruments) was employed to measure the surface topography both before and after UIT. Residual stress measurements were performed using an X-ray residual stress measurement device (LXRD-MG2000, Proto) with a Mn target and the {311} reflection. The azimuth angle of the diffraction crystal plane (ѱ) was set to 0°, 25°, 35°, and 45°, respectively. The 2θ scanning angles were defined as 150° for the initiating angle and 155° for the terminating angle, with a tube current of 25 mA, a tube voltage of 30 kV, and a spot size of 1 mm. To accurately measure residual stresses in the tensile direction (X) along the depth, surface layers were incrementally removed through electro-polishing with 10 vol% perchloric acid ethanol solution, exposing the sample surface at varying depths. Moreover, a dynamic explicit finite element model (FEM) was developed using Abaqus/Explicit software to simulate the residual stress distribution induced by ultrasonic impact treatment under single-point impact conditions. The model consists of a 5 × 5 × 2 mm 3IN718 alloy plate, meshed with 50 μm C3D8R (8-node linear hexahedral) elements, and a 3 mm diameter impact needle, meshed with 250 μm C3D10M (10-node modified quadratic tetrahedral) elements made of quenched martensitic steel. The impact needle was modeled as a rigid body due to its negligible deformation during impact. The stress field was simulated using the elastic-plastic model by using the mechanical property of IN718 alloy derived from the stress-strain curve of the as-LDEDed sample in Fig. 8c. To capture the transient dynamics of the impact process, the analysis time step was set to 0.001 s. For simplification, the impact force was assumed to be perpendicular to the center of the specimen surface. The bottom of the workpiece was completely fixed, while symmetric boundary conditions were used to reduce computational cost. The ultrasonic impact system operates by converting electrical energy into high-frequency vibrations through a transducer, where the ultrasonic output power is proportional to the square of the vibration amplitude. This relationship enables the control of the output powers, with specific vibration amplitude adjustments corresponding to distinct power levels: ∼14 μm for 400 W, ∼17 μm for 600 W, and ∼20 μm for 800 W, respectively. The maximum initial velocity of the impact pin is vm= 2 πAf, where Ais the vibration amplitude and fis the frequency of 18 kHz, respectively. To observe the UIT-induced microstructure characteristics, cross-sectional (YZ-plane) samples were ground using different grit sizes of sandpaper (from #180 to #2000) and mechanically polished with diamond paste. Afterward, samples were electro-etched with the solution consisting of H 3PO 4(70 mL) and H 2O (30 mL) for 5 s with an applied voltage of 5 V. Optical microscopy (OM, XJP-6A, COIC) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM, S-4800, Hitachi) equipped with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) were used to observe the near-surface microstructure. The depth-dependent grain orientation and dislocation density were evaluated using electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, C-Nano, OXFORD) with a sample inclination angle of 70° and an operating voltage of 15 kV. The EBSD samples were treated with electrochemical polishing for 20 s using the solution of 10 vol% perchloric acid ethanol, with an applied voltage of 20 V. The raw data were further processed using the MTEX package and a custom-designed graphical user interface. Detailed deformation nanostructures at different depths were carried out using transmission electron microscopy (TEM, JEM-2100F, JEOL). The TEM sample with depth ≥30 μm was fabricated by twin-jet electro-polishing in a solution of 8% HClO 4and 92% ethanol. To scrutinize the near-surface microstructure, as seen in Fig. 2d, a thin foil of ∼100 nm thick was lifted out from the UIT surface by focused ion beam (FIB, FEI Strata 400S) and further investigated using TEM. To analyze the surface grain structure, an area of ∼6 × 4.3 μm 2from the TEM foil was scanned by transmission Kikuchi diffraction (TKD, Bruker Optimus) with a step size of 15 nm. Dislocation density estimation from TEM micrographs was performed by using the line-intercept method: (1)ρ=NLtwhere ρis the total dislocation density, Nis the number of intersection points between dislocations and random lines with a total length of L, and tis the thickness of the TEM foil designated as ∼100 nm. Microhardness was measured on the YZ plane of samples before and after UIT using a Vickers indenter (HV-1000, Shanghai Taiming) by applying a load of 0.2 kgf for 15 s. Room-temperature tensile tests were performed using a universal material testing machine (INSTRON-5982) at a loading rate of 1 mm/min. The UITed tensile samples were fabricated through the procedure in Fig. 2e, that is, the as-LDEDed specimen blocks were sectioned into plates with a thickness of 2 mm and ground on both sides to remove the oxide layer, then the plate was subsequently subjected to double-sided UIT and machined to dog-bone-shaped tensile testing samples. Processing Text: The ingots with nominal compositions of Fe-0.05C-1.6Mn-0.25Si-0.3Cr-2.5Ni-0.25Cu-0.055(Nb + Ti) (wt%) were prepared by vacuum induction melting under high-purity inert atmosphere. The as-cast ingots were forged into 170 × 85 × 120 mm (length × width × height) rectangular square billets within the temperature range of 1100-1200 °C. The forged billet was homogenized at 1200 °C for 2 h, and subsequently rough-rolled (the first stage of rolling) to 84 mm-thick plate between 1100 °C and 1030 °C. The rough-rolled plate was then air-cooled to 830 °C (plate surface) and hot-rolled (the second stage of rolling) to 50 mm in three passes at this temperature. After rolling, the steel plate was ultra-fast cooling to ∼400 °C. Subsequently, the steel plate was reheated to 830 °C and held at that temperature for 30 min to achieve thermal equilibrium between the experimental steel core specimen and the surface of the steel plate, thereby ensuring temperature uniformity throughout the experimental steel plate. Here, the reheating temperature was selected at 830 °C, exceeding the Ac3 temperature (808 °C) by 22 °C, to ensure complete austenitization of the microstructure while maintaining a moderate thermal gradient that minimizes energy consumption and prevents excessive grain growth. After that, the plate was hot-rolled (the third stage of rolling) to a thickness of 32 mm by 2 passes and subsequently laminar cooling to ∼400 °C. Finally, the rolled steel was cooled in air to room temperature, which was referred to as TPS-three-stage rolling coupling inter-pass reheating process steel. Condition: room temperature; Microstructure: ferrite-bainite mixed microstructure

Processing Text: The coating comprises two types of powder materials. One is spherical 316 L stainless steel powder, with a particle size ranging from 50 μm to 150 μm. The other material is YSZ (Jinggao Advanced Materials Technology). Its particle size range is 50 μm to 100 μm, with a purity of 99.9 %. The chemical composition of the YSZ powder is provided in Table 2. Firstly, 316 L stainless steel powder was mixed thoroughly with YSZ powder using a ball mill for approximately 4 h, resulting in mixtures containing 2.5 wt% and 5 wt% ZrO₂. The mixed powder was subsequently placed in a vacuum drying oven and preheated at 150 °C for 2 h to remove moisture and enhance flowability. The powder was then deposited as desired coating using a self-built LDED equipment equipped with a laser of 4 KW and 1060 nm wavelength (Raycus RFL-C4000). The LDED technology utilizes a coaxial powder feeding method to ensure the stability of coating properties. The optimal parameters were identified as a laser power of 1700 W, a scanning speed of 10 mm/s, a spot diameter of 4 mm, a powder feed rate of 1.2 r/min, and an overlap ratio of 50 %. With these optimized parameters, the 316 L composite coating was fabricated via multi-layer, multi-track laser processing, yielding a well-formed surface. After completing the coating process, the uneven top surface of the coating was removed using an electrical discharge wire cutting, and then cut into samples measuring 10 mm × 10 mm × 10 mm and 5 mm × 5 mm × 10 mm for subsequent tests. The metallographic samples were sequentially ground with SiC sandpaper with grades from 240# to 2000#, followed by polishing with 2.5μm diamond polishing paste. Aqua regia (HCl:HNO 3=3:1 V:V) was employed to etch the sample surface for 10-15 s, followed by ultrasonic cleaning with alcohol. The polarization test samples were mechanically polished and subsequently ultrasonically cleaned with alcohol to remove any residual polishing paste and surface impurities. Processing Text: LPBF-fabricated 316L stainless steel typically exhibits a high yield strength of approximately 600 MPa due to its high dislocation density. The raw material used in this work was commercially available gas atomized 316L stainless steel powders. The average size was 42.3 μm for 316L powder. The steels were fabricated using a commercial LPBF machine, the ProX DMP 300 (3D Systems, US). Specifications of the laser are as follows: full power = 500 W, wavelength = 1.07 μm, spot size = 75 μm. Oxygen level in the printing chamber was maintained below 300 ppm using high purity Argon gas. The laser scanning direction was rotated by 90° between consecutive layers. The printing parameters are presented in Table 2. Grinding, polishing, and etching were conducted to the samples for microstructural analysis. Processing Text: LPBF-fabricated 316L-TiB 2composites, the core at the centre of the melt pool contains ultrafine grains and twin boundaries while the edge features columnar grains. The LPBF-processed 316L-TiB 2exhibits an excellent combination of high strength (yield strength: 858 MPa, ultimate tensile strength: 1095 MPa) and ductility (27%). Adding 1 wt% TiB 2particles significantly enhances yield strength while maintaining excellent ductility. The synergistic interaction of Ti and B elements and 316L matrix was found to drive the formation of a distinctive core-shell structure. The core is filled with fine equiaxed grains and the shell is filled with columnar grains. A detailed microstructure characterization was further carried out using SEM BSE mode before and after etching the sample. By incorporating 3 wt% TiB 2particles to 316L introduced approximately 30% ferritic phase. The X-Ray diffraction positions of TiB 2(#35-0741) are also labelled in Fig. 6. It can be concluded that no diffraction peaks belong to the TiB 2phase. By incorporating 3 wt% TiB 2, the melt pool edge became narrower. Significant grain refinement has been achieved in LPBF-fabricated 316L by doping TiB 2particles. By incorporating just 1 wt% TiB 2, the grain size was reduced to about 1 μm. The mechanism behind the enhanced efficiency of TiB 2particles in grain refinement warrants further discussion. During the LPBF process of 316L-TiB 2composites, micronsized TiB 2particles dissolve and react with the 316L matrix. The Ti released from the decomposition of TiB 2is primarily responsible for the observed grain refinement. Additionally, the B from the decomposition forms a complex network of M 2B borides (M = Fe, Cr). These borides are distributed along the grain boundaries and the cellular structure boundaries. This network of borides further enhances grain refinement through the Zener pinning effect. Adding 1 wt% TiB 2particles reduces its grain size from 25.9 μm to about 1 μm. A complex network of M 2B borides (M = Fe, Cr) forms along the grain boundaries, promoting grain refinement via the Zener pinning effect. Additionally, Ti, resulting from the decomposition of TiB 2, acts as a potent solute for further grain refinement. The addition of 1 wt% TiB 2particles significantly enhanced the yield strength of 316L to 858 MPa from 599 MPa while maintaining a high elongation of 27%. Further increases in TiB 2content improve strength but result in a reduction in elongation. Among the various particles evaluated, TiB 2demonstrated superior efficiency over other ceramic particles in grain refinement and strength enhancement for 316L. Processing Text: Alloy ingot (300 g) with a nominal composition of Ni50Co25Cr9.5Al9Ti5Ta1.5 was prepared by arc-melting a mixture of high-purity raw metals (purity > 99.99 wt.%) in a Ti-gettered argon atmosphere. The ingot was re-melted at least five times with electromagnetic stirring to ensure chemical homogeneity. The output arc current is about 600 A, and the melting duration of single cycle is about 1 min (for detailed casting process, see supplementary material). To carry out microstructure observation, the specimen was mechanically polished with SiC paper, from 60 grit to 3000 grit, to eliminate scratches. After that, the SEM sample was electrolytically polished in a mixed solution of 90 % C2H5OH + 10 % HClO4 at 30 V for 20 s and electrolytically etched using H3PO4(170 ml) + H2SO4(10 ml) + CrO3(15 g) mixed solution at 5 V for 10 s. For the EBSD sample, only electrolytic polishing was conducted to remove the surface stress layer. The preparation process of TEM sample is as follows: Firstly, the samples were mechanically ground to a thickness of 40 μm using 3000 grit SiC paper. Then, they were stamped into Φ3 mm disc, and ion-milling (Gatan 695) was carried out using a mixed solution of 90 % CH3OH + 10 % HClO4 at 15 V and 25 °C. The dog-bone-shaped tensile specimens with a gauge length of 18 mm, width of 5 mm and thickness of 1.8 mm were prepared from the ingot via wire electrical discharge machining. Quasi-static uniaxial tensile tests were performed on electronic universal tensile testing machine (Instron-5569) with a strain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1 at room temperature. The tensile samples were sequentially ground until no obvious defects could be observed. Three times tests were conducted to minimize errors, and the yield strength was determined using 0.2 % offset plastic strain method. Microstructure investigation and room-temperature tensile test with identical parameters to as-cast Ni50Co25Cr9.5Al9Ti5Ta1.5 were conducted on the annealed counterpart. Processing Text: Alloy ingots with nominal compositions of Cu 50Ni 17.375Al 9.375Co 17Cr 3.125Ti 3.125B 0.5(at%) were fabricated by using a vacuum arc melting furnace under a high-purity argon atmosphere, and the starting materials were at least 99.9 wt%. All the ingots were repeatedly melted for 5 times to promote the chemical homogeneity, and then sucked into water-cooled copper mold with a plate shaped cavity of 80 mm × 20 mm × 7 mm. The isothermal oxidation experiments were performed in a box-type resistance furnace and an electronic balance with a resolution of 0.1 mg, and the samples size were 16 × 10 × 3 mm 3. Processing Text: The Al-1.5Mn alloy with a gradient microstructure was fabricated by ultrasonic shot peening (USSP). Ultrasonic shot peening (USSP) was carried out using an ultrasonic shot peening equipment (SONIC JY-P20). The ultrasonic shot peening parameters listed in Table 1 were selected for this study. Note that the parameters were selected mainly based on the mechanical responses, i.e., for peening duration 2 min the alloy manifests the best strength-plasticity synergy. The combination of 3 mm shots diameter and 15 mm peening distance can guarantee a relatively large peening intensity and in the meantime not causing surface damage such as cracks on the specimen surface. The amplitude of USSP is fixed in our device. All the surfaces of tensile specimen have been uniformly shot peened. The microstructure of Al-1.5Mn alloys with and without USSP was observed and analyzed using scanning electron microscope (SEM, Thermo Scientific Phenom XL, USA). The chemical composition of the samples was analyzed using energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) in conjunction with SEM. Phase transformations and residual stress distribution of alloys were determined by using X-ray diffraction (XRD, Bruker D-8 Focus X-ray, German). The refined microstructure of the sample was characterized by transmission electron microscopy (TEM, FEI Talos 200X, USA), electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, ThermoFisher Verios 5UC, USA) and transmission Kikuchi diffraction (TKD, ThermoFisher Verios 5UC, USA) techniques to determine the grain size and orientation changes before and after USSP. The sample was thinned using ion milling (PIPS II, USA) to prepare TEM foils. TEM-BF (bright field) imaging, selected area diffraction (SAD), STEM-BF imaging and energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) mapping were utilized. TKD test samples were prepared using the same ion-milled specimens as those used for TEM analysis. For the preparation of EBSD samples, the surface was initially ground with 600#, 1000#, and 2500# sandpapers, followed by polishing with a cloth to achieve a mirror-like finish. The samples were then subjected to vibratory polishing for 2 hours. A Vickers hardness tester (Mitutoyo HM-101, Japan) was used for hardness testing with a load of 0.1 N. At least three indentations were made at each depth position, and the standard deviation was calculated to measure the changes in the microhardness of specimens before and after shot peening. The tensile specimens, whose size is depicted in Fig. 1(c), were prepared and subjected to double-sided USSP. Uniaxial tensile tests were conducted using a universal testing machine at an initial strain rate of 10 −3s −1. The true stress-strain curves were obtained using Eqs. (1) and (2), which could provide a quantitative description of the work hardening rate. After tensile tests, fracture morphologies of Al-1.5Mn alloys were characterized by using SEM (Thermo Scientific Phenom XL, USA). In the quasi-in-situ immersion experiment, the cross-sections of Al-1.5Mn alloys with USSP treatment were ground and polished to achieve a mirror-like finish. Note that, in order to avoid the well-known interference factor of surface contamination, surface contamination layer (∼5 μm in thickness) was firstly removed by polishing before electrochemical corrosion test. This can make the to-be-studied system simpler and enable us to specifically study the influences of microstructural and residual stress changes on corrosion performance. In addition, all the specimens used for electrochemical corrosion tests had the same mirror-like finish obtained by 80 nm SiO 2 polishing. The gradient Al-1.5Mn alloy was annealed at 200 °C for 2 hours to relieve the residual stress. Condition: untreated sample

Processing Text: Nickel 625 solid and the first-developed TiC-containing Ni625-core wires were utilized in this study for comparative analysis. Given the differences in deposition form and current density between solid and cored wires, particularly with non-metallic ceramic particles, deposition parameters for both wires were examined separately. The optimized deposition parameters are listed in Table 3. The Q235 substrate was polished to eliminate surface impurities and oxides. The deposited components were cut to precise dimensions using a wire-cutting machine. The sample surfaces were sequentially polished using grit papers of 200#, 400#, 800#, 1200#, 1500#, 2000#, and 3000#. Further refinement was achieved using cloth polishing and a 2.5 μm diamond spray polish. A custom FeCl 3 etchant (8 g FeCl 3 + 14 ml HCl + 20 ml C 2H 5OH) was applied. The treated surfaces were analyzed using a 3D profilometry optical microscope (OLYMPUS DSX1000). High-resolution field emission scanning electron microscopy (FSEM, MAIA3 LMH) was employed to analyze particle distribution, morphology, and microstructural evolution. The porosity distribution in rectangular samples from the top of the single-wall structure was analyzed using 3D-CT. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, OXFORD C NANO+) was employed on electrolytically polished surfaces to quantify particle distribution and structural characteristics. The test was performed at 20.00 kV with a 70° sample tilt, a scanning speed of ∼198 Hz, and a 5 μm step size. A transmission electron microscope (TEM, JEM-2100F) was used for microstructural characterization. Microhardness along the deposition direction was measured using a Vickers hardness tester (HVSA-1000A). Three equidistant horizontal points at the same depth from the surface or bottom were tested, and their average was recorded. Tensile properties were measured using an electronic universal testing machine (Zwick020). A tensile speed of 0.6 mm/min was applied. Three specimens per sample, taken from the top, middle, and bottom in both horizontal and longitudinal directions, were analyzed for mechanical properties and anisotropy. Multi-layer deposition was performed under different conditions using the parameters listed in Table 3. A PC210 industrial thermal imaging camera recorded weld bead temperatures during deposition, with data analyzed using ThermoTools software. To reduce thermal accumulation, careful control of interlayer temperature is required. In this study, each layer was cooled to near-room temperature before subsequent deposition. As shown in Fig. 6f, each layer was deposited after cooling to 'room temperature - 40 °C.' Thermal imaging and temperature analysis indicate that when the interlayer is sufficiently cooled, temperature differences between arc initiation and extinction points become negligible. Processing Text: The experimental material consisted of 316L austenitic stainless steel rods with a diameter of 30 mm. The material was hot-rolled to 4 mm in thickness, followed by solution treatment at 1050 °C for 1 h. Before each rolling pass, the initial material was immersed in liquid nitrogen for 10 min. The thickness reduction per pass was kept below 5 %. Surface cracks developed when the total thickness reduction reached 70 %. Consequently, the final thickness was reduced by 70 %, resulting in a thickness of 1.2 mm for the cryo-rolled sample, which was labeled as CryoR sample. After cryo-rolling, the samples were subjected to annealing at 700 °C 20 min, 750 °C 6 min, and a sequential 700 °C 20 min + 750 °C 6 min process, followed by water quenching. These samples were labeled as 700A, 750A, and 700A-750A, respectively. All heat treatment processes were performed in a muffle furnace without a protective atmosphere. Tensile tests were conducted using a universal testing machine (5105, SSANS-CMT) at room temperature (24 °C) and liquid nitrogen temperature (−196 °C) with a strain rate of 10 −3s −1. All tensile samples were cut along the rolling direction into dog-bone shapes with a gauge length of 34 mm, width of 10 mm, and thickness of 1 mm. Each test was repeated at least three times to ensure accuracy. To evaluate inhomogeneous deformation, load-unload-reload (LUR) tests were also performed under the same conditions as the tensile tests to quantify the back stress (σ B) component. The microstructural evolution of the samples along the rolling direction (RD) was characterized. XRD analysis was conducted to examine phase transformation with a diffraction angle range of 40°-100° and a scanning speed of 2°/min, using Cu-Kα radiation at 40 kV and 150 mA. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, Oxford) was employed for quantitative analysis of the phase microstructure. After mechanical polishing, samples were electropolished using a 10 % perchloric acid solution at 20 V for 20-25 s. EBSD measurements were performed on a Zeiss Auriga scanning electron microscope with a step size of 100 nm at an accelerating voltage of 15 kV. Processing Text: To obtain excellent fatigue resistance and mechanical properties, a gradient-nanostructured layer was fabricated by ultrasonic surface rolling process (USRP) at the gauge section and arc transition. Severe plastic deformation (SPD) was introduced on the specimen surface by the ultrasonic vibrating motion combined with static force on the specimen applied through a rolling ball tip. The ultrasonic surface rolling processing parameters are as follows: static force 400 N, vibration amplitude 10 μm, feeding rate 500 mm/min, and repeated processing 30 times. After USRP, fatigue and tensile specimens with a thickness of 2 mm are wire-cut from the blank specimen. Microhardness distribution was measured on the cross-sections (parallel to ND) of GNS-Zr with an applied load of 200 g and a holding time of 15 s using a digital microhardness tester at room temperature. Residual compressive stress along the ND was measured using an X-ray diffractometer (XRD) with Cu-Kα radiation at the Zr {211} plane, and the diffraction angle (2θ) range was 30°-90°. Tensile tests were performed at a strain rate of 1×10−3s−1 at room temperature using a universal testing machine. The tensile properties of coarse-grained and gradient-nanostructured Zr were measured with the dimensions of 15×4×2mm3 (as shown in Fig. 1(b)). Stress-controlled fatigue tests were conducted with a frequency of 20 Hz and a stress ratio R of 0.1 using an Instron 8801 fatigue testing machine under stress control. The crack propagation rate would be calculated by the slope of two neighboring data points of the crack length versus the cycle number. The crack propagation length ∆a under different fatigue cycles was measured using a two-part silicone rubber replica method in combination with a metallographic microscope. The stress intensity factor ∆K of the single-edge notched specimens can be calculated. The test stress σmax is 270MPa, the stress ratio R is 0.1, and the frequency f is 20 Hz. Life tests were performed on notched coarse grain specimens (CG-Zr) and notched gradient nanostructured specimens (GNS-Zr). The microstructure was investigated using a Zeiss Gemini 300 field emission scanning electron microscope (SEM) fitted with an Oxford Symmetry EBSD detector, and a Talos F200X transmission electron microscope (TEM). The physical quantities of microstructure at different locations in the gradient direction were investigated by EBSD characterization. The TEM specimens were mechanically ground down to 50 μm to characterize the fine microstructure. Then, the thin foil samples were fabricated by the Gatan695 precision ion thinning machine to obtain an electron-transparent TEM sample. Compared to CG-Zr, the yield strength increased by 18%; The material also exhibited satisfactory ductility with an elongation of approximately 24%.

Processing Text: W30Cu composite materials were prepared by mechanically mixing high-purity (purity >99.9 %) W powder (average particle size 5 μm) and Cu powder (average particle size 10 μm), followed by hot pressing sintering (HPS). After mixing 70 wt% W powder and 30 wt% Cu powder, the mixture was ball-milled with a ball-to-powder ratio of 3:1. The milling was conducted at a speed of 300 rpm for 2 h, using tungsten carbide balls and a silicon nitride milling pot to ensure efficient powder milling without contamination. The milled powder mixture was then placed into a hot pressing sintering mold, which had good sealing properties, a height of 6 mm, and was made of tungsten alloy. After vacuum evacuation, HPS treatment was carried out at 1350 °C and 150 MPa for 2 h. 6 mm thick W30Cu billets were obtained by cutting after cooling with the furnace. In the first step, the W30Cu billets prepared by HPS were cut to dimensions of 30 mm × 40 mm × 6 mm and then annealed in a muffle furnace for rolling. The heating temperature was set at 500 °C with a heating time of 30 min. After annealing, the material was sent to a double-roll reversible mill for unidirectional rolling and further annealing was carried out, depending on the rolling condition of the sample, until the material thickness was reduced to 1 mm. In the second step, the 1 mm thick plates were cut to 20 mm × 40 mm × 1 mm and annealed in a muffle furnace at the same heating temperature. The heating time was extended to 45 min and the material was then sent to a four-roll reversible mill for unidirectional rolling. Annealing was performed when the sample thickness reached 0.6 mm and 0.2 mm, depending on the rolling status, and the material was rolled further until the thickness reached 0.1 mm. Samples were taken for analysis from the raw material, the 1 mm (R83%) plates after the first rolling stage and the 0.6 mm (R90%), 0.2 mm (R97%) and 0.1 mm (R98%) plates after the second rolling stage. Processing Text: The chemical composition of A100 steel was shown in Table 1, and its heat treatment system was as follows: 885 ± 15 °C heat preservation for 60 min, quenching, oil cooling; Then, it was kept at −73 ± 8 °C for 60 min for cold treatment and reheated in air. Finally, 482 ± 3 °C insulation for 5 h tempering, air cooling. The mechanical properties of A100 ultra-high strength steels treated according to this heat treatment specification were shown in Table 2. The yield strength ( σ s), tensile strength ( σ b), elongation ( δ5) and section shrinkage (ψ) were 1920 MPa, 1998 MPa, 12.23 % and 65.82 %, respectively. In the USRP process, the static pressure and amplitude determined the intensity of ultrasonic energy, and the spindle speed and axial feed determined the coverage of processing. Parameters for the process were fine-tuned through prior orthogonal experiments and were as follows for this study: a spindle speed set at 45 r/min, an axial feed of 0.08 mm/r, static pressure fixed at 900 N, and an amplitude setting of 12 μm. Two samples were prepared for comparison—one treated with a single pass, labelled USRP-1, and the other with thirty passes, designated as USRP-30. X-ray diffraction phase analysis: The Rigaku Ultima IV X-ray diffractometer was utilized to study the specimen surface phases pre- and post-treatment, employing a Cu-Kα radiation source with a 1.5418 Å wavelength. The equipment operated at 40 kV and 35 mA, scanning at a speed of 1°/min across an angular range of 30° to 90° in 2θ. Surface topography and roughness analysis: The surface topography of USRP cylindrical specimens was observed with IFM-G4 white light surface topography instrument, and its surface roughness was measured. The average value of 3 measurements was taken as the test result of roughness. Scanning electron microscopy analysis: To scrutinize the alterations in the specimen surface microstructure pre- and post-treatment, the TESCAN LYRA3 XMU was employed, a dual-beam SEM, to capture images of the cross-sectional topography. Prior to SEM analysis, the cross-section of specimen underwent mechanical polishing utilizing a gradation of SiC sandpapers (ranging from 320 to 1200 grit), followed by a 1 μm diamond suspension. Subsequently, the sample was etched with a 4 % solution of nitric acid. Transmission electron microscope analysis: A Tecnai G2 F20 Transmission Electron Microscope (TEM) was utilized along with High-Resolution TEM to examine the surface microstructure modifications induced by USRP. Prior to TEM analysis, the specimens was meticulously prepared by grinding their surfaces to a thickness of 50 μm. Subsequently, a precision single injection thinning process on the interior perforations was employed for utilizing a solution composed of 10 % HClO 4+ 90 % CH 3OH (volume fraction). Hardness test: A Knoop HV-1000 microhardness tester was employed to gauge surface hardness pre- and post-treatment, applying a 25 g force with a 20 s dwell time. To verify the dependability of test data, five measurements for each datum was took. Residual stress test: The XL-640 system residual stress tester was utilized to evaluate surface stresses in variously processed samples. Employing Cr-Kα as the radiation source, the analyses was conducted based on the sin2ψ technique. To ascertain how residual stress altered with depth within the layers, the material was systematically stripped using an electrolytic method. This involved immersing the specimen in a concoction primarily composed of methanol (87.5 % by volume) with a sulfuric acid fraction of 12.5 %. Through this process, each layer of specimen was carefully peeled off to chart the residual stress profile depth-wise. Rotational bending fretting fatigue test method: A rotational bending fretting fatigue test was conducted using the PQ-6 tester, employing a custom fixture to facilitate the fretting fatigue load. As shown in Fig. 2, the interfacing geometry between the specimen and the bridge took the form of a curved contact, and the form of contact between the specimen and fretting pad was cylinder to camber. As the reference [20], throughout the test, the stress ring moved in unison with the specimen, and the normal forced was applied to the fretting pad by adjusting screws attached to the probing ring and was maintained at 3.6 KN using a tension sensor. The test maintained a speed of 2100 r/min, equivalent to 35 Hz, with a stress ratio set at R = -1. All testing occurred under standard room conditions, without any special atmospheric controls. The specimen size and observation method used in this paper are consistent with those in a previous paper published by us [22]. Prior to testing, all A100 steel samples were mechanically polished using a grinder to achieve the same low surface roughness. To characterize the cross-sectional surface microstructure, hardness, and residual stress distribution along the transverse direction (TD) after processing, the sample was also cut by electric discharge machining (EDM) along the TD with the Φ 6 mm × 10 mm. To study the PF and FF fracture, the samples were cut by EDM along the TD at a distance of 5 mm from the point of fracture. For the samples subjected to FF testing, the cut portion of the sample was also used to study the change in the fretting contact zone, which was located near the fretting fatigue fracture surface. In addition, to observe secondary cracks in the fretting fatigue test, the cut samples were cut in half again by EDM along the longitudinal direction (LD); these smaller sections were then mechanically polished to a mirror-like surface and etched using a 4 % Nital solution. In order to further elucidate the nano-mechanism of the martensite structure in USRP-treated A100 steel, the precipitated phase in A100 steel was characterized. In order to better confirm and characterize the morphology and type of precipitate phases, this paper focused on the analysis of the precipitate phase in the A100 steel substrate because the microstructure of the surface layer of the sample was severely refined after USRP-30 treatment, and the precipitated phase, nanocrystalline and dislocation defects were intertwined. To ensure chemical composition uniformity, each ingot was remelted at least six times before being cast into a water-cooled copper mold using a suction casting method. Initially, the cast ingots were polished to remove the surface contamination layer and then processed into rods with a diameter of 96 mm. TEM samples were prepared by wire cutting into discs with a diameter of 6 mm and a thickness of 0.5 mm, followed by grinding to 60 μm. Processing Text: The alloy ingot was fabricated by arc melting and 6 times of melting were done repeatedly to guarantee compositional homogeneity. The raw materials for melting are Ti ingot (99.99 %), Nb thin plate (99.99 %), Sn shot (99.99 %) and TiO 2 powder (99.99 %). The as-produced ingot is button-like and its weight loss after melting is less than 0.1 % and can be negligible, indicating the good quality of the ingot produced. The button-like ingot was encapsulated in a quartz tube in which a vacuum atmosphere of 1.5 × 10 −5 torr was produced. Homogenization heat treatment was carried out at 1000 °C for 2 h.
