Processing Text: This experiment used commercial 6061-T6 aluminum alloy with a thickness of 8 mm, rolled under ultra-low temperature conditions (−196 °C) with a total reduction of 85%. Unlike conventional rolling processes, this experiment employed a large reduction with fewer passes to achieve high strain rate deformation. The rolling was conducted in four passes, with a reduction of 25% in the first pass and 20% in the remaining three passes. The ultra-low temperature rolling process is conducted as follows: The experimental aluminum alloy sheet is immersed in liquid nitrogen for 3 min to ensure that the temperature of the aluminum sheet equilibrates with that of the liquid nitrogen. Simultaneously, liquid nitrogen is also sprayed onto the rolling mills to reduce their temperature. The aluminum sheet, now in an ultra-low temperature state, is promptly transferred into the rolling mill for rolling, with the transfer time not exceeding 0.5 s. After completing one pass of rolling, the aluminum alloy sheet is once again submerged in liquid nitrogen for cooling, and the other operational steps are consistent with those previously described. This process is repeated until the rolling experiment is completed. In this experiment, the rolling speed for ultra-low temperature rolling was set at 15 rad/s, with a roll diameter of 200 mm, resulting in a strain rate during rolling of 3.5s⁻¹. Processing Text: The gas-atomized SS 310 powder supplied by Indo-MIM with the elemental composition listed in Table 1 was utilized as raw material to fabricate SLM specimens for surface quality and mechanical characterization. Before SLM fabrication, the 310 powder was kept in vacuum-drying ovens at 120°C for 2 hours to remove the volatile impurities. The test samples were built by SLM EP-M100T machine equipped with a continuous wave Ytterbium (CW Yb) fiber laser with a maximum power of 200 W, wavelength of 1.07 µm, and spot diameter of 80 µm under the shielding gas of nitrogen. The striped hatch scan pattern with a 67° rotation between each consecutive layer was chosen because it enhanced part quality. The tensile samples were prepared horizontally with respect to build direction due to their superior tensile strength. After the SLM process, the as-built samples are removed from the substrate using wire electrical discharge machining. Microstructural analysis of the SLM specimens was performed using optical microscopy (Olympus BX53M) and field emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM) (FEI Quanta 250 FEG). Elemental composition was determined using energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) in conjunction with FE-SEM. For microstructural analysis, the samples were polished using SiC grinding papers and etched by standard metallographic techniques. The hardness was measured on both surface PBD and surface PPBD to understand the anisotropic properties of the SLM specimen. Processing Text: The Zr45Ti15Nb20Ta20 RMEA fabrication process was detailed in our previous work. The as-cast samples were initially solidified at 1673 K for 2 h and subsequently aged at 773-1173 K for 6 h, 12 h, and 24 h. For ease of indicating the different heat treatments of the RMEAs, they are termed A-x-y (x = 773, 973, and 1173; y = 6, 12, and 24). The microhardness of the aged-RMEAs was measured on a Vickers hardness tester (MHVS-1000AT) with an applied load of 0.98 N and a holding time of 15 s. High-temperature uniaxial compression tests were conducted using the Gleeble 3800 thermo-simulation machine, with cylindrical specimens measuring 8 mm in diameter and 12 mm in height. Compression tests were conducted at a constant stain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1 at 1273 K, with a true stain of 0.69 (50 pct reduction in the height). The room temperature tests were performed using a universal testing machine (Instron-5582, Instron, USA) at an initial strain rate of 10−3 s−1, stopping when the cylindrical height was reduced by 50% or when the compression sample failed to fracture. The phase constituents of as-homogenized and aged RMEAs were analyzed using X-ray diffraction (XRD, Bruker d8 X-ray Diffractometer) with Cu-Kα radiation. Diffraction angles between 20° and 100° (2θ) were collected with a step size of approximately 10° per minute. The microstructure of specimens before and after compression was examined using a field emission scanning electron microscope (SEM; XL-30FEG, Holland) equipped with an electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) and energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) detector. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) (Talos F200X) was employed for additional microstructural characterization using specimens prepared by ion milling. Processing Text: The Iron-based MEA was fabricated using a vacuum arc melting furnace, and each raw material was sourced from pure commercial elements with a purity of at least 99.9 %. The master alloy was turned upside down five times during melting to ensure chemically homogenized alloy. During the melting process, the alloy was melted upside down five times to ensure a uniform chemical composition. The as-cast ingots were sealed in an evacuated quartz tube, homogenized at 1150 °C for 24 h, and then water quenched to room temperature. The homogenized ingots were subsequently cold-rolled to 87 % reduction in thickness using laboratory-scale rolling equipment. To obtain various grain sizes of the MEA, the tensile specimens were sealed in a quartz tube and annealed at different temperatures for various durations. The specimens were annealed at 950 °C for 100 s, 25 min, and 1 h, respectively. Additionally, in order to achieve a larger grain size within a shorter annealing time, some specimens were subjected to annealing at 1050 °C for 5 h. TEM specimens were mechanically polished using 1200-grit sandpaper to reduce the thickness to less than 100 mm and then jet-polished by an Automatic Twin-Jet Electropolisher (FISCHIONE, Model 110, applied voltage: 27 V). Tensile tests were conducted using a 100-kN-capacity universal Material Testing System (MTS, Model: 810) at room temperature (25 °C) and cryogenic temperature (−100 °C & −196 °C), with a constant strain rate of 0.001 s −1. Processing Text: CBT specimens for AA6016-T4 were subjected to 2, 4, 6, 8, and 10 CBT cycles before the process was interrupted and each specimen was removed. A subsize specimen was then machined from the center of each interrupted CBT specimen and pulled in tension. The entire pre-strain process was repeated twice to produce two sets of subsize specimens which will be referred to as set 1 and set 2. CBT and ST specimens were cut from sheets of AA6016-T4 with thicknesses of 1 mm. The AA6016 alloy is heat treatable and arrived in the T4 temper state. The sheets were obtained from Commonwealth Rolled Products in 2021. The chemical compositions are shown in Table 1. The Mg and Si content in AA6016 produce Mg 2Si precipitates. The following sequence of precipitation strengthens the alloy: supersaturated solid solution → Guinier-Preston (GP) zones → needle-like β ”→ rod-like β ’+ lath-like precipitates → β + Si. These precipitates cause barriers to dislocation glide, with the β ”phases proving the most effective hardening. Optimizing parameters for AA6016-T4 was possible using one factor at a time (OFAT) testing. The maximum elongation occurs at a bend depth of 3.5 mm in RD and 4.5 mm in TD. For pull speed, the maximum elongation occurs at a value of slightly below 1.5 mm/s in RD and slightly above 1.5 mm/s in TD. To have an agreement in optimal values between the two directions the values of parameters in each direction were averaged. The result is a bend depth of 4 mm and pull speed of 1.5 mm/s as optimal parameters for AA6016-T4. The force displacement data recorded during several selected CBT tests in RD and TD compared to simple tension data is shown in Fig. 6. The optimal values of 4 mm bend depth and 1.5 mm/s pull speed are included for comparison to ST and several other CBT tests with different parameters. The CBT data shows characteristic sawtooth shapes due to the bending and unbending of the specimen as the rollers move over it. When the carriage stops to change direction after each pass there is a brief period where the specimen is not bending but is in pure tension producing the spikes seen in Fig. 6. The magnitude of bend depth and pull speed effect the tensile force required to deform the material. As bending depth increases, more plastic deformation is caused by bending rather than by tension which lowers the force output. Similarly, as pull speed decreases more deformation is caused by bending also reducing force. The forces are higher when pull speed is increased or bend depth decreased due to tension being the route of deformation. The effects of these variables allow the force on the specimen in CBT to be controlled, allowing the process to conform to any material to produce the maximum elongation. It is evident that CBT greatly increases elongation to failure of AA6016-T4. The experimental results also indicate some anisotropy between the RD and TD directions for this material. The TD direction exhibits slightly longer ETF at optimal parameters when compared to the RD direction. Fig. 10 shows the true and engineering stress strain response of the alloys obtained from specimens cut from the center of CBT specimens after CBT treatment. CBT specimens for AA6016-T4 were subjected to 2, 4, 6, 8, and 10 CBT cycles before the process was interrupted and each specimen was removed. A subsize specimen was then machined from the center of each interrupted CBT specimen and pulled in tension. The entire pre-strain process was repeated twice to produce two sets of subsize specimens which will be referred to as set 1 and set 2. The intent was to test two specimens after every pre-strain level for verification. However, the time t between testing one set of specimens to testing the other set was about three months. The specimens tested later belong to set 1, while those tested right after machining belong to set 2. The time between CBT pre-straining including machining to testing set 2 was within a month. It is known that 6xxx and 7xxx aluminum alloys are susceptible to natural aging with pre-strain influencing the aging process. The as-received specimens from 2021 did not show any natural aging effect as the natural aging processes in the alloys likely saturated. Therefore, the expectation was that the specimens will not undergo natural aging. Nevertheless, some natural aging effect on the mechanical properties is observed in the experimental results shown in Fig. 10. The observed effect shows some softening, which is the opposite of typically observed strengthening natural aging effect. Evidently the severely pre-strained structures of the alloy are unstable. The notable effect of natural aging of the pre-strained specimens in this study is seen in the decreased ultimate tensile strength (UTS) of set 1 compared to set 2. Aside from the combined pre-strain and aging effect, it is seen that the work hardening achieved via CBT results in significant increase of yield strength compared to the as-received AA6016-T4 in both RD and TD. Remarkably, yield strength exceeds 300 MPa after 10 CBT cycles, which is well above UTS. The residual ductility decreases with the increase in strength. Notably, 2 CBT cycles significantly strengthen the alloy, about 2x, but residual ductility is also appreciable, ∼10%. Fig. 12 shows the trends of plastic strain ratios r-ratios (or r-values) as a function of CBT cycles. For sheet metals the r-ratio is the resistance to thinning during plastic deformation which is important for selecting the right material for a sheet metal forming process. The r-ratio is defined as the ratio of true width strain (strain perpendicular to direction of applied load) and true thickness strain: r=εwεt. In this study DIC was used to obtain strain data in the length and width directions. Assuming volume remains constant, the equation for r ratio becomes: r=−εw(εw+εl). This equation makes it possible to calculate the r ratio without directly knowing the strain in the thickness direction. Sheet forming is impeded by pronounced anisotropic material behavior, characterized by r-ratio. It is generally understood that the anisotropy of AA sheets is mainly driven by the crystallographic texture of the sheets. However, it has been observed in 6xxx series AA that crystallographic texture by itself does not solely explain the anisotropic properties, especially for pre-strained sheets. In the present work, the r-ratio increases but then decreases with an increase in CBT cycles. The increase is likely owing to the change in texture, while the decrease could be owing to the damage accumulation. Similarly to strength, 2 CBT cycles are found to be beneficial for r-ratio. Optimizing parameters for AA6016-T4 was possible using one factor at a time (OFAT) testing. The maximum elongation occurs at a bend depth of 3.5 mm in RD and 4.5 mm in TD. For pull speed, the maximum elongation occurs at a value of slightly below 1.5 mm/s in RD and slightly above 1.5 mm/s in TD. To have an agreement in optimal values between the two directions the values of parameters in each direction were averaged. The result is a bend depth of 4 mm and pull speed of 1.5 mm/s as optimal parameters for AA6016-T4. The force displacement data recorded during several selected CBT tests in RD and TD compared to simple tension data is shown in Fig. 6. The optimal values of 4 mm bend depth and 1.5 mm/s pull speed are included for comparison to ST and several other CBT tests with different parameters. The CBT data shows characteristic sawtooth shapes due to the bending and unbending of the specimen as the rollers move over it. When the carriage stops to change direction after each pass there is a brief period where the specimen is not bending but is in pure tension producing the spikes seen in Fig. 6. The magnitude of bend depth and pull speed effect the tensile force required to deform the material. As bending depth increases, more plastic deformation is caused by bending rather than by tension which lowers the force output. Similarly, as pull speed decreases more deformation is caused by bending also reducing force. The forces are higher when pull speed is increased or bend depth decreased due to tension being the route of deformation. The effects of these variables allow the force on the specimen in CBT to be controlled, allowing the process to conform to any material to produce the maximum elongation. It is evident that CBT greatly increases elongation to failure of AA6016-T4. The experimental results also indicate some anisotropy between the RD and TD directions for this material. The TD direction exhibits slightly longer ETF at optimal parameters when compared to the RD direction. Fig. 10 shows the true and engineering stress strain response of the alloys obtained from specimens cut from the center of CBT specimens after CBT treatment. CBT specimens for AA6016-T4 were subjected to 2, 4, 6, 8, and 10 CBT cycles before the process was interrupted and each specimen was removed. A subsize specimen was then machined from the center of each interrupted CBT specimen and pulled in tension. The entire pre-strain process was repeated twice to produce two sets of subsize specimens which will be referred to as set 1 and set 2. The intent was to test two specimens after every pre-strain level for verification. However, the time t between testing one set of specimens to testing the other set was about three months. The specimens tested later belong to set 1, while those tested right after machining belong to set 2. The time between CBT pre-straining including machining to testing set 2 was within a month. It is known that 6xxx and 7xxx aluminum alloys are susceptible to natural aging with pre-strain influencing the aging process. The as-received specimens from 2021 did not show any natural aging effect as the natural aging processes in the alloys likely saturated. Therefore, the expectation was that the specimens will not undergo natural aging. Nevertheless, some natural aging effect on the mechanical properties is observed in the experimental results shown in Fig. 10. The observed effect shows some softening, which is the opposite of typically observed strengthening natural aging effect. Evidently the severely pre-strained structures of the alloy are unstable. The notable effect of natural aging of the pre-strained specimens in this study is seen in the decreased ultimate tensile strength (UTS) of set 1 compared to set 2. Aside from the combined pre-strain and aging effect, it is seen that the work hardening achieved via CBT results in significant increase of yield strength compared to the as-received AA6016-T4 in both RD and TD. Remarkably, yield strength exceeds 300 MPa after 10 CBT cycles, which is well above UTS. The residual ductility decreases with the increase in strength. Notably, 2 CBT cycles significantly strengthen the alloy, about 2x, but residual ductility is also appreciable, ∼10%. Fig. 12 shows the trends of plastic strain ratios r-ratios (or r-values) as a function of CBT cycles. For sheet metals the r-ratio is the resistance to thinning during plastic deformation which is important for selecting the right material for a sheet metal forming process. The r-ratio is defined as the ratio of true width strain (strain perpendicular to direction of applied load) and true thickness strain: r=εwεt. In this study DIC was used to obtain strain data in the length and width directions. Assuming volume remains constant, the equation for r ratio becomes: r=−εw(εw+εl). This equation makes it possible to calculate the r ratio without directly knowing the strain in the thickness direction. Sheet forming is impeded by pronounced anisotropic material behavior, characterized by r-ratio. It is generally understood that the anisotropy of AA sheets is mainly driven by the crystallographic texture of the sheets. However, it has been observed in 6xxx series AA that crystallographic texture by itself does not solely explain the anisotropic properties, especially for pre-strained sheets. In the present work, the r-ratio increases but then decreases with an increase in CBT cycles. The increase is likely owing to the change in texture, while the decrease could be owing to the damage accumulation. Similarly to strength, 2 CBT cycles are found to be beneficial for r-ratio. Moreover 4 CBT cycles reduce the anisotropy in r-ratio between RD and TD of AA6016-T4, which is noteworthy. As-received state

Processing Text: Fig. 11 contains the subsize ST curves recorded for AA7021-T79 which were created using the same process that was used for AA6016-T4. AA7021-T79 is much more brittle than AA6016 and was only able to be pre-strained up to 5 CBT cycles without fracture. The natural aging effect is once again observed as set 2 has higher UTS and yield strength compared to set 1. Appendix A contains numerical data for AA7021-T79. It is demonstrated that work hardening by CBT increased yield strength by over 100 MPa in both RD and TD. Evidently, the improvements are good but not as drastic as for AA6016-T4. CBT and ST specimens were cut from sheets of AA7021-T79 with thicknesses of 2.5 mm. The AA7021 alloy is heat treatable and arrived in the T79 temper state. The sheets were obtained from Commonwealth Rolled Products in 2021. The chemical compositions are shown in Table 1. Heat treatment of AA7021 (Al-Zn-Mg-Cu) results in a typical precipitation sequence as follows: supersaturated solid solution → GP zones (coherent) → η ’(metastable and semicoherent) → η (MgZn 2- incoherent resulting from over-aging). The use of AA7021 in industry is relatively small owing to its low formability at room temperature. Warm forming is a solution but increases the cost. The higher yield strength and the increased material thickness resulted in much higher forces during CBT testing. These higher bending forces resulted in the pull speed significantly changing as bend depth changed. Due to the presence of variable interactions the optimization of AA7021-T79 could not be as readily obtained using the OFAT method as it was possible for AA6016. A new method was employed that tests the effect of both variables at the same time. The Design of Experiments (DoE) method allows the experimenter to test the effect of multiple variables and their interactions on the response. The method is employed here for AA7021-T79. A 2 level, 2 variable ( 22) full factorial experiment with two center points and 1 replicate point was created using JMP statistical software for AA7021-T79 RD and TD directions. The experimental runs were set up based on two variables (bend depth and voltage) with each having two levels, a low and a high. Pull speed is not used as a variable because it is a measured response which is controlled by the voltage input to the hydraulic cylinder. Bend depth had a low of 1 mm and a high of 4 mm while voltage had a low of 1 V and a high of 9 V. The low and high levels for these variables were selected based on the machine capabilities. The purpose of low and high variable values is to be able to evaluate all possible combinations of variables in-between. For a 22 factorial experiment the area that these variable combinations form is a square with the x and y axis being the values of bend depth and voltage respectively. The area that the variable levels cover is called the experimental space. Experimental runs are carried out at combinations of low and high levels determined by the design generated in JMP. For this study the initial size of each experiment was 12 runs. After elongation data was recorded JMP can be used to analyze the results using a variety of statistical modeling techniques. A fit least squares response surface model was used to produce contour plots of the experimental space indicating regions of high elongation to failure. Additional experiments were then performed in selected regions to further close in on the optimal values of bend depth and voltage. The total number of runs to converge on optimal values for AA7021-T79 was 30 for RD and 24 for TD. The relationship between output force and the experimental variables is the same as previously explained for AA6016-T4. Evidently, the less ductile AA7021-T79 tolerated less bending and pulling speed compared to AA6016-T4. The optimal values of bend depth and pull speed were 2.5 mm and 1 mm/s for AA7021-T79. Under these conditions, the AA7021-T79 alloys elongated about 3x more compared to ST, respectively. The force displacement curves for these optimal values along with the ST test and a few other CBT tests at different combinations of bend depth and pull speed for comparisons. It is again evident that the CBT process produces much larger ETF compared to ST. It should be noted that the force displacement graphs could not be represented like those for AA6016-T4 in Fig. 6 due to the interaction between the variables. The sheet thickness and yield strength of AA7021-T79 were much higher than AA6016-T4 resulting in larger forces acting on the rollers during testing. It was discovered that these forces were large enough to slightly change the intended bend depth for a given test by moving the rollers. This created the slight variation observed between simulated and experimental results for AA7021-T79. As-received state

Processing Text: Cu-0.5Cr-0.05Zr alloys were prepared by vacuum melting. The hot-forged samples were cut into 5 mm thick plates and subjected to 80% reduction room-temperature rolling. Afterward, the rolled samples were vacuum aged at 350 °C-550 °C for 0-12 h. To ensure the complete dissolution of solute atoms and eliminate potential micro segregation in the as-cast structure, homogenization annealing was performed at 930 °C-990 °C (with 20 °C intervals) and at 900 °C-1050 °C (with 50 °C intervals). Considering that some second phases precipitate after hot forging at 870 °C, both alloys were subjected to solution treatment at 1000 °C for 1 h to ensure the complete dissolution of residual second phases. For TEM sample preparation, after mechanical grinding, electro-polishing was performed at −30 °C using a solution of 70% HNO 3+ 30% CH 3OH, followed by ion milling with argon ions. EBSD samples were taken from the center of the same position on the sheet under different aging conditions, and for EBSD sample preparation, the cold-rolled samples were cut and polished on the TD plane using diamond polishing paste, followed by electro-polishing with a solution of 50% H 3PO4 acid +25% C 2H 5OH + 25% water at a current of 0.1A. Aging condition: 450 °C × 1 h

Processing Text: The as-received steels were cast in vacuum furnaces and subsequently forged into billets with thicknesses ranging from 40 to 60 mm at ∼1100 °C. After homogenization at 1150 °C for two hours, the billets were hot rolled to 5 mm thickness via seven passes with the final rolling temperature over 900 °C, followed by air cooling to room temperature. Ultimately, the steels were cold rolled into 1.5 mm thick plates with a 70% reduction. The cold-rolled sheets were intercritically annealed at 680 °C for 30 min, followed by water quenching to room temperature. The temperature of 680 °C was selected to avoid cementite precipitation. Samples for synchrotron XRD and EBSD measurements were mechanically polished and then electro-polished at a voltage of 20 V for 10 s, with the electrolyte containing 10% perchloric acid and 90% ethanol. Samples for TEM characterizations were prepared using the double-jet electropolishing technique with an electrolyte containing 10% perchloric acid and 90% ethanol. The tensile samples had a gauge length of 3.4 mm, a width of 0.8 mm, and a thickness of 0.9 mm. The samples were electro-polished and then deposited using SiO 2 nanoparticles. The in situ tensile tests were performed at a strain rate of 2.75 × 10 −4 s −1 and were stopped at different global nominal strains to capture the corresponding images. Uniaxial tensile tests were carried out using an Instron 5967 machine equipped with a 30-kN load cell at room temperature with a strain rate of 1 × 10 −3 s −1. The tensile samples with the gauge length of 5 mm, thickness of 1.2 mm, and width of 2 mm were utilized. Interrupted tensile tests were also performed to investigate the deformed microstructure at different strain levels. Nanoindentation tests were performed using a Hysitron PI980 nanoindenter with a Berkovich-type tip at room temperature in a fast indentation mode. Processing state: intercritically annealed medium Mn steel; Microstructure: duplex-phase ultrafine microstructure consisting of ferrite and metastable austenite

Processing Text: AlCu xCrTiV HEAs were fabricated using vacuum arc melting with pure metal particles (≥99.9 wt%). The button ingots, with a diameter of approximately 30 mm and a mass of about 40 g, were produced using a stepwise melting process. Metals with similar physical properties were melted first, followed by the sequential addition of other raw materials for remelting. To ensure homogeneity, each master alloy was remelted five times. The vacuum degree of vacuum arc melting is on the order of 10⁻³ Pa to 10⁻⁴ Pa, with a power supply of 100 kW. Samples were machined into cylindrical dimensions (Φ6 × 3 mm) and polished with 400#, 1000#, and 2000# sandpaper. After immersion in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution for 30 min to stabilize, the open circuit potential (OCP) was measured until the curve showed minimal fluctuation. Polarization curve (PPC) tests were conducted at a scanning speed of 0.005 V/s with a sensitivity of 0.01 A/V. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) tests were performed at the OCP, with a signal amplitude of 0.005 A, a rest time of 2 s, high and low frequencies of 10 5Hz and 10 −2, respectively. Both PPC and EIS tests were repeated five times, with the samples polished before each test. Processing Text: A set of bulk ultrafine-grained Al alloys with nominal compositions of Al-8.5Mg-1X ( X= 0, Fe, Ti, Zr or Y) (in wt.%) were fabricated with a combined mechanical alloying and hot extrusion of powder compacts in a scalable way. Initially, powder mixtures of Al and Mg with and without the addition of Fe, Ti, Zr, or Y (purity > 99.9 %) were blended, followed by mechanical alloying under argon (Ar) atmosphere. These mechanically-alloyed powders were then compacted by a 200-tonnage hydraulic press into a cylindrical shape of 52 mm in diameter and 20 mm in height. The powder compaction was performed under a pressure of approximately 200 MPa for 5 min. Subsequently, such powder compacts were heated up to 773 K, using a conduction coil, with a heating rate of ∼30 K/min. To mitigate oxidation, the compaction, heating and extrusion were all carried out in a glove box filled with Ar, maintaining an oxygen content of below 200 ppm throughout the entire operation process. Processing Text: The CoCrNi MPR-MEA was fabricated using laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) on mixed elemental powder blends. The powders were mixed using a planetary ball mill at 200 rpm for 7 h to ensure thorough and homogeneous blending. The Co powder had a particle size distribution ranging from 15 μm to 45 μm, with an average particle size of approximately 30 μm. The particle size distribution of the Ni powders ranged from approximately 15 μm-45 μm, with an average particle size of around 29 μm. The Cr powder exhibited a particle size distribution between 20 μm and 50 μm, with an average particle size of about 40 μm. The mixed powders were fed into an AconityMini LPBF machine. During the LPBF process, CoCrNi MPR-MEA samples were fabricated using a 316L plate as the substrate, under a high-purity argon atmosphere to prevent oxidation. The hatch spacing was fixed at 120 μm, and the layer thickness was set at 30 μm. The combinations consisted of six different laser power levels (100 W, 140 W, 180 W, 220 W, 260 W, and 300 W) and six different scanning speeds (500 mm/s, 700 mm/s, 900 mm/s, 1100 mm/s, 1300 mm/s, and 1500 mm/s), which were randomly paired for evaluation. After parameter optimization, rectangular blocks were fabricated using a laser power of 260 W and a scanning speed of 700 mm/s. The samples were prepared and cleaned using ultrasonic vibration for 5 min to remove surface contaminants. The density was measured using the Archimedes method with an AKD-310G analytical balance and distilled water as the immersion medium. Each sample was weighed in air and then in water. The measurement was repeated three times for each sample, and the average value was recorded as the final density. The relative density was calculated by dividing the measured density by the theoretical density of the reference material, CoCrNi MEA. The phase composition and crystal structure of the LPBF-fabricated CoCrNi MPR-MEA specimens were investigated using X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis. The XRD patterns were acquired using a Rigaku SmartLab diffractometer with Cu-Kα radiation operating at 40 kV and 30 mA. The diffraction patterns were collected over a 2θ range of 10-100° with a step size of 0.02° and a scanning speed of 2°/min. The morphology and elemental composition of the CoCrNi alloy powders were characterized using a HITACHI SU-1510 scanning electron microscope (SEM) equipped with an energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) detector. The SEM images were obtained at an accelerating voltage of 15 kV, and the chemical composition of the powders was determined by EDS analysis. To investigate the microstructural evolution of the LPBF-fabricated CoCrNi MPR-MEA samples, both cross-sectional and longitudinal planes were prepared following standard metallographic procedures, which included cutting, mounting, grinding, and polishing. The microstructures were examined in both as-polished and etched conditions using an Olympus GX53 optical microscope (OM) and SEM. The samples were etched using a mixture of 30 ml HCl, 10 ml HNO3, and 20 ml H2O. The fracture surfaces of the tensile tested specimens were also studied using SEM to elucidate the failure mechanisms. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) analysis was performed using a HITACHI SU-1500 SEM equipped with an EBSD detector. The EBSD data were acquired with a step size of 1.5 μm and analyzed using the TSL OIM Analysis software to determine the grain size distribution, grain boundary characteristics, and phase constitution of the LPBF-fabricated CoCrNi MPR-MEA samples. The EBSD samples were prepared by mechanical polishing, followed by electrolytic polishing in a solution containing 10 % perchloric acid and 90 % ethanol at 20 V for 30 s. The TEM analysis is conducted using a FEI Tecnai F20 transmission electron microscope, which operates at an accelerating voltage of 200 kV to obtain high-resolution images of the specimens. Prior to this characterization, the samples are carefully prepared by first mechanically polishing them to a thickness of approximately 30 μm. This is followed by an electropolishing process using a solution of 5 vol% perchloric acid and 95 vol% ethanol at −35 °C and 20 V, resulting in final specimens with a diameter of about 3 mm. The mechanical properties of the LPBF-fabricated CoCrNi MPR-MEA samples were investigated using a combination of microhardness measurements and uniaxial tensile tests. Vickers microhardness tests were performed on a fully automated Struers Duramin-40 microhardness tester with a load of 500 gf and a dwell time of 10 s. The indentations were made on both the cross-sectional and longitudinal planes of the polished samples, maintaining a minimum spacing of 5 times the indent size to minimize the influence of neighboring indentations. To ensure statistical reliability, a total of 20 indentations were made on each sample. Uniaxial tensile tests were performed at room temperature using an MTS Systems Corporation CMT-5205 microcomputer-controlled electronic universal testing machine with a maximum load capacity of 50 kN. The tensile specimens were machined from the LPBF-fabricated CoCrNi MPR-MEA samples using wire electrical discharge machining (WEDM) with a gauge length of 25 mm and a diameter of 5 mm. The tests were conducted at a constant strain rate of 1 × 10−3s−1, and the strain was measured using a clip-on extensometer with a gauge length of 10 mm. This setup allowed for accurate determination of the elastic modulus, yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation to failure. To establish the reproducibility and reliability of the results, three tensile specimens were tested for each processing condition. Processing Text: Equimolar CoCrNi MEA was prepared by arc-melting Co, Cr, and Ni mixtures with 99.99 % purity in a high-purity argon atmosphere. The ingot was remelted more than five times before the drop-cast process to ensure homogeneity. Subsequently, the as-cast CoCrNi MEA ingot was cold-forged by a 50 % reduction in thickness. Afterward, the alloy was annealed at 1173K for 1 h to reduce deformation-induced defects and promote recrystallization. Quasi-static compression tests with strain rates ranging from 1.0 × 10^−3 s^−1 to 10^−1 s^−1 were performed on CoCrNi MEA samples with a diameter of 3 mm and length of 6 mm using an Instron 5969 testing machine. Dynamic compression tests with strain rates ranging from 2.6 × 10^3 s^−1 to 6.2 × 10^3 s^−1 were carried out on CoCrNi MEA samples with a diameter of 3 mm and length of 3 mm using a SHPB system. Stop-ring technology was introduced to control the strain during the dynamic compressions. The ramp wave and shock compression experiments were conducted using the CQ-4 magnetically driven system, delivering a pulsed current with a peak value of 4 MA and a rising time of 500 ns, developed by the Institute of Fluid Physics, China Academy of Engineering Physics. Multi-level characterizations were conducted to explore the intrinsic mechanisms of CoCrNi MEA. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) was performed using a JEOL JSM-7100F field-emission scanning electron microscope (SEM). An acceleration voltage of 20 kV, a specimen tilt angle of 70°, and a working distance of 15 mm were used in the EBSD observations. A JEM-2100F transmission electron microscopy (TEM) was operated at an acceleration voltage of 200 kV to uncover microscopic deformation mechanisms. Processing Text: Commercial 6082 aluminum alloy rod with a diameter of 12 mm was selected for the experiment. The alloy was sectioned into a sample measuring 25 cm in length for the purpose of the UVAT experiment. In the UVAT experiment, the initial step involved establishing a connection between the aluminum rod and the ultrasonic transducer by tapping one end of the rod. However, CAT samples did not require this tapping process, and were simply cut to a fixed length in preparation for the aging process. Following the preparation, the sample underwent SS treatment at a temperature of 555 °C for 1h under Ar conditions. Subsequently, the sample was rapidly quenched to room temperature to maintain the supersaturated solid solution state. Two different aging experiments were then conducted under vacuum at a temperature of 150 °C. The first experiment involved aging CAT samples under conventional conditions, while the second experiment utilized UVAT on the samples. The ultrasonic generator operated at a vibration frequency of 20 KHz, and the power was set to 100W. Room temperature tensile tests were performed on a servohydraulic testing machine at a rate of 5 mm/min. Vickers microhardness testing was used to assess the hardness of the samples, applying a load of 0.98N for a period of 15s. The micromorphology, fracture, and elemental composition were characterized using the FEI Nova Nano SEM 450 scanning electron microscope equipped with a 15 KV energy dispersive X-ray spectrometer (EDS). X-ray diffraction phase detection was performed on the samples, involving the following parameters: V = 40 KV, A = 40 mA, 2θ = 10-90°, and a scanning speed of 5°/min. The grain structure and morphology were characterized using EBSD with a step size of μ = 0.5 μm. The samples were electrosprayed within a temperature range of −35 °C to −25 °C, followed by low-voltage ion thinning and cleaning in an angle range of ±2° to ±4° using the ion thinning instrument to prepare a thin region of an amorphous layer. Finally, transmission electron microscopy (TEM) was employed to characterize dislocations and precipitated phases of the samples. Processing Text: The TiZrNbHf alloy used in this experiment is melted by Ti, Zr, Nb and Hf elements with purity greater than 99.9 %. Each melting was carried out at a vacuum of 5 × 10−3Pa, followed by the introduction of high-purity argon gas to generate an arc beam. In order to ensure the uniform composition of the alloy, the ingot was turned over and remelted for 6 times. The ingot was cold rolled into sheets (80 % thickness reduction) as shown in Fig. 1. Rectangular dogbone specimens for tensile testing were then machined using an electric discharge machining (EDM) method with a mark length of 12.5 mm and a cross-sectional area of 3.2 mm × 2 mm. The specimens were annealed in vacuum quartz tubes at a vacuum of 5 × 10−3μm at a temperature of 1000 °C for 30 min. The specimens were annealed in a vacuum quartz tube at room temperature at a strain rate of 1 × 10−3s−1 strain rate on INSTRON 3382 to obtain the room temperature tensile properties of the alloy. The phase composition of the alloys was measured by XRD using Co Kα radiation at a scanning rate of 2°/minute. The microstructure of TiZrNbHf alloy was observed by SEM and TEM. The samples for EBSD characterization were prepared by electrochemical polishing in 10 % HClO4 and 90 % CH4O solution for 5 s after grinding to 3000 mesh. For the preparation of TEM samples, the samples were first mechanically polished to 50 μm and finally subjected to ion-beam thinning at low temperatures to obtain rings with a diameter of 5 μm. Subsequently, the cold-rolled sample was subjected to heat treatment at 1000 °C for 30 min to recrystallize the alloy and remove the dislocations and residual stresses generated by cold rolling. Processing Text: Haynes 230, a nickel-based superalloy with a high melting point, is prone to forming microcracks during laser powder bed fusion (LPBF). After HIP, microcracks closed with the formation of nanoprecipitates at the closure sites, accompanied by increases in both grain and nanoprecipitate sizes, which were limited by pressure. M23C6 precipitates transformed into M6C, reducing lattice mismatch. To characterize the crack inhibition process, the as-deposited samples underwent HIP treatment at pressures of 60 MPa, 130 MPa, and 180 MPa at 1210 °C for 2 h ( Fig. 1d). The nanoprecipitates grew and shifted in composition, from Cr-rich M 23C 6in the crack generation state to W- and Mo-rich M 6C after crack inhibition. Due to its high Cr (23 wt%) and W (14 wt%) content, Haynes 230 exhibits a solid-solution strengthening mechanism ( σss) [45]. In LPBF samples, the high dislocation density contributes to dislocation strengthening ( σdis). In LPBF+HIP samples, the significant coarsening of precipitates leads to precipitation strengthening ( σOro) [46]. Therefore, the strength ( σLPBF) of the as-deposited state is mainly determined by three factors: σss, σdis, and grain boundary strengthening ( σGB). After HIP treatment, the strength ( σLPBF+HIP) is primarily determined by σss, σOro, and σGB. Dislocation strengthening dominated in the as-deposited Haynes 230, with a yield strength of 517 MPa, while precipitation strengthening dominated in the HIP state, with a yield strength of 502 MPa. After hot isostatic pressing, microcracks closed, and grain and precipitate sizes increased. Higher pressure suppressed grain growth. In the crack-inhibited alloy, the secondary phase was identified as M 6C, which formed via thermodynamically driven phase transformation and exhibited various orientation relationships with the matrix. During crack inhibition, nanoprecipitates formed at junctions, bridging microcracks. The M 23C 6phase in the as-deposited state transformed into M 6C, reducing lattice mismatch, with nanotwin boundaries forming within the nanoprecipitates. Analysis of the fractured zones of crack generation and crack inhibition samples revealed changes in the deformation mechanism, transitioning from dislocation slip to the accumulation of deformation twins, nano-growth twins, and stacking faults. Synergistic enhancement in strength and ductility was observed, with strength improvement resulting from the combined effects of crack closure and nanoprecipitates hindering dislocation motion, and ductility enhancement arising from crack closure, the formation of nanotwin boundaries, and the transformation of the deformation mechanism. Processing state: as-deposited; Elongation: 5.4 ± 1.2 %; Dominant strengthening mechanism: Dislocation strengthening

Processing Text: For thin, elongated metal tapes such as 50 μm Hastelloy substrate, rolling is the most commonly employed method. However, due to the inherent hardness of alloys like Hastelloy C-276, direct rolling to a thickness as low as 50 μm is challenging and may likely require intermediate annealing. Our private communication with REBCO manufacturers revealed that they only specify the thickness and surface roughness, indicating that different Hastelloy manufacturers may provide identical 50 μm Hastelloy tapes with significantly varied grain morphologies due to distinct intermediate annealing setups during rolling. Furthermore, while nearly all REBCO tape manufacturers utilize the IBAD process, the diverse methods of superconducting layer deposition, such as PLD, MOCVD, etc., introduce varying annealing temperatures and times to the Hastelloy substrate during the layer-by-layer fabrication of the final commercial REBCO product. This effectively leads the Hastelloy tapes into different recovery stages or even initial recrystallization stages. The differing initial grain conditions of the Hastelloy, coupled with varying heat inputs during the fabrication process, can result in markedly distinct grain morphologies of Hastelloy in the final products from different manufacturers, consequently yielding different strength values. Condition: 77 K
Processing Word: Condition: 77 K

Processing Text: An equiatomic CoCrFeNi ingot was prepared from raw materials with purities > 99.5 % in an arc melting furnace with an Ar-filled protective atmosphere, followed by solid-solution treatment at 1200 °C for 2 h. The actual composition of CoCrFeNi alloy was determined using energy dispersive spectroscopy inside the Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM), as presented in Table 1. The ingot was sectioned into two pieces and then rolled to a thickness reduction of 90 % at room and cryogenic (∼-160 ± 10 °C) temperatures, respectively, before annealing at 870 °C and 800 °C for 1 hour, respectively, followed by final quenching in water. The rolling process was carried out at cryogenic temperature to obtain a more refined grain structure as compared to room temperature due to retarded grain growth. In the following sections, the alloys rolled at the room temperature and annealed at 870 °C as well as rolled at the cryogenic temperature and annealed at 800 °C, respectively, are referred to as CG (Coarse-Grained) and FG (Fine-Grained) HEAs. The specimens for HRDIC were initially ground to #4000 grit, followed by polishing with diamond suspensions and a final chemo-mechanical polishing in a solution of 1:1.5 amorphous colloidal silica suspension to deionised water ratio to remove the surface deformation introduced during the abrasive stages of preparation. After EBSD analysis, the surface was coated with a nano-sized Au speckle pattern following the procedure developed by Gioacchino and da Fonseca [ 79]. Firstly, the specimen was coated with a ∼5 nm thin film of 99.99 % Au using an Edwards S150B sputter coater (40 mA for 315 s). The continuous film was remodelled by heating at 275 °C in a flow of water vapour for 4 h, leading to the formation of nano-sized Au speckles. CoCrFeNi HEA with coarse grains

Processing Text: The material used is annealed low-carbon steel (LCS) sheets with a thickness of 2 mm and a nominal composition (wt.%) of 0.2C-0.5Mn-1.0Si. In order to introduce a gradient distribution of interstitial atoms, a diffusion bonding treatment was used. The detailed process is given as follows: 0.1 mm graphite was stacked between two steel sheets to form a sandwich plate; then, the stacked sandwich was diffusion bonded under a pressure of 5 kPa and under the protection of argon gas. The target bonding temperatures of 1200 °C and 1220 °C were used, respectively, with a holding time of 30 min. Subsequently, the bonded plates were hot rolled at 1000 °C with a thickness reduction of 50 % to tailor the grain morphologies. Hereafter, the hot-rolled specimens via diffusion bonding at 1200 °C and 1220 °C are referred to as CGS1200 and CGS1220, respectively. Processing Text: The experiments utilized 2195 Al-Li alloy (Al-3.75Cu-1.07Li-0.52Mg-0.39Ag-0.12Zr), provided by the China Space Technology Research Institute. The sheets underwent solid-solution at 510°C for 30 min, followed by natural aging (NA) for at least three days to reach a steady state. After natural aging, the sheets were pre-rolled under either room temperature or cryogenic conditions, with reduction ratios of 3∼15 %. The rolling process was carried out with 80 mm diameter working rolls at a speed of 1 m/min. In regard to CPR, the sheets were immersed in liquid nitrogen for 30 min prior to rolling, with a transfer time of less than 5 s. After pre-rolling, artificial aging was performed at 160°C for 0.5 h ∼ 60 h. Samples that underwent RPR with rolling reduction ratios 0 %, 3 %, 6 %, 10 %, and 15 % were labeled as RPR0, RPR3, RPR6, RPR10, and RPR15 respectively. The CPR samples, with rolling reduction ratios of 3 %, 6 %, 10 %, and 15 % were labeled as CPR3, CPR6, CPR10, and CPR15. The microstructural examination and grain size analysis of the pre-rolled samples were conducted using optical microscopy (OM, Mshort MJ42). The RD-ND plane was mechanically polished and anodized in a fluoroboric acid solution (5 ml HBF 4, 100 ml H 2O). The aged samples’ microstructure was characterized using transmission electron microscopy (TEM, FEI TECNAI G2 T20, 200 kV). High-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) and high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) were used to observe precipitates. The samples were mechanically thinned less than 0.1 mm, and 3 mm diameter discs were wafered using a perforator. The wafers were then thinned using a twin-jet machine with a mixed solution (CH 4O: HNO 3= 7:3). The thinning process was conducted at −25℃, with a voltage of 25 V and a current voltage of 80 mA. X-ray Diffraction (XRD) tests were performed to determine the pre-rolled samples’ dislocation density using instrumentation (D8 ADVANCE Davinci). The scanning speed was 1°/min, with a scanning step of 0.02°, and an angular range of 30° ∼ 90°. The {111}, {200}, {220}, and {311} diffraction peaks were fitted using the Voigt method to calculate full width at half maxima (FWHM). The modified Williamson-Hall formula [24,25], was utilized for determining the dislocation density. Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) analysis was performed using a differential scanning calorimeter (Netzsch DSC 200 F3). The experiments were conducted in a high-purity nitrogen atmosphere, with the samples placed in a pure aluminum crucible. The heating rate was 10 °C/min, and the temperature range spanned from 50°C to 500°C. The sample weight was measured to be about 10 mg. A Vicker's hardness tester (HXD-2000TMC/LCD 181101X) was used to measure the hardness, applying a 300 gf load for a 15-s dwell time. Samples for tensile testing were prepared along the rolling direction and tested at 1 mm/min using a Shimadzu AGS-X 10 kN tensile machine. Each condition was tested three times, with strain monitored by a video extensometer (TRViewX). Scanning electron microscopy (SEM, TESCAN MIRA3 LMU) was employed to examine the fracture surfaces. Intergranular corrosion (IGC) test was performed in accordance with the ISO 8407 standard. Before the corrosion tests, samples were pretreated by immersion in a 10 wt% sodium hydroxide (NaOH) solution at 50°C for 2 min, followed by a brief immersion in concentrated nitric acid (HNO3, 1.4 g/ml) solution for another 2 min and thorough rinsing. Subsequently, the samples were immersed in a corrosive solution containing sodium chloride (NaCl, 30 g/L) and concentrated hydrochloric acid (HCl, 14 g/L) at ambient temperature for 24 h. Electrochemical characterization was performed utilizing a standard three-electrode setup within an electrochemical workstation. Polarization tests were conducted at a scan rate of 2 mV/s with an exposed electrode area of 1 cm². For the electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) measurements, the polished samples were briefly immersed in a sodium chloride solution (NaCl, 3.5 wt%) for 10 min to attain a stable open circuit potential. The EIS tests were performed with a sinusoidal perturbation amplitude of 5 mV, spanning a frequency range from 10 −2to 10 5Hz. All electrochemical tests were conducted three times to ensure reliability of the results. Peak-aged state, room-temperature pre-rolled (RPR) samples
Processing Word: Peak-aged state, room-temperature pre-rolled (RPR) samples

Processing Text: Spherical pre-alloyed FCC-type CoCrNi powders, with a particle size range of 15-45 µm, were utilized to prepare CoCrNi(Al0.6TiFe)x (x = 0, 0.13, 0.20, 0.28) alloys on 304 stainless steel substrate using an LDED system. The powders were fed with a double-hopper powder feeding system and mixed in a blender before feeding through the nozzle. All the bulk samples (50 ×20 ×6 mm 3) were fabricated with optimized process parameters where the laser power, scanning velocity, powder feed rate, and laser beam diameter were optimized and set at 570 W, 1200 mm min −1, 5.4 g min −1, and 1.3 mm, respectively. Deposit layer thickness was around 0.5 mm. A rotation of 90° was conducted between the adjacent layers. The overlapping rate was set at 50 %. Tensile coupons with a gauge dimension of 25 × 6 × 4 mm 3 were extracted from the bulk samples by wire cut electrical discharge machining. Uniaxial tensile testing was carried out on the MTS E45 universal test machine. The nominal engineering strain rate was set to be 0.6 mm min −1. A non-contact and digital image correlation (DIC) technique (Correlated Solution, Inc.) with one 12MP (3000 × 4000 pixels) camera was used to monitor the displacement and strain fields during tensile tests. The DIC system was synchronized with tensile test machine, and the frame capture speed was set to 2 Hz during loading. The microstructure observation was performed in the cross-section parallel to the build direction. The samples were ground with fine SiC papers and then polished with diamond polishing paste, finally etched with an etchant (5 g CuCl 2 in 100 ml HCl and 100 ml of ethanol) for 2 minutes. The phase identification was conducted by X-ray diffraction (XRD, PANalytical Empyrean) with Cu Kα radiation source at 30 kV and 30 mA with a step size of 0.01° and scanning speed of 0.6 °/min. The microstructures were observed using optical microscope (OM), scanning electron microscope (SEM, FEI Apreo2S Lovac), energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) and electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD). The accelerate voltage values were 10 kV and 20 kV for SEM and EBSD observation, respectively. The transmission electron microscope (TEM) foils were prepared by a twin-jet electro-polishing with a mixture of 5 vol% perchloric acid and 95 vol% ethanol. TEM, high-resolution TEM (HRTEM) and selected area electron diffraction (SAED) were performed by using a FEI Talos F200X G2 device at an acceleration voltage of 200 kV. High angle annular dark field (HAADF)-scanning TEM (STEM), annular dark field (ADF)-STEM, annular bright field (ABF)-STEM and EDS analyses were carried out by the same TEM instrument. Processing Text: Samples were fabricated using laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) additive manufacturing. The processing parameters included laser powers ranging from 114 to 264 W, scanning speeds varying between 323 and 1847 mm/s with a fixed hatch distance of 0.1 mm and a layer thickness of 0.03 mm. The parameters were designed based on the volumetric energy density (VED) concept. The VED values for these samples varied from 48 to 118 J/mm³. A bidirectional laser scanning strategy with a 67° rotation between adjacent layers was employed. Prior to printing, a grade 40 steel substrate was preheated to 80 °C. Throughout the printing process, the chamber was protected by high-purity argon, with oxygen content below 0.1 %. Thirty cubic samples were successfully fabricated, while two samples (No. 31 and No. 32) failed due to severe warping during fabrication. Following isochronal annealing at temperatures between 600 and 1150 °C for two hours, the AB steel underwent varying degrees of microstructure evolution. The AB steel was annealed at 700 °C for 2 h (marked as AM-700 samples), followed by water quenching. Both the AB samples and their recrystallized (Re) counterparts underwent isochronal annealing at various temperatures (ranging from 500 to 950 °C, with 50 °C intervals) for 2 h, followed by water quenching. Processing Text: With its inherent lightweight characteristics, magnesium (Mg) alloy has become a key material in industries such as aerospace and rail transportation. To broaden its application scenarios, adding various alloying elements has become a common method for customizing its performance characteristics [1-3]. Among them, the addition of heavy rare earth (RE) elements such as Gadolinium (Gd) and Yttrium (Y) has been proven to be extremely effective in improving the YS of Mg alloys. For example, Wang et al. [4]reported that by adding more than 12 wt% of rare earth elements and combining with the extrusion process, a YS as high as 385 MPa could be obtained. In addition, various elements such as Manganese (Mn), Tin (Sn), and Zinc (Zn) are also used to improve the performance of Mg alloys. Mn could effectively improve the corrosion resistance of the alloy. At the same time, it could act as a heterogeneous nucleation point in the alloy during solidification, and then refine the grains [5]. The Sn element could also form a new MgSnRE phase with RE elements, which could form fine grains and tiny precipitates within grains and boundaries, hinder dislocation slip, and improve the comprehensive performance [6]. The solubility of Zn element in Mg is very high, which has a good solid solution strengthening effect and helps to improve the tensile properties [7]. Five solute elements, including Sn, Zn, Ca, Mn, and Al, were adopted by our team in the early stage, to design an alloy with the proportions of these solute elements being nearly equimolar. Its specific chemical composition is Mg-0.29Sn-0.35Zn-0.52Ca-0.30Mn-0.36Al (at%). After extrusion, this alloy showed excellent mechanical properties, with a YS of 280 MPa, a UTS of 310 MPa, and an EL of 20.3 % [8,9]. The significant improvement in mechanical properties is mainly attributed to the synergistic effects of fine grain strengthening, dislocation strengthening, and the uniform and dispersed distribution of nanoscale granular phases in the alloy matrix. The strengthening and toughening effects of adding Gd, Y, Zn, Mn, and Sn to Mg alloys are fully documented and widely recognized in the literature [10-16]. However, there are relatively few studies on their addition to the Mg matrix in nearly equimolar ratio. In addition, at present, there are not many studies on the microstructure evolution, mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance of Mg alloys prepared by the above method. It is necessary to conduct in-depth research on these systems to broaden the application range of Mg alloys. The purpose of this study is to study the microstructure evolution of the Mg-Gd-Sn-Y-Zn-Mn alloy system synthesized in nearly equimolar ratio and evaluate its mechanical properties and corrosion resistance in the extruded state. Optical microscopy (OM), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), electron backscattering diffraction (EBSD), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) are used to clarify the comprehensive influence of these multi-element additions on the alloy microstructure and final properties. The nearly equal-amplitude addition of solute elements has caused obvious changes in the microstructure of VTWZM alloy, thus affecting the tensile properties and corrosion resistance of the alloy. Through the observation of SEM and TEM, it was found that after the concentrations of solute elements in this study increased nearly equal-amplitude, more key elements such as Gd, Sn, Y, and Mn would respectively promote the precipitation of the MgSnRE phase and Mn-rich phase in the microstructure. The second phase in the as-cast VTWZM-X (X = 1, 2, 3) alloy is mainly composed of MgSnRE phase and α-Mg phase. After approximately equal-amplitude increase in solute concentration, the formation of MgSnRE phase in the microstructure increases and the grains of the as-cast alloy are refined. The extruded alloy is composed of a large number of deformed grains and a small amount of DRXed grains. The nearly equal-amplitude increase in solute concentration results in the refinement and an increase in the proportion of DRXed grains, which creates conditions for intergranular deformation, weakens the basal texture, and improves the ductility of the alloy. The YS of VTWZM-3 alloy is 356 MPa, the UTS is 363 MPa, and the EL is 9.3 %. It exhibits good strength and acceptable plasticity. In addition, the extruded VTWZM-3 alloy shows the best corrosion resistance with a corrosion rate of 15.19 mm/a. The key is that the alloy has a low proportion of coarse grains and a high proportion of fine DRXed grains. The positive effects of the two are significant and they jointly dominate the change of the corrosion rate. Processing state: Extruded

Processing Text: The Ti54Nb14Zr15Mo17 alloys were prepared by arc-melting. The Ti54Nb14Zr15Mo17 alloys, with high Mo Eq, Bo, and Md values, fall within the range of β-titanium alloys. The crystal structures were identified by an X-ray diffractometer (XRD, Bruker D8 Advance, Germany). To study the hot processing behavior and microstructure evolution of the Ti54Nb14Zr15Mo17 alloys, single-pass compression tests on small bars were conducted using the THERMECMASTOR-Z100KN thermal simulation machine. Prior to the tests, graphite plates coated with tantalum sheet lubricant were placed between the specimens and the dies to reduce friction. Four different testing temperatures (950 ℃, 1000 ℃, 1050 ℃, and 1100 ℃) and four different strain rates (0.001 s⁻¹, 0.01 s⁻¹, 0.1 s⁻¹, and 1 s⁻¹) were utilized. After the hot compression tests, the deformed alloys were water-quenched immediately to maintain the deformation microstructure. True stress-strain curves were obtained through hot compression tests, and a constitutive equation was derived to relate flow stress to hot deformation parameters. A hot processing map was constructed based on the dynamic material model and verified by deformation microstructure. The mechanical properties of the alloys were tested by selecting the optimal hot processing parameters from the map, and the orientation distribution function (ODF) method was employed to quantitatively investigate the texture evolution under different deformation conditions. The DRX mechanisms were analyzed in detail by transmission electron microscopy (TEM). Optimized hot processing parameters; Compressive yield strength

Processing Text: The raw alloy ingots of Al 0.3CoCrFeNi (atomic percent, at%) with dimensions of 275 × 96 × 38 mm 3 were produced via arc-melting high-purity metals (purity > 99 % wt%) in an argon atmosphere. To ensure chemical homogeneity, the ingots underwent at least two re-melting cycles. To minimize casting defects, the ingots were held in a furnace a 1250 ℃ for 1 h and then underwent multi-pass hot rolling, reducing the thickness by 80-85 %. Subsequently, they were heat-treated at 1250 ℃ for 24 h to refine their microstructure. Following homogenization, the samples underwent severe cold rolling, reducing the thickness by 85-90 %. The samples were annealed at 700, 750, 800, and 850 °C for 1 h, followed by water quenching. Specifically, cold-rolled specimens were subjected to recrystallization annealing at 1150 °C, followed by 50 h of annealing at 600°C for the FCC+L12 microstructure; direct 50 h annealing at 600 °C after cold rolling for the FCC+B2 + σ microstructure; and direct 1 h annealing at 800 °C after cold rolling for the FCC+B2 microstructure. Processing Text: A 50 kg ingot of lightweight steel with a composition of Fe-18Mn-8Al-1C-5Ni (wt%) was prepared in a vacuum induction melting furnace (chemical composition analyzed by spark optical emission spectroscopy: Fe-18.20Mn-7.98Al-1.03C-5.02Ni wt%). The hot-rolled steels were homogenized at 1200°C for 1 hour and then cold-rolled to a final thickness of 1 mm with a total reduction of 80 %. Three types of heat treatment schedules were applied to the cold rolled specimens in the present study, as illustrated in the Fig. 1. The cold-rolled strips were at 1000°C for 50 minutes to obtain full recrystallization (referred to as "AN50"), and annealed at 850 °C for 5 minutes to induce partial recrystallization (referred to as "AN5"), followed by WQ. Pre-straining was conducted in the AN5 specimen with several tensile strains of 0 %, 5 %, and 15 %. Subsequently, these AN5 specimens with different pre-strains were annealed at 850°C for 7 minutes with WQ. These pre-strained and sequent annealed specimens were denoted as "0 %-AN7", "5 %-AN7", and "15 %-AN7," respectively. Processing Text: The base alloy (90W-7Ni-3Fe) and the alloy compositions with Mo and Nb addition of (1.25, 2.5, & 3.75 wt%) independently were sintered in a reducing atmosphere at 1500 °C for 60 min. Alloys of different compositions with Mo and Nb addition were prepared using elemental powders. The base composition was modified by adding elements Mo and Nb independently in the steps of 1.25 wt%. For all the compositions, a constant Ni to Fe ratio of 7:3 was maintained. The required quantity of powder for each alloy was measured carefully and hand-mixed in a mortar and pestle for 20 minutes. The hand-mixed powder was further mixed rigorously in a turbo mixer at 80 rpm for 60 minutes without any medium. The mixed powder was compacted using a uniaxial press at 350 MPa pressure to obtain cylindrical samples of a diameter of 6 mm and height of 3 mm and cylindrical samples for compression testing of 6 mm diameter and 8 mm height. Further, these compacts were sintered in a tubular horizontal furnace (Tehreek, India) at a sintering temperature of 1500 °C for 60 min under a flowing hydrogen atmosphere (0.1 lpm). Samples were heated at a heating rate of 5 °C/min from room temperature to 1000 °C and dwelled for 40 min. Further temperature increments were done as 4 °C/min till 1200 °C and 3 °C/min till 1500 °C. Finally, samples were furnace cooled at 5 °C/min. The samples were sectioned along a plane parallel to the vertical axis of the sintered sample for microstructure and phase analysis and hardness measurements. The sintered samples were ground using emery paper till 3000 grit size, followed by cloth polishing using alumina and colloidal silica. Processing Text: The Al-4Ni-0.4V-0.2Zr-0.2Ti (ANV-ZT) alloy was prepared from a commercial-purity Al ingot, an Al-10Ni master alloy, an Al-5V master alloy, and Al-5Zr and Al-5Ti master alloys. The alloy was melted in a ZnO-coated clay-graphite crucible in a resistance furnace at a temperature of 800 °C. Argon was used for degassing, and the alloy was allowed to settle for 10 min. The melted alloy was then poured into a permanent mold (cooling rate 7 °C/s) at 750 °C. The permanent mold was preheated to 220 ± 5 °C before the alloy was poured into it. Isochronous and isothermal annealing experiments were conducted on the ANV-ZT alloys. For isochronous annealing, the duration was 8 h, with temperature ranging from 200 to 500 °C, in 50 °C increments. After determining the optimum annealing temperature, isothermal annealing kinetics experiments were performed, varying the holding time from 2 to 120 h. The samples were positioned similarly to those used for microstructure observations. Sample dimensions were 8 × 8 × 8 mm. All annealing was carried out in air, and the samples were cooled in water at 60 °C after annealing. The sampling locations are shown in Fig. 1(a). After casting and annealing, the samples were ground, polished, etched with a 0.5 % HF aqueous solution. Their microstructures were observed using an optical microscope (DMM-580C, Caikon, China). The average grain size of the primary α-Al (as cast) was measured using a lineal intercept image analysis method (ImageJ), with the average calculated from ten visual fields for each sample. The eutectic Al 3Ni phases were observed using scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Nova Nano SEM 450, FEI, Netherlands), and the intermetallic compounds were analyzed using energy dispersive spectroscopy spectrometer (EDS). The samples were further etched with a 10 % HCl aqueous solution and the three-dimensional morphology of the eutectic Al 3Ni phase was observed using SEM. Multiple fields of view were selected for each sample, and at least 300 rod-like eutectic Al 3Ni phases from different eutectic colonies were measured using ImageJ software to determine the average diameter and spacing of the Al 3Ni phases. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM, Tecnai G2 F30, FEI, Netherlands) was used to observe the morphology and distribution of the precipitated phases. TEM samples were prepared from the ANV-ZT (isothermal peak annealing) alloy. The sample was initially to 50 μm and then thinned using a double-spray method (TenuPol, Struers, Denmark). The double-spray electrolyte was a nitrate methanol solution, with a voltage of 18-20 V, and a temperature of −25 °C. The microhardness of the alloys was measured under a load of 4.9035 N for 30 s using a Vickers hardness tester (430 SVD; Wilson, USA). Each sample had 10 measurement points selected randomly, and the average hardness value was calculated. Tensile tests were conducted using a universal testing machine (AG-IC/100kN, Shimadzu, Japan) at a loading speed of 1.0 mm/min, with a strain rate of 1.4×10 −6s −1. The positions and sizes of the tensile samples are shown in Fig. 1(b). The elevated-temperature tensile test tests were performed at 350 °C. The samples maintained at this temperature for 10 min before stretching, and the tensile strength and elongation were determined from the average of at least three samples. Processing Text: The alloy was developed through in-situ alloying with Al, Si, Ti, Mo and V elemental powders to fabricate quintenary alloy of Ti-Al-Si-Mo-V. The samples were deposited onto the metal plate substrates of Ti6Al4V alloy through in-situ laser alloy deposition of powders. The LENS machine deposition head has a four-way feeding nozzles made of copper which deposits powders co-axially on the base plate while a beam of laser instantaneously dissolves the powder materials. Using three externally attached powder feeders (GTV Verschleiss-Schutz Gmbh, Luckenbach, Germany), to supply the Si, V, and Mo powders while the Ti and Al powders were deposited by powder feeders of the LENS machine. This resulted in a five-way powder feeding system, as opposed to two that the manufacturer had originally installed. A heating platform was introduced to control and/or reduce thermal gradient during sample fabrication based on our observation from the simulation results. The ceramic heating platform had a heating element and thermostat controller attached to it; this was used to continuously keep the temperature of the base plate constant to prevent cracking. The samples were built based on the pre-programmed CAD file using a cross-hatch pattern of deposition strategy along axes of x and y. The alloys were generated at a laser power of 450 W, 10.58 mm/s scan speed, and 25 l/min center purge gas rate. With the intention of varying the composition of alloy samples deposited, each elemental powder flow rates were approximated following calibration of the powder flow rate in rpm (revolution per minute) and converted to mass flow rate in g/min. The samples were heat-treated for 60 minutes at temperatures of 1200 °C and 1400 °C, with subsequent furnace cooling (FC). The heat treatment furnace (Kejia Furnace, China) was applied for the post-processing in an inert atmosphere having an inlet for the continuous supply of Ar (99.99 % purity) to prevent contaminations and oxidation during HT. After ramping the temperature from RT to the desired temperature at 20 °C per minute, FC was done after holding for 60 minutes at the set temperatures. As shown in Fig. 3(a-c), the selected area electron diffraction (SAED) patterns verify that randomly distributed Mg 12Ce was formed in the Mg-9Li-0.6Ce alloy, The presence of coarse and fine Mg 12Ce precipitate distributed along the grain boundaries in the Mg-9Li-0.6Ce alloy can be observed from Fig. 3 (a) and (c). Fig. 5(b) presents the typical stress-strain curves for the alloys under tension. Processing Text: A series of Hf xNbTaTiV ( x= 0.00, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00 in molar ratio) alloy ingots with different Hf content were synthesized from high purity (>99.95%) metals by vacuum arc melting within a Ti-gettered ultra-high purity Ar (>99.99%) atmosphere. The as-cast ingots were flipped and remelted at least six cycles to ensure chemical homogeneity. The button-shaped ingots were rolled into thin sheets approximately 1 mm in thick at room temperature using a precision rolling mill (JH-RZH-110, China). More than three dog-bone-shaped samples were sliced from the rolled sheets for each alloy component along the rolling direction using an electrical spark erosion wire cutting machine (DK77, China). The size of the dog-bone samples was about 16 mm in length, 12 mm in width, and 1 mm in thickness. The dog-bone samples were sealed in an evacuated quartz tube maintained about 0.67 Pa vacuum and annealed at 1200 °C for 45 min and quenched in water to achieve recrystallized microstructures. The tensile tests of the annealed samples were performed at a strain rate of 0.001 s −1by an electronic universal testing machine (ETM205D, China). The microhardness (HV) of the as-cast alloys was tested using a Vicky MHV-1000 hardness tester. The phase composition of the alloys were determined by X-Ray diffraction with Cu-Kα radiation ( λ= 0.15406 nm) and a 2 θangle range of 20°-90° using an X-ray diffractometer (Rigaku Smartlab SE, Japan). A recrystallization anneal at 1200 °C for 45 min was applied to cold-rolled Hf xNbTaTiV sheets to eliminate deformation textures and defects. Condition: Annealed samples; Fracture strain ratio: 26.9%

The superior mechanical property can be attributed to the synergetic deformation of the eutectic structure, R characterization (abnormal yield effect) and the Ti alloying enhanced phase stability at elevated temperatures. The non-equilibrium solidification induced super-saturation also results in the super-high strength at room-to-medium temperature and a unique softening mechanism via the formation of the two-fold composite structure. Alloy ingots with nominal compositions (at. %) of Ni-25Al-7Ti, Ni-22Al-8Ti, Ni-22Al-7Ti, Ni-22Al-6Ti, Ni-Al and Ni-25Al were prepared by using the arc melting technique under Ar-atmosphere. The Vickers hardness was measured by a hardness tester (Leica Duramin 40 Micro-Hardness), with a load of 500 gf for 15 s. Processing Text: The experimental material consisted of 316L austenitic stainless steel rods with a diameter of 30 mm. The material was hot-rolled to 4 mm in thickness, followed by solution treatment at 1050 °C for 1 h. Before each rolling pass, the initial material was immersed in liquid nitrogen for 10 min. The thickness reduction per pass was kept below 5 %. Surface cracks developed when the total thickness reduction reached 70 %. Consequently, the final thickness was reduced by 70 %, resulting in a thickness of 1.2 mm for the cryo-rolled sample, which was labeled as CryoR sample. After cryo-rolling, the samples were subjected to annealing at 700 °C 20 min, 750 °C 6 min, and a sequential 700 °C 20 min + 750 °C 6 min process, followed by water quenching. These samples were labeled as 700A, 750A, and 700A-750A, respectively. All heat treatment processes were performed in a muffle furnace without a protective atmosphere. Tensile tests were conducted using a universal testing machine (5105, SSANS-CMT) at room temperature (24 °C) and liquid nitrogen temperature (−196 °C) with a strain rate of 10 −3s −1. All tensile samples were cut along the rolling direction into dog-bone shapes with a gauge length of 34 mm, width of 10 mm, and thickness of 1 mm. Each test was repeated at least three times to ensure accuracy. To evaluate inhomogeneous deformation, load-unload-reload (LUR) tests were also performed under the same conditions as the tensile tests to quantify the back stress (σ B) component. The microstructural evolution of the samples along the rolling direction (RD) was characterized. XRD analysis was conducted to examine phase transformation with a diffraction angle range of 40°-100° and a scanning speed of 2°/min, using Cu-Kα radiation at 40 kV and 150 mA. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, Oxford) was employed for quantitative analysis of the phase microstructure. After mechanical polishing, samples were electropolished using a 10 % perchloric acid solution at 20 V for 20-25 s. EBSD measurements were performed on a Zeiss Auriga scanning electron microscope with a step size of 100 nm at an accelerating voltage of 15 kV. Processing Text: In the present work, a single-pass multi-layer wall structure of Monel 400 alloy was deposited using the CMT-WAAM technique. The microstructure was analysed in the building direction, where finer equiaxed dendrites were observed in the bottom region, gradually transforming into coarse elongated dendrites in the top region of the deposited structure. Along with the change in microstructure, a variation in average microhardness was observed in the building direction, decreasing from 286 HV0.1 in the bottom region to 249 HV0.1 in the top region. The tensile specimens tested along the building direction fractured in the gauge length towards the top region of the wall, with an average yield strength of 353 MPa, ultimate tensile strength of 718 MPa, and percent elongation of 39 %. The electrochemical corrosion test in a 3.5 wt% NaCl solution was performed at the central region of the deposited structure. The CMT-WAAM deposited Monel 400 showed an exceptionally low corrosion rate of 0.03 mm/year. The experimental results confirmed that CMT-WAAM deposited Monel 400 exhibits mechanical and corrosion properties similar to or superior to conventional Monel 400, establishing the credential of the process for marine applications. In current study, a single-pass multi-layer wall structure of Monel 400 alloy was deposited using the CMT-WAAM technique. Systematic experimental work was conducted to examine the microstructural features and mechanical properties of the deposited structure at different locations within the build. In addition, the corrosion performance of the deposited Monel 400 alloy in a 3.5 wt% NaCl solution was evaluated. In the present work, Monel 400 has been deposited using CMT equipped Fronius TPS 400i metal inert gas welding machine integrated with an ABB IRB 1500 six-axis robotic arm also known as CMT-WAAM. This approach offers welding without spatter with minimal heat input, and rapid deposition rate. The wire feed rate was calibrated in accordance with the welding voltage and current, enabling the thorough fusion of the furnished wires. The 1.2 mm diameter Monel 400 (LINCOLN ELECTRIC, ERNiCu-7) wire is used for depositing the single wall structure. The elemental composition of Monel 400 feed wire is depicted in Table 1. The deposition process was carried out in an argon shielding atmosphere by keeping the torch perpendicular to the substrate and moving it horizontally. Layer-wise deposition was carried out on the horizontal plane by moving the torch along the Z-axis. In order to prevent the build-up flaws caused by the intermittent start-stop of deposition process at the extremities, the deposition direction was altered for each layer. The microstructure development may be controlled by the initial circumstances present before the deposition of each layer. Therefore, in order to reduce its impact, deposited material was cooled to nearly 93°C before the next pass. Additionally, this method has the benefits of maintaining a consistent thickness of the weld bead with reducing overflow.
