Processing Text: Spherical Fe36Ni35Al17Cr10Mo2 (at. %) pre-alloyed powders were fabricated via argon gas atomization, whose chemical compositions were analyzed using inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometry (ICP-OES). Powders with a particle size of 53∼150 μm were selected via sieving and dried at 120 °C for 6 h in a vacuum chamber to ensure liquidity. The experiment was conducted on an LSF-VI additive manufacturing system with a semiconductor laser, a coaxial powder feeder, and an inert atmosphere protection chamber (argon atmosphere with an oxygen content below 50 ppm). The following DED parameters were adopted: a 90° rotation between each successive layer, laser power of 1500 W, scanning speed of 480 mm/s, powder feeding rate of 10 g/min, elevated height of 1 mm, spot diameter of 3 mm and overlap of 50 %. Fig. 1(c) shows the formed single wall with dimensions of about 60 mm × 15 mm × 100 mm on the 316 L steel substrate plate. Crystalline structure was identified using X-ray diffractometry (XRD) (D8 ADVANCE) with Cu-Kα radiation at a scanning rate of 5° min−1. The metallographic samples were electrochemically polished in a mixture of 90 % ethanol and 10 % perchloric acid before examining the microstructure with an optical microscope (OM). The samples intended for backscattered electron (BSE) characterization, energy dispersive spectrometry (EDS) mapping analyses, and electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) were characterized by TESCAN MIRA-Ⅲ equipped with an EBSD detector. EBSD data were acquired with a step size of 0.6 μm for a large region and 0.04 μm for an individual grain and processed with Aztec-HKL software. A representative bulk sample with 10 mm × 10 mm × 10 mm was extracted from the deposited alloy via wire electrical discharge machining. Texture characterization was conducted on a neutron texture diffractometer at the China Advanced Research Reactor (CARR), the China Institute of Atomic Energy (CIAE). Using the Euler cradle, the pole density Pℎ kl( α, β) for a specified plane (hkl) can be obtained by rotating the sample through the χ(0°-90°) and φ(0°-360°) axis with a certain angle interval, which aligns the various sample orientations along the (hkl) scattering vector while recording the diffracted neutron intensities at each step using a detector set at the 2θposition of the (hkl) reflection. The step of the Euler cradle was set as 5°. The horizontal direction (X) of the chosen sample was φ=0°, and the deposition direction (Z) was parallel to the φ=90°. The pole figures and orientation distribution function (ODF) can be calculated from the diffracted neutron intensities and polar coordinates using LaboTex software. Ambient-temperature and elevated-temperature uniaxial tensile testing was conducted on a TSMT mechanical testing platform at a strain rate of 1 × 10−3s−1in air. The rectangular dog-bone-shaped tensile specimens with a gauge geometry of 12.5 mm × 3.0 mm × 2.0 mm were sectioned in the middle of the deposited sample along the Z direction and examined, and each sample was repeated at least twice to verify the reproducibility. An extensometer was employed to directly monitor the strains for ambient-temperature tensile tests, while for the testing at 600-800 °C, strains were determined indirectly from the load displacement. A thermocouple was used to measure the temperature of the upper, middle, and lower ends of the tensile sample to ensure an even distribution of circumambient temperature. To eliminate the effect of temperature fluctuation at the high-temperature tensile test, the samples were heated to the preset temperature at a heating rate of 10 °C/min and kept for 5 min before testing. Condition: room-temperature; Microstructure: hierarchical microstructure, including microscale lamellar structure and nanoscale BCC phases

Processing Text: The alloy ingots of these four compositions were prepared using vacuum arc melting in a water-cooled copper hearth under an argon atmosphere. Prior to melting, the raw materials (Mo, Nb, Ta, V, and Al) with a purity of 99.99 % were mechanically ground to remove the surface oxidation and then ultrasonically cleaned in ethanol for 3 min. High-purity Ti was employed as a degassing substance to remove residual oxygen in the vacuum chamber. In order to ensure chemical homogeneity, the button ingots were remelted for six times. Rectangular specimens with dimensions of 5 × 5 × 10 mm were machined from the button ingots. All surfaces were mechanically polished to a mirror-like finish. The microstructure were characterized using an X-ray diffractometer (XRD-6000, Shimadzu) with Cu-Kα radiation and a scanning electron microscope (SEM, Nova NanoSEM 450) equipped with an energy-dispersive spectrometer (EDS) and a backscatter electron (BSE) detector. Elemental micro-segregation was characterized by electron probe micro-analysis using an EPMA-8050G operating at an accelerating voltage of 15 keV. Vickers microhardness was examined by a 430SVD Micro-hardness test system on polished surfaces using a 136° Vickers diamond pyramid under 3000 g load applied for 15 s. 10 random indentations were inducted to get the average hardness. The ambient temperature compression properties were tested on a mechanical testing machine (AG-IC 100 kN) using the rectangular specimens with a strain rate of 10 −3s −1. Besides, the uniaxial compression tests at 600 °C, 800 °C, 1000 °C and 1200 °C were conducted on a Gleeble 3500-GTC system. During the tests, specimens were heated to the target temperature at a rate of 5 °C/s and held for 30 s, then uniaxially compressed with a strain rate of 10 −3s −1. The density measurements were performed on a JD200-3 electronic balance with a sensitivity of 0.1 mg, based on Archimedes' Law. Condition: before Al doping

Processing Text: In this research, focusing on low-carbon steel, a martensite-ferrite heterogeneous structure dual-phase (MFDP) steel with a network morphology where ferrite is surrounded by martensite was obtained via cyclic annealing and subcritical quenching heat treatment processes. With the initial microstructure of ferrite and lamellar pearlite, a spherical pearlite and martensitic structure surrounding the ferrite was first obtained by applying the cyclic annealing process near the Ac1 temperature. Subsequently, the annealed structure was subjected to subcritical quenching heat treatment, thereby establishing a network-like martensite-ferrite dual-phase heterogeneous structure and named N-760 °C and N-780 °C. The heat treatment experiment was carried out in a box-type resistance furnace, and the model was YFX16/120-GC. Through the previous heat treatment attempt, the microstructure obtained by different cycle time and cycle times was observed. Finally, it was concluded that the martensite can effectively wrap the ferrite structure after seven cycles of 690 °C holding for 2min and 700 °C holding for 8min. The specific process is as follows. (i)The sample is subjected to a heat treatment process in a resistance furnace at a temperature of 700 °C for 2 min, followed by cooling the furnace to 690 °C and maintaining it for 8 min. The temperature transition from 700 °C to 690 °C occurs over 7 min. Subsequently, the furnace is reheated to 700 °C and held for 2 min, during which the temperature rises from 690 °C to 700 °C over 12 min. This cycle is repeated 7 times to achieve a uniform ferrite-pearlite structure. After the cyclic annealing, the sample is air-cooled for 30 min.(ii)The sample was kept at the temperature of the two-phase region for 60 min, and finally water quenching was carried out to obtain the network martensite-ferrite dual-phase (MFDP) steel. The sample is subjected to a heat treatment process in a resistance furnace at a temperature of 700 °C for 2 min, followed by cooling the furnace to 690 °C and maintaining it for 8 min. The temperature transition from 700 °C to 690 °C occurs over 7 min. Subsequently, the furnace is reheated to 700 °C and held for 2 min, during which the temperature rises from 690 °C to 700 °C over 12 min. This cycle is repeated 7 times to achieve a uniform ferrite-pearlite structure. After the cyclic annealing, the sample is air-cooled for 30 min. The sample was kept at the temperature of the two-phase region for 60 min, and finally water quenching was carried out to obtain the network martensite-ferrite dual-phase (MFDP) steel. In Fig. 1 (b), the sample was placed in a heat treatment resistance furnace with a temperature of 950 °C for 30 min for homogenization heat treatment to eliminate internal defects in the structure and obtain a more uniform structure. Then the furnace was cooled to 690 °C and held for 60 min, where the temperature was reduced from 950 °C to 690 °C in 66 min. After the sample was held at 690 °C for 60 min, it was finally quenched with water to obtain a ferrite-martensite dual-phase (FMDP) steel and was named C-950 °C. In this study, the experimental steel was quenched at 720 °C, 740 °C, 760 °C, and 780 °C after cyclic annealing according to the heat treatment process in Fig. 1 (a)to form the network martensite ferrite isomeric structure. Processing Text: An 30 g ingot with a nominal composition of (CrHfMoNbTaTiVZr) 84Si 16was produced by vacuum arc melting of pure (> 99.95 wt%) metals. Rectangular samples measured 6 × 4 × 4 mm 3were cut from the as-cast ingot. Samples for XRD and SEM analysis were prepared by careful mechanical polishing to mirror surfaces using Buehler MasterMet 2 Suspension. For TEM examinations, thin foils were prepared using a Tenupol-5 twin-jet electro-polisher with an electrolyte containing a mixture of 600 ml of methanol, 360 ml of butanol, and 60 ml of perchloric acid at − 35 °C and 29.5 V; more details can be found elsewhere [ 17]. The surfaces of the samples for the hardness measurements were prepared by careful mechanical polishing to mirror surfaces using Buehler MasterMet 2 Suspension. Microstructural investigations were performed using X-ray diffraction (XRD, Rigaku Ultima IV; Cu Kα radiation having the wavelength of 1.5406 Å and a scanning rate of 3°/min from 20° to 80° (Fig. S1)), scanning electron microscopy (SEM; FEI Quanta 600 FEG and Nova NanoSEM 450), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM; JEM JEOL-2100 and Thermo Fisher Scientific™ Talos™ F200X G2) together with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS). The hardness measurements of constitutive phases were performed using a Shimadzu DUH-211S Dynamic Ultra Micro Hardness Tester fitted with a Berkovich tip. The measurements were conducted using a 10 × 10 grit with a distance of ∼50 μm between the indents. The maximum load of 50 mN was applied for 5 s; a loading speed was 6.6620 mN/s. The hardness and elastic moduli were obtained by using the Oliver and Pharr method [ 18]. After the measurements have been completed, the area was analysed by SEM (in a back scattered electron (BSE) regime) and EDS mapping to correlate the indents and phases (Fig. S2). The indentation fracture toughness, K C, also known as indentation fracture resistance, was evaluated at room temperature using by Digital Vickers Hardness Tester under a load of 98 N, following the formula [ 19]: (1)Kc=0.009EH0.4Phl0.5where E is the elastic modulus, which was equal to 120.1 GPa and derived from the indentation tests (using DUH-211S Dynamic Ultra Micro Hardness Tester under a load of 1961 mN and Oliver and Pharr method [ 18]); H is the measured microhardness; P is the indentation load; h is the length between the center and the corner of a remnant imprint; l is the length between the corner of the indent and the tip of the crack. For calculations, all the indents (10 independent measurements) that showed at least one crack were considered, according to [ 19]. Isothermal compression of the specimens measured 6 × 4 × 4 mm 3was carried out at 22, 800, 1000, 1200, and 1400 °C. Room-temperature compression tests were performed in the air using an Instron 5882 test machine. High-temperature compression test were conducted in vacuum (10 −4Torr or better) using a REM-600 A test machine. The specimens tested at 800, 1000, 1200, and 1400 °C were placed in the furnace, evacuated, heated (20 °C/min) to a target temperature, and held for ≈ 10 min to equilibrate the temperature before testing. The temperature of the specimen was controlled by a thermocouple attached to its side surface. No forced cooling was applied after the termination of the test. The initial strain rate was 10 −4s −1both for room- and high-temperature tests. Testing was carried out to the fracture of the specimens or to 50 % of strain. At least two samples at each temperature were tested. Oxidation tests were carried out using a Nabertherm furnace under the static laboratory air at 1200 °C. Priorto the tests, surfaces of the samples were mechanically gritted, polished, and ultrasonically cleaned in isopropanol. During the testing process, samples were placed in alumina boats, put into the preheated furnace, and removed after 0.5, 1, and 6 h of the oxidation test and cooled in the laboratory air for mass measurements. The mass of the specimens before and after oxidation was measured using an HR-200 analytical balance with an accuracy of 0.1 mg. Cross-sectional morphologies of the oxidised specimens were examined by SEM and EDS (Fig. S3). Compression test at 1000 °C

Processing Text: The steel was melted in a vacuum induction furnace into an ingot of 25 kg, followed by hot-forging and hot-rolling (HR) into 12 mm thick plate. The hot-rolled plate was firstly machined into a dilatometric sample with a diameter of 3 mm and a length of 10 mm. The dilatometric sample was then heated to 1100 ℃ at a rate of 10 ℃/min. For quenching and tempering (QT) treatment ( Fig. 1c), the sample was austenitized at 900 ℃ for 30 min followed by water-quenching, and then tempered at 650 ℃ for 30 min. For step quenching and tempering (SQT) treatment ( Fig. 1c), the specimen was initially austenitized at 900 ℃ for 30 min, followed by slow cooling (∼10 ℃/min) to the intercritical temperature (780 ℃) for 20 min, and then water-quenching to room temperature. Such quenching treatment is referred to as step quenching. Finally, the specimen was tempered at 650 ℃ for 30 min. Standard cylindrical tensile specimens with a gauge length of 44 mm and diameter of 7 mm were prepared from the QT and SQT plates. Uniaxial tensile testing (MTS machine) was carried out at ambient temperature using an initial strain rate of 10 −3s −1. To quantify the evolution of HDI stress, a load-unload-reload (LUR) process was conducted under tensile tests using the MTS machine at a strain rate of 10 −3s −1. Tensile strain was measured using an extensometer. The sample was unloaded in a load-control mode at various plastic strains up to 200 N, at an unloading rate of 1000 N/min, and then reloaded at the same strain rate as the previous loading to obtain stress-strain hysteresis loops. Standard Charpy V-notch impact specimens (10 × 10 × 55 mm 3) were chipped from the QT and SQT plates. The Charpy impact tests were performed using an Instron 9250 impact tester at −20 and −40 ℃. To unveil the local hardness distribution, nanoindentation measurements were performed on the SQT sample using KLA Nano Indenter G200X machine. A diamond Berkovich indenter was utilized at a constant loading force of 8 mN and a rate of 1.6 mN/s to access the nanohardness distribution within a matrix area. Nanohardness analysis was determined based on the Oliver-Pharr method [30]. Electrochemical tests were conducted utilizing a conventional three-electrode system on an electrochemical workstation (3000A-DX, PARSTAT), where a platinum electrode was used as the counter electrode, a saturated calomel electrode (SCE) was used as the reference electrode and the test steel was used as the working electrode. Prior to the electrochemical test, the sample surface underwent grinding and polishing to a mirror finish. The sample was submerged in a simulated marine solution to attain a stable state, and the open circuit potential (OCP) was monitored (solution temperature: 25 ℃). The exposed area of the working electrode is 1 cm 2. The potentiodynamic polarization (PDP) curves were measured at a scanning rate of 0.5 mV/s from an initial potential of −200 mV related to OCP until the current density increased to 1 mA/cm 2. Standard cylindrical tensile specimens with a gage length of 44 mm and diameter of 7 mm were mechanically polished using 400-4000 grit abrasive papers. Slow strain rate tensile (SSRT) experiments were carried out at a strain rate of 10 −6s −1using a Letry stress corrosion machine (WDML-1) in air and simulated marine solution at 25 ℃. Prior to each test, the tensile specimens were immersed for 30 h applied 0.5 σsconstant stress at 25 ℃ to investigate the role of corrosion in stress corrosion cracking. Initially, they were mechanically ground using silicon carbide abrasive paper, ranging from P400 to P5000. Following this, polishing was carried out using 3-1 μm diamond suspensions. Lastly, the quenched samples were etched with supersaturated picric acid and a sodium dodecyl benzene sulfonate aqueous solution at 90 ℃ for 15 s to observe the prior austenite grains using optical microscopy (OM, OLYMPUS-DSX500). The QT and SQT samples etched with 4 % nital, fracture and cross-sectional surfaces after SSRT tests were observed by a scanning electron microscope (SEM, FEI Apreo2S Lovac). The transmission electron microscope (TEM) foils were prepared by twin-jet electro-polishing with a mixture of 10 % perchloric acid and 90 % ethanol (vol%). The QT and SQT specimens electro-polished with an ethanol solution of 8 % perchloric acid were analyzed by electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD, JEM-7001F) at 15 kV with a step size of 200 nm. An X-ray diffractometer (XRD, Philips X Pert pro, CuKα, λ=0.15418 nm) was used to obtain the XRD patterns and analyze dislocation density. TEM, high-resolution TEM (HRTEM) and selected area electron diffraction (SAED) were performed by using a FEI Tecnai G2 F30 device at an acceleration voltage of 300 kV. The elemental compositions of carbide particles in the scanning TEM (STEM) images were recorded by energy dispersive spectrometry (EDS). Condition: step quenching and tempering treatment (SQT sample); Microstructure: hierarchical structure with ferrite and tempered martensite

Processing Text: The master FeCoCrNiCuAl0.4 alloys with a mass of 170 g were prepared by high-frequency induction melting using high purity of 99.99 wt% Fe, 99.99 wt% Co, 99.99 wt% Cr, 99.99 wt% Ni, 99.99 wt% Cu, and 99.99 wt% Al elements. The experiments were performed by a self-designed 3D ultrasonic solidification apparatus for metallic alloys. Three ultrasonic transducers with an operating frequency of 20 kHz were set up vertically by locating TC4 ultrasonic rods with 5 mm diameter end faces at the center point of the outer walls of the mold through X, Y and Z directions with elastic contact. There were two 1045 steel rods with fixed bases coaxially arranged on the opposite sides of the ultrasonic horns along X and Y directions, and a fixed cover plate using the same steel material with a central window to stabilize along Z direction. The mold was optimized to ensure the ultrasonic solidification system was in resonance, which internal and external sizes were 30×30×55 mm and 20×20×50 mm, respectively. During the experiments, the master alloys were melted and heated to 1873 K using high-frequency induction melting and subsequently poured into a cubic graphite casting mold, which was preheated to 1273 K and has a protective coating. The ultrasonic transducers were turned on, and one-dimensional Z, two-dimensional Y and Z, and three-dimensional X, Y, and Z ultrasonic waves, all with an amplitude of 18 μm, were selected to be applied to the melt through the casting mold. Meanwhile, a self-designed high-temperature sound field detecting system and K-type NiCr-NiSi thermocouple were used to monitored the acoustic field and temperature synchronously by immersing them at a distance of 30 mm below the highest alloy melt liquid level and 5 mm from the side wall. When the liquid alloys completely solidified and the temperature reached to 1273 K, the ultrasonic powers supply were turned off, and the solidified samples of FeCoCrNiCuAl0.4 alloy were finally obtained. After experiment, the alloy samples were cut longitudinally and polished. A Netzch 404 C Differential Scanning Calorimeter (DSC) was used for thermal analysis of static specimen at a scan rate of 10 K/min. The phase constitution was analyzed by a D8 discover A25 X-ray diffractometer (XRD) with a wavelength of 0.179021 nm. The solidification microstructures and crystallographic information were characterized by a Zeiss Gemini 500 scanning electron microscope (SEM). The electron backscatter diffraction images (EBSD) and energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS) results were taken by Oxford Instruments Nordlys detectors. The EBSD samples were electropolished with a mixed solution of HClO4: C2H7O2: CH4O=1: 2: 7 and the electric voltage of 18 V at 293 K for 15 s. A FEI Talos F200X transmission electron microscope (TEM) was used to characterize the crystal structure. Mechanical tensile tests were performed at the loading rate of 1×10−3s−1 by an Instron 3382 universal testing machine equipped with a Lve-Pro video extensometer. The gauge section of the dog bone-shaped sample was 10×3×1.2 mm. Electrochemical corrosion studies were performed in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution via a CHI660E electrochemical workstation. After the open circuit potential (OCP) was stabilized, the potential dynamic polarization curve was recorded at a potential scanning rate of 10 mV/s, and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was performed in the frequency range of 10−2∼105Hz, with a sinusoidal perturbation of amplitude 5.0 mV around the obtained OCP values for each sample. Processing Text: A commercial pure Mg cast ingot with a diameter of 80 mm was utilized in this work. The initial processing step involved extruding the an as-cast Mg ingot at 523 K with a high extrusion ratio of approximately 17:1 and the extrusion speed is 5∼6 mm / s. Following extrusion, the ingot was annealed at 573 K for 30 min, obtaining the as-annealed (AE) sample. This annealing treatment primarily aimed to recover intragranular dislocations and promote grain growth, without altering the strong basal-plane texture, along the normal direction (ND), induced by the extrusion process. Subsequently, we conducted compression deformation in the TD and tensile deformation along the ED at RT on this strongly textured AE sample, using the MTS 809 Axial/Torsional Test System. Due to the asymmetric crystal structure of hexagonal close-packed (HCP) pure Mg, a high fraction of twins and dislocations are induced in the matrix after plastic deformation under these two different stress conditions. For simplicity, we denote the pre-tension and pre-compression samples as PT and PC samples, respectively. As shown in Table 1, the numbers in the abbreviations represent the deformation strain. For example, PT3 denotes a 3% pre-tension deformation applied to the AE sample along the ED. Intentionally, we conducted combined deformations of pre-tension followed by pre-compression. Thin sections with the foil normal parallel to the ND were extracted from the PT3, PC7, PT3C4, and PT3C7 samples. Thin foils for TEM observations were prepared by ion-milling using a Gatan PIPS 691 after mechanical grinding to approximately 50 μm. The Mg samples were mechanically ground with grit papers ranging from 600 to 3000 grits, followed by electro-chemical polishing in an AC2 solution (10 ml isopropanol, 10 g hydroxyquinoline, 80 ml absolute ethanol, 18 ml distilled water, 75 g citric acid, and 41 g sodium hydrosulfide) at 20 V for 120 s and temperature was maintained at −25 to −30 °C. Processing Text: The Al0.2CrNbTiV high-entropy alloy was prepared by vacuum arc melting. The raw materials of Al, Cr, Nb, Ti and V elemental metal blocks with a purity in excess of 99.9 wt% was placed in a water-cooled copper crucible, evacuate to a vacuum degree of less than 2 × 10−3Pa, then melt in a high-purity argon atmosphere to avoid oxidation. The ingots were repeatedly melted and turned over at least 5 times to eliminate segregation and ensure the uniform distribution of different elements. The alloy ingot size obtained is about 56 mm in diameter and 20 mm in height. The annealing temperature was determined based on the thermal analysis results. During the annealing experiments, the Al0.2 alloy specimens were placed in a crucible and sealed in a vacuum quartz tube, heated to the corresponding annealing temperature at a heating rate of 5 °C/min, held for 12 h then cooled slowly with the furnace. The annealing temperatures of 650 °C, 850 °C and 1050 °C were determined in this paper to further analyze the changes in the structure and properties of Al0.2 alloy after annealing at different temperatures. Room temperature (25 °C) compression experiments were carried out using an MTS EM-type material testing machine with 6 × 4 × 4 mm3 rectangular specimens of the alloy, with an initial strain rate of 10−3s−1, and loaded to a strain of 50 %. The annealed specimens were ground and polished to a mirror surface using the mechanical polishing method, ultrasonically cleaned in ethanol for 30 min and dried. The hardness of the annealed alloy was measured using a micro-Vickers hardness tester with an experimental load of 200 g and a loading time of 15 s, each specimen was measured at least eight times to take the average value. The annealed alloy was subjected to reciprocal dry friction test at room temperature (25 °C) using UMT-TRIBOLAB multifunctional material surface mechanical property tester to analyze the friction and wear properties of the annealed alloy. Experimental normal load of 10 N, stroke of 5 mm, frequency of 2 Hz, time of 20 min, for Si3N4 ceramic balls of φ6 mm, each sample was repeated 3 times to calculate the average friction coefficient; meanwhile, the profile shape and volume loss of the worn samples were scanned using a matching 3D profiler. Processing Text: Mo compacts with different microstructures were prepared via SPS of the prepared Mo composite powders. Processing Text: Mg-1Zn-0.2Ca-1.0MgO (wt.%) was prepared by pure Mg (99.99 wt.%), pure Zn (99.99 wt.%), Mg-25Ca (wt.%) master alloy and MgO NPs (mean particle size ∼50 nm). A shear stirring equipment and an ultrasonic device were then used to disperse MgO NPs for 15 min. Finally, the melt was poured into a steel mold at 720°C. The ingot was firstly solution-treated at 420°C for 16 h and then was extruded using an extrusion ration of 56 and a ram speed of 0.2 mm/s at 270°C. Heat treatment was applied to the extruded samples at 200°C, 275°C, 350°C for 30 min. An ultra-fine grained (UFG) Mg-1Zn-0.2Ca-1.0MgO composite with an average grain size of 0.49 µm as well as an excellent combination of yield strength (379 MPa) and ductility (10.1%) was produced by one-step extrusion. Subsequent heat treatment at 200 ℃ for 30 min further improved its yield strength to 420 MPa and elongation to 12.1% with a slight grain growth to 0.76 µm. Processing Text: The Nb 25Ti 35V 5Zr 35HEA were fabricated by arc-melting of high-purity raw materials (Nb, Ti, V, Zr, all over 99.9 wt% purity) under an Ar atmosphere, remelted at least six times to ensure chemical homogeneity. To eliminate the cold work hardening and residual stresses induced by the rolling process, the sample rolled by 80 % was annealed at 1050 °C for 30 minutes. Processing Text: Molybdenum-rhenium alloys has a low recrystallization temperature and insufficient high temperature strength, making it unable to serve as structural parts for a long time in high temperature environments above 1300 ℃ for a long time. The Mo-5 wt% Re and Mo-5 wt% Re-1 wt% ZrO 2alloys were prepared by liquid-liquid doping method (Abbreviations are Mo-Re and Mo-Re-ZrO 2). (NH 4) 2Mo 4O 13(99.99 % purity, CMOC Group Limited), Zr(NO 3) 4·5 H 2O (99.99 % purity, MACKLIN), CO(NH 2) 2(99.99 % purity, MACKLIN), and Re powder (99.99 % purity, MACKLIN) as raw materials, the precursor powder of ZrO 2was prepared by hydrothermal method at 180 ℃ for 16 h. (NH 4) 2Mo 4O 13was then dissolved in distilled water. The Re powder was dispersed by a cell crusher for 30 min, and the obtained suspension was mixed and stirred with (NH 4) 2Mo 4O 13. The hydrothermal preparation of ZrO 2precursor powder mixing with the above solution, after ultrasonic oscillation and mechanical mixing, drying in vacuum drying furnace. After drying at 100 ℃ × 48 h, the mixed precursor powder was obtained, calcined at low temperature, and reduced at high temperature with two stages of hydrogen. Then, the composite powder was sieved and put into a rubber leather sleeve with an inner diameter of 30 mm, and compressed at a pressure of 200 MPa through a cold isostatic press for 20 min. The pressed blank was kept warm for 72 h in a medium frequency sintering furnace at 1900 ℃. The Mo-Re alloy rods obtained by sintering was cut into cylindrical compression samples of 6 × 9 mm along the direction parallel to the axial direction, and the samples were subsequently polished. The room temperature compression experiment used a SHI MADZU AG-I250 kN precision universal testing machine with a diameter of 6 mm and a length of 9 mm, and a strain rate of 1 s −1. The high temperature compression tests were carried out on a Gleeble 1500D thermal simulation tester. The specimens were subjected to heating to the deformation temperature and then tested at a heating rate of 20 ℃/s and a holding time of 5 min. The hot compression test temperatures were 1100 ℃, 1200 ℃, 1300 ℃, and 1400 ℃, with a strain rate of 1 s −1. Condition: room temperature compressive yield strength

Processing Text: The powder feedstock for L-PBF was supplied by the Volgograd-Russia Aluminum Plant (UC RUSAL) with the following particle size distribution: d 10= 17.3 μm, d 50= 26.7 μm, and d 90= 40.75 μm using the molten metal spraying method. Cylindrical bars having a diameter of 20 mm and a length of 100 mm were manufactured with the building direction (BD) parallel to the bar's length under a controlled Ar atmosphere. A commercial SLM280HL printer (Selective Laser Melting Solutions Group AG, Lübeck, Germany), was used to make samples, operating with the following parameters: a scan speed of 1650 mm/s, a power of 370 W, a hatch spacing of 130 µm, layer thickness of 50 µm and a scanning rotation of 67° between consecutive layers. These parameters yielded a laser energy density of 1.72 J/mm 2, leading to a porosity fraction lower than 0.18 %. Annealing in the temperature range of 20 °C to 500 °C for one hour led to evolutions in the as-built L-PBF cellular structure, including partial fragmentation of the cell boundaries between 20 °C and 300 °C; the breakdown and transformation into ultrafine Si-enriched particles in the range of 300 °C to 400 °C; and subsequently coarsening at temperatures exceeding 400 °C. Uniaxial tensile tests were conducted at room temperature at an initial strain rate of 1 × 10 −3s −1using miniature bone-shaped samples (4 mm in length, 1.3 mm in width, 2 mm in thickness and 1 mm radius (R)) oriented parallel to the BD. The samples for the mechanical testing were fabricated from the as-built bars using electrode discharge machining, which resulted in uniformly smooth surfaces. Vickers microhardness using a square-based pyramidal diamond indenter were carried out for the as-built and annealed samples. A constant load of 1.8 N and a dwell time of 15 s were used. In situ high-energy synchrotron X-ray diffraction (HEXRD) analysis was carried out during isothermal annealing heat treatments at 400 °C and 500 °C with a holding time of one hour each using cylindrical samples of 5 mm diameter and 8 mm length. To mitigate the impact of sample size on strain calculation, the so-called digital image correlation (DIC) method was used. The DIC system was implemented on a universal tensile machine employing a 12-megapixel digital camera operating at 32 frames per second with an acquisition time of 2 s and a pixel size of 0.04 mm. The acquired data was subsequently processed in Matlab, utilizing the open source software Ncorr. To ensure more reliable results, all tensile samples were tested in the weakest direction, i.e., the tensile loading direction parallel to the BD. In order to establish a correlation between synchrotron measurements and the microstructure and mechanical properties at various temperatures, a series of samples from the as-built material were subjected to annealing treatments with a holding time of one hour at temperatures of 200 °C, 300 °C, 400 °C, and 500 °C. Subsequently, these samples were evaluated using EBSD, hardness, and tensile testing. Condition: after annealing at 400 °C
Processing Word: Condition: after annealing at 400 °C

Processing Text: Cu 45Mn 8Ni 40Sn 7medium entropy bronze alloy was fabricated using copper, manganese, nickel, and tin powders as raw materials in a vacuum induction furnace (VIF-1, TianJin Muffle Technology Co.). The multi-stage heat treatment of the alloy is performed using a high-temperature box-type resistance furnace in air atmosphere. The appropriate temperature for each step in the heat treatment process was primarily determined based on differential scanning calorimetry (DSC, DMA242E, NETZSCH) analysis of the alloy and previous studies of Cu-Ni-Sn alloys [28,29]. To reduce compositional segregation, the ingots with dimensions of Φ25 × 20 mm were homogenized at 820 ℃ for 4 h, followed by furnace cooling. The solution treatment temperature was selected at 900 ℃, and water quenching was performed after holding for 1 h. Aging treatment was conducted at 450 ℃ for 5 h to ensure sufficient formation of the precipitated phase. The alloy, treated by homogenization (820 ℃/4 h)-solution (900 ℃/1 h)-aging (450 ℃/5 h), exhibits a hardness of 362 HV, yield strength of 626 MPa, ultimate strength of 1229 MPa, compressive strain of 47.2 %, fracture toughness of 20.7 MPa·m1/2, and maintains a low wear rate of 1.72×10−5 mm3·N−1·m−1. The processes of homogenization and solution treatment reduce dendrite segregation of elements and eliminate the detrimental lamellar structure at the grain boundaries. During the aging treatment of the alloy, sub-micron scale needle-like precipitates are formed, which play a significant role in enhancing its mechanical properties. Processing Text: To prepare the Ti/W composites, industrial pure titanium (D 50 = 10 μm) and tungsten (D 50 = 2 μm) powders are mixed using a planetary ball mill. The tungsten content is varied at mass fractions of 10 %, 15 %, 20 %, and 25 %. The ball milling process involves a rotational speed of 200 rpm, a ball-powder weight ratio of 10:1, and a total milling time of 10 hours. In order to minimize the temperature rise during the milling process, a single ball grinding time is 30 minutes, with an interval of 10 minutes between each milling session. Anhydrous ethanol is used as a process control agent. After milling, the powder and anhydrous ethanol mixture is vacuum dried at 60°C for 24 hours to obtain the composite powder. Next, the Ti/W composite powder is introduced into a graphite mold with a 20 mm inner diameter, and graphite foil is added to facilitate lubrication and facilitate sample removal after sintering. The composite powders are pre-compacted at 10 MPa uniaxial pressure for 10 minutes and then subjected to vacuum sintering using the sparking plasma sintering system (SPS-3 T-3-MN, Chen Hua, China). The sintering process involves a temperature of 1400°C, a heating rate of 100 °C/min, an applied pressure of 40 MPa, and a sintering time of 10 minutes. Subsequently, the samples are cooled to room temperature in the furnace. Processing Text: Solid cylindrical samples of AM 316H SS were fabricated using a Concept Laser Mlab 100R powder bed fusion system (GE Additive, Boston, MA, USA). The process employed a laser power of 90 W, a scan speed of 1275 mm/s, a layer thickness of 25 μm, and a laser focus diameter of 50 μm. Printing occurred in an argon gas environment, with all specimens printed vertically. For the AM SS specimens, we first 3D printed cylindrical samples measuring 3 cm in height and 1 cm in diameter. Subsequently, these samples underwent precision machining via electrical discharge machining (EDM) to attain final specimens with a diameter of 10 mm and a thickness of 2 mm. Tensile specimens were 3D printed in a vertical orientation with a nominal gage length section of 5 x 2.5 × 1 mm 3, employing printing conditions similar to those for the cylindrical specimens. The AM 316H SS and conventional SS specimens were mechanically ground and polished using a Struers Tegramin-25 automatic polisher. Grinding was done on an MD-Piano 220 grinding surface, while polishing was carried out using an MD-Plan cloth with 9 μm diamond suspension. Final polishing utilized an MD-Chem cloth with 0.25 μm fumed silica. The as-built polished AM SS and the conventional SS samples were irradiated using a 3SDH Pelletron accelerator (National Electrostatics Corporation, Middleton, WI, USA) at ambient temperature. Irradiation was performed with an H +ion beam, with fluences of 1.49577x1016and 1.49577x1017ion/cm 2corresponding to damage of 0.6 and 6 displacements per atom (dpa), respectively. During irradiation, the incident ions exhibited an average energy of 0.5 MeV with an average beam current of 300 nA. Hardness testing was conducted on AM and conventional SS specimens to assess the radiation damage and hardness changes before and following irradiation, using a Shimadzu HMV-M3 Vickers hardness tester (Shimadzu Scientific Instruments, Kyoto, Japan). Each measurement involved applying a 50 g indenter load with a dwell time of 15 s. The selection of the specific weight for the study was deliberate, ensuring that the penetration depth remained within the affected irradiated volume. For each irradiation level studied, at least five hardness measurements were conducted on two samples, ensuring a representative dataset for subsequent analysis. Uniaxial tensile testing was conducted using an INSTRON®servo-hydraulic (Instron Company, Norwood, MA, USA) load frame with a 100 kN load cell. All tension tests were performed under displacement control (0.1 mm/s). The strain was measured using digital image correlation (DIC), and the engineering strain was extracted using the digital extensometer method. The Young's modulus, yield strength (YS), total elongation (TE), and ultimate strength (UTS) were calculated from the resulting stress-strain curves. We employed an environmental scanning electron microscope (SEM), specifically the FEI Quanta™ FEG 450 ESEM(FEI Company, Hillsboro, OR, USA), to examine the cracked surfaces resulting from the uniaxial testing. Processing Text: This study aimed to explore the impact of in-situ formed nitride and oxide precipitates on the properties of Fe12Cr6Al alloy by using a nitrogen-rich atmosphere and incorporating nano-sized Y2O3 (0.45 wt %) during laser powder bed fusion (LPBF). As a result of adding Y2O3 nanoparticles to the Fe12Cr6Al alloy, the grain size decreased from 70 μm to 40 μm, and the Al-O, Al-N, and Al-N-O precipitates were replaced by Y-O, Y-Al-O, and Y-N precipitates. Additionally, the nitrogen contents increased from 220 ppm to 470 ppm. The sample with Y2O3 exhibited higher mechanical properties, with yield strength, tensile strength, and hardness (HV) increasing by 80 MPa, 112 MPa, and 23 HV, respectively. This study deviates from previous research on Y2O3-containing FeCrAl alloys by investigating the impact of in-situ synthesized Y-N nitrides on Fe12Cr6Al. The objective is to elucidate the combined effects of these precipitates on the properties of Fe12Cr6Al alloy in comparison to literature-reported oxide dispersion-strengthened (ODS) FeCrAl alloys, which were fabricated in an argon (Ar) atmosphere. Fe12Cr6Al powders were sourced from MK Co. in South Korea and fabricated using gas atomization, along with Y2O3 powders also sourced from MK Co. The Fe12Cr6Al powder ranged from 15 to 45 μm, while the Y2O3 powder had particle sizes from 50 to 100 nm. The test powder was prepared by blending Fe12Cr6Al powder with 0.45 wt % Y2O3 powder. The Fe12Cr6Al and Y2O3 powders were mixed at 6000 RPM for 6 min to ensure a uniform distribution. Two samples were fabricated using the LPBF machine (Metalsys-250, WINFORSYS): one without Y2O3 and one with Y2O3 in the Fe12Cr6Al alloy. The chamber was continuously supplied with N2 gas during the fabrication, maintaining the O2 content below 100 ppm. All samples were fabricated using the laser processing parameters (laser power: 200 W, scanning speed: 400 mm/s, layer thickness: 30 μm, scanning distance: 100 μm, spot size: 100 μm) identified as optimal for achieving superior properties. The alloys were printed in a striped pattern, with each layer's scan direction rotated by 90°, and were fabricated with dimensions of 30 × 10 × 10 mm³ for property examination. The elemental compositions of the powders and the as-built samples were determined using inductively coupled plasma-optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES, QSG-750, OBLF). The oxygen and nitrogen content in the as-built samples, particularly, was measured using a nitrogen/oxygen analyzer (LECO, ON-836, Japan). For tensile testing (three tests for each sample), the as-built dog bone specimens were precision-cut from the 316 L substrate parallel to the building direction, with a gauge length of 6.4 mm and a gauge width of 2.5 mm. Their tensile properties were evaluated at room temperature using a Universal Testing Machine (Instron-582, INSTRON) with a strain rate of 10⁻³ s⁻¹. Vickers hardness measurements were also conducted on cross-sections of the specimens using a Mitutoyo/HM-220B microhardness tester. Hardness values were determined by averaging the results of ten indentations made on each specimen under a load of HV 0.5 for a dwell time of 10 s. During the LPBF process, Fe12Cr6Al melts within a nitrogen atmosphere, promoting nitrogen absorption. This environment facilitates the dissociation of nitrogen gas molecules, leading to the formation of reactive nitrogen species that can subsequently interact with the molten metal and contribute to the formation of Al-N and Y-N precipitates. Processing Text: Alloy ingot with nominal compositions of AlCrFeNiTi 0.2 were prepared by non-consumable electrode arc-melting in a Ti-gettered, high-purity argon atmosphere on a water-cooled copper hearth. The ingot was flipped and remelted at least seven times to ensure compositional homogeneity. For microstructural analysis, specimens were cut from the as-cast AlCrFeNiTi0.2 ingot by electrical discharge machining (EDM). The metallographic specimens were abraded on SiC papers to 2000 grit, and then final polished on a Buehler Vibromet using 0.05 μm colloidal silica for 30 min. The slight alkalinity of the colloidal silica could potentially produce an etched surface; therefore, no additional etchant was applied prior to microscopic observation. In order to observe the dendritic microstructure more clearly, aqua regia etching was used to distinguish the two main phases (A2 and B2/L2 1) of the as-cast AlCrFeNiTi 0.2 HEA. A series of small cylinders with a diameter of Φ2.5 mm and a length of 5 mm were cut and polished from the as-cast AlCrFeNiTi 0.2 ingot for the purpose of conducting compression tests. Compression tests were conducted at a compressing speed of 0.5 mm/min on a SASTest CMT4305 universal testing machine. The microhardness of the as-cast AlCrFeNiTi 0.2 HEA was measured using a QATM Qness 60 A + EVO microhardness tester according to ASTM E384. The tester has an accuracy range of ±2% to ±5%. The applied load is 200 g and the holding pressure time is 15 s. Furthermore, an Agilent G200 nanoindentation tester was employed to assess the hardness of distinct regions. The maximum indentation depth was 1000 nm using the indentation depth control mode. Processing Text: The powders used in this investigation were a Mar-M247 superalloy with size distributions ranging from 15 to 53 μm. SLM-100 system (Shandong Charmray Laser Technology Co., Ltd) was used to prepare specimens with the following parameters: laser power 140-240 W, scanning speed 800-1200 mm/s, interlayer rotation angle 67°, reciprocating scanning strategy, layer thickness 30 μm, and hatch spacing 80 μm. Progressive remelting has been proposed to slowly raise the temperature field and reduce the peak stress by multiple cycling at low laser power. The identical parameters of progressive remelting: laser power 60-90 W, scanning speed 600-800 mm/s, interlayer rotation angle 60°-90°, layer thickness 30 μm, hatch spacing 60-70 μm and building parameters: laser power 120-150 W, scanning speed 700-800 mm/s, interlayer rotation angle 60°-90°, layer thickness 30 μm, hatch distance 70-80 μm. Cuboidal specimens 5 mm × 5 mm × 5 mm for microstructure characterization, tensile samples 8 mm × 2 mm × 55 mm along the building direction for room temperature, and tensile samples 15 mm × 1.8 mm × 48 mm along the building direction for 900 °C were fabricated on 316L stainless steel build-plates. In order to promote the nucleation and growth of γ′ phase and improve the mechanical properties at elevated temperature, a standard heat treatment used for investment casting is conducted in a KSL-1200X furnace with solution treatment at 1185 °C (below γ′ phases solvus and in order to ensure the complete dissolution of γ′ phase) for 2 h with air-cooling and followed by a double-aging treatment at 1100 °C for 4 h, and 871 °C for 20 h cooled in the air (to make the alloy close to the equilibrium state) as well. Optical microscopy (OM) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) were used to observe the microstructures of the samples and the square samples were cut along the building direction, after which the cut sample was ground and polished. In order to obtain the microstructure, the samples were etched with a solution of 5 g CuSO4 + 20 ml HCl +20 ml H2O. SEM images and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) data were obtained by a JEF 7800 field emission scanning electron microscope. TEM observation was performed using FEI Talos F200X to investigate the microstructures of Mar-M247. Tensile tests at room temperature were performed along the building direction using an Instron 5584 machine at a constant crosshead velocity of 0.02/s. Tensile tests at 900 °C were performed along the building direction using an AG-X Plus Series Dual Column Electromechanical Test Frame at a strain rate of 0.0008/s in accordance with ISO 6892-2:2011. Processing Text: The ingots of HEAs with a nominal composition of Al 0.4CoCrFe 2Ni 2/TiC were prepared using a vacuum arc furnace. Ceramic reinforcement phases were added to the alloy by mass percentage, including TiC (μm) at 2.5 wt%. TiC (μm) powder was mixed with Ni powder. These two groups of powders were blended thoroughly using a ball mill to ensure uniform dispersion within the alloy. The sphere to material mass ratio is 10:1. YLJ-15 T manual tableting machine was employed for mechanical pressing to obtain block preforms made from composite powder with the pressure holding time is 10 min. The total mass of the matrix alloy was 80 g. Al, Cr, Ni-TiC (μm), and Fe-TiC (nm) metal raw materials were placed inside a vacuum arc furnace and melted under protection from ultra-high purity argon gas at 1 × 10 -4Pa pressure level. The ingots underwent five repeated melting cycles to guarantee consistent chemical composition. The size of the tissue cut by the electric spark wire cutting machine was 10 * 10 * 10 mm. The tensile sample is shown as a dog bone in Fig. 3, and the size of the transmission test sample is 10 * 10 * 0.5 mm. The as-cast samples were ground, polished and electrolytically corroded. The transparent thin foil for transmission electron microscope (TEM) observation was prepared by mechanical grinding, polishing and double jet electrolytic polishing technology, after the sheet with a thickness of 500 μm was cutting from the alloy. The tensile samples like dog bone with a gauge length of 7 mm, a width of 4 mm, and a thickness of 2 mm were subjected to tensile tests at room temperature on a universal electronic testing machine (MTS-E45) with a strain rate of 10 −3mm·s −1. Processing Text: Bulk specimens were produced by BLT-S310 Selective Laser Melting machine from gas-atomized powder with compositions of Al-4Cu-2Mg-0.3Sc-0.7Zr (wt.%). The powder was dried in a vacuum drying oven at 120 °C for 15 h before SLM processing. Based on a series of process parameter optimizations, the parameters of preparing the bulk specimens (70 × 70 × 15 mm 3) were: a laser power of 200 W, laser scanning speed of 540 mm/s, layer thickness of 0.03 mm, hatch spacing and laser spot of 0.1 mm, and a scan direction rotation of 67°. The as-fabricated and aging treatment samples were cut, ground and polished for microstructure analysis and microhardness analyses. The microstructures of the samples were characterized by scanning electron microscopy (SEM, SIGMA 500 of Ziess Company) equipped with an energy dispersive x-ray spectrometer (EDS) and an electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD). The microstructure was further characterized using an Thermo Fisher Talos F200S G2 transmission electron microscopy (TEM) operating and high angle annular dark field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) with EDS. The tensile samples with a gauge length of 25 mm were tested on an Instron 3382 machine with a constant cross head moving speed of 1 mm/min. Strain was measured with a 12.5 mm gauge length extensometer. Samples were aligned perpendicular to the build direction as shown in Fig. 2. The phase transformation point was measured by differential scanning calorimetry (DSC). Differential scanning calorimetry was performed using a NETZSCH STA 449C Simultaneous Thermal Analyzer by heating rates of 4 °C/min in nitrogen inert atmosphere. The DSC sample weight is between 5 and 10 mg, was cut from the as-fabricated samples to fit into the alumina crucibles (Ф5 × 4 mm 3) for the analysis. Based on the DSC peaks observed, the temperatures for direct heat treatments were chosen in such a way that the peak temperature of each possible phase transition (local minimum points) and the possible phase transition termination temperature. The sample underwent a significant melting reaction after 520 °C, therefore, heat treatment at temperatures of 520 °C was performed. From all the above considerations, the aging treatment used were 203 °C, 225 °C, 282 °C, 320 °C, 440 °C, 465 °C, 496 °C and 520 °C for 2.5 h followed by water cooling. Furthermore, it is worth noting that despite a noticeable reduction in dislocation density, this heat treatment process significantly enhances yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, plasticity and hardness simultaneously, which could be attributed to the formation of nano-scale precipitates mentioned above. Processing Text: In this work, we developed a Ti20W alloy using powder metallurgy and hot extrusion, which combined remarkable mechanical properties and good corrosion resistance. High-purity powders of Ti (<45 μm), and W (<10 μm) were mixed for 6 h under an argon atmosphere to obtain the Ti20W (weight fraction, wt.%) powder mixture. Subsequently, the Ti20W powder mixture was compacted through cold isostatic pressing (CIP). The parameters for CIP included the pressure of 180 MPa, the holding time of 1 min, and the temperature of 298 K. Then, the compact Ti20W samples were set in a vacuum furnace for sintering. The details for the sintering process involved the heating rate of 10 °C/s, the sintering temperature of 1350 °C, the holding time of 4 h, and furnace cooling to the room temperature. The as-sintered billets were further machined into cylindrical samples with a diameter of 120 mm in preparation for extrusion. Before extrusion, the cylindrical samples were set into a die at 950 °C for 2 h. The subsequent hot extrusion process was conducted at 950 °C with an extrusion ratio of 4, followed by air cooling to the room temperature. Cylindrical samples with a diameter of 60 mm were obtained and labeled as Ti20W-60. Then, the Ti20W-60 samples were extruded at 950 °C to get the cylindrical rods with a diameter of 30 mm, labeled as Ti20W-30. Processing Text: High-purity elements (Co, Cu, Fe, Ni ≥ 99.99 wt%, and Ta ≥99.95 wt%) were used for casting. To ensure uniform dispersion of elements, the ingots were flipped over and remelted at least five times. The thoroughly homogenized ingots called the As-casted (Ac-) samples, were subsequently cast into copper molds to achieve the final dimensions of 4 cm × 4 cm × 9 cm. The Ac- samples were then annealed at 1100 °C for 2 h to optimize their microstructure and they were named Heat-treated (Ht-) samples. Compression tests were conducted on both Ac- and Ht-samples to evaluate the mechanical properties using a UTM4000 electronic universal testing machine from the Three-Sides All-Round Company. The tests were performed at a strain rate of 1 × 10 −3mm/s on cylindrical samples with a dimension of Ф6 × 9 mm. The Vickers hardness test used a TH-300 hardness tester with a 49.03 N (HV5) load. The final hardness value was determined by averaging five individual measurements. During heat treatment, Cu outwards diffused from γ′(Cu-rich) into γ matrix, γ′(Ta-rich) phase and δ phase. The accumulation of Cu and Ta into the δ phase strongly promoted its growth. After heat treatment, the γ′ phase became much less and was accumulated along the δ phase. Cu outwards diffused from the γ′(Cu-rich) phase into the γ matrix, γ′(Ta-rich) phases, and δ phases. Finally, γ′(Cu-rich) phases transformed into γ matrix. At the same time, the accumulation of Cu and Ta into δ phases significantly promoted its growth, which resulted in the increase of δ phase volume fraction from 3% to 6%. Processing Text: TC19 and Ti150 were used as the materials for this diffusion joining experiment. Fig. 2(a) outlines the experimental parameters related to diffusion bonding process, with the vacuum in the furnace maintained consistently below 5 × 10−3Pa. Bonding temperatures were designed based on the solution temperatures of the two alloys. All welding experiments in this study were conducted at a pressure of 10 MPa with a holding time of 60 min. After completing all welding experiments, metallographic specimens and tensile test samples were prepared. A field emission scanning electron microscope equipped with an electron backscatter diffraction system was used to observe the microstructure of the joints. To further illustrate the formation mechanism of the joints, a field emission high-resolution transmission electron microscope was used to analyze the elemental distribution at the joint interface and identify potential intermediate phase compositions. In-situ tensile tests aimed to explain the deformation behavior and fracture mechanisms of the joints were conducted using a field emission scanning electron microscope equipped with a tensile device at a rate of 0.05 mm/min. Uniaxial tensile tests were conducted on an electronic universal material testing machine to assess the ductility level of the joints. Processing Text: The AlCrCuFeNi high entropy alloy (HEA) with two FCC and BCC crystalline phases was successfully synthesized through 60 h of mechanical alloying (MA) followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS). The AlCrCuFeNi HEA was synthesized using elemental powders of Al, Cr, Cu, Fe, and Ni, each with a purity exceeding 99 % (Merck Co., Germany) and particle sizes below 45 μm. These powders were blended in equal atomic proportions (20 %) and subjected to MA using a planetary ball mill (QM-3SP4, Nanda Co., Ltd) within a steel vial containing hardened chromium steel balls, with a ball-to-powder weight ratio of 10:1. The powders underwent milling at a speed of 350 rpm for a duration of 60 h, all under a protective argon gas atmosphere to prevent oxidation. To prevent powder agglomeration, approximately 2 wt% of stearic acid was introduced to the powders as a process control agent (PCA). Following MA, the AlCrCuFeNi milled powders were compacted using spark plasma sintering (SPS) (KPFVT Company, Iran). The powders were pressed into a graphite die with a diameter of 40 mm under a pressure of 45 MPa for 6 min within a vacuum environment. This technique employs direct current (DC), low pulse voltage current, and uniaxial force in a low-pressure environment to achieve rapid powder sintering. The sintered samples were processed at three distinct temperatures of 850 °C, 900 °C, and 950 °C. The sample sintered at 900 °C, exhibiting a relative density of 94 %, was identified as the optimal sintered sample. This sintered AlCrCuFeNi alloy was determined to comprise two solid solution phases (BCC and FCC) alongside an intermetallic compound known as σ. Estimated using shear punch testing; Room temperature

Processing Text: In this contribution, we utilized the laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) technique to produce a high-Mo maraging steel with a nominal chemical composition of Fe-13Ni-12Co-10Mo-1W-1Ti (wt.%). Notably, the ultrafast cooling rate inherent to L-PBF successfully suppresses the formation of coarse Mo-enriched precipitates. The co-precipitation of high-density Ni3Ti and Mo-enriched nanoprecipitates within the direct-aged martensitic matrix was observed. As a result, despite containing ∼16% soft reverted austenite, the direct-aged samples exhibit an ultrahigh yield strength (YS) of ∼ 2.34 GPa and an ultrahigh ultimate tensile strength (UTS) of ∼2.57 GPa, with an acceptable uniform elongation (UE) of around 2.7%. Gas-atomized powders with particle sizes ranging from 15 to 53 μm were utilized to make bulk samples. The chemical composition of the pre-alloyed powder is detailed in the Table 1. Sample blocks with dimensions of 70 (x) × 22 (y) × 14 (z, building direction (BD)) mm 3( Supplementary Fig. S2) were fabricated in an L-PBF machine BLT-S210 (BLT, Inc, Xi'an, China). The printing was conducted with optimized parameters of a laser power of 170 W, a hatch spacing of 80 μm, a scan speed of 1000 mm/s, a layer thickness of 20 μm, and a scan strategy with 67° rotation between layers. Post-printing heat treatments were conducted using a DIL-805 A/D type dilatometer with both the heating and cooling rates set at 10 °C/s. In reference to aging parameter used by Kwon et al. [ 25] for an ultrahigh UTS of 2.4 GPa in a high-Mo maraging medium-entropy alloy (56.89 Fe-25.01 Co-9.96 Ni-8.14 Mo in wt.%), the as-built samples of this study were performed an aging treatment at 550 °C for 10 min, followed by cooling to ambient temperature (denoted as direct-aged samples). In addition, to replicate conventional heat treatment process, the as-built samples underwent annealing at 1000 °C for 1 h, followed by cooling to ambient temperature (denoted as annealed samples). This annealing temperature is higher than the standard 820 °C typically used for 18 Ni maraging steels, aiming to suppress the formation of Mo-enriched precipitates during the annealing. These annealed samples were then subjected to the same aging treatment at 550 °C for 10 min, facilitating comparative analyses between different fabrication techniques. Vickers hardness tests were performed under an applied load of 9.8 N and a dwell time of 10 s, and at least ten indentations were conducted per sample. Uniaxial tensile tests were conducted at a strain rate of 10 -4s -1at ambient temperature. Dog-bone-shape tensile specimens with the gauge dimensions of 8 × 2 × 1 mm 3were prepared along the x-axis direction using electrical-discharge machining, and then polished to 5000-grid SiC paper. Processing Text: We fabricated a non-equiatomic Ni35Co27.5Cr27.5Al5Ti5 HEA consisting of spherical L12 nanoprecipitates and FCC matrix using casting, homogenization and aging. Notably, both the homogenized and aged Ni35Co27.5Cr27.5Al5Ti5 HEA samples exhibit equiaxed grains, with the latter showcasing uniformly distributed spherical L12 nanoprecipitates in the FCC matrix. The average size and volume fraction of these nanoprecipitates in the aged HEA are ∼10.9 nm and ∼41.9 vol%, respectively. Mechanical testing reveals remarkable improvements in the aged HEA, with a yield strength of ∼916 MPa, an ultimate tensile strength of ∼1220 MPa, and a total elongation of ∼21.5 %. The non-equiatomic Ni35Co27.5Cr27.5Al5Ti5 (at%) ingot was fabricated by induction levitation melting using pure metals (with purities of ≥ 99.9 wt%) as starting materials, and the process was conducted under a high-purity argon atmosphere for protection. During melting, the metal raw materials were placed in a coil with high-frequency current, and then the electromagnetic force counteracted the gravity of the materials by controlling the high-frequency power supply to achieve materials suspension or quasi-suspension, avoiding crucible contamination and reducing burning loss, obtaining pure and homogeneous alloy with accurate composition. To ensure uniformity of composition, the ingot underwent at least five re-melting cycles, with flipping between each cycle. Finally, the molten alloy was poured into a steel die with a dimension ∼60 mm (length) × ∼25 mm (width) × ∼12 mm (thickness). Subsequently, the ingot was homogenized at 1120 °C for 12 h with flowing argon gas to mitigate elemental segregation during solidification, followed by quenching in cold water. Half of the homogenized ingot was then aged at 700 °C for 2 h under the flowing argon gas, followed by air cooling. Condition: Room Temperature; Phase: FCC+L12; Processing state: Aged at 700°C for 2 h

Processing Text: Equimolar CoCrNi MEA was prepared by arc-melting Co, Cr, and Ni mixtures with 99.99 % purity in a high-purity argon atmosphere. Quasi-static compression tests with strain rates ranging from 1.0 × 10^−3 s^−1 to 10^−1 s^−1 were performed on CoCrNi MEA samples with a diameter of 3 mm and length of 6 mm using an Instron 5969 testing machine. Processing Text: Alloy ingots with nominal composition of the Al x CrFe 2 Ni (x = 0.3, 0.4, 0.5 and 0.7 in mole ratios), denoted as Al x, or Al 0.3, Al 0.4, Al 0.5, and Al 0.7, respectively, were manufactured by arc melting in a high purity argon atmosphere with high purity (> 99.8 wt%) Al, Cr, Fe, and Ni raw materials. To ensure a homogeneous composition the ingots were repeatedly melted five times. Rectangular plates of 70 mm × 14 mm × 2 mm for the four MEAs were prepared by the copper mold injection casting. The crystal structure of the as-cast Al x CrFe 2 Ni MEAs was identified by X-ray diffraction (XRD, Shimadzu 7000) at a speed of 4 ◦/min with Cu K α radiation. The scanning electron microscopy (SEM) equipped with energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) was used to observe the microstructure and detect the elemental distributions of the alloys. The volume fraction and distribution of the different phases in the alloys were observed by electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD). Besides, the structure of each phase of the as-cast alloys was also characterized by the transmission electron microscope (TEM, JEM-2100). Hysteresis lines of different samples were measured using an integrated physical property measurement system (VSM, Micro Sense EZ9). The strain gauge type BX120-5AA (5×3) was used to measure the magnetostriction coefficient of the alloys with a resistance value of 120 Ω and a strain measurement range of 1-19999 ppm. The magnetic domains of alloys were tested using the magnetic force microscope (MFM) module of the atomic force microscope. The damping capacity of the as-cast alloys were characterized by the dynamic mechanical analyzer (DMA, Q800, single cantilever mode), and the damping capacity was estimated using the internal friction Q−1 (Q−1 = tan δ, where δ is the phase lagged between the applied cyclic stress and the resulting strain). A universal mechanical testing machine (MTS-E45) was used to test the tensile sample at tensile rate of 1 × 10 −3 s −1. Processing Text: Cu47.5Zr45.1Al7.4 and Zr41.2Ti13.8Cu12.5Ni10Be22.5 BMGs prepared by vacuum arc melting and vacuum die casting processes were purchased from Peshing New Metal Co., Ltd. The size of BMG samples was 20 mm × 20 mm × 2 mm. Before CE experiments, the samples were polished with water sandpaper and diamond paste to mirror the surface and then were ultrasonically cleaned in ethanol solution for 10 min. The CE test of two types of samples was carried out in deionized water by an ultrasonic vibration apparatus that conforms to ASTM G32-16 standard. The BMG samples were held stationary below the amplitude transformer with a diameter of 15.9 mm at a distance of 0.5 ± 0.01 mm and immersed in water at a depth of 12 ± 4 mm. CE tests were operated at a frequency of 20 kHz, an amplitude of 50 μm (peak-to-peak), a duration of 12 h and a water temperature of 25 ± 2 °C controlled by a circulatory system. After every interval of 1 h, the mass loss of the samples before and after CE was measured by an electronic analytical balance with an accuracy of 0.1 mg, and then converted to volume loss according to their densities. The amorphous structure of Cu47.5Zr45.1Al7.4 and Zr41.2Ti13.8Cu12.5Ni10Be22.5 BMGs was verified by X-ray diffractometer (XRD, D/Max-2400, Philips, Netherlands) with a Cu-Kα radiation (40 kV, 40 mA) over a 2θ range of 20°-90°. The thermal stability of the two types of samples was evaluated by differential scanning calorimeter (DSC, Netzsch STA 449 F5, Germany) from 298 to 1073 K at a heating rate of 20 K min-1 in high-purity nitrogen. Their morphologies and elements distribution of polished surfaces were measured by the JSM-5600LV scanning electron microscope (SEM, JEOL, Japan) coupled with an energy-dispersive spectrometer (EDS). A FIB-SEM system (Helios G4 PFIB, FEI, Netherlands) was used to prepare TEM samples of the CE zone of BMGs and a transmission electron microscopy (TEM, JEM-F200, JEOL, Japan) was employed to investigate the microstructure of BMGs and to study whether nanocrystalline precipitates were formed after CE. In addition, positron annihilation lifetime spectroscopy (PALS, Ortec, United States) measurements were performed using a fast-fast coincident method and a 12.5 μCi 22Na position source sandwiched between two pieces of the same specimen. The density values of the two types of samples were obtained by calculation, which can be expressed as the following formula: ρ=mV where m is the mass of the sample, accurately measured by an electronic analytical balance with an accuracy of 0.1 mg, and V represents the actual volume of the sample, measured with an AccuPyc 1330 Rycnometer-type densimeter (Micromeritics, USA) in high purity helium. The microhardness of polished surfaces of BMGs was measured by a microhardness tester (MH-5-VM) at a load of 300 g and a dwelling time of 10 s, and the average value of 10 points was taken. Their nanoindentation tests before and after CE were carried out by an NHT02 nanoindentation instrument with a triangular pyramid indenter at a maximum load of 30 mN, a loading/unloading rate of 60 mN min-1, a dwelling time of 10 s, and a collection frequency of 10 Hz, and each test was repeated five times at least. In addition, under the sinus mode of the NHT02 nanoindentation instrument, the true stress-strain curves of the two BMGs were tested to obtain yield strength using a spherical indenter with a radius of 10 μm at a maximum load of 50 mN, a sinus frequency of 10 Hz, an amplitude of 5 μm, a holding time of 10 s and a loading-unloading rate of 100 mN min-1, and each test was repeated five times at least. Processing Text: Ti 1.5Ta 0.5NbZrMo 0.5RHEA was prepared by LPBF. Specifically, this study focuses on how the structure of the precipitates and dislocation tangles affects the high-temperature creep resistance and microstructural evolution. The pure metal powder being used are Ti (20∼74 μm, purity: 99.9 %), Nb (20∼74 μm, purity: 99.9 %), Ta (20∼74 μm, purity: 99.9 %), Zr (53∼105 μm, purity: 99.7 %) and Mo (20∼74 μm, purity: 99.9 %), as shown in Fig. 1a. The powders were mixed according to the nominal composition of RHEA and stirred with a planetary ball mill (Pulverisette-4) for 40 h to achieve the purpose of mechanical alloying, as shown in Fig. 1b. Fig. 1c shows the powder morphology obtained after ball milling and it can be found that a large amount of crushed powder has adhered to the intact spherical powder particles. To check the mixing effect, EDS with a working voltage of 20 kV characterized the mixed powder and the results showed that the Ti 1.5Ta 0.5NbZr 0.5Mo RHEA powder had completed the preliminary mechanical alloying, which ensured the compositional homogeneity of the billet samples prepared by the subsequent rapid prototyping ( Fig. 1d). Cylindrical samples (diameter: 5 mm, height: 7.5 mm) were prepared using commercial LPBF equipment (M2 multi-laser) under an Ar atmosphere. The laser power, scanning speed and layer thickness were 240 W, 1700 mm/s and 0.05 mm, respectively. The Ti 1.5Ta 0.5NbZr 0.5Mo RHEA cylinders were prepared using the LPBF technique and the laser scanning strategy is shown in Fig. 1f. The Archimedes density (ρ A) of the as-built sample was measured by an analytical balance with pure ethanol, according to ASTM B962-08standard. The samples for microstructural characterization are mechanically polished using SiC papers up to 2000 grits and then are precision polished with Cr 2O 3. The microstructures were observed using scanning electron microscopy (SEM, TESCAN VEGA 3), energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), with a working voltage of 20 kV. The grain size distribution is investigated via electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) (MIRA 3, TESCAN, Czech Republic). The step sizes of the EBSD maps were 0.25 μm. The obtained EBSD data was analyzed using the channel 5 software. The nanoscale microstructures were characterized by Transmission electron microscope (TEM). The TEM samples were processed by EDM wire cutting, then ground to 50 μm thickness with abrasive paper, thinned to perforation with argon ions and observed by JEM 2100F. High-angle annular dark-field scanning TEM (HAADF-STEM) images were observed using a Talos F200X G2 with an operating voltage of 200 kV and the GATAN Digital Micrograph software was used to measure the crystal plane spacing and to calibrate selected area electron diffraction (SAED) patterns. Tensile Creep tests were carried out according to ASTM E139 and dimensions of the creep specimen are shown in the Fig. S1. The length direction of the creep samples is perpendicular to the building direction. The tensile creep tests were conducted at 923 K, 973 K, and 1023 K in vacuum of 1 × 10 -4Pa controlled by an oil diffusion pump. The tensile creep tests were conducted under stresses of 30, 60, 90, 120 and 150 Mpa, as shown in Table 1. The strain of the material during creep is measured by a resistance-strain high-temperature extensometer (2632 series, Instron). Experimental value; Prepared using LPBF; Error margin ± 14.7 MPa

Processing Text: The Ni 1.5FeCrCu 0.5HEA was fabricated using the vacuum induction melting (VIM) technology, employing high-purity Fe, Ni, Cr, and Cu metals at 99.5 %. The as-cast HEA ingot underwent machining to remove surface layers and was cut using a wire-cut machine into samples with dimensions of 80 × 30 × 50 mm³. Subsequently, the specimens underwent a process of cold rolling to achieve different thickness reductions of 24, 45, 65, and 85 %. A rolling machine, with a load of 20 tons and a roll diameter of 140 mm, was utilized for this process. Following each reduction, samples were strategically cut along the ND-RD cross-section to explore and analyze the intricate microstructure. To investigate the microstructure through the electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) technique, the specimens were polished with 6-, 3-, and 1-μm polishing pads for 3 min after sanding. Following this, the samples were placed on a vibratory machine with oxide polishing suspensions (OPS) for 16 h. Additionally, the central layer of the RD-TD section was mechanically polished to examine the bulk texture. Eventually, specimens for tensile testing were created, having a gauge length of 6.4 mm and a width of 2.5 mm. Deformed samples' phase and texture evolution were comprehensively analyzed with a Philips-XPERT X-ray Diffractometer (XRD) equipped with Cu-Kα radiation (λ = 0.15406 nm). The microstructure of the deformed alloys underwent study using a scanning electron microscopy (SEM) equipped with a high resolution (1244 × 1024 pixels) Oxford electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) Symmetry® S3 detector (CMOS sensor technology) integrated with the AZtecHKL software. Observation of the microstructure of deformed materials at 200 keV was undertaken using a transmission electron microscope (TEM) (JEM-2100F, JEOL, Japan). Using the same electrolyte as for EBSD samples, the TEM samples (about 100 mm thick) were created in a twin jet Tenupol-5 electrolytic polisher at 10 °C with a flow rate of 10, and voltage of 24 V. Micro-hardness tests were carried out under a force of 10 kg for 30 s to determine Vickers hardness. Tensile tests, conducted at room temperature according to ASTM E8Mstandard, utilized a universal uniaxial testing machine (Hounsfield H25KS). Subsequently, SEM was employed to assess the fracture surfaces after tensile tests. Processing state: 85 % cold rolled

Processing Text: The experimental material used in this study was Hastelloy C276 wire with a diameter of 6 mm produced by Nanye Metal products Technology Co., Ltd. (Jiangsu, China). A four-roll mill with a diameter of 70 mm was employed to carry out the cold rolling pre-experiments of three different series of deformations. The samples using 10% single-pass deformation have been conducted 20 passes in total and the final total deformation is 87.8%. The samples using 20% single-pass deformation have been conducted 10 passes in total and the final total deformation is 89.3%. The samples using 40% single-pass deformation have been conducted 4 passes in total and the final total deformation is 87.0%. In the subsequent heat treatment experiments, samples with a total deformation of 49.7%, 71.3%, and 79.9% were selected for strip samples A, B, and C. Hence, twenty sets of heat treatment experiments were performed. The final substrate is prepared by alternating heat treatment and rolling, and the surface of the substrate is mechanically polished using 0.5CR alumina solution and argon ion polished under 3-5 keV for 60 min by IM4000II to obtain the final nanoscale roughness. Processing Text: A Ti-23Nb at.% alloy was prepared by cold crucible levitation melting using 99.99% pure Ti and 99.9% pure Nb. Ingots were homogenized at 1273 K for 120 min followed by water quenching, and hot rolling at approximately 1173 K. The resulting ingot was cut into chips that were cold-rolled to a 60% thickness reduction, achieving a final thickness of approximately 2 mm at room temperature. These sheets were then fully recrystallized at 1123 K for 15 min in a pure Ar atmosphere, followed by water quenching to attain the solution-treated (ST) alloy. Some ST samples were cut into cuboids with cross-sectional dimensions of 10.5 × 2 mm, which were annealed at 573 K for 10 min and then cooled in air and furnace to produce the air-cooled (AC) and furnace-cooled (FC) samples, respectively. The samples with gage dimensions of 3 × 15 × 2 mm 3 for the tensile tests were cut by an electric discharge machine along the rolling direction (RD). Full α″-type ST samples of a Ti-23Nb alloy were annealed at 573 K to induce the α″ → β reverse martensitic transformation and ω precipitation. Thereafter, ω-strengthened β-type Ti-23Nb samples were acquired by slowly cooling the annealed samples via either air cooling (AC samples) or furnace cooling (FC samples). Processing Text: The bulk MoNbTaW RHEA was fabricated by laser energy deposition on the TC4 substrate. Prior to the process, the substrate was washed using alcohol and then dried in a drying furnace at 200 °C for 2 h. The raw powders were blended using a ball mill for 12 h to obtain the mixed powder, which was dried in a furnace at 120 °C for 3 h. The pre-experiments were conducted in order to obtain samples without any macroscopic cracks and holes on the surface. The deposition path has been designed to ensure the flatness of the sample surface and reduce the formation of cracks and holes. The optimized process parameters are as follows: a powder feed rate of 0.2 r min−1, a protecting argon gas flow of 15 L min−1, a laser power of 1200 W, and a scanning speed of 10 mm s−1. The wire-cutting method was utilized to prepare the cuboid samples measuring 12*12*5 mm3 for composition analysis and wear testing and 5*5*2 mm3 for oxidation tests. In addition, cylinder samples with a diameter of 3.6 mm and a height of 5.4 mm were prepared for the compression tests. The oxidation tests were performed with a heat-treatment furnace (KSL-1200×-M) in an air environment. The cuboid samples were ground with sandpaper to remove the oxide layer from their surfaces. Afterward, the processed samples were cleaned with alcohol to eliminate any impurities. To investigate the impact of temperature on oxide behavior, the oxidation tests were conducted using temperature gradients of 500, 650 and 800 °C. Additionally, the weight of the samples was recorded before and after the oxidation test to draw oxidation kinetics curves. The oxide scales collected from the surface on oxidation samples were ground using a circular glass container to obtain a mixed powder of oxidation products. This mixed powder was subsequently sieved to meet the XRD observation requirements. To improve the repeatability of experiments, each experiment was repeated three times to calculate the average value of mass gain. The wear behavior of the MoNbTaW RHEA was investigated through the reciprocating sliding wear tests at 500 and 600 °C. Under specific conditions, the wear tests are conducted using the multifunctional wear tester (UMT-TriboLab). The applied normal load is 4 N, with a wear time of 20 min, a wear frequency of 2 Hz, and a stroke length of 10 mm. The Si3N4 balls with a diameter of 6 mm have been chosen as frictional pairs. The 3D white light profiling system (Bruker Contour GT-K) is utilized to obtain the wear volume and wear coefficient. Additionally, the microstructure and composition of the wear surface are analyzed by SEM. Condition: at 1400 °C; Reported by Senkov et al.
