Processing Text: The wire-cut specimens were extracted from 10H2M steel pipe sections of 1 m long delivered in both, the as-received state and after extensive exploitation for 280,000 h at high temperature equal to 540 °C under the internal pressure of 2.9 MPa, as specified by the power plant maintenance service. The hourglass specimens used for either standard tensile or fatigue tests were wire-cut and machined from the as-received and exploited pipelines made of 10H2M steel. Uniaxial tensile tests were executed to determine material characteristics and typical strength parameters like the yield strength for example under strain rate equal to 2 × 10 −4s −1. Fatigue tests identified another important effect, namely, due to exploitation a significant decrease of the fatigue lifetime was observed for the entire range of stress amplitudes considered. Two sets of selected specimens (as-received and exploited) after fatigue tests at four stress amplitudes (±320 MPa, ±350 MPa, ±370 MPa and ± 400 MPa) were analysed. SEM analysis confirmed, that the long-term exploitation of the 10H2M steel in the power plant working conditions strongly effects its fracture mechanisms, and a consequence, its ability to further safe work. Processing Text: Metallic-glass-crystal composites of Cu47.5Zr47.5Al5 are obtained by flash-annealing of metallic-glass ribbons. Metallic glasses are typically prepared by rapid cooling from the liquid state. Master alloys with the nominal compositions of Cu47.5Zr47.5Al5 were prepared from high-purity elements (> 99.98%) by arc melting under Ar atmosphere (5 N). Glassy ribbons (1.2−1.4 mm wide, 30−35 μm thick) were obtained from the master ingots by using the melt-spinning technique. From these ribbons, ∼5.4 cm long pieces were cut for resistive annealing (an actively heated length was 3 cm) in a device custom-built at IFW Dresden. Cu47.5Zr47.5Al5 MGCCs with the predominant B2 CuZr phase were obtained via single-step annealing at Φ ≈ 1200 ± 100 K s−1. The power was shut immediately when Tx was reached, detected by a resistance drop. About 3 cm long samples were cut out from as-spun MG ribbons for the tensile tests. In situ high-energy XRD measurements during mechanical testing were carried out at the P21.1 beamline, PETRA III synchrotron radiation source at the Deutsches Elektronen-Synchrotron DESY Hamburg. In order to increase the strength of fully-crystalline Cu46.5Zr48Al4Nb1.5 samples while maintaining their ductility, more attention was subsequently paid to the role of the Cu10Zr7 phase. To eliminate the effect of the remaining glassy phase on mechanical properties and to further understand the role of the crystalline phases in the deformation mechanism, two-step annealing in vacuum was carried out with Cu47.5Zr47.5Al5 MG ribbons. The grain size and volume fraction of the Cu10Zr7 phase were controlled by adjusting the annealing time of the second step in which the phase transformation PT1 (Cu10Zr7 → B2 CuZr) and even PT2 (Cu10Zr7 → τ4) occurred. Cu47.5Zr47.5Al5 MG has a wide Φ-processing window for the formation of MG-B2 composites with a minimum Φ of ∼500 K s−1. To fabricate MGCCs containing predominantly the B2 CuZr phase, an optimum Φ of ∼1200 K s−1 was chosen in the present work. The volume fraction of crystalline phases identified by Rietveld-refinement of XRD data is given in Table 2. The measured stress-strain curves (σ-ε) are plotted in Fig. 2(a). The corresponding microstructures of fractured samples of a fully-crystalline sample (Al5C) and two composites (Al5GC#1 and Al5GC#2) are shown in Fig. 2(b-d). The measured mechanical properties are listed in Table 2. The introduction of B2 crystals into the glassy matrix decreased the yield stress σy but improved the ductility conforming to the study of flash-annealed MGCCs of Cu47.5Zr47.5Al5 MG ribbons. The higher strength of the MGCC in the present study can be explained by the significantly smaller diameter of B2 CuZr crystals, i.e., ∼10 µm on average. In situ XRD measurements of Cu47.5Zr47.5Al5 MGCC (sample Al5GC#1) carried out in the present study showed that tensile deformation was accompanied by a remarkable martensitic transformation (MT, B2 CuZr ↔ B19′/B33 CuZr) initiated upon yielding. Fig. 4 shows cycled tensile loading/unloading experiments of Cu47.5Zr47.5Al5 MGCC (sample Al5GC#2). The stress required for the MT onset showed an apparent decrease from 969 ± 20 to 514 ± 20 MPa between the 1st and 4th cycles. The volume fraction of the remained B19′/B33 martensite increased from ∼0% in the 1st cycle to ∼14% in the 4th cycle (∼41% remaining) after unloading. Processing Text: The SAF2507 duplex stainless steel with the heterogeneous structure is produced through cold rolling (ε = 90%) and subsequent 1-min normalizing at 1273 K. The original material with a thickness of 11 mm was normalized at 1523 K for 2 h to obtain the homogeneous coarse grains (CG) structure, refer as the CG sample. Then, the normalized steel plate was cold rolled (CR) with a thickness reduction of 90%, refer as the CR90% sample. The cold rolled plate was cut into the dimensions of 150 mm × 10 mm × 1.1 mm (length × width × height) using the wire-electrode cutting, and the small plates were sealed using a vacuum sealing machine (MRVS-3002, Partulab, Wuhan, China). Subsequently, in order to ensure that only partial recrystallization of the grains of the samples occurred, vacuum-sealed samples were placed as soon as the furnace temperature reached 1273 K and held for 1 min When the time was up, the samples were quickly removed and air cooled, refer as 90%-1273 sample. Dog-bone-shaped tensile samples with a gauge length of 49 mm, width of 9 mm, and thickness of 1.1 mm were cut from the steel plates with the longitudinal axes parallel to the rolling direction. Uniaxial tensile test and loading-unloading-reloading (LUR) experiment were performed at room temperature using a SHIMADZU-100kN Universal Tester (Shimadzu Corporation, Tokyo, Japan) with a quasi-static strain rate of 6.6 × 10 −4s −1, and used a dual camera non-contact extensometer as a strain gauge for mechanical property testing. The X-ray diffraction (XRD, Empyrean, Malvern Panalytical, Holland) with Cu Kα radiation, scan rate: 1°/min, step size: 0.02°, and 2θ angle ranging from 40° to 100° was carried out to confirm the fraction of constituent phases and determine the dislocation densities of the specimens. The microstructures in the RD-TD plane were observed using a field emission scanning electron microscope (FE-SEM, NOVA Nano SEM 450, FEI company, Hillsboro, OR, America) equipped with the electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, NordlysMax2 detector, Oxford Instrument, Abingdon, UK) and the X-ray energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS, X-MaxN50 electrically cooled, Oxford Instrument, Abingdon, UK) plugin. The EBSD tests selected step sizes of 2 μm, 0.2 μm, and 0.1 μm corresponding to CG, CR90%, and 90-1237K samples, respectively. The substructures of the steel samples were analyzed using a transmission electron microscope (TEM, FEI-Tecnai-F30, FEI company, Hillsboro, OR, USA) operated at 300 kV with selected area electron diffraction (SAED) and the EDS plugin. Processing Text: The experimental material is 3.6 % copper-containing austenitic antibacterial stainless steel. The electrolyte was 10 ml 70% perchloric acid and 90 ml anhydrous ethanol. In order to eliminate the residual stress on the surface of the sample and obtain high-precision calibration. The sample was cut into a thickness of 0.3 mm by wire cutting, and then ground to a thin sheet with a thickness of 30-50 μm by 2000# sandpaper. The thin sheet sample was punched into a circle of Ф3 mm, and the RL-2 electrolytic double spray thinning instrument was used for thinning. Processing Text: The width of the fusion region in bimetallic SS/IN parts joined using LPBF was reported to be 100-200 μm. Both additively manufactured SS and Inconel formed columnar grains in the z-direction because of the thermal gradient induced by the building process. However, stainless steel formed wider and more equiaxed grains compared to the finer Inconel grains due to the difference in thermal expansion between the two alloys. One of the first studies on dissimilar joining of SS/IN via LPBF was presented by Mei et al., in 2019, where the authors printed a 316SS/IN718/316SS sandwich structure and reported the presence of microcracks on both interfaces, specifically on the stainless-steel segment of each interface. This crack formation is likely caused by the residual thermal stresses at the interfaces. Notably, microcracks were more dominant at the IN718/316SS interface, while lack-of-fusion pores were more dominant at the 316SS/IN718 interface. A similar observation was made by Wits et al. in graded IN718/316L builds, where cracking occurred in the Fe-rich regions. Axial force applied parallel to interfaces

Processing Text: The IN718 components were fabricated using SLM Solutions 280HL machine, Germany. The powders were spread on the platform and melted layer by layer to generate the cylindrical specimens of dimensions 13 mm diameter and 80 mm length. An argon atmosphere was maintained in the chamber throughout the process to avoid oxidation during SLM process. A hatch style rotation of 67° was employed between the layers. The parameters utilized for SLM process like laser power of 200 W, scan speed of 1200 mm/s, hatch spacing of 90 μm and layer thickness of 30 μm. To maintain proper heat dissipation during the printing process a support structure were maintained for the samples with the same material and the supports were removed from the platform using wire cut electric discharge machine, once the printing process completed. The cylindrical specimens generated by SLM were friction welded by continuous drive KUKA friction welding (FW) machine. A facing operation was performed for the faying surfaces to remove any contaminations or oxides if present. The parameters employed for FW process such as, heating pressure of 50 bar, upset pressure of 60 bar, heating time of 6 s, upset time of 3 s and a rotary speed of 1125 rpm. An infrared thermographic (IR) camera (FLIR-make) was used to measure the temperature distribution at the interface during FW. Two cylindrical rods were considered whereas one was at stationery position and other was rotated with constant rpm during FW. The workpieces generate the frictional force in between the faying surfaces and an upset force was applied to forms the welds. The SLM samples after FW were examined for the microstructural characterization. The cross section of samples was grounded and polished with standard metallography practices to obtain scratch free surfaces. After etching with an etchant of HCl -10 ml and H 2O 2-3 ml for 10 s, the microstructures were observed under Olympus BX51 optical microscope (OM) and for higher magnification, scanning electron microscope (SEM) of Zeiss EVO MA 15 was used. The X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis was performed using Rigaku ultima IV with Cu-Kα radiation of wavelength 0.1542 nm. The step size of 0.02° was used during diffraction analysis at an angle ranging from 40° to 100°. For micro-texture analysis, a FEI TMQuanta 3D-SEM with TSL-EDX TMEBSD (electron back scatter diffraction) system was utilized. OIM Analysis TM(version 8.1) post processing software was used to analyse EBSD data. The Vickers microhardness tests were carried out with 500 g load and a dwell time of 10 s using Buehler Micromet indenter. The measurements were performed along the cross section of the specimen to cover all the zones present in the specimen. Room temperature tensile tests were conducted using Instron 8516 with a strain rate of 10 -4s -1for the as-built SLM and welded samples. The strain hardening behaviour was analysed using Kocks-Mecking plots from the tensile tests data and fracture analysis was performed on the tensile samples to evaluate the fractography features. The strength contribution from the various strengthening mechanisms were calculated for both the SLM as built and weld conditions of IN718 components. Reference baseline

Processing Text: The mixture of element powders of Co, Cr, Ni and nano-TiC powders was used to alloy the CoCrNi-TiC composite in-situ by LPBF. To begin with, the mixed powders were tumble blended for 4h, and ball milled for 4h at a powder ratio of 4:1 at 300 rpm. Then, the obtained powders were alloyed in-situ by LPBF on the BLT s200 laser printing machine with a laser wavelength of 1070 nm and a laser spot diameter of 80 μm. The hatch space was set to 80 μm, and the scan direction rotated 67° between each building layer. The strip scanning strategy with a strip width of 10 mm was adopted to minimize the thermal stress within the sample during preparation. According to the nominal composition of CoCrNi-4wt%TiC, the nano-TiC particles with an average diameter of 40 nm and spherical elemental powders of Co, Cr, Ni with an average diameter of around 40 μm were mixed. The laser scanning strategy that combines high scanning speed and high laser power can effectively disperse the agglomeration of the nano-TiC particles. Also, the high times taken by remelting in each building layers facilitates the in-situ alloying of the blended elemental powders containing high melting point Cr powders. This high depression force applied during the keyhole mode melting leads to the heterogeneous distribution of nano-carbides with a higher number density and a smaller particle size at the bottom of the melting pool. The addition of high fraction nano-TiC particles significantly improves the strength of the composite to 1886 MPa at 77K, 1456 MPa at 298K, 528 MPa at 1073K, 300 MPa at 1173K, respectively. Meanwhile, plasticity is maintained at a reasonable level. Test temperature: 77 K; Strengthening mechanisms include lattice friction, second-phase, grain-boundary, and dislocation strengthening

Processing Text: The Ti4Al3 MEA was fabricated in an arc-melting furnace (Shenyang Jinyan New Material Preparation Technology Co., Ltd). The starting elemental materials, at least 99.95 weight percent (wt. %) pure, were supplied by ZhongNuo Advanced Material (Beijing) Technology Co., Ltd. Before the arc melting, the furnace chamber was purified by melting high purity Ti. The melting of MEA ingots was repeated for five times to ensure the homogeneity of alloying elements. After the melting, the melt alloy was cast into a copper mold (50 mm × 20 mm × 5 mm in dimension). The alloy ingots were first homogenized at 1150 °C for 3 h in vacuum (less than 0.005 MPa), then water-quenched to room temperature, and finally cold rolled. The cold rolling was performed with the reduction in thickness per pass below 0.2 mm and a total reduction in thickness of 70 %. The HP heat-treatment was carried out in a CS-IB type cubic-anvil apparatus (Guilin Guiye Machinery Co., Ltd.). A specimen (20 mm in diameter and 1.5 mm in thickness) was compressed to a HP of 4 GPa by six orthogonal pistons. Under a HP of 4 GPa, the specimen was first heated to 1150 °C, held for 10 min for recrystallization, then cooled to 600 °C and remained at 600 °C for 60 min for aging, and finally water-cooled to room temperature to achieve the HP-treated specimen (named HP MEA). For comparison, the specimens were also synthesized using the above recrystallization-ageing treatments at atmospheric pressure (named AP MEA). As-processed (AP) condition

Processing Text: The Inconel 718 powders used in LDED. (a) Typical SEM micrograph, (b) particle size distribution. The Inconel 718 powders utilized in this investigation were fabricated using the plasma rotating electrode process (PREP). Table 1 shows the chemical composition (wt.%) distribution of these powders. The microscopic morphology and particle size distribution of the raw Inconel 718 powders were illustrated in Fig. 1(a) and (b). The average dimension of these powders was 82.637 μm, with Dv(10) = 52.994 μm, Dv(50) = 90.261 μm, and Dv(90) = 146.319 μm. Before LDED, the powders were desiccated in a vacuum drying oven at a preset temperature of 120 °C for 4 h and then cooled to room temperature in a vacuum. LDED processing was performed on a laser deposition system developed by Nanjing-Rui Optoelectronics Technology Co., Ltd. The system mainly combines a fiber laser (DF6000-60), a 6-axis robot (STAUBLI RX160), a laser water cooler (MCWL-200DTR), a powder feeder (HR-spfh-dt1h06), and a vacuum environment bin. The Ar gas of 99.99 % purity was used as a protective and powder feed gas during LDED. Meanwhile, the entire LDED process was conducted within an Ar-filled environmental chamber with a water and oxygen level under 50 ppm to eliminate oxidation. The TSH facility is a far-infrared graphite microcrystalline heating platform mainly composed of graphite microcrystalline panels and an induction heating coil. It can realize excellent heat transfer with the substrate and display the temperature of the substrate in real time on the LCD screen. Before LDED processing, the substrate was first placed on the heating platform, then heated to the preset temperature, and finally, LDED was performed. For accuracy, the temperature of the heating substrate was additionally assessed by an infrared temperature measurement instrument to verify that the predetermined temperature was achieved. Notably, the heating platform was continuously operated during LDED and kept the preset temperature constant. The optimized parameters used in LDED processing are illustrated in Table 2. Fig. 2(a) presents the schematic diagram of the TSH coupled with LDED, where the laser scanning paths of two neighboring deposited layers were perpendicular to each other for releasing RS. The LDEDed Inconel 718 alloy with the substrate at room temperature (RT), heating 100 °C, heating 200 °C, and heating 300 °C were named T RT specimens, T 100 specimens, T 200 specimens, and T 300 specimens, respectively. Meanwhile, to investigate the effects on the microstructures and mechanical properties of LDEDed Inconel 718 alloy in different building directions, the specimens perpendicular to the building direction and parallel to the building direction were named the 0° specimen and the 90° specimen, respectively. Firstly, original block specimens with a size of 35 mm × 35 mm × 30 mm (height) were fabricated by LDED at different TSH temperatures. Then, these original specimens were cut to avoid the influence of possible metallurgical defects (porosity, inclusions, etc.) in the peripheral regions, and only the centermost portion of 30 mm × 30 mm × 25 mm (height) was retained. The sampling positions of the block specimens for microstructure observations, microhardness tests, and residual stress tests are illustrated in Fig. 2(b). All test surfaces (10 mm × 10 mm red-marked surfaces in Fig. 2(b)) were abraded with 180 # - 3000 # SiC sandpapers and polished with diamond spray polish (1.5 μm). Subsequently, these polished surfaces were etched with aqua regia (HCl: HNO 3= 3:1, vol) for 15-20 s, immediately rinsing with anhydrous ethanol and air-dried in moving air. Microstructure observation was first performed using an OLYMPUS-GX71 optical microscope (OM) and a JSM-7800F scanning electron microscope (SEM). Then, the grain size, orientation, and boundary distribution were analyzed using a ZEISS-G300 type electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD). Eventually, a focused ion beam (FIB) prepared FIB flakes for further microstructure observation at the nanoscale in a JEOL 2100 PLUS type transmission electron microscope (TEM). Moreover, the primary dendrite arm spacing (PDAS) values of the typical OM images in the specimens were quantitatively analyzed using Image-J software. All the tested surfaces in the specimens were polished and sanded identically before the microhardness test. The microhardness was performed using an FM-ARS900 Vickers hardness tester with a spacing of 0.5 mm and a load of 100 gf for 15 s. The average of 10 measurements was taken as the definitive microhardness figure to ensure accuracy and rationality. Before the RS test, all the test surfaces were polished using a Leica EM RES102 argon ion polisher to avoid the introduction of excessive mechanical stress. The RS tests were performed on an X-350A X-ray residual stress tester. The fixed ψ method with angles of 0°, 25°, 35°, and 45° was used for residual stress measurements. The cross-correlation method determined the peaks, and the 2θ angle scanning step was set to 0.10° and the counting time to 0.50 s. The high voltage of the X-ray tube was 22.0 kV, the current was 6.0 mA, the collimator diameter was 2 mm, and the stress constant was constant at −601 MPa/°. The measurements were taken at 50 μm intervals on the surface of the specimen, and a total of four points were taken to obtain the residual stresses on the surface of the specimen. The three-dimensional dimensions of the tensile specimen are shown in Fig. 1(c). The tensile tests were performed on a Germany-DOLI-DDL200 tensile testing machine with a 0.5 mm/min tensile loading rate at room temperature. After the tensile experiments, the failed specimens were immediately examined with an SEM to get the fracture morphology without pollution. Specimen orientation: 90°; Condition: T RT (Room Temperature)

Processing Text: The steel bars were austenitized at about 900 °C for 1 h, quenched in water, and tempered between 650 °C and 700 °C to the desired strength for 2 h. Two kinds of specimens were produced utilizing different heat treatment routes. The first type of specimens was subjected to the conventional quenching and tempering procedure, described above, and these samples are denoted as SQT (single quenched and tempered). SQT samples were further exposed to a replicated tempering step, similar to the first one. In this way, a second type of specimens designated as DQT (double quenched and tempered) was obtained. After heat treatment, decarburized layers were removed in order to machine the specimens for hydrogen-related experiments. Processing Text: The Cu-18Ni-17Zn alloy ingot, with a thickness of 20 mm and a width of 300 mm, has been manufactured by horizontal continuous casting. The as-cast billet was cold rolled into a plate with a 50 % reduction. The rolled plate was then heat treated at 800 °C for 2 h and water quenched at room temperature. This step was followed by cold-rolling to a thickness of 2 mm. Finally, the cold-rolled samples were found to have a rolling strain (η) of 0.8. The formula for the rolling strain is presented in eq. (1): (1)η= (h0-h)/h0 where h represents the uniform thickness of the plate cross-section after rolling, and h0 is the initial uniform thickness of the plate cross-section. The cold-rolled samples were subjected to annealing treatments at temperatures ranging from 350 °C to 900 °C for various durations. Furthermore, Vickers hardness measurements were performed with a 200HVS-5 hardness tester, with an applied load of 1 kg for 15 s. The tensile tests were conducted at a strain rate of 10−3s−1 using a universal tensile testing machine at room temperature. In the EBSD analyses, the specimens were firstly ground with waterproof emery papers up to a grit of #5000. They were then ion milled using an ion mill at an accelerating voltage of 3 kV and a gun angle of 7°. The EBSD measurements were performed by scanning electron microscopy (SEM; Zeiss ΣIGMA); the microscope was equipped with an EBSD system. The applied voltage was fixed at 20 kV, and a nominal beam current value of 6.4 nA was used. The working distance, tilt angle, binning level, and step size were 15 mm, 70°, 4 × 4, and 0.5 μm, respectively. Furthermore, the samples were characterized by XRD with an X'pert X-ray diffractometer and Cu-Kα radiation. The scanning range and step size were 35°-100° and 0.02°, respectively. Processing Text: The original alloy ingots with nominal compositions of Mg-5Zn-6Cu were fabricated in an electric-resistant furnace under an argon atmosphere by melting high-purity Mg, Zn, and Cu at 750 °C. The melt was purified by bubbling argon gas, with a controlled gas flow to ensure the integrity of the melt surface. Subsequently, the molten metal was maintained at 750 °C for 20 min before removing any slag. The melts were then cast into a preheated mold at 200 °C. The resulting cast alloys had a diameter of 42 mm and a height of 150 mm. Their chemical compositions were measured using an inductively coupled plasma analyzer. For the metal fluidity test, another part of the Mg-5Zn-Cu melts was cast into a preheated spiral test mold. The size of the spiral test mold was 224 × 224 × 130 mm 3, and it included spiral grooves with a width of 10 mm and a depth of 5 mm. Processing Text: The Ti6Al4V scaffold was fabricated using laser-based powder bed fusion (PBF-LB), then immersed in molten Zn while utilizing an oxide film to prevent merging of the two materials. The pre-alloyed Ti6Al4V powder particles utilized in creating the Ti6Al4V scaffold were spherical powders produced through the gas atomizing method (D10=23.0μm, D50=36.2μm, D90=55.0μm, Avimetal Powder Metallurgy Technology Co., Ltd, China). Argon gas was employed to maintain an inert protective atmosphere during the PBF-LB manufacturing process ( Fig. 1a). A PBF-LB additive manufacturing machine was used to manufacture the specimens (S210, Xi’an Bright Laser Technologies Co., Ltd.). The parameters for laser power, scanning spacing, scanning speed, and layer thickness were set to 180 W, 60 μm, 800 mm/s, and 20 μm, respectively. This set of parameters is selected to achieve optimal density and mechanical properties. The open-cell rhombic dodecahedron structure was selected for processing, with a design porosity of 80 %. The PBF-LB-processed Ti6Al4V scaffold was immersed in a chemical solution with a fixed ratio ( Fig. 1b), containing nitric acid (HNO 3), hydrofluoric acid (HF), and deionized water in a volume ratio of 40:10:50. The initial concentrations were 4 mol/L for HNO 3and 22.5 mol/L for HF (Yantai Shuangshuang Chemical Co., Ltd., China). The chemical polishing solution was placed in a water bath and kept at 20°C with a magnetic rotor at 150 r/min. The chemical polishing process lasted 2 minutes. Subsequently, the polished Ti6Al4V scaffold underwent ultrasonication in ethanol for 15 minutes, followed by drying and weighing [66]. A Zn block was heated to 700°C in a graphite crucible, while a Ti6Al4V scaffold was preheated in a 700°C air environment for 30 minutes. 0.1 g of NH 4Cl is applied to the surface of molten Zn, followed by placing the Ti6Al4V scaffold and adding heavy objects on top to prevent floating ( Fig. 1c). The depth of molten Zn exceeds the height of the Ti6Al4V scaffold to ensure complete filling of Zn. Subsequently, the crucible was cooled in the air, and once the Zn solidified, the heavy object was removed. Water cooling aided in removing the IPCs from the crucible without miscible of Zn and Ti6Al4V. Sandpapers were used to smooth the surface, remove excess Zn on the surface, and expose the Ti6Al4V scaffold. Samples were encapsulated in epoxy resin, leaving only 1 cm 2of area exposed to the SBF solution [68]. Compression test

Processing Text: ARB process combined with subsequent low-temperature annealing was utilized to produce the HM/NLS in pure Cu. Firstly, fully annealed (annealing at 450 °C for 2 h) and 98% cold-rolled pure copper sheets with different initial thicknesses were used as the original materials for this work. To obtain CRed-Cu/FAed-Cu laminated composites with different layer thickness ratios, we fixed the initial FAed-Cu sheet thickness and changed the CRed-Cu sheet thickness. To promote bonding, both of the CRed-Cu and FAed-Cu sheets were ultrasonically cleaned in acetone bath. Then the CRed-Cu and FAed-Cu sheets were stacked in a sandwich-like structure with an order of FAed-Cu/CRed-Cu/FAed-Cu and roll-bonded at room temperature using 2-high rolling mill (Φ 200 × 300 mm) with a nominal thickness reduction of 50%. Subsequently, the roll-bonded tri-layer structural FAed-Cu/CRed-Cu/FAed-Cu sheet was cut in half along the rolling direction (RD). Thereafter, a repeating sequence of cleaning, stacking, roll bonding and halving was performed. Through repeating the above process to 6 cycles, FAed-Cu/CRed-Cu laminated composite sheets with average layer thickness h = 20 μm can be fabricated. The ARB processed FAed-Cu/CRed-Cu laminated composites were annealed at 200 °C for 30 min under vacuum protection and water quenched to finally obtain the HM/NLS. Through using aforementioned fabricate process, a series of HM/NLSed Cu samples with different layer thickness ratios (corresponding to different volume fraction of coarse/fine grains) can be obtained by changing the initial thicknesses ratio of the CRed-Cu sheet to the FAed-Cu sheet. Processing Text: Gas-atomized CM247LC powder (LPW Technology Ltd., Britain) was used for the LPBF process. An LPBF machine with an IPG-YLR-500 fiber laser and a Gaussian spot size of approximately 80 μm (DiMetal-100H, South China University of Technology, China) was used to manufacture CM247LC samples. The laser linear energy density El and volumetric energy density Ev was determined by: (1)El=Pv(2)Ev=Pvht where P is the laser power (W), v is the scan speed (mm/s), h is the hatch spacing (mm), and t is the layer thickness (mm). Different linear energy density values of remelting Er (i.e., 0.1 J/mm, 0.2 J/mm, 0.3 J/mm) and remelting scan strategies (i.e., parallel remelting PR, and orthogonal remelting OR) were used in the LPBF process. In the PR scan strategy, the rotation of 0° was applied between the prior melting and remelting, while the rotation of 90° was applied in OR. To remelt the layer sufficiently and eliminate lack-of-fusion pores, the hatch spacing of remelting (40 μm) was half of the prior melting (80 μm). A scan strategy with 90° rotation between layers was adopted in the prior melting. The laser remelting strategy was employed to each printed layer for manufacturing the CM247LC alloy via LPBF. The effects of laser remelting parameters on the microstructure, cracking behavior and mechanical properties of the LPBF-processed CM247LC alloy were systematically investigated. The impact of the energy density and scan strategies of remelting on the crack behavior and the underlying crack inhibition mechanisms of laser remelting were discussed. Based on the effects of laser remelting on the cracking behavior of LPBF-processed CM247LC samples, optimized-remelting parameters (P= 100 W, v= 1000 mm/s, h= 40 μm, remelting scan strategy = OR) were obtained. The LPBF-processed CM247LC samples with enhanced strength-ductility (ultimate tensile strength of 1280 MPa, yield strength of 885 MPa and elongation of 11.9%) were obtained by optimized-remelting parameters. Processing Text: Subsequent heat treatment was performed to adjust the microstructure and mechanical properties. The results show that the heat treatment caused the precipitation of nanoscale carbide within the martensite, which significantly increased the yield strength from 792 MPa to 1078 MPa. The Fe-5Mn HT sample exhibits equiaxed martensite grains with a similar average grain size of about 1.6 μm. The Fe-5Mn HT sample exhibits the presence of nanoparticles within the α′-martensite grains, as confirmed by the selected area electron diffraction (SAED) plot, indicating their precipitation from within the α′-martensite. The orientation relationship between these nanoparticles and the matrix is consistent with ε-carbides commonly found in α′-martensite, following a Jack orientation expressed as α′[011]//ε-carbide [1100]. Heat treatment induces the precipitation of ε-carbide particles within α′-martensite. This is attributed to the uniform distribution of C atoms within the grains at elevated temperatures. The rapid transformation of austenite to martensite during water quenching prevents C atoms from diffusing back to austenite, causing them to be trapped within the martensite structure. During tempering, C atoms precipitate out of the martensitic lattice as carbides, which reduces the distortion level of the martensitic lattice and enhances its stability. As a result, the Fe-5Mn HT sample exhibits the presence of nano-sized carbide particles within the martensite structure. Processing Text: The experimental material consisted of 316L austenitic stainless steel rods with a diameter of 30 mm. The material was hot-rolled to 4 mm in thickness, followed by solution treatment at 1050 °C for 1 h. Before each rolling pass, the initial material was immersed in liquid nitrogen for 10 min. The thickness reduction per pass was kept below 5 %. Surface cracks developed when the total thickness reduction reached 70 %. Consequently, the final thickness was reduced by 70 %, resulting in a thickness of 1.2 mm for the cryo-rolled sample, which was labeled as CryoR sample. After cryo-rolling, the samples were subjected to annealing at 700 °C 20 min, 750 °C 6 min, and a sequential 700 °C 20 min + 750 °C 6 min process, followed by water quenching. These samples were labeled as 700A, 750A, and 700A-750A, respectively. All heat treatment processes were performed in a muffle furnace without a protective atmosphere. Tensile tests were conducted using a universal testing machine (5105, SSANS-CMT) at room temperature (24 °C) and liquid nitrogen temperature (−196 °C) with a strain rate of 10 −3s −1. All tensile samples were cut along the rolling direction into dog-bone shapes with a gauge length of 34 mm, width of 10 mm, and thickness of 1 mm. Each test was repeated at least three times to ensure accuracy. To evaluate inhomogeneous deformation, load-unload-reload (LUR) tests were also performed under the same conditions as the tensile tests to quantify the back stress (σ B) component. The microstructural evolution of the samples along the rolling direction (RD) was characterized. XRD analysis was conducted to examine phase transformation with a diffraction angle range of 40°-100° and a scanning speed of 2°/min, using Cu-Kα radiation at 40 kV and 150 mA. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, Oxford) was employed for quantitative analysis of the phase microstructure. After mechanical polishing, samples were electropolished using a 10 % perchloric acid solution at 20 V for 20-25 s. EBSD measurements were performed on a Zeiss Auriga scanning electron microscope with a step size of 100 nm at an accelerating voltage of 15 kV. Processing Text: The heavy warm rolling promoted the transformation of metastable austenite (∼12.2 vol%) into hard domain α’ martensite. After 600 °C re-annealing, the hard domain α’ re-reversed to α + γ. The austenite content of WRA (71.9 %) significantly increased compared to WR. It was deduced that the hard domain α’ martensite was re-reversed into α + γ, and the heterogeneous microstructure disappeared during re-annealing. It was found that the austenite content (48.0 %) in WRT decreased slightly compared to WR, which was attributed to the decomposition of a small amount of metastable austenite into cementite and ferrite during tempering. In addition, the low temperature tempering further promoted C enrichment of soft domain γ without the re-reversion of α’ martensite (400 °C below Ae1 temperature point), thus further improving the thermal stability of soft domain γ while maintaining the heterogeneous microstructure. The microstructures of WR, WRA and WRT were characterized by the EBSD band slope (BS) images superposed by the inverse polar figure (IPF) maps of austenite. Austenite was represented by the color region. For WRA, the durable high-temperature re-annealing promoted the re-reversion of the hard domain α’ martensite into newly nucleated γ L, while the pre-existing γ Lin WR recrystallized and grew into globular grains (γ G) with random crystallographic orientations, the austenite size was also coarsened (0.45 → 0.57 μm). Processing Text: The NiCoCr multi principal element alloy (MPEA) was prepared by thermal-mechanical processing. Processing Text: The powder feedstock for L-PBF was supplied by the Volgograd-Russia Aluminum Plant (UC RUSAL) with the following particle size distribution: d 10= 17.3 μm, d 50= 26.7 μm, and d 90= 40.75 μm using the molten metal spraying method. Cylindrical bars having a diameter of 20 mm and a length of 100 mm were manufactured with the building direction (BD) parallel to the bar's length under a controlled Ar atmosphere. A commercial SLM280HL printer (Selective Laser Melting Solutions Group AG, Lübeck, Germany), was used to make samples, operating with the following parameters: a scan speed of 1650 mm/s, a power of 370 W, a hatch spacing of 130 µm, layer thickness of 50 µm and a scanning rotation of 67° between consecutive layers. These parameters yielded a laser energy density of 1.72 J/mm 2, leading to a porosity fraction lower than 0.18 %. Annealing in the temperature range of 20 °C to 500 °C for one hour led to evolutions in the as-built L-PBF cellular structure, including partial fragmentation of the cell boundaries between 20 °C and 300 °C; the breakdown and transformation into ultrafine Si-enriched particles in the range of 300 °C to 400 °C; and subsequently coarsening at temperatures exceeding 400 °C. Uniaxial tensile tests were conducted at room temperature at an initial strain rate of 1 × 10 −3s −1using miniature bone-shaped samples (4 mm in length, 1.3 mm in width, 2 mm in thickness and 1 mm radius (R)) oriented parallel to the BD. The samples for the mechanical testing were fabricated from the as-built bars using electrode discharge machining, which resulted in uniformly smooth surfaces. Vickers microhardness using a square-based pyramidal diamond indenter were carried out for the as-built and annealed samples. A constant load of 1.8 N and a dwell time of 15 s were used. In situ high-energy synchrotron X-ray diffraction (HEXRD) analysis was carried out during isothermal annealing heat treatments at 400 °C and 500 °C with a holding time of one hour each using cylindrical samples of 5 mm diameter and 8 mm length. To mitigate the impact of sample size on strain calculation, the so-called digital image correlation (DIC) method was used. The DIC system was implemented on a universal tensile machine employing a 12-megapixel digital camera operating at 32 frames per second with an acquisition time of 2 s and a pixel size of 0.04 mm. The acquired data was subsequently processed in Matlab, utilizing the open source software Ncorr. To ensure more reliable results, all tensile samples were tested in the weakest direction, i.e., the tensile loading direction parallel to the BD. In order to establish a correlation between synchrotron measurements and the microstructure and mechanical properties at various temperatures, a series of samples from the as-built material were subjected to annealing treatments with a holding time of one hour at temperatures of 200 °C, 300 °C, 400 °C, and 500 °C. Subsequently, these samples were evaluated using EBSD, hardness, and tensile testing. Condition: After one ECAP pass at room temperature; Additional context: Superficial cracks following room temperature ECAP processing without prior stress relief HT

Processing Text: Al 0·25FeCoNiV HEA was prepared as shown in Fig. 2(a). First, raw material particles with a purity greater than 99.9 % were used to prepare blocks in a vacuum induction levitation furnace. The melting and casting processes were protected by an argon atmosphere throughout, and the chemical homogeneity of the material was ensured by five repeated melting cycles. Subsequently, the flake specimens were treated under argon protection at 1373 K for 10 h to obtain homogenized specimens. Then, using a multi-roll mill at room temperature, the homogenized specimens were cold rolled to different degrees of 30 %, 50 %, 70 %, and 90 %, and represented by CR-30 %, CR-50 %, CR-70 %, and CR-90 %, respectively. Subsequently, the cold-rolled sheets were annealed under vacuum conditions with a holding time of 1.5 h at 1223 K, followed quickly by water quenching to obtain annealed state specimens with different cold rolling ratios (represented by CR30%-A, CR50%-A, CR70%-A, and CR90%-A, respectively). Processing Text: The ingot of the Co 68Al 18.2Fe 6.5V 4.75Cr 2.55alloys were fabricated by arc-melting the mixtures of high-purity constituent elements in a Ti-gettered argon atmosphere and the ingot was remelted at least five times to ensure chemical homogeneity. The samples were ground with SiC abrasive papers with grits of 400, 800, and 1,200, and finally polished with 0.25-μm-diamond suspension. The microstructure and fracture morphology of the as-cast MEA were observed by FEI Quanta 250F scanning electron microscope (SEM) with SE detector. The phase structure and chemical composition of the as-cast MEA were characterized by a FEI Talos F200X transmission electron microscope (TEM) at a voltage of 200 kV with an energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS). Electron back-scattered diffraction (EBSD) measurement was conducted on JEOL-JSM-IT800 instruments equipped with an Oxford Symmetry S2 detector. The scanning step size and the scanning area are 0.16 μm and 60 × 60 μm 2, respectively. The nanoindentation tests with the maximum load of 30 mN was conducted on KLA-Nano indenter G200 machine. Rectangular specimens with dimensions of 2 × 2 × 4 mm 3were cut from the as-cast ingot by electric discharge machine and tested for room-temperature compression and high-temperature compression tests. Room-temperature compression tests were conducted on an Instron 5969 universal testing machine at a strain rate of 2 × 10 −4s −1. Processing Text: This letter successfully used double-wire arc additive manufacturing technology to prepare a new type of Al20.33Co21.60Fe30.45Ni27.62 EHEA. In particular, the double-wire feeding system uses combined cable wire (CCW) as the main welding wire and locates the eutectic point by adjusting the bypass Al wire feeding speed, which greatly improves the flexibility of alloy design. For the first time, this paper adopts D-WAAM technology, using self-designed CCW as the main welding wire and Al wire as the side axis feeding wire to locate the eutectic point and prepare an Al20.33Co21.60Fe30.45Ni27.62 eutectic high entropy alloy with a strength plasticity balance. In this paper, cold metal transfer smart arc additive manufacturing equipment was used to prepare EHEAs. As the main welding wire, CCW is transported vertically by CCW equipment, and the Al welding wire is transported by a side-axis wire feeder. It consists of two Fe wires, two Co wires and three Ni wires. The wire diameters are all 0.6 mm. The wire feeding speed is 7 m/min. The Al wire is a pure Al wire with a diameter of 0.8 mm, and the wire feeding speed is 3.4 m/min. The phase structure of the deposited samples was analyzed using an X-ray diffractometer (XRD). The XRD test voltage was 40 kV, the current was 150 mA, the scanning angle range was 20°-100°, and the scanning speed was 6°/min. A universal testing machine was used to conduct tensile experiments with a tensile rate of 0.6 mm/min. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) were used to observe the microstructure and tensile fracture morphology. Processing Text: Commercially sourced gas-atomized CoCrNi pre-alloy powders were utilized, characterized by spherical geometry. The powders demonstrated a Hall flow rate of 18.8 s/50 g, a loose powder density of 4.31 g/cm³, and a tapped density of 4.80 g/cm³. Particle size analysis revealed a median particle diameter (D₅₀) of 43.4 μm, with a size distribution spanning from D₁₀ = 27.4 μm to D₉₀ = 65.5 μm, and an average particle size of 45.7 μm. Elemental distribution within the CoCrNi pre-alloy powders was found to be uniform. The SLM apparatus was equipped with a three-cylinder forming system and an IPG YLR-AC 1000 W laser, with a laser spot diameter ranging from 90 to 110 μm. A specific scanning strategy was employed, incorporating a 67° rotation angle between successive layers with a thickness of 40 μm to reduce anisotropy. An orthogonal experimental design was applied to systematically adjust the process parameters, namely laser power (p), scanning speed (v), and hatching space (d), set within the ranges of 80–140 W, 300–450 mm/s, and 80–110 μm, respectively. The parameter samples were fabricated with dimensions of 10 × 10 × 4 mm³ (length × width × thickness). The density of these samples was measured using the Archimedes drainage method, with at least three repetitions, and compared to the density of cast counterparts (8.2687 g/cm³). The optimal processing parameters were identified as p = 120 W, v = 350 mm/s, and d = 110 μm, achieving a density of 8.2191 g/cm³ and a relative density of 99.4%. Minimal microporosities were detected through electronic computed tomography (CT) imaging, indicating excellent forming quality. Processing Text: To produce the Al-20%Mg2Si composite, an ingot of A413 aluminum alloy was melted in a graphite crucible located in an electrical resistance furnace, and pure magnesium (99.9%) was immersed by a graphite-coated steel plunger at 750 ± 5 °C. The melt was protected from oxidation and gas absorption by using coverall flux. The melt was held for 10 min at 750 ± 5 °C for homogenization, then poured into a graphite-coated and preheated Y-block steel mold. In another set of experiments, the optimal amount of the Cu-8%P master alloy was added into the melt to investigate the effect of the modification. The specimens were annealed at 490 °C ± 2 for 8 h to eliminate any internal and residual stresses. The specimens were hot rolled at 400 °C for 10%. Deformed specimens were heated to the semi-solid temperature of 570 °C. The specimens were held at the semi-solid temperature for 25, 35, and 45 min, then they were quenched into the water. They were heated to the selected semi-solid temperature for the appropriate time in an electrical resistance furnace and placed in a 500 °C preheated H13 tool steel mold. Subsequently, they were hot pressed into 27% reduction by using a hydraulic press at the conditions of a cross-head speed of 20 cm/s, pressure of 40 tons, and specimens with the dimensions of 3 × 25 × 85 mm 3 were produced. The solutionizing treatment was carried out at 490 °C ± 2 for 4 h in an inert gas atmosphere then, the specimens were quenched into the water, and finally, they were age-hardened at 170 °C ± 1 for 2 h. Processing Text: Al 0.5CoCrFeNb 0.5Ni HEA ingots were prepared from high-purity (≥99.95 wt%) Al, Cr, Co, Fe, Nb, Ni metal particles (from Beijing Ryubon New Material Technology, LTD) by vacuum induction melting in a high-purity (99.9%) argon atmosphere. The ingots were remelted more than five times to achieve homogeneity and then solidified in zirconia crucibles, as explained detailed in the authors' previous studies [ 29]. Square specimens of 32.8 mm (length) × 10 mm (width) × 2 mm (height) and 5 mm × 5 mm x 5 mm were cut from the ingot using wire cutting. The surfaces were ground with SiC sandpaper to 5000 grit and then polished with diamond spray polish, followed by ultrasonically cleansing with ethanol and then drying and storing for characterization and high-temperature friction experiments. Room temperature quasi-static compression test was conducted using a universal testing machine (CMT 5205, US) at a strain rate of 0.1 s −1. According to the ASTM E209-18standard [ 30], a dynamic thermal simulator (Gleeble-3500, US) was used to test in an argon environment with a temperature range of 800-1200 °C (in increments of 100 °C). The strain rate was 0.1 s −1and the strain was 50%. Homogenized for 15 min before deformation to eliminate the thermal gradient of specimens. After cutting along the mid-plane parallel to the compression axis, the internal organization of the section was observed using SEM with equipped electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, Oxford Symmetry, US) to further investigate the microstructural evolution. Processing Text: The Ti-4V-2Mo-2Fe alloy (referred to as TVMF hereafter) was prepared in a vacuum suspension melting furnace utilizing high-purity Ti, V, Mo, and Fe particles as raw materials. Throughout the smelting process, argon gas serves as the protective atmosphere. The ingot undergoes six times of melting to ensure uniform chemical composition. The β phase transition temperature of the TVMF alloy was determined to be approximately 753 ± 3 °C via a differential scanning calorimeter (DSC). Subsequently, the alloy ingot undergoes three forging stages using a four-column hydraulic press, with temperatures maintained at 1000 °C, 950 °C, and 900 °C for 30 min before each forging cycle. Each forging pass induces approximately 40% deformation, and the alloy was air-cooled after the final forging. Next, the alloy was subjected to deformation using a two-high mill at temperatures of 700 °C, 750 °C, 800 °C, 850 °C, and 900 °C, denoted as 700HR, 750HR, 800HR, 850HR, and 900HR for ease of identification. Prior to rolling, the alloys were preheated in a muffle furnace for 30 min. The initial thickness of the alloy was 20 mm, with a pressure of 1 mm applied per pass and a total deformation of approximately 90% after a 3 min hold following each pass. Following the final rolling, the alloy was subjected to a 3 min keep warm and subsequently quenched in water. Processing Text: Ti40Zr25Nb25Ta5Mo5 (at.%) HEA was fabricated from commercially pure (purity ≥99.95 wt.%) nuggets of each element using an arc melting furnace (AM200, Edmund Bühler GmbH, using a Vario hybrid 400-DC-HF generator). The furnace was engineered to incorporate a water-cooled copper crucible equipped with multi-purpose mould cavities. Each ingot was prepared in a batch of 20 g and loaded in a water-cooled copper mould cavity in the order of high melting point metals stacking on top of lower melting point metals to minimize evaporation. After that, the chamber was closed, evacuated to about 5 Pa by a rotary pump, and then flushed with a flow of high-purity argon for 15 min. This process was repeated twice. Then, the chamber was further evacuated to a high vacuum condition (∼10 −4Pa) by a diffusion pump. Finally, the chamber was refilled with high-purity argon for the arc-melting process. CP-Ti nuggets were used as an oxygen getter. The materials were then melted by the arc which was controlled by the generator and an arc-driving arm. Each ingot (20 g) was melted six times and flipped after each melting. During each cycle of melting, the molten alloy was held in the liquid state for 10 min for chemical homogeneity (inverted each time before remelting). Five ingots were then melted together and cast into a water-cooled copper mould to form a cuboidal bar with dimensions of 90 × 12 × 8 mm 3. Finally, specimens were cut from the as-cast alloy bar, ground with SiC abrasive papers and mirror-polished with 0.04 μm colloidal silica suspension (OPS) with 30% H 2O 2(10:1 by volume) for characterisation. Processing Text: The material being studied in this current work is 2024 aluminum alloy in the 413 °C annealed state. To obtain better plasticity and toughness, the 2024 aluminum alloy was heated to 493 °C, held for a certain period, and then quenched in water. The quenched 2024 aluminum alloy was subsequently subjected to natural aging at room temperature for a duration of 12 h. The matrix material was first machined into a round bar sample using wire cutting and mechanically polished, then the microstructure of the polished specimen was characterized by electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD). The aluminum alloy stock was first wire cut to obtain aluminum alloy round bars. Then, mechanical polishing is performed on the round bars to remove surface defects. Next the polished aluminum alloy round bar was turned on a CAK3665 CNC lathe with a maximum spindle speed of 3000 r/min. The tool used for the test was a carbide tool with a tool front angle of 30 °and a tool back angle of 11 °. In order to obtain aluminum alloy specimens with different surface microstructures, the cutting speed vand feed rate fwere selected as the control variables for the turning experiments, with each control variable corresponding to three levels of variation, which could produce nine different sets of test conditions, with the specimens under each set of test conditions numbered C1-C9 in turn. The USRP test was carried out on a CA6140 CNC lathe. A 14 mm diameter WC-Co rolling ball was used to impact the surface of the polished sample. The cylindrical samples after turning and USRP testing were cut transversely using a wire-cut machine, the cut specimen blocks were set in conductive resin molds for metallurgical preparation, the set samples were polished using sandpaper and polished in a colloidal silica suspension, then ion etched using a Gatan precision etching system at 6 kV and 400 μA, and finally data was collected using EBSD to obtain the crystallographic characteristics of the specimens. A thin foil sample of approximately 100 nm thickness was extracted from the surface of the specimen after turning and USRP tests respectively using a plasma focused ion beam (FIB) system to make a transmission electron microscopy (TEM) specimen, and then the prepared sample was observed using a FEI Tecnai G2 F20 high resolution TEM to obtain bright field (BF), high angle annular dark field (HAADF) images and selected area electron diffraction (SAED) in TEM mode to determine the microscopic morphology, particle size and phase structure of the specimen. In order to obtain the mechanical properties of the specimens, monotonic tensile tests were carried out on 2024 aluminum alloy specimens using an MTS Bionix 858 servo-hydraulic system at a constant strain rate of 1.0 mm/min, with the loading direction parallel to the axial direction of the specimen, and the mechanical properties of the specimens were determined from the average of the two measurements. Processing Text: A commercially extruded Mg-Y-Nd-Gd-Zr alloy (∅15 × 100 mm) was utilized as the experimental specimen. The alloy underwent an initial partial solution treatment (450 °C, 2 h) in a resistance furnace (SX-G04133), followed by cooling in hot water at 80 °C (ST). The samples treated with a solid solution after the 1st, 4th, 8th, and 9th rolls are denoted as ST+1P, ST+4P, ST+8P, and ST+9P, respectively. The microstructures of the samples were examined by optical microscopy (OM, Olympus GX51) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Gemini300, Zeiss). The cross-sectional surface of the Mg alloy bar was observed. The microstructural evolution of the samples was analyzed by X-ray diffraction (XRD, D8 Advance), electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, C-nano, Oxford), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM, FEI Talos F200X, 200 kV). The XRD measurement utilized a Cu target as the radiation source, with an incident wavelength of 1.5406 A. The test voltage was set to 40 kV (in increments of 1 kV per step) and the tube current was maintained at 30 mA. The angle range (2θ) for scanning was specified as 20-80°, and the scanning rate was set to 2°/min. For EBSD sample preparation, argon ion polishing was performed on the OM samples at 5, 4, and 3 kV for 45 min with an inclination angle of approximately 4.5°. EBSD observations were conducted using an Oxford C-nano EBSD system (Zeiss) in conjunction with a Gemini300 scanning electron microscope operating at a test voltage of 25 kV. The image resolution was set to 311 × 256 pixels, and the scanning step size was 0.5 mm. The tensile properties and hardness of the samples were evaluated using an MTS Landmark material-testing system (MTS810, 250 KN) and an HVS-1000 digital Vickers microhardness tester. The surface of the ST sample, without undergoing the USRP treatment, has a rough texture with an arithmetic mean deviation (Ra) of 0.65 μm and a micro-roughness 10-point height (Rz) of 6.92 μm. Following the USRP treatment, the surface roughness of the ST+1P sample significantly decreases, with Ra and Rz values measuring 0.17 and 1.44 μm, respectively. The surface smoothness of the ST+4P sample improves as all burrs disappear, resulting in Ra and Rz values of 0.06 and 0.55 μm, respectively. With a further increase in the USRP-induced deformation, surface burrs reappear on the ST+8P sample, exhibiting a rougher texture than that of the ST+4P sample; correspondingly, Ra and Rz increase to 0.24 and 1.87 μm, respectively. However, spalling occurs on the surface of the ST+9P sample, leading to morphological damage; at this stage, the Ra and Rz values of the Mg alloy are approximately 3.29 and 20.59 μm, respectively. The optimal surface roughness of the Mg-Y-Nd-Gd-Zr alloy is achieved after four passes. The depth of the gradient layer increased with each additional USRP pass, ranging from 650 μm (1 pass) to 910 μm (8 passes). The USRP induced the largest plastic deformation at the top surface of the sample, leading to the continuous proliferation of high-density dislocations and stratification, which in turn triggered DRX and ultimately resulted in numerous dislocation-rich and stratified nanocrystals with HAGBs on the top surface. The plastic deformation in the subsurface layer was slightly lower than that in the surface layer, which still consisted of HAGBs nanocrystals wrapped in dislocations; however, their sizes were slightly smaller than those on the surface layer. Owing to the low fault energy of Mg alloys, abundant DTs were observed. As the depth increased, the number of DTs decreased while transitioning into tension twins with a relatively low CRSS. Eventually, a composite gradient structure, characterized by an increasing grain size, decreasing dislocation density, decreasing layer fault density, and decreasing twin density, was formed. The microhardness of the Mg alloy decreased exponentially with increasing depth from the surface treated using the USRP under the same number of rolling passes. Simultaneously, with an increase in the number of passes, a continuous enhancement in the microhardness of the topmost layer was observed, ranging from 106.3 Hv at one pass to 115 Hv at four passes and reaching up to 119.7 Hv at eight passes. After one USRP treatment, the YS of the Mg alloy increased by approximately 34.2%. As the number of USRP treatments increased, a continuous increase in the depth of the gradient layer and gradual consumption of the twin crystals was observed, resulting in an elevated work-hardening rate for the Mg alloy. Simultaneous transitioning from a brittle fracture mechanism to a ductile fracture mechanism resulted in ongoing improvements in the UTS and EL. Untreated ST sample
Processing Word: Untreated ST sample

Processing Text: The concentrations of Al and Ti are systemically adjusted for the propose to obtain high volume fraction of γ′ precipitates, good alumina-forming ability, and in the meantime minimizing the formation of harmful phases. Alloy ingots of 200 g were prepared from the constituent elements (Fe, Ni, Cr, Al, Ti, and so on, purity >99.9 wt%) by arc melting in an Ar atmosphere. The alloy buttons were flipped and remelted more than five times to ensure thoroughly mixing of all elements and then drop cast into a water chilled Cu mold (12.5 × 12.5 × 120 mm 3). The drop cast ingots were homogenized at 1225 °C for 8 h, then quenched in water. The homogenized ingots were cold rolled along the longitudinal direction to a thickness reduction of ∼70%. The cold rolled plates were recrystallized at 1000 °C for 1 h and then aged at 700 °C for 24 h. All the heat treatments were carried out in an argon-protected tube furnace. Dog bone shaped specimens with gauge sections about 3.2 × 2.0 × 12.7 mm 3 were cut from the aged plates by electro-discharge machining (EDM). The surface of the gauge section was mechanically ground by 1200 grits SiC paper to eliminate defects on the surface of the tensile specimen. Tensile tests were conducted in the laboratory atmosphere on a screw-driven mechanical testing machine equipped with an induction heater. Before load applying, the specimens were held at the testing temperature for 15 min to ensure the temperature being stable. All specimens were tested at a strain rate of 10 −3s −1, which corresponds to a displacement rate of 0.75 mm/min. For each alloy at each temperature, at least three specimens were tested to ensure data reproducible. The elongation to fracture (EF) was calculated by measuring the length of the specimen before and after fracture. The yield strength (YS) was obtained by using the 0.2% offset method. Specimens with a dimension of 10.0 × 10.0 × 2.0 mm 3 were cut by EDM and ground to 2000 grit SiC paper before test. Oxidation tests were conducted at 750 °C for 480 h in air. Before and after oxidation, weights of specimens were weighed by using an electronic scale with the accuracy of 10 −4g. The scanning electron microscopy (SEM) samples were ground with 1200 grit SiC paper and then mechanical polished or electropolished. TEM images and selected area electron diffraction (SAED) were captured with a spherical aberration corrected FEI Titan G 2scanning TEM and a FEI Tecnai G 2F20 TEM, both of which were operated at 200 kV and equipped with an annular dark field (ADF) detector and a high angle annular dark field (HAADF) detector. Temperature: 25°C to 650°C

Processing Text: The pure Cu and Cu-Al alloy are prepared by vacuum induction melting using high-purity (4 N) Cu and Al. Processing Text: Round extruded bars of these materials were machined down into billets measuring 70 mm in length and 9.8 mm in diameter. For CuCrZr alloy billets, a solution heat treatment was performed at 1000 °C for 1 h, followed by water quenching. ECAP was performed using an H13 steel die with an angle between channels (Φ) of 120° and an outer curvature angle (Ψ) of 22°, resulting in an equivalent strain of 0.67 in a single pass. The billets were pressed either at room temperature (RT-ECAP) or at a cryogenic temperature of approximately −80 °C (CT-ECAP). All ECAP procedures were carried out using an Instron 5500R testing machine, with an axial speed of 5 mm/min, following the B c route, and up to ten ECAP passes. Prior to pressing at room temperature, the billets were coated with a MoS 2 lubricant to minimize friction. In the case of CT-ECAP, the process was conducted within a cryogenic chamber, as described in [9]. Both billets and die were cooled down to −80 ± 1 °C and left to stabilize at this temperature without the application of any lubricant. A type-T thermocouple was placed near the region of the billet experiencing shear strain. Throughout the process, all samples were kept in liquid nitrogen between consecutive passes and reprocessed only after a short interval. After ECAP, ageing heat treatments were performed in the CuCrZr billets processed by RT- and CT-ECAP at 450 °C during 15 and 120 min, denominated as 450/15 and 450/120, respectively. Processing Text: The materials used in this study were from the same batch, and their chemical composition is provided in Table 1. The materials were prepared in a vacuum induction melting furnace, and heat isostatic pressing (HIP) was employed during the preparation process to reduce casting porosity that may affect tensile properties. Subsequently, a two-stage heat treatment, including solution treatment and aging treatment (1185 °C/2h/argon cooling and 871 °C/20 h/air cooling), was conducted to refine the γ-γ' eutectic structure at grain boundaries and increase the proportion of γ' for further enhancing the material strength. To accurately investigate the effect of SP on the microstructural evolution of the blade surface layer and the tensile fatigue properties, samples were taken from the BM along the blade direction in this study. In this study, the SP treatment was performed using S230 cast steel shots with a diameter of approximately 0.58 mm. The air pressure employed during the treatment was approximately 0.35 MPa, and the mass flow rate of the shot was around 12 kg/min. The coverage rate achieved was 150 %. Type A Almen specimens were used to assess the strength, and the average value of the three arc heights tested was found to be 0.32. SP was independently conducted on the sample plate, the high cycle fatigue specimen, and the tensile specimen. The specific areas subjected to SP treatment on different specimens are depicted in Fig. 1(c). The cutting method used in this study was Electrical Discharge Machining (EDM) wire cutting. For obtaining the micromorphology of the surface layer, the square specimens shown in Fig. 1(c) were mechanically polished using silicon carbide sandpapers with different grit sizes, namely 400 mesh, 1000 mesh, 2000 mesh, and 3000 mesh. After polishing, the specimens were corroded with a mixture of 10 ml HCl,10 ml HNO 3, 0.3 g H2MoO 4, and 15 ml H 2O. Finally, the micro-morphology of the surface deformation layer was observed by SEM (JEOL JSM-6510LV, Japan). For the EBSD analysis, the sample underwent the same milling process as described above. Electrolytic polishing was then performed to remove the residual stress layer generated during the grinding process. The polishing solution comprised 7 % perchloric acid and 93 % ethanol, and the current density was set at 450 mA/cm2 for approximately 1 min. To measure the microhardness on the surface layer of both the BM and the SP, a Vickers microhardness tester (SHIMADZU HMV-G31DT, Japan) was utilized. Prior to testing, the cutting surfaces were ground and polished to eliminate the effects of cutting on hardness measurements. A test load of 0.98 N, a dwell time of 15 s, and a test depth gradient of 50 μm were used. To ensure the accuracy of the test results, each depth was tested three times, and the average value was taken. In order to measure the residual stress after SP treatment, the Hole-drilling method was used, and the measurement standard was ASTM-E837-13A [38]. The SINT MTS3000 Hole-drilling strain gauge was employed to measure the shot peened samples. The distance between each test point was approximately 10 mm to avoid mutual influence between the test points. The BM and SP specimens were subjected to uniaxial tensile tests using a universal testing machine (AG-100KNXPSTDW/0, Japan) at RT besed on the standard of ASTM E8M [39], and the strain rate of both specimens was 2.5 × 10 −4s −1. In addition, high cycle fatigue tests were also carried out using a high-frequency fatigue testing machine (QBG-100, China) for BM and SP at RT (R = −1). Fatigue testing following standard ASTM E466-15 [40]. Specimen: BM (Base Material)

Processing Text: Pre-alloyed AlCo0.4CrFeNi2.7 (atomic percent %) hypoeutectic HEA powders produced via argon-gas atomization were used as raw materials for the L-PBF processes. The particle sizes were measured using a laser particle-size analyzer distributed in the range of 15-53 μm. The BLT-A300 apparatus (Xian, China) equipped with a maximum 500 W fiber laser operating in a continuous wave mode was employed for the L-PBF processes. A Gaussian energy intensity distribution and a focus beam-spot size of 76 μm were used during L-PBF. To reduce thermal stress, the substrate material of 304 stainless steel was preheated to 200 °C before printing. In addition, a 67° interlayer rotational angle was adopted during L-PBF. Based on our previous work [4], the following optimal scanning parameters were used during the L-PBF processes: laser power of 250 W, scanning speed of 800 mm/s, hatch spacing of 80 µm, and layer thickness of 40 µm. A block sample with the dimensions of 60 mm × 50 mm × 5 mm (length × width × height) was fabricated. Subsequently, to further improve the mechanical properties of the alloy, the as-printed sample was annealed at different temperatures (600 ℃, 700 ℃, 750 ℃, 800 ℃, and 1000 ℃) for 1 h in a tube furnace at a heating rate of 10 °C min−1 under an argon protective atmosphere, followed by water quenching. These samples were marked as HT600, HT700, HT750, HT800, and HT1000, respectively. The phase constitutions of the alloy were characterized using X-ray diffraction (XRD, BRUKERD8 Discover) with a Cu Kα radiation. The 2θ scanning was analyzed in the range of 20-100° with a scanning speed of 4°/min. The morphologies and phase constitutions of the alloy were investigated through a Zeiss Supra55 field emission scanning electron microscopy (SEM) equipped with an electron back-scattering diffraction (EBSD) spectrometer. The samples for SEM characterization were prepared using mechanically polished with oxide polishing suspension. The EBSD specimens were prepared by mechanically grinding them using 5000-grit SiC papers and then electrochemically polishing them in a mixture of 90 vol% (volume percent) ethanol and 10 vol% perchloric acid. A direct voltage of 22 V and a current of 1.5 A were used during the electrochemical polishing at room temperature. The scanning step of EBSD was 0.15 μm. The more detailed microstructures were characterized utilizing a transmission electron microscope (TEM, Tecnai F30). Disc-shaped TEM samples with a diameter of 3 mm were mechanically ground to a thickness of 40 μm and then thinned to be electron-transparent using double-jet electron polishing in a solution of 90 vol% ethanol and 10 vol% perchloric acid at a temperature of −25 ℃. The volume fraction and size of precipitates were measured from STEM images using Image J software. The tensile tests were carried out using a CMT4105 universal electronic tensile testing machine with an initial strain rate of 1.0 × 10−3 s−1 at room temperature. Dog-bone-shaped tensile samples were cut by electrical discharge machining and then were mechanically ground to 2000 grit size with lengths of 50 mm and cross sections of 5 mm × 1.5 mm. For each state of the alloy, at least three samples were tested. Before testing, the samples were fixed on a jig, and the strains were examined using an extensometer during tensile tests, with a gauge length of 15 mm. Processing state: as-printed; Microstructure: dual-phase nanolamellae (FCC + BCC)

Processing Text: The alloy ingots with nominal compositions of Ni30Co30Cr20Fe20-xRex (x=0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 9 at.%, denoted as Rex), and Ni30Co30Cr20Fe20-yMoy (y=2, 4, 6, 8, 10 at.%, denoted as Moy) were prepared by arc-melting method in Ti-gettered high-purity argon atmosphere. The purity of each metal is at least 99%. Co-Re and Mo-Fe intermediate alloys were first re-melted four times, then flipped and smelted at least five times with other raw materials to ensure compositional homogeneity. These ingots were drop-cast into a water-cooled copper mold with dimensions of 8 mm × 8 mm × 40 mm. The as-cast bars were homogenized at 1473 K for 12 h. To ensure a single-phase FCC structure, the homogenization temperature of Mo8 and Mo10 HEAs are selected as 1573 K for 12 h. Then all the bars were cold-rolled to a reduction 60% in thickness and annealed at 1473 K for 1 h. All the thermo-mechanical procedures were performed in vacuum and finally quenched with water. Phases identification and lattice parameters for these HEAs were conducted by X-ray diffraction (XRD) with Cu Kα radiation (Smart Lab 9 kV). The shear modulus and Poisson's ratio of the alloy were measured by UMS-100 ultrasonic echo analysis technique. The microstructures of the HEAs were characterized by ZEISS SUPRA 55 scanning electron microscope (SEM) equipped with an electron backscatter diffraction detector (EBSD). The SFE were measured via FEI Tecnai G2 F20 transmission electron microscopy (TEM) by the method of WBDF with a beam direction [111] zone on the (111) defect habit plane using <220>-type g-vectors. The EBSD data was analyzed using an AZtecCrystal data-analysis software. The EBSD samples were prepared by electrolytic polishing using an HClO4:C2H5OH = 1:9 solution with a direct of 20V and 29.5 V at room temperature. The TEM samples with 0.5 mm in thickness were first mechanically ground to a thickness of ∼60 μm using SiC papers. Then the samples were punched into 3-mm-diameter disks and further thinned by a double-jet electropolishing technique in a solution of HClO4:C2H5OH = 1:9 at a temperature of 233 K and an applied voltage of 30 V. The chemical homogeneity of Re8 alloy was examined using local electrode atom-probe tomography (APT) (LEAP 4000X SI) at the temperature of ∼50 K, a pulse frequency of 200 KHz, and a pulsing ultraviolet laser energy of 50 pJ. The sharp tip specimens for APT were made using an FEI Helios nanolab 600i focused ion beam (FIB) system by the lift-out method. The room temperature tensile tests of all HEAs were conducted on a CMT4105 universal electronic tensile testing machine at the strain rate of 10−3s-1. Dog-bone shape tensile specimens with a gauge geometry of 1.5 mm × 5 mm × 15 mm were cut from the sheets in the direction of rolling and polished down to the 2000-grit SiC papers. To study the microstructure evolution, some tests were interrupted at the engineering strain of ∼2%, ∼3% and ∼20%. Condition: room temperature; Comparison: ~127% increase compared to Re0 HEA
Processing Word: Condition: room temperature; Comparison: ~127% increase compared to Re0 HEA

Processing Text: A novel type of Ni-based alloy containing the gadolinium neutron absorption unit and the tungsten gamma ray shielding unit were successfully fabricated. The designed and fabricated Ni-based alloys had excellent hot workability between 1100 °C and 1200 °C. A series of Ni-based alloys with different Gd and W contents were designed and melted in a vacuum induction melting furnace and cast in a copper mould with water cooling. The raw materials for smelting were prepared using high-purity materials, namely pure chromium (99.9 wt%), pure gadolinium (99.9 wt%), pure nickel (99.9 wt%), and NiW (W content = 60 ± 0.1 wt%) alloy. The casting ingots weighing about 1 kg possessed a dimensions of 60 mm × 15 mm × L mm (L: length). The ingots were hot-rolled into thin plates with a thickness of 3 to 4 mm at 1100 to 1200 °C and then annealed at 1150 °C. After that, the partial annealed plates were cold-rolled into sheets with a thickness of about 1.5 mm and then solution treatment was carried out at 1150 °C. The density of all the prepared specimens was determined though the Standard Archimedes method. Tensile tests at room temperature were performed on an MTS-CMT 5205 testing machine with a tensile rate of 0.9 mm/min. High temperature tensile tests were carried out on a Gleeble 3500 testing machine with a strain rate of 0.001 s −1. The phase of the alloys was determined by D/max2200 X-ray diffractometer (XRD) analysis with Cu K αradiation. The microstructures were observed and analysed by Keyence VHX-100 optical microscopy (OM), Phenom XL scanning electron microscope (SEM), and JSM-2010F transmission electron microscope (TEM). Energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) was used to analyse the chemical compositions of the alloys. The phase diagrams of the alloys were calculated by Thermo-Calc thermodynamic simulation software. The ion-beam thinning method was used to prepare the TEM foils, including cutting thin slices from the specimens, mechanically grinding them, and finally thinning the samples with an argon ion beam under different angles. Condition: room temperature
Processing Word: Condition: room temperature

Processing Text: Commercial Ni, Al, and Cr powder were used as raw materials. The particle size of Ni powder and Al powder is 10 μm and the purity is 99.85%. The particle size of Cr powder is 45 μm and the purity is 99.5%. Weigh NiAl-30Cr according to the ratio of Ni: Al: Cr of 35 at.%: 35 at.%: 30 at.%, and mix them uniformly in a ball mill. The ball mill was set to run at 40 rpm for 8 h. Then, the uniformly mixed powder was pressed into a cylindrical prefabricated blocks at a pressure of 60 MPa. The prefabricated blocks were placed in a thermal explosion furnace for combustion synthesis and hot pressing. The furnace was programmed with a heating rate of 30 °C/min. As the temperature of prefabricated block increased rapidly, a pressure of approximately 40 MPa was promptly applied. Microhardness measurements were performed on a hardness testing system (HTS, 1600-5122VD Micromet 5104, USA) under a load of 50 g and holding time of 10 s. A servo-hydraulic universal material testing system (MTS, MTS810, USA) was used to test the room-temperature compressive properties of the specimens at compressive strain rate of 1.0 × 10−4s−1, fracture toughness (KIc) was also tested in this system. Another material testing system (MTS, DDL100, China) was used to test the high-temperature (at 1000 °C) compressive properties at a compressive strain rate of 1.0 × 10−4s−1. Temperature: 1000 °C

Processing Text: The starting material used in this work was a commercial AISI 316L stainless steel rod with a chemical composition of Fe-0.065C-2Mn-16.1Cr-10.02Ni-2.02Mo-Si-0.045P (wt.%). The rod with a diameter of 5.5 mm was drawn to 0.98 mm through 18 passes drawing with an average area reduction of 17% every pass. The drawing speed was set to be 0.1-0.2 m s−1, which is equal to a strain rate at a magnitude of 10−1s−1. The total drawing strain εis 3.44 (ε= 2ln (d0/ dw), where d0is the diameter of the rod, and dwis the diameter of the drawn wire). The 316L samples for X-ray diffraction analysis and electron microscopy investigation were sectioned along the longitudinal direction of the original rod and drawn wires. The samples were ground and polished. The samples were etched by Na2SO3: HCl: H2O solution before microstructural examination under scanning electron microscopy (SEM) using a second electron detector. For the transmission kikuchi diffraction (TKD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) experiments, the thin foil samples from the longitudinal section of the rod and wires were ground to a thickness of 50 μm and then prepared by double-jet electrolytic polishing or ion milling with a GATAN Model PIPS system. The tensile test of 316L samples were carried out using a CMT5105 universal material testing machine at room temperature (∼25 °C) and 120 °C (simulating the temperature during drawing). The total length and the gauge length of the tensile specimens are 15 mm and 5 mm, respectively. The strain rate of the tensile test was set to be 6.0 × 10−3s−1. Three samples for each strain were measured to ensure the accuracy and reliability of the mechanical testing results. X-ray diffraction (XRD) experiments were performed on a Rigaku D-max2100 diffractometer operating with Cu radiation, and the scanning speed was 5°/min. The SEM experiments were carried out in a FEI Siron-200 SEM. The electron back scattered diffraction (EBSD) and TKD were carried out in a ZEISS Crossbeam 550 SEM equipped with a Symmetry S2 detector. The scanning steps are at the range of 6-100 nm based on the boundary spacing of the microstructure in the samples. Acceleration voltages for EBSD and TKD were set to be 20 kV and 30 kV, respectively. The detailed microstructure and atomic resolution observation of the samples were examined using either an FEI-Tecnai G2 or Talos F200X high-resolution (HR) TEM, both operated at 200 kV.
