Processing Text: The ingots of (Ti-V-Al) 100-xN xshape memory alloys with different N additions (x = 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, at.%) were prepared by using a non-consumable arc-melting furnace under Ar atmosphere. High pure titanium (99.9%), vanadium (99.9%), aluminum (99.99%), and TiN particle powder were selected to be the raw materials. To ensure homogenization of the alloy composition, the ingots were melted and flipped six times. After melting, the (Ti-V-Al) 100-xN xsamples were sealed in quartz tubes under high vacuum. Then samples were solution treated at 1000 °C for 3 h, followed by water-quenching. Subsequently, the (Ti-V-Al) 100-xN xingots were hot-rolled to obtain thin plates measuring 4 mm in thickness. These plates were further cold-rolled to achieve a final thickness of 1 mm. Finally, the (Ti-V-Al) 100-xN xspecimens were cut into materials of different sizes (20 mm × 10 mm × 2 mm, 40 mm × 2 mm × 2 mm) using wire cutting to meet the requirements of various analytical experiments. After this, all samples were subjected to solution treatment at 900 °C for 3h under higher vacuum conditions, followed by water-quenching. The phase composition and structural information of the (Ti-V-Al) 100-xN xshape memory alloy were determined through X-ray diffraction (XRD) using the CuKα radiation source at room temperature. Optical microscopy (OM) was used to observe the microstructural evolution of the Ti-V-Al shape memory alloy with varying Nitrogen (N) content. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) combined with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) was utilized to examine the surface morphology, analyze the elemental composition of the second phase, and investigate the fracture surfaces. The specimens for SEM observation underwent polishing using SiC sandpaper with grit sizes ranging from #240 to #2000, followed by cloth polishing using a SiO 2solution with a particle size of 50 nm. To prepare the specimens for OM experiments, they were etched using a solution consisting of HF:HNO3:H2O in a ratio of 1:5:10. Bright-field transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images and corresponding selected area electron diffraction (SAED) patterns were used to study the martensitic variants and morphology of the second phase in the (Ti-V-Al) 100-xN xshape memory alloy. The twin jet-polishing was employed to prepare the specimens for transmission electron microscope (TEM) observations. The specimens were immersed in a solution containing 6% perchloric acid, 60% methyl alcohol, and 34% n-butyl alcohol, at approximately −20 °C. Furthermore, the martensitic transformation behavior of the (Ti-V-Al) 100-xN xshape memory alloys was investigated by conducting differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) analysis over a temperature range of −50 to 400 °C, with a heating/cooling rate of 20 °C/s. The mechanical properties of the (Ti-V-Al) 100-xN xshape memory alloy at room temperature, including tensile strength, were assessed using a tensile testing machine at a rate of 0.2 mm/min. The Vickers hardness of (Ti-V-Al) 100-xN xshape memory alloys was measured at room temperature using the nanoindentation technique with a 50g load applied for 10s. To ensure accuracy, measurements were taken at five different points on the same sample. To evaluate the friction and wear properties of the (Ti-V-Al) 100-xN xshape memory alloy under dry conditions at room temperature, a ball-on-disk tribometer (HSR-2M, Zhongke Kaihua) was used with a load of 10 N. Processing Text: CrMnFeCoNi HEA with 5 at.% SiC nanoparticles addition was fabricated by LMD. The size of the pre-alloyed spherical equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi powder and SiC powder that were analyzed using laser particle size analyzer (Microtrac s3500) are approximately 120 μm and 40 nm, respectively. Two powders were fully mixed and dried in a vacuum environment at 120 °C for 2.5 h prior to additive manufacturing. Under the protection of argon gas, the mixed powders were delivered into the chamber through a coaxial nozzle at an argon gas flow 15 L/min and a feeding rate of 7-9 g/min. Successive layers were deposited on a 316L steel substrate, ultimately forming walled-samples. The heat treatment processes of the samples were carried out in a vertical vacuum tube quenching furnace, which quenched immediately after 2-h heat treatment at different temperatures (700/900/1100 °C). The tensile tests of the samples were performed at an engineering strain rate of 10 −3s −1 in an Instron 5982 static testing machine. Each group of samples was retested three times to obtain their average value. The tensile samples with a gauge length of 10.0 mm, gauge width of 2.0 mm, and thickness of 1.6 mm were cut from to the center of LMD-fabricated wall, and the tensile direction was parallel to deposition direction (DD). The samples under different heat treatment temperature were subjected to corrosion treatment in equal proportion of FeCl 3-HCl-H 2O solution for 30 s before SEM observation. Condition: Room Temperature (25°C)

Processing Text: Electron beam freeform fabrication (EBF3) additive manufacturing technique has been successfully employed to print the non-weldable Al-5Cu thin-walled parts through an optimized set of process parameters. The process parameters were optimized, and the grain evolution mechanism with inherited characteristics is disclosed by both experimental and simulation methods. The composition of Cu: 4.90, Mn: 0.29, Ti: 0.14, V: 0.09, Cd: 0.29, Zr: 0.09, Fe: 0.08, Si: 0.03, Al: balance, wt% was determined by using the inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) method. The multiple sets of process parameters with various traveling speeds and feeding speeds were designed to build the single-track walls (height: 60 mm and length: 80 mm). Prior to the EBF3 printing, the wire material and the ground substrates were dried in an oven at 80 °C for 4 h. In order to obtain the temperature field of single-track walls, especially within melt pools, a numerical model was built using the ANSYS software. The “element birth and death” technique was applied to model the layer-by-layer deposition process. The numerical model was validated by the experimental results of melt pool morphology and in-situmonitored thermal cycle curves of substrate. The as-built sample with the optimum set of process parameters was subjected to solid solution treatment at 530 °C for 2 h and then water quenching at room temperature, followed by artificial aging treatment at 170 °C for 8 h. Post-heat treatment is conducted to engineer the desirable microstructure containing multiple nanostructures, i.e., the nanoscale θ"" and θ' precipitates, stacking faulted zones and Al-Cu-Cd clusters, leading to a high-strength Al-5Cu alloy with good ductility. After solution and aging heat treatment, Al-Cu-Cd nanoclusters (∼ 2 nm in Dia.) are generated, which facilitates the formation of nanoscale stacking faulted zones (∼11 nm). Meanwhile, as heterogeneous nucleation sites, Al-Cu-Cd nanoclusters effectively promote θ'-Al2Cu phase (∼ 19 - 114 nm) precipitation to enable the coexistence with fine θ""-Al3Cu precipitates (∼ 7 - 37 nm). Processing Text: In this paper, we present a straightforward method for fabricating graphene/Cu composites with an oriented bimodal structure through an in-situ synthesis process combined with hot rolling. Dendritic copper powder, mechanical exfoliation graphene and polyacrylonitrile were used as the raw materials. The graphene/Cu composite with oriented bimodal grains achieves a good balance between strength, ductility and electrical conductivity. Both the fine grains arising from the raised fine particles of dendritic copper powder and the graphene coated on the surface of fine grains facilitate the load transfer, resulting in improved strength of the composites. Furthermore, the formation of coarse grains during sintering and hot rolling deformation contributes to enhanced ductility. Simultaneously, the oriented structure of these coarse grains and graphene sheets establishes an efficient charge transport pathway, ensuring high electrical conductivity. The tensile yield strength of the oriented bimodal composite measures 315 MPa with 0.073 wt% carbon content, while its fracture elongation is 12.4%, and the electrical conductivity remains at 95.7% IACS. This study not only sheds light on the synergistic effects between graphene and copper in a bimodal composite system but also introduces a methodology for tailoring the microstructure to achieve a desired balance between mechanical strength, ductility, and electrical conductivity. Dendritic copper powder, mechanical exfoliation graphene and polyacrylonitrile (PAN) were used as the raw materials. PAN is a common raw material for the preparation of carbon fiber, which is easy to obtain and can be uniformly coated with copper powder and has a significant tendency to graphitization. Processing Text: The as-received 321ss rods were machined into a dog-shaped torsion specimens with a gauge dimensions of ∼60 mm in length and ∼5 mm in radius (R). The 321ss torsion specimens were austenitized at 1100 °C for 2 h to eliminate the effect of previous processing and obtain a single-phase γaustenitic coarse-grained (CG) microstructure. Then, the CG 321ss were subjected to small angle cyclic torsion (CT) processing with torsion angle of 5∼30°, torsion rate of 60°/min and cycle number of 200. The CT-treated samples were defined as CT-5, CT-10, CT-20, CT-30 (the numbers stand for CT torsion angle). The phase compositions and volume fractions of the strain-induced martensites at different radii in the radial direction of the CT-20 and CG 321ss before and after tensile deformation were measured by both micro-XRD (Bruker DB discover) with a diffraction beam of 1 mm and EBSD characterizations (JSM-7200F) with a step size of 0.3 μm and scanning region of 900 × 900 μm 2. The micro-XRD were taken at the cross-section of sample and the positions were shown in Fig. 1. To fix the position where micro-XRD is taken, the target positions are determined through an optical microscope, as a result, the fixed point measurement can be carried out. The volume fraction of α′martensite was estimated from the peak intensities Ihkl, and calculated using the formula, Vα′= Ibcc(110)/( Ibcc(110)+ Ifcc(111)) [ 25]. The EBSD raw data were further analyzed by OIM Analysis to acquire the average γgrain size, misorientation angle, grain boundary and GNDs density distributions. The microstructures at the surface of the CT-20 sample before and after tensile deformation with various strains were deeply characterized by TEM and SAED investigations (FEI Talos F200X). Interrupted tensile tests were carried out at various engineering strains to investigate the evolution of microstructures by TEM during tensile deformation. The samples for EBSD and TEM investigations were mechanically polished followed by ion thinning. The Vickers microhardness (HV) at different locations in the radial direction from the surface to the center of the CG and CT-treated specimens before and after tensile deformation were conducted with a load of 9.8 N and a duration of 10 s. Each HV average was obtained from four repeated measurements at the identical radius. The tensile tests of the CG and CT-treated samples were performed at a nominal strain rate of 5 × 10 −4s −1, and the tensile strain was measured by a contact-type extensometer with a gauge length of 25 mm. The loading-unloading-reloading (LUR) tests were conducted at a loading speed of 1.2 mm/min and an unloading speed of 2000 N/min. Condition: CT treatment of 5°

Processing Text: FeCrNi MEA was successfully fabricated using laser powder bed fusion. The pre-alloyed powders of FeCrNi consisted of Fe (32.97%), Cr (35.46%), and Ni (31.57%) in atomic percent. The powders were prepared by gas atomization. All samples were fabricated by the LPBF method. For the LPBF process, the as-building samples were fabricated by HBD − 150 (Shanghai Hanbang United 3D Tech Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China). The spot size of laser is 50 μm. LPBF samples were prepared on a building substrate pre-heated to 100 °C under protected Ar atmospheres. The FeCrNi MEA was manufactured using the same parameters as FeCrNi-TA MEA, which included a scanning speed of 800 mm/s, a layer thickness of 30 μm, and the scanning direction rotated 67° between each layer. X-ray diffraction (XRD, Bruker D8 ADVANCE) measurements were operated at 40 kV and 40 mA between 30° and 110° (2θ) with a step size of 3°/min. Specimens were mechanically ground and polished, and then electrically polished with a solution of 10% HClO4 and 90% C2H5OH at 25 V for 30 s at room temperature. The TEM samples were ground to a thickness of 30 μm, made to circle sheets (Ф3 mm), and finally thinned by a standard double jet polishing with an electrolyte solution of 90% ethanol and 10% perchloric acid. Room temperature uniaxial tensile tests (INSTRON 5982 tension machine) were conducted at an engineering strain rate of 1 × 10−3s−1. Three tensile tests were performed for each alloy. The as-built FeCrNi sample demonstrates a notably high relative density, reaching a maximum value of 99.976% (VED = 95.83 J/mm3). Processing state: as-built; Microstructure: single FCC structure

Processing Text: The Cast_33 superalloy was produced by arc melting under an Ar atmosphere. Then, the Cast_33 sample was homogenized at 1250°C for 24 h and subsequently aged at 900°C for 24 h (same heat treatments as for AM_33), to obtain a γ/γ' microstructure. The γ' microstructural stability of the Cast_33 superalloy at high temperatures was analyzed after long-term aging heat treatments at 800°C, 900°C, and 1000°C for 24 h, 100 h, 200 h, and 500 h. The homogenized samples were sealed in quartz glass capsules filled with Ar; subsequently, aging heat treatment was performed under the abovementioned conditions. The Cast_33 superalloy retained cuboidal γ' precipitates up to 1000°C for 500 h. Moreover, the γ' coarsening was confirmed to follow the LSW model at 800°C and the TIDC model at 900°C and 1000°C in terms of both the size and number density of γ' precipitates. By APT analyses, the sluggish interface diffusion of Co and corresponding interfacial energy reduction induced transition of γ'-coarsening mechanism from LSW to TIDC. Processing Text: Samples were fabricated on an SLM125HL machine with powders provided by Höganäs. Cylinders with a height of 96 mm and a diameter of 13 mm were manufactured under argon flux, with a pre-heating of the baseplate to 100 ∘C, and the LPBF parameters recommended by SLM for 316 L stainless steel. The baseplate used in this study was full of vertical samples (45 samples, dimension of baseplate: 125 mm × 125 mm) and so, the building time was approximately 48 h. The chessboard laser scan strategy with islands containing 20 scan vectors (2.4 mm × 2.4 mm) was used. A 67 ∘rotation of the pattern was applied between the layers. PMHT were conducted under secondary vacuum on AB samples. The furnace used is a secondary vacuum furnace which allows to realize heat treatments in a controlled atmosphere. It is equipped with a cold shelter and a sliding carriage facilitating the insertion of samples into the high-temperature zone once the desired temperature is attained, all while maintaining the furnace's vacuum integrity without necessitating its opening. The PMHT was conducted for a duration of 2 h at the prescribed temperature, after which the furnace was gradually cooled under vacuum conditions until the ambient temperature in the high-temperature region was reached. Specifically, in this investigation, samples are introduced into the preheated region of the furnace once it has reached the prescribed temperature, and subsequently held for a duration of two hours. Tensile specimens are machined from the cylinders built with the LPBF process (diameter = 13 mm, height = 96 mm). Heat treatments are realized after the machining in order to relief probable residual stresses induced by machining. Dislocation structures were studied by bright-field TEM for samples in the AB state, and after PMHT at 500, 650, 900 and 1200 °C. TEM analysis were carried out on thin foils extracted from samples in the AB state and heat treated at 500, 650, 900 and 1200 ∘C. Processing state: PMHT at 1200 °C; Contribution source: dislocations

In particular laser power was set in range 27-370 W (depends on the printing zone), scanning speed was set in range 500-7000 mm.s −1, hatching distance was determined in range 0.06-0.11 mm. The 3D printed samples exhibited a 1.2 mm allowance on their diameter. This allowance was removed by finishing operation using a cutting insert with 0.4 mm nose radius. The procedure of the heat treatment (prescribed by the powder supplier) was followed for the casted as well as for the 3D printed samples. The HIP operation was also included in the heat treatment of few samples, which combining the temperature of up to 2000 °C with a pressure of up to 2070 bar leads to the elimination of pores in the material and conversion of some undesirable structures, such as oxides, nitrides and some forms of carbides. The annealing heat treatment was performed by rapid heating (RH) to 1107 °C/2 h in a vacuum furnace followed by a slow cooling (3 °C/min) to 899 °C. After reaching a temperature of 899 °C a rapid cooling (RC) with Ar to the room temperature (RT) was carried out. Subsequent aging consisted of three steps i.e., RH to 913 °C/8 h plus RC with Ar at RT, RH to 982 °C/6 h plus RC with Ar at RT, RH to 803 °C/4 h, and quenching with Ar to RT. The HIP post-process operation was realized as a combination of the identical heat treatment with HIP at the temperature of 1200 °C/4 h and the pressure of 1000 bar. Few samples were subjected to the HIP process parameters at a temperature of 1200 °C/4 h and the pressure of 1035 bar in Ar atmosphere with a minimum purity of 99.995 %. The CrCoNi slurry was then vacuum-suction filtered and vacuum dried at 333 K for 24 h to obtain CrCoNi flaky powders. Processing Text: The material selected for the test was 45CrNiMoVA ultra-high-strength steel. The received materials were cylindrical bars with a diameter of 52 mm and a length of 200 mm. Surface morphology measurements were made using a 20× objective lens. The residual compressive stress on the specimen surface is measured by PROTO-LXRD X-ray. 1 mm aperture collimator is used. The diffraction angle is {211} Kα = 156.413°. Maximum beta is 25°. The number of beta angles is 5. Exposure time is 2 s. The surface normal residual stress was measured three times and the residual stress along the depth of the layer was measured one time. The cylindrical samples were inlaid, ground, and polished with argon ions, and the grain characteristics of the surface layers of the strengthened specimens were analyzed by using electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, JSM 7200F). The sample was subjected to 5 repeated pre-twists with an angle of 13.7° ( θpre), a torsion loading rate of 8°/min and an unloading rate of 200 N·m/min, releasing to zero torque each time. Processing Text: A novel high strength Nb3Cr2Ti0.9W0.4Fe6 HEA was developed in this work. The spherical powders were prepared by the dual process of mechanical alloying and high temperature remelting spheroidization (DP) since such technology has combined effect of mechanical milling (plastic deformation) and temperature lifting (atomic diffusion) to achieve the composition homogenization. At the same time, the powder prepared by gas atomization (GA) method is compared, and the printed parts are compared under the same parameters of laser powder bed fusion (LPBF). The yield strength (YS), ultimate tensile strength (UTS) and average elongation (ε) of the samples measured by DP-SLM were 953 MPa, 1159 MPa and 14.8 %, respectively. The hot compression test of Nb3Cr2Ti0.9W0.4Fe6 was carried out with Gleeble-3800 thermal simulation machine. The thermal processing diagram of the alloy under different stress variables was drawn by establishing the thermal deformation constitutive equation. The DP-SLM material recovers when the deformation temperature is 1000 ℃ with deformation rate stays at 0.01 s−1. Nb3Cr2Ti0.9W0.4Fe6 alloy processed at 1050-1150°C and a strain rate of 0.005∼ 0.1 s−1 shows high power dissipation efficiency (up to 37 %) and better dynamic recrystallization structure. Nb3Cr2Ti0.9W0.4Fe6 can be considered widely used in the engine combustion chamber, guide, turbine blade and turbo disk four hot end components. The RHEA spherical powders with uniform composition were prepared by mechanical alloying (MA) and High temperature remelting spherification technology (HTRS). MA technology achieves the composition uniformity of RHEA powder through the combined action of mechanical milling (plastic deformation) and temperature raising (atomic diffusion). Nb3Cr2Ti0.9W0.4Fe6 HEA powders were prepared by mechanical alloying process. After the alloyed powder was dried sufficiently, high temperature remelting equipment was used to prepare spherical powder, provided by Shaanxi Zhiqi Kaiwu Co. The printing parameters were set: laser power reached up to 550 W with 3200 mm/s scanning speed. laser wavelength is 1.06 μm, the thickness of each layer is 0.02 mm and spot diameter is 0.1 mm. 316 steel was regarded as the basic materials (BM) and its composition is shown in Table 3. In conclusion, MA can promote the alloying of refractory elements, while HTRS could change the powder morphology (spheroidization). Processing Text: The Fe-Cr-Mo-Mn steel used in this study are first heated by oxidation in an electric arc furnace, then decarbonized and desulphurized, with argon stirring to achieve deoxidation and desulphurization during the refining process. Subsequently, the steel ingot was subjected to multi-pass forging on a servo-hydraulic press. The forging process was initiated at an initial temperature of 1220 °C, with the final temperature reaching 800 °C, as illustrated in Fig. 1. The H1 sample undergoes QT based on the forged state, while the Ac1 and Ac2 temperatures for Fe-Cr-Mo-Mn steel are determined to be 710 °C and 780 °C, respectively. The H2 sample is subjected to an initial high-temperature normalization at 950 °C, followed by a near-Ac3 normalization at 770 °C, before proceeding to QT. In contrast, the H3 sample receives two successive high-temperature normalizations at 950 °C prior to the QT treatment. Following a single normalization, the resulting microstructure exhibits a combination of ferrite and pearlite. However, a significant refinement in both phases occurs after double normalization, as depicted in Fig. 1. The high-temperature tempering process engenders the formation of TS, characterized by the homogeneous dispersion of carbides within a ferritic matrix. The acicular martensite formed during the quenching process undergoes decomposition into a finer TS, which is uniformly distributed within the ferrite matrix during high-temperature tempering. Moreover, the elevated tempering temperatures facilitate enhanced diffusion of carbides, promoting the coalescence and growth of precipitated carbides within the ferrite matrix into a more uniformly dispersed granular morphology. Prior to the fatigue crack propagation tests, the initial microstructures of the H1, H2, and H3 specimens of Fe-Cr-Mo-Mn steel under varying heat treatment conditions were characterized using scanning electron microscopy (SEM). Following the fatigue crack propagation tests, the three groups of samples underwent characterization using SEM and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) to provide a comprehensive analysis of the microstructure evolution. Processing Text: A Cu-Ni-Si-Ca alloy was melted using a vacuum medium-frequency induction furnace and cast in a spheroidal graphite cast iron mold, resulting in a 30 mm-thick ingot, with the chemical composition listed in Table 1 obtained by using an Inductively Coupled Plasma-Atomic Emission Spectrometer (ICP-AES). The steel plate was solution-treated at 980 °C for 4 h, water quenched, and cold rolled with a 90 % thickness reduction. The plate was then cut into several 11 mm (parallel to the rolling direction) × 13 mm specimens, for the aging treatment in the temperature range from 450 °C to 550 °C for 15-1440 min. The addition of only 0.05 % Ca in this alloy is used to purify the alloy during the melting and casting process as a refinery. The DP process combined with thermomechanical treatment was exploited to expedite the precipitation kinetics, whilst the competition between DP and CP was utilized to inhibit the nucleation and growth of continuous precipitation phase (CPP). Cold deformation was conducted to further increase the nucleation rate by providing potential nucleation sites, such as dislocations and stacking faults. The growth of classic discontinuous precipitation phase (CDPP) was restricted due to the high nucleation rate of spherical discontinuous precipitation phase (SDPP) and the deformed microstructure. The aging time can be substantially shortened to introduce these metastable ordered t-Ni 3Si precipitates in the alloy. Processing Text: FeCoNiCr high-entropy alloys (HEAs) are often prepared by casting, resulting in a coarse-grained (CG) microstructure and low yield strength. The synthesis of FeCoNiCr HEA through mechanical alloying (MA) and spark plasma sintering (SPS) results in finer grain size, leading to high yield strength but low fracture strain. FeCoNiCr HEAs are often prepared by conventional casting, casting after purifying melts with B 2O 3, and occasionally by severe plastic deformation (SPD). Conventional casting of FeCoNiCr HEAs produces grain sizes ranging from 30 to 500 μm, yielding low strength (202 MPa) but high fracture strain (> 60 %). SPD processing of FeCoNiCr HEA can decrease the grain size to 50 μm, resulting in higher yield strength of 280 MPa and a lower fracture strain of 35 %. Casting after purifying melts with B 2O 3 causes supercooling, leading to a finer grain size of 7-20 μm, higher yield strength of 455 MPa, and a lower fracture strain of 16.8 %. FeCoNiCr HEA synthesized by MA and SPS techniques (MA-SPSed-FeCoNiCr HEA) leads to a grain size of 0.8 μm and significantly higher yield strength of 657 MPa. FeCoNiCr HEA containing 5 wt% nanoscale Y 2O 3 particles synthesized by MA and SPS techniques can even result in a grain size of 0.1 μm, leading to extremely high yield strength (1754 MPa), albeit with a low fracture-strain (5.8 %). CG FeCoNiCr (in equimolar ratio) HEAs were made via arc-melting a mixture of four elemental metal fragments. CG FeCoNiCr HEA was remelted five times to ensure uniformity and was made into an ingot weighing approx. 30 g in an electric arc furnace (Shenyang Jinyan JVAM-1B). Powders of FeCoNiCr HEA were prepared by mechanically alloying elemental Fe, Co, Ni, and Cr powders in a SPEX 8000D shaker mill for 24 h. A CS-IB cubic-anvil press was used to consolidate the as-milled powders into a bulk specimen for 30 min at 1000 °C and 4 GPa pressure. Processing Text: Al 0.7CoCrFeNi (at%) HEA ingot was prepared by levitation melting. During the whole melting process, the melt was electromagnetically stirred to ensure a uniform distribution of heat and thus the composition. Then the melt was cast into a graphite mold with dimensions of 200 mm × 200 mm × 25 mm. The alloy was set into a resistance heating furnace (SX-G 1300 ℃) holding at 1000 °C for isothermal and at 1050 °C to 1250 °C for non-isothermal treatments, followed by water quenching. The Vickers hardness was measured using a micro-hardness tester (3S-1000QZ) with a loading force of 500 g/N for 10 s. Prior to microstructure characterizations, HEA samples were prepared by the standard metallographic method. After grinding with SiC sandpaper up to 7000 grit and polishing with diamond paste. The X-ray diffractometer (XRD, D/max-2200) and the scanning electron microscopy (SEM-5000Pro) were employed to examine the microstructure and composition. The XRD analysis was performed using Cu Kα radiation (λ = 1.5418 Å, 40 kV, 40 mA) with the range (2θ) of 20° to 100° at a scanning speed of 8°/min, and a step size of 0.026°. To observe the microstructure, samples were etched with aqua regia (HCl: HNO₃ = 3:1) and then characterized utilizing the SEM equipped with an energy-dispersive (EDS) detector, operating in the back-scatter electron (BSE) mode at a working voltage of 15 kV and a working distance of 6 mm. The phase volume fraction, average lamellar thickness, and precipitation phase size were assessed using Image-J software. The isothermal treatment at 1000 °C indicates that the prolonged holding time promotes the transformation of the BCC/B2 phases to the FCC phase. The heat-treatment duration was strictly regulated to be within 3 h. In the initial stage of exploring the combined effects of the lamellar structure and B2 precipitates, the temperature interval for non-isothermal heat treatment was precisely set at 50 °C. Subsequently, with the intention of accentuating the influence of the lamellar-strengthening effect on the mechanical properties by highlighting the variances in the morphological distribution of the lamellar phase, the temperature interval was further augmented to 100 °C. Processing Text: Maraging 250 steel wire was used as a feedstock material and remotely fed under the electrode to coincide with the plasma arc during printing. Before printing bulk samples, 12 single tracks were printed as a preliminary study to identify optimized printing parameters. The optimized printing parameters were set as: welding current 182 A, voltage 30 V, welding speed 5 mm/s and wire feed speed 50 mm/s. During printing, argon (99.99% purity) was applied as both shielding and welding gas. Using these parameters, thin walls of about 80 mm (length) × 20 mm (height) × 10 mm (width) with a layer thickness of 1.2 mm were printed with different interlayer dwell times of 0 min, 1 min, and 3 min to exploit the effects of thermal history on the microstructure evolution and mechanical properties of the printed maraging 250 steels. By introducing a dwell time between adjacent layers, the maraging 250 steel is cooled below the martensite start temperature, triggering thermally-driven martensitic transformation during the printing process. Thermal cycling during subsequent layer deposition results in the formation of reverted austenite which shows a refined microstructure and induces elemental segregation between martensite and reverted austenite. The reverted austenite is metastable during deformation, leading to strain-induced martensitic transformation under loading. Specifically, a 3 min interlayer dwell time produces a maraging 250 steel with approximately 8% reverted austenite, resulting in improved work hardening via martensitic transformation induced plasticity during deformation. Meanwhile, the higher cooling rate and refined prior austenite grains lead to substantially refined martensitic grains (by approximately fivefold) together with an increased dislocation density. With 3 min interlayer dwell time, the yield strength of the printed maraging 250 steel increases from 836 MPa to 990 MPa, and the uniform elongation is doubled from 3.2% to 6.5%. This intermittent deposition strategy during PAW-DED allows us to achieve an outstanding strength-ductility synergy that outperforms conventional wrought and other additively manufactured maraging steel counterparts. Processing state: as-printed; Dwell time: 0 min
Processing Word: Processing state: as-printed; Dwell time: 0 min

Processing Text: The commercially available TC4 titanium alloy bars in an annealed state with the dimensions of Ф50 mm× 200 mm were used in this experiment. The annealing process was heating at 750 ℃ for 1.5 h and then air-cooled. The rectangular billets with dimensions of 35 mm × 35 mm × 37 mm were cut from the centre of the long bar for the subsequent MDF process. The relationship between DRX behavior and strain rate was determined by hot compression experiment. The deformation temperature was selected to be 940 ℃, 880 ℃ and 820 ℃. MDF was conducted on a four-column hydraulic press. The sample was rapidly heated in the furnace to the deformation temperature and then was soaked at this temperature for 5 min. Each forging pass was involved in three steps, and the forging axis was rotated by 90° step by step (i.e. Z to X to Y to Z). The true strain for each step was 0.22, calculated from ln(h 0/h 1), where h 0and h 1were the blank height values before and after forging, respectively. Therefore, the cumulative strain per pass was approximately 0.66. The samples were re-heated in a resistance furnace to the deformation temperature after each forging pass to compensate for the temperature loss during the MDF process. The microstructures of the alloys were characterized by optical microstructure (OM, Leitz MM-6), X-ray diffraction (XRD, D/MAX2500PC), scanning electron microscope (SEM, FEI Quanta 200), electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM, Titan G2 F20). The samples for OM observation were etched in a solution of 0.5 ml hydrofluoric acid, 1 ml nitric acid and 25 ml deionised water. TEM and EBSD foils were firstly ground to 80 µm and then further prepared with a twin-jet electropolisher (a solution of 6 % perchloric acid+34 % normal butanol+60 % methyl alcohol, vol%). Mechanical properties of the alloys were characterized by tensile tests. The room temperature tensile tests were conducted on an Instron 3369 electronic universal testing machine at a constant cross-head speed of 1 mm/ min. Processing Text: Raw Cu, Cr, Fe, Ni, Al and Ti blocks with purity>99.8 wt % were selected to prepare the 3.5 kg CuCrFeNiTi0.8Al1.2 HEA via magnetic levitation induction melting under high purity argon atmosphere. The melting process was repeated 4 times to achieve chemical homogeneity. In order to better study the organizational transformation behavior and solidification process during annealing, the obtained specimen was then annealed at 800 °C and 1000 °C for 24 h, followed by water quenching. As increase the annealing temperature to 1000 °C, relatively large quantities of secondary nano-particles precipitated from α phase not just the micro-particle from DR matrix. Processing Text: The maraging steel employed in this study was Fe-18Ni-8.5Co-5Mo-0.7Ti-0.2Al (wt.%). The steel was produced using a vacuum induction melting furnace and cast into ingots with a diameter of 50 mm and a weight of 2 kg. Before melting, the furnace chamber was evacuated to 10−3Pa and filled with 0.05 MPa of high-purity argon as a shielding gas. Processing Text: The 5356 aluminum alloy samples were fabricated utilizing WAAM and U-RE-WAAM processes, respectively. Prior to additive manufacturing, the substrate surface was mechanically polished and cleaned with alcohol to remove any oxide films and oil contamination. Deposition was conducted using three distinct processes: WAAM, RE-WAAM, and U-RE-WAAM. In each process, the filler wire was melted by an electric arc under a protective atmosphere of 99.99 % argon. The torch and the molten wire moved horizontally in the Y deposition direction to form the deposited layers. By elevating the torch height in the Z building direction, subsequent layers were deposited onto the previous ones. The specific parameters for the additive manufacturing process are listed in Table 2. The parameters for the ultrasonic rotating extrusion system are specified in Table 3. In the initial layer of the additive manufacturing process, a wire feed speed of 7.5 m/min is utilized. Subsequently, the wire feed speed is decremented by 0.5 mm/min with each additional layer, down to a minimum of 5.0 mm/min. This gradual reduction in wire feed speed is necessitated by the proximity of the initial layers to the substrate, where the melting pool experiences rapid cooling and limited spread, thus requiring a higher feed rate to ensure adequate deposition width. As the number of deposited layers accumulates, the cooling rate of the melt pool decreases, necessitating a reduction in wire feed speed to 5.0 mm/min to prevent the collapse of deposited layers. The additive manufacturing process incorporates a single stack path, with interlayer temperatures strictly controlled below 50°C to maintain material integrity and process consistency. Microstructure and mechanical properties remain important indicators for large-scale structural components in aerospace ( Ren et al., 2017). For the high-power/high-efficiency LDED process of titanium alloys, research hotspots mainly focus on the microstructural and properties ( Zhang et al., 2019), including the non-uniformity of microstructure, grain refinement mechanism, anisotropy of properties, and the improvement of mechanical properties ( Song et al., 2023). However, the drawback is that the tensile elongation is only 4.09%, indicating insufficient toughness ( Chen et al., 2024). Meanwhile, the introduction of external energy fields also contributes to grain refinement ( Tan et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2022, 2023). Applying high-frequency ultrasonic vibration during the deposition process can transform coarse columnar grains into fine equiaxed grains, thereby refining the grain structure and effectively enhancing tensile properties ( Todaro et al., 2020). In the LDED deposition of TC4 titanium alloy, the introduction of a transverse static magnetic field can refine the primary β grains and produce a discontinuous grain boundary α phase, thereby improving tensile ductility and reducing the anisotropy of tensile properties ( Yuan et al., 2021). Processing Text: Here, the cost-effective Si and Cu were used to modify an Al-5.5Mg alloy for laser-powder bed fusion (L-PBF), which achieved a synergetic combination of crack-free feature and high strength. Processing Text: The AFMAR alloys were prealloyed and gas atomized by CEIT (Spain). The powders were then sintered through Spark Plasma Sintering (HPD-25 equipment, FCT System GmbH, Germany) in a graphite die 20 mm in diameter. A tungsten foil of 25-50 µm was placed between the inner walls of the die and the powder, isolating the alloy from the graphite and preventing carbon contamination. A heating rate of 400 °C/min was used to reach a sintering temperature of 1100 °C and held for 5 min while applying a 50 MPa uniaxial pressure under a 10 -2mbar low vacuum. This sintering cycle was chosen because it had been previously optimized with the same die geometry for a similar alloy. AFMAR samples were cut into semi-circles of 20 mm in diameter and approximately 2 mm in thickness. All samples were grounded to a 1200-grit surface finish and cleaned with ethanol prior to the corrosion tests. The samples were placed in rectangular alumina crucibles with molten lead. Samples of commercial alloys 316 L and T91 were placed in a separate crucible from the AFMAR alloys and were used as reference. The lead exposure tests were conducted in a COSTA (COrrosion test STand for liquid metal Alloys) facility located at KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm, developed by the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT). The alumina crucibles containing the samples, and the lead were positioned inside a sealed quartz glass tube. To control the oxygen concentration in the atmosphere inside the tube, one extreme had inlet and outlet gas tubes. Since the oxygen partial pressures needed for the test are much lower than what can be provided in commercial bottles (≅ 10 -18bar), a flowing gas mixture of Ar, H 2and H 2O is used. An Ar gas flow is bubbled through water, carrying water vapor as it moves. Then, the humidified-Ar flow is mixed with an Ar-5 %H 2gas flow at the inlet of the gas tube. By controlling the flow rate of both gases, it is possible to adjust the H 2/H 2O ratio and achieve the desired oxygen partial pressure of the gas phase inside the glass tube (p O2). A Zirox SGM5 oxygen analyzer placed at the gas outlet was used to monitor the p O2. Corrosion tests at 550 °C and 650 °C were performed, lasting up to 1000 h each. Processing Text: The alloy components were weighed according to the designed composition and thoroughly melted in a ZG-25-A vacuum induction furnace at a temperature of approximately 1450 °C. The molten alloy was then poured into a sand mold to form 12 kg Al0.3CoCrFeNiTi0.15 ingots. A portion of the original ingot was subjected to further melting process to improve material homogeneity, remove impurities, and obtain the cast sample (noted as C-1 sample). For the LPBF process, the remaining primitive initial ingots were processed into 32 mm bars. The pre-alloyed Al0.3CoCrFeNiTi0.15 powders were generated by the plasma rotating electrode process (PREP) (the schematic view is shown in Fig. 1(a)) from the prepared bars. The particle size ranges from 10 to 53 μm. The 3 × 3 × 3 mm3 cuboid samples (noted as 0A ∼ 9J) were built on a commercial machine (TruPrint 1000) with a build chamber of Φ100 mm*80 mm (Figs. 2(a ∼ b)). Employing a laser power (P) of 175 W, and a layer thickness (h) of 30 μm, the laser was rotated at a 67° angle (α) for each scanning layer (Fig. 2(d)) for homogenous microstructure. The argon atmosphere was maintained during the deposition with an oxygen environment below 100 ppm to prevent oxidation. Meanwhile, the hatching space (d) ranged from 30 to 70 μm and the scanning speed (v) varied from 500 to 2400 mm/s, corresponding to changes in laser volumetric energy density (E=Pvhd) from 33.7 to 388.9 J·mm−3 (Table S1). These parameters were meticulously selected to build Al0.3CoCrFeNiTi0.15 specimens. In addition, to reduce the effect of pore characteristics (including shape, size, location and number) on stress concentrations (Fig. S1), the remelting technology was undertaken to further enhance the performance, as depicted in Fig. 2(c) (noted as R-2). Finally, 33 × 17 × 7 mm3 samples were deposited under the same optimized laser conditions to analyze their mechanical properties (Fig. 2(d)). The tensile test specimens perpendicular to the building direction, with a gauge length of 12.5 mm, a width of 4.0 mm, and a thickness of 1.5 mm (Fig. 2(d)), were cut out by a wire-cut electrical discharge machine. Then the tensile tests at 20 °C and 700 °C were conducted on the INSTRON 5982 and ZWICK universal testing machine (Z250SH) with a tensile rate of 5 × 10−3 s−1. A digital image correlation sensor was used to measure the strain at RT, the displacement at 700 °C tensile testing was measured by a ceramic contact extensometer. The microhardness was conducted by an XHVT-10Z Vickers hardness tester with a load of 1 kg for a dwell time of 20 s. Each reported hardness value is the average value of five measurements. The metallographic specimen was cut in the middle zone of cuboid samples, as depicted in Fig. 2(d), which were first ground with SiC papers up to 5000 grit and then polished. Defects and morphology (aqua regia etching: 15 mL HCl + 5 mL HNO3) were observed by optical microscope (OM) (SOPTOP RX50M). The microstructures and grain orientation were achieved using a TESCAN MIRA3 scanning electron microscope (SEM) equipped with an electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) detector and energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS). The grain size, texture, misorientation between grains, and Kernel average misorientation (KAM) map were investigated using EBSD analysis (MTEX). The microstructures and precipitations were also characterized by the FEI TALOS F200X transmission electron microscope (TEM). The 3 mm foils (thickness less than 50 μm) were polished to electron transparency by a twin-jet electro-polisher (5 % perchloric acid +95 % ethanol) at −15 °C and 30 V. Processing Text: The GH3535 nickel-based alloy, designed for molten salt nuclear reactors, was fabricated using wire arc additive manufacturing. Prior to the deposition process, the substrate undergoes meticulous surface preparation, which includes sanding to eliminate oxide layers and subsequent cleaning with acetone to remove any residual grease or dirt. A mixture shielding gas of Argon (Ar) and 50 % Helium (He) was used, with a flow rate of 15L•min−1. The deposition employed a reciprocating scanning strategy, with the torch rotated 90° between successive layers (Fig. 1c). An overlap rate of 35 % between adjacent weld beads was maintained to ensure consistent layer fusion. Throughout the deposition process, the inter-bead temperature was meticulously regulated to remain below 100 °C. The specific processing parameters are outlined in Table 2. Metallographic and tensile samples were extracted at three distinct vertical levels along the horizontal direction plane (as depicted in Fig. 1d), specifically from the bottom, middle and top, to evaluate the uniformity of the mechanical properties of the WAAM-fabricated GH3535 alloy. Specimens for tensile testing were meticulously prepared at deposition heights of 1 mm (representing the bottom layer), 25 mm (the middle layer) and 48 mm (the top layer), with three samples tested for each condition. Additionally, Vickers hardness tests were executed on the WAAM-fabricated GH3535 alloy samples, which were taken from various deposition heights with a consistent interval of 2 mm. Processing Text: The experiments were conducted using SS316L as both the powder bed material and the substrate material. The powder particles had a size distribution of 15-53 µm. In the first stage, nine cubic samples with dimensions of 10 mm x 6 mm x 5 mm were fabricated using the L-PBF process with processing conditions specified in Table 2. In the second stage, half of the top surface of each sample was polished using the LR parameters specified in Table 3. The L-PBF and LR experiments were performed using a Tong-Tai AM-160 machine, which is equipped with Ytterbium Fiber Laser YLR-1070 (wavelength 1070 nm) in a chamber filled with nitrogen and an oxygen concentration lower than 2000 ppm. For each as-built samples shown in Fig. 8, the top surface topology was measured using a confocal laser-scanning microscope (as shown in Fig. 13). and the corresponding values of Sa was determined as shown in Fig. 14. The feasibility of the proposed L-PBF+LR method is experimentally demonstrated using SS316L powder as the feedstock material. Tensile test specimens fabricated using the optimal processing conditions show an overall tensile strength of 550 ±7.8 MPa and an overall yield strength of 420 ±5.9 MPa. Compared to a conventional L-PBF process performed with a layer thickness of 30 µm, the mechanical properties of the optimal printed specimens are improved by 96 %, while the fabrication time is reduced by approximately 48 %. Tensile test specimens with the configuration and dimensions shown in Fig. 10 were fabricated using the L-PBF and in-situ LR process to investigate the effect of the re-melting process on improving the mechanical properties of the built parts. Tensile testing was performed at room temperature on an HT-2420 system at a displacement speed of 1 mm/min. In this study, the main purpose of density measurement is to observe the relationship between the SR and density of the L-PBF processed part. Thus, for each cubic samples, the average SR of each sample was measured, and the samples were then cut into two separate specimens to determine the density. In accordance with the procedure described in [55], polished cross-sectional images with different SR values were acquired using an optical microscope. The topology of the top surface of each specimen was measured after both the L-PBF construction process and the LR operation using a confocal laser-scanning microscope (KEYENCE VK-200) at 10-x magnification. The values of Sa and Sq, i.e., the arithmetical mean height and root mean square height, respectively, were computed from the measured surface profiles using MATLAB software. The autocorrelation function showing the spectral relationship between the surface height and the separation distance between surface points was also extracted from the SR profile. The correlation length, Cl, was determined as the point at which the autocorrelation function declined to 1/e [41]. The accuracy of the CFD model was verified by comparing the simulated depth of the melt pool ( Fig. 11) for three combinations of the L-PBF parameters with the results reported in [56]. The corresponding results are presented in Table 4 and Fig. 12. The reliability of the trained ANN model was evaluated by conducting a regression analysis of the ANN predictions for the melt pool depth and the SR results obtained by the CFD model. Note that the initial surface roughness was assumed to be 12 μm in both cases. The melt pool depth results presented in Fig. 19 indicate that the RSME has a value of 0.695. In order to examine the relationship between the SR and density of the built parts, a series of L-PBF experiments were conducted using different printing parameters to fabricate cubic parts with a size of 10 mm x 10 mm x T x No, as indicated in Table 5. After completing the printing process, the SR of each part was observed and the density value was calculated. In the present study, the mechanical properties and manufacturing efficiency were evaluated for three different printing strategies: LPBF30 (powder layer thickness of 30 µm); LPBF60 (powder layer thickness of 60 µm), and LPBF+LR60 (powder layer thickness of 60 µm and LR processing). Fig. 32 shows the arrangement of the different samples on the build table. Table 6 lists the L-PBF and LR parameters used for the different sample types. Finally, when the L-PBF and in-situ LR experiment finished, the tensile parts were conducted mechanical tests. Tensile strength was examined and compared between parts produced through L-PBF and in-situ LR and conventional L-PBF process. The mechanical properties of the samples fabricated using the different L-PBF and LR methods were evaluated through tensile testing. The results obtained for the yield strength, ultimate tensile strength (UTS), and elongation of the various samples are shown in Fig. 33. Fig. 34 shows the stress-strain curves for different methods namely LPBF60, LPBF30, LPBF+LR60 and EOS60. Note that the results for an EOS60 (powder layer thickness of 60 µm) standard components given in literature [62] are also shown for comparison purposes. The results have shown that the specimens fabricated using the LR method have an overall tensile strength of 550 MPa and an overall yield strength of 420 MPa. The corresponding standard deviation values are less than 7.8 and 5.9 MPa, respectively. These values are close to those of the optimal LPBF30 sample with no LR, that is, 564 ± 3.5 MPa and 425 ± 18.5 MPa, respectively. The elongation value of the LPBF+LR60 sample is greater (27 %) than that of the L-PBF60 and EOS60 samples. Processing Text: W/AlSi10Mg composite powders were prepared using a solvent-assisted dispersion method, followed by low-energy ball milling and drying processes. The procedure entailed dispersing W nanoparticles (average size ∼500 nm, 272 g, 6.4 wt%) onto the surface of spherical AlSi10Mg powders (average size ∼32 μm, 4 kg, 93.6 wt%) in an ethanol medium. Following this, low-energy ball milling was performed for 4 hours at 150 rpm, with a ball-to-powder ratio of 1:1. The composite powders were dried at 80°C and then sieved through a 200-mesh screen. W/AlSi10Mg composite samples were fabricated using an SLM 280 HL machine (SLM Solutions GmbH, Germany). This equipment, equipped with dual fiber lasers with a maximum power of 400 W and a spot diameter of 80 μm, enables high-precision and high-performance metal 3D printing. The forming chamber was evacuated and filled with high-purity argon, maintaining the oxygen content below 100 ppm to prevent material oxidation during fabrication. The substrate was preheated to 150°C to mitigate residual stress and deformation caused by rapid heating-cooling cycles. Considering surface quality, densification, and production efficiency, the following process parameters were determined: powder layer thickness (t) of 30 μm, hatch spacing (h) of 80 μm, and laser power (P) of 300 W. To investigate the influence of laser scanning speed on the microstructure and properties of the composites, three representative scanning speeds (v) were selected: 1800 mm/s, 2200 mm/s, and 2600 mm/s. A stripe scanning strategy was employed, with adjacent layers rotated 67° to improve the anisotropy of the fabricated parts. Based on these parameters, the volumetric energy density (Ev) was calculated using the equation Ev = P/(v·h·t). The calculated Ev values were 69.4 J/mm³, 56.8 J/mm³, and 48.0 J/mm³ for the three scanning speeds of 1800 mm/s, 2200 mm/s, and 2600 mm/s, respectively. Samples included standard tensile specimens for mechanical testing and 8 × 8 × 8 mm³ cubes for microstructural analysis. Processing Text: The examined material is 6061-T4 aluminum alloy, which is employed in the fabrication of battery enclosures for electric vehicles due to its outstanding combination of both strength and weight. The 6061-T4 alloy’s chemical composition is shown in Table 1. The common heat treatment procedure entails solutionizing for one hour at 530 ∘C, followed by aging and water quenching at room temperature [22]. This treatment dissolves alloying elements, such as Mg and Si, into a supersaturated solid solution, which subsequently promotes the formation of fine precipitates, such as Mg 2Si, during aging. These precipitates play a critical role in enhancing the alloy’s strength and mechanical properties. The first type is 76 mm × 19 mm × 3 mm samples, which are cut with a water-cooled abrasive cutter and ground with SiC paper of 1200 grit to an average roughness of 5.39 μm. The second type is 10 mm × 5 mm × 3 mm samples, which are cut using wire electrical discharge machining and polished to a mirror finish using an electrochemical polisher. These samples are used for microstructure characterization and microhardness testing. The third type is 20 mm × 20 mm × 3 mm samples, which are cut with a water-cooled abrasive cutter and ground with 1200 grit SiC paper to an average roughness of 5.39 μm, used for surface roughness and residual stress measurements. Samples are ultrasonically cleaned in denatured alcohol for 10 min before UNP treatment to eliminate surface contaminants including dust and grease. Ultra-high bonding double-sided tapes placed on the edges of the samples provide strong adhesion on the robot work table. To provide sufficient UNP energy, the peening device remains perpendicular to the surface of the sample. The ultrasonic generator power is set at efficiencies of 50 % and 100 %, corresponding to vibration amplitudes of 21 μm and 35 μm, measured via laser Doppler vibrometer (brand: Sunny Optical Technology). These amplitudes are selected to provide significant peening intensities that can be exploited to form and strengthen metallic components in the automotive industry. In addition, such vibration amplitudes can induce the desired level of plastic deformation, ensuring surface strengthening while preventing excessive damage or cracking at higher amplitudes. Additional manipulated variables that are fixed during the UNP process include the air pressure (0.5 MPa) and the standoff distance (2 mm) between the needle tips and the sample surface [19]. In addition, 16 translational UNP passes both forward and backward are executed by the end effector over the sample with a 50 mm/s robot travel velocity to ensure that the sample gets sufficient penetration energy. Before performing the test, the samples are polished using a motorized polisher (brand: Struers Tegramin-25) deploying grit papers of several grades until only a few indents remain to test the highly deformed surface layer. 100 gf of load and a 10-s dwell time are used for the test. Five indentation spots have been taken at various positions on the specimen surface for every test sample, with a distance of 500 μm between neighboring indents. Furthermore, 10 indentation spots are carried out at various points throughout the sample cross-section, following the recommendation of previous studies [24], with a 50 μm distance between two neighboring indents. According to ASTM International, tensile tests have been conducted on three type-1 samples in a longitudinal direction using an electronic universal material testing machine (brand: Zwick/Roll Z100) to evaluate their mechanical properties. For samples that exhibited bending after the robotic ultrasonic multi-needle peening process, we carefully flattened them before tensile testing to ensure accurate measurement of their mechanical properties. This approach is consistent with established practices for testing materials like Almen strips post-peening, where flattening procedures are employed to minimize the influence of residual stress-induced curvature on the tensile results [24,27]. The residual stress profiles of the UNP-0, UNP-1, and UNP-2 samples have been investigated using the incremental hole drilling strain gauge method. According to ASTM International [25], the SINT MTS3000 measurement system is used for all measurements. To eliminate distortion and edge effects and produce more accurate and reliable data, residual stresses are measured in the center of the samples rather than on their edges. The arc heights of the UNP-1 and UNP-2 samples have been quantitatively determined by employing an electronic indicator with a resolution of 0.002 mm. To ensure the stability and repeatability of the procedure, three iterations are taken into account for each of the samples. To compensate for initial arc heights, measurements are taken at three positions on each sample: the center and two adjacent points, both before and after the UNP process. Treated with robotic UNP at lower ultrasonic vibration amplitude (UNP-1); Young’s modulus: 145 ± 3.8 GPa; Ultimate tensile stress: 220 ± 1.8 MPa; Elongation: 21.5 ± 4.4 %

Processing Text: The AA 2024 alloy was melted using susceptor-assisted microwave heating, and the molten alloy was then directionally solidified in-situ at five solidification rates (50, 100, 150, 200, and 250 μm/s) under microwave irradiation. The target alloy was exposed to microwave at 900 W for 1200 s with a 300 s stabilization period; duty cycle was adjusted as shown in Table 3. Upon melting, the target alloy gets self-poured in-situ into the preheated mould which is adequately connected to the cooling and withdrawal system. The mould withdrawal system was equipped with a CNC controller to effectively maintain the targeted solidification rate by providing the physical movement to the mould using a stepper motor arrangement. The cooling system was designed to extract heat from the bottom of mould using a water jet at 30 °C. Initially, water jet cooling was applied at the bottom of the mould to induce nucleation, followed by withdrawing the mold from the applicator to the ambient environment at a predetermined rate to facilitate the growth of the nuclei. The phase identification of directionally solidified samples was carried out using an X-ray diffractometer (Model: Smart Lab, Make: Rigaku) diffractometer with Cu-Kα X-radiation at a scan rate of 1° min−1 scanning from 10° to 120°. The hardness of transverse and longitudinal sections was determined using a microhardness tester (Make: Omnitech, Model: MVH-SAuto) using a 50 g load and 10 s of dwell time in accordance with the ASTM E384 standard. Elemental composition was analyzed using the SEM images scanning the EDS point spectra to observe the distribution of alloying elements of various phases within the AA 2024 alloy. The chemical composition and ingredients of different phases were analyzed using multiple characterization techniques. The mechanical properties were determined in terms of hardness and tensile strength. Solidification rate: ∼125 µm/s; Microwave interaction during solidification

Processing Text: To investigate the impact of new phase addition of Invar 36, B4C particles, known for their high melting point, were used as reinforcement phases to fabricate B4C/Invar 36 composites through laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) technology, which offers high design flexibility. The Invar 36 powder (15-55 μm) and the B4C particles examined in this study were supplied by Shandong Lianhong New Material Technology Co., Ltd., China. As illustrated in Fig. 1(a), the gas-atomized spherical Invar 36 powder is uniformly distributed, with a mean particle size of 26.24 μm, making it well-suited for the LPBF powder laying process. Fig. 1(b) presents the 99.9 % purity irregularly shaped B4C powders. The chemical composition (in wt.%) of the precursor powders is detailed in Table 1 and 2. To achieve a homogeneously mixed feedstock composite powder containing 2 wt% B4C, a ball-milling process was conducted using a QM-3SP4-1 planetary ball mill at a rotation speed of 150 rpm for 2 h. Following this optimized ball-milling duration, the B4C particles were nearly all firmly embedded within the relatively soft surface of the larger Invar 36 powders, without any significant alteration to the original spherical particle shape or size distribution (Fig. 1(c)). It is noteworthy that the composite powder was dried at 80 °C for 120 min prior to the experiment. The LPBF apparatus utilized was the Hans-M100, which was equipped with a YLR-200/500 YAG fiber laser, featuring a wavelength of 1060 nm, a laser spot size of 70 μm, and a maximum power output of 500 W. The layer thickness, stripe width, and stripe overlap were consistently maintained at 0.03 mm, 10 mm, and 0.08 mm, respectively. Additionally, after the construction of each layer, the scanning direction was rotated by 67°. The influence of laser scanning speed on the relative density, microstructural evolution, and mechanical properties of the B4C/Invar 36 composites was systematically examined. The results indicate that B4C/Invar 36 composites with nearly full density (99.32 %) were successfully produced at a laser power of 150 W and a laser scanning speed of 700 mm/s. B4C particles exhibited a strong heterogeneous nucleation effect on Invar 36 grains; the increase in nucleation sites contributed to grain refinement, ultimately enhancing the mechanical properties of the samples. The yield strength of the samples reached 410.17 MPa, while the ultimate tensile strength reached 729.27 MPa. Calculations reveal that grain refinement strengthening is the primary mechanism by which B4C enhances the Invar 36 matrix, with other strengthening mechanisms serving as auxiliary contributors to achieve synergistic strengthening. Laser scanning speed: 1100 mm/s

Processing Text: Gas-atomized AISI 4140 powder was used as the additive material. The powder is spherical in shape, with an average particle size of approximately 40 μm. 95 % of the particles have diameters ranging from 25 to 53 μm. The experimental setup for conducting the LMD and EHLA processes is depicted in Fig. 2. The machine employed in this study consisted of a focusing optic PHFQ-H1-C, a coaxial powder nozzle, and a spindle. A diode laser with a maximum power of 4000 W was used as the beam source. Powder feed was accomplished through the coaxial powder delivery system of the laser head using a pneumatic twin powder feeder. Argon gas was used for powder delivery and specimen shielding to prevent oxidation, and the purity of argon gas is 99.99 %. A water-cooling system was implemented to cool the laser system and laser head. In the LMD process, the interaction time between the laser beam and the powder particles is short, resulting in a high ratio of laser energy being absorbed by the substrate. The powder particles melt in the melting pool, leading to a relatively large heat-affected zone. Conversely, in the EHLA process, the laser-powder reaction occurs along the powder delivery path. Consequently, most of the powder particles melt above the surface and enter the melting pool as liquid drops. The EHLA process employs higher laser power to ensure a pore-free, less-cracked, and metallurgical-bonded layer. We studied divergent parameter combinations for a single layer and investigated the microstructure (pores, cracks, bonding quality, thickness, etc.) of the cross-section of the deposition accordingly, and those results feeded back to the process parameters. Through trial and error, the process parameters for a single layer with low porosity, metallurgic bonding between the substrate and the layer, and without any cracks were finally selected. The parameters used for LMD and EHLA are presented in Table 2. In the process strategy, the workpiece rotates using a fixed lathe chuck while the powder nozzle moves horizontally above the substrate. The overlap ratio between two tracks in the same layer is approximately 70 %. All experiments were conducted using a meandering scan path. Case 1: a single layer with multiple tracks using LMD, following the process parameters outlined in Table 2(LMD process parameters). Case 2: a single layer with multiple tracks using EHLA, following the process parameters described in Table 2(EHLA process parameters). Case 3: a 3D structure using LMD on a cylindrical base material. The dimensions of the deposition were 10 mm in the thickness direction (BD, R) and 100 mm in the length direction (SD, Z). In order to mitigate potential hot cracking caused by high temperatures during continuous deposition and to conduct comparative IHT experiments, we fabricated a total of 22 layers (10 mm) and allowed a dwell time of 15 min for cooling the deposition to 60 °C. Case 4: a 3D structure using EHLA on a cylindrical base material. The dimensions of the EHLA deposition were identical to those of the LMD deposition. However, since the thickness of an EHLA layer is approximately one-fourth to one-fifth of an LMD layer, we deposited a total of 95 layers to achieve a structure with a 10-mm thickness. To study the IHT effect and compare the resulting microstructure with LMD, we implemented a cooling time of 15 min after each set of five continuous deposited layers in order to facilitate cooling to 60 °C. Due to the high-power input and limited time available for heat transfer, the EHLA deposited structure exhibited some burnt edges, with a zig-zag burnt position of 5 mm at a 45-degree angle to the horizontal direction at each edge. This phenomenon is primarily attributed to the zigzag scanning strategy, as it results in a brief period of secondary heating at both ends and insufficient time for heat dissipation. The as-built deposition was sectioned along the cross-sectional (R-Z) direction for microstructural characterization. The samples were carefully examined under a microscope (Axio Imager Objective A-Plan 50×) to ensure minimal pores, crack-free deposition, and a sound metallurgical interface. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM, ZEISS Sigma 300) was used to analyze the microstructural composition after etching with a 2 % Nital etchant (97 % ethanol and 3 % nitric acid) for 10 s. Electron dispersive spectroscopy (EDS, ZEISS) analysis was conducted to determine the element distribution in selected regions. Prior to texture analysis, vibration polishing with Al2O3 powders was performed. Texture analysis was carried out using an electron backscattered diffraction detector (EBSD, Oxford C-Nano) for both single-layer and multi-layer samples. Nanoindentation tests (FISCHERSCOPE HM2000, Germany) were used to measure the nanohardness of single layers, while the hardness of multi-layer samples was determined using a Vickers hardness tester as per DIN EN ISO 6507-1. To mirror the measurement errors, the hardness test was performed on three 3 positions from the edge to the middle (along Z direction) of the cross section, and three lines was defined for each position. The mean value of each point at three lines was used for the final results. The Vickers test was performed with a force of 0.98 N and a dwell time of 10 s. The distance between the clad edge ZB and testing position Z1 was approx. 2 mm. The horizontal distance between two testing lines Z1 and Z2 was 50 μm, and the vertical distance between two testing points R1 and R2 was 25 μm. A total length of approx. 3.5 mm consisting of deposition, heat affected zone (HAZ) and part of the substrate were tested. Similarly, three replicates were performed, and the mean value was used for the nanoindentation test, and a force of 300 mN was applied with a dwell time of 25 s according to standard ISO 14577-1 Metallic materials — Instrumented indentation test for hardness and materials parameters. A volume with thickness of 10 mm and length of 100 mm for the manufacturing of tensile test samples was produced for both LMD and EHLA process. Tensile tests were performed according to the DIN EN ISO 6892 standard, and the round tensile samples adhered to the dimensions specified in DIN 50125. Processing Text: The CoCrFeNi powder (Yijing New Material Technology Co., Ltd, China) with purity of 99.85 wt% and the AlTi powder (Zhongkeyannuo New Materials Technology Co., Ltd, China) were prepared by gas atomization. Processing Text: The present study utilized gas atomized pre-alloyed HX powder as the feedstock for the LPBF process. A BLT-S320 LPBF system (Xi'an Bright Laser Technologies Co., Ltd., Xian, China) was employed, with optimized process parameters to produce nearly fully dense samples: laser power of 300 W, scanning speed of 1000 mm/s, hatch distance of 0.09 mm, and layer thickness of 0.06 mm. A strip scanning strategy with a rotation angle of 67° was employed to perform sequential layer-by-layer fabrication, as illustrated in Fig. 1a. Tensile cylindrical bars with dimensions of Φ14 × 80 mm were built in both horizontal and vertical orientations. Following the LPBF procedure, the tensile sample bars underwent full heat treatments, consisting of HIP followed by ST. The HIP was conducted at 1180 °C and 150 MPa for 3 h with furnace cooling. Then, the ST was conducted at 1180 °C for 1 h with argon quenching. Both HIP and ST were performed under a vacuum of less than 1 × 10 −2Pa. To investigate the effect of temperature on deformation behavior, a series of tensile tests were performed on dog-bone shaped specimens ( Fig. 1c) machined from fully heat-treated (HIP + ST) tensile bars. These tests were performed at temperatures ranging from −50 °C to elevated temperatures. The tensile tests were conducted at a rate of 0.5 mm/min to ascertain the yield strength and 2.5 mm/min to fracture, using a universal testing machine. Specimens were cooled or heated to the test temperature and soaked for 15 min prior to the application of tension. The initial stage of tensile tests (first 0.2 % strain) was measured using an extensometer to ensure precise yield strength (YS) calculations. The tensile tests were repeated three times to quantify the standard error for each type of samples. The specimen used to examine the initial microstructure was obtained from the extremity portion of the tensile bar before testing. The specimen for deformation microstructure analysis was extracted from the gauge section of the tensile specimen, specifically near the fracture region. Processing Text: In this study, hierarchical heterostructures were introduced into CoCrFeMnNi HEA via an in-situ rolling (ISR) assisted laser cladding (LC) process. The coating was fabricated by overlapping individual tracks with a 30 % overlapping ratio. Following the preliminary testing, the distance D between the laser head and the roller was set to 13 mm. In this work, static pressures of 0 N, 1000 N, 2000 N, 3000 N, and 4000 N were applied, and the corresponding coatings were referred as un-ISR, ISR1, ISR2, ISR3 and ISR4, respectively. Annealed 45 steel with dimensions of 100 mm × 100 mm × 10 mm was chosen as the substrate. To minimize the interference of oxides and other impurities, an angle grinder was used to remove the oxide layer from the substrate surface, followed by cleaning with anhydrous ethanol. The powder used in this study was CoCrFeMnNi HEA powder with a particle size range of 45-105 μm, produced by high-temperature gas atomization. Before the experiment, place the powder in a vacuum drying oven (Shanghai Jiecheng Experimental Instrument Co., Ltd., DZF-6050) and dry it at 100 °C for 2 h to ensure its uniformity and fluidity. The coating was prepared by using a semiconductor laser (HWL-1500) with a wavelength range of 910-1050 nm and a DPSF scraper powder feeder to transport CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy powder coaxially. Laser spot diameter 2 mm, laser power 1500 W, scanning rate 3 mm/s, powder feed 7 g/min, overlapping ratio 30 %. High purity argon is used as melt pool shielding gas with a flow rate of 3 L / min. The prepared coating was cut into cuboid specimens with dimensions of 15 × 15 × 10 mm 3using a high-speed wire electrical discharge machining machine tool (Fangzheng CNC Machine Tool Co., Ltd., DK7720). The specimens were then hot - mounted using a metallographic specimen mounting machine (Laizhou Hengyi Test Instrument Co., Ltd., XQ-2B). Subsequently, the cross - section of the specimen was ground using SiC sandpapers of grit sizes 60 mesh, 400 mesh, 800 mesh, 1500 mesh, and 2000 mesh in a wet - grinding manner on a metallographic specimen grinding and polishing machine (Laizhou Hengyi Test Instrument Co., Ltd., MP-2B). After grinding, the specimens were polished with diamond polishing paste until no obvious scratches were visible under an optical microscope. The specimens were placed in anhydrous ethanol and cleaned in an ultrasonic cleaner for 5 min. To prepare the surfaces for electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) analysis, the specimen was pre-ground and polished using the metallographic pre-grinding machine (Hua Xing Test Instrument Co., Ltd.). The surface was then ion-polished with a precision ion thinning instrument (GATAN PIPS II 695) to remove the damage layer caused by mechanical polishing. The microhardness was measured using a Vickers hardness tester (Laizhou Hengyi Test Instrument Co., Ltd., NVM-1000 A). The load was set at 0.3 kg, and the dwell time was 15 s. Each value was measured three times to ensure accuracy. The tribological properties of the coatings at room temperature (25 °C) were evaluated by a ball-on-disk wear tester (Lanzhou Zhongke Kaihua Science and Technology Development Co., Ltd., HT-1000) with a Si 3N 4ball as the counterpart. The tests, performed under dry sliding conditions in accordance with the ASTM G99-17 standard, were repeated three times. The test parameters included a loading force of 10 N, a friction radius of 3 mm, a rotation speed of 600 r/min, and a wear time of 30 min. Processing Text: An irregular shape of pure Cr powder (>99% purity, JFE Material, Japan) was supplied as a starting material. The average particle size was measured using a Mastersizer 3000E particle size analyzer (Malvern Panalytical, UK), and the laser absorption of powder was determined using an ultraviolet-visible near-infrared spectrophotometer (V-770, Jasco, Japan). In addition, a rotary-drum-type powder flowability measuring device (Revolution Powder Analyzer, Mercury Scientific, US) was used to measure the rest fractal, avalanche angle. As described in Fig. 1(b), an L-PBF machine (EOS M290, EOS, Germany) equipped with a 400 W Yb-fiber laser as the primary heat source was used to fabricate the samples with dimensions of 10 mm × 10 mm × 5 mm along the x-, y-, and z-axes, respectively. Preheat temperatures of 80 °C and 200 °C were applied. The 80 °C preheat temperature was used to avoid unexpected temperature fluctuations caused by laser energy input during the manufacturing process and to maintain a constant fabrication condition. For the 200 °C preheat temperature, the maximum preheat temperature setting of the equipment used. Furthermore, shorter scan length samples were fabricated in size of 5 mm × 5 mm × 5 mm at a preheat temperature of 200 °C to maximize the heat accumulation effect. A bi-directional scanning with 90° rotation between layers was used to minimize the residual stress, and various input energy density (ED) conditions were attempted to optimize the process parameters. The densification of the as-built Cr samples was measured by the Archimedes principle using ethanol at room temperature. The theoretical density of 7.19 g/cm3 for pure Cr was used to determine the relative density. The specimens were then sectioned on the yz-plane representing the x-scan direction by wire electrical discharge machine, and prepared as mirror polish surface quality. The relative densities of specimens were additionally evaluated for representative samples using an optical microscope (OM; Eclipse LV-150, Nikon, Japan) and ImageJ software. The phase analysis of the as-built Cr specimens was carried out by X-ray diffraction (XRD, RINT-2500V, Rigaku, Japan) using Cu Kα radiation with a wavelength of 0.154 nm. The XRD data were obtained through point scanning in the 2θ angular range from 30° to 90° with a step size of 0.02° and a scan time of 2 s per step at room temperature. Microstructural characteristics were analyzed using FE-SEM equipped with electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD; NordlysMax 3, Oxford Instruments, UK), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM; JEM-ARM200F, JEOL, Japan). In terms of the mechanical properties evaluation, hardness was assessed using Vickers (HMV-G, Shimadzu, Japan) and nanoindentation (ENT-1100a, ELONIX, Japan) tests. The former test was performed with a test force of 0.2 kgf, while the latter test was carried out using a Berkovich tip at a force of 10 mN. Furthermore, compression tests (AG-X, Shimadzu, Japan) at room temperature were conducted at a nominal strain rate of 1.7 × 10−4s−1 condition employing the rectangular shape of the test samples with dimensions of 2 × 2 × 5 mm. The laser heat source behavior of multi-scan tracks was estimated by using a finite element thermal model simulation (COMSOL Multiphysics 6.1, COMSOL Inc., Sweden). Processing Text: Alloys with a nominal composition of Co 37Cr 14Ni 37Al 6Ti 6(at. %), hereinafter referred to as Al 6Ti 6, were prepared in a vacuum furnace by arc-melting a mixture of the constituent elements with a high-purity (>99.9% pure) supplied by Beijing Ryubon New Material Technology, LTD. All ingots were melted at least four times with magnetic stirring, then suctioned into a copper mold (10× 100 × 2 mm 3). The as-cast ingots were homogenized at 1200 °C for 2 h to eliminate elemental segregation during solidification, followed by oil quenching. The samples were cold rolled along the longitudinal direction with ∼65 % reduction in thickness, followed by a recrystallization annealing (RA) at 1050 °C for 2 min, and oil quenching, hereinafter referred to as Al 6Ti 6-RA. Part of the RA sheets was subjected to aging (RAA) at 700 °C for 4 h, followed by water quenching, hereinafter referred to as Al 6Ti 6-RAA. The aging temperature of 700 °C was chosen because it facilitates the formation of a hierarchical precipitation microstructure. All the heat treatments were conducted under an argon atmosphere in a high-temperature vacuum Muffle furnace. Notably, the heat treatment conditions of Al 6Ti 6alloy include solution treatment, cold rolling, RA, and aging, which were widely used for L1 2phase alloys in the previous reports [ 8-10, 14]. In addition, it is noted that the concentration of Cr element in the Al 6Ti 6alloy is lower than that of Co and Ni since an excessive concentration of Cr can result in the precipitation of a brittle phase.
