Processing Text: ER 2319 aluminum welding wire with a diameter of 1.2 mm was chosen as the fill wire, and a 2A12 plate with a thickness of 12 mm was used as the substrate. Before the WAAM process, the surface oxide layer and contaminants of the substrate should be removed by a weak alkaline solution and a special polishing wheel. Then, the treated substrate surface needed to be cleaned with alcohol and acetone and then dried for use. The WAAM system comprised a cold metal transfer heating source (TPS 400i, Fronius, Austria), a robot (ABB robot), a the wire feeding mechanism, and a control system. The welding wire was melted by the heat of the arc to form the molten pool, which solidified to build a deposition layer. Then, after forming a deposition layer, raising the torch, repeating the manufacturing process of the previous deposition layer to form the next deposition layer, and cycling the deposition layer by layer to fabricate the as-deposited wall of 150 mm × 220 mm in size. Finally, the as-deposited wall was milled on both sides into a thin plate with a thickness of 5 mm. The WAAM 2319 aluminum alloy underwent a T4 heat treatment process within the KSL-1200× muffle furnace prior to LSP, involving a solution treatment followed by natural aging. The sample was introduced into the muffle furnace at an initial temperature of 25 °C and then gradually heated to the solid solution temperature of 535 °C at a rate of 200 °C/h. Following a 60-min dwell time, the sample was extracted from the furnace and promptly immersed in a cooling medium for quenching, which consisted of water at a temperature of 20 °C. Subsequently, the sample was placed in a room temperature environment for a minimum of 48 h. LSP experiments were carried out by an SGR-Extra-15 Nd: YAG high power pulse laser (Beamtech, Beijing china) with a wavelength of 1064 nm, a pulse width of 10 ns, a frequency of 5 Hz, and a spot diameter of 3 mm. During the LSP experiment, a 100 um thick 3 M special aluminum foil needed to be pasted on the surface of the specimen as an absorptive layer. To raise the peak pressure of the laser shock wave, a confining layer of running water with a thickness of roughly 1-2 mm was applied to cover the peening area. Both sides of the thin plate should be subjected to LSP treatment. The other main experiment parameters used were: the number of impacts was 2 times, the laser energy was 5 J and 10 J, and the spot overlap rate of the longitudinal and transverse direction was 50 %. The tensile investigations of specimens before and after LSP with different energies were performed at room temperature with a constant strain rate of 10 −3s −1 and a tensile rate of 1.5 mm/min using the 8801 servo-hydraulic testing equipment (Instron, USA). The hole fatigue specimens were examined on a high-frequency fatigue machine (QBG-100, Qianbang, china) with a stress level of 130 MPa, a frequency of about 96 Hz, and a stress ratio of 0.1. Processing Text: The T42 RHEA sample was additively manufactured using a mixture of pure Ti, Hf, Nb, and V powders (all with purities exceeding 99.95 %). The particle size of the powder mixture was determined via a particle analyzer (Malvern Mastersizer 3000), giving an average particle size of ∼81 μm. X-ray diffraction (XRD, λ = 1.54 Å for Cu Kα) testing was applied, showing the phase structure of well-mixed elemental powders. During the LENS process, a remelting procedure involving ultra-high energy input was performed to maintain a uniform elemental distribution and prevent the presence of un-melted elemental powder. Argon was introduced into the LENS machine's (Optomec LENS MR-7) working chamber to maintain a low oxygen content (below 200 ppm). The fabrication process involved a scanning speed of 5 mm/s, hatching space of 381 μm, working laser power of 550 W, remelting power of 800 W, and a layer thickness of 200 μm. After the LENS procedure, a bulk RHEA sample measuring 70 × 12 × 5 mm was obtained for further testing. The tensile tests were conducted on the as-deposited samples at various temperatures, including RT, 673 K, 773 K, 873 K, and 1073 K, at a strain rate of 1 × 10 −3s −1. The tests were carried out using a ZwickRoell Proline universal testing machine equipped with a heating chamber, and strain evaluation was performed using digital image correlation (DIC). The tensile bar used in the experiments had a gauge length of 6 mm and a thickness of 1 mm. Prior to the hot tensile experiment, the tensile bar was preloaded at 30 N to compensate for thermal expansion during the heating process. A heating speed of 10 K/s was employed to reach the target temperature, and the hot tensile test commenced after a 10-min thermal insulation period at the target temperatures in the heating chamber. SEM specimens, including the deformed samples, were ground with 2000-grit SiC paper, polished with 1 μm micro-sized polycrystalline diamond solutions (Struers), and then finished with a finer polishing using a 50 nm sized SiO 2particle solution (OPS, Struers). Processing Text: The SPD processes can be classified as bulk-SPD, surface-SPD and powder-SPD methods. In bulk-SPD, the goal is to modify the bulk microstructure of a material with reasonably large sizes. In surface-SPD, only surface and sub-surface layers are modified. In powder-SPD, the material is in the form of powder, and strain is introduced on the surface layer and core of the powder particles usually by ball milling methods. Different methods based on rolling, torsion, forging and extrusion can satisfy the required conditions for SPD processing of bulk material. The most known method for inducing SPD in powders is high-energy ball milling. Recent trends in SPD methods include hydrostatic pressure methods, upscaling disc samples to rods using HPTE, pipe sample processing using t-HPS, sheet processing using IF-HPS, cryogenic-SPD, and ultra-SPD. Processing Text: The 24CrNiMoY alloy steel powder was prepared by vacuum induction melting gas atomization (VIGA), and the fine powder with a particle size of 15-53 μm was obtained by vibration sieving. The powder particle size distribution was measured by LA-920 laser particle sizer, and the powder morphology and particle size distribution are shown in Fig. 1. It can be seen that the powder particle size distribution ranges from 5 to 80μ m, and the average powder particle size is 34.3 μm, and the alloy steel powders are well sphericalized, which is suitable for the SLM printing block. The SLM 24CrNiMoY alloy steel samples with good surface formation and high tensile strength along with high elongation were printed by varying the laser power, i.e., energy density, using a 1000 W fiber laser SLM 3D printer with no change in other parameters. The SLM device used an AFS-M260 model equipped with a 1000 W fiber laser manufactured by Beijing Long yuan Company for sample preparation, and the standard x/y grating alternate scanning mode was used. In order to minimize porosity and further melt the upper layers of unfused powder and pore defects, a cross-scanning strategy was used, where the laser scanning direction was periodically rotated by 67° between adjacent layers. Q235 steel was selected as the substrate, which was preheated to 80 °C to reduce the temperature gradient. During the forming process, argon was continuously injected into the cavity as a protective gas to ensure that the oxygen content was less than200 ppm. Two kinds of samples were prepared, one of which was 10mm × 10mm × 10 mm for microstructure analysis and hardness testing, and the other was a tensile specimen of 30mm × 7mm × 1 mm for testing the mechanical properties. The wire-cut samples were ultrasonically cleaned with acetone solution, then sequentially sanded and polished, and then corroded using a solution of HNO3 (2 ml) and C2H5OH (48 ml) in conjunction for 3-5s. The cubic specimen blocks were ground and polished to reduce their surface roughness, and the microhardness of the samples was tested with a Qness Q10A + type microhardness tester under a load of 4.9 N and a holding time of 15S. The tensile specimens were designed according to the ISO 6892-1 standard, and the tensile tests were carried out at room temperature using an AG-X plus 100 kN electronic universal testing machine at a tensile speed of 0.5 mm/min, and the fracture morphology was observed using SEM equipment. The results show that with the optimized laser power over 400 W, the powder layer thickness can be increased to 60 μm, and the theoretical productivity reaches 7.2 mm3/s, which is more than two times of the normal SLM technology. As the laser energy density increases, the structure of melt pool changes from a thermal conduction mode to a keyhole mode, and the microstructure mainly consists of martensite, bainite and pre-eutectic ferrite, and the phase composition of the specimen is α-Fe phase and a small amount of Fe3C,with fine grain size and irregular orientation. When the laser energy density is 68 J/mm3, the microhardness of the specimen is 410HV0.2, the tensile strength reaches 1121 MPa and the percentage elongation after fracture is 11.5%, which realizes a good match between strength and ductility. The fine tempered martensite and lower bainite in the microstructure is the key to excellent strength and ductility. In order to avoid the keyhole mode of the molten pool, it is necessary to reduce the laser power or increase the powder thickness. The pristine powder was prepared by vacuum induction melting gas atomization (VIGA) technique and the powder quality was good. The relative density of 24CrNiMoY specimens shows a trend of increasing and then decreasing with the increase of EVD, and when the laser energy density is 68 J/mm 3, the density of the specimen is the highest, which reaches 98.42%, with the best surface molding quality and fewer internal defects. When the laser energy density reaches 72 J/mm 3, due to the high laser energy density, the "keyhole effect" appears at the bottom of the molten pool, which reduces the molding quality of the specimen. The microstructure of 24CrNiMoY specimen is mainly dominated by martensite, lower bainite and granular bainite, and with the increase of EVD, the HAZ area increases, and the proportion of bainite organization increases, which reaches the optimum when the laser energy density is 68 J/mm 3. At this time, the grain size is fine, the weaving strength is the weakest, and the orientation is irregular, thus obtaining a uniform specimen organization, which is conducive to improving the strength of alloy steel. Under the optimized scanning strategy, the best microhardness of 410 HV, tensile strength of 1121 MPa, yield strength of 1080 MPa, elongation after break of 11.5% were obtained for 24CrNiMoY specimens when the laser energy density was 68 J/mm 3. By increasing the layer thickness to 60 μm, not only can we obtain SLM specimens with good molding performance, but the molding rate also reaches 7.2 mm 3/s, which is 2 times higher than that of the low-layer-thickness molding. Processing Text: In this study, a Ti3Zr1.5NbVAl0.25 HEA was produced by DED. The DED equipment comprises an ytterbium fiber laser system (YLS-4000-U-K, Germany), a multi-axis linkage robot arm (KUKA, Germany), a coaxial powder feeder, circulating water cooling equipment, etc. ( Fig. 2(a) ). The molten pool forming process is shown in Fig. 2(b), where the high energy laser melts and deposits the powder onto the substrate. During the printing process, the shielding gas flow is maintained at 15 L/min, and the laser spot diameter is 3.85 mm. The process is conducted under high-purity argon, with an oxygen concentration below 50 ppm throughout. A total of 20 groups of experiments were designed, each requiring the printing of a 30 mm STCL. Microhardness testing was performed using a Vickers hardness tester (Innovatest Falcon 500) with a load of 200 g and a dwell time of 13 s, measuring at intervals of 0.5 mm between adjacent points. Nanoindentation experiments of the molten pool and HAZ were carried out using an Agilent G200 instrument, with 10 measurement points in each region and a spacing of 30 μm between adjacent points. For microstructure and elemental distribution analysis, a field emission SEM (Tescan MIRA3-LMH) was utilized. Processing Text: The Al-5.0Mn-1.5Mg-0.82Sc-0.76Zr (wt.%) alloy powder with a standard composition was prepared by gas atomization (Panxing New Alloy Materials Co., Ltd., China). Processing Text: In the present work, the AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 EHEA was hot rolled in multiple passes at different temperatures and reductions. Among them, the condition of 1200 °C and 60% reduction was tested as a control group to further explore the improvement of the mechanical properties. Taking the deformation of hot rolling at 1000 °C as an example, the sheet is heat-treated by annealing for 10 mins at 1000 °C, and then hot rolling operated at ∼10% reduction. The TEM specimens were prepared by means of ion milling on a GATAN 691. High purity elements (Al, Co, Cr, Fe, Ni with purity above 99.9%) were used to prepare AlCoCrFeNi 2.1EHEA ingots in a vacuum induction magnetic levitation melting furnace under high purity argon atmosphere. The material with Φ74 × 100 mm was cut from the center of the ingot as the raw material used in the experiment. Processing Text: Samples were manufactured using EOS Ti-6Al-4V grade 23 powder on an EOS M290 (EOS GmbH, Germany) LPBF machine housed at the ISO 13485 certified Centre for Rapid Prototyping and Manufacturing (CRPM) of the Central University of Technology in South Africa. Specimens were produced in three batches, and a representative portion of each batch and specimen type was selected to measure the oxygen content to ensure this was kept below 0.013 wt%. The base plate was preheated to 80 °C, and a high-speed steel blade was used as a scraper. The process parameters consisted of a 40 μm layer thickness, 280 W laser power, 1300 mm/s scan speed, 100 μm spot size and a hatch distance of 120 μm. Bidirectional scanning was used, and the scan direction was rotated by 67° between layers. This set of process parameters results in a material with less than 0.01 % porosity [ 23 ]. For tensile specimens, cylinders with a diameter of D = 10 mm and a length of L = 100 mm were produced in the vertical (Z) and horizontal (X) directions relative to the axis of the LPBF machine (and according to ASTM 59200) that is aligned with the direction in which the load is applied. For fracture toughness specimens, Compact Tension (C(T)) specimens were produced as rectangular blocks to allow for the final dimensions of a width of W = 25 mm. C(T) specimens were produced in three orientations, with the first letter indicating the direction in which the load is applied and the second letter indicating the direction in which the crack propagates, that is, ZX, XZ and XY [ 6 ], as shown in Fig. 1 . After printing, the specimens were stress-relieved (SR) at 650 °C for 3 h in a TSH 15/50/180 vacuum furnace (Elite Thermal Systems, England) and then wire-cut from the build plate. The SR treatment was chosen to allow comparison with the literature [ 15 ]. Subsequent heat treatments were conducted at the Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) in atmospheric air using a box furnace (Ultrafurn, South Africa). Therefore, at least 1 mm was removed by wire cutting or machining from all the heat-treated specimen surfaces to remove any α-case and oxide scale that may have formed. The heat treatment schedules, detailed in Table 1 , included the SR, an anneal (AN) heat treatment, chosen due to its simplicity combined with good tensile properties, and a duplex anneal (DA) heat treatment, chosen based on optimal tensile properties reported in the literature [ 6 , 25 ]. Furthermore, the heat treatments above T β (selected based on values available in the literature [ 9 , 15 ]) were combined with the stress relief (BtSR) and anneal (BtAN) heat treatments to mimic how SR or AN specimens would perform if the PBGs were equiaxed c . c It is acknowledged the above T β heat treatment is at the cost of PBG growth. Comparison to specimens with elongated PBGs is only based on orientation effects. After heat treatment, the specimens were machined and wire-cut to their final dimensions. Condition: as-received
Processing Word: Condition: as-received

Processing Text: The material used in this work is cold-rolled 316L austenitic SS seamless tubes with an outside diameter of 12 mm and a thickness of 2 mm. The 316L SS tubes were bright annealed at 1080 °C followed by rapid water quench and subsequently machined into specimens. The surface of the specimens was mechanically ground and polished to obtain a smooth surface by uniformly distributing the machining marks in the longitudinal direction, thus reducing the effect of surface quality. Multiaxial non-proportional cyclic pre-hardening (CPH) treatment was performed in a circular path, with a 90° phase shift between the axial and torsion loads, over 10 cycles at the strain amplitude of 0.4 %. At the end of the CPH process, the axial strain is at its peak value (0.4 %) and the equivalent shear strain is controlled to 0. Subsequently, the axial strain reaches the minimum value of the corresponding uniaxial fatigue tests to start the uniaxial stage while the equivalent shear strain is controlled at 0 throughout the whole uniaxial stage. Monotonic tensile tests were carried out under displacement control mode at a displacement rate of 0.06 mm/s. Strain-controlled uniaxial fatigue tests at the strain amplitudes of 0.2 % and 0.4 % were performed on AR and CPH materials in a fully-reversed triangular waveform (R = -1) with a fixed strain rate of 5 × 10 -3s −1. Microstructure observations were made using electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, Edax) equipped on a scanning electron microscope (SEM, Apreo S LoVac). The samples for EBSD observations were obtained along the axial direction of the specimen and at a distance of 5 mm away from the fracture surface. Mechanical ground and polished processes were carried out using 180, 400, 1000 and 2000 grit SiC sandpapers, followed by electrochemical polishing using a 10 % perchloric acid ethanol solution at a voltage of 20 V and a current of 5 A. The EBSD characterization were performed at a voltage of 20 kV, a working distance of 17.4 mm and a scan area of 400 μm × 300 μm with a step size of 0.8 μm. Due to the small scan area, two to four areas were scanned for each condition of the sample. The thin slices for TEM observation were also taken along the specimen axial direction at a distance of 5 mm away from the fracture surface. The sample preparation process consisted of mechanical grinding on both sides with SiC sandpaper grits of 400, 800, 1000, and 2000 under maintained horizontal conditions. Samples were thinned to ∼ 60 μm with 2000 grit, followed by twin-jet electro-polishing with a 10 % perchloric acid ethanol solution. Condition: As-received (AR)

Processing Text: Gas-atomised spherical 316 steel powder (size: 20-65 µm), sourced from SLM Solution Group AG, was used as the standard material for assessing the effectiveness of TiN in refining γ-austenite grains. Processing Text: The LDX 2101 material was prepared in an electric arc furnace, with an argon oxygen decarburizer, ladle refining furnace and continuous casting process. After casting, the LDX 2101 material was homogenized by heat treatment at 1250 °C for 1 h. After heat treatment, three samples were cut (10 mm thick) from LDX 2101 material for hot rolling at 1250 °C. In order to study the influence of different distributions of hot rolling reduction on the microstructure and mechanical properties, a reduction of 50 % is distributed in the first pass, and the thickness decreases to 10 mm→5 mm→4 mm→3 mm. In addition, a reduction of 50 % was distributed in the middle pass, and the thickness decreased to 10 mm→8 mm→4 mm→3 mm. Finally, the 50 % reduction is distributed in the last pass, and the thickness decreases to 10 mm→8 mm→6 mm→3 mm. After the rolling experiment, each sample was quenched in water to retain the deformed structure. After rolling, samples were prepared along the rolling direction (RD) for microscopy and mechanical testing. The microstructure of the specimens was analyzed by DM2500 optical microscope (Quanta FEG 450), and the specimens were etched in 10 % oxalic acid solution for 25 s. The dog bone-shaped tensile specimens with length of 15 mm, width of 5 mm and thickness of 3 mm were machined (by electric discharge machining) from the rolled plate along the RD. The tensile test at room temperature at a displacement rate of 1 mm/min was carried out on mTS810 tensile machine. The phase structure after deformation was determined by XRD. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) was used to analyze the grain, stress-strain distribution and deformation mechanism of the phases. In order to remove the surface stress, electrolytic polishing was performed in 10 % perchlorate ethanol at 30 V for 20 s. Lastly, transmission electron microscopy (TEM, 200 kV JEM-2200FS field emission electron microscope) was performed to investigate the microstructure of LDX 2101 material after different rolling distribution. Argon was chosen as the protective atmosphere to maintain an O2 content below 0.1 % during the laser powder bed fusion process. The study maintained consistent parameters throughout, including a laser power of 200 W, a hatch distance of 0.12 mm, a layer thickness of 0.03 mm, a stripe width of 10 mm, a stripe overlap of 0.08 mm, a scanning rotation of 67° between subsequent layers, and a stripe scanning strategy. Contouring, up-skin, and down-skin parameters were deactivated. Based on previous research findings, the laser scanning speed (mm/s) was adjusted to achieve different density levels. This adjustment allowed to produce specimens with keyhole (KH) flaws (speed of 400 mm/s) and lack-of-fusion (LoF) flaws (1500 mm/s). The polishing process was carried out on Buehler TexMet C polishing cloth. For the final polishing step, Allied High Tech products were utilized, including a 0.05 μm colloidal silica suspension and Chem-Pol polishing cloth. The plates with a size of 100 mm × 60 mm × 20 mm were prepared from the as-cast Zn-xCu (x= 0, 2, 4 and 8 wt%) alloys, and then were homogenized at 350 °C for 9 h. In order to crush coarse cast microstructure and obtain fine equiaxed grains, the as-cast Zn-xCu (x= 0, 2, 4 and 8 wt%) alloys plates were rolled down to 8 mm by 15 % reduction in thickness per pass after preheating at 200 °C for 5 min. Subsequently, the rolled samples were annealed at 300 °C for 1 h. The annealed Zn-xCu (x= 0, 2, 4 and 8 wt%) alloys plates were sequentially further rolled to 65 % rolling reduction in thickness by multi-pass after preheating at 250 °C for 10 min. The tensile specimens of the Zn-xCu (x= 0, 2, 4 and 8 wt%) alloys with a gauge length of 20 mm and a width of 3 mm were prepared from the rolled samples. The tensile specimens were cut along the rolling direction. The thickness of tensile specimens was equal to that of the rolled sheets. Specimens for microstructure characterization were ground, polished and etched with an acid solution (20 g CrO3, 1.5 g Na2SO4 and 100 mL distilled water), then were characterized by the optical microscope. The microstructure at high magnification and the chemical compositions of phase were analyzed by scanning electron microscopy with energy dispersive spectrometry (EDS). The phase compositions of the Zn-xCu (x= 0, 2, 4 and 8 wt%) alloys were identified using an X-ray diffractometer analysis (XRD) with a Cu-Kα irradiation and the XRD patterns were collected over the 2θ range of 30-80° at a scan rate of 2° per min. Moreover, microstructure and texture evolution of the Zn-xCu (x= 0, 2, 4 and 8 wt%) alloys during hot-rolling were characterized by the electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) analysis. To further characterize the microstructures of Zn-xCu alloys after hot-rolling, TEM observations were carried out by a Tecnai G2 transmission electron microscope. Processing Text: In this study, we used the powder metallurgy process to prepare HSLA steel to overcome this inherent problem. The samples were composed of 4340 powder, Fe powder, FeSi6.5 powder, FeCr60 powder, FeMn80 powder, and Mo powder. The alloy powder was weighed in proportion under a high-pressure and pure argon atmosphere, and 0.6 wt% zinc stearate was added for lubrication. The powder was mixed via a planetary ball mill at a rotational speed of 300 r/min, with a material-to-ball ratio of 1:5. To avoid excessive welding resulting from the high ball milling speed, grinding was stopped for 10 min every 60 min. The samples were pressed into balls with a diameter of 60 mm at a pressure of 800 MPa. The samples were heated to the predetermined sintering temperature (1200-1350 °C) at a speed of 4 °C/min and held at this temperature for 60 min. After the insulation process was complete, the mixture was allowed to cool to room temperature in the furnace. The phases in both the powder and sintered samples were analyzed via X-ray diffraction (XRD, XPERT). Cu radiation (λ = 1.54056 Å) was used to scan in the range of 20∼90° (2θ) at a scanning speed of 3°/min. Microstructure characterization was performed via optical microscopy (OM, DSX 510), field emission scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Gemini560), electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS, data analysis software: AZtecCrystal), electron probe microanalysis (EPMA, 1720), Auger electron spectroscopy (AES, PHI-710), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM, FEI Talos F200X). When the OM samples were prepared, sandpaper was used to polish the surfaces of the samples to 3000#. After the samples were smoothed by polishing, they were corroded with a 10 vol% nitric acid alcohol solution. The EBSD samples were prepared by 15 V electrolytic polishing for 15-20 s. The sample used for TEM was ground to a thickness of 50 μm and thinned via an ion thinning instrument (GATAN695). The Archimedes method was used to measure the density of each sintered sample. The hardness of each sample was tested via the Vickers hardness test. Ten points were measured on each sample, and the mean value was obtained. A rod-shaped tensile test sample with dimensions of 12 × 4 × 1.5 mm was machined in the center of the sample. Tensile testing of the HSLA steel was performed via an electronic universal testing machine (Instron 5967) at a strain rate of 0.5 × 10 −3s −1. A CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy (MEA) with gradient hetero-structure (GHS) composing of gradient nanostructured surface layer and hetero-structured matrix was prepared via a two-step process: pre-cold rolling (CR) deformation and subsequent annealing followed by surface mechanical grinding treatment (SMGT) and secondary annealing. The equiatomic CrCoNi MEA was electromagnetic levitation melted under a high-purity argon atmosphere and cast into ingot with dimensions of 10 × 70 × 800 mm 3. The chemical composition of the trial alloy is 32.05Cr-35.85Co-32.1Ni, in at.%. The 5 kg ingot was homogenized in an argon atmosphere at 1150 °C for 2h, followed by water cooling. The homogenized ingot was then cold rolled (CR) for multiple passes into sheets of 1.5 mm thickness with a total reduction of about 82%. The CRed sheets were then annealed at 650°C-800 °C to obtain HS samples, which were designated as HS650, HS700 and HS800 samples, respectively. The HS700 sample was selected for SMGT processing. A polished WC/Co ceramic ball with a diameter of 8.0 mm was pressed into the surface of the HS700 plate sample to obtain a gradient structured SL. The room-temperature SMGT processing was conducted under lubricating oil, with a pressing amount of 25 μm per pass and a total processing number of 15 passes. Both the surfaces of the plate sample were processed by SMGT, with the plates itself undergoing a synchronous alternation of positions in both the up-and-down and forward-and-backward directions at each processing interval. The sample obtained from the SMGT processing of the HS700 sample is designated as the GHS sample. In order to optimize the surface grain size gradient structure to maintain high strength and further restore intragranular dislocation plasticity in SL, the GHS sample was subjected to an additional annealing treatment at 625 °C for 1h, resulting in an optimized GHS sample, which is designated as the GHS625 sample. The designed Ti-4.5Al-4.5Mo-7V-1.5Cr-1.5Zr alloy was fabricated by a vacuum arc melting furnace. After casting, the ingot was subjected to two different forging processes. The first one takes place in the β-phase region, followed by water quenching (WQ). By contrast, the second one was performed with a starting temperature slightly above Tβ and a finishing temperature below it (β trans forging), followed by air cooling (AC). The single reduction for both processes was set to be ∼40 %. After the forging process, the alloy underwent an aging treatment at 480 °C for 6 h, followed by AC. The whole thermomechanical process is shown schematically in Fig. 2. The present forged and aged Ti alloys were subjected to various microstructure characterization facilities, including scanning electron microscope (SEM, Hitachi-SU6600), electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, Oxford instrument), transmission electron microscope (TEM, JEM-F200), and scanning transmission electron microscope (STEM, Hitachi-HF5000). The specimens for SEM and EBSD were prepared following standard metallographic procedures. For TEM analysis, the samples were ground to a foil with a thickness of ∼50 μm and punched into 3 mm discs. To produce electron-transparent regions in these punched disks, twin-jet polishing was conducted at -30 °C and 50 V in a solution of 65 % methanol, 30 % butyl alcohol, and 5 % perchloric acid. The X-ray diffraction (XRD, PANalytical X'Pert-PRO diffractometer) pattern was obtained using a Cu anode at 45 kV, the diffraction angular is in a range from 30° to 90°. The flat dog-bone tensile specimens with a gauge length of ∼12 mm and gauge width of ∼5 mm were cut using an electrical discharge machine (EDM). Quasi-static uniaxial tensile tests were performed on an INSTRON 1195 testing machine with a crosshead speed of 1 mm/min (corresponding to an initial strain rate of 1.4 × 10 -3) at room temperature. Tensile properties such as yield strength ( σ0.2), ultimate tensile strength ( σUTS), and total elongation at fracture ( ɛf) were measured using standard operation. Loading-unloading-reloading (LUR) cycles were conducted to measure the back stress evolution. In each cycle, the specimen was first stretched with a crosshead speed of 1 mm/min to a designated strain ε, and then it was unloaded using the load-control mode to 20 N at a rate of 200 N/min, followed by reloading at a rate of 1 mm/min again to the next designated strain. At least three samples were performed to ensure the repeatability of the testing. Processing state: aged

Processing Text: Green pellets with a diameter of 10 mm were produced using a 25-ton manual press (Kimaya Engineers, India) at a pressure of 520 MPa. The compacts were sintered in a tube furnace (Swam Equip, India) under a continuous flow of 99.99 % pure argon gas. The green samples were subjected to a sintering temperature range of 560-650 °C, with a 30 °C interval, at a heating rate of 5 °C/min. The duration of sintering was 90 min, followed by controlled cooling within the furnace. Bulk density measurements were performed using the Archimedes principle with a Sartorius Secura YDK03 instrument. Phase analysis was conducted using a Panalytical X-pert powder X-ray diffractometer (Make: Panalytical, Model: X-pert powder). The instrument was equipped with Cu-Kα radiation (λ = 0.15406 nm) for data profile acquisition. The process involved a voltage of 45 kV and a current of 30 mA, with a step size of 0.02 and a duration of 25s/step. Optical microscopy (Quasmo ISI Microscope) and scanning electron microscopy (VEGA 3 LMU TESCAN) were employed to characterize the microstructure. Quantification and mapping of elements were performed using a Field Emission Gun Scanning Electron Microscope (FEGSEM) (JEOL, model: JSM 7800F) equipped with an Energy Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDS) detector. For TEM analysis, specimens were obtained by cutting 300-micron-thick discs from the sintered samples, followed by metallographic polishing to a thickness of less than 100 μm. Subsequently, ion beam milling was applied to the specimens. The crystal structure and lattice imperfections, such as stacking faults, dislocations, and precipitation and their boundaries at the atomic scale, were investigated using a High Resolution- Transmission Electron Microscope (HR-TEM) (Model: JEOL JEM 2100, at an operating voltage of 200 kV). Nanoindentation measurements were performed using a Berkovich diamond indenter with a radius of 150 nm, featuring an included angle of 142.30° and a half angle of 65.27°, within a NANOINDENTER device (BRUKER'S HYSITRON TI PREMIER). A 2 mN load was used for the nanoindentation study and the distance between the two consecutive indentations was 3 μm to evaluate the hardness and modulus. The load-displacement curves were used to generate hardness and elastic modulus profiles across the matrix, intermetallic, and particle interfaces. The room temperature and isothermal compressive strength (at 200 °C, 250 °C, and 300 °C) of the composite were assessed using cylindrical samples (φ10mm x l = 15 mm) with an aspect ratio (l/d) of 1.5. The test was performed using a Universal Testing Machine (Jinan, WDW-100S) following the ASTM E−09standard. For the isothermal compression test, a furnace setup was employed. All samples were sintered at 620 °C due to its verified superior density in line with our previous findings. All samples were subjected to a strain of 0.5 and then water-quenched to facilitate microstructural observation. The strain rate for both room temperature and isothermal tests was set at 10 −4S −1. An in-house developed LMD printing system was employed, and the powder was fed into the laser melt pool on the GH4169 high-temperature alloy substrate using a coaxial nozzle under a high-purity argon gas atmosphere (≥99.99%). The variables that followed were the applied optimal process parameters: laser power of 1400 W, laser scanning speed of 400 mm/min, gas flow rate of 3 L/min and powder feed rate of 1.4 rad/min. The Ni43.9Co22.4Fe8.8Al10.7Ti11.7B2.5 alloy prepared by LMD consists of dendrite γ + γ′ phases, γ′ envelopes and interdendritic γ + γ′ phases, with discontinuous acicular TiB2 precipitates in the interdendritic γ + γ′ region. During the solidification process, TiB2 and γ dendrites preferentially precipitate, and the residual liquid phase reacts with γ dendrites to form γ′ envelope layer. Subsequently, γ and γ′ phases are co-precipitated from the residual interdendrite liquid phase. During the deposition process, the interdendrite γ′ phase coarsened and merged, and the cubic γ′ phase precipitated inside the γ dendrite. Processing Text: This work utilizes a consolidation technique that uses high-pressure & high-temperature (HPHT) to produce an ultrafine-grained (UFG) FeCrCoNi HEA. The high consolidation pressure has two effects: 1) reducing interparticle distances due to the enforced plastic deformation of individual granules, making for high bulk density, and 2) reducing the diffusivity, thereby reducing the growth speed of grains. The high strain is primarily the result of a reduction in the diameter and content of Cr-Mn-O-rich oxides - which reduce the interface area between the soft matrix and hard oxides, thereby suppressing the sources of crack generation - due to the utilization of high pressure. UFG FeCoNiCr HEA was prepared by MA and HPHT techniques. Applying a substantial consolidation pressure (4 GPa) leads to the UFG FeCoNiCr HEA achieving a relative density near 99 %. The consolidated UFG FeCoNiCr HEA exhibits an average grain diameter of approx. 181 nm and displays exceptionally high yield strength of approx. 1526 MPa - significantly higher than the yield strength (162 MPa) of CG FeCoNiCr HEA - and a high fracture of 35 %. The high yield strength is predominantly brought about by the UFG matrix. The achievement of the UFG matrix can be attributed primarily to the application of a high consolidation pressure, which has two effects: 1) reduces interparticle distances because of the enforced plastic deformation of the individual powder particles and 2) reducing the diffusivity, thereby reducing the rate of grain growth. The high strain is predominately induced by fine diameter and low content of coarse Cr-Mn-O-rich oxide. High sintering pressure suppresses the oxides to grow, reducing the interface area between soft matrix phases and hard oxides, and thus decreasing the sources of crack generation. Processing Text: Powder assembly and alloying process including elemental alloying and shift-speed ball milling is applied in fabrication of CNT/Al-xMg (x = 0, 2.5, 5, wt.%). The mass ratio of stainless-steel milling balls to powders is controlled to be 20:1. Low speed ball milling (LSBM) at 135 rpm flake the powders and provides sufficient surface areas for uniform dispersion of CNTs. High speed ball milling (HSBM) at 270 rpm assembles the powder flakes by cold welding. To avoid massive oxidation and cool down the planetary ball milling system, the ball milling jars are filled with Ar atmosphere and take rest for 30 min after every 2 h of working. After cooling down by water quenching, the extruded rods showing surface temperature of ∼300 K are preserved in freezers (∼273 K). Processing Text: The SPD processes can be classified as bulk-SPD, surface-SPD and powder-SPD methods. In powder-SPD, the material is in the form of powder, and strain is introduced on the surface layer and core of the powder particles usually by ball milling methods. The most known method for inducing SPD in powders is high-energy ball milling. Recent trends in SPD methods include hydrostatic pressure methods, upscaling disc samples to rods using HPTE, pipe sample processing using t-HPS, sheet processing using IF-HPS, cryogenic-SPD, and ultra-SPD. In this method, the TiN powder was initially blended with alcohol gel using ultrasonic stirring. Processing Text: A high-strength Co-free triple-phase Al10Cr12Fe35Mn23Ni20 high-entropy alloy (HEA) was successfully fabricated using Friction Surface Layer Deposition (FSLD), a bulk manufacturing method. Multiple single-layer deposits were produced by varying forging force (F) and traverse speeds (Tr) to optimize the process parameters. The optimized conditions (F = 40 kN & Tr = 200 mm/min) were then applied to manufacture a scaled-up multi-layer specimen. During FSLD, the FCC-matrix underwent continuous dynamic recrystallization due to high-temperature severe plastic deformation, forming finer equiaxed grains. Simultaneously, the BCC-dendrites fractured into smaller fragments, some of which experienced partial growth and coarsening under applied stress, resulting in an hourglass morphology. In contrast, the small B2-precipitates within the BCC-fragments dissolved during the elevated temperatures of FSLD and reprecipitated as substantially finer precipitates during continuous cooling post-FSLD. Processing Text: HEAs are generally categorized into two elements, as depicted in Fig. 6. Recently, HEAs have more potential in many industries than typical alloys. High entropy alloys (HEAs) are hard, strong, and have many properties, including thermostability and corrosion resistance. HEAs also had exceptional chemical and mechanical characteristics. As a result, these alloys offer enormous development potential [ 34]. Till Jan. 2022, more than 300 high entropy alloys have been processed along with more than 35 principal elements. The concept of HEAs is different from traditional alloys because HEAs are not made up of just one or two components. HEAs have been defined in two ways by researchers: the first is based on composition, while the second is based on entropy [ 35]. So, based on composition, high entropy alloys contain a minimum of 5 main elements in the equimolar or near equimolar ratios, as depicted in Fig. 7. The atomic % of each element for these alloys lies between 5 % to 35 %. Although several additional elements were included in the high entropy alloys, the overall percentage of these elements are <5 % [ 36]. However, based on entropy, the HEAs are defined as the random blending of distinct features that yields configurational entropy (ΔSconf.). Further, these alloys are categorized into three types of alloys, as shown in Fig. 8. These materials are termed as high entropy alloys owing to the fact that their random solid & liquid state has basically higher entropies as compared to those in conventional alloys. The evolution of HEAs from conventional alloys is shown in Fig. 9. The main properties of HEAs are as given below: a) High hardness and strength. In the case of HEAs, the uneven atomic radius of distinct elements causes an intensive lattice distortion effect. These types of effects obstruct the dislocation movement, leading to very high hardness and strength [ 34]. The lattice distortion of HEA containing chromium is shown in Fig. 10. Li et al. [ 35] also reported that severe lattice distortion could occur in the high entropy alloy, and each element has its unique and specific atomic size. Processing Text: AA7075 is widely utilized in aerospace and transportation due to its high specific strength, specific stiffness, and corrosion resistance. Hot forging is an efficient and cost-effective method for manufacturing AA7075 cylindrical rings. During hot forging, AA7075 cylindrical ring undergoes complex metal flow, resulting in anisotropy in both microstructure and mechanical properties. The present study investigated the anisotropic behaviors of microstructure and mechanical properties in AA7075 cylindrical rings along three directions: rolling direction (RD), transverse direction (TD), and normal direction (ND). The results indicated that the microstructural anisotropy contributed to anisotropy in mechanical properties both before and after hot forging. In the present study, an AA7075 extruded bar ( Table 1), measuring ø300 × 520 mm, was held at 435°C for 12 h before the initial upsetting was completed. Following the first upsetting, the material was held at 435°C for 1 h prior to the second upsetting. Processing Text: Plastic deformation at room temperature followed by post-annealing is one of the best methods to achieve fine-grained metals and alloys. In this research, the high-temperature annealing behavior of cold-rolled electrolytic tough-pitch (ETP) copper sheets was studied. 90 % asymmetric cold rolling followed by high-temperature post-annealing at 673 K for 1, 2, 5, 10, 30, 60, and 120 min were applied on the copper. The microstructure was significantly changed with increasing annealing time from 1 to 2 min owing to full recrystallization. With increasing the annealing duration, the grain size is increased. The formation of equiaxed grains with a smaller size (∼9 μm) compared to the full-annealed (initial) sample (∼68 μm) is observed after the longest time of post-annealing (120 min) due to the pinning effect of Cu2O particles. The post-annealed copper sheets processed by asymmetric rolling (in this work) exhibited a more homogeneous microstructure through the thickness compared to the symmetric rolling due to more uniform stored strain energy. The results showed that the first deformed grains that undergo recrystallization during post-annealing are Goss-oriented grains. With an increase in the post-annealing time, the S and Copper components were eliminated and a strong Cube and P texture orientations were formed. Interestingly, after 1 min of post-annealing, the yield and tensile strength enhanced to 410.2 MPa and 418.6 MPa owing to the annealing hardening phenomenon. The hardness and strength reached a constant value after the post-annealing for 10 min and above. With the increase of post-annealing time from 1 min to 120 min, the electrical conductivity was increased from 77.6 to 97.5 %IACS. From the obtained results, it can be concluded that the asymmetric cold rolling followed by high-temperature post-annealing is capable of strength improvement and maintaining electrical conductivity in copper. Meanwhile, the introduction of external energy fields also contributes to grain refinement ( Tan et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2022, 2023). Applying high-frequency ultrasonic vibration during the deposition process can transform coarse columnar grains into fine equiaxed grains, thereby refining the grain structure and effectively enhancing tensile properties ( Todaro et al., 2020). One kind of the main metallurgical defects of Al-Zn-Mg-Cu alloys manufactured by WAAM is pore. The presence of pores significantly reduces the mechanical properties of the materials. Strategies for reducing pore defects include vibrating the workpiece, using Cold Metal Transfer (CMT) technology, and applying thermal deformation.
